epoch-colossus-2.text: xAI operates Colossus 2, an AI data center in Memphis, Shelby County, Tennessee, that is already running and still expanding; the research group Epoch AI estimates it now draws about 946 megawatts of power, running Nvidia B200 and B300 chips worth an estimated $35.8 billion. Anthropic, Cursor and SpaceXAI use the computing power there, and Epoch AI projects the site will reach about 1,531 megawatts by early 2027. To power the site quickly, xAI installed natural gas turbines just across the state line in Southaven, Mississippi, which Epoch AI says may have been a way to secure faster approval for their operation. A company filing described the compute cluster as roughly 110,000 GB200 processors running on about 210 megawatts of power. In April 2026 the NAACP sued xAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech in federal court in the Northern District of Mississippi, saying the companies run 27 gas turbines in Southaven without an air permit that could emit more than 1,700 tons of smog-forming nitrogen oxides and up to 19 tons of formaldehyde a year near homes, schools and churches. "A data center should not be a potential death sentence for a community's health," said Abre' Conner, the NAACP's director of environmental and climate justice. The Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality has said the turbines are portable units covered by the Clean Air Act's mobile source provisions, and the NAACP asked in May for a preliminary injunction to stop them. In June 2026 the Department of Justice asked to join the case and have it dismissed, backed by a Defense Department official who said Grok, trained on Colossus 2, is used for national security work, while Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves wrote that the NAACP was "seeking to materially slow or outright stop the largest private investment in Mississippi's history." The federal judge in the Northern District of Mississippi has not yet ruled on the request to halt the turbines.

epoch-colossus-1.text: xAI's Colossus 1 data center stands on the site of a former Electrolux appliance factory in south Memphis, in Shelby County, Tennessee. The nearest neighborhood is Boxtown, about 2 miles away, in a part of the city whose cumulative cancer risk is already four times the national average. To power the building before the grid could, xAI brought in gas turbines, and the Southern Environmental Law Center found in August 2024 that they were running with no air permit at all. Aerial imaging on April 9, 2025 found 35 turbines on site, and thermal imaging on April 24 showed more than 30 running at once. Hundreds of residents came to an April 25, 2025 public hearing on xAI's permit application. Alexis Humphreys, 27, who lives in Boxtown, asked: "How come I can't breathe at home and y'all get to breathe at home?" xAI said its operations complied with all applicable laws. xAI removed the unpermitted turbines on June 17, 2025, after the law center sent a legal notice, and the Shelby County Health Department approved a permit for 15 on July 2. An appeal of that permit failed on December 15, 2025, when the Memphis and Shelby County Air Pollution Control Board dismissed it 6 to 1 as moot, with Yu Lin the only vote against. Twelve turbines fitted with selective catalytic reduction pollution controls remain in use at the site. "It allows large companies like data centers to install power plants without community input," said Amanda Garcia, a law center attorney. Bobby White of the Greater Memphis Chamber said the board had "applied existing law and policy." Colossus is still cooled with fresh drinking water because the water recycling plant xAI promised Memphis has not been built. The Daily Memphian reported in April 2026 that the plant was on indefinite pause, leaving xAI and the Tennessee Valley Authority drawing on the Memphis Sand aquifer, which supplies the region's drinking water. Elon Musk has said xAI must build Colossus 2 before it builds the water recycling plant. SpaceX paused construction of the plant in April 2026, and the City of Memphis has said it is confident SpaceX will finish it. The building is also getting busier: in May 2026 Anthropic announced a partnership tied to SpaceX that would add more than 300 megawatts of new capacity, over 220,000 Nvidia GPUs, at Colossus 1 within the month. xAI's larger Colossus 2 draws on turbines across the state line in Southaven, Mississippi, where the NAACP sued on April 14, 2026, alleging they too were running without an air permit.

epoch-microsoft-fairwater-atlanta.text: Microsoft's Fairwater Atlanta AI data center runs as a tenant inside QTS's 615-acre data center campus on Highway 54 West in Fayetteville, in Fayette County, Georgia. The Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported its opening in November 2025, describing a building of more than 1 million square feet. Fayetteville has since shut the door on any more: in March 2026 the city took data centers out of its business center zoning district, an effective ban on new ones within city limits. "As of right now, we don't have any sites that would be conducive to an additional data center," said Niki Vanderslice, president of the Fayette County Development Authority. The campus's water use came to light through the neighbours' taps: residents of the Annelise Park subdivision noticed unusually low water pressure, and when the county water system investigated it found two industrial-scale hookups feeding the campus, one installed without its knowledge and one not linked to QTS's account. Fayette County records reviewed by Atlanta News First showed one QTS water line had billed 20.6 million gallons since its meter was activated in February 2024, and all 13 lines on the campus combined had billed 109 million gallons, roughly the volume of 5,500 backyard pools. The county's own account shifted: it first said two of the lines were unauthorized and billed QTS about $147,000, then said the lines had been permitted and blamed a smart-meter upgrade. QTS paid $147,474 in back charges and was not fined, E&E News reported. "They're our largest customer, and we have to be partners. It's called customer service," said Vanessa Tigert, the county's water system director. QTS says that once the campus's closed-loop cooling system is finished, expected by 2030, monthly water use will fall to the equivalent of four households. "If my daughter down here tapped into that big pipeline down the road without putting a meter on it, she'd be in jail. A data center is not going to jail," said Willard Neal, an 87-year-old neighbor of the site. Neighbor Jesse Brooks said, "These giant things don't need to be in anyone's backyard." Georgia Tech researcher Ahmed Saeed said current use is under 1 percent of the county's monthly water supply, but warned that "once you have tens of such data centers coming up, then the water consumption becomes a problem."

epoch-anthropic-amazon-new-carlisle.text: Amazon Web Services operates Project Rainier, one of the world's largest active AI data center campuses, on the edge of New Carlisle, a St. Joseph County town of fewer than 2,000 people in Indiana. The campus runs on Amazon's own Trainium2 chips to train and run Anthropic's Claude models, and it plans to use up to 2.2 gigawatts of power once finished. On December 10, 2025, the county council voted 7-2 to reject rezoning 1,000 acres nearby for a third, $13 billion campus, and Amazon has filed nothing new since. The vote followed a meeting that ran past 4 a.m., with dozens of people signed up to speak. Council member Joe Thomas said the county already held what he called the nation's largest Amazon data center plus Microsoft facilities, and argued it should wait to see how those play out first. Resident Dan Caruso said the turnout gave the developer an uphill climb if it tries again, and that construction traffic had made once-quiet roads dangerous, with drivers gripping the wheel with both hands. Water has driven much of the debate. In July 2024, commissioners capped Amazon and a nearby General Motors plant at 24 million gallons of combined daily water use to protect the Kankakee Aquifer. In April 2025, Amazon asked state regulators to fill 9 acres of wetlands and reroute streams near Bendix Woods Nature Preserve for its expansion. On May 4, 2026, the drainage board approved pumping site water into the Niespodziany Ditch at up to 31 million gallons a day, with monitors to halt it if levels rise too high. AWS reported 935 full-time employees at the site as of December 2025, 80 percent of them Indiana residents, at an average wage of $40.99 an hour, and holds a 35-year property tax exemption. Amazon says the buildings use outside air for cooling and draw no cooling water from October through March, with limited use in warmer months, and it has not disclosed the campus's total water use.

epoch-meta-prometheus.text: Meta's Prometheus data center in New Albany, Licking County, Ohio is operating and is meant to be the company's first data center built to run more than one gigawatt of computing power. It sits on a 740-acre campus in the New Albany International Business Park, built by Sidecat LLC, a Meta affiliate, where Meta has had a presence since 2017. New Albany counts more than 40 data center facilities run by 15 companies. Neighbors can already hear it. In July 2026 the city was told about periodic noise from the campus after a temporary sound wall came down as construction neared completion, and the city and Meta agreed it had come down too soon. Meta put up a temporary wall along Morse Road, began turning up its cooling fans gradually instead of all at once, and is installing silencers while looking with the city at landscaped berms or a permanent sound wall. Much of Prometheus's power will not come from the electric grid. The Ohio Power Siting Board approved a 200 megawatt gas plant on the north side of Morse Road in June 2025, called Socrates South, built by Williams and Co. and fed directly by two 24-inch pipelines. The $1.6 billion plant is expected to reach two generation sites of 200 megawatts each at full build-out, with state filings projecting completion by the third quarter of 2026. Ohio regulators approved an AEP Ohio rate structure on July 9, 2025 requiring large data centers to pay for at least 85 percent of their contracted power every month, after AEP Ohio warned it will take years to build the grid infrastructure central Ohio's data centers need. Central Ohio residential customers could still pay about $36 more a month by 2027 in combined electric, gas and water bills if pending rate increases are approved. Meta has since bought another 429 acres in New Albany and Jersey Township near Prometheus, signaling more investment in the area.

epoch-google-pryor-north.text: Google's data center in Pryor, Mayes County, Oklahoma, has run since 2011 inside the state-owned MidAmerica Industrial Park and is the largest data center in the state. Google announced in August 2025 that it would expand the Pryor campus as part of a $9 billion, two-year investment in Oklahoma that also funds a new campus in Stillwater. The campus draws its water from the Neosho River under a contract through the industrial park. The campus uses evaporative cooling, which loses much of its water to the air. Utility records obtained by The Frontier show it used more than 1.1 billion gallons of water from July 2024 to June 2025, enough to fill about 1,666 Olympic-size pools, and discharged about 253 million gallons of wastewater into the Neosho River. Google was the industrial park's second largest water user, behind Associated Electric Cooperative; the park holds a state permit to withdraw up to 27.375 billion gallons a year. Nathan Cross, the industrial park's attorney, said the "contracted GRDA supply and available treatment capacity are adequate to meet foreseeable water requirements." Not everyone is reassured. Yohanes Sugeng, an engineer for the Oklahoma Water Resources Board, told state lawmakers in October 2025 that "the new and emerging users, such as data centers, will contribute to the strain depending on how data centers source water." The board projects statewide water demand will rise 18 percent over the next 20 years. Local reaction has been more positive. "They use a lot of electric," said Tim Lawson, editor of the Pryor Information Publication. "There's no denying that. But they generate that energy and our electric rates have not increased." Lawson said the tightest pressure has been on housing, with rents rising as workers moved in: "That's more shame on Pryor, not shame on Google." Mayes County's population has grown from 33,366 in 1990 to just over 41,000 as workers have moved in for the data center jobs. Oklahoma does not track data center water use closely. A July 2026 report by Investigate Midwest found a loophole leaves most of it untracked, including at Pryor, where the water permit is issued to the industrial park rather than to Google itself.

The board projects statewide water demand will rise 18 percent over the next 20 years.

Mayes County's population has grown from 33,366 in 1990 to just over 41,000 as workers have moved in for the data center jobs.

Oklahoma does not track data center water use closely. A July 2026 report by Investigate Midwest found a loophole leaves most of it untracked, including at Pryor, where the water permit is issued to the industrial park rather than to Google itself.

epoch-google-new-albany.text: Google's New Albany data center, at 1101 Beech Road SW in New Albany, Licking County, Ohio, was the company's first in the state when it broke ground in 2019 as a $600 million project. For neighbors the issue now is noise: since September 2025 residents near the Google campus have complained to the City of New Albany about its cooling fans, and a permanent fix is not due to be finished until December 2026. According to the city, Google brought in sound and mechanical engineers within two weeks of the first complaints and has since added sound monitoring, operational changes and sound-dampening materials. It also set up an email address for residents to report noise when they hear it and sends regular updates to city officials to pass on to the public. The permanent fix was scheduled for installation beginning in June 2026 and is designed to meet city noise codes, which limit sound at a site's boundary to the same decibel level as the nearest residential neighborhood. "We know residents want this resolved immediately, and we share that sense of urgency," the city says on its data center website. Google is not the only operator the city is dealing with: in July 2026 it was notified of periodic noise from Meta's campus south of State Route 161, after a temporary sound wall came down too soon, and that wall is being rebuilt. Google added data centers in Columbus and Lancaster and planned a $1 billion expansion at New Albany in 2021. In June 2025 it paid $63 million for nearly 85 acres at 2565 Harrison Road NW, about four miles north of the Beech Road campus. A Google spokesperson said of that purchase: "While we do not have a confirmed timeline for development for the site, we want to ensure we have the option to further grow, should our business demand it." The campus sits in the New Albany International Business Park, which spans 12,000 acres across the Franklin-Licking County line. Since 2010, companies have opened 40 data centers in the park, with 28 more planned or being built, according to the city, for 15 businesses including Google, Meta and Amazon Web Services. The city requires data center companies to make minimum annual payments in exchange for partial property tax abatement, and caps their water use from Columbus by agreement, community development director Jennifer Chrysler told News 5 Cleveland in May 2026. "It doesn't mean that it's going to be the experience that everyone has," Chrysler said of the city's record.

epoch-openai-stargate-abilene.text: OpenAI's Stargate data center campus in Abilene, Taylor County, Texas, built by Crusoe, is the project's flagship and most complete site, with an estimated four of its eight buildings operating. Epoch AI, a research group that tracks large computing sites, estimates current capacity at about 0.3 gigawatts (300 megawatts), with the site expanding toward 1.2 gigawatts by the end of 2026 using on-site natural gas, grid power and local wind energy. Construction began in 2024, and President Trump announced the project at a White House press conference in January 2025. OpenAI originally planned to expand the site further, to 2.1 gigawatts, before redirecting that added capacity elsewhere; Mortenson, the power-delivery contractor, energized the first Phase 2 transformer on December 19, 2025, and had five main transformers running by March 10, 2026. The Abilene City Council gave Stargate an 85% tax abatement; Oracle says the city will still get an estimated $30 million a year, and Oracle representatives said the project created 9,000 construction jobs and is expected to create 1,000 long-term ones. Average rent in Abilene has risen to nearly $2,600 a month, up almost 50 percent in a year. One renter, who asked to be identified only as "Steve Rogers" to protect his job, said of his family's finances: "We don't have anything left for savings. I'm in school and I work full-time, and it's just scary." Michael Prado, a case manager at Abilene Hope Haven, said it used to take just over a month to move a family from the shelter into a home and now can take up to six months. Lexi Smith, whose family's land sits across the street from the site, said: "[Our] house has no more residential value. If we were ever able to sell, it would be purely commercial." She said she resents the city for ever allowing the data centers to build: "There's no amount of money worth it. None." Epoch AI cut its estimate of the site's current power in April 2026 after an Oracle post, and it projects the site will reach its full 1.2 gigawatt target in the fourth quarter of 2026.

epoch-microsoft-fairwater-wisconsin.text: Microsoft's Fairwater data center in Mount Pleasant, in Racine County, Wisconsin, is operating, and three neighbors in Sturtevant are suing the company over its noise. The class action, filed in early July 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Wisconsin, seeks to represent everyone living within 1.5 miles of the campus, which the suit says includes more than 1,000 households. Fairwater sits on 315 acres of the former Foxconn site and has three buildings with a combined 1.2 million square feet under roof, according to Microsoft, which calls it the largest AI data center it has built. Microsoft says more than 90 percent of it is cooled by a closed-loop liquid system that is filled once, with 172 20-foot fans chilling the water. Equipment began coming online in April 2026, and the company said in June that the first building was fully operational with close to 550 full-time staff and vendors on site. A second building next door is under construction and set to be finished by 2028. Microsoft bought the 315 acres inside the village's Tax Incremental District 5 for $50 million in 2023 and guaranteed a minimum assessed value of $1.4 billion by 2028, the Racine County Eye reported. The noise started with the fans. "Once you hear it, you can't unhear it. It's like ringing in your ear. You can't get rid of it," Sturtevant village president Mike Rosenbaum said in April, when residents north of the campus reported a humming they could hear inside with the windows shut. Microsoft adjusted fan speeds, added sound-reduction parts and says the problem is resolved, and the village of Mount Pleasant said it had received no formal complaints about Microsoft's properties since those adjustments. The lawsuit disagrees, saying much of the "low hum" noise is low-frequency infrasound that is not detected and reflected in dBA measurements. Plaintiff Garret Ostergaard says the noise forced him to move from third shift to second because he could not sleep. Neighbors of the construction also complain of dust, lights and traffic; Larry Neumiller, across from the third-phase site, said the lights are "just super lights that even my blinds in the windows can't keep out". Sturtevant was never consulted before the project was approved and had no vote on it, the Racine County Eye noted. On January 26, 2026 the Mount Pleasant Village Board unanimously approved site plans for 15 more data centers: nine at 12023 Durand Avenue, about 5.2 million square feet, and six at 2700 International Drive, about 3.5 million square feet. Village attorney Chris Smith told the meeting the land had been zoned for industrial uses including data centers since 2017, and that the board was only judging whether the site plans met the technical code: "This is not something that can be legally denied by the board as long as the approval shows all the requirements or it's approved with conditions that they meet the requirements." Tony Martino of Mount Pleasant told the board the expansion "should not be approved until the other data centers come online and we see the real-world effects on the environment and the residents of the Village of Mount Pleasant and surrounding communities". WEC Energy Group, parent of We Energies, projects its regional electric demand will rise about 45 percent over five years, driven mainly by the Microsoft campus and the Vantage campus in Port Washington, and in April 2026 the Wisconsin Public Service Commission approved tariffs requiring data centers to pay the full cost of the energy infrastructure built for them. Eight miles southwest, in Kenosha, residents are pushing the city for a moratorium on a Microsoft data center planned on about 240 acres the company bought in early 2025. Jacqueline Semm told a city meeting: "Kenosha County should not be Microsoft's guinea pig." As of August 2026, the class action noise lawsuit remains open with no ruling issued. Construction of the 15 newly approved buildings cannot begin until Microsoft meets the site plan conditions and gets further permits from Mount Pleasant. Sturtevant, where most of the noise complaints come from, has no vote on any of it.

epoch-google-columbus.text: Google's data center on South High Street in Columbus, in Franklin County, Ohio, stands on what was Hartman Stock Farm, a 5,000 acre spread founded in 1903 by the patent medicine millionaire Samuel B. Hartman. The farm was on the National Register of Historic Places from October 9, 1974 until February 10, 2022, when the listing was removed. By then most of the farm buildings were gone, leaving the foreman's house, one dairy barn, a single room schoolhouse and one other residence. Columbus City Council approved a zoning change and a $54 million tax abatement for the project over protests from local residents and the Columbus Landmarks Foundation. The campus opened in 2022 as the anchor of Google's us-east5 cloud region. Google says it has put more than $20 billion into Ohio since breaking ground at New Albany in 2019, and now runs data centers in New Albany, Lancaster and Columbus. The company describes the staffing as hundreds of full term and contractor roles across the state rather than at any one site. On March 11, 2026, council president Shannon Hardin called an informational hearing at City Hall on what data centers are doing to the city, covering energy use, water demand, jobs and land. Robert Hackney, who moved to a south Columbus neighborhood next to the site in 2019, remembered it before Google began building: "It was country, you know, quiet, peaceful," he said. Of the change since, he said: "Oh, it's terrible. It's upside down." Asked whether he would want one near him, Hackney said: "I would say I wouldn't have it. I wouldn't have it in my backyard." Six months later the council chose rules over a ban. Council member Christopher Wyche brought forward measures to set new rates and charges for high volume water users including data centers, to require water conservation plans, to lay down how a large data center must be decommissioned, and to deal with the pollution from power generated on site behind the meter. The water rate measure had its first reading in the week of September 17, 2026 and could reach a final vote at the next meeting. "If we're only charging a mega user, for how much water they use, we're missing the broader point of how much infrastructure they're actually requiring," Hardin said, arguing that data centers should be fully covering their own cost. Wyche said that passing a moratorium "would be performative where we're trying to be constructive. We have the ability to create a regulatory framework." A Bowling Green State University poll of 1,000 likely voters found 78 percent in favor of a temporary ban on new data centers, including over 90 percent of Democrats, over 80 percent of independents and over two-thirds of Republicans, and 75 percent opposed a data center in their own community. Union members spoke for the work while backing tighter rules, and Michael Starks of Sheet Metal Workers Local 24 said data centers had "blessed me, put me in a position to take care of my family." Jessica Holes, who lives in Franklin Township, told the council "Prevention is what is desperately needed" and questioned approving more of them while the demand already on the system is hard to meet. Nobody from the industry spoke at the hearing. The pressure is not only from sites inside the city, because data centers in surrounding communities draw on the Columbus water system as well. Columbus is taking bids for a fourth water treatment plant, expected to cost billions of dollars, to meet demand from the data centers and from new housing.

sentences.t: Google's data center on South High Street in Columbus, in Franklin County, Ohio, stands on what was Hartman Stock Farm, a 5,000 acre spread founded in 1903 by the patent medicine millionaire Samuel B. Hartman.
The farm was on the National Register of Historic Places from October 9, 1974 until February 10, 2022, when the listing was removed.
By then most of the farm buildings were gone, leaving the foreman's house, one dairy barn, a single room schoolhouse and one other residence.
Columbus City Council approved a zoning change and a $54 million tax abatement for the project over protests from local residents and the Columbus Landmarks Foundation.
The campus opened in 2022 as the anchor of Google's us-east5 cloud region.
Google says it has put more than $20 billion into Ohio since breaking ground at New Albany in 2019, and now runs data centers in New Albany, Lancaster and Columbus.
The company describes the staffing as hundreds of full term and contractor roles across the state rather than at any one site.
On March 11, 2026, council president Shannon Hardin called an informational hearing at City Hall on what data centers are doing to the city, covering energy use, water demand, jobs and land.
Robert Hackney, who moved to a south Columbus neighborhood next to the site in 2019, remembered it before Google began building: "It was country, you know, quiet, peaceful," he said.
Of the change since, he said: "Oh, it's terrible. It's upside down."
Asked whether he would want one near him, Hackney said: "I would say I wouldn't have it. I wouldn't have it in my backyard."
Six months later the council chose rules over a ban.

Council member Christopher Wyche brought forward measures to set new rates and charges for high volume water users including data centers, to require water conservation plans, to lay down how a large data center must be decommissioned, and to deal with the pollution from power generated on site behind the meter.
The water rate measure had its first reading in the week of September 17, 2026 and could reach a final vote at the next meeting.

"If we're only charging a mega user, for how much water they use, we're missing the broader point of how much infrastructure they're actually requiring," Hardin said, arguing that data centers should be fully covering their own cost.
Wyche said that passing a moratorium "would be performative where we're trying to be constructive. We have the ability to create a regulatory framework."

epoch-google-mesa.text: Google's data center in Mesa, Maricopa County, Arizona, covers about 187 acres at Elliot and Sossaman roads, in the area the city calls the Elliot Road Technology Corridor. The company broke ground in July 2023 on the $1 billion project, previously known as Redhawk, after first applying for tax breaks on the site in 2019. The first phase was due to open in July 2025, with full build-out planned across three phases by 2030. Google chose air cooling for the site, citing the poor health of the region's watershed; a water-cooled data center of similar size can use more than 250 gallons of water per megawatt hour of electricity. Air cooling needs more electricity, so Google signed an eight-year deal with Salt River Project for 434 megawatts of renewable power, aiming for 80 percent carbon-free power within a year of opening. That renewable supply includes the 250 megawatt Sonoran Solar Energy Center and the 161 megawatt Babbitt Ranch wind project. An earlier estimate, reported by NBC News in June 2021 citing Bloomberg, had put the facility's water use at up to 4 million gallons a day; Google's later decision to cool the site with air rather than water was meant to avoid that level of use. Arizona paused new applications to its Computer Data Center Program from July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2029. On August 31, 2026, Attorney General Kris Mayes asked state lawmakers to go further and pause approval of new data centers statewide, citing rising water and power demand; no vote on her proposal has been scheduled.

epoch-dayone-nusajaya.text: DayOne's Nusajaya Tech Park data center campus in Iskandar Puteri, Johor, Malaysia, has been operating since 2023, and the research group Epoch AI estimates its newer AI buildings now run about 240 MW of IT power. DayOne says it has more than 478 MW operating across Nusajaya Tech Park and its second Johor campus at Kempas Tech Park. Epoch AI leaves out the three Phase 1 buildings and counts the Phase 2 buildings, which it estimates hold Nvidia H100 and B300 chips worth about $9.1 billion. Its satellite images from April 2026 showed buildings 3 to 6 complete, buildings 7 and 8 almost done and the shells of 9 and 10 still going up, and it projects the site will reach about 473 MW by the end of 2026. DayOne is also buying more land nearby: on June 23, 2026, Paragon Globe told Bursa Malaysia it would sell 26.42 hectares of vacant freehold land in Gerbang Nusajaya to DayOne Data Centers Malaysia III for RM398.11 million in cash. Paragon Globe expects the sale to be completed in the second half of 2027. It still needs planning approval from the local authorities, and no details of the data center DayOne plans there have been given. Johor's data center disputes have centered on sites built beside homes, such as the ZData and NTT plot near Taman Nusa Bayu, where residents protested on Feb. 7, 2026. Kota Iskandar assemblyman Pandak Ahmad said afterward that future data centers should go away from homes, pointing to Nusajaya Tech Park as one of the more appropriate places. No dispute over DayOne's own campus has been reported; the new land still needs local planning approval, and Epoch AI's latest satellite image of the site is from March 27, 2026.

epoch-google-council-bluffs-east.text: Google's data center at 10420 Bunge Avenue in Council Bluffs, in Pottawattamie County, Iowa, is registered with the state under a subsidiary name, Questa LLC. The campus used 1.3 billion gallons of water in 2025, more than Google's three Nebraska sites put together took that year. That is the kind of demand that worries the city's public works director. "So when we get a request, it's not for 100,000 gallons a day. It's for a million gallons a day or two million gallons a day," Matt Cox told the city council in June 2026. "So it only takes one or two big projects and we're at capacity." Mayor Jill Shudak had asked for a year-long moratorium on new data center projects so the city could review regulations first written in 2007 and adopt a comprehensive data center ordinance. At a special meeting the council rejected it unanimously. "They see a red stop sign and say, 'that's what we're going to do' and I'm not sure that's the message as a community that we would want to send right now that we're not open for business," said Councilman Douglas Rew. Council Bluffs is going the other way from much of Iowa: Linn County adopted an 18 month moratorium in June 2026, and Marshalltown and at least six counties have paused new data centers. The state tax breaks that drew Google here are now an election issue: on August 4, 2026 Rob Sand, the Democratic nominee for governor, proposed ending Iowa's sales and property tax exemptions for data centers and making companies cover the full cost of utility upgrades. "These major corporations should be paying full freight and carrying their own weight," Sand said.

epoch-coreweave-denton-tx.text: The CoreWeave data center at 8171 Jim Christal Road in Denton, Denton County, Texas, is operating on the site of a former bitcoin mine that Core Scientific converted into an AI computing campus, contracted to deliver about 262 megawatts of critical IT load to CoreWeave. Denton's city council approved the conversion in 2024 and expects $194 million in property tax revenue from it over ten years. Two years later, the same council is moving to pause the next one: it voted unanimously in early September 2026 to advance a moratorium on new data centers of 90 days, extendable to 180. The council held the first of two required public hearings on September 22, with a second set for October 27, before any vote on the moratorium. "When that data center [Core Scientific] was allowed to be built in our city, it doubled the amount of electricity," said Mayor Pro Tem Nick Stevens, who pitched the pause, adding that Texas exempts data centers' electricity from state sales tax: "That is millions of dollars that we're losing a year as a city." Denton County resident James Macfadzean told the Denton Record-Chronicle: "A lot of it just seems to be like build, build, build and we'll deal with repercussions later." Brian Beck, then a council member running for mayor, said he was not interested in attracting more data centers: "I think we need to be making sure that if you are going to come to town, then you need to follow the greenest rules possible." The city approved one more data center before the pause: a 20 megawatt QumulusAI facility on 4 acres of city land nearby, on January 13, 2026, with operations expected in 2028. The QumulusAI project runs on closed-loop cooling, and the city does not expect it to draw significantly on local water. The city council returns to the moratorium after its second public hearing on October 27.

epoch-qts-richmond-1.text: QTS Richmond 1, at 6000 Technology Boulevard in Sandston, in Henrico County, Virginia, is the data center campus QTS built inside the former Qimonda semiconductor plant, which it bought for $12 million at a bankruptcy-court auction in April 2010 and converted. QTS says the campus now covers 207 acres with 2.3 million square feet, is master planned for six buildings, and is powered for 238 MW. Three of the buildings share the Technology Boulevard address; the fourth, fifth and sixth are at 3560, 3540 and 3520 Portugee Road. QTS says its closed-loop cooling needs only a one-time fill of water and then recirculates it, eliminating ongoing water demand for cooling. Richmond 1 is the first of three QTS campuses in Sandston, alongside Richmond 2 on Technology Boulevard and Richmond 3 on Portugee Road. Across its hub at White Oak Technology Park in the Varina district, QTS has 12 buildings operating and more than 3 million square feet built, and plans 26 buildings and 8 million square feet in all, according to Richmond BizSense, which says Henrico has given administrative approval for eight of the remaining 14. The growth is on two new campuses: RIC4, up to 10 data centers on 478 acres across Technology Boulevard that QTS bought from the Henrico Economic Development Authority for $43.8 million in April 2024, and RIC5, up to seven on a 622-acre site straddling Williamsburg Road. QTS has asked the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality to permit 370 more diesel emergency generators, on top of 544 generators and 11 cooling towers it is already permitted to run. The company said in a statement: "These systems are for emergency back-up purposes only and do not continuously run." Residents of Varina have pushed back. More than 100 residents packed the meeting room at the Varina Area Library on May 19, 2026, filling every seat and the hallway, for a town hall with Varina Supervisor Tyrone Nelson that stretched nearly three hours. QTS's expansion of 17 data centers does not need to go through a public approval process because of local zoning laws. QTS is not the only builder nearby: at 6110 Technology Creek Drive, Iron Mountain is developing four data centers totaling 365,000 square feet on 66 acres. Meta also operates facilities in White Oak Technology Park. Since 2025 Henrico has required a provisional use permit for every new data center project in the county; RIC5 was the last major data center rezoning approved before that change. The generator permits rest with the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality, whose air permits carry a mandatory 30-day public comment period before they are issued. Because Richmond 1 is already built, the decisions that matter to its neighbors now are the ones on QTS's expansion: the DEQ generator permit and any new data center project, which would now need a provisional use permit from Henrico County.

epoch-qts-richmond-2.text: QTS Richmond 2 is an 85-acre data center campus at 6030 to 6070 Technology Boulevard in Sandston, Henrico County, Virginia, one of three QTS campuses on that street. QTS says the site is master planned for five buildings, DC1 through DC3 plus DC5 and DC6, totaling 180 megawatts of power once complete; its closed-loop cooling needs only a one-time water fill rather than ongoing evaporative cooling. Across Technology Boulevard, QTS is building its RIC4 campus, up to 10 more data center buildings on 478 acres it bought from the Henrico Economic Development Authority for $43.8 million in April 2024. QTS has asked the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality to permit 370 more diesel emergency generators at its Henrico campuses, on top of 544 generators and 11 cooling towers already permitted; the company says these systems "are for emergency back-up purposes only and do not continuously run." Residents of the neighboring Varina district have pressed for guarantees on air quality; at a June 2025 meeting with Varina Supervisor Tyrone Nelson, state regulators said they would work with Henrico to monitor emissions at QTS's nearby White Oak Technology Park campuses. Henrico has required a provisional use permit for every new data center project in the county since 2025, and DEQ's air permits carry a mandatory 30-day public comment period before it decides on the extra generators QTS wants at its Henrico campuses.

QTS says the site is master planned for five buildings, DC1 through DC3 plus DC5 and DC6, totaling 180 megawatts of power once complete; its closed-loop cooling needs only a one-time water fill rather than ongoing evaporative cooling.

Across Technology Boulevard, QTS is building its RIC4 campus, up to 10 more data center buildings on 478 acres it bought from the Henrico Economic Development Authority for $43.8 million in April 2024. QTS has asked the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality to permit 370 more diesel emergency generators at its Henrico campuses, on top of 544 generators and 11 cooling towers already permitted; the company says these systems "are for emergency back-up purposes only and do not continuously run."

Residents of the neighboring Varina district have pressed for guarantees on air quality; at a June 2025 meeting with Varina Supervisor Tyrone Nelson, state regulators said they would work with Henrico to monitor emissions at QTS's nearby White Oak Technology Park campuses.

Henrico has required a provisional use permit for every new data center project in the county since 2025, and DEQ's air permits carry a mandatory 30-day public comment period before it decides on the extra generators QTS wants at its Henrico campuses.

epoch-qts-richmond-3.text: QTS Richmond 3 is a 221-acre data center campus on Portugee Road in Sandston, Henrico County, Virginia, the newest of QTS's three campuses there, master planned for five buildings at 3525 through 3543 Portugee Road. QTS says the campus is planned for 240 megawatts of power once complete; in 2022 the company announced the project after buying another 200 acres at the site, Data Center Dynamics reported. About a mile north, QTS is also building its RIC5 campus, up to seven data center buildings on 622 acres straddling Williamsburg Road; QTS bought roughly 397 acres of that land for $118.8 million in 2024. QTS has asked the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality to permit 370 more diesel emergency generators at its Henrico campuses, on top of 544 generators and 11 cooling towers already permitted; the company says these systems "are for emergency back-up purposes only and do not continuously run." Varina residents have pushed for answers on air quality; at a June 2025 meeting, resident Sharon Klein told VPM News, "We know we're not going to kind of stop the data centers from coming. We just want to be safe in the environment." DEQ's Tamara Thompson said the agency's rules allow the emergency generators to run only rarely. Henrico has required a provisional use permit for every new data center project in the county since 2025, and DEQ's generator permits carry a mandatory 30-day public comment period before it decides on QTS's request for the extra generators.

epoch-meta-rosemount.text: Meta's data center at UMore Park in Rosemount, in Dakota County, Minnesota, is still under construction and due to be finished later in 2026, and the city has already said it wants to see how it runs before allowing another. On April 21, 2026 the city council voted unanimously for a one-year moratorium on new data center development, which does not touch the building going up now. "This pause gives us the opportunity to evaluate actual performance, things like water usage, noise levels, and overall community impact based on the one project already in motion," council member Tami Klimpel said. Residents had pressed for it because Meta has bought land north of County Road 42 that appears earmarked for a second data center, though no formal development application has been filed. At a March 3, 2026 council meeting a resident named Jeremie read a statement asking the council to reject it, and two others spoke with similar concerns. The worry is water: the city's Well No. 8 already tests above state limits for gross alpha radiation, and residents are wary of a facility that could use millions of gallons of water a year. They asked the council to wait for real operating data from the first building, and pointed to neighboring Eagan's one-year moratorium, passed unanimously on February 17, 2026. Meta says the first building is an $800 million-plus investment that will support about 100 jobs once completed, after 1,000 skilled trade workers on site at the construction peak. It says the Rosemount data center uses a closed-loop, liquid cooled system that will use zero operational water. It says it worked with Xcel Energy so the data center pays the full cost of its power, and with the city so it pays the full cost of its own water and wastewater service. At the state level, a bill by Senator Jen McEwen for a two-year statewide pause never gained momentum, and the 2026 session ended without new restrictions. Tom Dicklich of the Minnesota State Building and Construction Trades Council argued the buildings will go up somewhere: "If we can do them in Minnesota, where we have labor standards and we can build these more efficiently than anywhere else in the country, we should be bringing them here." Under the interim ordinance, city staff, consultants and the planning commission are studying data centers and will recommend to the city council whether and how to amend Rosemount's zoning; the moratorium lasts one year unless the council adopts data center rules sooner.

epoch-amazon-madison-mega-site.text: Amazon's data center campus on Nissan Parkway at Highway 22 in Canton, in Madison County, Mississippi, went up so fast that some of its neighbours say they learned what it was only once construction had started. "They didn't tell us anything, even when it was in the making," said René Johnson, a retired schoolteacher who lives across the highway. Joey Deeson, who runs the Madison County Economic Development Authority, said a non-disclosure agreement with Amazon kept him from sharing certain details during development; the authority has since hired a company to pick up trash around the site and handed out air purifiers to households dealing with dust. Johnny Sims, a county constable who lives 200 yards from the site, said his teenage daughter, who has asthma, has been to the emergency room repeatedly because of construction dust: "Amazon brought a lot of baggage with them." "They're just kind of putting us in an Alamo," said Cynthia Allen, the alderwoman for Canton's fourth ward, who lives across from the industrial park. "There's nowhere to go." Amazon's two Madison County campuses will house more than 700 diesel generators, over 300 of them in Canton, and permit applications estimate nitrogen oxide emissions at the Canton campus could exceed 240 tons a year. The county and the company are also fighting over what the buildings are worth. Tax assessor Norman Cannady valued each of the five data center buildings at about $292 million for the 2026 roll; Amazon's own appraisal put each at around $69 million. Amazon's tax representative, James Poliyanskiy, would not share the company's construction costs, citing competition, but agreed under questioning that its figure would "come down by a significant amount" if those costs were disclosed. On August 17, 2026 the Board of Supervisors upheld the assessor's value, keeping about $5.8 million of tax revenue this year that Amazon's figure would have cost the county. "There's no better way to determine replacement costs than the actual cost to replace that facility, which they have," Cannady said, adding that Amazon can still contest the decision in court. More is coming: Amazon says its Mississippi buildout now totals $25 billion, including an additional $11 billion for Madison County on top of the original campus.

epoch-google-bristow.text: Google's data center campus in Bristow, Prince William County, Virginia, known as Mango Farm, covers 250 acres at 13001 Rollins Ford Road, next to Gainesville High School and across from the Jiffy Lube Live amphitheater. One building of about 290,000 square feet has run there since 2023, and county filings show Google plans at least three buildings on the site. The county values the property at $1.2 billion. Google announced $9 billion of investment across Virginia on August 27, 2025, covering cloud and artificial intelligence work, a new data center in Chesterfield County, and expansion at its Loudoun and Prince William sites, though it did not say how much would go to new Bristow buildings. Governor Glenn Youngkin called the money "a powerful endorsement of our commonwealth's leadership in the AI economy," and Trevor Johnson, the county's deputy director of economic development, called it "a vote of confidence" in the county. Google's own site drew protest before it was built. In 2022 the company submitted plans for 11 buildings up to 75 feet tall on the property, bordering the Silver Leaf Estates and Amberleigh Station neighborhoods, and the approved rezoning left only a 100 foot buffer between the data centers and Silver Leaf Estates homes. Telma Zambrana, a 27 year resident of Silver Leaf Estates who learned of the plans only a week before, said: "I can't find any [other] development that's being encircled with data centers around them that are 80 feet high." Prince William County limits noise in residential areas to 60 decibels between 8am and 10pm and 55 decibels at night, but the ordinance exempts data center air conditioning units from the night limit. Kathy Kulick, a leader of the HOA Roundtable, a coalition of 50 homeowner and civic associations across Prince William and Loudoun counties, said residents had not come there to "live next to an industrial zone, let alone the world's largest data center industrial zone." The next change is on Google's doorstep. The Prince William Times reported in November 2025 that the 42 acre Bristow Industrial Park next door, which includes South Riding Nurseries, is to be razed and replaced with two 85 foot tall data centers and an electrical substation, under a pending rezoning application. Developer Scott Plein sold the land for $75 million in September 2023 to Black Chamber Group, the data center developer that also bought Merrifield Garden Center in Gainesville. Rezonings like that one go to the Prince William Board of County Supervisors.

epoch-microsoft-goodyear.text: Microsoft's Goodyear data center campus in Arizona, on nearly 300 acres south of MC 85 and Phoenix Goodyear Airport in Maricopa County, is planned for five buildings, and how to cool them in the desert has shaped the project since Microsoft bought the site in 2018. By March 2023 Microsoft had developed a 290,000-square-foot building, had a second of 250,000 square feet being built and planned to start a third of the same size soon, AZBEX reported. Water cooling for the whole campus would have needed up to 5 million gallons a day delivered to the site, and the city did not have the sewer line or wastewater plant capacity to take the company's wastewater. The Goodyear City Council voted unanimously for a revised development agreement on March 6, 2023, requiring the fourth and fifth buildings to be air cooled instead of using direct evaporative cooling. Microsoft agreed to pay $36 million toward an estimated $90 million expansion of the city's 157th Avenue Wastewater Treatment Plant, which gives it 1.2 million gallons a day of capacity at full build-out, plus a $5 million deposit toward a new sewer line and $800,000 for a city coordinator. It was the third revision of the agreement. How much water the campus actually uses is not public. The Atlantic reported in March 2024 that, at full build-out, Microsoft estimates the data center could use up to 56 million gallons a year, but that the city and state cannot disclose the amount, according to the Goodyear Independent. The Independent said city documents suggested those projections could be optimistic. Microsoft is growing elsewhere in Goodyear too; in 2026 it paid $131 million for 100 acres next to a 150-acre Microsoft campus under development near Citrus and Indian School roads, bringing its footprint in the area to more than 550 acres, DCD reported, citing CoStar. Vantage, Compass, Stack, QTS and Prime also operate in Goodyear, and Microsoft is building another campus in El Mirage. Decisions on the campus's water and sewer terms rest with the Goodyear City Council, which has revised the development agreement three times. No newer water-use figures for the campus have been published since April 2024.

epoch-meta-jeffersonville.text: Jeffersonville's city council voted 8-0 on August 3, 2026 to ban new data centers in the city for one year, but the ban does not reach Meta's $800 million data center already under construction at the River Ridge Commerce Center in Clark County. That site sits on former Indiana Army Ammunition Plant land, where federal and state military reuse law gives zoning authority to the River Ridge Development Authority instead of the city. "River Ridge has the ultimate say in the uses that go in that district," said Chad Reischl, Jeffersonville's planning and zoning director, and city attorney Les Merkley said the moratorium would not reach the commerce center because its own board approves its own development. epoch-google-kansas-city-east.text: Google's first Missouri data center is still under construction at the Hunt Midwest Business Center, just east of Worlds of Fun in Kansas City's Northland, in Clay County. Google broke ground in March 2024 and confirmed in February 2026 that the campus was still under construction. The project was announced at 1 billion dollars and is expected to create about 1,000 construction jobs and 1,400 jobs in all, once logistics and warehousing work tied to the site are counted. Port KC, the city's port authority, approved a ceiling of up to $25 billion in bonds over 35 years. That ceiling is separate from Google's $1 billion announced investment in the initial data center. The project can also use a 2015 Missouri law that exempts data center equipment, utilities and construction materials from state and local sales tax. A spokesman for then Governor Mike Parson said at the time that Google was not receiving direct incentives from the state. Google is bringing its free Skilled Trades and Readiness program to the region and giving more than 100,000 dollars to the North Kansas City School District's STEAM center. U.S. Senator Josh Hawley, a Missouri Republican who has often criticized big tech companies, said he had no problem with the project but hoped the jobs would be unionized. "If they actually want to do something to provide jobs for Missourians, that would be a nice break from their usual evil activities," he said. Google is also planning a second Northland campus nearby, called Project Mica, where Port KC's board is separately weighing a bond package; the tax terms at the Hunt Midwest site itself are already settled.

epoch-aws-new-albany.text: AWS New Albany is Amazon's original data center campus at 13360 Miller Rd NW in New Albany, Licking County, Ohio, part of the wave of large data center projects Amazon Web Services started when it arrived in the New Albany International Business Park in 2015. The city's construction list shows AWS Building A there, a 251,265 square foot data center at Miller and Beech roads, plus a security control building. Between 2015 and 2024 Amazon invested $6.2 billion in AWS data center infrastructure in Licking County, the city says, and in 2024 alone AWS paid $3.1 million in property taxes and fees there while supporting an average of 1,550 full-time equivalent jobs a year. "Amazon continues to be one of New Albany's most trusted and forward-thinking partners," Mayor Sloan Spalding said. The city trades partial property tax abatement for minimum annual payments, so a data center with 200 to 250 employees brings in as much as an office complex with 2,000 workers, community development director Jennifer Chrysler told News 5 Cleveland. The business park gets water and sewer service from Columbus, and every data center there, including this one, operates under an agreement capping its water use, Chrysler said. New Albany has received only four noise complaints since 2015, officials said. By May 2026 the business park had 40 data centers open and 28 more planned or being built, for companies including Google, Meta and Amazon. Across Ohio, local governments have moved the other way: Ohio had over 125 active data center moratoriums by September 2026, the Ohio Capital Journal reported. Tax deals for new AWS buildings in New Albany go through the New Albany City Council. Amazon's newer expansion on nearby Beech Road, bought separately in 2020 and 2022, is a different project from this Miller Road campus.

epoch-google-omaha.text: Google's data center campus in northwest Omaha, in Douglas County, Nebraska, sits north of 114th and State Street along the west side of Blair High Road. Google announced the $750 million project in April 2022, and it was still building out the 378-acre site as of January 2025. City planning documents showed 1.4 million square feet of buildings no taller than four stories, and planners waived the required parking down from 2,865 stalls to 642. Water is the local worry: Google's three Nebraska data centers, in Omaha, Papillion and Lincoln, used about 732 million gallons of water in 2025, up from 134.7 million in 2023 and 46.6 million in 2022, more than Omaha Metropolitan Utilities District customers use in an average week combined. That came as wide swaths of the state were in extreme drought, and Google says it is supporting water resilience in Nebraska through three projects in the Platte River basin, most aimed at making farm irrigation more efficient. At Omaha Public Works' annual World O Water event in September 2026, Jordan Anderson of Sierra Club Nebraska said: "We are concerned about what the potential long-term consequences of data center water use is, and the lack of oversight that has been currently put into place." Nebraska has also stopped offering data centers new tax breaks: on July 21, 2026 Governor Jim Pillen signed an executive order ending access to incentives under the ImagiNE Act for new data center applications and setting up a state task force on water and energy impacts. State Senator Mike Jacobson, who backed the order, said he plans to introduce legislation next session so that if a data center locates in Nebraska, "our taxpayers and communities should receive the full benefit of that investment."

epoch-google-lincoln.text: Google's data center campus in Lincoln, in Lancaster County, Nebraska, went by the code name Agate for four years before the company said it was behind it. Agate LLC filed for a $600 million data center campus in July 2019 and gained approval that September, but nothing was built on the site until groundwork began in 2023. Google confirmed the project in August 2023: roughly 580 acres near Interstate 80 and North 56th Street, as much as 2 million square feet of floor area, and at least 30 full-time jobs when complete. It is Google's third Nebraska site, after Papillion and Omaha, and the developers applied for state tax incentives for it. Google's Nebraska data centers used about 732 million gallons of water in 2025, up from 134.7 million in 2023, in a state where the supply is uneven and often under drought. That incentive program is now closed to data centers. On July 21, 2026, Governor Jim Pillen signed executive order 26-17, ending data centers' access to tax incentives under the ImagiNE Nebraska Act and requiring the departments of Economic Development, Revenue, and Water, Energy and Environment to review data center proposals together. "This is not a moratorium on data centers," Pillen said. The order also sets up a data center task force through the water department, which its director said would work with Nebraska's Natural Resources Districts. Figures from the governor's office put the estimated property tax exemptions given to Nebraska data centers between January 1, 2021 and June 30, 2026 at $519 million, on $15 billion of exempted personal property. The Google data center in Lincoln and Monolith, which has proposed a center at Hallam, had not responded to 10/11's requests for comment. A state auditor's report earlier in 2026 put the cost of business incentives to Nebraska at more than $1.2 billion in lost revenue, and from North Platte to Nebraska City local governments have been dealing with data centers through moratoriums and recall votes. The task force is to give its recommendations to the Legislature.

epoch-google-the-dalles.text: Google's data centers on the Columbia River in The Dalles, in Wasco County, Oregon, are back at the center of a water argument, as residents ask why they are the only ones asked to cut back in a drought. At the city council in September 2026, with Level 1 restrictions asking residents to stop or cut yard watering, Widge Johnson said: "Google doesn't participate in this. This is a Level 1 restriction. So that means that it's just the residents." She told councilors Google's share of city water had risen from 29 percent in 2021 to nearly 40 percent in 2025, figures that were not independently verified at the meeting. She asked whether the contract let the city cut Google's use in a drought; Mayor Rich Mays noted the roughly $28 million Google had put into local water infrastructure, and Johnson replied: "I know, and we can talk money all day." She added: "I would like to know what's in the contract." The mayor said he would get a legal answer. Google has run data centers here since 2006, now on three sites employing about 200 people, finished another building in 2025 and plans one more in 2026. Its use grew from 104 million gallons in 2012 to 434 million in 2024, a 316 percent rise, while the city's population grew 12 percent. In 2021, when Google announced two new data centers, it offered through a subsidiary, Design LLC, to spend $28.5 million on two groundwater wells, two storage tanks and pump stations, in exchange for deep tax cuts for the data centers' first 15 years and a commitment of water; its property taxes are discounted by 92 percent. To keep up, the city wants to triple its reservoir to about 3,000 acre feet by around 2040, at an estimated $70 million, which needs federal Mount Hood National Forest land. "Google is really not a factor in this at all," Mays said; John DeVoe of WaterWatch said: "Obviously, the great driver of demand for water in The Dalles is Google." The mayor called OPB's reporting inaccurate; OPB reviewed it and corrected one figure, finding that the city's own master plan projects residential water rates rising 99 percent by 2036, not 7 percent. The figures are public only because of a fight. When The Oregonian asked for Google's water records, the city refused, calling them a trade secret, and after Wasco County's district attorney sided with the newspaper the city sued to keep them sealed, with Google agreeing to pay the city's legal bills until it changed its mind about shielding the information. The city settled with the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press on December 15, 2022, releasing a decade of data and paying the committee's fees. Google then said it would stop treating site-level water use as a trade secret anywhere in its fleet.

At the city council in September 2026, with Level 1 restrictions asking residents to stop or cut yard watering, Widge Johnson said: "Google doesn't participate in this. This is a Level 1 restriction. So that means that it's just the residents."
She told councilors Google's share of city water had risen from 29 percent in 2021 to nearly 40 percent in 2025, figures that were not independently verified at the meeting.

She asked whether the contract let the city cut Google's use in a drought; Mayor Rich Mays noted the roughly $28 million Google had put into local water infrastructure, and Johnson replied: "I know, and we can talk money all day." She added: "I would like to know what's in the contract."
The mayor said he would get a legal answer.
Google has run data centers here since 2006, now on three sites employing about 200 people, finished another building in 2025 and plans one more in 2026.
Its use grew from 104 million gallons in 2012 to 434 million in 2024, a 316 percent rise, while the city's population grew 12 percent.

In 2021, when Google announced two new data centers, it offered through a subsidiary, Design LLC, to spend $28.5 million on two groundwater wells, two storage tanks and pump stations, in exchange for deep tax cuts for the data centers' first 15 years and a commitment of water; its property taxes are discounted by 92 percent.
To keep up, the city wants to triple its reservoir to about 3,000 acre feet by around 2040, at an estimated $70 million, which needs federal Mount Hood National Forest land.
"Google is really not a factor in this at all," Mays said; John DeVoe of WaterWatch said: "Obviously, the great driver of demand for water in The Dalles is Google."

The mayor called OPB's reporting inaccurate; OPB reviewed it and corrected one figure, finding that the city's own master plan projects residential water rates rising 99 percent by 2036, not 7 percent.

epoch-meta-montgomery.text: Meta's Montgomery data center is being built off Interstate 65 in Montgomery, Alabama, across from the Hyundai automotive assembly plant. Meta announced the project in 2024 as an $800 million, 715,000-square-foot facility in Montgomery County, optimized for AI. In September 2025 Meta said it would add two buildings, taking the campus to nearly 1.3 million square feet and its total investment to more than $1.5 billion. Meta says the campus will support more than 100 operational jobs once complete, with more than 1,000 skilled trade workers on site at peak construction; the Montgomery Area Chamber of Commerce put the construction workforce at more than 1,500. Meta says the site's energy use will be matched with renewable energy and that projects it supports are adding 227 megawatts of clean power in Alabama. Terri Michal, who is calling for a statewide moratorium on data center construction, worries that large data centers could overwhelm Alabama's power grid and pull attention from local problems such as sewers. "I feel like our priorities are off, and no one knows yet what this is going to look like," Michal said. Henry Thornton, Meta's community engagement manager, said the company pays for all the electricity and generation its facility needs, so no one's bills rise because of it, and that Meta restores a gallon of freshwater to local ecosystems for every gallon its cooling systems consume. WSFA reported in August 2026 that servers at the campus were expected to begin handling traffic within six months.

epoch-meta-kuna.text: Meta's data center in Kuna, a small city in Ada County, Idaho, south of Boise, opened in September 2026 and is now fully operational, serving traffic on Meta's platforms worldwide. Meta describes it as a facility of more than 750,000 square feet near Pleasant Valley housing its latest AI data center technology, and its global economic development director Bradley Davis called it "the culmination of 1.2 billion in capital investment into the state of Idaho." Construction began in 2022 and went through several phases, including a redesign of the cooling system. How much it will draw from the grid is not clear, but the Idaho Public Utilities Commission said earlier in 2026 that it expects the Kuna data center to become Idaho Power's single biggest customer as soon as it starts. The project was announced in February 2022 and never went to a public hearing. The land was already zoned for industrial use and already annexed into the city, so no rezoning and no public comment period were required. Meta negotiated under the code name Project Peregrine, and the Idaho Department of Commerce grants companies anonymity during negotiations to protect their strategic information and planned decisions from direct market competition. When the city announced who the company was, officials were sent more than 50 pages of emails from angry residents. Kuna resident Mychal Wilson asked what the project would do to the water the area depends on: "What is that going to do to the water that we need for crops and for animals and for local landscaping?" She also worried the facility would hurt local businesses, and said decisions taken "in shadow usually are done because they're shameful. Or they're immoral." Most of the Treasure Valley was rated abnormally dry at the time, with drought across much of Idaho. Mayor Joe Stear, who led the negotiations, said "Meta has been pretty good to work with" and called it one of the biggest projects in the state. Meta's initial investment was about $800 million for a 960,000 square foot building, to be certified LEED Gold. The company offered a new water treatment facility, funding for public services, about 1,200 construction posts, about 100 permanent ones and a commitment to use local vendors and suppliers. On the water, Meta says its data centers use 80 percent less than average facilities and need no additional water rights. The company has pledged to be water positive across its operations by 2030, restoring more water than it consumes to local watersheds, and says it is identifying restoration projects in the Treasure Valley. The building uses a closed-loop cooling system, which Davis said lets it use "virtually no water for the majority of the year." Because the site needed no rezoning, no Kuna vote ever decided it; the public body that now matters most is the Idaho Public Utilities Commission, which regulates how Idaho Power serves its new largest customer.

epoch-meta-temple.text: Meta's data center campus in Temple, Bell County, Texas, has become the focus of a fight over tax breaks for data centers. In July 2026, residents urged the Bell County Commissioners Court to stop giving data centers tax abatements, noting Meta holds one from both the city of Temple and the county. Meta says it has invested $1.2 billion in the Temple campus, where it broke ground in 2022. JE Dunn, the general contractor, says it began building the 386-acre campus in April 2022: three buildings with more than 750,000 square feet of space, totaling 152 megawatts of power, with up to 1,200 trades workers at peak construction. The campus is complete and uses dry cooling to limit water use, the contractor says. Meta says the site supports about 100 operational jobs, that it pays the full cost of its water, wastewater and energy use, and that it has given more than $1.7 million to Bell County-area schools and nonprofits. "I don't think any data center should be given a tax abatement. They were already granted money they wouldn't have gotten. So they're already ahead," farmer Alton Fowler told commissioners on July 7. Resident Joe Royer questioned why the county gave Meta its own abatement on top of the city's: "We also gave them a county tax abatement as if we are deliberately trying to attract them to our community." Commissioner Bobby Whitson said most of the Meta tax revenue is tied up in a Tax Increment Reinvestment Zone and "was never coming to Bell County anyway until the TIRZ expires." He said a tax abatement is the only lever the county has to require public safety measures or good-neighbor conditions from a project. County Judge David Blackburn has said dropping data centers from abatements would make the county "the wild, wild west" for them, with no other regulation it could impose. Texas counties have no power to impose a moratorium on data centers, the county says. A second developer, Rowan, is also building in Bell County; both Rowan and Meta get their water from the City of Temple and are subject to its drought rules, and Meta has pledged its Temple site will capture rainwater. The Commissioners Court held workshops on the issue on July 27, August 3 and August 17, and is asking the State of Texas for more authority to set land-use rules on data centers beyond tax abatements. A public hearing and vote on an amended tax abatement policy was scheduled for September 8, 2026; no result has been published.

epoch-meta-cheyenne.text: Meta's data center campus in the High Plains Business Park in Cheyenne, in Laramie County, Wyoming, has not opened yet, and it has already put the city's reclaimed water system out of service for a time. In February 2026 water flushed through the campus's new cooling pipework by Meta's contractor was discharged into the city sewer carrying a rare, metal-resistant bacterium, Cupriavidus gilardii, which routine testing then found in the system. The Board of Public Utilities suspended the reclaimed water that irrigates parks and golf courses, because of the risk of breathing it in as spray; drinking water was not affected, and some bacteria passed into Crow Creek, where officials judged the risk low. "As soon as we became aware of the bacteria, and then of where it was coming from, we shut them down immediately," said Frank Strong, the board's engineering manager. On March 24 the board revoked the discharge privileges of Goat Systems, Meta's company on the project, and suspended all data center fill-and-flush discharges into the city system. The public was not told where the bacterium came from until July 2. "We understand the frustration and the public wanting to know all this information," said Erin Lamb, the board's administrative and public affairs coordinator, "but we did have to go through a certain process to make sure that everything was done correctly." City councilman Pete Laybourn called it "a very, very unpleasant surprise," and Mayor Patrick Collins "a disappointment to everyone involved." Meta said its contractor, Fortis, stopped discharging and began hauling the wastewater off site as soon as the board raised it. Follow-up testing found no bacteria left in either treatment plant, and the reclaimed water system is running again. In July, Representative Harriet Hageman wrote to Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg demanding answers about the discharge. Meta announced the campus in July 2024 as a 715,000 square foot, $800 million-plus project expected to employ about 100 people once finished.

epoch-amazon-ridgeland.text: Amazon is building a data center in Ridgeland, in Madison County, Mississippi, part of a planned $25 billion investment covering four data center projects across three counties. The site is part of Amazon's roughly $25 billion planned investment in Mississippi data centers and has been linked in reporting to Project Rainier, the company's giant AI computing buildout for Anthropic, though Amazon has not confirmed Anthropic as the tenant. Amazon agreed to draw its water exclusively from the city of Ridgeland's system, estimating it will use about 93 million gallons a year, roughly what 800 Madison County households use annually. The company is paying $37 million toward expanding the city's water system, on top of a $3.6 million federal pandemic recovery grant and $1.2 million from the city itself, more than $40 million in total. The deal sets a maximum daily withdrawal of 3.67 million gallons and a peak wastewater discharge of 1.84 million gallons a day into the sewer system that flows on to Jackson, Mississippi. Jackson's water and sewer system, still recovering after a 2022 crisis that left more than 150,000 residents without safe water and led the state to hand control to the utility JXN Water in 2023, is one reason some experts are watching the arrangement closely. Haley Gentry, assistant director of Tulane's Institute on Water Resources Law and Policy, said the deal leaves Amazon free to use far more than its estimate: "There's no binding language that would prevent Amazon from using the peak more regularly." Ridgeland public works director Alan Hart said of Amazon, "They have given us everything we've asked for, and we demanded a lot." The agreement includes no enforcement mechanism if Amazon's water use exceeds its estimate and no requirement to disclose if it does; non-disclosure agreements common in the industry shield many of its specifics from public view. Ridgeland resident Elizabeth Partin said the arrangement made her uneasy: "It feels dirty. I understand economic pushes and things like that, but you can't do it at the deficit of the humans living here." Amazon has made what it calls a water positive pledge, meaning it intends to return more water to local systems than it draws from them. The nearby city of Jackson passed its own six-month moratorium on new data center construction on July 14, 2026, by a 5-2 council vote, the first in Mississippi.
