Ridgeland resident Elizabeth Partin said the arrangement made her uneasy: "It feels dirty. I understand economic pushes and things like that, but you can't do it at the deficit of the humans living here."
Amazon has made what it calls a water positive pledge, meaning it intends to return more water to local systems than it draws from them.
The nearby city of Jackson passed its own six-month moratorium on new data center construction on July 14, 2026, by a 5-2 council vote, the first in Mississippi.

epoch-meta-huntsville.text: Meta's data center campus in north Huntsville near Toney, in Madison County, Alabama, is adding a second phase, and a residents' group wants a moratorium on any new data centers. Construction is underway on two more buildings that will expand the campus to about 2.5 million square feet, and a meeting with city leaders in August 2026 drew questions about its water and power use, noise and jobs. Meta broke ground in 2018 in the North Huntsville Industrial Park and the data center has been operating since it opened in 2021. Meta says it has invested more than $1.5 billion in Huntsville and that the campus will support more than 300 operational jobs once completed. In December 2021 the city signed a project agreement for a $750 million expansion that city economic development director Shane Davis described as a second campus on 250 acres just north of the first, bringing the site to nearly 600 acres, with 50 new jobs at a required annual wage of $80,000. The city agreed to improve Monroe and Liberty Hill roads and add a traffic signal on Pulaski Pike, and Meta agreed to fund $2.5 million of a $2.8 million sewer extension. "When you take 27.5 mills annually of that investment and it's going to your school system, it's significant," Davis told the City Council, which was told the second campus would generate an extra $8 million to $10 million a year for local schools. Meta halted part of the expansion for a time in December 2022 to redesign it for AI, saying it would "result in a temporary construction pause of a portion of the project while we update our design". Meta buys its electricity from the Tennessee Valley Authority and its water from Huntsville Utilities. "They use about as much as a big retailer might use," said Joe Gehrdes, Huntsville Utilities' director of external affairs. Residents organized by Empowering Women's Causes were not reassured. "There are no regulations that regulate data centers", said the group's president, Lynn Anderson, listing "their water consumption, their power consumption, their noise pollution, quality of life". Naimah Russ said the project had been expected to provide about 100 jobs at an average salary of about $80,000: "We'd like to make sure that they are fulfilling this promise". "We would like a year moratorium on any other data centers that are planned," Anderson said. "We have more questions and really no answers to any of our questions." North Alabama's other hyperscale data center is Google's in Jackson County, near Bridgeport, which Google said in June it will expand by $1.5 billion in 2026 and 2027. The Tennessee Valley Authority's board approved a new rate structure for data centers in August 2026, effective Oct. 1, under which they are expected to pay about 10% more for power, and new or expanding data centers of more than five megawatts must pay a capacity charge of about $1.5 million per megawatt. State Sen. Sam Givhan said a poll of his Madison County district found 55% opposed more data centers, and that he expects the 2027 Legislature to consider cutting state tax incentives: "It's clear now that they want to come whether they get the incentives or not. So why should we give them incentives?" Huntsville City Council President Jennie Robinson said: "Honestly, the one hyperscale data center we currently have in Huntsville is plenty." She said any future proposal should be judged under a formal city policy on location, power and water use, noise, infrastructure costs, environmental effects, jobs and benefits to residents. "I am opposed, lock, stock, and barrel, to any additional data centers coming into the city of Huntsville. Period," said Councilmember Bill Kling. As of Sept. 16, Anderson said Robinson had promised a work session on the Meta data center but had not yet scheduled one.

epoch-meta-aiken.text: Meta's Aiken data center is an $800 million campus under construction in the Sage Mill Industrial Park at Graniteville, Aiken County, South Carolina, due to open in 2027. Meta announced the 715,000 square foot building in August 2024 as its 22nd data center in the United States, built for its AI workloads. Gov. Henry McMaster attended the groundbreaking, and DPR Construction is leading the build; Meta says the campus will support about 100 jobs once complete, with more than 1,000 construction workers on site at the peak. Power and water are the local questions: Aiken Electric Cooperative is the power provider, and Will Williams, president of the Western SC Economic Development Partnership, said a solar field in Orangeburg County feeding the Santee Cooper system will offset "some of the use that Meta will have, not all of it," adding that Meta had to pay for a power study before utilities agreed. Laura Warren, Meta's regional community development manager, said the company aims for the Aiken data center "to be water positive in 2030," meaning it would restore more water than it consumes. Meta also gave more than $600,000 in grants this August to 13 Aiken groups, including the school district. Two smaller data centers are also being built in the county: Oppidan Investment Company is building a $32 million, 60,000 square foot facility on Bettis Academy Road next to Sage Mill, needing 15 megawatts and six employees, and DC Blox is building on Atomic Road. Aiken County Council has approved incentive agreements for all three projects; Williams said Meta went through the county's industrial zoning process "just like any other industrial client does."

epoch-coreweave-helios.text: Galaxy Digital finished the first phase of converting its Helios bitcoin mine in Dickens County, Texas, into an AI data center that has been operating for CoreWeave since July 2026, delivering about 200 megawatts of power for 133 megawatts of the computing CoreWeave actually uses. The campus sits west of Afton in northern Dickens County, where work on a second, larger phase is now underway. Argo Blockchain broke ground on the 160-acre site in July 2021, and Galaxy bought it from Argo in late 2022 for about $65 million after bitcoin mining began there in May 2022. CoreWeave has committed to 526 megawatts of computing power across three phases, all under 15-year leases, and Galaxy says the campus could eventually reach 3.6 gigawatts of power capacity across more than 2,200 acres, well beyond what is built today. "Helios is now generating revenue across its entire 133MW of IT load, and greenfield work on Phase II is already underway," Galaxy founder Mike Novogratz said. For a county of fewer than 2,000 people, the money is large: under a ten-year agreement signed with commissioners on July 28, Galaxy is to pay Dickens County $18.5 million in lieu of taxes plus $2 million for housing. "As a result of the Galaxy/CoreWeave partnership, we should see tax breaks to property owners, improved housing availability, an increase of well-paying fulltime jobs," County Judge Kevin Brendle said. The Texas Spur reported the county also granted CoreWeave its own $19 million abatement in December, with $4 million more as seed money focused on housing, and Helios expects to hire more than 100 permanent workers. New power for the site needs sign-off from the Texas grid operator ERCOT, which cleared another 830 megawatts for Helios in January 2026, served by AEP Texas.

epoch-microsoft-project-osmium.text: Microsoft's Project Osmium data center at 5855 SW Kerry St in Cumming is operating, one of five Microsoft campuses around West Des Moines, Iowa. The address sits in Madison County, though the 2016 announcement covered 200 acres split between Warren and Madison counties for four construction phases. Microsoft has since built two more campuses nearby, and on November 20, 2023 the West Des Moines city council approved the first zoning step for a sixth, Ruthenium, just northwest of Osmium in Madison County. David Roach, 62, lives on his family's 40-acre farm two miles from the campus and says the light spilling from it at night is "polluting my dark." Microsoft's five West Des Moines-area data centers used nearly 70 million gallons of water in 2024, more than any other customer of the city's water utility, and Madison County put a moratorium on new data center permits from May 26, 2026 to May 26, 2027. Microsoft has invested an estimated $5 billion to $6 billion in its West Des Moines-area campuses since 2012, and the company has paid about $25 million toward water system upgrades while the city has spent more than $200 million on related infrastructure. Public radio counted more than 600 Microsoft employees across the five sites; Ryan Moffatt, the city's economic development director, said construction on Ruthenium is set to start in 2026.

epoch-meta-eagle-mountain.text: Meta's data center campus at 1275 North Community Circle in Eagle Mountain, Utah County, Utah, opened in 2018 and now covers more than 500 acres. On September 14, 2026 the company said it would add three more data center buildings, an administration building and a warehouse, on land the city council approved for expansion in October 2025; the council also let Meta buy another 125 acre-feet of water a year, raising its allocation from 500 to 625 acre-feet. Meta is giving the Lake Mountain School District $600,000 toward land for a new elementary school, about 30 percent of what is needed, plus $1.5 million to the district's education foundation once construction starts and $50,000 a year after that, $10,000 each to two neighboring districts for scholarships, and $450,000 to the Walden Park Observatory. Mayor Jared Gray said: "This is a company that showed up here eight years ago and has kept its commitments to us since." Separately, Eagle Mountain's city council raised the city property tax rate 183 percent on August 6, 2026, the first increase since 2010, to raise more than $5 million a year, mostly for added Utah County Sheriff's Office deputies. Residents angry about the size of the increase and the tax breaks data centers get organized a referendum; resident Alex Washburn, who led the drive with State Sen. Emily Buss, said: "It's like death by a thousand cuts." The council then repealed the 183 percent rate and set a new, lower one; residents will still pay about double the old rate. How much water and power the expanded campus will use has not been made public.

epoch-google-midlothian.text: Google's data center campus in the RailPort Business Park at Midlothian, in Ellis County, Texas, is getting a fifth building. The state filing by Sharka LLC, Google's company on the site, describes a 288,000 square foot building at 3411 Railport Parkway, started in January 2026 and due to be finished in February 2027, at an estimated $491.7 million. When the filing was first reported in December 2025 the figure was $880 million, at 3800 Railport Parkway. The first building opened in 2022 as part of Google's Dallas cloud region. Midlothian landed it in 2018 with a 10-year abatement of all personal property tax and 85 percent of improvement tax, in return for at least $500 million of investment and 40 jobs. "While we do not have a confirmed timeline for development for the site, we want to ensure that we have the option to further grow should our business demand it," Google's Andrew Silvestri said at the time. Across Ellis County the argument has since turned to what data centers owe in return. Compass Datacenters, which is planning another facility in Red Oak, gave Ellis County $15 million for a new animal shelter and donated a $12.6 million building to Texas State Technical College, while a county tax abatement for its proposed 890 acre property was withdrawn before the commissioners met on June 23, 2026, in response to what Compass called the noise around it. Susie Hall of Waxahachie told the commissioners: "I hate to think that we're going to be obligated to Compass because there will be something they're going to want in return." Governor Greg Abbott said data centers "got to bring their own money, bring their own power, reuse their own water," and that he intended to repeal the state's data center tax exemptions. Google also runs a second Ellis County data center at Red Oak, part of $40 billion it says it will spend in Texas through 2027.

When the filing was first reported in December 2025 the figure was $880 million, at 3800 Railport Parkway.
The first building opened in 2022 as part of Google's Dallas cloud region.
Midlothian landed it in 2018 with a 10-year abatement of all personal property tax and 85 percent of improvement tax, in return for at least $500 million of investment and 40 jobs.

"While we do not have a confirmed timeline for development for the site, we want to ensure that we have the option to further grow should our business demand it," Google's Andrew Silvestri said at the time.
Across Ellis County the argument has since turned to what data centers owe in return.

Compass Datacenters, which is planning another facility in Red Oak, gave Ellis County $15 million for a new animal shelter and donated a $12.6 million building to Texas State Technical College, while a county tax abatement for its proposed 890 acre property was withdrawn before the commissioners met on June 23, 2026, in response to what Compass called the noise around it.
Susie Hall of Waxahachie told the commissioners: "I hate to think that we're going to be obligated to Compass because there will be something they're going to want in return."
Governor Greg Abbott said data centers "got to bring their own money, bring their own power, reuse their own water," and that he intended to repeal the state's data center tax exemptions.
Google also runs a second Ellis County data center at Red Oak, part of $40 billion it says it will spend in Texas through 2027.

epoch-google-storey-county.text: Google's Storey County data center in the Tahoe Reno Industrial Center, east of Reno in Storey County, Nevada, has operated since 2021, and the research group Epoch AI estimates it now draws about 161 megawatts of power across two buildings. Epoch AI's satellite images show a third building's foundation under way, and it projects the campus will reach about 300 megawatts by the second quarter of 2027. The campus is one of Google's rare dry-cooled sites, using air rather than water to cool its servers, which Epoch AI calls likely an adaptation to water-scarce Nevada. Google says it began using geothermal energy to power the campus and has invested more than $6 billion in Nevada since building its Henderson data center in 2019 and this one in 2021. Water is the open question for the park as a whole: its developer and the Tahoe-Reno Industrial General Improvement District, which supplies water to its companies, are fighting in court over whether there is enough. The district says shortfalls have already happened and will grow as the park fills, while the developer says companies use less than they are entitled to, leaving "a substantial surplus of water rights." "If TRIGID loses this lawsuit, it will become increasingly difficult for TRIGID to serve the water entitlements sold by the Master Developer to TRI Center landowners," said Clay Mitchell, a Storey County commissioner and district board member. A jury trial in that water lawsuit is scheduled for May 2027 unless the two sides settle first.

epoch-google-lancaster.text: Google's data center at 105 Whiley Road in Lancaster, Fairfield County, Ohio, is operating. The company announced the site on May 3, 2023, alongside a second new data center in Columbus, saying the pair would bring its total investment in Ohio to more than $2 billion. Construction was already under way when Google made the announcement, and the company said the new centers would help power its artificial intelligence tools along with Search, Gmail and Maps. Google holds a statewide agreement with Ohio, in place since December 2018, that exempts its eligible data center equipment from the state's sales tax. Google confirmed to Governing magazine that it has a property tax abatement agreement, called a Community Reinvestment Area, with the city of Lancaster, though it declined to say how much the deal is worth. "Due to confidentiality, we cannot provide actual tax forgone related to this credit, even in the aggregate because it is such a finite number of taxpayers," said Andrea Lannom, a spokeswoman for the Ohio Department of Taxation, which administers the state's data center sales tax exemption.

epoch-meta-qts-hillsboro-2.text: QTS Hillsboro 2 is a four-building data center campus in Hillsboro, Washington County, Oregon, and all four buildings are now operating. The research group Epoch AI estimates the campus runs about 180 megawatts of power, likely for computer chips used by Meta, at a capital cost of about $6.8 billion. It is one of three QTS campuses in the Hillsboro area, and QTS says Avangrid's Tower Solar project, a 120-megawatt solar farm, delivers power to the local electric grid to help support its operations there. Hillsboro has 35 data centers, more than any other Oregon city, and on July 27, 2026, its City Council unanimously adopted a 120-day moratorium on new land use applications for data centers and battery storage sites, the first in the state. Mayor Beach Pace said the city gave only a day's notice of the meeting to keep companies from rushing in applications before it took effect; the pause does not affect existing data centers such as this one. A month earlier, the Oregon Education Association, 1000 Friends of Oregon, Tax Fairness Oregon and others sued Hillsboro and Washington County over 17 enterprise zone tax break approvals granted to data center companies including Adobe, Nvidia and Dropbox in March and April, before a state pause took effect. The City Council can extend the moratorium for another 120 days while it rewrites the city's development code for data centers.

epoch-google-waltham-cross.text: Ten months after Google's data center opened at Waltham Cross in Cheshunt, in the Borough of Broxbourne in Hertfordshire, the people living around it got a meeting with the company. In late July 2026, two Google managers, server operations site manager Dan Dale and DCOps site manager Tihomir Lazic, met residents and Broxbourne Borough Council representatives at the council offices, and heard complaints about poor consultation, noise and light pollution. "We haven't had the opportunity to object," one resident said, and another said of the planning process: "If you're working in planning, you would have planned this better." A council representative said only 12 people had come to the previous public meeting about the facility. Several residents said they could hear a hum from the site, worst in the evening, a problem often blamed on cooling equipment at data centers. One said the lighting was shining right into their bedrooms all night, and Dale said Google was working on changes so that lights would "be on when needed and when access is required." Asked about heat and other effects on the environment, Dale said an environmental impact study had been submitted with the planning application and that "we are constantly monitored to make sure that we are in line with environmental permits." One resident asked whether Google would buy his house so that he could move, saying the site was already affecting house prices. On water, Lazic described a closed loop, air-cooled system, "a loop of water pipes which run the same amount of water around" rather than losing it to evaporation, and Dale put the site's water use, mostly from its offices, at about 60 cubic meters a month, roughly what five houses use. The 33-acre site is expected to provide up to 77 megawatts of power when full, but is currently nowhere near that level, according to Google. The opening, on September 16, 2025, had been a different sort of occasion. Chancellor Rachel Reeves opened the site and called Google's two-year, £5 billion UK investment, which it belongs to, "a powerful vote of confidence in the UK economy and the strength of our partnership with the US." Google says more than 250 companies worked on the construction, and it set up a community fund managed by Broxbourne Council. The company says its air-cooled system limits water use to domestic levels and that it is equipped to send waste heat free of charge to local homes, schools or businesses; it projects its UK operations will run at or near 95% carbon-free energy in 2026, with Shell Energy Europe managing that supply. The planning decisions came years earlier: The Register reported that a data center application for the land was first filed in 2018, before Google bought the land for £33 million in 2020, and that Broxbourne approved the final reserved-matters application on November 30, 2023. Google and the council both say proper procedures were followed, and a Google spokesperson said public consultation took place before the council granted permission. Google's team promised residents further meetings and better communication.

epoch-vnet-bayin-ulanqab.text: VNET's data center campus at Bayin, in the Chahar High-Tech Zone of Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, China, is being expanded: in February 2026 the zone's economic development bureau approved a third phase, to be built from March 2026 to March 2028. The approval places it north of Bayin Wei Road 12 and west of Bayin Jing Road 6, with two server buildings, a diesel generator building and a research building. The demand behind it is ByteDance's: Bloomberg reported in March 2026 that VNET had won a deal to supply the TikTok owner about 500 megawatts of capacity across China for its Doubao chatbot and other AI systems. The South China Morning Post reported that ByteDance was separately discussing five to six gigawatts of capacity in Ulanqab's Jining district, for delivery by early 2028. Ulanqab, long known as China's potato capital, has turned itself into a data center town: by the end of June 2026 the city had signed 89 data center projects, 86 of them for AI computing, China Newsweek reported. Huawei, Alibaba, Apple and Kuaishou run data centers there, and ByteDance, Tencent, Baidu and DeepSeek have placed large AI model training projects in the city. In the Chahar zone, large industrial power costs 0.35 to 0.45 yuan a kilowatt hour, less than half the price in eastern China, and land runs 100,000 to 120,000 yuan for a mu, a Chinese land unit close to a sixth of an acre. Ulanqab has set out to be what officials call China's "Token capital," the hub for the computing that trains and runs AI chatbots, though Zhou Haifeng of the Inner Mongolia Economic Society said the city still falls short on talent, capital, industry and technology. The city averages 4.3 degrees Celsius, cool enough to use outside air to cool servers about ten months a year, and two dedicated fiber cables run to Beijing, 4.2 milliseconds away. VNET signed a strategic cooperation agreement with the Chahar zone for the campus on April 18, 2024. The third phase, with total investment of 3 billion yuan, 600 million of it VNET's own money and 2.4 billion in loans, was approved and recorded on February 2, 2026 by the zone's economic development and investment promotion bureau.

epoch-huawei-horinger.text: Huawei Cloud is building a data center in the Horinger New Area Cloud Valley Zone of Hohhot, the capital of Inner Mongolia, China, where ground was broken on October 8, 2023. The project covers 5,963 mu, about 398 hectares, with a planned capacity of more than a million servers, and China Daily reported it would be Huawei's biggest computing hub cluster in north China once complete. Horinger is not one data center but a growing cluster: China Telecom started building south of Hohhot in Horinger County in 2011, Inner Mongolia announced a provincial big data strategy in 2016 modeled on Guizhou's, and the area was branded China Cloud Valley. Huawei is building there alongside China Telecom and China Mobile, which have already opened facilities, with data centers for the Bank of China, the Agricultural Bank of China, China Construction Bank and U-Cloud also planned for the area. By August 2024, Hohhot officials counted data centers by China Mobile, China Telecom and Huawei Cloud among the New Area's key projects, with a combined computing power of 24,000P across the cluster.

epoch-google-arcola.text: Google's Arcola data center, a 400,000-square-foot building in Sterling in eastern Loudoun County, Virginia, is one of three Northern Virginia sites where Google said in 2024 it would spend $1 billion on improvements. Google confirmed in November 2017 that it had bought the 91-acre Arcola property, just west of Dulles Airport, for $58 million, along with a 57-acre site in the Stonewall Business Park near Leesburg for $31 million. "We've purchased property in Northern Virginia to increase our capacity and meet the growing demand for Google's services in the area," Google public affairs manager Liz Schwab said at the time. The purchase marked a shift for Google, which had previously leased wholesale data center space in the region. The Arcola campus, also called the Dulles Arcola Center, is permitted for up to 2.35 million square feet of data center space. The 2024 spending, announced with Gov. Glenn Youngkin, covered the Arcola site, Google's 200,000-square-foot data center in Leesburg and its facility near Gainesville in Prince William County, and brought Google's total investment in Virginia to $4.2 billion. Google said the money would go to "technical infrastructure" and did not say whether it meant expanding the buildings. Bisnow reported that Google also plans a second facility closer to Dulles International Airport. The Arcola site sits in the part of the county where two-thirds of residents live alongside nearly 200 operating data centers, and the county says noise and air quality are the complaints that come with that mix. Loudoun's noise rules cap sound at 55 dBA at a residential property line, and data centers must submit a noise study before construction and another within a year of opening. In September 2026 the Loudoun County Board of Supervisors voted 7-1-1 to pause new data center applications for 12 months, with Supervisor Kristen Umstattd voting against and Supervisor Caleb Kershner of the Catoctin district abstaining. "For years, I have been pushing for Loudoun County to get a handle on data center growth," said Algonkian District Supervisor Juli Briskman, who brought the pause forward. The pause covers new applications rather than existing campuses such as Arcola, and county staff are to bring a formal resolution to the board's October 20 business meeting. The county has already removed data centers as a by-right zoning use and is exploring removing by-right status from projects that were grandfathered in; those decisions rest with the Board of Supervisors.

Google confirmed in November 2017 that it had bought the 91-acre Arcola property, just west of Dulles Airport, for $58 million, along with a 57-acre site in the Stonewall Business Park near Leesburg for $31 million.

"We've purchased property in Northern Virginia to increase our capacity and meet the growing demand for Google's services in the area," Google public affairs manager Liz Schwab said at the time. The purchase marked a shift for Google, which had previously leased wholesale data center space in the region. The Arcola campus, also called the Dulles Arcola Center, is permitted for up to 2.35 million square feet of data center space.

The 2024 spending, announced with Gov. Glenn Youngkin, covered the Arcola site, Google's 200,000-square-foot data center in Leesburg and its facility near Gainesville in Prince William County, and brought Google's total investment in Virginia to $4.2 billion. Google said the money would go to "technical infrastructure" and did not say whether it meant expanding the buildings. Bisnow reported that Google also plans a second facility closer to Dulles International Airport.

The Arcola site sits in the part of the county where two-thirds of residents live alongside nearly 200 operating data centers, and the county says noise and air quality are the complaints that come with that mix. Loudoun's noise rules cap sound at 55 dBA at a residential property line, and data centers must submit a noise study before construction and another within a year of opening.

In September 2026 the Loudoun County Board of Supervisors voted 7-1-1 to pause new data center applications for 12 months, with Supervisor Kristen Umstattd voting against and Supervisor Caleb Kershner of the Catoctin district abstaining. "For years, I have been pushing for Loudoun County to get a handle on data center growth," said Algonkian District Supervisor Juli Briskman, who brought the pause forward. The pause covers new applications rather than existing campuses such as Arcola, and county staff are to bring a formal resolution to the board's October 20 business meeting.

The county has already removed data centers as a by-right zoning use and is exploring removing by-right status from projects that were grandfathered in; those decisions rest with the Board of Supervisors.

epoch-google-red-oak.text: Google's Red Oak data center sits on 166 acres where Farm-to-Market Road 664 meets State Highway 342 in Ellis County, south of Dallas. Google built it as a $600 million investment, Ellis County commissioners approved a 10 year tax abatement in 2018, and it employs about 30 people full time. It is operating, and an expansion announced in 2023 is under way. The existing buildings are evaporative cooled, which means they consume water. The expansion will be closed loop air cooled instead, as will Google's new Texas sites in Haskell, Wilbarger and Armstrong counties. In 2026 the company published a Texas water stewardship plan: a $10 million Texas Water Impact Fund for communities where it builds, a commitment to replenish more water than it consumes at its sites by 2030, annual public reporting of water use, and work on reclaimed water. Google says it has put more than $500 million into water infrastructure in communities where it has data centers. Ben Townsend, its global head of infrastructure and sustainability, said the company wants to "walk the walk and talk the talk" on water. Red Oak itself has been arguing about the industry, though not primarily about Google. The town's population more than doubled to 20,000 between 2018 and 2025, and there are now seven data center sites at various stages: two operating, one under construction and four in the pipeline, with projected investment of $13 billion. In May 2026 the city council voted 4 to 1 to rezone 830 acres of farmland for Compass Datacenters, which plans eight two storey buildings of 200,000 square feet each. More than 130 residents turned up at city hall meetings to object, raising noise, light pollution, the risk of water contamination, traffic and property values. Mayor Mark Stanfill defended the growth as deliberate, positioning Red Oak as a regional gateway and business hub. Google, Compass and DataBank have each been granted 10 year tax breaks; the most recent abatement backed campus is a $9.45 billion investment expected to add $405 million to the tax base across the abatement period. Nine data centers are operating or planned in Ellis County.

epoch-google-papillion.text: Google's data center in Papillion, in Sarpy County, Nebraska, stands at 14706 Schram Road near Highway 50, on a site first known locally as Project Wizard. Google announced it as a $600 million project that would initially employ 30 people, and it was built in 2019, before Google's Omaha data center in 2022 and its Lincoln project announced in 2023. The number that has changed fastest here is water. Google's Nebraska operations, covering all three of the company's sites at Papillion, Omaha and Lincoln and not broken out by campus, used 46.6 million gallons in 2022, 134.7 million in 2023, and 732.1 million in 2025. For comparison, Meta's four million square foot campus nearby withdrew between 26.7 and 37.5 million gallons a year from 2020 to 2024. Google says it uses evaporative cooling or closed loop air cooled chillers depending on how much water is available in a place. Large parts of Nebraska are in extreme drought. John Winkler, general manager of the Papio-Missouri River Natural Resources District, put it plainly: "From a logical, common-sense perspective, we really need to stop putting industry in areas where they can't be supported by natural resources like water." Anthony Schutz, a law professor at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, said that set against the water Nebraska pours on its fields, the data centers' draw "remains a small amount relative to that." Pete Marin, who runs T5 Data Centers, said most of the industry is "doing the right thing," though he allowed there is a share of bad actors. Until recently nobody had to say how much they used. A law passed in the Nebraska legislature's 2026 session requires data center developments to report annual water use and energy demand to the state Department of Water, Energy and Environment, starting later in 2026. The department's director, Jesse Bradley, said the state has a planning process in every area of Nebraska aimed at protecting all existing water users.

epoch-meta-gallatin.text: Meta's Gallatin data center sits in the Gallatin Industrial Center, four miles northeast of downtown Gallatin in Sumner County, Tennessee. The 900 acre campus has four buildings spanning nearly 1.7 million square feet and has been operating for about two years. Meta puts its investment in the campus at $1.5 billion. Utility records show the campus used more than 53 million gallons of water in 2025, about 2% of the city's total, ranking Meta among Gallatin's top five water users. "It's one entity and they can do more per the contract with the city, and they're still building," City Councilman Pascal Jouvence said. Meta says its closed loop cooling system uses 80% less water than a typical data center. The city granted Meta a 20 year payment in lieu of taxes package worth an estimated $19.5 million in tax breaks, and Meta paid an estimated $1.8 million in local taxes in 2025. "I probably wouldn't agree to a PILOT," Mayor Paige Brown said. Neighbors on Brights Lane describe brown dust during construction and a low hum at night; one, Elizabeth Holmes, said Meta sent her a $2,500 check after a blast shook her house, in exchange for a statement that she would not sue. In June 2026, Councilman Jouvence proposed a two year moratorium on new data center construction, and the council deferred the vote. In July the council annexed about 125 acres west of Brights Lane, just north of the campus, with no stated purpose, though Jouvence said the land "looks perfect to extend for a new Data Center." No expansion has been announced. The council approved a 60 day pause on new data center applications on July 28, and on August 25 the Gallatin Planning Commission recommended a 12 month moratorium. Mayor Brown has called moratorium talk "performative," saying no data center proposals are pending. The City Council has not yet voted on the Planning Commission's recommendation.

epoch-meta-los-lunas.text: Meta's data center at Los Lunas, in Valencia County, New Mexico, stands along the Rio Grande near Interstate 25, south of Albuquerque; the company announced the project in 2016 and is now expanding it. On February 13, 2025 the village council unanimously approved an amended water agreement for the site and an industrial revenue bond ordinance for Greater Kudu LLC, a Meta subsidiary, to cover two more buildings for artificial intelligence work. The water agreement holds Meta's allocation at 500 acre-feet a year, about 163 million gallons, cuts the peak daily draw allowed in extreme heat from 4.5 million gallons to 3 million, and limits that access to five days at most during an emergency. "This agreement ensures that they cannot exceed the existing amount that we've agreed upon," said public works director Michael Jaramillo. The campus runs or is building 10 buildings across 750 acres and employs more than 180 people, a figure Meta expects to reach 400 at full build-out; Meta community development manager David Williams said the site is using about 60 percent of its water allocation and, "We will not be asking for any additional water." Williams said, "On typical days, no water is used to cool our servers, even on hot summer days, water isn't needed when temperatures are below 85 degrees," and the company says it matches all of the site's electricity use with renewable energy. Not everyone trusts the numbers: when the village weighed tax breaks for the expansion in 2021, the local group Valencia Water Watchers said the village had not been open about how much water the data center would use. Meta's withdrawals for the site came to 59 million gallons in 2020, rising to about 67 million gallons by 2024, drawn from the village system, Meta told the fact-checking site Snopes. In 2026, as the Rio Grande dried early, social media posts claimed the data center had "completely drained" the river; Snopes rated that claim false in July, since the site buys municipal water from the village, whose system is supplied by groundwater wells, and Meta holds no Rio Grande water rights. A Bureau of Reclamation water operations supervisor told Snopes nothing indicated the data center was contributing to the drying, which the agency put down to low snowpack, reservoir storage, unusually warm temperatures and long-term drought.

epoch-coreweave-ellendale-nd.text: Applied Digital's Polaris Forge 1 data center campus in Ellendale, Dickey County, North Dakota, is operating under a long-term lease to CoreWeave, which is contracted for 400 megawatts of it in all. The first 100 megawatt building has run at full load since Applied Digital completed its second phase on November 24, 2025, the first of three contracted buildings on the campus. Applied Digital signed two roughly 15-year leases with CoreWeave in June 2025 for 250 megawatts of critical IT load, expecting about $7 billion in revenue, with an option for CoreWeave to take 150 megawatts more. Applied Digital delivered the campus's second building in May 2026 and energized a 75-megawatt phase of it in July. The company came to Ellendale in 2021 because the town sits near a substation collecting power from wind farms across North and South Dakota, and its first data center there hired 35 people. For a town of about 1,100 people, the stakes are large: Ellendale annexed the property in early 2025, and Mayor Don Flaherty said the city's taxable value of $3.5 million at the end of that year is expected to grow more than tenfold. "Could it blow up in my face?" Flaherty said of the town's bet on the company. "Absolutely." Jamie Walker, a former property manager in town, said construction workers doubled the rent on a one-bedroom apartment from about $600 to more than $1,200, pushing out lower-income families: "The regular Ellendale local is not winning as big as, say, Casey's or Cenex or the local bars." Montana-Dakota Utilities customers have received credits because the data center's added demand raises the utility's revenue under a state cap on returns; the average customer saved about $70 in 2025. Applied Digital says it will be North Dakota's largest property taxpayer by 2028 or 2029, at more than $25 million a year, and also has data center projects near Harwood, Jamestown and Oliver County. In July 2026 the North Dakota Public Service Commission approved a roughly $110 million power project tied to the campus's next phase, Polaris Forge 2.

For a town of about 1,100 people, the stakes are large: Ellendale annexed the property in early 2025, and Mayor Don Flaherty said the city's taxable value of $3.5 million at the end of that year is expected to grow more than tenfold.
"Could it blow up in my face?" Flaherty said of the town's bet on the company. "Absolutely."

Jamie Walker, a former property manager in town, said construction workers doubled the rent on a one-bedroom apartment from about $600 to more than $1,200, pushing out lower-income families: "The regular Ellendale local is not winning as big as, say, Casey's or Cenex or the local bars."

Montana-Dakota Utilities customers have received credits because the data center's added demand raises the utility's revenue under a state cap on returns; the average customer saved about $70 in 2025.
Applied Digital says it will be North Dakota's largest property taxpayer by 2028 or 2029, at more than $25 million a year, and also has data center projects near Harwood, Jamestown and Oliver County.
In July 2026 the North Dakota Public Service Commission approved a roughly $110 million power project tied to the campus's next phase, Polaris Forge 2.

epoch-meta-sarpy.text: Meta's Sarpy data center broke ground in Papillion, Sarpy County, Nebraska in 2017 and went online in 2019. The company has since expanded the campus toward nine buildings and 4 million square feet, most recently adding a building on land it bought in Springfield, also in Sarpy County. Meta says it has invested more than $2.5 billion in the site and supports more than 300 operational jobs. Meta says it worked with the Omaha Public Power District to plan its energy needs and pay their full cost, and with the Metropolitan Utilities District to pay the full cost of its water and wastewater service. The company says it matches its electricity use with clean energy, including a wind farm it has invested in in Dixon County. From 2020 to 2024 the Sarpy campus withdrew between 26.7 million and 37.5 million gallons of water a year from the local supply, Meta's own reporting shows, the Flatwater Free Press found. The campus uses a mix of evaporative and closed-loop cooling. Omaha's Metropolitan Utilities District, which supplies the area, can deliver about 320 million gallons a day against average demand of about 98 million gallons, and counts at least 10 data centers among its biggest water users. Nebraska lawmakers passed a law in 2026 requiring data centers to report their annual water use and power demand to the state. Jesse Bradley, director of the state Department of Water, Energy, and Environment, called it a "great start" and said the agency would then see what information gaps remain.

epoch-coreweave-chester-va.text: CoreWeave's data center at 1401 Meadowville Technology Parkway in Chester, Chesterfield County, Virginia, is operating under developer Chirisa Technology Parks, which is building two more CoreWeave buildings nearby at 1600 Digital Drive. County officials say they are done approving new data centers: "The board has indicated they don't have an appetite for these," Deputy County Administrator Jesse Smith said in August 2026. The 242,000 square foot building was built for Capital One in 2013 and refitted for CoreWeave under a $200 million construction loan in 2023, when CoreWeave signed a 12-year lease with two five-year extension options. Chirisa is now building two roughly 190,000 square foot buildings for CoreWeave at 1600 Digital Drive, one due in late 2027 and the other in mid-2028, on the site of the never finished Cartograf packaging plant. "It'll be a master campus for the one tenant that we have there," said David Kelly, Chirisa's head of U.S. real estate. Since the start of 2026, every new data center in Chesterfield has needed a conditional use permit voted on by the Board of Supervisors, instead of being allowed by right in industrial zones. In June the county's Board of Zoning Appeals unanimously rejected a landowner's claim to vested rights for a data center on 89 acres at 1931 Old Bermuda Hundred Road in Chester, meaning it needs that permit too. The county counts at least 10 data center buildings built or being built, including Google's first Chesterfield campus, next to Meadowville Technology Park, due to open in late 2027. The county wants to use data center tax revenue to cut the car tax, now $3.25 per $100 of value, by at least $1, but supervisors deferred the vote a second time on September 23, 2026, moving it to November 18. "Those data centers are not going to come out of the ground for a long time, because Dominion doesn't have the energy to power them," Vice Chair Kevin Carroll said. The Board of Supervisors, which must approve any new data center permit, returns to the car tax vote on November 18.

epoch-oracle-batam.text: DayOne, a Singapore-based data center developer, runs a data center campus in Nongsa Digital Park on the Indonesian island of Batam, built with Indonesia's sovereign wealth fund, the Indonesia Investment Authority. The banks that financed the project, DBS and UOB, say the campus will carry about 72 megawatts of power once complete, roughly 5% of Indonesia's projected data center capacity by 2029. In April 2026 DayOne signed Indonesia's largest power supply deal, about 450 megawatts, for a second, larger Batam campus at the nearby Kabil Integrated Industrial Estate. In June 2025 DBS and UOB lent 6.7 trillion rupiah, about 530 million Singapore dollars, to build and run three data centers at Nongsa, the largest such loan ever made in Indonesian rupiah for a data center. It was the wealth fund's first investment in the sector. "This landmark financing is a strong endorsement of DayOne's proven ability to deliver digital infrastructure at speed and scale," said Jamie Khoo, DayOne's chief executive. DayOne says the site sits in Nongsa's special economic zone, close enough to Singapore for direct fiber links and access to more than 15 undersea cables, and that one building has LEED Gold certification. The company markets Batam together with Singapore and Johor, Malaysia, as a single cross-border hub for data centers. Power for the new Kabil campus will arrive in phases from Indonesia's state utility, PLN Batam, between 2026 and 2027.

epoch-aws-berwick.text: Amazon Web Services is building a data center campus beside Talen Energy's Susquehanna nuclear plant in Salem Township, near Berwick in Luzerne County, Pennsylvania, after buying an existing nuclear-powered data center at the site from Talen in March 2024. Salem Township supervisors approved rezoning roughly 1,600 acres for industrial use on May 30, 2024, clearing the way for as many as 15 data center buildings over the next decade. The township expects up to 600 jobs and about $7 million a year in local tax revenue once Amazon's ten-year, 70 percent tax break runs out. Amazon has said the campus is part of a plan to invest at least $20 billion in Pennsylvania, creating at least 1,250 high-skilled jobs, and some residents at the rezoning hearing said turning farmland industrial would devalue their own land. Three data center projects are now in play in the township: the AWS campus being built, an approved QTS project, and a third proposed by former state representative Mike Cabell. On August 25, 2026, Luzerne County Judge Lesa Gelb ruled that the Salem Township planning commission had violated Pennsylvania's Sunshine Act by holding a meeting on a zoning overlay for the third project while people trying to get in were shut out. The eight residents who sued, with no lawyer between them, included Annie Vinatieri, Teri Barren and Nate Eachus. "What happened on Tuesday was an actual win for citizens everywhere across Pennsylvania," Vinatieri said. They then asked for a restraining order to stop a second planning commission meeting arranged after the first was invalidated; the judge refused, and the case continues.

epoch-coreweave-marble-nc.text: Core Scientific's Marble, North Carolina data center sits on the site of the former American Thread Company mill in Cherokee County, which closed in 2015; the company's own site lists it as 250,000 square feet on 70 acres with a total power capacity of about 117 megawatts. It converted a cryptocurrency mine there into the AI facility, and the company says it is still doing that conversion at similar sites even after a planned merger with CoreWeave fell through in October 2025. Rebecca and Tom Lash moved to the area eight years ago hoping to retire in the Blue Ridge Mountains, and say the noise from crypto mining has intruded on their lives since it opened in 2021. "There was nothing in this little pasture but these electric lines," Rebecca Lash said. "And it was just nice and quiet." Tom Lash said: "The big AI centers and the big data centers, there's some horror stories about people that live near those." The facility runs on more than 170 diesel generators, and draws municipal water along with pumping from wells on site, which state regulations limit to 12 hours of pumping a day, according to Marble Community Water System board president C.B. McKinnon. Andrews Mayor James Reid refused to connect the facility to the town's wastewater system because it lacked an environmental plan, forcing it onto septic tanks: "I wouldn't wish this on any county or entity, ever. It's absolutely destroyed Marble." The county received $268,000 in tax revenue from the facility in 2024, though revenue fell in 2025 during construction. Since January 2026, neighboring towns such as Boone and Clyde, counties such as Swain and Clay, and the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians have adopted temporary bans or moratoriums on new data centers, as officials in Cherokee County itself reconvene their planning board to look for limits without countywide zoning.

epoch-core42-lake-mariner.text: TeraWulf is converting a former coal-fired power plant on Lake Ontario in Barker, New York, into a large AI data center campus called Lake Mariner, built on 180 acres it leases from the original 1,800-acre Somerset power plant site. At its peak, the coal plant paid about $20 million a year in taxes to Barker and its school district, and its workforce had fallen to 55 people by the time it closed; TeraWulf now employs 120 people on site, including 20 former coal plant workers. Core42, a unit of Abu Dhabi's G42, signed long-term leases with TeraWulf for more than 70 megawatts of data center capacity at Lake Mariner, released in phases between the first and third quarters of 2025, with room to expand by another 135 megawatts. "This is the fastest ongoing data center build in the US right now," said Sean Farrell, TeraWulf's chief operating officer. Noise from early cryptocurrency mining equipment at the site brought complaints from neighbors, and the newer buildings now use quieter cooling equipment after the company added noise controls. The campus draws its power from the regional New York grid zone that includes Niagara Falls hydropower, which is 89 percent carbon free, and its closed loop cooling system takes no water from Lake Ontario, though the old plant's water intake is still in place. In July 2026, Governor Kathy Hochul signed an executive order banning new state permits for data centers for a year and said she wants to end tax breaks for hyperscale data centers, including ones issued by local industrial development agencies. Investigative Post reported that TeraWulf is not paying state or local sales tax on its multi-billion dollar expansion at Lake Mariner and gets discounted electricity from the New York Power Authority, and that Niagara County officials are looking into how much revenue they are missing. Hochul said a ban on data center subsidies could come in next year's state budget, which puts the question before the governor and the state Legislature.

epoch-microsoft-sat40.text: Microsoft's SAT40 data center sits on about 70 acres at 15000 Lambda Drive, in Texas Research Park near State Highway 211 on the far west side of San Antonio. It is one of eight Microsoft properties across Bexar and Medina counties, more than $1.2 billion of investment since the company's first two San Antonio data centers went up in 2015 at $90 million each. Microsoft registered the building with Texas accessibility regulators on March 3, 2023 as new construction of a 153,227-square-foot data center shell, at an estimated cost of $175.9 million, with work scheduled from June to September 2023. What nobody outside the utility can find out is how much water any of them use. KSAT asked the San Antonio Water System for three years of water records covering 36 Bexar County data centers and was refused under Section 552.1331 of the Texas Government Code, which SAWS reads as shielding smart meter data on commercial accounts. The provision was written about six years earlier by State Representative Diego Bernal to stop payday lenders getting at household water use. Asked whether the utility had read his bill correctly, Bernal replied: "Absolutely not." He went on: "At this point, especially because of your request, I think there's fair warning that something has to be fixed." He added: "Data centers are doing tremendous damage to Texas, to our water supply, to air quality." SAWS spokesperson Anne Hayden said the utility "is correctly interpreting and applying the law," and State Representative Cody Harris said at a legislative hearing: "The transparency of utilization of resources shouldn't be optional." Davin Hicks, a Cibolo resident opposing a data center near him, said: "People are outraged because nobody knows and they just pop up." Microsoft's other holdings in the two counties include Westover Link on State Highway 151 at an estimated $216 million, a site on the Bexar and Medina county line at $230 million, and SAT80-1 and SAT80-2 on 206 rural acres at Potranco Road and FM 471 near Castroville.

epoch-microsoft-sat14.text: Microsoft's SAT14 data center campus at 3545 Wiseman Boulevard in San Antonio, Bexar County, is operating, one of more than 20 data centers already built in the city. The state's building register lists SAT14's first phase as two building shells of 152,000 and 107,000 square feet, built for an estimated $154.9 million between October 2021 and December 2022. Microsoft is planning up to five buildings on the site, totaling around 350,000 square feet at a cost of more than $200 million, Data Center Dynamics has reported. On Aug. 25, 2026 the San Antonio City Council heard draft zoning rules that would confine data centers to industrial or commercial districts, keep them at least 500 feet from homes, schools, hospitals and assisted living facilities, and bar them from the Edwards Aquifer Recharge Zone. "My biggest concern is the 500-foot setback," said Deedee Belmares, a clean energy advocate at Public Citizen, who wants more study of noise, light, air pollution and heat first. "Data centers are one of the largest, fastest-growing threats to our communities," said Councilman Jalen McKee-Rodriguez, who backed a moratorium; other council members opposed a pause but favored new rules, and electrical union workers said a single data center could employ 200 to 600 of them for years. Development Services director Amin Tohmaz said zoning could address noise and light through setbacks but could not regulate water and power use, and that a moratorium would exempt at least 12 projects already negotiating for utility service. Statewide, Gov. Greg Abbott ordered a moratorium on Aug. 3, 2026 on new data centers connecting to the Texas grid until regulators audit them, though it does not apply to data centers with their own power. The city's Zoning Commission session on data centers was scheduled for Sept. 15, 2026; no result has been published. The City Council is set to vote on the new zoning rules on Oct. 15, 2026.

epoch-stack-infrastructure-nva02.text: STACK Infrastructure's NVA02 data center campus in Manassas, in Prince William County, Virginia, covers more than 200 acres and is planned for at least seven data centers providing 420MW across more than 2.3 million square feet, fed by two dedicated 300MW on-site substations, according to the company. Its existing buildings are along Hornbaker Road, and in September 2025 the county board refused to let STACK extend the campus south into Bristow. STACK had asked to rezone about 58 acres along Nokesville Road, bought in 2023 from the nonprofit Youth For Tomorrow, from agricultural to a planned business district for two data centers totaling about 540,000 square feet, with a height limit of 75 feet. The land sits outside the county's designated data center overlay district, and residents had objected to its closeness to homes, noise, environmental effects and property values. The Board of County Supervisors voted 4-2 on September 9, 2025 to deny the "Bristow Campus," the first time the board had turned down a rezoning to expand a data center campus outside the area designated for them, the Prince William Times reported. The application had been deferred three times, and STACK pulled it minutes before a June hearing. "I think we all know why this keeps being deferred," Chair Deshundra Jefferson said then. "This is just the wrong place for a data center, very simple," said Supervisor Tom Gordy, whose Brentsville District includes the site. Supervisor Kenny Boddye said of projects moving closer to homes: "We don't have that here." Supervisors Margaret Franklin and Victor Angry voted against denial. The county has since changed the rules for every future data center. On September 22, 2026 the Board of County Supervisors voted 8-0 for a zoning text amendment ending by-right data center development countywide, so future projects must come to the board for a special use permit. The amendment shrinks the data center overlay district, which dates to 2016; data centers already built or being built, and those with a site plan past the county's quality-control threshold, remain in it. The board kept a 90-day grace period, after Supervisor George Stewart's motion for none, meant to avoid a "gold rush" of proposals in that window, failed 3-5. Rachel Ellis of the Coalition to Protect Prince William County called the amendment "smoke and mirrors" and said "there's no teeth to this." Setbacks from homes and schools were left for later: the county planning director said staff aim for a Planning Commission hearing in November and a board hearing in January. Any new STACK building outside what is already built or permitted at NVA02 would now need a special use permit from the Prince William Board of County Supervisors.

epoch-anthropic-lake-mariner.text: TeraWulf's Lake Mariner data center campus in the Town of Somerset, near Barker in Niagara County, New York, had 102 megawatts of AI computing capacity running for its tenant Fluidstack by early July 2026, with another 336 megawatts under construction. Niagara County says TeraWulf has not paid sales tax on equipment bought for the campus since 2022, and the county is preparing to sue. TeraWulf completed its CB-3 building in early July 2026, meeting the conditions for $600 million of Google's credit support for Fluidstack's lease at the site, the company said. The first data hall of CB-4 has entered commissioning, with phased delivery expected in the second half of 2026, and CB-5 is due to begin phased delivery in early 2027. The campus began as a bitcoin mining operation before turning to artificial intelligence, and its 410-acre former coal plant site still has five cryptomining buildings. The campus has 750 megawatts of power allocated from NYSEG and the New York Power Authority, 90 percent of it from hydropower, the Lockport Union-Sun & Journal reported in October 2025. The AI buildings' cooling fans are rated at 45 decibels, quieter than the cryptomining buildings, and town officials said there would be no room for further expansion once the latest buildings are complete. The tax fight is local. TeraWulf says its purchases at Lake Mariner are exempt under a state law passed under Gov. George Pataki for internet data centers, which the company calls "an existing provision of New York tax law applicable to internet data center operations." County Manager Rick Updegrove disagrees. He says the exemption was meant for email and web hosting, not a facility like Lake Mariner. "Yahoo is not Lake Mariner," he said. "The sales tax revenues would have a significant impact on our budget," Updegrove said. For every $10 million in equipment, the normal sales tax would be $800,000, split between state and local governments, and TeraWulf did not apply to the Niagara County Industrial Development Agency for incentives. John Kaehny of Reinvent Albany said such tax breaks are "ripe for abuse and rarely clawed back if misused." The county hired the law firm Hodgson Russ to investigate, and in early August 2026 the Niagara County Legislature unanimously asked Gov. Kathy Hochul to order an independent audit of the exemption statewide. Updegrove wrote to the governor: "It is our position that Lake Mariner is clearly not an internet web hosting facility, as it relates to the intent of the original exemption." Hochul has said the state may act on the exemption next year, according to the county. New buildings on the campus still need approval from the Town of Somerset's planning board and town board, which met jointly in October 2025 on an amendment to the campus's planned unit development district, a site plan and a special use permit, Supervisor Jeffrey Dewart said. Whether TeraWulf owes the tax will be settled by the state Department of Taxation and Finance, or in court, which the county says it has already authorized.

epoch-microsoft-nebius-new-jersey.text: The data center DataOne is building in Vineland, in Cumberland County, New Jersey, for the AI company Nebius and ultimately Microsoft, has been fined more than $1 million by the state for running 62 natural gas generators without a permit. State inspectors found the generators on July 29, 2026; they had not been there at the previous inspection in December 2025. Environmental Protection Commissioner Ed Potosnak called it the largest enforcement action ever taken against a data center in New Jersey, one that "sends a clear message that these facilities will not be constructed or operated with impunity in this state." DataOne said the generators were temporary, disagreed with the state's finding, and would apply for the permits. Tiffany Leone-Vespa, who lives about a mile away, hears a constant hum and motor noise, including at night: "Knowing that they didn't have the proper permits, I'm concerned about what is emitting, what am I breathing in." The 300 megawatt campus, part of Nebius's $17 billion deal with Microsoft, is under construction with its first phases approved, and the planning board approved a liquefied natural gas tank on site in August. DataOne had a $6 million equipment loan agreement with the city, but canceled it after public outcry. More than 100 residents packed a town hall on January 21, 2026 to question chief executive Charles-Antoine Beyney about noise, air quality, property values and union labor. Beyney said the campus would run gas engines for 85 percent of its operations, while DataOne's own webpage says it runs on Bloom Energy fuel cells. The campus sits over the Kirkwood-Cohansey aquifer. DataOne says it expects to be operating by 2027 with about 200 permanent jobs. DataOne is in communication with the Department of Environmental Protection about a timeline for moving from generators to its Bloom Energy fuel cells, the company said.

epoch-coreweave-norway.text: CoreWeave, the American AI cloud company, is a tenant at Bulk Infrastructure's N01 data center campus at Stoleheia, between Kristiansand and Vennesla in Norway's Agder region, at Stolevegen 39 in Øvrebø. Bulk said it has secured 400 megawatts of capacity for CoreWeave at the roughly 300-hectare site, with room to grow toward 1 gigawatt, as part of a $2.2 billion investment CoreWeave announced across Europe in 2024. Bulk said the campus runs on hydropower with direct connections to hydroelectric stations and to one of Europe's largest transformer stations. The power grid to carry that load is now approved. On January 8, 2026, the Norwegian Energy Regulatory Authority granted Statnett and Glitre Nett a concession to build the Stemmen transformer station at Stoleheia, and gave N01 Utilities, a Bulk subsidiary, permission for two connecting power lines. Ingrid Myrtveit, a section chief at the regulator, said the station would give the Agder grid more capacity and flexibility, and the regulator attached conditions protecting meadows and wetland forest. Bulk has told grid operator Statnett the full N01 campus, of which the CoreWeave building is one part, could need 2 gigawatts of electricity in the 2040s, roughly what all of Agder produces today. The region already pays Norway's highest electricity prices and runs a power deficit. Bulk employs 83 people permanently at the site and pays Vennesla municipality 258,000 kroner a year in property tax. More than half of Bulk Infrastructure Holding AS is held through holding companies abroad: BGO Europe IV King II Holdco in Luxembourg owns 30 percent, BGO King Holdco Sarl in Luxembourg 15 percent, and Geveran Trading in Cyprus, controlled by shipping magnate John Fredriksen, 7.5 percent. Norway's minister of digitalisation and public governance, Karianne Tung, said she was pleased to hear of the CoreWeave collaboration and that the government's goal is a national AI infrastructure by 2030.

The power grid to carry that load is now approved.

epoch-southgate-melbourne.text: Southgate Melbourne is the first deployment of Project Southgate, the Australian AI data center program run by Firmus Technologies with CDC Data Centres and Nvidia, and in March 2026 Firmus signed a multi-billion dollar contract with an unnamed global technology company for about 18,400 Nvidia GB300 GPUs at the Melbourne facility. Firmus called it the second large-scale customer secured for Project Southgate. Firmus announced the alliance with CDC in October 2025, with an initial investment of A$4.5 billion to be delivered at Southgate Melbourne and a plan to scale to 1.6GW and up to A$73.3 billion across Australia through 2028. At the time, the first stages in Tasmania and Melbourne were under construction, with up to 150MW to be delivered by mid-2026. CDC provides the data center infrastructure, and DCD reported that it was unclear whether CDC would build new facilities or Firmus would take capacity in existing ones. Firmus later said it would place an initial cluster of 18,500 GB300 GPUs live at Southgate Melbourne in the first quarter of 2026, and that Nvidia's DGX Cloud would set up a region there. The deployments use LiquidCore, CDC's own cooling technology, which the company says does not consume water for primary cooling. Firmus says every stage of Southgate will run on renewable power. Firmus secured a $10 billion private debt facility led by funds managed by Blackstone, with support from Coatue, in February 2026, w.media reported. In August 2026 it announced a fully subscribed $2 billion equity round from Coatue, Nvidia, Blackstone funds and Jane Street to speed up the Southgate rollout across Australia. In September 2026 Firmus said it had more than 900MW of contracted capacity, with OpenAI signing as an anchor customer for two sites in Malaysia, and that two of its seven AI factories, in Australia and Singapore, are operational. Firmus is also building a greenfield campus in Tasmania for about 36,800 GB300 GPUs, due to be completed in late 2026.

epoch-stream-phoenix.text: Stream Data Centers' Phoenix campus, called PHXA, sits at 2950 S. Litchfield Road in Goodyear, Maricopa County, Arizona, on 157 acres planned for seven buildings; two are already built and serving tenants. At full build the campus would use up to 280 megawatts of power across more than two million square feet, fed by a dedicated Arizona Public Service substation built to carry 480 megawatts. The first building, Phoenix I, opened in January 2021 as a 418,000-square-foot data center; Stream has not named its tenants. Arizona offers a 20-year sales tax exemption on equipment to tenants that lease at least 500 kilowatts for three years or more, an incentive Stream markets on this campus. Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes asked state lawmakers on August 31, 2026 to pause approval of new data centers statewide, citing rising energy costs and cuts to the state's Colorado River water supply; the Legislature has not acted. Stream has not announced a construction date for the remaining five buildings planned for the campus.

epoch-vantage-tx1.text: Vantage Data Centers is building its TX11 data center at 14720 Omicron Drive in San Antonio, in Bexar County, Texas, a two-story, 32 megawatt building with four 8-megawatt data halls. State records list it as a $95.8 million project that was due to be completed by September 1, 2026. On September 18, 2026, residents near Texas Research Park, close to State Highway 211 and Potranco Road, reported a strong smell of natural gas from the site. "Oh my God, what is that awful? Oh my God, that's natural gas," resident Sarah Forsythe said of the moment she smelled it. Stuart Pennington, who represents the neighborhood's homeowners association, said Vantage had injected far too much odorant into the gas, and residents described the smell as strong enough to make people violently nauseous. Vantage corrected the injection error after the association contacted the company, and Pennington said there have been no further complaints since. Mark Freeman, Vantage's vice president of global marketing, said the company is "not aware of any incident at the site that has posed a risk to the surrounding community" and follows its permitting, inspection and safety procedures. Two months earlier, on July 22, 2026, the Environmental Integrity Project, the Sierra Club and Public Citizen filed notice of intent to sue Vantage and its power provider VoltaGrid, the required first step before a Clean Air Act lawsuit. The groups say the companies split the data centers and their gas turbines and diesel generators into smaller permits to avoid the stricter review a single large permit would require. "If Vantage and its power plants, which are owned by VoltaGrid, were permitted all at once, then you'd have a major permit," said Adrian Shelley of Public Citizen. Jen Duggan of the Environmental Integrity Project said the equipment could emit particulate matter, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide and formaldehyde. Vantage said it takes its environmental responsibilities seriously and is committed to complying with the law. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality held a hearing on the Omicron Drive campus's federal operating permit on August 17, 2026, in San Antonio; it was held as scheduled and no result has been published. The 60-day wait that began with the July 22 notice has also passed, so the environmental groups can now sue, though no lawsuit has been reported. Texas Governor Greg Abbott ordered a statewide audit of data centers seeking grid connections on August 3, 2026, freezing new approvals while it runs, though sites that generate their own power, like this one, can bypass it.

epoch-coreweave-dalton-1-2.text: Core Scientific's data center at 2205 Industrial South Road in Dalton, Whitfield County, Georgia, is operating in a 52,000 square foot building on 5 acres, where Core Scientific advertises up to 50 megawatts of computing capacity leased to its AI cloud tenant CoreWeave. It is one of several data centers Core Scientific runs in and around Dalton, growth that residents have spent 2026 asking the county to slow. Dozens of residents gathered outside the Whitfield County Courthouse before commissioners' regular meeting on Monday, June 8, 2026, to protest what they called unchecked data center growth. "We're asking for a two-year planning moratorium on accepting any future applications and making any future development approvals, until those strategic plans can be developed based on research, study, and best practices across the country," said Carmen Shuler, a Dalton resident who spoke for the group. Dalton City Commissioner Dennis Mock told the board the county's tax digest was so far out of line that "we in the city don't know where our money's coming from or how much we're getting." In a separate report in July 2026, resident and state House candidate Quentin Postell said, "With Dalton now having an AI center put in the city, we want to make sure that the next one isn't allowed, or if we can kind of create a moratorium." Whitfield County Administrator Bob Sivick told the same outlet the board saw no need for a moratorium because "there's nothing in the works, and there hasn't been any problems with data centers here either in the construction or their operation." Dalton Utilities' peak electricity load has nearly doubled since data centers arrived, from about 250 megawatts to 476 megawatts, Chief Operating Officer Mark Buckner told the League of Women Voters of the Dalton Area in May 2026. The Dalton-Whitfield Joint Development Authority voted in September 2025 to approve tax abatements tied to a roughly $200 million Core Scientific investment on Old Tilton Road, a separate project nearby. CoreWeave agreed in July 2025 to buy Core Scientific, but shareholders voted the deal down and it was terminated on October 30, 2025.

epoch-alibaba-zhangbei.text: Alibaba runs an operating data center in Zhangbei County, near Zhangjiakou in China's Hebei province, that the research group Epoch AI estimates has grown to about 169 megawatts of power. Epoch AI, which studies satellite images of the site, says new cooling equipment was added to six of its buildings between 2024 and early 2026, roughly doubling its estimated power use from 85 to 169 megawatts. The site is part of China's "Eastern Data Western Compute" program, launched in 2021, which favors Zhangbei County for its cheap wind and solar power. Alibaba Cloud opened the center in 2022 alongside a twin site in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, to run its Feitian computing platform for tasks such as training self-driving car software. Epoch AI's satellite images show chillers being installed on the first three buildings starting in July 2024 and a large substation linked to the power grid by September 2025, with the last three buildings finished by early 2026. Epoch AI puts the site's cost at about $6.4 billion and estimates it holds computing power equal to roughly 32,000 Nvidia H100 chips, likely running on Nvidia H20 processors sold to the Chinese market.

epoch-start-campus-sines-data-campus.text: Start Campus's data center campus at Sines, in Portugal, has one building running and a second going up: SIN01 is in operation, and Radio M24 reported that construction of SIN02 would begin early in 2026 and run about 24 months, to the first quarter of 2028. The plan is six data processing buildings, and the government has classed the project, SINES 4.0, as a Project of Potential National Interest. The first building went up over ground the state's nature agency had asked to be protected. Inspecting the site from November 13 to 17, 2023, the Institute for Nature Conservation and Forests found SIN01 had been built directly over a temporary pond it should have kept intact, that one of two ponds set aside as compensation had been partly filled in, and that the other had been invaded by exotic species. Start Campus said protected heathers had been moved to a nursery with 200 tonnes of soil, to be put back later. The felling of 1,800 cork oaks was approved at the EDP Renováveis Morgavel wind farm that is to supply the campus, and at full build the campus would consume about a fifth of the renewable electricity Portugal generated in 2022. The project also helped bring down a government. In November 2023 Prime Minister António Costa resigned over Operation Influencer, a corruption investigation that took in a green hydrogen plant, lithium mines and this campus. Two Start Campus executives, Afonso Salema and Rui Oliveira Neves, resigned while under investigation; the charges were later dropped. Start Campus says the whole campus runs on renewable electricity and cools with seawater, and that the 8.5 billion euro investment is its own, with no public subsidy. The second building has one tenant lined up: on May 5, 2026 Nscale announced it would take the 200 megawatt building, investing 465 million euros there and 230 million euros in shared infrastructure, to install more than 66,000 Nvidia Rubin GPUs for Microsoft from late 2027, on top of the 12,600 Blackwell Ultra GPUs it is deploying for Microsoft in SIN01. Start Campus has secured 1.2 gigawatts of grid capacity from REN, the national transmission operator, and Data Center Frontier reported in 2024 that all the buildings were expected to be in operation by 2030. Construction of the second building has begun, the Portugal Resident reported in May 2026 citing Expresso, which put the plan at six buildings by 2031 and noted that the prosecutors' investigation has not interrupted the development.
