The felling of 1,800 cork oaks was approved at the EDP Renováveis Morgavel wind farm that is to supply the campus, and at full build the campus would consume about a fifth of the renewable electricity Portugal generated in 2022.

The project also helped bring down a government. In November 2023 Prime Minister António Costa resigned over Operation Influencer, a corruption investigation that took in a green hydrogen plant, lithium mines and this campus.
Two Start Campus executives, Afonso Salema and Rui Oliveira Neves, resigned while under investigation; the charges were later dropped.
Start Campus says the whole campus runs on renewable electricity and cools with seawater, and that the 8.5 billion euro investment is its own, with no public subsidy.

The second building has one tenant lined up: on May 5, 2026 Nscale announced it would take the 200 megawatt building, investing 465 million euros there and 230 million euros in shared infrastructure, to install more than 66,000 Nvidia Rubin GPUs for Microsoft from late 2027, on top of the 12,600 Blackwell Ultra GPUs it is deploying for Microsoft in SIN01.

Start Campus has secured 1.2 gigawatts of grid capacity from REN, the national transmission operator, and Data Center Frontier reported in 2024 that all the buildings were expected to be in operation by 2030.

Construction of the second building has begun, the Portugal Resident reported in May 2026 citing Expresso, which put the plan at six buildings by 2031 and noted that the prosecutors' investigation has not interrupted the development.

epoch-xai-qts-atlanta.text: xAI and X run an AI computing cluster inside the QTS data center at 1025 Jefferson Street NW in Atlanta, Fulton County, Georgia, operating on about 17 megawatts of IT power, the research group Epoch AI estimates. Documents filed with Develop Fulton list about 12,448 Nvidia GPUs, mostly H100s, and $700 million in chips, cables and other equipment, with X contributing $442 million and xAI $258 million. The equipment trains large language models and search products for X; the deal that brought it says 24 jobs will be kept at the site and none added. Epoch AI estimates the cluster came online around early 2025, when Business Insider reported the buildout, and its satellite images show no significant change to the building since. The Development Authority of Fulton County approved a $10.125 million, 10-year tax break for X's equipment on January 23, 2024, voting 6-2, with Kyle Lamont and Erica Long against. An identical request had been rejected in November 2023, when X projected a $1.09 billion economic impact over 10 years, a figure it later cut to $241 million without explanation. X had threatened to move the project to Portland, Oregon, and nine Fulton residents spoke against the deal. "Gifting public money to a purveyor of hate speech is not simply wasting money as many of these deals tend to do," said Jim Martin, chairman of Neighborhood Planning Unit D. The abatement is split between X and xAI based on their share of the hardware, a Develop Fulton representative told Business Insider in 2025.

epoch-anthropic-barber-lake.text: Cipher Digital is building a 300-megawatt data center campus for Anthropic's Claude AI models at 951 County Road 204 in Mitchell County, just outside Colorado City, Texas. Fluidstack leases the site and Google backs the deal; the campus is under construction, with its first phase due to start delivering power in September 2026 and a second phase in January 2027. On September 14, 2026, the three companies put $10 million toward fixing Colorado City's failing water system. Water has been the local question. In July 2026, thunderstorms knocked out power and backup generators at a Colorado City well-pump station, and taps ran dry on top of years of aging pipes and pumps. Cipher says the campus uses only on-site, non-potable water and will not draw from the municipal drinking supply, and Mayor Ruben Hurt said the data center is not a city water customer. The $10 million funds a new well field, a new water tower and replacement of the town's aging water main. "The main thing that this money is going to do is we're going to create another water storage in town," Hurt said, adding that the funding lets the city make repairs without shifting the cost to residents. Cattleman Lee Roy Miller, the Republican nominee for Precinct 2 county commissioner, said he still runs fewer cattle than he did 20 years ago over water concerns, but called the project a necessary economic development for the area. Anthropic's head of economic development, Ryan Wilson, said at the ceremony that governments should avoid "making deals that deny the community resources, such as giving away tax abatements indefinitely," and suggested Texas limit its sales tax break for data center equipment to 10 years. Barber Lake sits north of Interstate 20, outside city limits, and does not connect to Colorado City's water system; the next milestone is the second phase's rent start in January 2027.

epoch-coreweave-muskogee-ok.text: Core Scientific and CoreWeave broke ground in November 2024 on a 100-megawatt data center at the Port of Muskogee in Muskogee, Muskogee County, Oklahoma, built to host CoreWeave's Nvidia computer chips. The project remains under construction. Core Scientific said in May 2026 that the first building, designed for Nvidia's newest chips, was in final testing and on track for delivery in the second quarter of 2026; no update on that delivery has been published since. The 100 megawatts of power split into about 70 megawatts to run the Nvidia chips and 30 megawatts for cooling and other support systems, part of 500 megawatts CoreWeave contracted from Core Scientific under 12-year deals worth up to $8.7 billion. Core Scientific projected about 150 jobs averaging more than $65,000 a year and over $12 million in property and sales taxes for Muskogee County, the Hilldale School District and the City of Muskogee, and Port Muskogee put the capital investment at more than $4 billion. The campus is growing. In August 2026, Core Scientific completed a $444 million purchase of Polaris DS, the neighboring Bitcoin miner, taking over about 440 megawatts of grid power it draws under agreements with Oklahoma Gas & Electric, plus 40 acres and an on-site substation. Construction has begun on a second building of 82.5 megawatts, which Core Scientific said in August it plans to deliver starting in the second half of 2027. The company has also secured about 250 acres for a plan to generate power on site rather than draw it all from the grid, and has grid studies under way to add more capacity. In July 2026, Core Scientific and AMD announced a partnership for more than 500 megawatts of Core Scientific's U.S. data center capacity beginning in 2027, without naming which of the company's sites, a list that includes its lone Oklahoma facility at Muskogee, would host it. Google has separately announced two data center campuses in Muskogee County, near Summit and Council Hill, as part of a $9 billion Oklahoma investment. In August 2026 the Cherokee Nation banned hyperscale data centers on its tribal land after a survey found 64 percent of citizens opposed them. The next steps at Port Muskogee are Core Scientific's: its grid studies, its on-site power plan and the delivery of the second building in 2027. Locally the project is a partnership with Port Muskogee and the City of Muskogee, whose mayor, Patrick Cale, Core Scientific thanked at the groundbreaking.

epoch-crusoe-abilene-expansion.text: Crusoe is building a 900 megawatt AI data center campus for Microsoft in Abilene, Taylor County, Texas, next to its existing campus, which would bring the whole Abilene site to about 2.1 gigawatts of power. Crusoe announced the project on March 27, 2026, and said land clearing was already under way, with the first of two buildings expected to be energized in mid-2027. The company plans to power both buildings with a 900 megawatt on-site gas plant paired with battery storage. In August 2026 the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality gave preliminary approval to expedited air permits for an expanded power plant on the campus, and neighbors began getting notices listing pollutants including carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and sulfur dioxide. The watchdog group Oil & Gas Watch says the application would take the plant from 10 gas turbines to 49, with an estimated 11,862 people living within three miles. State Rep. Stan Lambert asked TCEQ for an in-person public meeting in Abilene, and the agency agreed, extending the comment period until the meeting ends. Rents around Abilene have doubled and tripled as the AI boom has grown, and at a September Chamber of Commerce panel, resident Molly Cedillo held a sign reading "No More Backroom Data Center Deals." Taylor County commissioners gave the earlier Stargate campus a 20-year property tax abatement, and Judge Phil Crowley said abatements are the only way counties get any authority over the projects: "I understand abatements are unpopular, but if people want counties that have control over data centers, you have to have an abatement." The next public step is the TCEQ meeting on the power plant permits, which the agency must announce 30 days ahead; comments can be filed until the meeting ends, under permit numbers 182126, PSDTX1688 and GHGPSDTX263.

epoch-goodnight.text: Crusoe is building the Goodnight data center campus, also called Project Llano, at 10001 Lima Road near Claude, in Armstrong County, Texas, just east of Amarillo. At a September 2026 open house for residents, Crusoe's Jeremy Bachrach said the campus will have six buildings, the first to be turned over to Google in early 2027 and construction finished by the end of that year. More than 7,500 employees and craft workers were on the site. State filings list four buildings of 805,380 square feet and two of 484,955 square feet, filed under the Crusoe affiliate GN DC1, LLC; the two latest, Buildings 3 and 4, carry an estimated $500 million construction cost each. An Armstrong County tax-abatement agreement says the first phase may have four buildings drawing as much as 530 megawatts. Google has said it is developing a data center campus in Armstrong County as part of a $40 billion investment in Texas cloud and AI infrastructure through 2027. Google has committed to 50 permanent jobs once the campus is running, and figures shown at the open house put local tax revenue at more than $850 million over the life of the project, about $28 million a year. Power is the sharpest question. In January 2026 Crusoe filed for a permit to build a 933-megawatt gas power plant on the campus that would run off the grid and power at least two of the buildings, and its application shows the plant could emit as much as 4.5 million tons of carbon dioxide a year, more than the city of San Francisco. Crusoe has applied to the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality for air permits for the Goodnight site, covering nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, particulate matter and greenhouse gases. A Google spokesperson said, "We don’t have a contract in place for the plant in Texas." At the September open house the companies said the site's primary power will come from the nearby Goodnight 1 and 2 wind farms, with the ERCOT grid as backup. Bachrach said the campus uses closed-loop cooling that is filled once: "We fill that system up one time, and then that water recirculates for a period of about 15 years." Construction itself has used about 600,000 gallons a day during earthwork and foundations, expected to fall to about 275,000 as buildings are enclosed, and officials estimate each finished building will use about 2 million gallons a year, supplied by nearby neighbors. "We understand that this data center has had impacts on the community in terms of traffic and other impacts," Bachrach said. Claude ISD Superintendent Brent Kirkland said traffic and water remain concerns but the school stands to benefit, and that hearing from the companies directly helps: "if they’re the ones saying it, you can hold them accountable for that." In March 2026 a fire near the construction site forced a partial evacuation. Crusoe is also developing a 1.4GW campus in Childress and the Abilene site used by OpenAI. On September 21 Gov. Greg Abbott told the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to issue no permits sought by data center projects until the ERCOT and Texas Water Development Board audits are complete.

epoch-google-cedar-rapids.text: Google's data center at Cedar Rapids, in Linn County, Iowa, is going up in the Big Cedar Industrial Center on the city's southwest side, on Alliant Energy land near the Eastern Iowa Airport. The city council voted unanimously on June 11, 2024 to extend a 30 inch water main to the site and relocate a road there, before Google had publicly confirmed the project. The site is a 1,000 acre Alliant Energy parcel, the state's first certified mega site, and Google will pay $350,000 a building each year under a community betterment agreement. The airport is the complication. By June 2026 the city council was set to approve a separate agreement with Google covering the data center's possible effects on the Eastern Iowa Airport, after concerns that heat and steam plumes from the facility could interfere with landings and takeoffs. The deal would also let Google take a temporary certificate of occupancy for one building while those effects are studied. The county has since slowed things down. Linn County adopted a data center ordinance in February 2026, requiring large projects to complete a water study, sign a water use agreement with tracking and reporting, and sign an economic development agreement. epoch-google-fort-wayne.text: Indiana regulators on September 10, 2026, approved another request to fill wetlands for Google's $2 billion data center campus in Fort Wayne, Allen County, clearing the way for three more buildings in its third phase. The campus, in southeast Allen County on Adams Center Road, broke ground in April 2024 and is expected to grow to 12 buildings. The permit lets Hatchworks LLC, the campus developer, fill 2.13 acres of forested, isolated wetlands, with work expected to start by mid-September and run to December 2030. The project was known as Project Zodiac until Google revealed itself as the company behind it, and its investment has grown from "at least $845 million" to "at least $2 billion." The city granted Google a 10-year, 50 percent tax abatement. For the second phase, Google sought to fill about 2.47 acres of wetlands, bringing the total for the six buildings of the first two phases to 8.54 acres, and proposed buying mitigation credits in Eel River Township on the county's northwestern edge rather than near the site. In April 2026 the Indiana Department of Environmental Management also approved plans to add more than 140 emergency diesel generators to the campus after public pushback. Wetland losses are the heart of the local fight. "When you just take a quarter acre here and a quarter acre there, over and over again, it adds up," said Bruce Kingsbury, director of Purdue Fort Wayne's Environmental Resources Center, who says credits bought elsewhere do not help downstream neighbors who face more flooding. At IDEM's online hearing on the third phase in August, resident Linda Hathaway said: "Once wetlands are destroyed, you're not gonna get them back ... Buying a credit, trying to fix them somewhere else, it's not ever gonna be the same." Many commenters also worried about water contamination and how much water the campus will use, but IDEM said water withdrawal, supply, use and treatment are outside its authority in a wetlands permit. City Councilman Geoff Paddock asked IDEM to apply the "strictest possible environmental and permit review standards" and said the developers had not disclosed plans to take over wetlands when the council approved the project's rezoning. Hatchworks will buy 4.26 acres of credits from the Openings Mitigation Bank in Fort Wayne, must show proof of purchase within a year, and may not clear trees from April through September to protect the endangered Indiana bat and the threatened northern long-eared bat. IDEM said drone photos it requested confirmed the wetlands had not been disturbed before approval. The Fort Wayne City Council is weighing a one-year moratorium on approving new data centers, proposed by Councilwoman Rohli Booker, that would have the city's Department of Planning Services write development standards covering zoning, approvals, environmental concerns and safety; it would not affect the Google campus already under construction. The council put a three-week delay on the vote on September 23 after a lengthy debate over amendments, and the matter is due back before the council in mid-October 2026. Further expansion of the campus itself depends on state wetland and generator permits from IDEM, which has approved every request so far, and on Hatchworks carrying out the mitigation plan in its application.

epoch-meta-hyperion.text: Meta's Hyperion data center campus is rising near Diane Cobb's home in Holly Ridge, Richland Parish, Louisiana, where she has lived since 1961. "It's not Holly Ridge anymore," Cobb said. "It really isn't." She said residents found out when the digging started: "Nobody told us anything. They supposedly had a big meeting. The whole community was supposed to come. Nobody knew anything about it. Ever." "You can't get information," said Joe Williams, who lives across from the site, "and they did not send no letters out, no nothing before they ever started this." His wife, Robin Williams, said, "No one come knocked on our door." Residents told WWNO their water sometimes turns brown and their electricity shuts off without notice, sometimes for days at a time. The nearest state air quality monitor is 30 miles away, in Monroe. Meta announced the project, a $10 billion investment, in December 2024. The campus covers 2,250 acres of former farmland, and Meta has since bought roughly 1,400 more acres next to it for a second phase. In October 2025 Meta brought in Blue Owl Capital as a joint venture partner to finance, build and operate the campus, pushing the target cost toward $27 billion. As of March 2026, about 3,700 construction workers were on site, Fortune reported, with a peak of roughly 5,000 expected within a couple of months; some residents say they have heard estimates as high as 8,000. On July 13, 2026, Meta said it was expanding the campus again, to 5 gigawatts of computing capacity, its largest data center anywhere, in an investment of more than $50 billion, with over 7,500 jobs at peak construction and 1,000 once it is running. Chris Holyfield supplies septic services and restroom facilities for the workforce, 58 units so far, after construction company leaders told him "this area's about to explode." "No one believed it at first," Holyfield said. "Now we're all feeling the difference." Katie and Logan Stewart put more than $40,000 into a food truck to feed construction crews, then lost much of that business when DPR, one of the main contractors, brought in an out of state catering company. "You talk about supporting the local community, but then you outsource the work," Katie said. "It felt like a slap in the face." In nearby Monroe, 34 year old Erika James said her rent kept rising and she was given five days to vacate her mobile home after paying rent one day late. "We are now having to entertain the idea of leaving the area completely," she said. "There is nowhere to go if you can't pay triple prices." Meta says it has put more than $1 billion into local roads, water and wastewater systems, and that Richland Parish teachers' yearly bonus checks were 400 percent higher this year because of tax revenue tied to the project. On August 12, 2026, the Louisiana Public Service Commission voted 3 to 1 to overturn a judge's recommendation that Meta turn over the data behind its projected job creation, economic impact and electricity demand, according to BT News.

meta-meta-richland-parish.text: Meta's data center at Holly Ridge, in Richland Parish, Louisiana, near the junction of LA-183 and Interstate 20, is called Hyperion, covers more than 4 million square feet and is expected to cost $27 billion and be running by 2030. The first thing it changed was the rent. "A rental that might've been $600-$700/month is now $2,500/month," the parish tax assessor, Emmett "Lee" Brown, said. "So, it's not affordable for the people that were here, and I hate that." Joyce Piercy, who is 81, said Meta had moved residents out into trailer parks and that some could not afford to relocate. "It's helping the community, but it's making it rough for us old folks, trying to drive in all that traffic," she said. Brown said the parish collected $22 million in property taxes in total last year, and that Meta alone is expected to pay $30 million over three years once state incentives are counted. "I just didn't think we were going to get that," he said. Jesse Johns, who runs a restaurant, said his sales were up about 30 percent since building started. State leaders point to $2 billion in property taxes over the life of the project, $200 million for local infrastructure and 6,500 construction jobs, while Meta promises more than 500 operational posts and about 5,000 construction ones at peak. The power for it is being built from scratch. On December 6, 2024 Entergy Louisiana said it would build three combined cycle combustion turbines totalling 2,260 megawatts, two of them in Richland Parish, expected online between 2028 and 2029 subject to regulatory approval. It will also build two of its own substations and six customer owned ones, put in nearly 100 miles of 500 kV transmission line and eight new 230 kV lines, and upgrade existing infrastructure near Sterlington. Entergy put the work at 1,500 to 1,800 construction jobs on the generation and 3,500 to 5,000 on substations and transmission, against 44 permanent jobs. The utility said revenue from Meta would offset the cost of serving it and cut existing customers' costs by more than $300 million, and that Meta would match $1 million of shareholder contributions to its Power to Care assistance programme. Phillip May, Entergy Louisiana's president and chief executive, said: "Today marks a turning point for Northeast Louisiana. This is more than just an investment in infrastructure; it's an investment in the people, businesses and communities of our state." Entergy broke ground on the 55 acre Smalling Substation at Rayville on June 27, 2025, a substation Meta is funding entirely. Troy Heytens, vice president of hyperscale execution, said the transmission substation's output would be the equivalent of delivering power to over one million homes. Two 780 megawatt gas units at the Franklin Farms plant, which Entergy Louisiana is building nearby, are due onstream in 2028. Meta's own account of the campus is that it will deliver 5 gigawatts of computing capacity, more than 2 gigawatts of it for training open source large language models. The company says it has invested more than $50 billion in Louisiana data center infrastructure since the project began, that peak construction employed more than 7,500 skilled trade workers, and that there will be 1,000 permanent jobs when the site is complete. It says it is paying for a closed loop glycol cooling system that runs dry for most of the year, and covering its own power costs through a partnership with Entergy that it says will save Entergy customers $2.65 billion over 20 years. Meta says it has awarded more than $1.6 billion in Louisiana business contracts, put more than $1 million into local schools, and given $215 million to Entergy's bill assistance and energy efficiency programmes for low and fixed income customers. The Alliance for Affordable Energy has questioned whether ratepayers are protected over the long run, warning about overpaying for speed and about being left with the cost of the infrastructure if Meta were to withdraw.

epoch-microsoft-narvik-norway.text: Nscale's 230 megawatt AI data center campus at Kvandal outside Narvik, in Nordland in Arctic Norway, will serve Microsoft after OpenAI, the project's original customer, withdrew in April 2026. On April 14, 2026, Nscale expanded its agreement with Microsoft to add more than 30,000 Nvidia Rubin chips, the specialized computer chips that run AI programs, for delivery in 2027, and said it would now run the project alone after folding its joint venture with Aker. Microsoft first signed with Nscale and Aker in September 2025, in a five-year deal worth an estimated $6.2 billion with service delivered in stages from 2026; Microsoft says the site was chosen for abundant hydropower, low local electricity demand, a cool climate and existing industrial infrastructure. Norway's digitalization minister, Karianne Tung, laid the foundation stone on November 19, 2025. epoch-openai-stargate-lordstown.text: SoftBank is building a small proof-of-concept AI data center for OpenAI's Stargate program at the former General Motors plant, 2300 Hallock-Young Road in Lordstown, Trumbull County, Ohio. OpenAI, Oracle and SoftBank named Lordstown as a Stargate site in September 2025. The project is under construction, but in April 2026 the research group Epoch AI reported only limited site clearing, put its likely capacity under three tenths of a gigawatt, and listed its finish date as unknown. The data center is part of a larger SoftBank push at the plant. A SoftBank-affiliated company, Crescent Dune LLC, bought the 6.2 million square foot factory from Foxconn for $375 million in 2025, and the two companies are setting up a joint venture there to make equipment for Stargate data centers. Trumbull County Commissioner Rick Hernandez said SoftBank told him the plant could employ up to 1,700 workers, including about 400 already working there for Foxconn. The village has also fought a different data center proposal next door. Bristolville 25 Developer LLC filed plans in October 2025 for a $3.6 billion, 1,650,000 square foot campus on 133 acres of industrial land near the old GM plant. The Lordstown Village Council banned data centers on November 3, 2025, repealed the ban a month later, and on January 5, 2026 imposed a 180-day moratorium on new data center applications instead. Bristolville 25 has asked the Ohio Supreme Court to force the village to review its site plan under the rules that were in place when it was filed. The village says the application was incomplete, missing stormwater plans, utility information and wetland studies. Residents at public meetings raised concerns about the water and electricity demands of data centers, cooling noise, and the lack of long-term jobs compared with manufacturing. On June 15, 2026, the Lordstown Village Council voted to extend the moratorium another 180 days, through about January 1, 2027, while consultant Brian Frantz helps write zoning rules on setbacks, noise, water use and lighting for future data center applications. The Ohio Supreme Court has not yet ruled on Bristolville 25's case.

epoch-openai-stargate-michigan.text: Related Digital is building the OpenAI Stargate Michigan data center, known locally as "The Barn," on 250 acres in Saline Township, Washtenaw County, for Oracle and OpenAI. Three 550,000-square-foot buildings are under construction, and Related says the campus will deliver over a gigawatt of power, with all three expected online by the end of 2028. In December 2025 the Michigan Public Service Commission conditionally approved DTE Electric's contracts to supply the 1,383-megawatt data center, run by Oracle subsidiary Green Chile Ventures, and made DTE responsible for any costs it cannot recover from the company. The contracts run at least 19 years and require the data center to pay for at least 80% of its contracted demand even if it uses less. The township board first voted to deny rezoning the farmland, but Related Digital sued, and the township settled with a consent agreement requiring it to approve the project and a tax exemption. On July 14, 2026, the board approved a 12-year, 50% property tax abatement based on a $4.8 billion valuation, far below the $43 billion Oracle had offered. "Billionaires and greedy politicians are never going to be satisfied," Saline resident Tim Bruneau told the board. Later that month the board voted 5-0 to remove the cap after the township attorney warned it would violate the 2025 consent judgment and risk damages. Resident Kathryn Haushalter and attorney Ellis Boal then asked the Michigan State Tax Commission, on August 12, 2026, to deny the exemption, arguing the township skipped the public hearing needed to create the industrial development district the tax break depends on. Boal also pointed to Oracle's exemption application, which lists February 6, 2026, as the start of property improvements. The Michigan State Tax Commission has not yet ruled on the challenge.

epoch-openai-stargate-milam.text: OpenAI's Stargate data center in Milam County, Texas, is a 1,200-megawatt campus near Rosebud being built and run by SoftBank subsidiary SB Energy. The first building, code-named Freebird, is due to finish in October 2026. A filing with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation lists that first phase as a single-story, 548,950-square-foot data center with four data halls, costing about $470 million, with a completion date of October 15. The Austin American-Statesman describes the project as an $18 billion, 600-acre campus outside the former Alcoa site near Rosebud, next to an SB Energy solar project. OpenAI chose SB Energy to build and operate the site in January 2026, when OpenAI and SoftBank Group each invested $500 million in the company. SB Energy says it plans to build new power generation for the data center and protect Texas ratepayers, and that it designed the campus to use less water. Epoch AI, which tracks Stargate sites by satellite, reported steel framing and roofing on the first building in March 2026. Stargate leader Peter Hoeschele said that month that phase one of Freebird had topped out; by April he had left OpenAI, along with several other Stargate executives. The Milam project is part of a Stargate build-out that has hit trouble elsewhere: Oracle and OpenAI dropped plans to expand the flagship Abilene campus in March 2026, and OpenAI has pulled out of Stargate sites in the UK and Norway. SoftBank is also buying land nearby: an entity tied to it, Southridge Land TX LLC, bought more than 4,700 acres of the former Alcoa smelting site near Rockdale in April 2026, with plans that are not public. Other parts of that site are planned for T1 Energy's solar cell factory, a gas-fired power plant and a 200-acre data center whose first tenant is AMD. In June 2026, Milam County asked state regulators to require public disclosure of data centers' electricity demand, water use, cooling technology and impact on county infrastructure. Texas law limits what counties can do: a 2023 law, House Bill 2127, blocks local governments from making rules that go beyond state law, so any new requirements would have to come from the Legislature, which next meets in January.

epoch-openai-stargate-shackelford.text: On July 21, 2025 Shackelford County's commissioners voted unanimously to let Vantage Data Centers build a campus called Frontier at the intersection of Highway 604 and Highway 351 in Shackelford County, Texas, on about 1,200 acres. The vote created Reinvestment Zone 2025-1, accepted the company's tax abatement application and set out the county's intent to sign a formal agreement once the land was bought. Under the ten year abatement Vantage will pay the county $10 million a year in place of property taxes, money the county can spend as it likes, which could raise its annual operating budget by close to 200 percent. The site sits inside Clyde ISD boundaries rather than Albany ISD, so the county seat's school district gets no direct tax benefit from it. The company also committed to $150,000 a year for local charitable causes over the first ten years, up to ten college scholarships a year for Shackelford County students, local hiring and training, and fire mitigation support for the volunteer departments. A Vantage representative told the commissioners: "We are not just developers, we are long-term operators" in the communities where the company builds. The campus is expected to create 250 permanent jobs with a $25 million annual payroll, and to employ up to 6,500 workers at peak construction, which runs from late 2025 through 2029. Mark Brown, co-manager of the Blanton-Caldwell Trading Company in Albany, said: "The employment, particularly during construction, will be very helpful for the area and for a retail business like us, the increase in traffic folks coming through either way." Vantage planned two recruitment events, one by the end of 2025 and another in 2026. The campus is planned for 10 buildings, a few hours' drive from both Dallas-Fort Worth and Austin. Vantage says the finished campus will provide 1.4 gigawatts of computing capacity; Epoch AI, which tracks these projects by satellite and permit records, puts the eventual capacity at 2 gigawatts. It is expected to run largely on a natural gas microgrid on the site rather than draw mainly from the regional grid. Construction began in the third quarter of 2025, the first building is due by late 2026 and the full campus is targeted for the end of 2028. Texas froze new large load grid connections for data centers on August 3, 2026, after an audit ordered by Governor Greg Abbott, though projects generating their own power on site can bypass it.

epoch-openai-stargate-uae.text: Khazna Data Centers, the G42 subsidiary building Stargate UAE with OpenAI, Oracle, Nvidia, Cisco and SoftBank, is under construction on a 1,000 megawatt AI data center cluster in Al Dhafrah, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. It sits inside the 5-gigawatt UAE-US AI Campus, a 19.2-square-kilometer site that The National describes as about nine times the size of Monaco. The agreement was signed in May 2025 during President Trump's visit to the UAE, and the cluster will be operated by OpenAI and Oracle. "That first phase of 200MW will be in place and ready at some point in the third quarter of next year," Khaldoon Al Mubarak, managing director and group chief executive of Mubadala, said in December 2025. By then more than 5,000 workers were on site and more than 100,000 cubic meters of concrete had been poured, with steelworks weighing 1.5 times as much as the Eiffel Tower, he said. G42 said in October 2025 that it had completed procurement of all long-lead equipment and expected full buildout of Stargate UAE within three years. Hassan Alnaqbi, chief executive of Khazna, said the project is "about 10 square miles, not only to build the data center, but the entire ecosystem around it," and aims to serve more than 3 billion people within a 3,000-kilometer radius. In October 2025, Khazna's Gareth Dennison said that three months earlier the whole construction site had been covered by a 40-foot-high sand dune. The United States authorized the export of up to the equivalent of 35,000 Nvidia GB300 Blackwell chips to G42 in November 2025, which Al Mubarak compared to going from 5 to 250 kilometers an hour. The 200-megawatt first phase was scheduled for the third quarter of 2026; no result has been published.

epoch-openai-stargate-wisconsin.text: Vantage Data Centers is building the "Lighthouse" data center campus in Port Washington, Wisconsin, in Ozaukee County about 30 minutes north of Milwaukee, on 672 acres. The plan calls for four single-story buildings totaling 902 megawatts of IT capacity, due for completion in 2028. Vantage says 70% of the campus's power will come from solar, wind and battery storage, with the rest matched through renewable energy purchases. The City of Port Washington approved a $458 million tax incentive package for the project in November 2025, for a data center to be leased by OpenAI and Oracle. A local group called Great Lakes Neighbors United organized against the project's scale and the tax breaks it received. On April 7, 2026, city voters passed a referendum, by about 66%, requiring a public vote on any future tax incremental financing district worth $10 million or more. The referendum does not undo the $458 million package already granted to the data center already under construction. Christine Le Jeune, a founding member and spokesperson for Great Lakes Neighbors United, said the financing decision "should not be single-handedly decided by a handful of representatives who are failing to meet the community where we're at with all the questions that we have about this financing, how that will impact us and whether this is something that will truly benefit the community." Voters were reported to be skeptical about the project's water and energy use; Mayor Ted Neitzke did not respond to a request for comment for that story. The Metropolitan Milwaukee Association of Commerce sued in February 2026 to challenge the referendum's validity, and a judge's ruling could still strike it down.

epoch-qts-cedar-rapids.text: QTS is building its first Iowa data center campus on about 612 acres in the Big Cedar Industrial Park in Fairfax, in Linn County just outside Cedar Rapids. The project has seven single-story buildings, described as the largest in QTS's portfolio, and will use about 1.05 gigawatts of electricity, roughly what 800,000 homes use. The Gazette put initial construction investment at more than $750 million, with buildings ranging from 400,000 to 1.1 million square feet, phase one targeted for 2026 and phase two about a year later. A separate industry report, from ABI Research, describes the full build-out as a $10 billion campus, calling it the state's largest investment ever. QTS declined to say who will use its Cedar Rapids facility. Cedar Rapids Mayor Tiffany O'Donnell said, "When you talk about bang for the buck, it makes a lot of sense for us to be bringing in a company like this." QTS's own estimate puts construction employment at about 11,000 jobs, and the company has committed $18 million through a community betterment agreement. The city expects about $20 million a year in property tax revenue at first, rising to roughly $55 million once incentives expire. Linn County adopted new data center zoning rules in 2026, after a first public reading that February, requiring water studies, water-use agreements with the county, 1,000-foot setbacks from residential zones, payments into a community betterment fund, and limits on noise and light pollution. County planning director Charlie Nichols said, "These are generational uses with generational infrastructure impacts, and treating them as a normal warehouse or normal commercial user is just not working." Dorothy Landt, a resident of Palo, asked supervisors for a full moratorium: "Why has Linn County, Iowa, become a dumping ground for soon-to-be obsolete technology that spoils our landscape and robs us of our resources?" In June 2026, county supervisors went further and imposed an 18-month moratorium on new data center projects, running to January 2028, to study the cumulative effect of the projects already approved.

epoch-qts-eagle-mountain.text: QTS Data Centers is building a 193-acre data center campus in Eagle Mountain, Utah County, Utah, and placed the last beam on its first three buildings in April 2026, with about 2,000 construction workers on the site. The three buildings, of between 579,000 and 592,000 square feet each, have been under construction since the fall of 2025 by Layton Construction and are set to be finished later in 2026, not far from Meta's existing Eagle Mountain data center. QTS, a Virginia-based company, has committed $6 billion to the campus and estimates 100 permanent jobs once it is complete, counting its own staff, tenants and contractors. The nearly 200-acre campus is expected to be completed by 2029, and city officials say any future expansion phases will undergo additional review. "This QTS campus represents major investments in Eagle Mountain," Mayor Jared Gray said at the topping out. Water is the question in a region grappling with drought. QTS says the buildings will use a closed-loop cooling system that is filled once and then uses no more water for cooling, with city water going mainly to bathrooms, kitchens, irrigation and humidification. "It's great that we're seeing less water use at the data center itself," said Hilary Hungerford, an earth sciences professor at Utah Valley University. "But we have to follow it upstream and ask what water use looks like in terms of power generation." A nearby data center built in 2018 does not have to disclose its water use, and Utah's 2026 law requiring large data centers to report water consumption, House Bill 76, applies only to facilities that start operating after July 2026. "It's a start," said the bill's sponsor, State Representative Jill Koford. "It wasn't everything we wanted, but it's where we needed to begin to get the bill passed." The data centers also came up in a fight over the city's own taxes. When the Eagle Mountain City Council passed a 183 percent property tax increase on August 6, 2026, hundreds of residents turned out, and many voiced frustration over tax breaks given to data centers. Resident Alex Washburn joined State Sen. Emily Buss to organize a referendum against it. On August 18 the council repealed the increase and adopted a smaller one of 69.81 percent, the city's first property tax rise since 2010, to pay for a Utah County Sheriff's Office contract. "It affects all of us. Everybody's taxes are going to be going up," Washburn said. City officials say the campus is subject to local development agreements and state regulations, and the Eagle Mountain City Council is the local body residents take their concerns to; water reporting rules are set by the Utah Legislature.

gemini-xai-colossus-2-macrohard.text: xAI's Colossus 2 data center, nicknamed Macrohard, stands on Tulane Road in the Whitehaven area of Memphis, in Shelby County, Tennessee, in a former warehouse xAI bought in February 2025 for about $80 million. Its first big cluster, about 110,000 Nvidia processors drawing roughly 210 megawatts, came online around January 2026 after about 91 days of construction. Whitehaven has been living with it since. "We live in this vicinity, so what are we supposed to do? Slowly die? We have kids to live for," one resident told WREG in July 2025, as xAI prepared to switch the building on with gas turbines as backup power. Air tests at the time found no dangerous pollutant levels, but the Southern Environmental Law Center said they had not measured ozone. Another resident was blunter about the trade: "distribute us a check, so we can get up out of here then." Part of its power comes from across the state line, from turbines xAI's affiliate MZX Tech installed at a former Duke Energy plant in Southaven, Mississippi, where regulators permitted a permanent plant of 41 turbines, about 1.2 gigawatts, in March 2026. The NAACP sued xAI and MZX Tech in federal court in April 2026, represented by the law center and Earthjustice, alleging the turbines ran without Clean Air Act permits, and in June the Department of Justice moved to intervene and have the case dismissed on national security grounds. Under an agreed order with Mississippi regulators, the temporary turbines are to be phased out by July 2027.

gemini-xai-minihard.text: Elon Musk said on X on July 29, 2026 that xAI is building a fourth Memphis-area data center, Minihard, next to its Colossus 2 and Macro-harder sites along Tulane Road in Memphis, Shelby County, Tennessee. He said Minihard will hold the same 220,000 GB300 chips as Macro-harder, in a denser configuration, Action News 5 reported. The project is under construction. The power for the Colossus 2 site that Minihard is joining is under challenge in federal court. In April 2026 the NAACP and its Mississippi State Conference sued xAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech over gas turbines running without an air permit at Southaven, Mississippi, saying the emissions threaten homes, schools and churches in north Mississippi and the Memphis area. "A data center should not be a potential death sentence for a community's health," said Abre' Conner, the NAACP's director of environmental and climate justice. By May 2026 the turbine count had grown to 33 and the NAACP asked the court for an injunction to halt the pollution; Conner said xAI "showed no remorse by adding six more turbines." In July 2026 xAI said it would remove all 69 temporary turbines at the Southaven site between August 2026 and July 2027 and replace them with a permanent 1.2-gigawatt, 41-turbine power plant.

gemini-meta-mesa.text: Meta's data center campus in Mesa, in Maricopa County, Arizona, covers 396 acres at the southeast corner of Elliot and Ellsworth roads, bought in the summer of 2021 under the name Redale LLC for $123.2 million. The city approved it under that name: on May 17, 2021 the council passed the development, with a city source confirming the company was Facebook, and vice mayor Jenn Duff was the only vote against. "This has been the driest 12 months in 126 years," Duff said. "We are on red alert, and I think data centers are an irresponsible use of our water." The water agreement estimates the campus at full build out of five buildings might use 1,400 acre feet of water a year, sets maximum flow rates of up to 4 million gallons a day, and requires Meta to buy water credits and sign them over to the city before it connects. In May 2022 Meta decided to build out its whole option, adding three more data halls to the two already under construction for a total of 2.5 million square feet, the same week the Bureau of Reclamation announced emergency measures to protect Lake Powell. "We know water's a concern and it's something we take very seriously," Meta's David Williams said then, and Mayor John Giles told the crowd that "Mesa's an incredible place to set up a shop." Williams said the whole project would be finished in 2026. Meta says the campus represents more than $1 billion of investment and will support more than 200 operational jobs once completed. Mesa has since written rules for the ones that come after it. In July 2025 the council adopted zoning rules written specifically for data centers, after fifteen had been constructed, approved or proposed in the city in six years under rules that treated them as indoor warehousing and storage. On August 31, 2026 Attorney General Kris Mayes asked lawmakers and Governor Katie Hobbs to pass a law pausing approval of new data centers, citing rising power bills and a federal cut of nearly 30 percent to Arizona's Colorado River allocation. Any statewide pause would have to be passed by the Legislature and signed by Governor Hobbs. Hobbs's office said she wants to permanently end the data center tax credit and make data centers pay their fair share for water, while the Senate Republican majority dismissed the call, saying "Policymaking is the Legislature's job".

On August 31, 2026 Attorney General Kris Mayes asked lawmakers and Governor Katie Hobbs to pass a law pausing approval of new data centers, citing rising power bills and a federal cut of nearly 30 percent to Arizona's Colorado River allocation.

Hobbs's office said she wants to permanently end the data center tax credit and make data centers pay their fair share for water, while the Senate Republican majority dismissed the call, saying "Policymaking is the Legislature's job".

The city approved it under that name: on May 17, 2021 the council passed the development, with a city source confirming the company was Facebook, and vice mayor Jenn Duff was the only vote against.
"This has been the driest 12 months in 126 years," Duff said. "We are on red alert, and I think data centers are an irresponsible use of our water."

The water agreement estimates the campus at full build out of five buildings might use 1,400 acre feet of water a year, sets maximum flow rates of up to 4 million gallons a day, and requires Meta to buy water credits and sign them over to the city before it connects.

In May 2022 Meta decided to build out its whole option, adding three more data halls to the two already under construction for a total of 2.5 million square feet, the same week the Bureau of Reclamation announced emergency measures to protect Lake Powell.
"We know water's a concern and it's something we take very seriously," Meta's David Williams said then, and Mayor John Giles told the crowd that "Mesa's an incredible place to set up a shop."
Williams said the whole project would be finished in 2026.

gemini-meta-stanton-springs.text: Meta runs a data center campus at Stanton Springs in Newton County, Georgia, near Mansfield, part of an industrial park where the company broke ground in 2018. Meta says the site represents more than $1.5 billion of investment and supports about 200 operating jobs. Four families from Mansfield sued Meta and county development officials in Gwinnett County court at the end of August 2026, saying construction fouled their well water and cut their property values. Newton County's Board of Commissioners extended an emergency moratorium on new data center permits by another 180 days at an April 2026 meeting, giving staff time to rewrite zoning rules for future projects. Beverly and Jeff Morris live about 1,000 feet from the data center, and their well pressure slowed to a trickle within a year after construction began in 2018; eventually nothing came from their bathroom and kitchen taps. Jeff Morris traced the problem to sediment he believes came from the construction, and the couple has spent $5,000 on repairs since 2019 because they cannot afford the $25,000 a new well would cost. "It feels like we're fighting an unwinnable battle that we didn't sign up for," Beverly Morris said. "I'm scared to drink our own water." Chris Wilson, who lives three doors away, said his water is sometimes "so brown, you'd think it came from a creek." Mike Hopkins of the Newton County Water and Sewerage Authority said Meta's facility uses about 10% of the county's daily water, while nine companies have applied to build data centers in the county, some seeking up to six million gallons a day, more than the county's total daily use. The lawsuit describes Meta's development as two campuses, a 416-acre west campus and a more than 566-acre east campus across the street from the plaintiffs, both drawing on the same aquifer. Meta said its own study shows groundwater flows away from the families' properties and that water used during construction came from the local utility, not their wells. "While we are committed to being a good community partner, we will still defend ourselves from baseless lawsuits," the company said. Newton County's moratorium on new data center permits runs through early October 2026, when commissioners are expected to take up rules that would require data centers to sit at least 1,000 feet from homes. The families' lawsuit, filed in Gwinnett County court, is moving forward; no trial date has been set.

gemini-meta-dekalb.text: Meta's data center in DeKalb, DeKalb County, Illinois, sits on former farmland roughly a mile from the nearest homes and started operating in 2022; it is the company's only site in the state. City manager Bill Nicklas says the city has had no complaints about noise or pollution since it opened, because Meta worked before construction to make the building less noticeable, and the project drew no opposition when it was announced in 2020, before data centers became a subject Illinoisans argued about. The argument arrived with the next project. In December 2025 the DeKalb City Council approved Endeavour Energy's Edged division to build on 560 acres directly south of Meta, in the Chicago West Business Center. Megan Renwick, a lifelong DeKalb resident, told the council the new project would mean habitat loss and "light and sound pollution, both of which will disturb our natural environment along with the wildlife in it." Jake Castanza, speaking for Local 32 of the laborers' union, backed the project: "We are thankful for what the Meta Data Center has done and what we know this data center will do if accepted," pointing to a new elementary school, a fire station and road work paid for out of data center revenue. Edged says its ThermalWorks cooling system will nearly eliminate the site's water use and its TurboCell generators, with far fewer moving parts than a standard diesel unit, are meant to cut noise; portions of the campus are expected to be finished through 2032. DeKalb has so far avoided the noise fights that hit Aurora, 40 miles east, where 10 data centers must stay under 56 decibels at the property line by day.

gemini-meta-forest-city.text: Meta's data center campus in Forest City, Rutherford County, North Carolina, on U.S. 74A and Old Caroleen Road, was one of Facebook's first two data center sites in North America, and the company has invested more than $750 million there since breaking ground in 2010. The campus now supports more than 275 operational jobs across three buildings, the largest a 480,000-square-foot data center backed by more than $200 million in investment with support from the Town of Forest City, Rutherford County and the state. Meta says it worked with Duke Energy to pay the full cost of the energy the data center uses, and with the Town of Forest City to pay the full cost of its water and wastewater service. It says six projects in North Carolina are adding 410 megawatts of new renewable energy for it, and that it has given local schools and nonprofits more than $6.4 million since 2011. A state bill advanced in May 2026 would require North Carolina data centers using at least 100 megawatts to use closed-loop cooling, assess their noise on nearby homes, pay the cost of the electricity they use, and would bar local governments from subsidizing them, while letting local governments require assessments of a data center's effects on water and farmland. Local approvals for any further expansion at the Forest City site rest with the Town of Forest City and Rutherford County.

gemini-meta-bowling-green.text: Meta is building an $800 million data center on more than 280 acres in Middleton Township, north of Bowling Green in Wood County, Ohio, its second in the state. It has its own permitted natural gas plant behind the meter, built with Williams and fed from lines off the Nexus and Rover pipelines. Meta puts construction at more than 1,000 workers and the running campus at about 100 permanent jobs. County commissioners approved a tax abatement in September 2023, 75 percent for 15 years, and Meta was only named as the developer in the summer of 2024. The Eastwood and Otsego school districts are each estimated to receive about $900,000 a year. On January 6, 2026 about 150 residents filled the Wood County Planning Commission room past capacity and questioned the commission for more than two and a half hours. Mark Patton, who lives on Devil's Hole Road a mile from the site, said: "We can't leave. We can't sell our properties." Joe DeMare of Bowling Green said: "Data centers can suck up all the resources." Brittney Klockowski, of Weston village council, said of this kind of development: "It's a different beast." They asked for a moratorium on new data centers, for transparency in rezoning, and for the end user of a project to be disclosed before approval. The commission's answer was that it could not help. Commissioner Craig LaHote said: "We can be sympathetic. But we have no authority." Planning director Dave Steiner said of rezoning applications: "If it's 1,000 acres, it's probably a data center. If it's 50-100 acres, we don't know." Commission chair and county engineer John Musteric asked the room: "Do you want us to lie to you?" LaHote later said he understood the frustration, and that had officials known the potential downsides they might have been able to warn people. Economic development director Wade Gottschalk said that in 2023 "there was no 'anti data center' movement" and that data centers were sought after nationally. Port authority president Rex Huffman said, "What they were was never hidden. There were a lot of hearings along the way." On water the two sides do not even agree on the order of magnitude. Meta says the running campus is liquid cooled in a closed loop with dry coolers and needs no water to operate, using less in a year than two full service restaurants, and that it pays the full cost of its water and sewer. Opponents have cited a figure of up to 600,000 gallons a day, served by the Northwestern Water and Sewer District from Bowling Green's supply. Findlay and Tiffin both passed data center moratoriums on April 22, 2026, and Maumee, Monclova, Waterville Township and Lake Township passed their own earlier in the year.

gemini-meta-altoona.text: Meta's data center campus in Altoona, Polk County, Iowa, is about 5.5 million square feet of buildings along Interstate 80 on the north edge of the Des Moines suburb; Meta broke ground there in 2013 and says it has invested more than $2.5 billion in Iowa, supporting more than 400 operational jobs. The Altoona campus has become a model other towns visit before deciding on data centers of their own. Meta says it worked with MidAmerican Energy to pay the full cost of the energy the data center uses, and with the city of Altoona to pay the full cost of its water and wastewater service. Meta's annual water withdrawal in Altoona was 64 million gallons in 2024, and on a hot summer day it may use as much as 300,000 gallons, Mayor Dean O'Connor said. Meta and other big users might take 15 to 20 percent of Altoona's water supply on a high-use day, city utilities director Dan Scott said, and the city is spending $50 million on new wells and treatment to double its water supply for overall growth. The developer Tract has bought a 453-acre, fully entitled site in Altoona between Northeast 62nd and 70th avenues that it says can support up to 1 gigawatt of power. The city's Planning and Zoning Commission recommended rezoning about 370 acres of newly annexed farmland north of Interstate 80 from agricultural to limited industrial, and Altoona has approved a 10-year tax abatement for properties in the annexed area. In August 2026 the St. Joseph, Missouri, city council scheduled a visit to Altoona to study the city's experience with data centers; city utilities director Dan Scott said Altoona gets about one inquiry a month from would-be data center builders. Decisions on new data centers in Altoona, including rezonings, rest with the Altoona City Council.

meta-meta-henrico.text: Meta's Henrico data center is one of the largest sites in White Oak Technology Park, in Sandston in eastern Henrico County, Virginia, where Meta broke ground in 2017. Meta says it has invested more than $1 billion in Virginia, supports more than 200 operational jobs, and that construction peaked at about 1,500 trade workers. Meta says it worked with Dominion Energy to pay the full cost of the energy the data center uses, with eight projects in Virginia adding 700 megawatts of new renewable energy for it. It says it has given more than $4.2 million in direct funding to Henrico County area schools and nonprofits, and has provided more than 200 local grants and sponsorships since 2019. The park keeps growing. QTS, which already runs 12 operating buildings at its neighboring White Oak hub, is moving ahead with expansions that would add 1,100 acres and bring its campus to 26 buildings and about 8 million square feet of data center space, Richmond BizSense reported in May 2026. QTS has applied to the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality to add 370 diesel fired emergency generators, on top of the 544 generators and 11 cooling towers it is already permitted to run. "These systems are for emergency back-up purposes only and do not continuously run," QTS said in a statement. The Henrico County Board of Supervisors decides new data center cases in the county. On June 10, 2025, the board adopted a Data Center Comprehensive Plan Amendment to guide those decisions.

gemini-meta-fort-worth.text: Meta's Fort Worth data center is the company's first in Texas, a campus in north Fort Worth in Tarrant County where Meta broke ground in 2015 and is now operating. Meta says it has invested more than $1.5 billion there, had 1,200 skilled trade workers at peak construction, and supports more than 200 jobs. The company says it pays the full cost of the energy the campus uses and works with the Fort Worth Water Department to cover water and wastewater costs. On August 11, 2026, the Fort Worth City Council voted unanimously to start the process toward a 90 day moratorium on new data center construction. It voted 10 to 1 to require applicants to show approval from the Public Utility Commission and the state grid operator, and 10 to 1 to create a data center committee. The council is set to adopt the moratorium on February 16, 2027, by a three quarters majority; if adopted, the pause would run to May 17, 2027, and would not apply to projects already filed or approved. That six month wait before any pause begins is what residents came to object to. "We're here because the city has had a flawed approach to data centers this whole time," Kent DeCardenas told the council. Gary Hogan, who lives in southwest Fort Worth, asked, "I don't think there's one person on this city council that would like to have this data center 200 feet from their home. So why impose it on other neighborhoods?" Council member Elizabeth Beck told residents, "We are here to work with you on this. We aren't your enemy in this fight." Caleb Roberts of Downwinders at Risk said the long timetable would push developers to file their applications before any pause takes effect. The committee the council created is to study noise, what data centers take from local water supplies and how long that supply will last, and how the sites fit alongside other land uses. On August 3, 2026, Governor Greg Abbott ordered state regulators to audit data centers waiting for grid connections, freezing those approvals while the reviews run.

gemini-meta-prineville.text: Meta's Prineville campus in Crook County, Oregon began construction in 2010, when the sawmill town's economy was struggling, and has grown into the company's largest data center campus in the country. The campus is operating, and Meta says it has invested more than $2 billion in Oregon, employed up to 1,000 skilled trade workers at peak construction, and supports more than 350 operational jobs. The deal that brought it was a full property tax exemption under Oregon's Long-Term Rural Enterprise Zone program, created in 1985. Crook County assessor Jon Soliz puts the exempted value at more than $130 million a year, and Good Jobs First put the cost of the tax breaks to Oregon schools at $275 million in 2024. What the city collects instead is utility fees, which rose from about $430,000 in 2011 to about $11 million in 2026. Prineville now wants a different bargain. City manager Steve Forrester told a state advisory committee on June 26, 2026 that the city expects to roughly double its property tax revenue once the exemptions expire, the first in 2027, and city leaders say they will probably not grant a full tax break to the next data center that asks. In early June 2026 the Oregon legislature imposed a one year pause on the tax exemption program. On June 28, 2026, 66 workers at Meta's campus lost their jobs after the company ended a contract with an IT services contractor; Meta said it plans to rehire most of them through a different firm. "To me it hurts the economy, it doesn't help the economy. It's not like it's benefitting us from having that up there," said Karl Wilkerson, co-owner of Dad's Place, a Prineville diner. "We're not like Prineville," said Mickey Killingsworth, treasurer of the Jefferson County Farm Bureau. "We don't support data centers." Meta's campus used 70 million gallons of water in 2024, about the same as 420 Prineville households used in 2021. Meta says it aims to restore 200 percent of the water the campus consumes to local watersheds, working with the Crooked River Watershed Council and the Deschutes River Conservancy.

gemini-meta-zeewolde.text: Meta cancelled its planned data center at Zeewolde, a town in Flevoland in the Netherlands, in July 2022, three months after putting the project on hold amid public opposition, DutchNews reported. The campus would have spanned five data halls drawing 200MW at full build, the largest data center campus in the country. Zeewolde's council had approved the zoning change in December 2021, for a campus of 166 hectares on farmland expected to create 400 permanent jobs. In March 2022 a political party opposing the project won an absolute majority in the local election. Tom Zonneveld, chair of the local party Leefbaar Zeewolde, which had campaigned against the plan, called the pause "a postponement and not an adjustment." The fight moved to national politics. All but two parties in the Dutch Senate backed a motion asking Prime Minister Mark Rutte's government to halt the project until a national policy on data centres had been developed. Some environmental campaigners did not want the limited supply of sustainable power in the country to be used by a multinational. "This is a purely political decision," said Stijn Grove, managing director of the Dutch Data Center Association, adding that it had been made "largely because it is Facebook." The land Meta needed was owned by the government, and after lawmakers voted to stop site preparation, the government said it did not plan to sell it "at this time," DCD reported. "When considering a location for a data center, our priority is a good match with the environment. Ultimately, we decided that building a data center in Zeewolde is not the right investment," Meta said. The project had squeezed in just before a ban on new data center construction in Flevoland province.

gemini-microsoft-queretaro.text: Microsoft's Mexico Central cloud region, a group of data centers around Querétaro, opened in May 2024 as the company's first cloud region in Mexico. Microsoft first announced the $1.1 billion project in 2020. One of its data centers is in the semi-desert municipality of Colón, which has been in a two-year drought. Neither Microsoft nor Querétaro's government would tell the Thomson Reuters Foundation's Context how much water the Colón data centers use. Microsoft said its Querétaro data centers use water for cooling less than 5% of the year. "If there is no water for the population, much less will there be water for the companies," said environmental activist Teresa Roldán. Three years after the project was announced, Microsoft obtained a concession to draw 25 million liters a year from an aquifer for one of its two Colón data center units. That is 24% of the water Querétaro allocates to the municipality for public and urban use, according to Mexico's water regulator. Querétaro's minister of sustainable development, Marco del Prete, said "blaming data centers for water shortages oversimplifies the problem, as water issues predate their arrival." Residents of Viborillas, a town surrounded by data centers, say some homes get water only three days a week and have gone without it for a month, resident Brenda Almaraz told Mexico Business News. Groups including the National Antorchista Movement and Voceras de la Madre Tierra are pressing the state for transparency on how much water the data centers use. Querétaro has 12 operating data centers and plans for up to 10 more, including a $4.8 billion CloudHQ project announced in September 2025 to build six data centers by 2027.

gemini-microsoft-naivasha.text: Musa Olorkedienye lives near Lake Naivasha, in Nakuru County, Kenya, where Microsoft wants to build a data centre. "Currently, we are relying on water vendors to get water, our animals are walking for kilometres," he said. Microsoft and the Abu Dhabi firm G42 announced a $1 billion data centre campus at KenGen's Green Energy Park, in the Olkaria geothermal fields near Naivasha, in May 2024, designed to run on 100 percent geothermal power, with a first phase of 100 megawatts and a long term goal of 1 gigawatt. Neither company has published how much water it would use. KenGen's existing Olkaria operations were taking 153,918 cubic metres a month in July 2023. Lake Naivasha is already under pressure from farming, tourism, livestock and a growing population, and nearly dried up in 2010 from over abstraction; Kenya's freshwater availability falls below the United Nations water scarcity threshold. Grace Kimani, a patrol leader with Lake Naivasha and Oloiden, said the planned Microsoft and G42 data centre at Olkaria could create jobs and draw investment, but that its water demand would add pressure to needs that already compete, particularly in dry periods. Silas Wanjala, of the Lake Naivasha Riparian Association, said: "These industries, especially EcoCloud, which deal with data, will consume a lot of water at a time when rivers are drying." What stopped the project, for now, was electricity rather than water. The Kenyan government would not guarantee the annual capacity payments Microsoft wanted, and the talks over power supply broke down in May 2026. President William Ruto said powering the full 1 gigawatt project would mean switching off roughly half the country's electricity supply; Kenya's total installed capacity is only 3,000 to 3,200 megawatts against peak demand of 2,444. John Tanui, principal secretary at Kenya's Ministry of Information, said negotiations were continuing and the project had not been withdrawn, though it "requires further structuring."

gemini-google-douglas-county.text: Google's data center in Lithia Springs, Douglas County, Georgia, was the company's first data center in the state and is one of the first in the industry to cool its servers with recycled industrial water. In March 2025 Douglas County commissioners voted 4-1 for a 90-day moratorium on new data center applications after a developer sought 11 buildings and three warehouse data centers in western Douglas County, a project three times the size of the Mall of Georgia. The Lithia Springs site is operating today, though Google's own website gives two different years for when it began work there, 2003 and 2007. Google's site says it began building its Douglas County data center in 2003; elsewhere on the same site it calls the facility, established in 2007, its first data center in Georgia. In 2015 Google announced a $300 million expansion next to the existing 500,000-square-foot building, adding 25 jobs to the more than 350 people it then employed there, after county officials approved a package of tax breaks. "Much like Google, Douglas County continues to rapidly grow", said then-commission chairman Tom Worthan at the time. Google says it has committed more than $3 billion of investment in Georgia since 2003. "Next thing you know, I have 12 in my backyard," said Amy McCoy, a realtor who helped bring one of the county's first data centers to Lithia Springs. "This area deserves so much more." The moratorium covered new rezonings, special use permits and variances for data centers larger than 50,000 square feet, and commissioners set the pause at 90 days, running through about June 2025. It followed a fight over a data center in the rural Winston community that commissioners approved against their planning staff's advice. Google says its Douglas County site uses recycled wastewater for cooling, and that company-wide it aims to replenish more water than it uses by 2030. "We have a really strong commitment to protecting watersheds," said Ben Townsend, Google's global head of infrastructure and sustainability, "but we can't speak for everyone else in the space." The state Public Service Commission voted in December 2025 to let Georgia Power add nearly 10 gigawatts of power production, mostly for data centers, and critics fear ratepayers will help cover the cost. Any new data center proposal for the county, including an expansion of the Lithia Springs site, goes before the Douglas County Board of Commissioners.

gemini-google-quilicura.text: Google's Quilicura data center, at El Molino 2130 in the commune of Quilicura on the northern edge of Santiago, Chile, went online in January 2015, according to Google. In September 2018 Google announced a $140 million expansion of what was then its only Latin American data center, to triple the campus to 11.2 hectares, with 1,000 construction jobs and 120 permanent positions, at an event attended by President Sebastián Piñera, DCD reported. Google's Curie subsea cable links the Quilicura data center to Los Angeles. In 2019 Google began environmental permitting for a second, $200 million Chilean data center on land between San Bernardo and Cerrillos in the Metropolitan Region, InvestChile reported, citing El Mercurio. Water is the fight. The Quilicura wetland, one of Chile's largest at 468.4 hectares and partly protected, has been drying up, and a May 2026 Guardian report by Anna Heikkinen described it as "a stretch of dry, yellowed grass". "What you see here is a wetland without water," said Rodrigo Vallejos, a law student who investigated the causes with the group Resistencia Socioambiental de Quilicura. "I discovered that Quilicura is home to the largest concentration of datacentres in Latin America", he said. The Guardian reported that companies such as Google and Microsoft defend their water use, while residents point to few jobs, high power use and failed environmental offsets. Google says it has invested in wetlands restoration and precision irrigation projects in the area. New data centers in the Santiago region go through Chile's Environmental Assessment Service, as Google's second project did.

gemini-google-visakhapatnam.text: In Tarluvada, a village outside Visakhapatnam in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh, Google is building what it calls India's first gigawatt-scale AI hub through its subsidiary Raiden Infotech India, three data center campuses on more than 600 acres in the Visakhapatnam and Anakapalli districts, part of a $15 billion investment in India from 2026 to 2030. Raiden has announced partnerships with Adani Infrastructure and Airtel's Nxtra to build the hub, which displaced 51 households, most of them Dalit farming families who had worked the land for more than 50 years. "We were never told about any data centre," one resident said, according to Land Conflict Watch. Farmer Relli Ramakrishnan told Land Conflict Watch his family had cleared the land themselves: "We had to clear the jungle ourselves; it took us 15 years, 15 long years. We worked hard, shed our blood for this land." After the pushback, the state raised compensation to 20 lakh rupees an acre for recorded land and 10 lakh rupees an acre for unrecorded land, up from initial offers of 17 lakh and 8.5 lakh, and added house-site land and job or shop promises for 520 farmers. The project's environmental clearance was granted on April 18, 2026, nine days after Adani's subsidiary applied for it and ten days before an April 28 groundbreaking attended by Union IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw and Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu, The News Minute reported. The clearance was classified in a lower-scrutiny category that let it skip a public hearing and full environmental review, even though the site is 1.53 kilometers from the Kambalakonda Wildlife Sanctuary and nearly 90 percent of the Tarluvada parcel overlaps a reserve forest, the outlet reported. The Human Rights Forum said putting "a high-energy, heat-intensive complex of this magnitude in such a terrain is ecologically reckless" given the city's water stress and cyclone exposure, and called Google's promise of 100 percent renewable operation technically untenable. Visakhapatnam receives 410 million liters of water a day against a requirement of 480 million, the state government says, and residents and children have marched with banners reading "We cannot drink DATA." The dispute is before the Andhra Pradesh High Court and the National Green Tribunal. On August 24, 2026, a High Court bench led by Chief Justice Lisa Gill refused to halt construction but ordered the state to ensure all legal and environmental permissions are in place and to file a consolidated response from the departments that granted approvals. Petitioner Bolisetty Satyanarayana also challenges the use of about 160 acres of Simhachalam temple land and argues the environmental clearance covers building the data center, not operating it.

gemini-aws-queretaro.text: Amazon Web Services runs its AWS Mexico (Central) cloud region across three separate data center sites in the state of Queretaro, Mexico, not a single campus; AWS launched the region on January 14, 2025, saying it would invest more than $5 billion in Mexico over 15 years. AWS first announced the region in February 2024 after five years of work, and says it will add about $10 billion to Mexico's GDP and support more than 7,000 full-time equivalent jobs a year at outside businesses. AWS describes each of the three sites as having its own power, cooling and security, spaced far enough apart to keep working if one fails but close enough to keep response times fast. The company launched a $300,000 community fund in Queretaro, and Governor Mauricio Kuri said the investment puts the state "at the digital forefront of Latin America." AWS told the Thomson Reuters Foundation's Context in 2024 that its buildings use an air-cooled design that does not need ongoing cooling water, but the nearby municipality of Colon, which has drawn $10 billion in data center investment from Microsoft, Google and Amazon, was then in its second year of drought. In February 2026 Mexico Business News reported resident complaints about water rationing and power cuts near the state's data centers; Queretaro's sustainable development minister, Marco del Prete, said the water problems predate the data centers. Microsoft opened its own competing Mexico Central region in Queretaro in 2024, and in March 2026 AWS technology director Manuel Puron told El CEO that the company plans to keep growing its footprint there, with more than 110 AWS services then available from the region, including generative AI models through Bedrock.
