gemini-oracle-ashburn.text: Oracle rents 91,809 square feet inside a Digital Realty building at 43915 Devin Shafron Drive in Ashburn, Loudoun County, Virginia, where its data center has operated since 2010. On September 15, 2026 the Loudoun County board of supervisors voted 7-1-1 to direct staff to draft a resolution pausing new data center applications for up to 12 months; the pause is not yet in force, with a final vote due October 20, 2026. The lease covers three quarters of the building's power load, 6.75 megawatts of Oracle's use, runs through August 31, 2032, and costs about $9.47 million a year, with Morgan Stanley as the building's other main tenant. Loudoun County, home to unincorporated Ashburn, is known as "Data Center Alley" for its concentration of data centers; Ashburn's district supervisor Michael Turner counted 199 data centers in the county with another 117 in development. Those facilities took 24 percent of Dominion's Virginia electricity sales in 2023, and the utility plans to spend $50.1 billion on capital projects between 2025 and 2029 to keep up with demand. "This pause is a major step forward," said Algonkian District Supervisor Juli E. Briskman, who brought the proposal, adding it gives the county "the breathing room required" to rewrite its data center rules. The property last changed hands in 2022, when GI Partners bought it from Starwood Capital for $150 million; Oracle's cloud region there, us-ashburn-1, has three availability domains.

gemini-oracle-salt-lake-city.text: Oracle's data center in Utah is at West Jordan, in Salt Lake County, about eight miles south of Salt Lake City: a 179,000 square foot building known inside the company as Project Sequoia, cooled with air rather than water to make use of the dry climate. Oracle's own list of commercial cloud regions has none in Utah; in the United States it gives Ashburn, Chicago, Phoenix and San Jose. Utah decided in 2026 that it wants to know what these buildings use. HB 76, brought by Rep. Jill Koford, makes a new large data center tell the state where its water will come from, how it will be reused and how much it actually withdraws each year, with the figures published online. HB 507, brought by Rep. Cal Roberts, bars local governments from offering incentives to large data centers outside designated development zones and caps property tax incentives at 60 percent of new county revenue. "One thing that I think we're united on is we do not want a state full of data centers," said the House speaker, Mike Schultz.

gemini-oracle-iowa.text: Oracle has no data center of its own in Iowa, in Story County or anywhere else in the state. Its Iowa presence is racks inside Google's, at Council Bluffs: the company's own multicloud documentation pairs Google's us-central1 region at Council Bluffs with an Oracle region it labels US Midwest (Des Moines), and runs its database services there under the Oracle Database@Google Cloud arrangement. The commercial region list Oracle publishes separately, of data centres it operates itself, has no Iowa entry at all: in the United States it gives Ashburn, Chicago, Phoenix and San Jose. The campus the racks sit in is one of the largest in the state. Google's Council Bluffs site has been expanded repeatedly since 2009 and is approaching 300 megawatts. The city gave it a 20 year tax abatement on the original building and has renewed incentives at each expansion, with state exemptions running 20 years at 70 percent so long as job and employment thresholds are met, and the campus has taken more than $36 million in tax incentives. MidAmerican Energy serves it from the Council Bluffs 345 kilovolt substation, and Google contracted for up to 407 megawatts of wind power for the site. Council Bluffs is in Pottawattamie County, on the Nebraska line, about 130 miles from Story County.

gemini-oracle-montreal.text: Oracle runs a cloud data center region in Montreal, Quebec, which opened March 30, 2020 as the company's second Canadian region after Toronto. Oracle paired the two regions so Canadian customers could run backup and disaster recovery entirely inside Canada, without their data leaving the country. Quebec's power utility now wants to charge large data centers far more for electricity, and a regulator's decision on the new rate is due by November 1, 2026. "The new Montreal Region coupled with the Toronto Region enables Oracle to provide multi-region deployments in country to address Canadian organizations' disaster recovery and compliance requirements," said Don Johnson, then executive vice president of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, when the region opened. In December 2025 Oracle began offering its database services inside Google Cloud's Montreal region too, running on Oracle hardware placed inside Google's data center there. In February 2026 Hydro-Quebec asked the Regie de l'energie to approve a new tariff for large data centers averaging 13 cents per kilowatt-hour, about double the current large-power rate, starting in the second half of 2026, with a five-year transition for centers already connected. Hydro-Quebec said it expects data center power use in the province to grow sevenfold by 2035, and that large projects still must pass its selection process before getting power. A coalition of six operators running 23 sites in Quebec, including QScale, Vantage and Cologix, is fighting the tariff before the Regie de l'energie as too high and unfair, La Presse reported in May 2026.

Oracle paired the two regions so Canadian customers could run backup and disaster recovery entirely inside Canada, without their data leaving the country. Quebec's power utility now wants to charge large data centers far more for electricity, and a regulator's decision on the new rate is due by November 1, 2026.

In December 2025 Oracle began offering its database services inside Google Cloud's Montreal region too, running on Oracle hardware placed inside Google's data center there.

Hydro-Quebec said it expects data center power use in the province to grow sevenfold by 2035, and that large projects still must pass its selection process before getting power.

gemini-oracle-toronto.text: Oracle's Toronto data center, its first in Canada, opened on January 17, 2019 in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, to host the Oracle Cloud Infrastructure region there. Oracle did not say how big the Toronto data center is, DCD noted. "Enterprises in the region still have limited ability to run mission-critical applications in the cloud and are struggling to attain the level of performance they have on-premises without a major overhaul," Oracle's Don Johnson said at the opening. Cologix said it would offer private connections to the Oracle region from its Toronto data center, TOR1. Oracle added a Montreal region in March 2020 so Canadian customers could run disaster recovery across two regions inside the country. In December 2025 Oracle also began selling its database services from inside Google Cloud's Toronto and Montreal regions. Ontario is now setting rules for data centers. On August 13, 2026 Premier Doug Ford outlined a provincial framework under which new data centers must pay all their energy costs, could face a higher rate class than other industrial users, get no cash incentives, and must show local benefits to win approval. "But if any data centre thinks they’re coming into Ontario and getting a freebie: not happening", Ford said. Toronto and other municipalities had pressed the province for clearer rules, Oakville passed a one-year data center moratorium that week, and Mississauga was set to vote on its own pause. The grid operator said data center requests to connect had doubled since March and now equal more than a quarter of the province's peak demand. Under Bill 40, amendments to the Electricity Act that took effect on December 11, 2025 let the province prioritize and approve grid connections for data centers it deems to serve its economic interests, with the details left to regulations still to come. Oracle's existing Toronto region is already connected; the new framework applies to future projects, which Oracle has not announced in Ontario.

gemini-core-scientific-marble-falls.text: Core Scientific has no data center at Marble Falls, and none in Mills County, Texas. Its own list of sites gives three in Texas, at Austin, Denton and Pecos, where the Cottonwood buildings are, alongside Auburn in Alabama, Dalton in Georgia, Calvert City in Kentucky, Grand Forks in North Dakota, Muskogee in Oklahoma and one called Marble 1. Marble 1 is in North Carolina. The company puts that campus at 117 megawatts across 250,000 square feet on 70 acres at Marble, in the far west of the state, and sells it on fibre routes reaching Knoxville, Charlotte, Nashville and Atlanta. Across all its American sites Core Scientific gives itself more than 1,300 megawatts of power capacity, with racks available from 50 to more than 200 kilowatts. The Texas sites are not interchangeable: Cottonwood 1 and 2 at Pecos, in Reeves County, are the ones the company is turning from Bitcoin mining to artificial intelligence work, at 1.5 gigawatts of gross power.

gemini-core-scientific-dalton.text: Core Scientific runs three operating data centers in Dalton, Whitfield County, Georgia: Dalton 1 and 2 on Industrial South Road, with 50 megawatts combined, and Dalton 3 at 206 Boring Drive, this site, with about 142 megawatts. It is also building a fourth site, Dalton 4, on about 170 acres on Old Tilton Road, planned for roughly 145 megawatts with a target opening of July 2026, a date that has passed with no report that it opened. County commissioners rezoned the Old Tilton Road site from agricultural to heavy manufacturing in March 2025, after a public meeting where dozens of residents, some from farming families who had worked the land for generations, spoke against it. One resident told commissioners at that meeting: "If you're talking about the size facility that is being discussed, you've got a monster." Georgia's Environmental Protection Division is reviewing separate air permits for standby diesel generators: up to 80 at Dalton 4, and eight totaling 21.6 megawatts at the Industrial South Road site; the permits cover only generator emissions, not whether the data centers themselves may operate. Public comment on the Old Tilton Road permit closed April 24, 2026, and on the Industrial South Road permit June 26, 2026, and EPD's Sara Lips said on May 27, 2026 that the Old Tilton Road permit was "in the final stages of review." Carl Campbell of the Dalton-Whitfield Joint Development Authority said the company spends about $5 million a month on electricity in Dalton, and that "all that money from the power generation helps our city." Dalton Utilities says data centers cover the full cost of their own power supply. At a June 8, 2026 county commission meeting, resident Carmen Shuler said: "We now feel threatened by unplanned development of AI data centers in our community." Cathy Kott said: "These are billionaires coming in to make profit off of our community. They should be giving not just in assets but also in information." County Administrator Bob Sivick told them: "Electric power is not a finite resource kept in a warehouse somewhere. It's part of a regional pool, and electricity is routed to where it's needed or where it's not needed."

gemini-core-scientific-grand-forks-1.text: Grand Forks 1, Core Scientific's data center at 5601 11th Ave S in Grand Forks, in Grand Forks County, North Dakota, has 100 MW of total power capacity on a 20-acre campus with 90,000 square feet of buildings, according to the company. Core Scientific listed the data center in October 2025 at about 70MW of billable power with the status "Future Colocation Site", meaning space to be leased to customers. Core Scientific announced the site in May 2021 as a mining and hosting facility, developed in partnership with Nodak Electric Cooperative and Minnkota Power Cooperative, and said it would create up to 12 local jobs that year. Core Scientific is shifting its business from bitcoin mining to leasing data center capacity for AI: colocation made up 83 percent of its second-quarter 2026 revenue, and in July it signed 15-year leases with AMD for 529 megawatts at other sites. Grand Forks has two data centers today, this one and a cryptocurrency mine run by Sundog Mining, the Grand Forks Herald reported in September 2026. County Administrator Tom Ford said there are no plans at present for a new one, but Grand Forks County commissioners were shown a model data center ordinance in June, covering permits, use standards, fence locations, landscaping buffers and wastewater outlets. Ford said: "We need to have some kind of process and policy in place for when that time comes." City Administrator Todd Feland said AI data centers could bring more investment and jobs than cryptocurrency facilities, and the city and county have been talking with Minnkota Power, Nodak Electric and Xcel Energy about how much the grid can support. Elsewhere in North Dakota the boom is further along. Near Ellendale, Applied Digital runs two data centers and is building two more, and Mayor Don Flaherty described heavy traffic, worn roads and tight housing. "Right now, things are pretty hectic," Flaherty said. Applied Digital's $3 billion data center near Harwood has drawn criticism from residents, and a public forum on hyperscale AI data centers was held on August 28. Rules for any new data center in Grand Forks County would come from the Grand Forks County Commission, which is weighing a development policy like those it has for wind and solar farms.

gemini-applied-digital-jamestown.text: Applied Digital built its first data center in Jamestown, North Dakota, in 2021: an $82 million, 106-megawatt facility for blockchain computing in Stutsman County that now employs 40 people. It was the company's first site before Applied Digital expanded to Ellendale, to Harwood near Fargo, and to a site approved about 40 miles northwest of Bismarck. Statewide, the argument over new data centers is about noise, bills and water, and Applied Digital's Nick Phillips has pointed to an Electric Power Research Institute study that found data center growth pushed electricity rates down 6 percent between 2019 and 2024. Robert Mayo, a research specialist at North Dakota State University's Challey Institute who wrote a guide to the industry for the state, said his aim was that "citizens and policymakers have accurate facts so that they can, based on those facts, choose the policy that will get them the result they want." Senate Majority Leader David Hogue created an interim legislative committee on AI and data centers to study the subject ahead of next year's legislative session; it first met in mid-July 2026, and counties are updating their own data center application policies.

gemini-core-scientific-austin.text: Core Scientific's Austin data center, in Austin, Travis County, Texas, is a leased tier 3 building that formerly housed Hewlett Packard, which Core Scientific took on in 2024 to host GPU computing for CoreWeave. Under a multi-year contract announced in March 2024, Core Scientific agreed to supply up to 16 MW of data center capacity there to CoreWeave, with total potential revenue of more than $100 million. It was Core Scientific's first move from bitcoin mining into hosting for high-performance computing. Chief executive Adam Sullivan said when the deal was announced: "Our new data center in Austin will support CoreWeave's near-term requirements while also expanding and diversifying Core Scientific's hosting customer portfolio across two categories of high value compute: bitcoin mining and specialized GPU cloud compute." In an October 2025 investor presentation Core Scientific listed Austin at about 20MW of billable power, with a customer in place. Austin is one of the smaller sites in a company now leasing about 1.1 gigawatts of capacity to customers, according to CoinDesk, after a July 2026 deal with AMD for 529 megawatts at its sites in Pecos and Hunt County, Texas, and Muskogee, Oklahoma. Colocation made up 83 percent of Core Scientific's second-quarter 2026 revenue as its own bitcoin mining wound down. Texas has frozen new data center grid connections for now. Gov. Greg Abbott ordered an audit on August 3, 2026 of about 250 to 300 projects in ERCOT's first batch of large-load connection requests, most of them data centers, which must be completed before any data center in that queue can connect to the state grid. ERCOT said the audit would take several months and that it still aimed to finish studying the first batch by April. The audit covers projects seeking new connections; Core Scientific lists the Austin building as already serving a customer.

gemini-start-sines-4-0.text: Start Campus's Sines 4.0 data centre campus, in Portugal's Sines industrial zone about 90 kilometres south of Lisbon, where the transatlantic cables come ashore, has more grid power reserved for it than any colocation site in Europe, by the company's account. REN, the Portuguese transmission operator, raised the campus's allocation from 495 megawatts to 1.2 gigawatts in August 2024, enough for six buildings, the later five of up to 240 megawatts each. What that power means for the country is the argument. At full build the campus would consume 4,769.8 gigawatt hours a year, about a fifth of the renewable electricity Portugal generated in 2022, and approval was granted to fell 1,800 cork oaks at the EDP Renovaveis Morgavel wind farm meant to supply it. The cooling draws seawater from the Atlantic and returns it about a degree warmer, which is how the company claims to consume no water. The campus has also been caught up in the corruption investigation that brought down Antonio Costa's government in November 2023, and accused of building its first hall on a protected wetland; both are covered on this site's page for the Sines data campus.

gemini-ytl-green-park.text: YTL Power operates a large data center campus, YTL Green Data Center Park, in Kulai, Johor, Malaysia, built for up to 600 megawatts of power. The company had 298 megawatts already under contract with customers as of March 2026, The Edge Malaysia reported, and it is bringing more capacity online in stages. In August 2026 YTL Power announced a second campus nearby, at Sedenak Tech Park West. The park was first announced in August 2022. YTL Power says its AI facility there sits on a 1,640-acre site and runs on renewable power from a 500-megawatt solar plant. Singapore's Sea was reported to be the anchor tenant, and GDS was also building a data center on the campus, DCD reported. In October 2025 YTL Power completed Malaysia's first Nvidia-powered AI data center at the park, built with Nvidia's liquid-cooled GB200 chips, and its YTL AI Cloud began operating there. Managing director Yeoh Seok Hong said YTL AI Cloud will host government and citizen-facing AI services. The Sedenak project will sit on 145 acres that YTL Power's 70%-owned unit SIPP Power is buying from JLand Group, the property arm of the state-owned Johor Corporation, with an option on up to 400 more acres. "Together with our expanding Kulai campus, Sedenak will further strengthen Johor's position as a leading regional centre for artificial intelligence, cloud computing and digital innovation," Yeoh said. RHB Investment Bank said in July 2026 that YTL Power was exploring a stock listing of its data center unit in 2027. Johor's chief minister, Onn Hafiz Ghazi, said in March 2026 that the state will only approve data centers that use air cooling, which needs little water: "If a data centre demands a high intake of water, we will not approve it." He said 38 projects worth RM15.3 billion will shore up the state's water supply, and that a state committee reviews each applicant's water and electricity needs. In February 2026 residents of Gelang Patah protested outside a data center construction site over water, The Diplomat reported. Further data center approvals in Johor go through the Johor State Data Centre Development Coordinating Committee.

gemini-khazna-ajman.text: Khazna Data Centers, a unit of Abu Dhabi's G42, is building QAJ01, a 100 megawatt data center in Ajman, United Arab Emirates, its largest facility yet, with 20 data halls of 5 megawatts each and liquid cooling, a system that uses fluid instead of just air to handle the heat dense AI computer clusters produce. Khazna announced the project at the Gitex Global technology conference in Dubai in October 2024, when chief executive Hassan Al Naqbi said it would open in the third quarter of 2025. That date has passed with no opening announced; on February 24, 2026, Uptime Institute certified the facility's design under its Tier III standard, the first of two steps in checking a data center's build against its plans. Electricity for the site is to come from Etihad Water and Electricity, and Al Naqbi said the average construction cost across Khazna's projects is "between $8 million and $12 million" per megawatt. Khazna's chief technology officer Abdulmajeed Harmoodi said: "QAJ1 sets a new regional benchmark, combining high-density readiness, advanced liquid cooling, and globally certified design to support the next generation of compute." Al Naqbi said Khazna held about 74 percent of the UAE data center market in 2024 and expects the country's total capacity to reach at least 850 megawatts by 2029.

gemini-khazna-abu-dhabi.text: Khazna Data Centers, the G42-owned company building the Stargate UAE data center cluster, is also developing the wider 5-gigawatt UAE-US AI Campus that will surround it, a data center campus spanning 10 square miles in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, that Presidents Donald Trump and Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan announced on May 22, 2025. The campus is meant to be powered by nuclear, solar and natural gas power to cut carbon emissions, and will also include a science park for research and training. Its first cluster, the 1-gigawatt Stargate UAE, is being built with OpenAI, Oracle, Nvidia, Cisco and SoftBank and has its own page here; no timeline has been shared for the rest of the wider campus. G42's chair Tahnoun bin Zayed Al Nahyan, who is also the UAE's national security adviser, called the deal part of the US-UAE AI Acceleration Partnership, under which UAE entities are also expanding investment in US data center projects such as Stargate US. OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman called it the first Stargate site built outside the United States. US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said American companies will operate the data centers and offer American-managed cloud services across the region, with what he called strong security guarantees against the diversion of US technology.

gemini-ai71-abu-dhabi.text: AI71 is a software company rather than a data center operator. Abu Dhabi's Advanced Technology Research Council and its commercialisation arm VentureOne launched it to sell access to the Falcon family of large language models and to build decentralised data control for companies and governments, aimed first at medicine, education and law. Its compute is bought rather than built: the company sells credits for pay as you go access to Falcon through an API hub. The capacity behind that sits with others. Abu Dhabi is targeting a gigawatt of AI compute backed by up to $10 billion, inside a UAE and United States AI campus aiming at 5 gigawatts in total, with G42's cloud arm Core42 as the sovereign compute provider. Falcon itself is released under permissive open weights licensing, trained at the Technology Innovation Institute's expense and free for research and commercial use, which is the centre of the country's argument that it can be an AI power without depending on anyone else's models. The buildings that argument rests on belong to other parts of the same group. Khazna Data Centers, which is G42's, said in October 2025 that it would add more than a gigawatt of operating capacity over five years, including more than 400 megawatts in new markets such as Saudi Arabia and Italy alongside Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Ajman, supported by a $2.62 billion financing facility from Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank and First Abu Dhabi Bank.

gemini-quantum-frederick-park.text: Aligned Data Centers is building a 264-megawatt data center campus at Quantum Frederick Park, the former Alcoa Eastalco aluminum smelter site north of Adamstown in Frederick County, Maryland. Its first building, IAD-04, is a 72-megawatt facility on a 75-acre plot, and at full build-out the Aligned campus will have four multi-story buildings. Aligned broke ground on IAD-04 in February 2025 and began its second building, IAD-06, in October 2025; as of June 2026 none of the data centers in the park was yet operating. Aligned pitches the site as an alternative to Northern Virginia, linked to Ashburn by a new fiber ring called QLoop. The wider park was planned from 2021 as a 2,100-acre gigawatt-scale data center campus. Its original developer, Quantum Loophole, was pushed out in 2024 after a legal dispute, and Catellus Development Corporation became lead developer. Amazon Web Services and Rowan Digital Infrastructure have also broken ground there, and at full build the campus is expected to draw 2,400 megawatts, more than the 2024 average demand of Montgomery and Prince George's counties combined. Aligned's own path was not smooth. The Maryland Public Service Commission denied its application for 168 diesel backup generators, and Aligned pulled out of the project in mid-2023 after being granted only a provisional exemption for up to 70 megawatts of generators. After the state changed the rules, the Department of the Environment approved an application for 172 diesel backup generators in 2025. Nature Forward, an environmental group, counts at least 67 state inspections that found the Quantum Frederick site in noncompliance or needing corrective action, including boring crews releasing drilling fluid into nearby waterways, and notes that a promised 600-acre nature reserve planned with the University of Maryland has been put in doubt since its design contract was cancelled. The fight in Frederick County is now about what comes after the park. In December 2025 the County Council approved a 2,600-acre data center zone overlapping the campus, and residents who wanted data centers kept to the existing park collected more than 21,000 signatures for a referendum. On June 30, 2026 the Maryland Supreme Court upheld a ruling that the ordinance could not go to referendum and that the petition was unclear. "We felt a little betrayed," resident Nancy Evans said of the council's decision. In September the park's developer, Quantum Maryland, offered $110 million in community benefits and 20 per cent less data center development in exchange for an eight-year freeze on zoning changes affecting the campus. County Executive Jessica Fitzwater rejected it on September 14, 2026 after hundreds of public comments and extended the county's moratorium on data center applications to July 1, 2027. "Your comments also made it clear that you do not want to see any more decisions made about data centers, not until we have the next county council seated, and not until the state completes its impact study," she said. The moratorium applies to new data center applications, and residents have said data centers will be a deciding issue in the November county elections that seat that next council.

gemini-aligned-phoenix.text: Aligned Data Centers broke ground on Sept. 10, 2026 on Project Phoenix, a 2 gigawatt data center campus in Shippingport, Beaver County, Pennsylvania, built on the site of the former Bruce Mansfield coal-fired power plant. The three-building campus is in the Shippingport Industrial Park, about 30 miles northwest of Pittsburgh, next to the old Shippingport Power Station, which is being redeveloped into a natural gas energy campus. Phase one is under construction, and Shippingport's leaders have approved phase two of Aligned's land development plan, WPXI reported on Sept. 21, 2026. Shippingport Borough Council approved Aligned's conditional use application in January 2026, allowing up to three data center buildings totaling 2 million square feet. It was the first test of a data center ordinance the borough had passed in March 2025, before officials knew Aligned was coming. Aligned, which is based in Plano, Texas, closed on a 650.89-acre property in Shippingport in late July for $223,150,865.38, Beaver County Radio reported. Frontier Group of Companies, which owns the industrial park, bought the old plant site from Energy Harbor in 2022; the 2.49 gigawatt Bruce Mansfield plant opened in 1976 and shut down in 2019. Aligned puts the project at $10 billion in regional investment, 3,000 construction jobs and more than 640 full-time jobs once it runs. The company says the campus will use a dedicated onsite power source rather than the local electrical grid, and that its closed-loop cooling system needs no water for operational cooling. Frontier has said it will build a 2.7 gigawatt natural gas plant at the site and that the park can offer up to 3.6 gigawatts of behind-the-meter capacity. BizJournals reported in February that Aligned's buildings would not at first be powered by that new plant but by a separate National Fuel Gas line. In February Aligned told local officials it was still working to secure a customer for its data centers. Shippingport is a borough of about 160 people, and many residents first heard of the project indirectly, when some received notices about seismic testing to make sure blasting at the industrial park would not damage their foundations. "Someone jumped the gun," said Pat Lampe, the borough's emergency services coordinator. At a borough meeting days after Aligned filed its conditional use application in early December 2025, borough solicitor Rich Urick "emphasized that the project should proceed at a slower pace to allow proper review," according to meeting minutes. At Aligned's first information meeting in December, Lampe said, some people asked how the project would affect their property values, and others worried about landslides and stability in a hilly area that sits on top of mines. Resident Tim Goughnour saw the money the borough has missed: "We've lost so much revenue, we haven't been able to really care for the borough in the way we should have been able to all these years since … the loss of revenue from Bruce Mansfield". The Keystone reported that the groundbreaking went ahead despite concerns from some area residents. Jai-Ellen St. George of nearby Midland told WPXI: "I feel they're popping up everywhere like Dollar General stores." Shippingport Mayor John Erickson backed the project at the groundbreaking, saying the town had been defined by its history as "the birthplace of commercial nuclear energy" and that "Project Phoenix honors that legacy, opening a new chapter by taking a historic site and rebuilding it into a modern engine of innovation." Aligned is not the only data center interest in the Beaver Valley. Fezzik Energy, whose partners include land developer Chuck Betters, attorney Jonathan Kamin and Joanna Doven, is working to attract data centers to former J&L Steel sites in Midland and Aliquippa. In August 2025 a Vistra subsidiary paid $4.2 million for a 74-acre farm in Hookstown, a mile from the boundary of Vistra's Beaver Valley nuclear plant, and the company declined to say what it plans there. Vistra signed a 20-year deal in January 2026 to supply power from its nuclear plants, including Beaver Valley, to offset Meta's data center demand. Frontier has said it will build a 2.7 gigawatt natural gas plant at the site and that the park can offer up to 3.6 gigawatts of behind-the-meter capacity. BizJournals reported in February that Aligned's buildings would not at first be powered by that new plant but by a separate National Fuel Gas line. developers2-aligned-salt-lake-city-west-.text: Aligned Data Centers runs its Salt Lake City campus at 3333 West 9000 South in West Jordan, Salt Lake County, Utah, a 55-acre site that the company says holds its SLC-01, SLC-02 and SLC-03 data centers. Aligned markets the West Jordan data center campus as designed to Tier III standards with 24-hour access and a 100% uptime service agreement. Water is the local question. Records gathered by The Salt Lake Tribune show Aligned used 47.4 million gallons of water in West Jordan between October 2024 and September 2025, and 80 million gallons at its West Valley site. By comparison, the National Security Agency's data center in Bluffdale used more than 126 million gallons, and the nearby Novva campus in West Jordan, which fills a recirculating cooling system once, used 3 million gallons, two-thirds of it on landscaping. Power is the other. Rocky Mountain Power, the state's main utility, does not have the capacity to meet the surge in demand, so data center developers have turned to generating their own electricity, mostly from natural gas. Data centers in Salt Lake County, including Aligned's, have received approval in the last five years to install diesel backup generators, and environmental advocates warn new generators could push the region back out of compliance with air quality standards. In West Jordan itself, the expanding Novva campus won state approval in December 2024 to build a 200 megawatt natural gas plant. Aligned changed hands in July 2026, when a consortium of the AI Infrastructure Partnership, BlackRock's Global Infrastructure Partners and Abu Dhabi-based MGX completed a $40 billion purchase of the company from Macquarie Asset Management, the largest deal ever in data centers. The Dallas-based company has 51 campuses across North and South America and more than 6.4GW of operational and planned capacity, and CEO Andrew Schaap and his team stay on.

gemini-aligned-dfw-01-dfw-03.text: Aligned's DFW-03 data center at 3801 Britton Road in Mansfield, in Tarrant County, Texas, is a 429,600 square foot building on 27 acres with its own substation, registered with the state as a $120.5 million project built from June 2024 to January 2026. It was due to deliver its first capacity from the last quarter of 2025, cooled by air and liquid at densities above 350 kilowatts a rack. Water is the question people in Tarrant County have been asking. The Tarrant Regional Water District has said that while it supplies cities including Fort Worth and Mansfield, and some of that water ends up in data centers, it has signed no new supply contract for one. Fort Worth, about 20 miles away, voted unanimously on August 11, 2026 to take the first step toward a 90 day pause on new data center proposals, exempting projects already approved. Aligned's other two Dallas-Fort Worth buildings, DFW-01 and DFW-02, are on a 19 acre campus at 2800 Summit Avenue in Plano, in Collin County, about 50 miles away.

gemini-aligned-neo-01.text: Aligned Data Centers is building NEO-01, the first of up to four buildings on its data center campus in Perkins Township, just south of Sandusky in Erie County, Ohio, and expects to finish it in 2026. The company broke ground in May 2024 on the 129-acre site at 2509 Hayes Avenue, paying $52 million for the former manufacturing site in 2023, and is putting more than $200 million into the first phase, which it lists at 96 megawatts of power across 200,000 square feet. Aligned says its Ohio buildings use a closed-loop water system designed to use very little water for cooling. The site was an automotive bearing plant built around 1947, later run by Delphi and then Kyklos, that once employed about 5,000 people before closing around 2017. Township trustees, the school board and the career center agreed to put 70% of the new property-tax revenue from the buildings back into the project for 30 years and share the rest, and Aligned made a $325,000 upfront payment, most of which went to the schools. "From my lens, as an educator, this has been a godsend," said Perkins Local Schools Superintendent Lonny Rivera, whose district has failing boilers. Power and water remain open questions: the local newsletter StayTunedSandusky reported in 2025 that Aligned plans 15 natural gas engines on site capable of 282 megawatts rather than drawing from the local grid, and that officials had not said where the project's water would come from. The data center is expected to create 18 permanent jobs by February 2027. At least 138 Ohio municipalities and townships had active data center moratoriums as of September 17, 2026, the Ohio Capital Journal reported, though Perkins Township, governed by a three-member board of trustees, has not adopted one.

gemini-aligned-atl-01.text: Aligned's ATL-01 data center at 1551 North River Road in Lithia Springs, in Douglas County, Georgia, sits in one of the densest clusters of data centers in the Atlanta region, and the county has already paused new ones once. On March 19, 2025 the Douglas County Commission voted 4 to 1 for a 90 day moratorium, after an application for 11 buildings and three warehouse data centers in the west of the county. "Next thing you know, I have 12 in my backyard," said Amy McCoy, a Lithia Springs homeowner and realtor who had helped bring one of the first data centers there. Aligned publishes the plant rather than the size for ATL-01: no acreage, square footage, megawatt figure, water figure or employment number appears on its page.

gemini-prince-william-digital-gateway.text: The Prince William Digital Gateway would have been the largest data center campus in the world: 37 buildings across more than 2,100 acres near Gainesville, Virginia, next to Manassas National Battlefield Park. The developers, QTS and Compass Datacenters, said it would bring "tens of billions of dollars" in investment and thousands of long-term jobs. The Prince William Board of County Supervisors, then chaired by Ann Wheeler, approved the rezoning of roughly 1,790 acres in December 2023. The vote came after a public hearing that ran 29 hours. The Oak Valley Homeowners Association and the American Battlefield Trust sued, arguing that the county's hearing notices in The Washington Post did not meet state and county requirements. On August 7, 2025, Circuit Court Judge Kimberly Irving agreed and declared the rezoning void "ab initio," meaning it had never legally existed. The county went on to spend $1.72 million defending the rezoning in court. Deshundra Jefferson became board chair in January 2024 opposing the project, a reversal from Wheeler's support. On March 31, 2026, a three-judge panel of the Virginia Court of Appeals, consolidating the Oak Valley and Battlefield Trust cases, unanimously upheld Irving's ruling, finding the public notice requirement could not be waived even for people who had actually attended the hearing. The Coalition to Protect Prince William County said the decision proved "Our community never gave up and never gave in." Mac Haddow, president of the Oak Valley Homeowners Association, said developers "cannot treat communities as obstacles to overcome" and needed to design projects so a neighborhood's impacts are addressed as part of the plan. On April 15, 2026, the county's Board of Supervisors voted unanimously to drop its own appeal of the ruling. Compass Datacenters declined further appeal the same month, its president AJ Byers saying on April 29 that "Compass has reached the unfortunate conclusion that we cannot move forward with the Prince William Digital Gateway project." QTS, the last developer still fighting in court, withdrew its final appeal to the Virginia Supreme Court on July 2, 2026, ending the project. QTS's legal team wrote in its withdrawal notice: "… after careful consideration, QTS has made the decision to terminate the Digital Gateway project and withdraw its associated filings." The Coalition to Protect Prince William County called the outcome proof that "the rule of law and the common man have prevailed." Support in Virginia fell while the case played out: just 35 percent of voters now say they would be comfortable with a new data center in their community, down from 69 percent in 2023, according to a Washington Post-Schar School poll reported by Tom's Hardware.

On April 15, 2026, the county's Board of Supervisors voted unanimously to drop its own appeal of the ruling.

Compass Datacenters declined further appeal the same month, its president AJ Byers saying on April 29 that "Compass has reached the unfortunate conclusion that we cannot move forward with the Prince William Digital Gateway project."
QTS, the last developer still fighting in court, withdrew its final appeal to the Virginia Supreme Court on July 2, 2026, ending the project.
QTS's legal team wrote in its withdrawal notice: "… after careful consideration, QTS has made the decision to terminate the Digital Gateway project and withdraw its associated filings."
The Coalition to Protect Prince William County called the outcome proof that "the rule of law and the common man have prevailed."

Support in Virginia fell while the case played out: just 35 percent of voters now say they would be comfortable with a new data center in their community, down from 69 percent in 2023, according to a Washington Post-Schar School poll reported by Tom's Hardware.

gemini-compass-red-oak.text: The Red Oak City Council voted 4-1 near midnight in May 2026 to rezone about 830 acres of farmland at the edge of Red Oak, in Ellis County, Texas, for a Compass Datacenters campus, over a packed and vocal council chamber. Compass already runs a data center campus in Red Oak; the newly approved site would be its second. City staff said the buildings will use a closed-loop water-cooling system not connected to the city's utility lines, and the council's briefing said the project would bring $72 million in electric grid reinforcements. The council added lighting shields, decibel limits and a ban on cryptocurrency mining before approving the rezoning and a $2.82 million tax abatement spread over ten years, after its planning and zoning board had recommended denying the project weeks earlier. "It allows for better funded city services without increasing taxes for residents", City Manager Todd Fuller said, arguing the zoning approach lets the city impose stricter controls than unincorporated county land would allow. In June, Compass withdrew a request for a tax abatement from Ellis County on its roughly 890-acre property, which founder Chris Crosby said came after the "noise" around the project; Compass has since given $15 million for a new Ellis County animal shelter and a $12.6 million building to Texas State Technical College. "There is no strings attached", said Ellis County Judge John Wray. A Red Oak nonprofit, Say NO MORE Data Centers, has raised money through car shows and retained a lawyer for possible legal action; "we just know that they do not belong here, right next to established residences and farms", said Jazmin Villegas, a spokesperson for the group. Gov. Greg Abbott ordered the Public Utility Commission of Texas and grid operator ERCOT on August 3, 2026 to audit every data center seeking to connect to the state's power grid before any new approvals proceed, a statewide review that reaches this project too. The Red Oak rezoning stands approved; any renewed county tax abatement request would go back to the Ellis County Commissioners Court.

gemini-cyrusone-shaw-road.text: CyrusOne operates a data center at 511 Shaw Road in Sterling, Loudoun County, Virginia, one of several CyrusOne campuses clustered in the town. The company opened its first Loudoun County data center in 2015, and by early 2023 said it operated 10 data centers at five campus locations in the county. It was bought in 2022 by the investment firms KKR and Global Infrastructure Partners in a $15 billion deal. Loudoun County has more data centers than anywhere else in the country, a concentration that has drawn scrutiny over water use, noise and power lines. In 2000 the county's zoning administrator ruled that data centers would be treated like office buildings, letting them go up by right in office parks near homes, one reason sites like this one sit inside Sterling neighborhoods. Residents have since raised concerns about water use, noise, air quality, land values and power lines across the county. Loudoun now has about 233 data center buildings built or under construction, and data centers produced $1.2 billion in property taxes in fiscal 2026, 39% of the county's budget. In March 2025 the Board of Supervisors voted 7-2 to end by-right data center development, so new data centers now need a special exception with public hearings before the Planning Commission and the board. Applications filed before February 12, 2025 for sites more than 500 feet from homes were allowed to continue under the old rules. The county expects to finish its Data Center Standards and Locations project, which will set further rules for where new data centers can go, in spring or summer 2027.

gemini-stack-stafford.text: STACK Infrastructure topped out the first building of its Stafford Technology Campus in May 2026, a 500-acre site along Eskimo Hill Road east of Richmond Highway in Stafford County, Virginia. STACK says the campus will eventually hold 1.1 gigawatts of power across four sub-campuses fed by six 300-megawatt substations, with 19 data centers planned in all, calling it the largest project investment in the county's history. The Stafford County Board of Supervisors voted 6-1 in September 2024 to rezone 504 acres from agricultural to light industrial for a campus of 23 buildings, six electric substations and about 5.5 million square feet; STACK took over the site from Peterson Companies, which had first filed for the rezoning in 2023, in January 2025. The developer agreed to fund $58 million in county capital projects, including water and sewer lines for the center of the county, a connector road between Richmond Highway and Eskimo Hill Road, and land for a fire station. Supervisor Crystal Vanuch cast the lone vote against the rezoning, saying she was concerned about the project's phasing and about county drinking water being used while a reuse water system, being built by Amazon for its nearby Potomac Church Road facility, was still under construction. "It was never the county's intent to give access to our drinking water to data centers in perpetuity," Vanuch said. At a League of Women Voters forum in Fredericksburg in September 2026, University of Mary Washington sociology professor Eric Bonds said the campus, now under construction, will be able to draw and distribute 1 gigawatt of power, "enough energy to power 700,000 households, or as much as one nuclear reactor can produce." The Stafford Technology Campus is one of five approved data center projects in the county, and its 2024 zoning stands, so no further supervisors' vote is required for the campus itself. The local group Protect Stafford is tracking newer data center proposals before the board, working alongside Safeguard Spotsy in neighboring Spotsylvania County.

gemini-stack-svy02a.text: STACK Infrastructure's SVY02A data center in Santa Clara, California, was built for 48 megawatts of power on the site of the former Memorex headquarters at Ronald Street and Memorex Drive, but it has been waiting on power from the city's utility, Silicon Valley Power. The four-story, roughly 470,000-square-foot building has its own substation, and one report said the site "isn't expecting power until 2027." The problem is the electric grid. STACK's building and a nearby Digital Realty data center both have supply agreements with Silicon Valley Power but are waiting on network upgrades. "SVP is undertaking a $450 million system upgrade to meet the needs of these and other customers, and the project is currently on schedule to be completed in 2028," utility spokesperson Janine de la Vega said. The utility said it is sequencing power delivery among customers as new substations and transmission lines come online. Neighbors have also objected to the building itself; the city has documented complaints about noise, height and appearance from the facility on Memorex Drive, the street where SVY02A stands. Santa Clara has 58 data centers and collects an estimated $29.5 million a year from them, and Silicon Valley Power charges 18.2 cents a kilowatt-hour, 57 percent less than PG&E's 42.2 cents. What happens next depends mainly on Silicon Valley Power's $450 million upgrade, due to finish in 2028. STACK said it is coordinating with the utility to phase in power to the building as the upgrades progress.

gemini-lancium-clean.text: The Lancium Clean Campus outside Abilene, in Taylor County, Texas, is the flagship site of OpenAI's Stargate project, where Crusoe is building the data center buildings on Lancium's land for Oracle and OpenAI. The first eight buildings are planned at about 4 million square feet and 1.2GW, and Crusoe said in March 2026 that a separate 900 MW campus for Microsoft next door would bring the whole Abilene site to about 2.1 GW. Construction began in 2024, and in September 2025 Crusoe said the first two buildings, 980,000 square feet supporting more than 200MW of IT, were running for Oracle Cloud Infrastructure on behalf of OpenAI. Crusoe topped out the eighth and final building in November 2025, thanking "the 7,000 electricians, construction pros, and skilled tradespeople who come to Abilene every day." Crusoe said in March 2026 that the second phase of six buildings was expected to be complete by the end of 2026. Oracle and OpenAI had been expected to take the whole campus but decided in early 2026 to stop at 1.2GW, saying: "We considered expanding it further, but ultimately chose to put that additional capacity in other locations." Microsoft then signed for 900MW in two new buildings with an on-site power plant, on land adjacent to the existing campus, where land works were already underway and the first building is expected to be energized in mid-2027. Crusoe says that plant will provide 900MW of behind-the-meter power, paired with a battery storage system, and that the new buildings will use closed-loop, non-evaporative liquid cooling. The original campus is also getting its own gas power: Parker Hannifin said in October 2025 it would supply equipment for 29 GE Vernova gas turbines with a combined capacity of 1.015GW at the site. The campus carries large local tax breaks. At a February 2025 special meeting on a second abatement for Lancium, City Manager Robert Hanna explained the terms: "On the tax abatement side, it's 15% of their tax liability. So, we're abating 85%, and we get 15%." Hanna argued that without it, "there's no way they could build the property." Taylor County commissioners granted a 20-year property tax abatement of their own. Crusoe says the first eight buildings are expected to deliver up to 32% of the City of Abilene's and up to 25% of Taylor County's budgeted property tax revenue for fiscal 2025. Residents raised power and water from the start. At the city's February 2025 meeting, Abilene resident Samuel Garcia recalled the 2021 freeze, in which six people in Taylor County died, and asked: "What happens with the usage of electricity and water by this facility if we were to have one of these?" Hanna answered that the cooling is a closed-loop system and that the city was looking at industrial pretreatment for the water the site discharges. At the county's meeting the same week, resident Dr. Mark Teague worried about unreliable, more expensive power for consumers and about heavy metals reaching the groundwater. Two years into construction, the complaints are about housing and the cost of living. KUT reported in August 2026 that average rent in Abilene was almost $2,600 a month according to Zillow, up nearly 50% in a year, and that Abilene Christian University said more than 100 incoming students had nowhere to live for the fall. Lexi Smith, whose family lives across the street from the construction, told KUT it had brought traffic, damaged roads and worse air and water quality. A shelter case manager, Michael Prado, said he now sees families priced out or evicted and that finding someone housing can take up to six months, where it used to take just over one. When the Abilene Chamber of Commerce held a panel on the region's data centers on September 2, 2026, demonstrators came with signs calling for more transparency, and resident Molly Cedillo carried one reading "No More Backroom Data Center Deals." Some residents want a pause, but Taylor County Judge Phil Crowley said in June 2026 that the county cannot impose one: "The county would have to have permission from the state to be able to pass a local moratorium on data centers." He pointed to Hill County, which reversed its moratorium after a developer sued, and to the water restrictions negotiated for the Stargate project. "If the state put in a moratorium, I would look at possibly supporting that, if that's what the citizens are interested in," Crowley said. More is coming to the area: in July 2026 a new firm, PowerPlay AI, announced a 400MW natural gas-powered data center near Abilene in a joint venture with the Australian company Sharon AI, targeting power delivery by 2028. Locally, the decisions that shape the campus sit with the Abilene City Council, which grants the city's abatements, and the Taylor County Commissioners Court, which grants the county's. Crowley has said a moratorium would have to come from the state, so residents who want one have been told to press the Legislature. In September 2026, a Chamber panel heard from protesters and Crowley defended abatements as the county's only lever: "But if people want counties that have control over data centers, you have to have an abatement because that is the only way you're going to have any authority otherwise."

At the city's February 2025 meeting, Abilene resident Samuel Garcia recalled the 2021 freeze, in which six people in Taylor County died, and asked: "What happens with the usage of electricity and water by this facility if we were to have one of these?"
Hanna answered that the cooling is a closed-loop system and that the city was looking at industrial pretreatment for the water the site discharges.
At the county's meeting the same week, resident Dr. Mark Teague worried about unreliable, more expensive power for consumers and about heavy metals reaching the groundwater.
Two years into construction, the complaints are about housing and the cost of living.

KUT reported in August 2026 that average rent in Abilene was almost $2,600 a month according to Zillow, up nearly 50% in a year, and that Abilene Christian University said more than 100 incoming students had nowhere to live for the fall.
Lexi Smith, whose family lives across the street from the construction, told KUT it had brought traffic, damaged roads and worse air and water quality.
A shelter case manager, Michael Prado, said he now sees families priced out or evicted and that finding someone housing can take up to six months, where it used to take just over one.

When the Abilene Chamber of Commerce held a panel on the region's data centers on September 2, 2026, demonstrators came with signs calling for more transparency, and resident Molly Cedillo carried one reading "No More Backroom Data Center Deals."

Some residents want a pause, but Taylor County Judge Phil Crowley said in June 2026 that the county cannot impose one: "The county would have to have permission from the state to be able to pass a local moratorium on data centers."
He pointed to Hill County, which reversed its moratorium after a developer sued, and to the water restrictions negotiated for the Stargate project.
"If the state put in a moratorium, I would look at possibly supporting that, if that's what the citizens are interested in," Crowley said.

More is coming to the area: in July 2026 a new firm, PowerPlay AI, announced a 400MW natural gas-powered data center near Abilene in a joint venture with the Australian company Sharon AI, targeting power delivery by 2028.
Locally, the decisions that shape the campus sit with the Abilene City Council, which grants the city's abatements, and the Taylor County Commissioners Court, which grants the county's.
Crowley has said a moratorium would have to come from the state, so residents who want one have been told to press the Legislature.

In September 2026, a Chamber panel heard from protesters and Crowley defended abatements as the county's only lever: "But if people want counties that have control over data centers, you have to have an abatement because that is the only way you're going to have any authority otherwise."

gemini-black-mountain-energy-fort-worth.text: The Fort Worth City Council voted 7-4 on August 25, 2026 to approve an amended site plan for 187 acres of Black Mountain Energy's planned $10 billion data center campus in southeast Fort Worth, in Tarrant County, Texas, over months of objections from nearby residents. The approved plan adds an electrical substation, raises the maximum building height to 70 feet, and, at the request of council members Michael Crain and Chris Nettles, sets 300 feet between homes and the data center instead of the 150 feet in the docket. The vote came after the council had twice tabled the site plan, in May and June. Black Mountain, a Fort Worth energy company founded in 2007 and focused mostly on oil and gas, first filed in January 2025 to rezone 141 acres at the southeast corner of Lon Stephenson Road and Forest Hill Drive for data center use. It has since obtained and rezoned more than 450 acres from agricultural land to light industrial, stretching from just south of Esco Drive to Anglin Circle, between Forest Hill and Kennedale. The approved site plan places four buildings of just over a million square feet south of Lon Stephenson Road, east of Forest Hill Drive and west of Anglin Drive, down from a first draft of 18 buildings and 3 million square feet. A proposed 980-megawatt electrical substation on the site would power the data center only. CEO Rhett Bennett has told residents the campus would not use a gas-fired power plant and would rely solely on the grid, with a closed-loop cooling system; he said the company was conducting a water study to find out how much water the campus would need. No end user has been named, and at the April zoning hearing Jackson Weston, whose family runs Weston Gardens, said residents had never heard from the data center's operating partner despite promises from Black Mountain: “This has not happened yet.” Weston Gardens, a historic garden and wedding venue, sits roughly 100 yards from Black Mountain's land. "What's it going to do to the birds? Am I going to lose revenue from the weddings and things that we've developed over the years to pay for a lot of the improvements to keep up the walls?" its owner, Sue Weston, told CBS News Texas, adding that vibrations from the cooling systems would crack the rocks. “Last September 30th, y’all told me you would find a way to protect the gardens, and I am going to hold you to that,” Weston told the council in August. Nettles, who represents the district, supports the project: "We don't believe that it's going to affect the garden," he said. At a Black Mountain town hall in March, Forest Hill residents said they had only just learned of the project. “I know we do not own the land. I know Fort Worth controls that, but somehow Forest Hill is going to be connected,” said Brigette Mathis, who lives near Lon Stephenson Road. “People did not know that you were putting something down that street.” Letitia Wilbourn, an activist in the Echo Heights neighborhood, told zoning commissioners the campus adds to pollution next to a city landfill. “This should have never been approved at any level to begin with,” she said. Other residents raised power, water, noise, traffic and the loss of farmland, and residents have organized as DFW Communities Over Data Centers and the 2871 Community Coalition. Before the August vote, activist Ambika Sharma asked the council to wait for the city's new Data Center and Infrastructure Commission to write its rules, while local business owner Emerald Khan backed the revised plan. Council member Mia Hall, who supports a moratorium, said: “This is about a site plan. … I can’t stop a data center from being there.” On August 11 the council voted unanimously to begin a 90-day moratorium on new data center rezonings and permits, but city officials say it will not apply to projects whose zoning applications were already submitted or approved, which includes Black Mountain. Under the city's timeline, the Data Center and Infrastructure Committee reports on November 3, public hearings follow on November 10 and January 5, and adoption by a council supermajority is set for February 16, 2027. The council also required new data center applications to show approval from the Public Utility Commission of Texas and ERCOT for their grid connection, in line with Gov. Greg Abbott's directive. Black Mountain and Edged Data Centers, which plans a $1 billion facility on 186 acres in Veale Ranch in southwest Fort Worth, have drawn the most opposition among seven data centers planned for the city. Elsewhere in Tarrant County, a planned data center in Westlake near Keller faces opposition from Keller's mayor and council, and residents have pushed back on projects in North Richland Hills. A company called Fort Worth Power Core LLC, sharing Black Mountain's mailing address, holds state air permits for power generation in ten counties including Tarrant, Parker, Somervell and Jack. What remains is Black Mountain's request to rezone another 80 acres from agricultural to industrial, which would bring its land to about 530 acres; the council tabled it in February and it was pushed to a December meeting at the company's request. The project also needs permits from the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, including on air quality. On September 21, 2026, Gov. Greg Abbott ordered the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to stop issuing new permits for data centers until the state's grid operator, ERCOT, and the Texas Water Development Board finish their audits of the industry. The Fort Worth City Council decides the rezoning; reporting in September 2026 said the city's moratorium will not reach it.

gemini-rowan-bauxite-iii.text: Bauxite III is the third data center Rowan Digital Infrastructure is building at Quantum Frederick, a 2,100-acre data center park on the former Alcoa Eastalco aluminum plant near Adamstown, in Frederick County, Maryland. The county's Planning Commission voted 5-0, with one abstention, for its site plan in December 2024: three buildings totaling 591,913 square feet on 55 acres, next to Rowan's Bauxite I and Bauxite II. Rowan says the three Bauxite sites together will deliver more than 630 megawatts, with Bauxite I substantially complete in 2025 and Bauxite II and III advancing toward delivery in 2026 and 2027. The site plan includes an auxiliary water building, a guard booth, water storage and parking, and Bauxite III alone would need 297,000 gallons of cooling water a day. Rowan, formed in 2021 by Quinbrook and Birch Infrastructure, says the three projects will bring $19 million a year in county taxes. Bauxite III is the only one of the three inside the campus's soil management area, which is why Commissioner Carole Sepe abstained; Rowan is working with the Maryland Department of the Environment on an environmental plan for the site. The land has a contamination history: cyanide and fluoride turned up in groundwater in 1983, and five old waste disposal sites were found between 2003 and 2005. Water is the other constraint. The county's agreement caps the park's first phase at 1.3 million gallons a day of cooling water, and the three Bauxite buildings alone would use 1.081 million. "There is no data to substantiate the water allocations for this facility," said Adamstown farmer Steve Black of the Sugarloaf Alliance. "It's just a number that came from nowhere." Commissioners Sepe and Joel Rensberger pressed Rowan on why no solar power was in the designs. Rowan said it plans to buy a 13-acre parcel on the campus for a community solar array to be run by a third party. Aligned Data Centers is separately building a four-building, 260-megawatt campus on 75 acres of the park, and Amazon Web Services and Rowan are developing a 300-megawatt AWS campus on another 151 acres. As of June 2026, none of the park's data centers had opened, though all three developers had broken ground. Frederick County Executive Jessica Fitzwater turned down a $110 million community benefits deal with the park's site developer on September 15, 2026, after residents objected that it would lock in county zoning for eight years. That declined package had included a $30 million Carroll Manor Elementary School renovation and a new Adamstown park. Fitzwater extended the county's data center moratorium, first ordered in July 2026, to freeze new data center applications until July 1, 2027, while the state completes its impact study. Bauxite III's own site plan already has county approval, so the new moratorium covers future applications rather than its existing permits; it still needs sign-off from Maryland environmental regulators on its soil management plan. Frederick County voters go to the polls in November 2026, with several county council races contested over data center policy.

gemini-nsa-utah.text: How much water the National Security Agency's data center at Bluffdale, in Utah County, uses was a secret until a newspaper went to court for it. The City of Bluffdale, which sells the agency its water, argued that knowing how much water the cooling systems used could help someone estimate the computing power inside, and so compromise national security. Utah's State Records Committee voted unanimously for The Salt Lake Tribune on March 19, 2014. Ernest Rowley, the panel's representative of local government interests, said the water belonged to the public; Patricia Smith-Mansfield, the governor's designee, said releasing it would not in her opinion jeopardize the agency. Nate Carlisle, the Tribune reporter who led the fight, said the paper wanted an educated discussion in Utah about what the facility's presence meant, in the second driest state in the country, where the city sells the agency the water and its taxpayers have an interest in knowing what it earns. Before it opened, the estimates were already large: KSL reported in July 2013 that the center could require as many as 1.7 million gallons of water a day, and the Jordan Valley Water Conservancy District's chief engineer, Alan Packard, said it was planning for 1,000 to 2,000 acre-feet a year. It has not gotten smaller: the site used more than 126 million gallons between October 2024 and September 2025, about 390 acre-feet, enough to meet the indoor needs of nearly 800 Utah households for a year. Utah legislated in 2026 to make the rest of the industry publish the same thing: HB 76, brought by Rep. Jill Koford, requires a new large data center to report where its water comes from and how much it withdraws each year, with the figures published online. Bluffdale city manager Mark Reid said the government funded $7 million in infrastructure for the data center, plus $5 million more that lets a third of its water be recycled for the city park and lawns.

gemini-adani-noida.text: AdaniConneX, the Adani Group's joint venture with US company EdgeConneX, runs a Rs 744 crore data center in Sector 62, Noida, Uttar Pradesh, India, that has been operating since 2025 and draws an estimated 80 megawatts of power. Google leased 464,000 square feet at the site in 2022 for 10 years, starting at Rs130.98 crore a year, and AdaniConneX bought the 34,275-square-meter Sector 62 parcel in July 2021 for a planned Rs 2,400 crore investment, after being granted a separate 39,146-square-meter site in Noida's Sector 80 that April. In February 2026 Adani Group said it would spend $100 billion to expand its national data center capacity to 5 gigawatts by 2035, including more campuses in Noida, though it has not said where in the city or how large they would be. Adani Energy Solutions has applied for a license to sell electricity directly to the DC Park area of Noida that includes the Sector 62 site; the application entered public consultation in late August 2026. "We have applied for a distribution licence for a designated and bounded area occupied by DC Park in Noida, to serve specific data-centre needs, especially to supply reliable and uninterrupted power with a larger share of green electrons to these facilities," an Adani Power spokesperson said. research-wilderness-crossing.text: Wilderness Crossing is a 2,600-acre development planned for homes, data centers and warehouses near the intersection of Routes 3 and 20 in Locust Grove, Orange County, Virginia, beside the Wilderness Battlefield. Orange County supervisors approved the rezoning for developer KEG Associates III in April 2023, and a lawsuit by preservation groups and neighbors to void it has kept the project in circuit court since 2023. No trial date has been set, and Amazon Web Services is named as the project's tenant. The approved plan allows up to 5,000 homes and 732 acres of industrial use, built out in phases over about 40 years, with the industrial portion including what the Culpeper Star-Exponent describes as Amazon data centers. A Virginia Freedom of Information Act lawsuit by the Piedmont Environmental Council found that 10 local officials had signed nondisclosure agreements for "the benefit of Amazon.com, Inc. and its affiliates." No official power figure has been published; Blackridge Research, a market research firm, estimates the campus at 1,500 megawatts of power and up to 21 million square feet of data center space at full build-out. Chris Miller, president of the Piedmont Environmental Council, has questioned where the water would come from, saying, "We will need two more generation plants in Orange County." The Board of Supervisors voted 4-1 on April 25, 2023 to approve the rezoning, the largest in county history according to the council, after 37 people spoke against it, mostly about water supply and traffic. The lawsuit says changes made the night of the public hearing raised cash proffers from $6 million to as much as $24 million and removed a cap that had limited data centers and warehouses to 5 million square feet, expanding it to more than 30 million. The plaintiffs, the American Battlefield Trust, Friends of Wilderness Battlefield, the Central Virginia Battlefields Trust and neighbors Mark and Cheryl Nowacki and Robert J. Foster, say the property abuts the battlefield where more than 160,000 Union and Confederate soldiers fought in May 1864 and that the project would add more than 60,000 daily vehicle trips to nearby roads. "You can move a development, you can move a data center, we can't move where this country's history happened," said David Duncan, president of the American Battlefield Trust. Orange County has since removed data centers as a by-right use in its industrial zoning district, and the Town of Orange now requires a special use permit for them. In September 2025, Judge David B. Franzén dismissed three of the plaintiffs' seven claims and let four proceed, over how the rezoning process, hearings and taxation were handled. At a March 27, 2026 hearing, Franzén declined to rule on a request by the county and the developers to send the case to the Virginia Court of Appeals before a trial, saying he would rule only after that appeals court acted on appeals the county had already filed there; the Court of Appeals had not yet acted. Mike Brady, the plaintiffs' lead attorney, has said the case is going to trial and will be decided on the legislative record; as of that April 2026 update, no trial date had been published.

research-starwood-plaza-500.text: Starwood Capital Group filed permit plans in July 2026 for Plaza 500 South, the first of two data centers it wants on the 34-acre Plaza 500 site at 6295 and 6299 Edsall Road in Lincolnia, in Fairfax County, Virginia, just outside the Alexandria city line. The Starwood data center itself is allowed by right, so the fight has turned to the Dominion Energy substation it needs, whose Fairfax County Planning Commission hearing was pushed from September 24 to December 2, 2026 at Dominion's request. The first building would be 75 feet tall and 226,469 square feet, according to the Washington Business Journal. Starwood bought the property in 2022 for $165 million. The site has held warehouse, office and retail uses and was once home to a Social Security office and Smoot Lumber. Resident leader Tyler Ray says the roughly five-acre substation would sit 67 feet from the Ridges at Edsall townhouses and power 176 megawatts for the data center, and the State Corporation Commission has already signed off on nearly a mile of transmission line to the existing Van Dorn substation. "Because in 2022 the developer Starwood Capital wouldn't agree to not build a data center there by kind of adding what's called a proffer to the rezoning, they came back and submitted a site plan in 2024 to build a data center by right," said Tyler Ray, president of the Bren Pointe Homeowners Association and founder of the Save Bren Mar Coalition. "They are manipulating the process and going out of order intentionally to try to force the county to approve this despite the process not fully playing out yet," Ray said of the permit filing. More than 100 residents came to the Mason District Land Use Committee's July 28 briefing, and the coalition now counts five homeowner and civic associations representing about 1,000 homes. On August 27 the Fairfax County Federation of Citizens Associations voted to oppose both the campus and the substation, citing the 67-foot distance and a resource protection area along Turkeycock Run. Rep. Don Beyer, Mason District Supervisor Andres Jimenez, Alexandria Mayor Alyia Gaskins and City Council, state Sen. Elizabeth Bennett-Parker and House Majority Leader Charniele Herring have all opposed the substation. "However, as we continue to experience unprecedented growth in data center development, we must ensure that these projects are appropriately located outside of residential areas," Beyer wrote to the Planning Commission. "Our community supports a reliable electric grid, but reliability and thoughtful planning are not mutually exclusive," Jimenez said. Starwood is also buying nearly 42 acres of county land in Chantilly for $166.8 million for data centers and is developing a data center at the former Washington Commanders training site in Herndon. The Fairfax County Planning Commission rules on the substation in its 2232 review on December 2, and Dominion can appeal a denial to the Board of Supervisors, which adopted stricter data center rules in 2024 but exempted pending applications like Plaza 500. The building plans themselves go through Fairfax County Land Development Services for permit review.

research-amazon-warrenton.text: Amazon's planned data center on Blackwell Road in Warrenton, Fauquier County, Virginia, is still waiting on a judge, more than three years after residents sued to overturn the Town Council's approval. Judge Stephen Sincavage heard final oral arguments on June 15, 2026 in the suit brought by Citizens for Fauquier County and 10 residents against Amazon Data Services' special use permit, and had not ruled as of August 3. The Warrenton Town Council voted 4-3 in February 2023 to grant Amazon Data Services a special use permit for a 220,000-square-foot data center at Blackwell Road and Lee Highway, at the town's eastern gateway. Hundreds of residents turned out to oppose it. "I think it's important that we listen to our citizens. Otherwise we become an oppressive government," Council Member David McGuire said before voting no. The town's former manager, Brandie Schaeffer, had exchanged 3,142 emails with Amazon representatives before leaving to work for Amazon, and the town fought Citizens for Fauquier County in court over releasing them. The plaintiffs argue that the April 2021 zoning amendment that allowed data centers in Warrenton was void from the start because the town did not state its purpose, so the permit built on it should fall too. "Reliance on a void act is reliance on nothing," their attorney, Dale Mullen, told the court. Amazon's attorney, Matt Westover, argued the amendment was valid and that challenges had to be brought within 30 days, warning that open-ended challenges would create "chaotic conditions beyond all comprehension." The town itself has changed sides: its attorney, Philip Carter Strother, backed many of the plaintiffs' arguments and said Warrenton no longer shares Amazon's "litigation alignment." In July 2025 the Town Council removed data centers as a permitted use in its industrial districts, which did not undo Amazon's permit but makes future approvals harder. In 2025 the town also found that Amazon does not have vested rights to build on the 42-acre site; Amazon has appealed that finding in court, and on July 30, 2026 Judge James Plowman turned down Citizens for Fauquier County's request to join that case. "As I understand… the [special use permit case] is the primary suit, which would essentially nullify and would basically render unnecessary the other two," said Ali Zarabi, the group's president. The county around Warrenton is tightening too. On September 17, 2026 the Fauquier County Planning Commission unanimously recommended limiting new data centers to land zoned planned commercial industrial, now only the Vint Hill area, and requiring a special exception from the Board of Supervisors for each one. Two data center applications near Remington were pulled before that meeting. The data center's fate now rests with the Fauquier County Circuit Court: Judge Sincavage's ruling on the permit, and the separate case over Amazon's vested rights. The judge gave no date for his decision.
