research-blakely.text: Developers Jim Marzolino and Alpesh Patel withdrew their request to rezone land in Blakely, a borough near Scranton in Lackawanna County, Pennsylvania, for the Blakely data center campus on September 12, 2025, three days before the borough council was to consider it. They had planned a four-building data center campus on 209 acres near Terrace Drive and Business Route 6, each building about 70 feet tall and roughly 150,000 square feet. The campus would have needed an estimated 1.5 gigawatts, equal to the total output of the nearby gas-fired Lackawanna Energy Center, and up to 300,000 gallons a day from the town's water supply, according to borough manager Christopher Paone. The site sits behind the Assembly of God Church on the Scranton/Carbondale Highway; Patel owns about 44 acres of it and companies tied to Marzolino about 77. The first public meeting in August 2025 overflowed, with dozens of people in the parking lot. About 300 people came in person to a council meeting in a town of fewer than 7,000 residents, and another 200 watched online, Paone said. "The immediate response was, 'No,'" Paone said. "They did not want it." The developers' lawyer, Michael Mey, said the request was withdrawn after borough officials declined to schedule another information meeting where revised plans could be shown; Paone said the developers had a formal hearing with sworn testimony available to them and more than three weeks to prepare. Blakely then wrote its own rules. On November 17, 2025, the borough council unanimously approved a new zoning overlay for data centers, requiring large setbacks, environmental studies, emergency plans, strict generator rules, DEP permitting and road impact studies, with the borough allowed on site for inspections at least four times a year. The potential site under the overlay sits behind West Mountain Road, near about 30 homes. "We went around with the petition to all 30 homes that this will affect and we have everybody but one house on the signature", said neighbor Charles Gudaitis. Blakely distributes its own electricity, so any data center there would have to buy power from the borough. About a dozen data centers are proposed across Lackawanna County, according to a citizen-run tracker cited by the Bay Journal. Blakely has received no new data center proposals since adopting its rules, and Paone said he is fine with that. "Would I like an extra four, five, six, ten million dollars in my budget every year? Absolutely," he said. "But [if it means] this type of possible detriment to the town? No, it wasn't worth it." Any new proposal would go through the overlay and the Blakely Borough Council.

sentences.t: Developers Jim Marzolino and Alpesh Patel withdrew their request to rezone land in Blakely, a borough near Scranton in Lackawanna County, Pennsylvania, for the Blakely data center campus on September 12, 2025, three days before the borough council was to consider it.
They had planned a four-building data center campus on 209 acres near Terrace Drive and Business Route 6, each building about 70 feet tall and roughly 150,000 square feet.

The campus would have needed an estimated 1.5 gigawatts, equal to the total output of the nearby gas-fired Lackawanna Energy Center, and up to 300,000 gallons a day from the town's water supply, according to borough manager Christopher Paone.
The site sits behind the Assembly of God Church on the Scranton/Carbondale Highway; Patel owns about 44 acres of it and companies tied to Marzolino about 77.
The first public meeting in August 2025 overflowed, with dozens of people in the parking lot.
About 300 people came in person to a council meeting in a town of fewer than 7,000 residents, and another 200 watched online, Paone said.
"The immediate response was, 'No,'" Paone said.
"They did not want it."

The developers' lawyer, Michael Mey, said the request was withdrawn after borough officials declined to schedule another information meeting where revised plans could be shown; Paone said the developers had a formal hearing with sworn testimony available to them and more than three weeks to prepare.
Blakely then wrote its own rules.

On November 17, 2025, the borough council unanimously approved a new zoning overlay for data centers, requiring large setbacks, environmental studies, emergency plans, strict generator rules, DEP permitting and road impact studies, with the borough allowed on site for inspections at least four times a year.
The potential site under the overlay sits behind West Mountain Road, near about 30 homes.
"We went around with the petition to all 30 homes that this will affect and we have everybody but one house on the signature", said neighbor Charles Gudaitis.
Blakely distributes its own electricity, so any data center there would have to buy power from the borough.

research-chandler-active-infrastructure.text: The Chandler City Council voted 7-0 and blocked a proposed $2.5 billion AI data center campus by the New York developer Active Infrastructure on the former Orbital headquarters site at Price and Dobson roads in Chandler, Maricopa County, Arizona, on December 11, 2025. The vote came after a meeting of 4 hours and 38 minutes at which about 50 people spoke, only four in favor, and after about 256 residents emailed the council in opposition and 10 in support. Former U.S. Sen. Kyrsten Sinema lobbied for the project, speaking at the Planning and Zoning Commission hearing and to the council. "I am also the co-founder of a national coalition called the AI Coalition Infrastructure and we work hand and glove with the Trump administration," Sinema told the council in October, AZFamily reported, and she warned that President Trump could step in if the city did not approve it. The development agreement city staff negotiated would have required a closed-loop cooling system, the developer's own power supply, noise monitoring, and 750 jobs paying at least $75,000 by 2032, plus property and sales taxes even if a future law exempted them. Salt River Project said the substation the project needed would take at least five years, delaying opening to 2031, and would cost "north of $200 million," said economic development director Micah Miranda. Residents worried about power and water use, noise, rate increases and how few jobs data centers bring. "We have already had some real issues with some of our neighborhoods along Dobson who can hear a constant humming from the 160 acres of data centers we already have in the Price corridor," said Jeff Weninger, a former councilman. Councilman Matt Orlando said his objection was the business case: "You can't give me a viable business case, and that's my concern." The Price Road corridor already holds many of Chandler's data centers, including Aligned's PHX04 and PHX06. Since 2022, Chandler has required new data centers to win zoning approval as a planned area development, with sound mitigation and resident notice. Under that rule, any new proposal for the Orbital site would again need the Chandler City Council's approval.

research-compass-statesville-iredell-cou.text: Compass Data Centers won approval for a data center campus on a 350-acre tract on Stamey Farm Road in western Iredell County, North Carolina, inside the City of Statesville: five 270,000-square-foot buildings backed by an investment the company put at more than $1 billion. The Statesville City Council voted unanimously on September 15, 2025 to approve the rezoning after more than two dozen people spoke against it, following a unanimous recommendation from both the Planning Board and city staff. Sheila Shuford, a nurse living on Mount Hermon Road, told the Planning Board: "There's got to be a better place for it than in the middle of a community with three schools." Jeff Byers, of Greenwich Drive, said: "I don't trust anything a developer tells me. I don't trust anything a politician tells me." Thomas Hamel likened the project's 200 biodiesel backup generators to building a large bomb near a school, while Compass vice president Katy Hancock told the board the biodiesel burns 70 percent cleaner than standard diesel and that 40 percent of the 350 acres will stay open space. On August 10, 2026 the council approved a first reading of a 180-day moratorium on new data center proposals; planning director Erika Martin said none is currently planned but the city has fielded inquiries and its development code does not address them. The moratorium does not cover the already-approved Compass project, and several speakers asked the council to add it in; Christian Smith called the pause a Trojan horse, and Jeff Tucker urged the council to "pull a rabbit out of the hat and put Stamey Farm Road back in it." On September 14, 2026, the Statesville City Council unanimously approved the 180-day moratorium on new data centers at its second reading. It took effect that day and does not apply to the approved Compass project.

research-terranova-queretaro.text: TERRANOVA, the data center company the British investor Actis launched in December 2025, said in February 2026 it was building a second Mexican data center in San Miguel de Allende, Guanajuato, for delivery in early 2026. The company's first Mexican site, in the neighboring Queretaro region, went live that same month with 8.12 megawatts of IT capacity, after being designed in two months and built in ten. Guanajuato's economy ministry told the newspaper AM in September 2026 that two data centers operate in the state, both run by ODATA, in San Miguel de Allende and Apaseo el Grande, and that a third is being built in San Miguel de Allende by a company it could not name under a confidentiality agreement. The ministry did not confirm that TERRANOVA is behind that third project, and TERRANOVA has not said publicly whether its own San Miguel site has opened. The ministry put the three projects together at $630 million of investment and 200 direct jobs. On August 10, 2026, Governor Libia Dennise Garcia Munoz Ledo opened a new power plant at the same San Miguel de Allende business park, built by Corral Energy for more than $45 million in its first stage, with 60 megawatts of capacity and a 230-kilovolt connection. ODATA opened its QR04 data center in the same business park in August 2025, designed for 24 megawatts with a first 12-megawatt phase. Its operations director, Carlos Forero, said the company's water use was minimal. Asked on September 11, 2026 about local concern over water and energy use, the governor said such investments come with their own water treatment, reuse, power plants and substations, so they do not burden the town's supply. The state says any further details, including whether TERRANOVA's own site is complete, will be announced when the companies involved allow it.

research-rio-city.text: Rio AI City is a data center campus Elea Data Centers is planning in Jacarepagua, in Rio de Janeiro's West Zone, Brazil, near the Olympic Park built for the 2016 Games. Mayor Eduardo Paes announced the project on April 27, 2025 at Web Summit Rio, calling it a step toward the "Innovation Capital of Latin America." Paes signed a protocol with Elea and Oracle on August 14, 2025; the developers plan an initial 1.8 gigawatts by 2027, growing to 3 gigawatts by 2032, DCD and Eixos reported. The architecture firm Hyphen, which designed the campus's 10 buildings, told Dezeen the first phase will use 1.5 gigawatts, scalable to 3.5 gigawatts, inside a Rio de Janeiro state grid with about 8.5 gigawatts of total capacity. A university researcher told RioOnWatch the project could eventually need up to 3 gigawatts, more than the Rio region's average power use of about 1.8 gigawatts. Oracle and NVIDIA have each signed on as early partners, and it is not yet clear whether the power will come from wind, solar, nuclear or a mix, Eixos reported. Elea says its cooling systems use no water at all, but researchers who spoke to RioOnWatch said that claim does not address other costs for residents in areas already short on water and power. RioOnWatch pointed to two existing Rio data centers, run by Ascenty in the Pavuna neighborhood and Cirion in Sao Cristovao, sitting in or near favelas with a history of water shortages, power outages and inadequate sanitation. Licinio Machado Rogerio, president of the residents' federation FAM-Rio, told a public forum that water use, power use, noise and real job creation should be debated before such projects are announced, not after. RioOnWatch reported that City Hall has not released data on the project's expected energy use, water use or environmental impact after RioOnWatch requested it under Brazil's public records law, and that residents have not had a real chance to discuss the plan with the city. RioOnWatch also pointed to a similar dispute over a ByteDance-linked data center in Pecem, Ceara, where federal prosecutors recommended in May 2026 that authorities tighten environmental licensing and consult the Anaca Indigenous community. For now Rio AI City rests on the protocol City Hall signed with Elea and Oracle, and no construction timeline beyond the 2027 target for the first phase has been published.

research-scala-bahia.text: Nothing has been announced, licensed or built at the Camacari industrial pole in Bahia, Brazil, where trackers place a Scala Data Centers data centre. Scala's link to Bahia is power, not buildings: it signed long term contracts for wind power from the Assurua 4 and Ventos da Bahia 3 farms, 393 megawatts of installed capacity, which it and its suppliers call the largest renewable supply contract in Latin America. The company's large building programme is in the far south, at Eldorado do Sul in Rio Grande do Sul, a town wrecked by the 2024 floods, where it plans an initial 550 million dollars and an eventual 4.75 gigawatts. "We have to take into account that we are living in the midst of a climate crisis, which leaves us with very little room for error," said Heverton Lacerda, president of the Gaucha Association for the Protection of the Natural Environment. Data centres are not on Brazil's list of industries that trigger special environmental licensing, so a Camacari project would not necessarily surface through a licensing file.

research-tecfusions-puente-alto.text: TECfusions, a US data center operator, and Chile's Baeza Group plan a data center campus of up to 100 megawatts of power on a 40-acre site owned by the Baeza family in Puente Alto, in southeast Santiago, Chile. The companies signed a binding letter of intent on May 7, 2025, the framework for a future joint venture pending due diligence, and the campus would start with 10 megawatts of capacity plus 10 more available from the local grid. TECfusions estimates the build will cost about $13 million per megawatt, putting the first 20 megawatts at roughly $260 million and the full build above $1 billion, and describes the campus as AI ready with a zero water approach relying on natural gas. At 100 megawatts the campus would nearly match the 173 megawatts installed across the 43 data centers in the Santiago Metropolitan Region at the end of 2024, most of them in northern communes such as Quilicura, Colina and Huechuraba. "Partnering with TECfusions allows us to retain a stake in our family's land while unlocking its full potential for Chile's digital future," said Eduardo Baeza, CEO of the Baeza Group. TECfusions named permits, environmental concerns, water use, energy consumption, connectivity and the community as its main risks in Chile, and said construction would employ 500 to 1,500 people at its peak and the finished campus 200 to 500. Water has shaped data center debates in Chile; Google halted work on its own planned data center in the country to rethink its water use after concerns about scarcity. TECfusions estimated 18 to 20 months from filing an environmental impact study to construction permits and said it expects the first phase to run within a year of groundbreaking; no update on the joint venture or the permits has been published since the May 2025 land deal.

sentences.t: TECfusions, a US data center operator, and Chile's Baeza Group plan a data center campus of up to 100 megawatts of power on a 40-acre site owned by the Baeza family in Puente Alto, in southeast Santiago, Chile.

The companies signed a binding letter of intent on May 7, 2025, the framework for a future joint venture pending due diligence, and the campus would start with 10 megawatts of capacity plus 10 more available from the local grid.

TECfusions estimates the build will cost about $13 million per megawatt, putting the first 20 megawatts at roughly $260 million and the full build above $1 billion, and describes the campus as AI ready with a zero water approach relying on natural gas.

At 100 megawatts the campus would nearly match the 173 megawatts installed across the 43 data centers in the Santiago Metropolitan Region at the end of 2024, most of them in northern communes such as Quilicura, Colina and Huechuraba.
"Partnering with TECfusions allows us to retain a stake in our family's land while unlocking its full potential for Chile's digital future," said Eduardo Baeza, CEO of the Baeza Group.

TECfusions named permits, environmental concerns, water use, energy consumption, connectivity and the community as its main risks in Chile, and said construction would employ 500 to 1,500 people at its peak and the finished campus 200 to 500.

research-stargate-argentina.text: Stargate Argentina, the AI data center OpenAI and Argentine company Sur Energy announced for Patagonia in October 2025, still has no confirmed site, no filing under the government's large-investment incentive scheme and no public timetable. The two companies signed a letter of intent for a data center of up to 500 megawatts of power, with investment of up to $25 billion, and Sur Energy said it was evaluating sites in the provinces of Neuquen, Rio Negro and Chubut. President Javier Milei's office announced the project on October 10, 2025, two weeks before elections, calling it the biggest yet under the RIGI incentive regime, which offers 30-year fiscal and customs benefits. "This is our first Stargate project in Latin America, a region full of talent, creativity and ambition," OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said in a video message at the time. Sur Energy co-founder Emiliano Kargieman said the money would come from investment funds rather than OpenAI, with energy supply deals already signed with Central Puerto and Genneia. Information published in June 2026 placed the site search in the Confluencia department of Neuquen, near the Limay River, with Senillosa and Arroyito mentioned, though neither location was confirmed, the regional paper Diario Nuevo Dia reported. Argentina's Economy Ministry acknowledged in May 2026 that nothing yet backs up the government's statement of intent. "Stargate has not been presented. We do not even include it in the 'announcements' because there has really been no mention of timescale, sums or localities," said Dario Clemente, a researcher with the RIGI Observatory of the environmental group FARN. The observatory said it could not study the project's environmental effects because "like all RIGI projects, it is totally opaque." OpenAI and Sur Energy did not answer questions about progress, and Demian Reidel, the official Economy Minister Luis Caputo credited when the deal was announced, has since been indicted; he had led the state nuclear company until February 2026. A project under RIGI must be cleared and published in Argentina's Official Gazette, and as of May 2026, Stargate was not among the 17 RIGI projects approved or the 23 under evaluation. No site, final investment decision or start of construction had been announced as of September 2026.

research-apple-athenry.text: Apple's planned €850 million data center at Derrydonnell Woods near Athenry, County Galway, Ireland, will not be built: Apple dropped it in 2018, and in June 2022 the High Court quashed the extension of its planning permission, which has now expired. Reviving the data center would take a completely new planning application, RTÉ reported. The Supreme Court dismissed objectors' challenges in 2019, but by then Apple had already built a data center in Denmark instead, according to Friends of the Irish Environment. Apple bought the roughly 500-acre site for around $15 million in 2014, a fraction of the €850 million it said the finished data center would cost, DCD reported. Although Galway County Council cleared its plans, appeals kept taking the case to An Bord Pleanála and the courts. Apple first won permission in 2016 but decided in 2018 not to proceed after the delays. In June 2021, still seeking a buyer, Apple applied to extend its planning permission to November 2026. The council granted a five-year extension that August, but resident Allan Daly and the group Eco-Advocacy challenged it in the High Court, arguing the council had not assessed the plan's cumulative impact under EU law, and the court quashed it with the council's and the State's consent. "The EU legislation specifically requires an assessment of other plans or projects," said Kieran Cummins, Eco-Advocacy's director. Sinn Féin's Louis O'Hara has called for the State to buy the site for start-up businesses, saying it should not be left "lying idle." Athenry is still cited as an early example of successful local resistance to data centers in Ireland, where they used 23 percent of the country's electricity in 2025.

research-google-berlin-cancelled.text: Google has abandoned its plan for a data center in Mittenwalde, Brandenburg, Germany, a site about 20 kilometers south of Berlin's BER airport. The company had meant to build a new Berlin-Brandenburg cloud region on about 30 hectares in the Schenkendorf part of town, but pulled out in July 2025 after a "thorough review of feasibility, general market developments, and our business priorities," Data Center Dynamics reported. Google began buying the land in 2022, after a long search reported by the Tagesspiegel that September. A Google spokesperson confirmed the purchase but said there was then no development plan allowing a data center and no firm commitment from local utilities to supply enough power, the Berliner Zeitung reported. The land was farmland already earmarked for commercial use, and the project was expected to bring about 100 full time jobs. Entwicklungsstadt, a Berlin development news site, reported that Google had weighed feasibility, economic conditions and its own priorities, and pointed to the site's distance from existing network hubs and questions over power supply. Google's Berlin cloud region, which launched in 2023, runs in data centers it leases from other operators. In November 2025 the company announced a 5.5 billion euro investment in Germany centered on Frankfurt instead: a new data center in Dietzenbach and further building at its Hanau campus.

research-aws-european-sovereign-cloud.text: At Massen, near Finsterwalde in the Elbe-Elster district of Brandenburg, Germany, earthworks and a container village for construction workers were visible by May 2026 on the larger of the two data centre campuses behind Amazon Web Services' European Sovereign Cloud. The district issued the building permit after about four months; approval for a substation on the property was still partly outstanding. Massen is planned at about 200 megawatts and the second site, Baruth/Mark south of Berlin, at about 100. Both begin in leased buildings before AWS moves into its own. The cloud region, meant to keep European customers' data under European control, opened on January 15, 2026, and AWS puts its commitment at more than 7.8 billion euro through 2040. Brandenburg now has 15 data centre projects, seven in planning, five under construction and three paused, which could take the state from under 50 megawatts of computing to almost 900. Many Brandenburg districts appear on the Heisse Luft initiative's mapping as areas under structural or acute groundwater stress, and the regional power network is described as reaching its limits.

research-microsoft-germany-elsdorf.text: Microsoft's planned data center in Elsdorf, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, is still waiting for its building permit, while permits have been granted for its two sister sites in Bedburg and Bergheim. All three are in the Rhenish mining area west of Cologne, a coal region facing an uncertain future as Germany exits coal, Heise reported in July 2026. The town of Elsdorf agreed in 2025 to sell Microsoft two plots totaling about 26 hectares, one kilometer south of the village of Heppendorf, with a connection to the A4 motorway. The town council had already started the land use planning for a commercial area there in 2021, and Mayor Andreas Heller called the sale a major milestone for the small town. The three sites are meant to back each other up, so that if one fails another can take over, and partial operation at Bedburg and Bergheim could start in 2028. Microsoft is investing 3.2 billion euros in the three projects, a sum that also covers expanding an existing Frankfurt site and training programs. Microsoft broke ground for the cluster in Bergheim on March 12, 2026, with Elsdorf's mayor among the guests, and the state government presents it as the region's shift from coal to artificial intelligence. Microsoft says the data centers will use closed-loop cooling that needs almost no refilling once filled, and that it has secured replacement habitat for skylarks with the towns. The grid operator Westnetz is building a new substation in Bergheim to connect the data center there. Critics online doubt the promised jobs because data centers run largely automated, point to high power demand, and note that host towns get little trade tax because companies with several sites split it, a German industry news site reported. Germany's national data center strategy, adopted in March 2026, calls for examining a rule that would give host towns a larger share of that tax, which still needs approval from the Bundestag, the federal parliament. Elsdorf has not given its own jobs estimate, though several hundred jobs running the centers are expected at each of the other two sites. Kilian Vieth-Ditlmann of the group AlgorithmWatch told Heise that building ever more data centers as things stand endangers Germany's climate targets. Microsoft plans a fourth site in the region, in Grevenbroich, where it has signed a purchase contract for about 23 hectares of farmland that is conditional on a building permit; it could run in the early 2030s. The next step in Elsdorf is the building permit for the Heppendorf site; no decision date has been published.

research-ia-fouju.text: Campus IA, the data center complex planned on farmland at Fouju, a village of about 650 people near Melun in Seine-et-Marne, France, won the prefect's authorisation in the summer of 2026, and a collective of associations says it will challenge it in court. The Stop IA à Fouju collective, which includes France Nature Environnement Seine-et-Marne, the bird protection league LPO, the farmers' union Confédération paysanne and the Soulèvements de la Terre, calls the public inquiry "bâclée" (rushed) and says the nuisances were minimised in the file. The plan is for eleven buildings 20 metres high, backed by 613 generators and 680 cooling units, built in phases from 2026 to 2038, with 300 to 500 direct jobs and electricity use equal to 200,000 French households. The public inquiry ran from April 30 to May 30, 2026 and ended with a favourable opinion. Opponents put the power demand at 1.4 gigawatts, twelve times what the surrounding community of communes uses now, and the carbon footprint at 766,000 tonnes a year, twice the area's current emissions. They also point to refrigerant gases including PFAS, noise from cooling and generators, and generator emissions near a prison under construction. A local beekeeper, Jean-Noel Peche, told Vert that residents had no say and that the choice was driven by the nearness of the motorway and the power grid. Local officials back it. Fouju's mayor, Jonathan Wochenmayer, has said the nuisance will be far less than from earlier plans for the site that would have brought road traffic. Christian Poteau, president of the community of communes, told Vert his main condition had been that the campus take no groundwater, and that he had not given way on it. Behind it are the French public bank Bpifrance, the Emirati fund MGX, Mistral AI and Nvidia, who announced it in May 2025 with a stated investment of 50 billion euro. Work on the first phase was scheduled to begin in September 2026 and be delivered at the end of 2029, with further phases from 2030 to 2033 and 2034 to 2038. What happens next rests with the courts: the collective has said it intends to file a legal challenge against the prefect's authorisation, and it held a day of workshops and debates at Melun on August 29.

Opponents put the power demand at 1.4 gigawatts, twelve times what the surrounding community of communes uses now, and the carbon footprint at 766,000 tonnes a year, twice the area's current emissions.
They also point to refrigerant gases including PFAS, noise from cooling and generators, and generator emissions near a prison under construction.
A local beekeeper, Jean-Noel Peche, told Vert that residents had no say and that the choice was driven by the nearness of the motorway and the power grid.
Local officials back it.
Fouju's mayor, Jonathan Wochenmayer, has said the nuisance will be far less than from earlier plans for the site that would have brought road traffic.
Christian Poteau, president of the community of communes, told Vert his main condition had been that the campus take no groundwater, and that he had not given way on it.
Behind it are the French public bank Bpifrance, the Emirati fund MGX, Mistral AI and Nvidia, who announced it in May 2025 with a stated investment of 50 billion euro.
Work on the first phase was scheduled to begin in September 2026 and be delivered at the end of 2029, with further phases from 2030 to 2033 and 2034 to 2038.

What happens next rests with the courts: the collective has said it intends to file a legal challenge against the prefect's authorisation, and it held a day of workshops and debates at Melun on August 29.

research-mistral-bruyeres-le-chatel.text: Eclairion is building a data center in the park of the chateau at Bruyeres-le-Chatel, in Essonne outside Paris, France, on four hectares the town's local plan had protected as a natural zone until the council reclassified it for construction in 2018. Owned by High Performance Capital, Eclairion offers up to 60 megawatts of power in separate modular data centers. In February 2025 it said it would host Mistral AI's new training cluster, and DCD reported in March 2026 that the site was still under construction. The project was put together by historian and urban planner Michel Carmona, with developer Patrice Cavalier putting in the first 10 to 12 million euros; Francois Sabatino is Eclairion's president. Mistral AI takes half the computing power, with the rest meant for companies such as Safran, Thales, Dassault Systemes, Valeo, Air France and Renault. GPU cloud company Fluidstack said it would deploy a cluster at the 40 megawatt site, but Bloomberg reported in March 2026 that Fluidstack had cancelled that deal to focus on the US. The site's electrical capacity is 60 megawatts, which Le Chiffon compared to the yearly consumption of Bordeaux's 260,000 residents, and it draws about 90 cubic meters of water a day from the public network, up to 423 on some days, almost as much as the whole town uses. Nine diesel generators totaling 49.5 megawatts stand behind it, fed by nine buried tanks of 40 cubic meters each. The municipal opposition group Bruyeres-le-Chatel Ensemble criticized the plan at a December 2018 council meeting over water, electricity and the buried fuel, and has since declined to comment. Carmona says regional prefect Michel Cadot raised objections over concrete and damage to the forest before the project was pushed through as a matter of national interest, because the project is backed by the Commissariat for Atomic Energy (CEA), based nearby. In November 2024 the Ile-de-France region voted three million euros of support for Eclairion.

research-brookfield-data4-cambrai-e-vall.text: Brookfield and its data center company Data4 plan an AI data center campus at the E-Valley business park on the former Cambrai-Epinoy air base in Epinoy, near Cambrai in France's Hauts-de-France region. The site is set to host up to 1 gigawatt of capacity, and Data Center Dynamics reported in September 2025 that work could begin in 2026. Brookfield pledged 20 billion euros for French data centers at an AI summit in February 2025, 15 billion euros of it through Data4, and named Cambrai as one of the sites. At the Choose France summit in June 2026 it raised its planned French investment to 30 billion euros for two Data4 campuses, this one at Cambrai and a new one at Escaudain, which Data4 confirmed on June 12, 2026 at a cost of 5 billion euros for 700 megawatts. Data4 has told Data Center Dynamics it expects to build its largest AI campuses away from Paris, including at sites like Cambrai, because AI workloads do not need to sit close to end users. "We're probably going to build the large campuses outside Paris," a Data4 executive said. Data4 has been owned by Brookfield since April 2023 and runs more than 30 data centers in six European countries, totaling around 1.5 gigawatts.

research-brookfield-data4-escaudain.text: Brookfield/Data4 is building a 700 megawatt AI data center campus in Escaudain, in the Hauts-de-France region of northern France, on the site of the former Usinor steel plant. The local authority selected Brookfield/Data4 in December 2025 to study the 33-hectare site, and the company confirmed the 5 billion euro project in June 2026. It will be Data4's largest campus, alongside a second Brookfield-backed site the company is building at Cambrai, on a former air force base. At the Choose France summit in June 2026, Brookfield raised its planned investment in French AI infrastructure to 30 billion euros, up from the 20 billion euros it announced in February 2025. Most of that money runs through Data4. "The expanded funding will support the development of a large-scale 700MW AI factory in Northern France, strengthen local communities, and create 2,500 permanent jobs," said Sikander Rashid, Brookfield's head of AI infrastructure and head of Europe. The land had been vacant for 45 years, and the French government had listed it as one of 35 fast-track data center sites with a quick grid connection through the RTE network. Data4 plans four data centers on the campus and says it will use low-carbon concrete and recover waste heat from the servers. "With this major data center campus project dedicated to artificial intelligence, we aim to erase the last remnants of an industrial era and open a new, more technological chapter," said Aymeric Robin, mayor of nearby Raismes. Data4 has not set a construction timeline or given the capacity of the first phase; further site studies and preliminary work are expected over the next year.

research-atnorth-haugaland.text: atNorth plans a data center called NOR01 on a 36-hectare plot in Haugaland Business Park at Gismarvik, in Tysvær municipality, Rogaland county, Norway. The company announced the land purchase in June 2026, its first site in Norway, with initial phases of 120 megawatts of power rising to 350 megawatts, and says power for the site is expected in 2028. Haugaland Næringspark, the park's owner, said atNorth aims to invest about 11 billion Norwegian kroner ($1.1 billion) in the first phase. atNorth was acquired by Equinix and the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board in a $4.2 billion deal, the company's owners as of mid-2026. Power for the site will come through two new substations, one from national grid operator Statnett and one from regional grid company Fagne. "This is a major milestone for us. After almost 20 years of maturing and developing areas and infrastructure, we are now seeing the first major industrial establishments being realized in the park," said Tiril Fjeld, general manager of Haugaland Næringspark. Tysvær Mayor Monika Lindanger said the project would bring training, jobs and heat-reuse partnerships to the area. The park has courted data centers for years: Green Mountain took an option on land at Gismarvik in 2021, when a new transformer station was expected to give the region 500 megawatts of power within four to five years. As of June 2026 it was unclear whether work had begun on that site. atNorth's next named milestone is getting power at the Haugaland site in 2028.

research-microsoft-sweden-sandviken-gavl.text: Microsoft is building again at Tuna in Sandviken, Gävleborg, Sweden, where it stopped work on its data center halls in April 2025 because the electricity they need was not coming. Halls four and five, taking Tuna from three to five, were to start after the summer of 2026. What unblocked it was an airfield. Vattenfall's new power line had to cross Rörberg airport, which Gävle's council voted to close in September 2024; the decision was appealed three times and a flying club campaign for a referendum gathered 10,000 signatures. In October 2025 Gävle's council voted 35 to 30 against holding the referendum, and the flying club appealed. In April 2026 it became clear that the airport would close, and Microsoft's operations manager, Mattias Ersson, told Gefle Dagblad it meant the project was starting up again. The pause hit the town. About 1,500 people work on the site at full construction, according to the municipality's business chief, Jan Fagerström, and local machinery hire firms, landlords and restaurants lost trade. The Social Democrat councillor Peter Kärnström called it terribly sad for all the subcontractors and jobs. The five halls are expected to bring about 300 permanent jobs. Tuna is one of three expansion sites, with Ersbo and Stackbo in Gävle municipality, in an investment of more than 30 billion kronor presented with the prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, in 2024. At Stackbo, outside Gävle, residents said at a meeting in January 2021 that they felt thoroughly misled, having heard nothing new since the previous autumn. Paul Lind and Anna-Karin Löfstrand, who live nearest a planned transformer station, had been short of water at times during the preparatory work, and others objected that Microsoft paid for water and sewage connections for 16 households along the new mains while theirs, at 130,000 to 160,000 kronor, were not covered. The area draws data centers because the big lines carrying hydropower from Norrland meet around Gävle and Sandviken. The power itself depends on Vattenfall Eldistribution, which the Energy Markets Inspectorate has licensed to build lines from Stackbo in Gävle to Tuna on condition that the airport closes. Vattenfall's project leader, Annelie Thomsson, told Gefle Dagblad in October 2025 that it planned to start building the following autumn and expected everything to be finished by mid-2028, while warning of many uncertainties.

research-microsoft-finland-pure-dc-seina.text: Pure DC, a British developer, is building a data centre campus at Seinajoki in South Ostrobothnia, western Finland. The city says the first phase is 110 megawatts on about 22 hectares in the Kivenneva area along the eastern highway, with the campus able to grow beyond 550 megawatts. The city says two more data centre developments are at the building permit stage in the same Kivenneva area, and it names the surroundings of the current site and the Roves and Rahkola areas as possible future data centre areas. Microsoft is among the companies taking capacity in the first phase, which is reported as fully leased. The city expects the first phase to start operating in 2027 or 2028 and about 200 jobs with it, rising to roughly 600 if the full campus is built, which would take about a decade. On the things people ask about, the city's answers are these. Cooling runs in a closed loop and uses almost no water, about what an office building uses for its staff. Noise comes from the cooling plant and the backup generators, and is to be handled with barriers, walls and planting, with measurements required near houses once the site is running. Pure DC buys its electricity from large producers on the market rather than locally, and talks about using the waste heat in the district heating network are still going on. An earlier data centre already running in Seinajoki recovers more than 90 percent of its waste heat and supplies about four percent of the city's district heating. The town turned out for this. So many people came to the residents' evening at the city library that dozens were turned away at the door and the rest watched online, with the mayor Jaakko Kiiskila, the general plan director Jyrki Kuusinen and representatives of Pure DC answering questions. What residents asked about was whether there would be enough electricity and whether their bills would go up, who pays to extend the grid, whether local young people would get the jobs, and whether a foreign-owned company would leave anything behind. Aila Laine asked how the change would affect nature and animals. Vaino Kuoppala hoped it would bring some stimulus to the area; Reino Elomaa was sceptical about the burden on taxpayers and about the foreign ownership.

So many people came to the residents' evening at the city library that dozens were turned away at the door and the rest watched online, with the mayor Jaakko Kiiskila, the general plan director Jyrki Kuusinen and representatives of Pure DC answering questions.

What residents asked about was whether there would be enough electricity and whether their bills would go up, who pays to extend the grid, whether local young people would get the jobs, and whether a foreign-owned company would leave anything behind.
Aila Laine asked how the change would affect nature and animals.
Vaino Kuoppala hoped it would bring some stimulus to the area; Reino Elomaa was sceptical about the burden on taxpayers and about the foreign ownership.

research-nebius-finland-factory.text: Nebius runs its first data center in Mantsala, in southern Finland, and said on August 13, 2026, that it is building a second one in the town, with up to 70 megawatts of power coming online from 2027. Nebius said in March 2026 that it had finished expanding the first Mantsala data center to up to 75 megawatts of power earlier that year. Nebius announced on October 8, 2024, that it would triple the Mantsala site's capacity to 75 megawatts, saying the expansion would let it place up to 60,000 GPUs, the computer chips used to run AI, there, with annual revenue potential of over $1 billion at full use. Nebius says the facility recovers server heat to warm nearby homes: in 2024 it said the system recovered about 20,000 megawatt hours a year, enough to heat 2,500 Finnish homes, and in March 2026 it said the heat recovery avoided about 4,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions in 2025 and cut heating costs for connected households by about 10%. The company also says its power usage effectiveness, a measure of how much of a data center's electricity reaches its computers rather than being lost to cooling, is as low as 1.1 under high loads, using outside air for cooling instead of machines. Nebius says the Mantsala site houses Europe's first working installation of Nvidia's GB300 NVL72 system, a newer generation of AI computer hardware. "Mantsala is where we built our first data center, and our experience there has helped shape how we build and operate sites around the world," Nebius said of the new building. Nebius's other Finnish project is a planned AI factory of up to 310 megawatts on about 100 acres in Lappeenranta, in South Karelia, with first capacity expected in 2027; with the second Mantsala building, the company says its total capacity in Finland will reach 455 megawatts across three sites.

research-qts-blackstone-cambois-northumb.text: QTS, owned by Blackstone, is preparing a data center campus of up to 10 buildings at Cambois, a village in south-east Northumberland, United Kingdom, on the site of shuttered coal power stations. The investment could reach £10 billion, and QTS told DCD the site will support 720MW of critical IT load. The project was announced in 2024 at the site of the former Blyth Power Station, after the battery company Britishvolt cancelled its factory plans amid bankruptcy proceedings. Northumberland County Council granted planning permission in March 2025 and approved preparatory works on the site in August 2025. In December 2025 councillors approved the first phase of development, the first two of up to ten data centre buildings. Enabling groundworks began in October 2025. In an April 2026 planning statement, QTS said it intends to accelerate delivery, with construction of the first two data centres scheduled to begin later in 2026, operations slated for 2029, and two more due by 2030, a year ahead of the original schedule. The campus would total up to 540,000 square metres and use QTS's closed-loop water system. The council expects hundreds of long-term operating jobs and 1,200 construction jobs, and will receive a £110m fund for investment along the new Northumberland Line as part of the deal. The North East was designated one of the UK's AI Growth Zones in 2025, which increases a project's grid connection priority. Local leaders have backed the scheme. "We want this development from QTS to take place as soon as we possibly can," said Ian Lavery, the Labour MP for Blyth and Ashington. "It is integral that local people come first in the construction phase and operation phase," Lavery said. Another developer, Wansbeck Regeneration, has proposed a second data centre just north of the QTS site at West Sleekburn. Planning decisions on later phases rest with Northumberland County Council's Strategic Planning Committee.

research-nscale-loughton.text: Nscale's planned two billion pound AI data center in Loughton, in Epping Forest district, Essex, has full planning permission, but the 90 megawatt grid connection it needs will not be ready in time for the planned 2027 opening. Nscale has held talks with Bloom Energy about using solid oxide fuel cells that burn natural gas to power the site until the connection arrives, Data Centre Review reported in July 2026. Epping Forest District Council granted planning permission in June 2026 despite objections from town councillors, local committees and residents, after Investment Minister Lord Stockwood wrote to the council's chief executive that "this Government is keen to see the successful delivery of this site." Loughton Town Council's planning officers had asked for a fresh application, since the building Nscale wants is about half again as large as the one already permitted, and wanted independent proof that the power draw would not strain the grid or raise bills. The site is meant to hold tens of thousands of Nvidia processors for Microsoft, which the companies say will make it the largest AI supercomputer in the UK, supporting 500 construction jobs and up to 250 permanent ones. Nscale has pushed the expected completion from late 2026 to early 2027, saying it needs time to upgrade hardware, and the timetable now depends on when enough electricity can reach the site.

research-stargate-uk-cobalt-park.text: Stargate UK, the data center that OpenAI, Nvidia and the British firm Nscale said they would develop at Cobalt Park, a business park in North Tyneside in the north east of England, United Kingdom, has been on hold since April 2026, when OpenAI paused the project citing regulation and energy costs. "We continue to explore Stargate UK and will move forward when the right conditions, such as regulation and the cost of energy, enable long-term infrastructure investment," an OpenAI spokesperson said. OpenAI announced its Cobalt Park plan in September 2025, as part of a £31 billion government package that made the North East an AI growth zone. Nscale said at the time that OpenAI would explore offtake of up to 8,000 Nvidia GPUs (graphics processing units) in the first quarter of 2026, with the potential to scale to 31,000 GPUs over time, across several UK sites of which only Cobalt Park was named. Cobalt Park already holds about 35 megawatts of data center capacity, but Computer Weekly reported in April 2026 that no planning applications had been lodged and no construction was underway for new capacity there. A Guardian investigation in July 2026, based on freedom of information requests, found that neither OpenAI nor Nscale had met the local authorities at the North Tyneside site; only Nvidia met the North East Combined Authority, in February 2026. A request to the National Energy System Operator suggested the site had no grid connection and had instead submitted an alternative way to power itself, the Guardian reported. "There's just not the infrastructure there to be able to actually support it," said John Johnsson, leader of the Conservatives in North Tyneside. "It's now looking highly unlikely whether the project is going to come to North Tyneside." The government told the campaign group Spotlight on Corruption that £20 billion of the growth zone's touted £30 billion was the sum the site would need to use its 1.1 gigawatt power supply, not investment already committed. The rest of the North East growth zone is moving. Northumberland Council signed off reserved matters in December 2025 for the first phase of the 6 million square foot QTS campus at Cambois, on the former Blyth Power Station site, financed by Blackstone's Renaissance Land, and QTS said it would install piling for the first building in spring 2026. Plans for two further buildings there have been lodged, and Wansbeck Regeneration has applied for a facility of almost 4 million square feet less than two miles away. Whether Stargate UK returns is up to OpenAI, which says it will move forward only when regulation and energy costs allow. A government-backed taskforce co-chaired by the technology secretary and North East mayor Kim McGuinness says the wider growth zone will still reach 1.1 gigawatts of power, with over 400 megawatts of capacity coming online in 2028.

research-culham-data-centre.text: The UK Atomic Energy Authority is looking for a private partner to build an AI data center at Culham Campus near Abingdon, Oxfordshire, the country's first AI Growth Zone, a designation meant to speed up approvals and guarantee power. UKAEA plans to release at least 10 acres with spare grid capacity for about 100 megawatts of power at first, and is exploring a larger plot that could allow up to 500 megawatts. It expects up to 20 megawatts of the facility could be made available on demand for fusion and other research at the site. UKAEA closed its call for investment partners on September 15, 2025, and said it would follow in October 2025 with an invitation to participate setting the final terms for bidders; no partner has been announced since. The site was chosen because decommissioning JET, the fusion reactor that ran there, freed up its 400kV grid connection, which UKAEA's Tim Bestwick said carries enough power for tens of thousands of homes. South Oxfordshire District Council hired a study on using the data center's waste heat to warm nearby homes; the study ran from March 2 to June 30, 2026, and no findings have been published since. The council's local plan allows 3,500 new homes on land next to the data center site that could also use that heat. Amazon Web Services and CloudHQ are also developing data centers near Culham.

research-vantage-newport-south-wales-agz.text: Vantage Data Centers' CWL1 campus in Newport, Wales, is one of Europe's largest data center campuses, with 148 megawatts of power under management. In August 2026 Vantage agreed to lease capacity there to the cloud company Nebius, its first announced commercial deal in the South Wales AI Growth Zone, a government designation meant to speed up planning and grid connections. The campus has operated since 2010, first as Next Generation Data in a former LG Electronics factory, before Vantage bought it in 2020. Newport City Council approved four three-story data centers behind the main building in September 2020, and in March 2021 approved a two-story "Data Centre 3" with ten data halls for a single hyperscale customer, backed by six 1.6-megawatt diesel generators per hall. When the council approved Data Centre 3, Councillor John Guy said: "It's fantastic to see this futuristic development but my concern is the scientific emissions and the actual sound," according to the South Wales Argus. Vantage says the campus's electricity use is matched with certified renewable energy and that its newest buildings use closed-loop cooling to limit water use. UK AI minister Kanishka Narayan said of the Nebius deal: "The infrastructure at Newport will create new high skilled jobs in South Wales." An August 2026 review of government records found little sign yet that AI Growth Zone status had sped up planning activity in South Wales.

research-humain-dammam.text: HUMAIN, the artificial intelligence company of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, broke ground in August 2025 on a 100-megawatt data center in Dammam, in the kingdom's Eastern Province, one of its first two sites alongside a matching facility in Riyadh. CEO Tareq Amin told Bloomberg the Dammam site was expected to go live in the second quarter of 2026, a target that has now passed with no result published. At groundbreaking, HUMAIN was still buying the chips for the sites from the United States, including 18,000 Nvidia GB300 chips, and Amin said the timeline for receiving them depended on "the governance and the protocols and the approval of the US government," formalities he said the company would begin "very, very soon." HUMAIN, launched in May 2025, aims to deliver 6.6 gigawatts of data center capacity over the next decade; it has also partnered with AWS on a $5 billion AI Zone and signed a deal with AMD for 500 megawatts of computing power.

At groundbreaking, HUMAIN was still buying the chips for the sites from the United States, including 18,000 Nvidia GB300 chips, and Amin said the timeline for receiving them depended on "the governance and the protocols and the approval of the US government," formalities he said the company would begin "very, very soon."

HUMAIN, launched in May 2025, aims to deliver 6.6 gigawatts of data center capacity over the next decade; it has also partnered with AWS on a $5 billion AI Zone and signed a deal with AMD for 500 megawatts of computing power.

research-reliance-jamnagar-data-centre.text: Reliance Industries is building a data center in Jamnagar, Gujarat, India that Meta will lease, the two companies announced June 10, 2026. The facility's first phase will have 168 megawatts of power, with an option for Meta to scale up, and Reliance expects to deliver it within two years. It is Meta's first built-to-suit data center in India. Meta said Jamnagar was chosen because it sits near undersea internet cable landing stations and Reliance's Jio fiber network, and because Reliance's existing operations there already provide land, utilities and power. The data center will run on renewable energy and be cooled with desalinated seawater, and Meta will pay the full cost of the energy and water it uses. Meta also signed contracts for almost 1 gigawatt of new clean power in India, including 837 megawatts of solar and wind projects with CleanMax and 88 megawatts with Fourth Partner Energy. Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg said the Jamnagar facility would help the company scale its AI infrastructure globally while deepening its long-term investment in India's economy. In January 2025, Bloomberg had reported that Reliance was planning a considerably larger data center at the Jamnagar site, one that could become the world's largest, at a cost of $20 billion to $30 billion, powered by an adjacent green energy complex and using Nvidia chips under a partnership signed in October 2024. That larger plan has not been confirmed since the smaller Meta deal was announced.

research-microsoft-hyderabad-adani.text: AdaniConneX, the data center venture of India's Adani Group, is building a campus for Microsoft on Pargi Road in Elkatta, on the edge of Hyderabad, Telangana, India, according to an Adani announcement in February 2026 that listed campuses "with Microsoft spanning Hyderabad and Pune." No capacity or completion date has been announced for the campus. AdaniConneX is a joint venture between Adani Enterprises and the US operator EdgeConneX. In January 2024, at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Adani signed an agreement with the Telangana state government to invest more than Rs 5,000 crore, about $600 million, in a 100 megawatt data center powered by renewable energy over five to seven years. The February 2026 announcement placed the Hyderabad campus within a wider pledge by the Adani Group to invest $100 billion in renewable-powered, AI-ready data centers across India by 2035. That builds on AdaniConneX's existing 2 gigawatt national data center platform, which the company aims to grow to 5 gigawatts.

research-yondr-sedenak.text: Vantage Data Centers now owns the data center campus in Sedenak Tech Park, Kulai, Johor, Malaysia, calling it JHB1 after completing its purchase from developer Yondr Group in November 2025. The site is operating, and Vantage says the nearly 73-acre campus will deliver more than 300 megawatts of power across three buildings once fully built. Yondr, which developed the campus, financed a first phase of about 98 megawatts in December 2024, expected to be ready for service in 2025, before selling the site to Vantage. Johor's data center growth has put water and power under scrutiny. Chief minister Onn Hafiz Ghazi said in March 2026 the state approves only data centers that use air cooling and will reject projects that demand high water use, and a state committee reviews each project's water and electricity needs. Residents of Gelang Patah protested over water outside a data center construction site in February 2026, The Diplomat reported. New developments in Johor need approval from the Johor State Data Centre Development Coordinating Committee. Yondr entered Malaysia in March 2022 and energized the Sedenak campus substation in March 2024, under an August 2023 electricity supply agreement with Tenaga Nasional Berhad for more than 300 megawatts of IT load through a 275-kilovolt substation. In December 2024 Yondr raised more than $900 million from lenders including DBS, Deutsche Bank, HSBC and the IFC to build that first phase. Vantage's purchase was funded in part by a $1.6 billion investment in its Asia-Pacific platform from GIC and the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, and made Johor Vantage's third campus in Malaysia. The campus uses direct-to-chip liquid cooling and is on track for EDGE certification, a green-building standard.

research-princeton-digital-jh1-sedenak.text: Princeton Digital Group's JH1 data center campus in Sedenak Tech Park, Johor, Malaysia, has grown to a planned 200MW across four buildings, and the operator topped out the third building and began the fourth in December 2025, DCD reported. The first 52MW phase was completed in July 2024. PDG bought 31 acres in Sedenak Tech Park in May 2023 from JLand Group, the property arm of the state-owned Johor Corporation, for a campus first planned at 150MW, with RM2 billion, about $450 million, earmarked for the first phase. It broke ground in October 2023 and delivered the first phase in 12 months, and says the full campus will see $1.5 billion invested. PDG signed an energy supply agreement with Tenaga Nasional Berhad for the whole campus, took a RM1.276 billion green loan, and says it will put solar panels on the roof. Johor's chief minister, Onn Hafiz Ghazi, opened the first phase in 2024, calling it "one of the fastest projects to be launched in Johor." Since then his government has tightened its rules: in March 2026 he said the state will approve only data centers that use air cooling and will reject those demanding a high intake of water. Residents of Gelang Patah protested over water outside a data center construction site in February 2026, The Diplomat reported. Sedenak Tech Park is one of Johor's busiest data center sites. Vantage Data Centers bought Yondr's campus of more than 300MW there in November 2025. YTL Power announced a gigawatt-scale campus at Sedenak Tech Park West in August 2026. PDG raised $1.3 billion from Stonepeak and a $1.2 billion debt financing in 2025 to fund its expansion across Asia. New data center developments in Johor need the approval of the Johor State Data Centre Development Coordinating Committee, which reviews water and electricity needs.

research-aws-malaysia-johor.text: Nothing published places an Amazon Web Services data centre in the YTL Green Data Center Park at Kulai, in Johor, Malaysia, where trackers list one under construction. AWS opened its Malaysian region on August 21, 2024 with three availability zones and did not say where they are. The park is YTL's own: 1,640 acres at Kulai, to be fed by a 500 megawatt solar plant with 600 megawatts of grid backup, where YTL Power completed its first Nvidia building in November 2025 and in April 2026 said it wanted to double the planned 500 megawatts within three years. YTL Power also controls Ranhill Utilities, which runs all 46 of the state's water treatment plants. Water is the argument in Johor. In November 2025 the state asked investors to hold water-cooled expansions for at least 18 months, until mid-2027, amid drought. The mayor of Johor Bahru, Mohd Noorazam Osman, said people were too excited about data centres and that the area does not have enough water and power.

research-nextdc-openai-western-sydney.text: NextDC has proposed S7, a 612-megawatt data center campus in Eastern Creek, a logistics hub in Sydney's western suburbs in New South Wales, Australia, according to planning documents reported by Data Center Dynamics in July 2026. OpenAI is set to be the initial anchor tenant under a memorandum of understanding signed in December 2025 that would make S7 an Australian Stargate site. The project still needs approval from the New South Wales government before construction can begin. NextDC bought the 255,135-square-meter parcel, south of Honeycomb Drive and east of Future Archbold Road, for AU$353 million in October 2024, and said then it would offer up to 550 megawatts of power at full buildout. A preliminary plan shows nine data center buildings spread across three blocks, plus a substation. The state planning portal describes three two-story data storage buildings with 340 back-up diesel generators, diesel fuel storage and an on-site substation. The project has been valued at AU$7 billion, and the first phase is expected to be delivered in the second half of 2027 if it is approved. NextDC says the campus will use closed-loop, high-density liquid cooling that will not require ongoing drinking water for cooling, and will draw power through long-term purchase agreements for new wind, solar and battery projects. It pitches S7 as a sovereign AI facility that keeps data and computing within Australia's jurisdiction, available to other organizations that need sovereign computing capacity. NextDC chief executive Craig Scroggie called it a "world leading piece of sustainable digital infrastructure that will demonstrate that Australia can be a leader in digital infrastructure and artificial intelligence." The neighborhood is filling up: Goodman filed in January 2026 for its own Eastern Creek campus, Project Atlas, of up to 500 megawatts. S7 is a State Significant Development, meaning the New South Wales government, not Blacktown City Council, decides on it. NextDC is now preparing an Environmental Impact Statement, a report on the project's effects on land, water and traffic, which will go on public display before the state takes public comments and makes a decision.

research-china-telecom-inner-mongolia-in.text: China Telecom's Inner Mongolia Information Park is a data center complex in the Horinger New Area, on the southern edge of Hohhot, Inner Mongolia, China. The plan calls for 42 data centers and 19 supporting buildings at a cost of 17.3 billion yuan, about $2.59 billion, holding more than 100,000 racks and over a million servers when finished, China Daily reported. As of June 2022, eight data centers, one multipurpose building, two power centers and other support buildings had gone up, and more than 70 companies, including internet firms, financial traders and government cloud operators, had taken space there, China Daily reported. Each finished data center is meant to hold 2,700 racks and close to 36,000 servers, a later China Daily report said. The park sits in Inner Mongolia, one of eight areas China has designated as national computing hubs under a plan to move computing demand from its crowded eastern cities to its resource-rich west, Bloomberg reported in September 2026. The wider Horinger New Area now holds 62 computing centers with a combined capacity of 150,000 petaflops, The Next Web reported, citing Xinhua and local authorities.

research-china-mobile-hohhot-horinger.text: China Mobile's Hohhot Intelligent Computing Center, a data center in the Horinger New Area of Hohhot, Inner Mongolia, China, is built to train artificial intelligence models and run big data analytics for sectors including transportation, healthcare and finance. It has a peak computing capacity of 6,700 petaflops, which China Daily said in 2025 made it the world's largest single-unit computing center run by a telecom company. Power is its biggest cost. The center paid about 290 million yuan, roughly $40 million, for electricity in 2025, more than 70 percent of its operating expenses, according to a Hohhot city government release reported by The Next Web. Horinger has become one of China's main computing hubs under a national plan to move computing demand from the crowded east to the resource-rich west. The district now holds 62 computing centers with a combined capacity of 150,000 petaflops, Xinhua reported, citing local authorities. In August 2026 Inner Mongolia signed 186.46 billion yuan, about $27 billion, of new green computing projects with companies including ByteDance's Volcano Engine, Cambricon and China Telecom. Researchers question how much the buildout helps residents nearby. Data centers do not necessarily create a "huge spillover effect" on local jobs, Andrew Stokols of Singapore Management University said; both in China and elsewhere, he said, "immediate benefits have been elusive."

research-envision-galaxy-ulanqab.text: Envision Group's Galaxy Campus, an AI data center in Ulanqab in China's Inner Mongolia, entered operation on August 6, 2026, with a planned total capacity of 2 gigawatts. Envision, a Chinese green technology company, describes it as the world's largest single AI computing facility: 120,000 square meters, roughly 20 football fields, built to run 1 million GPUs in parallel. Ulanqab is about 240 kilometers from Beijing in a straight line, Global Times reported, while the Chinese outlet Huxiu put the distance at about 320 kilometers. Global Times reported the project launches Envision's "Mission Gobi" initiative, which the company says targets 5 gigawatts of green computing capacity in desert regions worldwide by 2030. Global Times reported that the campus relies on directly connected green electricity for more than 80 percent of its power. Electricity for data centers in Ulanqab costs about 50 percent less than in the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region, Global Times reported, and the area gets more than 3,200 hours of sunshine a year. Qbitai, a Chinese technology outlet, put the wider region's green-power share at 67 percent. Huxiu reported the city had about 109 committed data center projects by August 2026, with total committed computing capacity rising from roughly 3.3 gigawatts a year earlier to about 12.5 gigawatts. Huxiu also reported the city signed 12 new smart-computing projects worth more than 130 billion yuan in August 2026 alone. Huxiu reported that DeepSeek plans about 1 gigawatt of data center capacity in Ulanqab. Global Times reported that Huawei, Alibaba and Apple have also set up computing operations in the area, citing the region's cheap electricity. Huxiu reported that GPU utilization at China's smart-computing centers nationally averages below 30 percent, and that officials have acknowledged such projects remain unprofitable during this investment phase.

research-alibaba-cloud-ulanqab.text: Alibaba Cloud's Ulanqab data centre campus sits in the Chahar high technology zone in Inner Mongolia, on what was sandy waste ground before the industry arrived. The first building, a 114,000 square metre, two floor structure with individual rooms exceeding 20,000 square metres each, went into service in 2020, one of three hyperscale sites Alibaba added to its Chinese network that year. That building runs roughly 924 server racks at 15 kilowatts each. The city's argument is electricity. The average temperature is 4.3 degrees, the summer average 18.8, and free air cooling works for close to ten months of the year, which the local account puts at a 20 to 30 percent saving; Ulanqab's delivered industrial tariff is less than half the eastern seaboard's, and it sits inside the Mengxi system, the only provincial grid in China outside the two national operators, which sets its own prices and allows direct connections to wind and solar. Alibaba's data centre general manager, Wang Chaoyang, has said that a one gigawatt site in Ulanqab would save as much as 5 billion yuan a year in electricity against other cities. The city paid for its own links to Beijing. Huawei signed in 2013, when officials in a farming and herding prefecture of two million people, whose best known product was the potato, had barely heard of big data; the city then paid for two 144 core fibre cables of its own to Beijing, 240 kilometres away, finished in 2016 and 2018. "We did not do it to make money," said Liu Huansuo, deputy director of the municipal big data bureau. "We wanted to provide a good service to the data centres." By the end of June 2026 the city had signed 89 data centre projects with 68 companies, worth more than 500 billion yuan, and the main streets of the zone are named Huawei Avenue, Apple Avenue and Alibaba Avenue. Data centres took 7.3 percent of the city's electricity in the first seven months of 2026. Goldman Sachs put operating and planned capacity at about 12.5 gigawatts. What the city keeps is narrower than the investment figures suggest. A gigawatt scale campus employs a few hundred people once built, most of them posted in from elsewhere; the tax comes mainly during construction, and afterwards from land, buildings and payroll, because the computing is sold by head offices in other provinces. The price of the power that drew Alibaba is set inside the Mengxi grid, run by Inner Mongolia Electric Power Group, which can set its own prices and trade independently, and can connect data centers directly to wind and solar.

research-china-mobile-ulanqab-hub.text: China Mobile is among the operators building data centres in the Chahar high-tech zone at Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, China, a city of fewer than two million people about 350 kilometres northwest of Beijing, and it has published no capacity, cost or completion date for its hub there. On the ground the building does not stop. A stallholder surnamed Yin, who sells 10 yuan plates of chicken, egg and tofu skin at a junction on the eastern edge of town, said there are hundreds of workers every day and it never stops, and asked how this could not be good. Ulanqab was named in February 2022 as part of one of eight national computing hubs, meant to process data where power and land are cheap, and now runs 172,000 petaflops, more than 95 percent of it for AI. Alibaba, Huawei, Apple and Kuaishou already have buildings there, and ByteDance's cloud arm, Cambricon and China Telecom are among the newest arrivals. New data centres in the region must take more than 80 percent of their yearly electricity from renewable sources.

research-deepseek-ulanqab.text: Chinese AI developer DeepSeek is planning a 1-gigawatt data center in the city of Ulanqab, in Inner Mongolia, China, according to a Bloomberg report at the end of July 2026. The Hangzhou-based company aims to build its own new facility in Ulanqab, about 350 kilometers northwest of Beijing, while leasing additional capacity from other companies, according to people familiar with the matter. DeepSeek is pushing to bring at least part of the capacity online by the end of 2027 or early 2028, two of those people said. It is unclear what kind of chips DeepSeek will use for the project. The people asked not to be identified discussing private information. More than a dozen firms have projects planned in the city, according to a third-party compilation of local government approvals. Inner Mongolia is one of the provinces in China's Eastern Data, Western Compute program, which seeks to place large-scale computing in the country's western regions.

research-vantage-jnb2-isando.text: Vantage Data Centers is building JNB2, its second Johannesburg data center campus, in Isando, in the City of Ekurhuleni, Gauteng, South Africa, near OR Tambo International Airport. The first building is a 20 megawatt, two-story data center of 355,000 square feet, built partly by reusing part of an existing warehouse, and it sits about 17 kilometers from Vantage's 120 megawatt JNB1 campus in Midrand. Vantage announced construction in December 2022 and said the building would open in mid-2024. That date has passed, and as of September 2026 Vantage's own website still describes JNB2 in the future tense, with no report yet that it has opened. Power comes from the Municipality of Ekurhuleni through an on-site substation, and the campus is cooled by a closed-loop water system designed to use outside air to cut water use, which Vantage says keeps water use near zero.

research-africa-data-centres-samrand.text: Africa Data Centres is expanding its Samrand data center in Centurion, Gauteng, South Africa, from 10 megawatts of power to 40 megawatts. The site, part of the Africa Data Centres network run by Cassava Technologies, is now listed as operating while the buildout continues. Africa Data Centres bought the campus from Standard Bank in 2020 and broke ground on the expansion on August 30, 2022. "The construction of the first phase is starting today and will deliver 20MW across eight data halls by 2023," said Tesh Durvasula, then Africa Data Centres' chief executive, at the groundbreaking. He said the next phase would add 10 more megawatts of power by the end of 2025. In August 2024, South Africa executive Angus Hay told TechCentral the facility, originally built for 10 megawatts, would gain another 20 megawatts of power when the upgrade finished in 2025. Cassava Technologies, the pan-African group that owns Africa Data Centres, runs two data centers in Johannesburg and one in Cape Town. In October 2025 Cassava announced an investment from Stanlib Infrastructure Investments to expand its AI-ready data centers in Johannesburg and Cape Town, after Nvidia delivered 3,000 graphics chips to a Cassava-built South African site in June 2025.

research-kasi-cloud-los1.text: Kasi Cloud Datacenters opened LOS1, the first building of its planned 100 megawatt data center campus, in the Maiyegun area of Lekki, Lagos State, Nigeria, in May 2026. Lagos Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu, who presided over the 2022 groundbreaking, returned to officiate the flag-off ceremony, which Kasi described as LOS1's move from construction into operational readiness. The campus covers about four hectares next to six subsea internet cables, including Equiano and 2Africa. Kasi broke ground in April 2022, when the project was reported to be backed by $250 million of investment, and the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority, which manages the country's sovereign wealth funds, is among its investors. Kasi has said the facility will be powered by gas, solar and battery storage, aiming for a power usage effectiveness rating (a measure of energy efficiency) below 1.6. "For too long, Africa's data has powered someone else's economy. Today, that changes," said Johnson Agogbua, Kasi's founder and CEO. Kasi pitches the site as an in-country option under Nigeria's National Cloud Policy 2025, which it says requires sensitive government and financial data to be hosted in Nigeria. Finance Minister Taiwo Oyedele and NSIA chief executive Aminu Umar-Sadiq also attended the ceremony. Most of Nigeria's data centers are clustered around Lagos, where Equinix, Digital Realty, MTN and Rack Centre also operate, and Kasi is developing another data center in Eket in southern Nigeria. The rest of the campus is to be built out toward about 100 megawatts of IT capacity, and LOS1 now goes through phased commissioning, systems integration and customer readiness work before full commercial operations.

research-nxtra-by-airtel-lagos.text: Nxtra, the data center arm of Airtel Africa and its parent Bharti Airtel, is building a 38 megawatt data center at Eko Atlantic City on Victoria Island in Lagos, Nigeria, now under construction and due to go live in 2028. research-open-access-dc-lagos-lekki.text: OADC, part of the West Indian Ocean Cable Company (WIOCC), is building a 24 megawatt data center expansion in Lekki, Lagos, Nigeria, at a cost of $240 million. The Tier III expansion is under construction as twin 12 megawatt stages; chief executive Ayotunde Coker said in March 2025 that piling had begun on the second stage and the work was expected to take about 18 months. The four-hectare Lekki campus, known as OADC Lagos LOS1, is where Google's Equiano subsea cable lands in Nigeria. Power comes through a dedicated transmission line into the facility, with a second line from Ajah in Lekki for backup, and the project is funded with equity and debt, including the International Finance Corporation and Proparco. "While on-site solar generation is limited due to space constraints, OADC is evaluating power wheeling options to source hydroelectric and solar power from external locations," Coker said. OADC operates six hyperscale data centers and more than 30 edge sites in South Africa, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Nigeria. In December 2025 ThisDay reported that the twin 12 megawatt Tier III facility was expected to be completed in 2026.

research-khazna-benya-maadi.text: Nothing has been reported from Maadi Technology Park in Cairo, Egypt, since Khazna Data Centers of Abu Dhabi and the Egyptian contractor Benya Group said in May 2023 they would build the country's first hyperscale data centre there. Construction was meant to start later in 2023 and take about three years, which would put completion around now. The plan was 25 megawatts of IT load across 40,000 square metres, at 250 million dollars. Egypt's General Authority for Investment and Free Zones placed it within a national plan to bring data centre industries into the country. For Khazna, formed in 2021 from the data centre arms of Etisalat and the Abu Dhabi AI company G42, it was the first project outside the United Arab Emirates.
