meta-meta-singapore.text: Meta's Singapore data center at Tanjong Kling, where the company broke ground in 2018, has been operating since 2022 and covers 170,000 square meters. Facebook, now Meta, announced it in September 2018 as its first purpose-built data center in Asia: an 11-floor, S$1.4 billion building in the western part of Singapore that would use 150MW when fully running, the largest single data center in Singapore at the time. To save land, the company built upward on a 12-acre plot, and Meta said the building would be a candidate for the world's largest data center under one roof. It was the first Meta data center to use StatePoint Liquid Cooling, developed with Nortek Air Solutions, which Meta says cuts peak water use by more than 20% in a climate like Singapore's, for a projected power usage effectiveness of 1.19. Meta says the site supports more than 100 operational jobs and drew 3,000 skilled trade workers at the peak of construction. Power is the pressure point in Singapore. Singapore halted new data center development in 2019, allowing only already authorized projects such as Meta's to go ahead, and relaxed the ban in 2022 with a pilot allocation that gave Equinix, GDS, Microsoft and an AirTrunk-ByteDance consortium 80MW in 2023. In December 2025 the Economic Development Board and the Infocomm Media Development Authority opened a second call for at least 200MW, requiring new facilities to be at least 50 percent powered by green energy; applications closed on March 31, 2026. On August 21, 2026 the two agencies provisionally allocated that capacity to four operators, Digital Realty, Equinix, Keppel Data Centres and ST Telemedia Global Data Centres, whose data centers will be built in a low-carbon park on Jurong Island. Meta buys renewable power for the site. In March 2025 its subsidiary Malkoha Pte signed a 25-year agreement with Sembcorp for a 150MW floating solar project on the Kranji Reservoir, with construction expected to start in the first half of 2027, subject to approvals. Meta earlier signed a 5MW floating solar deal and a 100MW rooftop solar deal with Sunseap. Any new data center capacity in Singapore is allocated by the Economic Development Board and the Infocomm Media Development Authority through their calls for application.

meta-meta-odense.text: Meta's Odense data center, in Odense in the Region of Southern Denmark, is a three-building campus that came online in 2019 and is best known for heating thousands of local homes with its servers' waste heat. Meta says its investment in the Odense data center exceeds 10 billion Danish kroner and that the site supports 175 operational jobs. The first 55,000-square-meter building opened in 2019, and Meta announced a 30,000-square-meter expansion in 2020. In December 2021 it said it would add two more buildings of about 90,000 square meters, taking the campus to nearly 200,000 square meters and its total investment to more than 13 billion kroner. A year later Meta stopped that plan. Its contractor Aarsleff said in December 2022 that its 2.4 billion kroner contract had been terminated and work "will be stopped immediately," after earthworks, concrete work and cable trenches were already done. "We have decided not to move forward with the planned expansion beyond three buildings and we will be ending construction work on the two additional buildings," Meta's Nordics communications manager Peter Munster told DCD, adding that AI workloads require "a different type of data center." The campus is connected to the Odense district heating network. Meta says 165,000 megawatt hours of surplus heat from its server halls go to the system run by Fjernvarme Fyn and reach up to about 9,000 households in Odense. It says three new solar projects in Denmark, totaling about 210 megawatts, are part of the renewable energy it buys to match its data centers' electricity use. Meta also owns 212 hectares of land at Andrup in Esbjerg, bought in 2021 for 277 million kroner as a possible site for a future data center.

meta-meta-clonee.text: Meta's Clonee data center in Clonee, County Meath, Ireland, is an operating Meta campus whose first buildings were already running when the company announced two more in 2019. Meta says it has invested 1.4 billion euro in the Clonee campus in Meath, which it says supports more than 300 operational jobs and drew 1,500 skilled trade workers at the peak of construction. In March 2019 Meta announced two new buildings at Clonee that would bring the facility to nearly 150,000 square meters, and said all its Clonee buildings would run on 100% renewable energy. Meta says three wind and solar projects it supports in Ireland are adding 219 megawatts of new renewable energy to the grid to match the data center's electricity use. Clonee has also been the scene of a labour dispute. In October 2024 engineers in the Connect trade union called a 24-hour strike over a new four-week shift cycle that meant more weekend and night work, saying Meta had imposed it without agreement. The strike was deferred and the dispute referred to the Labour Court. "While we respect our employee's right of association, we do not engage with third party representative bodies," Meta said at the time. In March 2025 Meta said it was proposing to make a "small number" of roles redundant at Clonee; RTÉ reported that 14 roles were at risk. The bigger question around Clonee is the grid. Ireland's 121 data centres use about one-fifth of the country's electricity, and almost all of them are in the congested Dublin-Meath area, The Irish Times reported in June 2026. The Commission for Regulation of Utilities said data centre demand grew from 5% of national electricity demand in 2015 to 22% in 2024 and is forecast to reach 31% by 2034. In December 2025 the CRU set new rules for data centres connecting to the grid: they must provide generation or storage to match their demand, meet at least 80% of annual demand with new renewable projects in Ireland, and be judged on whether their grid location is constrained. Friends of the Earth and two other groups have been granted leave to judicially review the State's data centre energy policy, with a hearing scheduled for April 2027. Under the CRU's policy, any new or larger grid connection for a data centre in the Dublin-Meath area is assessed by the system operators EirGrid and ESB Networks, who must now publish where the network has spare capacity.

meta-meta-lulea.text: Meta's Lulea data center in Norrbotten, a coastal region in northern Sweden, opened its first server hall in 2013, the company's first data center outside the United States; a second hall followed in 2014. The site is cooled with outside air and runs on hydroelectric power, which Facebook said was reliable enough to let it cut backup generators by more than 70 percent. In May 2018 Meta announced a third server hall and an expansion of an existing building, and Lulea's mayor, Niklas Nordstrom, said the town had made sure there was land and energy for it to grow. The campus grew on the promise of jobs. Early projections ran to 30,000 jobs, but by 2020 the halls employed 56 people on maintenance and service work, the Finnish broadcaster Yle reported. Thomas Lovgren, an editor at the Swedish paper NSD who had followed the site for years, said it had turned out differently from what was promised, counting the 8.7 billion kronor of company money and state support against it. A Swedish government evaluation published October 31, 2017 put the wider effect at about 240 new jobs in the region, with more work every third year when equipment is replaced, and recorded state investment support awarded in 2011 and 2014 against a total investment of nearly 11 billion kronor. Goran Lattman of the agency Tillvaxtverket said the support was granted while the company was weighing several locations, and that the site had since made the region more attractive for similar investment. Meta's own September 2026 fact sheet puts its investment in Lulea at more than 8.7 billion kronor and says the campus supports more than 300 operational jobs. It says Meta has given more than 31 million kronor to nonprofits, schools and community initiatives in Lulea and Norrbotten since 2012, through more than 210 grants and sponsorships.

gemini-xai-macrohardrr-colossus-3.text: xAI is converting an 800,000 square foot warehouse on Stateline Road West in Southaven, DeSoto County, Mississippi, into a data center called MACROHARDRR, its third site in the greater Memphis area after Colossus 1 and Colossus 2. Governor Tate Reeves's office announced the project on January 8, 2026 as an investment of more than $20 billion, and xAI said it planned to begin operations there in February 2026. The data center draws power from gas turbines at a separate plant on Stanton Road that also powers the neighboring Colossus 2 site. The Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice, representing the NAACP, say the Stanton Road turbines were installed without an air permit and could emit more than 1,700 tons of nitrogen oxides a year, likely the largest industrial source in the Memphis area, from a plant half a mile from homes and a mile from an elementary school. "Our communities are not playgrounds for corporations who are chasing profit over people," said the NAACP's Abre' Conner. Mississippi signed off on a permanent plant of 41 turbines at the site in March 2026. Three residents, Jason Haley, Preston Herrington and Taylor Logsdon, filed a class action in federal court in Oxford in June 2026 over turbine noise, on behalf of a class that could include more than 10,000 people. Their attorney, Robert Wright, said, "our homes are supposed to be a sanctuary for us against the world, but when they are invaded by noise 24 hours a day, it takes that fundamental peace of a good and decent life away from us." Southaven Mayor Darren Musselwhite said recent readings were in the 50 decibel range, below limits for an industrial zone. In July 2026 xAI began removing all 69 turbines from the Stanton Road site, with the work due to finish by July 2027, replacing them with a permanent 1.2 gigawatt plant of 41 turbines. Mississippi's Department of Environmental Quality is requiring emissions tests on the 14 cleanest turbines and barred xAI from adding new turbines after July 15, 2026. The law center said that "while xAI claims it is 'rapidly removing' its unpermitted gas turbines in reality the company has been continually expanding adding nine new turbines in July bringing the total to 69." The noise lawsuit remains before the federal court in Oxford.

gemini-meta-kansas-city.text: Meta's data center in Kansas City, Missouri, opened in August 2025, a $1 billion investment in the state, inside the Golden Plains Technology Park in the city's Northland. The park sits at the southwest corner of Northwest 128th Street and U.S. Highway 169, spanning Platte and Clay counties on more than 760 acres, and Meta's local project company, Velvet Tech Services, has since bought the park from its developer, Diode Ventures. Kansas City Council approved up to $8.2 billion in tax incentives in 2021 for the park's full planned buildout of up to 5.5 million square feet in 16 buildings; the data center that opened in 2025 is the first phase, a single 601,955-square-foot building, with the incentive package covering further construction only if Meta builds later phases. Meta says the site supports more than 100 jobs now that it is operating, and that construction peaked at about 1,500 trade workers. The incentive deal runs through a payment-in-lieu-of-taxes program, or PILOT, in which the data center pays a set fee instead of standard property tax; PILOT money from Golden Plains and a second Diode project nearby, Rocky Branch Creek, will cover nearly a quarter of the $74 million cost of a new Northland Kansas City Career Center. The Smithville School District says Golden Plains revenue let it add 7.5% to its base staff salary schedule, according to Diode Ventures. The Northland is becoming a data center cluster: Rocky Branch Creek, a nearby 500-acre site, was rezoned in 2022 and sold to a hyperscale data center client in 2023, and Meta says its next generation of AI-optimized data centers, the first set to open in 2026, will be built for its AI work. The Kansas City Council, which approved the Golden Plains incentives, decides on any new data center incentives in the city.

gemini-aws-threemile-exascale.text: Amazon Web Services has proposed what would be Oregon's first exascale data center campus in Morrow County, on former grazing land near the Boardman Airport south of the Columbia River. Threemile Canyon Farms, the dairy operation that owned the land, filed a land use application with the county before Amazon bought the roughly 1,300 acre site in March 2026. The application describes 4 million square feet of data centers in 16 to 20 buildings, priced at $8 billion to $12 billion and drawing 1,000 megawatts of power. Pacific Power told the county it could serve the site using transmission lines already permitted for other data centers nearby. The application seeks access to 35 million gallons of water a year from the Port of Morrow, up to 1,300 gallons a minute at peak, in a county already fighting nitrate contamination in its drinking water from decades of large scale farming. “We can find 1,300 gallons per minute for an exascale data center? It just doesn't make sense,” said Kaleb Lay, policy director at Oregon Rural Action. Amazon already runs about 800 acres of data centers around Boardman, and Oregon's land conservation agency has counted 9,100 acres of new data center land moving through the pipeline statewide. Morrow County has approved more than $1 billion in tax breaks for other Amazon sites; this application has none yet, though it says Amazon would likely seek relief through the state's Strategic Investment Program. County commission chair David Sykes said he knew of no incentive discussions for the site. Amazon has confirmed the purchase and told GeekWire its “development plans are not final” as it carries out its normal due diligence. The land use application remains before Morrow County, which will decide whether to approve it.

gemini-aws-bwi.text: AWS BWI, an Amazon Web Services data center building at 5601 Manor Woods Rd in Frederick, Frederick County, Maryland, is under construction inside the Quantum Frederick data center park. The Maryland Department of the Environment approved an air permit for the building's 99 diesel backup generators on March 25, 2026, and barred the generators from running as a primary power source. "We heard the concerns of residents, and are confident that this permit protects air quality and public health," said Secretary of the Environment Serena McIlwain. The building sits inside Quantum Frederick, the county's biggest fight over data centers. County Executive Jessica Fitzwater rejected a $110 million community benefits deal from the developer, Quantum Maryland, on September 14, 2026, after residents told her they did not want more data center decisions made before a new county council took office. "So today, I am also extending the moratorium on data center applications until July 1st, 2027," Fitzwater said. The rejected deal would have paid for $30 million in Carroll Manor Elementary School renovations, a $40 million community center and $14.5 million for workforce training. Two weeks earlier, on September 1, 2026, the county announced Catellus had agreed to shrink its planned buildout of the Eastalco site from 18.3 million square feet to 15 million square feet. More than 21,000 residents had signed an earlier petition for a referendum on the county's data centers, though the Maryland Supreme Court struck it down as too unclear, and the issue is now central to Frederick County's 2026 elections.

gemini-core-scientific-marble-1.text: Core Scientific converted its cryptocurrency mine in Marble, Cherokee County, North Carolina, into a data center for artificial intelligence, inside a former American Thread Company mill that closed in 2015, taking hundreds of jobs and hundreds of thousands of dollars in annual taxes with it. The facility spans 250,000 square feet on about seven acres and uses as much electricity as a medium-sized town. Cherokee County commissioners and a public records request by Commissioner Ben Adams show the company's site plan included more than 170 diesel generators, most meant to provide backup power. C.B. McKinnon, president of the Marble Community Water System board, said the site draws a small amount of water from the rural utility and most of its supply from wells on site, which the state limits to 12 hours of pumping a day. Andrews Mayor James Reid said the town refused to connect the facility to its wastewater system because the company lacked an environmental plan, so it runs on septic tanks instead. "I wouldn't wish this on any county or entity, ever," Reid said. "It's absolutely destroyed Marble." The county received $268,000 in taxes from the Marble facility in 2024, its last full year of crypto mining, with revenue falling sharply last year during data center construction. Adams, who ran on an anti-crypto platform in 2022 and did not seek reelection, asked colleagues in January 2026 to renew an expired crypto-mining moratorium and extend it to AI data centers: "If we don't do something, our little peaceful town's going to turn into something else and people are going to come here looking to put stuff in our town." Commissioners took no action that night, and Adams has since reconvened the county planning board to look for ways to limit new data centers without adopting countywide zoning. Since January 2026, neighboring communities including Boone, Clyde, Swain County, Clay County and the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians have adopted temporary bans on new data centers, and a state bill introduced in April 2026 would scale back data center tax incentives and require companies to pay the full cost of their energy use. Decisions on further local limits rest with the Cherokee County Board of Commissioners, which Adams is pressing to take up a new ordinance.

amazon-aws-boardman-gar-swanson.text: Amazon Data Services' PDX109 data center, operating at 75242 Gar Swanson Road in Boardman, Morrow County, Oregon, draws 40 megawatts of power from its utility, Umatilla Electric Cooperative. Its diesel backup generators run under a state air quality permit that was due for renewal by August 1, 2026; no result has been published. In March 2026 Amazon agreed to pay $20.5 million, without admitting guilt, to settle its part of a lawsuit over nitrate-contaminated well water in the area. The permit, issued August 27, 2021, allows 112 diesel emergency generators rated at about 266 megawatts combined, far more power than the site actually draws, and bars the generators from selling power to the grid. In 2023 Amazon told regulators the site was limited to 40 megawatts from the grid and asked to add about 24 megawatts of on-site fuel cells until transmission lines are upgraded, pointing to the planned Boardman to Hemingway line from Idaho. Cooling water that evaporates at the site returns to farm fields more concentrated with nitrate that predates Amazon's arrival in the area, the Oregon Capital Chronicle reported. "Communities in Eastern Oregon have faced groundwater quality issues for decades, long before we opened our data centers," Amazon spokesperson Kylee Yonas said, denying the company caused the contamination. Plaintiff Michael Pearson, who learned in 2022 his well held more than four times the federal nitrate limit, said: "When we bought the place, they didn't say a darn thing about nitrate." The lawsuit continues against the Port of Morrow and other defendants, including Lamb Weston, Threemile Canyon Farms and Portland General Electric, with plaintiffs seeking a state-backed cleanup and health monitoring program.

amazon-aws-calvert-cliffs-lusby.text: Amazon Web Services withdrew its plan for a data center campus at the Calvert Cliffs nuclear plant in Lusby, Calvert County, Maryland, on August 4, 2026. The withdrawn plan, filed in May as the Calvert Technology Center, called for eight buildings across three campuses on land owned by Constellation Energy, and would have drawn up to 500 megawatts of power supplied by the nuclear plant next door. Residents learned of the plan from a job posting in February 2026, and a petition by resident Melissa Emmal gathered more than 10,000 signatures against it. In the June 23 primary, voters ousted all three county commissioners who had voted against pausing data center development. Six weeks later Amazon pulled out, calling it a business decision. "After careful evaluation, Amazon has decided not to move forward with the proposed site development in Calvert County at this time," the company said. On August 18, before a packed room, the county commissioners adopted a six-month moratorium under which no new data center site plans will be accepted. "This moratorium is a first step, but it cannot be the last," said Danielle Pak, vice president of Citizens for Calvert. On September 22, the outgoing board told staff to advertise a vote to extend the moratorium by two years at its December 15 meeting, the day the newly elected board is sworn in. Across Maryland, Prince George's County has a two-year hold, Harford County a ban with no time limit, and Frederick County a pause that now runs through July 1, 2027.
paragraphs: Amazon Web Services withdrew its plan for a data center campus at the Calvert Cliffs nuclear plant in Lusby, Calvert County, Maryland, on August 4, 2026. The withdrawn plan, filed in May as the Calvert Technology Center, called for eight buildings across three campuses on land owned by Constellation Energy, and would have drawn up to 500 megawatts of power supplied by the nuclear plant next door.

Residents learned of the plan from a job posting in February 2026, and a petition by resident Melissa Emmal gathered more than 10,000 signatures against it. In the June 23 primary, voters ousted all three county commissioners who had voted against pausing data center development.

Six weeks later Amazon pulled out, calling it a business decision. "After careful evaluation, Amazon has decided not to move forward with the proposed site development in Calvert County at this time," the company said.

On August 18, before a packed room, the county commissioners adopted a six-month moratorium under which no new data center site plans will be accepted. "This moratorium is a first step, but it cannot be the last," said Danielle Pak, vice president of Citizens for Calvert.

On September 22, the outgoing board told staff to advertise a vote to extend the moratorium by two years at its December 15 meeting, the day the newly elected board is sworn in. Across Maryland, Prince George's County has a two-year hold, Harford County a ban with no time limit, and Frederick County a pause that now runs through July 1, 2027.

oracle-oracle-west-jordan.text: Oracle's data center at 6136 West 10120 South in West Jordan, in Salt Lake County, Utah, has run since 2012 after a stop-start build that the state and city helped pay for. The Governor's Office of Economic Development board awarded a state tax rebate of more than $15 million, and the city added nearly $10 million through an economic development area that paid back part of the new property tax over several years to cover land and site work. Oracle broke ground in October 2008 on what it called the Utah Compute Center, a 179,000 square foot, 285 million dollar building promised with about 100 jobs at wages more than double the county median. The site sat idle for a year. Oracle stopped work in the spring of 2009 while it was buying Sun Microsystems, whose data centers in Colorado and Las Vegas gave it the option to buy capacity rather than build it, and state officials said the company had put the project on hold for a little while. Construction resumed in the spring of 2010 under the name Project Sequoia, and the building came online in 2012. In 2016 Oracle added a 40,000 square foot section, Cells 2.1 and 2.2, with a multi-level plenum cooling system that its structural engineers, Salas O'Brien, said cut energy and water use in the city's desert climate. State officials projected $73.6 million in new wages over 10 years and $50.4 million in new state revenue over 12. West Jordan went after a much larger data center four years later, on a different site. In August 2016 the city courted a project code-named Discus, widely taken to be Facebook, on 232 acres between 9000 South and Old Bingham Highway, which would have drawn 180 megawatts and about 5.3 million gallons of water a day. Salt Lake County Mayor Ben McAdams and the county council voted against the city's $250 million incentive offer, objecting to the tax breaks for 70 to 130 jobs and to a commitment of 4.8 million gallons of water a day, and the state school board capped its share at $100 million. A competing bid from Los Lunas, New Mexico offered a full property tax abatement for 30 years. The city still wants the industry. An economic development plan presented to the West Jordan City Council on June 24, 2025 lists data centers among the preferred uses for several of its redevelopment areas, while naming their heavy energy use as a weakness and finite resources and the city's dependence on Rocky Mountain Power and Dominion as threats.

apple-apple-ulanqab.text: Apple's data center in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, opened to store iCloud data for northern China, built in the big data zone of the city's Chahar Industrial Park. Apple signed the deal with Ulanqab at a ceremony in Hohhot in early February 2018, agreeing to build and run the center through a local company using 100 percent renewable energy. Ground broke on March 15, 2019, power was switched on that December 17, and the site now covers 101,012 square meters of buildings, generators and a diesel tank yard, fed by its own 110-kilovolt substation. The center exists because of China's cybersecurity law, which requires iCloud data for Chinese users to stay in the country; China Daily named the operator as Guizhou-Cloud Big Data, owned by the Guizhou provincial government, which also runs Apple's first Chinese data center in Guizhou. Apple handed Chinese iCloud accounts to the Guizhou company on February 28, 2018, and Reporters Without Borders urged journalists and bloggers to move their accounts out of the country or close them. "Apple promises that it will never give governments a backdoor to content, but there is no way of being sure about this," said Cedric Alviani, head of the group's East Asia bureau. Ulanqab calls itself the Grassland Cloud Valley; Huawei was already in the area when Apple arrived, and by 2022 the city had signed 17 data center companies to 26 projects worth about 73.2 billion yuan, including Alibaba, Kuaishou and Xpeng. The city sits less than 300 kilometers from Beijing and has an average annual temperature of 4.3 degrees Celsius.

neoclouds-coreweave-hammond.text: Hammond approved the largest economic development project in the city's history, and then watched the deadline pass. The city council approved the development agreement 8 to 0 in June 2025, for a data center at 301 Digital Crossroads Drive in Hammond, Lake County, Indiana, built to CoreWeave's specifications and expanding the company's existing presence at the campus. On July 1, 2026 the city announced that the agreement had expired. It bound four parties: the City of Hammond, the Hammond Redevelopment Commission, Decennial Group and CoreWeave. Certain milestones and obligations had to be met by June 30, 2026. They were not, and two extensions had already been granted. The city said no further extension would be offered, and did not say which milestones were missed. Mayor Thomas M. McDermott Jr. said: "While we are disappointed that the project did not move forward under the terms of this agreement, we appreciate the time and effort invested by all parties throughout the process." The city said it will keep looking for development at the site, which it calls one of the premier locations for large scale economic development in the Midwest.

neoclouds-core-scientific-pecos-cottonwo.text: Core Scientific's Cottonwood campus outside Pecos, in Reeves County, Texas, was built in 2022 to mine Bitcoin and is being converted into a data center for artificial intelligence. In April 2026 the company announced plans to grow the campus to about 1.5 gigawatts of power; about 300 megawatts currently mine Bitcoin, and the site already has several buildings and its own electrical substation. Core Scientific has also contracted a further 300 megawatts of power from its utility and secured more than 200 acres for the expansion, with the rest to come from generators built on site rather than drawn from the grid, what the industry calls power generated "behind the meter." "By expanding in a market where we already control power, infrastructure, and operations, we can execute with speed to meet market demand," said Adam Sullivan, the company's chief executive. Foundations for the first data hall are finished and precast concrete wall sections have begun arriving, with the first capacity expected online in early 2027. In July 2026, Core Scientific signed 15-year leases with chipmaker AMD covering 529 megawatts of AI computing capacity across its US sites, a deal the company said could bring in more than $14 billion in revenue. AMD directly leased 377 megawatts of that capacity at Core Scientific's Pecos and Hunt County, Texas, sites and its Muskogee, Oklahoma, site, and can reserve up to 1,925 megawatts more through the end of 2028. CoreWeave remains the company's largest tenant overall, and Core Scientific was billing customers for 437 megawatts across all its sites as of mid-July 2026. Microsoft is also building a much larger, roughly 2 gigawatt campus in Pecos, announced June 22, 2026, expected to employ more than 6,000 people at the peak of construction. "We are excited to welcome Microsoft to Pecos," said Reeves County Judge Leo Hung. "This investment reflects the strength of our region and its ability to support innovation at a global scale."

neoclouds-core-scientific-calvert-city.text: Core Scientific runs a data center in Calvert City, Marshall County, Kentucky, inside the former Gerdau steel rolling mill that closed in 2016. The company announced the site in November 2019 as a large-scale blockchain facility and named the Tennessee Valley Authority and Jackson Purchase Energy as partners in developing its power supply, with TVA's gas turbine plant on Ky. 1523 nearby. The Kentucky Lantern's July 2026 survey of the state's large data centers lists the campus as operating at 150 megawatts since 2019. Matthew Bishop, the company's chief administrative officer, told the Paducah Sun the site opened with about 30 employees on site and far more contractors, and that reliable electric power was one of the main reasons for choosing Calvert City. Josh Tubbs, president of Kentucky Lake Economic Development, called the project "a significant capital investment in our community." Kevin Turner, then chief executive, said: "We are investing in the infrastructure and software solutions that help our customers maximize the performance of their servers." Core Scientific now lists Calvert 1, 2 and 3 among the sites where it offers high-density colocation for artificial intelligence and enterprise customers. Riot Platforms runs a second, smaller data center near Calvert City, a 25-megawatt site it bought from another Bitcoin miner in 2024, according to the Kentucky Lantern's survey.

neoclouds-nscale-glomfjord.text: Nscale's Glomfjord data center, in the small industrial town of Glomfjord in Nordland, northern Norway, just above the Arctic Circle, is operating at 30 megawatts of power, and the company is expanding it to 60 megawatts. Nscale inherited the site from the cryptomining company Arkon Energy, which it was spun out of in 2024. In March 2025, Nscale and the modular builder InfraPartners announced a liquid-cooled 30 megawatt building next to the existing facility, built from modules made off-site. "With an existing 30MW site and access to an abundance of hydroelectric power, this expansion to 60MW allows us to provide sustainable AI compute with European data sovereignty at a more affordable cost compared with competitors," said Alex Sharp, then Nscale's chief operating officer. Nscale says the town of about 1,000 people grew up around a 120 megawatt hydropower plant built at the end of the fjord more than a century ago, and that the data center runs entirely on the region's hydropower with adiabatic cooling. The company says it is investing in local infrastructure and jobs and is looking at reusing the data center's heat, for example to warm the local swimming pool. Glomfjord is Nscale's first Norwegian site but no longer its largest; the company's biggest Nordland project, a data center campus for Microsoft near Narvik, was called one of Europe's biggest AI data center projects by TIME in June 2026.

neoclouds-nscale-korgen.text: Aker Nscale, the joint venture between the Norwegian industrial group Aker and the AI company Nscale, plans a 250 megawatt AI data center at Vesterli, just outside Korgen in Hemnes municipality, Nordland, Norway, near the Nedre Rossaga hydropower station. Hemnes council approved the detailed zoning plan on June 10, 2026, as case 34/2026, after the municipal executive board took it up on June 2. Hemnes put the plan out for public consultation on September 26, 2024, with a deadline for comments of November 28 and an open public meeting in between. The plan, drawn by Tom Langeid of the consultancy Multiconsult, sets aside land for a data center or other power intensive industry, and the documents on display included impact assessments for landscape, biodiversity, farmland and reindeer herding, plus noise, traffic, geotechnical and water and wastewater studies. The council added a condition that heat from the data center must be made available to warm buildings and businesses inside the plan area wherever technically possible, and that the developer must justify in writing any heat not used. The decision was published on June 22, 2026, with three weeks to appeal, to the municipality at Sentrumsveien 1 in Korgen. Rana Blad reported in October 2025 that the project is costed at around 100 billion kroner and that Aker is aiming to have it running in 2028, on the same scale as the campus the venture is building at Narvik (Kvandal). The site is still waiting for a power allocation from Statnett, the national grid operator, before large scale construction can begin. Nscale also runs a 30 megawatt data center at Glomfjord, expandable to 60, where it is looking to reuse waste heat, for example to warm the local swimming pool.

Hemnes council approved the detailed zoning plan on June 10, 2026, as case 34/2026, after the municipal executive board took it up on June 2.

Hemnes put the plan out for public consultation on September 26, 2024, with a deadline for comments of November 28 and an open public meeting in between. The plan, drawn by Tom Langeid of the consultancy Multiconsult, sets aside land for a data center or other power intensive industry, and the documents on display included impact assessments for landscape, biodiversity, farmland and reindeer herding, plus noise, traffic, geotechnical and water and wastewater studies.

The council added a condition that heat from the data center must be made available to warm buildings and businesses inside the plan area wherever technically possible, and that the developer must justify in writing any heat not used. The decision was published on June 22, 2026, with three weeks to appeal, to the municipality at Sentrumsveien 1 in Korgen.

Rana Blad reported in October 2025 that the project is costed at around 100 billion kroner and that Aker is aiming to have it running in 2028, on the same scale as the campus the venture is building at Narvik (Kvandal). The site is still waiting for a power allocation from Statnett, the national grid operator, before large scale construction can begin.
Nscale also runs a 30 megawatt data center at Glomfjord, expandable to 60, where it is looking to reuse waste heat, for example to warm the local swimming pool.

neoclouds-nscale-fauske.text: Aker Nscale, the joint venture of the British company Nscale and Kjell Inge Røkke's Aker, has bought land in Fauske, Nordland, in northern Norway, for a data center, DCD reported in November 2025. The site is the old Krokdalsmyra trotting track, which only ever served as a training track for a few years. It has a 13MW grid connection and would need more capacity from Statnett to grow; the company hopes to start work in 2026 and open some time in 2027. Nscale's chief executive, Alex Sharp, told NRK that Aker Nscale would invest 12 billion kroner in construction alone if all goes to plan. In 2018 Åsmyra Industripark AS agreed with Fauske municipality to buy the track for 6.5 million kroner, on the condition that data center business was developed there. Its owners included Odd Emil Ingebrigtsen, mayor of Bodø and a former Conservative minister, and Lasse Bang, who each held 36.5 percent. On August 15, 2025 they sold the company to Norsk Data AS for 20 million kroner, and later the same day Norsk Data sold it on to Nscale for 4 million euros, 46.7 million kroner at the time. Bang told E24 he knew Norsk Data would sell to Nscale but not at what price. On October 8 the shares passed into the new Aker Nscale, owned half each by Aker and Nscale. Fauske's contract gave the municipality a share of the proceeds if the land was sold out of Åsmyra, and in July 2025 the executive committee voted unanimously not to drop that clause. On October 16, 2025 the council, meeting behind closed doors, gave it up for 1.5 million kroner, bringing what Fauske has received for the land to 8 million. Councillors worked from the 20 million kroner figure and were not told the company had already been sold on to Nscale. Tom Erik Holteng, the municipal director, told E24 the municipality had not been informed of the share sale. The mayor, Marlen Rendall Berg of the Centre Party, said what was done was probably not illegal but was "rå business", raw business. Fauske, with just under 10,000 people, ended 2024 with a deficit of 16.1 million kroner. Aker has booked its half of Aker Nscale at 2.9 billion kroner, and the venture is also planning data centers in the Narvik area with OpenAI and Microsoft.

developers-qts-ashburn-broderick-drive.text: QTS's Ashburn 1 data center, known as ASH1 DC1, stands at 22271 Broderick Drive in Sterling, Loudoun County, Virginia, on a 28-acre campus the company says will hold two buildings. QTS lists more than 55 MW of critical power capacity in the Broderick Drive data center, and its site lists a second building, ASH1 DC2 at 22280 Randolph Drive, with more than 22.5 MW as coming online in the second quarter of 2026. The company markets the campus with liquid cooling available for high-demand workloads, and describes the buildings as LEED certified. QTS runs several other campuses nearby, including Ashburn-Moran on Moran Road in Sterling and larger Ashburn 2 and Ashburn 3 campuses. Loudoun County is home to 233 data centers, the largest concentration in the United States, and data center development has been an incredibly contentious issue there, NBC Washington reported. On September 15, 2026, the Loudoun County Board of Supervisors voted 7-1-1 to have staff draft a resolution pausing new data center applications for 12 months, with Leesburg's Kristen Umstattd voting no and Catoctin's Caleb Kershner abstaining. The pause would apply only to new applications, and the county attorney said an indefinite moratorium would not be legal. Residents have complained about health problems from living close to data centers, while the construction industry argued it needs the jobs. Others object to the high-voltage transmission lines the power demand brings near homes, schools and backyards. The Loudoun County Board of Supervisors still has to take a final vote on the resolution, and it was to take the matter up again on October 13, 2026. The pause covers new applications only, not facilities already operating, such as the Broderick Drive building.

developers-qts-glendale.text: QTS, the Blackstone-owned developer, is building its PHX 3 data center campus in the Glendale area of Maricopa County, Arizona, north of Camelback Road and west of the Loop 303 along Cotton Lane. The plans QTS filed with the city of Glendale call for 16 buildings of about 180,000 square feet each, nearly 3 million square feet in all, with 750 megawatts of critical capacity and a 29 acre substation. QTS put the campus at 375 acres, and bought the land in July 2022 for $255.3 million. AZBEX, which puts the site at 391 acres in the C|303 industrial park, reported that it lies next to the Allen Ranches community and that the buildings will go up in pairs, starting at the southern end of the property. QTS now lists several PHX 3 buildings, among them DC1 at 17408 W. Camelback Road, with Litchfield Park mailing addresses. The company says its closed-loop cooling needs only a one-time water fill and does not draw water for cooling after that. A QTS spokesperson said the company was investing in Arizona "as a long-term partner" and would keep working with local governments "to ensure growth is additive to the area." "We choose markets like Glendale because of access to a highly skilled and motivated workforce," the company said. On April 7, 2026 Governor Katie Hobbs visited QTS's data center campus in the Phoenix area to see its water-saving cooling and hear its commitment to pay for its own energy infrastructure. The louder argument in the Glendale area is over a different project: Project Baccara, a $36 billion data center with its own 700 megawatt gas power plant, one mile north of Luke Air Force Base, which Maricopa County supervisors approved with Supervisor Steve Gallardo voting no. The Glendale City Council unanimously approved a pre-annexation agreement for it, and the Project Baccara Opposition Coalition has spoken out against it. For QTS's own campus, the site plans for each phase go to the city of Glendale, where QTS first filed in early 2023. No organized opposition to PHX 3 itself has been reported; the most recent public event was the governor's visit in April 2026.

developers-qts-santa-clara.text: QTS operates a small data center campus on Mission College Boulevard in Santa Clara, Santa Clara County, California, in the heart of Silicon Valley. QTS lists the Santa Clara data center campus at 4 acres with several buildings and 7.5MW of critical power, and says it is LEED Silver and Energy Star certified with seismic protection for equipment. Santa Clara has more standalone data centers than any other California city, and the city-owned utility, Silicon Valley Power, has hit its limit. In 2025 the utility's chief operating officer, Nico Procos, said it had requests to add 500 megawatts of load on top of a peak of about 720, and Councilmember Karen Hardy said there would be no new data centers beyond those the utility had already approved. Two new data centers in the city, built by Digital Realty and Stack, stood finished but empty in late 2025 while they waited for power; the utility says its $450 million system upgrade is on schedule for 2028. "Have we overpromised and underdelivered?" Vice Mayor Kelly Cox asked at a November 2025 council meeting. City officials have also raised the land, water and diesel backup generators data centers use; the city says it receives $40.9 million a year from them. Silicon Valley Power's major spending comes before the Santa Clara City Council, which pressed the utility on the delays in November 2025, the most recent reporting on the question.

developers-vantage-warsaw.text: Vantage Data Centers' Warsaw campus sits in the Bielany district of Warsaw, Poland, on part of the grounds of the former Huta Warszawa steelworks. Built out, it will be two four-story buildings totaling 390,000 square feet and 48 megawatts of power; the campus opened to customers in June 2022, alongside the company's Berlin campus. It was Vantage's first facility in Poland, taking the company to five operating campuses across Europe, the Middle East and Africa, out of nine then in hand. "Launching new facilities in Berlin and Warsaw creates much-needed outlets for pent-up demand from companies desiring a local presence in these regions," said Antoine Boniface, Vantage's president for the region. Bielany expected more than a million zloty a year in tax from the campus. "I'm very happy that a campus with data centers has been built in the Bielany district. We need new technologies, and as a district office, we support this development," said Grzegorz Pietruczuk, the mayor of Bielany. Vantage says the site offers renewable energy options and cools with outside-air economization, using minimal water, and gives customers electric vehicle charging, workspaces and meeting rooms on site. No expansion or new phase at the Warsaw campus has been reported since it opened in 2022.

The plan calls for three buildings with 28,000 square meters of space on a 7-acre site, and 80 megawatts of power at full build. Vantage had set the first phase, 8 megawatts, for completion in the second quarter of 2024, a date that has now passed. A 2026 guide from a Japanese data center construction manager says Vantage's only site running in Japan is Osaka's KIX1, with the Sagamihara campus still in the planning stage. Vantage's own list of its Asia-Pacific locations includes Osaka but no Tokyo or Sagamihara site. Vantage has not said when construction on the Sagamihara campus will begin, and no updated timeline has been published since the 2024 target passed.

developers-vantage-cyberjaya-kul2.text: Vantage Data Centers' second Cyberjaya, Malaysia campus, known as KUL2, is under construction next to its first campus and will offer 436 megawatts of computing power on 52 acres once complete. Vantage announced KUL2 in May 2023 with a planned $3 billion investment and broke ground in August 2024; the first of its data centers was scheduled to open in the fourth quarter of 2025, and no result has been published. Vantage broke ground at a ceremony attended by Malaysia's investment, trade and industry minister, Tengku Zafrul Tengku Abdul Aziz, along with officials from the Malaysian Investment Development Authority, Cyberview and the utility Tenaga Nasional Berhad. "We warmly welcome Vantage Data Centers' plan to build an AI-ready data center at their KUL2 campus," the minister said at the groundbreaking. KUL2 will use a closed-loop chilled water system designed for near-zero water use, with its own substation on site. Next door, Vantage finished its first Cyberjaya campus, KUL1, in December 2025, when its fourth building, the 16-megawatt KUL14, opened fully leased to a single customer.

developers-vantage-atlanta-fayetteville.text: No Vantage data center has been reported on Highway 54 in Fayetteville, in Fayette County, Georgia, where trackers list a 1.7 million square foot Vantage campus; the campus on Highway 54 West belongs to QTS, which is building it on 612 acres at number 1435, bounded by the highway, Tyrone Road and Flat Creek Trail. Fayetteville council adopted the development agreement unanimously on June 15, 2023. "At buildout the property may encompass approximately 7,000,000 square feet of data center storage facilities, supporting office space and associated substations," it says. Every internal road, parking area, sidewalk, sign and piece of landscaping is private and maintained by the developer or an owners association, and all the utilities run underground. The argument in the county has been less about the buildings than about the poles needed to power them. Georgia Power is running new lines to the Highway 54 development on poles nearly 200 feet tall, across land in front of people's houses. "I can't live next to those power lines," said Judy Drohn, who lives along the route. Owners keep their land but give up easement rights and may plant only low growing vegetation in the strip; some were offered around $3,000 for several feet of property and say they had no say in the decision. Georgia Power said its experts spent months choosing the route, weighing safety, reliability, construction timing and community impact, that the alternative would have displaced people entirely, and that it was still negotiating terms with the owners affected. At its January 2026 work session the council passed a 90 day moratorium on new data center applications. "Because of the expansion of QTS, we held back on taking the data centers totally out of [unified development ordinance], and we are now asking for a moratorium because I think we can all agree we do not want anymore data centers in our community," city manager Ray Gibson said. Councilman Emmett Spurlock asked whether the moratorium could be extended if the rewritten ordinance was not ready, and city attorney Patrick Jaugstetter said an extension would need public notice and the usual zoning procedure. Fayetteville then rewrote the ordinance to take data centers out of the business center district, which amounted to a permanent ban inside the city limits. That puts it with Palmetto and Atlanta as the only Georgia cities to have banned them outright. Fayette County passed its own ordinance in December and has four data centers proposed; residents went to court in May 2026 over the approval of Project Sail.

developers2-cyrusone-talkington-township.text: CyrusOne's planned $500 million data center campus in Talkington Township, near Waverly in Sangamon County, Illinois, is now being fought in court. The Sangamon County Board approved it on April 7, 2026, by a vote of 17 to 10, letting CyrusOne build six one-story buildings of 250,000 square feet each on about 280 acres of farmland in the 13000 block of Thayer Road, a campus that would use about 600 megawatts once fully built. Waverly residents sued in July to overturn the approval. Sangamon Circuit Judge Adam Giganti set an October 9, 2026 hearing on the county's motion to dismiss the lawsuit. The plaintiffs, members of the Caruthers family, who have farmed in southwest Sangamon County for close to two centuries, and Cathy Bettis, owner of Joette Kennel, are asking the court to void the approval and grant an injunction against the project. The lawsuit describes "an industrial facility of extraordinary scale," with an electrical load of about 634 megawatts and about 420 diesel backup generators, and argues the project fails the county's 50-decibel property-line noise limit, that the application was incomplete, and that it needed a rezoning rather than a conditional-use permit in an agricultural district. The county's lawyers want the suit dismissed, arguing the county "proactively researched potential issues" before approving it. More than 60 people signed up to speak before the April vote, but comment was cut off after about a quarter of them had addressed the board, and some who shouted objections were escorted out. "Listen to the community," Maribel Cruz-Hine told the board. "Take more time for research." Board member Tracy Sheppard, who voted no, said "decisions of this magnitude must be made with full clarity." CyrusOne has not asked for local tax breaks and plans a closed-loop cooling system. The plaintiffs had until September 25 to respond to the county's motion, the county until October 2, and Judge Giganti hears the motion to dismiss on October 9, 2026. The project still needs other permits, including one for construction.

developers2-cloudhq-manassas-mcc1-mcc2.text: CloudHQ's MCC data center campus in Manassas, Prince William County, Virginia, includes the company's first two buildings there, MCC1 and MCC2, part of a seven-building campus planned for about 2.23 million square feet and 382 megawatts of computing power. MCC1 and MCC2 are both operating, and CloudHQ says 96 megawatts of capacity remains available to lease across the campus. CloudHQ says the next building, MCC5, already has its site plan in hand and is ready for construction, and that MCC7 was slated to break ground in mid-2025 for delivery in the third quarter of 2026, though it has not published an update on either building since. The MCC campus connects to CloudHQ's second Manassas campus, MDC, and to local and long-haul fiber routes. Prince William County adopted zoning limits on new data center rezonings on March 4, 2026, after the Virginia Court of Appeals voided the rezoning behind the county's separate Digital Gateway project near Manassas National Battlefield Park. That ruling does not affect the already-operating MCC campus, which sits within an area already zoned for data centers and needs only routine county site plan approval for further buildings, as MCC5 has already gotten.

developers2-cloudhq-ashburn-lc1.text: CloudHQ's LC1 building, the first on the company's LC data center campus in Ashburn, Loudoun County, Virginia, is operating; CloudHQ plans up to fourteen buildings on the campus for more than 1,700 megawatts of power in all, with two more, LC3 and LC4, now under construction. CloudHQ lists the full campus at 1,256 megawatts of total capacity, of which 756 megawatts remains available to lease, though it does not break out how much LC1 alone provides. CloudHQ was founded in 2016 by Hossein Fateh, the former co-founder and chief executive of DuPont Fabros Technology; in 2022 a company tied to CloudHQ sought to more than double allowed data center space on the nearby 96.8-acre Dulles Berry site, from 1,671,000 to about 4,050,000 square feet. Loudoun County has 233 data centers, the largest concentration in the country, and on September 15, 2026 its Board of Supervisors voted 7-1-1 to have staff draft a resolution pausing new data center applications for 12 months. The pause would only affect new applications, not buildings like LC1 that already operate, and the county attorney says an outright moratorium would not be legal. The Board of Supervisors was scheduled to take a final vote on the resolution on October 13, 2026.

developers2-cloudhq-paris-lisses.text: CloudHQ operates a data center campus called the CDG Campus in Lisses, in the Essonne department south of Paris, France. The developer's two buildings share 148.8 megawatts of power in the Leonard de Vinci business park, and the first phase was inaugurated in June 2025. CloudHQ says 74 of those megawatts are still available for new customers, meaning the second building is still filling up. The specific 13.7-hectare parcel sits at the edge of Lisses, bordering the neighboring commune of Vert-le-Grand, in the Les Folies development zone west of town. Two 225-kilovolt lines feed the site, one main and one backup, and regional officials capped the power RTE could deliver at 240 megawatts, or 120 per building. Ground was broken in late 2022, and the first stone was laid in July 2023 after four years of work among CloudHQ, local agencies and the town of Lisses, the Essonne chamber of commerce said. Waste heat from the campus will supply the Corbeil-Essonnes district heating system, warming as many as 7,000 homes. "This data center is a pride for our territory. It is exemplary both ecologically and in its ability to create synergies," said Michel Bisson, president of Grand Paris Sud. The chamber said 62,000 square meters there will become green space, with 800 trees planted. CloudHQ's own campus page still lists 74 of the site's 148.8 megawatts as available to lease, so the second building keeps filling rather than standing finished.

developers2-cloudhq-frankfurt-hattershei.text: CloudHQ's first Frankfurt-area data center campus sits on Lammerspieler Weg in Offenbach am Main, Germany, just southeast of Frankfurt; it holds two data center buildings of 56 megawatts each, 112 megawatts and 108,000 square meters of floor space in all, built at a cost of 1.1 billion euros. The site is about 8 kilometers from the DE-CIX internet exchange in Frankfurt, one of the world's busiest. Construction on the first building began in spring 2021, and CloudHQ's campus page says it entered service in 2023, powered by a new substation built on the grounds. developers2-cloudhq-sao-paulo-barueri.text: No CloudHQ data centre has been reported in Barueri, west of São Paulo; CloudHQ called its campus at Paulínia, in the Campinas metropolitan region, its first data centre in Brazil when construction began on March 1, 2023. That campus is planned at 288 megawatts of IT load in two phases of three 48 megawatt buildings, with the first phase due in the first half of 2024. Vice-President Geraldo Alckmin, who attended the start of work with Governor Tarcísio de Freitas, said construction alone would create almost a thousand jobs. JLL counts about 221 megawatts of data centres operating in Barueri and 64 more under construction, against about 410 operating and 285 under construction around Campinas. Barueri itself is crowded with other operators' buildings, and land and available power are running short closer in to the city, which is pushing smaller projects out toward Barueri and Osasco. About a third of Brazil's data centres are in São Paulo state, which went through an acute water crisis about a decade ago, and that history is why the arrival of more of them worries people there.

developers2-compass-raleigh-wake-county.text: Compass Datacenters' first data center is a 22,000-square-foot building inside Research Triangle Park in Durham, Durham County, North Carolina, completed in 2013 and leased by Windstream Hosted Solutions. Compass built it in six months, with 10,000 square feet of expandable raised floor, 2,500 kVA of utility capacity and 300 tons of cooling power, according to the company. Durham County has since tightened its rules for projects like this one: on August 24, 2026 the Board of County Commissioners voted 4-1 for a nine-month moratorium on new data center construction, exempting buildings under 100,000 square feet that use closed-loop cooling and non-diesel backup power. The county counts 14 confirmed data centers, most in Research Triangle Park, and only three are larger than 100,000 square feet; Commissioner Nida Allam voted no and won an amendment requiring builders to disclose their water use, fuel consumption and fuel source. "We do not want to be Loudon County, but that doesn't mean that every data center presents the same risk", said Ramsay Ritchie of the Durham Chamber of Commerce, which backed the exemptions. Resident Pablo Friedmann said the growth of data centers is "burdening the residential ratepayer". The county's nine-month pause is due to run to about May 2027, while the Board of County Commissioners and the joint city-county planning department write permanent data center rules.

developers2-compass-montreal-levis.text: Compass Datacenters owns a data center at 19701 Clark Graham Avenue in Baie-d'Urfe, Montreal, Quebec, that it acquired in 2019 when it bought the Montreal wholesale data center provider Root Data Center. Compass completed the Root purchase on July 23, 2019, its first acquisition after announcing a plan to develop up to $3 billion in new data center campuses; financial terms were not disclosed. Root operated two data centers in Montreal, known as MTL-R1 and MTL-R2, with combined capacity of about 65 megawatts of power once its MTL-R1 building finished expanding; Root said MTL-R2 was the largest wholesale data center in Canada. Root claimed its facilities exceeded Uptime Institute Tier III requirements, though the Uptime Institute had not certified them, Data Center Dynamics reported. "Montreal's ample fiber capacity and inexpensive supply of renewable power via Hydro-Quebec enables cloud/hyperscale companies to achieve their sustainability goals while also growing at the pace necessary to meet demand", said AJ Byers, Root's chief executive, who joined Compass as president, international. "With this acquisition, Compass immediately becomes one of the top three wholesale providers in Montreal and gains an experienced management team there that can enable continued expansion in the area and beyond", said Kelly Morgan, vice president of research at The 451 Group.

developers2-stack-johor-jhb01.text: STACK Infrastructure's JHB01 data center campus is planned for Iskandar Puteri in Johor Bahru, in the southern Malaysian state of Johor, about 10 minutes from the border crossing into Singapore. The developer announced the 220 megawatt campus in January 2025, its first in Malaysia, with two buildings totaling 1 million square feet on 10.8 hectares. The first building is a two-story, 120 megawatt data center, followed by a second 100 megawatt building; STACK scheduled initial delivery for the fourth quarter of 2026. The campus is to draw power from Malaysia's national grid operator, Tenaga Nasional Berhad, through an on-site substation connected to its high-voltage network. In August 2025, Malaysia's Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Tengku Zafrul Abdul Aziz said STACK planned to invest about 7 billion ringgit, roughly $1.66 billion, in the Johor project, though details were scarce, W.Media reported. "We are excited to bring STACK's proven expertise to Malaysia's rapidly growing data center market," said Preet Gona, CEO of STACK APAC. Johor has become a large data center hub as development spills over from nearby Singapore, with companies including AirTrunk, Equinix, Keppel, Yondr and NTT already operating sites in the area, four AirTrunk data centers within about 2 kilometers of the STACK site.

developers2-aligned-chicago-northlake.text: Aligned Data Centers runs an operating data center, ORD-01, at 505 Northwest Avenue in Northlake, Cook County, Illinois, the first building on the company's 18.5-acre Chicago-area campus. The building opened in 2022 with 220,000 square feet and 48 megawatts of power, expandable to 60 megawatts. Aligned broke ground the same week on a second building, ORD-02, aiming for more than 100 megawatts of power across 520,000 square feet. When construction began in 2021, Northlake Mayor Jeffrey Sherwin called it the city's third data center development: "Their success is our success." Aligned points to Illinois sales-tax exemptions for qualifying data centers as one reason it built in Northlake, but Gov. JB Pritzker has since used his executive authority to pause the state program that grants those breaks to developers. Aligned changed hands in July 2026, when a group made up of the AI Infrastructure Partnership, BlackRock's Global Infrastructure Partners and Abu Dhabi's MGX completed a $40 billion purchase of the Dallas-based company from Macquarie Asset Management, the largest data center deal on record. Chief executive Andrew Schaap and his team stayed on after the sale.

developers2-aligned-ashburn-iad-01.text: Aligned Data Centers runs an operating data center called IAD-01 at 21890 Uunet Drive in Ashburn, Loudoun County, Virginia, on a 26-acre campus it shares with a second building, IAD-02. Aligned says it built the site to handle heavy cloud and AI computing loads, with backup power that can run it without the electric grid. On September 15, 2026, the Loudoun County Board of Supervisors voted 7-1-1 to have staff draft a resolution pausing new data center applications for 12 months. Leesburg's Kristen Umstattd voted no and Catoctin's Caleb Kershner abstained; the county attorney said an indefinite moratorium would not be legal. The pause would apply only to new applications, not to IAD-01, which is already operating; Loudoun County has 233 data centers, the most of any county in the country. Residents have complained about health problems from living near data centers, while construction industry supporters say the projects are good for local employment, and some neighbors object to the high-voltage power lines the sites need near homes and schools. Aligned changed hands in July 2026, when a group made up of the AI Infrastructure Partnership, BlackRock's Global Infrastructure Partners and Abu Dhabi's MGX completed a $40 billion purchase of the Dallas-based company from Macquarie Asset Management, the largest data center deal on record. Chief executive Andrew Schaap and his team stayed on after the sale. The Board of Supervisors still has to take a final vote on the pause, expected in October 2026.

developers2-edgecore-mesa.text: EdgeCore Digital Infrastructure is shrinking its data center campus at the southwest corner of Elliot Road and Everton Terrace in Mesa, Maricopa County, Arizona, to make room for the utility Salt River Project (SRP) to expand its substation. In March 2026, Mesa's Planning and Zoning Board approved EdgeCore's request to cut the project by 800,000 square feet to 1.2 million, on its consent agenda with no debate. The revised plan is two buildings of 618,480 square feet each, down from three approved in 2024. EdgeCore, based in Denver, already had one data hall running and two more under construction in January 2024, when it secured $1.9 billion in financing for a campus it then described as more than 3.1 million square feet and 450 megawatts of power. No source has given a new power figure for the smaller, 1.2 million-square-foot plan. The site sits in the Eastmark community between an Apple data center and a Meta data center on Mesa's technology corridor. The March approval requires a noise study, limits generator testing to 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., and calls for murals and equipment screening before the buildings can open; city staff said no neighbors within 750 feet objected. Mesa has had 15 data centers built, approved or proposed on 1,500 acres in under a decade, and the City Council has since limited new ones to industrial land, a rule EdgeCore applied before. Nearby, residents are fighting a separate, unrelated NTT Global Data Centers campus proposed at Pecos and Crismon roads, citing water use and health concerns; that project still needs City Council approval. Gov. Katie Hobbs has called for ending Arizona's data center tax incentives, but Republican lawmakers have rejected the idea, the Mesa Tribune reported. What remains for EdgeCore's Mesa campus is meeting the March approval's conditions, including a Federal Aviation Administration review of every structure because the site is near Mesa Gateway Airport, before the city issues certificates of occupancy.

developers2-edgecore-reno-sparks.text: EdgeCore Digital Infrastructure is building a 216 megawatt data center campus on 56 acres along USA Parkway in the Tahoe-Reno Industrial Center at McCarran, Storey County, Nevada, about 250 miles from Silicon Valley. Construction began in August 2023, nearly five years after EdgeCore first planned the site, with NV Energy supplying power to an on-site substation. The company said completion was expected as early as late 2025; as of September 2026 its own site still describes the three buildings in the future tense, saying, "Upon completion, the campus will total nearly 1M sq ft of space." EdgeCore says the campus uses a closed loop, air-cooled system that needs almost no water, and it has given the Storey County Sheriff's Department radios and a search and rescue vehicle and supported county health and veterans' services. The industrial center already hosts or has land held by Switch, Google, Tract, Novva, Vantage, PowerHouse, Apple and Microsoft, and NV Energy's Greenlink transmission line, whose cost grew from an estimated $2.5 billion to $4.2 billion, ends at the Comstock Meadows Substation there. NV Energy has promised Switch, Novva and other companies up to 4,000 megawatts for data centers around Reno. Water is the bigger local worry: Storey County averages about 11 inches of rain a year, and the industrial center draws from the Truckee River, which also supplies the Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe downstream. The tribe and groups including the Water over Data Alliance have pushed back against new development in the corridor.

developers2-edgecore-culpeper.text: EdgeCore Digital Infrastructure, a Denver-based developer, is building a data center campus on 120 acres on Nalles Mill Road in the Culpeper Technology Zone in Culpeper County, Virginia, on land the county rezoned for data centers in December 2023. Virginia Business reported in April 2026 that construction had begun. EdgeCore says the campus will support 196 megawatts of power in two buildings totaling 920,000 square feet, with capacity available beginning in mid-2029. Cielo Digital Infrastructure first bought the land in 2023 and won the rezoning; EdgeCore bought the project in May 2024 and cut the plan from an earlier 216-megawatt, 432-megawatt-expandable design. Power is expected from Rappahannock Electric Cooperative in early 2028, and the Town of Culpeper will provide water and sewer. The company says it will use a closed-loop cooling system that needs almost no water, and the campus includes a 30-acre conservation area. The rezoning came with binding conditions: noise may not exceed 60 decibels at the property line, the main entrance must be on Nalles Mill Road, and the owner must set aside up to $300,000 for road improvements. "All the proffers are binding. I expect that the new owner will be doing exactly what was presented in the rezoning case," County Administrator John Egertson said when EdgeCore took over. The deal also promises up to $392,000 to county fire and rescue. In July 2026, residents urged the Board of Supervisors to keep the county rural and reject more data centers, citing power and water use, noise and electricity bills. "It felt like a personal insult to the community when our entire community is completely enraged by the data center development," said a resident identified only as Amanda. Supervisor Gary Deal said much of the opposition came from misinformation about the project. Two data centers already operate in the county, which expects seven more campuses in the 1,000-acre technology zone plus an approved Amazon campus nearby. The Board of Supervisors, which approved the Culpeper rezoning 5-2, is the body residents keep pressing, including on a proposed tax on data center computer equipment like the ones Loudoun and Prince William counties already charge.

developers2-edgecore-santa-clara.text: EdgeCore Digital Infrastructure opened the first building of its 72 megawatt Santa Clara data center campus, at the corner of Juliette Lane and Laurelwood Road in Santa Clara, Santa Clara County, California, in September 2025. The two-story SV01 offers 36 megawatts across 255,200 square feet; a second building is planned to bring the campus to its full 72 megawatts. "EdgeCore is setting the standard for how companies should conduct themselves in our community," Santa Clara Mayor Lisa Gillmor said at the opening. EdgeCore broke ground in January 2023 and said the campus uses a closed loop cooling system that needs almost no water. Santa Clara has more standalone data centers than any other California city, and the city-owned utility, Silicon Valley Power, told the city in 2025 it had requests to add 500 megawatts of load on top of a peak of about 720, chief operating officer Nico Procos said. Two other data centers in the city, built by Digital Realty and Stack, stood finished but empty in late 2025 waiting for power, and the utility's $450 million system upgrade is on schedule for 2028. "Have we overpromised and underdelivered?" Santa Clara Vice Mayor Kelly Cox asked at a November 2025 council meeting about Silicon Valley Power's spending. Councilmember Karen Hardy said the city has turned away proposed data centers because of grid limits and there will be no new ones beyond those Silicon Valley Power has already approved; the city says it collects $40.9 million a year from its existing data centers.

aligned-aligned-mink-street-etna.text: Pataskala City Council has blocked Aligned Data Centers' proposed 200-megawatt data center on Mink Street, an address in Etna Township that sits inside Pataskala's city limits in Licking County, Ohio. The company had said the three-building campus would bring more than 100 permanent jobs and more than $5 billion in investment. At a meeting that stretched more than three hours on Tuesday night, August 25, 2026, the council voted unanimously to accept the Planning and Zoning Commission's earlier 5-2 recommendation against the project. Council president Brandon Galik said the power plan was incomplete: "There was big concerns with the power alone. The design was incomplete. We didn't have the full design for the power." Galik said state regulators, not just the city, control decisions like this, citing what he called Ohio's siting board. Residents cited water use, land and the substations and transmission lines the site would need; one told a reporter, "My entire block will be destroyed." Holly Wenzinger said, "We don't have studies on the potential long-term effects of these facilities," and Brandyn Bernard objected to a four-story building "among the corn and wheat fields." The fight is not over: after residents gathered more than 500 signatures, Pataskala placed a ballot measure banning any future data center that draws more than twenty-five megawatts of power on the November 3, 2026, ballot. Pataskala's measure is one of nine local petitions, alongside Conneaut, Defiance, Granville, Oregon, Piqua, Sunbury, Trenton and Upper Sandusky, that mirror a statewide push by Conserve Ohio, which is aiming for a 2027 statewide ballot after missing a signature deadline in July. Pataskala voters decide the ban on November 3, 2026.

gemini-digital-realty-par8.text: PAR8 is a Digital Realty data center at 2 Avenue Marcel Cachin in La Courneuve, near Paris, France, and one of four connected data centers on the company's Paris Digital Park campus. It was announced in April 2020 by Interxion, a Digital Realty company, as a three-phase building with 9,600 square meters of equipped space and 19MW of power available to customers, the French trade site DCmag reported. Interxion said the whole campus would hold four data centers, about 40,000 square meters of equipped space and up to 85MW of customer power. It put the investment in PAR8 at about 207 million euros, not counting land and other shared site costs, and planned to open the first phase of about 3,200 square meters at the end of 2021. Interxion said the campus would draw on the network connections of its seven existing interconnected Paris data centers, including the nearby PAR7. Construction ran slightly late. In February 2022 the Irish general contractor Mercury said it had completed the first two phases of PAR8, after delays that DCmag put down to Covid and to a foreign contractor adapting to French practices and rules, and customers were already in the first two floors. A lightning protection contractor that worked on the building describes PAR8 as the flagship of the park with 76MW of IT power, a figure close to the 85MW Interxion gave for the whole campus rather than the 19MW it gave for PAR8. The later buildings, PAR9, PAR10 and PAR11, have opened in stages, and Digital Realty has dropped the Interxion brand since buying the Dutch company, Le Monde Informatique reported in May 2023. Digital Realty France chief executive Fabrice Coquio said about 20 percent of PAR10's 10,000 square meters had been fitted with a liquid cooling loop for high-performance computing, adding 8 to 9 percent to the building's construction cost. Digital Realty is now building a second large campus north of Paris. Work began in December 2025 on PAR15 at the Dugny Digital Hub, on a former French Air Force site, the first of three buildings there planned to total 176MW of IT capacity, DCD reported in May 2026. Digital Realty operates around a dozen other data centers across Paris.

research-teraco-bredell.text: Teraco's Bredell Campus in Ekurhuleni, east of Johannesburg, South Africa, holds the company's JB2 and JB4 data centers, with 64 megawatts of critical power load. In August 2025 Teraco, a Digital Realty company, completed the second phase of JB4, which it calls the largest standalone data center built in Africa; the 30 megawatt addition took JB4 to 50 megawatts of critical IT power load. Teraco broke ground on JB4 in November 2020 and completed its first phase in 2022, with 30,000 square meters of building, 8,000 square meters of data hall space and 19 megawatts of critical power load; work on the second phase started in July 2023. JB4 now has 80,000 square meters of building, 80 megawatts of utility power supply and 14 data halls totaling 17,000 square meters, according to the company. Each of the six new halls supports 5 megawatts of critical IT load, which Teraco says is a first in Africa, and the halls can run liquid-to-liquid cooling for direct-to-chip AI workloads. Teraco says JB4 uses a closed-loop chilled water system with free air cooling and zero water during ongoing cooling, "an important feature on a continent facing water scarcity and supply reliability." "South Africa has become the technology and data centre hub for sub-Saharan Africa, acting as a springboard for cloud, AI and content provision into Africa," said Teraco chief executive Jan Hnizdo. The campus sits in Ekurhuleni's Aerotropolis, alongside the R21 business corridor, with fiber links to Teraco's Isando Campus 20 kilometers away. Teraco's South African platform totals 189 megawatts of critical power load, including 70 megawatts at Isando, 53 megawatts in Cape Town and 2 megawatts in Durban. Digital Realty acquired a majority stake in Teraco in January 2022, in a deal valuing the company at about $3.5 billion.

blocked-cerrillos-2024-09-17.text: Google is trying again to build a data center in Cerrillos, in Chile's Santiago Metropolitan Region, after an environmental court blocked its first design in 2024. Its Chilean unit, Dataluna, asked Chile's environmental regulator on June 17, 2026 whether the new $200 million project must go through a full environmental review. The site is the same 23 hectare lot on Camino a Lonquen, on the Cerrillos and San Bernardo boundary near Avenida Lo Espejo, that Google first proposed in 2019. Two environmental groups, OLCA and Mosacat, say the new plan is not really new: it uses the same land, the same $200 million budget and the same link to the Chena electrical substation in San Bernardo. They want regulators to order a full environmental study rather than accept Dataluna's own filing, citing 44 backup generators rated at 120 megawatts and 63 air cooling units with undisclosed refrigerant. They also want the regulator to weigh possible effects on three wetlands within about 2 to 4 kilometers of the site. Google dropped its original design in September 2024, after Chile's Second Environmental Tribunal ruled that February that regulators had not shown the project would avoid harming the Santiago Central Aquifer, the water source its cooling system would have tapped at up to 169 liters a second.
