blocked-iver-buckinghamshire-2026-01-22.text: Greystoke's plan for a 90MW data center on the former Woodlands Park landfill site in Iver, Buckinghamshire, next to the M25 and off Slough Road, has been in the courts since the United Kingdom government overruled Buckinghamshire Council's refusal in July 2025. In January 2026 government lawyers conceded that the decision contained a "serious logical error" and that permission should be quashed, after the campaign groups Foxglove and Global Action Plan brought a legal challenge. In April 2026 Greystoke, which had kept contesting the case, accepted that its measures to limit the data center's environmental impact must be made binding through a contract with the council. The scheme is for up to 72,000 sqm in two buildings, each up to 18m high, on land south of Slough Road between junction 14 of the M40 and junction 15 of the M4. It is a cut-down version of a 163,000 sqm, three-building plan the Secretary of State refused in October 2023; Buckinghamshire Council refused the smaller scheme in 2024 on Green Belt grounds. Angela Rayner, then housing secretary, called the application in and gave the plans a green light, accepting that they would "materially alter" the character of the Green Belt land. The council received 63 letters of objection to the 2024 plan, including from MP Joy Morrissey and Ivers Parish Council. The campaigners argued that the Government's decision letter gave only one paragraph to the facility's power and environmental cost and that no Environmental Impact Assessment had been carried out. "The reasons given by the Secretary of State [Ms Rayner] for considering the development did not require an EIA were inadequate," the government's letter said. Greystoke director Anthony Crean has called the Green Belt a "theological" concept that blocks developments in areas he believes are suitable for data centers. "While we are very pleased to see renewable energy commitments introduced for Woodlands Park, at the end of the day the community is still having to tolerate being neighbours with Big Tech, without clarity on the need or utility of the development," said Oliver Hayes of Global Action Plan. The groups are calling for a mandatory Environmental Impact Assessment for every new data center and a moratorium until the Government decides how many are needed. The Government has conceded that its approval was flawed, and Greystoke has accepted that its environmental measures must be made binding through a contract with Buckinghamshire Council; the campaigners called it a precedent for data centre developers' green claims to be concrete and enforceable.

blocked-edinburgh-south-gyle-former-rbs-.text: Shelborn Drummond Ltd's appeal against Edinburgh's refusal of a data center of about 210 MW on the former Royal Bank of Scotland headquarters site at South Gyle cannot go forward until the developer produces a full Environmental Impact Assessment, the Scottish Government ruled in August 2026. City of Edinburgh Council councillors unanimously refused the hyperscale data center at 1 Redheughs Avenue, in the Edinburgh Park business district, in early February 2026, even though the council's planning officials had recommended approval in principle. Shelborn had until August 20, 2026, to say whether it would submit that assessment; if it did not respond, the Scottish Government's Planning and Environmental Appeals Division would no longer have to consider the appeal. The proposal, brought forward by landowner Shelborn Asset Management, was marketed as a "green" data center alongside wider works including a new public park, and the developer said it would be powered by renewable electricity and could supply waste heat to homes and offices at Edinburgh Park. Its peak electricity demand of 210 to 213 MW is equivalent to the combined annual household consumption of Glasgow and Edinburgh, and committee papers put projected annual emissions at about 200,000 tonnes, roughly 10% of the city's total. Councillors found it failed the tests for a green data center. "On power from renewable energy sources, we've been told there is something in place but we haven't been given the figures on this, we haven't been able to hear from the power providers," said Green councillor Alys Mumford, adding that there had been no pre-engagement with Scottish Water and no real detail about cooling. "So if this isn't a green data centre, which I believe it isn't, there are major issues with this proposal which can't be balanced out by that national consideration," Mumford said, also objecting that the plan would remove a quarter of the site's trees. "If you look at guidance on green data centres, who the hell knows?" said Conservative councillor Joanna Mowat. The campaign group Action to Protect Rural Scotland argued that running the site's backup generators at scale would equal "100,000 idling cars-worth of diesel" being burned, and the council's report found potential significant noise effects on nearby homes and offices. The Scottish Government's decision to require an assessment came as calls grew for a moratorium on data centers in Scotland, where 24 proposals are in various stages of planning. "We now need to see the Scottish Government make EIAs mandatory for all similar developments so that local authorities also have access to adequate information for their own decision making," said Kat Jones, director of Action to Protect Rural Scotland. The appeal is decided by the Scottish Government's Planning and Environmental Appeals Division. That decision had been expected in September 2026; whether Shelborn met the August 20 deadline to confirm it would submit the assessment, and the appeal's outcome, had not been published as of September 29, 2026.

blocked-montour-county-2026-02-10.text: Talen Energy's plan for a data center in Montour County, Pennsylvania, was stopped on February 10, 2026, when the three Montour County commissioners unanimously denied the company's request to rezone farmland in Anthony Township from agricultural to industrial. Talen says it still intends to build a data center in the county, and in 2026 it applied to add a 1,310-megawatt gas plant at its Montour power station, which state regulators say is meant in part for data center demand. Talen first asked in August 2025 to rezone about 1,300 acres near its Montour power plant, saying the change could support future development "which could include data centers." The land included a 100-acre parcel next to the Montour Preserve, a wildlife reserve, and the Middle Susquehanna Riverkeeper Association warned of harm to its ecology and to Chillisquaque Creek. Talen later dropped 25 acres in Derry Township from the request, and the Montour County Planning Commission voted against recommending it in November 2025. By the time of the February vote, the request the commissioners denied covered more than 800 acres, according to Inside Climate News. Opposition grew at every stage: commissioners received a petition against the rezoning with 3,000 signatures and letters from two school boards and several municipalities, and some of the more than 50 people at the vote wore red shirts reading "Say No! Industrial Zoning." Commission chair Rebecca Dressler said the claimed jobs, taxes and economic benefits "were presented in general terms, without binding commitments, guarantees, or quantified physical analysis," and that Talen had been sparse on water use, noise and land impact. Commissioner Scott Lynn said the company never explained why it could not use land already zoned industrial elsewhere in the county, and Ginny Kerslake of Food & Water Watch called the result a "David and Goliath" moment. Talen said the denial "allows us to take the time to listen, incorporate feedback from the Commissioners, engage with the community, and refine our plans so they reflect local priorities," and that it remains committed to "a path forward in Montour County." In June 2026 it told commissioners in a letter that it had applied to PJM to connect two new natural gas units within the footprint of its Montour plant in Derry Township, a request PJM is expected to validate through December 2026. Its affiliate Montour CT Project LLC has applied to the Department of Environmental Protection for an air permit for two turbines of about 655 megawatts each, with construction expected to begin in 2028 and operation in 2031. DEP took comments on the air permit through September 21, 2026; no hearing had been scheduled, but one can be requested. A future data center would still need rezoning, which goes first to the county Planning Commission for a recommendation and then to the Montour County Board of Commissioners for a final decision. The air permit decision rests with DEP's Northcentral Regional Office in Williamsport, and under Governor Josh Shapiro's data center executive order, DEP will not review permits for a data center until the developer has all local approvals.

blocked-gross-gerau-2026-02-10.text: The Groß-Gerau town council, in Hesse, Germany south of Frankfurt, voted 18 to 14 on February 3, 2026, against opening contract negotiations with Vantage Data Centers over a 174-megawatt data center campus in the Lausböhl industrial area. Vantage owns the roughly 14-hectare site near Dornberg station, a former vehicle depot, and had planned about 2.5 billion euros of investment in five buildings up to about 30 meters high. The CDU and Kombi-FWG voted in favor while the SPD, Greens, FDP, Free Voters and Left voted against, after a debate of nearly 90 minutes watched by more than 70 people. "The business model is one in which others would generate very high added value, but the tax revenue would not remain in Groß-Gerau," said SPD group leader Susanne Theisen-Canibol. "We're missing out on millions in tax revenue, we're missing out on a good investor," said CDU group leader Thomas Hlubek. Residents objected that the site lies in a fresh-air corridor; Wolfgang Zwer of the Lausböhl citizens' initiative said the group was not against data centers as such, only against one of this size. The local Greens called the plan a "noisy, ugly monstrosity that would have overshadowed everything else." Vantage said it would first process the decision and settle its next steps internally, and Mayor Jörg Rüddenklau said the town would seek talks on how the site, which Vantage still owns, could be developed for the town's benefit. Any new data center plan for the site would need a fresh agreement with the Groß-Gerau town council.

blocked-new-brunswick-jersey-sandford-re.text: The New Brunswick City Council voted unanimously on February 18, 2026 to block a proposed 27,000-square-foot data center at 100 Jersey Avenue in New Brunswick, Middlesex County, New Jersey, less than two weeks after the plan became public. The council amended the redevelopment plan for the Jersey-Sandford area to remove data centers as a permitted use and restore plans for a public park. The redevelopment area covers 22 acres of long-vacant industrial land along Jersey Avenue, from Sandford Street to Railroad Avenue. The city's planning director, Dan Dominguez, told the council the data center had been included to help carry the cost of redeveloping the site, and that administrators recommended restoring the park instead. Officials said the data center had not been finalized and would have needed Public Service Electric & Gas approval showing the utility needed it. The council voted 5-0 to amend the plan and again to adopt the ordinance. Residents, Rutgers students and civil rights leaders packed the meeting, with dozens left outside City Hall chanting. Several speakers tied the data center to rising electric bills, and some said they had learned about it only days before the vote. A Rutgers student named Lauren said the site, near homes and the campus, raised environmental justice concerns. "I'd like to thank the council for deciding to scrap what many people did not want in their neighborhoods," said Bruce Morgan, president of the New Brunswick Area Branch NAACP. What goes on the land now is housing, small business space and the park. The plan calls for apartment buildings totaling 660 units on the north side, 10% of them affordable, commercial use on the south side, and four acres of public park under an easement from the redeveloper. Residents pressed for 20% affordable housing; the city said it already exceeds its state obligations. Boca Raton, Florida-based Amzak Capital Management took control of the properties at 90, 100, 120 and 298 Jersey Avenue in September 2025 through a deed in lieu of foreclosure, after the previous owners failed to repay a $27.8 million note. Neither city officials nor Amzak have said who would lead the redevelopment, and no company has been named to build on the site. The owner still has to bring a site plan to the New Brunswick Planning Board, and there is no word yet on when construction might start.

The council amended the redevelopment plan for the Jersey-Sandford area to remove data centers as a permitted use and restore plans for a public park.

The redevelopment area covers 22 acres of long-vacant industrial land along Jersey Avenue, from Sandford Street to Railroad Avenue. The city's planning director, Dan Dominguez, told the council the data center had been included to help carry the cost of redeveloping the site, and that administrators recommended restoring the park instead. Officials said the data center had not been finalized and would have needed Public Service Electric & Gas approval showing the utility needed it. The council voted 5-0 to amend the plan and again to adopt the ordinance.

Residents, Rutgers students and civil rights leaders packed the meeting, with dozens left outside City Hall chanting. Several speakers tied the data center to rising electric bills, and some said they had learned about it only days before the vote. A Rutgers student named Lauren said the site, near homes and the campus, raised environmental justice concerns. "I'd like to thank the council for deciding to scrap what many people did not want in their neighborhoods," said Bruce Morgan, president of the New Brunswick Area Branch NAACP.

What goes on the land now is housing, small business space and the park. The plan calls for apartment buildings totaling 660 units on the north side, 10% of them affordable, commercial use on the south side, and four acres of public park under an easement from the redeveloper. Residents pressed for 20% affordable housing; the city said it already exceeds its state obligations.

Boca Raton, Florida-based Amzak Capital Management took control of the properties at 90, 100, 120 and 298 Jersey Avenue in September 2025 through a deed in lieu of foreclosure, after the previous owners failed to repay a $27.8 million note. Neither city officials nor Amzak have said who would lead the redevelopment, and no company has been named to build on the site. The owner still has to bring a site plan to the New Brunswick Planning Board, and there is no word yet on when construction might start.

blocked-san-marcos-2026-03.text: The vote came at 2.14 in the morning, after eight hours. San Marcos City Council voted 5 to 2 to refuse the land use change for a $1.5 billion data center on 200 acres at Francis Harris Lane, between San Marcos and New Braunfels, next to the Hays Energy power station. The applicant was Highlander SM One LLC. Hundreds of people demonstrated. 125 signed up for citizen comment and 57 more for the public hearing. Water was the argument. The Edwards Aquifer is under strain and officials warned that continued drought could trigger emergency measures. Hays County Judge Ruben Becerra proposed a moratorium on building permits for anything needing large amounts of water. Torrie Martin, a rancher next to the site, told the council: "You are either going to greatly harm your relationship with your community or you're going to buckle down and work with us and come up with an alternative which we are all willing and eager to help you on." Resident Melanie Babot asked the council what kind of city it wanted to be: "Is it one ... that values natural resources for people, not AI?" The developer could have refiled within six months. The city closed the door first. On June 16, 2026 the council voted 4 to 3 to define data centers in its zoning law and make them ineligible in every district in the city, citing water and energy being drawn away from the community. San Marcos became the first city in Texas to ban data centers outright, a test of how far local control goes.

blocked-olds-2026-03-06.text: The Alberta Utilities Commission has turned down the natural gas power plant that Synapse Real Estate Corp. needed for its planned AI data center campus in the town of Olds, Alberta, Canada, ruling on August 17, 2026 that the site was too close to the community. "The project is too close to the surrounding community, and Synapse failed to demonstrate any compelling justification for selecting that location," the commission said. "The site is simply not suitable for the proposed development." Synapse planned 10 data centers of 100 megawatts each, offering up to 1,000 megawatts of capacity, and an onsite gas plant of 1,400 megawatts, on 121 hectares in the town's northeast at Highway 2A and Highway 27. The company promised a $10 billion investment and 1,000 jobs in a town of about 10,000 people roughly 85 kilometers north of Calgary. The plan also included 1.8 gigawatts of emergency and backup diesel generation. The commission counted 3,200 megawatts of installed generation in all, including 600 emergency diesel generators. The site boundary was about 30 meters from the first row of homes across a residential road, and near shops, restaurants and hotels, with more than 700 residences within 800 meters, the commission found. About 1,500 parties applied to take part in the hearings and more than 900 were granted standing, far more than usual. Residents raised noise, pollution, home values, safety and strain on health care and emergency services. "There is no way they should have been placing a 1.4-gigawatt power plant right inside the boundaries of a small heritage town. It's blasphemy. It's monstrous," said resident Carol Edwards, who said she told Synapse CEO Jason van Gaal to move it five kilometers outside town. "I'm feeling sick about the lack of transparency, and then all of a sudden this is thrust on us," resident Rachel Sorenson said at an open house in February. Olds council had rezoned the land for light industrial use despite the objections, and the town saw the project as a boost to its tax base. Mayor Dan Daley said the land will stay industrial and the town will keep seeking industrial projects there, because its tax base is about 80 percent residential. A second company, Data District Inc., has bought land in Olds and is working with Invest Olds on early planning, but has filed no application. The commission decides only on power infrastructure; zoning and land use for data centers belong to the town, which says it has never received a development permit application from Synapse and would review one against its Land Use Bylaw.

blocked-indiantown-13820-silver-fox-rd-2.text: Project Silver Fox, a hyperscale data center planned on 606 acres in Indiantown, Florida, is back before residents after developers withdrew an earlier, smaller version of the plan in April 2026. Developers Panattoni Development Co. and Ferreira Construction held an open house on September 21, 2026, in this Martin County village, and Adam Kramer, a Panattoni managing partner, said they plan to sell the finished project to Crux AI, a joint venture between Google and the private equity firm Blackstone. Kramer described a 1-gigawatt campus, with the facility taking about 34 percent of the land and 66 percent left undeveloped, about 3,000 construction workers and 300 employees, and $44 million a year in local utility franchise taxes. He said cooling would run through a closed-loop system and that the facility would not rely on Indiantown's water supply. "We're very confident this is going to happen because we chose a site that is by right to build a data center here," Kramer said, and he told TCPalm his company would fight a moratorium. The land is the problem for many neighbors. Records WPTV obtained in March 2026 for the earlier 2-million-square-foot plan at 13820 Silver Fox Road showed that about 230 of the 606 acres are wetlands, and South Florida Water Management District officials found wood storks, sandhill cranes, gopher tortoise activity and a bald eagle's nest there. Matthew Schwartz of the South Florida Wildlands Association called it the wrong place for a data center: "These areas are rich in wildlife because they're in a very rural area." "I still hate the idea," said Carroll McAllister, who keeps cattle within three-quarters of a mile of the site. "It's the noise. It's the water. It's the light." Julie Roberts, whose family bought land nearby in 1918, said they live less than two miles from the site and have concerns "about the health, about the heat, about the noise level." Mayor Phyllis Waters Brown said she came for answers: "I am not for or against. I have an open mind." The developers say the next step is site plan review with village staff. The Village Council is expected to take the first of two required votes on a one-year data center moratorium in October 2026.

blocked-amlwch-anglesey-former-octel-sit.text: Anglesey County Council refused Carbon3.ai's plan to turn the former Octel chemical works at Amlwch Port, on the island of Anglesey in north Wales, United Kingdom, into an AI data center, in a decision notice dated April 20, 2026. The notice said: "Insufficient information has been submitted to demonstrate that the proposal will not harm the landscape, special designated sites, ecology, Welsh Water apparatus as well as the amenity of adjacent nearby residential properties." The 61-acre site used to produce bromine from seawater and has lain empty since it closed in 2004. Carbon3.ai applied in January 2026 for a change of use to reuse the existing buildings for what its consultant described as a "modern, energy-efficient AI centre, delivering a high-capacity, secure and low-carbon AI computing facility". The application gave no target capacity or opening date, and the site plan appeared to show a single data hall. The site has tax site status within the Anglesey Freeport, and the application pointed to the UK government's decision in November 2025 to name north Wales an AI Growth Zone. Little is known about how Carbon3.ai is funded; it appears to be a subsidiary of Valencia Energy, which runs power plants around the UK, and it claims a 4.5-gigawatt pipeline across a planned network of UK sites, DCD reported. The company has also announced a modular AI data center in Derbyshire. The council's concerns were the landscape, protected sites, ecology, Welsh Water's infrastructure on the site and the effect on neighbors, and it found the proposal conflicted with planning policy and technical advice. The decision rests with Anglesey County Council, the planning authority.

blocked-hazelmere-city-of-swan-2026-05.text: GreenSquareDC withdrew its application for a 120MW data center on Stirling Crescent in Hazelmere, in the City of Swan about 15km from central Perth, Western Australia, on May 14, 2026, days before a state development assessment panel was due to decide it. The City of Swan received 1,897 submissions on the plan, 1,836 of them objections, and the city's planning staff had recommended refusal because the backup diesel generators would be too loud. The day before the withdrawal, councillors voted 11-2 for Mayor Tania Richardson to speak against the proposal at the panel meeting on May 19. The roughly 15,000 sqm building was planned north of Stirling Crescent, south of the Helena River and east of the Helena River Steiner School, a kindergarten and primary school. A GreenSquareDC spokesperson said the site sits next to existing power infrastructure at the Guildford power terminal, so the facility could connect without new transmission corridors. It would have been the company's first data center in Western Australia; GreenSquareDC launched in October 2022 and was acquired by the Swiss private equity firm Partners Group in March 2025. "However, city staff cannot accept that the potential for noise exceedance by the operation of the data centre in an emergency back-up power scenario and its potential nuisance and adverse impact to the amenity of so broad a residential area should be tolerable," wrote Phillip Russell, the City of Swan's statutory planning manager. "It is approximately 40m from the river channel, adjacent to a conservation wetland, located on two Aboriginal heritage sites, next to a primary school and in close proximity to private residences," said Francesca Flynn, executive director of the Bibbul Ngarma Aboriginal Association. Residents also raised water demand, diesel storage and the short consultation period, and a petition signed by more than 1300 people led the city to extend the deadline for submissions to March 30. CEO Charles Penny wrote that the method used to assess generator noise was "unrealistic and impractical" and that the company still believed the development was "an appropriate use for this established industrial site in Hazelmere." Hasluck MP Tania Lawrence called the withdrawal "a major win off the back of community coming together." City of Swan councillor Sarah Howlett said she remained concerned that Western Australia classifies data centres as "warehouses" for land purposes. In September 2026, Business News reported that CDC Data Centres had unveiled plans for a separate 192-megawatt data centre in Hazelmere, its second planned development in the state.

City of Swan councillor Sarah Howlett said she remained concerned that Western Australia classifies data centres as "warehouses" for land purposes.

blocked-hanover-county-13074-mountain-rd.text: The Hanover County Board of Supervisors voted 4-3 on May 27, 2026 to deny Tract's rezoning request for the Mountain Road Technology Park, a 900 megawatt data center campus proposed on nearly 430 acres at 13074 Mountain Road and 12517 Winns Church Road in western Hanover County, Virginia. Tract, a Denver-based data center developer, had won a recommendation of approval from the county planning commission the month before. The site is a seven-parcel, mostly undeveloped and wooded assemblage. Tract asked to rezone it from agricultural to limited industrial, with a permit for substations. It lies near the former Tyson Foods processing plant and the Henrico County line. Most of it is owned by Henrico-based Marchetti Properties, with Tyson Foods and G. M. and Brenda Tribble owning other parcels. Tract planned five buildings and committed to air cooling or recirculating evaporative cooling. The campus would have drawn an average of 600,000 gallons of water a day from the county system, with a peak of 2 million gallons. A Dominion Energy spokesperson said the first phase would be energized toward the end of 2029. Tract projected $901 million in tax revenue for the county between 2025 and 2044, up to 350 direct jobs and 1,100 construction jobs, though a full build-out was not expected before 2036. To win votes it offered $15 million for a booster pump station and water storage tanks, $6 million for land conservation and parks, limits on commercial vehicle traffic, payment for sheriff's traffic control during construction, and yearly noise studies at its own expense if the planning director asked. More than 30 people spoke against the project during a two-hour hearing and eight spoke for it, the opponents citing the water supply and the environment and the supporters tax revenue and jobs. The opposition was organized by Friends of Hanover, a coalition formed in response to industrial development in the county. "A 'Yes' vote will put us squarely on the irreversible path to lose our rural county", resident Jane Kirchner, who moved to Hanover from Loudoun County, told the board. At the planning commission in April, the vote was 6-1, with Ashland Commissioner Alan Abbott saying: "I think having too many data centers when we don't know the impact of it is problematic". Beaverdam construction worker Simon Strong spoke for the project there: "They're a good thing for the tax revenue of the county." Board chair Sean Davis of the Henry district cast the deciding vote, joined by Faye Prichard of Ashland, Danielle Floyd of Chickahominy and Jeff Stoneman of Beaverdam. Sue Dibble of South Anna, where the site is, Ryan Hudson of Mechanicsville and Michael Herzberg of Cold Harbor voted in favor. "Good revenue doesn't make a bad project good, and bad revenue doesn't make a good project bad," Davis said. Stoneman said: "I do think the water concern is a valid issue here," and that Tract's water offer was welcome, "However, I don't know if it goes far enough to meet the needs." Prichard acknowledged that the residents' campaign played a role in the decision that blocked the project: "I don't think this many citizens coming forward to say, 'This is really something we don't want,' is something I have the ability to ignore". Dibble said the revised plan answered residents' concerns and would be "our first step in the implementation of the vision for the Route 33 corridor". It was the second large data center plan turned back in Hanover in 2026: a 400-acre HHHunt proposal near the Wyndham community was rejected by the planning commission in January and then withdrawn. By late June LS Power had withdrawn its zoning request for a 200-acre data center site at 10165 Old Ridge Road, near Kings Dominion, and the supervisors had unanimously restored the county's data center equipment tax at 45 cents per $100 of assessed value. Tract itself is under construction on a 1,200-acre campus near Ashland that won zoning approval in 2024. The next case is Iron Horse, a data center campus on about 78 acres off East Patrick Henry Road in the Beaverdam district, which the planning commission recommended for approval 5-2 in August 2026 over objections from Friends of Hanover. "It's turning it into a corridor right there, just like a small data center corridor a mile long with residential neighbors sandwiched in the middle," Friends of Hanover's Jennifer Corpus said in June of Iron Horse and the approved Hickory Hill Road tech park nearby. Corpus told VPM News on June 1, 2026 that she wants firmer rules: "We really would love to stop playing whack-a-mole with data centers and instead get a data center ordinance, policy and guardrails passed in Virginia". The final decision on Iron Horse, as on Mountain Road, rests with the Hanover County Board of Supervisors.

blocked-hoffman-estates-higgins-rd-and-r.text: Karis Critical withdrew its request to rezone the 186-acre Plum Farms property at Higgins Road and Route 59 in Hoffman Estates, Cook County, Illinois, for a data center on July 1, 2026, notifying the village after community backlash, and the Village Board's scheduled vote was called off. "We heard the feedback clearly, including the call for a more specific plan before any rezoning," Karis spokesman Patrick Skarr said, adding that any future proposal would come with the details the village and community need. Karis bought the land, the former Plum Farms site at the northwest corner of Route 59 and Higgins Road, for $45 million in early 2025; it had earlier been planned for more than 1,000 homes and commercial space. The request, filed through H.E. Holdings LLC, which Karis advises, sought to change the zoning from commercial mixed-use and traditional neighborhood to manufacturing, and residents were told there was no specific site plan. The site sits on the edge of the village, bordering South Barrington and Barrington Hills, which have no official say in Hoffman Estates' decisions. Residents packed a three-hour Plan Commission hearing on June 3, and the commission voted 4-2 to recommend against the rezoning, raising traffic, noise, light, air quality and water use, and the lack of any studies. "Nobody here is saying, 'Don't do a data center,' everyone's saying, 'Don't do it here,'" Barrington Hills resident Karen Trzaska said. Records obtained by opponents showed village staff talking with Karis about a data center some 18 months earlier, including a comfort letter Village Manager Eric Palm signed the day before Karis bought the land, pledging that staff would support "necessary zoning and development approvals for a data center project." "It just seems like we're doing all this for just for political theater," said Amanda Pollard of Barrington Hills, who organized neighbors and filed an Open Meetings Act complaint with the Illinois Attorney General's office. Mayor William McLeod said it is normal for staff to work with developers for months before projects reach the board, and that "just because the staff or the village manager express support for a development that does not mean the village Board will approve the development." Hoffman Estates already has two other data centers under construction in areas zoned for manufacturing, and Microsoft is developing two more nearby. Karis Critical had a similar data center plan turned down by Naperville's City Council in January 2026. With the request withdrawn, any new plan for the land would go back to the Hoffman Estates Plan Commission and then to the Village Board, which makes the decision. State Sen. Darby Hills of Barrington Hills has introduced Senate Bill 1050, which would bar data centers within 3 miles of another municipality's boundary without its written consent, and said it could move in the fall veto session. Gov. JB Pritzker paused state tax incentives for new data centers from July 1, 2026 and asked lawmakers to pass reforms in that session.

blocked-babenhausen-former-continental-a.text: STACK Infrastructure dropped its plan for a data center campus of up to three billion euros on the former Continental site in Babenhausen, in the Darmstadt-Dieburg district of Hesse, Germany, in early July 2026. The landowner, the auto supplier Aumovio, said the plans had to end with great regret because of a lengthy and uncertain process that prevented reliable delivery, Hessenschau reported. STACK had planned three buildings on the roughly 270,000-square-meter former Continental plant, plus space for smaller businesses, promising 150 to 200 direct jobs. The project stalled in the town parliament: in March the CDU and Free Voters majority declined to pass the resolution needed to start the zoning process, asking first for a letter of intent and guarantee payments from STACK. Their conditions covered alternative water cooling, the power supply and renewable energy, use of waste heat, noise and contributions to local infrastructure; they wanted cooling with drinking water ruled out by contract and the planned business area handed to the town. Mayor Dominik Stadler, an independent, blamed the CDU's demand for a 250 million euro guarantee, which he called unjustified and unlawful, saying politicians' behavior had given the impression a data center was not wanted in Babenhausen. Free Voters leader Wolfgang Heil insisted they were not saying no. Contracts with Aumovio had been due to be signed in April 2026, and in May a STACK representative, Rebecca Schulz, warned that competitors would not wait. Aumovio is now looking for a new investor and is preparing applications to the town so zoning resolutions can be passed for the site, leaving open whether and with whom the former Continental land will be developed. Those resolutions would go before the Babenhausen town parliament (Stadtverordnetenversammlung). Stadler won re-election in September 2026 with 66.12 percent of the vote against the CDU's Frank Zick, and begins a second term in January 2027.

blocked-eisenach-stockhausen-2026-07-02.text: Eisenach's city council, in Thuringia, Germany, voted 19 to 16 against the Blue Future technology park, a planned data center site of about 80 hectares of farmland near Stockhausen, at its July 1, 2026 session, backing a residents' petition to keep the land as farmland. The Leipzig developer FAB had wanted to prepare the site and sell it to a data center investor; after the vote, Mayor Christoph Ihling withdrew his own proposal for the next planning steps. The city had proposed designating 86 hectares between Stockhausen and Hotzelsroda as an industrial area next to an electrical substation, for one large or several smaller data center buildings up to 22 meters tall, though no investor or operator had been named and the land still had to be bought from its owners. The city said up to 150 jobs could be created; FAB claimed wider effects of up to 360 jobs. The residents' petition, with 432 valid signatures, opposed both the zoning plan and a change to the city's land-use plan, and SPD council member Jonny Kraft cited the large area to be sealed, the blocked fresh-air flow to the city, and the data center's water and power use. Hotzelsroda's mayor, Sabine Heep, said the benefits would go to international corporations while the burdens stayed local, and about 60 supporters of the petition protested on the market square before the vote. Ihling had argued the zoning plan would only test whether the land was suitable, not decide on construction; petition organizer Steffi Wiegand said she expects him to bring the proposal back and that the initiative will prepare for it. Whether a new zoning plan is drawn up and a development contract signed with FAB is for the Eisenach city council to decide.

Ihling had argued the zoning plan would only test whether the land was suitable, not decide on construction; petition organizer Steffi Wiegand said she expects him to bring the proposal back and that the initiative will prepare for it.

blocked-douglas-county-i-20-at-liberty-r.text: Douglas County commissioners voted 4-1 in July 2026 to reject EdgeConneX's plans for a 700-acre data center campus near Liberty Road and Interstate 20 outside Villa Rica, in Douglas County, Georgia, the second time in seven months they turned down a large data center on the property. District 1 Commissioner Henry Mitchell cast the only vote against denial, and the county's Planning and Zoning Commission had unanimously recommended against the plan. The applicant, East Village Dothan LLC, asked to change the land from Rural Places to Commerce Center in the county's growth plan, rezone it from residential agriculture to a planned unit development, and get special use permits for a substation and buildings over 50,000 square feet. The campus would have held six buildings, by the Sentinel's count (other outlets reported five), totaling 4.4 million square feet on land bordered by I-20, the Clinton Nature Preserve and Liberty and Suddeth roads, with part of it inside Villa Rica and in the Dog River Basin, which feeds the county's main water source. When the project first surfaced, in a regional impact filing, it called for 11 data center buildings totaling 6.2 million square feet and four warehouses. EdgeConneX said more than 570 acres would stay green space, with the campus itself on about 130 acres. The developer's representatives promised 200 to 300 permanent jobs. Planning and Zoning Manager Allison Duncan said the plan conflicted with the county's long-term growth plan and could hurt traffic, public safety, fire protection and water quality. “We do not feel that Commerce Center is compatible with the Dog River Basin character area,” she said, adding that staff believes the county risks overbuilding data centers. Unincorporated Douglas County already has about 2.5 million square feet of data center space in eight buildings, with 3.3 million more square feet being built and 3.1 million under review, not counting Douglasville. Eileen Roberts of Post Road played commissioners a recording of industrial whirring: “That’s what a data center sounds like,” she said. “That’s 365 days a year, 24/7.” “At what point do we stop saying yes to every proposal and decide that preserving our community is more important than continuing to industrialize it for outsider profit?” asked Ashley Rencher of Chapel Hill Road. Supporters argued for the revenue: “This is a good thing for the county,” said Donald Vaughn, who has lived on Liberty Road for 40 years. EdgeConneX's Todd Workman said the company runs 90 data centers in 20 countries: “Yeah, we’re going to generate a lot of tax revenue,” he said. The developer's attorney, Anamaria Meanes, asked for a deferral to address residents' concerns; commissioners voted instead. The fight is part of a wider one in west Georgia, following data center protests in neighboring Paulding and Haralson counties and an extended data center moratorium in Carroll County. EdgeConneX, founded in 2009 and owned by EQT, has partnered with TA Realty on a 324-megawatt campus in Atlanta. The land stays zoned residential agriculture, and any new try would need the Douglas County Board of Commissioners to change both the growth plan and the zoning. No new application or appeal has been filed since the July 2026 vote.

blocked-prince-william-county-dulles-clo.text: Prince William County's Board of County Supervisors voted 8-0 on July 7, 2026 to deny the comprehensive plan amendment for the Dulles South Innovation Center, a nearly 2,000-acre data center campus that Sanders Lane Assemblage I LLC put forward along Sanders Lane in the Gainesville District of Prince William County, Virginia. The data center project, also called Dulles Cloud South, would have allowed 43 million square feet of data centers near the Loudoun County border, and a unanimous denial is a rarity for data center proposals. The amendment would have changed the long-range land use of about 252 parcels on roughly 1,940 acres from agriculture and forestry to industrial and mixed-use, followed by a rezoning from agricultural to a planned business district. More than 60 landowners had joined their properties into the assemblage. Many told the board their once-rural neighborhoods had become riddled with traffic and that selling to data centers could help both them and the county. "Voting no today does not restore those protections; it simply prevents the county from studying one coordinated alternative," said Brian Dunbar, a property owner within the site, referring to the rural protections a previous board removed in 2022. County staff recommended denial, noting the land lies outside the county's Data Center Opportunity Zone Overlay District, and a staff report cited "substantial concerns regarding infrastructure adequacy, environmental and rural character impacts, and land use compatibility." About 100 people rallied outside the county government center in Woodbridge before the vote, joined by U.S. Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, who urged the board to "just say no," and state Sen. Danica Roem and Del. Josh Thomas. Elena Schlossberg of the Coalition to Protect Prince William County said the industry should pay for its own infrastructure, including the roughly 6,000 diesel generators the campus would have needed. "Forests, farms and empty space are not open land to fill with data centers," said Ashley Studholme of the Prince William Conservation Alliance. Gainesville District Supervisor George Stewart led the opposition on the board, first by objecting to the applicant's last-minute request for a deferral, which the board then turned down 7-1. "Prince William County is not a Formula 1 vehicle, and this board is not a pit crew," Stewart said. "We cannot pave over the headwaters for the Occoquan – 8 million people depend on that." Brentsville Supervisor Tom Gordy pointed to the strained grid: "Right now, we have data centers that are not operating because we cannot get power." Supervisor Kenny Boddye said the area deserves time to plan "without another mega proposal looming over their heads." The vote came less than a week after the nearby PW Digital Gateway data center complex ended when developers dropped their legal fight over it. Prince William is home to more than 40 data centers with dozens more on the way, and Roem said the two decisions "will have statewide ramifications." The denial ends this application: the board was deciding only whether to begin the comprehensive plan amendment, the first step before any rezoning or data center applications. Any new attempt to bring data centers to the Sanders Lane area would have to come back to the Prince William Board of County Supervisors, which has said it wants to plan the area's future through the county's 2040 Comprehensive Plan.

blocked-alixan-rovaltain-2026-07-10.text: A judge at the administrative court in Grenoble on July 10, 2026, froze the building permit for Sesterce's AI data center at the Rovaltain business park in Alixan, in the Drome department of Auvergne-Rhone-Alpes, France, next to the Valence TGV station. The mayor of Alixan had granted the permit on December 18, 2025, for a data center of 40 MW at first, with a possible extension to 80 MW. The judge found that a project of this size should have had an environmental impact study, and saw serious doubt that the local zoning plan allows the plant it needs on that plot. The judge noted that at full build the facility would need more than 60 megawatts of electrical power. Sesterce, a Marseille start-up in computing infrastructure, puts the investment at 450 million euros for the first phase and nearly 1.5 billion euros in the long run. The company says the site's power was set at 40 MW with state officials, with backup plant of 19.80 MW thermal in the first stage, below the thresholds that would require a full environmental authorization, and that the plan removes two gas boilers now on the site. The case was brought by the collective Assez Datacenters Rovaltain, made up of residents and groups including Les Amis de la Terre and Attac, which warned of noise and of higher temperatures within 200 meters of the site. The court accepted that Les Amis de la Terre France had standing to seek the freeze because the project could harm the environment. The regional employers' federation MEDEF Drome-Ardeche called the court fights a worrying obstacle to freedom of enterprise, a position Sesterce welcomed. On July 27, 2026, Sesterce said it was appealing to the Conseil d'Etat, and it has asked the government to declare the campus a project of major national interest under a May 2026 economic simplification law. The freeze does not cancel the permit; it holds until the Grenoble court rules on the permit's legality.

blocked-le-bourget-2026-07-28.text: Segro's planned data center at the former H&M warehouse in Le Bourget, Seine-Saint-Denis, France, remains blocked after the administrative court of Montreuil refused on July 28, 2026 to suspend the new mayor's withdrawal of its building permit. The judge found the plans included a building more than 23 meters high in its central section, breaking the height rules in the local plan, so the mayor had been obliged to withdraw the permit, actu.fr reported. The Segro data center would have converted a 3.7-hectare former industrial site into three technical buildings with 25,300 square meters of floor space, 33 backup diesel generators and a 75MW grid connection. Its expected consumption of about 526 GWh a year was more than three times the whole commune's consumption in 2019, DCmag reported from the environmental authority's review. That review, by the regional environmental authority (MRAe), questioned the use of R1234ze, a refrigerant in the PFAS family of forever chemicals, and why Segro planned to recover heat from only 12MW of the 75MW the site would use. The former mayor, Jean-Baptiste Borsali, granted the permit on March 13, 2026, pointing to the jobs and cheaper heat for the district network. Residents had campaigned for months against it, and a petition passed 18,000 signatures, more than the commune's population, warning of harm to nearby homes, schools and daycare centers. The newly elected mayor, Mehdi Nezzar, withdrew the permit on June 12, saying he refused to let Le Bourget become a place where heavy industrial infrastructure keeps piling up at the expense of residents' health, environment and quality of life, and that he rejected the project in its current form. The site would have been the 30th data center in Seine-Saint-Denis, where the state and the Île-de-France region are both pushing for more of them. Segro is also working on a 70MW data center in Val-de-Marne, southeast of Paris. The July ruling was an emergency decision on an application brought by Segro, and the judge did not rule on the merits of the case. The town says it will keep defending its position in the proceedings.

blocked-kota-damansara-section-9-2026-07.text: The planning application for a business data center in Section 9, Kota Damansara, Petaling Jaya, in Selangor, Malaysia, was withdrawn on July 28, 2026, after residents objected. Petaling Jaya City Council (MBPJ) said the project's consultant, acting for the unnamed developer, withdrew it so the developer could re-evaluate the site's feasibility. The Kota Damansara data center was to be two three-story blocks on 19 private lots and part of a government road reserve along Jalan Rimba Riang 9/6. The site is zoned for business and services and for transport under the Petaling Jaya Local Plan 2, and PlanMalaysia's 2024 guidelines require a 50-meter buffer between a data center and homes. Residents found out from a notice board with wrong reference numbers and contact details and only a week to object. "The deadline for objection was stated as July 15. I quickly alerted a local residents' coalition and we submitted a written objection the same day," said Mohd Razif Mohd Lazim, who spotted the board on a morning walk. MBPJ ordered the errors fixed and extended the feedback period to July 27, and had received about 290 formal objections by July 21. Gabungan Penduduk Kota Damansara, a coalition of more than 500 households, raised noise, round-the-clock operation, heat, high energy use near the Kota Damansara community forest, traffic and the use of government road reserve, and asked for the shops in the original plan instead. Sungai Buloh MP R. Ramanan, Kota Damansara assemblyman Muhammad Izuan Ahmad Kasim and councillor Muhamad Shazwan Suhaimi also objected, citing non-conformity and a lack of early engagement. "It was particularly concerning that all the representatives publicly stated that they had not been informed of the proposed project," coalition spokesperson Narindera Pall Singh said. Under the Town and Country Planning Act 1976, MBPJ has the authority to approve or reject such applications, and an aggrieved party can appeal to the Appeals Board. "The developer can still submit a fresh application in the future, as long as it complies with whatever is permitted under the local plan," outgoing Petaling Jaya mayor Mohamad Zahri Samingon said, adding that residents could again object. The coalition has asked the Selangor government and MBPJ to strengthen how the public is told about planned developments.
paragraphs: The planning application for a business data center in Section 9, Kota Damansara, Petaling Jaya, in Selangor, Malaysia, was withdrawn on July 28, 2026, after residents objected. Petaling Jaya City Council (MBPJ) said the project's consultant, acting for the unnamed developer, withdrew it so the developer could re-evaluate the site's feasibility.

The Kota Damansara data center was to be two three-story blocks on 19 private lots and part of a government road reserve along Jalan Rimba Riang 9/6. The site is zoned for business and services and for transport under the Petaling Jaya Local Plan 2, and PlanMalaysia's 2024 guidelines require a 50-meter buffer between a data center and homes.

Residents found out from a notice board with wrong reference numbers and contact details and only a week to object. "The deadline for objection was stated as July 15. I quickly alerted a local residents' coalition and we submitted a written objection the same day," said Mohd Razif Mohd Lazim, who spotted the board on a morning walk. MBPJ ordered the errors fixed and extended the feedback period to July 27, and had received about 290 formal objections by July 21. Gabungan Penduduk Kota Damansara, a coalition of more than 500 households, raised noise, round-the-clock operation, heat, high energy use near the Kota Damansara community forest, traffic and the use of government road reserve, and asked for the shops in the original plan instead. Sungai Buloh MP R. Ramanan, Kota Damansara assemblyman Muhammad Izuan Ahmad Kasim and councillor Muhamad Shazwan Suhaimi also objected, citing non-conformity and a lack of early engagement. "It was particularly concerning that all the representatives publicly stated that they had not been informed of the proposed project," coalition spokesperson Narindera Pall Singh said.

Under the Town and Country Planning Act 1976, MBPJ has the authority to approve or reject such applications, and an aggrieved party can appeal to the Appeals Board. "The developer can still submit a fresh application in the future, as long as it complies with whatever is permitted under the local plan," outgoing Petaling Jaya mayor Mohamad Zahri Samingon said, adding that residents could again object. The coalition has asked the Selangor government and MBPJ to strengthen how the public is told about planned developments.

blocked-salem-mill-creek-corporate-cente.text: This one was stopped by the governor, not the council. Oregon owned the land, and Tina Kotek ordered the state to pull out of the sale. The California company Verrus had contracted in May 2025 to buy 32.23 acres at the Mill Creek Corporate Center in southeast Salem for a $5.1 billion data center, with the sale due to close in October 2026 and 75 permanent jobs promised. Kotek announced the withdrawal on July 30, 2026: "This decision is about my responsibility to make sure state actions reflect Oregon's values and serve the public interest." She said she supports economic development, but "growth has to make sense for the community, for our infrastructure, and for our natural resources." Salem resident Brian Hines said the protests were the most intense and emotional the city had seen on any subject. Another resident, Hannah Shooting Bear, put the objection in terms of the state's reputation: "when you start bringing these data centers in, that's not gonna be clean and green anymore." Verrus said the decision was "made unilaterally and without consultation," before the company could present its design, infrastructure plan and community benefit proposals.

blocked-pinal-county-south-of-eloy-2026-.text: Mary Eileen Flanagan told the supervisors what the water situation already is where she lives: "Many of my neighbors' wells have gone dry and require additional depth." On August 26, 2026 the Pinal County Board of Supervisors voted 4 to 1 to reject the rezoning and development plans for the La Osa Energy Center, a data center campus proposed by Vermaland on about 3,300 acres outside Eloy. The scheme covered 11 data center buildings, a 500 megawatt natural gas plant and battery storage, against a total demand of 1 gigawatt, which the reporting compared to powering a large city. The revised proposal capped fresh water use at 600 acre-feet, roughly 200 million gallons, for the data centers and the gas plant together. On offsetting that, the developer committed only to considering the purchase of effluent water. The power did not add up either. The developers said they had secured 500 megawatts of natural gas, half the 1 gigawatt demand. Supervisor Jeffrey McClure doubted the rest could be found in solar: "My understanding is that's dedicated to some other companies." Robin Davis, from Hidden Valley, suggested the developers had asked for more than they wanted so they could settle for their real target. Mark Seidel, from Florence, told the board: "I don't want an incomplete and hastily built and ever-changing proposal." Pinal County has no zoning definition or development requirement for data centers at all, which left water limits, noise rules and energy protections to whatever the developer chose to offer.

blocked-travagliato-2026-09.text: East Gate withdrew its application for a 120 megawatt data center on a 130,000 square metre site outside Travagliato, in the Brescia province of Lombardy, Italy, and the withdrawal was reported on September 14, 2026. Mayor Renato Pasinetti said the municipality had asked for the environmental and grid data for ten months and never received it, and that the province would now have to shelve the grid connection request. East Gate, a Brescia company, had filed on land in Travagliato that had been buildable since 2011, and at 120 megawatts the center would have used about a billion kilowatt hours a year, as much as 300,000 homes. In July Pasinetti said he wanted to know who the end customer was, amid rumors of Amazon or Meta, and raised the health of residents, the water needed for cooling and the waste heat. More than 300 people demonstrated at the council meeting of July 22, 2026, interrupting it three times, and the Province of Brescia froze East Gate's grid connection request because no environmental assessment or technical specification had been filed. The proposal offered 11 million euros in compensation, which the municipality refused, and included 648 parking spaces. When the council said no in August, Pasinetti pointed to a newly formed company with share capital of only 10,000 euros, a grid connection request made without municipal authorization, and power figures that had shifted from 300 to 120 megawatts. Residents of Travagliato and neighboring Castegnato, Ospitaletto and Roncadelle had gathered 450 signatures to force an extraordinary council meeting. An online petition against the project gathered nearly 10,000 signatures, and the friction is regional, with recent protests against a 240 megawatt facility at nearby Magenta.

blocked-killala-2026-09-17.text: Ireland's planning appeals body, An Coimisiun Pleanala, has overturned Mayo County Council's permission for Mayo Data Hub Ltd's 50-megawatt data center outside Killala in north County Mayo, ruling in September 2026 that it breached national climate policy. Mayo Data Hub, part of the US firm Avaio Digital, had won permission from the council in April 2025 despite numerous objections, including one from the author Sally Rooney. The appeal was brought by Colin Doyle of Ennis, County Clare, who had raised concerns about greenhouse gas emissions, energy use and Ireland's net zero commitments. The 29,000 square metre facility would have included a data center, administrative buildings, electrical and mechanical plant rooms and 56 parking spaces on the outskirts of the town. Avaio Digital had put the investment at 1.5 billion euros, with 300 construction jobs and up to 35 permanent jobs, and chose north Mayo because its wind farms generate surplus power while the grid around Dublin's M50 is constrained. The company planned its own backup generators running on fossil gas and/or biodiesel. The commission found the applicant had not shown a fixed grid connection agreement, enough capacity in existing infrastructure, significant on-site renewable power or a corporate power purchase agreement with a renewable supplier. The ruling said the applicant had not shown the project would accord with the overarching objectives of the Climate Action Plan 2025, and called it premature without evidence that it could use locally generated renewable power. Rooney had argued the data center's power demands would add to the "catastrophic planetary crisis that is global warming". Aontu TD Paul Lawless welcomed the ruling, saying Ireland was being used as "Europe's data centre", while Minister Alan Dillon said, "People want to see good jobs within reach of where they live and opportunities for young people to build their futures locally." Data centers used 22 per cent of all electricity in Ireland in 2024, more than all urban homes combined, Lawless noted. The ruling can be challenged only by judicial review, which must be sought within eight weeks of the decision being formally published.

ft-1779305646902-5353.text: Stak Energy, an Alaska start-up, wants to build an AI data center on about a square mile of state land just off the Dalton Highway, some 25 miles south of the oil hub of Deadhorse on Alaska's North Slope. There are no towns or villages within 50 miles of the site except Deadhorse, whose population is oil workers living in camps. A new pipeline would bring North Slope natural gas to a power plant on site, and the project could ultimately produce up to three gigawatts for its own use. The lease covers a 715-acre plot. Of that, 640 acres would become a gravel pad, built up about 5 feet above the permafrost with an estimated 7 million cubic yards of gravel, according to Native Movement. Stak Energy was founded by Sparrow Mahoney, a graduate of Wasilla High School, the Anchorage Daily News reported. Mahoney previously worked in cryptocurrency, according to Alaska Public Media. The company recently hired John Boyle, Alaska's natural resources commissioner from 2023 to 2025, as chief strategy officer, and Jim Shine, a former state Department of Natural Resources official. State documents put the cost at $500 million; Boyle later said it would be more than $10 billion. Its power plant could use more than twice as much natural gas as urban Alaska uses for electricity and heating combined, the Anchorage Daily News reported. Stak says the North Slope's cold climate, with an average annual temperature of 12 degrees Fahrenheit, would let it cut water use by 90 percent or more compared with data centers elsewhere. The state estimates the project would employ 1,500 workers at peak construction and about 60 people permanently. The Alaska Department of Natural Resources' Division of Oil and Gas took public comment on Stak's lease application, extending the deadline to July 17, 2026. More than 500 comments came in, and fewer than a dozen supported the project, agency spokesperson Sean Clifton said. The Northern Alaska Environmental Center, the Alaska Public Interest Research Group and the Alaska chapter of Backcountry Hunters and Anglers all filed formal opposition. One commenter wrote simply, "No," adding, "You may build one in Canada though." Another wrote that the site's remoteness "pretty well leaves NIMBY out of the equation." Stak's chief strategy officer, John Boyle, said the vast majority of the comments were "form letters lacking substance other than reflecting an individual's point of view." Native Movement, a nonprofit with offices in Fairbanks and Anchorage that works on the unceded lands of the lower Tanana Dene and Dena'ina peoples, organized against the project. The group said the gravel pad would use roughly double the material regulators authorized for ConocoPhillips' Willow oil project, and warned of harm to permafrost, caribou migration and more than 200 species of migratory birds. "Alaska lands are not disposable and they are certainly not for sale," the group said. Native Movement also disputed the jobs figure, saying the roughly 60 permanent positions were unlikely to benefit local communities. "We have no clue what the long term impacts of such a project would be in this region, from permafrost melt, to caribou migration impacts, to water contamination," the group said. The department issued its preliminary decision to lease the land on May 12, 2026; that is not final approval, and no final decision on the lease had been reported by September.

ft-1779306105674-8821.text: Far North Digital, LLC is promoting the Prudhoe Bay Data Center, a proposed modular co-location data center at Prudhoe Bay, in Alaska's North Slope Borough, that would run on the oil field's stranded natural gas. The company says it would start with a 120-megawatt power plant, built to tier 3 to 4 standards, with room to expand later. The pitch rests on gas that has nowhere else to go. Alaska Gasline Development Corp. authors, quoted on the company's own site, wrote that more than 8 billion cubic feet of gas produced daily at Prudhoe Bay must be reinjected into the ground for lack of a way to ship it to market. Far North Digital says the site could generate enough electricity to power New York City for more than 90 days. ft-1771618379668-1750.text: Nebius, an AI cloud company, has its 300 megawatt BHM01 data center under construction in the Oxmoor Valley area of Birmingham, Jefferson County, Alabama, on the site of the former Regions Lakeshore Operations Center. Three lawsuits are trying to stop the project, and Jefferson County Circuit Judge Javan Patton Crayton has set March 8, 2027, for a hearing on whether to halt it permanently. Nebius plans two phases, 100 megawatts first and then 200 more, with full build-out by 2028, and expects to spend nearly $36 billion over 30 years on the campus. The company says the project will bring more than 100 jobs and an estimated $80 million for Birmingham city and Jefferson County schools. "This is 900 feet from my home. We didn't find out until February 9th," John Hilley said at an April protest outside City Hall. The Greater Birmingham Humane Society, which had planned an animal medical campus nearby, told the council that the noise studies data centers rely on discount the high frequencies and vibrations that animals hear. Patrick Anderson of the Southern Environmental Law Center warned that if all four of Nebius's backup diesel generators were modeled running, "it could be really hard for them to not show a violation." Birmingham gave public notice of a data center moratorium on December 16, 2025, and Nebius requested its permit on January 7, before the council approved a six-month moratorium on March 3 that exempted projects already in permitting. On June 9, 2026, the council voted 6-3 to adopt the city's first data center zoning rules, banning routine on-site gas and diesel generation and setting a 500-foot buffer from homes, but the rules do not apply to BHM01. Construction continues while the case moves forward, and the decision on BHM01 now rests with the March 8, 2027, hearing before Judge Crayton. Nebius spokesperson Leah Davis told WBHM in September that the company believes it "followed every legal and valid process."

ft-1769466294729-7743.text: A developer identified only as WHP is studying the Childersburg Industrial Park, a former World War II munitions and Manhattan Project site on the Coosa River in Talladega County, Alabama, for a $6 billion, 500-megawatt data center. Council members say they have been in talks with the group for 14 months, but as of July 2026 no deal had been signed and no offer to buy the property had been made. "There is no data center," Councilman Tommy Ivey said. Mayor Ken Wesson said the city has signed a purchase service agreement with the developer for 486 acres in the park, worth about $17 million, and that the project would use a glycol-based cooling system and could bring around 220 permanent jobs. He called it "an agreement in principle," pending the developer's own site assessment. The developer's representative, Joshua Harrelson, would not confirm a company name; Inside Climate News reported WHP may be Western Hospitality Partners. That company withdrew a $6 billion, 600-megawatt data center called Project Lincoln in Oldham County, Kentucky, in June 2026 after local opposition, and later filed for a smaller version nearby. In January 2026 Childersburg's council added a line to the park's zoning naming data centers a permitted use; Wesson said the site was already zoned for industrial use and a data center "would have been permitted anyway" without the change. The site's history worries residents. It was placed on the EPA's national priorities list for cleanup in 1987, and a 2023 Army Corps of Engineers report warned that without further work, "industrial workers may be exposed to contaminants" there. Hundreds have joined a Facebook group opposing the project, and resident Noah Beckham said people "just want them to listen and be transparent with us about the process." Any sale would need an ordinance passed by the Childersburg City Council, Wesson said: "the city has not sold any property to anybody as of yet, that would take an ordinance." The developer's feasibility and environmental studies were still under way as of the council's July 7, 2026 meeting.

ft-1783368725536-2775.text: Beacon Data Centers' Calvert Infrastructure Hub, a proposed 95-acre data center complex between Calvert and Mount Vernon in northern Mobile County, Alabama, drew residents to the Mobile County Commission again on July 28, 2026, where commissioners said they have no authority to stop it. Construction of the data center campus is slated to begin by the end of 2026, according to South Alabama Utilities. Beacon plans two data center buildings and supporting infrastructure on 95 acres of a 650-acre site between Highway 43 and Shepard House Road, leaving the rest as wooded buffer and open land, and puts the initial construction cost at $6 billion. The company says the first building is targeted for 2027, and that the campus would create up to 1,000 construction jobs and about 250 permanent jobs averaging $115,000 a year. Beacon, launched by investment firm Nadia Partners in March 2023, also has campuses planned in Alberta and New Brunswick, Texas and California. Commission President Connie Hudson said the county cannot prevent the project because it lacks home rule, does not issue the construction permits because the land is in an industrial zone, and has not been asked for tax abatements. At an earlier meeting on July 13, three women urged commissioners to stop the project over its power and water use, bears pushed into neighborhoods, higher local temperatures and harm to livestock. Cathy Odom told the commission she does not trust the county to act in residents' interests. "It just seems like it's a done deal, we can't do anything about it," she said. Gina Daniels of Mount Vernon said the county should press Beacon to invest in services such as an ambulance company and a full-time fire brigade. Terry Williams of Mount Vernon said he went to a community meeting expecting to hate the project and left thinking Beacon was operating more positively than earlier data centers. The utilities offered assurances. Donnie Cunningham of South Alabama Utilities said the campus would use roughly 7,500 gallons of water a day and that Beacon would pay for any water and sewer upgrades. How much water would cool the servers is not clear; Beacon says it will use a closed-loop system. Alabama Power's Erin Delaport said Beacon would pay to improve the local grid but did not say how much power the campus would use, adding that the utility will not sign a contract until an engineering study is done. Beacon told the Mobile Chamber and Commissioner Randall Dueitt it will not seek tax breaks, and the chamber said the county could expect $49 million and the county schools $50 million a year in taxes. The next decision point is Alabama Power's engineering study and power contract; the county commission says it has nothing to approve unless Beacon asks for tax abatements, which Beacon says it will not.

ft-1782768008253-2482.text: Sovereign Gazelle LLC, working with VoltCore, wants to build a 50-megawatt bitcoin mining data center on 15 acres at 369 Union Road outside Somerville, in southeast Morgan County, Alabama, near where State Roads 36 and 67 meet. Four homeowners would have to grant easements for 75-foot utility poles, and all have refused offers of cash, free internet for a year, a natural gas line and land restoration. "It just changes the entire environment right now. Right now, it's beautiful, it's peaceful, it's country setting," said Will Hutson, and his wife Lyndsey said, "This road isn't rated for heavy trucks, so it would tear up our road." "There are more rules if I wanted to put a chicken house on my property, than there are if I wanted to install a data center," said neighbor Brock Wilson. VoltCore said the center would not create noise pollution, raise power bills or draw on water resources, and would create 20 to 30 jobs. On June 23, 2026, the Morgan County Commission voted 4-0 for a 12-month moratorium on data centers in unincorporated Morgan County, which Chairman Ray Long called "a pause button" while the county studies the impacts. Joe Wheeler EMC's chief executive, Gene Kanikovsky, said the cooperative cannot refuse a member that meets its bylaws. Residents traced the owners: probate records show Texas-based Sovereign Global Solutions bought the land in August 2025 and moved it in May 2026 to Sovereign Gazelle, both tied to Kevin Mohan of Texas, and Sovereign Gazelle's agent is the man who had visited them for VoltCore. By August, Long said the county had no legal authority to stop the project and called the moratorium just words, while homeowners raised money for an environmental study.

ft-1777852614752-9350.text: NorthPoint Development, a Kansas City real estate company, wants to build a 1,008 megawatt data center on land in and around Wilsonville, in Shelby County, Alabama, off County Highway 61. Planning documents describe a 664 acre site with 14 buildings of 219,000 square feet each. NorthPoint holds a two year purchase option on about 687 acres from landowner Richard Cashio, reached in February 2025 and running to February 27, 2027, and as of September 2025 had filed no formal application with the town or county. The land lies along Lick Branch, a tributary of the Coosa River, about 2.5 miles from Alabama Power's Gaston plant; the project's projected peak demand of 1,008 megawatts is more than half the plant's 1,880 megawatt capacity. Town leaders have acknowledged gaps in water supply and fire protection for a project that size. More than 100 residents packed the Aug. 18, 2025 council meeting, many carrying signs reading "No Wilsonville Data Center," and residents packed a second meeting on Sept. 4. Former mayor Lee McCarty said the project would be "extremely detrimental to the community." Resident Renny Stanhope said, "All I know is, the people selling this land and the people brokering the deal, that's going to be their legacy, to potentially destroy a small town." Lifelong resident Alicia Towndrow told the council in September, "I know that this is agricultural land, it was zoned that for a reason. We want to keep it that way." Residents have also asked council members to pledge not to sign non-disclosure agreements; Mayor Ricky Morris says he has not signed one. Who decides depends on where the land lies: about a third is inside Wilsonville and the rest is unincorporated Shelby County land known as Fourmile. An annexation or rezoning request would go to the Wilsonville Town Council. Shelby County Manager Chad Scroggins said the county land is zoned agricultural, that a rezoning would be "very difficult," and that any proposal would get public advertising and comment periods. Neither NorthPoint nor Cashio has responded to reporters' requests for comment, and Mayor Morris has told residents, "When we have something to discuss, it will be on the agenda."

ft-1764304493710-2258.text: Serverfarm is building a $6.6 billion data center campus beside Johnson Regional Medical Center in Clarksville, Johnson County, Arkansas. Construction is underway on the first of four buildings, due for completion by January 2028, with a total of 432 megawatts of power. Residents are now petitioning for a public vote on the up to $55 billion in industrial revenue bonds, a type of tax-exempt bond issued by the city on the company's behalf, that the City Council authorized for it on July 30, 2026. The four phase-one buildings will need about 432 megawatts combined, against a peak demand of about 50 megawatts for the whole city utility. Because the utility's lines cannot carry that, the project includes a power island, a set of 40 on-site natural gas turbines that generate power for the campus itself. The utility's commitment letter provides up to 50,000 gallons of water a day at first, rising to 1.45 million gallons a day by July 2027. Many residents learned of the project only when a hillside next to the hospital was cleared in January 2026. "And then I just looked out the window and it was just, it was happening," said Karen Fawley, who watched it from her mother's hospital room. Resident Bryan Connerly told a July town hall, "I don't think I'm the only one that believes big corporations don't always keep their promises." The council's bond deal gives Serverfarm a 65% property tax break for up to 30 years through a payment-in-lieu-of-taxes agreement, or PILOT, under which the company pays the city a set amount instead of standard property taxes. It also pays $1 million each to the city, the county and the hospital. Resident Becky Kraft asked the council to wait: "Once you approve these bonds, we're committed, not only to phase one but to two and three as well." Organizers led by Heather Fresard are collecting signatures for a referendum on the bonds; each petition needs 291 valid signatures from Clarksville voters. On September 14 the council pulled an ordinance to set a special election because the signatures had not yet been certified. The Clarksville City Council meets next on October 12, when it could set a special election once the Johnson County clerk verifies the signatures.
