ft-1779972865110-6579.text: Conway's city council approved in April 2025 a memorandum of understanding with Forgelight Ventures LLC for a $1 billion, 300,000-square-foot data center on Lollie Road in southwest Conway, Faulkner County, Arkansas, for a Fortune 100 company it has not named. The memorandum promises about 50 jobs and a tax abatement of at least 65 percent for 30 years, with a high-voltage electric franchise fee set with Entergy Arkansas, and lets the company add more buildings on the same terms. Conway Corp is to build a pump station and pipeline from the Tupelo Bayou wastewater plant to supply cooling water, using treated wastewater rather than drinking water, and a pipeline to discharge blowdown water to the Arkansas River; Lollie Road will be moved. Jamie Gates of the Conway Development Corp. said in 2025: "Over the course of the next year, we have a lot of work to do. There will be a number of public milestones as we develop the necessary ordinances." A year later, residents packed a May 12, 2026 council meeting so full the city capped attendance at 80 people. Jeremy Rice, who lives about 500 feet from the site, said: "It has now been over a year since I stood at this podium asking questions about this project. To this day I still do not have real answers." Leia Morshedi of the Conway First Advisory Group asked: "What are we getting for this? How are we benefiting from this?" Emily Lane, a University of Central Arkansas professor, said: "Pre data center, this area has toxic air releases in the 98th percentile nationally." Mayor Bart Castleberry said the project remained speculative: "Economic conditions, the availability of power, etc. could cause the project to be delayed indefinitely." Conway Corp was still assessing whether it could supply enough water and electricity for a facility that size. Residents have also protested every other Saturday morning, including on May 16, 2026, over the tax incentives, the water and the power and the lack of information about any of them. Kris Mallory, who organized the May 16 protest, said the council had "passed this without the consent of citizens." As of the May 2026 meeting the project remained in the design phase, with no ordinances filed yet. No date has been set for the next council vote or for the ordinances Conway Development Corp promised.

ft-9.text: The Brightspeed data center at 214 South Denver Avenue in Russellville, Pope County, Arkansas, a former CenturyLink telecom building, went up for sale in April 2025 in a sale-leaseback deal, brokers Cushman & Wakefield and Sage Partners said. The two-story, 44,650-square-foot building was built in 2000 and offered with a 20-year lease covering the whole property, plus at least 20 more years of renewal options. The asking price was $4.5 million, and the lease would bring in about $360,000 a year in rent. The listing did not name the tenant, but images of the building point to CenturyLink, which rebranded its local phone business as Brightspeed after selling it, along with operations in 20 states including Arkansas, to Apollo Global Management in 2021. Brightspeed's own website says it has taken over CenturyLink's offerings in Russellville. The business traces back to the Oak Ridge Telephone Company, founded in 1930, and later passed through US West and Qwest before becoming CenturyLink and then Brightspeed.

ft-1777384607756-2066.text: Clean Cloud Energy, an Austin, Texas-based company, has proposed an 800-megawatt data center on a 753-acre site outside Sheridan, in Grant County, Arkansas, valued by county officials at $8 billion to $12 billion. County Judge Randy Pruitt told the Quorum Court in July 2026 that global developer EdgeConneX had signed a letter of intent for the project, and said the county had not begun negotiating with the company over taxes. Clean Cloud Energy first proposed a 500-megawatt data center and 400-megawatt solar farm a year earlier, estimated at $5 billion to $6 billion; the data center grew to 800 megawatts after the Arkansas Electric Cooperative Corp. secured more electrical capacity. The Quorum Court passed a resolution in October 2025 letting county leaders learn more about the plan, without finalizing any agreement, and residents protested outside the courthouse in Sheridan. "It's concerning. It's nerve-wracking in what it's going to do to our property values and our way of life," said Brody Channell, who lives near the proposed site. An advisory group Pruitt assembled, drawing on public surveys, wrote six conditions a company must meet to be considered for a tax abatement, a reduction in property taxes. "We don't want to see it, hear it or smell it," said Justice of the Peace Mike Nevens, one of the advisers. "We don't want it to ruin our water table, we don't want it to raise electric rates for our citizens, and we don't want it to ruin our internet." Meeting all six conditions qualifies a company for a 20% tax abatement. To reach the full 65% abatement allowed under the state's Act 9 bond law, the end user would have to pay the county close to $57 million up front, including $7.5 million to cut $1,000 off each property owner's taxes, plus $12.4 million a year afterward. Breaking the conditions would cost $1 million in fines and could void the abatement. "We want the public to know that there is going to be teeth in this agreement," Pruitt said. The county requires a closed-loop, air-chilled cooling system, and Pruitt said no Grant County official has signed a nondisclosure agreement. EdgeConneX's letter of intent gives it 120 days of due diligence, with an option for 30 more, and its representatives have visited the site and begun environmental tests. "But we have not negotiated with them at this point; it's just too early for that," Pruitt said.

ft-1771257815409-6897.text: Fortescue, the Australian mining and energy company, is weighing a data center on 158 acres at the northwest corner of State Route 85 and Patterson Road in Buckeye, in Maricopa County, Arizona, land it bought to make hydrogen. In March 2026 the Buckeye City Council voted to lift the conditions that had limited the site to hydrogen production, clearing the way for other heavy industrial uses, including a possible data center. No capacity has been disclosed. Nikola Corporation and its partner TC Energy bought the property in 2022 for a hydrogen plant to fuel Nikola's trucks, and Fortescue paid a reported $24 million for the project's assets in July 2023. Fortescue held a ceremonial groundbreaking in May 2024, but construction never began, and it called off the $550 million plant in the summer of 2025. In an October letter to the city, Fortescue's Christy McDonough pointed to the federal tax and spending law signed in July 2025, which she said tightens and speeds the phase-out of the clean energy tax credits that had supported renewable hydrogen. The company told the city it "is currently assessing multiple development options for the property, including a potential data center and other industrial developments." The applicant, Fortescue subsidiary Phoenix Hydrogen Hub LLC, has a site plan under review for an Arizona Public Service substation on the property, which city staff said would primarily serve an eventual data center campus. Fortescue's letter says a data center would draw water from on-site groundwater wells and treat wastewater on site rather than use city utilities. Nobody came to the neighborhood meeting in December 2025, and when the staff report was written the city had received no public comment for or against. Cepand Alizadeh of the Arizona Technology Council told the council, "The signs of a good tech company are ones that know how to pivot and they know how to read the tea leaves." Buckeye resident Sasha Diann Wootton started an online petition to halt approval of water-hungry data centers, which had fewer than 100 verified signatures. "We are on our own well and this could cause us thousands of dollars if we have to drill deeper and then no guarantee," one commenter wrote. A data center is a conditional use in the site's heavy industrial zoning, so it would need a conditional use permit from the Buckeye Planning and Zoning Commission and site plan approval. Expanding onto the surrounding 920 acres would need a general plan amendment and further rezoning from the Buckeye City Council, which has not set a hearing date.

ft-1773462534738-4516.text: Vintage Partners has dropped its data center plan for 63 acres at the southwest corner of Loop 202 and Lower Buckeye Road in Laveen, Phoenix, in Maricopa County, Arizona, after the city asked it to. The Scottsdale developer, through VP LB & 202 LLC, now proposes neighborhood commercial and retail uses on about 22.6 acres along Lower Buckeye Road and employment uses on the remaining 41.8 acres. Its latest filing, a public hearing draft dated August 31, 2026, would bar data centers on the site entirely. Vintage bought the land from the Arizona Department of Transportation, and it came with transmission lines and an electrical substation that made the site look well suited for a data center under how city staff then read the zoning. Partner Walter Crutchfield told the Phoenix Business Journal the company had spent a year and a half building toward the project and the site was "almost ready to switch on." Phoenix adopted new data center rules on July 2, 2025, after Mayor Kate Gallego called for ending tax incentives for data centers, and Crutchfield said those rules, plus changes to how projects wait in line for power, left Vintage responsible for grid upgrades as part of a user "cluster." Vintage filed a claim for the property's lost value; the city asked it to drop the claim and scrap the data center. The rules Phoenix's Planning Commission recommended defined data centers, required a utility's written "will-serve" letter before site plan approval, barred them within 300 feet of homes where ambient noise is already high, and kept them 2,640 feet from high capacity transit stations. Deputy City Manager Alan Stephenson said, "Any land within these centers and the village cores should be focused on creating a significant number of jobs or housing units." In its own filing, Vintage said it agreed to the new plan "following coordination with City Council and City staff" despite "the substantial financial impacts associated with a change in development direction." Phoenix rezonings go to the Laveen Village Planning Committee and the Planning Commission before a final vote by the Phoenix City Council, which has not yet scheduled a vote on the August 31, 2026 draft.

Phoenix adopted new data center rules on July 2, 2025, after Mayor Kate Gallego called for ending tax incentives for data centers, and Crutchfield said those rules, plus changes to how projects wait in line for power, left Vintage responsible for grid upgrades as part of a user "cluster." Vintage filed a claim for the property's lost value; the city asked it to drop the claim and scrap the data center.

The rules Phoenix's Planning Commission recommended defined data centers, required a utility's written "will-serve" letter before site plan approval, barred them within 300 feet of homes where ambient noise is already high, and kept them 2,640 feet from high capacity transit stations. Deputy City Manager Alan Stephenson said, "Any land within these centers and the village cores should be focused on creating a significant number of jobs or housing units."

In its own filing, Vintage said it agreed to the new plan "following coordination with City Council and City staff" despite "the substantial financial impacts associated with a change in development direction." Phoenix rezonings go to the Laveen Village Planning Committee and the Planning Commission before a final vote by the Phoenix City Council, which has not yet scheduled a vote on the August 31, 2026 draft.

ft-1768192510392-2116.text: The data center campus approved at Marana, in Pima County, Arizona, is the second home for a project Tucson turned away. Beale Infrastructure is the developer of both, working through a company called Humphrey's Peak Properties, LLC. In June 2025 the Pima County Board of Supervisors voted 3 to 2 to rezone a 290 acre parcel near the county fairgrounds, half a mile south of Interstate 10, and then 3 to 2 again to sell it to Humphrey's Peak Properties for nearly $21 million. The city of Tucson refused to annex that site in August, which the project needed for city water service. The county supervisors said plainly why they voted as they did. Steve Christy said that "as far as the county is concerned, from a business proposition, it's a good deal." Board chair Rex Scott said he supported it enthusiastically because of what it could do to the local economy, while acknowledging that most of the constituents who contacted him were against it. Jen Allen, voting no, warned that "data centers beget data centers" rather than bringing broader growth, and pointed to regrets voiced by California officials. Andres Cano, also against, said "We are not just building in the desert, we're building on a legacy." At that meeting the project's representatives declined to say how much water or power it would use. The Marana campus covers more than 600 acres across two properties. About 300 acres west of Interstate 10 on North Luckett Road belong to the Kai family trust, and 310 acres at 14990 West Hardin Road belong to the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. The town council approved the rezoning 6 to 0, with Councilmember Herb Kai recusing himself because his family owns the south parcel. The vote came on the night of Tuesday, January 6, 2026. More than 50 people spoke at the hearing, and the overflow crowd was sent to the Marana Police Department. Union workers held signs supporting the data center, which Arizona Public Media reported were provided by the developer. The application is filed under the name Luckett Road Project and was known internally as the Jaguar West Project. On power, the Arizona Daily Star reports 550 to 750 megawatts supplied by Trico Electric Cooperative. Arizona Public Media reports up to 750 megawatts per site and up to 1,500 megawatts across both parcels, from Trico and Tucson Electric Power. On water, the developer says the buildings will be air cooled with no potable water used for cooling, drawing about 40 acre feet a year against the roughly 2,000 acre feet the land currently uses as farmland. The company also projects nearly $1 million in one time impact fees, 4,200 construction jobs, 400 permanent jobs and about $15 million a year in taxes at full build. Opponents tried to put the rezoning to Marana's voters. On February 4, 2026, Arizonans for Responsible Development, a group sponsored by the advocacy organization Worker Power, filed two referendum petitions with about 2,800 signatures each, well over the number required. Worker Power then tried to withdraw them, and on February 18 the town rejected both, saying they did not include the legal description of the properties that Arizona law requires. Fremont Peak Properties, a Beale Infrastructure subsidiary, sued the town for refusing the withdrawal, and residents sued over the rejection. In May 2026 a Pima County judge upheld the town clerk on both counts, so Marana voters will not get a vote on the data center. "We're committed to continuing to fight for the people of Marana and for their right to have control over the future of the town," said Jackie McGuire, a Marana resident and plaintiff in the case, who said the ruling was disappointing.

ft-1764303051982-5528.text: Huntley LLC is evaluating a data center on roughly 500 acres of city-owned land southwest of Page near Highway 98, about two miles from Horseshoe Bend. Page approved a $7 million land-sale agreement in October 2025, but has not approved a final site, zoning, construction, utilities or water supply. The proposal has been described as a potential 1,000-megawatt campus; that is planned capacity, not power in use. Page residents filed a referendum petition with 405 hand-signed signatures after the land-sale vote. The city rejected it in December 2025 over defects in the signature sheets, so the ordinance did not go to a ballot. The neighboring LeChee Chapter of the Navajo Nation voted in February 2026 to oppose the sale, citing concern about water and the lack of consultation. Page says it has committed neither municipal water nor power to the project; Huntley must secure lawful supplies itself. The developer had described closed-loop cooling in 2025, but the city's current FAQ says no cooling method has been submitted or approved. The sale cannot close until zoning issues are resolved, and the agreement lets the city repurchase the land if the developer misses construction milestones. The next public meeting is a September 29, 2026, work session on proposed data-center zoning rules at City Hall, 697 Vista Avenue, at 5:30 p.m. The Planning and Zoning Commission will hold a public hearing October 6 at 5:30 p.m., followed by City Council on October 28 at the same time and place. Any site-specific rezoning would require separate hearings afterward.

ft-30.text: The Pinal County Board of Supervisors voted 4-1 on August 26, 2026 to reject the rezoning for the La Osa Energy Center, a data center campus that the Phoenix land developer Vermaland planned on more than 3,300 acres near Eloy, in Pinal County, Arizona. The vote blocked the project even after Vermaland cut its plan from 59 buildings and two gas-fired power plants to 11 buildings and one 500-megawatt gas plant, capped at 1 gigawatt of total energy demand, and offered new water and noise conditions. Supervisor Stephen Miller cast the only vote in favor. When Vermaland announced the project in the summer of 2025, it described La Osa as a $33 billion data center industrial park that would support up to 3 gigawatts of power and become the largest such development in the United States. Vermaland's chief executive, Kuldip Verma, said the company was building "the next generation of digital infrastructure," and a separate 1,700-acre part of its land had already received zoning for data centers, gas plants, battery storage and solar. A rural-to-industrial rezoning ordinance for La Osa was proposed in April 2026, and the county's Planning and Zoning Commission approved an earlier, larger version of the plan; by the August 26 vote the project had been cut to 11 buildings, a 500-megawatt natural gas plant and battery storage. Robin Davis, who lives in Hidden Valley, said she thought the reduction was "probably planned all along. Ask for more than you want and settle for what you really wanted." Mark Seidel of Florence told the board, "I don't want stipulations that are unenforceable or not enforced. I don't want promises from a lawyer or seller that have no meaning after the sale." Between the May hearing and the vote, Vermaland added 22 development conditions, including a 600 acre-foot yearly cap on fresh water use, close to 200 million gallons. Antonio Ramirez of Rural Arizona Engagement raised the closed loop cooling system: "There's also water quality issues because the closed loop systems use PFAS, and if that water is injected back into the ground, groundwater system, then that could contaminate other people's water supply." Mary Eileen Flanagan, an area resident, said the aquifer already suffers from overdrawing and land subsidence. Vermaland's Robert Clang told the board the developer had secured 500 megawatts of natural gas from a broker and the turbines for the plant, and would try to get the rest from nearby solar farms or the Palo Verde nuclear plant, more than 100 miles away. Supervisor Jeffrey McClure doubted it: "My understanding is that's dedicated to some other companies." At an August 13 special session, planning commissioners Robert Klob and Gary Pranzo said they did not know enough about the county's energy picture to recommend large data centers. "Are we robbing resources from residential? Who's going to take precedent if we have power failure or not enough power?" Pranzo asked. Planning commissioner Karen Mooney said the county had received incomplete information and inaccurate job and economic figures in the earlier applications: "Nothing was mentioned about the data center, and data centers hadn't come here yet." Union members spoke in favor, pointing to construction jobs; Bill Ruiz of the Workforce Arizona Council said the project would provide "hard hats that [are] going to pay the bills here." Supervisor Stephen Miller, who cast the only vote for the project, said, "Individuals have a right to use their property the way they want. I really truly believe that all the negativity on these data centers has been from our adversaries around the world." Pinal County's zoning code has no definition of a data center and no rules written for one; every water, noise and energy limit in the La Osa plan was offered by Vermaland rather than required by the county. Any new data center plan on the site would have to go back before the five county supervisors, and residents are pressing the county to write data center rules before it considers another proposal.

ft-31.text: Arizona Land Consulting's Hassayampa Ranch data center, a campus of up to 1.5 gigawatts (1,500 megawatts of power) planned on about 2,000 acres of desert near Tonopah in Maricopa County, Arizona, was approved for a second time by the county Board of Supervisors on April 8, 2026. The supervisors had already voted unanimously on December 10, 2025 to allow industrial use on the land, and no end user has been named for the site. Developer Anita Verma-Lallian told Data Center Dynamics the campus could cost $25 billion at full build out, though she said estimates were hard to give before planning and design. Neighbors fought the December change: two adjacent landowners spoke against it and two petitions carried about 100 signatures from Tonopah and Buckeye residents, citing air and noise pollution, property values and water use in a community that depends on groundwater. Water attorney Michele Van Quathem said the project would likely partner with Global Water Resources or that the tenant could supply its own water, and that water sources must comply with Arizona's groundwater laws for the Phoenix Active Management Area. Tonopah resident Tonya Pearsall said her main concern is water because everyone there is on wells, and neighbor Cherisse Campbell, who raises turkeys next door, gathered nearly 200 signatures over light and noise pollution and traffic. Buckeye city staff and the White Tank Mountains Conservancy first opposed the change over a wildlife corridor along Jackrabbit Wash and the Hassayampa River, and the city withdrew its objection after the developer agreed to work with it and the Arizona Game and Fish Department on wildlife movement. By April, former opponents including neighbors Ron and Kathy Fletcher wrote in support, citing buffer zones and limited-use designations, and several who had opposed the project spoke in favor at the hearing. The April approval lets Arizona Land Consulting move to a detailed zoning application and site plans, and neighbors will get another chance to weigh in during that site-plan review.

Neighbors fought the December change: two adjacent landowners spoke against it and two petitions carried about 100 signatures from Tonopah and Buckeye residents, citing air and noise pollution, property values and water use in a community that depends on groundwater.

Water attorney Michele Van Quathem said the project would likely partner with Global Water Resources or that the tenant could supply its own water, and that water sources must comply with Arizona's groundwater laws for the Phoenix Active Management Area.

Tonopah resident Tonya Pearsall said her main concern is water because everyone there is on wells, and neighbor Cherisse Campbell, who raises turkeys next door, gathered nearly 200 signatures over light and noise pollution and traffic.

Buckeye city staff and the White Tank Mountains Conservancy first opposed the change over a wildlife corridor along Jackrabbit Wash and the Hassayampa River, and the city withdrew its objection after the developer agreed to work with it and the Arizona Game and Fish Department on wildlife movement.

By April, former opponents including neighbors Ron and Kathy Fletcher wrote in support, citing buffer zones and limited-use designations, and several who had opposed the project spoke in favor at the hearing.
The April approval lets Arizona Land Consulting move to a detailed zoning application and site plans, and neighbors will get another chance to weigh in during that site-plan review.

ft-33.text: The U.S. Air Force is offering about 300 acres on the west side of Davis-Monthan Air Force Base in Tucson, Pima County, Arizona, for a private company to build a data center, one of five military bases it put up for lease in October 2025. Proposals were due November 14, 2025, and the Air Force has not named a developer since. The site borders a Tucson Electric Power plant, and the base pumps its own well water rather than drawing from the city. The same lease offer covers Arnold Air Force Base in Tennessee, Edwards in California, Joint Base McGuire-Dix-Lakehurst in New Jersey and Robins in Georgia. Under President Trump's executive order on federal data center permitting, each project must involve at least $500 million in spending and clear the federal size threshold for a data center. Applicants must bring their own water and power supply, and the Air Force did not say where either would come from. Environmental surveys would be paid for by whichever company wins the lease. Because the base supplies its own water, the Tucson City Council's refusal to supply water to the nearby Project Blue data center may not apply here, though state regulators could weigh in if pumping affects the city's supply. "We'll need to review the details coming up, but our stance has always been not one drop for data," said Vivek Bharathan of the No Desert Data Center Coalition, which is also fighting Project Blue nearby. "No matter where these things are built, you'll see our community show up," Bharathan said.

ft-35.text: The data center once planned at the Guadalupe Quarry on San Bruno Mountain in Brisbane, San Mateo County, California, has been dropped: developer Orchard Partners now says its renamed Quarry Innovation Center "is intended to be 100% Advanced Manufacturing and related uses. It does NOT include a data center." The City of Brisbane's revised environmental notice, circulated on August 6, 2026, describes a light fabrication building with offices, research, storage and distribution uses, a parking garage and an electrical substation, with no data center. The quarry, which has supplied rock since 1895, including for San Francisco International Airport, would close under the plan. The data center was itself a revision. Orchard Partners first planned a 1.3 million-square-foot, three-story warehouse, then in July 2025 swapped it for two two-story buildings of about 900,000 square feet, one a data center and the other warehouse and advanced manufacturing space, after opposition over noise, traffic and the mountain's endangered butterflies. The data center in that version was to be 180,000 square feet. The current plan is a single two-level building of 892,000 square feet on about 61 acres to be annexed into Brisbane, with about 82 acres set aside as protected open space, according to the developer. Environmental groups opposed the earlier versions, and San Bruno Mountain Watch says its goal is to end all industrial activity on the mountain. "To us, it's not really as much about the type of industrial use," said Ariel Cherbowsky Corkidi, executive director of San Bruno Mountain Watch, "it's that there will be an industrial use in a place that has potential to be a mountain again." Del Schembari of the Mountain Butterfly Collective called it the "wrong project, wrong place." Concerns center on rare and endangered plants and animals on the mountain, including several butterfly species. The developer argues that without the project the quarry's owner holds permits to keep mining through at least 2055. The project now goes through a recirculated draft environmental impact report, and Orchard Partners says it will complete a full review rather than seek the exemption state law offers advanced manufacturing. The project would go before the Brisbane City Council, and the developer also needs county, state and federal permits. The latest update is the city's August 2026 revised notice.

ft-1776267030921-7400.text: Stronghold Power Systems proposed the Coachella Valley Technology Campus, a data center project on more than 240 acres of farmland near Fillmore Street and Avenue 52 in Coachella, Riverside County, California, that grew in city filings to as much as 450 acres and six buildings. On August 25, 2026, the Coachella City Council passed a permanent citywide ban on data centers, ending the project and making Coachella the first city in the valley with such a ban. Hundreds of people packed the council chamber on May 27, 2026, where Alex Rodriguez, a government affairs adviser for Stronghold, said, "There is a requirement for a large load to be brought in, and the data center fits perfectly with that," arguing California's environmental rules made the project different from data centers elsewhere. Indio resident Elizabeth Humphreys questioned whether firm rules were even in place, noting Gov. Gavin Newsom had vetoed AB 93, a bill that would have required data centers to report their actual water use. "We will not take no for an answer. We will recall city council members if we have to," Coachella resident Stephanie Ambriz told the council. On June 4 the council passed a 45-day moratorium on new data center development, directed staff to draft a permanent ban, and voted to terminate the utility agreement it had approved in February with Stronghold's affiliate, Coachella Valley Power Services LLC. "We know you're hurt, we know you're angry, we know you're disappointed, and you have every right to be," Councilwoman Denise Delgado said before the vote, while resident Maria Duarte said in Spanish, "We don't want our prices to go up. We don't want our water contaminated." In July the council unanimously extended the moratorium by 10 months and 15 days, though Cherie Cabral of the California Labor Management Trust urged it to weigh each project's economic benefits. In late August 2026 the council passed Ordinance No. 1231, the permanent ban, which took effect 30 days after the vote.

ft-36.text: The Air Force is offering land at Edwards Air Force Base, in Kern County, California, to private companies for AI data centers, under a request for lease proposals it posted on October 15, 2025. Edwards holds most of the roughly 3,100 acres on offer at five bases: Defense News put the Edwards share at more than 2,100 acres, and Defense One reported 2,115 acres across seven sites there. The Air Force set a proposal deadline of November 14, 2025, and said it would announce a selection or selections in January 2026; that month has long passed and no result has been published. To qualify, a project must add more than 100 megawatts of new power load and be worth at least $500 million, and leases can run up to 50 years. Developers must bring their own power and water, submit a plan to protect local utilities, pay fair market value plus $250,000 to the government, and show they have built three AI data centers of more than 100 megawatts within the last three years. Robert Moriarty, the Air Force's deputy assistant secretary for installations, said: "AI is transforming the modern world, and these data centers are crucial for America to remain at the forefront of innovation." Edwards is where the Air Force tests aircraft such as the B-21 Raider bomber, and that worries some analysts. Stacie Pettyjohn of the Center for a New American Security said: "If you're letting a lot of people on the base, there is a lot of room for potential espionage, let alone sabotage or things like that." She added the deal "is potentially ceding land that the U.S. government will actually never get control over again," and an Air Force spokesperson said the service will "ensure the proper security precautions are taken to protect the installation and its assets."

ft-1787747578563-7945.text: Canon Partners, the owner of a 300-acre industrial site in northeast Fairfield, Solano County, California, is considering a 150 MW data center there, marketed to investors as Project North Bay Solutions, the Vallejo Sun reported in August 2026. The project would sit between Vanden Road and North Gate Road near homes at the outer edge of Vacaville. The city has received no formal development application beyond a 2023 master permit, city spokesperson Bill Way said, and any application would need a public hearing before the City of Fairfield, not the county. The pitch came in presentation slides distributed by the real estate firm Jones Lang LaSalle and the Kansas City developer NorthPoint Development, offering the project to investors or to clients seeking server capacity, with room to expand beyond 150 MW. The slides say the site's zoning allows a data center "by right" and that entitlements are nearly complete. The slides also say PG&E began an engineering study in 2025 and that the city would supply water, with 1 million gallons a day of spare wastewater capacity near the site. Jones Lang LaSalle did not respond to the Vallejo Sun's questions. Canon Partners is controlled by Andrews Lando & Associates and Stroud Properties, longtime Fairfield developers. In 2023 the Fairfield Planning Commission approved Canon Partners' master development permit for a 4.6 million square foot industrial park on the site, finding it consistent with the general plan. That permit sets conditions on utilities, traffic and architecture but contains no detailed construction plans, and requires the city to provide water at its normal rates. "There are no specific limitations," Way said. "This would be determined by the type of industrial facility and its capacity needs." Way said Canon Partners is studying the cost of bringing in the PG&E infrastructure a high-power use would need.

ft-1768323204639-1816.text: A judge has ordered a full environmental review of the Imperial Data Center, the 330 megawatt data center that developer Sebastian Rucci's company, Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing, wants to build near the city of Imperial in Imperial County, California. On September 9, 2026, Imperial County Superior Court Judge Brooks Anderholt overturned the county's April approval of the project's lot merger, ruling the county had illegally skipped review under the California Environmental Quality Act. The ruling does not ban the project, but requires the more detailed study first. The plan is for a nearly 1 million square foot complex on a 75 acre site, using about 750,000 gallons of water a day and drawing almost double the electricity the whole county used in 2024. The Board of Supervisors approved the lot merger 4 to 1 on April 7, 2026, after residents were removed from the hearing by sheriff's deputies. The city of Imperial and the Sierra Club sued over that vote, and Judge Anderholt agreed the county had abused its discretion. In June 2026 the Board of Supervisors reversed course and imposed a moratorium on new data centers in the county through mid-2027, and Rucci sued over that too; in August a judge found the county had not shown the "current and immediate threat" an emergency moratorium requires. The company also sued the Imperial Irrigation District in June after it denied a request for Colorado River water. Rucci said he would seek a new trial or appeal, and is also looking at other sites away from homes.

ft-1783369238463-6397.text: The RB Inyokern Data Center, a 99-megawatt data center proposed by R&L Capital near U.S. Highway 395 and State Route 178 in Inyokern, an unincorporated community in Kern County, California, is under review by the California Energy Commission and facing opposition over the valley's overdrawn groundwater. In August 2026 the Indian Wells Valley Groundwater Authority said it had warned the commission about adding significant new groundwater demand to a closed, critically overdrafted basin. R&L Capital plans a single-story, 238,000-square-foot building with six data halls and an on-site substation on a 50-acre site between U.S. 395 and North Brown Road. The first phase would offer 60MW, and construction could start in April 2027 for a November 2028 opening. Its filing with the Energy Commission lists 40 diesel generators of 3 MW each for up to 99 MW of emergency backup power, and the project would use both liquid and air cooling. News of the project surfaced in May 2026, and a Change.org petition against it had more than 1,140 signatures by early July. Water is the central worry. The Indian Wells Valley basin's state-approved sustainable yield is 7,650 acre-feet a year, but reported pumping has run near 21,000 acre-feet, and the basin is in adjudication. The Groundwater Authority's board voted unanimously to tell the commission that if the project's demand exceeds the Inyokern Community Services District's allocation, the developer would be expected to help pay for imported water, and that any project wells would owe the authority's replenishment and extraction fees. "Our board acted unanimously on this because protecting the basin is core to what SGMA charges us to do," said chair Scott Hayman. ft-1768851231126-6169.text: NewYork GreenCloud has scaled back its plan for a data center at the former Buena Vista Biomass Power plant in Ione, Amador County, California, next to Harrah's Northern California casino. A company spokesperson told the Calaveras Enterprise in September 2026 that it had dropped the pyrolysis process it announced in January and would instead seek Amador County permits to renovate the existing 18 megawatt biomass plant, supplying up to 16 megawatts to the data center. The company said it was aiming to finish construction by the end of August or early September 2026, but as of a July site visit, District 3 Supervisor Jeff Brown wrote, "they still have not applied for a construction permit or completed an Environmental Impact Report for the AI Center." No county permit approval or construction start has been reported since; about $4 million had been spent on refurbishment by August 2026, with another $171 million planned. The Plattsburgh, New York company, founded in 2024, bought the plant in January 2026 and said it would use pyrolysis technology from BucSha Energy to feed a "carbon-negative" AI data center, partnering with Atlas Cloud AI to host 2,304 Nvidia Blackwell GPUs. The plant began as a coal plant, was decommissioned in the 1990s, and was converted to burn wood waste in 2011 after an environmental review found significant impacts. Neighboring Calaveras County passed a 45-day moratorium on data center permits on August 25, 2026, citing demands on energy and water and questions about jobs created; Angels Camp moved toward its own 45-day moratorium. The company still needs to apply to Amador County for the renovation permits before construction can proceed.

ft-1787243731897-3645.text: NorthPoint Development's interest in building a data center on the former FMC chemical plant site at 1200 Graphics Drive in Modesto, Stanislaus County, California, has drawn a march, a petition and a packed council meeting, though no application has been filed. After a four-hour Modesto City Council meeting in August 2026 attended by about 200 people, five of the seven council members said they favor a moratorium on data centers, and city staff are gathering information for a future council vote. Councilman Chris Ricci posted on Facebook in late July that NorthPoint, a data center developer with an office in Sacramento, was lobbying council members about a data center. "If you have opinions about data centers, now is the time to let your council know," Ricci's post said, and it drew 319 comments within five hours. City officials later confirmed NorthPoint's interest in the Graphics Drive site near the Modesto Junior College East Campus. The 45-acre site has been empty since 1984; its cleanup of barium, strontium, arsenic and fuel contamination ended in 2007, and an application from NorthPoint to split it into two parcels was deemed complete in December 2025. The size, capacity and operator of any data center have not been confirmed. Residents organized fast. Elizabeth Miranda Morales, a lifelong Modesto resident, started a Change.org petition against data centers in Modesto and Stanislaus County that passed 1,700 signatures in less than a week. "To think of a data center just running water 24/7 whenever they want, with probably no repercussions, is not fair to the residents," she said. Students with MJC Pirates for Peace, Modesto 50501 and the Central Valley Black, Indigenous and People of Color Coalition marched from Five Points to City Hall before the August 11 council meeting. Hannah Methvin of Pirates for Peace said a data center "is going to drive up energy and water costs for our residents." The city says data centers are not an allowed land use under its municipal code, though residents and some council members worry the code could change once an application arrives. Mayor Sue Zwahlen said she had agreed to meet with a data center developer and needed more information. The Modesto Irrigation District said developers must pay for a study of their energy demand and impact before it decides whether it can serve them without harming existing customers. Nearby Patterson imposed a 45-day data center moratorium on July 16, 2026. Whether a data center could be built in Modesto rests with the Modesto City Council, which would have to change the land use rules and is weighing a moratorium, and with the Modesto Irrigation District on power.

ft-1771911668943-4728.text: HMC Capital, through its StratCap unit, withdrew its application for a data center at 1977 Saturn Street in Monterey Park, Los Angeles County, California, at the end of March 2026, after months of community opposition. In June, Monterey Park voters went further and banned data centers outright: preliminary returns on June 4 showed more than 86 percent backing Measure NDC, a permanent citywide prohibition. The withdrawn project would have been a 247,000-square-foot data center, with a new electrical substation and about two dozen backup diesel generators, built by the Australian asset manager on a site it bought for $39 million in 2024. The group No Data Center in Monterey Park formed in December 2025, collected 5,300 petition signatures and argued the costs in electricity, noise and property values outweighed a small number of permanent jobs. Co-founder Steven Kung, who lives a few minutes from the site, texted his husband "Yikes, let's fight this" when he learned of it. The City Council adopted a 45-day moratorium in January 2026, then on March 4 voted 5-0 to extend it by 10.5 months and put a ban to voters, with City Attorney Karl Berger calling the combined steps a "belt, suspenders and girdle approach." "We're glad HMC StratCap is going to work with the city to find other land uses for their purchase," Councilmember Jose Sanchez said after the withdrawal. The fight has spread: El Monte passed its own 45-day citywide moratorium on March 18, 2026, and a regional alliance, the No Data Centers San Gabriel Valley Coalition, now links opposition groups across several cities, including in the City of Industry, where residents are organizing against a data center proposed for the Puente Hills Mall site. The measure passed with wide support, and Mayor Elizabeth Yang said the city has no pending data center applications: "We're hoping that our actions here in our little city are going to set an example for other cities that are dealing with similar issues." What happens to the Saturn Street land now rests with its owner and the City Council; HMC StratCap had not told the city its plans for the property after withdrawing.

ft-1782743502353-9741.text: An unnamed company approached Mount Shasta, Siskiyou County, California, about building an AI data center at the former Crystal Geyser bottling plant, but the idea is dead: Mount Shasta City Manager Todd Juhasz told the company the city was not interested, and Siskiyou County supervisors said in July 2026 that nothing was pending before the county. "We are well aware of the community's opposition to that," Siskiyou County Supervisor Ray Haupt said at the board's July meeting, adding: "We have nothing pending before the county or county departments regarding data centers." The inquiry reached the city's planning director in June, and Juhasz said the company was likely drawn by the property's water rights and a high-producing well: springs fed by the volcanic aquifers around Mount Shasta form the headwaters of the Sacramento River. "We'll hear them out," Juhasz said. "But unless there's some magical thing they do that other data centers don't, I can't imagine this would be good for the community," adding there's "no ROI for the city." The site has fought this fight before: Crystal Geyser bought it in 2013 to bottle Mount Shasta water and gave up in 2021 after years of opposition led by the Winnemem Wintu Tribe, which quickly spoke out again over water, power, fumes and noise. A petition against a data center there passed 7,500 signatures, and the Mount Shasta Police Department said officials had received death threats over the proposal, even though no one in city government supported it. The property lies in unincorporated Siskiyou County, so the county holds approval power, and Mount Shasta has begun looking at annexing it, which would give the city more control over development and water. If a data center application is ever filed, it would go to the Siskiyou County Board of Supervisors unless the city annexes the land first; no application had been filed as of July 2026.

ft-1786566307591-8402.text: Behring Companies' plan to put a data center in the former Oakland Scientific Facility at 415 20th St. in downtown Oakland, Alameda County, California, has set off the city's first organized fight over data centers. On September 22, 2026 a City Council committee unanimously approved a 45-day moratorium on new data centers citywide, and the full Oakland City Council takes up the moratorium on October 6. The four-story, roughly 83,000-square-foot building once housed a Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory supercomputing center, and Behring bought it vacant from Hines in December 2025 for $6.8 million. Behring plans to use about 20,000 square feet of it as a data center within a larger AI campus of three neighboring buildings that would also include a 39-story apartment tower above the 19th Street BART station and 20 stories of offices. The site already supports up to 20 megawatts of computing power because of its past use, according to Behring, which said it was boosting the building's power from 4.5 megawatts for dense AI computing. Chief executive Colin Behring argues nothing new is proposed: "Nothing has changed, and our proposal at this point is to use the same building doing what it used to do the same way." He says the project would provide up to 2,300 jobs, and the company is hoping the city will let it proceed without a conditional use permit on the strength of the building's past use. The proposal went to city staff in August and has not reached the City Council. Opponents say a downtown data center could strain the city's grid and water system, bring noise to nearby residents, and create few jobs for the utilities it would use. A No Data Center in Oakland campaign, with much of the organizing led by the Party for Socialism and Liberation, has a petition, canvassers and flyers in downtown bar windows: "This fight is about who decides the future of Oakland: the people, or the ultra wealthy," its website reads. Councilmember Carroll Fife, who represents downtown, stood beside Behring in August and said the project "is not the large-scale mega-facility that people have expressed, and legitimately so, concerns." On September 11 she introduced the urgency moratorium, which would stop the city from approving land-use agreements or entitlements for data centers anywhere in Oakland for 45 days while it writes rules on energy, water, air and noise pollution, land use and public health. "I've always stood for development without displacement," Fife said at the committee. Dozens of residents at the committee urged a permanent ban. "Why are we doing a moratorium?" asked Toshia Christal, an Oakland teacher, artist and business owner. "Why are we not just saying no?" Medina Munoz of East Oakland's Sobrante Park, whose daughters have asthma, said: "Before you approve anything, we need you to study what contaminants would be released." Eric Negomir of the Silicon Valley Leadership Group urged the committee to engage with the industry rather than add barriers, and mayoral candidate Mindy Pechenuk said the city should regulate data centers rather than stop them. Nearby, Oakley has banned data centers, San Francisco is weighing a similar moratorium, and a much larger data center is under development in Hayward. In the same week, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed bills aimed at keeping data centers from passing electricity costs on to residents and requiring them to report water and electricity use. Whether Behring's building needs a conditional use permit at all is still a question for the city; Fife said in August that it may not need more approval if its use matches the laboratory's. If the full council adopts the moratorium on October 6, the city could not approve land-use agreements or entitlements for new data centers while it drafts permanent rules, and any extension would need another council vote.
paragraphs: Behring Companies' plan to put a data center in the former Oakland Scientific Facility at 415 20th St. in downtown Oakland, Alameda County, California, has set off the city's first organized fight over data centers. On September 22, 2026 a City Council committee unanimously approved a 45-day moratorium on new data centers citywide, and the full Oakland City Council takes up the moratorium on October 6.

The four-story, roughly 83,000-square-foot building once housed a Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory supercomputing center, and Behring bought it vacant from Hines in December 2025 for $6.8 million. Behring plans to use about 20,000 square feet of it as a data center within a larger AI campus of three neighboring buildings that would also include a 39-story apartment tower above the 19th Street BART station and 20 stories of offices.

The site already supports up to 20 megawatts of computing power because of its past use, according to Behring, which said it was boosting the building's power from 4.5 megawatts for dense AI computing.

Chief executive Colin Behring argues nothing new is proposed: "Nothing has changed, and our proposal at this point is to use the same building doing what it used to do the same way." He says the project would provide up to 2,300 jobs, and the company is hoping the city will let it proceed without a conditional use permit on the strength of the building's past use. The proposal went to city staff in August and has not reached the City Council.

Opponents say a downtown data center could strain the city's grid and water system, bring noise to nearby residents, and create few jobs for the utilities it would use. A No Data Center in Oakland campaign, with much of the organizing led by the Party for Socialism and Liberation, has a petition, canvassers and flyers in downtown bar windows: "This fight is about who decides the future of Oakland: the people, or the ultra wealthy," its website reads.

Councilmember Carroll Fife, who represents downtown, stood beside Behring in August and said the project "is not the large-scale mega-facility that people have expressed, and legitimately so, concerns." On September 11 she introduced the urgency moratorium, which would stop the city from approving land-use agreements or entitlements for data centers anywhere in Oakland for 45 days while it writes rules on energy, water, air and noise pollution, land use and public health. "I've always stood for development without displacement," Fife said at the committee.

Dozens of residents at the committee urged a permanent ban. "Why are we doing a moratorium?" asked Toshia Christal, an Oakland teacher, artist and business owner. "Why are we not just saying no?" Medina Munoz of East Oakland's Sobrante Park, whose daughters have asthma, said: "Before you approve anything, we need you to study what contaminants would be released."

Eric Negomir of the Silicon Valley Leadership Group urged the committee to engage with the industry rather than add barriers, and mayoral candidate Mindy Pechenuk said the city should regulate data centers rather than stop them.

Nearby, Oakley has banned data centers, San Francisco is weighing a similar moratorium, and a much larger data center is under development in Hayward. In the same week, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed bills aimed at keeping data centers from passing electricity costs on to residents and requiring them to report water and electricity use.

Whether Behring's building needs a conditional use permit at all is still a question for the city; Fife said in August that it may not need more approval if its use matches the laboratory's. If the full council adopts the moratorium on October 6, the city could not approve land-use agreements or entitlements for new data centers while it drafts permanent rules, and any extension would need another council vote.

ft-1773459686943-1188.text: Amazon paid $78.8 million in late 2025 for the two-story, 168,000 square foot building at 2964 Bradley Street in East Pasadena, in Los Angeles County, California, along the 210 freeway, and at first said nothing about what it was for. Residents worried it would become a cloud and AI data center, and on March 6, 2026 AWS said it would be a "research-and-development facility that expands our quantum computing work in Pasadena." The building went up in 1981, was renovated in 2018 and was once home to the internet provider EarthLink; the apparel company Max Studios occupies about half of it through 2027, and the French aerospace firm Thales is also a tenant. The seller, Alvarez & Marsal Capital Real Estate, had bought it from Graymark Capital for $33 million in early 2021, a gain of about 139 percent in four years. The site is separate from Caltech, where AWS opened a Center for Quantum Computing of about 21,000 square feet on campus in 2021. The question pushed the city to act. In the spring of 2026 the city council directed staff to take data center zoning to the Planning Commission, and AWS said it would work with the city on permitting for the Bradley Street building.

ft-1781283258160-3335.text: AVAIO Digital is building the AVAIO Perseus Data Center, a 99-megawatt data center on the former Delta View Golf Course in Pittsburg, Contra Costa County, California. The first phase, 347,000 square feet, anchors AVAIO's 76-acre Pittsburg Technology Park. The Pittsburg City Council approved the project 5-0 in November 2024, with 37 backup diesel generators, a switching yard and a PG&E substation with access to seven 230 kV lines. AVAIO put the investment at over $800 million, with construction starting in 2025 and energization in 2027. Many residents only learned of the project in 2026, through social media and an online petition that passed 14,000 signatures. More than 200 people crowded a June 15, 2026 council meeting and gave over 100 public comments, most against the project, on transparency, water, power, pollution and noise. Mayor Dionne Adams told the room, "I know there are strong feelings about the data center project and I recognize as the mayor many residents have questions or concerns." The Center for Biological Diversity sued in December 2024, arguing the city's environmental review ignored greenhouse gas emissions, water, wildlife and nearby wetlands. Under a settlement signed in December 2025, AVAIO must use recycled water as the sole source for cooling, install rooftop solar, buy 100 percent carbon-free electricity, and pay $750,000 toward regional climate projects. The anger has turned personal. Council member Arlene Kobata told NBC Bay Area in September 2026 that a woman grabbed and shoved her at a public event and that she has received death threats. Mayor Adams condemned the threats. As of September 2026, Pittsburg has paused further action on the project while it does more community outreach.

ft-44.text: Nautilus Data Technologies runs a floating data center on a barge moored beside the San Joaquin River at the Port of Stockton, in San Joaquin County, California. It is cooled by the river: water is drawn upstream, filtered with systems used in power plants and naval vessels, and run through a heat exchanger feeding rear-door coolers on each rack, without touching the servers or taking on chemicals. The water spends less than 15 seconds in the system and goes back about 4 degrees Fahrenheit warmer, at a discharge point chosen with wildlife in mind, and the operation was certified by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife and other state and federal agencies. The cloud storage company Backblaze said in September 2022 that it would keep more than an exabyte of data on the barge. In April 2024 Nautilus signed a 2.5 megawatt deal to host AI hardware from the chipmaker Cerebras at 30 kilowatts a rack, deployed within 60 days. A Cerebras press release of 11 March 2025 announcing its inference data center locations lists Stockton as already online, alongside Santa Clara and Dallas.

ft-1782348677413-3761.text: Beacon Data Centers and California Resources Corporation announced in June 2026 the Golden Valley Technology Hub, a 275-megawatt data center development on the Elk Hills Oil Field about 20 miles west of Bakersfield, in Kern County, California. The 600,000-square-foot campus would sit on 100 acres of the field, more than a mile from the nearest homes. Elk Hills was discovered in 1911, covers 75 square miles and has produced more than two billion barrels of oil. CRC's Elk Hills plant, running below capacity, would supply almost all the campus's electricity, with the grid as backup and fifteen 2.5 megawatt diesel generators behind that. Cooling would be closed loop, which the companies say would consume enough water to fill an Olympic swimming pool over ten years, and noise barriers are planned round the site. Chris Gould, CRC's chief sustainability officer, made the case for reusing an industrial site: it means "creating jobs and tax revenue in Kern County, utilizing dedicated on-site power, and employing one of the industry's most water-efficient cooling systems." CRC submitted about 150 residents' signatures in support; at least five of those people are connected to the local oil industry. Nina Robertson of Earthjustice said: "You should be powering any data centers in California with zero-emission energy." Earthjustice, the Center for Biological Diversity and other groups have sued Kern County over its approval of a related CRC carbon capture project, and that litigation is ongoing. Gabriel Collins, a researcher at Rice University, summed up the argument: "Where you stand on these things depends on where you sit." CRC has held community meetings with residents of nearby Taft and Buttonwillow, and the project faces strict environmental review as part of its permit application, which could take about a year.

ft-1775785975978-4389.text: Raeden's Project Taurus, a 50MW data center that would reuse a 451,217-square-foot building on about 22 acres at 1565 High Tech Way in Colorado Springs, El Paso County, Colorado, won city planning approval on June 11, 2026, but a final decision now waits until April 2027. On Sept. 17 the City Council voted 7-2 to push its decision on appeals of that approval to April 13, 2027, a week after the city's municipal election. The site is already zoned for a data center, and Raeden's co-founder Jason Green has said it would use closed-loop cooling. Sound was the main worry: resident Matt Martin said city noise rules measured in dBA filter out the low hum data centers make, and council members recalled noise hardship permits the mayor granted the Ford Amphitheater. Green said a 40-megawatt data center already sits 100 feet from homes in the city, but Colorado Springs Utilities chief executive Travas Deal said its largest data center customer uses about six megawatts. "I don't think this is a location that's appropriate for a data center, even if we study this for 6 months or 8 months," said Councilor Dave Donelson, one of three who backed granting the appeal outright. Police arrested four people after a scuffle in the audience at the Sept. 17 meeting; the appeal group Integrity Matters said they were not affiliated with it. Raeden said it would use the extra time to keep engaging while "carefully evaluating whether or not this is the right partnership for RAEDEN," and the City Council holds the final say on the appeals in April.

ft-1779200831736-3704.text: Granite Renewables, a New York company, wants to build a data center campus on about 4,000 acres roughly 21 miles northwest of Sterling, in Logan County, Colorado. It says the project could need up to 2,000 megawatts of electricity, at an estimated cost of $15 billion. The two nearest power plants are wind farms, Peetz Table Wind Energy and Logan Wind Energy, a combined 401 megawatts about 15 to 19 kilometers away, a fifth of what the project alone could draw. The region's grid authority, the Western Area Power Administration's Rocky Mountain region, serves a peak load of about 3,362 megawatts today across its entire territory, so this one project could need close to 60% of that again. County officials say they did not know about the project until Granite Renewables began meeting with them in September 2025. The following month, Logan County commissioners imposed a moratorium on new data centers, battery storage, solar and wind projects while they wrote rules for how to site them. "You have to understand, this is all new to us," Commissioner Jim Yahn said. "You don't want to look back 10 years down the road and have regrets because we did something in haste." The county's new rules, Resolution 2026-5, took effect on February 17, 2026, and cover any data center facility of one megawatt or larger. Applicants must map the site, submit a wildlife impact plan for review by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and Colorado Parks and Wildlife, notify property owners within a mile of the project, and carry liability insurance covering construction and operation. In December 2025, commissioners separately approved an agreement with the Sterling Urban Renewal Authority allowing tax-increment financing to help pay for infrastructure tied to the project. Andrew Fritzer, who chairs the county's economic development board, called the project a "once-in-a-generation opportunity to transform the local economy." The board's executive director, Trae Miller, said the moratorium itself sent "a negative message to the market." Granite Renewables says the project could create up to 1,000 construction jobs and 50 to 100 permanent technical and management positions. The site sits about 1.2 miles from the South Platte River, the area's main water source. The river is already the subject of disputes over its allocation. Commissioners have also raised concerns about the project's proximity to Minuteman missile silos in the area, and the farmland the campus would take out of production. Colorado Governor Jared Polis has said he wants to streamline permitting for energy projects, which critics worry could weaken local governments' say over where projects like this get built. "One of the reasons we can't have nice things is we don't let them be built," Polis said. As of the most recent reporting found, Granite Renewables had not filed a formal application for the project.

It says the project could need up to 2,000 megawatts of electricity, at an estimated cost of $15 billion.
The two nearest power plants are wind farms, Peetz Table Wind Energy and Logan Wind Energy, a combined 401 megawatts about 15 to 19 kilometers away, a fifth of what the project alone could draw.

The region's grid authority, the Western Area Power Administration's Rocky Mountain region, serves a peak load of about 3,362 megawatts today across its entire territory, so this one project could need close to 60% of that again.

The following month, Logan County commissioners imposed a moratorium on new data centers, battery storage, solar and wind projects while they wrote rules for how to site them.
"You have to understand, this is all new to us," Commissioner Jim Yahn said.
"You don't want to look back 10 years down the road and have regrets because we did something in haste."

ft-1772679253414-7249.text: Weld County approved zoning for a Global AI data center near Windsor in September 2026, after ordering the company to stop construction three times. Global AI, a New York company, bought the 438 acre former Kodak and Carestream Health site at 2000 Howard Smith Avenue West for about $15.6 million in November 2025, and plans a 41 acre data center there. The first phase needs 27.5 megawatts, and Global AI aims to have a gigawatt in its network by 2029. The county posted stop work orders on May 7, 2026, and June 11, 2026, and a third with no date given in county records. On July 20, 2026, it sent a formal order to abate, giving Global AI until July 31, 2026, to comply or face termination of unlawful occupancy. The abatement letter said the company had added chiller tanks and piping, data center specific work, without the zoning approval or building permits that phase required. Weld County would not detail its inspections or say whether Global AI had complied, citing a pending investigation. Angela Snyder, a county planner, said of residents' objections: "We sorted the public comments into categories of what is within our jurisdiction to address and what isn't. Those things that we have the ability to address ... we will not approve it unless those things are addressed." Scott Simmons, a retired information technology architect who lives about a mile from the site, said: "This is not the place to put a data center, right in the middle of all these communities." Of the county's oversight he said: "It couldn't be more 'Nightmare on Elm Street,'" adding, "These people don't care." The Board of Commissioners approved the zoning 5 to 0 in September 2026, after more than 400 written comments came in against it, on water, electricity, environmental impact and noise. Chair Scott James said: "It repurposes an industrial facility that has been vacant for years. It will spur economic activity." Commissioner Lynette Peppler said site visits and research had overcome her concerns. The approval came with conditions: closed loop cooling, an initial water fill of 65,000 gallons and an annual top up of 6,500, noise held to ambient levels with 65 decibels in normal operation, and a decommissioning bond. The Poudre Valley Rural Electric Association has committed 35 megawatts in a will serve letter, but can supply only that much until mid 2028, dropping to 27 megawatts in early 2028. Global AI says it will run the site with Nvidia and Humain, an Arabic language artificial intelligence company backed by a Saudi sovereign wealth fund, and has not said publicly who its customers will be. The company estimates 1,500 construction jobs and 200 long term jobs, and puts the investment at $2 billion to $20 billion.

ft-49.text: Atlas Capital Group, a commercial developer based in New York, has floated a data center with more than 900,000 square feet of data processing space on a 44.5-acre site at 132 Griffin Road North in Bloomfield, Hartford County, Connecticut. The company presented the idea to Bloomfield's Town Plan and Zoning Commission as an informal, conceptual discussion on June 26, 2025, a step before any formal application. Commissioners called the project "worthy of consideration" if it would "not be incompatible with the community surrounding it." The concept shows a 60-foot-tall building off Route 189 with a 127,000-square-foot open-air substation, two generator yards for backup power, and chillers on the roof. About 40 people would work there. Atlas representative Marisa Fontaine said the substation was needed for a project of this size and that the company had held preliminary talks with the utility Eversource about power. In 1987 the town accepted a master plan for a mixed-use development on the same property, but that project never moved forward. Bloomfield's Town Plan and Zoning Commission has not taken further public action on the Griffin Road North plan since that June 2025 presentation. A formal site plan application would have to go before that same commission, which decides what, if anything, gets built there.

ft-50.text: GotSpace Data Partners, a Groton, Connecticut company, planned a data center in Bozrah, in New London County, Connecticut, as one of five it hoped to build across the state, but in October 2021 Bozrah turned down the company's request for a new zoning category that would have allowed it. The GotSpace owners and representatives did not attend the Bozrah planning and zoning commission meeting on the request, telling town officials the company was going through a change in leadership. GotSpace had host agreements with Bozrah, Groton, Griswold and Wallingford, and also aimed to build in Norwich. The same year, Gov. Ned Lamont signed a data center tax exemption law offering sales, use and property tax exemptions for 20 or 30 years, depending on a project's size and location. Founded in Boston in January 2021, GotSpace lists real estate developers Thomas Quinn and Nicholas Fiorillo as partners and had not delivered any data centers. Quinn previously led Verde Group, which won site plan approval for a data center in Montville in 2019 but never broke ground. Bozrah's refusal spread. Wallingford's town council looked into rescinding its own host agreement for a GotSpace campus of five buildings totaling nearly 1 million square feet, after the Bozrah vote. Wallingford Town Attorney Gerald Farrell said, "Gotspace has some internal issues going on within itself." The town's lawyer said there was no legal basis to rescind the agreement, which could only end if GotSpace failed to apply for a building permit within 36 months. For a data center to come to Bozrah, the town's planning and zoning commission would first have to create a zoning category allowing one. CT Examiner reported in August 2022 that Bozrah, facing a budget squeeze, was weighing whether to approve the data center; the town has not announced a decision.

ft-51.text: NE Edge's plan to build a 300 megawatt data center at the Millstone nuclear power station in Waterford, New London County, Connecticut, is effectively canceled: the developer never filed a building permit application, and its host fee agreement with the town has run out. First Selectman Rob Brule announced the termination on Facebook, saying the agreement expired "by its own terms" and that he would not support any future host fee agreements for data centers in Waterford. NE Edge CEO Thomas Quinn said the company still had a $3 billion financing commitment lined up and interest from potential customers, while Dominion Energy, which owns Millstone, said it has "no current plans to develop a data center" there. Waterford's Representative Town Meeting and Board of Selectmen unanimously approved the host agreement in March 2023, promising the town $231 million over 30 years in place of property taxes that Connecticut's 2021 data center incentive law waives; it covered two two-story buildings and a switchyard on about 55 acres of the 526-acre Millstone site, buying power directly from Dominion's reactors. Residents objected from the start over noise, traffic, fire risk, flooding and the power the campus would draw, forming Concerned Citizens of Waterford, later Concerned Citizens of Waterford and East Lyme. The group's founder, Bryan Sayles, found in grid operator ISO New England's records that both Millstone reactors had been offline for five weeks, which he said undercut NE Edge's argument that a direct reactor connection meant it needed no backup generators. The Connecticut Siting Council, whose approval Dominion needed to supply the data center directly from the reactors, rejected the request without prejudice in January 2024, and Dominion never refiled. The council's executive director, Melanie Bachman, called it "premature" to review the plan given "the lack of information surrounding the proposed data centers and their direct interconnection to Millstone Power Station Units 2 and 3." NE Edge has also pursued data center sites elsewhere in Connecticut, including in Killingly, where the town approved selling it land in August 2023, and Quinn said the company intends to keep developing in the state. For the Millstone site to return, a new developer would need a host fee agreement from Waterford, which Brule has said he will not support, and Dominion would have to seek Siting Council approval again.

ft-1786763855689-3289.text: Parkway Gravel Inc. wants to turn the St. Georges Business Park, land that includes the Frightland Halloween attraction near Middletown in New Castle County, Delaware, into an industrial site that could become a data center. The company's engineering firm, Verdantas, filed revised plans in November 2025 covering 3.2 million square feet along U.S. Route 13, arguing that data centers need "far less" parking than other industrial uses, and county planners say they have "not received any clarification on the proposed use." County Council members split on the plan: Janet Kilpatrick said "we need to get our tax base up, and we need to get people jobs," while Dave Carter said "we're losing ground, but it could get a whole lot worse if we don't get some reasonable controls in place." In March 2026 the county council passed Carter's data center rules 12-0, requiring new data centers to sit at least 1,000 feet from the nearest home unless a noise study allows 500 feet, plus closed-loop cooling and money set aside for eventual demolition. The rules apply only to new projects, and whether they cover the St. Georges site, which entered the pipeline as warehouses, remains unclear; the county's land use department did not answer the question. Delaware's Coastal Zone Act is the other hurdle: the state ruled that Starwood Digital Ventures' nearby Project Washington violated the 1971 law, a state board upheld that ruling, and Starwood dropped its court appeal in July 2026, leaving that project unable to proceed as designed. The St. Georges site would also fall under the Coastal Zone Act, and whether the law stops it will likely depend on how the site is powered. New Castle County's land use department is reviewing the plans, and the state Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control will rule on the Coastal Zone Act question.

ft-1786764095148-3335.text: The Newark Project, Shelbourne's plan to replace the White Clay Center business park at the end of White Clay Center Drive near Newark, in New Castle County, Delaware, with an 850,000-square-foot data center campus, has been suspended under a handshake deal, but the company is still seeking county approval for it. In September 2026 the New York-based developer filed plans to turn half of one existing building into a 10-classroom vocational school for the Christina School District instead. The 44-acre site, reached from Ogletown Road (Del. 273) across from CarMax, holds seven office and industrial buildings from the 1980s and sits just across the railroad tracks from Kimberton, Greenbridge, Newark Oaks and several apartment complexes. Exploratory plans filed in late 2025 would demolish them for three light industrial buildings and a guard shack, with the proposed use listed as a data center. The engineering firm Verdantas filed the land use application, which also describes a switchyard. ft-52.text: The thing that killed this project was not the data halls. It was 516 diesel generators. Starwood Digital Ventures proposed Project Washington, a data center at Delaware City, in New Castle County: 11 two storey buildings, 6 million square feet, 1.2 gigawatts. The backup power was to be 516 generators, against a maximum of eight used by any single entity in the state at the time, served by a fuel tank farm of more than 5 acres holding 2.5 million gallons. Delaware's Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control refused the permit, citing the Coastal Zone Act, a 1971 law that keeps heavy industry off the state's shoreline. The department said the smokestacks serving the diesel generators would be "the largest source of nitrogen oxide emissions in the entire state, with the sole exception of the Delaware City refinery". Dustyn Thompson of the Sierra Club said "The Coastal Zone Act is a recognition that our coastal ecologies, and the tourism and benefits of resiliency that they provide to the state, is well worth protecting and preserving." County Councilman Kevin Caneco called the decision a victory for his constituents and the environment. Starwood said the project "is proud to have the support of the Delaware unions and trades, the business community, and hundreds of New Castle County residents". Starwood appealed, and lost again. On 26 March 2026 the Delaware Coastal Zone Industrial Control Board unanimously upheld the secretary's refusal. Board member Willie Scott said the generators were emission points collectively large enough to count as a major source of pollution. Starwood's attorney Katharine Mowery argued that "The Secretary has distorted what Project Washington is, and ignored binding case law in order to find a way to prohibit this project." Lawyers following the case expect appeals to the Delaware Superior Court and then the state Supreme Court, which could take between 18 months and three years to work through. The company could also redesign the project to comply.
