ft-53.text: Stonebridge has city approval for a 4.4 million-square-foot AI data center in Fort Meade, Polk County, Florida, and three of the city leaders who approved it now face a recall. On April 15, 2026, the Fort Meade City Commission voted unanimously for a development agreement with Stonebridge for the data center, which would sit on more than 1,300 acres, after a four-hour meeting at which dozens of people spoke against it. The land, owned by Florida Eco Park and Polk Industrial Park and used for cattle grazing, was rezoned in June 2025 for up to 4.4 million square feet of data centers, and the end user has not been named. Stonebridge must build certain water and wastewater improvements, and the city will reserve water and wastewater capacity for the campus. Vice Mayor Petrina McCutchen called her vote a leap: "Unfortunately, there are some questions that will go unanswered that I don't even have, that you don't even have, but does that mean I don't take a leap because I'm gripped by fear?" Water is the open question. Stonebridge first said it would need about 140,000 gallons a day and later said 50,000. The Southwest Florida Water Management District told the city in April that under rules adopted in December it cannot serve the data center from its existing water permit; the demand must go into a new permit approved by the district's governing board at a public meeting. Days after the vote, Florida Commerce Secretary Alex Kelly wrote to the commission that the project "presents significant risks to Central Florida's energy capacity, water resources, and transportation infrastructure" and that its projected water demand "appears woefully underestimated." "These facilities introduce persistent low-frequency noise, large substations, and transmission lines," real estate agent Danielle Evans told the commission. Residents have gone to court and to the ballot. The group Watchdogs of Fort Meade sued the city in May over what it calls a lack of transparency and lawful review, and asked the state Department of Environmental Protection for an environmental review. A recall committee then filed petitions against Mayor Jaret Williams, Vice Mayor McCutchen and Commissioner Matthew Taylor, and its vice chairman, George McNerney, said residents had asked repeatedly for a moratorium. The Polk County Supervisor of Elections certified enough first-round signatures on August 14, and in early September Taylor sued to stop the recall, calling it retaliation for his support of the data center and "a gross abuse of the process." Taylor has defended the project as keeping Florida ahead in the global AI race. The data center cannot proceed until the Southwest Florida Water Management District's governing board approves a water permit that covers it. For the recall to reach a ballot, organizers must next gather signatures from 15% of Fort Meade's registered voters. A judge has not yet ruled on Taylor's challenge.

ft-1763321276591-6787.text: Sentinel Grove Technology Park, also known as Project Jarvis, is a proposed data center campus of up to 15 million square feet on a former citrus grove outside Fort Pierce, in St. Lucie County, Florida. Its developer, Timberline Real Estate Partners, needed the land changed from Agricultural-5 to a Special District, and the St. Lucie County Planning and Zoning Commission rejected that change 4-2 at its October 16 meeting. That vote came in October 2025, against the recommendation of county staff. In February 2026 the application was withdrawn, the applicants choosing to wait and see what the Florida Legislature would do about data centers. The 1,218-acre site lies on the east side of Minute Maid Road, extending about 2,600 feet north of Orange Avenue (State Road 68), south and east of the South Florida Water Management District's C-25 Canal. The land is zoned AG-5 agricultural and is owned by Epic Estates 68 LLC; Epic Estates, a Tallahassee-based land banking investment firm, bought it for $15 million in July 2024, according to the St. Lucie County Property Appraiser's Office. The architecture and planning firm HJA Design Studios submitted the request alongside Timberline. One notice said the zoning would allow up to 15 million square feet of development, about 5 million of it in the first phase. The buildings would stand about 60 feet tall. The project reportedly represented a long-term private investment of $13.5 billion "for the first 1,000MW of data center capacity." The county would not have supplied its water: the plan called for private, self-contained package treatment plants for water and wastewater. At the October hearing, county Senior Planner Thad Crow called it "a large-scale technology park" and "a low-traffic generator", and Patty Tobin, presenting the project, said: "This project would put SLC on the map." Scott Bullock of Timberline said there was no tenant at the time, and told the commission: "We anticipate a very large decrease in water consumption." Residents were not persuaded. "That's the last agricultural area we have left in St. Lucie County, please don't destroy it," said Cynthia Adams. Charles Paschal, who has property on Orange Avenue near the site, said: "If you read this plan, this is like a teenager writing their own permission slip to a party". Peter Harrison, an Orange Avenue resident who owns an 18-acre homestead and is an officer of the nearby 4-H ranch, said: "The size and scope of the project is just unprecedented. The numbers are just off the chart." In February, St. Lucie County Commissioner Cathy Townsend said the "data center pulled out because they knew that there was going to be legislation coming out in Tallahassee," DCD reported. That legislation, SB 484, became law in May 2026, narrower than Gov. Ron DeSantis had wanted. It requires data centers to pay for their own utilities rather than shift the cost to other customers, does not ban nondisclosure agreements between data center companies and state agencies, and continues to let local governments regulate land development for data centers. The nearest fight now is inside Fort Pierce. Willow Lakes LLC, owner of 203 acres off West Midway Road and Interstate 95, applied in June 2026 to rezone 174 acres to light industrial for a data center; the land was once planned for the Koa Bay Surf Park Community. Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick said he wants the developers to show there will be no impact on groundwater, utility fees or noise: "If they don't, then I will not be supportive of it". More than 200 people crowded the Fort Pierce Planning Board meeting on the request in September, and the applicant's attorney, Lee Dobbins, asked for the item to be tabled to an unspecified date. City Planning Director Kevin Freeman said Fort Pierce has no zoning classification that specifically addresses data centers, and that a decision "may be some time away". Fort Pierce activist Kevin Keene has asked the city commission to draft an ordinance requiring a unanimous 5-0 vote for any future "high-impact data center development." In February 2026, DCD reported that the Sentinel Grove applicant was choosing to wait and see how the legislative process played out. The planning commission's vote was only a recommendation; the decision belongs to the St. Lucie County Board of County Commissioners. In January 2026 the county's communications director, Erick Gill, said the developer could still bring the project to that board by submitting its plan to county staff, and that no meetings were scheduled.

ft-54.text: A data center that Cielo Digital Infrastructure wants to build on Marion Road in Haines City, Polk County, Florida, is on hold because the city does not have enough water to supply it. Cielo asked the city about utility service for a 300 megawatt campus on about 74 acres near Marion Road and State Road 544 East, which would need up to 150,000 gallons of water a day. Deputy City Manager James Keene said Haines City can produce 10 million gallons of water a day and already uses just over 7 million, with about 8,000 more homes coming. The city has asked the Southwest Florida Water Management District since June 2022 to raise its permit to 16.42 million gallons a day; the water district disputed that the city's application includes Cielo's 150,000 gallons. "Haines City and surrounding areas are already having a water problem by not having enough and stuff," said resident Jule Cortez, who asked, "if there's not enough water, why are you trying to make it worse?" In nearby Lakeland, commissioners voted 4-3 in August 2026 for a one-year moratorium on new data centers after an uproar over a separate proposed data center called Project Swan. The water district's board must first act on the city's permit request; Keene said Cielo is "still in their phase waiting on SWFWMD's Board of Directors' approval." If water is approved, the project would still need zoning and environmental review and would have to go before the Haines City Commission, which Keene said has not yet reviewed any data center proposal. City officials said residents will be notified if the project moves forward.
paragraphs: A data center that Cielo Digital Infrastructure wants to build on Marion Road in Haines City, Polk County, Florida, is on hold because the city does not have enough water to supply it. Cielo asked the city about utility service for a 300 megawatt campus on about 74 acres near Marion Road and State Road 544 East, which would need up to 150,000 gallons of water a day.

Deputy City Manager James Keene said Haines City can produce 10 million gallons of water a day and already uses just over 7 million, with about 8,000 more homes coming. The city has asked the Southwest Florida Water Management District since June 2022 to raise its permit to 16.42 million gallons a day; the water district disputed that the city's application includes Cielo's 150,000 gallons.

"Haines City and surrounding areas are already having a water problem by not having enough and stuff," said resident Jule Cortez, who asked, "if there's not enough water, why are you trying to make it worse?"
In nearby Lakeland, commissioners voted 4-3 in August 2026 for a one-year moratorium on new data centers after an uproar over a separate proposed data center called Project Swan.

The water district's board must first act on the city's permit request; Keene said Cielo is "still in their phase waiting on SWFWMD's Board of Directors' approval." If water is approved, the project would still need zoning and environmental review and would have to go before the Haines City Commission, which Keene said has not yet reviewed any data center proposal. City officials said residents will be notified if the project moves forward.

ft-1782754581724-6170.text: Deltona Corporation has withdrawn its plan to open the way for a data center at the Holder Industrial Park near Hernando in Citrus County, Florida, after residents packed hearing rooms against it. Deltona withdrew its applications for the Holder Industrial Park in a letter to the county on June 23, 2026. The request would have turned almost 800 more acres of agricultural and residential land into heavy industrial use, growing the park from about 557 acres to a little over 1,300, which could have allowed a data center. The July 14 hearing before the Board of County Commissioners was cancelled. The withdrawal came a day after commissioners unanimously refused Deltona's request to put off a decision until November, and a week after the county's Planning & Development Commission unanimously recommended denial. The land lies between North Lecanto Highway, North Tram Road and North Florida Avenue, near U.S. 41, and Deltona is known mainly as a homebuilder. Joanna Coutu, the county's deputy growth manager, told the planning commission the area is low-density residential, rural residential and agricultural: "That's not where heavy industrial goes so definitely there are concerns about that." Residents raised the effect on nearby homes and businesses, the county's water supply, the electrical grid and the area's long-term environmental health. "We don't want any industrial sites near our homes. We want to protect our environment, our resources and our health," Hernando resident Tracy Landry told the planning commission. A group called No Data Center Citrus organized the opposition with meeting alerts and public comment templates. Deltona's attorney, Clark Stillwell, argued that many of the concerns about noise, vibration and water were based on older data centers. In May 2026 Citrus County commissioners imposed a one-year moratorium on data centers and on zoning changes that would enable them, and it remains in effect. Deltona's application had been filed before the moratorium, so it still had to be heard. "I think this is good news because now they are under the moratorium for data centers," Commissioner Holly Davis said, noting Deltona would have to start over to pursue a data center again. Elsewhere in the region, residents in Fort Meade in Polk County have launched a recall petition against three city officials over the approved Stonebridge data center. On September 4, 2026, the county released draft data center regulations and began taking public comments for about 30 days. The draft would allow data centers only on land zoned for heavy industry and with special county approval, bar them from agricultural land, and keep them at least 1,000 feet from homes, parks, schools, libraries, daycares and hospitals. It would cap noise at 50 decibels at the property line, limit backup generators to emergencies and 40 hours a month, require cooling with reclaimed or recycled water, and make developers post 115 percent of the estimated cost of dismantling a facility. There are no pending data center applications in Citrus County, and after the comment period the rules go to public hearings before the Planning and Development Commission and, ultimately, the Citrus County Board of County Commissioners. Florida's new data center law, which took effect July 1, 2026, also governs how data centers are permitted, powered and financed.

ft-1780879082497-8845.text: Project Swan, a proposed data center of up to 600,000 square feet at 923 Wilkinson Road in west Lakeland, Polk County, Florida, set off the one-year data center moratorium the Lakeland City Commission passed 4-3 on August 3, 2026. Kimley-Horn filed the concept plan on May 5, 2026 on behalf of developer Ryan Companies US, and the moratorium, which took effect immediately, stops the city from accepting or reviewing data center applications while it writes permanent rules. The plan shows three data center buildings, large mechanical yards, stormwater ponds and an electrical substation on 60.5 acres near Old Tampa Highway and Wilkinson Road, the first hyperscale-style data center proposed within Lakeland's city limits. The application names no tenant or operator and gives no figures for water, electricity, traffic or noise; the roughly 3.8-acre substation area is the only hint of its power demand, said Brian Rewis, the city's community and economic development director. The land is owned by Holmes Beach Family Tides LLC, controlled by Lutz investor Joel Schachter, and part of it lies in unincorporated Polk County and would have to be annexed. The site abuts the city's West Lakeland Wasteload Reduction Facility, with the McLane distribution center to the north and at least six homes across Wilkinson Road, including a beekeeping business. Lakeland's code does not list data centers at all, and Rewis said, "To our reading of our own code, there is no comparable use to a data center." The city's review comments said the project would need annexation, rezoning and a Planned Unit Development; after receiving the city's 13-page response, the developer canceled its June 3 review meeting, but the city said it remained an active project under review. More than 50 residents came to the June 1 City Commission meeting even though the project was not on the agenda, and 18 spoke against it, from Polk County Republican Party chairman Sam Romain to members of the grassroots group Defund Oligarchy. "The prospect of running a hyperscale data center in the midst of these concerns, as well as Florida being in the longest drought since 2001, doesn't just bother me, it scares me," Defund Oligarchy member Atheena said. The moratorium vote split the commission: Mayor Sara Roberts McCarley and Commissioners Terry Coney, Chad McLeod and Guy LaLonde Jr. voted for it, while Commissioners Stephanie Madden, Mike Musick and Ashley Troutman voted against, saying they backed a pause but found the ordinance too broad. "Nothing wrong with pumping the brakes, guys," LaLonde said. Lakeland Electric's acting general manager Scott Bishop supported the pause, saying the power large data centers need would be unlike anything the city-owned utility has handled. The moratorium applies inside the city and to projects outside it that seek service from Lakeland utilities, which matters because nearly 70 percent of Lakeland Electric's service area lies outside the city limits. It can last up to 12 months from August 2026, and commissioners may end it sooner once city staff finish rules on whether and where data centers may go; any revived Project Swan would then need further staff review, public hearings and a commission vote on annexation and zoning.

ft-1765431719795-7285.text: Project Tango, the hyperscale AI data center PBA Holdings wanted to build at the Central Park Commerce Center near Loxahatchee, is not finished: after Palm Beach County commissioners blocked it on July 15, 2026, the developer filed an appeal under Florida's Land Use and Environmental Dispute Resolution Act. The 202-acre site is at 20125 Southern Boulevard (State Road 80) in western Palm Beach County, next to the Arden community and roughly 900 to 1,200 feet from Saddle View Elementary School. PBA Holdings asked the county for nearly 3.6 million square feet of development: 2.35 million square feet of warehouses, 1.03 million square feet for an AI data center and 216,000 square feet of supporting utility structures. The campus was projected to draw 600 megawatts. PBA put the value of the finished data center and warehouse complex at $34.5 billion. A 2016 county approval already gives the owners the right to build 1.2 million square feet of warehouses and a 206,000-square-foot data center on the site, and that approval was not affected by the vote. "Well, that project goes forward. This vote doesn't have any effect on that," PBA project manager Ernie Cox said after the vote. The county commission voted 5-1 after a hearing of about 12 hours, with Commissioner Maria Marino the only vote in favor. County Mayor Sara Baxter, who represents the district, recused herself after publicly opposing the project before the hearing. The Zoning Commission had already voted unanimously on July 2 to recommend against it, arguing that a hyperscale AI campus works more like a heavy industrial facility than a light industrial one. Vice Mayor Marci Woodward said the development was not "compatible" with the county's comprehensive plan and needed too many conditions just to be approved. "We're trying to make it fit. [The current zoning code] is not that. We're going to create that. But it is not that," Woodward said. Residents organized for months against the project, arguing it would strain local infrastructure, and raised water use, electricity demand, noise and its closeness to homes and an elementary school. Opposition organizers wrote that the data center "will be constructed within 1,200 feet of Saddle View Elementary School and the preexisting Arden community and neighborhood". Opponents told the commission the campus threatened the 2,300-home Arden community with noise, vibration, heat, lighting and possible water contaminants. The developer said its closed-loop cooling would use 100,000 gallons of potable water a day and that its low-frequency hum would stay below sleep-disturbance levels; an independent review by Dr. Santiago Lattanzio called the developer's noise claims wildly inaccurate, finding its acoustic model covered only five fans and five chillers when cooling would take about 180 modules. Christina Reichert, a senior attorney with Earthjustice who spoke against the project, said heavy industrial uses belong "in places where that is appropriate, and that's not next to communities and elementary schools." PBA's appeal, filed August 5, argues that the commission judged Project Tango against what it wished the rules were. "It is readily apparent from the conduct of the board, and the comments of the board's members, that the board reviewed the Project Tango application not pursuant to the regulatory provisions actually and legally governing such review, but measured against what the board wished those provisions were", PBA attorney Ethan Loeb wrote, adding that what the board wished for was a total ban on data centers. Under the act, a special magistrate hears the challenge, with PBA and some opponents able to call witnesses, and then reports to the County Commission; if the commission turns the rezoning down again, PBA can sue or refile. PBA has also sued WPB Logistics Owner, the TPA Group affiliate that bought 60 acres of the site in 2023, claiming a breach of their 2021 contract. That company had earlier sued PBA, and county documents show a TPA-affiliated entity explored replacing an approved 1.2 million-square-foot warehouse with four data center buildings through an administrative review with no public hearing. "It's horrifying, because for one, it's wrong," said Rachel Smith, who created the No to Project Tango website. The county has moved to stop the next one. New data center proposals have been halted since July 9, and on August 27 commissioners voted unanimously to pursue a yearlong moratorium on large-scale data centers, defined as those with a monthly peak load of 50 megawatts or more. The final commission vote on the moratorium was scheduled for September 24, 2026. Martin County, to the north, advanced its own moratorium after backlash to the Silver Fox Data Center, and Clay, Hernando and Lake counties have adopted similar pauses. The Palm Beach County Board of County Commissioners decides both the moratorium and, after the magistrate's report, Project Tango's appeal.

That company had earlier sued PBA, and county documents show a TPA-affiliated entity explored replacing an approved 1.2 million-square-foot warehouse with four data center buildings through an administrative review with no public hearing.
"It's horrifying, because for one, it's wrong," said Rachel Smith, who created the No to Project Tango website.
The county has moved to stop the next one.

New data center proposals have been halted since July 9, and on August 27 commissioners voted unanimously to pursue a yearlong moratorium on large-scale data centers, defined as those with a monthly peak load of 50 megawatts or more.
The final commission vote on the moratorium was scheduled for September 24, 2026.
Martin County, to the north, advanced its own moratorium after backlash to the Silver Fox Data Center, and Clay, Hernando and Lake counties have adopted similar pauses.
The Palm Beach County Board of County Commissioners decides both the moratorium and, after the magistrate's report, Project Tango's appeal.

ft-55.text: HostDime, an Orlando-based company, is finishing a seven-story, 100,000-square-foot data center on the edge of Eatonville, Orange County, Florida, with a Maitland mailing address on Wymore Road, near Interstate 4 and Lee Road. The building missed its July 2025 opening deadline under HostDime's agreement with the Town of Eatonville, and the town has fined the company $250 a day since, with fines reaching $99,250 by September 1, 2026. HostDime CEO Manny Vivar told Channel 9 on September 3 the data center could open as early as October if it passes final inspection. A day earlier, Eatonville Mayor Ruthi Critton said HostDime is expected to hold a ribbon-cutting and open the facility this month, and that the town is "still hopeful nevertheless that we can get it all worked out." At a September 1 council meeting, Councilman Tarus Mack addressed Vivar, who was not there: "I'm extremely disappointed in everything that has been taking place with you not showing accountability, disrespecting my community. Don't make your mouth write a check that you can't cash." Vivar called the fines "salt to a wound" and said the town using them as leverage isn't helping, though HostDime wants the project done as much as anyone. The council put off a vote on doubling the fine to $500 a day until it meets with the developer. A proposed amendment would make it legally binding for the town to withhold the final certificate of occupancy unless HostDime meets commitments on sound dampening, water use and utility standards. The town gave HostDime $200,000 to reimburse it for designing and building water and sewer connections, and Critton said the flooding, noise and water concerns residents raised have been addressed, though some infrastructure work is still underway. HostDime broke ground on the site, the former home of a historic Eatonville school, in 2016, when it described an 88,000-square-foot building expected to open in 2018; the company says the finished facility will become its flagship Orlando data center.

ft-1777315563905-2542.text: Okee-One, the data center campus Indian River State College planned on the 205-acre former Florida School for Boys property along U.S. 441 in Okeechobee County, Florida, was canceled in April 2026 after the state pulled its support. At the April 23 county commission meeting, Commissioner Terry Burroughs announced: "IRSC will return almost 50 percent of the money that was in the Rural Infrastructure Funds to the state. The data center is not going to be built." The college took over the land from the state in 2023 with help from the county and its economic development corporation, and Governor Ron DeSantis awarded it $1.5 million in December 2024 for site preparation. The college billed Okee-One as both a working data center and a training lab for its students. In February 2026, IRSC's Andrew Treadwell told commissioners the first data center would use 9 to 10 megawatts, the most Florida Power & Light said the site could support, and that demolition of the old reform school buildings would begin in March. He said the college was exploring on-site generation to "fire up more of the site," and mentioned Nvidia while saying he could not break nondisclosure agreements. Those remarks alarmed residents. A petition against the project neared 2,000 signatures, and residents filled the April 9 commission meeting. "This town is more than just open land on a map. It's our home. And once we give that up, we won't get it back", said resident Korinne Curren. "Is there something to protect the citizens from it becoming a mega data center?" asked Elizabeth Canright. The site carries its own history: the Okeechobee reform school, where students were systematically abused, was the sister campus of the Dozier School for Boys in Marianna. Then the state reversed itself. The Florida Department of Commerce declined a second round of funding and accused the college of misleading it. "After further review, it became clear that (the college)'s plans, much like the data center industry around the nation, is based on falsehoods and pretenses about energy and water," department spokesperson Emily Hetherington said. College President Timothy Moore said the governor "would be mistaken" and that the campus was meant as a training site. The same day Okee-One was declared dead, commissioners voted to drop "Special Technology Opportunity Centers," a proposed comprehensive plan designation that would have opened county land to data centers, and the crowd applauded. Florida's new data center law, SB 484, requires data centers to pay for their own utilities without shifting costs to customers, but lets companies keep their plans confidential for a year, and it leaves land use decisions to local governments. The college has held the property since 2023, and county officials say they do not control what happens there. "Whether it be this one or any other when it may want to come to town, we're going to do our due diligence", said David Hazellief, chairman of the Okeechobee County Board of County Commissioners. Other parts of the county's comprehensive plan update remain in hearings.

ft-1772678463697-4680.text: The data center at 655 North Franklin Street in Tampa, in Hillsborough County, Florida, is on the tenth floor of an office block. The Franklin Exchange Building, 22 storeys, was the tallest building in Tampa when it was finished in 1966, and H5 Data Centers runs 27,300 square feet of it as a carrier hotel: a place where networks meet and hand traffic to each other. It houses the Tampa Internet Exchange and is Florida's main interconnection point outside Miami, carrier neutral, with 22 networks on net. The plant is modest by the standards of a campus: 750 kilowatt diesel generators on site and cooling towers at N+1 redundancy. It changed hands at the start of 2026. The Canadian private equity firm Novacap and H5 formed a joint venture called HyscaleIX Data Centers to buy and run carrier hotels across North America, anchored by four of them, three bought from 365 Data Centers at Buffalo, Nashville and Tampa, each hosting its local internet exchange. Terms were not disclosed.

ft-214.text: Project Sassy is a data center campus that Atlas Development has proposed for about 178 acres between Plainville Road and Ga. 53, across from the Lowe's Distribution Center, outside Rome in Floyd County, Georgia. Atlas's plans call for seven buildings of about 72 megawatts each, up to 504 megawatts across 2.49 million square feet, and the company sought to rezone the land from suburban residential to heavy industrial. Atlas withdrew that rezoning request in February 2025, the day the Rome-Floyd Planning Commission was to hear it, and a resident who filed a Floyd County records request said in August 2026 that the minutes show the request was pulled and that the county's response did not show it was resubmitted. Single-family homes and farmland sit near the site, and residents have raised concerns about noise, the strain on natural resources and how few workers data centers employ. Woodward Creek and its wetlands cross the property, so an environmental report would be required, and some residents called for a moratorium until the county's development code addressed data centers. Planning Director Brice Wood said that if Atlas reapplies, the request would be advertised again, with new letters sent to neighboring property owners and new signs posted on the property. On August 25, 2026, in front of a packed room, the Floyd County Commission adopted rules for any future data center in the unincorporated county: they are allowed only in heavy industrial zoning, buildings must sit at least 600 feet from an existing home, and noise at a residential property line is capped at 65 decibels by day and 55 decibels at night. No permit can issue until utilities confirm in writing that power and water are available, and the ordinance bars private wells and direct surface-water withdrawals and requires a bonded decommissioning plan. Most speakers at the hearing supported the rules, though some said they did not go far enough. Atlas has two other sites nearby in Floyd County: the seven-building, 2.4-million-square-foot Project Gracie campus planned behind Coosa High School, and the former Battey Business Complex on North Division Street in Rome, which the Rome-Floyd Development Authority agreed in August 2025 to sell to Atlas for $5.7 million. If Atlas reapplies for Project Sassy, the request would go before the Rome-Floyd Planning Commission and then the Floyd County Commission, and it would have to meet the new ordinance; none has been filed since the 2025 withdrawal.

ft-57.text: Project Springbank was Atlas Development's proposal for six data center buildings on 588 acres of farmland near Adairsville in Bartow County, Georgia, about an hour northwest of Atlanta. The $4.5 billion plan called for six buildings of 379,000 square feet each, using up to 78 megawatts per building and 432 megawatts in total, enough power for about 324,000 homes. The Bartow County planning commission recommended denial, and Atlas Development withdrew the proposal in May 2025. Atlas Development, founded in 2017 in Whitesburg, filed a Development of Regional Impact request on February 14, 2025; the land was zoned agricultural and miles from any industrial zone, so the company needed a rezoning. Bartow County resident Josh Cauthen told the planning commission, "If this goes through, you've placed an industrial zoning in the area, and it'll open up the floodgates for all the properties around it." Bartow County has had its own zoning limits on data centers in place since January 1, 2025, with no set end date, as more Georgia counties adopted or considered similar rules.

ft-60.text: GI Partners bought the data center at 4905 North Point Parkway in Alpharetta, Fulton County, Georgia, for $253 million in October 2025, according to court records reported by Bisnow. The seller, Principal Asset Management, describes it as a 15.2-megawatt, 185,000-square-foot single-story building on 39 acres. The deal changes only the building's owner; it keeps operating for its two tenants. The site is leased to two unnamed tenants, a Fortune 100 financial services company and a high-performance computing company. Principal says it raised the power capacity to 15 megawatts and that land next to the building would allow more expansion if a future owner wanted it. "We substantially increased the site's power capacity, further meeting the demand of today's tenants," said Devin Chen of Principal Asset Management. The companies involved declined to comment on the deal, according to Bisnow's reporting. The building went up in 2009 for the phone maker BlackBerry, with an initial design for 4 megawatts of power. Ascent bought the building from BlackBerry in 2017 for $30 million, with help from TowerBrook Capital Partners, and named it ATL1. In 2018 Ascent hired JLL to market about 34,000 square feet of available space and said the site could expand to 30 megawatts in two phases. A fund managed by Principal, working with Lincoln Rackhouse, bought the building in August 2022 for about $63 million, before selling it to GI Partners in October 2025.

ft-61.text: The data center rezoning at the White Oak Technology Park in Appling, Columbia County, Georgia, has been in court since it was granted. Commissioners approved it in early February 2026, and on February 25 a county resident, Gregory P. Guido Jr, filed petitions for judicial review of that decision and of a second rezoning at Pumpkin Center. The petitions allege procedural defects, incomplete analysis and conflicts with the county's comprehensive plan. On White Oak specifically they say water use and sewer capacity were never verified, that the county leaned on a traffic study from June 2025, that the school district was not given proper notice, and that the site's main access was moved to 1635 Appling Harlem Road without anyone assessing what that would do. ft-62.text: Trammell Crow Company, a subsidiary of CBRE, filed plans in April 2025 for a data center and technology park on about 1,900 acres off Morris Callaway Road and Innovation Parkway at Appling, in Columbia County, Georgia. The Development of Regional Impact application puts the campus at 8.076 million square feet of buildings, 8.004 million of it data centers, with the first phase inside two years and the rest over the next decade and beyond. It goes next to the existing 612 acre White Oak Business Park, where Amazon already has a fulfillment center. Commissioner Alison Couch of District 4 said she had researched technology parks for months, including visits to data centers around the state. "Based on my observations, I have concluded this use of land offers extremely low overall impact to the surrounding area, while generating tremendous tax revenues in return," she said. At a hearing in November 2025 the county put the revenue at $118 million and said Georgia Power had approved the power consumption model. Chairman Doug Duncan said the end user would bear every cost of infrastructure, construction and utility use, with no financial burden on residents, and that he expected the land to be bought before December 19. County manager Scott Johnson described what was being created: "It is creating a zoning by right, but each of those zonings would be heard at a later date." Vin Muller, a resident, went at the noise standard: "Noise is cumulative. Each additional device, building, generator, or HVAC unit that they put in there will add to that noise." The county attached conditions when it rezoned: lower noise limits, more space between the project and existing homes, and a landscaped berm for privacy. It also asked the state for property tax relief legislation for residents, which passed both chambers of the Georgia General Assembly. In August 2025, before the rezoning, an Augusta paper reported that no end user had been secured, that the developer or end user would carry the water and sewer costs, that about 30 percent of water could be recycled, and that newer closed loop cooling was being encouraged. On July 23, 2026, the Development Authority of Columbia County announced that Google would be the "sole end-user and operator" of the data center. The authority had sold the land to Trammell Crow for roughly $78 million in a deal ratified in December 2025, and the company in turn sold it to an entity listed as Kinetic Infrastructure for nearly half a billion dollars. Two more data center projects followed nearby: in February 2026 the commission gave the Pumpkin Center project the county's new data center zoning and voted down the Byrd Farms request. "This is one of the most significant investments in our county's history," Duncan said in the announcement.

ft-1766109846803-1450.text: Joel Harber, whose Athena Studios film campus sits in northeast Athens in Clarke County, Georgia, has submitted plans to turn it and surrounding land into a data center, as film production in the state has slumped. The 185,000-square-foot site already has power and air conditioning in place, and Georgia film and television spending in the year to June 2025 was down by nearly half from 2022, according to the Georgia Film Office. Harber said the studio has "an oversupply of space and an undersupply of demand," and estimates about three-quarters of Georgia's soundstages are now empty, compared with none when construction began in late 2021. Any data center there needs a rezoning: the parcel is zoned E-I, and County Manager Bob Cowell said staff determined a data center requires industrial zoning, which county rules have allowed in heavy industrial zones since the commission replaced its moratorium with new regulations in April 2026. The Athens-Clarke County Commission had passed that moratorium unanimously in December 2025, worried that data centers use excessive water and electricity and lower neighbors' quality of life, before replacing it with rules requiring closed-loop cooling. Commissioner Tiffany Taylor pointed to Pittard Road, where residents found in 2024 that a former industrial project had contaminated their well water, saying "we don't want a repeat of what happened with pollutants in communities, especially marginalized communities." Any project at Athena Studios must first go through that rezoning process, starting with a pre-application conference with county planning staff before the application reaches the Athens-Clarke County Planning Commission and then the Mayor and Commission for a vote.

ft-89.text: The ATL1 data center at 40 Perimeter Center East, in Atlanta's Perimeter Center area of DeKalb County, Georgia, is owned by Lincoln Rackhouse, runs 15 megawatts of power and is operating, with colocation company Internap holding a master lease and Coca-Cola as a significant tenant. In December 2025, CBS News Atlanta reported that DeKalb County had two existing data centers, one an 88,000-square-foot facility owned by Lincoln Rackhouse, as the county debates how to handle large new ones. DeKalb County commissioners voted on July 7, 2026 to extend a moratorium on new data center development to March 30, 2027 while county departments study the industry's impact, and any new rules must account for the Department of Watershed Management's water and sewer protocols. Internap once ran its corporate headquarters from the building before shifting to Virginia; its then chief executive, Pete Aquino, told analysts some Atlanta employees would move to "our new suburban data center anchored by Coca-Cola," while the company also operated a flagship downtown data center at 250 Williams Street at the time.

ft-68.text: Coloblox Data Centers, an Atlanta colocation company that has rented server space since 1998, runs its SMY1 facility at 1100 Circle 75 Parkway in Atlanta, Cobb County, one of two Atlanta sites the company calls ATL1 and ATL2. Coloblox does not publish SMY1's size or power draw; customers rent shared rack space or private cabinets and can have new equipment running within 72 hours. The site connects to several network carriers, including AT&T, Verizon and Hurricane Electric, and Coloblox says customers can bring their own network provider in directly rather than being locked to one carrier. Cobb County is not accepting new data center applications for now: the county board extended a moratorium on new permits by 180 days in August 2026, pushing the freeze to at least early February 2027. The moratorium, first adopted in February 2026, does not affect facilities already running like SMY1, and it was extended as the Marietta City Council weighed a separate data center proposal off Delk Road.

ft-79.text: Edged's ATL01-2 data center at 1760 Thomas Street NW in Atlanta, Fulton County, is the largest of three buildings on the company's 80-plus-acre campus near downtown, offering 100 megawatts of the campus's 169 megawatts of total capacity. ATL01-2 is still under construction; Edged has not announced when it will open, while the smaller ATL01-1 opened in August 2024 and ATL01-3 topped out in April 2026 for an early 2027 opening. The campus, on the former Tilford rail yard that Edged bought from CSX for $40 million in 2021, is fully leased and cools with glycol and air-cooled chillers instead of evaporating water, from Edged's sister company ThermalWorks. Edged was first planned as a 180 megawatt campus when it broke ground in 2023; the company now lists it at 169 megawatts once fully built and leased. Georgia Power supplies the campus through two dedicated substations, and founder Jakob Carnemark says the waterless design saves an expected 663 million gallons a year compared with an industry-average data center. The campus sits in the fastest-building data center market in the country: in September 2026, CBRE research put metro Atlanta at 1,803 megawatts of operating capacity with another 2,882 megawatts under construction, more than anywhere else in the country. Atlanta has banned new data centers in parts of the city since October 1, 2024, part of a wave of local moratoriums across Georgia.

ft-102.text: Lumen's Doraville 1 data center is an existing, operating building at 6855 Crescent Drive, with an Atlanta, Georgia postal address, in the Doraville area of DeKalb County. DeKalb County has had a moratorium on new data center development since 2025, and on June 23, 2026, commissioners voted 7-0 to reject a proposed set of data center rules that would have limited them to industrial zoning and set standards for noise, water and energy, after residents urged an outright ban instead. "Please do not let the monster in," one resident told commissioners, and Commissioner Ted Terry said the county "can't put our heads in the sand" because "data centers are knocking on our doors." On July 7, 2026, commissioners voted to extend the moratorium on new data center development through March 30, 2027 while officials keep studying the industry's impact on water and sewer capacity; Terry cast the only no vote. DeKalb's moratorium on new data center development runs to March 30, 2027 unless commissioners extend it again or pass new rules first.

ft-111.text: QTS Data Centers is building a $2 billion, six-building data center campus at 2883 Gordon Highway in Augusta, Richmond County, Georgia, on the site once planned by T5 as Project Eisenhower, between the Hayne's Station and Captain's Corner neighborhoods near Fort Gordon. The Augusta Commission adopted new data center rules by a 6-5 vote on September 15, 2026. Those rules do not apply to the QTS campus, which received its zoning approvals before the city's moratorium took effect. The land was first rezoned for a data center in 2022 under T5, and QTS, which worked through Eagle South LLC, received updated approvals in 2024 and 2025 after enlarging the project. The revised plan filed with the state calls for six two-story buildings totaling about 2.15 million square feet. The campus covers more than 170 acres, with the first building planned for as soon as 2027. QTS told residents that tree clearing would start in spring 2026 and grading that summer, with construction of the first building expected in 2027 and about 160 to 220 permanent jobs. QTS said the campus would use closed-loop cooling and put its maximum daily water use at about 18,000 gallons, rejecting a figure of 18 million gallons a day that had circulated. Many Hayne's Station residents were surprised when groundwork began, and then learned the data center had been approved before their homes were built. "None of us would have purchased our houses here if we would have known a data center was going into our backyards," Hayne's Station resident Zakiya Mabery told commissioners in June. At a packed February town hall, residents raised traffic, noise, wetlands, generator fumes, power and water bills and property values. "I would like for the elected officials to talk to us and explain to us how this happened," said Lacey Gaines. Mayor Garnett Johnson said it was a misconception that the commission had approved the deal, pointing to the economic development authority, and authority president Cal Wray said a private landowner had zoned the site and sold it to QTS. In February city staff said grading permits were still under review, no building permits had been issued, and wetland approvals from the Army Corps of Engineers were still needed. Residents pushed for a 12-month moratorium; on June 2 the commission instead passed a 49-day pause on new data centers that did not cover QTS. The final draft released a week before the vote bars data centers from residential and agricultural areas, requires a public hearing and commission approval in most other zones, sets noise limits of 65 decibels by day and 60 at night, and requires 500-foot buffers from homes and farmland and closed-loop cooling. The Augusta Press reported that some said the nearly three-month moratorium was not long enough. QTS is also developing campuses near Fayetteville and in Blakely, Georgia. QTS says it is holding a series of community meetings and events for Augusta residents, including a community panel session at Belair Elementary on June 24. The permits still outstanding in February, for grading, buildings and wetlands, are handled by Augusta's planning and permitting staff and the Army Corps of Engineers.

The campus covers more than 170 acres, with the first building planned for as soon as 2027. QTS told residents that tree clearing would start in spring 2026 and grading that summer, with construction of the first building expected in 2027 and about 160 to 220 permanent jobs. "None of us would have purchased our houses here if we would have known a data center was going into our backyards," Hayne's Station resident Zakiya Mabery told commissioners in June. At a packed February town hall, residents raised traffic, noise, wetlands, generator fumes, power and water bills and property values. "I would like for the elected officials to talk to us and explain to us how this happened," said Lacey Gaines. Mayor Garnett Johnson said it was a misconception that the commission had approved the deal, pointing to the economic development authority, and authority president Cal Wray said a private landowner had zoned the site and sold it to QTS.

QTS is also developing campuses near Fayetteville and in Blakely, Georgia. QTS says it is holding a series of community meetings and events for Augusta residents, including a community panel session at Belair Elementary on June 24. The permits still outstanding in February, for grading, buildings and wetlands, are handled by Augusta's planning and permitting staff and the Army Corps of Engineers.

ft-1765217894086-3055.text: The Forsyth City Council approved the Forsyth Technology Campus 5-1 on February 2, 2026: a 12 million square foot data center campus that CBRE-owned Trammell Crow Company plans on about 1,600 acres west of Interstate 75 in Forsyth, the seat of Monroe County, Georgia. The developer's filing called it a $21 billion project of up to 21 buildings, one of the largest proposed in Georgia, with power still unsettled. The land belongs to local timber firm H & H, which has it under contract to Trammell Crow. About 1,200 of the 1,632 acres already carried the agricultural zoning Forsyth requires for data centers; H & H asked the city to rezone the rest and grant a conditional use permit for the whole tract. H & H's filing projected $1.4 million a year in property taxes to the city, county and school board at the start, rising to an estimated $21.2 million a year to the city alone at full build-out, and put water use at 1.5 million gallons a day. The approval was close at every step. In January the Forsyth Planning and Zoning board split 3-3 on the conditional use permit, with one member recused over ties to the landowners, which counted as a no. "It's going to be developed one way or the other," board member Hal Clarke said. "What you need to do is choose the lesser of two evils." Longtime resident Joshua Pruitt, who opposes data centers, said promises of jobs and tax revenue "you can't take to the bank." Monroe County has become a data center battleground beyond this project. Google paid about $42 million for roughly 950 acres off I-75 and Rumble Road at the end of September 2025, and in November the county commission unanimously refused to sign a nondisclosure agreement Google had asked for. Trammell Crow still has to settle its power supply and bring detailed site plans back to the Forsyth City Council for approval before construction can begin; no groundbreaking has been reported as of the latest coverage in February 2026.

ft-1766554337607-2193.text: Project Blue Hole is QTS Data Centers' planned campus of up to 12 million square feet on undeveloped land off Martha Berry Highway near the Early County Airport in Blakely, Early County, Georgia. In August 2026 the Blakely City Council approved an agreement under which QTS will pay the Early County Development Authority $7.5 million for the first phase and then $7 million a year, to be divided among the city, the county and the school system. QTS, which is owned by Blackstone, filed a Development of Regional Impact application with the state for the campus, with full build-out by the end of 2035. The site came through John Engler of McKnight Engler in Augusta, who evaluated the McKnight-Blakely property and approached the city in 2024. Local officials said the campus would use closed-loop cooling with about 5,000 gallons a day for domestic use, and that QTS was still working with power providers on supply. QTS says it will fund the energy infrastructure and electricity the campus needs so that costs are not passed to residents, and it has pledged a $28.75 million Community Betterment Fund for park improvements and the old Washington High School building, among other projects. The project has divided Blakely. At a packed meeting at the Early County Theatre in July, Leighanne Willis, who lives across from the site and learned of it after noticing activity in a nearby field, said: "I'm scared to death." "Bringing it within the city limits and bringing it too close to homes out in the county, I do not go for that at all," Willis said. Lauren Dorminey of neighboring Mitchell County raised concerns about water drawn from area aquifers, possible contaminants and soil and air pollution. Commissioners pointed to the loss of Early County's Georgia-Pacific paper mill and more than 500 jobs, which they said cut about 10% of the county budget. On July 13, 2026 the Early County commissioners unanimously adopted a data center ordinance that requires water-efficient cooling, sets noise limits and sets a 1,000-foot buffer between any data center and homes, schools and churches. Chairman Hank Jester said that without clear rules development could become "like the Wild Wild West," and that the ordinance can be updated. The August agreement is only a first step. "We've got to meet with the company and decide on certain things like water, sewer, transportation, other development issues like that," city attorney Tommy Coleman said, adding that the three governments must agree on how to split the money. Those decisions rest with the Blakely City Council, the Early County Board of Commissioners, the Early County Board of Education and the Development Authority of Early County. QTS is also building a campus on Gordon Highway in Augusta and developing one near Fayetteville.

ft-1772085526952-5781.text: Project Ruby is a proposed $5.18 billion data center campus that Choose Columbus, the marketing arm of the Development Authority of Columbus, wants to build on 865 acres in Upatoi, near Box Springs in northeast Muscogee County, Georgia. Habitat Real Estate Partners bought the land, and WRBL reported that Atlas Development, which also has data center sites in Rome, Villa Rica and Temple, is involved too; the campus is planned for construction between 2027 and 2030. The developers have asked Flint Energies for a 600 megawatt grid connection, more power than all of Columbus now uses. Residents packed a town hall organized by Clean Energy Columbus on March 8, 2026, where resident Shaun Tarkington said he was against the project because "they're extremely loud ... and they have to compete for power." He asked why residents "have to compete with something that drives up our prices for water and electricity during a recession ... and we still haven't seen the hard data." Columbus Water Works said it can draw the water the project needs from the Chattahoochee River but lacks the pipes to deliver it, and its wastewater plant has had no major upgrade since the 1960s. Clean Energy Columbus asked the city for a moratorium on the project until it set standards for power use, cooling, water and tax breaks. On June 16, 2026 the Columbus Council instead voted 6-2 to create a technology overlay district, with a 500-foot buffer, noise limits of 55 to 75 decibels depending on the time of day, on-site water pre-treatment and Tier IV diesel generators. Councilor Joanne Cogle, who voted no, said: "This is a premature thing, and I'm not completely satisfied the enforcement will protect citizens." "This is a tool," said Mayor Pro Tem Gary Allen. "We have no applications (for a data center)." Project Ruby can be built only if it meets the new ordinance and the council approves the developer's rezoning request, which had not been filed as of the June 16 vote; no update has been published since.

ft-1782858901235-6061.text: An Atlanta-based developer is pursuing a 500,000-square-foot data center on 11 acres of a 57-acre tract off Highway 53 in Calhoun, Georgia, next to Fair's Auto Services & Repair, despite moratoriums on data centers, the Chattanooga Times Free Press reported in June 2026. The property, about 57.27 acres at 1401 Hwy. 53 Spur between the Brookstone Subdivision and Fair's Auto, lies inside Calhoun's city limits in Gordon County, where the county's own moratorium on data centers does not apply. The Gordon Gazette first reported the site in April 2026, when it was being cleared and a driveway had been installed. "The proposed use of the property to construct a data processing center would be a legal conforming use for the zoning district," City Building Official Joey Moore said of the land, which is zoned IND-G, Industrial General. Discussion of the site followed reports of possible negotiations over energy rates between the city and North Georgia EMC, and of a possible will-serve letter from the city to the utility. A host of residents attended the City Council meeting that month, and every member of the public who spoke opposed a data center, several fearing one was already underway. "I will assure you to my knowledge and to the council's knowledge that none of us have been approached or have any knowledge of a data center in any way," Mayor Jimmy Palmer told the crowd. The council's four members then unanimously adopted a moratorium on "all applications for zoning decisions, land disturbance permits, and licenses for data centers" through at least July 27, 2026, while City Attorney Brandon Bowen drafts an ordinance. Bowen said the ordinance would include a public notice and hearing process and was meant "to create an ordinance that will be protective of the city." On June 8, 2026, the council voted 3-0 to extend the moratorium by six months, halting data center permits, approvals and construction in the city through mid-January 2027. The Gordon County Board of Commissioners adopted its own moratorium near the end of March 2026. Across Georgia, 34 counties and 23 cities had moratoriums or ordinances in place or in draft as of June 5, 2026, and Atlanta, Palmetto and Fayetteville have banned data centers. Whether the Highway 53 project can go forward depends on the Calhoun City Council, which can issue no data center permits until the extended moratorium ends in mid-January 2027 unless it acts sooner. The Gordon County Board of Commissioners has no authority over the site.

ft-114.text: Digital Realty's Project Bunkhouse is under construction on the former Gaines family cattle farm along Taff Road in Bartow County. Sole Commissioner Steve Taylor approved a rezoning requested by Taurus DC SPE LLC on June 4, 2025. In an August 2026 statement, the county described the Stilesboro-area campus as planned for about 1.3 gigawatts of computing capacity and roughly $18 billion of investment over a buildout projected to take about ten years. The county said the campus was still in construction and had not begun operating. The project's early state filing proposed 12 buildings with almost 8.7 million square feet of floor space on about 877 acres. The county's later rezoning approval capped floor space at 8.3 million square feet and required buffers before buildings open, water-efficiency measures and compliance with county data-center rules. Main access must come from Taff Road; Floyd Creek Church Road is limited to secondary and emergency access. These conditions changed the scale and layout proposed in the first filing. Neighbors raised concerns about the loss of farmland, water and power use, and possible new transmission lines near Plant Bowen. At the rezoning meeting, a project representative told one neighbor that the needed power infrastructure was already in place. The county says it has granted no local tax abatement for the campus; Digital Realty forecasts more than 800 jobs once the buildout is complete. Those jobs and the county's investment estimate are projections, while the buildings are still being developed. Bartow County adopted stricter data-center standards in July 2026, including closed-loop or equivalent cooling, a 200-foot buffer next to residential districts and nighttime noise limits. The county's August statement says the Digital Realty campus remains under construction and that only its land value has entered the tax digest so far. Building and equipment values will be assessed as the campus is completed, so the county's projected investment is not current tax revenue.

ft-1782187196919-6153.text: The Cartersville City Council unanimously approved rezoning for Project Indo, DataBank's planned 200 megawatt data center campus on about 69 acres at 218 Industrial Park Road in Cartersville, Bartow County, Georgia, on September 3, 2026. The council also approved variances and attached three conditions: the project is limited to the site plan, the land may be used only as a data center, and no certificate of occupancy will be issued until a power source is lined up. Dallas-based DataBank filed a Development of Regional Impact application for 1.1 million square feet valued at $2.4 billion at full build-out, and has applied for a 288 megawatt grid connection. The open question is power. The city's electric provider, MEAG, is still studying whether 288 megawatts is available. "None of our open capacity is going to serve this facility," Mayor Matt Santini said at the August 20 hearing, and City Manager Dan Porta added: "Our ratepayers are not going to subsidize their power needs." At the September 3 hearing, DataBank's attorney Brandon Bowen said each building's closed-loop cooling holds about 300,000 gallons, 600,000 for the site. Resident Jason Barton, who lives less than two miles away, was the only speaker against the project at the final hearing, raising Pettit Creek, a tributary of the Etowah River along the property's edge, nearby homes in the unincorporated county, and infrasound. DataBank executive Justin Puccio told the council the company does not flip sites and serves banks, health records and emergency communications rather than AI: "We are not a flipper." With zoning approved, the project now turns on power. MEAG is still studying routing and usage, and under the council's condition, no building can open until a power source is secured.

ft-115.text: Switch, the Las Vegas data center company, is building its Keep 2.0 Atlanta North campus on 126 acres south of Old Alabama Road and Bates Road in Cartersville, Bartow County, Georgia, running to the Paulding County line. Switch plans to invest $772 million in the data center campus, with a first phase due in the second quarter of 2026 and build-out continuing to 2046. The first phase is a single data center building about 1,620 feet long, with driveways, detention ponds and an electrical substation. The Cartersville City Council created a new technology zoning district for the project and, at Switch's request, voted unanimously in November 2023 to rezone the 1,946 undeveloped acres left in the Carter Grove Planned Development to it. The land had been meant for later phases of the Carter Grove neighborhood, planned in the early 2000s for as many as 2,500 homes, of which about 400 lots exist. The filing put annual local tax revenue at $15 million. Paulding County residents objected to a data center so close to homes. "This area is zoned as residential and should stay residential," Vicki Cox wrote to the city planner, citing frequent power outages nearby and "the noise and the environmental impact, as well as ongoing traffic nightmares." Mayor Matt Santini said Switch offered buffers twice the size the city usually requires, and Switch's local counsel, Brandon Bowen, said the campus would not use Carter Grove Boulevard for access. Officials say Switch's cooling system recycles water rather than relying on continuous withdrawals. Bartow County officials have welcomed data centers. "It’s basically a warehouse with computers," said County Administrator Peter Olson, who hopes data center revenue could one day eliminate property taxes. In July 2026 Sole Commissioner Steve Taylor signed an amendment to the county's data center ordinance requiring each data center to provide its own power source, use a closed-loop water system, obey a strict noise ordinance and turn lights off at 9 p.m. A separate proposed data center in the Etowah Valley Historic District has drawn protests and petitions, and resident Marty Knight, who leads the opposition, said: "I don’t know anybody who wants a data center." "I want to see a moratorium," said Bella Bautista, a candidate for Georgia House District 14. Switch has said it will keep building the campus in phases through 2046. Olson says at least three more data centers are approved or proposed elsewhere in Bartow County, and the Etowah Valley site would need a rezoning before a data center could be built there. As of August 2026, the campus was under construction.

ft-118.text: Vantage Data Centers has proposed a 105-megawatt data center at 4380 Stacks Road in South Fulton, Fulton County, Georgia, on a 24-acre site at Stacks and Mallory roads, just north of the CSX railroad. Vantage filed it with the state in August 2024 along with a second filing, Westlake, about 10 miles away; Stacks Road was planned for completion in January 2027. South Fulton's City Council later paused new data center applications, but Stacks Road was filed before that pause took effect. The city's moratorium on new data center applications began December 9, 2025, and was extended in May 2026 to September 9, 2026, a date that has since passed with no further extension published. Whether construction has started at Stacks Road is unclear; the most recent published reporting on the project is from early 2025. Decisions on data centers in South Fulton rest with the mayor and City Council. The Atlanta Regional Commission's review found the project "not aligned" with the region's policy of preserving forested land, and recommended waterless or near-waterless cooling to ease the burden on drinking water supplies. It estimated the project would bring South Fulton about $7.3 million a year in revenue and generate 690 new vehicle trips a day.

ft-121.text: DC BLOX is under construction on the first phase of its Atlanta East data center campus at 1726 Farmer Road in Conyers, Rockdale County, Georgia, the only data center campus so far cleared to build in the county. The company announced the campus in December 2023 with 216 megawatts of power committed by Georgia Power, and county filings put the full project at just over a million square feet across seven buildings. A hyperscale company will be the first phase's anchor tenant; DC BLOX has not named it. In November 2025 a DC BLOX affiliate asked state and federal regulators for permits to build three more 40-megawatt buildings, five stormwater ponds and a large substation on about 53 acres next to the Rockdale Regional Youth Detention Center. That work would permanently fill wetlands, a pond and more than 1,200 feet of streams draining toward the Yellow River, which the developer proposes to offset by buying wetland mitigation credits. The county's fact sheet says DC BLOX has agreed to pay for a substation, transmission lines and four miles of water and sewer lines, and that the campus will have 50 to 60 staff. Rockdale County has barred new data center applications since January 2026. On September 22, 2026, commissioners adopted most of a new development ordinance but put off its data center rules, extending the moratorium through October 9. The draft would require a special permit for new data centers, closed-loop cooling, noise limits and setbacks of 250 feet from homes and 1,000 feet from schools. Resident Roderick Bohn objected to a clause exempting projects already underway that show "extensive discussions" and "significant expenditures": "Those words are not defined anywhere in this 300-page document." Commissioner Tuwanya Smith said, "I just don't understand why we have to rush." The Rockdale County Board of Commissioners takes up the data center rules at 10 a.m. on October 6 at Assembly Hall, 901 Main St. in Conyers.

ft-122.text: Rockdale Technology Park 1 is a three building data center campus of about 837,500 square feet that SDP Acquisitions LLC, an affiliate of Atlanta based Strategic Real Estate Partners, planned on 52.78 acres at the southwest corner of Farmer Road and Lester Road near Conyers, in Rockdale County, Georgia. The Rockdale County Board of Commissioners approved the rezoning and a special use permit for the project in September 2024. The board rezoned the land from single family residential to office institutional and approved a special use permit for a 4 acre substation pad. Georgia Power found the campus's electricity use would not interfere with existing customers nearby, and the developer said it hoped to create a technology park where students could learn about STEM; when the plan was filed in early 2024 its IT capacity and end customer were not disclosed, and the developer expected to finish in 2028. The Atlanta Regional Commission, reviewing the plan in April 2024, said it did not fit the area's "Established Suburbs" designation, which stresses preserving single family neighborhoods, and estimated about 800 new vehicle trips a day. It urged waterless or near waterless cooling and asked for a revised site plan showing the wetlands the project would affect. In November 2025, DC BLOX, through DCB Atlanta East LLC, filed for state and federal wetlands permits for a three building, 216 megawatt data campus on 52.84 acres described as west of Farmer Road and Lester Road, the same intersection as SDP's site. Rockdale County's May 2026 fact sheet counts only "DC BLOX on Farmer Road" as an approved data center in the county. Rockdale County has paused new data center and battery storage applications since January 2026 while it writes new rules requiring a special use permit, closed loop or similar cooling, noise limits and a 250 foot setback from homes. On September 22, 2026, commissioners extended the moratorium through October 9 and put off a vote on the data center rules to an October 6 meeting at Assembly Hall in Conyers, after residents questioned a clause that would let some in-progress projects keep the old rules.

ft-123.text: Residents near the Project Splice data center site outside Cordele, in Crisp County, Georgia, are organizing again more than a year after the county rezoned the land, and the site has changed hands on paper: Premier Data Center Development is now the developer of the site Red Wolf DCD Properties first proposed. Carla Baker, who helped organize an August 2026 meeting of concerned residents at Midway Church, said: "Our next steps are to see if anyone's willing to get organized and possibly try to get this on the ballot for a vote for Crisp County." Crisp County commissioners voted unanimously on June 10, 2025 to rezone 583.62 acres off Cemetery Road and Ninth Street, outside Cordele in Georgia, for a data center campus. Red Wolf DCD Properties had filed for it in March that year as Project Splice: seven buildings of 300,000 square feet each, 2.1 million square feet in all, with a substation, valued in the filing at $6 billion and phased to finish in 2029, 2031 and 2033. Residents living near the site had spoken against it at a public hearing on May 13, and the ordinance the commission passed is largely a list of answers to them. "If it does decrease in value by you rezoning it and you putting it there, do you plan on compensating us for the devaluation of our property," Baker, who lives on a four-generation farm on Cemetery Road, asked commissioners at that hearing. "This is going to be a 24/7 noise factor in our life and it is going to affect us," her neighbor Rhona Bernecker told them. The first phase must sit 325 feet back from Old Nesbitt Road; the main way in during construction is from Ninth Avenue; fast growing evergreens must screen the noise and the view; noise must stay inside the county code; the outside lighting is to be inspected so it does not spill onto neighboring homes; daily construction is limited to 6:30 a.m. to 8 p.m., with exceptions for concrete work and interior build-out; the agricultural wells are to be sealed; a fire plan has to be agreed with county fire and rescue; and the site managers must give out 24 hour contact numbers. Interim county administrator Mickey Dunnavant took the commission through the eight standards the state requires for a rezoning. "The west and south sides of the property are surrounded by commercial and industrial zoning," he said, and "Exit 102 is experiencing a burst with commercial growth." "Water usage is estimated at .3 million gallons a day," he told them. The campus is put at 180 to 200 jobs averaging about $80,000 a year, with roughly 270 more in the wider community. ft-127.text: John B. Williams is proposing the Gregory Road Data Center on Gregory Road and Flat Rock Road outside Covington, in Newton County, Georgia: 1,410,000 square feet of data center buildings and 307 acres of housing on a 520 acre site, with a power capacity of 360 megawatts, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported when the plans were filed in March 2025. Universal Planning and Development, the development arm of John B. Williams, is behind the plan; his other Covington projects include the Amazon data center campus next to this site. The plan is five data center buildings, two maintenance buildings, an electrical substation, a switch yard, a wastewater treatment plant and 27 houses on lots of two and a half to four acres, built in three phases to 2036, on ground that is now woodland and farmland with eight houses and a barn on it. The developer wants the land annexed into Covington and rezoned from agricultural to heavy industrial and residential, which triggered a regional review that put the finished value at $5.7 billion and the annual local tax at about $19.17 million. The site sits beside Lake Roy Varner, a drinking water reservoir, inside both the Cornish Creek and Alcovy River watersheds. Daily demand is 1.08 million gallons of water, which existing capacity covers only for phase one, and 0.36 million gallons of sewage, for which the county has no designated treatment provider. Some of the buildings would sit on top of critical water lines, and the project would require moving a 30 inch transmission main that feeds northern and western Newton County and links to Walton County. Newton County's development services director, Shena Applewhaite, told the review she could not recommend the plan as proposed: heavy industrial is the county's most intensive use and could hurt the protected watersheds and drinking reservoir, and there is no end user identified for the data center. She recommended zoning the whole project residential at a ten acre minimum until a user is identified, then rezoning the industrial part with conditions on buffers and stormwater. The county's transportation office said closing Gregory Road would turn a half mile trip into a five mile detour one way, nine the other, and the developer has no power to buy the right of way it would need to fix that. Granite outcrops on the site would have to be blasted out, and the regional review recommended a survey for rare lichens and mosses growing on them. The site still needs to be annexed into Covington and rezoned before it can move forward. Those decisions rest with the city of Covington, and no decision on the annexation has been reported since the plans were filed in spring 2025.

ft-138.text: On Thursday, September 18, 2025, Twiggs County commissioners approved rezoning 291.5 acres from agricultural land to general industrial for the Pine Ridge Technology Center, a data center planned by Eagle Rock Partners in the unincorporated county near Dry Branch, Georgia. The developer valued the project at up to $5 billion and said it would double the county's tax revenue and bring 500 to 600 new jobs. About two dozen residents spoke against it at a hearing the day before, raising the environment, energy use, water and the local black bear population. Ken Loeber of Eagle Rock Partners told the commissioners the jobs would not all require advanced degrees: "There is a perception that everyone that works in these things has a Ph.D. in Computer Science, and that's just not factual." He said noise from the site would not exceed 55 decibels. Question and answer sessions were held September 16 and 17, and the commission voted at the courthouse on September 18. Resident Meg Couillard Bevan said: "If we have to have a new data center here let's make sure that we have everything in order and that we're doing the right things." John Wilson, who has spent nearly four decades arguing for land preservation, led the opposition: "The data center - you can build it anywhere. So why would you put it in an important place like this," he said. He said the facility would need deep wells drawing water on the scale of a town of thirty thousand people. His case rested on the Ocmulgee River corridor, land historically inhabited by the Muscogee Creek Nation, and the fencing the campus would need, which he said would split the local black bear population into what he called upper bears and lower bears. To win approval, the developer offered a guaranteed property tax return of at least $175 million, $100,000 for school career training and another $100,000 for fire, public safety or recreation, and agreed the site would not be used for cryptocurrency mining. Residents who believed the commission rushed the rezoning sued to overturn it, arguing the county skipped a regional impact review that a state panel added for data centers in November 2025 and that commissioners' actions "were an abuse of its police and zoning powers." Eagle Rock's Ken Loeber had told commissioners that waiting "would kill" the project, and the county's attorney, Kerry Howell, argued the review requirement did not apply while it was paused for data centers. In its December 2025 response, the county denied the rezoning was made in haste or through "fraud, corruption, or a manifest abuse," and denied that residents have a substantial interest in the case; the county's filing is the newest word on the lawsuit, which remains before the court. Nancy Lubeck, one of the plaintiffs, said communities are left "flying blind" on what these facilities will do to the state's power grid and water supply.
