ft-140.text: The DeKalb County Board of Commissioners unanimously denied the $1.6 billion data center that PCC-DeKalb LLC proposed for 95 acres at 4280 and 4358 Loveless Place and 2281 Pineview Trail in Ellenwood, south DeKalb County, Georgia, on August 13, 2026. The vote capped nearly a year of deferrals, and the room erupted into applause. The denial means the site keeps its existing zoning; PCC-DeKalb cannot immediately revise and resubmit the application, but could challenge the vote in court. The plan, filed as "Project Preserve" on June 16, 2025, called for a 1 million square foot campus of three two-story buildings and an electric substation, in a majority Black community surrounded by homes. Brett Embry of E-Data Company told commissioners in 2025 the site was chosen because a Georgia Power transmission line runs beside it: "That's the driving force behind all data centers: it's the energy and the power." He promised sound-dampening fencing, 40 acres left undeveloped, cooling with treated gray water and dark-sky lighting, and said the project would add about $28 million a year to the county's tax roll, roughly $14 million of it for schools. Opponents said the application understated its size: "This application has been misrepresented by the SLUP application for a 1 million square-foot [data center], when in fact it's a 2 million square-foot data center," said Jan Dunaway, DeKalb's soil and water conservation supervisor. DeKalb's code has no data center category, so PCC-DeKalb applied under "utility structure," and county planners recommended denial: the land is zoned for about 300 homes and sits in Tier 5 of the Bouldercrest Overlay District, which protects established subdivisions. "[S]taff doesn't believe this is your typical utility structure," Senior Planner John Reid said. Residents came for months to oppose it, raising water, power bills, air pollution, noise and property values. "We are surrounded by a lot of things that are not compatible to our neighborhood," said Pat Culp, president of the Cedar Grove Neighborhood Association, whose community already lives with odors from the Seminole Road Landfill and noise from Hartsfield-Jackson airport traffic. "We are dealing with too much," said Jackie Malcom, an organizer with the DeKalb Citizens Coalition who lives less than a quarter mile from the site. Her fellow organizer Gina Mangham pointed to DeKalb's water system: "We have both capacity issues as well as we have a lot of sewage overspills. We've had a lot of water main breaks." The county still has no data center rules: commissioners voted down a draft ordinance in June 2026 after residents asked for stronger protections, and have extended the moratorium on new data center applications, in place since July 2025, to March 30, 2027. The Ellenwood application went forward only because it was filed three weeks before the moratorium began. Elsewhere in south DeKalb, Shadowbox Studios sued the county in August 2026 to overturn the moratorium so it can build a data center on nearly 200 acres at 3600 International Park Drive, saying county planners had told it the zoning would allow it. On September 9, 2026, the DeKalb Zoning Board of Appeals affirmed the county's denial of Shadowbox's permit request, leaving the dispute to DeKalb County Superior Court. What happens next turns on two things: whether PCC-DeKalb challenges the Ellenwood denial in court, and whether the Board of Commissioners writes data center rules before the moratorium expires on March 30, 2027. "If the BOC and the administration are truly committed to DeKalb residents, they need to defend the Shadowbox lawsuit," Mangham said.

ft-1775151442981-9276.text: Crow Holdings Development and CHI/Acquisitions withdrew their plan for a data center on Highway 85 North in Fayetteville, Fayette County, Georgia, after the city's Planning and Zoning Commission rejected the site plan in late January 2026. The developers gave up their appeal to the Fayetteville City Council on March 20, 2026, days before the council was set to hear it. The plan was a single two-story, 300,000-square-foot building and a substation on 37.4 acres, with cryptomining barred and no power figure released. The land was already zoned for a data center, so the commission's rejection of the site plan left an appeal to the City Council as the developers' only path forward. The City of Fayetteville said on Facebook that Crow Holdings Development and CHI/Acquisitions, LP had "officially withdrawn their appeal to build a new data center north of the Fayette Pavilion shopping center along Highway 85 North." ft-148.text: Project Turbo, a $1.2 billion data center planned on O'Kelly Road outside Gainesville in Hall County, Georgia, was withdrawn in December 2025 after significant opposition from residents over water use and traffic. Williams Brothers Development had presented the plan to the Hall County Planning Commission as three buildings of about 300,000 square feet each, 900,000 square feet in all, promising about 150 jobs. Its developers say they still want to build there, and Hall County has since put a moratorium on data centers, extended in August 2026 for another 180 days. The applicant, Project Turbo LLC, applied in 2025 for a special use permit and a rezoning from planned industrial development to light industrial on roughly 119 acres at 2400 O'Kelly Road, off Candler Road; its listed organizers are Cameron Grogan, owner of Atlanta-based Williams Brothers Development, and Christopher Hoag. It also filed for a state Development of Regional Impact review for the site, which is about 55 miles northeast of downtown Atlanta. The plans included a new substation; Georgia Power high-voltage transmission lines and a natural gas transmission facility border the southern part of the site. Water was the fight. The developer acknowledged that the City of Gainesville, which would supply the water, said it would not have enough capacity if the data center reached the high end of its estimated use, and residents worried about roughly 225,000 gallons a day for cooling. "It wasn't that long ago we had a drought, and we were thirty feet down [at Lake Lanier] and we here in Hall County were in desperate shape where water is concerned so what's going to happen then?" resident Mandy Harris asked. "They're not giving us answers," said Jody White, another resident. Planning Commission member Shannon Davidson said: "What kind of issues are we gonna have in the County if the City is saying they can't do it?" Residents also questioned a possible conflict of interest because Planning Commission Chair Chris Braswell works for Norton Commercial, which was selling the land to the developer; Braswell recused himself from the item. The planning commission eventually approved the application, but the developers withdrew it before the county commission's vote. "We withdrew our application not because we want to walk away, but because it's just clear that the county has not yet decided if it wants a data center, and if it does, then just we need to all take a step back and come up with some rules and regulations of how those will be developed in the future," developer Cameron Grogan said on WDUN. Grogan said annexation into the City of Gainesville would be needed for sewer, which the Lake Lanier Association wanted so the water could be returned to the lake, and he argued the plant's maximum water use would take 12 and a half years to lower the lake by an inch. At the county commission meeting, residents learned the developers would seek a light industrial zoning change instead, and many remained skeptical. "I'm very happy they pulled the plug," said neighbor Kerri McCoy. The same applicant, Project Turbo LLC, is linked to Project Azalea, a six-building data center campus proposed on 200 acres on Randall Hunt Road in Thomson, McDuffie County, outside Augusta. Hall County commissioners approved a 180-day moratorium on data centers on February 26, 2026, and on August 27 voted to extend it by another 180 days while they work on a data center ordinance. At an August 14 public hearing, many residents said the draft ordinance did not go far enough, and some wanted an outright ban. "It's so we can go and do our due diligence and our homework," Commissioner Gregg Poole said of the extension. Any return of Project Turbo would go either to the Hall County Board of Commissioners under the ordinance it is now writing, or to the City of Gainesville if the land were annexed.

ft-149.text: Eagle Rock Partners and Thomas and Hutton Engineering withdrew their application to rezone more than 600 acres for a data center in Jones County, Georgia, before the planning and zoning board could hear it. The Crooked Creek Technology Park would have been about 1.8 million square feet at the intersection of Highway 18 and Bethlehem Church Road, on 634 acres, and Eagle Rock had put it at an investment of $5 to $7 billion. The withdrawal came by email to the county's planning and zoning director, Tim Pitrowski, with the hearing days away. A residents' group calling itself No Data Centers in Jones County had organised against it. The same engineering firm worked on a 900 acre scheme at Bolingbroke in Monroe County, which the planning and zoning board there refused in early August after resident opposition and objections about the environment. EagleRock is also behind Pine Ridge Technology Park in Twiggs County, approved a month before the Jones County withdrawal despite local opposition; objectors there say commissioners broke county ordinances in approving it and plan to go to law. The Jones County proposal can be filed again. EagleRock declined to comment on the withdrawal, and some residents have moved on to trying to change the county's ordinances to make a data center harder to build there at all.

ft-1765203657910-6182.text: Eagle Rock Partners' Crooked Creek Technology Park, a data center campus of up to 1.8 million square feet on more than 600 acres in Jones County, Georgia, was withdrawn on October 20, 2025, less than a day before its zoning hearing. Eagle Rock and Thomas & Hutton Engineering had filed on September 25, 2025 to rezone the farmland at Highway 18 and Bethlehem Church Road, saying the project would bring "an investment of $5 to $7 billion." It withdrew by email to Planning and Zoning Director Tim Pitrowski and has not said why. The same developer has since agreed to buy the county's Griswoldville Industrial Park, a deal now tied up in a residents' lawsuit. Residents organized fast. Dustin Riley's Facebook group "No Data Centers in Jones County" drew more than 1,500 members within weeks, and farmer Alexandra Lefholz started a petition. "The fact that it's just 'Bam!' and popped up is what's really rubbed a lot of people the wrong way," Riley said. After the withdrawal, the county adopted a 90-day moratorium, then on January 16, 2026 unanimously approved data centers as a conditional use only in a new industrial district at Griswoldville, with closed-loop cooling and lower noise limits. April Lipscomb of the Southern Environmental Law Center called the new 200-foot setback "utterly inadequate," and in February 2026, 17 residents including Lefholz and Riley sued the county, arguing officials gave improper notice and engaged in unlawful "contract zoning" with the developer. The development authority's chairman, Eric Varnadoe, had signed a letter of intent to sell the 956-acre Griswoldville park to Eagle Rock for $25 million, but the authority voted in March to put the sale on hold. "We essentially have a lame duck property right now," Varnadoe said in June. What happens next depends on the court. The county has moved to dismiss the lawsuit, and a hearing may not come until 2027, according to the development authority. Any data center at Griswoldville would still need conditional use approval from the Jones County Board of Commissioners, chaired by Chris Weidner.

ft-1772657752383-8906.text: The 75 South Data Center Campus, proposed by Industrial VI Enterprises, a Hillwood affiliate, on Tomochichi Road in Griffin, Spalding County, Georgia, will not be built. The company had applied to put seven two-story buildings totaling 2.24 million square feet on land in the county's southeast corner, but by September 3, 2026 county zoning attorney Newton Galloway said the rezoning and special exception applications had been withdrawn and the developers do not plan to come back. Commissioner James Dutton says Spalding County's strict water and zoning rules, written after a moratorium, are why no data center has broken ground in the county even though it has approved three others. "Because our rules are so high, you'll notice that there are no data centers in Spalding County," Dutton said. "Why would you come and build here, when Butts County is going to give away the farm... and there is no tax incentive to come here." Community development director Touissant Kirk said the county has "not received any applications, plans, or other submittals related to a Land Disturbance Permit" for any of its approved projects either.

ft-150.text: Project Spalding is a data center campus of about 2.4 million square feet that Montana Property Group LLC plans on 133 acres at High Falls Road and Alicia Drive outside Griffin, in Spalding County, Georgia. The Spalding County Board of Commissioners approved the project in 2025, the first of three data center campuses the county has approved along High Falls Road, and the latest plan shows three buildings plus a power station. The land belongs to Alan R. Mobley, who owns 86.81 acres on High Falls Road and 46.1 acres on Alicia Drive, and the county rezoned it from agricultural-residential and single-family residential to C-1C light manufacturing for the data center. Montana Property Group's state filing put the value at build-out at $1.875 billion, with about $26.859 million a year in local taxes, and build-out by 2030; no end user has been named. The plan came to light in March 2025 through a state filing, and resident Greg Berns pressed commissioners in April 2025, asking, "Why has there been no public discourse about this?" Berns warned the campus would use more power and water than the entire county and make noise "equivalent to a small airplane." Spalding County approved a second campus across High Falls Road, Spalding Investments LLC's data centers, in 2025, and in January 2026 approved a third, larger campus nearby over objections from residents and the Altamaha and Flint Riverkeepers. Inside the city of Griffin itself, the city commission passed a 180-day moratorium on data centers in January 2026 and is weighing rules to allow only smaller data centers by special permit. The Spalding County Board of Commissioners requires acoustic walls and sidewalks of this campus, conditions a commissioner later asked be added to the county's other approved campuses too.

ft-1767937475006-5182.text: Spalding Investments LLC plans a data center campus of about 1.42 million square feet on 127.45 acres bordered by High Falls Road, South McDonough Road and Highway 16 outside Griffin, in Spalding County, Georgia. The Spalding County Board of Commissioners approved the Spalding Investments data center campus in 2025, one of two it approved that year. The company first proposed eight two-story buildings, six with 170,000-square-foot footprints and two with 200,000, plus a power transfer station, and the developers put the campus's value at $1.5 billion with about $22.9 million a year in property tax. Because the site lies in the flight path of the new Griffin-Spalding County Regional Airport, the developer redesigned it with six buildings of the same total size and proposed lowering the ground to keep the buildings under height limits. Its attorney, Steven Jones, said it would use a closed-loop water system, with water and sewer from the Spalding County Water Authority, and access from High Falls Road and South McDonough Road. Details about the campus's power capacity were not provided with the application. Four people spoke against it at the August 2025 hearing, asking who pays for its power, when the county would see tax revenue, whether data centers could be obsolete in five years, and why the entrance could not come off Highway 16 instead of High Falls Road; they noted no resident had spoken in favor of data centers. Commissioners tabled the rezoning 4-1 that day. Commission Chair Clay Davis wanted the zoning to revert if nothing was built within three years, and Commissioner Gwen Flowers-Taylor asked for the acoustic wall and other conditions required of the first data center. The county's zoning attorney said the zoning cannot revert automatically, but the county can start the process if the data center is not built in time. ft-1767936670789-7174.text: The Wallace Jackson Data Center Campus, 10 buildings totaling 4.986 million square feet on 189 acres at Jackson Road and Wallace Road in Griffin, Spalding County, Georgia, was approved by county commissioners on January 22, 2026. It is now tied up in two lawsuits filed by neighbors, and developer Wallace Jackson LLC has not yet applied for a land disturbance permit. A state Development of Regional Impact review estimated the campus's value at build-out in 2035 at $3.65 billion, with $51.656 million a year in local tax revenue; build-out is expected to take 10 years. The buildings would range from 297,000 to 780,000 square feet, and the state filing lists the landowner as Havenwood Holdings. Attorney Steven Jones said nondisclosure agreements kept him from naming an end user, though the site had drawn interest from one. The site sits at the corner of the Butts County/Towaliga River Watershed District and has wetlands, though county rules exclude data centers from its watershed and wetland protection districts. Commissioners voted 4-0 to grant a variance with conditions, including marked buffers and diesel fuel stored away from the protected area, then 4-0 to rezone the land and grant a special exception. Neighbors warned that blasting the granite on the site could release radioactive elements into their wells and asked for regular well testing. "It's taking precious land that people have lived here for generations to farm, and they're turning it into a data center that's not going to provide any jobs of substance to the county," said resident Gregory Berns. County Attorney Steven Ledbetter framed the project as a way to lower residents' taxes. Two lawsuits filed in Spalding County Superior Court on February 17, 2026, by attorney Robert Fricks Sr. on behalf of nearby residents argue the commissioners ignored their own procedures and data center rules, and ask the court to vacate the zoning and bar a data center on the site. The parties were waiting in September for a judge's decision on a joint motion by the county and the developer, which Fricks expected within weeks.

ft-153.text: The Hampton Data Center is a planned three-building data center campus by Southeast Property Holdings LLC on 133 acres north of Georgia 20 at McDonough Street in Hampton, Henry County, Georgia, which city officials approved with a conditional use permit in 2025. It was the first data center approved in Henry County, and it is still unclear which company is behind Southeast Property Holdings. The site is part of Henderson Farms, a 900-acre mixed-use development that was never built, and a data center is allowed under its existing mixed-use zoning. The plan calls for three buildings of about 195,000 square feet each and an electrical substation, and city documents say the applicant has discussed a hydroponic farm and training facility on the campus with the University of Georgia. The developer is responsible for negotiating its own power supply. The city attached conditions: a buffer of at least 100 feet along the property line, landscaping to screen the buildings and substation, a noise impact study, green roofs, strategies to minimize water use, pedestrian improvements on nearby streets, land along the Towaliga River for a city park, and a $75,000 contribution to Hampton. Several large campuses have since been proposed around Hampton and Henry County. Equinix is developing a 240MW, four-building campus in the area, and Hampton Technology Park Owner LLC has filed for a 603-acre, five-building, 4 million-square-foot campus along Lower Woolsey Road. Construction of a data center near South Lee Road and Lower Woolsey Road has drawn protests over its closeness to a historic Black cemetery holding 54 documented names and 16 undocumented enslaved people, FOX 5 Atlanta reported in August 2026. "It hurts. It hurts. We're out here advocating and trying to save these cemeteries and they're constantly ignoring us. Nobody is hearing us," said advocate Shawndrea Gay. Mayor Ann Tarpley said the city set a 50-foot buffer and hopes to get the cemetery on the national and state historic registers. Residents have organized. The group Conserve Henry GA, which runs a petition against data centers in Henry County, says none of Hampton's three known data center sites filed revised regional impact reviews and that only Southeast Property Holdings held the required conditional use permit hearing. Hampton has been considering a 120-day moratorium on data center development to give the city time to assess its impact. Henry County, which governs the unincorporated land around the city, has a moratorium on data centers there until it adopts a data center ordinance, the group says. Decisions on data centers inside the city belong to the Hampton City Council, and those in unincorporated areas to the Henry County Board of Commissioners.

ft-1781101739670-6807.text: The Pumpkin Technology Campus, also called the Pumpkin Center data center or Project Pumpkin, is a 420-acre data center site near Harlem in Columbia County, Georgia. Applicant Piedmont DevCo LLC, backed by Cloverleaf Infrastructure, plans four data center buildings, two warehouses and a substation on land owned by the Prather family. Columbia County commissioners approved the rezoning 4-1 on February 3, 2026, over the strongest opposition of any of the county's three data center proposals. Greenpoint residents say they bought homes near the site expecting shops and restaurants, as the original development plans showed. "There's a place for a data center. It's not in a residential area," resident Kyle Brucks told WRDW before the vote. A change.org petition against the campus had 195 signatures in January, with residents citing utility costs, environmental harm and the character of the area. Commissioner Allison Couch cast the lone vote against the rezoning. The approval carries conditions: a 500-foot natural buffer along Highway 221 and Wrightsboro Road with a 12-foot berm planted with evergreens, a 65-decibel noise limit at the property line, and a requirement that the owners remove residential uses planned for the east side of Highway 221. Approval did not clear the way to build right away. In February the county sent back the site plan with reviewers' comments. "They have the ability to go disturb the land. They don't have the ability to build anything yet," County Manager Scott Johnson said. Building plans still have to pass county staff review, and Georgia Power is studying the approved projects. Greenpoint resident Gregory P. Guido Jr. sued on February 25, arguing the rezoning was approved despite an incomplete state regional impact review and without timely notice to the school district. "I felt like the only way to actually do this was to file a lawsuit," Guido said. A Superior Court judge dismissed the case on March 25, and Guido filed a notice of appeal to the Georgia Court of Appeals on April 13. The Pumpkin site should not be confused with Project Squash, a separate, roughly 325-acre data center site about a mile west at 6423 Wrightsboro Road. State filings from May 2026 name Whiting-Turner as Project Squash's contractor, with land clearing expected to finish in 2027; it is a different project from the Pumpkin Technology Campus.

ft-1764596671092-5385.text: Hogansville's city council is still rewriting the rules any data center would have to meet, nearly a year after residents learned that a developer, Fertile Ground Investments LLC, wanted 437 acres of city land on Hightower Road for a 600-megawatt data center in Troup County, Georgia. At a September 21, 2026 work session, council members agreed to add special-use permits, a ban on Sunday construction, a 500-foot wetlands buffer and noise controls to a draft ordinance that would create a heavy-industrial zoning district for data centers. The site is the city's old wastewater spray field off Hightower Road, on the outskirts of a town of about 3,000 people. Records obtained through an open records request by resident Al Prado showed that Luis Matta, a Fayetteville developer who works for Fertile Ground Investments and sits on the board of the Fayette County Development Authority, had agreed with the city on a purchase of 437 acres at $12,000 an acre, contingent on rezoning from residential to industrial, the Ledger-Enquirer reported. A power study by MEAG, the city's municipal power supplier, assessed bringing 600 megawatts online and found no generation currently available for it. The city uses about 25 MW a year and owns 36 MW under its MEAG terms. The study put the cost at $300 million, with a customer bearing $153.75 million, and service four to five years after funding. Residents objected first to the secrecy: the council signed a non-disclosure agreement in January 2024 in executive session, Council Member Mark Ayers said at a December 2025 town hall, and Council Member Michael Taylor Jr. said the council and the development authority got out of it just before the November 2025 election. Resident Roseanna Prado told the Ledger-Enquirer, "I'm not sure what their definition of transparency is, but mine certainly isn't keeping something like this from the public." About 20 residents spoke against the project at a December 2, 2025 town hall, citing light and noise, wells drying up and the loss of the road's rural character; resident Stacey Smith said "Hightower Road is not industry. It's residential, it's homes, it's families, it's people, it's bonfires." Tina Payton, whose land borders the site and whose children run a 30-acre zoo across the road, said: "My thing is that, it's not ever gonna be quiet or dark." Taylor was then the only council member openly opposed, saying the deal would bring about $400,000 a year in taxes but only "about 30 to 35 jobs." Gage Bailey, founder of the Troup County Anti-Data Center Coalition, has attended council meetings with members of the coalition, including Hogansville residents. On February 2, 2026, the council adopted a 90-day moratorium on all data center applications, including any for the Hightower Road spray field. City Attorney Alex Dixon said the moratorium would not automatically push back March deadlines in the purchase option and development authority agreements, that the developer would still need a rezoning, and that those agreements were not legally binding because the council had never voted on them in a public meeting. On August 17, 2026, the council voted 4-1 to reject the draft ordinance as too weak and extended the moratorium to its September 8 meeting, after residents cited a Southern Environmental Law Center letter asking for stronger standards. Councilmember Mandy Neese said, "My biggest concern is that I don't feel like this ordinance is strong enough at this point. It's not," and said the city has no inspectors or city engineer to manage a data center's construction, while Mayor Jake Ayers said he felt it "is in a good spot and keeps our citizens safe." Hogansville is not alone in Troup County: the county government adopted its own 90-day moratorium on data center projects in 2025 and the city of LaGrange adopted a 180-day moratorium, both after public concern. What happens next is in the hands of the city council and the Planning and Zoning Commission. City staff are to bring the revised ordinance back by the October 5, 2026 work session, after which it goes to the Planning and Zoning Commission, another public hearing, and votes by the commission and the council. Councilmember Kandis Strickland has said she wants no data centers in city limits or on city-owned property, while Councilmember Mark Ayers said he is not ready to rule them out "until one actually comes with a zoning request and a preliminary plat with what they actually want." Any data center on the Hightower Road land would still need its own rezoning and public hearings before it could proceed.

ft-155.text: Google is building Project Pegasus, a data center under construction at 411 Pegasus Parkway in LaGrange, Troup County, Georgia, which it confirmed in April 2026. In July 2026 it filed to add a second building of 470,000 square feet, valued at $1 billion, with construction that could run until 2029 while work continues on the first building. The site is the former LaGrange plant of Jindal Films, which made packaging films and closed in 2024, leaving the city without its largest electric customer. Thor Equities bought the 270-acre property in 2024, including a 506,220 square foot building and a substation capable of 100 MVA transformation, and planned it for its data center arm, Form8tion, though Thor has since told Data Center Dynamics it is no longer involved. Thor had said the first building could total 50 megawatts and go live in late 2026 or early 2027, with an eventual 400 megawatts targeted. The project was led by the Development Authority of LaGrange, which had already validated bonds for it by September 2025, City Planner Mark Kostial said. In early April 2026 emergency crews rescued a construction worker who was severely injured on the building's roof. The city has no property tax and relies on utility revenue, and City Manager Patrick Bowie said the power contract could double that revenue. "Google's decision to locate here fills a vital void in our utility system left by the closing of our largest electric customer," Bowie said. Google says it will cover the full cost of the site's power and infrastructure, and it is giving $1 million to Groundswell's Save On Utilities Long-term program for upgrades for at least 50 LaGrange families. Water is the open question. Google's own report shows its Douglas County data center returns only about 17% of its water to the supply, with the rest evaporating, WSB-TV reported. Katie Ottenweller of Google said the company would "replenish 120% of all of the water that we use at a certain data center site," and Bowie said the former textile town has water to spare. Many residents felt the project got through without a say. When the city council adopted a 180-day moratorium on new data centers in September 2025, City Attorney Jeff Todd said it could not apply to this site: "You can't apply a moratorium to someone who already has vested rights in the system." Councilmember Darby Pippin said in April 2026 there had been "a great deal of public outcry" that the project had "somehow slipped through the cracks," even though it went through three public hearings. Cyndie Hutchings of the Troup County Anti-Data Center Coalition told the council: "There was also nothing about community benefits agreements, which we feel was something that we really missed out on with the Google data center." Councilman Leon Childs recused himself from the city's data center votes after colleagues noted that his employer, Groundswell, is backed by Google. LaGrange's own 180-day moratorium, which explicitly did not cover this site, ended in March 2026 when the city council voted 3-2 to require a special-use permit, with an advertised public hearing, for every new data center in the city. Troup County's separate moratorium on the unincorporated county, extended in February 2026, was lifted in May 2026 when commissioners adopted permanent rules requiring a special-use permit, heavy industrial zoning, closed-loop cooling and 1,500-foot setbacks from homes, schools and other sensitive sites. Also in the LaGrange area, Project West WHP-GA LLC filed in March 2025 for a 1.5 million square foot data center campus whose end user has not been named. The second Pegasus building has been filed with Georgia's Department of Community Affairs as a development of regional impact; the filing called any later phases "speculative at this time."

ft-156.text: Project West, a $9.7 billion data center campus proposed on 513 acres south of Interstate 85 near LaGrange in Troup County, Georgia, has stalled since March 2025, when the LaGrange City Council declined to take up the developer's request to annex the land into the city. The applicant, Project West WHP - GA LLC, had filed plans for six 252,000-square-foot industrial buildings, 1.5 million square feet in all, with their own electrical substation. The buildings were estimated to need up to 600 megawatts of power. The land lies between Hamilton Road and Whitesville Road, bordered also by Bartley Road and GA-403, and a transmission line crosses it. The filing with the state's Development of Regional Impact program set out three phases, finishing in 2028, 2030 and 2033. The developer and property owner, LaGrange entrepreneur Joshua Harrelson, lives on the property. "My farm is really big. Nobody will see it," Harrelson told the LaGrange Daily News. "It's a huge place. The size of these structures, while they might seem big, we're setting them back a very long way away from anybody else. Nobody will even know that they're there." He estimated about 580 jobs at an average salary of $80,000, and the regional impact documents projected about $60 million a year in tax revenue for the county. A study by the Economic Impact Group LLC, released by the developers, put the net economic benefit to the city and county at $762 million. The developers did not say which companies might be involved. Power was the sticking point. The whole city of LaGrange uses about 100 megawatts, so the campus would have needed roughly six times the city's load. City Planner Mark Kostial said at the outset that the developer still had to complete a water study and a study of whether upwards of 600 megawatts could actually be provided. Asked by Councilman Tom Gore whether the data center would drive up the cost of electricity, City Manager Patrick Bowie answered: "Yes." "There's going to be pressure on the power markets. There's going to be pressure on the natural gas markets, regardless of where these things are located in LaGrange or South Carolina," Bowie said. When Mayor Jim Arrington asked for a motion to notify the county of the annexation request, Councilman Nathan Gaskin made it and no other member seconded, so it died. By January 2026 the LaGrange Daily News described the project as "effectively nixed" by that vote, which blocked the route the developer had chosen. Public concern over data centers only appeared after Project West was proposed in rural Troup County, the LaGrange Daily News reported, even though the city had long known about Project Pegasus, the data center at the former Jindal Films site that turned out to be Google's. At a standing-room-only town hall in September 2025, the Sierra Club, Science for Georgia and Chattahoochee Riverkeeper warned about the power and water such campuses use, and Science for Georgia's Amy Sharma urged residents to push for a moratorium: "If they show up, make them pay." LaGrange, Troup County and the other cities then passed moratoriums while they wrote rules, and county commission chairman Patrick Crews said he, like many others, had been caught unaware by Project West. In April 2026 he told residents no data center application was on file in unincorporated Troup County, "and particularly down on Bartley Road." On May 5, 2026, the Troup County Board of Commissioners unanimously adopted a data center ordinance and lifted its moratorium. Every data center in unincorporated Troup now needs a special-use permit from the commissioners; average-size and hyperscale centers are limited to heavy industrial zoning, must use closed-loop cooling and public water and sewer, must keep buildings, substations and parking lots 1,500 feet from the property lines of homes, schools, daycares, hospitals, places of worship and parks, may be no taller than 40 feet, must use "four-tier" backup generators to cut noise and emissions, and must run noise studies once operating. Because the Project West site is in unincorporated Troup County, a data center there would now fall under the county's rules, unless a city annexed the land, in which case, Crews has warned, the county has very little say. While the city was drafting its rules, LaGrange planned to limit hyperscale data centers to heavy industrial zoning, and Mayor Jim Arrington said that if a developer asked to rezone land "over here on Hamilton Road" for heavy industry, "we're going to be like, 'No, that's not a spot for heavy industry.'" LaGrange has since adopted an ordinance that requires a special-use permit, and so a public hearing, for every data center. Other data center plans in the area are moving. Google's Project Pegasus in LaGrange had broken ground by September 2025, and Sharma said it was getting a 50 percent tax abatement for 20 years. In August 2026 the LaGrange City Council voted 5-1 to call a September 8 public hearing on a special-use permit for a data center at the Lafayette Logistics Center off Old Hutchinson Mill Road, proposed by Grandview Partners and Farpoint with no end user named, stressing that calling the hearing did not signal support. In Hogansville, the city council voted 4-1 on August 17 to reject its draft data center ordinance after members said it was not strong enough, and extended its moratorium on applications. If Project West comes back, the deciding body depends on the route: the Troup County Board of Commissioners, chaired by Patrick Crews, through a special-use permit, or the LaGrange City Council, under Mayor Arrington, through annexation and a special-use permit with a public hearing.

ft-1785164164773-4269.text: Stillwater Development's plan for a 1,250 megawatt data center campus at 11760 Panhandle Road in Lovejoy, Clayton County, Georgia, has been withdrawn after weeks of resident opposition. The Lovejoy City Council accepted the withdrawal at a special meeting on August 6, 2026, and the developer says it will pursue a residential plan for the land instead. The campus would have covered about 400 acres with up to 15 buildings totaling 3.465 million square feet and two substations, according to the developer's filing with Georgia's Department of Community Affairs. Central Georgia EMC was to supply the power, which could have reached 1,250 megawatts, with a first phase finished by 2031 and the project valued at up to $13 billion. The site sits across Panhandle Road from Michelle Obama Elementary and Eddie White Middle academies. In its own review of the project, the city of Lovejoy warned of "high traffic congestion on Panhandle already experienced due to the Michelle Obama and Eddie White school traffic." The land was annexed into Lovejoy in 2024 for a residential project, then rezoned for the data center, which Mayor Marci Fluellyn said was pitched to her as a way to raise up to $10 million a year in city revenue. Residents packed Lovejoy City Hall before the vote. "We want to make sure our water stays clean, and we don't suffer from any additional noise that comes with a data center," said Attania Jean-Funny, a community activist. Ken Worrell, who lives near the site, said, "We don't need something like that within our community right here." The council voted unanimously to start rescinding the project. Clayton County has had a moratorium on new data center applications in its unincorporated areas since September 2025, extended three times, though it does not cover Lovejoy. Fluellyn said the city council planned to update its zoning to prohibit data centers, with the change set to come before the council in September 2026; no result has been published.

ft-171.text: Monroe County commissioners unanimously rejected the Bolingbroke Technology Campus on August 5, 2025, refusing to rezone about 970 acres of forest near the unincorporated community of Bolingbroke, in Monroe County, Georgia, for a data center. Bolingbroke Technology Center LLC had proposed nine buildings totaling 5.4 million square feet along US Highway 41, Wadley Road and Interstate 475, about 15 miles northwest of Macon, at a cost of $5.8 billion. The county's planning and zoning board had already voted 5 to 0 against the rezoning on July 28, 2025, pointing mainly to predicted noise levels, while hundreds of residents packed the hearing in "Say No To Rezoning" T-shirts. Opponents cited cleared forest, the Ocmulgee skullcap and tricolored bats on the land, and a power demand they compared to adding a city the size of San Jose. "While we are disappointed by the board's recommendation, we remain confident that the Board of Commissioners will make a fact-based decision about the positive impacts this project offers," said Ben Sheidler, speaking for Bolingbroke Technology. Supporters pointed to about $60 million a year in taxes and 200 to 250 jobs, in a county whose biggest taxpayer, Georgia Power's Plant Scherer, is due to close within a decade. The landowners said after the vote: "This project is a thoughtful, community-driven proposal designed to bring meaningful long-term benefits to Monroe County." Henry Davis Properties, LLC, and other landowners sued Monroe County in Monroe County Superior Court on September 3, 2025, arguing the county's development ordinance was never properly adopted and that commissioners had no rational basis for approving a rival data center on Rumble Road the same night while refusing this one. No trial date has been set, and no ruling has been published since the suit was filed.

ft-174.text: Grind Capital Group's data center at 1751 Bells Ferry Road in Marietta, Cobb County, Georgia, is approved and moving toward construction over resident objections. The Marietta City Council voted 7-0 on June 17, 2025, to rezone the 31.4 acre site from retail commercial to light industrial for two buildings totaling 347,200 square feet and 108 megawatts of power. The developer, Grind Capital Group, also operates as MMM Acquisitions LLC. The council would have to take new action to reverse the zoning, and none has been reported. The site holds a cell tower built around 1994 and five billboards along Interstate 75; the tower would be moved near the site's entrance driveway. With homes on the east side, the campus would be graded so most of the 105 foot buildings sit below their eyeline, with new trees planted to screen the view. Grind Capital plans a closed loop cooling system and is paying for an on-site substation, and Cobb County Water has confirmed it can serve the site, though no daily water figure has been made public. A group called Not For Us - Cobb County organized against the project, citing public records that put the permanent jobs at 5 to 20, against the developer's estimate of 40. No independent environmental or health study was required before the 2025 vote. At the rezoning hearing, Ward 6 council member Andre Sims asked about heat from the buildings, and the developer acknowledged it would produce "a lot of heat"; Sims voted yes anyway. Opponents packed the June 10, 2026, council meeting even though the agenda had no data center item, and city officials called the groups' claims "misinformation." Cobb County paused new data center applications on unincorporated land starting in February 2026, then extended that pause 180 days on August 12, 2026, now running to early February 2027; it does not cover this site, which sits inside Marietta's city limits. Marietta's own council passed its own six-month moratorium on new data centers in July 2026, but that freeze also excludes the Bells Ferry Road project because it was approved before the vote.

ft-1784069628664-5291.text: Prime Storage Powers Ferry Place Marietta, LLC filed to turn part of a self-storage site at 1155 Powers Ferry Place in Marietta, the county seat of Cobb County, Georgia, into an 18 megawatt data center. The Marietta City Council approved it 5 to 2 on 12 August 2026, a month after adopting a six month moratorium on new data centers, because the application was filed before the freeze took effect. The 10.7 acre site holds a one-story concrete building, a 100,000 square foot Pace Warehouse store converted to storage in 1996, and rows of outdoor storage units. About 40 percent of the building would become data center space, around 21,570 square feet of white space and 15,365 of grey space, while the rest stays in storage and most of the outdoor rows come down for an equipment yard with enclosures meant to cut noise and a closed loop air cooled system. Prime Group Holdings, which owns hundreds of storage sites, lists the building as GA10 on its edge computing website, with service possible as soon as the third quarter of 2026. The application went in on 19 May 2026, and the planning commission recommended it by 4 votes to 3. City staff found it did not fit the comprehensive plan and lacked detail on how heat would be managed. Jean Allred of Marietta Blue Ladies United said the group wanted "a moratorium until the energy drain, the pollution and the environmental concerns can be addressed and regulations put into place." State Rep. Gabriel Sanchez said: "There's better uses of the very limited resources the city has for the data center projects." On 8 July 2026 the council tabled the vote 7 to 0 until August, and Councilwoman Cheryl Richardson said she wanted to consult a sound engineer first. Prime Storage offered a closed loop water system, sound barriers, enclosed generators, a 10 foot fence and limits of 60 decibels by day and 50 at night. Former NFL player Chris Conley listed the risks as "air pollution, noise pollution, water contamination, water storage, rising electricity rates." At the August vote Richardson and Daniel Gaddis were the two against. State Rep. Mary Frances Williams told the council: "I've read the most recent submission letter outlining more details about the proposed project, and I continue to have concerns that, in my opinion, have not been fully answered." The Cobb Chamber of Commerce backed the plan, saying "Data centers are an important opportunity to strengthen and future-proof our local economy." Residents raised noise and pollution of Rottenwood Creek, and about 2.5% of the property lies in the creek's floodplain. The chamber was full, people shouted "shame" after the vote, and police escorted some protesters out.

ft-175.text: Grading has begun at the Northern Data data center site in Maysville's industrial park, and Rum Group, the company formerly called Rumble that took over Northern Data in 2026, says it will start construction and hiring in late November or December. The site is on the Jackson County side of Maysville, Georgia, at 121 Industrial Drive and on Meeks Road behind it, and residents of the town of just over 2,000 have fought it since spring 2026. Northern Data announced the Maysville campus in December 2024 as a 63-acre site delivering 120 megawatts of power, with room to expand to 180 megawatts, and fully operational in the first quarter of 2027. The company holds a conditional use permit for two buildings of 125,000 square feet each, and its executives put the cost at $5 billion to $7 billion. Rum Group bought 85 percent of Northern Data's shares in June 2026, and in August it disclosed a contract worth up to $13.7 billion over six years with an unnamed US cloud customer for GPU services at the Maysville site. The zoning was approved in January 2025, according to the city. Water is at the center of the fight, because Maysville already struggles to supply its own. "Welcome to Maysville, don't drink the water," Gary Miller of Justice for Water shouted at a May 16 protest across from City Hall. "We might be small, but we are loud. We have no water for our town, so how will we have any for a data center?" The property reportedly backs up to Maysville Elementary School. At a May 28 meeting a resident asked whether the city's franchise revenue, which Mayor Richard Presley put in the neighborhood of $350,000, was worth their children's potential health; "Yes it is," Presley replied. The city then canceled a special question-and-answer meeting, saying its code "does not authorize additional public hearings for zoning matters that have already been approved." At a July 28 town hall, Northern Data chief executive John Hoffman and Rum Group chief operating officer Tyler Hughes said the buildings would use a closed-loop cooling system, that no municipal water would be used, and that water would be trucked in from providers within 100 to 200 miles. They offered $15 million through a community benefit agreement, estimated $20 million to $26 million a year in property taxes, and Hoffman said the company would not take tax abatements. Two council members were not persuaded: "I feel disgusted. I feel like they betrayed our people, and I feel like leadership has let us down," Ward 4 Councilor Brodriche Jackson said afterward, and Ward 2 Councilor Amanda Farley said, "I feel like we're not being told everything." Residents also pressed on the company's past: European authorities had investigated Northern Data over tax incentives tied to Nvidia chips, and Hughes said, "It's not an excuse. There was previous leadership before us, and we really want to acknowledge where we were." Noise is the other worry, because a crypto mining data center run by Peak Mining already operates in the same industrial park. "I hear humming all the time," said Peggy Cooper, who lives next to it; Hoffman said Northern Data and Rumble no longer own Peak Mining but agreed to pass on her concerns. For the new buildings the company plans sound barriers inside and outside, and says it has a customer lined up that it cannot yet name. The city has since put a 180-day moratorium on any future requests, but that does not reach this already-permitted project. Instead the council formed a Community Based Agreement committee, chaired by Darrell Scoggins, to decide how the $15 million is spent; ideas include city water improvements, wastewater treatment and protection for the elementary school. "With all due respect, I don't want your data center here," Scoggins told Hoffman in September. "If it's going to be built, I will squeeze you for all I can so that the citizens, schools and locals can benefit." The company says it will present design plans to the Maysville City Council and the public, and construction still needs a building permit. The Community Based Agreement committee meets through October 25 to settle its list of projects, which the company's attorney will then review with the city. Residents who want a say can reach the committee at [email address removed]

The city then canceled a special question-and-answer meeting, saying its code "does not authorize additional public hearings for zoning matters that have already been approved."

At a July 28 town hall, Northern Data chief executive John Hoffman and Rum Group chief operating officer Tyler Hughes said the buildings would use a closed-loop cooling system, that no municipal water would be used, and that water would be trucked in from providers within 100 to 200 miles.
They offered $15 million through a community benefit agreement, estimated $20 million to $26 million a year in property taxes, and Hoffman said the company would not take tax abatements.

Two council members were not persuaded: "I feel disgusted. I feel like they betrayed our people, and I feel like leadership has let us down," Ward 4 Councilor Brodriche Jackson said afterward, and Ward 2 Councilor Amanda Farley said, "I feel like we're not being told everything."

Residents also pressed on the company's past: European authorities had investigated Northern Data over tax incentives tied to Nvidia chips, and Hughes said, "It's not an excuse. There was previous leadership before us, and we really want to acknowledge where we were."
Noise is the other worry, because a crypto mining data center run by Peak Mining already operates in the same industrial park.
"I hear humming all the time," said Peggy Cooper, who lives next to it; Hoffman said Northern Data and Rumble no longer own Peak Mining but agreed to pass on her concerns.
For the new buildings the company plans sound barriers inside and outside, and says it has a customer lined up that it cannot yet name.
The city has since put a 180-day moratorium on any future requests, but that does not reach this already-permitted project.

Instead the council formed a Community Based Agreement committee, chaired by Darrell Scoggins, to decide how the $15 million is spent; ideas include city water improvements, wastewater treatment and protection for the elementary school.
"With all due respect, I don't want your data center here," Scoggins told Hoffman in September.
"If it's going to be built, I will squeeze you for all I can so that the citizens, schools and locals can benefit."
The company says it will present design plans to the Maysville City Council and the public, and construction still needs a building permit.
The Community Based Agreement committee meets through October 25 to settle its list of projects, which the company's attorney will then review with the city.
Residents who want a say can reach the committee at [email address removed]

ft-213.text: Central Coweta Industrial LLC, a Senoia company tied to Brent Scarbrough & Company, put a $4 billion data center development, later nicknamed Project Oak, into Georgia's regional development review in October 2025. The plan, officially called Central Coweta Industrial Phase II, called for eight data center buildings totaling 2.4 million square feet on 458 acres near Newnan, in Coweta County, bounded by Bullsboro Drive, Coweta Industrial Parkway, US 29 and Interstate 85, with three substations and projected annual local tax revenue of $40 million. Three Rivers Regional Commission planner Stephanie Wagner told the developers that, unlike past reviews, citizens could no longer comment directly: "Although past DRI reviews had been open to citizen comments, we have adjusted the procedure." By August 2026 the developers had cut the project to a 255-acre industrial parcel zoned in April 2024, around Lake Amlajack, and asked the county to lift a zoning condition that limited the site to about 2.1 million square feet of office and warehouse use so it could be built as a data center instead. Homeowners near Walt Sanders Road formed a group called Stop Project Oak; a county filing projected the site would use 28,000 gallons of water a day. "I don't want a big giant industrial building with bright lights and loud noises right in our backyard," said resident Robin Angus, while Michelle Lore said her biggest worry was the strain the project would put on water and air quality: "what our children breathe in." The Coweta County Board of Commissioners denied the rezoning unanimously on August 25, 2026, despite the developers' offer to fund extensions of the boulevards that serve the site; zoning coordinator Nicole Blackwell said the county had received 121 letters of opposition from 112 individuals and none in support. Commissioner Jeff Fisher, who had voted for two other data center projects in the county, explained his vote: "Project Peach, Project Sail and Project Oak are three different projects, and supporting one doesn't mean I'm automatically going to support the next one." The land stays zoned industrial, limited to office and warehouse use, and under county rules the developers must wait six months before applying again.

ft-176.text: Coweta County commissioners voted in April 2026 to rezone 832 acres near Newnan, Georgia, for Project Sail, a data center campus first put forward by Atlas Development, and residents have gone to court to undo it. On Tuesday, May 5, 2026 they filed a petition in Coweta County Superior Court against the county and Atlas Development LLC, asking a judge to void the rezoning. Seventeen residents, farmers, longtime landowners and neighbors are asking the court to throw out the decision and block the project entirely. The land matters because of what is under it. The site, near Welcome Sargent and Wagers Mill roads inside the Middle Chattahoochee River basin, is designated by the state as a Most Significant Groundwater Recharge Area, one of Georgia's highest environmental protection designations, and the rezoning took it from rural conservation to industrial use. The petition says the original regional review stated the property was not in a significant groundwater recharge area, and that Atlas's amended application in January 2026, which changed the request from light industrial to full industrial zoning, should have triggered a new regional review. It cites a peer reviewed study projecting a $118 million fall in residential property values across about 1,215 parcels within 1.25 miles of the site, and notes construction could last up to 10 years by the developer's own estimates. "This is not how rezoning should take place in Coweta County," said plaintiff Steve Swope, one of the organizers of Citizens for a Rural Coweta. Commissioners Al Smith, Jeff Fisher and John Reidelbach, who voted for the rezoning, declined to comment because of the pending litigation, and the county said it does not comment on pending litigation. The version the commissioners approved is a nine-building campus of 4.34 million square feet on 832 acres, about 900 megawatts, 45 miles south of Atlanta. Prologis, the industrial real estate trust, is lined up to buy the site from Atlas, though DCD reported in April 2026 that it had not yet closed on the purchase. The first plan, revealed in a Development of Regional Impact filing on December 31, 2024, was bigger: 13 buildings of 378,000 square feet each, more than 4.9 million square feet in all, which is more than twice the floor space of the Mall of Georgia, at a cost of $17 billion. The tax estimates in the first filing were questioned and later revised in new filings with the Three Rivers Regional Commission. Citizens for a Rural Coweta organized the opposition through months of hearings and has formed a political action committee to campaign against the commissioners who voted for the project. The case now sits with the Coweta County Superior Court, filed under Georgia's zoning procedures law, and the county's legal costs in defending it will be paid by taxpayers.

ft-1776887365551-1592.text: The Irwin County Board of Commissioners voted 5 to 0 on May 20, 2026 to grant a special exception for Project Arrowhead, a data center campus planned for farm and forest land near Ocilla in south central Georgia. The developer, Premier Data Center Development LLC, plans five buildings totaling 4.22 million square feet on about 1,000 acres outside the community of Mystic, with up to 1.25 gigawatts of capacity and up to $6 billion invested. The first phase could open in 2030, with the campus complete by 2034. Georgia Power is carrying out an energy study for the site. The state filing of April 10, 2026 covers about 1,066 acres across five parcels and gives water use of 0.05 million gallons a day from the Floridan Aquifer, wastewater of 0.03 million gallons a day treated on site and discharged under permit, 200 full-time jobs and $20 million a year in local taxes. The land belongs to the Fletcher Marcus D Trust and Sirrom Farms LLC. Part of it was first proposed as the Irwin Forward Tech Park, a 17-building project the applicant withdrew in March 2026 even though the county planning commission had recommended approval. That first application, by James Russell Bryant for the Marcus D. Fletcher Trust, covered about 546 acres zoned agricultural, and it came as the county moved in February to dissolve its industrial development authority, which officials said was unrelated. Residents asked then about traffic, noise from cooling equipment, rural roads and groundwater in drought, while officials noted the site might use less water than the center-pivot irrigation already on farmland. Fifteen people sent comments on the new application, all opposed, citing the aquifer, power bills, farmland, habitat and the small number of jobs. The Georgia Water Coalition said this would be "the first data center in Georgia that we are aware of that will withdraw water directly from the Floridan Aquifer." WWALS Watershed Coalition, led by Suwannee Riverkeeper John S. Quarterman, asked for the water estimate to be checked independently and warned that the treated wastewater "is likely to be a significant tributary of the Alapaha River, especially in drought conditions." Irwin County's own ordinance permits only closed loop cooling and requires an independent hydrogeologic study before a certificate of occupancy is issued. At the special called meeting, Commissioner Don Hickey, on the phone, moved approval, Aldene Tyson seconded, and Chair Vince Thompson, Paul McIntyre and Chris Paulk joined them. Asked about water, Thompson said the filing specified 50,000 gallons a day but that commissioners "didn't get all the questions like that answered" on their site visit. County attorney James Banner said enforcement beyond a $1,000-a-day fine could include withholding a certificate of occupancy or seeking an injunction. After the meeting the applicants said they had no end customer yet, only two or three candidates; a Change.org petition started by Audrey Wynn on February 4, 2026 against a 1-gigawatt Google data center in the county had drawn 926 signatures by then. Any certificate of occupancy will still require the independent hydrogeologic study the county's ordinance calls for, and Georgia Power's energy study for the site continues.

ft-182.text: Project Peach, a data center campus of up to eight buildings and 2.1 million square feet at 300 Johnston Circle near Palmetto in Coweta County, Georgia, was filed in October 2024 by Strategic Real Estate Partners through North Coweta Investors LLC. The Coweta County Board of Commissioners approved its rezoning 3 to 2 in April 2025, with Bob Blackburn, Jeffrey Fisher and John Reidelbach for and Bill McKenzie and Al Smith against. The developers promised 500 construction jobs, 50 permanent ones and $100 million in taxes over ten years from a campus drawing about 700 megawatts of power and phased to 2036. The Three Rivers Regional Commission's review, completed on February 4, 2025, describes about 320 acres in unincorporated Coweta County beside SR 14/US 29 and Weldon Road, rezoned from rural conservation to light industrial, and estimates 2,080 new trips a day on a stretch the county already lists as congested. Chattahoochee Riverkeeper told the commission that the 105,000 gallons a day the county water authority can supply comes from the Chattahoochee, while some of the 52,000 gallons of daily wastewater could be returned to the Flint River basin, an interbasin transfer. Palmetto's mayor and council led the opposition, and residents in yellow shirts filled the seats at the rezoning hearing. Mayor Theresa Thomas-Smith asked commissioners, on behalf of all Palmetto, to "please consider the long time cost to our quality of life, our environment and our residents." Ten residents spoke against the project and six developer representatives for it. Commissioner Fisher pointed to the county budget: "We had to cut over $10 million." Commissioner Reidelbach added two of the rezoning's 21 conditions: a power purchase agreement within six months, or the land would revert to rural conservation, and noise of no more than 45 decibels at the property line. That six-month deadline ran out on October 15, 2025 with no contract. That month the board voted 4 to 1, with Al Smith against, to give the developers 12 more months, until October 15, 2026. Brad Hall, representing CyrusOne, which by then the Times-Herald described as the project's developer, said talks with Georgia Power had slowed because "the end user of the data center is undetermined." If commissioners had not granted the extension, county staff would have started rezoning the land back to rural conservation, and that is what would happen again if the October 2026 deadline is missed. Resident Tina Mann asked what deadlines were for: "When you do not follow through with them, they are meaningless." Palmetto council member Jessica Wilbanks urged commissioners to refuse the extension so the project would fall under the county's newer data center rules. The mayor warned about construction traffic on the city's 100-year-old infrastructure, and Reidelbach called the extension "a learning curve for us."

ft-184.text: T5 Data Centers filed a state review in September 2023 for a data center campus, later named Project Pegasus, on 200 acres at Weldon and Palmetto-Tyrone roads in Coweta County, Georgia. ft-1784759411642-3058.text: As of September 22, Effingham County commissioners had not approved the site plan for OpenAI's proposed Project Camellia near Rincon. The plan calls for four buildings totaling 4.4 million square feet on a roughly 1,400-acre site within Savannah Gateway Industrial Hub, with construction phased from 2028. The state review estimates 3,210 megawatts of peak electric demand, close to the 3.2-gigawatt supply announced by OpenAI and Georgia Power. The county development authority approved a deal giving OpenAI a 50% property-tax abatement for 15 years. County and company officials project 400 long-term jobs and say OpenAI will provide $80 million for community programs; these are forecasts and commitments, not benefits already delivered. Residents have questioned the water and power demands and how little notice they received before the project was announced in July. Two lawsuits challenge the local approval process. The later case, brought by residents and the environmental group One Hundred Miles, alleges that the development authority listed its July meeting item as 'Project Gateway' without identifying OpenAI or the tax deal, then rescheduled that meeting without the legally required notice. An earlier suit by three residents challenges the county's August change allowing data centers on industrial land, alleging it passed without required public hearings; both cases were pending in state court as of September 22. The regional-impact review projects about 30,000 gallons of daily water use with a system that recycles cooling water, but it also identifies wetlands, flood-prone land and a state-protected plant on the site. Savannah Riverkeeper has asked for binding assurances that the campus will use treated surface water rather than groundwater. The state review does not approve the project; county commissioners postponed site-plan consideration at the developer's request while drafting stricter rules and had not announced a new decision date as of September 16.

ft-185.text: Atlas Development has ended its agreement to buy the Battey Business Complex in Rome, Georgia, for a data center, Rome-Floyd County Development Authority Chairman Jimmy Byars confirmed in August 2026. The site was the remaining 100 acres of the former Northwest Georgia Regional Hospital campus along North Division Street in West Rome, in Floyd County. The reason was power: Georgia Power moved the property down its connection queue, Rome City Attorney Andy Davis said. "The Battey property had been put into the queue and got moved down further in the queue with Georgia Power," Davis told the development authority. "So, it was going to be 3 to 4 years before Georgia Power expected that they would be able to do power if there was going to be a data center there." That was longer than the deal's 19-month due diligence period. The authority had signed a term sheet in August 2025, worth $5.7 million for the land, with a $150,000 payment from Atlas and the deed restricted to data centers. Because the site was already zoned heavy industrial, the plan needed no extra approval from the planning department. Residents, especially in the nearby Summerville Park neighborhood, raised concerns about transparency, utility demand, noise and the environment, and an online petition against the project gathered more than 2,200 verified signatures. The site's future is open again. The authority has more than $7 million in federal grants to remove asbestos and demolish the old hospital buildings, though a bid challenge has held up the work. The land stays zoned heavy industrial and must be used for job creation; Rome Mayor Jim Bojo said officials can now reconsider its best use, Coosa Valley News reported. Atlas is still pursuing other Floyd County data centers, including Project Gracie, a seven-building campus along Vann Road NW between Rome and Coosa. On August 25, 2026 the Floyd County Commission adopted rules for unincorporated Floyd County limiting data centers to heavy industrial zoning, a 600-foot home setback, and noise limits of 65 decibels by day and 55 at night. That ordinance does not cover Battey, since it lies inside Rome; the Rome-Floyd County Development Authority, which is selling the land, decides what happens there next.

ft-186.text: Microsoft's Project Firecracker is a data center campus planned on 347 acres on Huffaker Road, outside Rome in Floyd County, Georgia. Microsoft announced it at the Rome-Floyd County Development Authority's meeting on October 30, 2023, and the authority voted to issue $1 billion in bonds and a 12-year tax abatement. The company said it would invest more than $1 billion and create 150 jobs, and expected the facility to take about three years to build. Microsoft agreed to pay $40,000 an acre, about $13.9 million in all, for land the authority had worked since 2021 to get zoned Heavy Industrial with the owner, Floyd County 118 LLC. "Rome and Floyd County's industrial zoning and strong infrastructure led to our decision to locate our data center campus there," said Paul Englis, Microsoft's director of community engagement. "Ratepayers and taxpayers should not foot the bill for this project," Englis said. Rome City Commissioner Mark Cochran said the data center "represents the future of investment for our area," pointing to technology jobs that do not require interstate access. A Microsoft spokesperson said the company did not "have anything definitive to share at this time." At Berry College, about five miles away, chief information officer Penny Evans-Plants said residents' worries about water and power were fair: "I think those are legitimate concerns, because of what we've seen happen at other locations around the country where data centers are located, the amount of power and water they use." Floyd County commissioners approved an 80-day moratorium on new data centers on June 9, 2026, then adopted a data center ordinance on August 25, 2026 after a public hearing. It allows data centers only on Heavy Industrial land, keeps buildings at least 600 feet from homes, limits noise at a residential property line to 65 decibels by day and 55 at night, bars private wells and direct withdrawals from surface water, and requires a bond or other guarantee to pay for cleanup when a site closes. The rules apply to future projects in unincorporated Floyd County. The Huffaker Road land was already zoned for heavy industry before Microsoft's purchase was announced.

ft-189.text: Project Gracie is Atlas Development's plan for a seven-building data center campus on greenfield land along Vann Road NW, between Rome and Coosa in Floyd County, Georgia. The state filing describes 2.395 million square feet of data centers, built out by the end of 2032. Atlas, based in Carrollton, had no track record of building data centers, and Gracie was its fifth large proposal in Georgia since January 2025, Bisnow reported. The site, more than 200 acres of unused land off Vann Road, sits right beside Coosa Middle School. The Floyd County Board of Education sold 114 acres behind Coosa High School for the data center at a reported price of around $40,000 an acre, after approving the sale at a November 26 meeting. Before the Rome-Floyd Planning Commission, Atlas attorney Brandon Bowen put potential tax revenue at up to $50 million a year for the county and its school system, and the plans called for about 20 employees per building at average salaries of $120,000. Superintendent Glenn White told the board: "I wouldn't support it if I thought it posed any danger to our students." Neighbors raised traffic, noise, light pollution, environmental harm and a natural spring that runs through the property, and the commission voted 4 to 3 to recommend heavy industrial zoning. Coosa residents packed the room when the Floyd County Commission heard the rezoning on May 27, 2025, and it was approved. "We have experienced burning bans, we have experienced watering restrictions where we could not water our lawns," said Alan Brinson, who was worried about "using an additional several million gallons of water." "The risks to our neighborhood, our schools, our water, our power, and our quality of life are simply just too great," said Wendy Lignell. Commissioner Scotty Hancock said the developers came for the county's water: "Floyd County did not recruit them. They came to us with this project." He said the board had discussed a moratorium "because there are only so many of them our community can absorb." The approval limits the land to data center use, requires dark-sky lighting and noise limits, and imposes a 100 foot undisturbed buffer to adjacent properties and the full 200 foot buffer along the southern line. Atlas later backed out of a second Rome site: in August 2026 it ended a preliminary agreement to buy the remaining 100 acres of the Battey Business Complex on North Division Street for $5.7 million, and neither Atlas nor the development authority gave a reason.

ft-1784074529300-4979.text: CleanSpark is turning its bitcoin mining site in Sandersville, the seat of Washington County, Georgia, into a data center under a 20-year lease with Meta for 175 megawatts of computing power. CleanSpark, which has run the Sandersville site since 2022, announced the lease on July 14, 2026, with an expected $6.6 billion in revenue over the first 20 years and two five-year renewal options. CleanSpark first described the tenant only as a "high investment-grade, leading global technology company," but a September 2026 SEC filing named it as Anviran, a Meta subsidiary, with Meta as guarantor of the lease. The same Meta subsidiary has also signed a letter of intent for 885 megawatts at CleanSpark's Sealy and Brazoria campuses in Texas, part of a wider push by Meta to lock up computing capacity. CleanSpark is seeking $2.227 billion to help pay for the Sandersville build, which it expects to cost $2.08 billion in all, with rent starting in November 2027 and the full build finished by March 2028.

ft-190.text: An Athens-Clarke County plans review notice for 20 July 2023 lists application PR-2023-07-1387, a new data center with office space at 0 Voyles Road and 105 Old Elberton Road, Shoals Crossing, with Kevin Conway of Brasfield & Gorrie as the contact. The builder's project list describes the Athens Shoals Crossing data center as a 75,000 square foot design-build enterprise building with 20,000 square feet of white space, 10,000 more for a future data hall, and 3 megawatts of critical IT load, for a confidential client. The building is owned by Atlanta Gas Light, and Athens had no formal definition of a data center in its zoning code when it went up. The building stands in the same area as the old DuPont plant that Pittard Road advocate Tawana Mattox believes poisoned her neighborhood's well water, and no one in the neighborhood was told about the data center while it was being built. "We're watching this building come up, [but] nobody can tell us what the building is," Mattox said at a town hall in Winterville. Mattox's community had struggled for years with PFAS contamination, likely from industrial runoff; that danger had been resolved, and now the data center had arrived. The commission voted unanimously in early December 2025 to pause new data centers. "The first data center snuck up on us," Commissioner Ovita Thornton said. "It should have set off some alarms for us." Thornton, who represents District 9, later said she had not known it was running: "A lot of people did not know that [a data center in Athens] is currently up and running. I'm on the commission and I didn't even know." "When the data center on [Voyles Road] was built, by right, there [were] no ordinances, there [were] no check-ins," she said. The commission extended the pause unanimously on 3 March 2026, to 5 June, while residents at a packed meeting asked for renewable energy rules, community benefit agreements and an end to nondisclosure agreements. In April 2026 commissioners voted unanimously to lift the pause and replace it with an ordinance that allows data centers in heavy industrial zones and requires closed loop cooling. ft-195.text: Vantage Data Centers' Westlake project would put a 754,220 square foot data center on undeveloped land west of Plummer Road and north of Riverside Drive in South Fulton, Fulton County, Georgia, east of the existing Quaker facility. The company filed it for state review in August 2024, alongside a second South Fulton campus on Stacks Road, and gave Westlake a completion date of January 2028. The city of South Fulton submitted the Development of Regional Impact form on August 13, 2024, the state found on November 12 that it warranted regional review, and the Atlanta Regional Commission issued its finding on February 21, 2025. The transportation study filed with the review shows two buildings, labeled GA21 and GA22, on a 35.42 acre lot, with 16.1 acres paved or built over, 27.63 acres disturbed and two driveways onto Plummer Road. In a preliminary report dated January 27, 2025, the commission said the project did not fit its policy for the area, a Regional Center where it wants more housing, mixed use and parks close to residents, and that clearing the heavily forested site would worsen local heat. It recommended replacing the trees and putting some of the estimated $7.4 million a year the project would bring the city toward buying natural land elsewhere, while crediting the plan with keeping about 8 acres of natural space and all stream buffer areas. South Fulton adopted an ordinance in June 2025 setting noise and distance-from-homes rules for future data centers, and council member Linda Pritchett said some colleagues wanted a moratorium. "I don't think that we need to rush to continue building up data centers because of the fact that we have a lot of raw land," Pritchett said. "By the time we find out about a data center, it's often a done deal," said Wanda Mosley of the Black Voters Matter Fund, who has been gathering residents to share information on data centers being voted on in the area.
