ft-1787747120516-1685.text: Statesboro's mayor broke a 2 to 2 tie on Aug. 18, 2026 to rezone 26.49 acres at 6539 Burkhalter Road from high-density residential to office and business, so developers can keep pursuing a data center there, in Bulloch County, Georgia. The owners, 4AM Development LLC partners Bobby Bagwell of Augusta and Charles C. Way of Savannah, mainly residential developers until now, propose a two-story data center with roughly 230,000 square feet of floor space. Council members Ginny Hendley and Tangie Reese Johnson voted for the change, Sharri Barr and John Riggs voted against, and Mayor Jonathan McCollar cast the deciding vote. "I've been in much prayer regarding this data center," said Johnson, who works at Georgia Southern University. "I'm not against data centers." About 100 people protested outside City Hall before the vote, and opponents filled the council chamber and the second floor corridor to the 133-person fire code limit. At the Planning Commission on Aug. 4, which recommended the change 5 to 1, Lori Braselton, who bought a home in the area in May, said: "I just see my investment and my retirement going down the tubes." Way answered: "The idea that there's going to be noise heard from this thing a half a mile or a mile away is simply not true." Before the council, Ogeechee Riverkeeper urged a denial, and neighbors raised home values, noise, water, electrical demand, wetlands and traffic. The concept plan puts the power requirement at 40 to 90 megawatts, and the developers have applied to Georgia Power for 99 megawatts from the transmission lines beside the property. A water plan by Thomas & Hutton projects a closed-loop cooling system needing 30 to 100 gallons a day of makeup water, and a total average demand of 330 to 400 gallons a day. A fiscal study obtained through the Development Authority of Bulloch County, at the developers' request and expense, projects $1.2 billion of investment over 10 years and 12 full-time jobs. "Well honestly, I don't know if it's realistic or not," said Benjy Thompson, the authority's CEO. "I've never worked a data center project." The developers have no operator yet, and Way said they are "zoning it speculatively, but there is zero chance that they're going to build this speculatively." The city's data center ordinance, passed 3 to 1 on June 2, still requires a special use permit with a further hearing and council approval, and limits any data center to a 50 acre site. On Sept. 1 City Manager Charles Penny said no application had been received and the council should not decide it without knowing the end user: "I don't believe that this council will sign a blank check." Bulloch County's own moratorium, extended to Dec. 31, covers only unincorporated land, and on Sept. 1 county commissioners voted 4 to 3 against turning it into a permanent ban.

ft-1770386692559-2351.text: Atlas Development withdrew Project Bus, a proposed data center campus of up to 12 buildings and two substations on about 350 acres near Temple, Georgia, in Carroll County, in February 2026 after heavy local opposition. Atlas had filed a Development of Regional Impact application with the state saying the campus could be worth $11 billion at full build-out and finished by 2036. Atlas describes itself as a developer of power-ready sites for hyperscale and enterprise clients and claims 18 sites under control, including a 428-acre technology park outside Villa Rica. "There's no reason for us to request annexation, because they've withdrawn their request," Temple Mayor Michael Johnson told the Times-Georgian after Atlas notified the city. Opponents packed the Temple Senior Center that Thursday evening to celebrate and plan for any future proposal. "Tonight was a win for rural, agricultural America. It proved that informed, organized communities still have a voice," wrote Zack Martin, organizer of the Carroll County Anti-Data Center Coalition, warning of "a second attempt to refile under a different path." "Data centers haven't been around long enough for us to know the full impact (on the area)," said Dee Perry, founder of the Georgia Agricultural Land Trust. Atlas has finished the state review for its Avemore data center in Villa Rica, where the city took jurisdiction after approving an annexation and a zoning overlay, while in Temple the project had hinged on the city requesting annexation of the land.

ft-210.text: The Upson County Megasite is a 1,443 acre farm at 795 Windsweep Farm Road outside Thomaston that is being marketed for sale as a site for a data center campus. The Upson Beacon reported on 27 August 2025 that SugarOak Realty was selling the former W.R. Bean and Son property as a megasite, and that although the tax assessor lists Manty Tree LLC as the owner, the land is held by Dominion Capital, an Atlanta holding company that bought it in 2021. Marketing material posted on LoopNet sketched 13 data center footprints of roughly 250,000 square feet each, a 10 acre and a 20 acre substation and a 10 acre power generation plant, laid out around wetlands, a stream, a gas line and water retention bays. SugarOak's own listing gives 1,450 acres, up to 619 of them buildable, with direct access to 230 kV and 115 kV transmission lines, fiber already in place and a natural gas pipeline on site. The Beacon put 74.7 megawatts of available capacity on the 115 kV line and 741 megawatts on the 230 kV line, and noted the Edward L. Addison power plant 3.2 miles away. The county had changed its rules a month before the listing surfaced: on 22 July 2025 the Upson County Board of Commissioners voted unanimously to create a technology overlay district that technology businesses can seek on agricultural-residential land, and to amend the M-1 and M-2 manufacturing districts. Commissioner Chris Biggs promised a town hall and set out the questions: "One of my questions is about water usage. The volume of water needed will come from the City of Thomaston, but how will it be disposed of, or will it be recycled?" Biggs also raised fire cover, saying Rock Hill "is a volunteer fire department and does an excellent job, but if there were a fire, additional resources would be needed." Slade Gulledge, executive director of the Thomaston-Upson Industrial Development Authority, said the authority is "in the opportunity business" and will "carefully explore and evaluate every potential prospect and or project that could strengthen our local economy." At the 28 October 2025 commission meeting a resident identified only as Kevin said a data center was planned across Andrews Chapel Road from his home: "This data center is gonna go right across the road from me." "There's gonna be 12 of them over there. They're gonna be lit up all night, fans running, air conditioning. Where's the water coming from?" he asked, adding that neighbors had not been contacted. Biggs told the meeting: "I can assure you that there hasn't been any more discussion about a data center. None whatsoever." By the summer of 2026 residents wanted a pause; at the 23 June meeting Rusty Blackson asked for a moratorium of at least 12 months so the county could write rules before a project arrived, and commissioners said they would rather write a data center ordinance than adopt an emergency moratorium. At a 14 July 2026 work session county attorney Heath English called the draft ordinance "very restrictive", and the board asked staff to add a development agreement, a decommissioning plan backed by a bond or other financial assurance, an emergency response plan and a letter of commitment from the utility. The draft discussed on 6 August 2026 would allow data centers in industrial districts only by special exception, on at least 100 acres, with 50 foot natural buffers, a 500 foot setback from homes, public water and sewer instead of wells or septic, closed loop cooling, sound studies and a decommissioning bond. Commissioners were still weighing whether to make data centers a permitted use with supplemental standards or to require a special exception for every one.

ft-1768319637494-3478.text: Project Azalea is a plan for six data center buildings on 200 acres at 2660-2358 Randall Hunt Road in Thomson, in McDuffie County, west of Augusta. The developer is Williams Brothers Development, founded by Cameron Grogan, and McDuffie County commissioners approved the rezoning 4 to 1 on March 17, 2026. The project first came to light through a Development of Regional Impact application to the Georgia Department of Community Affairs. That January 2026 filing was linked to Project Turbo LLC, which had proposed and then withdrawn a 145-acre data center at Gainesville in Hall County, and projected completion by 2029. The regional commission's review warned that "sufficient energy supply is not available to serve this project" and said studies were under way with Georgia Power, Georgia Transmission Corporation and the EMC to find out what upgrades were needed. The same report noted that no traffic study had been done and listed 18 outside parties that could be affected, among them Fort Gordon, Augusta-Richmond County, Jefferson County and Columbia County. In answers published by the McDuffie Progress on February 11, 2026, the project team said the campus would cost more than $1 billion, likely scale to 300 to 500 megawatts of power, use closed loop cooling and less than 1 percent of the municipal water capacity, and pointed out that the county's schools receive roughly 40 to 45 percent of all property tax revenue. The project's own website puts water use at 30,000 gallons a day, about what 120 homes use, drawn from the municipal system rather than wells. Carrie Davis, who owns land in both McDuffie and Columbia counties, told WRDW in January: "How do you do research if it's not out there?" Davis also asked what becomes of the buildings once the demand passes, since "there's no kind of bond that keeps them accountable." The planning commission voted 5 to 1 on March 3, 2026 to recommend approval, after Grogan told the room "We don't have any NDAs" and "We want to answer every question." Gary Norris said the rural roads could not take the heavy equipment, Barbara Wilcher worried about the effect on future generations, and Davis again said residents had not been told. The county collected 74 written questions before a listening session on March 10, where commissioners put them to the developers. On decommissioning the developer promised that "whether we start, we leave, or it ceases to be a data center, we will remove anything that makes it a data center," taking out computing equipment and generators and leaving the shell buildings. Preston Lingle left unconvinced: "I think they told people what they wanted to hear and I think there are some elements of truth in it." At the March 17 hearing, Gloria Thompson said: "I'm absolutely in favor of this data center and what it will bring to McDuffie County, and not only just in taxes, but in job opportunities." Kim Silva listed the fears as "The noise pollution, all the health issues that they cause, the seepage from the loop system." The McDuffie County Board of Commissioners approved the rezoning 4 to 1 that night. "When all the questions are answered, and we've agreed to every condition, there's nothing to negotiate, it feels like it was time to take a vote," Grogan said. The Augusta Chronicle gave the campus 1.5 million square feet, 125 full-time jobs and about $25 million a year in local taxes, $4.6 million of it county property tax and $9 million school tax, with power from an adjacent Jefferson Electric Cooperative substation. Grogan expected work to begin in about a year and to be finished within three to four years.

ft-200.text: Project Rita, the Microsoft data center approved in March 2024 for the town of Tyrone in Fayette County, Georgia, still has no construction application: as of June 2, 2026, Microsoft had filed no site plan, land disturbance permit or building permit, the town says. Two years after the approval, residents have begun to push back, asking the town for independent studies and a moratorium on future data centers. The Fayette County Development Authority brought the project to Tyrone, asking the town to annex 145.5 acres of undeveloped land and rezone it to Business Technology Park for two one-story data center buildings totaling 490,000 square feet, an on-site substation and 96 megawatts. The site lies west of Georgia Highway 74, between Kirkley Road and the Fairburn city limit on the Fulton County line. Of 161 acres planned, about 147 are within Tyrone and the rest in Fulton County. The Planning Commission held a public hearing on Feb. 22, 2024, and the Town Council held its hearing on March 21 and approved the rezoning on March 28, 2024. Microsoft estimates the campus will use about 4,000 gallons of water a day once it is running, and the town says Microsoft did not request, and was not offered, a tax abatement. More than 12 residents spoke against the project at the Town Council meeting on May 21, 2026. "My husband and I begged the council to wait, do more research, learn lessons from QTS, but here we are," said resident Molly Larson, listing concerns from power and water use to noise, drainage, wetlands and oversight. Hannah Schilsky, who said transmission lines along Graves Road led her to sell her home, told the council: "I am not against progress, but if Georgia Power is going to do what they want without any oversight, I would extremely recommend putting a moratorium on data centers." Mayor Eric Dial defended the 2024 decision, saying the Highway 74 corridor had long been planned for business technology park zoning: "If we stablish this long-term land use plan and then deny a rezoning, it is highly likely that if sued, we would have a limited defense." "Many residents said they did not fully understand the scope, scale, or intended use of this project until the public hearings were underway," resident La'Shawn Dudley said at the July 16 council meeting. Officials noted the site is in a groundwater recharge area, as is most of northwest Fayette County. The town says it cannot revoke the zoning, because legal rights vested with the approval. Tyrone's Business Technology Park rules cap each building at 300,000 square feet, and staff presented a comparison of Georgia data center ordinances to the Town Council on Aug. 6, 2026. Nearby in Fayetteville, where QTS is developing a data center campus, Fayette County said in May 2026 that QTS's water use over the past year was less than 1% of the county water system's production and permitted capacity. What happens next depends on Microsoft. "They have not indicated a timeframe," Assistant Town Manager Phillip Trocquet said in July when asked when the company would submit engineering plans. When it does, the site plan and architectural review will come before the Tyrone Planning Commission in a public meeting, and the Town Council will not vote again unless Microsoft seeks substantive changes to its plan. Water service is decided by the Fayette County Water System, not the town.

ft-202.text: The public hearing signs for this data center rezoning went up thirteen days before the hearing, and the law requires fifteen. That is what a local group found after asking Lowndes County for the rezoning file under Georgia's open records law. The signs were photographed on 25 June 2025 and the county commission heard the case on 8 July. The application, REZ-2025-11, covers 719.46 acres on Coleman Road North, across the Withlacoochee River from Langdale Park, for a data center. The applicant is Langdale Capital Assets Inc., which received the property from The Langdale Company on 30 December 2009 for, in the deed's words, "TEN DOLLARS and other valuable consideration". The dates run: application lodged 9 May 2025, fees of $908.48 paid on 19 May, completeness determined 9 June, adjacent owners notified by certified mail on 20 June, planning commission on 30 June, county commission on 8 July. The county first quoted $250 for the documents, which are the kind normally included in a board packet, and in the end charged $40.85. Water is the reason the site matters. The rezoning materials document the land's closeness to the Withlacoochee River and its position over the Floridan Aquifer. The developer is named as Langdale Capital Assets, with organised local advocacy logged through a group called Lowndes Citizens Against Data Centers, and a Valdosta moratorium running from 25 August to 24 October 2026. This is the only data center site recorded in Lowndes County. The nearest generation is a 70 megawatt biomass plant at a Valdosta paper mill, 21 kilometres away, and two 150 megawatt solar plants at about 30.

ft-206.text: Atlas Development's Avemore project is a 428-acre technology and data center park on the Carroll County side of Villa Rica, Georgia, along Highway 61, Hickory Level Road and South Van Wert Road. Villa Rica annexed and rezoned the land on May 13, 2025, despite residents speaking against it, while neighbors in Carroll County were already fighting it in court. More than 30 Carroll County residents had petitioned Carroll County Superior Court in February 2025 against the city, Embry Development Company and another landowner over more than 200 acres between Hickory Level and South Van Wert roads, arguing the annexation and rezoning would directly harm their land. At the May hearing, resident attorney Jefferson Allen said the city had not given timely notice; Atlas attorney Brandon Bowen replied: "In Georgia, the power to zone is placed directly in the city council. It's not in the court system." Paul Cutler, a 27-year Villa Rica resident, questioned the water supply: "Villa Rica gets 80% of their water from Douglas County." Dan Christner, who gathered 500 signatures door to door, said the developer's own filings put water use at 1.1 million gallons a day. An online petition against the $4 billion to $7 billion project has more than 1,737 verified signatures. Atlas has since filed a Development of Regional Impact application for Avemore, with a first construction phase set for 2028. Carroll County commissioners adopted a 100-day moratorium on data center permits by a 7-0 vote on March 3, 2026, and extended it for another 100 days on June 3, 2026, running through September 11, 2026. The moratorium covers only unincorporated county land, so it does not affect Villa Rica, where Avemore sits.

ft-204.text: Atlas Development wants to put a data center campus where Villa Rica, in Carroll County, Georgia, once zoned land for a housing project called Avemore. The city council cleared 200 single family homes, 300 multi-family and live/work units, and a retirement community with independent living and memory care on the site in 2018, then raised the housing limits in 2020 and cleared more senior housing in 2021. Avemore GA LLC now wants seven data center buildings on roughly the same 432 acres instead. On August 20, 2024, Avemore GA LLC asked the planning and zoning commission to extend the 2018 zoning, due to expire September 12, 2024, and to add light industrial zoning for the data center buildings. Community development director Nina Shabazz recommended denying both requests, writing that the data center was a "completely new project that was never reviewed or approved" and telling the applicant to start over with a full application. Site plans in the packet showed seven buildings of 350,000 square feet each, about 2.45 million square feet total, on parcels held by Avemore GA LLC, Jerry Tolbert and Brenda Matthews. The application was later withdrawn and refiled, and city staff then recommended approval. In April 2025 Atlas Development filed a Development of Regional Impact application with the state for a 428-acre technology and data park on the site, with a first phase planned for 2028.

ft-205.text: The Hickman Property data center plan covered about 700 acres near Interstate 20 and Clinton Road in Douglas County, partly inside Villa Rica. Douglas County commissioners have now refused it twice in seven months, the second time on 7 July 2026, when representatives of EdgeConnex spoke for it as the developer. The applicant, East Village Dothan LLC, was registered in 2022 by James Hickman, who does not own the land. The first filing, in March 2025, described 6.2 million square feet, eleven data center buildings and 66,000 square feet of warehouses, with no megawatt figure, no timeline and no build out value, on land zoned residential and agricultural. By the first vote the plan was seven buildings of 320,000 to 1.2 million square feet, 4.7 million in all, with a substation and a water treatment system, on 700 acres off Tyson Road. On 2 December 2025 the planning and zoning commission and then the county commission each voted 4 to 1 to deny rezoning from rural agriculture to light industrial. Planning and zoning manager Allison Duncan recommended denial: "The scale and intensity of the proposed project is not contemplated or supported by the comprehensive plan or future land use map." District 4 commissioner Mark Alcarez, whose district held the site, said: "To know that our fire department cannot adequately keep you safe and service that area at this time is something that I have to go to bed with at night if something was to happen to y'all." District 2 commissioner Whitney Kenner Jones, whose district has many data centers, said they "still have not generated enough revenue to build out the appropriate number of fire stations across the county." Villa Rica resident Natalie Hays called the promised green space "a lot of lipstick on a pig" and pointed to the diesel generators data centers depend on, while law student Moses Dotson argued for it: "There is nothing here in Douglas County for us." The second application asked for a land use change from Rural Places to Commerce Center, a planned unit development and special use permits for six buildings totaling 4.4 million square feet and a substation. EdgeConnex said more than 570 acres would stay green space, and its lawyer Anamaria Meanes asked for a deferral "so that we can address the concerns of the community and further discuss the project." Duncan again recommended denial, saying "We do not feel that Commerce Center is compatible with the Dog River Basin character area"; part of the site lies in the basin that feeds the Dog River Reservoir, the county's main water source. Donald Vaughn, who has lived on Liberty Road for 40 years, backed it: "This is a good thing for the county." The commission voted 4 to 1 to deny each request, with District 1 commissioner Henry Mitchell the only vote against denial.

ft-207.text: Robins Air Force Base in Warner Robins, Houston County, Georgia, is one of five Air Force bases where the service has offered to lease land to a private company for an AI data center. The Department of the Air Force published its request for proposals on October 15, 2025, listing three parcels at Robins of 30 to 135 acres, and said it expected to choose lease applicants in January 2026. As of late September 2026, no developer has been named and the Air Force has not announced which company, if any, won a lease. Defense One put the land available at Robins at 219 acres. Proposals had to add more than 100 megawatts of power capacity and at least $500 million in capital spending, thresholds set by executive order 14318, and were due November 14, 2025; leases could run up to 50 years, with the lessee paying for utilities and services that must stay "accessible and affordable" to the base and surrounding community. Benjamin Kindt, the Air Force's chief of real estate development, said the department is "focused on swiftly, yet effectively, selecting an industry leader as a lease applicant." Stacie Pettyjohn of the Center for a New American Security warned that letting more people onto a base creates "a lot of room for potential espionage, let alone sabotage or things like that." At Arnold Air Force Base in Tennessee, another of the five sites, officials said on June 1, 2026 that no company had submitted a proposal for its parcels by the May 29 deadline. Outside the fence, Warner Robins City Council approved a six month moratorium on data center applications on July 20, 2026, running through January 20, 2027. Mayor LaRhonda Patrick said the city wants to hear from experts on the water table, sewer system and electric grid before any project moves forward: "We can't allow someone to come in and suck up all our water resources, and be left with water with low pressure, for example."

ft-1771618149523-4077.text: Servpac, a Hawaii cloud and colocation company, is adding a second building to its MTP Data Center in Mililani Technology Park in central O'ahu, Hawaii. The site is in Honolulu County, and the first building has been operating since 2021. Building 2 broke ground on Jan. 22, 2026: a $13 million, 15,500-square-foot building on a 5-acre parcel of company-owned land that will increase the facility's size by 50 percent, with completion expected in the second quarter of 2026. The existing 30,000-square-foot Building 1 is the state's only Tier IV Uptime Institute-certified data center, and Servpac expects Building 2 to receive that designation too. Servpac's website puts the current facility at 1MW, and the company told DCD the expansion would provide an estimated 10 times more cabinet and power capacity. The first phase, completed in September 2021, was designed to produce about 1MWh of power a day from 500 solar panels, and the new building is designed to withstand Category 5 hurricane winds with its own power supply. President Richard Zheng said Hawaii's "particular vulnerabilities because of threats from hurricanes to tsunami and rising sea levels" create a great need for a geographically secure data facility. Ralph S. Inouye Co. is the general contractor. Hawaii's argument over data centers is about much bigger facilities. On Hawaii island, Hawaii County Council member Heather Kimball's Bill 170 would state that data centers "are not a permitted use in the County," while exempting those serving public institutions and leaving existing ones alone. "There has been a clear indication from some of these entities that they intend to build data centers in every state in the country, including Hawaii," Kimball told the Windward Planning Commission, which on Sept. 3, 2026 voted 4-0 to defer the bill until October. County Planning Director Jeff Darrow suggested allowing standalone data centers only in the general industrial district, up to 10,000 square feet, with larger ones needing a use permit, and he warned that an outright county ban could push developers to seek state approval instead. Those rules would apply only on Hawaii island, not on O'ahu, where Servpac's expansion is already under way.

ft-220.text: Edged is building a 13 megawatt data center in Ankeny, Polk County, Iowa, just north of Interstate 80, at a cost of $187 million. The Ankeny City Council approved a development agreement with Edged Des Moines LLC on March 3, 2025, the last step before site work could begin. Edged had bought the 17.5 acre parcel for $3.7 million in late 2024, and the building is expected to open in 2026. The agreement gives Edged a five year sliding scale tax increment financing package worth up to $2 million and requires 22 jobs paying $29.76 to $35.71 an hour. Edged is paying to extend water and sewer to the site, opening another 120 acres to development, and the city expects the project to add $41 million of taxable value and about $1.25 million a year in tax once the incentive ends. Derek Lord, Ankeny's economic development director, said the city had worked with Edged for more than three years, "so we're very excited for it to get to the finish line." Edged's chief operating officer Mitch Fonseca said Iowa's draw was "cheap power, which is a huge factor, skilled labor is a huge factor, and fiber connectivity is also helpful." Edged broke ground at 9100 Southeast Four Mile Drive in May 2025 and topped out the building's structural frame that August. The facility uses a waterless closed loop cooling system that moves heat with glycol to rooftop air cooled chillers, which Edged expects will save more than 52 million gallons of water a year compared with a conventional data center. Backup generators use Tier 4 Final engines, which Edged says cut emissions by up to 99 percent. A second, larger project is planned at the same intersection of Southeast 90th Street and Southeast Four Mile Drive: the I-80 Commerce Center, where Commerce Center LLC, owned by Signature Real Estate, wants to build two data centers of 535,555 and 775,520 square feet and a substation on about 35 acres. The Des Moines Register has reported Edged as the likely operator, and Kye Nielsen of the Will Group told the Ankeny planning commission the buildings would run entirely on air cooling and use water only for domestic needs. City staff recommended approval and the planning commission agreed, but the Ankeny City Council still has to give final approval, and no vote date has been announced.

ft-1775148054695-4922.text: Simple Mining, a bitcoin company based in Cedar Falls, plans to put about 40 crypto mining containers on roughly four acres of the Cascade Industrial Park in Cascade, Iowa, a town of 2,386 people that lies partly in Dubuque County and partly in Jones County. "Simple Mining is not putting in a data center," Ken McDermott, president of the Cascade Economic Development Corporation, said, though the Telegraph Herald later reported the company had bought 15 acres in the park, about a third of it for the mining facility, with six to eight jobs. The corporation has called a public forum on the project for Thursday, October 1, 2026, from 6 to 7:30 pm at the KC Hall in Cascade, with questions to be sent in by September 25. Each container would be about 160 square feet on a concrete pad, self-cooled to use less water and power, and an agreement caps noise leaving the property at the level of a normal conversation and requires Simple Mining to disclose the project's maximum possible electricity use before the land sale closes. Joan Hoffmann, who lives next to the park in the Oak Hill neighborhood, said she worries about the water and power the project would use: "I spend a lot of my time in the summer out on the porch and I love the sound of the birds and the kids playing at the park nearby. I hope that wouldn't interfere with that." At a May 26, 2026 council meeting, resident Mireille Gudenkauf said, "Should the center be built, it's my understanding that it's not going to just affect the people that live on Oak Hill, but the other people in Cascade," and asked when the promised community meeting would happen. The Telegraph Herald obtained the development agreement, filed in redacted form at the Dubuque County Recorder's Office, which shows the economic development corporation would get financial incentives if Simple Mining builds; Cascade's mayor has said the financial details are not public. The Cascade City Council passed a 12-month data center moratorium in June 2026 while the town writes rules, and a resident's letter to the Telegraph Herald argued the deal's 60-decibel noise cap at the property line is far louder than the 30 to 45 decibels normally heard in Oak Hill. Simple Mining says it runs five mining sites with 100 megawatts of power under management and is aiming for 500 megawatts by the end of 2026; its larger plan in Cedar Falls failed when that city council unanimously rejected the zoning changes it needed on May 18, 2026.

ft-1775147721305-8550.text: The Cedar Falls City Council voted unanimously on May 18, 2026 against the zoning changes that would have let Simple Mining, a Cedar Falls bitcoin company, build a crypto mining data center in the city's industrial park. The site was more than 38 acres near the West Viking Road Industrial Park, in Black Hawk County, next to where Cedar Falls Utilities plans a natural gas power plant called the Viking Energy Center. The city mailed letters to neighboring owners on March 19, 2026, and the draft rules would have required buildings to stand at least 200 feet from any residential district. Nathan Nebbe lives on 22 acres directly across from the industrial park, land his family has worked since 1981 to restore for ducks, beavers and other wildlife. "I was flat-out hurt when, a couple days ago, we [got] this letter telling us that [the property in question] is for a crypto mine. I'm sorry, that's what it is," Nebbe told Iowa Public Radio. "We've been here 40 years. That was a gut punch." His father, Dennis Nebbe, said the plant and mine were "something that we didn't sign on for, something that is going to probably destroy the value of our property and undo what we've tried to do over 40 years." Tom Risse, project manager for the Viking Energy Center, said: "It's all closed-loop water systems. We're not digging any onsite wells. We don't have any water discharge." Matt Hein, Simple Mining's director of energy infrastructure, said the site would need at least 50 employees and that larger, slower fans would cut the noise: "Our large consumption of electricity is an economic benefit to the city of Cedar Falls," he said. "We help pay for schools. We help pay for roads by our operations." Karen Howard, the city's planning manager, said crypto is already mined at three places in Cedar Falls even though city code does not allow it: "When they were presented, we didn't really know what we were permitting and what the actual use was." The planning commission pushed its hearing from April 8 to April 22, 2026 after residents raised noise, environmental and property value worries. Before that meeting, Cedar Falls Utilities withdrew its request to rezone the roughly 48 acres for heavy industry and asked instead for public zoning, which rules out crypto mines. "Under this zoning classification, cryptocurrency mining, data centers, and other private IT infrastructure would not be permitted on this property," utility chief executive Susan Abernathy wrote to the commission. City documents also recorded that the utility did not support large data centers, because the power they need would likely exceed its capacity. The commission then recommended denying the crypto mining rules, and the council followed it. At the May 18 hearing, Simple Mining founder and chief executive Adam Haynes said the facility would use about as much water in a year as seven homes. Resident Dave Deibler told the council: "What really concerns me is losing control of our city." Mayor Danny Laudick said a council member had also filed a referral asking staff to look at "explicitly disallowing cryptocurrency data centers, especially the hyper scale, larger facilities." Two days after the vote, Simple Mining held an open house to show residents its cooling and the noise levels of its Manchester site. "There's a lot of misconceptions and maybe misunderstanding nationwide about data centers," Haynes said, while resident Axel Hoogland said he was glad the ordinance failed and wanted a better one: "As long as they write the code well, you know, I think, you know, whatever the business is, it can operate within a well-written code."

ft-222.text: Edged topped out the first of two buildings at Project Lola, its roughly 200 megawatt data center campus at College Road and East Kanesville Boulevard in Council Bluffs, Pottawattamie County, Iowa, in late June 2026, with the second due in September 2026. No report on the second building's completion has been published. The Council Bluffs city council adopted the original plan for two 450,000 square foot buildings on June 10, 2024, then approved a smaller redesign, two 285,444 square foot buildings and owner-operated substations, in June 2025. "These updates allow us to deliver a highly efficient, purpose-built solution while maintaining the same 200MW capacity for the campus," Edged chief operating officer Mitch Fonseca said; Edged broke ground in October 2025 with Turner Construction as general contractor. A July 2026 Substack investigation by James P. Brainard, built on county deeds and city records, found Google named as the tenant in a lender agreement recorded on August 4, 2025, though every other public record lists only "tenant." Brainard reported Edged's letter of intent promised cooling "that use no water" and that Council Bluffs Water Works agreed to supply 3,500 gallons a minute at peak demand, while neither Water Works nor Edged has disclosed actual operating water use. On June 15, 2026, Mayor Jill Shudak, who had voted for the project twice as a council member, asked the council for a moratorium of up to a year on new data center projects; it would not have affected Project Lola, and the council rejected it unanimously. "We're running very high at capacity for both water and sewer," Shudak said, and public works director Matt Cox said data center requests for a million or two million gallons a day mean "it only takes one or two big projects and we're at capacity," putting a new wastewater plant at $200 million to $300 million. County resident Roger Williams told the council that vibrations from soil compaction at a data center build had damaged his home, and Councilman Douglas Rew said a pause would show developers "a red stop sign."

ft-1783823589544-7821.text: The City of Maquoketa, in Jackson County, Iowa, ended talks on a data center proposed for 46 acres in the industrial park south of Maquoketa off Highway 61. City leaders and Gronen, the city's development consultant, called off the talks on August 18, 2026, about six weeks after residents packed a city council meeting to object. City Manager Josh Boldt said no solid plan was ever formally presented to the council. The plan, presented to the council in July, was for a small to mid-sized facility with no end user secured yet and no cryptocurrency mining, on land already zoned heavy industrial. The land could have sold for $25,000 an acre, and city officials said the unnamed developer sought no incentives and would pay for any infrastructure upgrades. "We have no local incentives in this agreement," Boldt told residents, saying a data center would add hundreds of thousands of dollars a year to city, county and school budgets strained by inflation. Dozens of residents filled the council chambers to object. "I think when people think of Maquoketa, a data center is not going to be on the list of positives for us," said Forrest Grey. Angie Petit Lichter of the county conservation board asked: "My main concern is when you project this long term, 20 years from now, how many people are they expecting to employ?" "Maquoketa can think bigger and more creatively, and Maquoketa can choose a better future for our people," said Marie Young. When the talks ended, officials said no city staff member or council member had signed a nondisclosure agreement. The land remains available for other development, Boldt said. Council members and staff plan to review the rules for the heavy industrial district, including for data centers, so the city is ready for future proposals. Boldt said it remains likely that other developers will approach the city with similar proposals. The council has not set a date for that review.

ft-1782755707189-2976.text: The company that looked at hundreds of acres of farmland east of Dubuque Regional Airport for a data center is Karis, a national real estate firm, emails obtained by the Telegraph Herald showed in June 2026. Dubuque County officials had declined to name it, but the records show Karis sent "site info for our proposed project east of the airport" to county zoning administrator Ben Kober on May 15, 2026. The land discussed lies near Old Davenport Road between Laudeville Road and Feeney Road. Kober told KCRG that Karis had contacted the county in mid-May but had not applied; the Florida-based company also approached the city of Dubuque. Public records obtained by KCRG show the data center would need up to 3 million gallons of water to fill its closed-loop cooling system and up to 250,000 gallons a year after that, with Karis asking to connect to city water and sewer. The city says it will take no action on any data center until it has an ordinance. Rumors of the land deal had already moved the county. After a packed zoning meeting, the planning and zoning commission unanimously asked for a halt, and on May 26, 2026 the supervisors voted 2 to 1 for a 12 month moratorium, lengthened from the 120 days auditor Keith Lucy had drafted. "I do not support data centers and I have said that in the past repeatedly," said Supervisor Ann McDonough, who moved the change; Wayne Kenniker voted no, saying the motion had not been reviewed by the county's lawyers. Kim Mangers, who lives near the site, said: "My house is worth zero. Zero, because nobody is going to buy my home." Nearly 300 people came to the county's first town hall, at the Peosta Rec Center on June 23, and about 30 spoke on water quality, property values, utilities and the county's economic future. Stephanie Grutz, who owns The Health Spa in Peosta, said the moratorium was too short: "It's like a race to see who can throw these up the fastest without taking a pause and actually looking at the data." Matt Moore, a commercial airline pilot, said a day earlier: "I choose to live here because I want to live next to farms, not server farms." On July 13 airport director Todd Dalsing warned that heat plumes, vapors and cooling ponds near the airport could cause turbulence, low visibility and icing, while the Greater Dubuque Development Corporation presented a consultant's estimate of $6.2 billion in local economic impact and 400 permanent jobs. The supervisors instead agreed to ask the county attorney to hire outside counsel to explore a ban, with Kenniker saying: "Let's decide. I'm willing to decide." By September Karis had turned to Peosta, where developer Jim Conlan said he and Karis Critical had already acquired at least 194 acres south of U.S. 20 off Cox Springs Road. "Build a strong ordinance," Conlan told a packed council work session on September 16. "We're not going away, so if the ordinance takes a year, it takes a year." In a city survey of nearly 300 Peosta residents, 87 percent said they did not support any data center, and the city may extend its own moratorium, due to expire in December.

ft-1782767279002-6514.text: MidAmerican Energy holds options, through its affiliate Midwest Capital Group, on about 900 acres of farmland at Salix, Iowa, that the city annexed from Woodbury County in April 2026, bounded by Old Highway 75, 260th Street and Charles Avenue, to sell on to a data center customer. On August 3, 2026, MidAmerican named that customer as Google, which it said had expressed interest in exploring a data center in the Salix area. Salix has about 300 people and sits south of Sioux City. MidAmerican first told the council in a letter of June 8 that the site was "being evaluated for possible development as a data center site," and that any customer would be "required to pay the full cost of the infrastructure needed to serve its load." Council minutes from June 10 record that residents "have many concerns of a data center coming in," many of them with homes near the annexed land. A petition against the plan had more than 540 signatures by the end of June. Woodbury County supervisors passed a 12 month moratorium 5 to 0 on June 23, 2026, but it covers only unincorporated land and so does not reach the annexed site. Supervisor Matthew Ung questioned how Salix handled the annexation, saying the city never set a time to consult the county. Woodbury County is challenging the annexation in court, arguing that Salix failed to notify residents properly and took in land that does not border the city. On August 6 three residents also asked a judge to declare the annexation void because they were given no notice; the city has moved to dismiss, saying they missed a 30 day deadline. Google's Trent Fellers told residents the company would not seek local property tax abatements or rebates: "All property tax revenue will go directly to the city of Salix, Woodbury County, local school districts and all other local taxing entities." A council meeting set for August 12 to vote on a one year moratorium was postponed after death and terroristic threats against the city government were posted on social media, and Mayor Kevin Nelson said the sheriff was investigating. On August 20 the council voted 3 to 2 against the moratorium. Council member Gene Monk, who backed the pause, said: "It's too big of a decision for us five people [on the council]." Keely Bassette Purscell of the Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska, which owns land nearby and opposes hyperscale data centers near its reservation, told the council: "Whatever you guys do will affect us." The land would still need rezoning for a data center. On September 9, after Nelson had three people removed under new decorum rules, the council agreed to have the regional planning agency SIMPCO draft a data center ordinance for public comment. Supervisors tabled a memorandum of understanding until October 14, 2026.

Council minutes from June 10 record that residents "have many concerns of a data center coming in," many of them with homes near the annexed land. A petition against the plan had more than 540 signatures by the end of June.

Woodbury County supervisors passed a 12 month moratorium 5 to 0 on June 23, 2026, but it covers only unincorporated land and so does not reach the annexed site. Supervisor Matthew Ung questioned how Salix handled the annexation, saying the city never set a time to consult the county.

Woodbury County is challenging the annexation in court, arguing that Salix failed to notify residents properly and took in land that does not border the city. On August 6 three residents also asked a judge to declare the annexation void because they were given no notice; the city has moved to dismiss, saying they missed a 30 day deadline.

Google's Trent Fellers told residents the company would not seek local property tax abatements or rebates: "All property tax revenue will go directly to the city of Salix, Woodbury County, local school districts and all other local taxing entities." A council meeting set for August 12 to vote on a one year moratorium was postponed after death and terroristic threats against the city government were posted on social media, and Mayor Kevin Nelson said the sheriff was investigating.

On August 20 the council voted 3 to 2 against the moratorium. Council member Gene Monk, who backed the pause, said: "It's too big of a decision for us five people [on the council]." Keely Bassette Purscell of the Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska, which owns land nearby and opposes hyperscale data centers near its reservation, told the council: "Whatever you guys do will affect us." The land would still need rezoning for a data center.

On September 9, after Nelson had three people removed under new decorum rules, the council agreed to have the regional planning agency SIMPCO draft a data center ordinance for public comment. Supervisors tabled a memorandum of understanding until October 14, 2026.

ft-1765218735449-8207.text: Deep Atomic, a small nuclear reactor developer, has asked the US Department of Energy for a long-term lease at Idaho National Laboratory to build a data center campus that would eventually run on its own 60 megawatt reactor, the MK60. The laboratory sits near Idaho Falls, in Bonneville County, Idaho, though the reactor test site itself is a 900 square mile stretch of remote desert, about the size of Rhode Island. Deep Atomic's consortium submitted the proposal to the Department of Energy's Office of Nuclear Energy in early December 2025, and the department has not yet announced a decision on it. The plan is to open the data center first, within 24 to 36 months, running on grid, geothermal and solar power, while the MK60 reactor goes through the licensing steps needed before it can operate. Deep Atomic told the Nuclear Regulatory Commission on March 20, 2025 that it was starting that process, and said it aimed to file the required paperwork by the end of 2027. Clayco joined the consortium in February 2026 to help plan construction, and its chairman Bob Clark said the goal was "a buildable, delivery-ready proposal for this groundbreaking, first-of-kind project." Shane Todd of Parker Tide, a member of the consortium, called the lab "the perfect home for this historic first." Near the laboratory, residents of Atomic City, the closest town, say they are not worried about new test reactors running there this summer: "I live 10 miles away, and I'm fine," said Vickie O'Haro, who runs the town's bar. Edwin Lyman, nuclear power safety director at the Union of Concerned Scientists, was less reassured, saying "I have no confidence in the Department of Energy and its oversight of this at all." Those test reactors are separate from Deep Atomic's plan; they are part of a Department of Energy pilot program that required four companies to reach criticality, a self-sustaining chain reaction, by July 4, 2026. One of those companies, Aalo Atomics, hit that deadline at the laboratory and is now working with Crusoe to install one of Crusoe's small prefabricated data centers there in 2027, powered by an Aalo reactor, a plan further along than Deep Atomic's. The Department of Energy opened this kind of bidding on September 8, 2025, offering companies long-term leases on about 44,000 acres of laboratory land if they pay to build, run and eventually dismantle their own projects and secure their own power connections. No date has been set for a decision on Deep Atomic's proposal.

ft-1788614497039-3418.text: Sherry Agnew has lived beside this land in Kuna, in Ada County, Idaho, for 25 years, and what worries her about the data center is her electricity bill. "I'm just worried being a senior citizen, I don't want my power rates to go up," she said, describing the scale of what is planned as mind-boggling. Diode Ventures is developing the Gemstone Technology Park on 620 acres of farmland in southeast Kuna, and the city approved the rezoning in 2025. The company had not broken ground on any infrastructure or buildings when that report was published. The legislature took up the rate question. Idaho House Bill 756 would require customers needing 20 megawatts or more, Gemstone among them, to pay for their own infrastructure so the cost does not fall on other ratepayers. The developer's own project page says it will take on all of the cost of the grid interconnection upgrades, and that Idaho Power has run a feasibility study on the power needed. It gives no megawatt figure at all. On water, the company says the land's historical groundwater irrigation rights are being converted to industrial use, which cuts the maximum allowable usage by 33 percent, so the total volume falls while the diversion rate stays the same. Cooling water would be treated to Idaho Department of Environmental Quality standards, and the site would not use the city of Kuna's utilities. The company puts the investment at more than $1 billion, with 800 to 1,200 construction jobs at peak and more than 100 permanent ones. It offers $30 million to the Kuna Rural Fire District over 13 years, $10 million to Kuna Police over 20, and $500,000 to the school district for athletics and technology. It promises phased development, setbacks, berms, landscaped screening, dark sky compatible lighting and noise dampening enclosures around the generators.

ft-1784071383967-5023.text: Lex Developments' proposed AI data center at the former Hoku plant, 1800 River Park Way in Pocatello, remains blocked. On September 17, the City Council again upheld the May denial of a conditional use permit, voting 3–2 on the company's request for reconsideration. The council waived the usual 12-month wait to reapply, so Lex can submit another application even though this one was denied. The proposal called for seven buildings and 100 megawatts of power by 2031; that figure is a plan, not power in use today. The Shoshone-Bannock Tribes opposed the permit after reviewing the application and hearing testimony. They said Lex had not supplied enough information to judge possible effects on electricity rates, water use and the nearby Portneuf River. Council member Ann Swanson also cited the lack of detail about the project's effects when explaining her September vote. Lex argued that the site's industrial zoning did not require a conditional use permit. A motion to grant one failed 3–2 before the council voted to uphold the denial and let Lex reapply sooner. The council's decision is scheduled to become official on October 1, 2026. When it becomes official, Lex will have 28 days to seek judicial review.

ft-1771258984530-9087.text: Brennan Investment Group, a Rosemont developer, pitched a 110 acre artificial intelligence data center campus at Penny Road and Route 68 in Barrington Hills, Cook County, Illinois, in December 2025. The $2 billion plan was withdrawn in late January 2026, before a special plan commission meeting on February 2 where Brennan was to present it, and the developer said it was acting "based on initial feedback." Brennan told village trustees the land was under contract and put the return to Barrington Hills at $20 million to $40 million a year in property tax and more than $10 million a year in utility tax, against the $3,000 a year the parcel pays now. He called the project "very low impact" and said it would be "fully enclosed with abundant privacy landscaping." Trustee Laura "AB" Ekstrom led most of the questions that followed his five-minute presentation. Residents pushed back hard: a Change.org petition from a group calling itself Barrington Hills Against Data Centers argued that a large site can use 3 to 7 million gallons of water a day in a village that depends on groundwater, and cited diesel generator emissions and the village's own tree and groundwater rules. By January 28, 2026, the petition had 1,303 signatures; it has since passed 2,000. Brennan has built data centers in Elk Grove Village and Rolling Meadows. The village said only, "At this time, the village considers this matter closed and does not anticipate any further discussion," and CBS Chicago reported it remained unclear whether Brennan had dropped the project altogether or only declined to present it at that meeting.

ft-1769465678151-7354.text: Western Hospitality Partners' planned eight-building data center campus near Interstate 55 and Reed Road in Braidwood, Will County, Illinois, has been suspended since January 2026, a pause the city blamed on "ComEd's internal demands and regulations regarding its infrastructure." The New York developer, working with Found Digital, is drawn by the nearby 2.2 gigawatt Braidwood Nuclear Generating Station. A public meeting planned for May 2025 was called off before Western Hospitality Partners closed on the land. County records show the company paid $3,150,000 for a 158 acre parcel at 26125 W. Kennedy Road, and the sale closed on August 28, 2025, according to the Braidwood Journal. On November 12, 2025, the City Council passed an inducement resolution, a formal statement that the city might issue tax-exempt bonds, opening the door to a possible fourth tax increment financing district. City attorney Bryan Wellner said the city was only exploring that option and thought it unlikely to create the district unless the data center went ahead within the city. The pause followed new ComEd rules, introduced January 6, 2026, that require firm financial commitments from projects of at least 50 megawatts of power and a letter of credit covering 10 years of transmission service revenue. "After taking office, I shared publicly that the city was exploring a potential annexation related to this project and that additional research was needed," Mayor Todd Lyons said. The developer has closed on the land while the city is still deciding whether to annex it, and Lyons said the city would hold a public meeting for community input at a later date.

ft-1786415749791-9416.text: Chicago investor Igor Gabal wants to convert the second through sixth floors of the landmarked office building at 300 W. Adams St., in the Loop, Cook County, into a data center. The Commission on Chicago Landmarks' Permit Review Committee signed off on the plan on August 6, 2026, but the full commission still has to give final approval, and no construction timeline has been set. The developer, Chilled AI, would fill in the building's light court, install ten backup generators on the roof, and build a ComEd vault that Gabal says will supply no more than 50 megawatts of power, though the building's brochure lists the vault at 20.4 megawatts. Preservation Chicago, which backed the building's 2009 landmark designation, opposes the conversion; executive director Ward Miller called it a "dangerous precedent" for other landmarks and wants the space turned into housing instead. Gabal, who bought the 1927 building for $4 million in 2023 when it was nearly 60% vacant, says "no one wants to lease space" in Class C office towers like this one. In July 2026 his venture sold its interest for $12.5 million to a new joint venture with Greenwich, Connecticut-based Strategic Value Partners, which is partnering with him on the data center, according to Illinois property records. The Chicago Tribune editorial board has also come out against the plan. On August 11, 2026, days after the committee vote, Mayor Brandon Johnson signed an executive order asking for a moratorium on new or expanded data centers in Chicago, but the city's planning department says the Adams Street proposal is not subject to the new review because data center use is already allowed under the building's zoning. Zoning committee chair Gilbert Villegas called the mayor's order a "political stunt."

In July 2026 his venture sold its interest for $12.5 million to a new joint venture with Greenwich, Connecticut-based Strategic Value Partners, which is partnering with him on the data center, according to Illinois property records.
The Chicago Tribune editorial board has also come out against the plan.

On August 11, 2026, days after the committee vote, Mayor Brandon Johnson signed an executive order asking for a moratorium on new or expanded data centers in Chicago, but the city's planning department says the Adams Street proposal is not subject to the new review because data center use is already allowed under the building's zoning.
Zoning committee chair Gilbert Villegas called the mayor's order a "political stunt."

ft-235.text: Karis Acquisitions asked DeKalb in July 2024 to allow a seven building data center campus on 132 acres at the northeast corner of Peace and Gurler roads, which would be the city's second after Meta's. The City of DeKalb's development list records a planning and zoning recommendation on July 15, 2024, and council approval on July 22, 2024, for an amendment allowing a 1,750,000 square foot data center in seven buildings, filed by Steven Goldin and Karis Acquisitions. Jake Finley presented the petition for Karis, which also sought a 17.5 acre ComEd substation; city staff and Jerry Krusinski, manager of the neighboring ChicagoWest Business Center, wanted it moved from the corner to a screened spot inside the site. It ended up at the southeast corner, which officials said would keep "a nice campus look" for drivers heading south on Peace Road. David Dicks, vice president of development for Karis Acquisitions, said traffic would mainly be employees' vehicles and that "The impacts were very, very minimal," and the company projected 75 to 100 jobs per building. Roy Jones of Earlville questioned whether the plan met "best practices in land management stewardship" and warned against leasing resources to "out-of-state entities at a flat rate." At the council, former city clerk Lynn Fazekas urged the city to protect its water supply first: "Meta's only been operational for less than a year." Deborah Ridder asked about landscaping and fencing and objected to losing farmland. City manager Bill Nicklas answered that a data center brings far less truck traffic than a warehouse, and pointed to a 300 foot setback from Gurler Road, a detention basin and landscaped berms. The land had been annexed and zoned for planned industrial development in 2023; the council's vote added data centers as a permitted use and raised the allowed floor area, and a separate vote on the development itself is still needed before construction. The city's March 2026 development list gives no construction dates for the Karis project, while other projects on it carry grading and building years. Karis's own website now markets a 250 acre DeKalb site next to Meta's campus as shovel ready and available for sale or joint venture, with power details offered only to qualified parties.

ft-1767322980321-2337.text: Gail Technology's solar-powered data center at 15244 E. 1700th Avenue, on the north side of Effingham, in Effingham County, Illinois, is under construction. It is the one project Effingham's new data center moratorium does not reach, because the city council's 12-month pause, passed 5-0 on June 2, 2026, exempts permit petitions already filed before that date. City Planner Greg Koester said the site runs on a 4.63-acre solar array and battery storage, sends extra power to the grid, and uses no water for cooling. Residents have pushed the city to go further anyway. Nicholas Tkachuk of Altamont told the city council data centers could bring pollution, consume farmland and strain water and electricity, saying, "I think it's incredibly important that we make sure that these data centers don't spiral out of control." City Attorney Tracy Willenborg said the 12-month moratorium, which covers the city and the mile and a half around it, gives officials time to study the issue before writing permanent rules. Effingham County has not followed suit. Pat Lewis of the EASE Community Alliance asked the county board to adopt a moratorium too, but board chairman Josh Douthit said Effingham County has no zoning and does not believe it can approve one. Gail Technology, based in Bannockburn, says the solar array and batteries should run the data center around the clock, with Ameren paying for surplus power sent back to the grid. The company says the center will serve artificial intelligence and Web3, the term for blockchain-based computing, and that it has 10 similar projects in central Illinois, with this one expected to take 10 to 15 months to build. Chief Financial Officer Nick Mahoney said Effingham was chosen for its utilities, permitting, flat land and distance from neighbors, and that the land can return to farming when the 25-year lease ends. IAG Investments is leasing the land to a solar developer that will build the array and the data center shell, and Gail Technology will then lease access to the finished data center to customers. The Effingham City Council is due to write the city's permanent data center rules before the 12-month moratorium expires in June 2027.

ft-243.text: Nexstar Media Group and its development affiliate, IL_720 Rohlwing Rd. LLC, are building toward a data center campus on part of the WGN radio tower site at 720 Rohlwing Road in Elk Grove Village, Cook County. The Elk Grove Village plan commission approved a three-building campus in June 2023, and years of power-supply delays have pushed the developer's deadline to start construction to September 30, 2027. WGN and Nexstar announced in June 2022 that they would sell 35 acres of the 100-acre tower site, then in unincorporated Schaumburg Township in Cook County, to an unnamed data center developer. Mayor Craig Johnson said the village had worked with the broadcaster for about eighteen months to find a buyer, and that residents at a meeting on June 2, 2022 "gave a standing ovation for the proposal." He said data centers "have few employees, generate little traffic, and make little noise." The plan commission unanimously approved the three-building campus by IL_720 Rohlwing Rd. LLC on June 5, 2023, with pickleball courts for the park district included on the site. A redevelopment agreement signed in July 2023 set a phased timeline, but the first deadline passed with nothing built. The village has since moved the construction deadline to September 30, 2027. Power issues have continued to dog the project. Johnson said Nexstar now envisions four data center buildings spread across a larger portion of the 102-acre site and no longer needs to replace the old towers, since radio transmission can be handled other ways. To bring in power, the village agreed in January 2026 to sell Commonwealth Edison a vacant 1.2-acre parcel at 300 East Devon Avenue for about $3.6 million. At the village board meeting of August 11, 2026, residents living near the site voiced concerns over continuous noise, wildlife and water use. Martinique Pozniak played a recording of noise from Microsoft's Oakton Street data center at 10 p.m. and asked the village to study low frequency sound and its effect on people and wildlife. Johnson declined to pay outside consultants for noise or water studies, saying modern data centers recirculate deionized water in closed loops. Late that evening he and a reporter visited the Microsoft and T5 sites, and found the Microsoft noise comparable to a home air conditioner. Johnson's answer was the alternative: Nexstar first wanted to sell the land to a trucking and logistics operator, and he said he steered it toward a data center to keep up to 850 trucks a day out of the neighborhood.

ft-1769465345105-8259.text: New York City-based Western Hospitality Partners wanted to buy about 320 acres of Pekin's 1,000-acre Lutticken Farm, between Illinois Route 98 and Sheridan Road in Tazewell County, Illinois, to build a data center, offering $4.5 million, about $14,000 an acre. By May 2026 the deal was dead: Western Hospitality Partners sent the city a letter dated May 5, 2026 terminating the agreement and asking for its $85,000 deposit back. "It's a clean break. This contract is over. It's terminated. It's done," city attorney Jim Vasselli told the council on May 12. Opposition built quickly in January 2026, when residents delivered nearly 2,000 petition signatures to the council, and the Tazewell County Data Center Opposition group passed 2,200 members on Facebook. In February, council member Dave Nutter said he would vote no after hours of public comment: "It is not the right fit for Pekin, Illinois." On March 9, 2026, Mayor Mary Burress announced the city would not pursue the project, saying, "When a project creates this level of uncertainty and division, it's important to step back and carefully consider whether moving forward is truly the right path." The city had bought the whole farm for $14 million in 2025, and officials had said the data center would bring about $20 million a year in property taxes and more than 100 full-time jobs. With the deal off, the city is looking for other developers for the farm, and still owes the first payment, due in May, on the $12.5 million loan it took out from Morton Community Bank to buy the land. "We did hear your voice, please don't think that we did not," Burress told residents. Tazewell County has since stopped accepting data center petitions while it drafts a zoning ordinance; the county board passed a resolution, not a moratorium, in early May 2026 barring new petitions until the ordinance is finished. "You can't replace it," land use committee chairman Russ Crawford said of the Mahomet Aquifer, a concern the ordinance is meant to address.

ft-1770097908572-5270.text: Miami-based Hut 8 Corp. wants to build Logan Prairie, a $5 billion, 500 megawatt data center on farmland in Laenna Township near Latham, an unincorporated community in Logan County, Illinois. About 250 people packed a hearing at the Logan County courthouse in Lincoln on January 5, 2026, and most who spoke were against it. The Logan County Board has the final say on the zoning Hut 8 needs, and as of late September 2026 it had not voted. Sebastian Scassiferro, of Mount Pulaski, told the hearing: "I see farm land turning into asphalt, and I don't like it." Other residents raised concerns about electricity rates, power disruptions, noise, light pollution and the loss of farmland. Rachel Smith, who lives near Latham, said she was glad county officials had slowed the process: "I'm glad to see it looks like there will be a little more transparency." The county board passed a 60-day moratorium on data center applications on February 24, 2026, then a full 12-month moratorium on May 19. After Hut 8 emailed county officials on June 16 threatening legal action, State's Attorney Bradley Hauge told the board on June 18 that the May moratorium was invalid because it had skipped a required advisory vote and public hearings. The county's zoning office deemed Hut 8's applications complete on June 29. Hut 8 also tried annexing the site into the village of Latham, which would let it bypass the county board. Village President Theodore Allen said in July that trustees would vote down the plan, and Hut 8 agreed to focus on winning approval at the county level instead, though the company's attorney said on July 28 that the application had not been withdrawn. Village Trustee Ryan Virden, who opposed the annexation, said: "People move out to the rural areas for peace and quiet." At the county level, officials found technical errors in Hut 8's zoning applications, which Hut 8 disputes, and canceled votes that had been scheduled for August. County Zoning Officer Allan Green said Hut 8 could correct and resubmit its applications for consideration in September 2026 at the earliest; no county vote has taken place since. Hut 8 has promised Latham, a village with annual revenue of $291,000, between $8 million and $11 million a year for 15 years if the project goes forward.

ft-1769227209572-8586.text: Cloud Centers LLC wanted to build a 256,000-square-foot, 50-megawatt data center on the former Lockformer site at 711 Ogden Avenue in Lisle, DuPage County, Illinois, but withdrew its application on March 11, 2026. The site sits across the street from a subdivision and carries a history of contamination lawsuits from the old Lockformer metal fabricating plant, which residents linked to cancers and deaths in the early 2000s. At a January 21, 2026 hearing that had to be postponed once for the size of the crowd, Mayor Mary Jo Mullen said the site's history "weighs on residents," and a Change.org petition with more than 1,900 signatures raised the 20 backup generators and 40 air chillers the plan called for. After the withdrawal, a village spokesperson said officials "continue to explore additional opportunities for future redevelopment of the site." Lisle then moved to remove data centers as a permitted use in its I-1 industrial district, a change village documents said would effectively bar new ones unless the zoning code is amended for a specific project. At a May 20, 2026 hearing on the change, several residents spoke in favor and no one against, and the planning commission recommended it unanimously. Village trustees were scheduled to vote on the amendment on June 1, 2026; no result has been published since.

ft-246.text: Naperville's city council rejected the Karis Critical data center proposed for 1960 Lucent Lane on January 20, 2026, ending months of debate. The DuPage County council voted 6 to 1 against a conditional use permit: Mary Gibson, Ian Holzhauer, Supna Jain, Patrick Kelly, Ashfaq Syed and Benny White voted no, Josh McBroom voted yes, and Mayor Scott Wehrli and Nate Wilson abstained. The 40.87 acre parcel holds the former Nokia/Alcatel-Lucent building. Karis first proposed two buildings with 72 megawatts of power in September 2025; the planning and zoning commission approved a 36 megawatt version in November, and by the council vote the company had cut it to 24 megawatts in one building. The commission had voted 8 to 1 for a 211,000 square foot building, with Commissioner Naumes the only no, and Karis spokesperson Patrick Skarr pointed to a "$250 million" investment. Karis also offered to cut the diesel generators from 24 to 12, running them only during power cuts and for monthly tests. Greg Strom of Karis said: "We have no interest in building and developing a facility that causes trouble within the community." A petition against the plan had more than 3,700 signatures by November 20, 2025, and more than two dozen local doctors spoke against it at the November 5 hearing. By the time it reached the council more than 5,000 residents had signed, citing more than 200 homes, nature preserves and three playgrounds within walking distance. Rich Janor said: "We're not opposed to data centers. We're pro-business. We like AI, but we don't want it so close to homes." Organizers of an older petition against housing near the Herrick Lake and Danada forest preserves turned it on the data center, calling supporters to a December 16, 2025 council meeting for a 30 minute presentation against the plan. More than 40 people spoke at the final meeting; oncologist Sujay Shah warned: "Diesel exhaust is a known carcinogen; that is not debatable." Anthony Giunti, for electrical workers, spoke for the construction jobs, while Hiba Suleman put the residents' case plainly: "mitigation is not elimination." Kelly said locating the data center "this close to four and soon to be five neighborhoods" would harm public health, safety and welfare. Jain objected to design changes that had not gone through the planning commission: "When does it end, then? It could continually be changed, and when are we really able to make a decisive vote on it?" Wehrli moved to put the vote off to February 17, and that failed 3 to 6. Karis said afterward: "We are disappointed by the outcome of the vote, which overturned the city plan commission's recommendation." The DuPage County Building Trades said "six officials took years of high-paying, high-skilled work away from the men and women of the trades." City attorney Michael DiSanto said Karis "retains the opportunity to resubmit a revised proposal for a data center development," with changes or at another location.

ft-1782187388649-2944.text: Karis Critical, the developer whose Lucent Lane data center plan Naperville's City Council rejected in January 2026, is exploring the purchase of the 168-acre former BP campus at 150 W. Warrenville Road for a data center and an advanced manufacturing hub. "We have no pending proposal for the 168-acre campus," Karis spokesperson Patrick Skarr said in June 2026. "We've made no decision about whether to pursue an investment in the corridor or not"; the company does not own the land. According to a May 29 city memo obtained by the Naperville Sun, Mayor Scott Wehrli, City Manager Doug Krieger and representatives of the Naperville Development Partnership and JLL, which is listing the property, were briefed on Karis' concept in May. Skarr described a stand-alone data center of 100,000 to 125,000 square feet and, at full buildout, about 1.5 million square feet of advanced manufacturing space that he said could bring 1,000 to 1,500 jobs. The site, contaminated from prior use by the U.S. Army and BP Amoco, has buildings that would need to be demolished. "We were bullish on the potential opportunity for some advanced manufacturing to basically be the identified use for the site," Wehrli said, adding that the data center part was viewed less favorably because of community sentiment from the Lucent Lane fight: "Anything that gets promoted in that space is going to bear a high degree of attention." That fight is why the city is wary: the City Council voted 6-1 in January 2026 against a Karis data center on the former Alcatel-Lucent site at 1960 Lucent Lane after residents packed hearings over diesel generators and health concerns. Skarr said "everything is on the table from our perspective" for the BP site and that the company was weighing the city's feedback. Karis is active elsewhere in the Chicago area: in Hoffman Estates, the company withdrew a separate rezoning request for a data center on July 1, 2026 after residents and the Plan Commission pushed back, and it is also developing a data center in DeKalb. The former BP campus has sat vacant for eight years, and only three developers contacted the city about it in the past year, none of which submitted plans. Nothing has been filed for the BP campus. Any data center proposal Karis brings would go first to the Planning and Zoning Commission, then to the City Council for a final vote, as happened with the Lucent Lane plan.
