ft-1781206965427-5855.text: The shuttered AMC Pekin 14 cinema at 1124 Edgewater Drive in North Pekin, in Tazewell County, Illinois, was sold in December 2025 to North 52 LLC, and by June 2026 a rumor on Facebook had it becoming a data center. North 52's owner, Jeff Agan, said no data center was planned; what he wanted was to rezone the building from retail to light industrial so that it could be sold. Tazewell County property records show the Indiana company paid $575,000 for the 44,556 square foot building, and Agan said he was thinking of turning it into warehouse units of 5,000 to 7,000 square feet. "It's very tough to generate a second-generation user on a theater," he said. The theater sits around the corner from the Lutticken property in Pekin, which was planned as a data center until Pekin officials paused it. Western Hospitality Partners had withdrawn that proposal a month earlier, and the Central Illinois Data Center Opposition Group urged residents to go to the North Pekin Village Board and ask for no zoning change without an independent community impact study. On Monday 8 June 2026 residents in "NO Data Center" t-shirts filled a room where usually only a small group attends. "There is no plan to discuss any future data centers in any meetings," Village President Steve Flowers told them. "We don't have the area nor the infrastructure to accommodate such a facility." "It won't be a data center, because if it is, I would just be finding out the news," Agan told 25News. "But, no, we have no intention and no connection with anyone operating a data center." Dave Milam, who had been due to live next to the Pekin project, told the board: "Please be diligent this is what they prey on." The village attorney, William Anderson, said he would not advise a blanket rezoning without knowing the exact use proposed for the property. The next night the North Pekin Planning and Zoning Commission voted 5 to 3 to table the rezoning after more than two dozen people spent almost two hours asking about traffic, barriers at the property line and, again and again, how to keep a data center out. "Can you write it in, whatever zoning you guys choose, can it be written in, that there is no data center, [that] no service center is to be on that property, no matter what zoning it is?" asked resident Kelly Sonderman. "We will not be considering a data center. That's not in the cards," Anderson said. In July the commission held off again and asked Agan for more information, and Flowers said Agan had offered to put a clause in the deed barring a data center. The village is also writing its first data center ordinance, which Flowers said would define a data center, limit size and set requirements for water and power, with the draft due at the Planning and Zoning Commission on 11 August 2026. "We do not have a data center ordinance [right now]. There is no recommendations or nothing that really clarifies what a data center is," Flowers said. Tazewell County is moving the same way: on 9 September 2026 its land use committee sent a nine month data center moratorium to the Zoning Board of Appeals for a hearing, on top of an April zoning amendment that already bars any use the code does not explicitly allow. "It's a moratorium without calling it a moratorium. And it's temporary," said Jackie Workman, who runs the county's community development department.

The reporting gives the address as 1124 Edgewater Drive, not the 1224 in our record. ft-1780879611564-2991.text: Eagle Rock Partners, a North Carolina company, gave up on August 12, 2026, on its $6 billion Meridian Technology Park, planned for farmland near Palmer in Christian County, Illinois, southwest of Taylorville. The project would have been a 1,000 to 1,100 megawatt data center on 475 acres, built over five to seven years. The company said it had lost its planned electricity supply and had never filed a formal zoning request. The power was to come from the Lincoln Land Energy Center, a gas plant near Pawnee that was permitted in 2022 but never built, whose entire output Eagle Rock had agreed to buy. County board chairman Bryan Sharp said the company told him a state law requiring gas plants to close or reach zero carbon emissions by 2045 made the plant too hard to finance. "Due to circumstances beyond our control, the delivery of the power infrastructure on which the project depended is no longer certain," Eagle Rock said. Palmer Mayor Mike McKinney told the county board months earlier that water is the village's biggest source of revenue. "I'm concerned if there's any damage to the water. That could put Palmer in jeopardy, closing doors, because that's our biggest revenue stream," McKinney said. About 400 people, almost all opposed, filled the Taylorville High School cafeteria on June 16 when Eagle Rock partner Ken Loeber made his first formal appearance before the county board. Resident Maureen Tarrant, who lives just over a mile from the site, said: "I love the place we live. I don't want it changed. It's a fairy tale, and I don't want it turned into a horror story." Sharp said the opposition was not the reason for the withdrawal: "I know they were very aware of it, but I don't think that had an effect on their decision." Christian County had temporarily restricted data center construction since August 2025, and in late August 2026 the board approved a one-year restriction on both data centers and carbon sequestration while it writes new ordinances. Sharp said he expects more proposals because "Christian County has the infrastructure and a willing seller."

The power was to come from the Lincoln Land Energy Center, a gas plant near Pawnee that was permitted in 2022 but never built, whose entire output Eagle Rock had agreed to buy.
County board chairman Bryan Sharp said the company told him a state law requiring gas plants to close or reach zero carbon emissions by 2045 made the plant too hard to finance.
"Due to circumstances beyond our control, the delivery of the power infrastructure on which the project depended is no longer certain," Eagle Rock said.
Palmer Mayor Mike McKinney told the county board months earlier that water is the village's biggest source of revenue.
"I'm concerned if there's any damage to the water. That could put Palmer in jeopardy, closing doors, because that's our biggest revenue stream," McKinney said.
About 400 people, almost all opposed, filled the Taylorville High School cafeteria on June 16 when Eagle Rock partner Ken Loeber made his first formal appearance before the county board.
Resident Maureen Tarrant, who lives just over a mile from the site, said: "I love the place we live. I don't want it changed. It's a fairy tale, and I don't want it turned into a horror story."
Sharp said the opposition was not the reason for the withdrawal: "I know they were very aware of it, but I don't think that had an effect on their decision."

Christian County had temporarily restricted data center construction since August 2025, and in late August 2026 the board approved a one-year restriction on both data centers and carbon sequestration while it writes new ordinances.
Sharp said he expects more proposals because "Christian County has the infrastructure and a willing seller."

ft-1782347277521-3270.text: The trash incinerator that closed in 2000 at 13400 South Kedzie Avenue in Robbins, in Cook County, Illinois, has drawn at least five parties interested in buying it for a data center this year, according to its owner, Paul Duggan. He is asking $25 million to $30 million for the 16 acre site on the Cal-Sag Canal. "The model we are looking at is three buildings on the property," Duggan said. "Or it could be one owner and three tenants or one owner and one tenant, like a Microsoft." Robbins has fought over this ground before. The incinerator was proposed in 1990 by Reading Energy of Philadelphia, which later sold its interest to Foster Wheeler, and the town was told it would receive as much as $2 million a year and up to 100 jobs. Residents of Robbins and of Beverly and Mount Greenwood on Chicago's far south side formed the South Cook County Environmental Action Coalition and spent years fighting the state's 1988 "retail rate" law, a subsidy worth about $20 million a year to the Robbins plant, until the legislature repealed it in 1996. "They said the state's going to pump about $20 million [per year] into it in return for 20 jobs and $2 million for Robbins," said Gloria Scott, who grew up in the town. The plant opened anyway in June 1997, and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency alleged it broke air pollution rules 779 times in the six months it ran that year. Built to burn more than 1,000 tons of trash a day, it closed in 2000 after its tax subsidies were removed, and around 2021 the site was earmarked for conversion to a natural gas and fertilizer plant. That plan, by Sustainable BioWorks, was for an anaerobic digester turning food waste into gas and fertilizer pellets, with 135 jobs and a training center for local residents. Mayor Darren Bryant has not ruled out a data center. "I know there are a lot of negative stories out there, but my job as mayor is to be innovative," he said. "Water, electricity, noise, pollution, and environmental all are concerns of mine too, but we are in the discovery phase. If we cannot solve those issues, it will never enter Robbins." Bryant said the village, as a home rule municipality, could offer its own tax incentives on top of credits from the Cal Sag enterprise zone, and that any project would need the zoning board and the full village board, possibly with town hall meetings first. The site has a natural gas line that could serve as a power source. Jason Sticha, who has lived in Robbins for four years, was not persuaded. "I am not against bringing business and jobs," he said. "But we need to live in reality. I have seen no positives from data centers."

ft-1784670808582-1700.text: White Rose Partners, a Dallas developer, wanted to annex 20 acres at 33W304 Kenyon Road, at the northwest corner of Kenyon Road and Illinois Route 25, into South Elgin in Kane County, Illinois, for a data center on farmland owned by former Kane County Board member Mike Kenyon. In August 2026 the South Elgin Village Board of Trustees unanimously rejected the annexation and a special use permit for the project, which the developer called Project Kilo, and the village paused all new data center proposals. The building would have covered 200,000 square feet, with 40 chillers on a rooftop platform and 20 emergency generators, and the developer had asked Commonwealth Edison for 48 megawatts of power, which its application said the Bartlett substation could supply. Kenyon, 81, a dairy farmer who represented the area on the county board as a Republican for 18 years, knew what was coming. "My wife is mad at me," he said. "I'm expecting people to be mad at me." Managing partner Jeff Eigenbrood said the building would use closed loop cooling filled once with less than half an Olympic pool of water, that "ongoing operational water usage will be less than that of two single-family homes in South Elgin," and that it would pay more than $1 million a year in property taxes. The company's project website put the noise at 30 to 35 decibels at the property line, about 600 construction jobs at peak, and noted the land now pays under $8,000 a year in property tax. Anthony Saccomanno, president of the nearby Prairie Pointe subdivision, started a petition that drew 4,800 signatures in under 48 hours. "We are sitting on a water table that is a community well, and they want to draw off of that," he said, pointing out that the village staff report put daily use at 247 to 342 gallons. The site is less than half a mile from South Elgin High School, Kenyon Woods Middle School and Clinton Elementary School, where Saccomanno has children at all three: "I'm not against data centers, and I'm not against AI, just not right next to us." By July 28 the change.org petition had 8,347 signatures and White Rose had launched a website, with Eigenbrood saying "there has been a lot of misinformation circulating online." When the concept plan reached the village board, trustees rejected both the annexation and the special use permit. "I'm voting no almost only because of the location," said Trustee Greg Lieser. "AI is here to stay. America needs to lead the AI industry, and we need data centers to do that." Wendy Man, a resident of 30 years, said "we should not have to choose between economic development and protecting public health." White Rose's senior development manager, Alejandro Fuentes, had said 60 percent of the site would be green space and the project would generate $7.8 million to $28 million in tax revenue for the village. Richard Williams, a Geneva attorney for the company, said it was evaluating its options, would neither confirm nor rule out suing the village, and complained the plan had not been judged on its merits.

ft-1770385806911-4545.text: Cloverleaf Infrastructure, a data center land developer based in Houston and Seattle, wants to build a 500 megawatt data center on farmland on the southwest side of Troy, in Madison County, Illinois, near the US 40 and Interstate 55-70 interchange. Troy has since capped any data center in the city at 30 megawatts and extended a moratorium on data centers to next March, and Mayor David Nonn says no council member supports the project. Jeff Lake, Cloverleaf's principal development manager, laid out the plan to 40 to 50 residents at a special planning commission meeting on January 8, 2026: "Our business model is to identify sites based on power; power is the king in this space." He said 500 megawatts would need 250 to 300 acres, with a first phase of six buildings on 165 acres and a full build of four buildings on 275 acres that would close part of Collinsville and Formosa roads and mostly surround Bethel Church. Lake promised 1,000 to 2,000 construction jobs, up to 200 permanent jobs paying at least $80,000 a year, closed loop cooling, completion in late 2028, and no nondisclosure agreements for public officials. Bobby Williams, chief executive of Southwestern Electric, said the local cooperative peaks at 118 megawatts, so the data center would be four times its size. "I can tell you, standing here today, if this data center comes in or it does not, electric rates aren't going to stabilize," he said. On January 20, more than 100 people packed the council chamber to hear 15 speakers, although data centers were not on the agenda, and Bethel Baptist Church sent a contingent. "Though it's still its beginnings, this is an existential crisis for us," said Nicholas Martin, head of school at Bethel Academy. "My son goes to daycare right across the street from where this is proposed," said Viktor Varnaitis. Hundreds more filled Triad High School on February 10, 2026, for a session Cloverleaf hosted. "We're not an industrial town. We're a small rural town. There is nowhere you can put this here that it won't impact somebody," said Derrick Ramert, of Troy Residents for Responsible Growth. Chuck Hopper asked: "Now, who's going to buy my house when they sit on that back porch and they're faced with this humming big building?" Lake said there was a process to widen buffers, add trees or otherwise reduce sound, and a large group of union members came in support of the jobs. Police were at that meeting because days earlier a 33-year-old Trenton man had been charged with intimidation, a felony, and electronic harassment, after charging documents said he used public Facebook pages to threaten to kill Troy officials or contractors over the project; he is presumed innocent. On February 10, Mayor Nonn and three aldermen met Cloverleaf and asked what it would commit toward a $50 million sewer plant, water plant upgrades, electric bills and property tax relief. "Once again, they did not have any answers," Nonn told the February 17 council meeting, adding: "I can tell you at this point that no council member is [and I'm not] in support of a data center in the City of Troy." The same day, Madison County Board chairman Chris Slusser said the two Troy sites were not compatible with data center development and proposed redeveloping the Route 3 corridor instead. The council adopted a six-month moratorium on March 16, 2026; building and zoning director Ann Byrd said city attorney Fred Keck "is able to defend six months." In June, the Times-Tribune reported there would be no hyperscale data centers in Troy, with data centers capped at 30 megawatts, and city engineer Tom Cissell laid out a three-step approval process for new industrial zoning, with two council readings and three chances for the public to speak. On September 10, the planning commission voted 5-0 to extend the moratorium until next March, so the city can see what the state legislature does after Illinois paused its data center incentives. The extension goes to the city council next.

ft-253.text: Provident Realty Advisors of Dallas withdrew its $1.3 billion data center proposal for the former Brassie Golf Course on Pearson Road in Chesterton, Porter County, Indiana, on June 10, 2024, after the Chesterton Town Council said it "could never support this project" at its proposed scale and location. Its request to annex the southernmost 27 acres of the golf course site was withdrawn too. Provident had proposed eight buildings of 150,000 square feet each and had expected to break ground in early 2026. The campus was to cover a 200-acre parcel, with a bank of backup generators for each building. Company representative George Gonzalez told the Chesterton Plan Commission it would not fence the whole site and would landscape the eastern boundary against noise, and he said the generators would have noise suppressors to hold sound to a maximum of 42 decibels. Neighbors organized fast. Sixty to 75 people gathered in Dogwood Park on Memorial Day to raise noise, air, water, energy, wetlands, wildlife, home values and the stress of the fight. "I don't think you wanted to be on the town council to make people want to move out of our town which countless citizens will do if this project moves forward," Dogwood Estates resident Jenny Hansen wrote to the council. "But wait, no one will buy our homes." The council held public forums and then wrote that if the proposal were to receive any serious consideration, "the number, size, and height of the buildings would need to be significantly reduced." Reaction to the withdrawal was mixed, with some residents relieved and others lamenting the lost tax dollars and worrying about what else might be pitched for the site. Porter County has kept pushing back since. In September 2025, QTS dropped plans for a $2 billion data center on 800 acres in Union Township near Wheeler High School after hundreds of residents turned out at a county meeting in Valparaiso, and Agincourt's plan for a data center in Valparaiso was rejected by the local authority that year. On August 10, 2026, the Valparaiso City Council unanimously adopted a data center moratorium that lasts until the city rewrites its zoning, which the planning director expects to take about 18 months to two years. Neighboring Portage created a new Technology Park zone and restricted data centers to it. The town council statement noted that no data center was on the agenda of either the Chesterton Plan Commission or the Town Council. The land has since drawn housing plans instead: in October 2025 a group led by Michael Herbers of PMM Chesterton LLC, an owner of the former golf course, pitched 632 homes for the site, while a rival group led by Mark Markovich of Mark I Construction proposed a golf course community with 61 single-family homes and 26 paired patio homes. Town spokesperson Kevin Nevers said the owner's proposal of more than 600 units was still in the early stages. Any new data center proposal for the golf course land would go to the Chesterton Plan Commission and Town Council, which set out in 2024 what a smaller plan would need to be considered at all.

ft-256.text: Karis Critical's proposed data center campus on 101st Avenue in Merrillville, Lake County, Indiana, has its zoning: the Merrillville Town Council voted 7-0 in September 2024 to allow a data center on the 180-acre site east of Deep River County Park. The campus could total nine buildings, each costing $100 million, and no timeline or end customer has been named. The town's Data Center Citizen Advisory Committee, nine residents plus town officials and development professionals, endorsed the proposal. Town council president Rick Bella said of the committee that "The preparation and thoughtful participation they brought to the discussion were invaluable." Plan commission member Brian Dering estimated about $1 million in annual property tax revenue for each building, and said the impact on town services would be small. Councilman Shawn Pettit called it "a low impact/high reward development." Power is the open question: Karis has been working to make sure it can get enough from NIPSCO, and the existing transmission lines can serve only the first two buildings, with more needed for all nine. It is one of three. Province Group of Newport Beach plans up to $500 million on a million square foot technology park near Colorado Street and Harms Road; Wylie Capital of Chicago plans 1.2 million square feet at Broadway, 93rd Avenue and Georgia Street for about $600 million and up to 200 jobs; and Karis Critical plans up to $900 million on 180 acres at 101st Avenue. A thousand housing units are being built at Liberty Estates for the workers. Bella said the three together were "a huge boon to the tax base of course once these buildings are totally finished and operational", and Stephen Muenstermann of the town's data center advisory board said the $2 billion of direct investment "could end up having an $8 billion economic impact." The town has since grown more cautious about new proposals: the Merrillville Town Council placed a one-year moratorium on new data center project approvals from June 1, 2026, through May 31, 2027, to give officials time to study impacts, after four separate developers approached the town. In July 2026 the council voted unanimously to extend the moratorium by six months, to January 1, 2028. Lake County has also limited where data centers can be zoned countywide since August 12, 2025. Karis Critical's zoning was already approved before either measure took effect, and no construction date has been announced.

ft-255.text: Wylie Capital, a Chicago real estate firm, wants to turn the Merrillville Commerce Center, at Broadway, 93rd Avenue and Georgia Street in Merrillville, Lake County, Indiana, into a data center campus of up to six buildings. The $600 million, 1.2 million square foot plan calls for buildings up to three stories, two of them in a first phase, and could employ up to 200 people. Merrillville's data center advisory committee gave it preliminary approval in November 2024, but on May 26, 2026 the town council voted to pause all data center projects instead. The council's moratorium, adopted unanimously on a motion from councilman Shawn Pettit, runs from June 1, 2026 to May 31, 2027 so the town can study what a data center would do to infrastructure, utilities, traffic, noise, tax revenue and neighborhoods. In July 2026 the council voted unanimously to extend the moratorium by six months, to January 1, 2028. Four developers, including Wylie Capital, Province Group and Karis Critical, had approached Merrillville with data center proposals, and one had advanced further than the others. Council President Rick Bella pointed to the neighboring city of Hobart, where officials have clashed with residents over a data center's environmental and traffic impacts, as a reason to wait and learn first. Residents split at the podium. Jennifer Gross handed out what she said were Harvard University studies on the effects of data centers and urged neighbors to "open their eyes" to the industry's impact on towns. An informal poll of a Merrillville Facebook group found 280 people against a data center, 11 for and eight undecided. Another resident said no one objected when factories and warehouses went up elsewhere in Lake County and argued the town should "rethink this and rethink about taking opportunity when opportunity comes knocking." The Northwest Indiana Forum held an information session for residents at the Dean and Barbara White Community Center on June 11, 2026, with expert speakers and question sessions. Pettit, who proposed the moratorium, said he favors the tax revenue a data center would bring but that the decision rests with residents: "If they don't want it, they don't want it... We just need to listen to residents." The moratorium now runs through January 1, 2028.

ft-258.text: On 20 January 2026 the Clinton County commissioners unanimously refused to rezone 715 acres of farmland north of Frankfort for a data center campus proposed by Logix Realty. Logix Realty is an affiliate of the developer Logistix, whose president, Doug Swain, had said the project would bring more than $10 billion of investment. Swain laid out the plan on 15 July 2025 to about 30 landowners and others in the Chamber of Commerce meeting room in the Iron Block Building: more than 700 acres north of the Conagra plant, up to 7 million square feet in several buildings, as much as 600 megawatts, and a buyer to be found among well capitalized firms such as Meta or Amazon, with everyone involved under a nondisclosure agreement. Asked about water, he said newer data centers use less and some are air cooled; asked about noise, he compared it to road traffic; asked where residents could see something similar, he said "you may have to at least go to Ohio". He put the jobs at half a job per megawatt, about 300, paying around $100,000 a year, and said of the tax effect: "we are studying that right now". The first application, filed by Logix Realty on 3 July 2025, asked Frankfort to rezone 833 acres from agriculture to general business and bring the land inside the city, and was due before the city plan commission on 23 July. Mayor Judith Sheets put out a statement on the "frustration, fear, and anger circulating throughout our community regarding the proposed data center project", and Logistix rescinded the request, saying it would go to the county instead. The county commissioners said at the time that they were "not for or against the proposal at this time" and needed more information. In early September 2025 Logistix brought the county area plan commission a smaller plan, the Logix I campus on 155 acres across the railroad from the Conagra plant, with about 170 jobs and $1 billion of investment. More than 100 people came, more than a dozen spoke about noise, light and water, and Kevin Myers, a plan commission member who is also a county commissioner, said: "There's too many unanswered questions that I don't feel like I could be in favor of anything but a negative recommendation." The board deadlocked and sent the request on with no recommendation, after member Jeff Chynoweth, the one vote against a negative recommendation, was booed for saying some people would say no to anything on that land. On 18 November 2025, before the commissioners voted, Logix withdrew it; the area plan director, Liz Stitzel, said a revised filing would follow and could grow to about 1,200 acres with a casting company involved. The new petition covered 714.55 acres in Washington and Union townships, named DataOne as the intended user, and described a three part campus: a data center, a precast concrete plant and a hydroponic "gigafarm". At the 6 January 2026 hearing supporters put the first investment at $10 billion to $12 billion, rising possibly to $50 billion, and neighbors raised aquifer depletion, noise and the loss of farmland. The developer agreed in principle to 14 binding commitments, among them a 65 decibel limit at the property line, closed loop water and a decommissioning plan backed by financial security, and Stitzel told the board: "Staff would strongly caution against any favorable recommendation without a full set of clear commitments." The commission voted to send a favorable recommendation. Two weeks later commissioners Bert Weaver, Kevin Myers and Jordan Brewer turned it down. Myers said: "Given what this has put our community through and given that the majority of our residents are against this project, I cannot support the rezone." Weaver said the project "could be a tremendous boost" but that he had grown "uncomfortable" with the negotiations, and Brewer said: "We want development, but we want to work with partners we trust on projects that are economically beneficial to the community as a whole." Weaver also objected that the developer had offered to pay for only half of the road in front of the entrance, which he called a red flag, and reportedly said it wanted to "nickel and dime" the county. The denial bars the same request for 12 months. Inside the city, the Frankfort Board of Zoning Appeals had granted Logix a variance for a data center on land east of Conagra on 23 April 2025. On 2 February 2026 Mayor Sheets set conditions for any DataOne proposal in the city industrial park, including public town halls and published economic and environmental impact studies, saying: "Our community deserves facts and not assumptions when evaluating a project of this magnitude." In September 2026 DataOne asked the city to approve a $7.5 billion "AI factory" on 115 acres of the Logix Innovation Campus, land already zoned for light industry, with an 800,000 square foot building and about 200 permanent jobs. Its chief executive, Charles-Antoine Beyney, promised closed loop cooling using about 22,000 gallons a day, on-site fuel cells and no diesel generators, and two new substations paid for by the company, and named the chief complaints at its Vineland, New Jersey campus as "Lack of communication, number one by far," followed by noise. At the company's open house on 21 September 2026, electrical engineer Kevin Thomas put the draw at 350 megawatts from the grid through IMPA plus 175 megawatts from Bloom Energy gas fuel cells. The city's financial adviser, Gary Smith of Reedy Financial Group, projected about $331 million for Frankfort through 2054, against a shortfall of $4.3 million to $4.5 million in 2030 from state tax changes that could otherwise cost about 40 city jobs. Deborah Pearson, a county council candidate from Center Township, said she was "adamantly opposed", and a masked protester outside called data centers "a cancer in the community". Sheets, who votes only to break a tie, said "This is not a perfect project," and "There is no perfect project." Council members are holding listening sessions at the Chamber of Commerce from 23 to 25 September. The council is expected to take up the proposal at a special meeting on 28 September 2026. Councilman Steve Beardsley said: "We want your voices to be heard and look forward to some fruitful conversations."

Its chief executive, Charles-Antoine Beyney, promised closed loop cooling using about 22,000 gallons a day, on-site fuel cells and no diesel generators, and two new substations paid for by the company, and named the chief complaints at its Vineland, New Jersey campus as "Lack of communication, number one by far," followed by noise.
At the company's open house on 21 September 2026, electrical engineer Kevin Thomas put the draw at 350 megawatts from the grid through IMPA plus 175 megawatts from Bloom Energy gas fuel cells.

The city's financial adviser, Gary Smith of Reedy Financial Group, projected about $331 million for Frankfort through 2054, against a shortfall of $4.3 million to $4.5 million in 2030 from state tax changes that could otherwise cost about 40 city jobs.
Deborah Pearson, a county council candidate from Center Township, said she was "adamantly opposed", and a masked protester outside called data centers "a cancer in the community".
Sheets, who votes only to break a tie, said "This is not a perfect project," and "There is no perfect project."
Council members are holding listening sessions at the Chamber of Commerce from 23 to 25 September.
The council is expected to take up the proposal at a special meeting on 28 September 2026.
Councilman Steve Beardsley said: "We want your voices to be heard and look forward to some fruitful conversations."

ft-260.text: Jumping Bison LLC plans a data center on a 550-acre site in Greensburg's Business Enterprise Park, in Decatur County, Indiana, across Interstate 74 from Honda's Indiana Auto Plant. Greensburg City Council approved a 10-year, 60 percent property tax abatement for the project by a 7-0 vote in December 2024. The company, described only as U.S.-based, plans two phases of construction at $400 million each, and it has not said how many jobs the project would create. The Coalition to Protect Decatur County Against AI Data Center started a Change.org petition in September 2025 that reads, "We deserve to have a vote in this and our voices should be heard." It had more than 950 signatures by the end of October 2025 and had grown to 2,595 by September 2026. Economic Development Corporation director Bryan Robbins told the council, "We're excited that the city council is supportive." No new decision, permit or hearing on the project has been reported since the December 2024 abatement vote; the petition's growing signature count is the clearest sign of how the project stands as of September 2026.

ft-263.text: Project Redline is the code name the Indiana Economic Development Corporation used on 25 June 2025 for a hyperscale data center in Hancock County, Indiana, whose owner it would not name. The unidentified end user pledged 50 jobs and $1 billion of investment by 2029, and the agency's business development committee approved a tax break it valued at $42 million over an initial 35 years. The break, created by the legislature in 2019, exempts a data center from sales tax on its servers and other equipment and from utility tax on the electricity that runs them, and can be renewed for three further five year periods with more investment. Redline was one of four approved that day, with Project Louie in Morgan County, Project Flo in Marion County and Project Maize in LaPorte County, $168 million in all. Agency spokeswoman Erin Sweitzer declined to name the companies and said it could not confirm whether the projects were ones already reported. The Hancock County project in the news in the months before had been proposed by Surge Development of Shelbyville, which withdrew its rezoning request in May 2025 after significant public opposition. That was a 775 acre MegaSite in Buck Creek Township, around 3400 West 500 North just east of the Indianapolis Regional Airport, and the only data center images in its filings were of Google facilities. Opposition centred on Tuttle Orchards next door, and Surge said it would focus "on working directly with the specific users who have expressed interest in the site." Surge's principal, Chris King, sits on the agency's board and recused himself before the data centers came up, so he did not vote on Redline. Data Center Dynamics wrote that Project Redline "likely refers" to the Surge site. Hancock County's commissioners answered by building a gate: on 16 June 2026 they passed an ordinance, unanimously and effective at once, limiting data centers to land zoned industrial general, creating a data center overlay district and giving themselves the final vote on any project. A developer must now write to the commissioners first, and they decide whether the project promotes public health, safety and welfare, fits the comprehensive plan and the character of the industrial general district, is the most desirable use of the land, conserves property values in the district and counts as responsible development. Only then does it reach a technical review, a plan commission public hearing and a final commissioners' vote. County planning director Kayla Brooks said the old definition had lumped data centers in with "communication service exchange" and made them a permitted use in several districts: "Before, they could just go to the Board of Zoning Appeals and get it approved without coming to (the commissioners)." Commissioner Gary McDaniel said afterwards that an overlay was chosen over a moratorium because a pause would tie the county's hands, and that two data center companies were looking at Hancock County without having approached the commissioners. A citizens committee on data center siting is to report to the plan commission by the end of 2026 with the development standards the ordinance does not yet carry.

ft-1778639294240-2778.text: The Lake County Council voted 6-0 on June 9, 2026, to rezone a 162-acre farm site near Hebron and Lowell in unincorporated Eagle Creek Township, Lake County, Indiana, for Sentinel Data Centers' proposed $5 billion data center, known as Project Shirley. The site lies on the south side of State Road 2, just east of Clay Street and nearly two miles east of Interstate 65. The New York-based company plans a 500-megawatt center of four buildings, in a township of about 1,700 people. Much of the argument has been about the utility: regulators approved a NIPSCO subsidiary, NIPSCO Generation LLC, that negotiates data center contracts confidentially and has funded new gas generation for Amazon projects. Opposition organized fast, with a Facebook group passing a thousand members within weeks, and after a February hearing Sentinel postponed the rezoning vote to May. "The reason I think people are so skeptical and have pushed back with such fervor is because they've been lied to so many times," said Randy Niemeyer, a Lake County councilmember who sits on the plan commission. In May the plan commission took the unusual step of sending the rezoning to the council with "no recommendation." Opponents packed the council meeting in Crown Point, but the vote passed before many in the standing-room audience realized it. Sentinel must still win a special exception and site development plan approval under the county's data center ordinance, which sets noise limits, setbacks and electricity and water rules, before it can build.

ft-265.text: Metrobloks, a Los Angeles data center developer, won final approval on May 4, 2026 from the Indianapolis City-County Council to build two data halls on a nearly 14-acre lot on Sherman Drive in the Martindale-Brightwood neighborhood of Indianapolis, in Marion County, Indiana. The Metropolitan Development Commission had approved the rezoning on April 1, 2026 after months of objections over noise, power, water, jobs and home values. The $500 million campus sits on a vacant lot that was once a drive-in theater. Several Martindale Brightwood residents and the Hoosier Environmental Council filed a petition on May 1, 2026 in Marion Superior Court for judicial review of the commission's decision, arguing it "failed to properly apply variance standards" and that Metrobloks had not done adequate studies of environmental impact, water use, utility use and traffic. "We feel as though we have been sidelined and that this has not been reviewed properly and that it may have been predetermined," said Cierra Johnson, president of neighborhood group One Voice Martindale Brightwood. No ruling on the petition has been published since it was filed. Metrobloks has pledged $2.5 million for affordable housing and infrastructure, rising toward $20 million depending on a tax abatement the company receives. It says the data halls will draw power from AES Indiana under contract rather than the residential grid, and will cool on a closed loop using about 19,000 gallons for the first building and about 47,500 for the second, which it argues is less water than the warehouses already allowed on the site under its industrial zoning.

ft-266.text: Lifeline Data Centers, a colocation company, runs its Indianapolis data center from the building it calls Eastgate, at 401 North Shadeland Avenue in Marion County. The company bought the 40 acre former Eastgate shopping center in May 2008 from JTL Capital of Dallas, and in 2011 the City-County Council voted 23 to 6 to lease 76,000 square feet of it for 25 years as a public safety complex, at $685,000 a year for the first ten years. Lifeline says the site is powered by a 4 megawatt solar farm at the facility, backed up by IPL's coal fired power fed from more than one substation, and offers security "anything from FISMA, to Top Secret". In 2016 it said it had 120,000 square feet across its Indianapolis sites, and its owners, Rich Banta and Alex Carroll, were then shielding a new $17.5 million data center in Fort Wayne against electromagnetic pulse. Lifeline also used to rent space in the downtown carrier hotel at 733 West Henry Street, and in July 2022 it told customers it would leave at the end of the year because the new owner, Netrality, was raising its rent by 300 percent; its other two Indiana data centers were at 401 North Shadeland Avenue and in Fort Wayne. Netrality answered that the lease had run "for over 15 years without any escalation in the rental rate" and in January 2023 bought Lifeline's colocation business there. Southwest of the corner of Washington Street and Shadeland Avenue, on a former Ford factory site near Irvington Community Elementary School, DC Blox has proposed a $2 billion data center campus. The Metropolitan Development Commission approved it on 15 July 2026, and on 14 August neighbors and Irvington Community Schools went to court for a judicial review. A month later, on 19 August 2026, the same commission voted 6 to 0 for a moratorium on new data centers in Indianapolis through 2027.

ft-1776266211604-5792.text: DC Blox, a data center developer from Georgia, won approval from the Indianapolis Metropolitan Development Commission on July 15, 2026 for a data center campus at 305 Fintail Drive in the Thunderbird Commerce Center, the old Ford plant site near Irvington on the east side of Indianapolis, in Marion County. The approved plan, worth $2 billion, is smaller than the one first filed: a one story, 70,000 square foot building due in two years and a two story, 250,000 square foot building in five. The Ford Visteon plant opened on the site in 1957, made car parts until 2007 and was demolished in 2017, and Lauth Group and Covington Group bought the land in 2021 for an industrial park. DC Blox filed in April 2026 for three buildings of 80,000, 140,000 and 190,000 square feet, and Bill Thomson, its vice president of marketing, described the cooling: "Rather than continuously pulling from utility water, we'll fill up our water system one time from the utility, and then we continue to recirculate the water within the system." The land is zoned heavy industrial but Indianapolis has no zoning class for data centers, so the company asked for a variance of use, which the Metropolitan Development Commission decides and the City-County Council cannot call down. At a Warren Township meeting on May 21, 2026 some residents held signs reading "Block DC Blox," and Julie Watson said "these meetings happen, and then regardless of how the residents feel, the data center goes in anyway." The company's David Armistead answered: "Not all data center companies are the same, and not all data centers are the same." On June 11, 2026 the commission's hearing examiner, Judy Weerts Hall, recommended approval. Residents shouted "Shame on you"; Dawn Briggs said "promises are not the same as proven facts, and assurances are not the same as enforceable commitments"; and Councilor Andy Nielsen cited his own survey in which 83 percent of respondents opposed the campus, while Councilor Michael-Paul Hart, whose district shares the site, held off. DC Blox then published 20 commitments: to pay all utility costs and enroll in AES's green power program, use closed loop cooling, draw no groundwater, test generators only outside school hours, and give at least $20,000 a year for five years to the Pennsy Trail. Mikey Hess, a lifelong east sider, said: "I just don't trust it at all." On July 9, 2026 the company cut the plan from three buildings to two, from 56 diesel generators to 31, and cut power demand from about 80 megawatts by 28 megawatts, to about 52 megawatts, moving the buildings toward the middle of the park, away from the trail and Irvington Community Elementary School. The school, with about 300 students, is 850 feet from the site according to a later lawsuit, and the approval conditions require vapor mitigation, a two foot soil barrier on open ground, and a sound study showing no more than 65 decibels at the campus edge. Rachel Maldonado, the charter network's chief executive, visited a DC Blox center in Atlanta and heard a generator from 700 feet away, and said: "We're only getting a snapshot." The city's moratorium on new data centers, passed by the development commission 6 to 0 on August 19, 2026 and running through 2027, does not reach this already-approved campus, and DC Blox is also pursuing tax abatements. The commission approved the campus 6 to 1 a week after the cuts. Heather Rodriguez, who chairs the Irvington Community Schools board, told it: "What they are really asking for, a permanent change to what this land may be used for, next to an elementary school, is a rezoning dressed up as a variance." On August 14, 2026 two neighbors, Irvington Community Schools and Eastside Community Action, filed for judicial review in Marion Superior Court 5 and asked for construction to be halted while it is heard. Megan Lapa, a plaintiff who lives near the site, said the objections raised on July 15 were "disregarded so pretty carelessly."

Residents shouted "Shame on you"; Dawn Briggs said "promises are not the same as proven facts, and assurances are not the same as enforceable commitments"; and Councilor Andy Nielsen cited his own survey in which 83 percent of respondents opposed the campus, while Councilor Michael-Paul Hart, whose district shares the site, held off.

Megan Lapa, a plaintiff who lives near the site, said the objections raised on July 15 were "disregarded so pretty carelessly."

ft-267.text: US Signal runs a data center it calls IN02 at 6325 Morenci Trail on the northwest side of Indianapolis, in Marion County. The company bought the single story, 9,600 square foot, 2 megawatt building in December 2023 as its second data center in Indianapolis. It had been the only site of Rack Bunker, a local colocation firm founded in 2019, and before that was used by the disaster recovery company BlueLock, which InterVision bought in 2018. US Signal said it bought the building and land from the previous ownership group, not Rack Bunker's business, and planned 300 cabinets once upgrades were done, with room on the several acres for up to 600 more as demand allowed. The upgrades were managed by Etzel Engineer and Build, ran more than six miles of new fibre out to over 500 enterprise locations, and added ten to twelve jobs. The building was cut open to visitors on 11 July 2024 and opened that August, with customers buying cabinet space before it did. Chief operating officer John White said the site was "another step in our five-year plan to build additional digital infrastructure in our Midwest footprint." US Signal, founded in 2001 with its own 9,500 mile fiber network, had itself been bought earlier that year by Igneo Infrastructure Partners. The company now lists the building as built in 1975 and updated in 1984, 2006, 2010 and 2024, with 2,500 kilowatts of generators, 1,600 kilowatts of UPS, a 2,500 kVA utility feed, 500 tons of cooling and six carriers on site. It pairs the building with IN01, its space in a downtown carrier hotel, for customers who want a second site in the same city. On 10 August 2026 the City-County Council voted 23 to 1 to stop new data centers in Indianapolis through the end of 2027 while it writes rules on sound levels and on plans for water and electrical capacity. Council President Maggie Lewis said the pause would give councilors time to fine-tune those rules, and the lone vote against came from Councilor Michael-Paul Hart, who said: "If we had development standards in place, you could always pick a more restrictive set of commitments."

ft-1763572480079-2104.text: Prologis's proposed data center near Leesburg in Kosciusko County, Indiana, was blocked when the county said no twice to rezoning more than 500 acres of farmland from agricultural to industrial for it. The land, on the north side of CR 700N west of CR 300W in Prairie and Jefferson townships, belongs to Tim Polk, Polk Family Farms and Murphy Place LLC, and adjoins a NIPSCO substation on a 20-acre tract. The Area Plan Commission recommended denial on April 2, 2025, with about 100 people in an overflow annex, more than 350 watching on YouTube, many in neon hats reading "No data center," and a petition against the project with more than a thousand signatures. "We're gonna lose over 500 acres of really good farmland and there's a lot of homes up there," said opponents Lisa Hay, Gary Parker and Craig Charlton, who said it would change life for the Amish farmers in the area. On April 22, 2025, the county commissioners upheld the recommendation 3-0 before 114 people in an old courtroom that holds 120. Commissioner Bob Conley gave three reasons: the citizens had spoken, the plan commission had spoken, and now the commissioners were speaking. Commissioner Sue Ann Mitchell said she supported data centers in logical locations, then added: "The rezoning of property should be denied because it is not a reasonable and prudent location for this type of development." Commissioner Cary Groninger, who had visited five data centers in Indiana and Illinois, said the problems with this location "have not been overcome by the petitioner." Attorney Steve Snyder put the petitioners' case on the land itself: "We have the convergence of three 345,000 watt transmission lines on these parcels, and that is what is essential to what is being proposed." He offered to limit the rezoned ground to a data center only, and said $10 billion would go into 10 buildings with 30 jobs each paying over $100,000. JC Witt, Prologis's data centers vice president, said the site was the least disruptive because it needs no new high-voltage lines, and that if refused, "it's not going in another location." "We're not against a data center. We're against a data center in this location," said attorney Jack Birch, for the objectors, who argued that power lines can be moved or extended. Courtney Van Cleave asked the commissioners for a one-year moratorium on data centers while they are researched, and afterward Chris Polk said the decision told Warsaw businesses that "Kosciusko County is closed for business." The commissioners' April 2025 denial is the latest reported decision; had the rezoning passed, the project would still have needed a special exception from the Board of Zoning Appeals.

ft-1779197186556-7045.text: The Ford family of Dupont wants to build a data center campus on 549 acres of the old airfield at the former Jefferson Proving Ground, outside Madison in Jefferson County, Indiana. The development plan filed with the county planning and zoning office in February 2026 shows nine buildings totaling 7,175,657 square feet, built in phases over three to four years, and the family says the campus would create about 300 full time jobs and pay about $60 million a year in property tax, more than double the county's $29,718,559 budget for this year. The company that would build and run the campus has not been disclosed; the Fords own the land and say they have asked for no tax abatements. Building inspector Josh Cline approved the application on February 25, 2026, judging it sufficiently similar to uses already permitted in the heavy industrial zone, such as chemical processing and hazardous storage; classed that way, the project needed no public notice. Neighbors appealed, and on May 20, 2026, the Board of Zoning Appeals unanimously denied the appeal after a hearing that ran more than five hours, finding the data center fits within the zoning. Attorney Laureen White, representing appellant Debra Jones, argued that "the proposed data center campus is not simply a warehouse, not simply a research facility, not simply an office, and not simply manufacturing." Resident Elijah Chandler of Madison asked at a County Council meeting, "Can they guarantee us no rate hikes in the county? How much water will they use?", while Jack Hartwell, who lives half a mile from the site, said, "The county needs this money. It needs roads, it needs bridges. It needs it for the schools." Dean Ford, who bought the land after the Army closed the proving ground on September 30, 1995, told the zoning board the company "will rebuild the roads, rebuild the sewer, rebuild the water, rebuild all electric inside JPG containment area," and the family says the buildings would use closed-loop cooling from the existing JPG water tower with no groundwater drawn. After the ruling, organizers said Daniel Ford had stayed away from a town hall citing death threats against his family, and Jill Koren of Jefferson County Concerned Citizens said, "I feel like the whole ethos of a data center of that scale is very counter to what we care about most here in Madison and Jefferson County." On September 1, 2026, the county Plan Commission voted 5 to 3 against starting work on a data center moratorium, even though 63 of 64 written submissions had asked for one. Commission president Warren Auxier said a pause would change nothing at the proving ground: "A moratorium would have no impact on the JPG data center because a development plan has already been submitted." With the zoning appeal denied and no moratorium in place, the development plan already has county approval and no further public hearing is scheduled; Chandler, an opponent of the project, is running for a County Council seat.

ft-272.text: The farmland at North 400 West and West 500 North, near McCordsville in Hancock County, Indiana, is where Surge Development wanted to build the Hancock County MegaSite, a data center campus. The Shelbyville developer pulled its petition to rezone 775 acres in Buck Creek Township on 13 May 2025, five days after a four-hour public information session, and before the plan commission could vote. The site ran across 24 parcels immediately east of Indianapolis Regional Airport, with Buck Creek along its western edge. The preliminary plan showed four buildings for IT systems surrounded by cooling equipment and electrical yards, three administrative buildings and several stormwater ponds, up to 75 feet tall, with the rest of the land held for future industrial uses. Citizens Energy Group was named to supply water, which project leaders said would not come from wells, although a Citizens spokesperson said the company did not yet serve the site. Surge's principal, Chris King, said no company had signed on as an end user. The land backed directly onto the pick-your-own fields of Tuttle Orchards, a fourth-generation family business, and some residents first heard of the plan on the evening of 15 April 2025, when the orchard's owners, the Roney family, posted a statement opposing it. At the session on 8 May at Greenfield-Central High School, Mike Roney asked officials "to seriously consider if this project brings such an overwhelming benefit to the community that it can constitute sacrificing a longstanding business in the community that cannot be replaced." Nearby resident George Langston said: "We don't have a lot of tourism at all here, and we cannot afford to lose Tuttle's." Not everyone was against it: Tom Redmond said his mother, nearly 90, had agreed to sell her land because it was "a cohesive plan", after turning down a solar developer years earlier. Erin Brier, a doula who buys the orchard's quiches and pot pies for the families she works with, said: "It feels like it would be two completely different worlds right next to each other." Luke Lomax of Mt. Comfort said a project of that size should bring its own resources: "They should have their own sustainable power grid. They should have their own water source." Gary Kingen, whose family has farmed beside the orchard since 1903, made about 50 "No Data Center" yard signs and worried about drainage: "It doesn't flow very good from 500 North all the way to 900 North." The Save Hancock County Facebook group grew from about 700 members in April to 1,700 by July, and its founder, Leah Lederman, who lost her own house to an earlier warehouse project that was never built, kept a motto: "If you think they're not listening, speak louder." In its withdrawal statement Surge said it would work with specific users so the community could judge individual projects "with specific details available", and called the MegaSite "a strategically important opportunity to advance the County's economic development and infrastructure goals." In late June 2025 Governor Mike Braun appointed King to the board of the Indiana Economic Development Corp. for a term ending 23 June 2029. In April 2026 the county plan commission voted 5 to 0 to set up a data center study committee, due to report by October, after residents asked the commissioners for a one-year pause. The county has also adopted a data center overlay district that requires Industrial General zoning and a multi-step public process in which the commissioners have the final say. The next proposal arrived in August 2026, nearby: EQT Real Estate filed a letter of intent for a 130 acre campus northwest of County Roads 500 North and 500 West, next to Walmart's IND3 distribution center, offering a one-time payment of $22.2 million and $22 million a year at full buildout.

ft-273.text: Province Group, a developer based in Newport Beach, California, proposed the Merrillville Technology Park in November 2024, a data center campus of four 250,000 square foot buildings near Colorado Street and Harms Road in Merrillville, in Lake County, Indiana, close to the Hobart line. By May 2026 the project presented for that same corner was Project WayPoint, put forward by PowerHouse, a subsidiary of the fund manager and developer AREP, still evaluating feasibility. The Merrillville Town Council put a one-year moratorium on approving any data center project on May 26, 2026, and extended it on July 14, 2026 to noon on January 1, 2028. Province put its original plan's investment at up to $500 million over five to seven years and said it was aiming to offer up to 400 megawatts of power, depending on a transmission study it had commissioned from NIPSCO. Province vice president Tim Ramm said: "It would be low intensity compared to other uses. It doesn't impact schools, parks, police fire, or emergency services." The Times of Northwest Indiana reported the campus would pay workers up to a projected $175,000 a year. At the May 2026 informational meeting attended by about 40 people, PowerHouse's team showed 10 buildings of about 330,000 square feet each, set 500 feet off Harms Road and 1,700 feet off Colorado Street, near the Polycon plant, the new fire station and a NIPSCO substation with three power lines dedicated to it. The developer's attorney, Richard Anderson, said NIPSCO had reported it could handle the load but was not guaranteeing it. Council president Rick Bella said that because the campus would be built on spec, it would not happen until the developer could name its customer. Councilman Shawn Pettit tied the project to the town budget and said he had asked the county election board about a November referendum: "We need to get on board with this, because if we don't, this council will have to implement an option income tax." Resident Jennifer Gross, who lives in the proposed area, answered: "I've lived here for 25 years, and every time some developer brings up a pie-in-the-sky project, we get burned." A week later, on May 26, 2026, the Town Council voted unanimously for the one-year moratorium, running from June 1, 2026 to May 31, 2027 at first. Pettit, described as the council's biggest data center supporter, said a conversation with an investor in Polycon had changed his mind: "If (residents) don't want it, they don't want it. It's that simple." Residents Jennifer Gross and Pablo Payan thanked the council for the pause; Bryon Mesarch said he was disappointed. On July 14, 2026 the council voted unanimously to extend the moratorium by six months, to noon on January 1, 2028, when a new council takes office. Pettit told the meeting: "A couple months back, we had a lot of controversy about data centers, and when I made the motion (to put a moratorium on them), I made it for one year. I would like to extend that."

ft-274.text: Google is building a data center, Project Maize, in Michigan City, Indiana, on the 67-acre former ANCO windshield wiper factory site at 402 Royal Rd, in LaPorte County, after the Common Council approved the project in September 2025. Google confirmed on April 16, 2026 that it had taken over the site, which had stood empty for more than fifteen years after Federal Mogul left it. Broderick Green, Google's data center public affairs manager, said the company would cover all power and infrastructure costs: "We don't just build data centers; we become part of the community." Google was not the first developer here. Phoenix Michigan City Industrial Investors LLC, which bought the site for about $1.25 million in late 2022, had offered an earlier $832 million project with 30 jobs by 2034 against $42 million in tax abatements spread over 35 years. Mayor Angie Nelson Deuitch turned that offer down on July 14, 2025, after negotiations broke down over the abatement terms: "Any major project of this magnitude must bring tangible value and benefits to Michigan City residents," she said, calling the job creation limited and the tax impact unproven. Because the land is already zoned light industrial, Phoenix could build without the city's approval and without the incentives, and the Common Council approved the company's plans that September. As construction neared, the argument shifted to who was doing the building. Operating Engineers Local 150 picketed over the use of out-of-state contractors, saying the public tax incentives made the hiring a public matter. The developer's attorneys sent strikers a cease and desist letter on October 17, 2025, and on October 29 two Local 150 members who would not move their truck were arrested for criminal trespass, police chief Steve Forker said. At a news conference on November 4, Mayor Deuitch called the picket a stunt: "This is unacceptable, and we won't be bullied. Michigan City will not be bullied." David A. Fagan, Local 150's financial secretary and a member of the Indiana Economic Development Corporation board, said the union wanted "solid participation in the project" rather than "a small part of the work", and that a public right of way had been treated as private land. Deuitch, who had turned down the abatement the previous July, welcomed Google's arrival as a community partner and said the city was "spotlighting Michigan City as a hub for digital infrastructure."

ft-279.text: A petition to rezone about 1,057 acres of farmland northeast of New Carlisle, in St. Joseph County, Indiana, for a data center was denied 7 to 2 by the St. Joseph County Council on December 10, 2025, after a meeting that ran ten hours and ended after four in the morning. The land belongs to Mall-O-Manor LLC and Randall, Betty and Scott Szczypiorski; the prospective buyer, put by DCD at $13 billion for the project, listed an address on Broad Street in New York and was not otherwise named in county records. A conceptual plan called for fourteen buildings, each about the size of Notre Dame Stadium. Nearly four dozen people spoke, three minutes each, most against it on environmental grounds; public comment ran from around 11:30 p.m. to just after 3 a.m. "[The turnout] had an influence on the vote tonight," resident Dan Caruso said afterward. Only two council members backed the rezoning, Democrats Diana Hess and Mark Catanzarite; no Republican did, although county Republican chair Jackie Horvath and Republican commissioners' president Carl Baxmeyer had endorsed it. Republican council member Amy Drake said she was with the people of New Carlisle and that the opposition was overwhelming. Council member Joe Thomas pointed to the Amazon data center already being built nearby: "So, let's just wait until we see that the dust settles, and see what happens." The case for the project rested on property tax revenue to offset state funding cuts, and was pressed with television advertising, door-to-door canvassing and targeted messaging. The refusal was the third against a data center rezoning in the area: the county's Area Plan Commission and a county council committee had each recommended against this project, and in October 2025 the New Carlisle town council had filed a resolution opposing it after unanimous opposition from its own plan commission, with residents citing water and electricity use and the loss of farmland. Tom Miles, who runs a business near the Amazon campus, said his worry was traffic: "All I could think of was the 300 residents down at Hamilton Grove ... a cement truck hits her, and pow, dead." South Bend Mayor James Mueller warned of the county's finances: "There's going to be a 4 a.m. conversation in a couple years when we don't have the money, and this council's going to have to choose, do you raise income taxes? Do you close fire stations?" Drake said that before the vote, people claiming to be from child protective services had come to her home, a false report she said was made against her family. Mueller said in December 2025 that the developer could bring the proposal back to the council within six months; no new rezoning petition has been reported since.

ft-1767729868771-4781.text: RadiusDC, a data center company launched by IPI Partners in 2022, plans two buildings of 100,835 square feet each on 31 acres at the southeast corner of Smith Road and AllPoints Parkway in Plainfield, Hendricks County, Indiana. The Plainfield Plan Commission unanimously approved the primary plat on January 5, 2026, after more than a dozen residents spoke against it. The developer calls the two buildings AllPoints 18 and 19 and describes them as edge data centers, with precast structures, a preserved corridor along Clark's Creek between the sites, and closed-loop cooling it says will use minimal water. The land was zoned for office and warehouse uses, and power is to come from a new substation under development next to the property. A week after the vote, the company announced the campus as a 24 megawatt colocation site, starting with a first building named Indy I on the same design as its Nashville facility, with space for a matching Indy II. Long-time Hendricks County resident Madeline Garcia told the commission, "Biggest concerns for me are the data center usage of electricity, taxpayers subsidizing that, the tax breaks that we already have in the state code and water usage." She added, "There's very little that I expect to see as a Plainfield citizen to come back in a benefit to me in the coming years, and I'm very concerned about that." A Change.org petition started by Michelle Rollings and addressed to town council members Robin Brandgard, Lance Angle, Dan Bridget and Tom Kingseed says the main worry is "the immense water and electricity this facility would consume, potentially driving our bills up to unsustainable levels." It had 43 signatures after less than a day online, according to Data Center Dynamics. In a statement, the town said all proposed data centers go through the same multi-step review as other major developments, and that "the Town of Plainfield does not support development that places an undue burden on public infrastructure or water utilities." The plan commission's vote was the final decision: the project will not go before the town council, because the land was already zoned industrial and only zoning changes, not permitted uses, require council review. The town says Radius DC expects to use about 700 gallons of water a day, and that Duke Energy sent a formal "Will Serve" letter confirming it has enough electrical capacity without hurting existing customers. The Board of Zoning Appeals has since granted Radius DC variances for both buildings to allow outdoor storage and operations beyond the 10% limit set in the office and warehouse district. RadiusDC also has sites in Denver, Miami, Nashville and Atlanta; IPI Partners, which launched the company, was acquired by Blue Owl.

The developer calls the two buildings AllPoints 18 and 19 and describes them as edge data centers, with precast structures, a preserved corridor along Clark's Creek between the sites, and closed-loop cooling it says will use minimal water.
The land was zoned for office and warehouse uses, and power is to come from a new substation under development next to the property.

A week after the vote, the company announced the campus as a 24 megawatt colocation site, starting with a first building named Indy I on the same design as its Nashville facility, with space for a matching Indy II.

Long-time Hendricks County resident Madeline Garcia told the commission, "Biggest concerns for me are the data center usage of electricity, taxpayers subsidizing that, the tax breaks that we already have in the state code and water usage."
She added, "There's very little that I expect to see as a Plainfield citizen to come back in a benefit to me in the coming years, and I'm very concerned about that."

A Change.org petition started by Michelle Rollings and addressed to town council members Robin Brandgard, Lance Angle, Dan Bridget and Tom Kingseed says the main worry is "the immense water and electricity this facility would consume, potentially driving our bills up to unsustainable levels."
It had 43 signatures after less than a day online, according to Data Center Dynamics.

In a statement, the town said all proposed data centers go through the same multi-step review as other major developments, and that "the Town of Plainfield does not support development that places an undue burden on public infrastructure or water utilities."

The plan commission's vote was the final decision: the project will not go before the town council, because the land was already zoned industrial and only zoning changes, not permitted uses, require council review.

The town says Radius DC expects to use about 700 gallons of water a day, and that Duke Energy sent a formal "Will Serve" letter confirming it has enough electrical capacity without hurting existing customers.
The Board of Zoning Appeals has since granted Radius DC variances for both buildings to allow outdoor storage and operations beyond the 10% limit set in the office and warehouse district.
RadiusDC also has sites in Denver, Miami, Nashville and Atlanta; IPI Partners, which launched the company, was acquired by Blue Owl.

ft-281.text: In July 2024, Provident Realty Advisors, the Texas developer whose plan for a data center in nearby Chesterton had just collapsed, asked Burns Harbor to rezone about 100 acres of Worthington Steel property for a data center campus. The site's mailing address lists Porter, but the project went before the Burns Harbor Plan Commission and Town Council, not the town of Porter. Provident withdrew the proposal on October 7, 2024, and it remains withdrawn. The plan called for up to seven buildings on 102 acres at the corner of Babcock and Haglund roads, on land zoned residential, and was first introduced to the Plan Commission on July 8, 2024. Provident gave no investment figure, and its representative Nick Farris said: "It is our company policy not to comment on sites in the land use process." Town Council president Jennifer McHargue said: "This is the first developer that has shown interest in that property in a decade." Annette Hansen, executive director of the Izaak Walton League's Porter County chapter, who lives about a mile from the site, wanted to know how much water it would use, whether refrigerant would be added to cooling water, and whether diesel generators would run during power cuts. Chapter president Gary Brown said: "Provident people aren't totally stupid. They've got to know there's a reason why Chesterton didn't do it." Ed Orlando, who fought the Chesterton plan before moving to Burns Harbor, asked how many local people it would employ and said: "Before we sign off on these things, we've got to understand them." More than 100 people came to the Plan Commission on August 5, 2024, and 20 spoke against the plan, questioning what the town would gain and raising fire risk. The buildings could have reached 120 feet; commissioners floated a 60 foot limit, and Provident spokesman Todd Leeth said such a limit would kill the project. The commission continued the rezoning request, to a new S8 Technology District classification, to September 9. Provident withdrew the proposal on October 7, 2024 but said it would return with changes that would "respond to concerns that have been brought to light in public meetings." Objections had centered on the 120 foot height, setbacks of only 50 feet, noise, and the effect on the nearby Indiana Dunes National Park. The firm became eligible to refile after January 10, 2025, but by February Plan Commission president Jeremy McHargue, who is also the town's police chief, said: "We haven't had any communication." Any new proposal would have to start the process over.

ft-1767730502747-3818.text: Prologis, the California-based industrial real estate company, wants to build a data center campus of up to 13 buildings on 576 acres in Shelbyville, in Shelby County, Indiana, about 30 miles southeast of Indianapolis. The land lies east of the State Road 44 and Interstate 74 interchange, and 429 acres of it needed to be annexed into the city and rezoned from agricultural to industrial. Two Duke Energy transmission lines already cross the property, built for a manufacturing plant on a neighbouring site that never came to fruition; no tenant or power figure has been disclosed. The Shelbyville Common Council approved the plan on Monday, April 6, 2026, with a crowd of objectors in the room. By 4-2, with one member abstaining over a conflict of interest, it approved an economic development agreement giving Prologis a 30-year, 100 percent personal property tax abatement and a 10-year, 50 percent abatement on real property. In return the company must spend at least $2 billion and create 25 jobs for every data center building; it says the finished 11-building campus would employ 450 people full time at an average salary of $100,000. The city said construction would still need separate applications, permits and regulatory approvals. Connie Lindsay, a Shelbyville resident of more than 30 years and a real estate agent, started a petition against the annexation that has passed 7,500 signatures. "The environmental issues, health and safety issues, we're losing valuable farm ground," Lindsay told WRTV. A lawsuit over the annexation and rezoning went the city's way on July 29, 2026, when Shelby Superior Court No. 2 Judge David Riggins ruled for Shelbyville in a 15-page order. The mayor made things worse. A video that went viral on June 3, seemingly filmed without his knowledge, showed Mayor Scott Furgeson holding a "No Data Centers" sign and saying: "I've seen a lot of these all over the town, but I only see them in sh***y houses." "It doesn't matter if they're rentals or not, they're still human beings," a woman at the table told him. His first statement said only that he "regrets that his choice of words may have caused offense"; two weeks later, in a video, he called his remarks "disrespectful," "hurtful" and "wrong." "I take full responsibility for what I said," Furgeson said. "I sincerely apologize to all of you."

ft-1763577844897-4160.text: Agincourt Investments' plan for a data center campus in Valparaiso, Porter County, Indiana, collapsed within days of residents packing a city council meeting to oppose it, and the project is cancelled. The developer had an option, signed in January 2025, to buy 180 acres of city-owned farmland east of Indiana 49 for four two-story buildings of 157,000 square feet each. More than 500 residents filled Valparaiso's City Hall on March 10, 2025, and the council heard more than 90 minutes of opposition even though the data center was not on the agenda. "I don't like this deal. It stinks," said Greg Kuehl, who described himself as the largest landowner next to the site. The next day, Mayor Jon Costas said Agincourt had agreed to withdraw its option: "Our citizens have spoken decisively that they believe this is a project that is not in the best interests of the city." City attorney Patrick Lyp said Valparaiso would not have to repay the federal pandemic relief money it had used to buy the 248-acre tract for an earlier, abandoned sports complex. Development director George Douglas had said on March 3, 2025, that the city had "no design and no site plan," and Valparaiso University political scientist Jennifer Hora called the handling "not transparency." In July 2026 the Valparaiso council voted 6 to 1 on first reading to strip the two-year end date from a proposed data center moratorium and sent it to the Plan Commission for a hearing. Councilman Peter Anderson cast the lone no vote: "The whole idea behind a moratorium is that it's temporary. It requires an end date." The measure now awaits a Plan Commission hearing before it can return to the council for a final vote.
