ft-1783829909593-7384.text: Blue Ladder is planning a data center campus, called Project Wolcott, on 322 acres near U.S. Highway 24 at Wolcott, in White County, Indiana, with four data halls of about 327,600 square feet each, a 50,000-square-foot office and a 100,000-square-foot warehouse. The company's own project website says the buildings would sit at least 797 feet from the highway, and it does not give a megawatt figure or say who would operate the site. On water, the website is specific: closed-loop and dry-cooled, no water for cooling and no wells, with water used only by the people who work there; on power, it says the project will pay for its own electrical infrastructure without saying where the power comes from. It promises about 1,000 construction jobs, hundreds of permanent ones with local hiring given priority, tens of millions of dollars a year in property tax once built out in 2029 or 2030, and noise under 50 decibels. The White County plan commission backed rezoning about 287 acres at Mid-America Commerce Park west of Wolcott by a 6-4 vote on August 12, 2025, after officials had signed non-disclosure agreements with developers and met behind closed doors three times since mid-June. County council member Joanne Mosher asked why a legitimate business would need to hide its arrival, and residents on the county's water-short western edge wanted the rezoning held until a water table study was finished; commissioner Mike Smolek answered that the rezoning was procedural, not a project approval. In August 2025 Wolcott residents Bart and Amy Snyder sued the county commissioners and the redevelopment commission to overturn the rezoning of about 184 acres near U.S. 24 and County Road 1100 West, saying the applications skipped the notarized authorization and site plan the county requires. A hearing on summary judgment in the Snyders' lawsuit was set for July 27, 2026; that hearing was scheduled for that date, and no result has been published. Blue Ladder and county officials held a community open house at the Best Western in Monticello on June 29, 2026, which county economic development president Randy Strasser confirmed.

ft-1768319342629-2737.text: Project Pilot is Beale Infrastructure's data center campus at the northwest corner of 103rd Street and Edgerton Road in De Soto, Johnson County, Kansas, just south of Kansas Highway 10 and west of the Panasonic plant. Construction began in April 2026, and by then the plan had grown: what the city council was shown in August 2025 as four buildings totaling 1.14 million square feet is now four buildings totaling nearly 2.9 million square feet. Pilot KC Holdings LLC, another company tied to Beale, bought the land in September 2025, according to property filings reported by the Kansas City Business Journal. Beale, backed by the asset manager Blue Owl, announced the first phase at the end of April 2026, with Evergy supplying the power and a large technology company signed as tenant on a long-term lease. City planners approved the site plan that week, on condition Beale bring a new landscaping plan to the planning commission before it gets an occupancy permit. The first phase is a 300,000 square foot building and an 863,000 square foot building, due for completion in 2028; the second phase adds two more buildings of 864,000 square feet each, with no timeline given. The growth in size is what residents object to. "They (Beale) are proposing a facility larger than what was originally presented," Toni Caldwell told the city council on May 7, 2026, calling it "a breach of understanding that they created with this community." A Beale spokesperson said the August 2025 designs were "preliminary and subject to change, and not part of the formal application," which the planning commission approved in April and May. City administrator Mike Brungardt told KSHB 41 the binding agreement approved in August 2025 "does not limit building size," and that because the project fit existing zoning, the change did not have to go back to the full council. Rob Daniels, the former council member who made the motion to approve it, said the franchise fee cap the council negotiated "didn't necessarily account for them using potentially two and a half times the power." Michelle Kauk, Beale's director of public policy, said the air-cooled, closed-loop cooling design chosen for the site is what increased the square footage. Beale held an open house at De Soto High School on June 18, 2026, and more than 150 people came. Tony Burkart, Beale's senior vice president for public policy, said water came up often, and that daily use at the site would be akin to a restaurant's. The city's project page puts the first phase at about 15,000 to 20,000 gallons a day, roughly two or three sit-down restaurants, and says the cooling system is filled once rather than drawing water continuously. Sara VanDeCreek told the council that evening the open house had been "geared a lot toward our families and our children," with balloon artists and face painters, and that she got no new information from it. "I mean, we've been lied to so much. I don't know what's real and what isn't any more," Caldwell told KMBC at the event. Payments in lieu of taxes are tied to floor area, so the larger plan pays more: a Beale spokesperson put the figure at $163 million for the city and $78 million for USD 232, plus a further $250 million in sales tax on power and franchise fees. A statement quoted by KSHB 41 also lists $10 million to replace the city's 80-year-old cast iron pipeline across the Kansas River, which carries most of De Soto's raw water. Beale puts construction employment at 400 to 800 and says each phase will support about 50 jobs once running, plus more than 100 contract positions. VanDeCreek and Caldwell are now asking the council for noise, lighting and environmental ordinances and a moratorium. A second, larger proposal is coming: on June 4, 2026 Digital Realty presented plans for a 1,400-acre campus just down the road from Beale's site.

ft-1784674300198-1510.text: DAMAC Digital, the digital infrastructure division of Dubai-based DAMAC Group, plans to turn an existing 400,000 square foot warehouse at Logistics Park Kansas City in Edgerton, in Johnson County, Kansas, into an $860 million data center it calls the Heartland Data Center Project. Edgerton's planning commission refused the final plans, and on July 16, 2026 the city council overrode that refusal unanimously at a special meeting. Public comment was not permitted at that meeting. The site plan shows two medium voltage intake buildings, a guard shack, 60 outdoor diesel generators, an electrical substation and an Evergy switching station. DAMAC says the cooling will be a sealed closed loop filled once, with public water otherwise used for restrooms and break rooms; it has not given the volume of that first fill. It has not said how many people it will employ, only that annual payroll should reach about $2.4 million. Because Logistics Park is already zoned for data centers, the planning commission rather than the council was the approving body, and city attorney Todd Luckman warned that denying a plan that met code could open the city to litigation. More than 75 people filled City Hall for the first hearing on May 12, 2026; 15 spoke against the project and two in favor. "The people of Edgerton, the vast majority, do not want it," resident Shane Mizer said. A motion to approve failed 2 to 2, chair Tina Mathos and Ray Soemer for, Jeremy Little and Adam Draskovich against, and the plan was tabled for answers on the generators and noise. Asked for decibel figures, DAMAC's director of land acquisition, Chelsea Kulhanek, could give none. "If you can't provide a number," Draskovich said, "that gives me all the information that I need." On June 9, 2026 the commission denied the plan 3 to 2, Draskovich, Little and Jordyn Mueller against Mathos and Soemer, after Draskovich found no fuel storage shown in the plans, which the city's zoning code requires to be below ground. Days later the council refused a six-month moratorium on data centers 3 to 2, Josh Lewis, Clay Longanecker and Bill Malloy voting to deny it and Deb Lebakken and Ron Conus against, with no discussion before the vote. Lebakken said she had pushed for the pause "because we still don't have the environmental answers our community deserves." At the override DAMAC's representative, Charles Renner, said the tanks would be underground. "They found a problem that did not exist," he said. "This is incredibly disappointing, as it was the citizens that voted them in and that they are supposed to represent," said resident Kim Twente. Twente, Carrie Schmidt and Twente's nonprofit, Public Trust Collective, then gathered 208 signatures for a petition ordinance declaring data centers "industrial nuisances," and the county election office confirmed the signatures. The council declined to adopt it on July 23, and on August 4 the city sued the two women and the group in Johnson County District Court, arguing the ordinance was administrative and could not go to a vote. Judge Stephanie Goodenow struck the suit in early September under the Kansas Public Speech Protection Act, the law against lawsuits meant to silence public participation. "The City of Edgerton should respect the petition process instead of treating citizen participation as a problem that needs to be litigated away," Schmidt said. The city says the ordinance "exceeds the City's authority and misstates facts over water and power." Whether it reaches the November ballot now turns on a separate suit by Eric Twente against the city clerk, Dusti Callahan, whose hearing was set for after the September 19 ballot cutoff. Twente said DAMAC has filed a motion to intervene in the court fight.

ft-1782187847377-5528.text: The Flint Hills Digital Campus is a proposed gigawatt-scale data center on about 1,000 acres on the north side of Emporia's Industrial Park IV, just west of Americus Road, in Lyon County, Kansas. Kanza Park Place LLC announced it on June 2, 2026, and regional development officials said it had been under discussion for close to eight months. The project website describes a "combination of dedicated grid infrastructure and on-site generation," without further detail. Spokesman Garrett Nordstrom has put the construction investment at about $3 billion and permanent employment afterwards at around 250 at most, and City Manager Trey Cocking has spoken of a possible $500 million rise in assessed value. No end user has been named; Nordstrom said in September that one would be announced before a development agreement is finalized. On water, Nordstrom said in June that a daily figure could not yet be given because the rights would be negotiated with the city, while Cocking said use would be on par with Emporia's other big water users. The city is meanwhile weighing its aging treatment plant at 24th and Industrial Road, where a rehabilitation would cost almost $75 million and a new plant more than $135 million. Who stands behind the project has been a running question. Local landowner Gary Pinkston was introduced as the developer and called the campus a "legacy project" for his family on KVOE in June, but in a June creditors' meeting in an unrelated Chapter 11 case in Georgia he said under oath that he had no interest in it and no ownership in Kanza Park Place. Nordstrom confirmed that Pinkston's two adult daughters own Kanza Park Place and described Pinkston as its president with no financial interest, though Pinkston's signature is on the May 21 rezoning applications as owner and applicant. By September Nordstrom said Pinkston and his daughters may step away as the project turns to a master developer. On July 22, 2026, after hours of public comment, the Emporia City Commission voted unanimously for large volume water and wastewater policies, a Digital Infrastructure Overlay, the rezoning of 11 tracts and the application of the overlay to them. Mayor Becky Smith said commissioners were voting on land use and protection policies, not a green light for any project, and Commissioner Tammi Ogle said: "However, feelings are not facts and we are looking for facts." Jay Vehige of Emporia Neighbors United called the decisions disappointing, and when police removed one person for what commissioners deemed disruptive behavior, Vehige, who said the person had only clapped, called it "outrageous." The group's first petition to ban high-impact data centers and battery storage, with more than 1,400 signatures, was ruled invalid by the Lyon County clerk on July 10 because of how the pages and affidavits were submitted. A second petition was verified before the July 22 vote. The city asked the court to hold the question back until a judge decides whether the ordinance is legislative or administrative, but on August 20 Senior Judge Glenn Braun ordered it onto the November ballot, ruling that if voters approve it, it will not be enacted until that question is decided. On August 26 the commission voted unanimously to put both the 10-year data center ban and a ban on battery energy storage systems to voters on November 3. Separately, Lyon County commissioners adopted a six-month moratorium on data centers and battery storage in the unincorporated county on July 23, after a North Carolina developer approached the county zoning office. Nordstrom says interest from outside has not slowed, with "almost every end user in the country" taking a look.

ft-285.text: Residents beat half of this data center on a technicality the law gave them, and the other half turned on eight people changing their minds. Red Wolf DCD Properties proposed six buildings totalling 1.8 million square feet on land north and south of Parallel Parkway in western Kansas City, Kansas, in Wyandotte County, which would have been the largest development in the county's history. The campus would total some 600 megawatts across 1.8 million square feet, with two on-site substations, three buildings north of Parallel Parkway and three south, west of the Kansas Speedway. Protest petitions were filed against both halves, which required a supermajority of the eleven member planning and zoning commission. On 31 July 2025 the north side rezoning failed to reach it on a 7 to 3 vote. The south side never faced the same test, because eight signatories took their names off that petition. Neal Palmer and Haskell Farms LLC then sued, alleging the applications contained "numerous errors and insufficiencies" and "failed to adhere to the Unified Government's municipal code", and that the commission rushed its review "without sufficient study of short and long-term impacts". The suit also alleges that a commissioner was "unduly pressured" to recuse himself from planning commission hearings, and that Red Wolf orchestrated the effort to have those signatures withdrawn. On 29 October a district judge refused the Unified Government's motion to have the case thrown out. Greg Kindle, president of the Wyandotte Economic Development Council, argued the return: the site is in the Piper school district, the second fastest growing in the state, and each of the six buildings would pay more than $2 million a year in property tax. "General Motors pays about $3.5 million annually in property taxes on four million square feet," he said. "We're looking at one data center generating $2.4 million a year on 330,000 square feet." He put the jobs at 40 to 60 confirmed and possibly 100, technical work at around $100,000 a year, and said the water demand would be set by the tenant: "These folks aren't planning to use a significant amount of water. They're going heavier on power and less on water." Ty Gorman of the Sierra Club's Beyond Coal campaign answered that the campus would double the county's energy use, and that the objection was to who would own it: "The risk to our health and the risk to our bills of just inviting this kind of real estate flipper style of data center from Red Wolf is great." His preference was that the commission force a sale to an end user like Google that had committed to green energy and would invest in the grid around it. Zack Pistora, who directs the Sierra Club in Kansas, framed the wider question: "We're trying to figure out, if we're going to welcome data centers to Kansas, how we can make sure that we're not doing any harm to the communities, to the ecosystems and the environment." Kasia Tarczynska of Good Jobs First, who studies data center subsidies, said there had been a great deal of buildup and talk of a bubble. Power is the next test. In January 2026 the Unified Government and the Board of Public Utilities said they were in the pre-development phase with three proposed data centers, code-named Red Wolf, Yardbird and Linda, in a system that now peaks at about 500 megawatts. BPU officials said existing ratepayers would be protected and developers would pay all on-site costs and substations.

On 31 July 2025 the north side rezoning failed to reach it on a 7 to 3 vote.
The south side never faced the same test, because eight signatories took their names off that petition.

Neal Palmer and Haskell Farms LLC then sued, alleging the applications contained "numerous errors and insufficiencies" and "failed to adhere to the Unified Government's municipal code", and that the commission rushed its review "without sufficient study of short and long-term impacts".
The suit also alleges that a commissioner was "unduly pressured" to recuse himself from planning commission hearings, and that Red Wolf orchestrated the effort to have those signatures withdrawn.
On 29 October a district judge refused the Unified Government's motion to have the case thrown out.

Greg Kindle, president of the Wyandotte Economic Development Council, argued the return: the site is in the Piper school district, the second fastest growing in the state, and each of the six buildings would pay more than $2 million a year in property tax.
"General Motors pays about $3.5 million annually in property taxes on four million square feet," he said. "We're looking at one data center generating $2.4 million a year on 330,000 square feet."

He put the jobs at 40 to 60 confirmed and possibly 100, technical work at around $100,000 a year, and said the water demand would be set by the tenant: "These folks aren't planning to use a significant amount of water. They're going heavier on power and less on water."

Ty Gorman of the Sierra Club's Beyond Coal campaign answered that the campus would double the county's energy use, and that the objection was to who would own it: "The risk to our health and the risk to our bills of just inviting this kind of real estate flipper style of data center from Red Wolf is great."
His preference was that the commission force a sale to an end user like Google that had committed to green energy and would invest in the grid around it.

Zack Pistora, who directs the Sierra Club in Kansas, framed the wider question: "We're trying to figure out, if we're going to welcome data centers to Kansas, how we can make sure that we're not doing any harm to the communities, to the ecosystems and the environment."
Kasia Tarczynska of Good Jobs First, who studies data center subsidies, said there had been a great deal of buildup and talk of a bubble.
Power is the next test.

In January 2026 the Unified Government and the Board of Public Utilities said they were in the pre-development phase with three proposed data centers, code-named Red Wolf, Yardbird and Linda, in a system that now peaks at about 500 megawatts.
BPU officials said existing ratepayers would be protected and developers would pay all on-site costs and substations.

ft-1772687054523-4633.text: Project Catalyst is Alcove Development's plan for a data center campus at Osawatomie, in Miami County, Kansas, first set out on about 115 acres of land the city acquired from the state of Kansas. It has since grown to 283 acres and a 500 megawatt, multi-phase campus, after Alcove added a privately owned tract next door. The city council signed off on a pre-development agreement in January 2026 giving Alcove the exclusive right to develop the site for three years, and the city agreed not to market it to anyone else. Alcove, based in Lawrence, mostly builds housing and has never developed a data center. The agreement offers a 50 percent property tax abatement for 10 years and industrial revenue bonds, and commits the city to supply a million gallons of water a day and 150 megawatts of power. The city says about 100 development leads for the Northland property were pursued between 2007 and 2025, and none of them led to construction. About 80 percent of the city's tax base is residential property. "One of the things we have not been able to successfully do is land a big commercial development," said City Manager Bret Glendening. Alcove says the city would receive $30 million or more a year, Miami County more than $10 million and the Osawatomie school district, USD 367, more than $10 million in property tax. It says the campus will be air cooled, with day-to-day water use limited to restrooms and handwashing, and that all new transmission, substation upgrades and any generation it needs will be paid for by the project. KCUR reported that the city would supply 80,000 gallons a day for cooling, about 10 percent of its usual production, and that all seven buildings would employ about 90 people. "They're just going to sit on the edge of town and print money for the city," said Charles Tinsley, a vice president of MDH Partners, the Atlanta firm financing the proposal. Troy Harp, who lives next to the site, fears the developer will tap the natural gas pipeline on his property for a power station. In early June he began a petition to limit the project's scale. "It's so small, the resources are so limited, and it's just something that's not the right fit for this town," he said. Mayor Nick Hampson said he first saw Alcove's press release announcing that Project Catalyst would "move forward" on a Friday morning, and that no applications had been filed and no permits pulled. At the June 25, 2026 council meeting with the developer, comments were limited to three minutes and questions had to be sent in advance; resident Lee Brewer was escorted out by police, and Glendening said Brewer "elected not to follow the rules." The council meeting with the developer stretched for four hours, and residents asked whether their water would run dry, whether they would still have enough electricity to heat their homes, and whether the hum of the servers would disturb patients at the state mental hospital in town. Miami County's moratorium on data centers does not reach the site, because it is inside the city limits. The city planning commission is now weighing whether to recommend the project to the council, and the developers would still have to interest a builder. "This town has to do something," said John Fletcher, a retired engineer who volunteers at the city historical museum, "or it's probably going to go under."

ft-1783827632129-9082.text: HyperDataGrid, a Texas company, wants to buy at least 20 acres in the Tolen Creek Industrial Park at Parsons, in Labette County, Kansas, for what the city calls a micro data center. The company says it can bring a 20 megawatt facility online within 12 months. A six-month purchase option, with a possible six-month extension, went to a City Commission work session on July 2, 2026 and the regular meeting on July 6. The commission approved the option, which gives the company time for due diligence; building the data center would need a separate approval. During the option the company is to study utility availability, review land use and survey the site, while the land price and the exact location in the park were still being discussed. Clay Roberts of HyperDataGrid told commissioners the company intends to be "as upfront and as transparent as we possibly can." Two water options were put forward, one using very little water and the other up to 50,000 gallons a day as the project grows. "50,000 gallons would take just about an hour a day to make with our water plant at its current operating status and in no way limits water production," said City Utilities Director Derek Clevenger. The Parsons plant can make three million gallons a day and produces about 1.5 million at the summer peak. HyperDataGrid says its facilities use closed-loop systems and direct-to-chip liquid cooling that can support up to 600 kilowatts a rack. The city estimates up to $150,000 a year in extra water sales, and utility franchise fees that could reach another $150,000 a year at peak. "This doesn't solve all our problems, but it is a nice start in bridging some of those gaps we have in our budgeting process," said City Manager Jeff Cantrell. Mayor Kevin Cruse called it "exactly what we're looking for, some higher paying jobs, immediate property tax input and purchasing the city's only utility, water, with no risk or financial burden on residents." A city official said the company is also prepared to partner on housing or neighborhood revitalization elsewhere in Parsons. Beyond Parsons, HyperDataGrid lists two Texas developments, and the Angelina County judge says it has secured power and water agreements and begun clearing a former 40-acre chip mill site on Highway 103 West outside Lufkin. Parsons officials point to a similar-sized project in Pittsburg that produces about $20,000 a month in franchise fees and taxes.

ft-1775094586984-7529.text: The Rochelle City Council in Ogle County, Illinois, voted unanimously on April 27, 2026, to deny a development agreement for a 48-megawatt, 300,000-square-foot data center planned by Midwest Power Investors, an affiliate of New York real estate company LFF Industrial. The site lies north of Steward Road, west of the BNSF railroad and south of Interstate 88, and optional later phases could have taken it to 100MW and then beyond 150MW. The council had first voted 4-3 on March 23 to table the agreement, with Mayor John Bearrows and council members Dan McDermott and Tom McDermott voting against tabling. "We are putting a lot of trust in a development firm that is located in New York City to be good stewards for our community's resources," resident Megan Sneyd told the council. At the April 27 meeting the developers dropped the later phases, but several members said 48 megawatts was still too much for Rochelle Municipal Utilities, whose largest electric customer uses about 10. "I don't think 48 megawatts is a project we need in this community," said council member Kate Shaw-Dickey, and Bearrows cited Illinois's projected power capacity shortage in early 2029. "The developer does not live here," said Christian Bailey. "We do. This agreement is our leverage. Once it is signed, our leverage is gone." A petition against the data center had 1,018 signatures by April 28, and members said they would consider a smaller development if one came back before the council.

ft-1773459882465-1893.text: Bullock Capital and Colossus Data Center Advisors withdrew their plan for a data center at 191st Street and Renner Road in Spring Hill, Johnson County, Kansas, after the city said on March 6, 2026 that no zoning request remained on file for the property. The companies had asked to rezone about 316 acres there from rural residential to general industrial, and a public hearing on the request had been moved to a special meeting set for March 25. "We have decided to withdraw our application and are no longer pursuing the opportunity near 191st and Renner," the companies said in a statement. Colossus, a site selection firm founded in March 2024 by Jake Wagner and Dillon Zahler, never named an end user for the project, and fierce local opposition and the threat of a lawsuit drove the withdrawal, according to KMBC's reporting. The land had been annexed in December 2025, and neighbors learned of the rezoning request from a letter in the mail, then lined the road with signs reading "Protect our children. No data center." "The open land, the dark nights, and our quiet," said Lindsay Museousky, on why her family moved there, adding that Wolf Creek Elementary and Forest Spring Middle School are a mile and a half away. The city's Facebook post on March 6 ended the plan before the special March 25 hearing was ever held. "This is probably round one," neighbor Jennifer Caldwell said. "My question is, what's next? And where is it going?" Laura Harrell, who lives down the road, said, "Yay! So, so happy, and I know the dogs will be happy."

ft-1784063102452-6016.text: Cloverleaf Infrastructure's proposed Project Bluestem is a hyperscale data center and power plant on more than 1,000 acres of the former Tailgate Ranch south of Tonganoxie, in Leavenworth County, Kansas, near the Tonganoxie/Eudora interchange on Interstate 70. Cloverleaf told the Journal-World the center could need up to 1.2 gigawatts of power. The developer's site promises closed-loop cooling, to pay for any power and transmission upgrades, more than 1,000 construction jobs over two-plus years, and more than 50 permanent jobs at first and over 200 at full build-out. A county moratorium on data center applications was allowed to expire, and the project is still early in the county's application process, with no timeline for a decision. On Sept. 16, 2026, more than a thousand people packed or crowded outside the administration building at the Leavenworth County Fairgrounds for a three-hour forum held by the County Commission. Residents raised noise, energy and water use, property values and the heat the project would give off, and the area is full of "no data center" yard signs. Commissioners Mike Stieben, Vanessa Reid and Jeff Culbertson said they shared several of the concerns but stopped short of opposing the project, and said they would do more research before the Leavenworth County Commission decides.

ft-1785191559906-1126.text: PowerHouse Data Centers and the Louisville real estate firm Poe Companies want to build a $9.6 billion data center campus, the Carrollton Industrial Campus, on 550 acres east of Interstate 71 on Greens Bottom Road outside Carrollton, in Carroll County, Kentucky. It is the pair's second Kentucky campus, after a planned 150-acre, 400 megawatt site in Louisville's Rubbertown district. Part of the site is city land beside Carrollton Utilities' regional wastewater treatment plant, bought in 2019 for a plant expansion that is no longer needed. "We believe that this location is well suited for a data center, due to the poor agricultural and development qualities of the property; its location sandwiched between the Interstate and a large, regional sewage treatment plant; and the availability of resources which will not result in any increase in local utility costs," the city said. In July 2025 Mayor Robb Adams signed an unrecorded option contract to sell 340 acres of public land for the project, after the council spent almost two hours in executive session and then voted to sell or buy several unnamed properties. The development team did not announce the plan until July 2026. Hank Hillebrand, president of Poe Companies, told Carroll County Fiscal Court that the company has an agreement to buy 800 megawatts of power from Kentucky Utilities, and that no site plan has been shown because it could depend on the eventual tenant. Any transmission upgrades will reportedly be paid for by the developers. County economic development director Matthew Dusing called it the second hyperscale project showing significant interest in the county. ft-1782768716724-7542.text: Kentucky Industrial Alliance wants to build a $4.8 billion, 1,200 megawatt data center campus called Cave Point Commerce Center just north of downtown Cave City, Barren County, Kentucky, the gateway town to Mammoth Cave National Park. After Cave City passed a 12-month moratorium on data centers in May 2026, the company sued the city, its council and the joint city-county planning commission on June 8, 2026. The two lawsuits, over the moratorium and over a 2024 annexation, have been combined, and the next status conference is set for November 23, 2026. The joint planning commission had drafted rules for where data centers could go, but the city council voted those down on May 11, 2026 in favor of a pause, and passed the moratorium on second reading on May 20, halting all zoning, conditional-use, building and site-plan approvals for data centers in the city for a year. "A moratorium was our only option to get something passed quickly in a special called meeting," said council member Leticia Cline, who said rewriting the zoning ordinance the normal way could have taken up to 120 days. The company's plans were not public when the council acted; they came to light through the lawsuit and describe a 600 acre campus of ten 200,000 square foot buildings, half powered by a gas-fired plant Kentucky Industrial Alliance would build on site and half by Farmers Rural Electric Cooperative. The company says the project would pay $45.2 million in property tax, give Cave City about $2.9 million a year, which city documents show as more than three quarters of the city's operating budget, and create about 360 direct and indirect jobs. Cave City's lawyers argue the company filed only a two-page application on May 11 with no development plan attached, calling it "a woefully incomplete (and potentially inaccurate) development plan application" filed in "an apparent rushed effort to frustrate Cave City's legitimate authority to attend to the health, wellness and safety of its residents." Angie Dawn Herald, whose family farms just southeast of the site, has counted seven sinkholes on her own land: "With the constant vibration of a data center and a power plant above, I feel like we're going to have more and more of these sinkholes that keep falling in. I don't want my home to end up like the Corvette Museum," a reference to the 2014 sinkhole collapse under the National Corvette Museum in Bowling Green. Council member Leticia Cline said her own worry is eminent domain for new substations or transmission lines: "There's going to have to be land taken from somewhere," and added, "I'm 100% against a data center being the identity of the entrance to Mammoth Cave."

ft-1763323509256-4676.text: A plan to rezone 135 acres of farmland at Joe Prather Highway and Garrett Road in Ekron, Meade County, Kentucky, for a data center from PowerHouse Industries was voted down on October 14, 2025, the same day it was heard. The Thomas A. Hobbs Living Trust had asked to change the land from agricultural and residential zoning to light industrial for what the application called an IT infrastructure facility that would run around the clock and employ about 100 people. So many people came to the planning and zoning commission's hearing at the Meade County Fairgrounds that it had to move to a larger building; more than 150 people signed up to speak, and none spoke in favor. Neighbors worried most about their wells: "They expel wastewater, which is going to go right in the ground and I'm going to pump it out. I'm on a well," said Donnie Dowell, whose property backs onto the site. "We are already struggling as farmers," another resident said at the hearing. "We don't need something else to fight against. A lot of farms use well water." The commission voted unanimously to recommend denial, and the county's magistrates on the fiscal court, which has the final say, voted unanimously against the rezoning that same night. Bridget Blake, who lives across the street and started a Change.org petition against the project, said: "The last thing that we need here is a big AI data center that is not only gonna affect our utilities but our health." Trey Webb, the District 6 magistrate, wrote on the petition page: "The Fiscal Court has voted down the proposed construction, and the project will not be moving forward as originally planned." Meade County's fiscal court then adopted a countywide moratorium on data centers, effective January 13, 2026 and running one year, giving officials time to write zoning rules before another data center proposal can come forward.

ft-1773461556521-5226.text: TenKey LandCo's plan for a data center campus in Franklin, in Simpson County, Kentucky, is now in the hands of a judge. On March 3, 2026 the Franklin-Simpson Planning and Zoning Commission approved TenKey's preliminary development plan for about 200 acres on Steele Road near Exit 2 of Interstate 65: three buildings of 200,000 square feet each, built over three years, with power generation on the site. Residents packed the community room of the Franklin police department for the vote; hours of raucous, expletive-laced comment followed, and officers removed some of those present. The vote itself went badly before it went through. Commissioner Derrick Kepley tried to table it for a third time, board attorney Bob Link ruled that tabling was no longer available, and county judge-executive Mason Barnes disputed that reading and said people in the room were talking about ethics complaints. A motion to approve found no seconder and a motion to deny tied; only then did the board vote unanimously to approve with conditions. The conditions require TenKey to file monthly status reports with the commission, make those reports public, hold monthly meetings with planning and zoning staff, and provide more information on stormwater drainage, power generation and the regulatory framework. "We will hold your feet to the fire," chairwoman Debbie Thornton told the company. The developer is Adam DeSimone and the company's attorney is Greg Dutton. TenKey describes the scheme as "the next generation of data infrastructure, providing high-paying jobs, generating millions in tax revenue," with closed loop cooling. Two lawsuits now run against each other over the same ground. TenKey sued Simpson County over an ordinance requiring a conditional use permit before a data center can be built. In April a residents' group, Franklin Citizens for Responsible Development, sued to overturn the March approval, arguing the commission's decision "was arbitrary, capricious, and inconsistent with the City of Franklin Zoning Ordinance" and that only the board of adjustments can grant such a permit. Riley Bright, who owns Bright's Antique World, gave the complaint its physical form: "These generators produce a silent noise that can penetrate walls and vibrate windows." The county case was argued in Simpson Circuit Court in August 2026, where TenKey attorney Gregory Dutton said a planning commission "controlled by the city has exclusive jurisdiction within its own borders," and the county's attorney, Aaron Smith, said the county may regulate where its rules are stricter than the city's. Judge Mark Thurmond took the matter under advisement and said he hoped to rule before an October 14, 2026 status conference; in the residents' case, TenKey argues under new state law HB 321 that the group lacks standing to appeal, so the rulings could decide both whether the county can add conditions inside Franklin and whether neighbors can challenge such projects at all.

ft-1772034500997-4053.text: The Mercer County data center is a proposed 645 megawatt campus on a 555-acre farmland site at Bailey Pike and Handy Pike near Harrodsburg, in Mercer County, Kentucky. A private landowner has been marketing the property, advertised on LinkedIn by a JLL Data Center Services broker; Mercer County Judge-Executive Sarah Steele has said no formal application has been submitted. On August 11, 2026, the Mercer County Fiscal Court passed a one-year moratorium on new data center applications in the unincorporated county, running through August 11, 2027. The stables across the road became part of the fight: "I've had mares and babies run through fences, and it's just not safe to have a data center right across the street that's going to produce that much noise day in and day out," said Caitlyn Cooper, co-owner of Desmar Stables. Diane Floyd's petition passed 2,000 signatures, a group called We Are Mercer County formed, and more than 50 people spoke at a February 2026 planning and zoning meeting. Burgin Independent Schools Superintendent Chris LeMonds wrote that the facility could generate an estimated $25 to $30 million a year in new tax revenue for the district, a message school board members privately mocked residents opposed to the plan for sending. On July 30, 2026, the Harrodsburg-Mercer County Joint Planning and Zoning Commission unanimously recommended a data center ordinance that bars use of A1 farmland for data centers and adds fines of up to $25,000 a day. Two days earlier the fiscal court gave the moratorium its first reading; Magistrate Susan Barrington, whose front porch is a mile and a half from the site, said the county needed a moratorium "without a doubt." The moratorium does not cover the nearby town of Burgin, which has no zoning rules of its own; the developer Panattoni has pitched a data center called Project Bluegrass for land next to the site, and Burgin's council gave first reading in July 2026 to annexing that land into the city. Burgin's council has not scheduled a final vote on the annexation.

Burgin Independent Schools Superintendent Chris LeMonds wrote that the facility could generate an estimated $25 to $30 million a year in new tax revenue for the district, a message school board members privately mocked residents opposed to the plan for sending.

On July 30, 2026, the Harrodsburg-Mercer County Joint Planning and Zoning Commission unanimously recommended a data center ordinance that bars use of A1 farmland for data centers and adds fines of up to $25,000 a day.

Two days earlier the fiscal court gave the moratorium its first reading; Magistrate Susan Barrington, whose front porch is a mile and a half from the site, said the county needed a moratorium "without a doubt."

The moratorium does not cover the nearby town of Burgin, which has no zoning rules of its own; the developer Panattoni has pitched a data center called Project Bluegrass for land next to the site, and Burgin's council gave first reading in July 2026 to annexing that land into the city.

ft-1785254902468-1607.text: Panattoni Data Centers, a California-based developer, has proposed a data center campus called Project Bluegrass on roughly 900 acres of farmland northwest of Burgin, near Harrodsburg/Burgin in Mercer County, Kentucky. As of a September 8 meeting, the land had not yet been annexed into Burgin and no formal data-center plan had been submitted to the city. That meeting ended when council member Melinda Wofford walked out, breaking quorum before a vote on drafting a new annexation ordinance. Mercer County's Fiscal Court passed a one-year pause on new data-center applications in unincorporated areas on August 11, 2026, which covers the Project Bluegrass site while it stays outside city limits; annexation into Burgin would move it outside that pause. Burgin gave an initial reading on September 17 to an agreement rejoining the Harrodsburg-Mercer County planning and zoning commission, but has not finalized it. Panattoni has said the project would bring more than 1,500 construction jobs and about 100 permanent jobs, while residents have raised concerns about water, electricity and noise. The county had scheduled a second reading of an ordinance creating a data-center zoning district for September 28, 2026, at a meeting at the Campbellsville University-Harrodsburg gym; no result of that vote has been published yet.

ft-1763324182750-5583.text: Western Hospitality Partners announced in late March 2025 what became known as Project Lincoln, a large data center on 267 acres of farmland on Highway 53 near La Grange, in rural Oldham County, Kentucky: two million square feet in eight buildings, 600 megawatts of power, $6 billion. By July 2025 local opposition had pushed the project off that site and then out of the county. On Monday, June 2, 2025, the company announced it was moving to 3210 DW Griffith Lane, a 30-acre former drive-in cinema site between La Grange and Buckner, with two buildings instead of eight. It did not say how much power the smaller version would need or what it would cost. Abie Kassin of the company said the plans changed "after hearing the community's concerns about the Highway 53 site and working closely with numerous leaders within the community." Nate Oberg, whose family's land adjoins the original site, had founded We Are Oldham County in April 2025, and it grew to thousands of members. Oberg called the move only a "slight victory," adding: "The fight still goes on. It's always been my position that without regulation in place, Oldham County is still at risk." He also called the move "a last ditch effort to circumvent the process, to circumvent any moratorium that will be coming down the road soon." County Judge-Executive David Voegele, who had opposed the Highway 53 location, called the new one "an appropriate location" and correctly zoned. House Speaker David Osborne, whose district covers both sites, said: "It was obvious from the beginning that the original proposal was poorly conceived." On July 1, 2025 the Oldham County Fiscal Court approved a 150-day moratorium on data centers, amending it 4-2 to remove an exemption that would have let the drive-in application go ahead. Two days later the company withdrew that application too, saying "in keeping with WHP's commitment to the community, the project will be withdrawn and will not proceed." Its statement added that "WHP currently has no plans to develop a data center in Oldham County." Voegele said a draft data center ordinance would go through the county Planning Commission before a vote by the Fiscal Court, which will decide the rules any future data center must meet: "Some people call it progress, others call it disruption. But you have to have jobs and you have to have economic development."

ft-286.text: Western Hospitality Partners' fallback site for its Oldham County data center was the Sauerbeck Family Drive-In, and that plan ended the way the first one did, with the company withdrawing its application. The company, known as WHP, had moved there in June 2025 after opposition drove it off 267 acres at 3557 North Highway 53, cutting a $6 billion, 600 megawatt project called Project Lincoln to a $1.5 billion one just south of the original land. The drive-in occupies 30 acres at 3210 DW Griffith Lane between LaGrange and Buckner, next door to Louisville Gas and Electric's Buckner substation and East Kentucky Power Cooperative's Bluegrass Generating Station. The company said the new plan would include its own electric substation, and County Judge-Executive David Voegele said it would have two buildings instead of eight. Voegele called the site zoned industrial, but the county property valuation office listed it as commercial. The company meant to seek the same conditional use permit as a "private utility" from the appointed board of adjustments, a route that bypasses a rezoning vote by the elected fiscal court. That route was what residents had objected to at the first site: "The fact that this was submitted as a conditional use permit, rather than going through planning and zoning, was extremely intentional. It was to take it out of the hands of elected officials," Sarah Little said at a packed technical review committee meeting in May 2025. State Senator Lindsey Tichenor said then that "there's really not a place that I've been able to see that is already prepared to welcome a data center", while the company's representative, Cliff Ashburner, said it had tried to keep communication open through community meetings and a project website. On July 1, 2025 the fiscal court passed a 150 day moratorium on all data center developments, after an exemption for projects already in progress was taken out of the draft, which put the drive-in plan on hold. Nathan Oberg, president of We Are Oldham County, called it "a win for the group" and said: "It's very reasonable for the county to establish a true moratorium, inclusive for all data centers." The vote was 4 to 2, with Voegele and several other officials recused. The vote came amid a dispute over a May 22, 2025 meeting between officials and the developer, which the deputy judge-executive, Joe Ender, had secretly recorded; he was fired, and accused Voegele and others of corruption and bribery, saying the developer had offered to build the county a sports complex in exchange for zoning approval. Voegele denied it and asked the Attorney General's office to investigate, and state investigators found no evidence of bribery or other criminal wrongdoing. WHAS11 later reported that the developer "ultimately withdrew its application for the Commerce Parkway site as well, ending the Project Lincoln proposal." The county has since written its own rules: two weeks' notice to anyone living within 1,000 feet of a proposed site, data centers only in commercial or industrial zones and set away from schools, farms and hospitals, and a 10 megawatt cap on power that would keep out hyperscale campuses. "The regulations that we put together and proposed, that I expect to be passed by the court, are all reasonable regulations that will control any small data center that might want to come here in the future," Voegele said. Some magistrates wanted them tougher; at an August 2026 special meeting Stephanie Hawkins said, "We don't know the detriment they'll bring. We don't know the low hum that is present and how that will affect school children and people at work and people in their homes moving forward." The county's moratorium was still in effect then, and the proposed rules had gone back to the planning commission. The fiscal court is scheduled to vote on them on October 6, 2026.

ft-287.text: The switch and data center building at 151 Martin Luther King Boulevard in downtown Lexington, Kentucky, is an operating telecom hub that JLL put up for sale in 2024 as part of an eight-building portfolio leased to a home internet provider, which DCD identified as likely Windstream. JLL said the Lexington building serves "as the switch and data center hub for the tenant's east coast operations", and that it and a Colorado Springs site "serve as key data center locations for the tenant's wholesale services". The eight sites total 379,000 square feet on 26 acres in seven states, with seven leased through 2034 and one through 2031, and they generate $5.7 million a year in rent, DCD reported in August 2024. The tenant has occupied all eight buildings since at least 2014, and JLL described them as interconnected transmission facilities that route telecommunication traffic across the tenant's network. Whether the portfolio sold, and to whom, has not been reported. Lexington is in the middle of writing its first data center rules. In June 2026 the Urban County Council voted unanimously to pause data center development through at least October 31, 2026, and directed the Planning Commission to draft zoning changes. The Planning Commission's July recommendations would cap a minor data center at 40,000 square feet and add an energy capacity cap, raise set-backs from 1,000 feet to 1,500 feet, and hold noise at the property line of an adjoining residential zone or use to 30 decibels, 24 hours a day. At a Sept. 8 committee meeting, 1st District Councilmember Tyler Morton pointed out that many of the B-4 and I-1 zones where minor data centers would be allowed as a conditional use are concentrated in his district, and questioned whether equity was considered. The council will hear from residents at a public hearing on October 6, 2026 at 5:30 p.m. in the Government Center at 200 East Main Street before making a final decision. The draft rules deal with new data centers; the Martin Luther King Boulevard building is an established telecom facility, and no change to it has been reported.

ft-1774675197474-8739.text: Mason County, Kentucky, approved rezoning 28 farm properties, about 2,080 acres north of Germantown Road near Maysville, to rural industrial for a hyperscale data center campus, adopting Fiscal Court Ordinance 26-03 after a second reading set for May 22, 2026. The six-building complex would be built and run by an unnamed Fortune 50 company, kept anonymous under nondisclosure agreements, with the city-county industrial development authority applying on its behalf. Tanner Nichols, an attorney for the applicants, said it would create 2,000 construction jobs and 400 permanent jobs, with the company covering the full cost of more than $555 million. Not every landowner sold: Ida Huddleston, 82, and her daughter Delsia Bare turned down $26 million for about half of their 1,200-acre farm, roughly ten times the local rate of about $6,000 an acre. "Stay and hold and feed a nation," Bare said. "$26 million doesn't mean anything." Bare said the company revised its plans using land from owners who agreed to sell. The Joint Planning Commission heard the case over two nights, March 25 and 26, then voted on April 1 and approved the development plan with a condition on April 22. "I would rather look at the country setting that I look at now," said Melissa Humphries, whose home faces the proposed complex, doubting a planned berm would hide it. The fiscal court adopted data center regulations for unincorporated Mason County in February 2026; no construction start for the rezoned campus has been reported.

ft-289.text: Soluna's Project Sophie is a 25 megawatt data center at Murray, Kentucky, that went live in the last quarter of 2021. It came up in July 2026 when the Calloway County Fiscal Court held the first reading of a 12 month moratorium on data centers. Soluna called Sophie its first greenfield project, named it for Sophie Wilson, who helped invent ARM chip technology, and prefabricated its buildings at a factory in Kentucky so they could be bolted together on site. In October 2025 it agreed to run about 3.3 megawatts of bitcoin mining machines at Sophie for KULR Technology Group, a company that keeps bitcoin in its treasury, with operations expected to begin in the last quarter of that year. Magistrate Paul Rister, who brought the moratorium, described Sophie as a bitcoin mining facility rather than a hyperscale data center and said the moratorium would block any expansion of its footprint. ft-1768855509323-6256.text: Riot Platforms operates a Bitcoin mining data center at 5600 Commerce Drive in McCracken County's Industrial Park West, just outside Paducah, Kentucky, one of two Kentucky sites it gained in 2024 by buying Block Mining Inc. for $92.5 million. The two sites together had 60 megawatts of operating capacity at the time of the sale, with room to grow to 110 megawatts and, with a planned third site, past 300 megawatts, Riot said. In May 2026 Riot named the Paducah operation among the sites where it may pair a future data center with a small nuclear reactor from Terrestrial Energy, though WKMS reported it as Riot's only existing Kentucky facility and no timeline for a reactor has been released. Riot's operation runs on grid power under two power purchase agreements CEO Jason Les signed this year with Jackson Purchase Energy Corporation, extending through 2043. Les said in a release that Riot's data centers "require reliable and predictable energy at the scale demanded by today's hyperscale customers." Greater Paducah Economic Development, which has backed Block Mining since it opened in 2021, called the 2024 sale "a testament to the strength of our community." Much bigger plans are moving nearby. In July 2026 the Department of Energy announced a 1.8-gigawatt hyperscale data center campus at the former Paducah Gaseous Diffusion Plant, a Superfund site, with Brookfield developing it and NextEra Energy adding two gigawatts of gas fired power. Two nuclear fuel startups, General Matter and Global Laser Enrichment, are also planning operations near the DOE site. Residents in a group called Protect McCracken County want an independent environmental study of all the projects. "Our biggest concern with all of these projects is that you're doing it on a Superfund site," said Erica Moore, who helped start the group. Paducah Mayor George Bray, running for McCracken County judge-executive, has said residents can be protected through local regulation, though for the DOE site "the Department of Energy is leasing the land and choosing the partners."

ft-1768855290900-5209.text: Riot Platforms' Bitcoin mining site on Coleman Road, in McCracken County's Industrial Park West just outside Paducah, Kentucky, could one day run on a small modular nuclear reactor. In May 2026 Riot and Terrestrial Energy announced a partnership to pair Riot's future data centers with Terrestrial Energy's advanced reactors and named the Paducah operation among the sites they may consider, though WKMS reported this is "Riot's sole existing Kentucky facility" and no timeline has been set. Riot acquired its two Paducah sites in 2024 when it bought Block Mining Inc., the Kentucky company that built them, for $92.5 million: $18.5 million in cash and $74 million in Riot stock, with up to $32.5 million more if Block Mining added power capacity. The two sites had 60 megawatts of combined operating capacity at the time, and Riot said it could expand them to 110 megawatts, plus a third Kentucky site, for a total above 300 megawatts. Riot's operations run on grid power under two power purchase agreements CEO Jason Les signed this year with Jackson Purchase Energy Corporation, extending through 2043. Whether a reactor is ever built depends on Riot and Terrestrial Energy, which have set no date for announcing or building one. McCracken County has also become a draw for nuclear fuel investment, with General Matter and Global Laser Enrichment each announcing billion-dollar uranium enrichment plants near the former Paducah Gaseous Diffusion Plant, where the Department of Energy announced a separate 1.8-gigawatt data center campus in July 2026. Residents organized as Protect McCracken County are asking for an independent environmental study of all the projects because the site carries Superfund contamination.

ft-1784847703607-3659.text: Rubix Data Centers, a subsidiary of Barcelona's Submer Group, wants to build a 2-gigawatt data center at the former AK Steel mill in the Westwood area and has agreed to buy the 500-acre site from Cleveland-Cliffs for $55 million. Most of it is in Russell, with the rest in Boyd County and Ashland. Russell's council imposed a six-month moratorium on data centers in June 2026; Rubix needs it lifted by August 31 to close the sale, and it was still in place heading into the August 27 meeting, with no outcome published yet. About 100 residents, including the full Russell council, attended a nearly three-hour town hall on July 21. Chris Honstain of Gateway City Energy said the first 155 megawatts could run by November 2027 through Kentucky Power, and that Rubix would pay Russell about $70 million a year in property tax at full operation. The company's written answers to the council put total local property tax nearer $40 million a year. Councilman Ryan Biederman said he would not lift the moratorium until residents told him they wanted it. A week later, at a meeting devoted to public comment, mill veteran Ken Smith said the projected noise falls well short of what the steel plant once produced. Resident Jack Patterson said, "If you decide no, we don't want these people here, then I don't know who we will get to clean up that site at AK Steel." Bren Martin worried Kentucky Power would raise rates and blame data centers, and Harry Rudolph, calling himself "not against it and not for it," asked what guarantee the company's promises carried. Boyd County finalized its own 180-day moratorium the day of the town hall, and Judge-Executive Eric Chaney said he had had "zero conversations with Rubix." Ashland's planning commission has recommended zoning that would leave only 20 acres of the wider site open to data centers. Unlike TeraWulf's nearby 1-gigawatt EastPark project, announced in May under a nondisclosure agreement, Honstain said there were no such agreements this time.

ft-1789394660686-8699.text: Azimuth Renewables, a St. Louis company, has taken options on more than 1,100 acres north of Moss Bluff, near Lake Charles in Calcasieu Parish, Louisiana, for a proposed data center, though the land is zoned agricultural and the parish has no rule allowing data centers outside its towns. “Calcasieu Parish is one of many areas where we have secured land options to explore data center development opportunities,” Azimuth president David Bunge said in a statement. “There's nothing wrong with having a data center. It's just there's a certain place for it and it's not Moss Bluff in a community of homes where people are raising their families,” said Lana Bodin, a longtime Moss Bluff resident. State Rep. Brett Geymann said his constituents “don't want anything industrial or heavy commercial. That's not what that community wants.” Ward 1 police juror Darby Quinn, whose property borders the land, said he is “against any industrial-sized development in Ward 1.” No rezoning application has been filed, no parish data center ordinance exists and no timetable for writing one has been proposed, parish spokesman J.P. Booth said. Gov. Jeff Landry has signed an executive order setting requirements for data center developers, including that they supply their own power without raising other ratepayers' bills. Geymann said Azimuth has not met those standards, so he does not expect the proposal to be seriously considered for now.

ft-1788647482524-3261.text: Near the RiverPlex MegaPark outside Donaldsonville, in Ascension Parish, Louisiana, ONE Nuclear Energy wants to build Project Cayman: a 2.88 gigawatt natural gas power plant, a battery storage system and a data center campus beside them. The parish was already looking for a firm to write a voluntary relocation and buyout plan for homes inside the MegaPark's industrial overlay, which Parish President Clint Cointment described as transitioning the rural area ahead of expected growth. RiverPlex is a 17,000 acre industrial tract with more than 10 miles of Mississippi River frontage in the Modeste area, about nine miles northwest of Donaldsonville, where Hyundai Steel plans a mill of nearly $5.8 billion and CF Industries a roughly $4 billion ammonia plant. Chris Hansmeyer, the company's chief development officer, told the Baton Rouge Business Report in September that the preferred site covers more than 400 acres and that final locations have not been chosen. He said he first looked at the land about seven years ago while developing solar projects in Louisiana, including Lightsource bp's Oxbow project in Pointe Coupee Parish, and found it a poor fit for solar. Working from industry benchmarks rather than a project estimate, he put the cost at roughly $4 billion to $6.5 billion, with 1,500 to 2,500 construction workers at peak and 125 to 200 permanent jobs. He described the preferred sites as on the edges of the parishes, away from homes, and said the company would design around existing trees, wetlands, drainage and canals. Hansmeyer said he had met landowners and begun talks with Iberville Parish officials, with Ascension officials next and public information meetings from October. "None of this is a forced thing," he said. The Florida company said on August 31, 2026 that it had signed a binding letter of intent with a "prominent Louisiana landowner group" for control of the site, and did not disclose details about the data center, including the companies involved. The batteries would be rated at 700 megawatts and 2.88 gigawatt hours. The Donaldsonville Chief placed the project in the Donaldsonville area, northeast of SpaceX's announced expansion. The company has also announced Project Amberjack, two small modular reactors on roughly 750 acres in the same Ascension and Iberville corridor, which would need review by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. ONE Nuclear, which announced a business combination with Hennessy Capital Investment Corp. VII in August, has other projects in Washington state, Texas and New Mexico.

ft-1775695942354-9936.text: MS Solar Grid Data proposed a data center near Interstate 10 and Read Boulevard in New Orleans East, Orleans Parish, Louisiana, on land zoned for residential use. The plan surfaced in January 2026, and the New Orleans City Council stopped it on January 28, 2026 by creating a one-year interim zoning district that pauses any data center, server farm or crypto mining operation in the city. The company later withdrew the plan. Both the site's own zoning and the city's zoning ordinance would have needed to change for the project to proceed, according to the Alliance for Affordable Energy, which noted the company "does not appear to be a solar developer." ft-291.text: DartPoints runs its SHV01 colocation data center at 601 Milam Street in downtown Shreveport, Louisiana, in a former Selber Brothers department store building that opened as a data center in 2016. The site is in Caddo Parish, and it is an existing, operating facility, not a new project. DartPoints took it over in May 2023 when it acquired the Louisiana operator Venyu, which also brought it two data centers in Baton Rouge. DartPoints says the Shreveport site delivers 2.2 MW of utility power, with 4,000 kW of generator capacity and 760 tons of cooling, and up to 20kW per rack across more than 200 racks, and it bills it as the only Tier III-rated data center in Louisiana. DCD described the building as 87,000 square feet and Tier III-certified. The investment fund Nova Infrastructure bought a majority stake in DartPoints in April 2025, and Nova and Orion Infrastructure Capital said they had invested a total of $250 million in the company. The data center story around Shreveport now is Amazon. Gov. Jeff Landry announced in February 2026 that Amazon would invest more than $12 billion in three interconnected data center campuses across Caddo and Bossier parishes, promising to pay for its electricity and limit its water use. On Aug. 18, 2026 Amazon Web Services announced a further $6 billion campus at Resilient Technologies Park in west Shreveport, bringing the total to $18 billion, with STACK Infrastructure as construction partner and completion set for the middle of 2028. "This is not going to cost the people of Louisiana any more on their utility rates," Landry said. Caddo Parish has no zoning rules for its unincorporated areas, which means Amazon can build there with no local restrictions. On Aug. 31, 2026 the parish commission voted 6 to 4, with two members absent, against a resolution asking the Planning and Zoning Commission to consider pausing data center construction. "There's no zoning whatsoever outside of that boundary," Stephen Jean of the Metropolitan Planning Commission said, describing the planning limit that runs roughly five miles beyond Shreveport's city limits. It is unclear when commissioners could take up zoning changes, which concern the unincorporated parish rather than downtown Shreveport, where DartPoints' building sits.

ft-1768933943301-3941.text: Markley Group's data center at One Summer Street in Boston's Downtown Crossing, in Suffolk County, Massachusetts, is a 920,000 square foot carrier hotel above a Macy's with a total capacity of 30 megawatts. Markley calls it New England's primary telecommunications facility and only carrier hotel, home to more than 90 carriers and network providers. Markley describes itself as New England's largest multi-tenant data center and carrier hotel, with a second site in Lowell that is linked to One Summer by three dark fiber routes. The Boston building has been the subject of a lease fight with one of its tenants. In April 2023 zColo, owned by DataBank, sued Markley, claiming a "years-long harassing letter-writing campaign" and an invoice for $70 million on a lease whose monthly payments had been set at $63,708. zColo leases about 0.5 megawatts and 8,090 square feet of raised floor in the building, a lease originally signed by its former parent, Zayo, in 2014. Markley said it "strenuously denies all allegations in that complaint." In August 2023 it countersued Zayo for $80 million, arguing the lease could not be transferred and asking that Zayo vacate. Markley's expansion at its other data center, a 352,000 square foot building in a dense residential area of Lowell, has drawn a resident lawsuit. On Aug. 10, 2026 Superior Court Judge C. William Barrett halted the installation of four new diesel generators there while residents challenge the state's air permits, arguing regulators did not properly weigh the pollution's effects on an environmental justice community. "This ruling is a win for the entire community", said Jake Fortes, a third-generation Lowell resident whose home directly abuts the data center. Markley chief executive Jeff Markley said the decision was "based on a limited set of facts and arguments" and that the company would prevail. The Lowell case now sits with the Massachusetts Superior Court, where Conservation Law Foundation, Yale Law School's Environmental Justice Law and Advocacy Clinic and Fitch Law Partners represent the residents against Markley and the state Department of Environmental Protection.

ft-1769137398193-3423.text: No company has proposed a data center in Everett, in Middlesex County, Massachusetts. The city spent the first half of 2026 writing rules so that none could be built as of right. The land in question is the Everett Docklands Innovation District, about 100 acres of former industrial ground beside the Mystic River that the city carved out of its zoning code in 2024 to encourage redevelopment. The Davis Companies holds a master plan special permit there allowing a range of uses. On January 12, 2026, city councillors questioned a plan for a data center in the district and referred the matter to the planning board for study. Councillor at large Katy Rogers told the meeting the city had to be cautious because data centers "use astronomical amounts of water and electricity to create noise." Ward 2 councillor Stephanie Martins opposed the idea, saying "It's not time for this" and that the employment would be insignificant. Planning board member Stephanie McColaugh called them "risky for the long-term security of our water and grid infrastructure", and said one could use as much electricity as 80,000 to 800,000 homes. On April 6, 2026, the planning board voted unanimously for an ordinance that would make a data center a discretionary use in the district, requiring a special permit. It would cap any such building at 20,000 square feet or five megawatts, whichever is smaller, and allow it only as part of a larger mixed use development rather than on its own. Applications would be reviewed for noise, water use, electricity demand and jobs. Planning director Matt Lattanzi said the point was to avoid a building that sits alone: "We didn't want to see a standalone data center, because that kills any type of activation of the site." McColaugh put it more bluntly: "I'm pro development in the city, but I think it's clear that this is not the development that Everett is looking for." Both Lattanzi and McColaugh said the developer had not in fact proposed a data center. The ordinance has to pass the city council twice before it takes effect, and a citywide version was being drafted separately. The Everett entry stands as a proposal with no developer, no capacity and no acreage, resting on that January council discussion. Markley Group's operating Boston data center is five kilometres away, and a small operating site in Medford is two kilometres off.

ft-1768935043811-8257.text: The building that holds Markley Group's Lowell data center, at 1 Markley Way in Middlesex County, Massachusetts, made pasta for most of the twentieth century. It was the Prince pasta plant from the late 1930s until the mid 1990s, then stood empty for about two decades. Markley Group moved in in 2015 with a $77 million tax incentive package running 20 years, and turned it into 352,000 square feet of data center, the largest in Massachusetts. It occupies 14 acres in the Sacred Heart and Back Central neighbourhoods, with houses immediately alongside. The fight is about diesel. The Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection approved a permit allowing the data center up to eight more diesel generators, bringing its total to 27. One of the diesel stacks stands 84 feet from the home of Jake Fortes. The company says the generators run about five minutes a week for testing. Fortes says the tests run five to 10 minutes a week and send fumes into his home. They also describe constant noise from the generators and cooling fans, chemical smells, and mist from the cooling towers settling on their yards. The dispute is older than the lawsuit. At a planning board hearing on September 19, 2024, dozens of residents turned out against a proposal to add four generators, nine modular chiller plants and a water treatment plant at 2 Prince Avenue and 1 Markley Way. Nancy Fortes, of Iowa Street, told the board: "They present themselves as neighborhood friendly when actually they've been a public nuisance to me and other residents since their arrival." Board chair Tom Linnehan said earlier conditions had not been met and that unauthorised work had been done, and the board held the case over to October 21 for a site visit. Markley executive vice president Jeff Flanagan told the board the company had committed more than $350 million to the Lowell site, of which more than $225 million was already spent, and that the project had created 47 permanent jobs that would rise to 100 by 2035. In March 2026 the city council passed a 360 day moratorium on data center construction and expansion, unanimously. On April 26, 2026 a group of residents including Jacob Fortes, whose home is at the fenceline, sued in Massachusetts Superior Court, represented by the Conservation Law Foundation, the Environmental Justice Law and Advocacy Clinic at Yale Law School and Fitch Law Partners. The complaint says the state environment department unlawfully approved an air permit for 27 diesel generators and 16 cooling towers in a residential neighbourhood, dismissed the residents' appeal without letting them present evidence, and allowed Markley to install and run generators before final approval under an undisclosed side agreement. Fortes said at the time: "This is an important step forward in getting the respect our neighborhood has not had for the past 11 years. It didn't have to come to this, but Markley refused to listen to the neighborhood or respect state laws." Markley challenged the moratorium, and in July 2026 reached an agreement with the city allowing it to go ahead with expansion plans that predated the ban. Residents rallied outside City Hall on Tuesday, July 28, 2026, ten days after a national day of action on July 18 that counted 142 protests across 42 states, and the next day residents in the lawsuit asked a Middlesex County Superior Court judge to step in. "The people of Lowell do not want this data center," said Lowell resident Amada Moundele. Another resident, Sienna Herbert, said the expansion "will essentially make us a corporate town." On August 10, 2026, Superior Court Judge William Barrett ordered a halt to the installation of four generators that were not yet in place, while letting four already installed continue to operate. Jake Fortes said of the order: "It's finally somebody recognizing that the rules haven't been followed." The data center keeps operating, including the four generators already installed, subject to the permit's special conditions, while the case continues.

ft-1768935396866-3153.text: The data center proposed at 199 Servistar Industrial Way in Westfield, Hampden County, Massachusetts, was never built. An investigation published December 30, 2025 by The Shoestring found a mailed copy of the project's special permit was refused delivery and there has been no contact between developer Servistar Realties and the city since October 2021. Servistar's limited liability company was administratively dissolved by the Secretary of the Commonwealth's office at the end of 2024 for failing to file annual reports two years running. Servistar Realties had proposed ten buildings, each 86 feet tall, totaling 2.7 million square feet on 156 acres assembled from 16 separate lots. It would have drawn more than 300 megawatts, roughly ten times the output of the largest data center then operating in Massachusetts and four to five times Westfield's own peak demand of 85 megawatts, Westfield Gas and Electric said. The three equal members of Servistar Realties were Erik Bartone, Paul Corey and Connecticut state senator John Fonfara; in March 2025 Fonfara told CT Insider the project had been dead for two years for lack of financing and that he was no longer involved. Five months later the president of Westmass Area Development Corporation, the project's consultant, told NBC Boston that predevelopment could start within six months, an account The Shoestring found no permit or filing to support. Westfield had already given the project a great deal: in October 2021 the city council approved a 40-year payment in lieu of taxes agreement worth $352 million and a special permit, with the tax clock not starting until the buildings opened. At-large council member Kristen Mello voted against, calling the project as proposed "an environmental nightmare." Former council member Dave Flaherty, who also voted against, called the tax deal "ridiculous, way more than any other business, in both dollars and percentage," and said it was put to the council as take it or leave it. City planner Jay Vinskey said of the project's status: "I don't have any insight on the status of this." The 156 acres sit on the Barnes Aquifer, hold habitat for endangered turtles, and are crossed by two 115,000-volt Eversource transmission lines. Tom Flaherty, general manager of Westfield Gas and Electric, said rejoining the queue for grid service with ISO New England would take at least two years, and that the substations serving the area date from 1975 and run at 90 percent of capacity. No building permit had been pulled, against a deadline of October 2026.
