ft-295.text: No data center has been proposed at Baltimore Peninsula. What exists is an idea the developers floated for part of the site, and MAG Partners, the developer named on the entry, has since left the project. Baltimore Peninsula is the 235 acre waterfront redevelopment on the south side of the city that used to be called Port Covington. About 1.1 million square feet has been built there, including 407 apartments, an 81 room hotel, CFG Bank's headquarters, Under Armour's global headquarters and the Rye Street Market. On August 5, 2025, MAG Partners chief executive MaryAnne Gilmartin told Bisnow she was in discussions with data center developers about a limited portion of the site, that no deal had been finalised and that she had not decided how many acres. She described multi-tenant colocation buildings rather than a hyperscale campus, and said the interest was there because "we have a lot of land, we've got access to power." She also said of the project's 14 million square foot vision: "Am I going to try to convince you that Baltimore can produce 14M SF of demand? I'm not sure I can say that, certainly not over the next decade." A week later the development team said it was exploring a stadium, townhouses and industrial uses including data centers for small fractions of the site, that the size and programme were undetermined, and that it was committed to environmental mitigation if it went ahead. On October 30, 2025, MAG Partners announced it was leaving the project, after lead investors Sagamore Ventures and Goldman Sachs decided not to renew its contract as master developer with the first phase close to stabilisation. The Baltimore Peninsula Partnership, the site's business improvement district, is guiding the neighbourhood while new development partners for later phases are identified. The data center idea was still listed among the possible uses for the undeveloped parcels when MAG Partners stepped back. Since then the ground has moved under the idea. On May 11, 2026 the Baltimore City Council passed a one year moratorium on data centers drawing 10 megawatts or more, sponsored by council president Zeke Cohen, alongside a nine month study of the effects on energy infrastructure, ratepayers, the economy and public health. Neither Baltimore Peninsula nor Port Covington was named in the measure. The 1,273 megawatt Brandon Shores coal plant is 11 kilometres from the peninsula and the 841 megawatt Herbert A Wagner station 12 kilometres, with the Wheelabrator refuse to energy plant a kilometre away. The entry stands as a proposal across 235 acres, with no capacity figure and no year.

ft-1772066586254-4342.text: Atmosphere Data Centers wants to build five data centers totaling 360 megawatts of power on the old Dickerson power plant site in Montgomery County, Maryland. The Montgomery County Council voted on July 28, 2026 to replace County Executive Marc Elrich's six-month executive moratorium with an 18-month ban on data center permits, running through January 2028. The council also passed a zoning measure that, for now, bars hyperscale data centers in the county, and Atmosphere is separately appealing how the county handled its permit applications. The Montgomery Countryside Alliance says the full build could use up to two million gallons of water a day from the Potomac River, with backup diesel generators of about 1.2 gigawatts. Council President Natali Fani-Gonzalez said the pause would let the council "deliberate on appropriate guardrails for large data centers in the County." Councilmember Evan Glass said the moratorium was needed to "protect the Potomac River, prevent an exorbitant rise in electric bills, and chart a more sustainable path forward." Atmosphere argues the county "impermissibly [changed] its mind" on zoning that had allowed its plans to move forward, and its stormwater and fire access plans remain unprocessed at the county's Department of Permitting Services. As of late July 2026, no ruling date had been set for that appeal. The new 18-month moratorium runs to January 28, 2028, giving the council time to write a full data center policy before the project can move forward.

ft-1773974568351-8688.text: GI Partners now owns the Eternal Rings data center at 9800 South Eternal Rings Drive in Laurel, Howard County, Maryland, after buying it from Harrison Street along with a second site in Severn for a combined $221.9 million, GI Partners announced on March 4, 2026. GI Partners' Mike Armstrong said the portfolio is 100% leased to a single user it did not name, citing "durable demand from government, defense, and regulated cloud users." The Howard County Council unanimously passed a temporary moratorium on new data center development on June 1, 2026, running through November 2, 2027, sponsored by council member Christiana Rigby. Rigby said the county's data center zoning dates to 1993 and does not fully account for modern facilities: "We're not looking at just a ban for a ban's sake. We're saying how and where data centers will be in Howard County." Rigby said the pause will not affect existing facilities or already approved projects. The council cannot change its zoning code until after the November 2026 election. Rigby said the pause gives the incoming council time to hear testimony and vote on a task force's recommendations, though no date has been set for that vote.

ft-1773974437562-2868.text: The Sandy Farms data center at 7665 Sandy Farm Road in Severn, Maryland, is an operating hyperscale powered shell that Harrison Street began building in 2020 and sold to the private equity firm GI Partners in early 2026, with Oppidan developing an added shell on the campus. It sits in Anne Arundel County, about 3 miles from Fort Meade, on a site of nearly 50 acres. Harrison Street finished the shell, about the size of two football fields, two years after breaking ground, and a 2025 letter from the project's consultants, Kimley-Horn, told the county zoning office the center had been operating for more than a year and that an added shell was planned "as an extension to the existing building." GI Partners bought Sandy Farms together with a powered shell in Laurel, Prince George's County, for a combined $221.9 million, with a $113 million acquisition loan from Capital One Bank, DCD reported on March 2, 2026, citing trade publications and county property records. Harrison Street said both campuses are fully leased to a hyperscale user, and GI Partners said they are leased to a single user, but neither named it. The Baltimore Banner reported that it is not clear who operates the Severn building, although a 2023 report said Amazon occupied a portion of it. On Sept. 21, 2026 the Anne Arundel County Council voted unanimously to impose a 15-month moratorium on data centers, choosing it over council member Nathan Volke's original bill to write data centers out of the county zoning code entirely. The moratorium does not affect data centers already in development, and it will not stop existing centers from expanding their buildings or onto adjacent lots, so the Sandy Farms extension is not blocked by it. "Now that we know these things are causing problems everywhere they go, it's time to pump the brakes," Volke said before the vote. "What concerns me isn't only the data centers themselves, but everything that comes with them," Brenda Cintron of Hanover said in public comment. Advocates for Fort George G. Meade pushed back on an outright ban over concerns it would stifle defense contractors and the cybersecurity industry, and Microsoft's Kaitlin Monaghan said future phases of the company's Annapolis Junction campus could be stifled by a moratorium. The new law sets up a work study group to look at data center practices elsewhere and recommend legislation to the county executive and council, and council member Julie Hummer said the moratorium would lift early if that report is finished before the 15 months are up. Anne Arundel joins Howard, Prince George's and Calvert counties with temporary bans, while Harford County has banned data centers outright.

ft-299.text: The Prosperity Drive Data Center is an existing data center in an industrial area on Prosperity Drive in Silver Spring, in Montgomery County, Maryland. St. Louis-based Sansone Group and Priseda, a local data center operator, bought the 214,000-square-foot building in August 2025 and plan to expand its power to as much as 100 megawatts. Their June 2026 leasing brochure promises 35.2 megawatts in phases by the end of 2027. Most of the first power would come from an on-site natural gas plant: 4 megawatts in early 2027 and 20 megawatts in the second quarter. Another 11.2 megawatts would come from the grid late in 2027, with 49 more from the grid in design. The brochure also lists a study under way for 100 megawatts of on-site gas generation. On July 28, 2026 the Montgomery County Council voted unanimously for an 18-month moratorium that bars the county from issuing data center permits, including for approved projects that do not yet have a building permit. It also banned the very largest data centers in the county for now. "We are not going to do things that shut existing data centers down," council member Dawn Luedtke said.

ft-1765432117824-7143.text: The data center Security Land and Development Co. has proposed at 1500 Woodlawn Drive in Woodlawn, Baltimore County, Maryland, would go on the site that housed the Social Security Administration's headquarters and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services until 2023. ft-1773438713365-3524.text: DeepGreen Western Passage SPV LLC wants to put a data center on the sea floor in the Western Passage, off Eastport, in Washington County, Maine, powered by tidal turbines. The company applied to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission in February 2026 for a 48-month preliminary permit to study the site, and on August 19, 2026 the commission accepted the filing as complete, a step short of a construction permit, and set October 19, 2026 as the deadline for public comments and motions to intervene. Eastport's City Council had already voted unanimously on August 12, 2026 for a 180-day moratorium on any data center application, permit or license in the city, on land or underwater. The man behind the project is Louis Wolfson, a luxury real estate developer and managing member of DeepGreen Holdings LLC, who is also pursuing a similar underwater project in Alaska's Upper Cook Inlet. After federal regulators found the first filing deficient, DeepGreen cut the plan from a 400-acre operational envelope to 27.1 acres and from 51 megawatts to 15, phasing in 16 turbines at first and 34 later. The downsized project is now put at $100 million. At a May 13, 2026 council meeting, resident Suellen Hendrix said, "This man (Wolfson) is a one-percenter. He doesn't care about us. There's a reason he isn't building it in Cape Cod, where he lives, and he's choosing Eastport." The Washington County Commission had already written to Wolfson on April 9, 2026 that the project "would be too risky for this region and its waters and the people of Washington County who live and work here." The Eastport Coalition for Healthy Oceans, which filed citizen petitions against the project, says data centers "try to circumvent local bans by calling themselves things like co-location storage facilities," and that its petition means "We the People keep approval power over future large-scale development." Not everyone in Eastport is opposed: Chris Gardner, executive director of the Eastport Port Authority, said in May 2026 that "if the Port Authority is so inclined to say we want to partner with an AI company, our charter allows it." Public comments on DeepGreen's federal permit application are due October 19, 2026, and Eastport's moratorium runs into mid-February 2027 while the city reviews citizen petitions for a permanent ban.

ft-1766087804541-4477.text: Lewiston said no. On December 16, 2025 the city council in Lewiston, in Androscoggin County, Maine, voted unanimously against MillCompute LLC's Tier III AI data center, planned for Bates Mill No. 3, the historic mill building in the middle of town, holding 85,000 square feet of servers alongside office and innovation space for technology companies. Much of the objection was to the money. The deal included a 20 year tax increment financing agreement that would have returned 90 percent of the project's taxes to the developer for ten years, then 85 percent for the following decade. City administrator Bryan Kaenrath, who had supported the project for the tax revenue, had said beforehand it would bring the city just under $800,000 in tax revenue and 20 to 30 jobs. "This had the potential for being a great project," Ward 6 council member David Chittim said. "It may still have, but not within the time frames and the constraints that have been imposed on it." Hunter Bouchard, the sophomore class president at Lewiston High School, told the council he had talked to as many classmates as he could and all of them were against it: "I want to remind you who they are. These are not just high school students; this is the next generation. They are going to be affected by this change 10 and 20 years down the line." After the vote, Kaenrath said future proposals would have to be looked at "very carefully": "There are many other options for development in these buildings. Making them financially feasible is the biggest challenge." No one from MillCompute LLC spoke at the meeting, and the plans, submitted by the mill building's owner, had been public for only a week. A memo to council members said the company's team included "local leadership and experts from across the country in data center construction, operation, and finance," without naming them.

ft-300.text: The data center at Old Ferry Road never got as far as a planning application, and it still cost Wiscasset $240,000 meant for housing. The 300 acres opposite the remains of Maine Yankee, in Lincoln County, Maine, once belonged to the atomic power company, and the town bought them in 2013. Wiscasset has about 4,000 residents. On November 5, 2024 Lincoln County awarded the town $240,000 of American Rescue Plan money for a feasibility study on affordable housing, against a proposal for 110 units. Two days later the town's economic development director, Aaron Chrostowsky, began discussing a data center for the same land instead. On February 4, 2025 he told a regional planning staffer he intended to use the federal housing money to study a data center instead; the staffer warned him against misappropriating government funding, and he asked for secrecy. By March 3, 2025 Lincoln County had noticed the plans had significantly changed, and town manager Dennis Simmons defended the pivot on March 24. The county withheld the money on March 27 and formally rescinded it on May 29, 2025, saying it no longer had confidence in the town's housing commitment. On August 19, 2025 the town signed a nondisclosure agreement with an unnamed California site evaluator, and the plans became public the following month. Protect Wiscasset formed to oppose the project, co-founded by Richard Davis, alongside RePower Wiscasset, started by Peter Arnold to push renewable energy on the Maine Yankee land instead. A public survey run for a state economic recovery program in January 2025 had found residents wanted parks, shops and culture on the land, not technology. As of May 2026 nothing had been built, and Chrostowsky said he had not heard from the site evaluator since talks paused in November 2025. On March 3, 2026 Lincoln County gave the $240,000 to Waldoboro and Newcastle instead. Commissioner Evan Goodkowsky said Wiscasset would not be a power player in any new housing project for years; Peter Arnold said the episode still clouds other development and has eroded trust in the town's governance. Wiscasset's selectboard paused conversations about developing the Old Ferry Road property in November 2025. At the state level, Governor Mills vetoed an 18-month moratorium on data centers above 20 megawatts on April 24, 2026.

ft-1767888648251-8640.text: Allen Park's planning commission voted 7 to 2 on June 4, 2026 to reject the preliminary site plan for Solstice Data's 26 megawatt data center at 7500 Enterprise Drive, south of I-94 in this Wayne County city, near Melvindale High School, homes, Inter-City Baptist Church and Maple Heights Senior Living Facility. Five days later, on June 9, the city council adopted an emergency ordinance imposing a six-month moratorium on any data center in the city, through December 9, and tightened its noise control ordinance. Commissioner Madison LaPalm, who moved to deny, cited the need for extensive revisions to comply with the zoning ordinance, missing information, a lack of adequate engineering studies, and a sound study that failed to show the noise would be mitigated. The 45,000-square-foot facility would have had a closed loop cooling system and 12 backup diesel generators. David Gibson, Solstice Data's senior vice president for power and land, argued the data center could be built by right if it met the city's zoning rules, and left the meeting with a police escort after boos from the crowd. The city's planner said Solstice could take the denial to the Zoning Board of Appeals, and Solstice did not say whether it would challenge it. The fight began in earnest at the planning commission on January 8, 2026, when more than 125 people came and about 40 spoke, almost all opposed; the meeting ran four hours and ended with the commission voting to postpone its decision, with commissioner Fred Frank the only vote against the delay. Solstice Data had planned to open the data center in the first quarter of 2027 with 30 to 35 staff on site, with backup power from 12 generators and 12 above-ground fuel tanks and closed loop cooling, with municipal water used only for the offices. The site sits beside the Ecorse River with the Reeck Drain crossing its southern edge, and the developers said regulated wetlands may be present and were running a delineation study. Abbas Alawieh, a candidate for the Michigan Senate, asked directly: "There is an elephant in the room: will this raise our rates?" Joanna Whaley, a candidate for the Michigan House, said "The corporations are doing really well right now, and all the rest of us are doing worse and having to make decisions about what bill we might pay." Asked whether the plant would cause air pollution, Solstice Data chief executive Phil Harvey said it would not. Before the hearing, the group Indivisible: Downriver United 734 organized a protest outside. The commission asked for more before it would decide: a further sound study, a fire department assessment, outreach to neighboring communities, and more detail on planning and water use, as recommended by its consultants at Carlisle Wortman. The moratorium the council passed June 9 runs through December 9, 2026, when the city must decide whether to let it lapse, extend it, or adopt permanent rules.

The city's planner said Solstice could take the denial to the Zoning Board of Appeals, and Solstice did not say whether it would challenge it.

The fight began in earnest at the planning commission on January 8, 2026, when more than 125 people came and about 40 spoke, almost all opposed; the meeting ran four hours and ended with the commission voting to postpone its decision, with commissioner Fred Frank the only vote against the delay.

Solstice Data had planned to open the data center in the first quarter of 2027 with 30 to 35 staff on site, with backup power from 12 generators and 12 above-ground fuel tanks and closed loop cooling, with municipal water used only for the offices.
The site sits beside the Ecorse River with the Reeck Drain crossing its southern edge, and the developers said regulated wetlands may be present and were running a delineation study.
Abbas Alawieh, a candidate for the Michigan Senate, asked directly: "There is an elephant in the room: will this raise our rates?"

Joanna Whaley, a candidate for the Michigan House, said "The corporations are doing really well right now, and all the rest of us are doing worse and having to make decisions about what bill we might pay."
Asked whether the plant would cause air pollution, Solstice Data chief executive Phil Harvey said it would not.
Before the hearing, the group Indivisible: Downriver United 734 organized a protest outside.

The commission asked for more before it would decide: a further sound study, a fire department assessment, outreach to neighboring communities, and more detail on planning and water use, as recommended by its consultants at Carlisle Wortman.
The moratorium the council passed June 9 runs through December 9, 2026, when the city must decide whether to let it lapse, extend it, or adopt permanent rules.

ft-1763327086525-1547.text: On August 4, 2026, Augusta Township, in Washtenaw County, Michigan, voted down the Thor Equities data center, 2,314 to 269, or 89.5 percent against. The vote overturned the rezoning of 522 acres of farmland near Milan from agricultural residential to general industrial, and left the land zoned as it was. Thor Equities, a New York real estate firm, sought about 810 acres of farmland and wetland southeast of Ann Arbor for the project, with at least five large buildings for artificial intelligence and computing, potentially for a company such as Google or Microsoft. The township board rezoned 522 acres of that land from agricultural to industrial in July 2025; the rest was already zoned for industry. The project might have used a million gallons of water a day and would have had large diesel generators. The township board had been entirely in favor. It approved the rezoning unanimously in July 2025, despite the objections already being made. Township clerk Kim Gonczy said of the project: "It would just be so huge for us." Officials played down the concerns, saying lighting would be directed at the ground and the noise ordinance would be complied with. Travis Matts, who learned of the proposal in May 2025, set up Protect Augusta Charter Township and went door to door. In about two weeks in August 2025 the group collected 957 signatures, well above the 561 needed to force a referendum, from an estimated 1,200 to 1,400 residents contacted. Matts said: "It's sad that we residents have to fight as hard as we do to keep these facilities out of our backyards, but if we don't then who will?" Another opponent, Deborah Fuqua-Frey, described the response to the campaign as harassment: "Calling the cops, that's harassment." The residents were not finished after the vote. Petitions were submitted to recall all seven township trustees, under review for a possible place on the November ballot. Wendy Taylor Albers, who organized the petition, said the vote itself had been the point: "But I would have accepted anything that the residents of Augusta Township decided. This was all about giving the people of the township a voice in this rezoning decision. So, I'm ecstatic."

ft-1775150502593-4665.text: Microsoft wants to rezone nearly 104 acres in Gaines Township, Kent County, Michigan, near Caledonia, for a data center campus, and already owns about 356 acres there zoned for that kind of development. In March 2026 the company said it was working to buy 57.8 more acres next to its site, land that includes part of the former Steelcase wood plant, with the purchase likely to come up at the township's April 15 planning meeting. That night the Gaines Township Planning Commission voted to table its decision on the rezoning after hours of public comment at a hearing moved to South Christian High School to fit the turnout. Microsoft said it could not yet confirm whether the facility would be used for artificial intelligence. Hundreds of residents filled the auditorium, most of them opposed to the project. Many called for a moratorium, questioned whether a data center campus counts as light industrial, and said litigation would be the township's only way to enforce conditions against a company worth trillions of dollars. A group from a local building trades union spoke in favor, and one resident called the project a "generational investment." Microsoft presented a draft conditional rezoning contract that would cap noise at 65 decibels at residential property lines, set a 150-foot setback for server buildings and cooling equipment, add an 8-foot landscaped berm, avoid drawing on local groundwater, skip local tax abatements and pay for water and electrical upgrades. The township attorney said the contract language, drafted by Microsoft, still needed tightening and that the conditions were an offer, not a finished legal document. If the land is rezoned, Microsoft would have 10 years under the draft contract to begin development. The planning commission would then need to recommend approval or denial to the Gaines Charter Township Board, which would hold its own hearing before a final vote. The township attorney said it was not yet clear whether another special meeting would be scheduled or the item would appear on a regular meeting agenda, but that it would be announced ahead of time.

ft-1782766364343-7627.text: An unnamed technology company wants to build a data center campus, known in county emails as Project Peninsula, in Solon Township, Kent County, Michigan, just outside Cedar Springs and about 20 miles north of Grand Rapids. County emails released under a public records request describe an 800-acre site near US-131 and 17 Mile Rd for a campus of 600,000 to 800,000 square feet costing more than $1 billion, and say only that the end user is not Microsoft. Solon Township signed a nondisclosure agreement with Venerly LLC, and talks have run through the economic development group The Right Place since 2025. News of the project surfaced in January 2026, and in February the township paused new data center proposals for six months. It extended that pause in July 2026, and it now runs through February 9, 2027, directly affecting Project Peninsula. In June 2026 the planning commission tabled a draft data center zoning ordinance until July; no result has been published since. The Stop Solon Township Data Center group worries about light, sound and air pollution, water and electricity use, tax breaks and the lack of transparency about who is behind the project. "We just want to maintain the rural character of our community and make sure that the businesses and developments that come in, they care about our community the same way that we do," said group member Katie Valtchev. Randy Thelen of The Right Place said residents' questions "have been addressed in other communities" with Microsoft data centers. Any new proposal still needs the township's data center zoning ordinance, which does not yet exist.

ft-1775150882369-7465.text: Microsoft's planned data center in Dorr Township, Allegan County, Michigan, on farmland off 144th Avenue near U.S. 131, is stalled by a 12-month township moratorium on data center development that started February 26, 2026 and runs until February 26, 2027. The board acted after Microsoft paid about $48 million for a 272-acre parcel of farmland across from Walnutdale Family Farms and Frontier Truck Parts in 2024, and after Microsoft and the economic development group Lakeshore Advantage said in December 2025 they had been working with local leaders on a data center there. More than 75 people cheered when the township board approved the moratorium. Treasurer Sheila Reitz argued the Planning Commission needed more time to draft a zoning ordinance amendment, and her position won out over Supervisor Jeff Miling and Trustee John Tuinstra, who backed the shorter six months the township's attorney had suggested. Resident Nick Barlow told the board, "I just don't want the damn thing to go in... period." Resident Michelle Holcomb said her property tax assessment rose by $3,000 and that she was told it was because of the expected data centers. Microsoft's proposal calls for developing 128 of the 272 acres, and the company has not submitted a finalized development plan, announced a construction schedule, or disclosed the site's water and electricity needs. Dorr Township has no municipal water or sewer, so homes rely on private wells, and resident Linda Dumond, who leads the group Dorr Township MI, We the People, said, "I'm very concerned that it could affect all of our wells." Supervisor Miling has said the township's master plan designates the parcel commercial and industrial, zoning that would allow a data center, and that a court challenge would likely fail because Microsoft could win approval by right. Protesters gathered outside Dorr Township Hall as about 110 elected and appointed officials from Allegan, Barry, Kent and other counties attended an invitation-only seminar on data centers, run by the township's contracted planning firm. Dumond said residents asked for the seminar to be opened to the public and were turned down: "We're worried about what gets said behind closed doors." While the moratorium runs, the Dorr Township Planning Commission is drafting a zoning ordinance amendment for data centers, and the Dorr Township Board will decide on it before the moratorium ends. Miling has said no action can or should be taken until Microsoft submits a formal site plan.

ft-1766553396160-9385.text: The complaint about Hyperscale Data's data center at 415 East Prairie Ronde Street in Dowagiac, in Cass County, Michigan, is a sound. Mitchell Gourley, who lives across the street, said: "It's almost like having a vacuum cleaner running all the time." Neighbors report 60 to 70 decibels in front of the facility, about the level of an air conditioner or a dishwasher running nonstop. Residents filed a class action lawsuit in May 2026 against Alliance Cloud Services, a Hyperscale Data subsidiary, saying the plant's cooling fans emit unreasonable and excessive noise with insufficient barriers. Philip Cunningham said he started hearing the noise randomly, with no idea what it was until a neighbor told him it was the new data center. Dowagiac revised its noise ordinance in March 2026, and Gourley said what he wants is simple: "I would just like there would be less noise." Hyperscale's chief executive, Will Horne, came to a public meeting on July 13, 2026. He said the plant would stop all cryptocurrency mining within three months and shift to AI computing and robot training, cutting noise and adding about 500 jobs. "I want something better for my kids, and I'm sure everyone here wants something better for theirs," he told the room. The room was not soothed. "How is this better for our community?" one resident called out. Another told Horne: "If you think this is such a great idea for Dowagiac, why haven't you built it in your own backyard to impact your family?" The company offered to buy nearby homes on Louise Avenue from residents who remained unhappy. On September 1, 2026, Hyperscale confirmed it had shut down all Bitcoin mining at the site, ahead of the three-month deadline Horne had given, to prepare for a California AI company that signed a 20 megawatt lease in June, with an option to grow to 52 megawatts. Hyperscale has also bought 48.5 more acres to expand the site, which it acquired as a 1972 manufacturing building in May 2022. Mayor Patrick Bakeman said if the noise came down and the jobs came too, "I think that would be the best scenario for everybody."

ft-1114.text: Cloverleaf Infrastructure withdrew its agreement for Project Ironwood, a data center it had examined on a 750 acre site spanning Dundee and Milan townships in Monroe County, Michigan, in October 2025, after local opposition. Dundee Township, where the Village of Dundee sits, later put its own moratorium on data center projects, running from December 9, 2025 to June 22, 2027. Cloverleaf, a powered land company, had a pre-development agreement with the Village of Dundee, but pulled it before a council vote after dozens of residents turned out to protest. "They needed water from us and everything from Monroe [County], we're just going to say no now," Dundee Village President Tim Bordine told WTOL11. Development principal Michael Evans wrote to the village council: "In hindsight, Cloverleaf should have done more public communication and listening prior to bringing this forward." Cloverleaf's own project site still describes Project Ironwood as in the development phase, on about 350 acres already zoned industrial, with a closed-loop cooling system and more than 200 long-term jobs claimed. Asked why residents did not know the end user, the company said after an October 8, 2025 town hall that it would look for one to build and operate the data center once it had local approvals and power. Other Monroe County townships have followed Dundee with their own moratoriums: Erie Township's began March 16, 2026. Frenchtown Township drafted its own data center moratorium in March, and Berlin Township's planning commission has taken up a data center ordinance. A statewide tracking effort by the news outlet Gander Newsroom, last updated in September 2026, lists Project Ironwood among the Michigan data center proposals that have collapsed.

ft-1765383091599-7166.text: The Southfield City Council, in Oakland County, Michigan, sat through nearly six hours of public comment on Metrobloks' data center before it voted. On Monday, December 15, 2025 it approved the site plan 5 to 2. The developer is Metrobloks, of Los Angeles, and the building is 109,683 square feet on 12.19 acres on the east side of Inkster Road between 11 Mile Road and I-696. Metrobloks' Jeff Mandel said it would draw 100 megawatts and cost roughly $1.5 billion across two phases; the project could bring 35 permanent jobs, and city officials estimated about $400,000 a year in property tax. Council president Charles Hicks voted against: "I'm just concerned there's too many unknowns, not enough fact based information to make a good decision." Council president pro tem Coretta Houge voted for it: "We have to consider new technologies, new ideas, because that's just the way the world is going." Resident Lysa Davis asked: “This is a little scary ... Why do we have to be the first one?” An IT engineer, Terrance Francis, told the council: "Right now they're saying 100 megawatts ... it's 150 megawatts that they're really actually looking at by the time they break ground going forward." At an earlier packed meeting, Metrobloks did not turn up, having presented its plans the week before. Sherry Evanscafe, who lives within walking distance, told the council: "I'm asking council to protect our neighborhoods. If the data center proposal is adopted that this area will be protected from pollution, noise and disruption." One Inkster Road resident supported the project but worried about traffic on a road already congested. Southfield already has about nine data centers, and Hicks put the proposal in that line: "For decades, our city has supported both large and small data centers as part of the broader technology ecosystem that serves residents, local businesses, hospitals and regional institutions." Residents and the councillors who opposed it asked for a community benefits agreement and a health impact study, and questioned whether the infrastructure was ready. Mayor Ken Siver said Metrobloks did not yet have all the money it needs: “Now that they've got a site that they can develop, they've got to find their customers, they've got to raise the rest of the money. They've got to do something within 18 months, or they've got to come back and renew it.” Its next step is submitting building plans to the city, which Siver said would oversee each permit: “No, the city will continue to monitor this.”

ft-1763326509042-3634.text: The developers of a $1 billion data center campus in Howell Township, Livingston County, Michigan, withdrew their request to rezone more than 1,000 acres of mostly agricultural land on both sides of Grand River Avenue, pulling the application late on December 7, 2025, the night before the township board was to vote on it. The developers, Stantec Consulting Michigan Inc. and Randee LLC, said in a statement: "We believe the right thing to do now is to honor the current moratorium, which will give the township and its residents the time needed to develop thoughtful, well-considered regulations for any future data centers." The township board had passed a six-month moratorium on data center development on November 20, 2025, after the Planning Commission voted unanimously against the rezoning in September following a seven-hour meeting, and more than 3,700 people signed a petition against the project. The Livingston County Planning Commission also recommended rejecting the rezoning in November, and Howell Township trustee Bob Wilson told the Michigan Advance that Meta was behind the project; Meta did not respond to the Advance. Howell Township resident Cory Alchin called the withdrawal a victory: "We are setting a precedent for people to follow and have faith in, across the country. The key was that people kept showing up and kept showing up." Township Treasurer and Zoning Administrator Jonathan Hohenstein said the developers may return: "The communication from the applicant makes it sound like once the regulations are complete, they will resubmit their application; time will tell." In January 2026 township planners began drafting a data center ordinance with a residents' research committee, which suggested confining data centers to an overlay district along about 1.4 miles north of I-96 and east of M-59, near existing industrial land. Committee member Kristen Dennison said the area "feels appropriate" because it is near the interstate, train tracks and Grand River Avenue, and that packing large data centers too densely elsewhere would let noise "spill beyond the borders that they were intended to be confined to." Planners said a draft ordinance will go to a public hearing, and the Howell Township board will have the final vote.

ft-1115.text: Franklin Partners' planned data center on South 26th Street and East N Avenue in Pavilion Township, Kalamazoo County, Michigan, has been on hold since October 2025, when the real estate company paused it after residents objected. "Public displeasure is not a way we look at doing business. We want to make sure our interests are aligned with the community," co-founder Don Shoemaker said at the time, adding that the company was considering other uses for the site. The land is an industrial-zoned plot Franklin Partners has owned for about three years. In August 2025 Franklin Partners and the economic development group Southwest Michigan First asked the township to add data centers as a special exception use in its Industrial-2 district; the company said it was marketing the property for data centers and might build on speculation to attract a tenant. Franklin's Will Schumacker told planners a 138 kilovolt power line runs along N Avenue and said a data center would pose "zero cost" to the township. Franklin had not submitted formal site plans; the request was only for the zoning change, and the size and exact location of any data center were not shared. A planning commission meeting on the change drew so many people that its chair, Stan Strzalkowski, counted the crowd to make sure it stayed within the fire code limit. "We are not all on the same side of a lot of issues. We're all here on the same side of this one because we all know that we can't live for seven days without drinkable water," resident Elizabeth Clark told Michigan Public. Residents of Pavilion Estates worried about their already high water bills and about contamination, and Vicksburg resident Katelyn Clarey cited electricity costs and emissions from generators: "People felt very surprised and blindsided in that it was going very, very quickly." Township Supervisor John Speeter said a data center's bills should not spill onto neighbors: "If anything, there might be some economies of scale that their bills may go down because of the larger wires and additional usage." Since then, other Kalamazoo County governments have paused data centers. Comstock Township adopted a one-year moratorium on accepting or processing data center applications on March 16, 2026, while it studies regulations. The City of Kalamazoo adopted a one-year pause on data centers, battery storage, crypto mining and AI data centers by resolution on August 17, 2026, and is writing it into its zoning code; a public hearing and second reading are set for October 5, which would restart the one-year clock. The city's planning commission also recommended a cross-functional task force of residents, utilities and industry to help draft the eventual rules. Any revival in Pavilion Township would start with the zoning change: the township planning commission would make a recommendation and the Pavilion Township Board would decide. Speeter said the item would be off the township board's agenda for the rest of 2025, and as of March 2026 the Pavilion Township project was "on hold until further notice," according to a notice on the township's website reported by WOOD TV.

ft-1764303510176-1505.text: Rocklocker proposed a multi-billion-dollar data center with its own power plant on 1,440 acres of state land near Island Lake and South River roads in Kalkaska County, Michigan, and dropped it in November 2025 after three days of public backlash. Matt Rine, whose work is focused on carbon sequestration, put it forward through a consortium called Kalkaska Go, hoping it could run with net-zero carbon emissions. Rine told residents the project would create work and tens of millions of dollars a year in tax revenue, and that the region's geology suited a data center using carbon capture to reach net zero. The Michigan Department of Natural Resources had already refused Rocklocker's earlier request to buy the state land. The first forum, at Garfield Township Hall in Fife Lake on Monday, November 17, 2025, drew a packed crowd, and most who spoke opposed the project. One attendee told the presenters: "We're gonna fight like hell, so y'all should stop. It's gonna be expensive." Willow Lund, who is 17 and from Kalkaska, asked: "What are our other land options other than pulling down a forest?" Ryan Harper asked how much the cooling would raise the temperature of the ground, the groundwater and the springs that keep the Boardman River cool. Another man said he could hear DTE Energy's Kalkaska compressor facility from his house: “we're probably five miles away as the crow flies from there.” State Sen. Jon Bumstead sat in the front row and told the crowd: “The DNR does not plan on selling or leasing any of that land over there.” Sen. Michele Hoitenga said in a statement that she stood “in firm opposition of this project,” and Rep. Ken Borton reposted an article about it with the message “Not on my watch!” Residents also worried about what would be left behind, citing companies that had come to the area before and gone, leaving scars on the landscape. On Thursday, November 20, Rine announced: “And we heard you. That is why my company and Kalkaska Go will end its pursuit of a data center.” A second statement said concerns about building on public lands were “significant and, ultimately, decisive,” and that some feedback had been “personally distressing to Rocklocker personnel and their families.” The last forum, at the Coldsprings Township Branch Library in Mancelona, was cancelled; the state land stays with the Michigan Department of Natural Resources, which would have had to agree to any sale or lease.

ft-1764610070998-6215.text: Deep Green, a UK company, withdrew its plan for a $120 million, 24 megawatt data center in downtown Lansing, Ingham County, Michigan, on April 6, 2026, hours before the city council was due to vote on rezoning the site. "What this means: the data center proposal downtown will not move forward," Council President Peter Spadafore wrote that afternoon. Three months later, on July 13, 2026, the council voted 7-1 for a 182-day moratorium on new data centers while it writes rules. The project, announced in November 2025 with the municipally owned Lansing Board of Water & Light, was a two-story, 25,000-square-foot data center on a 2.7-acre city-owned parking lot between Kalamazoo, Cedar and Larch streets. Deep Green would have given its waste heat free to BWL's downtown hot water system, which General Manager Dick Peffley said meant "about $1.1 million in savings that will allow us to reduce our budget." Mayor Andy Schor backed the project without asking the city for an incentive or tax break, crediting Deep Green with heat capture, closed-loop cooling and paying for the infrastructure the site needed. Opposition built through late 2025. Ingham County Commissioner Chris Trubac said, "Really my concern is just that I want to make sure that peoples' voices are heard and that we really take the time to scrutinize these contracts and these agreements to ensure that people are protected." In December the Planning Commission recommended selling the land to Deep Green but voted against the rezoning it needed. After the withdrawal, Deep Green chief executive Mark Lee said "our commitment to building data centers the right way has never been stronger," while the Lansing Regional Chamber of Commerce called it "a deeply disappointing outcome for our community." The land remains parking lots, and Schor has asked residents who suggested housing there to bring forward proposals. Councilmember Jeremy Garza cast the lone vote against the later moratorium, arguing the city should not single out one type of development. The Lansing City Council will decide the permanent zoning rules that come out of its 182-day review.

"What this means: the data center proposal downtown will not move forward," Council President Peter Spadafore wrote that afternoon. Three months later, on July 13, 2026, the council voted 7-1 for a 182-day moratorium on new data centers while it writes rules.

The project, announced in November 2025 with the municipally owned Lansing Board of Water & Light, was a two-story, 25,000-square-foot data center on a 2.7-acre city-owned parking lot between Kalamazoo, Cedar and Larch streets. Deep Green would have given its waste heat free to BWL's downtown hot water system, which General Manager Dick Peffley said meant "about $1.1 million in savings that will allow us to reduce our budget." Mayor Andy Schor backed the project without asking the city for an incentive or tax break, crediting Deep Green with heat capture, closed-loop cooling and paying for the infrastructure the site needed.

Opposition built through late 2025. Ingham County Commissioner Chris Trubac said, "Really my concern is just that I want to make sure that peoples' voices are heard and that we really take the time to scrutinize these contracts and these agreements to ensure that people are protected." In December the Planning Commission recommended selling the land to Deep Green but voted against the rezoning it needed. After the withdrawal, Deep Green chief executive Mark Lee said "our commitment to building data centers the right way has never been stronger," while the Lansing Regional Chamber of Commerce called it "a deeply disappointing outcome for our community."

The land remains parking lots, and Schor has asked residents who suggested housing there to bring forward proposals. Councilmember Jeremy Garza cast the lone vote against the later moratorium, arguing the city should not single out one type of development. The Lansing City Council will decide the permanent zoning rules that come out of its 182-day review.

ft-1765216543175-2908.text: Microsoft's proposed data center at the Covenant Business Park in Lowell Township, Kent County, Michigan, is on hold while a township committee writes the rules any data center there would have to follow. The site is a 237-acre industrial parcel at 4687 Alden Nash Ave. SE, where the developer Franklin Partners began drawing interest from data center tenants in 2025. A Microsoft spokesperson has described a current plan of five data center buildings, subject to change, in what Spectrum News has called a potential $1 billion project. The land is owned by the Barnabas Foundation and has been zoned for industry since the early 1990s but has no municipal water or sewer, which the city of Lowell would have to extend. The site won about $17.5 million in state site readiness grants, and the city and township approved a land transfer agreement for it in 2024. Residents learned of the data center only in November 2025, when the applicant asked the township to rezone the park, and the reaction was overwhelmingly negative. A December 8, 2025 hearing had to be rescheduled because the venue was too small for the crowd, and on December 18 the township said the applicant had requested an "indefinite suspension of the application and its approval process." In January 2026 Microsoft said publicly it was the company behind the plan and that it had asked the seller to pause the rezoning process so it could spend time with the community before proceeding. Residents have raised power demand and bills, water and the aquifer, generator noise and emissions, wetlands and farmland, and whether the local fire department could handle a data center fire. A group called Residents United for a Healthy Lowell formed to oppose the project, and an online petition against it has drawn thousands of signatures. In May 2026 the Lowell Township Board set up an advisory committee, instead of a moratorium, to recommend a data center ordinance. "It's going to take quite a long time to get to the point where there actually is an ordinance that we can make public," Planning Commission Chair Dave Simmonds said in August 2026. Committee member Julie Echtinaw, who lives across the street from the site, said: "We cannot just exclude Microsoft. That's exclusionary law in the state of Michigan." Microsoft is pursuing other sites nearby: it owns about 316 acres in Gaines Township, Kent County, where a rezoning request has also been put on hold, and nearly 272 acres in Dorr Township, Allegan County, where it plans to develop 128 acres for a data center. The Lowell Township Planning Commission holds a public hearing on any rezoning and makes a recommendation, and the Lowell Township Board has the final say on both rezoning and any data center ordinance. The Lowell City Council must separately approve new water and sewer agreements before the site can be served. No date has been set for the ordinance's first public reading.

ft-1766256114879-1116.text: Alterra Development's proposed data center at Brooks Industrial Park in Marshall, Calhoun County, Michigan, is on hold for at least a year after the City Council voted on Aug. 3, 2026, for a 365-day moratorium on approving data centers. On Oct. 30, 2025, Marshall's Local Development Finance Authority unanimously approved selling the Ontario-based developer 270 acres, including 112 buildable acres, for $1.12 million. Alterra pitched a shovel-ready site designed for 1 gigawatt of onsite power generation and a 1.5-gigawatt technology park, a minimum investment of $10 billion to $15 billion with 300 to 500 full-time jobs. The deal gave it a 180-day due diligence period, with extensions, to study power and a wetland mitigation framework with the state environment department. The site sits near wetlands and a lake, and Mayor Scott Wolfersberger said the finance authority had not considered the environmental concerns when it sold the land. Wolfersberger said Alterra has since dropped the gas plant, cutting the project's energy use by 60%: "It's no longer a hyperscale data center by, you know, most definitions." The moratorium cites uncertainty about electricity, water use and heat discharge, and the city plans to write an ordinance limiting low-frequency noise during the pause. "We want to make sure they come and they talk to us and they have this conversation," Wolfersberger said. Days after the vote, Marshall police alerted council members to death threats tied to the dispute that they judged credible, and Councilmember Ryan Traver wrote that "we are neighbors first." Alterra is still in due diligence, and no data center can be approved in Marshall until at least August 2027, though pending legislation in Lansing could affect how much local control the city keeps.

ft-1765821873733-6952.text: Verrus wants to build a 525-megawatt data center called Project Flex on 172 acres in Lyon Township, near New Hudson, in Oakland County, Michigan, six buildings totaling 1.8 million square feet south of Grand River Avenue. The Lyon Township Planning Commission gave conditional site-plan approval on September 8, 2025, the first meeting it considered the project, without holding a public hearing; the township says none was required because data processing centers are a permitted use in the industrial district. Neighbors did not learn about the project until December 2025, after Craig Kreutzberg saw a neighborhood Facebook post and Melisa Noble heard from a friend whose property backs up to the site; the two had never met, and went on to help build the group No Data Center Lyon Township. The site is between South Hill and Milford Roads, with a new DTE substation of its own, and backup power would be battery storage for outages under four hours and diesel generators in acoustic enclosures for anything longer. Noble said the development does not belong "next to an elementary school, two daycares, and literally in the backyards of homes." The sound study projected 44 decibels in normal operation but left out the diesel generators, which can reach 110 decibels. Final approval depends on an independent review of that study and an energy audit, and the township has said the planning commission may revisit its site-plan approval to make sure conditions have been properly addressed. Nancy Hopkins, who lives about a mile away, worries about the cooling system and generator fuel reaching her well water, and about relatives with asthma. Kelley Haynes called for a twelve-month moratorium: "The red flags are going up all around us." Verrus spokesperson Emily Hebert said the company was working to set a new industry benchmark for responsible development, through cooling and power systems with little to no water consumption or emissions, and said it was the backup batteries, not diesel generators, that would support grid reliability. About 125 people came to the planning meeting on January 12, 2026, and the township held further sessions at South Lyon East High School on January 15 and January 22. The township hired K&S Engineers to review Verrus's sound study, and in March 2026 the firm concluded it did not adequately show the project would meet the township's noise ordinance; a fire-code consultant separately raised issues with fire-truck access and the large battery systems. "It allowed us to finally have proof of what we've been saying," Noble said of the noise review. Verrus warned that continued delays or denials could lead to litigation, and Noble answered: "We've had multiple residents say in public comment, 'Sue us.'" Verrus is backed by Sidewalk Infrastructure Partners, whose investors include Alphabet, StepStone and the Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan. In early August 2026 the township board extended for another six months the moratorium on new data center applications it had enacted in March; the moratorium does not apply to Project Flex. On August 13 Verrus submitted revised plans with an 18-foot acoustic wall around parts of the substation and more sound attenuation on rooftop equipment, and asked the township to approve them administratively. The planning commission was not scheduled to take up Project Flex at its September 14, 2026 meeting, and no new hearing date or decision has been published; No Data Center Lyon Township says it will challenge any final site-plan approval before the Zoning Board of Appeals.

ft-1782841480971-3749.text: On June 26, 2026 the Oakland University board of trustees in Rochester, Michigan, voted to advance a 20 to 26 megawatt data center on campus, seven votes in favor, with trustee Stefen J. Welch abstaining because he still had questions and was not ready to vote either way. The vote opens a year of due diligence with the developer Fairmount Properties, working with DTE Energy. President Ora Pescovitz told the meeting: "This is a project that we desperately need in order to sustain our current position and for us to see ourselves in the future." Dozens of people, many of them students, held protest signs through the presentation. Cullen Black, president of the student congress, said: "Students resoundingly have said no [to the data center], and we're here to echo that statement." Megan L. Peiser, an associate professor of English and a member of the Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma, accused the board of "ignoring native people's opposition to this data center" and told them "shame on you." The site, parking lot P37, lies next to the campus Native American heritage site on Anishinaabe ancestral land. Ten percent of the computing capacity would serve the campus and the other 90 percent would go to partner companies, which is most of what the campus objection is about. The university says the building would take less than two percent of its land, and due diligence was expected to start in September or October 2026 before design and construction. If the project passes due diligence it would move into design and then construction. Each of the three agreements with Fairmount, including the ground lease, runs through the university's board of trustees.

ft-1766108459741-7894.text: Panattoni Development Co. proposed Project Cannoli, a 1-gigawatt data center, for a site north of I-94 between Haggerty Road and I-275 in Van Buren Township, in Wayne County, Michigan. On March 17, 2026 Google confirmed it was the company behind it. The facility would be 800,000 square feet on 282 acres and use around 2 million to 3.6 million gallons of water a day, according to the township, and DTE says it would begin taking service in December 2027, “with max load being achieved by December 2028.” Google announced the project alongside a DTE Energy deal for 2.7 gigawatts of new solar and storage resources. It said existing customers would see nearly $1.7 billion in affordability benefits, and pledged $10 million for energy affordability work in Michigan communities. Michigan attorney general Dana Nessel said Google had "obviously learned a lesson from the Oracle/Open AI boondoggle", referring to the fast-tracked approvals given to the Saline Township campus. The township planning commission gave preliminary site plan approval on February 11, 2026, and approved the DTE and ITC substation and switching station on the site in May after a five-hour meeting. “Our job is not to debate the moral aspects of whether you think AI is a good thing or bad thing,” planning commissioner Jeff Jahr said. Commissioner Jackson Pahle's motion to deny the substation failed: “I'm still concerned about the burden placed on nearby residents through cumulative community and environmental impacts as well as infrastructure strain.” Nearly 1,700 people have signed a petition against the data center. Residents planned a protest outside the township hall on January 14, 2026, when they still did not know who the customer was. Sanjay Singh, who lives in the township, told Planet Detroit that “the general community sentiment is currently a resounding 'no,'” adding: “If the township only receives standard water/sewer fees and basic property tax, this is a waste of land.” The objections were that the outreach had been inadequate, that a gigawatt would strain local utilities, and that residents already dealing with higher bills and outages would carry the cost. The township has approved a $125 million local tax break for the project, which Supervisor Kevin McNamara defends as leverage for requirements on landscaping, water use and noise. Because the data center is a use by right under township zoning, officials say the planning commission must approve the final site plan if it complies with the ordinance. That vote, pushed back from August 26, is likely on October 14, 2026, according to township municipal services director Ron Akers. The Michigan Public Service Commission decides whether to approve the DTE energy contracts with Google.
paragraphs: Panattoni Development Co. proposed Project Cannoli, a 1-gigawatt data center, for a site north of I-94 between Haggerty Road and I-275 in Van Buren Township, in Wayne County, Michigan. On March 17, 2026 Google confirmed it was the company behind it. The facility would be 800,000 square feet on 282 acres and use around 2 million to 3.6 million gallons of water a day, according to the township, and DTE says it would begin taking service in December 2027, “with max load being achieved by December 2028.”

Google announced the project alongside a DTE Energy deal for 2.7 gigawatts of new solar and storage resources. It said existing customers would see nearly $1.7 billion in affordability benefits, and pledged $10 million for energy affordability work in Michigan communities. Michigan attorney general Dana Nessel said Google had "obviously learned a lesson from the Oracle/Open AI boondoggle", referring to the fast-tracked approvals given to the Saline Township campus.

The township planning commission gave preliminary site plan approval on February 11, 2026, and approved the DTE and ITC substation and switching station on the site in May after a five-hour meeting. “Our job is not to debate the moral aspects of whether you think AI is a good thing or bad thing,” planning commissioner Jeff Jahr said. Commissioner Jackson Pahle's motion to deny the substation failed: “I'm still concerned about the burden placed on nearby residents through cumulative community and environmental impacts as well as infrastructure strain.” Nearly 1,700 people have signed a petition against the data center.

Residents planned a protest outside the township hall on January 14, 2026, when they still did not know who the customer was. Sanjay Singh, who lives in the township, told Planet Detroit that “the general community sentiment is currently a resounding 'no,'” adding: “If the township only receives standard water/sewer fees and basic property tax, this is a waste of land.” The objections were that the outreach had been inadequate, that a gigawatt would strain local utilities, and that residents already dealing with higher bills and outages would carry the cost. The township has approved a $125 million local tax break for the project, which Supervisor Kevin McNamara defends as leverage for requirements on landscaping, water use and noise.

Because the data center is a use by right under township zoning, officials say the planning commission must approve the final site plan if it complies with the ordinance. That vote, pushed back from August 26, is likely on October 14, 2026, according to township municipal services director Ron Akers. The Michigan Public Service Commission decides whether to approve the DTE energy contracts with Google.

ft-1767583568638-1135.text: Prologis, a San Francisco real estate company, wants to build a technical campus and data center on 312 acres on the south side of 32 Mile Road, between M-53 and Powell Road, in Washington Township, Macomb County, Michigan. Prologis withdrew its rezoning application on May 19, 2026, saying it would wait until the township adopts a data center ordinance before trying again. Washington Township trustees passed a six-month moratorium on all data center applications on May 23, 2026, running through November 23, 2026. More than 100 residents packed a December 11, 2025 planning commission hearing after over 170 people had emailed in, most of them opposed, and the commission postponed a decision for a month rather than vote that night. Almont resident John Ardelean said the project "would take us backwards 40 years, instead of propelling us forward 20 years," and Washington Township resident Corinne Graper, who started a Facebook group against it, called the slow rollout "death by a thousand paper cuts." Not everyone opposed it: retired IT worker Fred Hakim argued the power and water upgrades the project would force utilities to make would help the whole township, since "DTE has no incentive to improve our infrastructure" otherwise. No megawatt figure for the project was ever published; before the December hearing, Prologis told Planet Detroit it was "still early in evaluating what could work best on the site." In its May 19 withdrawal letter, Prologis said it plans to reapply once the township adopts rules for data centers.

ft-305.text: The University of Michigan and Los Alamos National Laboratory plan a $1.2 billion computing center on Textile Road in Ypsilanti Township, Washtenaw County, Michigan, on the south bank of the Huron River. The state is putting in $100 million and the university is financing $850 million, with construction and completion projected between 2028 and 2031. On August 11, 2026 the university affirmed it will build on the 144 acres it bought next to the river, over the objections of township officials who want the project moved. Ypsilanti Township passed a moratorium on new data center approvals on April 22, 2026, one of two local moratoriums now in effect along with the City of Ypsilanti's. The township wants the project moved east to the American Center for Mobility, away from the river and the West Willow neighborhood. State representative Jimmie Wilson Jr introduced legislation December 11, 2025 to rescind the grant: "The University of Michigan has not been fully transparent with this project and has refused to collaborate with the Ypsilanti Township officials throughout this planning process." Township attorney Doug Winters said after the announcement, "We're going to fight," and Supervisor Brenda Stumbo called it a "call to action." Township officials said they learned of the university's decision by text message moments before it was made public. The university planned a community town hall in the township for September 9, 2026, to discuss the project. No report on what happened at that meeting has been published.

ft-1775095642594-1332.text: Apple Valley, Minnesota, has blocked Oppidan's plan for a data center campus of up to five buildings on gravel-mining land in Dakota County, after the City Council unanimously denied the project's permits on March 26, 2026. The council then passed a one-year moratorium on new data center proposals on July 9, 2026, halting any further consideration on the site. Oppidan and landowner Rockport LLC had proposed the Apple Valley Technology Park in early 2025, with five buildings totaling 1.05 million square feet and 250 to 300 megawatts of power. The city's objections were land use and water: Apple Valley's 2040 Comprehensive Plan guides the site, between Flagstaff Avenue, 150th Street and Pilot Knob Road, for retail, hotel, office, medical and housing, not a data center of that size. A city analysis found it could not supply the water the project would need; the city says it already needs $106 million in water treatment work and has shut two of its 14 wells over PFAS contamination. Rockport disputed that analysis and proposed private wells on the site; the city asked for an escrow payment to fund a study of the idea. The city received more than 100 comments, mostly opposed, and residents raised water, electric supply, noise, traffic and land use at meetings. The Planning Commission voted 5-1 against the plan in April 2025, and the City Council denied it in January 2026. Oppidan and Rockport withdrew their rezoning requests on March 6 and 10, 2026, days before Oppidan's last extension ran out. On March 18 the Planning Commission unanimously recommended denial of the remaining permits, and on March 26 the City Council unanimously denied them. Oppidan had said the campus could bring thousands of construction jobs, about 200 permanent jobs and a $4.5 million increase in city taxes by 2030. Apple Valley joins Eagan, Rosemount, Inver Grove Heights, Elk River and Minneapolis among Minnesota cities that have passed data center moratoriums. A lawsuit seeks to void Eagan's moratorium, arguing it is invalid because it pauses proposals above a 20-megawatt threshold; a Farmington data center proposal faces separate lawsuits over an annexation agreement and environmental review. During the one-year moratorium, which runs to July 9, 2027, Apple Valley staff are studying how to regulate data centers and will recommend any new rules to the City Council, which can shorten or end the pause.

ft-309.text: Centra is converting the former Thomson Reuters data center at 610 Opperman Drive in Eagan, Dakota County, Minnesota into MSP1, a data center using 12 megawatts of power for network and cloud connections. Centra broke ground in August 2025, and the network provider Arvig said in March 2026 that the facility, then under construction, was set to open in the summer of 2026. That summer target has passed; no result on the opening has been published. The 150,000-square-foot building, built around 1989, will house multiple tenants and network providers on land Thomson Reuters sold to Ryan Cos., which is redeveloping the rest of the site for industrial and residential use. Centra plans refrigerant-based cooling, with free cooling for nearly half the year, and green power under Dakota Electric's renewable programs. Centra, formerly Deep Edge and backed by Columbia Capital, also runs network connection sites in Reno, Portland, Maine, Charlotte and Columbus. In February 2026 the Eagan City Council voted unanimously for a one-year pause on new data center projects using more than 20 megawatts of power or sited within 500 feet of homes; MSP1, a 12 megawatt conversion already under construction, was not covered. Resident Leo Caravello told the council: "Water is a reason many data centers here today have been coming to Minnesota, and while we have an abundant supply of water, we do not have an infinite amount." Eagan already has four data centers, two built and two under construction, all 20 megawatts of power or smaller. The pause, which Mayor Mike Maguire's council approved to study the industry's effects on energy, water and zoning, ends February 17, 2027.

ft-1783825562487-1869.text: Elk River Capital LLC and Swervo Development have withdrawn their plan to convert a vacant former injection molding plant at 19178 Industrial Boulevard NW in Elk River, Sherburne County, Minnesota, into a 33-megawatt data center. The Elk River City Council voted unanimously against the zoning change the project needed on July 6, 2026, and the developers pulled the application afterward. The facility would have been run by Swervo-affiliated Irongate Data Centers. Timothy Jones, whose brewery sits yards from where one version of the plan put its cooling equipment, said a consultant's study found the noise there would exceed 70 decibels, under Minnesota's 80-decibel limit. "I think it would mean either closing this location and moving or closing completely," Jones said. Elk River Municipal Utilities general manager Mark Hanson told the planning commission the project was "a substantial opportunity" for the utility, but the commission recommended against the zoning change and asked for a moratorium. Residents raised noise, energy use, diesel generator pollution and the closeness of homes and schools to the proposed site. "There are other communities that are investigating this for us. There's a lot to learn, but there's no reason for us to rush into this," resident David McClellan said. Council member Jennifer Wagner said the vote was not a verdict against data centers generally: "Good community planning sometimes means saying yes. It also means sometimes saying no, or not yet, or we just don't have it right yet." After the vote, the council directed city staff to draft a one-year moratorium on new data center applications, to come back for review at the council's August 3, 2026 meeting; no result of that meeting has been published.
