ft-311.text: Hermantown, in St. Louis County, Minnesota, was asked to rezone 220 acres for a data center to be developed by Mortenson Co. for a customer nobody would name. Several city and county officials had signed nondisclosure agreements with the developer, and the project went by the name Project Loon. More than 300 people came to the city council on October 20, 2025, filling the chamber and the overflow rooms. City officials would say only that the customer was a United States based Fortune 50 company. The council voted unanimously to rezone the land from suburban to business and light manufacturing, and the audience stood and shouted "Shame". Less than 24 hours later the city delayed considering the permits. Assistant city administrator Joe Wicklund explained: "Our approach was, hey, the request is valid. Let's just pause." He said the city would take the next legal steps to see whether the work done in preparation for the alternative urban areawide review met the mark, and that everything was on pause while it took a deep look at the next environmental step. The project would likely be built in three phases and could reach 1.8 million square feet. The first plans showed four buildings, each up to 50 feet tall and 300,000 square feet, and a first phase costing $650 million. At full capacity it would use 30,000 to 50,000 gallons of water a day. Dan Lessor, a vice president at the developer Mortenson, told the meeting data centers are "critical pieces of our local and national infrastructure", and the city projected $50 million to $100 million in economic stimulus. Nicholas Rinehart, a resident, put the objection in one question: "Is this the Hermantown we want to become?" A group called Stop the Hermantown Data Center formed against it and petitioned the state Environmental Quality Board, saying noise, light, air and water had been inadequately addressed, with some homes within 350 feet of the site. On March 3, 2026, Google said it was the company behind the project, which had been dubbed Project Loon, and called Hermantown "a natural fit for this project, offering a climate that supports energy-efficient air cooling, a resilient power grid and a dedicated and motivated workforce." Minnesota Power announced an agreement to supply the campus, under which Google will help fund 700 megawatts of new clean energy, 300 megawatts of wind and 400 megawatts of battery storage; Google did not say how much electricity the data center would use. Stop the Hermantown Data Center and the Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy have sued to block it, and the group's Jeffrey Donahue said: "The fact that Google wants to come into our community without completing an environmental impact statement is obscene." In May 2026 the council heard about three hours of public comment on agreements that would give Google a property tax break estimated at about $70 million and possibly as high as $80 million, in return for about $130 million toward utilities and infrastructure and about $70 million for Hermantown schools over 28 years. Councilors voted unanimously to table the vote, some of them unsure whether the city could approve the agreements while an environmental review and two lawsuits were pending; the city expects three phases over eight to 10 years, with a total investment of around $2 billion. In August 2026 Google said it had cut the campus from four buildings to three and from 1.8 million square feet to 1.66 million, reducing the wetlands and land it would disturb. At its open house that month opponents interrupted the presentation and several were escorted out by police, after the Duluth Monitor published leaked recordings in which Police Chief Jim Crace called an opponent an "idiot"; Mayor Wayne Boucher said the city would ask for an outside investigation. The project still needs city council approval.
paragraphs: Hermantown, in St. Louis County, Minnesota, was asked to rezone 220 acres for a data center to be developed by Mortenson Co. for a customer nobody would name. Several city and county officials had signed nondisclosure agreements with the developer, and the project went by the name Project Loon. More than 300 people came to the city council on October 20, 2025, filling the chamber and the overflow rooms. City officials would say only that the customer was a United States based Fortune 50 company. The council voted unanimously to rezone the land from suburban to business and light manufacturing, and the audience stood and shouted "Shame".

Less than 24 hours later the city delayed considering the permits. Assistant city administrator Joe Wicklund explained: "Our approach was, hey, the request is valid. Let's just pause." He said the city would take the next legal steps to see whether the work done in preparation for the alternative urban areawide review met the mark, and that everything was on pause while it took a deep look at the next environmental step.

The project would likely be built in three phases and could reach 1.8 million square feet. The first plans showed four buildings, each up to 50 feet tall and 300,000 square feet, and a first phase costing $650 million. At full capacity it would use 30,000 to 50,000 gallons of water a day. Dan Lessor, a vice president at the developer Mortenson, told the meeting data centers are "critical pieces of our local and national infrastructure", and the city projected $50 million to $100 million in economic stimulus.

Nicholas Rinehart, a resident, put the objection in one question: "Is this the Hermantown we want to become?" A group called Stop the Hermantown Data Center formed against it and petitioned the state Environmental Quality Board, saying noise, light, air and water had been inadequately addressed, with some homes within 350 feet of the site.

On March 3, 2026, Google said it was the company behind the project, which had been dubbed Project Loon, and called Hermantown "a natural fit for this project, offering a climate that supports energy-efficient air cooling, a resilient power grid and a dedicated and motivated workforce." Minnesota Power announced an agreement to supply the campus, under which Google will help fund 700 megawatts of new clean energy, 300 megawatts of wind and 400 megawatts of battery storage; Google did not say how much electricity the data center would use. Stop the Hermantown Data Center and the Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy have sued to block it, and the group's Jeffrey Donahue said: "The fact that Google wants to come into our community without completing an environmental impact statement is obscene."

In May 2026 the council heard about three hours of public comment on agreements that would give Google a property tax break estimated at about $70 million and possibly as high as $80 million, in return for about $130 million toward utilities and infrastructure and about $70 million for Hermantown schools over 28 years. Councilors voted unanimously to table the vote, some of them unsure whether the city could approve the agreements while an environmental review and two lawsuits were pending; the city expects three phases over eight to 10 years, with a total investment of around $2 billion. In August 2026 Google said it had cut the campus from four buildings to three and from 1.8 million square feet to 1.66 million, reducing the wetlands and land it would disturb. At its open house that month opponents interrupted the presentation and several were escorted out by police, after the Duluth Monitor published leaked recordings in which Police Chief Jim Crace called an opponent an "idiot"; Mayor Wayne Boucher said the city would ask for an outside investigation. The project still needs city council approval.

ft-1785527745587-6440.text: The Minnesota Star Tribune stopped printing at 800 North First Street in Minneapolis, Hennepin County, Minnesota, in December 2025, moving the work to Iowa and affecting about 125 jobs, and a data center developer moved to buy the building. In July 2026, Legacy Investing, of Arlington, Virginia, agreed to purchase the 13-acre printing site in the North Loop, expecting 20 megawatts of capacity; the same company had already turned the nearby Sleep Number building into a 30 megawatt data center. Adam Duininck, president and chief executive of the Minneapolis Downtown Council, welcomed it: "I think it's an exciting opportunity just to rethink how a data center development can help spur a different use." He said it could lead to hundreds of millions of dollars in additional valuation and tens of millions of dollars of property tax. The neighborhood did not agree. Kaitlyn Cooper, who lives next to the site, said: "I think environmental concerns of course is like number one, also just like hearing other news reports of like, noise and things like that." Hundreds of city residents took part in the opposition at forums in August 2026, raising environmental effects and how few jobs the building would create. Minneapolis had already imposed a six month ban in May 2026 on data centers larger than 350,000 square feet. Legacy Investing withdrew its land use application on September 11, 2026 without comment, and emails to the company bounced back. City spokesperson Jess Olstad said: "The city looks forward to working with other partners who may wish to look at the future of this site." The Star Tribune still owns the building, and vice president Chris Iles said the company "remains committed to maximizing the value of the Heritage Printing Facility for the benefit of our community and our journalism."

ft-312.text: US Internet, a Minnetonka-based fiber internet provider, plans a small data center of about 4,000 square feet at 3819 West Broadway in Robbinsdale, Hennepin County, Minnesota, on the site of the former Robbinsdale Clinic. The Robbinsdale City Council rezoned the lot on December 3, 2024 and approved a variance and conditional use permit for the project on March 4, 2025. The remaining steps are demolition and construction. The company's chief financial officer, Tim Martin, told the council the building "isn't like data mining, which is a heavy user of power," calling it "really a switching station that our fiber is coming into." It will anchor a fiber network the company plans to lay underground across Robbinsdale over about three years, and US Internet has about half a dozen similar buildings around the Twin Cities. The site was the Robbinsdale Clinic, which closed in early 2025 after it could not raise enough money to stay open. The 1925 building was later used as a dental office before US Internet's purchase. As of an August 2025 report the clinic building was expected to be demolished to make way for the new facility; no update since has been published.

ft-1772134804921-7396.text: Monticello's first formal data center decision is coming: the city lists Monticello Tech's technology campus, known as Project Groundhog, as an applicant under consideration, with a public hearing scheduled for Tuesday, October 6. Monticello Tech LLC, run by Nick Frattalone, chief executive of the commercial developer Frattalone Companies, is proposing a data center campus called Project Groundhog on about 550 acres east of Highway 25 and south of 85th Street, inside Monticello's orderly annexation area, in Wright County, Minnesota. About a tenth of the land would be built on, with the rest kept as buffers and infrastructure. Three large technology companies are being considered as tenants under nondisclosure agreements, and none has been chosen. The power question was still open in January: Monticello Tech applied to Xcel Energy for a study in June 2024 and was waiting on the results, and Frattalone said a data center is developed on "how much power is available and when." No cost figure has been given, and the company says nothing will be developed in 2026, with construction no earlier than the second quarter of 2027. About 100 residents came to an open house on January 7 and left without much. Nancy Friesen said: "I was hoping to get some answers, but any questions I've heard, I've only heard 'I don't know' from the people presenting." Jenna Van Den Boom made the same point differently: "Depending on who it ends up being, this could look very different." On April 27, 2026 the city council voted 4 to 1 to adopt a data center ordinance that opens the door to such projects while adding restrictions. A developer must first get the land rezoned and then apply for a conditional use permit, show there is enough water and energy, and meet standards for buffers, screening, noise and lighting; the city will not offer tax incentives, and developers must pay for any new infrastructure. Council member Tracy Hinz called it "one of the best, most well-framed ordinances in our state, if not broader," while residents at the hearings warned about property values, water and electricity, and constant noise. The next step is the city's public hearing on October 6, and under the new ordinance the land would then need rezoning and a conditional use permit from the city.

ft-313.text: Project Skyway is a 482-acre technology park that Ryan Companies is developing on the north side of Pine Island, a small city in Goodhue County north of Rochester, Minnesota. Google signed on in February 2026 as the first tenant, its first Minnesota data center: a 250,000-square-foot building with a 35,000-square-foot office on about 88 acres of the site, cooled with air rather than water. Construction has been on hold since May 22, 2026, when a Goodhue County judge issued a temporary restraining order sought by the Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy, which argues the city should have ordered a fuller environmental review; as of September 11, 2026 the case was still before the court. On February 4, 2026, the city council voted 5-0 to approve a $36.6 million tax abatement for the project, and City Administrator Elizabeth Howard told the council the city would collect more than $131 million in new taxes over about two decades; the agreement requires the developer to create at least 38 full-time jobs paying a minimum of $31 an hour. Google has separately said the project will bring 100 permanent jobs and about 500 construction jobs, and has committed $20 million to infrastructure and $25 million over 20 years to Pine Island's public schools. Several residents spoke against the abatement before the vote: Mary Bakeberg warned that "this data center could be obsolete by the time the building is even finished," and the Reverend David Derksen said: "Let's not move fast and break things. Let's slow this down." At an April 2026 council meeting the debate grew tense enough that police were called, the Star Tribune reported, and in June the council adopted rules limiting public comment to 20 minutes total and barring name-calling. Mayor David Friese resigned the day before that vote, citing the demands of the job rather than the data center dispute; Brandi Veith Staloch is now Pine Island's mayor. In September 2026, a survey of 656 respondents conducted by resident Susanne Blazek, who has a doctorate in social psychology, found 75.8 percent opposed the project and 19.2 percent supported it; critics called it a self-selected sample partly shared through an opposition Facebook group. Data center supporter Rod Steele disputed the survey, saying concerns about water, electricity and noise had "been dealt with and debunked." The case remains before Goodhue County District Judge Patrick Biren, who is weighing whether the city should have ordered a fuller environmental review before construction can resume.

ft-1765219039814-2361.text: Nobles County, near Reading, Minnesota, said no to the data center, and Geronimo Power said it would look elsewhere. On April 21, 2026 the county commissioners voted 3 to 2 to uphold the planning commission's refusal to change the agricultural preservation zoning ordinance, which killed the proposal. The land is zoned for agricultural preservation, and that zoning is what stopped it. Commissioners Chris Dybevick and Robert Demuth were the two against the motion, preferring an option that upheld the refusal but also told staff to work on alternative amendments. Geronimo Power had proposed a campus in the Summit Lake, Elk, Bloom and Seward townships near Brewster and Reading, on a site of about one section, 640 acres, and possibly more, with no parcel settled when it came to the county. The campus was put at 400 to 450 megawatts of power, with a 400 megawatt facility targeted for 2030 and an end user possibly involved as early as 2027. It was pitched alongside Geronimo's Lime Creek and Plum Creek wind farms and a proposed Summit Lake solar farm near Reading, about 1,500 megawatts between them once running. The capital infrastructure was put at more than $4 billion, with hundreds of construction jobs and more than 100 permanent ones. Jordan Burmeister of Geronimo said the company's mission is to bring economic development to rural regions. After the vote, Emily Morissette, Geronimo's senior manager of marketing and communications, said: "Throughout this process we have listened and learned from local leaders and community members in Nobles County." She said the company would consider alternative options, including some other communities that have expressed interest.

ft-1763324793343-5887.text: A rezoning that could have brought a data center to 63 acres of farmland at 3815 Hinkson Creek Road, northeast of U.S. 63 and Paris Road in north Columbia, Boone County, Missouri, was blocked when the City Council split 3-3 on Nov. 17, 2025, with Sixth Ward council member Betsy Peters absent. The owner, Gordon Arbuckle, said he wanted to build a technology hub there, and the developer representing him said a data center would fall under light industry. The request, filed on behalf of the J Gordon Arbuckle Living Trust, sought to change 63.11 acres of an 83.66-acre property from agriculture to industrial, and city staff noted the applicant had said a data center may be pursued on the site. The city's Planning and Zoning Commission recommended the change in October after residents questioned putting a possible data center on working farmland. "We've seen places like Memphis and Texas, places that are already suffering from high utility rates," said Columbia resident James Gordon. Isaac Ellis, a farmer who lives southeast of the site, described cows and calves, hay storage, a big barn and a house on the land, though he added, "I think industrial land is needed in Columbia." On the night of the council vote, people handed out stickers reading "Save Farmland: No Data Center" outside the packed chamber. "There's a commodity that is being sold, bought and eaten on that farm right now, and we have no clue what will come after," Ellis told the council. The council later voted 6-0 for the city's first data center definition and zoning criteria, which require a conditional use permit for any new data center, and asked staff to bring forward a six-month pause on applications. In May 2026 it adopted a one-year moratorium instead, pausing any data center permits or plans from being processed until April 2027; the rezoning of the Arbuckle land, like any future one, is the City Council's call.

ft-1776036204429-9677.text: CRG has won approval to build a data center on about 240 acres north of Highway 67 in Festus, Jefferson County, Missouri, on land the city annexed in November 2025. The city council approved a framework of requirements for CRG on March 30, 2026, but four Festus residents and the group Wake Up JeffCo sued the city and CRG on April 9, 2026, seeking to reverse both the rezoning and the city's contract with the developer. No end user for the data center has been identified. The lawsuit accuses the city of holding unlawful private meetings with the developer to avoid Missouri's Sunshine Law. Attorney Steve Jeffery, who represents the plaintiffs, said officials met in small groups "so that they wouldn't have to comply with any of those Sunshine Law requirements." Mary Fakes, who lives 300 yards from the site and joined the suit, said she fears for her daughter's health if the project goes forward. Voters had already responded. In the April 2026 city election, all four council incumbents who backed the project were defeated by candidates who ran against it, including Dan Moore, who said: "People are awake now, and we're not going to let this continue on anymore." Opponents then filed recall petitions in May against Mayor Sam Richards and three council members who backed the project, and the council rejected them. Estimates of the project's cost have grown: officials described it in February as at least $1 billion, and by April CRG's plan was valued at $6 billion. After the June 8 council meeting, Richards said CRG had still not submitted plans or asked for permits: "We don't have any plans submitted or any permit requests." The Wake Up JeffCo lawsuit in St. Louis County Circuit Court continues, with no trial date set.

ft-1768323532709-2448.text: Nebius is building an 800 megawatt data center on about 400 acres in the Eastgate Commerce Center in Independence, Jackson County, Missouri, with construction underway since the project broke ground in May 2026. Nebius's site plan allows for up to 10 buildings that could eventually total 1.2 gigawatts, though only the approved 800 megawatt phase is under construction now. Three Independence City Council members have since lost their seats over tax breaks the city approved for the project. In March 2026, council member John Perkins was one of five who voted to approve more than $6 billion in tax breaks for the planned $150 billion data center; two others who backed the breaks, Bridget McCandless and Jared Fears, lost their races for mayor and reelection that April. On September 1, Perkins was recalled, with nearly 70% of his district voting to remove him, according to unofficial results from Jackson County. Perkins urged voters to judge him on his full record, writing in a Kansas City Star op-ed that "disagreement isn't a crime." On July 6, 2026, the Independence City Council voted 7-0 for a six month moratorium on new data center approvals, sponsored by councilman Brice Stewart; it does not affect Nebius, which was already approved, or a second pending application. Stewart said, "I understand their frustration. I don't think anybody could have imagined what a data center would be now compared to what it was then." The planning commission was due to take up zoning changes that would require large data centers, those over 2.5 megawatts, to get a special use permit instead of approval as of right, with a council vote possible as early as mid-August; no result of that vote has been published. Residents living beside the site say the moratorium came too late to help them. Daniel Moorehead, who lives on Bly Road and leads the Independence Guard Alliance, said, "When you have a moratorium that doesn't stop current items, you're effectively saying I have special interest in keeping the current items active." Howard Hoff, who has lived near the site for nearly 30 years, said, "I don't personally know that we can do anything about what's going on now," and described a nearby road closed since April 1, 2026, to make way for the project. Nebius said it has sent updates to Bly Road residents and posted guards at Bly and Bundschu roads to keep construction traffic out of the neighborhood.

ft-1782767669801-3250.text: Patmos, a Kansas City-based company, is under contract to buy an empty warehouse at 2500 Little Blue Parkway in Independence, Missouri, from developer NorthPoint and turn it into a $107 million data center. It applied for a commercial permit on June 2, 2026, before the city's later moratorium, so the company says the project can proceed. The Independence City Council voted 7-0 on July 6, 2026 for a six-month pause on new data-center approvals that exempts projects already submitted. The data center would start at 17.5 megawatts and could expand to 70 megawatts, Councilmember Brice Stewart said. "While the land is currently zoned correctly for a data center to be added there, the city does not currently have the power to supply it," Stewart wrote. Patmos vice president Monica Brisimitzakis said the company would rather buy power from the city's utility, Independence Power & Light, and pay for a grid upgrade, but could otherwise generate its own power with on-site fuel cells. Patmos hopes to break ground November 15, 2026 if it buys city power, or April 1, 2027 if it must generate its own. The building's exterior would stay the same, with data halls inside and six backup generators in a fenced yard, each rated at 93.6 decibels at 23 feet and tested for half an hour monthly. The project would use a Chapter 100 bond with payments in lieu of taxes, which Brisimitzakis said the company plans to give up later. Some residents first learned of the project from postcards inviting them to a town hall in late June 2026. Rachel Gonzalez, an organizer opposing data center construction locally, raised "significant concerns" about generator noise and air pollution and asked the city to press for answers on power demand, water use, fuel storage and future expansion. "The community deserves a transparent process and confidence that any costs or impacts associated with the project will be borne by the developer," Gonzalez said. Patmos would be Independence's second data center; Nebius is building one on about 400 acres nearby that will grow to at least 800 megawatts. Daniel Moorehead of the Independence Guard Alliance called the moratorium "only a half measure" because it exempts both the Nebius project and the Patmos application already filed. The Independence City Council still must approve any power upgrade before Patmos can move forward, and is separately weighing a zoning change that would require public review for data centers above 2.5 megawatts.

ft-1769227962763-8860.text: Neighbors have sued to undo Joplin's rezoning of land at West 20th Street and Central City Road, in Jasper County, Missouri, where Wildwood Ranch LLC wants to sell land for a data center. The Joplin City Council annexed 540 acres of the property in January 2026 and rezoned a total of 600 acres from residential to heavy industrial, and a Mokan Partnership listing puts the project's power at 200 megawatts or more. The rezoning is approved; a circuit court judge is now reviewing a lawsuit seeking to void it. The land belongs to Wildwood Ranch LLC, whose owner, James "Jimmer" Pinjuv, requested the annexation and rezoning; he has said a sale for a technology or data center site was not finalized, so he does not know who the developer or end user would be. City documents said the owner wants to sell to a developer "interested in developing the site for heavy industrial use," and the planning commission recommended approval in January 2026. About seven hours of public comment preceded the council's approval, and hundreds of residents raised the volume of water and electricity the campus might use; Pinjuv and officers of Missouri American Water and Liberty, the local electric utility, said rates would not rise, and Pinjuv said the developer or end user would pay for utility service. State Rep. Cathy Jo Loy and U.S. Rep. Eric Burlison sent letters supporting the project. The Joplin Sustainable Technology Alliance tried to force a citywide vote, gathering 2,832 signatures to repeal the annexation and 2,348 to repeal the rezoning, each far short of the roughly 5,032 required, and the council certified both petitions insufficient. "While we didn't hit the required goal of 5,032 signatures, we still showed the council that there is a lot of concern about data centers in the community," said Rebecca Collins, the alliance's director. The lawsuit comes from inside the development: Derek and Laura Snyder own two lots in Forest View Estates, a subdivision Wildwood Ranch created and sold as a quiet, nature-preserving single-family area that borders the south side of the data center land. Their suit against the city, Mayor Keenan Cortez, the council members and Wildwood Ranch LLC alleges the council fast-tracked the project without required traffic, environmental or utility studies and approved heavy industrial zoning with no site plan, though the city's own code calls heavy industry incompatible with homes. It also argues the council gave up its legislative powers by basing the rezoning on a 2009 agreement made by a prior council, and that the rezoning violates the development's own land-use agreement, which requires owners to preserve the land's natural state. The Jasper County circuit court now decides whether the rezoning stands; no ruling has been published.

ft-317.text: Project Kestrel is a planned campus of six data centers, up to 1.8 million square feet, on 379 acres of the KCI-29 industrial site north of Kansas City International Airport, in Platte County, Missouri. The developer is Shenandoah Computing LLC, which asked Port KC, Kansas City's port authority, for up to $100 billion in conduit bonds to build the campus in phases over twenty years. The end user has not been named; Port KC calls it one of the world's leading technology companies, and the Kansas City Business Journal has reported it may be linked to Google, which did not comment. KCI-29 is a Hunt Midwest logistics park at 13231 NW Roanridge Road, about an eight-minute drive from downtown Platte City. Port KC granted the project a 35-year tax abatement, and Shenandoah also sought sales tax exemptions on construction materials. Port KC says the campus will generate more than $110 million in tax revenue over the life of the bonds, against $1,400 a year from the land now, starting with $2.62 million for a new Northland Career Center. It adds a 25-cent-per-square-foot charge for workforce training, worth about $15.75 million at full build-out. Port KC says the developer will draw at least half its energy from carbon-free sources, pay standard city water and wastewater rates, and create about 50 jobs per phase paying more than $100,000 a year. "This data center represents more than just a technology investment, it's a long-term partnership with our community," said Port KC chief executive Jon Stephens. Platte County's presiding commissioner has come out against it. Scott Fricker said in November 2025 that he "can't support 'Project Kestrel'" because of the property and sales tax subsidies it gives to some of the world's largest corporations, and warned that households would end up paying for new power plants, grid upgrades and water treatment. ft-1775186170925-3942.text: Revitalization Unlimited, a Miami developer, wanted to demolish the three-story Western Newspaper Union building at 304 West 10th Street in the Quality Hill neighborhood of Kansas City, Jackson County, Missouri, and put up a 20-story, 384-foot data center with shops on the ground floor. The Kansas City Plan Commission voted 6 to 0 to reject the plan on August 5, 2026, after 55 people testified and the city received 475 letters opposing it, with none in support. Megan Haave told the commission: "It will not house, feed, or clothe residents. It will not increase civic pride or public trust." Ethan Starr, executive director of Historic Kansas City, pointed out that the building had been bought on a preservation argument: "The Western Newspaper Union's building acquisition was presented as a preservation-oriented investment ... Now, instead, the city is being asked to approve demolition." Commissioner Matt Hasek said: "It's not a productive use of downtown space. And I find it ironic, too, that the historic building that you're wanting to tear down has more productive capacity than what you're offering, almost twice as much as the 20-story building." The developer can appeal to the city council, though Mayor Quinton Lucas said a reversal was "highly unlikely and would not have my support." Two groups, Sunrise Movement KC and KC Data Center Watchdog, are pressing for a complete ban, and a data center transparency task force ordinance went to a council committee on August 11.

ft-1775149605384-7770.text: Metrobloks plans Liberty's first data center at 2515 Old Hughes Road in Liberty, Clay County, Missouri: three buildings on about 29 acres, starting with a two-story, 177,000-square-foot building that received planning permission in December 2025. The Los Angeles-based company announced the $1.4 billion campus in March 2026. The city says the three buildings are projected to use 150MW of electricity. Liberty officials approved $1.4 billion in bonds and $202.7 million in tax abatements over 25 years, and Metrobloks agreed to contribute $28 million over that time to the nonprofit Liberty Institute for Science and Ethics. Development director Brandon Smith said the city won't be on the hook to repay the bonds, which Metrobloks will buy. "We believe this is the first step in building a high-tech foundation to our city's economy going forward," Mayor Greg Canuteson said. The city says the site was already zoned industrial, so the project went through the Planning & Zoning Commission on Dec. 9, 2025, and the City Council on Dec. 15, both with public hearings, after a legal notice and letters to owners within 185 feet. The city, which says it has heard residents' concerns about data centers, says a closed-loop cooling system will put little demand on its water plant, with higher rates or reduced flow if the site exceeds set limits. The City Council has already approved the project and its incentives, and Metrobloks has not shared a timeline or a construction start.

ft-1779304562667-7801.text: Swarm Systems has paused its plan for a data center in the industrial park in Marshfield, in Webster County, Missouri. "We're going to take a beat," company official Amir Atefi told the Springfield Business Journal in May 2026, calling it "not an active project" and promising that "If we choose to reengage, we will have a public forum first before we get to any city submittals." The company had been looking at an 8.2-acre portion of a larger parcel at 630 George St., and its website showed renderings of a Missouri campus promising 20 megawatts, "ready for service in mid-2027," until the images and text were removed on May 18. A January email to the city described a building of about 60,000 square feet, up to 39.5 feet tall, with standby generators and a largest shift of about 15 employees. City administrator Sam Rost said no formal plans were submitted, and that Swarm had first asked about hooking into city facilities at an unincorporated site: "That was pretty well basically a no." On April 23 the Marshfield Board of Aldermen passed a measure requiring a conditional use permit for data centers inside the city limits, which Rost said came out of those first conversations. "Until we have something set in stone, this is just another inquiry," Rost said. Marshfield had already had its first data center fight. On May 11, 2026 hundreds of people filled the high school auditorium over a different project, a five acre facility on Rifle Range Road north of the town being built by Lumon Solutions, where site preparation had begun with no public announcement. Dale Fraker, an associate commissioner for Webster County, explained the limits of what the county could do: "Because there's not a lot of county oversight here with planning and zoning or anything like that. What folks in Webster County do with their personal property is their business." Christine Vande Griend left unconvinced: "Those answers did not put me at ease. In fact, I think it probably raised more questions than answers." Seth Atkison's worry was heat: energy that is used, he said, cannot be destroyed or created, so it has to be put somewhere. That developer said it would draw only a few gallons a day from a 500 foot well through a closed loop, and afterwards declined to comment further. If Swarm returns to the George Street site, it will need that conditional use permit from the city of Marshfield.

ft-1776913850649-9361.text: White Cloud Acres, an AI data center with a co-located 600 megawatt natural gas power plant, is planned along US Highway 71 about eight miles south of Maryville in Nodaway County, Missouri. First put at $4 billion in early 2026, the cost had grown to $6.3 billion by June, and its developer, Scale Microgrids of New Jersey, had bought the Chicago company that started the project, ReLoad, in February. A county moratorium has halted construction since July 21, 2026. The landowners here have signed nondisclosure agreements, so the county commission has discussed a project it cannot fully describe. ReLoad, a Chicago company that says it sites, designs and permits gigawatt-scale data center campuses, met Nodaway County commissioners on December 16, 2025 about land in the south of the county near Maryville, with plans for several buildings of about a million square feet each. North District Commissioner Chris Burns said the reaction was divisive, with people "either 100% for it or 100% against it," and that without zoning the county's hands are tied: "If the landowners choose to sell their land or lease their land for that purpose, without zoning, we don't have a lot of control over that." Separately, Evergy is building a 440 megawatt gas plant eight miles south of Maryville on US Highway 71, due by 2030, which the utility says is for existing demand rather than any new customer. Scale showed the plan to the public for the first time at an open house in June, and many who came left frustrated with the format. The company said the closed loop cooling would need an initial fill of 1.5 million gallons of water and that it planned to treat reclaimed water from Maryville's treatment plant on site, asking for about 100,000 gallons a day in all. Billy Mires, a retired veteran and rancher, said the sound study left out the power plant next door: "That's a lot of DBs from two sources within a mile of each other." "I have state regulations I have to follow to be a rancher," he said. "These guys have none." The county commission passed the moratorium unanimously on July 21, 2026, running six months with an option to extend six more, and blocking construction while it seeks answers on drainage, noise, light and the strain on utilities. Presiding Commissioner Bill Walker said he would also insist the facility's end user be named first, and Scale's attorney said no end user had yet been agreed. On September 15 Commissioner Burns said Scale was getting close to announcing a hyperscale partner, which could change the design, and Scale has said it plans to start construction in early 2027.

ft-1765662789346-3319.text: Construction is under way on Project Spade, a Google data center campus on the former Hoette Farms tree farm off Interstate 70 at New Florence, in Montgomery County, Missouri. The developer for the Google project is Related Digital. The county completed its administrative review in January 2026 and delivered construction permits in March, and by June excavators and dump trucks covered the site. The campus sits in the southeast quadrant of the I-70 and Highway 19 interchange, on about 780 acres in unincorporated Montgomery County and 130 acres inside New Florence. The plan was amended from three buildings of 1,080,920 square feet to two of about 800,000 square feet each, with a closed-loop air-cooled system, two on-site wells mainly for employee use, and both an Ameren substation and an applicant-owned substation. Related Digital says the campus will deliver 1.2 gigawatts of utility capacity. Google has pledged $15 billion for Missouri infrastructure including the New Florence data center, and says it will work with Ameren to add 500 megawatts of new power capacity to the state grid; the company expects 2,000 construction jobs. Across the interstate, Amazon Web Services is building Project Green, which would span roughly 1,000 acres. Amazon plans 17 buildings there; together the two campuses cover 1,900 acres of land the county made shovel-ready in 2023 with $5 million in COVID-19 recovery funds. Montgomery County agreed to a plan for Google to pay all of its real estate property taxes in exchange for a 70% abatement on personal property taxes. As late as December 2025 the company behind Project Spade had not been disclosed, and county commissioners had signed a non-disclosure agreement for the south site. “We signed an NDA, looked at over by legal council for the south project. Why? Because the people that are over here screaming right now, they would have been over there screaming at the land owners because they wanted to sell their properties,” Presiding Commissioner Ryan Poston told a heated December 2025 town hall. “Is it going to affect our well pressure? We have a lot of irrigation systems around here and they say sometimes that can affect things,” resident Tammy Ridgley asked at the same meeting. Brenda Buechele, who lives less than 3 miles from the Google site, said she had trouble with road conditions until she asked the county commission to limit traffic: “I feel like we win little battles every day, all day long.” The residents' group Preserve Montgomery County sued the county and the Missouri Department of Economic Development in February 2026 to halt the Amazon data center, claiming inadequate public notice, Sunshine Law violations and a failure to weigh the tax abatement. In September 2026 Cole County Circuit Judge Cotton Walker ruled the group has standing and can pursue most of its claims, including that the county did not adequately inform the community about the data centers' water and electricity use, while dismissing the state department from the case. More than 100 people came to the group's town hall in the Montgomery County High School gym in September. Harry Cope, a longtime resident, is running this fall for presiding commissioner against Poston, who supports the projects. The lawsuit continues against Montgomery County in Cole County Circuit Court, the latest development as of late September 2026, while construction goes on.

ft-1773978372506-6542.text: Franklin County commissioners voted on Sept. 15, 2026, to approve rezoning for Beltline's Meramec Valley Technology Park, a hyperscale data center planned on the Crooked Creek farm property along Highway O south of Pacific, Missouri, along with a second data center near Villa Ridge. BLE Landholdings, the Beltline Energy subsidiary behind it, had asked to rezone 12 parcels totaling 490 acres around 684 Phelan Road. The county's planning and zoning commission had voted 5-4 against recommending the Crooked Creek rezoning, even as it backed the Villa Ridge project. Separately, Beltline withdrew a $16 billion, 500-acre rezoning application with the city of Pacific on Aug. 7, 2026, two days after the city passed a one-year data center moratorium. Opponents also raised a possible conflict of interest, since landowner William McLaren sat on the county planning and zoning commission when the application was filed. "It's just the wrong piece of dirt and the wrong way to go about it," said Gene Elkins, who lives a few hundred yards from the site and depends on a well for water. Elkins said he does not see the vote as the end of it, and that neighbors have "several different things that might help us from a legal standpoint" to slow or stop the project.

ft-319.text: Diode Ventures planned Project Harper, the Harper Road Technology Park, as a $1.5 billion data center campus on the west side of Harper Road between 203rd Street and a future 211th Street in Peculiar, in Cass County, Missouri, beside a new Evergy substation and 345 kV transmission lines. Mayor Doug Stark revealed the 504 acre project in January 2024, and site plans showed up to seven buildings of about 300,000 square feet each. Diode executives told residents over wine slushies at the town winery in July that the campus would bring new jobs and more than $1 billion in tax revenue, most of it for the school district, while its internal documents showed it was seeking 25 year tax abatements for a data center creating about 100 jobs. Emails released under a public records request show Diode had been working with Stark and city administrator Mickey Ary since September 2023, and both men signed a nondisclosure agreement with a data center company called IPI before meeting the client. Becky Wiseman, whose land abuts the site, said Diode required neighbors to sign nondisclosure agreements to keep talking, and after visiting Meta and Google campuses in Nebraska and Iowa she described them as "Like living next to a maximum-security prison." Chad Buck and his neighbor Vicki Howe started a Facebook page called Don't Dump Data on Peculiar that quickly passed 1,000 members, and meetings moved from City Hall to the Lions Club to fit the crowds. At a September meeting Stark told the room, "I hope everyone understands that while shooting from the hip like this, you're destroying any future development that might want to come to Peculiar," and talk of a recall petition followed, though none was formally submitted. Patti DiPardo Livergood, who lived next to the site, told the aldermen she had taken her home off the market after the data center scared off buyers. In October 2024 the Board of Aldermen, before a standing room crowd, took out the data center definition it had earlier added to the light industrial zoning code, so data centers are no longer permitted in the city. The six member board's vote was unanimous, and Peculiar became one of the earliest documented communities in the country to defeat a data center through grassroots pushback. Diode later said it would not discuss Peculiar because there was no active application. "You're not going to stop progress," said Glenn Yoakum, who runs a farm feed store downtown. "But they should make sure it's at least a good deal for the town."

ft-1774580479532-3628.text: Geronimo Power, based in Bloomington, Minnesota, is evaluating land south of the La Russell Energy Center in eastern Jasper County, Missouri, for a 400 megawatt data center park, plus a solar and battery farm to power it. The company told the Sarcoxie City Council about the project on March 3, but the site is outside city limits, so the council has no say. Whether Jasper County grants Geronimo tax breaks called Chapter 100 bonds is the open question, after commissioners told residents in March they opposed any such deal. In March 2026 the Jasper County Commission signed a letter to Geronimo Power saying it was "unanimously opposed to any special tax treatment including Chapter 100 bonds for this or any development in Jasper County." By September, Rhys Hine said, Commissioner Jimmy Morris had told him the commission was now looking at Chapter 100 bonds at the company's request: "We just want them to be true to their word." The commission did not respond to KOAM's requests for comment. Its own project page says the data center would use about 400 megawatts and promises closed-loop cooling, with sound at the property line similar to a household dishwasher. The solar farm and batteries would cover about 2,000 acres west and north of La Russell, 1,360 of them in Jasper County and 640 in Lawrence County, and could generate about 150 megawatts. Ryan Butterfield, Geronimo's vice president of strategy, told the Lawrence County Record that the solar would cover only part of the load, so another power project would be needed or the data center would draw from the grid, and that neither project had yet found a customer. Rhys Hine, who owns land within about half a mile of the site, heard about the project from a co-worker at the March 3 council meeting, posted the company's map on Facebook and started a group, "Say No to Data Centers: Keep Jasper and Lawrence Counties Rural," that drew 679 members in its first week. Hine said water use was the big worry, since "we're all in wells out there, so the water table will deplete," and listed noise and light pollution as well. "Ultimately, we want to be where people want us and see value in what we're doing," Butterfield said, after dozens of residents turned out against the plan at the Lawrence County Commission on March 30. "Come talk to us. Our doors are open," said Lindsay Smith, Geronimo's vice president of external affairs. Jasper County has no zoning, and Commissioner Jimmy Morris said, "Since we have no zoning, our main role is just being an advocate," pointing to road and decommissioning agreements. By late May opponents were pressing the county to use section 192.300 of state law, which lets a county of its class write ordinances on public health. A coalition, Southwest Missouri Citizens Against Data Centers, held a town hall at the Gene Taylor Community Building in Sarcoxie on May 28, raising utility bills, well water, noise and health. No date has been set for the Jasper County Commission to vote on the Chapter 100 bond request.

ft-320.text: Project Cumulus was a data center proposed by the developers Clayco and CRG on 440 acres near Elm Point Road and Route 370 in St. Charles, St. Charles County, Missouri, on top of the Elm Point well field that supplies the city's drinking water. The developer withdrew the project after public pushback, and on May 19, 2026, the St. Charles City Council voted 7 to 1 to ban data centers anywhere in the city, making permanent a one-year moratorium adopted in fall 2025. The city's seven wells can produce more than six million gallons a day, but four have been shut down, two of them in 2022 after chemicals from nearby properties leaked into the groundwater, and the Environmental Protection Agency is overseeing the cleanup. The end user was never named, described only as a Fortune 100 company, in what project officials called a $1 billion deal. Project spokesperson Korb Maxwell said: "This is the new base of the economy." Scott Stratton-Henderson, a neighboring resident and Lindenwood University student, started an online petition in August 2025 that gathered more than 5,000 signatures inside a week, raising concerns over diesel stored on the site, flooding and runoff, generator noise, emissions, light and traffic. "Everyone is under a non-disclosure agreement. There is just so much risk as opposed to reward around this project," he said. The county's Planning and Zoning Commission had partly recommended the project for approval on July 14, 2025, but denied the permit needed to store diesel fuel near the wells. The St. Charles City Council was set to decide on August 19, 2025, whether to grant that conditional use permit for diesel storage and well-treatment chemicals; the developer withdrew before a vote happened. Ward 3 councilman Vince Ratchford called the May 2026 ban "a straightforward step that closes a gap in the code and provides clarity for residents, staff, and applicants." Stratton-Henderson went on to found a nonprofit on accountability, transparency and integrity in the city.

ft-1782841054762-7833.text: Capstone Technology Campus, a company owned by St. Joseph businessman Steve Craig, has withdrawn its applications for the STJ Data Center campus, which would have annexed about 130 acres at 6321 Pickett Road into the city and rezoned that land and 5701 Pickett Road in Buchanan County, Missouri. "At the developer's request, both applications have been withdrawn," the city of St. Joseph said on June 26, 2026, adding that any future proposal would need new applications. The campus would have had four data center buildings and a substation, developed by Atmosphere Data Centers, an operator led by Chuck McBride, formerly of Radius DC. The developer's fact sheet promised more than 1,000 construction jobs, 150 to 250 permanent jobs and an estimated $50 million a year in taxes. Opponents cited the environment, noise and the limited economic payoff, and argued the land would suit other development better; two petitions against it drew more than 720 and 1,500 signatures. "They need sewer, they need water, they need city infrastructure. Anything going in there would," Eastern District Commissioner Scott Burnham said, since the site would need annexation into St. Joseph to get city utilities. On July 20, 2026, the St. Joseph City Council voted 8-0 for an emergency ordinance pausing all applications to build or expand data centers in the city for 12 months while it hires outside help to update its zoning code. Many residents had asked for 18 months and a citizens advisory committee, and City Manager Mike Schumacher said a work session on forming that committee would be held in August 2026. Any new plan for the site would have to wait out the pause, then start over with new applications through the city's standard review, ending with the City Council.

sentences.t: Capstone Technology Campus, a company owned by St. Joseph businessman Steve Craig, has withdrawn its applications for the STJ Data Center campus, which would have annexed about 130 acres at 6321 Pickett Road into the city and rezoned that land and 5701 Pickett Road in Buchanan County, Missouri.
"At the developer's request, both applications have been withdrawn," the city of St. Joseph said on June 26, 2026, adding that any future proposal would need new applications.
The campus would have had four data center buildings and a substation, developed by Atmosphere Data Centers, an operator led by Chuck McBride, formerly of Radius DC.
The developer's fact sheet promised more than 1,000 construction jobs, 150 to 250 permanent jobs and an estimated $50 million a year in taxes.
Opponents cited the environment, noise and the limited economic payoff, and argued the land would suit other development better; two petitions against it drew more than 720 and 1,500 signatures.

"They need sewer, they need water, they need city infrastructure. Anything going in there would," Eastern District Commissioner Scott Burnham said, since the site would need annexation into St. Joseph to get city utilities.

On July 20, 2026, the St. Joseph City Council voted 8-0 for an emergency ordinance pausing all applications to build or expand data centers in the city for 12 months while it hires outside help to update its zoning code.
Many residents had asked for 18 months and a citizens advisory committee, and City Manager Mike Schumacher said a work session on forming that committee would be held in August 2026.

ft-1781278847242-2340.text: The former Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield building at 1831 Chestnut Street in downtown St. Louis, Missouri, which housed the insurer's primary Missouri data center for 32 years, has been empty since January 1, 2026 and was sold this summer at a court-ordered auction. The building is in downtown St. Louis city, beside Energizer Park and Enterprise Center and near the redeveloped Union Station. The six-storey property sits on a 4.24-acre site and has 53,000 square feet of data center space, with two interior generators, one exterior generator and two Liebert cooling units, according to a Colliers brochure cited by DCD in June 2026. The building was in receivership, and Newmark and RI Marketplace offered Unit 1 of the 1831 Chestnut Condominium, 336,392 square feet covering the lower level and floors 1 to 5 and 8 to 9, for the court-appointed receiver with a starting bid of $250,000; floors 6 and 7 are separately owned. RI Marketplace says the property was part of its June 24, 2026 auction and resulted in a transaction that closed in 42 days, but the buyer and price have not been reported. The sellers pitched it for office lease-up, "data center re-use or expansion," residential conversion, hotels or education, so it is not known whether any data center use will resume. Any new data center use would now fall under rules St. Louis passed this month. On Sept. 11, 2026 the Board of Aldermen passed comprehensive data center regulations that restrict where new data centers can be built, limit noise and heat, and require renewable energy, plus a companion bill banning city tax incentives for data center projects. "The people of St. Louis have been pretty clear, by and large, about how they feel about data centers, and it's our job as representatives to listen to the people we represent," said Alderwoman Anne Schweitzer. An amendment adopted in July created a case-by-case path for some downtown buildings to exceed a 30% cap on ground-floor building use if they sign a community benefit agreement with the city. The regulations went to Mayor Cara Spencer for her signature after the vote.

ft-323.text: The Netrality data center at 210 North Tucker Boulevard in downtown St. Louis, Missouri, is the city's main carrier hotel, an operating building where competing networks physically connect. Netrality has run the building since 2016, when it bought it and 900 Walnut Street from Digital Realty, along with 365 Data Centers' colocation space inside 210 North Tucker. The building offers 442,000 square feet of colocation space, more than 61 network providers, and a carrier-neutral meet-me room where those networks connect to each other. In 2022 Netrality added two data halls totaling 11,600 square feet at the building, Data Center Dynamics reported. "St. Louis' rapidly evolving market in technology, biotech, and healthcare will increase the demand for edge computing in the state," Netrality's chief revenue officer, Amber Caramella, said at the time. St. Louis passed its first citywide data center rules on September 11, 2026, after a larger fight over a separate, much bigger data center planned for the old Famous-Barr warehouse in Midtown. The rules limit where new data centers can be built, cap noise and heat, require renewable energy and bar city tax incentives for data centers. Under the ordinance, data centers already operating continue as legal nonconforming uses, but any enlargement, including more backup generator capacity, must fully comply with the new rules.

ft-325.text: Netrality's data center at 900 Walnut Street in downtown St. Louis, Missouri, is an operating carrier hotel and colocation building that the company pairs with its larger interconnection hub at 210 North Tucker. Netrality and TierPoint both run data centers near 11th and Olive downtown. Netrality markets 900 Walnut to network operators, cloud providers and enterprises, offering space from single cabinets to private suites and direct links to six cloud connection providers, including Cloudflare, Megaport and Zayo CloudLink. The company describes itself as the largest privately held owner of core interconnection facilities in the U.S. On September 11, 2026, the St. Louis Board of Aldermen passed zoning rules restricting where new data centers can be built, limiting noise and heat, and requiring renewable energy, plus a companion bill banning city tax incentives for data centers. "The people of St. Louis have been pretty clear, by and large, about how they feel about data centers, and it's our job as representatives to listen to the people we represent," said Alderwoman Anne Schweitzer, the bill's sponsor. The rules classify data centers by size, cap ground-floor data center use in most buildings at 30%, and allow exceptions for buildings that sign a community benefit agreement with the city. Existing data centers, including 900 Walnut, continue as legal nonconforming uses, though any enlargement must fully comply. The bill now goes to Mayor Cara Spencer for her signature.

ft-324.text: St. Louis's Board of Public Service gave final approval on April 21, 2026 to a data center planned inside the former Famous-Barr warehouse on Market Street in St. Louis, a $3 billion conversion with the neighboring Armory building becoming offices. St. Louis Magazine reported the data center would total 120 megawatts of power, and under the approval it is expected to open by the end of 2028. The approval carries unusual conditions: cooling must run as a closed loop with air-cooled chillers, at least half the power must come from renewable sources within five years, and there can be no on-site generators in normal operation. Backup power must come from batteries, noisy equipment must be enclosed, and the roofs must be green, cool or solar. The city projects $27.4 million in first-year tax revenue for itself and $33.4 million for St. Louis Public Schools, according to the mayor's office. Mayor Cara Spencer said she shares concerns about data centers but that the city negotiated hard on what it could control: "As mayor, I cannot responsibly ignore the amount of good this amount of tax revenue will do for city services, SLPS students and some of the most important amenities and services that our community depends on." Opponents watched from a City Hall conference room while the board met electronically, without public comment. The approval came while St. Louis was still writing separate zoning rules for data centers, and the project was exempt from those draft rules.

ft-322.text: TierPoint's St. Louis-Olive data center at 1111 Olive Street in downtown St. Louis, Missouri, is an operating colocation facility the company took over when it bought Cosentry in January 2016. The building is in the city of St. Louis, and it was converted into a data center by Xiolink, which bought it in 2009, before passing to Cosentry in 2014. TierPoint lists more than 124,000 square feet in total and more than 11,000 square feet of raised floor, backed by two redundant generators with at least 48 hours of runtime. The site is linked by 10G waves to TierPoint's other data centers in the region, including its Millpark Drive site in St. Louis. TierPoint is also growing downtown: in August 2024 it bought the 135,800-square-foot former NSI Building at 2300 Locust Street to convert into a data center in phases, with an unnamed Fortune 100 anchor tenant and up to $150 million of investment. When the city first debated data centers in September 2025, First Alert 4 noted that two already stood off 11th and Olive, TierPoint's and Netrality's. Mayor Cara Spencer said then that she supported a pause but not a ban, citing concerns about the environment and utility prices, and Planning Commission head Don Roe wrote that the city needed regulations quickly or a pause. The city chose rules, and on Sept. 11, 2026 the Board of Aldermen passed comprehensive data center regulations that restrict where new data centers can be built, limit noise and heat, require renewable energy, and bar city tax incentives for data center projects. Earlier amendments, over the objections of sponsors Anne Schweitzer and Alisha Sonnier, let developers seek a waiver from the 10-year 100% renewable energy requirement. In the version the Planning Commission approved on June 10, 2026, any data center lawfully in use when the rules take effect becomes an existing nonconforming use that may continue, but enlargements, including more backup generator capacity, must fully comply. The regulations went to Mayor Spencer for her signature after the Sept. 11 vote.

ft-1782184685957-7279.text: Crusoe, a Denver-based AI company, wants to build a $4.5 billion data center on 200 acres in the northwest Kingdom City area of Callaway County, Missouri. "It's not an absolute done deal," Western District Commissioner Christopher Scott said in late July 2026, adding that to his knowledge there had been no land purchase and no agreement with the water district. Crusoe's site plan has changed more than once, from one 800,000-square-foot building to two shown at a July open house, and Scott said it may become three smaller buildings. Callaway County has no planning and zoning outside its towns, so it has no say over whether the data center is built on private land; its main lever is taxes. Presiding Commissioner Gary Jungermann said the commission wants a Chapter 100 agreement, a tax abatement that is also a contract guaranteeing payments, with no abatement on real estate but close to an 80 percent abatement on the servers. Power may decide the matter: Crusoe plans to connect through Callaway Electric Cooperative, which Jungermann said has told the county there is no additional power available. "Until there's more generation brought on, it kind of imposes its own moratorium for where we're at," Scott said, and the water district would also need larger pipes before the data center could connect. The deals still to come are with Callaway Electric Cooperative, the water district and the county commission on the tax agreement.

ft-1773978119961-7743.text: The Franklin County Commission voted on Sept. 15, 2026, to approve rezoning for Provident Data Centers' Gateway Digital Campus near Villa Ridge, Missouri, by the Shaw Nature Reserve off Interstate 44, along with a second data center project south of Pacific. Provident's proposal rezones about 575 acres of agricultural land at Diamond Farms on Robertsville Road for the data center development. The county planning and zoning commission first took up both projects on March 17 in a meeting at Union High School that ran nearly 11 hours, with about 174 speakers, the vast majority opposed, before adjourning at 4:39 a.m. without a vote. "I really love my sleep but I love my community more. And that's why I'm still here at 4 a.m.," Elisabeth Bennett said. On April 21 the commission voted 5-4 to recommend rezoning Diamond Farms and 5-4 against the Crooked Creek site near Pacific. "We did not intend to move to an industrial complex, a hyper-scale data center," said Max Baxa, who represents residents of Desloge Estates near the Diamond Farms site. Before the final vote, Dana Bowers of Pacific, whose parents live next to the Villa Ridge project, said: "I want them to just say no." She objected that the latest county rules measure the 1,000-foot setback from an inhabited home rather than a property line. The county's new data center rules add noise standards, construction hours and a development agreement with fines of $20,000 a day and a $10 million escrow, and opponents near the Pacific site say they are weighing legal steps to slow or stop the projects.

ft-1782184370358-2124.text: The Warrenton Board of Aldermen approved Crusoe's site plan for a data center campus of about 337 acres at 22151 NW Service Road in Warrenton, Warren County, Missouri, voting 6 to 0 on January 20, 2026. The approved plan is two 805,000-square-foot data center buildings and a 40,000-square-foot administration building, with the first building and administration building due in 2027 and the second in 2028. Crusoe's Matt Fields told the board the project would be "the largest private investment in the city's history" and committed to seek no abatement of real property or gross receipts taxes. Resident Laura Gierer, whose property touches the site's eastern edge, told the board, "The county residents surrounding this parcel have been ignored and forgotten," and asked for the vote to be tabled. Alderman Christine Wait objected that Crusoe's environmental site assessment would stay confidential: "It just screams to me there is something in there that you don't want us to see." In April 2026 the board voted 4 to 2 for a Chapter 100 plan giving Crusoe a 75 percent abatement of personal property tax on the computing equipment, with the city's cost-benefit analysis putting that equipment at about $8.366 billion. Newly elected alderman Josh Chandler called the 75 percent abatement too high, while project backers projected $77.8 million a year in new property tax, most of it for the Warren County R-III School District. Computer equipment is due to start going in from spring 2027, and Crusoe's Conor Bates has said its environmental studies remain confidential under an agreement with the landowner.

ft-327.text: AVAIO Digital Partners is building the Taurus Data Center Hub, a $6 billion, 116-megawatt data center campus on 329 acres in Brandon, Rankin County, Mississippi, east of Jackson. AVAIO announced the project on August 19, 2025, broke ground in September 2025 with Yates Construction building it and Entergy Mississippi supplying power, and its project page now targets first occupancy in August 2027. The Mississippi Development Authority cleared the project for the state's Data Center Enterprises tax exemption, and AVAIO is also seeking a fee in lieu of property tax that needs sign-off from the county, the city and the development authority. Rankin First, the county's economic development group, estimates about $23 million a year in new local tax revenue once the campus is on the rolls, most of it for the school district; AVAIO promises at least 60 direct jobs, water-efficient cooling, rainwater recapture and rooftop solar. Nathan Rester, who lives a few miles from the site with his wife, Larkyn Collier, and their toddler, started a Change.org petition asking county leaders to guarantee no rise in utility bills or pollution; it had nearly 1,000 signatures by late October 2025. "People genuinely just want answers and transparency here. And they want safeguards in place," Rester said. "I'm even more concerned about the secrecy surrounding this process," resident Bailey Henry said. "If this is such a great development for Mississippi, then why have Mississippians been kept in the dark on this?" Rankin First's project page reports an independent noise study found ambient levels near the closest neighborhood of 42 to 56 decibels, expects the campus to stay within city noise limits, and says AVAIO has set up a Community Advisory Group. Brandon Mayor Butch Lee called the investment a "major step forward for Brandon," and Gov. Tate Reeves' office said the state reviews data center projects "on a case-by-case basis to ensure Mississippi has the resources needed to sustain them."

ft-1773980337121-4985.text: On March 23, 2026 Clarksdale's Board of Mayor and Commissioners rezoned 648 acres between the Sunflower River, U.S. 278, Tallahatchie Street and the Roundyard neighborhood from commercial and agricultural to light industrial, the first step in what the city calls "The Data Center Project." The vote did not approve a data center, and its capacity, layout and end user are unknown. Clarksdale is the county seat of Coahoma County, Mississippi, near the Arkansas line. The rezoning application, filed in December 2025 by local surveyor Terry Smith for three landowners, did not mention a data center, according to court records. Residents' complaint says Jon Levingston of the Crossroads Economic Partnership spoke for the project at the planning commission without naming its use, citing a nondisclosure agreement; the commission recommended approval 4 to 2. Any developer must pay a one-time $5 million impact fee, cover utility upgrades, obtain emissions permits and keep a buffer of at least 1,000 feet from residential districts. Curtis Boschert of Clarksdale Public Utilities said a data center could bring a tenfold increase in demand on the city's grid. Hundreds came to a March public forum, and most speakers opposed the project. "We got plenty of companies who come to Clarksdale, get their tax cuts, and stay around long enough to get paid back and leave," said resident Voneshay Walker. About 15 residents have since sued the city, alleging the public was not properly told the land's intended use; the case is pending. It still has to go back before the Planning Commission and the board before construction could begin, according to an official close to the matter.

ft-1782768383796-6279.text: On August 11, 2026, the Starkville Planning and Zoning Commission denied a zoning exemption that would have let Starkville Energy LLC build a cryptocurrency mining data center on Industrial Park Road in Oktibbeha County, Mississippi. The commission found the application lacked transparency and had not addressed residents' concerns. Mandy Jiang, a representative for the project, told the commission it would use at most 73,000 gallons of water a day in the hotter months. Jiang later told the Commercial Dispatch that Starkville Energy plans to keep pursuing the project, with more transparency, because of the money already invested. The plant would have drawn up to 30 megawatts of power, making it Starkville Utilities' second-largest customer after Mississippi State University, on about half of a seven-acre plot near a utility substation. In June, Starkville Utilities Director Edward Kemp put water usage at up to 20,000 gallons a day, less than a tenth of one percent of the utility's capacity; by the August hearing Jiang gave a higher hot-weather figure of up to 73,000 gallons a day. Mayor Lynn Spruill had been open to the project. "The revenue that we get from the business is such that we would not necessarily have to do a rate increase to cover some of our capital costs," she told the Dispatch. About $800,000 was to pay for the transmission line from the substation to the site, under three separate power agreements. Ward 1 Alderwoman Kim Moreland asked for a safeguard: a clause letting the city "shut power off to that data center" and supply Starkville residents instead if something failed on the Tennessee Valley Authority's end. Opponents included Ward 3 resident Carys Snyder, Mississippi State professor Jane Moorhead, former resident Lishman Heathcock and members of the Oktibbeha Humane Society. Heathcock dismissed the tax argument: "The crypto mine would've brought in tax money; however, any job would bring tax money." Douglass Carswell, president of the Mississippi Center for Public Policy, said most arguments against data centers focus more on an anti-free-market ideology than on environmental and economic concerns, while Josh Wotten of the Tennessee Valley Authority said the center would not strain Starkville's grid.

ft-1783825074231-3258.text: Krambu, an Idaho company, applied to build a data center in the former UFP Edge building at the Bonner Mill Industrial Park in Bonner, Missoula County, Montana, where a cryptocurrency mine ran from 2017 to 2020. Because the site sits within 500 feet of a residential property boundary, the county's Consolidated Land Use Board had to review the project before any permit could be issued, with a hearing set for July 1, 2026. On July 6, 2026, Mike Heisey, general manager of the industrial park, withdrew his signature from Krambu's application, leaving the project withdrawn: "Bonner Property will not be moving forward with the data center proposed by them." Krambu's application said the facility would start at about 7 megawatts of power and could grow to as much as 100 megawatts, and county zoning required the power to come from a new renewable source. The data center would run around the clock with no regular staff, using a closed loop cooling system with evaporative and dry towers; the evaporative towers would need about 500 gallons of water to fill and be recharged three or four times a year. More than 100 people came to a University of Montana panel on May 19, 2026 to raise concerns about the project. "If we aren't diligent and firm and seeking strong sideboards around data centers, we could end up paying the financial and environmental cost, with the economic benefits largely accruing to out-of-state tech billionaires," said Derek Goldman of the North West Energy Coalition, who helped organize the panel. Anne Hedges of the Montana Environmental Information Center said three data centers seeking to connect to NorthWestern Energy were together asking for 1,400 megawatts of power by 2030: "It's mind-numbing to think that we would have to provide that much power to these companies. We simply cannot supply this amount of energy." County planner Jennie Dixon said she had encouraged Krambu to stay the course, asking, "wouldn't it be fantastic if Missoula could be the poster child for how to do a data center the right way?" County officials said the issues found while reviewing Krambu's application partly prompted a proposed interim zoning pause on new or expanding data centers; commissioners were set to vote on it July 9, 2026, and no result has been published in the sources reviewed.

ft-1775695533341-7374.text: Quantica Infrastructure began construction in September 2026 on its data center campus on a nearly 8-square-mile property outside the town of Broadview, in Yellowstone County, Montana. Quantica Infrastructure is planning a 5,000 acre campus it calls Big Sky Digital Infrastructure, starting at 500 megawatts of renewable power and battery storage and expandable to a gigawatt, with construction expected to begin in 2026. In July 2025 NorthWestern Energy announced a letter of intent to supply up to 1,000 megawatts to the project. NorthWestern supplies about 760 megawatts on an average day and peaks at around 1,300. The utility says folding the data center into its regulated business will "improve cost efficiency by spreading the fixed costs of operating Montana-based energy infrastructure across a broader customer base". Anne Hedges, who runs the Montana Environmental Information Center, does not accept that: "We have what we need. Adding [new data centers] to the system should cost them, not us." Alana Lake, executive director of the Montana Public Service Commission, said: "New data center loads of this size represent a significant change to NorthWestern's energy service obligation." NorthWestern's chief financial officer Crystal Lail had argued in a March 2025 letter that the commission has no legal authority to require approval for a large new customer, citing House Bill 25 and the Reintegration Act; the commission says it is watching closely but has opened no docket. Quantica's founders are Damon Obie, a Montanan, and John Chesser, with Charlie Baker as chief financial officer. The company describes hundreds of miles of new fibre-ready underground conduit and diverse routes to major metropolitan areas. No tenant is named in its announcement, which describes the campus as serving AI, hyperscale and data center operators generally. NorthWestern was at the same time negotiating with TAC Data Centers for 600 megawatts near Great Falls and Atlas Power for 150 megawatts in Butte, the Butte project expected to be running within the year. Postcards mailed to residents said the company began staging equipment in early September 2026, with access roads and a well first and drilling possibly “as early as the end of September.” Opponents have crowded into county commission meetings to boo commissioners and demand action, but Yellowstone County Attorney Scott Twito advised against the interim zoning Missoula County adopted in July, saying any county move to stop the project would trigger a lawsuit and possibly hefty fines. Quantica plans to draw water from the deep Madison Aquifer, 1,300 feet below the Eagle Aquifer that Broadview homes use, and expects to need up to 150,000 gallons a day during construction and 20,000 a day once operating. Retired Montana Tech professor Jon Reiten said the deep well should not affect shallower wells if done properly, but warned the water is salty and its treatment waste costly to dispose of: “if they just dump it on the ground up there, it's not going to be good.” Quantica signed a June 2026 agreement to use local union labor where possible, but the building trades council said job numbers and wages will not be known until Quantica secures an end user to buy the facility.

Retired Montana Tech professor Jon Reiten said the deep well should not affect shallower wells if done properly, but warned the water is salty and its treatment waste costly to dispose of: “if they just dump it on the ground up there, it's not going to be good.”
