Quantica Infrastructure is planning a 5,000 acre campus it calls Big Sky Digital Infrastructure, starting at 500 megawatts of renewable power and battery storage and expandable to a gigawatt, with construction expected to begin in 2026.
In July 2025 NorthWestern Energy announced a letter of intent to supply up to 1,000 megawatts to the project.
NorthWestern supplies about 760 megawatts on an average day and peaks at around 1,300.

The utility says folding the data center into its regulated business will "improve cost efficiency by spreading the fixed costs of operating Montana-based energy infrastructure across a broader customer base".
Anne Hedges, who runs the Montana Environmental Information Center, does not accept that: "We have what we need. Adding [new data centers] to the system should cost them, not us."
Alana Lake, executive director of the Montana Public Service Commission, said: "New data center loads of this size represent a significant change to NorthWestern's energy service obligation."

NorthWestern's chief financial officer Crystal Lail had argued in a March 2025 letter that the commission has no legal authority to require approval for a large new customer, citing House Bill 25 and the Reintegration Act; the commission says it is watching closely but has opened no docket.
Quantica's founders are Damon Obie, a Montanan, and John Chesser, with Charlie Baker as chief financial officer.
The company describes hundreds of miles of new fibre-ready underground conduit and diverse routes to major metropolitan areas.
No tenant is named in its announcement, which describes the campus as serving AI, hyperscale and data center operators generally.

ft-1765288165990-8143.text: Sabey Data Centers has backed out of its plan for a data center at the Montana Connections business park in Butte, Silver Bow County, Montana. Silicon producer REC Silicon used a right of first refusal to buy part of the land in April 2026, ending Sabey's agreement to buy about 600 acres at German Gulch Road and Rick Jones Way. The plan called for two buildings of 500,000 square feet each, under an option to buy the city-county had agreed to in April 2025. "This could be upwards of over $1 billion of investment into our community," said J.P. Gallagher, the Butte-Silver Bow chief executive. NorthWestern Energy had cleared Sabey to use 50 megawatts, with eventual expansion to 250. "250 megawatts is approximately one-third of what Northwestern Energy is serving all of its Montana customers currently," said Ben Catton of the Montana Environmental Information Center, which wants state regulators to put data centers in their own rate class so households do not subsidize them. Sabey said it would use under 30 million gallons of water a year from Silver Lake, not connected to Butte's drinking water; community organizer Sarah Borduin wanted that written into a contract. Gallagher told the Montana State Exponent after the sale that Sabey was still looking at sites in southwest Montana, including Silver Bow and Deer Lodge counties.

ft-329.text: Ardent TAC Data Centers, an Atlanta company, proposed Project Cardinal in June 2025: a 2 million square foot data center campus on 569 acres next to the AgriTech Park in Great Falls, Cascade County, Montana, seeking 500 to 600 megawatts of power and costing $1 billion to $1.5 billion. It was the largest data center proposed in Montana at the time, but that much power was not readily available in northcentral Montana, and TAC dropped the proposal by the fall of 2025. The withdrawal did not end the debate. On July 28, 2026, the Golden Triangle Resource Council brought Cascade County commissioners a petition with about 250 signatures asking the county to press state regulators on consumer protections and to adopt its own moratorium on hyperscale data centers until rules exist. "We had a petition that about 250 signed that they want the county commission to take some steps to safeguard ourselves, our pocketbook and our natural resources and put some positive steps in place before the hyperscale lands on us," council member Steve Grout said. Fellow member Gordon Whirry asked commissioners to schedule a public hearing on the request "quite soon." Commissioners had not set a hearing date or voted on the moratorium request by the time of that meeting, and no county decision on it has been published since. Great Falls Development Alliance president Brett Doney described a different response to the cancelled project: "We formed a data center task force to learn about the potential benefits and potential negative impacts, so if we do have another proposed data center project, we're better informed."

ft-331.text: DartPoints' Asheville data center, AVL01, is an operating colocation facility in the Biltmore Park Technology Center at 100 Technology Drive in Asheville, Buncombe County, North Carolina. The company lists 23,000 square feet of white space, 1.5 MW of utility power, 2,050 kW of generators, 975 kW of UPS and a 330-ton cooling system, with seven network providers and five fiber entries. DartPoints pitches the site's location on a high plateau between the Great Smoky and Blue Ridge mountains as natural protection against severe weather. Asheville now has a pause on new data centers. In June 2026 city leaders approved a one-year moratorium on all new data centers, regardless of size, because the city's Unified Development Ordinance had no definition or rules for them, and city staff cited the strain on electric and water utilities and the noise and heat data centers can put on neighbors. Planners are to spend the first three months mapping where data centers would cause the least conflict, then up to nine more writing standards on buffers, soundproofing and daily water use before the council adopts final rules. Data centers "are forever," Mayor Esther Manheimer said, "so I think we need to take a pause and make sure we put in measures that address all the concerns that we have as a community." Local officials doubt the area suits large data centers: "Data centers look for cheap, flat land, two things that are rare in our area," said Buncombe County planning director Nathan Pennington, whose county restricted data centers in 2024 after a moratorium. Asheville's water system can supply about 40 million gallons a day against average demand of about 25 million, but a city spokesperson warned that running treatment at full throttle can only be done in short bursts. The moratorium covers new data centers while the rules are written, and the Asheville City Council will adopt the final zoning.

ft-1768322840623-4794.text: The Fort Bragg data center is an Army proposal to lease unused land on the North Carolina base to a private developer for an AI data center; as of July 2026 it remained a solicitation with no developer chosen. The Army offered six sites on the base, which spans Cumberland and Harnett counties, ranging from 78 to 205 acres and totaling 734 acres, with proposals due January 22, 2026. Procurement documents describe the sites as mostly pine and hardwood forest, rate the base's water risk as "High," and note that several possible locations sit within a mile of civilian areas and half a mile of civilian housing. The Army's terms differ from commercial projects off base: proposals must include net-zero water use and a power plan that does not draw on the local grid, and bidders must describe local outreach and assess "any risks or opposition" to the project. Of the four Army bases the Army sought bids for in January, only two had picked developers by March: Carlyle at Fort Bliss, Texas, and CyrusOne at Dugway Proving Ground, Utah, each in exclusive negotiations on projects estimated at about $2 billion; Fort Bragg was not among them. Any Fort Bragg lease is the Army's decision, with the Army Corps of Engineers negotiating terms and conducting environmental review for whichever site is selected; the Association of Defense Communities plans further discussion of military data centers at its Installation Innovation Forum in October 2026.

ft-1786993215278-6354.text: Beacon Partners, which owns the 13-acre site at 3101 Jones Sausage Road in southeast Raleigh, Wake County, North Carolina, withdrew its request for the city to annex the land on August 15, 2026, canceling that week's planned City Council hearing. About 70 or more residents had signed up to speak about the proposed data center, and hundreds of emails poured into council members' inboxes once the agenda went public, according to council member Mitchell Silver. Beacon Partners later said it is not the developer: "We have no involvement in the proposed development project," Walker Gorham of Beacon Partners said, adding that the firm sold the parcel under contract in 2025. The withdrawn plan called for a three-story, 100,000-square-foot building on land already zoned for industrial mixed use, valued at about $180 million, roughly two miles from Interstate 40 near Rock Quarry Road and Big Branch Creek. The Parrish Manor neighborhood sits across the road and the Chelmshire Downs subdivision about 1,000 feet away. "The vast majority were opposed," Silver said of the residents who signed up to speak. Who, if anyone, is now planning to develop the site is unclear.

ft-1776888239501-7805.text: The Vance County Board of Commissioners voted 6-1 on April 20, 2026, at a special meeting, to rezone a 40-acre parcel on US-158 Business near Henderson, Vance County, North Carolina, potentially clearing the way for a data center there from developer Natelli Investments. The county planning board had approved the rezoning unanimously in March, and commissioners postponed a decision at their April 6 meeting before approving it two weeks later; Natelli has not said what it will build and has not confirmed the rezoning is for a data center. At the meeting, one resident shouted, "You just sold out. I'm leaving. I'm leaving. But shame on all of you and every single one of you up here," drawing applause from other attendees. When another resident asked commissioners to say who cast the lone vote against the rezoning, the board declined, calling it not "appropriate." Natelli Investments pulled out of a much larger project the month before, withdrawing its 250 megawatt New Hill Digital Campus in Apex, beside the Shearon Harris nuclear plant, after opposition from residents and the town government. Little is known about Natelli Investments LLC beyond its link to Natelli Communities, a developer of residential and commercial property in the Southeast. Residents later raised their concerns about the Henderson-area proposal, along with drought and data center water use, at a rural listening session Governor Josh Stein's office held in Henderson on April 29. Whatever Natelli proposes next will still need separate permitting approval from Vance County.

ft-1786991748772-7428.text: WhiteFiber's NC-1 data center in Madison, Rockingham County, North Carolina, is a retrofit of the former Unifi textile plant at 805 Island Drive, and its first tenant, the AI cloud company Nscale, signed an $865 million, 10-year deal for 40 megawatts there. Nscale was to start paying for 20 megawatts in April 2026 and a further 20 megawatts the following month, and it could double its deployment by the end of 2027. WhiteFiber, the high-performance computing arm of former bitcoin miner Bit Digital, bought the 96-acre, 1 million square foot property from Unifi for $45 million in 2025. Unifi had announced in February 2025 that it was closing the plant after more than 30 years and laying off 91 people. Bit Digital said the site would offer 99 megawatts in the short term, with an eventual 200 megawatts, and the companies said they had invested $150 million by late 2025. "In Madison, I run emergency generators for one hour, once a week. That's it," Jonathan Collins, the site's operations manager, told Yadkinville's town board in September 2026. Collins said the data halls are built as a building inside the old plant's walls to contain the sound, and that cooling uses outside air: "We're not using 100s of 1000s of gallons of water a day for cooling, it is all done by the fresh air around us". He said the company buys abandoned industrial properties because it is faster than building new: "So we're a little selfish. It gets us to market quicker so that we can start earning some money". WhiteFiber is now buying parts of Unifi's manufacturing plants in Yadkinville, which it plans to turn into data centers, and residents there are wary. "What happens when this becomes archaic in four to five years and they have a building they've retrofitted and then abandoned?" asked Boonville resident Worth Shover. "I'm not here because I'm against technology or progress", said Rebekah Shover. "... But I keep coming back to one question, what kind of future are we creating for our children?" "This is all a bubble. It's a money model. It's an AI bubble", said Paul Freer of the Lone Hickory community. WhiteFiber scheduled a town hall forum at the Madison plant for Sept. 19, 2026, open to residents who registered in advance.

Nscale was to start paying for 20 megawatts in April 2026 and a further 20 megawatts the following month, and it could double its deployment by the end of 2027.
WhiteFiber, the high-performance computing arm of former bitcoin miner Bit Digital, bought the 96-acre, 1 million square foot property from Unifi for $45 million in 2025.
Unifi had announced in February 2025 that it was closing the plant after more than 30 years and laying off 91 people.
Bit Digital said the site would offer 99 megawatts in the short term, with an eventual 200 megawatts, and the companies said they had invested $150 million by late 2025.
"In Madison, I run emergency generators for one hour, once a week. That's it," Jonathan Collins, the site's operations manager, told Yadkinville's town board in September 2026.

Collins said the data halls are built as a building inside the old plant's walls to contain the sound, and that cooling uses outside air: "We're not using 100s of 1000s of gallons of water a day for cooling, it is all done by the fresh air around us".
He said the company buys abandoned industrial properties because it is faster than building new: "So we're a little selfish. It gets us to market quicker so that we can start earning some money".
WhiteFiber is now buying parts of Unifi's manufacturing plants in Yadkinville, which it plans to turn into data centers, and residents there are wary.
"What happens when this becomes archaic in four to five years and they have a building they've retrofitted and then abandoned?" asked Boonville resident Worth Shover.
"I'm not here because I'm against technology or progress", said Rebekah Shover. "... But I keep coming back to one question, what kind of future are we creating for our children?"
"This is all a bubble. It's a money model. It's an AI bubble", said Paul Freer of the Lone Hickory community.
WhiteFiber scheduled a town hall forum at the Madison plant for Sept. 19, 2026, open to residents who registered in advance.

ft-343.text: Project Accelerate's developers withdrew their request to rezone 123 acres along East John Street in Matthews on October 7, 2025. The site south of Interstate 485 was zoned for residential use, and the application sought conditional industrial zoning for a data center. Mayor John Higdon announced the withdrawal; commissioners had been due to consider the application on October 13. Crosland Southeast, Crow Holdings and Engineered Land Solutions had proposed five two-story buildings, with as much as 600 megawatts of electricity needed for a full campus. That figure described a possible project, not power already in use. The town's staff report said the plan was generally inconsistent with the East John Street small-area plan, which calls for a mix of business, housing and open space along the corridor. Nearby residents questioned the project's demand for water and power, its noise and its fit beside neighborhoods. Town commissioners asked for more information about electricity supply, taxes, noise and building design rather than advancing the rezoning after a September hearing. At a public meeting, a restaurant across the street welcomed the prospect of more customers, while other residents feared higher bills and a changed landscape. The developers' withdrawal ended that rezoning request without approval of a data center on the tract. The land remained zoned R-12 residential under the town's September 2025 staff report; a data center there would need a new land-use decision. Crosland Southeast said the team would explore other options, without announcing a replacement design.

ft-1773461117966-4882.text: On March 5, 2026, Natelli Investments withdrew its applications for the New Hill Digital Campus, a 250 megawatt data center planned next to Duke Energy's Shearon Harris nuclear plant in the New Hill area of unincorporated Wake County, North Carolina, near Apex. The company cited the town of Apex's unfinished zoning changes needed to allow data centers. The plan called for six buildings up to 70 feet tall and about 80 generators of three megawatts each on 189 acres of farmland off Old US Highway 1. Natelli had filed for annexation, rezoning and a land use amendment with Apex, arguing the property was already marked for industrial use on the town's 2019 land use map. Executive vice president Michael Natelli said: "Data Storage Facilities are modest users of public facilities. Not only do they generate far less traffic than residential communities, but they create high-wage technology jobs and strengthen the technology eco-system in their region." The company said cooling would use recirculating non-potable water and that power would come off Duke Energy's grid without straining the town's supply. More than 100 residents wore red shirts to an Apex town council meeting, and an online petition against the project gathered nearly 2,000 signatures in two weeks. Doug Stewart, of the Jordan Pointe community, told the council: "Just like this birdhouse here, our community is handcrafted. It's imperfect, but it's also built to last, just like our town is." Neighbors formed the Protect Wake County Coalition over concerns about water, diesel fumes and who would pay for infrastructure. US Representative Valerie Foushee said: "Plainly, I don't support a new data center in the heart of our district." After the withdrawal, campaigner Melissa Ripper said: "We thought we had, probably, another six [or] eight months of trying to push back." Apex council member Terry Mahaffey said he would bring a motion on March 10, 2026 for a one-year moratorium on data center applications, permits and construction, to "finish the work that we started" on the town's development rules. No result of that vote has been published. Wake County adopted its own year-long data center moratorium in June 2026, which covers the unincorporated area where the site sits.

ft-1764178421499-3631.text: Five years on nothing has been built, and nothing published describes the Research Triangle Park project as a data center. Apple announced a $1 billion East Coast hub at Research Triangle Park in April 2021, promising 378 jobs in the Triangle by the end of 2024, 990 by the end of 2025, at least 2,700 by 2031, and at least $500 million spent on a Wake County site by 2031. The company paused the development in June 2024. On November 26, 2025 North Carolina's Economic Investment Committee, part of the Department of Commerce, granted Apple about four more years to meet the hiring and investment targets. Apple has added more than 600 employees to its existing Raleigh operations over three years, but no campus has gone up. Scott Levitan, who runs Research Triangle Park, said: "Research Triangle Park is a great home for so many companies, and we're thrilled that Apple will be among them." Gerald Cohen, chief economist at the UNC Kenan Institute, was more measured: "We have a skill set. We have people that they want to tap into. The negative is that it's going to be slower going." The entry is recorded as suspended at $1 billion, with no capacity and no acreage, and marks pushback as unknown. The same report says Apple has plans to build a data center in the Charlotte area, which is a different project from this one. The ground around it has shifted while Apple waited. Thirteen jurisdictions within reach of the park now carry data center moratoriums or zoning limits, including Durham from June 16, 2026, Apex from April 14, Garner from May 19, Chatham County from February 11 and Orange County from April 21. An operating Compass data center is five kilometres away, CyrusOne's Durham buildings nine kilometres, and the cancelled New Hill campus 22 kilometres. The 964 megawatt Harris nuclear station is 25 kilometres off.

ft-1775148797572-2455.text: The Drox Group asked Forsyth County, North Carolina to rezone 129 acres across from Rural Hall Town Hall for a data center campus called Project Iron Spur. On July 30, 2026, county commissioners voted 5 to 2 to deny the rezoning, following a planning board recommendation to deny it on June 11. Only commissioners Don Martin and Gloria Whisenhunt voted in favor. The refusal came after six months, more than 400 emails and dozens of speakers. Company representative Michael Foess said the buildings would keep noise below 60 decibels and use less water, and that plans had been revised after meeting with neighbors to lower one building and add a public recreation area. He said the county would gain nearly $80 million in tax over ten years. Planning board member Lindsey Schwab said the proposal conflicted with the county's land-use plan: "I don't question the economic impact that this project would bring a $3 billion investment and millions and millions of dollars into the coffers of Forsyth County, which we desperately need ... However, I question the cost of that today." Commissioner Gray Wilson said: "I don't know that we make the decision that this is something that they ought to have and we just cram it down everybody's throat." Commissioners said they were not against data centers but needed to decide where such sites would be most appropriate. The July 30 vote was the final decision on the rezoning.

ft-1769472104271-6330.text: This one would burn its own gas, from a well drilled in 1998. Deep River Data, a company incorporated in Alamance County on April 30, 2025, wants to put a data center on a 643 acre forested tract just south of US Highway 421 near the Lee and Chatham county line, powered from Butler Well Number 3, a vertical well sunk 2,655 feet into black shale and old coal deposits. The land belongs to Ed Myrick of Pompano Beach, Florida; the mineral rights belong to Dan Butler of Southern Pines, who holds rights under more than 2,700 acres in Lee County. The company's adviser, Dan Spuller, a crypto entrepreneur and natural gas landman, contacted the state Oil and Gas Commission about the project in September 2025. Spuller said the company was evaluating whether the well can safely and efficiently produce gas by conventional methods rather than fracking, and that it remains in a pre-feasibility phase. Fracking is legal in North Carolina, and Lee County's own fracking moratoriums, from 2017 and 2019, have both expired. The site sits less than a tenth of a mile from the Deep River and Patterson Creek. Nearly 23 miles of the Deep River are on the federal impaired waters list, carrying 1,4-dioxane, a likely carcinogen. Stephanie Stephens, the Deep River riverkeeper, said the county should be choosy about the industry it takes: "We already have a polluted river." Therese Vick of the Blue Ridge Environmental Defense League said: "The Oil and Gas Commission must look carefully at this proposal to exploit the gas well near the Deep River, as well as those who want to develop it." Duke Energy has projected that data centers could add nearly six gigawatts to North Carolina's demand, which is the wider reason a company would go looking for its own gas rather than wait in a utility queue. The entry stands as proposed with no acreage, no capacity and no cost. Eleven jurisdictions within reach now carry moratoriums or zoning limits, including Lee County itself from June 16, 2026 and Sanford from August 5, plus Chatham County from February 11. The 964 megawatt Harris nuclear station is 29 kilometres away, and a CyrusOne site sits 14 kilometres off.

ft-1771357617687-3210.text: Energy Storage Solutions had pitched a $19.2 billion, 900 megawatt data center for the Kingsboro area of Edgecombe County, near Tarboro, North Carolina, powered onsite by up to 1,800 megawatts of mostly natural gas turbines built for redundancy, president Dan Shaffer told commissioners. The company withdrew; County Manager Eric Evans told commissioners on July 6, 2026 that Energy Storage Solutions had backed out, and the board voted to return its deposit on the land. Shaffer said investors "insisted that we move forward with other projects that we have in friendlier communities" because of delays and opposition in Kingsboro and in Tarboro, where the town council had voted 6-1 in September 2025 to deny the company a permit for a separate data center. Community organizer Janice Bulluck said: "When you come in, and you present this, then make it sound as though it's the best thing since sliced bread, when we start really looking into this, and it didn't even come close." Leggett resident James Wrenn compared it to the hog farms and slaughterhouses that once threatened the same land in the 1990s: "Data centers of the 2020s are like the hog farms and slaughterhouses of the 1990s, coming with the promise of much-needed funds for the county government while exposing the citizens of the surrounding community in Edgecombe County for serious environmental hazards." Residents raised air and noise pollution, water use and where the natural gas would come from, pointing to xAI's data center in Memphis, Tennessee, and its 35 unpermitted gas turbines. On August 3, 2026, after a public hearing, five of Edgecombe County's seven commissioners voted for a two-year moratorium that bars the county from accepting, processing or approving data center development applications or permits until August 3, 2028. Commissioner Donald Boswell, who was absent for that vote, had pushed back on the idea at the July 6 meeting: "I am a little tired of hearing that it's going to use all of our water or it's going to take all of our electricity and all the things that they've used since day one." He said he was not advocating for a data center, only against locking the county out of future options.

The company withdrew; County Manager Eric Evans told commissioners on July 6, 2026 that Energy Storage Solutions had backed out, and the board voted to return its deposit on the land.

Shaffer said investors "insisted that we move forward with other projects that we have in friendlier communities" because of delays and opposition in Kingsboro and in Tarboro, where the town council had voted 6-1 in September 2025 to deny the company a permit for a separate data center.

Community organizer Janice Bulluck said: "When you come in, and you present this, then make it sound as though it's the best thing since sliced bread, when we start really looking into this, and it didn't even come close."

Leggett resident James Wrenn compared it to the hog farms and slaughterhouses that once threatened the same land in the 1990s: "Data centers of the 2020s are like the hog farms and slaughterhouses of the 1990s, coming with the promise of much-needed funds for the county government while exposing the citizens of the surrounding community in Edgecombe County for serious environmental hazards."
Residents raised air and noise pollution, water use and where the natural gas would come from, pointing to xAI's data center in Memphis, Tennessee, and its 35 unpermitted gas turbines.

On August 3, 2026, after a public hearing, five of Edgecombe County's seven commissioners voted for a two-year moratorium that bars the county from accepting, processing or approving data center development applications or permits until August 3, 2028.

Commissioner Donald Boswell, who was absent for that vote, had pushed back on the idea at the July 6 meeting: "I am a little tired of hearing that it's going to use all of our water or it's going to take all of our electricity and all the things that they've used since day one."
He said he was not advocating for a data center, only against locking the county out of future options.

ft-1776915601648-9828.text: On September 14, 2026 the Stokes County Board of Commissioners voted 3-2 to rezone roughly 1,800 acres of farmland near Walnut Cove, in Stokes County, North Carolina, for Engineered Land Solutions' Project Delta data center. It was the same margin as the board's first vote in January, which was later voided after a legal challenge. The land came from Triad developer David Couch's company, DFC Stokes, and ELS is the data center proponent. Hundreds of people came to the January rezoning meeting to oppose it, and graves tied to the Hairston Clan lie on the land, along with concerns about water and air pollution. The Southern Coalition for Social Justice and the Southern Environmental Law Center then sued for the National Hairston Clan, Cleanaire NC, the Dan River Basin Association, 7 Directions of Service and more than a dozen residents, alleging the rezoning was not done by the book. “Both amendments were not properly noticed, so that made it harder for concerned residents to participate in the process, especially because it basically took place from Thanksgiving to New Year's,” said Anne Harvey David, the coalition's chief counsel. The commissioners rescinded the rezoning and voided the text amendment that had made data centers a permitted use in heavy manufacturing districts, and ELS warned the county stood “to lose $20–$40 million in potential annual tax revenue” and said it would resubmit. Residents who spoke before the September vote were uniformly opposed. Chairman Wayne Barneycastle and Commissioner Brad Chandler voted no again, Chandler saying the board had too little time to review changes: “I hope, I pray to God, that if we continue down this road tonight with this hyperscale data center, that y'all are right if you vote for it as is.” Commissioner Keith Wood voted after the county attorney found no conflict in his past work at CMC Rebar, a possible supplier, and Commissioner Sonya Cox, a former school board member, noted that voters had rejected several attempts to raise taxes. Resident Tim Smith cited an economic analysis, funded by the Southern Environmental Law Center, that projected far less tax revenue than ELS estimates: “It is not going to bring the money in that they say it is.” ELS CEO Drew Nations said the proposal had changed since January to include stricter standards on noise, energy generation and water use. The county's rezoning decision is made, and David would not say whether another lawsuit is planned, only that the group's fight over the project is not over.

ft-1786991491104-5317.text: WhiteFiber plans to turn two former Unifi warehouse properties in Yadkinville, Yadkin County, North Carolina, into data center campuses called NC-2 and NC-3, under a $60 million deal announced in August 2026. The announcement came the same day county commissioners voted 5-0 for a two-year moratorium on data centers, but the moratorium covers only unincorporated parts of the county, and the Unifi properties sit inside the town. "The moratorium only addresses the unincorporated areas of the county, which fall underneath our zoning areas," County Manager Michael Silverman told WFDD. The deal, made through WhiteFiber's subsidiary Enovum Data Centers, covers about 120 acres and 500,000 square feet of warehouse space at two locations, and is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026. It says it is in advanced discussions with prospective customers but has named none. WhiteFiber says the sites would start with a combined 60 megawatts of power, 30 each, and could support up to about 200 megawatts of power over time, with first capacity targeted for the third quarter of 2027. WhiteFiber, founded in 2024 by the Bitcoin mining company Bit Digital, already runs a 40 megawatt campus, NC-1, in a former Unifi plant at Madison in Rockingham County, about 55 miles away, which went live in the summer of 2026; the Yadkinville sites would be modeled on it. More than 20 people spoke at the county's moratorium hearing, most of them against data centers, citing heavy water use and its effect on farmers, the loss of farmland, property values, noise and the county's rural character. "My family has been farming since the 1800s," said Janet Robbins. "We need our farmers, and we don't need to use our land for data centers." Dean Swaim argued for a shorter pause and for data centers to bring tax revenue: "For the longest time, Yadkin County has always gotten the crumbs from the counties around them." Jon Collins of Enovum said reusing warehouses means an abandoned facility does not become a drag on the community, and that "we're not taking Bobby Baker's tobacco field and making a data center out of it." The decision on the Yadkinville sites sits with the town, whose board has said it will neither hold a hearing nor impose a moratorium. On August 27, 2026, the Yadkinville Board of Commissioners said in a position statement that it "will not initiate a separate public hearing concerning data centers at this time, nor will it impose a moratorium on data centers," because a proposal alone does not establish grounds for one and state law bars down-zoning a property without its owner's consent. The Yadkin Ripple reported that because the Unifi land is already zoned industrial, there is no legal or zoning hurdle to using it for a data center. If the town does later propose a change to its own data center rules, it must hold a legislative hearing first, where residents could speak.

ft-350.text: Aurum Capital Ventures, an Iowa data center developer, told the Burleigh County Commission on June 16, 2025, it was looking at 300 acres of county-owned land in east Bismarck, North Dakota, near the Buckstop Junction historical village, for a new data center. Land agent Charlie White said the draw was a nearby electrical substation, and that Aurum was also considering several hundred acres of state land to the north. Commissioner Steve Schwab questioned the tax benefit: "It sounds to me like the state would get more taxes out of this thing than the county ... I'm sorry that doesn't sound good." White answered that the project would add 50 to 300 high-paying tech jobs. Commissioner Steve Bakken said data centers now need to supply their own power on site, "because once it's on the grid, that's when the grid gets even more destabilized." Commissioner Jerry Woodcox said the county received the land from the state under restrictions tying it to fairgrounds use, which would need a legal opinion before any sale. Aurum's chief executive is listed on the company's site only as "JP;" the Bismarck Tribune reported he appears to be John Paul Baric, founder of the cryptocurrency company MiningStore. White said Aurum aims to spend about $25 million a quarter placing data centers. Within days, the Bismarck Tribune's editorial board wrote that the county should reject selling land inside city limits for a data center. The Burleigh County Commission was set to take the proposal up again on July 7, 2025; no result has been published.

ft-1783368254228-4571.text: Nixxy, the company behind the proposed Nakota data center campus about 5 miles west of Williston in Williams County, North Dakota, ended its merger agreement with developer Tachyon 9 on July 30, 2026. Nixxy said it will instead buy the site directly and pay for the permits the project still needs. The campus is planned to reach up to 1 gigawatt of power, but no permit application has been filed yet, and the Williams County Commission would have to approve one before construction could start. Williams County has more data center activity than anywhere else in North Dakota, with ten projects tracked and nine still in the pipeline, according to a Valley News Live count from August 2026. Nearby, the Atlas Power data center has become a cautionary example: its power draw strained the local grid and pushed up energy costs, and noise complaints led to a lawsuit, the North Dakota Monitor reported. Public Service Commission chair Randy Christmann said he "cringed" when he learned about that facility because the region already had grid congestion. At least four western North Dakota counties have placed temporary bans on data center projects, though some have since lifted them. As first proposed, the Nakota campus would cover about 620 acres and generate its own electricity rather than draw from the grid, using turbines that can burn hydrogen along with natural gas that would otherwise be flared. Cooling would use a closed-loop liquid system that needs only an initial fill of water rather than continuous fresh water. The first 120 to 150 megawatts were targeted for the second quarter of 2027, "subject to financing, regulatory approvals and completion of the proposed transaction." Nixxy, formerly known as Recruiter.com Group, moved into AI infrastructure in 2024. Under the original deal, Tachyon 9 was to contribute about $64 million in equipment and land rights, and had lined up Nidar Infrastructure, parent of India's Yotta Data Services, as the anchor customer for the first 100 megawatts, a deal it valued around $2.34 billion. Nixxy's SEC filing said it ended the Tachyon 9 agreement "to pursue other potential business opportunities" and paid no penalty, and that it is negotiating to acquire the full project itself. North Dakota requires no state environmental review for data centers; developers need only a conditional use permit from local government, here the Williams County Commission. The county has approved permits for other data center projects and expects developers to work with nearby residents. "There should not be a lot of discontent. If you make your neighbors happy in this process, then it should be a good project," Commissioner Beau Anderson said in 2025, approving a different project. Nixxy has not yet filed a conditional use permit application for the Nakota site.

ft-353.text: Applied Digital's Polaris Forge 2, a $3 billion, 280-megawatt AI data center between Fargo and Harwood in Cass County, North Dakota, was nearing completion in September 2026, with about 1,800 workers finishing two buildings of 907,000 square feet each. The facility is leased to Oracle; Applied Digital first announced the lease without naming the tenant in October 2025, and Valley News Live reported the Oracle name in March 2026. The Harwood City Council, meeting in a city hall that held 40 people, voted unanimously and without discussion to rezone the land on September 10, 2025, refusing to take public comment or postpone to its regular October meeting. Mayor Blake Hankey, attending by video from Portugal, said, "Our decision isn't going to change," and Harwood resident Michael Swartz said of the council, "They're acting like good little lap dogs right now." Crews broke ground five days later. Fargo then tried to annex about 300 acres including the site, a fight that ended in December 2025 when the Fargo City Commission unanimously withdrew after Mayor Tim Mahoney raised who would maintain roads and supply water, electricity and emergency response. Cass County Electric Cooperative president Paul Matthys said the data center would roughly double the co-op's peak demand but would not raise rates for existing customers; Applied Digital is paying for the Agassiz substation and transmission line, which it put at $112 million in September 2026. At a February 2026 meeting, resident Michael Swartz said residents still felt left in the dark, and Hankey replied, "I think we followed every ordinance and law and everything we needed to follow." As of February 2026, city officials could not accurately project the tax revenue the center would bring, though Applied Digital says it expects to be the largest single taxpayer in the state by 2029. The Harwood City Council, led by Hankey, is the body that approved the rezoning and continues to oversee the project as construction finishes.

Mayor Blake Hankey, attending by video from Portugal, said, "Our decision isn't going to change," and Harwood resident Michael Swartz said of the council, "They're acting like good little lap dogs right now."

Crews broke ground five days later. Fargo then tried to annex about 300 acres including the site, a fight that ended in December 2025 when the Fargo City Commission unanimously withdrew after Mayor Tim Mahoney raised who would maintain roads and supply water, electricity and emergency response.

Cass County Electric Cooperative president Paul Matthys said the data center would roughly double the co-op's peak demand but would not raise rates for existing customers; Applied Digital is paying for the Agassiz substation and transmission line, which it put at $112 million in September 2026.
At a February 2026 meeting, resident Michael Swartz said residents still felt left in the dark, and Hankey replied, "I think we followed every ordinance and law and everything we needed to follow."
As of February 2026, city officials could not accurately project the tax revenue the center would bring, though Applied Digital says it expects to be the largest single taxpayer in the state by 2029.
The Harwood City Council, led by Hankey, is the body that approved the rezoning and continues to oversee the project as construction finishes.

ft-1768499921572-5394.text: Neighbors of the Atlas Power data center near Williston, North Dakota, were receiving settlement payments in March 2026 after suing the cryptocurrency-mining facility's owner over excessive noise. Twenty-two neighbors had sued, saying Williams County was not enforcing its own rule that all noise stay inside the site's heavy-industrial zone. Terms are confidential, Atlas attorney Doug Daniels told the court on March 13, and the data center is still operating as normal. Gov. Doug Burgum announced the $1.9 billion project in January 2022. It was built by Montana-based FX Solutions to be owned and run by Atlas Power, planned in three phases from 240 megawatts up to 700 megawatts, with about 65% of its computing power mining cryptocurrency. The Bismarck Tribune reported in 2024 that the site was drawing 200 megawatts of power and that the regional grid operator had limited how much more it could draw until power lines in the area were upgraded. The land had been an alfalfa field zoned heavy industrial for years, but most neighbors said they had no idea what was coming. "It still sounds like a jet plane taking off," said Corey Seidel, whose property line is 420 feet from the site. Lacie White, who measured 67 decibels by her daughter's bedroom window, said: "My daughter wakes up in the middle of the night and she struggles to go back to sleep because that's all she hears." In 2023 the county granted a temporary certificate of occupancy after Atlas paid $232,000 in fines for building code violations and promised acoustical panels and security fencing. A settlement was reached in June 2025, a month before a scheduled jury trial. By March 2026, attorney Daniels said three settlements were finalized, more were coming, and three were still being negotiated.

ft-1768500717091-1569.text: Project Fighting Pike, the proposed data center campus of 455 megawatts that Critical Data House plans at the northern entrance to Williston, North Dakota, is not expected to open until late 2028 or early 2029, because the company still does not hold clear title to the land, the Williston Herald reported on September 17, 2026. The Williston project in Williams County was filed as seven 65MW buildings on a 300-acre site at the corner of 56th Street NW and US Highway 2. City documents describe buildings of 275,000 to 500,000 square feet, cooled by a closed-loop system with direct-to-chip liquid cooling, built in three phases over ten years with two buildings in the first. Critical Data House could invest as much as $5 billion in the buildings, with another $5 billion possible on computer hardware. The Williston City Commission approved the plans in March 2025, requiring noise mitigation to be in place before operation and maintained for a year after, with a third-party consultant working on it. "Hopefully we spent the time on it and got it right," Mayor Howard Klug said then. The land is the problem. Over 1,100 people, mainly from Malaysia and Singapore, invested $18 million in a 322-acre planned community on the lot southwest of U.S. Highway 2 and the U.S. 85 Bypass, then abandoned it when demand for oil workers fell and Williston's population declined. After the city approved the subdivision plat on March 25, 2025, the company learned it had to serve each of those investors under the Hague Conventions, an international legal process that is still going on. CEO Chris Hardin told the Herald that if a pending decision allows notice to be served through newspapers in Malaysia and Singapore and the title arrives around January 2027, the campus could run between October 2028 and January 2029, on a 20 to 24 month build; the company had once said it would be operating by January 2027. He said five to seven companies were in talks to use the facility but that nondisclosure agreements kept him from naming them. Dale Haugen, the former Mountrail-Williams Electric Cooperative general manager who represents Williston on the project, said he wanted the abandoned lot cleaned up: "This is the entrance to our community that I worked with and love." The worry in Williston is noise, because the city has lived with it. Residents near the Atlas Power data center sued in 2023, saying its noise hurt their property values and quality of life, and settlements, whose terms are confidential, were going out to them in March 2026 while the facility kept running. Atlas's power use also strained the grid and contributed to higher energy costs, the North Dakota Monitor reported. Protesters gathered near Harmon Park in May 2026 over what they saw as a lack of transparency about the project's environmental and economic safeguards and its delays. Haugen said the planning documents gave thorough assurances and that there had been no way to tell the public about the delays before the Herald interview; the company says it will start a website for updates and hold more public meetings. Hardin said Fighting Pike would not mine cryptocurrency: "The Atlas situation is truly a Bitcoin facility. It's not a data center." Williams County has more tracked data center facilities than any other county in the state, ten, nine of them not yet running, Valley News Live reported in August 2026. Atlas Power's facility near Williston is one that is already operating. Nixxy has also announced the Nakota campus of up to 1GW in what it calls North Dakota's energy corridor. At least four western North Dakota counties have put temporary bans on data center projects, though some have since lifted them, and the only permit a developer needs in the state is from local government. The next step is a legal one, not at City Hall: the Williston City Commission has already approved the plat, and construction waits on the title. Hardin said every month of delay in serving the investors pushes the opening back by the same amount. The noise conditions the Williston City Commission attached in 2025 apply once the campus operates.

ft-1784072046513-8603.text: Monolith, a carbon black producer, wants to expand its Olive Creek facility in Hallam with a data center. The 35-megawatt co-located data center would be built with the Denver AI company Crusoe, alongside four more carbon black units. The data center would be up to 36 modular units the size of shipping containers on about ten acres at the northeast corner of the site, using an estimated 770,000 gallons of water a year, with either air cooling or a closed loop. The carbon black expansion would use more: about 62 gallons a minute in its first phase and 250 in its second, which at 80 percent is around 105 million gallons a year, and the second phase would spread east across Southwest 42nd Street. Chief development officer Anna Wishart said the plan is “significantly lower profile” than the ammonia facility Monolith had planned, and put the jobs at about 15 for the data center and 150 for the carbon black expansion. The chief executive Russell Webb said of choosing Crusoe: "we wanted to try to pick a partner that does those type of things," meaning efficiency and the right scale. Residents lined up out of the Hallam auditorium for a town hall in July 2026. Kathy Stevens, a lifelong resident whose land backs up to the plant, and landowner Cami Slauson, who said transparency had been missing, spoke for many of the worried neighbors. The planning commission delayed its vote on August 19 after a public hearing that drew concerns about water, sound and the future of Hallam land, then unanimously recommended the special use permit in September. Crusoe's Steve Buster said the conditions of approval, including a community benefit fund controlled by three Hallam residents, “are our contract with the village of how we will operate this project.” Commissioner Cynthia Heier voted yes but said: “I mean, this portion of Nebraska is under attack from big companies who just think we're just throwaway people.” The Hallam Village Board is set to decide whether to give Monolith the final green light at its October 5, 2026 meeting.

ft-1772681077912-7681.text: Sequitor Edge, a Nebraska company, is building a 40,000-square-foot edge data center on 16 acres the Kearney City Council sold it in the Tech oNE business park in northeast Kearney, Buffalo County, Nebraska. The building is due to open in early 2027 and, Mayor Jonathan Nikkila said after a May 2026 council meeting, will use around five megawatts of power. Sequitor Edge plans 18 such edge centers across the Midwest and chose the site for its access to Nebraska Public Power District lines and fiber. The project drew a 600-signature petition from resident Josh Lillyman, who asked the council to restore an old nuisance ordinance, update the noise code and release the development agreement. "The deal Kearney sets as a template now will shape what shows up next, it will be larger more impactful and harder to negotiate from a weaker position," Lillyman told the council in May 2026. Nikkila said afterward that a purchase agreement is in place but the developer has not yet decided whether to build, and council member Alex Straatmann said the nearby Central Nebraska Veterans' Home is of "paramount concern." In August 2026 the council adopted a data center zoning ordinance, shaped partly by Lillyman's work on a citizen advisory committee, that caps noise at 55 decibels and requires a conditional use permit. "It'll just be an ongoing battle to ensure that they abide by all the codes we put in place," Lillyman said. "And that'll be the community's job to hold them accountable." The first project to go through that permit process is far bigger than Sequitor Edge's: Worldwide Mission Critical wants to build Tech One Crossing, a multiphase campus in the same park that would reach 368 megawatts, replacing the 100 megawatts now used by Marathon Digital's bitcoin mine there.

ft-1763168180527-7934.text: H5 Data Centers is offering colocation space in a former Yahoo data center at 10917 Harry Watanabe Parkway in La Vista, Nebraska, on the edge of Omaha. H5 lists it as a single building of 234,500 square feet on 32 acres with 17.3 megawatts, DCD reported in January 2025. Yahoo acquired the shell around 2008 to convert it into a data center, opened it in 2010 and expanded it in 2015. Unlike Yahoo's "chicken-coop" buildings in Lockport, New York and Quincy, Washington, the La Vista property has a flat roof design. H5 added the La Vista site to its website around the turn of 2025, alongside the two Quincy sites, after buying Yahoo's two data center properties in Lockport for $49 million in a sale-leaseback deal in which Yahoo signed a long-term lease. DCD said H5 and Yahoo had not given details on the La Vista deal. Elsewhere in the Omaha area, Google already runs data centers in Papillion and Omaha, and documents obtained by the Flatwater Free Press in March 2026 showed it considering a fourth Nebraska data center that could need 1,000 to 3,000 megawatts. That would be more than three times the power the whole city of Lincoln uses at summer peak, and it would run on a privately built natural gas plant developed by the Omaha company Tenaska.

ft-1780877798165-4320.text: Tom Moulton's proposal for a data center in Nottingham, Rockingham County, New Hampshire, was withdrawn on Wednesday, May 27, 2026, hours before the planning board was due to discuss it. His lawyer's letter said the withdrawal would "allow the applicant to conduct additional research, further evaluate the property and the proposed use, and determine whether this is an appropriate use for this site," and Moulton told NHPR he wanted to come back with more information before possibly reintroducing it. Moulton, a Seacoast businessman, had asked the town's planning board for a conceptual consultation about a data center at Nottingham Business Park on Old Turnpike Road, off Route 4, on a property of more than 100 acres of which about 40 would be used. The plan was to convert a vacant warehouse there, and opponents warned the site contains wetlands in the Lamprey River Watershed, a federally designated Wild and Scenic River system. ft-359.text: Comcast Cable is converting a vacant former TD Bank building at 92 West Main Street in Clinton, Hunterdon County, New Jersey, into a small, unmanned data center to house computer servers and equipment. The Clinton Town land use board approved the conversion, My Central Jersey reported. The single-story building sits on just over an acre and covers 2,170 square feet; online listings suggest it was built around 1975 and last renovated around 2017 after standing vacant for eight to ten years. Comcast plans to install two generators and remove the drive-through lane at the back of the building. The building will not be staffed around the clock, matching how Comcast runs its other small, unmanned server sites. With the land use board's approval in hand, what remains is the conversion work itself; as of the August 2025 report, no construction timeline had been made public.

ft-360.text: The Department of the Air Force is weighing private data center proposals for land at Joint Base McGuire-Dix-Lakehurst, home to Fort Dix in Burlington County, New Jersey. The base's 73-acre and 120-acre parcels were offered to developers in an October 2025 solicitation, one of five Air Force sites in that round. By late July 2026 no lease had been awarded and no company chosen; only two military-base data center deals anywhere, at Fort Bliss, Texas, and Dugway Proving Ground, Utah, had moved past the proposal stage, Military.com reported. No project is planned yet at the New Jersey base beyond the solicitation itself; the Air Force said it would review proposals and negotiate lease terms with any bidder chosen. Bidders were required to plan for net-zero water use, power that does not draw on the local electric grid, and local outreach addressing "any risks or opposition," terms that do not apply to commercial data centers built off base, Military.com reported. There is no public report of who, if anyone, bid on the McGuire-Dix-Lakehurst parcels or when a decision might come.

ft-1785457888414-6619.text: Hexa Builders is suing Monroe Township in Gloucester County, New Jersey, for $300 million after the township banned data centers and its planning board turned down Hexa's application for a 1 million-square-foot data center and a warehouse at 3043 Black Horse Pike in Williamstown. The Hexa data center case is now in federal court in Camden, where the township asked in late July 2026 for it to be dismissed. Hexa, a Princeton-based developer led by CEO Dipal Patel, bought about 170 acres of farmland on Black Horse Pike for $5 million in 2022, under a township redevelopment plan for warehouses and distribution. In early 2025 the township amended that plan to allow data centers. Hexa planned two warehouses, one of about 522,000 square feet and one of about 1.1 million, and intended to convert the larger one into a data center. Residents objected to the water, pollution and noise a data center could bring, and a January 2026 planning board meeting ran more than four hours, though the board still granted a preliminary site plan for the warehouse project. "We are here as elected officials this evening, saying that we're going to do everything in our power to stop all data centers from coming here," Mayor Gregory Wolfe said at a March 25 meeting, according to Hexa's lawsuit. On April 22 the township passed two ordinances, one banning data centers and one repealing the 2025 change, and in May the planning board deemed Hexa's amended application incomplete. Williamstown resident John Romano, who said the data center would be right in his backyard, told the planning board in July: "This has got my wife and I really concerned." Hexa's 20-count suit, filed June 5, says the ban is arbitrary and violates the 14th Amendment and the First Amendment, arguing that "data centers are a medium of expression" and that banning them burdens free speech rights. Rutgers law professor Ronald Chen called the free-speech argument a long shot: "The data center is not speaking. It's not generating content." The township's attorney, Todd Gelfand, wrote that the ban does not regulate the content of speech, a speaker, a message, or Hexa's ability to engage in expressive activity. Hexa's lawyer, Jim Maley, has asked for the state-law claims to go back to New Jersey court. Other South Jersey towns have moved the same way: Medford banned data centers in June, Millville banned large-scale ones in May, and Collingswood banned data centers and small computing nodes in August, while Cherry Hill was considering a ban. In Vineland, a large data center is due to be finished by the end of the year. What happens next is up to U.S. District Judge Edward Kiel, who has yet to rule on the township's request to dismiss the case or Hexa's request to send part of it back to state court. The ban stays in force meanwhile, and Monroe's mayor and council say they will defend it.

ft-1763166934482-3928.text: DataVerge, a Brooklyn colocation company, runs a small backup and disaster recovery data center called NJ1 at 111 Town Square Place in Jersey City, Hudson County, New Jersey, with 10,000 square feet of space, 600 kilowatts of power and a matching diesel generator for backup. The site mainly lets customers at DataVerge's Industry City headquarters in Brooklyn replicate their data across the river, and the hosting company InterServer also leases space there. Jersey City's new ban on data centers exempts NJ1 because it sits inside a shared office building rather than standing alone on industrial land, so no vote on this site is pending. The City Council voted unanimously on August 19, 2026 to pass Ordinance 26-057, removing "cyber hotels" and data centers as allowed uses on industrial land, after the Planning Board recommended it 6-0 on June 30 and the council passed a first reading on July 15. Mayor James Solomon said the city already has five data centers inside shared office buildings, which the law does not affect: "Data centers eat up power, drive up utility bills for every ratepayer in this state, and employ almost nobody." Resident Abril Rios supported the ban: "I think a lot of A.I. data centers have been going up without confirmation of the community, so it is really important that we have input before anything happens." Resident Brenden Clark asked the council to regulate rather than ban data centers, pointing to a 15.5% property tax increase: "We are telling homeowners we need more reoccurring revenue, yet at the same time we are considering an ordinance eliminating a category of capital-intensive development from our industrial property." Jersey City is now the 34th New Jersey municipality to ban data centers, joining Bayonne and more than 30 other towns and cities across the state. Some council members have called for a statewide moratorium similar to the one New York Governor Kathy Hochul put in place in July 2026.

ft-361.text: The Comcast data center at 650 Centerton Road in Moorestown, Burlington County, New Jersey, occupies the first floor of a three-story office building outside Philadelphia that Comcast uses as an Xfinity facility. Built in 2001 on 5.1 acres, the 74,240-square-foot building went up for sale in November 2023 in a sale-leaseback deal, with Comcast keeping the ground-floor data center under only an initial 12-month lease while the rest of the building was marketed to investors. The listing described that first floor as a data center with mostly raised flooring, 14 Liebert HVAC units, four Liebert battery systems and four Liebert power systems, and local property taxes assessed the building at just over $10 million. Avison Young marketed the property through LoopNet without listing a sale price, and the building is or was the site of Comcast's Cybersecurity Operations Center, according to an incident-response forum cited by Data Center Dynamics. That 12-month leaseback on the data center floor was due to end around November 2024.

ft-1780317709189-8508.text: The Andover Township Committee banned data centers everywhere in town on May 28, 2026, stopping a planned data center on the 97-acre former Jump Airport site at 248 Stickles Pond Road, outside Newton in Sussex County, New Jersey. National Land Developers LLC, the Pennsylvania company that wants to build there, sued the township in Sussex County Superior Court on July 10, 2026 to overturn the ban. The court has not yet ruled. The site had sat empty for nearly 13 years before the owner applied in 2024 to build a 650,000 square foot warehouse with 130 loading bays. The Township Committee amended its Route 206 Redevelopment Plan in September 2025 to allow a data center there instead, and in April 2026 raised the height limit for data centers to two stories or 65 feet, according to the developer's lawsuit. Officials said a data center could bring in up to $5 million a year. At a packed public meeting, a speaker cursed at officials and scuffled with two police officers as he was led out. Mayor Thomas Walsh said afterward: "But we also agree that no project, no money is worth tearing a town at its seams." The committee introduced the township-wide ban on May 12, 2026 and adopted it unanimously on May 28 as Ordinance 2026-13, making data centers a prohibited use in every zone. Walsh put the lost payment in lieu of taxes at $5 million a year for 30 years, saying: "Many people supported the idea, and many didn't and I'm not about to tear the town apart over money." The Sussex Visibility Brigade, which organized against the project, said: "Make no mistake: we dragged them to this decision." National Land Developers argues the ban had no valid land use purpose and was adopted without proper notice. "The Township Committee intends to vigorously defend the allegations and has no interest in settling," the mayor and committee said. By August 2026, developers had also sued Montgomery and Monroe townships to overturn their data center bans, among nearly three dozen New Jersey municipalities that have passed bans or restrictions, the New Jersey Monitor reported. Whether the Andover ban stands is now up to the Superior Court in Sussex County.

ft-363.text: Prism Capital Partners has approval to use an 11-acre parcel at 275 Kingsland Street, at Cathedral Avenue in Nutley, Essex County, New Jersey, for a "major data center and other permitted uses" on its ON3 campus. No further details of the proposed data center have been announced. The data center plan replaced a warehouse that critics called a "truck depot." Residents had opposed the depot over traffic congestion, and Diaz said that plan was "dismissed and withdrawn." Prism withdrew the warehouse application, and in June 2025 the Nutley Board of Commissioners introduced an ordinance creating an overlay zone that would let 275 Kingsland become a data center, with public comment at its July 1 meeting. Prism announced in July 2025 that Nutley had approved its plan for the 11 acres. ON3 is the 116-acre former Hoffmann-La Roche complex on Route 3, straddling Nutley and Clifton, which Prism has owned since 2016. It houses the Hackensack Meridian School of Medicine and Ralph Lauren offices, among other tenants, with an on-site co-hybrid power plant supplying electricity, heating and cooling. The same round of approvals allows up to 1,074 apartments and about 90,000 square feet of retail in Clifton. ft-1116.text: Midland, Texas-based New Era Energy & Digital has a land option on about 3,500 acres near the unincorporated community of Caprock in Lea County, New Mexico, and proposes a data center campus of up to 7 gigawatts for artificial intelligence. The company, previously called New Era Helium until it rebranded in August 2025, announced the plan in November 2025. Chief executive E. Will Gray II told the Albuquerque Journal the site, about 45 minutes east of Roswell, is on private land and would need federal and state permits before construction. New Era says the site would be powered by more than 2 gigawatts of natural gas generation plus a planned nuclear installation of 5 gigawatts or more, with the reactor technology still being chosen. Spokesman Jonathan Paterson told the Roswell Daily Record the campus would be built in "tranches" as partners agree to lease parts of it. "I think in terms of a budget or cost, we will know more later on," Paterson said. Lea County officials learned of the plan from New Era's news release, and County Manager Corey Needham said no commissioner had met with the company: "I can say there have been high-level discussions with some data center developers, but we haven't spoken to them (New Era)." Water and power are the county's biggest worries; at a January 2026 meeting, Xcel Energy's James Lackey said the utility was about 7,500 megawatts short of regional power demand, a gap that could grow to 20,000 megawatts within 10 years. Commission chair Tyson Pierce said the water table at his house "has dropped considerably," and that the commission would do everything in its power "to come out on top, no matter what." In February 2026 the county commission adopted its first data center rules: banning evaporative cooling, requiring annual water use reports, and requiring any project to either build its own power or negotiate with utilities so its load does not raise other customers' rates. Any project seeking industrial revenue bonds or tax breaks must share those payments with every school and hospital district in the county. Commissioner Dee Ann Kimbro said: "I like this. I like that we are doing this. I think it is a great deal." Needham said commissioners will not be involved in New Era's project until "much later stages," and any tax deal the company seeks will have to meet the county's February water and power rules, reviewed by the Board of County Commissioners that Pierce chairs. New Era has not released a budget, tenant list or site plan for the Caprock campus.

ft-370.text: Zenith Volts Corp., a company based in Cheyenne, Wyoming, plans a data center campus powered by an on-site solar farm and battery storage on ranch land about 20 miles south of Roswell, near Lake Arthur in Chaves County. The Chaves County Commission approved a special use permit for the project in August 2025, with Commissioner Richard Taylor casting the only vote against it. Data Center Dynamics reported the project's capacity at 1.24 gigawatts. The approved solar facility covers 1,265 megawatts on the north side of West Pearson Road, next to a 250-acre battery storage system, on about 8,500 acres of grazing land owned by Wade Berry, who filed the permit application. County staff estimated the data center itself would need about 632 megawatts during the day, requiring roughly 633,000 solar panels across more than 6,000 acres to supply it. Zenith project manager Nick Coleman told the Albuquerque Journal the data center would support 1.3 gigawatts, at an estimated cost of $11.7 billion. Central Valley Electric Cooperative, the utility for the area, wrote that it lacks the transmission lines and power capacity to serve the site: "CVE currently doesn't have suitable electric transmission line infrastructure or sufficient power capacity to serve the facility's primary or standby power needs," wrote Ransom Spencer, the cooperative's manager of distribution engineering. Coleman said the site will not connect to the grid instead, which he said avoids passing costs to the general public. Apart from company representatives and Berry, no one spoke in favor of the project at the county hearing. One neighbor who spoke against it told commissioners, "I'm not totally against it; I'm not totally for it. I just want more transparency," and asked how hail, wildlife and weather would affect the site. Commissioner Hub Corn said the permit should be limited to a set number of acres, since neither the start date nor the site of initial construction had been decided. Louis Jaramillo, the county's planning and zoning director, said the county offered no incentives to Zenith ahead of approval. Zenith will own and operate the campus and was still in discussion with potential tenants as of October 2025. A Zenith acquisitions officer told the Wyoming Tribune Eagle that the company itself would not be the end client and was only beginning its search for a tenant. The county attached 17 conditions to the permit, including a two-year deadline to break ground. Coleman said in October 2025 that the first phase, the solar farm and battery storage, would begin within weeks. No report since October 2025 has confirmed that construction started or that a tenant signed.

ft-1776268068120-6733.text: Green Data's 2-gigawatt data center planned for 10,000 acres of New Mexico Tech land at Socorro, in Socorro County, New Mexico, was cancelled on June 2, 2026, when the university said it would not go forward. The Canadian company, led by chief executive Jason Bak, had proposed a 10-gigawatt solar and data center project west of M Mountain and north of U.S. 60, with battery storage for round-the-clock operation and water drawn from the desert air. "During the initial phase of this process, we identified several material considerations that led both parties to mutually conclude that proceeding under the current framework is not the right path at this time," said New Mexico Tech president Michael Jackson. He cited the university's available acreage, the difficulty of integrating other renewable sources and of vetting so large a project, and said NMT remained open to revisiting the idea. A petition against the project had passed 4,600 signatures. On May 11, the Village of Magdalena, about 27 miles west, formally opposed the project unless it could be shown not to harm local water, the environment or community character. A week after New Mexico Tech's announcement, on Tuesday, June 9, the Socorro County Commission unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on data centers and related infrastructure, and formed a Blue Ribbon Committee to study the issue. Fourteen residents spoke for the moratorium, urging protection of water, ranch land and scientific assets such as the Very Large Array, and the crowd of more than 80 applauded the vote. "We understand that some Socorro County residents are skeptical," Bak said, promising about $50 million a year in community benefits and saying he wanted to join the committee. Cecilia Rosacker of Inform Socorro called the moratorium a big win, and the group plans to ask the city of Socorro to adopt its own. Bak said Green Data would not make any decisions and would "get a sense of what emerges from the moratorium."

ft-1775096275548-3508.text: Townsite Solar 2, a subsidiary of Skylar Energy Resources, walked away from its plan to build a data center on Boulder City-owned land and instead won federal approval to build on nearby Bureau of Land Management land in the Eldorado Valley, in Clark County, Nevada. The company withdrew its city application on July 6, 2026, after a planning board vote against it, and BLM approved a switch of its 2023 solar-and-battery permit to a two-building data center campus with a peak demand of 167 megawatts. The Interior Department's Board of Land Appeals halted the project on September 1, 2026, after Boulder City and environmental groups appealed. Boulder City had projected about $1.46 million a year in added lease revenue from the data center against $611,000 for the solar project it would have replaced, since land lease revenue funds more than a third of the city's budget. "This feels so unprecedented for us to have a project placed in our city without the chance to weigh in," said city spokesperson Lisa LaPlante. The city council and a citizens' group aided by the Sierra Club and the Center for Biological Diversity are pursuing separate appeals of BLM's approval. The Board of Land Appeals will decide whether to keep the project on hold while it reviews the case; if it does not, opponents said they could seek a stay in court.

ft-1767731168400-3957.text: Jet.AI, a company that pivoted from aviation software to data center development in 2025, plans a 50 megawatt data center campus on about 20 acres in Moapa, an unincorporated community in Clark County, Nevada, in a joint venture with the construction firm Choo Choo Express. Under the agreement announced in December 2025, Choo Choo Express would provide the land, subject to definitive agreements and due diligence, and Jet.AI expects to put in about $10 million over two years toward a project costed at about $500 million, roughly $400 million of it debt. Jet.AI says it builds only after tenants are secured, and none has been announced for Moapa; no construction timeline has been given. The site sits beside the former Reid Gardner coal plant, once rated the nation's dirtiest for carbon dioxide emissions, which NV Energy shut down in 2014 after the Moapa Band of Paiute Indians and the Sierra Club sued over contamination, and demolished in 2020. The property now holds the Reid Gardner Battery Energy Storage System, which stores up to 220 megawatts; Jet.AI has not said whether the battery system would supply power to its planned data center. Clark County has become the site of a broader fight over data centers: more than a dozen people spoke at a Commission meeting in June 2026 to protest a Switch data center expansion, and in July the commission discussed data center rules at Commissioner Tick Segerblom's request but took no action on a moratorium the Sierra Club and others had asked for. "We need some type of ordinance," Segerblom said. "Let's try to get ahead of the game." Commissioner William McCurdy II said: "I believe that we should look for a uniform standard of what we would require of those looking to construct data centers here in our valley." The Clark County Commission, which oversees Moapa as an unincorporated town, has not adopted a data center ordinance or moratorium, while Reno, Henderson and several rural Nevada counties have adopted or are considering their own. Jet.AI's website says a power study for the Moapa site is under way and the project is advancing toward final documentation; no tenant or construction date has been set.

sentences.t: Jet.AI, a company that pivoted from aviation software to data center development in 2025, plans a 50 megawatt data center campus on about 20 acres in Moapa, an unincorporated community in Clark County, Nevada, in a joint venture with the construction firm Choo Choo Express.

Under the agreement announced in December 2025, Choo Choo Express would provide the land, subject to definitive agreements and due diligence, and Jet.AI expects to put in about $10 million over two years toward a project costed at about $500 million, roughly $400 million of it debt.
Jet.AI says it builds only after tenants are secured, and none has been announced for Moapa; no construction timeline has been given.

The site sits beside the former Reid Gardner coal plant, once rated the nation's dirtiest for carbon dioxide emissions, which NV Energy shut down in 2014 after the Moapa Band of Paiute Indians and the Sierra Club sued over contamination, and demolished in 2020.
The property now holds the Reid Gardner Battery Energy Storage System, which stores up to 220 megawatts; Jet.AI has not said whether the battery system would supply power to its planned data center.

Clark County has become the site of a broader fight over data centers: more than a dozen people spoke at a Commission meeting in June 2026 to protest a Switch data center expansion, and in July the commission discussed data center rules at Commissioner Tick Segerblom's request but took no action on a moratorium the Sierra Club and others had asked for.
"We need some type of ordinance," Segerblom said. "Let's try to get ahead of the game."
Commissioner William McCurdy II said: "I believe that we should look for a uniform standard of what we would require of those looking to construct data centers here in our valley."
