ft-1764305284386-6651.text: Centra's RNO2 data center at 265 Keystone Avenue near downtown Reno is still under construction, and the company now lists its first 4.4 MW of capacity for the fourth quarter of 2026, later than the early second-quarter opening it announced at groundbreaking. Centra broke ground on the 90,000 square foot Keystone data center in Reno, Washoe County, Nevada, in November 2025, and says the 12MW figure attached to the site represents its full potential. Centra, formerly known as Deep Edge and backed by Columbia Capital, already manages the meet-me room and carrier hotel at 200 South Virginia Street in Reno. It pitches RNO2 as Reno's first purpose-built interconnection data center, with two meet-me rooms, more than 15 fiber carriers and liquid cooling for racks up to 150kW. The building will use air cooling and liquid cooling in a closed-loop system with free cooling for part of the year. In February 2025 the Nevada Governor's Office of Economic Development considered tax abatements for the Centra company behind the project, CADC Reno 265, LLC, worth an estimated $5.09 million over 10 years, on a planned $58.1 million in equipment spending and 11 jobs. The application said the company would use an air-based cooling system rather than a water-based one. Some neighbors say they were never told. "Despite being a neighbor, I had no warning about the project and have received no information about impacts to air, water and noise pollution, which are going to impact my neighborhood as well as Reno High School," Tara de Queiroz said in April 2026, when she urged the city to consider a ban. "I think there's a lot of concerns with sound, a lot of concerns with water, with how close it is to the river," resident Allison Hartmann told 2 News Nevada; she said she lost her job after posting TikTok videos about the Keystone project and that it seemed some contractors had called to get her fired. Cullin McGinnis of the Sierra Club's Toiyabe Chapter objected that it is "right on the river, and also that it was approved before there were regulations on the books." The backlash produced a pause. On June 1, 2026 the Reno City Council voted 6-1 to keep a moratorium on accepting, processing and approving new data center applications until August 31, 2027 or until the city adopts data center rules, with Councilmember Kathleen Taylor voting no. Data centers already built or under construction, including the Keystone Data Center and the recently approved Oppidan Data Center, are not affected. "They're looking for certainty," said Councilmember Devon Reese, who asked for the extension. Councilmember Meghan Ebert insisted the pause be tied to new regulations: "My community does not have trust that this body will follow through on any promises." Mayor Hillary Schieve said the city will also "have to address how we are going to deal with the existing ones." In the 18 months before the pause, Reno approved three data centers, run by Colovore, Oppidan and Centra, all smaller than others in the state. In January 2025 the council also upheld a conditional use permit for the Webb Data Center in the North Valleys, and that March it approved the Oppidan Data Center. Officials in rural Humboldt County have taken initial steps toward a moratorium of their own. City planning staff are drafting rules on about a dozen topics, including noise, air quality, water, energy use, fire and building safety and community benefit agreements, and the Reno City Council will vote on them. Tax breaks for data centers are offered by the state, not the city, a senior city planner noted. Centra's own site gives a fourth-quarter 2026 date.

ft-376.text: The Webb Data Center, the first data center the City of Reno approved, is under construction at 9710-9730 North Virginia Street in the North Valleys of Reno, in Washoe County, Nevada, next to an Amazon warehouse off North Virginia Street and Stead Boulevard. Its developer is the California-based company Ellis Partners, and the city puts the 82,000-square-foot building's needs at 28.5 megawatts of power and 2 acre-feet of water a year, about enough power for 11,400 homes by the city's own comparison. The project has its building permits and is under construction. Webb was contested from the start: the Reno Planning Commission granted it a conditional use permit in December 2024, and the Sierra Club Toiyabe Chapter appealed, arguing the city had added data centers to its zoning without public input. "The folks who live nearby this data center never had an opportunity to comment on ... the permitting of data centers," said Olivia Tanager, the chapter's director. In January 2025 the Reno City Council upheld the permit 5-2, with council members Meghan Ebert and Naomi Duerr voting no; Duerr said the developer needed to do more to reduce environmental effects in what has been called the fastest-warming city in the nation. In March 2025 the council unanimously overturned the planning commission's denial of the Oppidan Data Center next door, which plans to use 8 acre-feet of water and 8 megawatts; Mayor Hillary Schieve said then that she wished data center applications were not coming so quickly. Reno has since stopped taking new data center applications: on June 1, 2026 the council voted 6-1 to keep a moratorium on accepting, processing and approving new applications until August 31, 2027, or until the city adopts new data center rules, with Councilmember Kathleen Taylor voting no. Data centers already built or being built, including Webb, are not affected, so the pause does not reach this project. "My community does not have trust that this body will follow through on any promises," said Ebert, who pushed to tie the end of the moratorium to the adoption of new rules. The Reno City Council will decide the new rules on energy use, water, noise and air quality that the pause is meant to lead to.

ft-381.text: Stream U.S. Data Centers' Project Double Reed, a $19.46 billion data center campus planned for the STAMP industrial park in the town of Alabama, in Genesee County, New York, is waiting on revised plans after state regulators changed how they read the wetlands on the site. The campus would put three two-story buildings, 2.2 million square feet in all, on about 130 acres, with about 500 megawatts of power split between a North Campus and South Campus on either side of Crosby Road. On September 14, Alabama Town Supervisor Rob Crossen said Stream was revising its plans "to try to comply with the most recent determination by the DEC on how wetlands are looked at." The state Department of Environmental Conservation has told the development center that construction cannot begin without a stormwater permit, which it will not grant until it reviews an updated wetland study. In an August 24 letter, the development center's attorney said the state no longer considers STAMP grandfathered from new wetland rules. The land was meant for Plug Power's hydrogen plant, which stalled amid funding problems; Plug sold it to Stream for $132.5 million. Stream says it is working with an unnamed "prominent existing tenant, a Fortune 50 company with an S&P credit rating of at least AA-." The project has grown from a $6.3 billion, 60-acre plan approved by the county's development board in March 2025 to today's $19.5 billion version, and Stream has asked for $1.46 billion in state and local tax breaks. Water, noise and the land's neighbors are at the center of the fight; the STAMP site borders the Tonawanda Seneca Nation, and the Nation and the Sierra Club oppose the project over effects on wetlands and wildlife. "The misinformation is mainly on their side," said Jim Joyner, who has lived near the site about 35 years, disputing residents' figures on water use and noise. Neighbor Cheryl Cordes told 13WHAM her family would leave if the project is built: "We're leaving the home that we built." At a packed hearing in April 2026, one resident asked whether the 20,000 gallons of water a day in the application was "per building or in total"; the development center's chief executive said engineering calculations put use closer to 13,000 gallons a day. "They're going to jack up my electric bill even more," said Adrienne Yocina of Indian Falls, a few miles from the site. Two things changed in July 2026: Governor Kathy Hochul issued an executive order on July 14 pausing state environmental permits for new large data centers for up to a year, and a day earlier the Tonawanda Seneca Nation, the Sierra Club and an Alabama resident sued to challenge the 2012 agreement that created STAMP. "It is a past IZA that really does lock out future boards from making decisions for their people, and that's not right," said Grandell Logan, a spokesperson for the Tonawanda Seneca Nation. The project still needs final environmental and site plan approval from the Alabama Planning Board and approval of its tax incentives from the Genesee County Economic Development Center. Crossen has said the governor's order appears to exclude local approvals, so the town's review continues, while the Seneca Nation's lawsuit and the dispute over the state stormwater permit remain pending.

ft-1777412785651-2157.text: EKG Group's Guild Ventures wants to redevelop the 76-acre Kenwood Commons hilltop off Southern Boulevard in Albany, New York, the former site of the Doane Stuart School and Kenwood convent that burned down in 2023, into a multibillion-dollar mixed-use technology campus anchored by a data center. No formal application has been filed with the city of Albany, but the developer has asked the New York Independent System Operator to study up to 180 megawatts of electric demand for the whole site, a figure Guild Ventures calls a theoretical ceiling; the data center itself could use up to 100 megawatts. That is twice the 50-megawatt threshold in Governor Kathy Hochul's one-year moratorium on state environmental permits for large data centers, which she signed July 14, 2026 while New York writes rules on energy demand, water and air quality, and effects on utility customers. About a week before Hochul signed the order, the Albany Common Council passed a resolution supporting a statewide moratorium on data center permit siting, and Albany's mayor has also backed it. Owusu Anane, who represents Albany's 10th Ward on the Common Council, said: "We've seen many promises being made as it relates to data centers, but it's had an adverse impact on various communities, particularly when it comes to the water or even the utility bills." Asked whether data centers benefit Albany residents, he said the decision "needs to be led by the residents of those communities that are going to be impacted the most," adding: "This pause, I believe, is a step in the right direction." In a statement, Guild Ventures director Michael-Henry Elghanian-Krayem said the company is still reviewing the governor's order but designed Kenwood "to be a project others could model themselves on, one that treats responsibility to the community as a starting condition rather than an afterthought, with no air impacts, limited water use, and protections for ratepayers." City officials say they have met with the property owner, but there is still no formal development application before Albany, so how the moratorium will apply to the project remains unclear.

In a statement, Guild Ventures director Michael-Henry Elghanian-Krayem said the company is still reviewing the governor's order but designed Kenwood "to be a project others could model themselves on, one that treats responsibility to the community as a starting condition rather than an afterthought, with no air impacts, limited water use, and protections for ratepayers."
City officials say they have met with the property owner, but there is still no formal development application before Albany, so how the moratorium will apply to the project remains unclear.

ft-1779984485357-9169.text: No data center has been proposed at Camp Monterey, and no developer has put its name to one. What exists is a set of emails obtained under New York's freedom of information law and published on May 27, 2026, between Judy McKinney Cherry, executive director of FLX Gateway, and Greg Hering, co-founder and director of development at ClearPath Energy, discussing data barns at Beaver Dams, in Schuyler County, and other places in the Southern Tier. In November 2025 Hering asked about industrial electrical service, water storage and the capacity of the wastewater treatment plant; on January 23, 2026 the exchange turned to data barns, data center conferences and fibre plans. The former Camp Monterey property has three productive wells yielding about 140,000 gallons a day, sits near a 115 kilovolt line and has natural gas about half a mile off. One message says simply: "I only need 4 acres, lots of power and gas." Seneca Lake Guardian, the group that has spent years fighting the cryptocurrency operation at Dresden, obtained the emails and shared screenshots publicly. FLX Gateway is an economic development body rather than a data center company, which is why the emails matter: they are the only public record of the interest. FLX Gateway's own listing describes Camp Monterey as a 25 acre redevelopment site at 2150 Evergreen Hill Road in the Town of Orange, with its own water and wastewater system, more than 86,000 square feet of buildings and access to a $5 million reimbursable grant.

ft-1763170035575-2992.text: Indian Point stopped making electricity in 2021, and Holtec wants to sell 200 megawatts of it to a data center instead. The company, which took ownership of the site at Buchanan, in Westchester County, in May 2021 to decommission it, told the Indian Point Decommissioning Oversight Board on December 5, 2024 that it had asked the New York Independent System Operator that October for 200 megawatts of grid power. The plan is for the 240 acre site, and specifically the training building area, to anchor an initiative Holtec calls HI-CLOUD: a million square foot, 200 megawatt utility-ready data center. There is no customer. Holtec vice president Frank Spagnuolo told the board: "Currently we have no offer. We're not working with any outside Amazon, Microsoft, nobody, for a data center or anything." The board had other things on its mind. Richard Webster of Riverkeeper raised caesium-137, found in July in one surface soil sample near the training building: "It's never good when you find radioactive materials that you don't expect to be there." Spagnuolo said the area "was not identified as an area of concern. We did not expect to see any cesium or any radioactive components there at all." The environmental lawyer Susan Shapiro framed it as a choice: "AI has no interest in human life, so we have to choose, are we going to support AI that really has no use for us as human beings and life and the health things that we need to live like clean water and clean air." New York State's moratorium, running from June 4, 2026 to June 4, 2027, covers data centers of 50 megawatts and above, and East Fishkill has a three year moratorium from June 25, 2026.

ft-1768453625879-6878.text: Tesla's plan to put $500 million of its Dojo supercomputer, including a cluster of servers, at its state-owned factory in South Buffalo, in Erie County, New York, ended when Elon Musk shut Dojo down in August 2025 to focus on Cortex, a supercomputer at Tesla's plant in Austin, Texas. The Dojo data center pledge was part of a pending update to Tesla's lease on the Buffalo factory, and its collapse set the talks back. Dojo was to run on specially designed chips and analyze data from more than a million Tesla vehicles to help develop the company's self-driving software. "They backed away from the Dojo and that was a problem for us because that was a big part of why we were coming to this extension of the agreement," said Kevin Younis, chief operating officer of Empire State Development, the state's economic development agency. Younis said the state still wants Tesla to commit to some kind of computer in Buffalo, and that Tesla is doing a supercomputer with somebody else's chips instead of its own. In February 2026, Tesla said it has invested $350 million in supercomputers on the site. The state built the factory for almost $1 billion as the centerpiece of former Gov. Andrew Cuomo's Buffalo Billion program and rents it to Tesla for $1 a year in exchange for a promise of 3,460 jobs across the state. The plant was meant to make solar panels and mostly makes chargers for electric vehicles. In February 2026, Tesla reported it had hired more than 300 more people in Buffalo and had met its jobs target at the end of 2025, with 2,399 full-time workers at the factory and 1,060 at other Tesla sites in the state. Assemblymember Pat Burke said he is skeptical of the jobs report, which the state had not yet verified. Critics want the state to walk away or enforce penalties. Assemblymember Micah Lasher has called for the state to collect $41.2 million in penalties for Tesla's past shortfalls, and John Kaehny of Reinvent Albany wants the state to seek proposals from other possible tenants. Kaehny said the point of the deal was manufacturing jobs, "not subsidizing the sale and maintenance of Tesla vehicles." Buffalo Mayor Sean Ryan has pushed for a payment in lieu of taxes to the city. "The original vision may have changed, but we still expect Tesla to do everything it can to maximize jobs and investment here in Buffalo," Ryan said. The most recent public draft of the lease update, from January 2025, would extend the lease five years to 2034 and raise the rent to $2 million a year and eventually $5 million. Empire State Development president Hope Knight said the state was still weighing whether to fine Tesla.

ft-1763415612655-9636.text: The former Greenidge bitcoin mine and gas power plant at Dresden, in Yates County, New York, is being turned toward AI data centers by its owner, which changed its name in August 2026 from Greenidge Generation to Vulcan Infrastructure and Power. Atlas Holdings bought the plant in 2014, and a bitcoin mine started there in March 2020. Vulcan says it has left its historical bitcoin mining behind and has secured approval for 60 megawatts of non-curtailable grid power at Dresden, working with New York State Electric and Gas on the upgrades needed. The plant can generate about 106 megawatts and previously sent up to 60 megawatts to its bitcoin miners while selling electricity to the grid; Vulcan said the power plant's operation would not change under the data center conversion. For years the fight was over its air permit. Greenidge applied to renew its Title V air permit in 2021, and the state Department of Environmental Conservation denied it in 2022, finding renewal inconsistent with the greenhouse gas limits in New York's climate law. The denial was upheld on appeal and then overturned by the state Supreme Court in November 2024, and Greenidge and the DEC have since settled: the DEC will issue a renewed permit after public process, requiring a 44% cut in permitted emissions and a 25% cut in actual emissions by 2030, and Greenidge dropped its appeal. Yvonne Taylor's drinking water comes out of Seneca Lake through a pipe that runs down the hill from her house. She is vice president of Seneca Lake Guardian, and her worry about the power plant and data center is specific: "If there's a harmful algal bloom in front of my water source, I can't use my water at all. I can't flush the toilet, I can't shower, I can't bathe." The plant discharges warm water into Seneca Lake and into nearby Keuka Lake, which is what residents fear will feed cyanobacteria and set off algal blooms. "They're behaving like a petulant, rich child, because they don't like the answer that they get," Taylor said of the company's appeals. Seneca Lake Guardian, the Sierra Club and the Committee to Preserve the Finger Lakes sued under the Clean Water Act in 2023; the case was dismissed, the court finding the company's permit application sufficient. The next hurdle is New York's own. In July 2026 Governor Kathy Hochul ordered the DEC to hold discretionary permit applications for data centers of 50 megawatts or more while the state studies their environmental impact. The DEC told Gothamist it had not received a new application for the Vulcan conversion and did not say whether it would fall under the pause.

ft-1772679409535-8250.text: A Global AI data center on the Huron Campus in Endicott, in Broome County, New York, is getting its own power plant. Bloom Energy built a 9.36-megawatt natural gas fuel cell system next to a NYSEG substation on Clark Street, west of Hayes Avenue, to supply it. Chris Pelto, who oversees Huron Campus operations, said the site needs more power. Construction began in a Huron Campus parking lot in February 2026, and by early April Keeley Construction had finished building it while NYSEG crews worked at the site. Bloom says its fuel cells convert fuel into energy without combustion, built to give data centers a reliable power source. Broome County Executive Jason Garnar said he expects more on-site generation in the future because it would take NYSEG a few years to supply the extra power that companies hoping to locate in the county will need. The Village of Endicott has moved to slow data centers down. In July 2026 Mayor Nick Burlingame said the village attorney was drafting a 12-month moratorium on AI data centers, citing water and energy use in a village with a long history of water contamination. "We have a long history of pollution, and we just have to make sure that we are good stewards of our environment locally," Burlingame said. What prompted it was a small data center in Building 46 on the Huron Campus that recently changed businesses without needing zoning, planning or village board approval, because code enforcement saw no change of use; it has existed for more than a decade. "But, if that little center came in so effortlessly, this is a trigger for the moratorium," Burlingame said. New York's own one-year moratorium on large data centers took effect July 14, 2026. Burlingame said the village would still act because the state measure limits only large data centers and the village wants to limit all of them for now. Much of Endicott is zoned industrial, which could make it a target for more data centers. The Endicott Village Board was set to vote on the moratorium on July 20, 2026, at its regular meeting; no result has been published. If it passed, Burlingame planned a committee of businesses and residents to study data centers and report back before the village decides whether to change its rules.

ft-1771292292832-1038.text: Treetop Companies, a New Jersey developer, asked New York's grid operator in July 2025 to study a 1,000 megawatt data center on 137 wooded acres it controls in East Fishkill, near Hopewell Junction in Dutchess County, but never filed an application with the town. On June 25, 2026, the East Fishkill Town Board passed a three-year moratorium on data centers, running to July 1, 2029, that has effectively blocked the proposal. Treetop wanted a 1 gigawatt facility, with 500 megawatts of power open by 2028 and the rest by 2030. That is more than 10 times the size of the largest existing data center in New York. A drawing on Treetop's website showed a 1.16 million square foot data center south of Old State Road, off Donovan Drive. The project would connect to ConEd's grid, though the grid study also looked at its effect on Central Hudson and NYSEG. Through the landowner, Donovan Drive Holdings LLC, Treetop had first sought approval in 2023 for two warehouses totaling 765,000 square feet on the same industrial-zoned land, a plan later paused when the town adopted a separate industrial moratorium in August 2024. ft-1776884122303-9139.text: The Village of Ilion scheduled a public hearing for September 28, 2026 on a proposed moratorium on large-load electric development, the latest turn in the fight over whether the former Remington Arms gun factory in Herkimer County, New York, becomes a data center. The site's owner, Turin Hoefler Avenue LLC of Turin Management, has filed state brownfield cleanup applications describing a data center, but says "no data center end user is involved or committed to this site." The plant at 14 Hoefler Avenue covers about 32 acres and 1.1 million square feet, and it closed in March 2024 after more than two centuries of gun making; Turin bought it the following year. State filings describe a 250,000-square-foot data center on Site C, a second phase of the same size on Site E, and a substation on Site D, totaling 200 megawatts of power with $2 billion to $3 billion invested. Investigators found arsenic, lead and copper in the Site C soil above state cleanup standards for commercial use. A large crowd came to the Village Board of Trustees meeting on April 27, 2026, after the filings were reported. Resident Carrie Burling asked about cooling chemicals, pointing to a high concentration of cancer in the area, and a Change.org petition asking officials to pause approval and study the plan had more than 1,000 signatures by late April. "It's marketed as an economic opportunity, but after construction it will provide minimal jobs," wrote signer Peter from New Hartford, who had moved from northern Virginia. Mayor John Stephens has played the plan down, saying there is "not an interested party at this early stage," and that any future power for the site would be kept separate from the village's electric system. The Herkimer County Industrial Development Agency said Turin explored a data center and entered the state grid operator's power queue, but has since pivoted to back a multi-tenant office and light industrial park instead. Turin itself is still weighing a data center: an Empire State Development study "found a data center to be the strongest option for the site," and it had tried and failed to attract a manufacturer, chief executive Kristen O'Neill told residents. O'Neill wrote that Turin is "a small, women owned business" that has invested millions of dollars without a profit and cannot fund the cleanup alone, and argued the moratorium "sends investors and manufacturers a clear message to stay away from Ilion." The Village Board of Trustees scheduled a public hearing on the moratorium for 5 p.m. on September 28 at the Municipal Building on Morgan Street; no result has been published yet. Separately, the state Department of Environmental Conservation is reviewing the brownfield applications, with review and comment periods scheduled through 2026 and 2027.

ft-1763167673373-9089.text: H5 Data Centers owns the former Yahoo data center campus in the Town of Lockport's industrial park in Niagara County, New York, which it bought for a reported $49 million in a sale-leaseback deal that closed on Dec. 30, 2024. Yahoo is still operating on the site under a five-year lease. The Town of Lockport, meanwhile, is working on an 18-month moratorium on any new data centers. The campus sits at Upper Mountain and Junction roads. Yahoo first built it in 2009 on 30 acres for $150 million, and expansions in 2014 and 2019 grew it to 10 buildings on 43 acres totaling 409,200 square feet. The buildings use the passively air-cooled "chicken-coop" design, and H5 lists two on-site substations offering up to 44 megawatts. Of Yahoo's employees, 15 moved to H5 and 140 remained with Yahoo on the site. "This entity, H5 Data Centers, purchased all of Yahoo's land and buildings, i.e. real estate. It didn't do anything with the operations of Yahoo! itself", said Tom Sy, the town's economic development coordinator. Yahoo's two tax agreements with the Lockport Industrial Development Agency, which had spared it town, county and Starpoint Central School District taxes for years before phasing in payments, were ended with the sale, and H5 receives no tax incentives for now. H5 could still ask the IDA for incentives for future expansions, and Sy said the 2019 building is nowhere near full: "There is room in the 2019 data center for H5 to go out and identify other companies that need data center storage". In 2026 the Niagara County Planning Board backed data center moratoriums sought by the towns of Lockport and Cambria, 18 months in Lockport and nine in Cambria, and neither town had received any new data center requests. Other data centers in Niagara County include the Digipower X facility in North Tonawanda, the Lake Mariner complex in Somerset and Blockfusion in Niagara Falls, and the Town of Lewiston enacted its own 18-month moratorium earlier in 2026. The Lockport Town Board scheduled a public hearing for Aug. 5, 2026 on a local law establishing an 18-month moratorium on data center permitting and approval in the town. New York State's year-long moratorium on approving large new data centers applies only to state permitting, so data centers could still go through local review.

ft-1779021406073-5441.text: Ranalli Super DC, LLC, a company controlled by Syracuse developer James Ranalli, has asked the state grid operator to connect a 300 megawatt data center on vacant industrial land near Route 48 and Hencle Boulevard in Lysander, Onondaga County, New York. The Town of Lysander answered with a six-month moratorium on data storage facilities, passed May 7, 2026, that runs until November 7, 2026. The 124-acre site at Hencle Boulevard and Oswego Road is listed for sale at $60 million, and Ranalli plans to sell it to a data center developer he says he cannot name because of a non-disclosure agreement. Ranalli, who would not build the data center himself, put its possible cost at $4 billion to $8 billion and said it would be good for the town because of the property taxes it would pay. "We don't understand data centers. It's not what we do," Ranalli said, calling for a town meeting with a representative of the developer. The sale listing describes the land as a "300 MW Data Center Site" next to 345-kilovolt transmission lines, with a National Grid gas regulator station beside the property. Ranalli Super DC applied to the New York Independent System Operator in May 2025, and the project is projected to connect to the grid in 2028. It is the second plan for the same land: in 2021 the company proposed a 1-million-square-foot auto parts warehouse, distribution and retail center there. After community opposition and a lawsuit, a smaller version was approved with tax breaks, and the company canceled it in 2023. Residents organized as Citizens Against Lysander Data Center and gathered more than 1,800 signatures on a petition for a moratorium, pointing to the site's closeness to the Three Rivers Wildlife Management Area, noise from cooling systems and backup diesel generators, energy costs, property values and water. "Water pollution, limited natural resources, and the impact during droughts are concerns, especially for many of the Lysander residents on wells and not village water," the petition states. More than 350 residents attended the May 7 meeting where the moratorium passed unanimously. "So we as a community could have issues and we wouldn't have anywhere to go to," said Johanna Bock of Citizens for Lysander, who worries about who would answer for problems if the facility changed hands. No application for the data center is before the town. "A data center would be an allowed use under our current zoning regulations on an industrial parcel," Supervisor Kevin Rode said in April, adding that any application would go to the planning board, not the town board. Rode said the town chose six months because an entity is seeking utility and grid operator approvals for the project, and that the moratorium law lets applicants seek a hardship exception from the Town Board. The town has set up a data center advisory committee to review its code, and Onondaga County has funded a $500,000 study of data centers. New York's one-year statewide moratorium on permits for big data centers does not stop local review. "That does not preclude local governments from moving forward in their local permitting process," said State Sen. Kristen Gonzalez. The Lysander Town Board has said that because no application was before the town before the governor's executive order, it believes the state pause holds in Lysander, and that it knows of no state environmental permit request for a data center on the parcel. The town moratorium expires November 7, 2026; after that, any application would go to the Lysander Planning Board, which Rode has said would treat it as an entirely new application and a lengthy process.

ft-1763172695674-8393.text: A data center planned in the former Sears store at the St. Lawrence Centre mall in Massena, St. Lawrence County, New York, won site plan approval from the St. Lawrence County Planning Board in August 2020, but nothing has been reported on it since. The developer was Tareo Capital Management LP of New York City, which described the project only as a new electronic data processing center; a county planning official said at the time, "I don't know for sure if this is a Bitcoin mining data center or a data processing data center." The mall itself has since closed to the public. By April 2024 it had been renamed the St. Lawrence Industrial Complex, advertising more than 600,000 square feet of industrial and warehouse space, with JCPenney as its remaining store. Work that began in 2022 turned the former Hills store and food court into warehouse space for goods resold to Amazon and Walmart, with self-storage, and spaces from 30,000 to 200,000 square feet are now offered for lease across the former mall; no data center has been reported there since the 2020 approval. Massena's data center debate has since moved to a much larger project nearby. North Country Colocation Services wants to build a 1.5 million-square-foot, 635-megawatt data center at the former Alcoa East site near the St. Lawrence River. On September 16, 2026 the Massena Town Board voted 3-2 against a six-month moratorium that would have restricted it, after more than an hour of public comment. "We need at least three years to do this research. We need substantial time. We need a moratorium," said Marina Johnson Zafiris of Akwesasne, with the group Mohawks United in Safety and Health. Fire Chief Tom Millar argued the other way: "We gotta find a way, we gotta get jobs here, so the fire department, the rescue squad, can flourish again." Site plans in Massena are decided by the Massena Planning Board, with review by the St. Lawrence County Planning Board, and zoning questions go to the Massena Town Board and its Zoning Board of Appeals.

ft-1763170918062-5222.text: North Country Colocation Services, backed by Coinmint/NYDIG, wants to expand its bitcoin mining and data center site in Massena, St. Lawrence County, New York, on the old Reynolds/Alcoa smelter site along the St. Lawrence River. The project is on hold: New York's one-year moratorium on new data center construction, the Responsible Data Center Development Act, took effect July 14, 2026, and blocks new work at the site until July 2027. On September 16, 2026, the Massena town board separately voted 3-2 against its own proposed six-month local moratorium, but that vote does not lift the state freeze. NCCS's original plan called for three buildings totaling close to 1.5 million square feet and 635 megawatts of power, drawing from the New York Power Authority's hydroelectric supply. After community pushback, the company dropped a building and cut the footprint by about 400,000 square feet, redesigning to the 400 megawatts now listed for the site. The company says the project would use a closed-loop cooling system that does not draw from or discharge into local waterways. Councilmember Jared Hollander, who voted against the local moratorium, said of the developers: "I've had a chance to speak to the developers. They've seemed willing to work with us and earnestly try to make the community better." Fire Chief Tom Millar backed the project for the jobs it could bring, saying "we gotta get jobs here, so the fire department, the rescue squad, can flourish again." Bill Fiacco, owner of Gristmill Brewery, said "the only thing a moratorium does is start scaring the developers away from the area." Marina Johnson Zafiris, of Akwesasne, told the board: "We presently do not know the long-term social, environmental, and political risks of allowing hyperscale data centers into our communities." A resident group, Massena Data Center Watch, says capped smelter contamination on the site, including PCBs, dioxins and metals, sits next to a federal river cleanup that construction could disturb. The group also disputes the developer's jobs figures, noting Coinmint promised 150 jobs within 18 months but employed only 65 by 2020 and about 60 today, against a projection of 200 permanent jobs. St. Lawrence County stopped short of its own moratorium on June 1, 2026, instead passing a resolution affirming local control over data center siting. Because the state moratorium runs through July 14, 2027, no new construction can begin at the Massena site before then unless the law changes.

ft-1763170364459-3434.text: ZeroC Data Centers, whose majority owner is Petawatt Holdings, has prepared an industrial site at 417 County Route 42 in Massena, St. Lawrence County, New York, for a future data center. The company won approval in February 2025 for a roughly $30 million substation on the site, but no data center itself has been approved, and the 300 megawatt grid connection the substation was meant to protect was later withdrawn. Petawatt's plan is to prepare the land and then sell or lease it, not build the data center itself. "They are not going to be the ones building and running the data center. What they're doing is simply doing the site prep so it's ready to pass on to a developer," the company's architect, Brooks Washburn, told the St. Lawrence County Planning Board in January 2025. The site already held two cryptocurrency mining containers, and county planning director Jason Pfotenhauer noted the town's industrial zone did not list crypto mining, utilities or substations as permitted uses, sending the question to the town's Zoning Board of Appeals. When the Massena Town Planning Board took up the site plan on February 20, 2025, members pressed the company on what the substation was for; board member David Grant said it seemed strange to spend $30 million with no idea what the substation would connect to. Asked the difference between a data center and a crypto mining center, the Petawatt representative answered that "a crypto mining operation is a data center," though he offered to sign an agreement guaranteeing no cryptocurrency mining if the project were approved, and the board approved the substation 4-0. The Petawatt case pushed Massena to draft a local law allowing data centers in industrial zones, since they were not a permitted use before, and by May 2026 ten data center proposals were under review in the Massena area. The furthest along is a separate proposal, North Country Colocation Services, for three buildings totaling close to 1.5 million square feet next to the former Alcoa East plant, needing about 635 megawatts. On September 16, 2026, the Massena Town Board voted 3-2 against a six-month moratorium on new data centers after more than an hour of divided public comment, clearing the way for North Country Colocation Services' project to keep moving. "We presently do not know the long-term social, environmental, and political risks of allowing hyperscale data centers into our communities," said Marina Johnson Zafiris of Akwesasne, who led the push for a pause; Fire Chief Tom Millar argued the other side, "we gotta get jobs here, so the fire department, the rescue squad, can flourish again." New York State has its own moratorium on new data centers statewide, from July 14, 2026 to July 14, 2027, which covers this site along with the rest of the state. For now, only the substation at 417 County Route 42 is approved; no developer has taken over the site to build a data center there, and the grid request tied to it has lapsed.

ft-384.text: Oxford Quantum Circuits (OQC) installed New York City's first quantum computer in September 2025 inside a data center that Digital Realty runs in the Google-owned carrier hotel at 111 8th Avenue in Chelsea, Manhattan, New York County. The system is paired with an Nvidia Grace Hopper superchip, and OQC's chief executive, Gerald Mullally, called it "the industry's first quantum AI data center." Mullally said OQC expected to spend "tens of millions of dollars" over three to five years, partly on Nvidia chips, and planned to open the center to the wider market in 2026 after starting with select customers. Google bought 111 8th Avenue, a carrier hotel, in 2010 in a deal reported at around $1.8 billion. Mullally said banks were among the interested customers: "We are embedding it within their secure infrastructure in New York so they can access it in the same way they access the rest of their computing infrastructure." OQC, spun out of the University of Oxford in 2017, raised $40.5 million in 2022 and $100 million in 2024, and plans to install a more powerful quantum computer by 2028. The installation sits inside an existing building and is far smaller than the scale New York's statewide pause targets: in July 2026 Gov. Kathy Hochul signed an executive order blocking construction of data centers above 50 megawatts for up to a year while the state writes new environmental and grid rules.

ft-1768452919400-6955.text: 9 Lives Digital Group (9LDG), the company behind the proposed 9Lives Data Center, bought the shuttered Globe Metallurgical plant at 3807 Highland Avenue in Niagara Falls' North End, Niagara County, New York, in July 2024. President Michael Bagley said the company would build an artificial intelligence data center, logistics hub and warehouse on the 22-acre site, which already has a 100 megawatt substation. The $3 million sale closed on July 16, 2024; Bagley said the data center would cost about $100 million, create roughly 500 construction jobs, and take 18 to 24 months to build. "This is a comeback story for me, and part of a comeback story for Niagara Falls," Bagley told the Buffalo News. Bagley was sentenced to four years in federal prison in February 2019 for helping launder drug-trafficking proceeds for people he believed were tied to a Mexican cartel, and published reports say he served about two years; he says people shouldn't believe everything they read and that he is now focused on redeveloping the region. Buffalo Business First reported that a mortgage document names Gjergj M. Hajati, who has served two prison sentences for fraud, as a management member of the company that bought the property. Instead of a data center, neighbors reported bitcoin mining containers and heavy equipment moving onto the site, and as of January 2025 no building permits had been pulled for it. City administrator Anthony Restaino said Niagara Falls had received no site plans or demolition permits for the project and would be "monitoring what activity is taking place out there." Any data center on the site still needs city permits, and nothing has surfaced publicly since.

ft-1763419229850-2546.text: The Niagara Falls City Council voted unanimously in October 2025 to approve a high-energy use overlay for the BlockFusion data center and bitcoin mine at 5380 Frontier Avenue in Niagara Falls, Niagara County, New York, clearing the way for its operator, North East Data LLC, to apply for the city permit it needs to keep running. The vote followed a unanimous recommendation from the city Planning Board and ended a three-year fight over noise. Complaints about mining noise led the city in 2022 to confine data centers and bitcoin mines to industrial zones with a 65-decibel cap at the nearest home, and BlockFusion shut down when the rules took effect that November. The company sued the city and the two sides settled in December 2023 on an environmental review process; the company's noise consultant found the plant does not raise sound levels at nearby homes, though resident Sarah Zelensky disagreed. Zelensky described "a horrible, mechanical, grinding noise" from the site; the city's Zoning Board of Appeals later found the company in compliance anyway. In September 2026 BlockFusion's subsidiary signed a 15-year anchor lease with the AI cloud company CoreWeave, firming up a June letter of intent for up to 300 megawatts that includes 85 megawatts of guaranteed capacity, with the first 25 megawatts expected in 2027. BlockFusion is going public through a $450 million merger with Blue Acquisition Corp. and has an exclusivity deal to buy adjacent land that would grow the site from about 5 acres to roughly 40. New York also put a moratorium on new data center construction in place statewide from July 14, 2026, to July 14, 2027, but it targets new proposals rather than BlockFusion's plant, which already holds its city permits. With the overlay cleared, BlockFusion can now seek the city's high-energy use permit to keep the site running long term.

ft-1763171931545-6175.text: The Niagara Digital Campus, a $1.5 billion, 135-megawatt data center proposed by Niagara Falls Redevelopment (NFR) in the South End of Niagara Falls, Niagara County, won the zoning it needed in June 2026 as part of a settlement ending years of litigation between the company and the city. The deal rezoned NFR's land east of 907 Falls Street for the data center campus, while NFR handed the city the 10-acre property at 907 Falls Street for its planned Centennial Park arena in return for $4.029 million. NFR, a subsidiary of New York City-based Milstein Properties, owns more than 140 acres in Niagara Falls and plans the campus with Urbacon, a Toronto construction company with data centers in Canada. The plan calls for about 600,000 square feet of data center space, with its first phase now planned on NFR land on 15th Street, behind the Holy Trinity Roman Catholic Church complex on Falls Street. Its 2024 zoning application described eight two-story buildings and one one-story building, 1,232,715 square feet in all, across about 53 acres bounded by John B. Daly Boulevard, Falls Street, 15th Street and Buffalo Avenue, built in five phases. NFR says the campus would bring at least 500 permanent jobs, and Urbacon has pointed to Niagara's hydroelectric power and a northern climate that needs less mechanical cooling. The fight was over land, not only the data center. NFR unveiled the campus as the city moved to take 907 Falls Street by eminent domain for Centennial Park, and Mayor Robert Restaino said then: "It's not the best use for that property. That's a gateway into the city." The land sits in an area zoned for residential, commercial and other non-industrial uses, and the city's 2022 High Energy Use Law put tough noise and other restrictions on high-energy-use industrial facilities. The Niagara Falls Planning Board found NFR's revised application incomplete, and both the city and Niagara County planning boards rejected the company's request to loosen the High Energy Use Law. Court-sanctioned mediation this year led to what some have called the "Two-Project Solution," and the settlement commits the city to grant NFR the approvals for its Planned Unit Development, subdivide parcels and close streets at the company's request. NFR paid $1.43 million for the two parcels it is handing over for $4.029 million. At a contentious council meeting on June 3, speakers split: one said both projects "will create a significant number of jobs for the building trades," and another warned that "These machines require and contaminate a lot of water, and once it's gone, we don't get it back." Marybeth Nugent, whose Gadawski's Restaurant is surrounded by NFR property, was unconvinced: "They haven't done anything in all this time, so maybe they just made $4 million off of us." Restaino has said the settlement was not a green light for construction: "Last night wasn't the approval of a data center. There are still things that have to happen for that to occur." NFR has controlled more than 140 acres of South End land for more than two decades without completing a development, and Restaino said nothing in the agreement requires it to build. A majority of the city council later balked at authorizing the $4.029 million payment from the city's fund balance. The bigger obstacle may now be Albany: in July 2026 Gov. Kathy Hochul signed an executive order blocking construction of data centers operating above 50 megawatts for up to a year while state officials write new rules on the environment and the grid, and an NFR spokesperson said the company had not yet seen the order and had no comment. City officials say NFR must still obtain local and state approvals before construction on the Niagara Digital Campus can begin.

ft-1763418819550-7661.text: DigiPower X, the company formerly called Digihost, wants to turn its cryptocurrency mining data center at the former Fortistar gas power plant on Erie Avenue in North Tonawanda, in Niagara County, New York, into an AI data center, and the city has extended a moratorium that blocks it. On June 8, 2026 the company presented a plan for a two-story, 80,000-square-foot building on the property to replace its cryptocurrency mining computers with AI supercomputers. The $250 million building would replace much of the existing site and employ 50 to 70 people, against 17 today, according to the company's application to the city planning commission. The application proposes removing the computer fans "that were previously creating higher than desired noise levels", and says the new design would use emergency-only backup diesel generators and closed-loop air-cooled cooling towers. The company bought the rarely used 55-megawatt Fortistar gas plant in 2022 with the approval of the state Public Service Commission. Noise is what neighbors have fought for years. The site's cooling fans produce a loud, droning noise, according to a class-action lawsuit that residents filed in federal court in Buffalo in April 2026 on behalf of everyone living within three miles. "My family and I are under attack," plaintiff Mark Polito said in the lawsuit. Of the AI plan, Polito said: "None of us want an AI data center, none of us want the crypto data center that's there now". Deborah Gondek, a local advocate, said the company "didn't have a lot of specifics" about whether the change would bring the noise within the city's new ordinance. Police cited the company for exceeding the nighttime noise limit in July 2025, but in June 2026 a city court dismissed three of the four citations because the old ordinance had since been replaced; the company pleaded not guilty to the remaining one, issued in June under the updated law. The state climate law is a second front. On May 28, 2026 the Appellate Division, Third Department, ruled that the Public Service Commission must examine the emissions impacts of the 2022 plant sale under the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act, and found the commission still had not completed that analysis. The ruling was a win for the Clean Air Coalition of Western New York and the Sierra Club, represented by Earthjustice. North Tonawanda's Common Council first passed a two-year moratorium on new data centers and expansions of existing ones in July 2024, and in June 2026 voted to extend it by a year while the city rewrites its zoning. Mayor Austin Tylec said: "I think we're in a good position now to have controls in place to make sure we're not the guinea pig anymore with new industries coming in." The company could still seek the moratorium's "extraordinary hardship" exception, Tylec has said, and the city planning commission has made itself lead agency for the project's environmental review and referred it to the Niagara County Planning Board. At least seven data centers operate in Erie and Niagara counties, and more are planned, including a $2 billion AI data center at the old Tonawanda Coke site.

ft-1763168488100-6067.text: The Riverview Innovation & Technology Campus, a proposed 300 megawatt AI data center on the former Tonawanda Coke site on River Road in the Town of Tonawanda, Erie County, New York, is suspended behind a grid study and a town moratorium. On August 3, 2026, the Town Board voted unanimously for a one year moratorium on data centers of 20 megawatts or more, two months after the site's owners, developers Jon Williams and John Yensan, paused the town's review of their application. Riverview said after the vote it would keep reviewing its options with legal counsel. The plan, filed with the town planning board in spring 2026, calls for a 500,000 square foot data center on the 140 acre campus at 3800 and 3875 River Road, with up to $2 billion invested. Williams and Yensan bought the site at auction in 2019 for $1, the only bid, and their remediation firm has led an estimated $100 million cleanup of the former coke plant, which closed around 2018 after Tonawanda Coke Corp. went bankrupt and was fined about $25 million for hazardous emissions. The developers, who have not named their data center partner, hope to break ground late in 2026 and finish by the end of 2027. The project includes a planned $50 million electrical substation and, the developers say, would run on about 91% emission free electricity from the Niagara Power Project and the Nine Mile Point nuclear station without raising electricity prices. The Clean Air Coalition of Western New York opposes the project and wants the corridor used for unionized renewable power and storage instead. "We have no say in this," said Jim Jones, a former town engineer who chairs the coalition's board. "These computers, they burn out. Is this just going to be adding to our hazardous waste?" asked Bridge Rauch, the coalition's environmental justice organizer. Resident Jamie Moore told the packed June 3, 2026 planning board meeting that cooling systems for such projects "typically operate at 75 to 105 decibels or greater." State Sen. Jeremy Zellner, who represents Tonawanda, said the project's 300 megawatt power load is "going to be just about as much electricity as my entire district uses." In early June, Town Supervisor John Flynn said the developer had asked to pause its application because of a "backlog" at the New York Independent System Operator, which studies the project's grid impact; Riverview said its SEQRA and site plan reviews were only "temporarily delayed" while it awaits word from NYISO and National Grid on transmission upgrades and cost. Tonawanda's moratorium mirrors a state one Gov. Kathy Hochul signed in July, pausing new data centers above 50 megawatts for up to a year. The Town Board plans to write new data center zoning rules during its moratorium year, which runs through August 3, 2027; when Riverview's review resumes, its site plan goes back to the planning board under any new rules, and its power supply still depends on NYISO's grid study and National Grid.

ft-1763171550036-9496.text: Wildflower's plan for a $1 billion, 176 megawatt data center at its warehouse campus on Expressway Drive North in Yaphank, Suffolk County, is on hold. The Town of Brookhaven adopted an 18-month moratorium on data centers on July 16, 2026, and a state moratorium covering projects of 50 megawatts or more took effect two days earlier. Town Attorney Annette Eaderesto said Wildflower's application was incomplete when the moratorium passed and will not be processed while it lasts. The company, formally WF Industrial XII, wants to convert three warehouses on 71 acres into what it calls the Brookhaven Digital Infrastructure Facility, using a closed-loop cooling system that would need a one-time fill of about 700,000 gallons of water. It has not selected a tenant. Wildflower's director of development, Michael Bowden, told the town the project would bring more than 1,000 union construction jobs and 50 permanent jobs, and that annual property taxes would rise from $1.8 million to $40 million. Councilmember Jonathan Kornreich said the plant "would represent 50% of the total electricity use of the entire Town of Brookhaven," and that its 78 proposed backup generators, all running, would be "comparable in emissions output to [approximately] 12,000 trucks." A noise study found the site would need sound mitigation "especially at night and especially along the western side of the property," he said. About 70 people rallied outside Town Hall for a permanent ban before a six-hour hearing on the moratorium. The moratorium runs until early 2028 while the town's planning department writes the first zoning rules for data centers, coordinating with the electric utility LIPA and the Suffolk County Water Authority, which says the developer has not yet applied for the water it would need. Wildflower said it was reviewing the state order but has not said whether it will try to move the project forward.

ft-1773440681171-2299.text: Amazon Web Services' Aberdeen data center would rise in Sprigg Township, Adams County, Ohio, about two miles from the village of Manchester, though the public did not learn Amazon was behind it until opponents' records requests uncovered it. A February 3, 2026 filing from AES Ohio to grid operator PJM says the project, near the former Stuart power plant, would draw 100 megawatts of power starting in 2028, rising to 1.3 gigawatts by March 2032, and the US Army Corps of Engineers has since issued a permit for construction. Adams County's own project webpage says Amazon is evaluating the county, will fund the energy and infrastructure the data center needs, and expects the campus to create at least 500 long-term jobs from a $10 billion investment. At that size the project would use about 11.4 million megawatt hours of electricity a year, roughly 31 times Adams County's entire 2025 consumption, according to WCPO's analysis of the AES filing. Ben Murray, a Food & Water Watch researcher who is building a house on family land near Manchester, has helped lead the opposition; he said emails about the project went back to 2024, but the developer "remained entirely nameless and faceless until the records requests found that it's going to be an Amazon data center." In February 2026 Sprigg Township trustees agreed to a one-year voluntary pause with the developer, and neighboring Monroe Township passed a binding one-year moratorium; both townships have since started zoning processes that could restrict where a data center could be built. "The voluntary pause and the initiating of the zoning, those came about just because people spoke up and turned out to these meetings," Murray said.

ft-1774482485361-4747.text: Viking Data Centers runs a crypto-mining and AI data center at 428 Seiberling St. in East Akron, in Summit County, Ohio, inside what was once Goodyear's largest tire factory. The 380,000-square-foot building also houses Viking's headquarters and uses 150 megawatts of power around the clock, according to the company's website. Viking says it opened in 2021 and grew from 20 megawatts that year to 150 megawatts in 2024. The company says it is "actively mining the capacity available on the site" and is a top-three customer of the electric utility. In March 2026 Viking chose Atlantic Energy as its retail power supplier, in a deal Atlantic said would support up to 150 MW of computing capacity "with further expansion potential." "We selected Atlantic Energy as our provider for a long-term agreement because of their ability to structure a comprehensive and forward-thinking energy solution aligned with Viking's strategic growth plans," said Kazim Tahir-Kheli of Viking Data Centers. The facility's 150 megawatts is enough to power about 63,000 homes, Signal Akron reported. Akron has since tightened its rules. On July 27, 2026 the City Council passed a zoning change that makes data centers a defined land use needing conditional-use approval, with a Planning Commission review and public hearings before any new one is built. Applicants must now disclose expected electricity demand, water use and wastewater, backup power and projected noise; the new requirements do not apply to expansions of existing facilities, Signal Akron reported. "Our zoning code was written before facilities like modern data centers became a significant planning consideration," Mayor Shammas Malik said in a city release. Residents who spoke for the rules raised health, energy and noise concerns. "Overall, I'm concerned about hyper-scale data centers," said Abigail Drennen of Highland Square, who said a moratorium would be appropriate. Theresa Augustin of Summit Lake said she worried the historic Firestone Plant #1 could become a data center. Planning director Kyle Julien said he expects the city to go further and explicitly limit data centers near schools or parks. Viking is one of four data centers operating in Akron. The company ark data centers, which has two locations in the city, received a $4.5 million tax break to expand its operations in Akron and Independence. Any new data center in Akron now goes to the Planning Commission and City Council for conditional-use approval; expansions of existing ones, like Viking's, are not covered by the new process.

ft-1784757848477-2555.text: Amherst's Board of Zoning Appeals on July 30, 2026, rejected the use variance Cervenka Development Partners needed to turn three buildings on the former Nordson Corporation campus in Amherst, Lorain County, Ohio, into a data center, a day after more than 100 residents packed a hearing at City Hall. The Illinois-based developer had described a data center with a potential power capacity of 45 megawatts at 100, 200 and 300 Nordson Drive, on a 36.58-acre parcel Nordson has listed for sale. Nordson, founded in Amherst in 1954 and now based in Westlake, is moving out; its older manufacturing buildings at the south end of the campus sit empty and are set to be demolished, while the three newer buildings Cervenka wants are still in use. A Cervenka spokesperson said the company had not bought the property and the zoning request was part of due diligence; the firm, run by Tom and Sasha Cervenka, describes itself as a woman-owned commercial real estate firm. "It's a small community, and we love how it is," resident Judy Heiser told the zoning board. "And we don't need data centers and noise. We just don't need it." Cervenka argued the buildings, built for Nordson, would be hard for another manufacturer to use, but acknowledged under questioning: "Am I gonna tell you that there is no other user that can use these buildings? No." The board's written decision said he had undermined his own case, and member John Jeffreys noted the buildings had only gone on the market in April. "The board has spoken. The people have spoken," Mayor Mark Costilow said, adding that if Cervenka sues, "the city will defend its position." Cervenka had 30 days to appeal to the Lorain County Common Pleas Court, a deadline that passed in late August with no further public update since. Costilow said a moratorium on data centers is up to Amherst City Council, though he believes the city's existing zoning code, which does not list data centers as a permitted use, already works.

ft-1771179164518-9722.text: Ashville's village council has moved to repeal its agreement with EdgeConneX for a data center campus and gas power plant on about 195 acres in the village, in Pickaway County, Ohio, rather than put it to a public vote in November. In early September 2026 the council introduced Resolution 16-2026 to repeal the deal, which under Ohio law takes the citizens' referendum off the November 3 ballot. EdgeConneX plans two data center buildings on the parcel, and through an affiliate is seeking state approval for a natural gas power plant next to it. The Ohio Power Siting Board lists that plant, PowerConneX's Ashville Energy Center, at up to 800 megawatts of power on about 110 acres. The company originally planned a larger, 680-acre campus reaching into Harrison Township, but in early 2026 the council voted 4-2 against annexing about 400 acres of that farmland into the village. Money was the village's reason to deal. On April 6, 2026 the council voted 5-1 to approve a term summary in which EdgeConneX offered up to $102 million to the village, Harrison Township and the Teays Valley Local School District. Village Administrator Bert Cline warned that without it, residents could face water bill increases of nearly $125 a month to pay for about $35 million in required water and sewer upgrades. The deal also exempted EdgeConneX from Ashville's data center moratorium. Residents gathered 875 signatures for a referendum, and 669 were verified. The village's fiscal officer refused to certify the petition because the council had passed the resolution as an emergency, but on August 7 the Ohio Supreme Court unanimously ordered it certified, ruling the council never gave specific reasons for the emergency. On August 24 the Pickaway County Board of Elections voted 4-0 to put the question on the November ballot. Repealing the term summary does not end the project. The repeal resolution says it does not affect other proceedings, including the gas plant case before the Ohio Power Siting Board, which held its local public hearing at Teays Valley High School on August 19. The siting board, not the village, has final authority over the gas plant and has approved projects in the past over local opposition. The next decisions are the village council's final vote on the repeal and the siting board's ruling on the PowerConneX gas plant, case 26-196-EL-BGN.

ft-387.text: Project Triton, Quantum HPC's planned data center at the former PPG limestone mine at 3700 Limestone Drive in Norton, Ohio, was dropped in October 2025, days after a town hall where residents confronted the developer. Norton City Council announced on October 17 that the data center project was not moving forward, after a resident showed that statements by the developer's representative were untrue and the developer said that person no longer worked for it. Quantum HPC had planned a 485,000-square-foot data center and a 157,000-square-foot power yard with six natural gas turbines on a 90-acre site off South Cleveland-Massillon Road, a limestone mine that closed about 50 years ago. It promised about 280 construction jobs and 110 full-time jobs. About 200 residents came to the October 13 town hall and raised noise, pollution, the drain on natural resources and the plant's round-the-clock operation, along with questions about the developer's earlier proposals that had not gone ahead. Law Director Justin Markey determined that statements made by Quantum HPC founder Dale James Hobbie were not true, and council later honored resident James Helmick for raising questions about Hobbie's education and litigation over his other projects. Quantum HPC said through spokesman Dan Williamson that it was engaging a new development team and remained "committed to building a highly secure, highly efficient data center in Ohio". "I'll just say there's nothing to fight. It's a done deal. It's over with," Council President Doug DeHarpart told a packed council meeting on October 20. Both cities then moved to pause data centers. Norton City Council gave a first reading on November 3, 2025 to a 180-day moratorium on zoning certificates for data processing and hosting, to give the city time to update its zoning code. The council enacted the six-month moratorium in December 2025, News 5 Cleveland reported, and city leaders declined to discuss how they plan to proceed. Barberton City Council passed an indefinite moratorium on data centers on November 10, 2025, which Councilman Thomas Heitic said would last until data center rules are added to the city's new development code. "If [a data center] can work within the parameters [established by the city], then welcome to Barberton," Heitic said. Across Ohio, at least 138 municipalities and townships had active data center moratoriums as of September 17, 2026, and 23 communities have effectively banned them, the Ohio Capital Journal reported. A Bowling Green State University poll found 78% of Ohioans support moratoriums until more is known about data centers' effects. Any new data center at the mine would need a zoning certificate from the City of Norton under whatever rules Norton City Council and its Planning Commission adopt.

Barberton City Council passed an indefinite moratorium on data centers on November 10, 2025, which Councilman Thomas Heitic said would last until data center rules are added to the city's new development code.
"If [a data center] can work within the parameters [established by the city], then welcome to Barberton," Heitic said.
Across Ohio, at least 138 municipalities and townships had active data center moratoriums as of September 17, 2026, and 23 communities have effectively banned them, the Ohio Capital Journal reported.
A Bowling Green State University poll found 78% of Ohioans support moratoriums until more is known about data centers' effects.
Any new data center at the mine would need a zoning certificate from the City of Norton under whatever rules Norton City Council and its Planning Commission adopt.

ft-1778247647739-3538.text: Lakeland Equity Group proposed a $1.6 billion, 150 megawatt data center on a 35-acre site at 3560 East 55th Street in Cleveland's Slavic Village, Cuyahoga County, Ohio. Cleveland's Mayor Justin Bibb administration rejected the permit application in May 2026 for failing zoning review, blocking the project, and a citywide moratorium on new data centers runs through October. City Council holds its final public hearing on permanent data center rules October 7 at the Gunning Recreation Center, after earlier hearings on September 24 and September 29. Lakeland filed on May 5 for three two-story buildings totaling 300,000 square feet on the former Morabito Enterprises trucking property between Interstate 77 and East 55th Street, and held an option to buy the site if the city approved. The company said $1 billion would go to the data center itself, that it would pay for grid upgrades, and that closed loop cooling would cut water use 80 to 90 percent compared with older systems. It forecast 1,500 to 2,000 construction jobs over 30 to 42 months and 65 to 115 permanent jobs. Dorothy Blackwell and Witold Sztalkopr, who have lived in Slavic Village since 1985, said they want to know how a project this size would affect water, power and traffic. "Is this beneficial for the area or causing more trouble? How is it going to impact utilities?" Blackwell asked. Councilman Charles Slife of Ward 15, who introduced the moratorium in late April, said the developer appeared to be racing to get approved before the rules changed. "I remain skeptical," he said. "If I were a resident of that immediate area, I would have a lot of questions." The city's statement said "Mayor Bibb has serious concerns about hyperscale, standalone data centers being placed in residential neighborhoods." A city source told NEOtrans the application was rejected because no site plans were submitted. Lakeland called the rejection "abrupt" and said it was "considering our options for immediate next steps." The land is zoned semi-industry, which allows buildings up to 115 feet, more than twice the floor area Lakeland proposed, so a similar plan might be legal there without variances. In late June, council's utilities committee cut Slife's proposed one-year moratorium to three months, covering new data centers and expansions but not companies' own in-house data centers. Ward 12 Councilmember Tanmay Shah tried to extend it to six months and questioned whether the city's electrical grid could handle data centers. Construction trades workers packed the room in support; IBEW Local 38's Mike Bremmer said, "We could be the tech capital of the Midwest." Council President Blaine Griffin said, "We do want to make sure that we get this right, but we also don't want to say that Cleveland is closed for business." Council passed the moratorium, which runs through October unless extended. Utilities Committee chairman Brian Kazy scheduled three public hearings on how to regulate data centers: September 24 at the Collinwood Recreation Center, September 29 at City Hall, and October 7 at the Gunning Recreation Center, plus an online survey. The September 24 hearing has been held; no result has been published. City Council's decision on the rules, and whether it extends the pause, will determine whether a plan like Lakeland's can be filed again in a residential neighborhood.

ft-401.text: DartPoints runs a colocation data center at 565 Metro Place South in Dublin, in Franklin County, Ohio, a building it bought in October 2020 when it acquired Metro Data Centers. DartPoints lists the Dublin data center, which it calls CMH01, as a 40,000-square-foot facility with 3 MW of utility power, a critical IT load of 345 kW, a 5,900-square-foot data hall and 11 network providers on site. Metro Data Centers was a carrier-neutral data center with 22,000 square feet of technical space when DartPoints, then newly backed by the private equity firm Astra Capital, bought it. "The acquisition of MDC is a prime example of how we are executing on our strategy for regional growth aimed at improving interconnectivity," DartPoints CEO Scott Willis said at the time. Metro co-founder and president Rob Kopp said his team was "fully committed to integrate our solutions with the expanding DartPoints' portfolio of interconnection points." The building is small next to the cloud campuses around it: Data Center Frontier noted it sits about 20 miles from the New Albany cluster that includes data centers for Facebook, Google and Amazon Web Services. DartPoints says the site is staffed around the clock and offers colocation, cloud and interconnection services. Dublin has since closed its door to new data centers in its western corridor. In June 2025, residents of the Ballantrae neighborhood pushed back on a plan to rezone the West Innovation District for industrial uses that could include data centers, citing traffic, noise and property values. "We know that Amazon is looking at this area. They have a data center just down the street on 161 in Houchard. They have a data center on Cosgray Road in Hilliard. And we're right between those two," resident Amy Swank said. On July 1, 2026, Dublin City Council passed Ordinance 33-26, which removes data centers as permitted or conditional uses in the West Innovation District, and rezoned about 370 acres there. The city's Planning and Zoning Commission is expected to review further updates to the district's ID-2 and ID-3 zoning on October 1, with a recommendation to City Council expected on October 15. The latest DartPoints listing, which gives no opening date, shows the Metro Place data center in service.

ft-403.text: The owners behind the PRSM data center proposal on about 298 acres of farmland along Orphans Road near Eaton, in Jefferson Township, Preble County, Ohio, withdrew their rezoning request on September 29, 2025, two days before the county commissioners were due to vote. PRSM Land Development Group, the land developer behind the data center, says the project is not over. The case was Preble County Zoning Case #1630. The request would have rezoned 270.34 acres south of Interstate 70 to limited industrial to allow a computer data storage center, and 27.98 acres north of the interstate to a special use under agricultural zoning. The land has frontage on Oxford-Gettysburg Road, Eaton-Gettysburg Road and the north side of Orphans Road. The Preble County Planning Commission voted 11-0 against it on August 21, 2025, and the Rural Zoning Commission 5-0 against it on September 2. The September 2 public hearing drew an overflow crowd worried about the environment and their energy bills. "I don't think the citizens of the county will support it," said Jesse Morland, who lives on the 300 acres. "They didn't support this go around. I don't see why anyone would expect anything else." In their withdrawal, the owners wrote that they "believe this process requires a different approach and will be re-evaluated sometime in the future." "Interest in having a data center on that land has not gone away," said Patrick Scanlon of PRSM Land Development Group. "The threshold for this development is the rezoning. And without that nothing happens." Scanlon said PRSM hopes to resubmit when it has a more favorable plan. A new application would start over. Brad Kramer, the county's director of land use management, said any similar case would have to go back through the Planning Commission, the Rural Zoning Commission and then the Preble County Board of Commissioners, and that the owners could reapply at any time. "The Planning Commission meeting is open to the public. That's not part of the advertising process by law," Kramer said, urging neighbors to spread the word if an application returns. A February 2026 Ohio statewide report pointed to Preble County as a place where data centers must pass several planning commission approvals, unlike townships with little zoning.

ft-1786993666588-1903.text: AWS Data Center, an Amazon Web Services data center proposed for Madison Township, in Butler County, Ohio, just south of Trenton, was stalled when the City of Trenton withdrew its petition to annex about 600 acres of the land on September 14, 2026. The city's attorney said it reserves the right to refile after the November 3 election, when Trenton voters will decide whether to ban data centers above a 25-megawatt threshold in the city. Amazon is planning 18 buildings of about 220,000 square feet each on 601 acres along Wayne Madison Road and Hawkins Road, near a Duke Energy substation and gas-fired power plant, in Madison and St. Clair townships. Both townships turned down the annexation in August 2026; Madison Township trustees voted 3-0, and board president Jeff Willoughby said the petition would create an island of township land and contained errors in its legal description. "If you walk out your front door, what are you going to see? Are you going to see concrete? Are you going to see trees? Are you going to see a fence?" Willoughby said, citing residents' worries about noise, stormwater and the view. Amazon had offered each township $5 million. Butler County enacted a six-month moratorium on data centers in June 2026 covering Madison Township, set to expire in December, and St. Clair Township adopted its own 12-month moratorium in May. If Trenton voters pass the November ban, Amazon could still try to build through the townships instead of annexation, and Amazon Web Services did not respond to questions about whether it will continue pursuing the site.
