ft-405.text: Logistix Property Group's plan for a data center on 29 acres of city-owned land at 1380 University Boulevard in Hamilton, Butler County, Ohio, is suspended. On January 15, 2026, the developer asked the city to pause a feasibility study into supplying 240 megawatts of power to the site, after an earlier study found it would take at least 24 months to deliver just 45 megawatts. Hamilton City Council has not voted on the project, which still needs city and state approval. City Manager Craig Bucheit said the new impact study showed "it's going to take a significant amount of time, money and infrastructure to meet the project needs that have been set out." Logistix said in a statement that it was "evaluating the information and that no decision has been made with respect to the project." Hamilton resident Jay Kidd urged the city to drop the project: "We can just not build it at all. We are not willing to sacrifice our children for economic growth." The city entered a development agreement with Logistix for the 29-acre site, and the project would be paid for by the developer, which would become a customer of Hamilton's own electric utility. More than 600 people have joined a Facebook group called the Coalition Against Data Centers in South Ohio, circulating petitions and turning out at city council meetings to demand the city scrap the project.

ft-1778014585820-4803.text: MARA Holdings, the bitcoin miner moving into AI data centers, wants to take over the Long Ridge gas plant at Hannibal, in Monroe County, Ohio, and build a data center campus there starting at 200 megawatts of power. MARA agreed to buy the plant from Long Ridge Energy & Power for about $1.5 billion, including $785 million of assumed debt. The deal needs approval from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, which has not yet ruled. The deal covers a 505-megawatt gas plant and more than 1,600 acres on the Ohio River, once home to the Ormet aluminum smelter. MARA says the site could grow to 600 megawatts of power through grid expansion and on-site generation, and eventually support more than 1,000 megawatts combined. MARA already owns a bitcoin mining facility at the same site, bought from Arkon Energy in November 2024. The plant employs about 20 people, whom MARA said it would keep. The main objection so far has come from the grid's own watchdog, not from neighbors. Monitoring Analytics, the independent watchdog for the regional PJM power grid, told regulators in May 2026 that MARA could pull the plant's power out of the shared grid to feed its own data center, raising costs for other electricity customers. "The Transaction should not be approved without a commitment from MARA not to remove the Long Ridge capacity and energy from the PJM markets to serve data center load," the monitor wrote, calling MARA's public statements vague and not binding. MARA says it does not intend to reduce the plant's supply to the shared grid. Jason Hamman, Monroe County's economic development director, said MARA already leased a bitcoin mining facility in the area for several years, and believes that is the same site now described as a 200-megawatt data center. He said the acquisition could bring more jobs, though he had no estimate, and noted the county has seen a data center promise fall through before: DP Facilities announced one at Hannibal in 2019 that Hamman said never happened. In neighboring Washington County, a company called Hashworks Powered Land Waterford LLC bought nearly 500 acres where officials confirm a data center is expected. A group called Conserve Ohio is gathering signatures for a state constitutional amendment to ban large data centers in Ohio. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission has not set a date to rule on the sale, in docket EC26-92. MARA said in its second-quarter 2026 shareholder letter that it expected to complete the purchase in the second half of 2026, once FERC approves it.
paragraphs: MARA Holdings, the bitcoin miner moving into AI data centers, wants to take over the Long Ridge gas plant at Hannibal, in Monroe County, Ohio, and build a data center campus there starting at 200 megawatts of power. MARA agreed to buy the plant from Long Ridge Energy & Power for about $1.5 billion, including $785 million of assumed debt. The deal needs approval from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, which has not yet ruled.

The deal covers a 505-megawatt gas plant and more than 1,600 acres on the Ohio River, once home to the Ormet aluminum smelter. MARA says the site could grow to 600 megawatts of power through grid expansion and on-site generation, and eventually support more than 1,000 megawatts combined. MARA already owns a bitcoin mining facility at the same site, bought from Arkon Energy in November 2024. The plant employs about 20 people, whom MARA said it would keep.

The main objection so far has come from the grid's own watchdog, not from neighbors. Monitoring Analytics, the independent watchdog for the regional PJM power grid, told regulators in May 2026 that MARA could pull the plant's power out of the shared grid to feed its own data center, raising costs for other electricity customers.

"The Transaction should not be approved without a commitment from MARA not to remove the Long Ridge capacity and energy from the PJM markets to serve data center load," the monitor wrote, calling MARA's public statements vague and not binding. MARA says it does not intend to reduce the plant's supply to the shared grid.

Jason Hamman, Monroe County's economic development director, said MARA already leased a bitcoin mining facility in the area for several years, and believes that is the same site now described as a 200-megawatt data center. He said the acquisition could bring more jobs, though he had no estimate, and noted the county has seen a data center promise fall through before: DP Facilities announced one at Hannibal in 2019 that Hamman said never happened.

In neighboring Washington County, a company called Hashworks Powered Land Waterford LLC bought nearly 500 acres where officials confirm a data center is expected. A group called Conserve Ohio is gathering signatures for a state constitutional amendment to ban large data centers in Ohio.

The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission has not set a date to rule on the sale, in docket EC26-92. MARA said in its second-quarter 2026 shareholder letter that it expected to complete the purchase in the second half of 2026, once FERC approves it.

ft-1768320725363-3199.text: Strata Expanse, a Texas company, opened a data center it calls an AI Center of Excellence west of Hanging Rock, near Ironton in Lawrence County, Ohio, with a ribbon cutting on December 19, 2025. The site produces about 10 megawatts of computing power now and could grow to 80, running largely on hydrogen, natural gas, geothermal, solar and battery power, chief revenue officer Ellen Taylor said. The site sits in Hamilton Township, which has no zoning code, so the company needed no permit, public hearing or vote before building. Ironton residents said they only learned about the project after it was already built; a petition titled "Stop the AI data centers in Lawrence County, Ohio" passed 5,000 signatures, and 30 to 50 people attended a special city council meeting on January 8, 2026. Development corporation director Bill Dingus told the council Strata Expanse did not need or want tax breaks, so the county commission was never notified, and he had not personally seen the company's power numbers. "To me it was a clear indication that public support for this project is non-existent," said Councilman Jacob Hock, who added that Dingus "seems to be pretty ill-informed about data centers and their potential impact on the community." Ironton City Council passed a moratorium on AI data centers on February 12, 2026, written to end automatically once the city adopted permanent zoning rules for data centers. The council adopted those rules, Amended Ordinance 26-09, unanimously on May 14, 2026, which ended the moratorium. Neither measure ever covered Hamilton Township, where the Strata Expanse site sits, so the project itself was never subject to either one.

ft-1773979949074-3633.text: Google is building Project BOSC, a $500 million data center on more than 200 acres near North Cole Street and Bluelick Road in American and Sugar Creek townships north of Lima, Allen County, Ohio. The Allen Economic Development Group revealed Google as the company behind the data center on March 16, 2026, after months in which it was known only through Bistrozzi LLC, a company created for the project, while local officials cited nondisclosure agreements. Construction is under way; Allen County Sanitary Engineer Brad Niemeyer said in May 2026 that completion was projected around January to March 2028. The Lima News reported in July 2026 that construction of the data center is expected to be completed by 2030. Bistrozzi bought three parcels in August 2025 for a combined $14,435,300, including just over 200 acres at 4110 N. Cole St. from Neff Farms. Google agreed to a 15-year tax abatement and to pay Elida Local Schools $250,000 a year, and the project includes about $50 million for local infrastructure near Cole Street and Bluelick Road. The project is expected to create 50 full-time jobs. AEP Ohio is planning a new 345-kilovolt substation, the Lyka transmission station, and about four miles of transmission line between North Cole and North West streets, close to the data center, though it would not name the customer. The air permit drew the loudest objections. The permit the Ohio EPA has since released calls for 115 diesel-fired generators and 36 cooling towers between North Cole Street and West Bluelick Road, and the agency says its modeling shows emissions "will not exceed any National Ambient Air Quality Standard." The draft version the agency took comments on in March also listed four emergency fire pumps and electrical generators and 113 fuel storage tanks. At a standing-room-only EPA hearing on March 11, residents objected that the application was heavily redacted. "The application for the permit is heavily redacted, and I don't think it's fair for the EPA to make a decision on a highly redacted application," said resident Jessica Cruikshank. Catherine Adams of the Buckeye Environmental Network said the area already has an 11% asthma rate against 8% statewide: "We already have the refinery, the ammonia plant and a bunch of chemical facilities." A Google spokesperson said the generators will run only in "rare cases of an emergency or during periodic testing." Construction brought its own complaints. Ohio EPA inspectors visited the site over lime kiln dust used to stabilize wet soil blowing off the property, and the construction company added water trucks and wind monitoring after the agency asked it to contain the dust. American Township resident Charlene McCoy said the dust made her "sicker and sicker" and that she plans to sell her home: "It's life-changing. I'm tired." Google is paying for roundabouts on North Cole Street at state Route 115, Beery Road and Bluelick Road, and neighbors said they serve Google's construction traffic more than residents. "This is all about Google trying to address the traffic issue that Google is creating with construction," said David Streeter of Sugar Creek Township. Water is handled through county agreements. A water ordinance for five million gallons a day was secured for the project in September 2025. In July 2026 Allen County commissioners signed off on an $8 million, Google-paid change to the $31 million sewer contract that splits up to 500,000 gallons a day of the center's wastewater between two county plants and sends any excess to the City of Lima's plant; Niemeyer said the county has promised Google 2.5 million gallons a day on its worst day. "We're not maxing ourselves out," Commissioner Cory Noonan said. The remaining public decisions sit with the Allen County commissioners, who control the sewer and road contracts, and AEP Ohio's routing of the new transmission line.

ft-1782755291382-6186.text: The county commissioners are against it and cannot stop it. Guernsey County has no countywide zoning, so the commissioners cannot approve or refuse a data center on private land; their only lever is a request for a property tax abatement. Commissioner Jack Marlin put their position anyway: "I would say the people have spoken. They're against data centers. We said we were against it. So I don't see how we come back from that." Commissioner Bill Cowgill agreed: "If it were to be put on the ballot, it would probably not pass here by a large margin." Commissioner Dave Wilson made the wider point: "When you see a deal has been cut like that, and plus Ohio already has I believe it's 217 data centers, we don't see where it's a good value for Guernsey County." Smart Energy Partners, led by chief executive Rich Stokey, is advising a local estate agent, Jason Miller, on using 425 acres he controls for a data center. No site has been announced, though meeting minutes refer to development in the area of Cambridge municipal airport, and describe a closed loop system needing minimal water with behind-the-meter power generated from natural gas. More than fifty residents have organised as Guernsey County and Ohio: Data Center Developments, co-led by Amy Kissinger and Geno Riley. They worry about farmland, green space and the water supply, particularly the Pleasant City aquifer, which the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency has designated a sole source aquifer, meaning it is the only viable drinking water source for at least half the area's population; withdrawals from it need no EPA review and are governed by Ohio's reasonable use doctrine. Amy Kissinger was careful to say the group is not against the industry: "We understand that technology is advancing and that this is an industrial movement that is happening and needs to happen."

ft-1782182999139-2340.text: Bitdeer Technologies Group, a Singapore-based bitcoin miner and AI company, wants to build a 15-building data center campus of up to 750 megawatts on 257 acres of the Turnpike Commerce Center in Shalersville Township, near Mantua in Portage County, Ohio. On September 10 the township zoning commission voted unanimously to recommend defining any use of 25 megawatts or more as heavy industry, which would effectively keep the data center out because no land in Shalersville is zoned for heavy industry. The first phase would be two data halls of about 48,000 square feet each and a 51,500-square-foot office, drawing about 150 megawatts; a second phase would add 12 more data halls. Bitdeer says the campus would cost more than $300 million, employ 150 to 200 people, is not asking for tax breaks, and would bring in $2.17 million a year in real estate taxes from phase one. Meetings have repeatedly drawn more people than Shalersville Town Hall can hold; at a June 16 town hall a room full of hands went up when one resident asked who opposed the data center. "We're about to celebrate 250 years. What does that mean if we can't say no?" one woman asked. Noise is the sharpest dispute: Bitdeer says the campus would add 43 to 48 decibels at the nearest residential property lines behind sound walls, but trustee Jack Bias said the township has repeatedly asked for the source of those figures without an answer. In August the trustees hired an acoustics firm for $9,000 to measure the township's existing noise and critique any study the developer provides. Only the Shalersville Township trustees can enact the zoning change; they hold a public hearing at 7 p.m. on October 6 at Shalersville Town Hall, and the Portage County Regional Planning Commission takes up competing conditions on October 14. The township's moratorium on data centers runs until early November, and trustees said in August they would extend it by six months if the noise study is not finished.

ft-1782183424777-9963.text: Bitdeer's bitcoin mine at 1115 Industrial Avenue SW in Massillon, Stark County, Ohio, is a crypto mining facility that works much like a data center; the first mining machines went to work in November 2025. By June 2026 the site was about half built, using up to 221 megawatts, which site manager Jon Wonsettler compared to a steel mill's electric usage; all 24 mining buildings were due to finish by the end of summer 2026, and no completion has been announced since. Bitdeer bought the 31-acre site in 2023 for $1.6 million, land once owned by Republic Steel that borders homes in Perry Township, and received no property tax break to build the nearly $100 million facility. When Bitdeer asked City Council in March 2024 to replat part of the property, some neighbors and council members objected to the location: "I don't feel this is the proper site," said Councilwoman Julie Harwig-Smith. The council voted 8-1 on April 1, 2024, to approve the replat. Noise was the main worry; after residents raised it, Bitdeer built a sound wall of 30 to 40 feet by the nearest homes and pledged to keep noise at 60 decibels or less at the property line. "That's kind of our main concern, in terms of being good neighbors," Wonsettler said. About 40 people worked on site in June 2026, with up to 70 expected at full operation, at starting wages of $22 an hour. A fire on November 11, 2025, damaged two of the 24 buildings under construction before any servers were installed; investigators found no signs of arson, and Bitdeer's chief executive said the fire was caused by welding. Massillon is Bitdeer's only Ohio site now running; the company is also developing sites in Niles and Clarington and has proposed a much larger campus in Shalersville Township, Portage County.

When Bitdeer asked City Council in March 2024 to replat part of the property, some neighbors and council members objected to the location: "I don't feel this is the proper site," said Councilwoman Julie Harwig-Smith. The council voted 8-1 on April 1, 2024, to approve the replat.

Noise was the main worry; after residents raised it, Bitdeer built a sound wall of 30 to 40 feet by the nearest homes and pledged to keep noise at 60 decibels or less at the property line. "That's kind of our main concern, in terms of being good neighbors," Wonsettler said. About 40 people worked on site in June 2026, with up to 70 expected at full operation, at starting wages of $22 an hour.

A fire on November 11, 2025, damaged two of the 24 buildings under construction before any servers were installed; investigators found no signs of arson, and Bitdeer's chief executive said the fire was caused by welding. Massillon is Bitdeer's only Ohio site now running; the company is also developing sites in Niles and Clarington and has proposed a much larger campus in Shalersville Township, Portage County.

ft-420.text: Site work is underway on Vantage Data Centers' $2.1 billion OH2 data center campus, which is under construction on 500 acres of former farmland in the village of Millersport, Fairfield County, Ohio, about a mile from the Millersport school. The campus would hold up to four data centers totaling 2.5 million square feet and 696 megawatts of capacity. The state must still decide whether to permit the 1,300 megawatt gas plant that would power it, with a ruling due from the Ohio Power Siting Board by November 26, 2026. The land came into the village in May 2025, when Fairfield County commissioners voted to annex 500 acres from neighboring Walnut Township for the project. Gov. Mike DeWine confirmed Vantage as the company, calling it a $2.1 billion investment with 37 full-time positions, and said Vantage received a 50 percent tax exemption for 10 years on certain purchases. Vantage says construction began in the summer of 2026 and will continue into early 2030. The power plant, the Fairfield Energy Center, would be built by Advanced Power, a Boston-based developer, on land leased from Vantage, with up to 1,300 megawatts of gas generation and 1,000 megawatts of battery storage on about 100 acres. Signal Ohio reported the plant would run 40 gas turbines and 132 diesel generators and would not feed the public grid, sending all its power to Vantage. Oil and Gas Watch estimates the plant would discharge 1,600 tons of air pollutants and 6.6 million tons of carbon dioxide. At the board's local hearing on August 17, 2026, in the cafeteria of Millersport Junior/Senior High School, residents raised concerns about emissions near schools, playgrounds and Buckeye Lake. "There is no local necessity to have a private, 1,350-megawatt fossil fuel generating station. It's tech infrastructure dumping noise, heat and air pollution onto our families," said resident Lorrie Hoover. Wayne Harris of Pleasantville objected to the tax breaks: "We don't get tax abatements. Our taxes go up." Most of the support at the hearing came from union trades who expect to build and maintain the projects. "As data centers continue to expand because of the growing demand for artificial intelligence and other high-tech industries, it is important that new development also brings infrastructure to support its own energy needs," said Dorsey Hager of the Central Ohio Building and Construction Trades Council. The plant's developers told the board they expect about 6,600 construction jobs over three years and 20 long-term jobs running it. The siting board held its evidentiary hearing in the case, number 26-0160-EL-BGN, on September 17, 2026, in Columbus; it must rule within 195 days of receiving the application, setting a deadline of November 26. No decision has been published yet. Two days after the Millersport hearing, the board also heard from the public on the PowerConneX Ashville Energy Center, an 800 megawatt plant in Pickaway County that would power a co-located data center.

ft-1778089927585-6375.text: Monclova Township, in Lucas County, Ohio, adopted a 12-month moratorium on any data center on February 17, 2026, though no data center had been proposed there. Trustee Deborah Stevens-Laux moved Resolution 02172026-01, Chair Barbara Lang seconded, and all three trustees voted yes, after Chuck Hoecherl noted that Ohio law allows at most 12 months. The audience clapped and cheered. Lang explained why the board had waited: the township's first aim is to avoid being annexed and to keep control of zoning, conditional use approvals and site plans. She said: "Rejecting concepts prematurely or taking symbolic actions without considering annexation risk can unintentionally push development across our borders, where township residents lose any voice or protection." She added: "Now that the City of Maumee has enacted a moratorium on this type of development, the landscape has changed." Lang doubted the township would still have a say in a year, because state and federal governments seemed to be moving away from local zoning for data centers.

ft-1771913845055-5122.text: Pacifico Energy's plan for a data center and power plant on London Road at Pherson Pike in Muhlenberg Township, Pickaway County, Ohio, cannot go forward for now after the township trustees passed a 12-month moratorium on data centers in February 2026. The moratorium, Resolution 2026-10, bars the "receipt, processing, issuance or approval of any application for a zoning certificate for a data center" until February 3, 2027. Township zoning inspector Kevin Steward told the trustees on December 29, 2025 that he had been approached about a data center and power plant at the site, and Pacifico Energy of San Juan Capistrano, California, asked for a zoning change application and a variance application. Trustee Jeff Wippel said the draw appeared to be the natural gas line through the property and the electric lines overhead. The land is zoned farm-residential and owned by a trust, and no zoning application had been filed. "I can't tell you what they're building, how big it is, how small it is," Steward said, adding that he knew only "that it's going to be a data center and a power plant, and somehow AEP is involved." Pacifico, the energy arm of the Pacifico Group, is also behind GW Ranch, an off-grid natural gas plant planned on 8,000 acres in Texas. Residents filled the trustees' meetings. A petition against the plan gathered more than 700 signatures, DCD reported. Its organizer, Brian Cooper, told the trustees at the February meeting that he held "over a thousand signatures." Cooper said "we're not anti-progress. We're not opposed to technology or economic development." Speakers worried that heated water from cooling systems could harm the Charles O. Trump Wildlife Area and Big Darby Creek, a State Scenic River near the site, and Patty Hamilton of Stoutsville objected to tax abatements for data centers. "We have 12 months to continue to make sure they know we are serious about our resistance," Carolyn Loxley told the trustees. Wippel said the pause would "hold things off for a year where we can get our zoning and all that kind of stuff in line, and see what other kind of transparencies happen with the state," pointing to Ohio House Bill 646, which would create a commission to study data centers' effects on communities. Elsewhere in Pickaway County, EdgeConneX and Amazon are pursuing developments. The village of Ashville adopted another 180-day data center moratorium in July 2026 while EdgeConneX's PowerConneX affiliate seeks Ohio Power Siting Board approval for on-site generation there. Pacifico may not come back. In July 2026 Community Impact reported that a Pacifico affiliate had applied in Texas for a 2,842-acre data center and natural gas power campus in Cedar Creek, Bastrop County, and that the company was weighing that site against Muhlenberg Township. In its Texas application, the company said the Ohio site could still be considered when the moratorium expires in February 2027, and that state and local incentives will factor into its final choice. Any rezoning at the site would go first to the township Zoning Board for a hearing, with notice to owners within 200 feet, and the final decision on a zoning change rests with the three Muhlenberg Township trustees. A variance would go separately to the Board of Zoning Appeals, where the trustees have no say.

ft-422.text: Capacity LLC has been trying to build a 500 megawatt data center campus on about 168 acres at the northwest corner of Wynn and Corduroy roads in Oregon, Lucas County, Ohio, land the city spent years assembling. The Oregon City Council denied developer Will Turner of Capacity LLC a six month extension in February 2026, giving him until March 31 to finalize plans, and by July 2026 city officials had named Vantage Data Centers as the prospective developer of three buildings on the site. City administrator Brodin Walters called the deal "a really complicated math problem that we have to convince, you know, the community and city council that it's a good deal." The city describes the project at full build as about 500 megawatts of power, $2 billion to $3 billion of investment, and 20,000 to 30,000 gallons of water a day with closed loop cooling; Oregon has spent about $8.6 million of its own money assembling the land over ten years. One resident whose home sat near the planned site said: "Due to the picture that they painted us, we sold the home...I wouldn't have done it if I would have known what I know now." United Neighbors of Oregon gathered signatures for a charter amendment capping data centers at 25 megawatts and steering them to brownfield and industrial land; organizer James Davis said, "We're okay with data centers as long as they're suitably sized for the communities." Oregon is one of nine Ohio communities with petitions on the November 2026 ballot that mirror a statewide effort to ban data centers drawing more than 25 megawatts.

ft-1775186735797-5852.text: SoftBank's subsidiary SB Energy is developing the PORTS Technology Campus, a data center planned for up to 10 gigawatts at the former Portsmouth Gaseous Diffusion Plant south of Piketon, Pike County, Ohio, on land owned by the U.S. Department of Energy. In August 2026 Nvidia confirmed it would financially back the first 4.25 gigawatts of the campus, which is expected to be fully leased to OpenAI. Pike County commissioners held a community open house on the project from 5 to 7 p.m. on September 28 at the Pike County Fairgrounds Multipurpose Building, with SoftBank and AEP expected to attend. The Department of Energy and Department of Commerce announced the partnership with SoftBank and AEP Ohio in March 2026. SB Energy plans 10 gigawatts of new generation, 9.2 gigawatts of it from natural gas, funded with $33.3 billion in Japanese money under the U.S.-Japan trade agreement, and says it will spend $4.2 billion with AEP Ohio on new and upgraded transmission lines in southern Ohio. SoftBank says the full project will cost $30 billion to $40 billion including chips and will employ 35,000 construction workers and more than 2,500 people once complete. U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright spoke at a groundbreaking ceremony at the site on March 20, 2026, and the first phase, 800 megawatts, is expected to come online in 2028. The site was built in the 1950s to make enriched uranium for weapons, Navy submarines and later commercial reactors; much of the 3,775-acre plant is shut down and undergoing decontamination. The campus is not limited to federal land: WOUB reported SB Energy filed a permit application with the Ohio EPA on May 28, 2026 for a 10 gigawatt data center complex on about 1,016 acres of mostly farmland north and east of the plant, and the company would pay no property tax on the DOE land. Vina Colley, a former PORTS electrician and president of Portsmouth/Piketon Residents for Environmental Safety and Security, told The Post Athens the site needs to be cleaned up and victims addressed before construction starts. Paul Mobley, a former Air Force-trained engineer, warned the plant would draw water from the Scioto River: "The main issue is Little Beaver Creek flows right into Big Beaver Creek, and Big Beaver Creek flows right into the Scioto River and the Scioto River flows the entire length of Scioto County." SoftBank spokesperson Ally Copple said "SB Energy has committed to paying for accelerated cleanup and remediation at the site," and that construction on the first phase would begin later in 2026, with work across the campus continuing through 2032. At a July 2026 open house on the gas plant in Waverly, attended by more than 100 residents, Inside Climate News found no sign of an organized campaign against the project. "We do not need all these data centers," said Terri Slater of Jackson. Dennis and Deborah Hopkins, who will see the power plant from their windows, turned down an offer to buy their property. "I want to keep my house," Deborah Hopkins said. Pike County commissioner Tony Montgomery said officials had asked what happens if the project stops being viable: "How is our community not stuck with a bunch of buildings that maybe we can't use for anything else? We're trying to address that." Several decisions are still ahead, made in Columbus rather than in Piketon: the Ohio Power Siting Board must approve the gas plant, and the Ohio EPA must rule on the permit for the private land because the project would affect wetlands, streams and wildlife. AEP Ohio's transmission lines also need Power Siting Board approval after environmental and land-use studies, and AEP has said it will seek feedback from nearby landowners on the route. Pike County tied the September 28 open house to its Pike 2040 planning effort, which included a station for public feedback.

ft-1770130909274-3596.text: Piqua voters will decide on November 3, 2026 whether to amend the city charter in a way aimed at stopping a planned data center in Piqua, Miami County, Ohio. The data center is being developed by J5 LLC, doing business as Shaytura LLC, north of Farrington Road and east of Washington Road. The proposed amendment would limit data centers to 25 megawatts; Meta's Piqua project would demand around 1,400 megawatts of power, according to the Ohio Capital Journal. The Piqua Commission approved a development agreement with J5 on November 3, 2025, after a meeting of more than four hours, for a site in the I-75 Exit 78 Business and Industrial Park. City officials said then that a non-disclosure agreement kept the company's name from them, and City Manager Paul Oberdorfer said he did not know who it was. The plan is for two buildings of about 350,000 square feet each on land along the north side of Farrington Road, built in overlapping phases over three to five years. The city says the project will make a $735,000 payment in lieu of taxes for each building every year of a 15-year abatement and will pay $76 million to extend water, wastewater and power lines and build roads. Water was the first worry. In November 2025 the utilities director said the city might supply up to 2 million gallons a day at peak from a plant that makes 6.7 million and uses about 2.2 million. By August 2026 the city's economic development director described a closed-loop system using the equivalent of two full-service restaurants. "Is that in the contract?" someone in the audience shouted. On August 18, 2026 the commission voted 4-1 to grant AES Ohio a 30-year franchise, with a $1 million annual fee paid by the customer, to build and run the electric lines serving the data center; Commissioner Paul Simmons voted no, saying 94.5% of those who spoke had opposed it. "I am going to urge you to reconsider this deal," resident Val Mullikin told the commission, and resident Jonathan Wessel said: "For me, this is the last piece of leverage that the city has in this deal." Vice Mayor Frank DeBrosse, who moved the vote, said: "I support this project. I support the opportunities this investment means for our community and our future." Meta has pledged $8 million to the city, which the interim city manager said would go toward needs such as a new ladder truck and police equipment. The citizen group Save Piqua has answered with petitions: the charter amendment now headed to the ballot, a referendum on the AES franchise, and recall petitions against Mayor James Vetter, Vice Mayor DeBrosse and Commissioner Rick Walker. Petition organizer Alisha Lange said: "Even though the data centers are driving us apart, the petitions are bringing us together." Piqua is one of 18 Ohio communities voting on data centers in November, and nine of them, including Piqua, have petitions modeled on the Conserve Ohio 25-megawatt limit. Amazon is also pursuing a data center campus in Sidney, in neighboring Shelby County. What happens next: the charter amendment goes to voters on November 3, though the city's law director warned that a pending Ohio Supreme Court case on signature rules could affect its certification, and she has said the courts, not the commission, decide whether such an amendment is constitutional. The Piqua Commission would have to act on the recall and referendum petitions once they are certified.

ft-1767026476511-2974.text: Prologis is building Project Mila, a 250-megawatt data center campus for Amazon Web Services on 141 acres in the Trenton Industrial Park in Trenton, Butler County, Ohio, even as the city's voters prepare to decide on November 3 whether to ban any new data center that needs more than 25 megawatts. The ban would not affect the Prologis project, which is already under construction and calls for four single-story buildings totaling 893,034 square feet. Prologis bought the land from the city for $7.7 million in October 2025, about a mile south of downtown Trenton off Woodsdale Road, east of Molson Coors' Trenton Brewery, with the first building opening in 2028 and all four by 2029. Mayor Ryan Perry has said the project would bring 150 jobs and hundreds of thousands of dollars in taxes and water sales, and the city said the campus was expected to use about 15 million gallons of water a year, subject to review. On March 30, 2026, the Trenton Planning Commission approved Prologis' site plan unanimously in a 10-minute meeting, with no time for public comment and no questions from commissioners, while residents filled nearly every seat. "It's like they don't care about what's going on with us or within parks or within [the] city or [with] citizens," said Barry Blankenship of the Woodsdale and Trenton Environmental Resistance group, who wants answers on health, the environment and the campus's closeness to Chrisholm MetroPark. In July the city council approved a Community Reinvestment Area agreement giving Prologis a 75 percent property tax exemption on each building for 15 years. "Without the abatement, we would be getting more from them," Perry said, "but... every business that we have in the city of Trenton has an abatement of some kind." Blankenship and his wife Lorie helped build a resident group, W.A.T.E.R., to nearly 2,000 members on Facebook, which petitioned for a city charter amendment banning data centers over 25 megawatts. The Butler County Board of Elections certified 336 valid signatures, but in July the city council refused to advance the petition, arguing it needed about 820. On September 1 the Ohio Supreme Court ruled unanimously that 128 signatures were enough and that the council had a "mandatory constitutional duty" to certify the petition, and on September 3 the council voted to put the measure on the November 3 ballot. "It feels like finally we have been heard," Barry Blankenship said after the ruling. Trenton had also petitioned to annex about 600 acres in neighboring Madison and St. Clair townships for a second Amazon Web Services campus, and after both townships rejected the request, the city withdrew it on September 14, reserving the right to refile after the November 3 vote. St. Clair Township trustee Dustin Gadd has warned that the Prologis site alone is expected to bring more than 1,200 construction workers a day, and that a second campus could mean 4,000 to 5,000 on township roads; St. Clair adopted a 12-month data center moratorium in May. Butler County enacted a six-month moratorium in June for Madison and five other townships, set to expire in December. Trenton voters decide the charter amendment on November 3, 2026. Any annexation for the second Amazon campus would go to the Butler County Board of Commissioners, and if Amazon pursued the land in Madison Township instead, the county commission would decide under county zoning.

The city had welcomed it at first: in April 2025 the council annexed Thor's land, rezoned it for manufacturing and made data centers a permitted use there, and in November it approved a tax abatement agreement. The zoning board had rejected Thor's site plan in February 2026, and the council passed a 12-month moratorium on data centers in March. On June 16, 2026 the council went further and voted to repeal Ordinance 4621-25, banning data centers from the city. Three days later, on June 19, Thor Equities filed a federal lawsuit against the city, its council and its board of zoning appeals, alleging Urbana broke state and local law by changing the rules after the company had applied. The company's complaint says: "The City's actions have caused lost investment, delayed project timelines, impaired business relationships, and deprived the local community of jobs, tax revenue, and the benefits of planned infrastructure improvements." In a statement Thor said it rejected "the misinformation and outright nonsense being spread online about data centers," and that it "looks forward to resolving this matter fairly so it can continue being a strong partner for Urbana and help build a brighter future for the city." Thor has also appealed the site plan rejection in Champaign County Common Pleas Court, where in July a judge ordered the city to add a full transcript of the April zoning appeals hearing to the record. Under that schedule the city's response is due by October 2, 2026, and the project remains on hold while the courts decide.

ft-1778088996829-8003.text: An unnamed company wants to build a data center in Waterville Township, in Lucas County, Ohio, township trustee Toby Miller confirmed in April 2026, though officials say they still do not know who it is or exactly where it would go. No application has been filed, and the township is using a one-year moratorium, from December 17, 2025 to December 17, 2026, to write tougher zoning before a developer arrives. The Waterville Township Zoning Commission held a public hearing on the new rules, case Z22-C141, on September 14, 2026; that hearing was scheduled for that date, and no result has been published yet. The Board of Trustees, Toby Miller, Julie Theroux and Kyle Hertzfeld, will review the amendment next and make the final decision. "Is there a data center coming to Waterville Township?" Miller told a standing-room-only trustees meeting on April 22. "Yes. There is a company interested." He said environmental studies were under way, that the interest dates to 2024, and: "We know it's not Meta or Google." Residents pushed back from the start: Janice and Anthony Braida urged the trustees to adopt a moratorium in October 2025, and Monclova Township resident Lyn Cox, who started a Facebook page against the project, said, "As residents, we're pretty much madder than hell." Trustee Kyle Hertzfeld said he would recuse himself from any vote because his family owns property there, and Miller, whose own house sits in an area suspected to be under consideration, told residents, "I stand to be screwed substantially." The new rules would replace the township's existing path for data centers, a conditional use permit on agricultural land decided by the appointed Board of Zoning Appeals. Instead, a developer would have to ask for land to be rezoned to a new M-3 campus industrial district, which Miller said means residents could gather 327 signatures to force a referendum. The draft required a nonrefundable fee of $500 an acre, an escrow of 1 percent of the project's cost, and a closed-circuit, non-evaporative cooling system. "Hopefully it dissuades a data center from coming in, but if a data center does come in, they have a lot of hurdles to jump through and a lot of money they're going to have to put out," said Brian Gowing of the township's advisory committee. At least 138 Ohio municipalities and townships had active data center moratoriums as of September 17, 2026, according to the Ohio Capital Journal.

ft-1778596422570-8176.text: The company that was eyeing 51 acres between the Creek Turnpike and State Highway 51 in east Broken Arrow, Oklahoma, for a data center has walked away, city officials said in June 2026, after the letter of intent to buy the land expired and was not renewed. No reason was given, and no application for a Broken Arrow data center has been filed. The city learned of the interest on April 21, 2026, when a site selector asked about a pre-development meeting for the privately owned tract at 8521 S. 209th East Avenue, just east of the Blue Bell plant. The land is zoned agricultural, so any data center would have needed rezoning to Industrial Light, with public hearings before the Planning Commission and the City Council. The company was never identified. City Manager Michael Spurgeon went public early, acknowledging "the concerns citizens have about the potential impacts related to noise pollution, utility usages including water and electricity, and the environment." He also promised: "no City Councilor, myself, or members of my staff have been asked to sign a non-disclosure agreement about this potential project, and we will not sign an NDA." Gary Camfield, who has lived on the east side for more than 30 years, listed his worries: "Higher electric bill, higher water bills, noise and we don't get much out of it". In the end, the city said, no pre-development meeting was ever requested and no formal discussions took place. Nearby in Rogers County, the Claremore City Council backed Beale Infrastructure's Project Mustang data center at the Claremore Industrial Park on May 18, 2026, after nearly two hours of public comment, and Google is planning two campuses in Muskogee County. Oklahoma City's data center moratorium appears to have affected the planned CloudBurst campus there. If any company returns to the site, it would have to seek rezoning through the Broken Arrow Planning Commission and City Council in public hearings; the city says it will keep studying data centers and follow its established process.

ft-426.text: Project Anthem, Meta's data center under construction in east Tulsa near the Creek Turnpike, is a more than $1 billion investment that Meta confirmed as its own on April 21, 2026, with Gov. Kevin Stitt at the announcement. The site's plat places it in the city of Tulsa, Wagoner County, Oklahoma, with a Catoosa mailing address, and lists the owner as Atmoss LLC. The campus, at 21304 E. 11th St., is expected to be finished in 2028. The first phase covers 340 acres at the Fair Oaks Industrial Park and was approved in March 2024, with a city tax incentive district that exempts the owner from 85 percent of its annual property tax bill. Meta says it will bring about 1,000 construction jobs and around 100 permanent jobs, and it is partnering with Tulsa Tech and Tulsa Community College on trade training. Meta said the campus will support Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp and AI workloads, and that it is committed to building infrastructure so it does not overburden local power and water. The Tulsa World reported in September 2026 that the data center estimates a need of about 1 billion gallons of water a year, and a city permit was issued for an industrial water management building on the site. East Tulsa residents have pushed back. Cheyenna Morgan, who lives about three miles away, worries the campus will overuse city water and cause pollution, and protested outside the April announcement: "Electric rate increases, there will be noise pollution, construction out there is incredible dangerous." Before Meta's name was public, some city officials signed nondisclosure agreements with the developers, and city staff turned down the project's requests to change Tulsa's noise and nuisance ordinance, according to memos obtained by the Tulsa Flyer. "Those handful people who live by that, it is going to be hell, excuse my language," electrical engineer Buchanan Dowling said of a possible expansion. In March 2026 the Tulsa City Council passed a nine-month moratorium on new data centers, which exempted both phases of Project Anthem. Atmoss had sought to rezone about 375 more acres between East 11th and East 21st streets for a second phase, but withdrew that application on March 31, 2026; a city spokesman said the developer was "exploring options." The first phase needs no further zoning vote, and construction continues. Any second phase would need rezoning from agricultural to industrial through the Tulsa Metropolitan Area Planning Commission and the Tulsa City Council.

ft-1767731765455-3760.text: Beale Infrastructure's Project Mustang data center in the Claremore Industrial Park, Rogers County, Oklahoma, was approved by the Claremore City Council on May 18, 2026, and construction was expected to begin within days, the Tulsa World reported on August 28, 2026, after the city finalized the land sale. The company that will use the data center has still not been named. "I don't know when the timing of that will be," City Manager John Feary said. "I honestly don't know." The agreement calls for construction over roughly five to seven years and a contractually obligated investment of at least $1 billion, a city release said, and Beale has executed a $21.552 million irrevocable letter of credit to secure its obligations to the city. The campus will sit on about 290 acres of the industrial park, about three miles north of downtown along Route 66, on land zoned industrial for decades. Beale has said the project could include up to three data centers built in phases, air-cooled and using about 20,000 gallons of water a day, with about 50 permanent jobs per phase. Power will come from Claremore's public utility, which buys from the Grand River Dam Authority; the city says the site will have a dedicated GRDA-owned substation and that Beale pays upfront for all infrastructure. The city says the end user is a domestically owned, publicly traded company. The fight was over taxes and transparency. At a second public hearing that filled City Hall to standing room, the council approved the project plan and a tax increment district, letting Beale seek a 25-year property tax exemption for each phase. Beale said the project would still contribute more than $250 million to Rogers County schools, municipal services and community programs over time. "How are you going to compensate me and my neighbors? We get no benefit from you at all. We get destruction of our lifestyle, destruction of our property values," Rogers County resident Debbie Cassita told the council. Some residents asked for a moratorium until more is known about data centers' effects, while supporters pointed to jobs and investment. Opponents then tried to force a public vote. Activist Ron Durbin filed nine recall petitions, one against each council member, and referendum petitions on the three ordinances that cleared the project. Organizers gathered 702, 730 and 763 signatures, more than double the 356 each required. In June the city declared all three referendum petitions legally invalid because true copies had not been filed with the city clerk before signatures were gathered. "I think that the process was very secretive for a long time, and then all of a sudden we just kind of rubber-stamped it through as a council," said resident Alex Miller. The project plan does not exempt Beale from planned unit development, code enforcement and zoning approvals needed before it builds, so the remaining permits run through the City of Claremore. Miller said opponents would fight the ruling in district court and, if necessary, at the Oklahoma Supreme Court.

ft-1767733393101-9707.text: Beltline Energy, a renewable energy firm, wants to build a data center on a 400-acre parcel near an Oklahoma Gas and Electric power plant in Luther, in Oklahoma County, Oklahoma. Its zoning and special-use permit applications are filed, but on June 17, 2026, before an estimated 300 to 400 people on a closed-off Main Street, the Luther Board of Trustees approved a moratorium that freezes any decision on new or pending data center applications, including Beltline's, through December 31, 2026. Beltline's applications formally entered the town's review process in early June 2026. The site lies between North Triple X Road and North Luther Road, and a 40-mile transmission line from Luther to Piedmont is also planned, to be finished in 2027. Beltline, described by the Luther Register as a Georgia company, told the town it would build the data center and hand it to another company to operate; that operator has not been named. Beltline's application says the town's drinking water would not be used for cooling; it proposes buying wastewater from Oklahoma City for that purpose, under an agreement it has not yet secured. Town Manager Rian Harkins said he would have "a hard time as zoning administrator and town manager recommending approval if they didn't have that." Opposition began a year before any application. When Beltline first pitched the idea to trustees in May 2025, former mayor Jenni White, who lives about a mile from the power plant, called it "really an enormous concern," pointing to the town's past water troubles and battery fire risk. At a January 2026 meeting, residents raised water use, pollution of water sources, who pays for the power, and round-the-clock noise and light. "We don't want it. We're here and we're going to make a stand," resident Shannon Hopkins said at the June meeting, as the crowd chanted "let us vote." Records obtained by News 9 showed Mayor Terry Arps had signed a non-disclosure agreement with Beltline on May 29, 2025, a year before the company's application became public. The town said it never received proprietary information under the agreement, and Arps said the board never approved it, so it never took effect. Oklahoma City and Edmond also have data center moratoriums in place while they write their own rules. Gov. Kevin Stitt signed the Data Center Consumer Ratepayer Protection Act in May 2026 to keep grid-upgrade costs for data centers off other customers' bills; critics say it does not address water, noise or rural character. The Luther Board of Trustees decides Beltline's rezoning and special-use permit; Town Manager Harkins has said the permit process lets the town negotiate conditions and seek impact fees. The town is using the moratorium to review and possibly revise its zoning rules for data centers and battery storage before the moratorium ends December 31, 2026.

ft-427.text: ValorC3 Data Centers runs a colocation data center at 4442 Newcastle Road in Oklahoma City, in Oklahoma County, near Will Rogers World Airport, in a building Devon Energy originally owned. The company, then called Tonaquint, officially opened the renovated data center with a ribbon-cutting in May 2024. Tonaquint got the building in late 2023 when it bought EdgeX Data Centers, and it converted the facility from a single-client building to one serving many clients. The 65,000-square-foot building sits on a four-acre campus, and the company says it can withstand tornado-force winds of up to 310 mph. At the opening, Tonaquint Chief Commercial Officer Mike DeVito said the company's mission was "to provide the absolute best data center solutions in emerging markets like Oklahoma City." ValorC3 now lists the site with a 5MW critical load, expandable to 12MW with a new substation, fed by primary and secondary substations from Oklahoma Gas and Electric. Backup power comes from five 2,000 kW diesel generators with two 15,000-gallon fuel tanks, and cooling from water-cooled and air-cooled chillers with three cooling towers, according to the company. The city around it has grown more wary of data centers. A June 2026 News 9 roundup listed ValorC3 among the data centers operating in Oklahoma City, and said construction of the planned 200MW CloudBurst campus near South Council Road appeared to have been impacted by the city's data center moratorium. Gov. Kevin Stitt has pointed to Google's campus in Pryor as an example of the jobs, tax revenue and school funding such projects can bring. A News 9 roundup in June 2026 described ValorC3 as operating the Newcastle Road site.

ft-429.text: On August 19, 2026, Google confirmed that it is the end user of Project Clydesdale, a 506 acre data center campus that Beale Infrastructure is building in unincorporated Tulsa County, Oklahoma, just west of Owasso and next to the Cherokee Industrial Park. Beale broke ground in October 2025, and until that day the end user had not been publicly identified. Cheyenne Morgan, coalition coordinator for Stop Data Colonialism, who became involved during the rezoning more than a year earlier, said: "Despite community pushback, Project Clydesdale got pushed forward anyways, without us knowing who the end user was for that proposed project." She added: "I don't believe that there was true community consent or engagement around this project." County Commissioner Stan Sallee called it "a tremendous boost to northeast Oklahoma" and said of the site: "It is next to an industrial park. The zoning matches, it works. It has the water needs for this company. It has the utility it needs as well." Trystine Payfer, Google's public affairs manager for Oklahoma, said: "This project is far more than an infrastructure investment; it is a long-term commitment to Tulsa County's future." Google said it had invested more than $15 billion in Oklahoma since 2011 and that its 2025 spending supported $2.6 billion of state economic activity. The project includes a new on-site substation funded by Beale, about 1.5 miles of new water lines and upgrades for Washington County Rural Water District No. 3, and a training partnership with the electrical training ALLIANCE aiming at more than 160 apprentices in Oklahoma by 2030. Stacy Smith of the Tulsa Regional Chamber argued the benefit was wider than the direct jobs: "This isn't just a 100, 200 direct jobs. This is an ecosystem of activity and additional jobs that's going to follow." The announcement gave no power or cost figure for the campus; Morgan said residents have raised concerns about water, power and noise, and construction is ongoing.

ft-1779111700697-5716.text: Cloverleaf Infrastructure's proposed Project Open Sky data center campus near Piedmont, in Canadian County, Oklahoma, is on hold after the City Council voted on July 27, 2026, to send a key land-use change back to the Planning and Zoning Commission for more study. Cloverleaf has asked Piedmont to annex and rezone a 633-acre parcel between Azalea Road NW, Richland Road NW and Moffat Road NW for six 352,800-square-foot data center buildings, warehouses and a substation. Company representatives said the campus would need about 1.4 gigawatts of electrical capacity to support a 1-gigawatt cloud data center, and could take in another 393 acres. At a packed June 22 meeting, Cloverleaf's Aaron Bilyeu said the closed-loop cooling would use 75,000 gallons of water a day for up to four months in the first phase and that the facility would run at 60 decibels. "Data centers are not making money. They are taking money," one resident told the council, which the Planning Commission had advised to deny the rezoning. Cloverleaf, a powered land company founded in 2024, says it prepares sites and then transfers them to a company that will build and run the data center, and that it does not sign nondisclosure agreements with local governments. It recently walked away from two data center projects in Wisconsin after local objections. Cloverleaf wants the site annexed so it can receive city services including water, and annexation and zoning remain for the Piedmont City Council to decide once the land-use map comes back.

ft-1767732134204-9106.text: Beale Infrastructure withdrew Project Atlas, its planned 270-acre data center campus at 16192 State Highway 51B near Coweta in Wagoner County, Oklahoma, on March 30, 2026, after the city's planning commission refused to back the rezoning. "In plain terms, no re-zoning means Project Atlas is not moving forward in Coweta," the city said. The campus would have had at least one phase of about 200,000 square feet, with three more possible, and Beale is backed by the private credit firm Blue Owl. Beale first approached city officials in 2024 and later bought more than 250 acres with the data center in mind. At the January 19, 2026 planning commission meeting, Beale offered $500,000 for a water plant master study and at least $3 million for upgrades to the city's water system, and said the city and schools would take in at least $1 million to $2 million through franchise fees. "The general consensus of residents is that Beale has been non-committal and less than transparent," resident Julianne Davis told the commission, which voted 4-1 to recommend denying the rezoning. Supporters included Eric Lemley of Iron Workers Local 584, who said, "If Coweta passes this up then I really feel sorry for them." Secrecy became the bigger story. City Manager Julie Casteen signed a nondisclosure agreement with IPI Management LLC, later known as Beale Infrastructure, on May 20, 2024, which made even the agreement's existence confidential. Mayor Naomi Hogue and Vice Mayor Jeremy Barnett signed their own nondisclosure agreements on September 3, 2025, and the project was not announced until October 22, 2025. An open records request later showed Casteen had called anti-data center advocates "just not very smart and can't accept change," for which she apologized. After the withdrawal, residents demanded Casteen's firing, and Police Chief Mike Bell investigated their allegations involving the city council and the city manager. On June 29, 2026, Bell called the allegations "unsubstantiated": "The evidence did not support the findings that state law, criminal statutes or applicable regulations have been violated." Casteen acknowledged signing the nondisclosure agreement in 2024 and said, "Coweta was a guinea pig in this regard, where we are the first ones presented with this. At the time, it seemed like a normal, standard thing. Turns out it wasn't." Beale has pursued other campuses around Tulsa. It has been in talks with Claremore over Project Mustang in the Claremore Industrial Park and has been named as the firm behind Project Clydesdale, a planned 506-acre campus in Owasso. Across Oklahoma, The Frontier found other cities where officials signed data center nondisclosure agreements months before projects became public, and an assistant district attorney in Wagoner County cautioned officials against signing such deals. Any new data center proposal for the site would need a rezoning from the Coweta City Council after a planning commission recommendation.

ft-430.text: TierPoint runs a data center at 12151 E. State Farm Boulevard in Tulsa, in Tulsa County, Oklahoma. The company finished the 16,000-square-foot building in early 2018 as its fourth Oklahoma site, working with Compass Data Centers as a construction partner and setting aside $20 million for the project. TierPoint now lists the site at more than 32,000 square feet total, including more than 16,000 square feet of server floor space. The building has dual utility power feeds backed by two 2.5-megawatt diesel generators with 3,500-gallon fuel tanks, and it connects by a dedicated fiber line to TierPoint's other Tulsa data center on Archer Street and its Oklahoma City sites. A June 2026 roundup by News 9 and News On 6 listed the State Farm Boulevard site among Tulsa's operating data centers. Nearby, Meta's proposed Project Anthem campus near 11th Street and the Creek Turnpike would be a more than $1 billion investment; developer Atmoss LLC withdrew its zoning application for the project's second phase in March 2026, city officials said.

The building has dual utility power feeds backed by two 2.5-megawatt diesel generators with 3,500-gallon fuel tanks, and it connects by a dedicated fiber line to TierPoint's other Tulsa data center on Archer Street and its Oklahoma City sites.
A June 2026 roundup by News 9 and News On 6 listed the State Farm Boulevard site among Tulsa's operating data centers.

Nearby, Meta's proposed Project Anthem campus near 11th Street and the Creek Turnpike would be a more than $1 billion investment; developer Atmoss LLC withdrew its zoning application for the project's second phase in March 2026, city officials said.

ft-434.text: The Roundhouse data center, a $100 million project that the startup Roundhouse Digital Infrastructure pitched for the Port of Cascade Locks in Hood River County, Oregon, was cancelled in July 2023 after residents turned against it and voted out the port commissioners who backed it. The port and Roundhouse jointly announced on July 20, 2023 that they were ending the project, and new port manager Jeremiah Blue said: "We just didn't feel like there was enough public support to continue with it." Roundhouse had sought a 25-year lease of the port's vacant 43,000-square-foot Flex 6 building and 10 nearby acres, planning $40 million in computers and upgrades there and $60 million for a new building, at 10 megawatts of power capacity. The port needed a tenant: it was paying $53,000 a month in loan payments and upkeep on Flex 6 after the previous tenant, a clothing company, walked away from its lease. "Things come and go, and we need to be diverse," port commission president Jess Groves said when the plan was announced. Many residents worried about what the data center's power needs would mean for their future electricity supply, and about whether Roundhouse could deliver. "I personally think it's a power grab and a water grab and a land grab," resident Rachel Najjar said. Roundhouse was a new venture led by Stephen King, who had little experience in data hosting, had not raised the money for the project and had a history of business disputes with former partners, The Oregonian reported. In June 2023 voters recalled two port commissioners who had supported the data center, and two others who had backed negotiations lost re-election. Cascade Locks is a scenic community about 40 miles up the Columbia River from Portland, and data centers have become one of Oregon's largest industries, drawn in large part by property tax breaks. Earlier attempts to diversify the port's economy, a casino and a Nestlé bottling plant, also failed in the face of opposition. After the collapse, Blue said the port would "likely entertain anything in there that isn't a data center." By May 2025 the port's budget message reported that Flex 6 is now leased. The port, which owns the land, is governed by a five-member commission.

ft-435.text: Crane Data Centers broke ground in July 2025 on a two-building, 100-megawatt data center campus on a 35-acre field at 3975 Heather Street in Forest Grove, Washington County, Oregon, bordered by houses on two sides and across the street from Neil Armstrong Middle School. The first building, 180,000 square feet and 40 feet tall, was due to finish in 2026; no update on its completion has been published since. A second building of 363,000 square feet, up to 75 feet tall, would follow. Crane, a San Francisco startup building its first data center, switched from evaporative to air cooling after residents raised concerns about water use, and its financial backer is Principal Asset Management. Forest Grove Light & Power Director Keith Hormann said the first building would start at about 8 megawatts and rise to a cap of 47, with Crane paying for all power upgrades; the second building would need a new substation, also at Crane's expense. City planning staff approved the site plan in July 2024, the planning commission upheld it after an appeal, and the city council voted 5-0 on October 14, 2024 to deny a second appeal from resident Dale Feik. "It blocks out the sky. It puts my house in the shade of this giant building," neighbor David Haworth, 70, told the council. Mayor Malynda Wenzl said, "My job as a presiding officer and as an elected person in Forest Grove is to uphold our code. I'm not gonna lie, a 75-foot building? I feel you." In nearby Hillsboro, data centers have consumed more than 300 acres of the city's industrial land, and Hillsboro has since enacted a temporary ban on new data centers. Crane must still finish a Heather Street extension and meet the city's drainage and noise rules before it can occupy the building; no work session on possible zoning changes had been scheduled as of August 2025.

ft-1779562814193-6454.text: On May 27, 2026, the La Pine City Council, in Deschutes County, Oregon, voted unanimously against selling 20 acres in the La Pine Industrial Park to Boxminer.io for a 20-megawatt data center, to applause and cheers. At a May 13 hearing, public comment ran nearly three hours, most of it opposed, and the next day Boxminer.io chief executive Jeff Keller wrote, "I'm not sure there will ever be a data center in La Pine after last night's meeting and the land sale has not yet been approved by the city." A March 25 city memo said Boxminer would buy the 20-acre parcel for $1.5 million, half to the city and half to Deschutes County, which must also sign off, and that site construction would cost $286 million. Midstate Electric Cooperative could guarantee at least 20 megawatts of power, enough for about 16,000 homes, according to Midstate. Keller told the hearing, "We are here to create jobs in the community. A data center is a clean factory with no pollution, very little noise, a lot less noise than the sawmill and the freight train, and a positive effect on the community." City Manager Geoff Wullschlager said the company had not provided specific examples of how its closed loop cooling technology worked elsewhere. Boxminer had floated up to 200 full-time jobs if the site expanded, but Keller estimated 50 to start, adding, "I'm not 100% sure we will get to 50, but it will be considerable." Wullschlager's report found that by Amazon's job-to-square-foot ratio the facility would produce only about five jobs: "In both the revenue and employment categories (comparable by way of data), Boxminer's estimates fail to yield dependable information." "You have to understand, we do listen to you," City Council President Cathi VanDamme told the crowd. The land is owned by Deschutes County, and any sale needed approval from both the La Pine City Council and the Deschutes County Board of County Commissioners; the council's May 27 vote ended the sale process.

ft-1784230987783-1009.text: Verrus cannot build its planned data center campus in Salem, in Marion County, Oregon, while the city's new data center moratorium lasts, the city attorney told councilors before they passed the 120-day ban on September 21, 2026. The Verrus data center, called Oakline at Mill Creek, is planned for the Mill Creek Corporate Center at Turner Road SE and Deer Park Drive SE. The ban runs until January 19, and during it the city cannot approve any data center application. Verrus, backed by the Alphabet spin-out Sidewalk Infrastructure Partners, first described three buildings and a substation on 75 acres, starting at "dozens of megawatts," with closed-loop cooling and battery backup instead of diesel generators. The city had been under a non-disclosure agreement with Verrus since March 2025, and the project became public only in July 2026 after details surfaced on social media. On July 30, Gov. Tina Kotek directed the state to cancel its contract to sell Verrus about 32 acres of state land at Mill Creek, about half the land the project needed. "This decision is about my responsibility to make sure state actions reflect Oregon's values and serve the public interest," Kotek said. Verrus spokesperson JP Newmann said the decision "was made unilaterally and without consultation." Within days, an applicant filing on Verrus's behalf, Alderstone, LLC, submitted plans for two one-story buildings with a combined 600,000-square-foot footprint on 100.2 acres owned by Capstone Mill Creek Logistics LLC and Scannell Properties, valuing the project at $394 million. Verrus says the campus would bring 75 permanent jobs. Residents packed the July 27 council meeting in outrage over the project, and public comment at the August 3 meeting ran more than four hours. "We do not want your data center in our town," one resident said; others warned the Santiam River, the city's drinking water source, could be threatened. City Attorney Dan Atchison told councilors that "there is a potential that our water supply will be imperiled" by pending drawdowns of the Detroit Reservoir. State Sen. Deb Patterson, a Salem Democrat, said the project had moved "under a cloak of secrecy" and said she would bring legislation on public officials' use of NDAs. Salem joins Hillsboro and Woodburn in pausing data centers, and Kotek has told state agencies to hold off on unapproved requests for data centers on state land until next year. A statewide study found Oregon's 111 data centers in operation used more than 14 terawatt-hours last year, about 71% of all electricity sold to Oregon households. The council can extend the moratorium by six months before the end of the year, and it will reconsider the freeze in January. A nine-member city Data Center Task Force is due to recommend data center policy to the Salem City Council by the end of 2026, and the council decides what follows.

ft-1767584334287-8832.text: Edged wants to build Project Atlas, a data center campus of three buildings totaling 725 megawatts of power, on about 410 acres of farmland at 2493 N. Cedar Crest Boulevard in South Whitehall Township, Lehigh County, outside Allentown, Pennsylvania. On September 23, 2026, before more than 100 people at Parkland High School, across the street from the site, the township's planning commission took the plan under advisement without a decision, and the deadline for a decision moved from October 31 to December 31. Edged first proposed six data centers of more than 5.1 million square feet before cutting the plan to three buildings of about 492,000 square feet each, plus an administration building, a warehouse and an on-site substation screened by a 12-foot berm. The company says it will invest more than $8.9 billion and pay about $16.5 million a year in taxes, and Chief Investment Officer John Callahan said in July that no electricity costs "will be passed on to local residents." Residents have opposed the plan since it surfaced. "As a voter in South Whitehall, I can absolutely say I do not want this in my backyard," resident Spurgeon Dunbar told the Lehigh Valley Planning Commission in January. Regional planning staff raised noise, nighttime lighting and possible sinkholes, and committee member Christopher Amato said he had "significant concerns about electrical rates" and the site's karst topography. A Change.org petition against the project had more than 9,150 signatures in July. In July, after a planning commission meeting, text messages disparaging residents' appearance and intelligence circulated on social media; WFMZ reported they were sent by a now-former senior development manager for Scannell Properties. Edged's head of marketing, Marcie Kaplan, said the comments were his own and did not reflect the company's values. Edged says the Parkland School District faces a $15.7 million funding gap for 2026-27, and representative Garland Christopher asked, "Who is going to bridge that if Project Atlas is not here?" Elsewhere in Lehigh County, in Upper Macungie Township, the zoning board rejected a similar data center on Air Products' former headquarters site, and the company confirmed in August 2026 it would not appeal. Edged has said it will return to South Whitehall with a revised plan. The township's planning commission now has until December 31 to make a recommendation, but the South Whitehall Township Board of Commissioners has the final say on the land development plan.

Petrucci Company has proposed a 100 megawatt data center, a 146,000 square foot building with its own electrical substation, at 1024 North Bradford Street on Allentown's East Side in Lehigh County, Pennsylvania, next to Coca-Cola Park, recently renamed Jefferson Park. The Lehigh Valley Planning Commission's planning committee reviewed the plan in September 2026 and warned Allentown not to approve it without basic facts about how it would run. The full commission was scheduled to take up the review on September 24, 2026; no result has been published, and the decision itself rests with Allentown, whose planning department must first settle which zoning rules apply. Allentown's City Council unanimously passed Bill 52 on August 5, hours after the Petrucci application arrived, confining data centers to the Industrial Manufacturing district, raising the setback from homes, schools and child care sites from 200 feet to 500 feet, and setting an 8 acre minimum lot for larger facilities. Council solicitor Maria Montero has said the new rules apply to the Bradford Street plan under the pending ordinance doctrine, but a 2022 Commonwealth Court ruling that the doctrine does not cover land development plans leaves it unclear which version governs. The Executive Education Academy Charter School sits across Bradford Street, within the setback under either version, and at 500 feet it would be virtually impossible to build the 146,000 square foot facility. The regional planners found the submission left out the cooling system, water demand, total electrical demand, standby generation, the location of mechanical equipment, and expected noise, vibration and heat. Given the region's drought, they asked whether the building would be air cooled, water cooled, evaporative or hybrid, and asked the developer to show PPL Electric Utilities can carry the load without hurting service to existing customers. The plan's 94 car and 36 truck spaces, they noted, look like a layout for a freight heavy industrial use rather than a data center, and nearby Union Boulevard is already a "high crash corridor," with the ballpark and the school adding to traffic. A spokesman for the developer said the project "would pay its own way for power and use advanced cooling systems, such as closed-loop technology, that dramatically reduce water usage and do not require local water for cooling," and that the missing requirements "will be completed in the coming weeks and months." An LLC registered to Petrucci's New Jersey business address owns the 9.5 acre site, marketed as the Allentown Flex Center; the Allentown Planning Commission gave a warehouse there conditional final approval in 2022.

ft-1785374952695-7873.text: Quantm Group wants to turn a vacant 224,000-square-foot warehouse at 2401 West Emaus Avenue in Allentown, Lehigh County, Pennsylvania, into an 80-megawatt data center with a 23,000-square-foot addition. The Allentown Planning Commission reviewed Quantm's revised plan on Tuesday, September 8, 2026, and reached no verdict, and a zoning appeal about the project set for the zoning hearing board on August 31 was postponed with no new date. The Allentown Planning Commission decides the land development plan, and the zoning appeal is still waiting for a hearing date before the zoning hearing board. The revised plan moves an electrical substation from the Emaus Avenue frontage to the south side of the property, adds sound walls around mechanical equipment and more landscaping, and lists 66 employees and 32 backup generators. Quantm says it will use 42 rooftop chillers with a closed-loop cooling system, which its attorney Anthony Maras said it would accept as a deed restriction, and 35-foot sound walls to stay within the city's limits of 57 decibels by day and 52 at night. Maras said PPL had indicated the project would not raise rates for other customers, and he has put the data center's tax revenue at about $4 million a year. About three dozen residents spoke at a special evening meeting of the planning commission on July 16, raising noise, water and electricity use and utility costs. "I am very concerned about our community. I want to be somewhere where we can live and thrive," resident Alexx Knight said. City planners have questioned how few jobs the data center would bring to an area the city has designated a major employment hub, and its fit with neighbors such as Camelot for Children, a nonprofit for children with special needs, and the Wynnewood Greens housing complex. Allentown City Council adopted data center standards in June 2026 covering water and electricity use, noise and environmental studies, but they do not apply here because Quantm filed before the council took up the issue. Council is now working on a change to the city's noise ordinance aimed at the continuous hum of data centers, which would cover the Quantm site and every other property in the city.
