ft-446.text: Data Centric LLC, a New York City company, cancelled its planned data center at the Great Stream Commons industrial park near Allenwood in August 2025, pulling out of a deal to buy a 37-acre lot there, in Union County, Pennsylvania, for $2.7 million. The sale agreement, backed by the real estate and investment firm KSR Capital, was signed in May 2025 with a 180-day due diligence period and $100,000 held in escrow. "We received an official termination notice from the data center at Great Stream Commons. They have pulled out of the deal", said Shawn McLaughlin, Union County's planning and economic development director. "They are stating that in their sole and absolute discretion, they have decided not to proceed with the acquisition of the property as per the executed agreement. Because it was within the contingency period, they can do that, and do not lose their initial deposit held in escrow." "It is challenging to land any project with significant infrastructure demands in rural Pennsylvania because it is rare for a development site to have all the necessary utilities at the capacity the industrial user needs", he said. Little is publicly known about Data Centric, DCD noted. Union County Commissioners Chair Preston Boop said in March 2026: "We were told once before that (PPL Electric Utilities) does not have the ability or the will to provide enough electricity for a data center there." The industrial park has since drawn a far larger plan from another New York City developer, PNK Group, which wants four data centers in Great Stream Commons, starting in a vacant 500,000-square-foot warehouse at the southern end of the park. More than 100 people, many wearing red, came to the Gregg Township supervisors' meeting on May 4, 2026 to oppose it. On August 20, 2026 the three supervisors unanimously suspended new data center development for at least 180 days while they review the zoning ordinance; the pause does not affect PNK's application. PNK has asked for a curative amendment and conditional use approval that would permit data centers in the commercial manufacturing district, and the supervisors closed their hearing on it on September 14, 2026. They have until October 29 to decide whether to allow data centers in the commercial manufacturing district at Great Stream Commons, by adopting PNK's ordinance or writing their own, and will announce the decision at a special meeting in October.

ft-472.text: Site work is underway at the former Highway Auto Parts junkyard on Eynon Jermyn Road in Archbald for Project Boson, a proposed 619,925-square-foot data center from PDC Realty LLC, a company affiliated with Kriger Construction, while Pennsylvania regulators have flagged deficiencies in its stormwater permit application. PDC Realty bought the 83.5-acre junkyard in Archbald Borough, Lackawanna County, for $1.575 million in August 2025 to build the data center, first filed as the Archbald Data & Energy Center. The original April 2025 plan called for three two-story buildings under 70 feet tall, a 20,000-square-foot office and an equipment yard for substations, with 200-foot buffers from homes to the east and south; the three buildings have since been merged into one. Because the project applied before Archbald tightened its data center zoning in November 2025, it is grandfathered as a permitted use and skips the conditional-use hearings other campuses face, though it still needs final land development approval from the borough and permits from the state Department of Environmental Protection. The DEP's August 26, 2026 letter on the stormwater permit listed deficiencies in 23 categories and about 140 comments, including soil contamination and a lack of investigation into possible groundwater contamination from a junkyard that operated for nearly 70 years. Across the road, Kriger Construction president Jim Marzolino applied in March 2026 through Essential Energy LLC for a natural gas power plant with four 66,000-square-foot turbine pads, less than 1,000 feet from Staback Park and about half a mile from Valley View Intermediate School; unlike the data center, it needs a conditional-use hearing before borough council. In August, Gov. Josh Shapiro, who had visited Archbald, ordered data center developers statewide to meet his GRID standards through the DEP. "These kids are never getting away from these," said Madonna Munley, a fifth-generation Archbald resident, of the children in nearby housing who would live, play and go to school beside the data centers and plant. Council President Louis Rapoch said, "We don't want it there, like we don't want the data centers there. These are speculators that are coming in here, hoping that we'll just lay down." Archbald now has six data center campuses proposed, 51 buildings in all, most along a stretch of less than a mile of Eynon Jermyn Road and Business Route 6; in September 2026 Lackawanna County commissioners hired EmPower Analytics Group to study the combined air and health effects of the county's proposed data centers and power plants. What decides Project Boson now is the DEP's review of its stormwater permit and the borough's final land development approval.

ft-447.text: Corscale, a data center developer with campuses in Northern Virginia, now owns the 186-acre Project Gravity site in Archbald Borough, Lackawanna County, Pennsylvania, and says it will submit final land development plans for the campus “imminently.” The site was sold on December 23, 2025 by Archbald 25 Developer LLC, the Western Hospitality Partners entity that first proposed it, to US Gravity Purchaser LLC, tied to Corscale's investment partner Affinius Capital. The plan is five one-story and two two-story data center buildings on mine-spoiled land, and Corscale says it is in serious talks with a large computing tenant. The first developer told the state it expected to invest $5 billion and create 300 permanent jobs. Corscale's Erik Draaisma said the campus is on track for closed-loop cooling and will use a fraction of the diesel backup generators allowed. Project Gravity was expected to draw 360,000 gallons of water a day from Lake Scranton, which serves 134,570 people. The site takes in the Valley View Estates mobile home park and borders 18 homes and State Game Lands 307. Park residents received eviction notices in July 2025, shortly after Project Gravity was announced, with an April 15, 2026 deadline to leave. “These people have no resources,” said Archbald resident Ann Beynon. Draaisma said the design will keep most operations away from the northeast corner of the property, where most of the homes are. “It's something new, and it's something different, and it's something that's become easy to dislike,” he said. Project Gravity was a permitted use under Archbald's previous zoning rules, so it skipped the borough's conditional use process. Residents of Stop Archbald Data Centers, which has more than 5,000 members, pushed for tighter rules, and some have appealed the borough's updated data center zoning in court. At the end of April 2026 the state removed Project Gravity from the PA Permit Fast Track program, telling the developer its “lack of responsiveness and unwillingness to provide a transparent overview of the project” led to the removal. Governor Josh Shapiro later said Archbald had the most impact on his thinking when he issued his data center standards executive order in August 2026. Archbald has six proposed data center campuses, the most of any municipality in Pennsylvania. Project Gravity would be bordered by Project Scott and Project North, with Project Boson across Eynon Jermyn Road and the Wildcat Ridge AI Data Center Campus further down the road. Together the campuses would cover 14 percent of the town. The project still needs final land development approval from Archbald Borough, plus wetland and waterway permits from the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, before construction can begin.

“It's something new, and it's something different, and it's something that's become easy to dislike,” he said.

ft-1774058965456-7910.text: Archbald Borough Council's hearings on Project Green Mountain, a seven-building data center campus that Green Mountain 6 LLC wants to build at the Stavola Quarry in Archbald, Lackawanna County, Pennsylvania, resume on September 30, 2026, after a three-month pause. It will be the fourth conditional use hearing on the L-shaped, nearly 271-acre campus east of the Casey Highway, and the process ends with council voting to approve or deny it. It is one of six data center campuses proposed in Archbald, amounting to 51 buildings, and six more are proposed elsewhere in Lackawanna County, in Clifton and Covington townships, Dickson City, Jessup, Olyphant and Ransom Township. The application, filed January 26, calls for seven two-story data centers, each with a 138,000-square-foot footprint and 65 feet tall, drawing a projected 525 megawatts of power, or 75 megawatts per building. Cooling would be a closed loop of water and glycol, and the campus would take up to 14,000 gallons of water a day from Pennsylvania American Water for sinks and toilets. For outages it would have 196 diesel generators, each with a tank of up to 10,000 gallons, for 1.96 million gallons of diesel on site. The developer has offered Archbald a $2.25 million community benefits agreement: $1 million on signing and $250,000 for each of the first five data centers when they get temporary occupancy permits. Who is behind it has been a question from the start. The application named only a limited liability company, but during the first hearing in March a presenter's shared screen showed a file directory that included “Western Hospitality,” appearing to link the project to Western Hospitality Partners, which first proposed Archbald's Project Gravity before selling that site to Corscale in December 2025. Green Mountain also proposes seven data centers with 138,000-square-foot footprints. “Project Green Mountain is a wholly and independently owned entity. Our standalone business is exclusively focused on the proposed project,” said Nicole Schomburg of FTI Consulting. Noise has been the sharpest issue. The developer's sound study found the campus would stay under Archbald's 55-decibel residential daytime limit even with all 196 generators running, but Justin Richards, attorney for members of Stop Archbald Data Centers, said the predictions were “at the very margin,” equal to the maximum at some homes. Asked whether any comparable campus had a completed post-construction sound study, the developer's acoustics engineer said, “As far as I know, nothing we have done this process for has been constructed.” More than 300 people, many in yellow-and-black “No Data Centers” shirts, packed the first hearing. Green Mountain is the only Archbald campus on the side of the Casey Highway away from homes, which is one of the main requests of residents who oppose the borough's data center standards. Council amended its zoning in November 2025 to regulate data centers, putting an overlay on the quarry site that allows them as conditional uses. After the developer finishes its testimony, the borough and opponents can present their own experts, followed by public comment. Archbald Borough Council then has 45 days to vote and issue a written decision. The next hearing is at 5 p.m. on September 30 at Valley View High School, 1 Columbus Drive.

ft-1774025698970-5215.text: Project North is one of six data center campuses proposed in Archbald, a Lackawanna County borough of about 7,500 people in Pennsylvania's Lackawanna Valley, where developers plan 51 buildings covering 14% of the town. Anthony Domiano Jr., whose family runs a chain of local car dealerships, sold a large amount of land to Project South and Project North. Project North's developer, size and power have not been made public; it applied to the borough as a principal permitted use under Archbald's 2023 zoning, which lets a data center proceed with preliminary and final land development approval and no conditions tailored to the industry. The people with most at stake live at Valley View Estates, a trailer park whose owner has agreed to sell to a data center developer and which is set to be surrounded by data centers; residents were told they would be evicted on April 15, 2026. Sharon Williams, a home health aide making $17.50 an hour, pays $390 a month in lot rent there, and the county's public housing is roughly 98% occupied. "Everybody's worried about where they're going to go," said resident Matthew Bucksbee, who with his fiancée, Candace May, may be able to move to a friend's land in Forest City. The borough's rules were written with developers in the room. Documents published by DeSmog show developers played a significant role in the data center overlay ordinance passed in November 2025: Council President Dave Moran requested a 1,000-yard buffer between data centers and neighboring properties, and it was whittled down to 300 yards in the final language. Council member Erin Owen, who opposed the data centers from the outset, said: "All the impacts will be terrible." At a hearing, Nick Farris of Provident Real Estate Advisors, representing the developer of the neighboring Project Scott, kept telling a jeering crowd, "It's going to be away from everyone," and put the tax payoff at roughly $20 million a year for Archbald, $50 million for Lackawanna County and $100 million for the Valley View School District. Since then the ground has shifted. On March 27, 2026 the borough council voted 5-0 to deny Project Scott, an 18-building campus next to a borough park, as more than 200 residents cheered. All four council members who voted for the November ordinance have since left office or resigned, and in April residents presented a petition with more than 800 signatures calling for the removal of several borough officials. The borough has now drafted a stricter 26-page data center ordinance that would, among other things, remove the noise exemption for backup generators. It will not apply retroactively to projects already filed such as Project North, though any project that is denied or withdrawn would have to meet it if it came back. Council must first vote to advertise the ordinance for a public hearing before adopting it, and Project North's own land development approvals also rest with the Archbald borough council.

ft-1774058434144-4902.text: Project Scott is an 18-building data center campus on about 400 acres that Provident Realty Advisors of Dallas, operating as Archbald I LLC, has proposed on Eynon Jermyn Road next to Staback Park in Archbald Borough, Lackawanna County, Pennsylvania. Archbald has 51 of the more than 90 data centers proposed in Lackawanna County, 30 of them along the roughly one-mile stretch of Eynon Jermyn Road near Valley View School District's schools. The Archbald Borough Council voted 5-0 in March 2026 to deny Project Scott's application, but the developer has asked the Lackawanna County Court of Common Pleas to rule the project automatically approved over a missed hearing deadline, so the project remains blocked while the court decides. Provident's Nick Farris told a crowd at Valley View High School: "I think that this is the best data center site in this area of the country, by far," and the audience began to laugh as he described data centers as a boon for communities. The Valley View School District, which has four schools serving about 2,400 students, has asked to join both the borough's fight against the deemed-approval claim and residents' separate challenge to Archbald's zoning ordinance, arguing the campuses sit "dangerously close" to its schools. In November 2025, Archbald's council adopted a data center zoning ordinance despite heavy opposition; every member who voted for it has since left office or resigned. In July 2026, Lackawanna County Judge Mark Powell ruled that eight residents living 1,600 to 5,200 feet from the overlay districts have standing to challenge the ordinance, rejecting developers' argument that they lived too far away. The Lackawanna County Court of Common Pleas will now decide whether Project Scott was automatically approved, whether the council's denial stands, and whether the 2025 zoning ordinance survives. A hearing on whether the school district and the Lackawanna County Housing Authority can join the case was scheduled for September 3, 2026; no result has been published.

ft-1763999888960-6008.text: TierPoint runs a data center at 3864 Courtney Street in Bethlehem, Northampton County, Pennsylvania, one of two data centers it operates in the city. The colocation facility has more than 25,000 square feet, including over 12,000 square feet of raised floor, backed by three redundant generators with at least 48 hours of runtime. Bethlehem is writing new rules for data centers after city staff and the Lehigh Valley Planning Commission presented a draft zoning amendment in August 2026 that would allow them only by special exception in the Industrial district. The draft would keep data centers at least 1,000 feet from homes, schools, daycare centers, parks and hospitals, cap their height at 80 feet, and require an environmental review covering karst, air, water and wildlife. Assistant planning director Craig Peiffer said the city cannot regulate utilities overseen by the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission, and said Bethlehem is largely built out. "We have no room for data centers," resident Bill Sheirer told the city's Community Development Committee, arguing that vacant land should go to affordable housing instead. Councilmember Justin Amann said the city should be open about residents' concerns: "Making sure we are open about that and candid about those concerns upfront is a really critical piece of this process." The draft goes next to the city planning commission and the Lehigh Valley Planning Commission, then to a public hearing and a vote of City Council.

ft-1763999128335-5701.text: TierPoint, a St. Louis data center company, is carrying out a 100-megawatt power expansion at its Tek Park data center at 9999 Hamilton Boulevard in Upper Macungie Township, near Breinigsville, Lehigh County, Pennsylvania, after buying the 137-acre campus for $175 million in October 2025. TierPoint told the Lehigh Valley Economic Development Corporation it expects to finish the expansion in the second half of 2026. The existing data center has more than 122,000 square feet, more than 96,000 of them raised floor, backed by 23 redundant generators with at least 36 hours of runtime, according to TierPoint. TierPoint had leased the building before the purchase, which it financed alongside a new $240 million asset-backed securities issuance; Data Center Dynamics called it TierPoint's largest data center in Pennsylvania. The 508,000 square foot campus was built in 1987 as a Bell Laboratories site owned by AT&T and passed to Lucent, Agere and in 2003 TriQuint Semiconductor before Hamilton TEK Partners bought it in 2005; real estate firm MRA Group owned it before TierPoint. TierPoint said it will add around 100 jobs, and that the expansion, including work on the utility substation, could support 350 or more construction and engineering jobs. "TierPoint continues to build on its exceptional growth trajectory, with strong demand for our digital infrastructure solutions, including market-leading enterprise, wholesale, and high-density colocation services that support artificial intelligence and other compute-intensive workloads," chair and CEO Jerry Kent said. Along the same stretch of Hamilton Boulevard, the township has just turned away a far larger proposal. Air Products wanted three data center buildings totaling about 2.6 million square feet on its vacant 194-acre former headquarters nearby, but the Upper Macungie Zoning Hearing Board ruled in July 2026 against treating a data center as a "similar use" in that district, and Air Products let its appeal deadline pass. No hearing is required for the Tek Park expansion, since it is adding capacity to a campus already used for data center operations; TierPoint's own timeline points to the second half of 2026 for completion.

"TierPoint continues to build on its exceptional growth trajectory, with strong demand for our digital infrastructure solutions, including market-leading enterprise, wholesale, and high-density colocation services that support artificial intelligence and other compute-intensive workloads," chair and CEO Jerry Kent said.
Along the same stretch of Hamilton Boulevard, the township has just turned away a far larger proposal.

Air Products wanted three data center buildings totaling about 2.6 million square feet on its vacant 194-acre former headquarters nearby, but the Upper Macungie Zoning Hearing Board ruled in July 2026 against treating a data center as a "similar use" in that district, and Air Products let its appeal deadline pass.

No hearing is required for the Tek Park expansion, since it is adding capacity to a campus already used for data center operations; TierPoint's own timeline points to the second half of 2026 for completion.

ft-1776918405079-1325.text: Popca LLC's proposed two-building data center campus on Newton Road outside Clarks Summit was blocked by Newton Township's zoning officer in February 2026, and the Archbald company appealed to the township zoning hearing board, which scheduled a hearing for April 27, 2026. The campus, the tenth proposed in Lackawanna County, Pennsylvania, would sit on about 90 acres known as the East Newton Ira Tripp Tract, in the township's rural resource zoning district. Mark Gawron, the land's former owner and the company's contact, filed the zoning application on January 21, 2026 and estimated the project's cost at $280 million. Zoning officer D. Scot Haan found that a data center is not an allowed use in the township's rural resource district. Gawron's lawyers argued the use fits the township's commercial, institutional, utility or light industrial categories. Lackawanna County is weighing the cumulative effect of more than a dozen data centers and power plants proposed there. In September 2026 the county commissioners hired a firm to study the air quality and health effects, with a report due in 90 days. "The people who live in Lackawanna County don't breathe air one project at a time. They breathe the cumulative air of Lackawanna County," said Commissioner Bill Gaughan. The Newton Township Zoning Hearing Board decides the appeal; the hearing was scheduled for April 27, 2026, and no result has been published.

ft-454.text: 1778 Rich Pike LLC, the developer behind Project Gold Data Center, sued Clifton Township in Lackawanna County, Pennsylvania in April 2025, arguing that the township's zoning ordinance illegally excluded data centers, their equipment and private power generation. The township's supervisors rejected a first settlement 2 to 1 in August 2025, with chair Jill Zindle the only yes vote, then approved a revised settlement unanimously on January 2, 2026. The settlement raises the township's height limit for data centers from 35 feet to 65 feet, with rooftop equipment adding another 15 feet, for 80 feet in all. Zindle said the settlement covers zoning only: "This does not stop the process for them having to go through all land development... it doesn't mean they pour concrete tomorrow." Matt Gruenloh, an incoming supervisor and planning commission member, said: "I understand that what you did is legal. I just don't think it was appropriate." Howard Ives said: "My family owns 150 acres. I'm fourth generation. This data center will destroy the value and the habitat of my property." June Ejk held the supervisors to their own rules: "We have a township ordinance that does not allow buildings to go over 35 feet... you are violating your own township ordinance." Matthew Chase asked for time: "Give the public time to read these settlements, to read these proposals, give the public time to comment," and residents said they would take the supervisors to court. Project Gold is planned on at least seven properties along Route 380 between Clifton and Covington townships; the settlement splits the Clifton portion into three campuses with five two-story buildings, a utility switchyard and an administration building. The developer, based in Doylestown, now describes an 11-building campus, and a company sharing its address, Gouldsboro Land LLC, bought 456 acres in the two townships between December 2025 and June 2026. On August 19, 2026, Lackawanna County Judge Mark Powell ruled the township's May 2025 data center ordinance void, which the township solicitor said means "effectively it never became law." The supervisors are writing a new ordinance, and at its first hearing the next day residents asked for wider woodland buffers than the draft's 100 feet, tighter water limits and a 35-foot height cap, while the developer's lawyer sent the township his own marked-up version.

ft-456.text: Peach Bottom Township, in York County, Pennsylvania, adopted rules for data centers on August 5, 2026, a year after Energy Capital Partners announced a $5 billion data center at its Calpine York 2 Energy Center near Delta. The Board of Supervisors voted 3-0 for Ordinance No. 2026-02 after an hour-long public hearing, and confirmed that no formal data center proposal or application has been submitted to the township. Energy Capital Partners said in July 2025 that it would develop the data center through Calpine, its energy business, on the site of the 828-megawatt gas-fired York 2 plant. The project was among $90 billion in Pennsylvania investments announced at an energy and innovation summit in Pittsburgh, and officials said it would create 2,500 construction jobs. Peach Bottom is also home to the Peach Bottom nuclear plant, owned by Constellation Energy and PSEG. "This project is just another example of how we're building a better York County that's at the leading edge of economic progress," York County President Commissioner Julie Wheeler said at the time. No end user, building size or power figure for the data center itself has been made public. At the August hearing, residents asked why data centers could not be prohibited. According to the minutes, they also raised water usage, groundwater depletion, noise, electric rates, air pollution, diesel generators, health impacts, property values, farmland, traffic, and proximity to homes and schools. The supervisors answered that Pennsylvania zoning law does not allow a township to completely exclude a lawful use, and that electric rates and withdrawals from the Susquehanna River are regulated by state agencies, outside the township's control. In July, Mary Schultz of Drumore Township and Bob Williams submitted recommendations on the draft, particularly on noise standards and resident protections. Under the adopted ordinance, a data center is allowed only by special exception in the Industrial District, on a parcel of at least 50 acres, and must win approval from the township's Zoning Hearing Board. Rezoning any more land for one would take a separate vote by the supervisors. The May 2026 draft set a 60-foot height limit and a 1,000-foot setback where a site abuts a home, school, park, place of worship or other sensitive receptor, and capped noise at 58 decibels at the boundary of such properties. It allowed wells only for drinking and washing, required any cooling water to come directly from the Susquehanna River, and required baseline testing of at least four private wells within half a mile. If a data center fouled nearby wells, the draft required its owner to supply drinking water to affected residents, and to equip and train the Delta-Cardiff Volunteer Fire Company for emergencies at the site. Peach Bottom is one of several York County townships writing rules ahead of proposals. By late 2025, data center proposals in Fairview, Windsor and West Manchester townships were awaiting zoning approval, and East Manchester Township drew hundreds to a hearing over rumors of one near the Royal Manchester Golf Links. York County ranks first among Pennsylvania's counties in power generation, according to GridInfo figures cited by Keystone Newsroom. The board is Chairman Michael E. Kahl, Vice Chairman David E. Gemmill and Andrew K. Jarvis. Any application for the York 2 site would now go to the Peach Bottom Township Zoning Hearing Board for a special exception under the new rules, with the Board of Supervisors deciding any rezoning. The township told residents that future applications would appear on posted meeting agendas and the township website, and that the ordinance could be amended as technology changes.

ft-1774024346254-5098.text: Dickson City Development LLC, tied to Kriger Construction, wants to build four data centers along Bell Mountain above Business Route 6 in Dickson City, Lackawanna County, Pennsylvania, and the borough has denied every application so far. In May 2026 the borough's Zoning Hearing Board upheld the borough's data center ordinance and rejected the developer's appeals of all four denials. The developer's separate court challenge to the ordinance is still pending in the Lackawanna County Court of Common Pleas. Borough council limited data centers in February 2026 to a light manufacturing district near Enterprise and Railroad streets, which excludes Bell Mountain. The developer's attorney, Michael Mey, argued that district lacks the land and power lines a data center needs, but borough planner Thomas Shepstone testified it would fit: "We've identified land where you can put this use, and the bottom line is that it has been done before." Three companies called Dickson City Power, also tied to Kriger Construction, are separately seeking approval for natural gas plants totaling 600 megawatts on the same stretch of Bell Mountain. Asked whether the power could go to a data center, their witness, power executive Randall Holmes, said, "In theory, it could be a data center," though he said no arrangements had been made. Resident Tim Pfleiderer, who lives less than 1,000 feet from one proposed plant, asked Holmes if he would want the plant in his own backyard; Holmes answered yes. The Zoning Hearing Board was scheduled to reconvene on the power plant applications on July 22, 2026; no result has been published. The data centers' fate now rests with the Lackawanna County Court of Common Pleas, where the developer can also appeal the May denials.

ft-1778599430491-3948.text: MRP Industrial has proposed a data center campus of ten buildings, each 138,000 square feet, on 288 acres near Duncannon in Perry County, Pennsylvania, land where the company had earlier planned a logistics hub called Susquehanna Crossings. The plan went to the Watts Township planning commission on April 8, 2026, and no approvals have been granted. The Watts Township Board of Supervisors will decide a proposed data center ordinance and, under it, MRP's plans. More than 125 residents packed an April 1, 2026 supervisors meeting, forcing it outside the Watts-Buffalo Community Center, mostly to oppose the ordinance that would allow data centers. Supervisors put off a full hearing until May. Susan Fulmer, who moved to the township in 2020, said she fears for her property value, electricity bills, noise, light and the Susquehanna River: "Now it seems like everything we spent our entire lives working for to achieve is going to be taken." MRP vice president Nate Chadsey, who says he also part-owns the site, told supervisors the property has "significant visual buffering and distance from residents" and that a data center would create jobs and support the tax base. Volunteer fire chief Kevin Bissonnette supported the project, saying it would "enhance electrical capacity, upgrade roadways and utility expansion." Daniel Welliver, who has led opposition to this and other MRP projects, said his goal is stricter ordinances to protect current residents, not blocking all development. An April 2026 draft ordinance would treat data centers using 50 megawatts of power as developments of regional impact, requiring at least 20 acres, a 200-foot front yard and a 200-foot setback next to homes or farms. Gov. Josh Shapiro ordered data center developers statewide in August 2026 to meet new environmental standards and file plans with the state, saying only five of more than 100 proposed projects had the needed permits. The township canceled planned hearings on curative amendments to the ordinance and moved its September supervisors meeting to September 21, 2026, at the Watts-Buffalo Community Center. That meeting has passed; no result on the ordinance has been published.

ft-1773441380040-9264.text: The Smithfield Gateway data center, a 250,000-square-foot building proposed by developers DEPG Mosier Associates LP and DEPG of Shawnee II LP for the Mosier Farm Drive corridor near East Stroudsburg, Smithfield Township, Monroe County, Pennsylvania, is waiting on a conditional use hearing before the township's Board of Supervisors. The township says the hearing must be scheduled within 60 days of receiving the application, that dates are still pending, and that it is looking for a larger venue because it expects a big turnout. The conditional use application describes a single two-story data center of 250,000 square feet, though an earlier sketch plan for the Smithfield Gateway site showed two data center buildings, each with a 125,000-square-foot footprint, plus a power substation. The application includes an acoustical evaluation of sound emissions, and the township posts the documents, engineer reviews and the developer's responses on its website. A petition to stop the data center was circulating by March 2026, and the township has since rewritten its data center rules. On May 6, 2026, the Board of Supervisors adopted Resolution No. 621, starting the state's curative amendment process to revise the ordinance, after at least two hours of public comment, Township Manager Julia Heilakka wrote. She told residents Pennsylvania law does not let townships ban a use outright the way some other states can. ft-479.text: Pennhurst Holdings LLC wanted to build a 1.9 million square foot data center on the grounds of the former Pennhurst State School and Hospital in East Vincent Township, Chester County, Pennsylvania, now a Halloween attraction. In November 2025 the township supervisors put forward an ordinance to set rules for it: height and setback requirements and limits on various kinds of pollution, with a vote scheduled for December 17, 2025. Residents did not want rules; they wanted a refusal. Dina Hitchcock said: "In my opinion, creating this ordinance could be viewed as a red carpet invitation to a data center," and: "I'd rather this just be turned down outright." She was not against them everywhere. "I do understand there is a need for them," Hitchcock said. "I am just saying this is not the appropriate place." Joanna Binelli said: "I don't believe, strongly, that there's anything that you can put in the ordinance that will prevent these things from happening." State Senator Katie Muth said: "People here deserve better. They live here. They deserve to live in peace and quiet, and also not to have to subsidize this through utility bills." John Quigley, of the University of Pennsylvania's Kleinman Center, put the water question where it matters locally: "Whether it's being drawn from streams, rivers, or whether it's, especially if it's from groundwater, there are over one million Pennsylvanians that get their water from wells." On December 17, 2025 the supervisors shelved the ordinance, as residents had asked, and sent the application to a conditional use hearing instead. The township planning commission recommended against the plan, citing a lack of detail, technical deficiencies and conflicts with the zoning ordinance. On May 21, 2026, at the second hearing, the three supervisors unanimously rejected it as failing to meet the zoning standards, to cheers from more than 100 people; residents of the Southeastern Veterans' Center a few hundred feet away had opposed it. The developer's spokesman said it would appeal: "We plan to appeal the decision and we look forward to presenting the merits of the project in a court of law." Its attorney, Matt McHugh, said the appeal would go to the Chester County Court of Common Pleas, arguing the township is legally obliged to allow for data centers.

ft-1776917809954-2894.text: Earth-moving has begun on the Sentinel Green Fig data center, a campus of about 1.5 million square feet that Sentinel Data Centers and Green Fig LLC are building on the former Foote Mineral Superfund site at 13 South Bacton Hill Road in East Whiteland Township, near Exton, in Chester County, Pennsylvania. The township halted the early work in July 2026 over its review of soil and health safety plans, then let it resume on July 29 after issuing an erosion and sedimentation permit with conditions on soil monitoring, dust control and protection of the Superfund remedy. The 2024 plan, which won preliminary approval on June 12, 2024 and final approval with conditions on August 14, 2024, shows two two-story buildings with basements and a footprint of 1,544,700 square feet, next to PECO's Planebrook substation near Swedesford Road. The Board of Supervisors says it was legally obliged to sign the plan in March 2026 once staff found the conditions met, and it was recorded with the county on March 31, 2026. That plan would use about 3 million gallons of water a day for cooling. The land was zoned for a data center of up to 1,860,000 square feet, and the project dates to 2022, when Fifteenfortyseven Critical Systems Realty and Green Fig Land Company began planning it; Sentinel joined in 2024. Foote Mineral processed ores there from about 1941 until 1991, leaving lithium, boron, arsenic, hexavalent chromium and low-level radiation, and the site remains on the EPA's National Priorities List. The EPA told the developers any reuse must not interfere with the cleanup remedy and asked for a health and safety plan and a soil management plan before work began; it says the development is limited to parcels next to the capped quarry and that there have been no violations of the environmental covenant. Malvern resident Kelly Donia said, “No one seems to be concerned, but I mean, we live right here, we work right here,” adding that there are children and a daycare nearby. Faced with opposition, Sentinel filed a smaller amended plan in late 2025, and in April 2026 CEO Josh Rabina warned that if approval was delayed or further appeals were filed, “we will simply have no choice but to continue building the current plan.” The developer then withdrew the amended plan and said it would build the 2024 plan it already had permission for. In July it returned with a “field change” to swap cooling towers for rooftop air-chilled units, which it said would cut water use to effectively none, and a smaller total footprint of 536,000 square feet; the supervisors voted 2-1 to table the request. “This isn’t moving a pipe from five feet away to have some mud moved on top of it. This is a half-a-million-square-foot change,” said Tony Gianino. “This is a completely new project.” “In either event, Sentinel is proceeding with development,” said Lou Colagreco, the developers' attorney. A Chester County judge dismissed appeals challenging earlier approvals. The developers still need construction permits for work such as pouring footings and foundations, which the township says it must process. The East Whiteland Township Board of Supervisors decides the cooling “field change,” which was still pending as of August 19, 2026. Opposition to the project also drove a petition, signed by at least 500 residents, that puts a question on the November 3 ballot asking whether to expand the board from three members to five. That same week Gov. Josh Shapiro signed an executive order requiring local approval for data center projects to receive state permits.

ft-1763753707040-1765.text: Fairview Crossroads LLC has proposed a 750,000-square-foot data center worth about $500 million at Interstate 83 and Lewisberry Road in Fairview Township, York County, Pennsylvania, according to representative Kevin Brown. Fairview Township supervisors changed the zoning ordinance in July 2025 to allow data centers as a conditional use, but as of the township's September 1, 2026 planning agenda, no one has filed an actual data center application for the site. Any project here still needs a conditional use hearing before the Board of Supervisors. Brown, a partner in the Florida-based real estate firm Elysian Partners LLC, presented a concept plan to the Planning Commission in July 2025 for an 84-acre tract along Lewisberry Road. He said the project would raise more than $6 million a year in tax revenue, lifting the township's take from $396 to $396,000 and the West Shore School District's from $4,054 to $4,066,415, with about 120 jobs. The Planning Commission recommended the zoning change 5-1, with Chairman Williams opposed, and asked for 150-foot setbacks from homes, height limits of 55 to 65 feet, sound berms and noise studies before and after opening. Supervisors adopted Ordinance 2025-03 unanimously. Resident Brandon Freistat backed the zoning change but not a data center at this site: "A data center is closed off," he said. "It doesn't bring in foot traffic." Brown said in 2025 that grants the company held for Lewisberry Road improvements would expire June 30, 2026; that date has passed with no public update on the grants or a formal application. The Planning Commission's September 1, 2026 agenda still lists no data center proposal for the site.

ft-1762786214697-6167.text: Project Hummingbird is a 910 megawatt data center that International Electric Power (IEP) wants to build on 1,400 acres of the former Robena coal mine at Alicia, in Monongahela Township, Greene County, Pennsylvania. IEP, of Pittsburgh, wants gas turbines, backup generators and a water treatment plant on the site, with cooling drawing eight to nine million gallons a day from the Monongahela River, about 17 million gallons a day once the servers are added. The Greene County Planning Commission voted 8-1 on December 17, 2025 to approve the first phase, grading and reclaiming 309 acres, after nearly ninety minutes of public comment. IEP promises 1,500 construction jobs a year over six years, 150 to 200 permanent data center jobs and 40 to 50 running the turbines. County commissioners chair Jared Edgreen backs the project for its tax revenue: "For so many years, this county thrived on coal tax revenue, and we've seen that go down (along) with the jobs as well." Nearby resident Kimberly Barton disagreed: "For (a few) viable, long-term jobs, you have 28 houses of people that are being affected by the environmental impacts," and asked whether it would hurt the soil for growing crops. The gas turbines and the data center buildings still need separate approvals; planning commissioner Brian Sokol, who voted yes on the first phase, said of the rest, "Will they for Phase 2? I don't know. We'll see." As of December 2025, IEP said it hoped to have permitting done by early 2026, start building the data center and power plant in 2026, finish the data center by 2028 and have the turbines running in 2029. No public update on permits or construction has been published since that vote.

ft-459.text: The Dauphin County General Authority agreed in August 2025 to sell the Dauphin Highlands Golf Course, about 250 acres in Swatara Township and Steelton just outside Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, for $45.6 million to Harrisburg I, LLC, a buyer formed by Dallas-based Provident Realty that plans a data center there. The sale is not final: the data center developer still has to secure water, power, a highway occupancy permit and land-use approvals, and the course would stay open until a tentative closing at the end of 2027. The authority said Provident's offer was one of six proposals after it issued a request in February 2025, and that the sale would let it pay off $13 million of debt on a course that has consistently lost money. "Harrisburg I, LLC's proposal is approximately 10 times higher than the recorded value of the land," said board chair Barbara Zemlock. Because the authority is a public owner, the course pays no property taxes, and the authority says a private owner would produce significant revenue for the Central Dauphin School District, the township, the county and the state. Board member Eric Epstein put the open questions plainly: "They need to get water. They're going to need to get power. They need to get a highway occupancy permit, navigate land use." Provident has had data center plans turned away before: a 200-acre proposal in northwest Indiana was turned down, and it then pitched a seven-building campus in Burns Harbor, Indiana. Swatara Township's Board of Commissioners has since drafted rules for data centers: a July 2026 version of a zoning amendment would cap data center buildings at 105 feet, set them back at least 210 feet from adjoining lot lines, require a landscape buffer at least 70 feet deep and require sound studies. Elsewhere in Dauphin County, Londonderry Township weighed a data center overlay district in 2025, and resident Richard Sauerwine warned that cooling towers "can use up to 20,000 gallons of water a day." What happens next: Provident's due diligence, the township's final vote on its data center ordinance, and any land development plan, which would go to the Swatara Township Board of Commissioners and, for the Steelton portion, the borough.

ft-460.text: On November 14, 2025, the Hazle Township Board of Supervisors in Luzerne County unanimously rejected NorthPoint Development's land application for Project Hazelnut, a data center campus beside the north zone of the Humboldt Industrial Park. More than 200 residents packed the meeting where the vote happened. The stated reason was procedural: data centers were not specifically permitted on the property, and the application should have first gone to the zoning hearing board for a special exception, which had not happened. Ginny Marcille-Kerslake, the eastern Pennsylvania senior organizer for Food and Water Watch, which worked with residents on the campaign, said: “There is a reason why communities are pushing back on data centers, with residents showing up and speaking out, filling township meeting rooms in opposition: they serve private interests at the expense of the community.” NorthPoint told the county the buildings would rely mainly on air cooling, with gray water from the West Hazleton wastewater treatment plant as a backup water source instead of the public water system, and diesel generators for backup power during outages. The company said normal operations would sound like a dull conversation, and it put permanent employment at about 900 jobs. Before the township vote, NorthPoint had also been seeking a Luzerne County tax break on the site. In a February 2025 proposal it asked for relief on county real estate taxes at 90 percent for the first seven years, tapering to 80, 70 and 60 percent, plus payments of $2,500 an acre for land carrying buildings; township and school district tax breaks had already been approved. County council's infrastructure committee, chaired by Jimmy Sabatino with Harry Haas and Patty Krushnowski, advanced the request to a council work session set for March 11, 2025. No result from that session has been published, and the county tax question became moot once Hazle Township rejected the project itself in November 2025.

ft-1782348217275-9736.text: HCI DP Land Acquisition LLC, a Texas-based developer, has asked South Hanover Township in Dauphin County, Pennsylvania, to allow a data center campus on about 250 acres of the former Pennsy Supply quarry off Wagner Street, near Hummelstown. The township's Zoning Hearing Board scheduled hearings on HCI's two data center requests for August 17, 2026. A residents' group, Protect South Hanover, reports that both hearings have since been postponed indefinitely at HCI's request. The quarry tract, in the township's industrial park along the Swatara Creek near Derry Township and Hummelstown, would hold two data centers of 401,800 and 195,000 square feet and a substation. HCI had earlier sought to build distribution warehouses there and withdrew that plan in favor of the data center. Its first application asks for a special exception, arguing that the township's zoning neither permits nor prohibits data centers, so the use is "not provided for." Its second is a substantive validity challenge claiming the township's zoning illegally excludes data centers, and it says HCI is the equitable owner of 12 parcels totaling 496 acres. The residents' group says the extra land includes farmland and residentially zoned parcels. Residents have said they felt "blindsided" by the switch from warehouses to data centers. More than 100 people turned out for a special supervisors' meeting in early July 2026, and neighbors including the Milton Hershey School Trust raised water, the electric grid, noise, light and pollution. "While we understand the township has to provide for data centers," said Joe McMullan, director of real estate for the Milton Hershey School and its trusts, "we want to make sure the community understands the devil's in the details". Protect South Hanover says a June 8 noise study HCI submitted modeled a layout of eight data center buildings across the draft overlay area, including residential parcels, though that plan has not been filed as an application. Hummelstown Borough, which borders the site, says it is ready to support the township in defeating HCI's requests before the Zoning Hearing Board and has reserved the right to intervene. Nearby East Hanover Township scheduled a hearing and vote on August 18, 2026 on its own zoning rules for data centers and battery storage. South Hanover's supervisors are writing their own rules. In early July they voted unanimously to advertise an ordinance creating a data center overlay district, with data centers allowed only as a conditional use, kept at least 400 feet from residentially zoned property, capped at 55 feet tall, and required to submit sound reports and prove sufficient water. "Good zoning is proactive, not reactive," Supervisor Kevin Busher said. Residents asked for larger setbacks, lower heights and the removal of non-industrial parcels from the overlay. The South Hanover Township Zoning Hearing Board rules on HCI's special exception and validity challenge, and the five-member Board of Supervisors decides the ordinance after a public hearing.

ft-462.text: Jessup's zoning hearing board has rejected the Breaker Street Associates LLC data center campus in Jessup Borough, Lackawanna County, Pennsylvania, because the project's planned substation sat on residentially zoned land north of Breaker Street. The West Conshohocken company had applied in June 2025 to build six data center buildings, nearly 1.1 million square feet, on 131 acres south of Breaker Street, drawing 600 megawatts of power. Jessup's zoning officer denied the application on June 25, 2025, the company appealed, and the five-member zoning hearing board voted unanimously against it on December 23, 2025, issuing its written decision in January 2026. The board held that the substation was not a public utility facility under Pennsylvania law because the proposed use was not "to or for the public for compensation." Borough council has since adopted an ordinance creating an energy and information technology overlay district that confines future data centers to industrial land near the Valley View Business Park and the Lackawanna Energy Center gas plant, makes them conditional uses needing a public hearing, and caps their height at 50 feet. "We wanted to make sure that it was as thorough as possible," council member Curt Camoni said. Applications filed before the vote, including this one, are grandfathered under the old zoning. The project was one of at least six data centers proposed in Lackawanna County, with three in Archbald, one in Blakely and a large campus in Clifton and Covington townships. The developer's option after the board's decision was to appeal to county court, and no appeal filing has been reported since.

ft-463.text: Catalyst Commercial Development LLC, a West Conshohocken developer, has filed plans for a 487,000-square-foot data center on 48 acres at Sunnyside Road and Alberigi Drive in Jessup Borough, Lackawanna County, Pennsylvania, directly next to Invenergy's Lackawanna Energy Center gas-fired power plant. The August 2025 land development application, filed by an affiliate called Sunnyside Road Associates, projects construction starting September 1, 2026 and finishing a year later. The site already had approvals for a 334,800-square-foot warehouse, and the data center, under 50 feet tall, would take a similar footprint. Catalyst bought the 48.3 acres from Pompey Coal Company in 2024 for $3.4 million; Pompey had earlier sold the neighboring land for the 1,500-megawatt power plant. Catalyst's larger Jessup plan has already failed. Its affiliate Breaker Street Associates sought six 130-foot data centers totaling nearly 1.1 million square feet on 131 acres off Breaker Street, and in December 2025 the Jessup Zoning Hearing Board unanimously refused the zoning relief it needed for a switchyard and substation on residential land. That developer can appeal to county court. The Sunnyside Road site is where Jessup now wants data centers to go. In August 2025 the Borough Council unanimously created an overlay district that limits future data centers to industrial land south of the Casey Highway, including the land around the Lackawanna Energy Center, and makes them conditional uses that need a public hearing. The rules cap buildings at 50 feet, require proof from utilities that they can serve a data center without cutting service to residents, keep diesel generators at least 500 feet from homes and require noise studies. "It's not like we don't want one, we just want it in the industrial park where it belongs," Councilman Gregg Betti said. The Midvalley is crowded with proposals: in Archbald, the Wildcat Ridge campus would cover nearly 400 mountainside acres, and Project Gravity and the Archbald Data & Energy Center are also planned, while another large campus is proposed along Interstate 380 in Clifton and Covington townships. The Sunnyside Road application is dated August 13, 2025, six days before the council adopted the overlay rules on August 19. Applications received before that vote are grandfathered under the borough's 2020 zoning, which allowed data centers as principally permitted uses in light industrial zones. Catalyst could not be reached for comment in January 2026.

ft-1770305022079-6376.text: Mele Brothers Realty, based in Montgomery County, plans a data center campus along Route 903 and Maury Road in Penn Forest Township, Carbon County, Pennsylvania, where homes rely on private wells and there is no public water supply. Records obtained by the Times News show the company paid more than $2 million for properties around Maury Road. "One way or the other, we're going to pursue a data center development on this site, whether it's through this ordinance or through the validity challenge," attorney Matthew McHugh told the township in January 2026. Mele's challenge argued the township's zoning was unconstitutional because it excluded data centers entirely. The township answered on March 2, 2026 when supervisors unanimously adopted a curative amendment creating a data center overlay on about 500 acres, including Mele's land. "We determined that it is simply the least worst option," vice chairman Christian Bartulovich said, since the township's own industrial zone covers only about 50 acres next to state game lands. The ordinance sets a 30-acre minimum lot size, a 60-foot height cap, setback and buffer rules, noise standards, an emergency response plan, water and power feasibility studies with well testing, a 50 percent cap on clearing woodland, a decommissioning plan, and a public website giving 24 hours' notice before backup generators run. "We've written an ordinance that is as expansive as is legally possible to write," Bartulovich said. Residents who spoke mostly backed the rules while opposing any data center outright. Jacob Peterzak of Mayer's Well Drilling said, "There is not enough groundwater in this area to provide for a data center." Linda Christman, president of Save Carbon County, said the opposition "is not going anywhere" and cited two federally protected bat species and a wildflower on the site. Resident Ashleigh Davis questioned the water rule: "How are we going to determine where the aquifer spanned to?" No application to build a data center has been filed. A separate challenge to the new overlay itself, filed by resident William John Fontaine, went before the township's zoning hearing board on August 19, 2026. The board put off ruling on who could join the case and continued the hearing to September 1, 2026, and no report of that hearing has been published.

ft-1763416338551-2868.text: About 40 residents of southern Venango County filled a courthouse annex meeting room in Kennerdell, Pennsylvania on June 16, 2026 to ask questions about a data center that Keel Infrastructure, formerly known as Bitfarms, is considering at its Scrubgrass power plant site in Scrubgrass Township. Keel stopped mining cryptocurrency at Scrubgrass on June 29, 2026, though the plant still earns money selling electricity, and as of the meeting the county planning department had not received any application or plans for a data center there, so its size and layout are not yet public. In its August 2026 second-quarter results, Keel named a 110 megawatt data center in Sharon and a 350 megawatt campus at Panther Creek as its Pennsylvania priorities; Scrubgrass was not among them. Venango County Commissioner Tim Heffernan told the meeting there is "an incredible amount of speculation on data centers right now" and put the odds of the Scrubgrass project actually being built at less than 20 percent. Commissioner Ken Bryan said the county is "not for or against the data center" and is weighing power costs, environmental impact, water use and noise. Resident Scott Gearhart asked: "Who knew about it? Why here? What is the impact going to be on area residents and the environment? How far along are the plans?" Sandra McStraw said she doubted the jobs benefit: "The data center would only generate a few jobs for technicians." Rockland lawyer Mallory Piercy told the commissioners: "We are concerned not hearing from you that you are against it, as we are."

ft-1784071829364-1788.text: PA Data Center Partners filed plans on July 10, 2026, for a data center off Loop Road in Granville Township, Mifflin County, Pennsylvania, two days before township supervisors had planned to invoke a curative amendment process aimed at such developments. The Cumberland County firm, through its subsidiary Lewistown Development LLC, proposes six buildings totaling 1.54 million square feet on about 245.5 acres between the Mifflin County Industrial Park and homes along the Juniata River, and has promised $22.5 million in tax revenue to the county, school district and township. About 100 people came to an emergency supervisors meeting that Sunday, and several speakers urged Granville to become the first Pennsylvania municipality to take a stand against large-scale data center development. "It takes just one voice, one person, one municipality to stand up for the people," said Tony Dastra, the Green Party candidate for governor. Resident Nate Fisher alleged "backhanded deals," and Cori Hockenberry asked the township solicitor, Fred Lighty, about what she called a "gentleman's agreement" for the developer to wait until a new data-center ordinance was adopted; Lighty said he assumed the developer saw something in the draft it did not like. Supervisors dropped plans to invoke the curative amendment on Lighty's advice, since the ordinance the township was writing would not apply to an application already filed. The township then adopted a zoning amendment defining data centers for the first time, and less than 24 hours later its zoning officer returned the application as incomplete because it lacked a traffic study certification. A town hall with the developers was canceled. On August 13 the developer appealed, arguing the plan should be judged under the old ordinance, and said it would also challenge the amended ordinance in the Mifflin County Court of Common Pleas. The Granville Township Zoning Hearing Board will hear the developer's appeal at 7 p.m. on October 1, 2026, at the township building on Helen Street.

ft-1782834056806-8487.text: Liberty Energy, developer Imperial Land Corporation and gas producer Range Resources announced an alliance in April 2025 to build a natural gas power plant at the Fort Cherry Development District, an industrial park in Robinson Township near McDonald, Washington County, Pennsylvania. The plant would burn Marcellus Shale gas to supply data centers and other large energy users at the park, but the companies have not disclosed its capacity or timeline, and no data center has been proposed for the site itself. Range Resources' Alan Engberg said the site sits close to the Ohio River, the city of Pittsburgh and a newly renovated airport. Imperial Land says the park, off the Southern Beltway and PA-576, could eventually hold about 6 million square feet of industrial and flex space, with three pad-ready sites built in its first phase. U.S. Sen. Dave McCormick visited the park in May 2026 with Washington County Commission Chairman Nick Sherman to promote a federal energy bill, and called critics of data centers "naysayers." No data center tenant, capacity or construction timeline for the plant has been announced since.

ft-467.text: Ardent Data Centers, part of Germany's Northern Data Group, opened a 41,000-square-foot AI data center at 615 McMichael Road in McKees Rocks, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, with a ribbon cutting in June 2025. The company bought the 1980s building and its 7.5-acre site for $7.12 million in January 2024 and retrofitted it for computing use. It opened with 5 megawatts of power, with plans to reach 20 megawatts in phases. The retrofit uses liquid cooling piped straight to the computer chips, letting racks draw more than 135 kilowatts each, far more power than an older data center could handle. "In today's market, it's about speed and delivery," said Northern Data vice president Wayne Ginders, of the choice to redo an existing building rather than build new. Data centers are now contested across Allegheny County. Allegheny County Council introduced a ban on hyperscale data centers on county-owned land in August 2026 and passed it unanimously in September; it does not affect Ardent's existing private site. Public land "should be for all of us to enjoy, not just for large corporations to speculate off of," said co-sponsor Dan Grzybek. County Executive Sara Innamorato said she supported protecting public land and would sign the bill, while asking council to clarify its definitions and scope. At least 13 new data centers have been planned across western Pennsylvania, including in Springdale and Stowe in Allegheny County, where a divided Springdale Borough voted for a contentious project. Zoning for private land like the McMichael Road site is set by each municipality, not the county, so any expansion here would go to local officials. Grzybek said residents who want to keep data centers out should tell their municipal officials to update the zoning code.

ft-1771604056602-1877.text: Big Digital Energy runs a data center in Midland, Beaver County, Pennsylvania, built by its predecessor Mawson Infrastructure Group beside Allegheny Technologies' idled steel melt shop. Mawson renamed itself Big Digital Energy in April 2026, and a March 2023 lease amendment brought the site to 120 megawatts of power. Mawson leased 6 acres on the west side of the idled ATI melt shop in September 2021, paying $1.2 million a year with renewal options for up to 15 years. "It's 100% nuclear powered; we don't want to put any emissions into the air," said chief operating officer Liam Wilson, who signed a five-year power purchase agreement with Energy Harbor, then owner of the nearby Beaver Valley nuclear plant. The company planned to offer its power to the PJM grid as a balancing resource, and Wilson said Big Digital chose Midland for the power nearby, the cool climate and the borough's welcome. In May 2026 Big Digital signed a deal with an affiliate of the Endeavor Group to run about 25,000 mining computers on roughly 75 megawatts across its sites, ending a legal dispute that began in January when Mawson sued Endeavor Blockchain in Delaware federal court over a change-of-control plan it alleged. By April the two sides had agreed on a reconstituted board, with Endeavor's Joshua Kilgore as executive chairman and Phil Stanley as chief executive. Big Digital's latest annual filing put its total data center capacity across all sites at about 129 megawatts, with 24 more under development.

ft-468.text: Amazon wants to put 280 gas fired generators on a site in Bucks County that already has 76 diesel ones, and add three more diesel on top. The complex, up to 10 new one- and two-story buildings plus 1 million square feet of retrofitted warehouse space, is more than half built at the Keystone Trade Center in Falls Township, the site of a former U.S. Steel mill. It is one of two initial Amazon sites in Pennsylvania, with the other beside the Susquehanna nuclear plant in Luzerne County, under the company's plan to invest at least $20 billion in the state. The Department of Environmental Protection intends to approve the generator application, with a 30 day comment period expected to open in the Pennsylvania Bulletin on July 18, 2026. Amazon has agreed to hold annual emissions of volatile organic compounds and nitrogen oxides below 25 tons a year, which keeps the plant a synthetic minor source. Jillian Gallagher, the department's air quality environmental program manager, said: "The annual emissions from Amazon are projected to be similar to the various hospitals, universities and snack food manufacturing facilities that we already have in Pennsylvania." Seema Kazmi, who lives nearby, did not find that reassuring: "This is already a pollution-stressed area, and this is going to add to it." Residents raised their concerns at a meeting at Pennsbury East High School. Bob Campbell, an engineer with Pennoni Associates, described the request as an amount of water equivalent to that used by about 70 homes, drawn from the Delaware River rather than the drinking supply. Glen Murphy, PECO's senior manager for economic development, was careful about it: "When it comes to this particular project, we think it's going to be a net benefit to customers, when you look at transmission and distribution together. We think that ... it's going to bring down rates a bit."

ft-1785380999931-4842.text: Slate Belt Holdings, a joint venture between Talen Energy and River Pointe Logistics, proposes 23 data center buildings of 201,500 square feet each, with five substations and stormwater areas, on 753 acres between River Road and Potomac Street in Upper Mount Bethel Township, Northampton County, Pennsylvania. The campus has a goal of two gigawatts of capacity; Slate Belt bought the land, previously earmarked for an industrial project, from River Pointe earlier in 2026. In July 2026 Slate Belt Holdings filed a zoning validity challenge arguing the township's ordinance unlawfully excludes data center uses; the developers have said they would drop the challenge if a memorandum of understanding with the township is approved. That memorandum would pay the township $50 million if the campus reaches two gigawatts, under a community benefits agreement; the township's supervisors have been revising the draft, with versions dated August 10, 18 and 25, 2026. Board chairman John Bermingham has said more changes are coming before the memorandum is shown publicly and put to a vote; the developers launched a website, slatebelttechcampus.com, saying the project "is intended to bring significant private investment to an existing industrial park while setting clear, responsible standards for data center development."

ft-1781016607653-3665.text: Two neighbors have gone to court over the Muncy Data Center, a three-building data center complex proposed by the Williamsport developer Danko Holdings II LP and Fishlips LLC off John Brady Drive near the West Branch of the Susquehanna River in Muncy Township, Lycoming County, Pennsylvania. In September 2026 Rae-Ellah B. and Sean S. Tetreault, whose land adjoins the site, filed a land use appeal in the Lycoming County Court of Common Pleas asking a judge to overturn the project's "deemed approval." The developer filed a conditional use application on April 28, 2026, hours before township supervisors voted for a moratorium of up to nine months on data center applications. The plan shows three data center buildings, six water tanks, two stormwater basins, water and sewage treatment facilities, a substation and a security building, between private homes to the northwest and southeast. Both companies are owned by The Liberty Group, headed by Daniel Klingerman. At the April 28 meeting, Fire Chief Scott Oldweiler asked whether any application had come in, and Chairman Terri Lauchle said no; the Sun-Gazette later reported that a zoning permit application dated April 15 was already at the township office. Under Pennsylvania's Municipalities Planning Code, the township had 60 days to hold a hearing on the application or get an extension, and it did neither. In July the developer published a legal notice claiming the application was therefore deemed approved. The township's solicitor, Joseph Orso III, called the developer's filings "inconsistent" and said: "we can't ban data centers. We have to allow them somewhere." The Tetreaults say the data center would threaten their property values, safety and quiet with unmitigated industrial noise, very heavy loads on the power grid and large amounts of cooling water. They argue the township failed to hold the required hearings, and that the developer's proposed curative zoning amendment amounts to spot zoning with too few protections, including on noise. They ask the court to set aside the approval or send it back to the supervisors for full public hearings with strict conditions on noise, setbacks and water use. The developer is contesting the appeal, which is before Judge William P. Carlucci. Meanwhile the township is writing its own rules. The supervisors declared the zoning ordinance invalid on July 8, starting a curative amendment process under which the Muncy Township Planning Commission and the Lycoming County Planning Commission review the change, a public hearing follows, and the supervisors plan to adopt it on December 9; the process must be finished by January 4, 2027. If the project goes to a conditional use hearing instead, the Muncy Township Board of Supervisors can approve it with conditions, Orso said.

ft-1763416659575-1529.text: Keel Infrastructure, formerly known as Bitfarms, is waiting on state water permits for Carbon Node East, a 350 megawatt data center it wants to build next to its Panther Creek power plant in Nesquehoning, Carbon County, Pennsylvania. The Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection held a public meeting and hearing on the project on August 20, 2026, at Panther Valley High School, and is taking written comments on the permits through September 4, 2026. If the permits are granted, Keel expects construction on the four-building campus to start sometime in 2027 and take up to 20 months, using about 400 workers. Keel says the finished data center would employ 297 people full time, in jobs including security, janitorial, administrative, manufacturing and operator roles, with no plan to cut that number over time; the company has also said construction alone would cost $7.5 billion before computers are installed. Keel promises a closed-loop cooling system, but holds a permit to discharge 18,600 gallons a day from equipment condensation and would draw about 7,500 gallons a day from the public water system for employees; filling the cooling loop the first time would take 700,000 gallons bought from the borough, or trucked in if that would hurt the residential supply. The group Save Carbon County calls the discharge permit a "bait-and-switch" by a company that promised a data center that would not consume water, and says the project threatens Nesquehoning Creek and the Lehigh River. Nesquehoning's zoning board granted a special exception for the project in February 2026, the Carbon County Planning Commission recommended conditional rejection in April because the plan did not yet meet borough ordinances, and the borough planning commission voted for conditional preliminary approval in May, giving Keel a list of items to answer. Borough council voted 5-0 in June 2026 to approve the project's sewage facilities plan, projecting 18,662 gallons a day of wastewater to the borough treatment plant. Keel has said it will pay for the PPL power infrastructure the site needs and repair any roads damaged during construction, and that noise from the running campus will stay within the borough's 65 decibel daytime limit and 55 decibel evening limit. Nesquehoning Borough Council must give clean preliminary plan approval before Keel can begin site work, and the state must still decide the stormwater and stream encroachment permits after its September 4, 2026 comment deadline.

ft-1784230337213-5766.text: Stonebridge Associates' plan for a 16-building data center campus at the former Powder Mill Works near New Castle, in Lawrence County, Pennsylvania, lost two zoning appeals in September 2026. The Mahoning Township Zoning Hearing Board voted 2 to 0 on September 15 to reject the appeal from Stonebridge, of Bethesda, Maryland, and its affiliate S.S. Penn LLC, days after the North Beaver Township board unanimously denied its appeal there. The site is 569 acres at 3478 Howard Drive and McClelland Road, next to and surrounding the Hickory Run Energy power plant; about 85 percent of the land is in North Beaver, and half of the 16 buildings would be in Mahoning. The land once held an American Cyanamid plant that made explosives, including dynamite, until 1972. Stonebridge says it would spend more than $15 billion over up to six years, with power from Penn Power, and has not disclosed the campus's computing capacity. "We don't have a customer yet. But it's Meta, it's Oracle, it's Amazon, AWS," Stonebridge's Doug Firstenberg told about 150 people at a meeting in New Castle in July, promising 3,000 construction jobs, 400 permanent ones, water bought from Aqua rather than drawn from wells, and noise of 55 decibels at the property line. Residents were not persuaded. "It's a significant health risk to our children. It sucks up resources," said Torry Argiro of Mahoning Township, who handed Firstenberg a lawsuit demanding evidence and design plans. "There's no research that's backed anything he said, and everything that we've researched says the opposite," said Jessica Main of North Beaver Township. "So we don't want this in our community." The legal fight turns on timing. Mahoning's zoning office rejected Stonebridge's June 2 and June 9 applications as incomplete, over a wrong fee check and a missing $3,000 escrow deposit, and accepted one only on June 15, after the supervisors had tightened their April data center ordinance to make data centers a conditional use. Stonebridge argues it should be held to the original rules, while township solicitor Lou Perrotta says that once a proposed ordinance has been reviewed by a planning commission and properly advertised, developers must follow it, a principle known as the pending-ordinance doctrine. The company has 30 days to take the Mahoning decision to the Lawrence County Court of Common Pleas, and Perrotta indicated it plans to. It has also appealed to the state Commonwealth Court after Common Pleas Judge Bradley G. Olson Jr. dismissed its lawsuit against the townships in July.

ft-470.text: KRNL Data Centers, based in New York City, has bought an 89-acre wooded tract in New Castle Twp, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, for $600,000, land that had been owned by Mount Laurel Enterprises of Mahanoy City. The site sits behind the Schuylkill Technology Center North Campus and Broad Mountain, between Interstate 81 and the Laurel Street homes of neighboring Frackville. In May 2026, New Castle Township rezoned the land so a data center could be built there as a conditional use requiring a hearing before the township's supervisors, though no formal application has been filed and no megawatt figure or tenant has been published. The 89-acre parcel is wedged between the Walnick Manor section of Butler Township to the north, Interstate 81 to the south, a PPL Electric Utilities high-voltage line to the west and the Schuylkill Technology Center North Campus to the east; plans obtained by Coal Region Canary in 2025 showed four long buildings and a substation on the site. The people who would live closest to the site are not New Castle residents. Frackville's council voted unanimously in September 2025 to oppose the project, and West Mahanoy Township's supervisors wrote that they worried about the electricity and water use, round-the-clock fan noise from cooling and the loss of trees that buffer Interstate 81 noise. Frackville residents argue that New Castle Township and the Saint Clair Area School District would get the tax revenue while Frackville absorbs the losses. "These developers are from New York City and they have no ties to our people," Ryan Twardzik, who leads the Frackville-area residents, said. "What they see is relatively cheap land next to a substation, and they do not care what's around it." On May 5, 2026, before a standing-room crowd, New Castle's supervisors voted 2-0, with one abstaining, to create the Highway Industrial district along Interstate 81 near Frackville, replacing Conservation zoning on the KRNL parcel and requiring a hearing before the supervisors for any data center there. The rules require 200-foot setbacks, environmental studies before approval, and limits on woodland clearing and lighting. "You make this decision, you don't live beside it," Bobbie Cicioni told the supervisors. "Imagine if you did." "Frackville will not be Frackville anymore if that build this data center," Bernie Karpovich said. "I will be facing this data center every time I look out the window or sit on my front porch." Solicitor James Conville said the township had to act: "If we don't do something and we don't do it very quickly, they come in with no restrictions." KRNL is one of several data center prospects in the area; State Sen. David Argall has counted nine potential sites in his district, which includes Schuylkill County. If KRNL files a formal application, the New Castle Township Board of Supervisors will hold the conditional use hearing and decide; many of the people who packed the May meeting live in Frackville and Butler Township, where the effects would fall, not in New Castle, which decides.
