ft-471.text: TECfusions is building a data center campus at the former Alcoa Technical Center in Upper Burrell, a Westmoreland County township of about 2,000 people. The Florida company closed on the roughly 1,400-acre site on December 2, 2024 and says it could eventually add up to 3,000 megawatts of computing power over as long as 20 years. Its first tenant, the AI cloud company TensorWave, has moved into Building J with about 10 megawatts running today, supporting more than 100 skilled trade jobs. Upper Burrell passed a 180-day moratorium on new data center approvals in May 2026, running through November 11, 2026, after residents raised concerns about noise, water and unanswered questions on the plan's scale. The moratorium does not cover work already permitted for TECfusions; on August 5, while it was still in effect, supervisors approved a land development plan letting the company upgrade electrical and mechanical systems at Building J. A July 1 environmental study projected an on-site gas power plant would emit 15.6 million tons of greenhouse gases a year. Resident Sue Baxter told the township, "It's been three months, and they still have nothing to show." Township chairman Ross Walker said, "We don't have answers because (TECFusions doesn't) have answers. We can't read their minds." Founder Simon Tusha has said the company wants to feed power "back to the grid, if they need it in the community." Protect PT and residents Guy Fuller and Allen Uhler filed a land use appeal in Westmoreland County Court of Common Pleas, arguing supervisors should have sent TECfusions to the zoning hearing board before approving its building plan. Separately, TECfusions is asking Commonwealth Court to seal a $250,000 proposal it submitted to Pennsylvania's economic development office, arguing it contains trade secrets. Upper Burrell's moratorium runs through November 11, 2026, and the township's data center ordinance was still moving through review in mid-September.

The Florida company closed on the roughly 1,400-acre site on December 2, 2024 and says it could eventually add up to 3,000 megawatts of computing power over as long as 20 years. Its first tenant, the AI cloud company TensorWave, has moved into Building J with about 10 megawatts running today, supporting more than 100 skilled trade jobs.

Upper Burrell passed a 180-day moratorium on new data center approvals in May 2026, running through November 11, 2026, after residents raised concerns about noise, water and unanswered questions on the plan's scale. The moratorium does not cover work already permitted for TECfusions; on August 5, while it was still in effect, supervisors approved a land development plan letting the company upgrade electrical and mechanical systems at Building J. A July 1 environmental study projected an on-site gas power plant would emit 15.6 million tons of greenhouse gases a year.

Resident Sue Baxter told the township, "It's been three months, and they still have nothing to show." Township chairman Ross Walker said, "We don't have answers because (TECFusions doesn't) have answers. We can't read their minds." Founder Simon Tusha has said the company wants to feed power "back to the grid, if they need it in the community."

Protect PT and residents Guy Fuller and Allen Uhler filed a land use appeal in Westmoreland County Court of Common Pleas, arguing supervisors should have sent TECfusions to the zoning hearing board before approving its building plan. Separately, TECfusions is asking Commonwealth Court to seal a $250,000 proposal it submitted to Pennsylvania's economic development office, arguing it contains trade secrets.
Upper Burrell's moratorium runs through November 11, 2026, and the township's data center ordinance was still moving through review in mid-September.

ft-1763989849342-6605.text: TierPoint's Valley Forge data center is an operating colocation and cloud facility at 1000 Adams Avenue in Montgomery County, Pennsylvania, with a Norristown mailing address about 25 miles northwest of Philadelphia near I-76. The building totals more than 137,000 square feet, including more than 61,000 square feet of server floor space and more than 24,000 square feet of business continuity workspace. It runs on nine backup generators with at least 48 hours of fuel, and it hosts one of TierPoint's shared cloud pods. TierPoint does not publish the site's total power capacity, and it also runs data centers elsewhere in Pennsylvania, in Philadelphia, the Lehigh Valley, Bethlehem and Allentown. Montgomery County has since tightened its rules for future data center projects: the Montgomery and Chester county planning commissions published a guide recommending towns treat data centers as a conditional use with performance standards and siting requirements. On August 18, 2026, Gov. Josh Shapiro signed an executive order requiring developers to win local approval before the state issues permits for data center projects.

ft-455.text: Developer Brian O'Neill is back before Plymouth Township's Zoning Hearing Board with a second application for a 2 million-square-foot data center in ten existing buildings at the closed Cleveland-Cliffs steel mill, on 66 acres along the Schuylkill River in Plymouth Township, Montgomery County, Pennsylvania. The Plymouth Township data center site at 900 Conshohocken Road is about a mile from downtown Conshohocken, and this is O'Neill's second application for it. The township's planning board unanimously refused to recommend his first plan in fall 2025. At the zoning hearing board on November 17, 2025, O'Neill's attorney Edmund Campbell pulled that application after Cleveland-Cliffs' attorney Heather Fine said he had no standing because no sale had been agreed. “The signed agreement that was transmitted to my colleague at 5:51 p.m. this evening had redline changes. Those have not been accepted by my client,” Fine said. “It is the smallest of small wins, because we're making it harder for something bad to happen to our community,” said resident Nick Liermann. “But we will be back in this room in a few months.” The new application seeks a special exception in the Heavy Industrial district, which requires the zoning board to find the data center meets the ordinance's standards; if granted, it would still have to go through the township's land development process. O'Neill has also filed a challenge to the validity of the zoning ordinance, arguing that it unfairly fails to provide for data centers. He estimates the data center would bring in $420 million in taxes over 20 years and 800 permanent jobs, and says he is in talks with a top-five technology company and would use on-site natural gas generators. The first hearing on the new application, in August 2026, was repeatedly interrupted as residents booed and shouted at O'Neill's attorney and his planning witness, who testified that data centers resemble manufacturing because “Data is a raw material, which is used to manufacture a product. AI is a product.” “They just don't care. They want the money, they want the win at this point,” said Ardis Leukens, who lives about 500 feet from the site. A petition against the data center has more than 4,000 signatures. “The direct impact on our air is my biggest concern,” Genevieve Boland, who helped lead the petition, said in 2025. “At that rate we simply can't build enough power generation to keep up, so prices will continue to rise rapidly,” said Tom Schuster, president of the Pennsylvania chapter of the Sierra Club. O'Neill's five data center sites in neighboring Upper Merion Township were voted down by that township's supervisors in August 2026. In Plymouth the decision belongs to the Zoning Hearing Board, an independent body appointed by the township council. The hearings were set to continue in September 2026; no result has been published.

ft-1768850919550-7994.text: Constellation Energy's proposed data center on New Schuylkill Road and Sanatoga Road near Pottstown, in East Coventry Township, Chester County, Pennsylvania, was withdrawn on February 17, 2026. Constellation Energy Generation pulled its application asking the Board of Supervisors to amend the township's zoning code to allow data centers, and the public hearing set for March 9, 2026 was canceled. Plans for a data center on the site surfaced in November 2025. Constellation had not shared full details of the campus, but its application said each building would be up to 150,000 square feet, on land near the Route 724 highway. In December 2025 the East Coventry Township Planning Commission voted 4-0 to recommend rejecting the zoning change. Planning commission chairman Lawrence Tietjen said the township was under no obligation to change its zoning, because as a member of the Pottstown Metropolitan Regional Planning Commission it does not have to zone for every use, and neighboring Douglass Township already allows data centers. Any new attempt to build a data center on the East Coventry land would need a zoning change from the East Coventry Township Board of Supervisors. Gov. Josh Shapiro's data center executive order also requires developers to obtain all local approvals before the Department of Environmental Protection will review their permits.

ft-1768850376310-8876.text: Project Laurel, a data center campus proposed by MDC 7 LLC on about 191 acres in Limerick Township outside Pottstown, Montgomery County, has been before the township's Board of Supervisors in a conditional use hearing since April 2026, with the next session on October 1, 2026. The application calls for eight two-story data center buildings totaling just under 2.8 million square feet, three substations and 80,000 square feet of support buildings, on seven parcels between the Philadelphia Premium Outlets and the Limerick nuclear plant. The site has reportedly secured 750 megawatts of power from the utility PECO and lies less than a mile from Constellation Energy's Limerick Generating Station. The land has road frontage on Lightcap, Sanatoga, Evergreen and Possum Hollow roads, and the plan would vacate and relocate parts of Sanatoga Road and Possum Hollow Road and move a gas transmission line; the campus would be served by public water and sewer. WFMZ reported the campus would stand 85 feet tall and use at least 750,000 gallons of water every day. On July 7, hours before the supervisors voted on a stricter data center ordinance, MDC 7 filed two more applications for the same land, splitting the project into a first phase of one 300,000-square-foot building on the southwest corner along Evergreen and Sanatoga roads and a second phase of seven buildings, 2.7 million square feet in all. The township's summary puts the first building at about 36 emergency generators and 42 rooftop chillers. Who would run the campus is still not public: at the July hearing, MDC 7's attorney Ed Campbell said several possible end users and development companies were evaluating the site and that the applicant expected to partner with one after winning approval, but he declined to name them. "I'd like to determine if these people that are coming in were good neighbors where they're currently at," Supervisor Patrick Morroney said. The applicant's own witnesses left much unsettled that night: project manager A.J. Magnotta of LaBella Associates said the water, sewer, stormwater and other utility systems were not fully designed, that the relocation of an Energy Transfer gas pipeline was not final, and that he knew of no completed hydrogeological study of the effect on nearby private wells. Project principal Anthony Maras said the 750 megawatt figure came from a 2024 feasibility study that was preliminary and not a guarantee, that he did not believe a fully updated sound study had been done, and that if PECO asked the campus to cut its demand it would curtail operations rather than run its diesel generators. The applicant has not received an updated PECO service letter since 2024. The developer is also preparing a large-load application to Pennsylvania American Water to find out what new pipelines, pumping stations, storage and wastewater capacity would be needed. Neighbors have fought the plan since it surfaced in January, when a Change.org petition against it passed 680 signatures. "Where is the power coming from? Is my electric bill going to go up? I have well water, should I be concerned?" asked Meagan Smolsky, who lives about two miles from the site, at a May protest outside the township building. Smolsky, of the group Prevent Limerick Data Center Development, was denied party status, the legal standing that lets a resident question witnesses in the hearing. In April the township moved every data center hearing from the Spring-Ford Area High School auditorium to the much smaller township building, citing online threats; opponents said the move was meant to limit how many residents could attend. Township Manager Daniel Kerr described threats that politicians should be violently removed from office, and a threat of a Molotov cocktail at the township building; Smolsky's group said it had nothing to do with them. At the August 18 session, which ran more than four hours, the board declined to recognize the developer's expert witness, a landscape architect, after attorneys for the township and the Spring-Ford Area School District questioned her credentials; Patch reported the project would clear some 38 more acres of woodland. State Sen. Katie Muth said residents were still waiting for a credible, qualified expert to assess the risk of putting a data center a few hundred feet from the nuclear plant. The Limerick Township Board of Supervisors decides whether Project Laurel gets its conditional use approval, and the hearing continues October 1, 2026, at 6:30 p.m. at the Limerick Township Building; Connie Lawson chairs the board. As of July, the applicant's team said experts on sound, vibration, air emissions, generators, cooling, fire hazards, emergency planning and traffic would testify later, and no hearing dates have been set for the two phased applications. Even with approval, the project would still face land development hearings and environmental approval from the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection, which Kerr said could take another year before construction begins.

ft-1784918201918-3695.text: A company tied to the Mudiita Group bought 528.6 acres in Ransom Township, Lackawanna County, Pennsylvania in July 2026, planning a data center campus advertised at 750 megawatts of power on more than 930 acres. By late July, the deal appeared in flux: the White Haven man listed on the buyer's incorporation papers, Shatrughan Sinha, told WVIA he no longer owns shares in the company, would not name its shareholders, and said there are no current plans for the land. The Mudiita Group's websites have since been taken down. Mudiita Land Venture LLC paid $2.4 million for the land south of Ransom Road and west of South Keyser Avenue, under a deed dated July 14, 2026, buying it from KF Real Estate LLC. The site sits on Bald Mountain near the Old Forge border, less than half a mile from the Austin Heights neighborhood and about a mile from the Old Forge School District. Sinha said of the data center plan: "Because of the Scranton Material ordinance, they couldn't get it, so [we] decided the other way around." Most of the land is zoned for open space and conservation or agriculture, not the commercial or light-industrial use the Mudiita Infra website had claimed, and Ransom Township's zoning does not allow data centers at all. Township supervisors chairman Dave Bird said in a text that no one from Mudiita had come to the township. Any data center there would need a zoning change from the township board, the same board that rejected a data center rezoning for Scranton Materials LLC's quarry site in January 2026 after residents' objections; that denial is under appeal. Part of the same land also appears in a hydroelectric proposal: on July 7, 2026, Pittston-based Renewable Energy Aggregators Inc. filed federal paperwork for a pumped-storage plant using mine water from the Old Forge Borehole, with its upper reservoir on the Mudiita property. Sinha said he first learned of that project the Friday before his interview and does not know whether the land's previous owner had an agreement with its backers. paragraphs: A company tied to the Mudiita Group bought 528.6 acres in Ransom Township, Lackawanna County, Pennsylvania in July 2026, planning a data center campus advertised at 750 megawatts of power on more than 930 acres. By late July, the deal appeared in flux: the White Haven man listed on the buyer's incorporation papers, Shatrughan Sinha, told WVIA he no longer owns shares in the company, would not name its shareholders, and said there are no current plans for the land. The Mudiita Group's websites have since been taken down.

Mudiita Land Venture LLC paid $2.4 million for the land south of Ransom Road and west of South Keyser Avenue, under a deed dated July 14, 2026, buying it from KF Real Estate LLC. The site sits on Bald Mountain near the Old Forge border, less than half a mile from the Austin Heights neighborhood and about a mile from the Old Forge School District. Sinha said of the data center plan: "Because of the Scranton Material ordinance, they couldn't get it, so [we] decided the other way around."

Most of the land is zoned for open space and conservation or agriculture, not the commercial or light-industrial use the Mudiita Infra website had claimed, and Ransom Township's zoning does not allow data centers at all. Township supervisors chairman Dave Bird said in a text that no one from Mudiita had come to the township. ft-1769139372684-6188.text: Scranton Materials LLC, which runs a stone quarry at 819 Newton Road in Ransom Township, Lackawanna County, Pennsylvania, is fighting in court to overturn the township's January 2026 refusal of a zoning change that would have allowed a six-building data center campus on its 251-acre property. The site borders West Scranton and is zoned S1, an open space and conservation district. The concept plan shown to the township planning commission had six buildings, each 214 by 732 feet and 120 feet tall, stepping up a hillside, with two stormwater ponds of about 10 and 17 acres and retaining walls 50 feet high within 70 feet of the property lines, planning commission chair James Murphy testified. Murphy said the plans referred to cooling towers not shown on the drawings, that an access road ran into Newton Township, and that the ordinance had no analysis of the effect on water, sewage or emergency services. "The ultimate recommendation with the planning commission was that they (supervisors) do not accept this ordinance as written," Murphy said. More than 100 people packed the township garage for the January 20 hearing, many wearing yellow "NO DATA CENTERS" pins, after the municipal building proved too small the week before. Attorney Laura McGarry, representing her mother, Scranton resident Susan Magnotta, argued the company had presented no witnesses and could not authenticate its exhibits: "This is a hearing, nothing's been heard. They haven't presented any evidence," she said. Against the advice of solicitor Kevin Conaboy, Supervisors Robert Wells and Gerald Scott Jr. voted to deny the application, and chairman David Bird voted to let it proceed. "When the solar people came to present their case, they had the environmental study done, they had the hearing study done, they had the glare study done," Wells said. In its appeal to the Lackawanna County Court of Common Pleas, the company's attorney Michael Mey argues the supervisors had no authority to dismiss the application that way and that the township's zoning unlawfully excludes data centers, a use Pennsylvania municipalities must allow somewhere within their borders. The company also argued Magnotta had no standing because she does not live in the township, but in June 2026 Lackawanna County Judge Margaret Bisignani Moyle ruled that she does; she lives less than a mile from the property. Elsewhere in the township, Mudiita Land Venture LLC bought more than 500 acres along Ransom Road, above Waste Management's Alliance Landfill, for $2.4 million in July 2026, and a Mudiita website had advertised a 930-plus-acre all-electric data center campus in Lackawanna County. Sinha Shatrughan, whose name is on Mudiita's incorporation papers, said the Scranton Materials outcome changed its plans: "Personally, I didn't want to go ahead with any sort of data center there right now." Mey has asked the county court to reverse the supervisors and grant zoning relief for data centers on the Scranton Materials land, so the appeal now rests with the Lackawanna County Court of Common Pleas.

ft-1763997352536-7966.text: Omega Systems, a managed IT services company, runs a private data center from its headquarters at 1121 Snyder Road in Reading, Pennsylvania. The site is in Berks County, and it is an existing facility serving Omega's own IT customers, not a new data center project. Directory listings describe biometric access control, video surveillance, redundant fiber internet, N+1 UPS and generator backup, A+B power distribution and Novec fire suppression. No floor area or power capacity has been published for it. The data center fights in this part of Pennsylvania concern much larger buildings. "From Upper Macungie to the Poconos, public resistance to data centers continues to grow," WFMZ reported in June 2026, noting that Upper Macungie Township had turned down an appeal for a large data center, as had East Vincent Township in Chester County. State Sen. Katie Muth, who represents parts of Berks and Montgomery counties, has called for legislation to stop data centers from becoming public utilities, which would give them eminent domain powers. "If eminent domain were to happen, developers could just come in and take land," said Karen Feridun of the Better Path Coalition, a grassroots group tracking data centers. Elsewhere in Berks County, Tilden Township has been writing a data center ordinance and scheduled a special meeting on it for July 28, 2026. For Omega's Snyder Road site nothing is pending; no expansion, rezoning or new power request has been reported as of September 2026.

ft-1782833129282-7913.text: The Champion Data Center Campus is an advertisement, not a project: a land broker, Brian Patten of Next Generation Land Company, is marketing 1,000 acres of industrially zoned brownfield about ten minutes from Pittsburgh International Airport in Pennsylvania to data center developers. His company's business is finding large powered sites and selling them on. Every figure attached to the site is the seller's: on-site natural gas generation of 5 gigawatts, scalable to 16, a 138 kV line on the site, gas pipelines on and near it, and a possible ten-year tax break through a Keystone Opportunity Zone. No buyer, tenant or municipal filing has been reported.

ft-1772660913394-2532.text: Keel Infrastructure, the company formerly known as Bitfarms, is developing a 110MW data center on 18 acres of the former Westinghouse Electric plant on Clark Street in Sharon, Mercer County, Pennsylvania. Sharon City Council approved the final land development plans for Keel's two data centers in July 2026, and the company said in August that transformers had been delivered to the site. Keel acquired the site in October 2025 and has run a 30MW data center there. It stopped bitcoin mining at Sharon on June 29, 2026, as it moves from crypto mining into AI and high-performance computing. WFMJ reported the proposal as a $5 billion data center near the old Westinghouse building, with construction expected to start in October 2026. Two 80MW substations are targeted for completion by the end of 2026, and Keel plans to install Nvidia Vera Rubin hardware. Alex Brammer, Keel's executive vice president of operations, said the closed-loop cooling would use about 1,000 gallons of water a day, and the company said it would pay for the power infrastructure upgrades it needs. Keel's chief operating officer, Liam Wilson, pitched it as fixing an eyesore: "The fact that this piece of land has no future use, the fact that we're fixing up an eyesore, the fact that we're essentially, you know, giving this Brownfield facility another lease on life, I think that's all great". The zoning board approved the plan in April 2026 with conditions, including a 70-decibel noise limit and a ban on using water from the nearby river. Residents at an information meeting worried about noise and utility bills; one told WKBN: "I've heard it causes noise. I have heard it makes your electricity bill go up. I have heard it makes your water bill go up, and it makes a lot of humming noise." A Change.org petition to stop the data center had passed 2,100 signatures by May, and resident Stefanie Blair said opponents planned to take the fight to the state. Sharon cannot ban the project: under Pennsylvania law a municipality cannot outlaw a lawful business, and city solicitor Brett Stedman said zoning can only "limit where they are and to provide adequate controls as to their use within the municipalities". In July council unanimously adopted the Mercer County Regional Planning Commission's land development ordinance for data centers, and the same month approved zoning changes covering water, electricity, noise and lighting for any future data center. Keel's expansion is not bound by those new rules, but City Manager Bob Fiscus said the company agreed to them anyway. "We cant stop the data center but lets make the best of it," Fiscus said. Keel CEO Ben Gagnon said in August that the company's priority sites, including Sharon, were nearing full permitting, with multiple prospective tenants negotiating for capacity. Sharon's broader rewrite of its zoning ordinance, covering water, electricity, noise and lighting standards for any future data center, was still under way in July.

ft-1776914850279-3949.text: The $1.7 billion South Annville data center that Inch & Co. planned off Mount Pleasant Road in South Annville Township, Lebanon County, Pennsylvania, was withdrawn on May 12, 2026, after a grass-roots campaign against it. The developer's lawyer wrote to township supervisors that "the Petitioner has decided to no longer pursue the development of a data center in South Annville Township." The township is now writing a zoning ordinance to regulate any future data center. The petition came from 1235 Martina Drive Owner LLC, a joint venture between the York-based developer Inch & Co. and Eastern Land & Resources Co., owner of the site. It sought about 58 acres of new industrial zoning across four parcels totaling about 99 acres, on the western side of Mount Pleasant Road near U.S. Route 422, just west of Annville Borough. The plan was for five buildings of about 150,000 square feet each, with fans, chillers and generators on the roofs. Inch told Lebanon County Commissioners the campus would be built in three phases from 2027 to 2029 and would bring more than $17 million a year in taxes, and its handout told residents they would face regional electricity rate pressure whether or not the data center was built in their township. Opposition grew from the first Planning Commission presentation on April 7. Organizer Michael Schroeder said more than 500 people signed a petition, which he put at over one-third of the township's adults. At the Planning Commission, members addressed electricity, water, noise, infrasound and property values, Schroeder said. On May 5 the Planning Commission voted 6-0 to recommend that supervisors deny the rezoning, and a week later the developer withdrew. "The developers were able to see the tremendous popular opposition to this proposed data center," Schroeder said. Lebanon County Commissioner Jo Ellen Litz, who spoke of protecting bald eagles near the site, said: "I just think a whole community is exhaling." Neighboring North Annville Township adopted a data center ordinance on September 14, 2026, allowing data centers only by conditional use in its manufacturing district near the railroad and Route 422, with a 50-foot height limit and a 100-acre minimum lot. Its solicitor said the ordinance resembles those in North Lebanon, Union and Jackson townships, and that "it's unconstitutional to exclude a certain use from your municipality." The township Board of Supervisors, which had the final say on the rezoning, is also the body that will adopt the new ordinance. Its members are chairman Dale Hoover, vice chairman John Harrell and second vice chairman Garry Rhine. In August Hoover said the draft would go to the Lebanon County Planning Department and the township Planning Commission before the supervisors' September meeting, followed by a public hearing. "We're trying to discourage anything we possibly can, but we can't downright outlaw it in our township," Hoover said. Supervisors meet on the second Wednesday of each month.

sentences.t: The $1.7 billion South Annville data center that Inch & Co. planned off Mount Pleasant Road in South Annville Township, Lebanon County, Pennsylvania, was withdrawn on May 12, 2026, after a grass-roots campaign against it.
The developer's lawyer wrote to township supervisors that "the Petitioner has decided to no longer pursue the development of a data center in South Annville Township."
The township is now writing a zoning ordinance to regulate any future data center.
The petition came from 1235 Martina Drive Owner LLC, a joint venture between the York-based developer Inch & Co. and Eastern Land & Resources Co., owner of the site.
It sought about 58 acres of new industrial zoning across four parcels totaling about 99 acres, on the western side of Mount Pleasant Road near U.S. Route 422, just west of Annville Borough.
The plan was for five buildings of about 150,000 square feet each, with fans, chillers and generators on the roofs.

Inch told Lebanon County Commissioners the campus would be built in three phases from 2027 to 2029 and would bring more than $17 million a year in taxes, and its handout told residents they would face regional electricity rate pressure whether or not the data center was built in their township.
Opposition grew from the first Planning Commission presentation on April 7.
Organizer Michael Schroeder said more than 500 people signed a petition, which he put at over one-third of the township's adults.
At the Planning Commission, members addressed electricity, water, noise, infrasound and property values, Schroeder said.
On May 5 the Planning Commission voted 6-0 to recommend that supervisors deny the rezoning, and a week later the developer withdrew.
"The developers were able to see the tremendous popular opposition to this proposed data center," Schroeder said.
Lebanon County Commissioner Jo Ellen Litz, who spoke of protecting bald eagles near the site, said: "I just think a whole community is exhaling."

ft-1762807694034-3914.text: No buyer has come forward for Zediker Station, the roughly 1,400-acre tract off Zediker Station Road in South Strabane Township, Washington County, that CNX Resources owns and the real estate firm JLL has marketed as a site for a large AI data center. But the prospect alone rewrote the township's rules: in June 2026 the South Strabane Board of Supervisors voted unanimously to adopt a data center zoning ordinance and an updated noise ordinance, after more than six months of public outcry. CNX, a natural gas company based in Washington County, teamed up with Chicago-based JLL in October 2025 to market and lease the site, about 20 miles south of Pittsburgh. The pitch offered 400 buildable acres, natural gas reserves, plenty of water, and methane captured from coal mine ventilation, which the companies say can blend with natural gas for carbon-neutral power. The land is zoned for industrial use and has two rail lines; it had been marketed before for manufacturing and mixed-use projects that never went ahead. A JLL brochure showed layouts with more than 40 buildings. Washington County Commissioners chair Nick Sherman welcomed the listing, saying in a news release that the property "is primed for development and represents significant economic opportunity for our community." Residents did not welcome the pitch. At a packed supervisors' meeting in December 2025, Diane Ecker warned that "these data centers emit decibels that range from 75 to 96 decibels, when 85 decibels can cause hearing damage." Dan Adamski of JLL answered that the noise would be "much lower" than other permitted uses of the land: "At the property line, you won't even know it's there." Township solicitor Dennis Makel warned that an outright ban would not survive in court: "Whatever we do must be legal. You cannot say, 'We can't have data centers in this township,'" he said. At a planning commission meeting in February, Kristin Prezel objected that a revised draft had cut the setback from homes from 1,000 feet to 850 feet: "The current data center draft ordinance is insufficient." In April, resident Cynthia Rossi said a data center campus she had visited in Ohio "looked like Armageddon; it was unbelievable." CNX fought parts of the ordinance. In a March 19 letter, its attorney Blaine Lucas of Babst Calland argued that a required community benefit agreement was illegal and that the proposed setbacks would "eliminate most portions of CNX's Zediker Station property from development." Another Babst Calland attorney, Robert Max Junker, called the rules a "death by a thousand cuts" for any developer. At the June hearing Junker asked the board to cut the setback from homes to 1,000 feet and allow neighbors to waive it; the supervisors kept it at 1,500 feet, the same setback the township applies to oil and gas well pads. Makel said that leaves only 651 of the roughly 1,400 acres available for a data center. Chairman George Rowand called the result "right in the middle" between residents who wanted more and the landowner who wanted less. The February draft published by the township made data centers a conditional use in its light and general industrial districts, requiring noise and vibration studies, a water feasibility study for any private water source, and a decommissioning bond. Makel has said other Washington County municipalities, including Amwell Township, are using South Strabane's ordinance as a template. One piece is still unfinished. A third ordinance, regulating fossil fuel power generation such as on-site generators at data centers, was tabled in July after residents asked for changes, and again in August when sections of the draft turned out to be missing. At its September 2026 meeting, the board again declined to act after Rossi pointed out that parts of the text were still missing; Makel said the error was likely an unintended typographic mistake by his staff and took full responsibility. Any data center proposal for Zediker Station would come before the South Strabane Board of Supervisors, whose vice chairman, Jeff Bull, has urged neighboring townships to follow the township's example.

ft-480.text: On December 16, 2025 Springdale borough council, in Allegheny County, voted 5 to 2 to grant Allegheny DC Property Company a conditional use permit for a hyperscale data center on the site of the former Cheswick Generating Station, a coal plant. Jeffrey Hartz, one of the two who voted against it, said: "The way I look at it is, if you have to sue a small community like ours to invade it then you should probably not come." Jason Overly voted yes and gave the other half of the argument: "We're gonna be sued. We can't afford it. We can't afford to put roads in. I'm going to vote 'yes' because of that." The borough manager Terry Carcella put the council's position in law: "Pennsylvania law is clear that upon an applicant demonstrating compliance with a specific criteria expressed in the zoning ordinance, approval of the application is mandatory and not discretionary." The building is 565,000 square feet and about seven stories tall including the rooftop cooling equipment, with a power demand the reporting put at the equivalent of more than 140,000 homes at once. Carole Brennan, who has lived there more than 50 years, was talking about the council members who had not come to the community's town halls: "Their absence spoke loudly and their absence said, 'We really don't care. That's why we're not here.'" Devon McCullough, who works in computer science, asked what happens if the demand is not there: "If all of this development suddenly bottoms out, all of this money being spent, all of the lives that are going to be impacted by this data center won't mean anything if there's no cause for using the data center anymore." James Binnix and Kailyn Wood said they were considering moving away. The concerns raised were health, noise, the promised property tax revenue that nobody could yet count on, and the effect on daily life. The plans have grown since the vote. By August 2026 the Springdale data center, now developed by Dynamo DC, formerly Allegheny DC Property Co., called for a 652,000 square foot building 75 feet tall, with 124 generators and the potential to draw 330 megawatts, the Mon Valley Independent reported. The developer says it has changed the design to reduce noise and improve the site's look with landscaping and steel construction meant to reflect the region's heritage, and it held a public open house in Springdale in June 2026. Opponents have turned to Allegheny County, but its sustainability director, Brittany Prischak, said a county model ordinance would not be legally enforceable and that most of the issues residents raise are handled at the federal, state or municipal level. The borough's permit stands; the project still needs further approvals, and the county says a team is assigned to hold data center developers to their promises.

ft-482.text: LBT Investment Group LLC of Chicago wants to build a $4.8 billion data center on 185 acres along Tomhicken Road in Sugarloaf Township, Luzerne County, Pennsylvania, and has taken the township to court to force its zoning to allow one. The township's zoning did not address data centers, so in 2025 LBT filed what Pennsylvania law calls a curative amendment, a legal request to fix the zoning map, so data centers would be allowed in the I-1 industrial zone that includes its site. The supervisors refused to adopt it, and LBT appealed to Luzerne County Court, where the case is still pending; no data center application has been filed with the township. LBT's May 2025 proposal described six buildings of 200,000 square feet each, 10 acres of electrical substations, 180 jobs paying $80,000 to $150,000 a year, and completion by 2032. LBT has said the project would connect only to existing 230-kilovolt power lines, not the larger 500-kilovolt line PPL has proposed through the valley, and that closed-loop cooling would use about 100,000 gallons per building. "The township does not need to rush into a settlement or adopt a developer-driven ordinance," said resident John Zola after supervisors tabled a joint township-LBT ordinance in February 2026 following a meeting where more than 50 residents objected. "The people making the decisions don't live here. They don't own land here. But it's people like my 85-year-old parents who will be stuck paying these bills and dealing with the environmental destruction, water, air, soil, you name it," said resident Andy Sanko. Attorney Jack Dean, who represents several residents, told the board LBT is not registered to do business in Pennsylvania: "This morning, I filed a motion on behalf of my clients to strike their land use appeal because they are not registered in Pennsylvania." Supervisors Joseph DiSabella Sr., Rick Weaver and Jennifer Pecora are still weighing the joint ordinance while the court case and Dean's motion to strike LBT's appeal are both pending in Luzerne County Court; no date has been set for either decision.

ft-483.text: Management Science Associates runs a data center at 400 MSA Drive in the Rock Pointe Business Park in Tarentum, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, offering data center hosting, colocation and disaster recovery through its Information Technology Systems and Services Division. MSA, a Pittsburgh company, says it has been in business since 1963 and has more than 500 software and technology staff; the listing gives no size, power or opening date for the Tarentum facility. Southwestern Pennsylvania's rush of data center proposals has pushed nearby towns, including East Deer, Oakmont, Tarentum, Upper Burrell, Murrysville and Gilpin, to make moves to shield themselves from the industry, the Mon Valley Independent reported in August 2026. Allegheny County is drafting its own model zoning ordinance for data centers, though county sustainability director Brittany Prischak said it would not be legally binding and each of the county's 130 municipalities could choose whether to adopt it. "At the present, there is a lack of strong regulations around data centers and their energy usage," the county said in a statement, "so it's incumbent upon the county to ensure data center developers are held accountable for their promises to communities."

ft-1763999583583-5345.text: Air Products has dropped its plan for the Cetronia Road Data Center, a 2.6 million square foot campus on its former headquarters site in Upper Macungie Township, Lehigh County, Pennsylvania, after the township zoning hearing board blocked it and the company let its time to appeal run out. The project would have put three buildings on 194 acres along Hamilton Boulevard and Cetronia Road, the largest about 1.23 million square feet. Regional planners found the application thin. "Due to the haste with which the plans were submitted, they did not include essential information that is expected with a hyperscale data center submission," said Lehigh Valley Planning Commission planner Jill Seitz; the review asked Air Products to state the campus's total electrical load, confirm PPL could serve it, and show its water use under drought conditions. Commissioner John Gallagher called it "a 'spaghetti on the wall' proposal here, just thrown together to beat the rules." Air Products asked the zoning hearing board to treat a data center as a use similar to those allowed in the Light Industrial district, which required showing the use would "clearly be less intensive in external impacts and nuisances" than permitted uses. At a standing-room-only hearing in May 2026, the company's attorney arrived an hour late and asked for a third continuance; the board refused and unanimously denied the request. State Sen. Jarrett Coleman told residents, "I don't think Pennsylvania is the right fit, and I certainly don't think the Lehigh Valley is the right fit." The board confirmed the denial in writing in July, and Air Products said in August 2026 it would not appeal: "Air Products has a long history in the Lehigh Valley, and we remain committed to maintaining positive relationships in the communities where we operate." It has not said what it plans to do with the site. Upper Macungie had already taken action on a new data center zoning ordinance before the Air Products filing became public, so any future proposal on the site would need to meet the township's newer rules.

The project would have put three buildings on 194 acres along Hamilton Boulevard and Cetronia Road, the largest about 1.23 million square feet.

Regional planners found the application thin. Commissioner John Gallagher called it "a 'spaghetti on the wall' proposal here, just thrown together to beat the rules."

It has not said what it plans to do with the site. Upper Macungie had already taken action on a new data center zoning ordinance before the Air Products filing became public, so any future proposal on the site would need to meet the township's newer rules.

ft-1787244336673-6262.text: Upper Merion Township's Board of Supervisors on August 13, 2026, turned down developer Brian O'Neill's plan for five data centers totaling more than 4.6 million square feet near King of Prussia, in Montgomery County, Pennsylvania. O'Neill, who heads MLP Ventures, called the proposal the Renaissance Park and Innovation Data Center Campus. He told 6ABC he plans to appeal. The campus would have been built at Discovery Labs, a health care and life sciences office run by O'Neill's company, and was planned to generate its own power with natural gas turbines and diesel backup generators; O'Neill said it would use scrubbers to control emissions and a closed-loop cooling system. He estimated it would bring in $55.4 million a year in local taxes, nearly $38 million of it for the Upper Merion Area School District. The applications were filed before Upper Merion adopted data center restrictions in March 2026, so they were reviewed under the old rules. "The plans that were submitted prior to the ordinance change are vested," Township Manager Tony Hamaday said. Residents fought the plan for months, citing air pollution, water use, noise and property values, and a petition against it drew more than 17,000 signatures. "There is absolutely nothing he could say to make me amenable to multiple power plants being constructed in my own backyard," resident Courtney Smith said in July. O'Neill said then that he was not getting a fair hearing from township staff and planning commission members. In July the planning commission voted not to recommend three of the five projects. The night before the final vote, O'Neill sued the township for an extension; a Montgomery County judge vacated the injunction the next afternoon, and the supervisors then voted down the extensions and the preliminary plans. Chairperson Tina Garzillo said the township had received no landscape, traffic impact, emergency management or sanitary sewer plans: "The data centers at best are speculative and conceptual in nature, as evidenced by the lack of necessary details on the plan." Vice chairperson William Jenaway accused O'Neill of "bullying" the board. "I know it's not over. This is a very important first step," Smith said after the vote. O'Neill is also pursuing a 2 million-square-foot data center at the former Cleveland-Cliffs steel plant in neighboring Plymouth Township, which Gov. Josh Shapiro has publicly criticized. O'Neill can appeal the decision in court or file new or revised plans, which would come back before the Upper Merion Board of Supervisors for review.

ft-1770776013460-3256.text: Montour County commissioners unanimously blocked Talen Energy's plan for an Amazon data center campus near Talen's Montour power plant at Washingtonville, Pennsylvania, on February 10, 2026, refusing to rezone more than 800 acres of farmland from agricultural to industrial. The rezoning was meant to allow Amazon data centers next to Talen's natural gas-fired plant, the same arrangement Talen uses to supply Amazon at its Susquehanna nuclear plant, and it would also have allowed an expansion of the coal- and gas-fired plant to power the data center. Residents learned of the plan in summer 2025 by word of mouth, when neighbors began getting offers for their land at six to seven times market rate, and used right-to-know requests to confirm a data center was the goal. They formed Concerned Citizens of Montour County, and more people signed a petition against the rezoning than voted in the 2024 election; farmer Mike Leighow, whose farm relies on a well, said: "If we can't get water, we can't survive." Commission chair Rebecca Dressler said Talen had not met its burden: "No evidence was provided demonstrating that the benefits outweigh documented and foreseeable public harms." Talen said it still plans a data center in the county: "We remain committed to pursuing a path forward in Montour County," and analysts at Capstone said they expected Talen and Amazon to "either redouble their efforts in Montour County or pursue an alternative brownfield site elsewhere in Pennsylvania." Since the denial, Montour County commissioners have approved a data center amendment to the county zoning ordinance, amending it again after residents objected, and Derry, Limestone and West Hemlock townships adopted a joint data center ordinance in July. Any new Talen or Amazon proposal in Derry Township would go through the township's new ordinance and the county's rules, decided by the Derry Township supervisors and the Montour County Board of Commissioners.

ft-484.text: Comcast runs data centers on its Boot Road campus in West Chester, Chester County, Pennsylvania, a three-building site that also houses engineering departments and back-office operations, the company says. The contractor Hatzel & Buehler, which supports power and cooling work there, says its projects on campus have included backup battery upgrades, elevated flooring built to run cables underneath, switchboards, generators and transformers. In 2024 Comcast installed its own SmartKit AI energy management system across the campus to control heating and cooling and flag unusual energy use. The system turned up higher-than-expected energy use on weekends, and the facilities team adjusted heating and cooling schedules for unoccupied hours, according to Comcast. "Based on what we were able to accomplish in energy reduction during peak demand events, we're looking to scale the energy reduction across the campus on a regular basis for additional cost savings and efficiency," said Billy Osborne, Comcast's director of facilities and workplace.

ft-1763000249590-6997.text: KDI Wyalusing Power LLC, an affiliate of New Fortress Energy working under its Klondike Digital Infrastructure business, is developing a data center on a 335 acre property along Route 6 in Wyalusing Township, Bradford County, Pennsylvania, about 20 miles from Towanda. The data center would run on its own gas-fired power plant, the Wyalusing Energy Center, which received Pennsylvania's air quality approval on October 9, 2025. The state's review memo says the plant "will be used to generate up to 218 megawatts of electricity to power a data center" and will not connect to the electric grid. The plant would have eight natural gas turbines of 31 megawatts each, 248 megawatts of total capacity. When New Fortress filed the application, the data center itself was to be "owned and operated by a third party whom at this time is unknown," and the exact spot on the 335 acres has not been made public. The same land had a 2019 air approval for a liquefied natural gas plant that was never built; that approval expired. The project still needs a water withdrawal approval from the Susquehanna River Basin Commission, the four-state agency that oversees water use from the river, and a Chapter 105 permit, Pennsylvania's approval for work that affects a stream or wetland, for its water intake. It is not clear whether KDI has filed a land development application with Bradford County. Anyone objecting to the air permit had 30 days from its October 25, 2025 notice to appeal to the state's Environmental Hearing Board. Bradford County commissioners unanimously adopted rules for data centers on July 9, 2026, requiring a 200 foot buffer next to homes, closed loop cooling where feasible, proof from a utility that it can supply power, and a decommissioning plan backed by financial security. The rules apply only to future applications. Asylum Township resident Sue Corie told commissioners, "There are so many unknowns about data centers and the potential harm that they can create, that I wish there was some way we could slow them down." Commissioner Daryl Miller said he opposes tax abatements for data centers. Bradford County's planning director has identified possible data center sites in Wysox and Asylum townships as well, though no formal applications have been filed there. The next decisions on the Wyalusing project rest with the Susquehanna River Basin Commission on water and with local zoning review.

ft-486.text: Terra Nexus Ventures, a Charlotte developer, withdrew its request to rezone 162 acres at 771 Park Road near Camden, in Kershaw County, South Carolina, for a data center in the fall of 2025, before the county council could vote on it. A year later, on September 22, 2026, Kershaw County Council unanimously passed a one-year moratorium on data centers, cryptocurrency mining and data processing facilities while it writes rules; the pause runs through September 22, 2027. The data center was to go on vacant land across from the county landfill, about 30 miles northeast of Columbia. The company said it was working with Black River Electric Cooperative and Santee Cooper to secure power, and representatives told planners they would build two warehouses to hold computer servers, employing 10 to 15 people. The rezoning would have moved the land from a rural residential district to general development, which allows a wide range of residential, retail, industrial and commercial uses. The county Planning Commission recommended it unanimously on September 8, 2025. Terra Nexus's founders, Hemal Badiani and Brandon Maxwell, are affiliated with the investment firm Sage Equity. Neighbors spoke against it at the September 2025 council meeting. "There are a lot of factors we don't have any guidelines for in our community," said Lynne Conto, who lives near the site, and another resident raised water use and electricity consumption. Councilman Derek Shoemake warned that if the data center fell through, "now you have 100 acres that can be used for anything." Councilman Brant Tomlinson, whose district includes the site, said he told the developers he opposed it, citing how much water data centers can use. "I'm glad that they withdrew it," Tomlinson said after the withdrawal. "The community concerns are heard." Andrew Yablonski, who lives less than a mile away, said of data centers: "There's no service, there's no product, there's nothing." The developers did not respond to requests to explain why they withdrew. The moratorium passed its first reading on August 25, 2026, its second on September 8 and its third unanimously. "And that'll give us a year to look into things and see where we need to go from there," Councilmember Danny Catoe said. Counties across the Upstate and Midlands are passing similar one-year pauses, and Colleton and Fairfield counties are considering them. Any new data center proposal in the county would now wait for the rules Kershaw County Council writes during the one-year pause. Shoemake has said data centers "may be a good use in the right zoning districts in Kershaw County" if water and the grid can be properly managed.

ft-1775616979269-7668.text: Stream Data Centers has dropped Project Liberty, the $2.4 billion data center that Marion County Council in South Carolina approved in January 2026 before most residents knew what it was. On June 11, 2026 the developer said it would no longer move forward, citing utility timing constraints, and that the funds it had committed to Marion County would still go to the county to benefit families and institutions. The council approved the project at a meeting on January 22, as a rare winter storm bore down on the state, bringing ice and snow that caused hazardous roads, closures and at least two cold-related deaths. ft-1769702647022-9251.text: TigerDC will not build Project Spero, its planned $3 billion data center in the Tyger River Industrial Park in Spartanburg County, South Carolina, after the county council turned against the tax deal the company needed. The New York-based company withdrew on February 27, 2026, two hours before the council voted against offering it a property tax abatement, and said it would pursue other sites. TigerDC, which has run a bitcoin mining facility in Spartanburg County since 2022, announced the project publicly on January 26, 2026: a high-performance computing data center focused on artificial intelligence, with about 50 full-time jobs. Its first phase was to open in 2027 at 100 megawatts, with some power generated on site from natural gas and a closed-loop cooling system. Lockhart Power said the project would not raise its customers' rates. The fight was over the tax break. The fee-in-lieu-of-tax agreement would have cut the company's property tax rate from 10.5 percent to 4 percent for 40 years. Council passed first reading in November 2025, and on February 16, 2026, in front of a crowd that spilled into the hallway and frequently shouted and booed, voted 5 to 2 for second reading. "We're going to be the ones paying for it," resident Allison Herb told the council. Councilman Paul Abbott, who voted no, said: "I think that this is a bad business deal." A petition, "Stop Data Centers Coming to Upstate, SC", gathered more than 1,200 signatures and called for a moratorium on data centers in Spartanburg and Cherokee counties until regulations are in place. In the week after second reading, council chair Manning Lynch and Monier Abusaft, who had both voted yes, said they would vote no, and on February 26 council members held a news conference with state legislators to say they would let the state take the lead on regulating data centers. "We're thrilled with this no vote by our County Council," said Eric Allison, who started the No Data Centers in Spartanburg Facebook page. "Major infrastructure investments require alignment among stakeholders," the company said. "Project Spero recognizes that alignment has not been achieved." The door is not closed. "We're certainly not shutting the door on data centers," Abusaft said, adding: "Hopefully when another project like this comes, we have clear guidelines from the state." South Carolina lawmakers were debating a bill, S.867, that would change how the state regulates data center development. Spartanburg has other proposals, chief among them a $2.8 billion facility proposed by NorthMark Strategies.

ft-490.text: DC Blox, an Atlanta data center company, bought 27.5 acres in the Camp Hall commerce park near Ridgeville, in Berkeley County, South Carolina, from the state-owned utility Santee Cooper in 2023 for $4.7 million to build a proposed data center campus with about 45 megawatts of power. It never broke ground, and within months asked to trade up: an offer of about $17.7 million for a larger 64.5-acre parcel in the park's northwest corner, handing back its original land at no extra cost. The bigger deal needed approval from the General Assembly's Joint Bond Review Committee, a panel of state legislators that must sign off on land sales at Camp Hall, which was expected to review it in March 2024. Santee Cooper's real estate director, Dan Camp, told the utility's board the bigger investment was being driven "by AI," saying, "because of the ... significant increase in demand for data centers, they stepped back and said, 'Is this big enough?'" Berkeley County Supervisor Johnny Cribb welcomed the project, saying Camp Hall "is proving to be a prime location for industrial development and investment in our County." DC Blox's own website no longer lists a Camp Hall campus among its Southeast hyperscale sites, naming only Atlanta East, Atlanta West and Birmingham. The Joint Bond Review Committee's vote on the land swap was scheduled for March 2024, and no result has been published.

ft-1776707659042-4442.text: Volt Edge Energy's Project Alpaca, a proposed 49 megawatt data center campus at the Midway Green Industrial Park in Union, Union County, South Carolina, is on hold after the County Council tabled its tax deal on April 28, 2026. Company representative Ankit Joshi pitched it as a $410 million private investment with more than 500 construction jobs and more than 50 high-wage jobs once running. The company's fact sheet said the campus would use closed-loop cooling with "a specialized coolant mixture" from Texas rather than the local water system, while resident Braeden Jones, who has worked at such facilities, said local water would be used and would give off an odor. "Everybody's concerned about our water, about the noise pollution," said Jones, whose petition gathered hundreds of signatures. At a listening session hosted by the South Carolina Energy Justice Coalition, more than 50 residents raised noise, air and water quality and the rising cost of power. The council tabled the first reading of a fee-in-lieu-of-tax agreement for more time to evaluate the project, and canceled the public hearing set for May 12. "If the opportunity for reintroduction of the project arises, a public information forum will be scheduled and advertised accordingly prior to any advancement of any Fee in Lieu of Tax agreement," the council said.

ft-1767851240920-5564.text: Eagle Rock Partners' proposed Walterboro data center campus would put nine buildings on 859 acres of timberland along Cooks Hill Road, southeast of Walterboro in Colleton County, South Carolina, at the head of the ACE Basin. The $6 billion project would be the state's first gigawatt data center, and Ken Loeber, co-founder of the Charlotte-based firm, estimated it would need 1,000 megawatts of electricity. The ACE Basin, a 350,000-acre estuary named for the Ashepoo, Combahee and Edisto rivers, is home to nine federally endangered species, including wood storks and leatherback turtles. "To the extent that they use any water at all it will pose a great risk to the Ashepoo River system and the ecology of that river system," state Sen. Chip Campsen told the county zoning board on Dec. 18, 2025. Loeber said the campus would use about 12,000 gallons of water a day and touch just 1 1/2 of the site's 235 wetland acres. Opponents filled the rest of the three-hour meeting. "The answer is not here, not now, not ever," said Richard Burke, whose parents live near the site. The request came about a month after the county council amended its zoning code so rural data centers could be approved as a special exception in a single Zoning Board of Appeals vote, which the Southern Environmental Law Center's Robby Maynor said offered little public oversight. Santee Cooper paid about $1.2 million for a 99-acre plot on the same tax parcel to build a new substation. The zoning board took no action that night, saying it would vote at an unspecified future meeting; no vote on the Eagle Rock campus has since been reported. The county council passed a six-month data center moratorium in July 2026, then in September approved a Digital Infrastructure Overlay District opening much of the county's rural land to data centers and repealing the moratorium outside a few protected zones. Any approval still rests with Colleton County, which would also require state water and well permits and a power study from the project's electric provider.

ft-1772680694340-1860.text: Sequitor Edge, a Nebraska company, plans a small data center of 2 megawatts, expandable to 10, in the Black Hills Industrial Center on the south side of Rapid City, Pennington County, South Dakota. The city is now rewriting the rules it would be built under: on September 10, 2026 the Rapid City Planning Commission put off a new data center ordinance until November 5. Sequitor Edge, based in Bennington, Nebraska, announced the project on February 11, 2026: a 30,000-square-foot building on 10 acres south of Old Folsom Road and east of Highway 79, just down the road from the Rapid City Landfill. The company's Victoria Blatchford told the Rapid City Journal it would cost about $52 million and take 14 months to build once construction starts. Blatchford said it is a colocation center for local businesses such as banks, health care providers and government agencies, with one data hall of about 240 cabinets at first and up to five halls later. Cooling is a closed loop filled once with about 19,000 to 20,000 gallons of water, and power comes from Black Hills Energy. The company expects three to five full-time jobs averaging around $100,000. Because the land is already zoned industrial, the project needs only a building permit, approved by city staff with no vote by the Planning Commission or City Council, Community Development Director Vicki Fisher said. At a July 29 committee meeting a resident asked the city to require a conditional use permit for large data centers, calling it "a mandatory legal mechanism designed to give the citizens of Rapid City notice, public hearings, and the right to evaluate severe impacts on our grid and water resources." City Council President Rod Pettigrew said in February he is not "pro" data center and hopes the city gives no tax breaks, while Councilwoman Lindsey Seachris called the project "a win all the way around." Lisa Tiger of Dakota Rural Action said the group is "not anti-data center" but wants local control and transparency, and welcomed the closed-loop cooling. Mayor Jason Salamun proposed in April that large data centers need a conditional use permit, with public hearings and studies of water and electricity. The draft ordinance would ban hyperscale data centers of 50 megawatts or more, and would allow micro data centers of up to 10 megawatts and 4,000 gallons of water a day if they are at least 500 feet from residential zoning; larger centers would need a conditional use permit, evaporative cooling would be banned, a sound study would be required, and the electric utility would have to give a letter of approval. Fisher said after the September meeting that some residents feel the city has not gone far enough, and that "you know you've written a good ordinance when nobody's completely happy with it." Construction had not started as of July, when KOTA reported it was not expected until late 2026. The ordinance goes back to the Planning Commission on November 5 after an open house and a working session with the City Council, then to the Legal and Finance Committee and the full Rapid City Council for a final vote.

The city is now rewriting the rules it would be built under: on September 10, 2026 the Rapid City Planning Commission put off a new data center ordinance until November 5.

Sequitor Edge, based in Bennington, Nebraska, announced the project on February 11, 2026: a 30,000-square-foot building on 10 acres south of Old Folsom Road and east of Highway 79, just down the road from the Rapid City Landfill.
The company's Victoria Blatchford told the Rapid City Journal it would cost about $52 million and take 14 months to build once construction starts.

Blatchford said it is a colocation center for local businesses such as banks, health care providers and government agencies, with one data hall of about 240 cabinets at first and up to five halls later.
Cooling is a closed loop filled once with about 19,000 to 20,000 gallons of water, and power comes from Black Hills Energy.
The company expects three to five full-time jobs averaging around $100,000.

Because the land is already zoned industrial, the project needs only a building permit, approved by city staff with no vote by the Planning Commission or City Council, Community Development Director Vicki Fisher said.

At a July 29 committee meeting a resident asked the city to require a conditional use permit for large data centers, calling it "a mandatory legal mechanism designed to give the citizens of Rapid City notice, public hearings, and the right to evaluate severe impacts on our grid and water resources."

City Council President Rod Pettigrew said in February he is not "pro" data center and hopes the city gives no tax breaks, while Councilwoman Lindsey Seachris called the project "a win all the way around."
Lisa Tiger of Dakota Rural Action said the group is "not anti-data center" but wants local control and transparency, and welcomed the closed-loop cooling.
Mayor Jason Salamun proposed in April that large data centers need a conditional use permit, with public hearings and studies of water and electricity.

The draft ordinance would ban hyperscale data centers of 50 megawatts or more, and would allow micro data centers of up to 10 megawatts and 4,000 gallons of water a day if they are at least 500 feet from residential zoning; larger centers would need a conditional use permit, evaporative cooling would be banned, a sound study would be required, and the electric utility would have to give a letter of approval.
Fisher said after the September meeting that some residents feel the city has not gone far enough, and that "you know you've written a good ordinance when nobody's completely happy with it."
Construction had not started as of July, when KOTA reported it was not expected until late 2026.

The ordinance goes back to the Planning Commission on November 5 after an open house and a working session with the City Council, then to the Legal and Finance Committee and the full Rapid City Council for a final vote.

ft-492.text: Gemini Data Center SD LLC wants to build the first hyperscale data center in Sioux Falls, in Minnehaha County, South Dakota, on land it bought from Xcel Energy near Rice Street and Veterans Parkway. The company is connected with a California-based family office listed under the name Michael Anvar that invests in real estate, renewable energy and technology. The site, marketed as the Sioux Falls Technology Park, is about a mile south of the Veterans Parkway exit from Interstate 90, just south of Xcel's Split Rock substation and Angus Anson power station, which allows it to support a 500 megawatt power load. The city has said yes at each step so far. In October 2025 city councilors annexed the land into Sioux Falls after the company promised to cover the cost of extending utilities to the site. "Any future property owner, if Gemini would walk away, would get that notice of claim that indicates that they are responsible for all the future improvements with water, sewer and roads," said Jason Bieber of the city's planning department. In January 2026 the council unanimously approved rezoning about 164 acres to a light industrial district. A group calling itself Let Sioux Falls Vote circulated a referendum petition to put the rezoning to the city's voters and submitted 5,012 signatures against the 6,704 needed; the city said: "Even assuming each signature is legally valid and the petition has met all other legal requirements, the total number of signatures submitted of 5,012 is not sufficient to submit the ordinance to an election", and that the city clerk had to reject it by law. Across the state, a Facebook group called South Dakota for Data Center Transparency had about 3,600 members by March 2026, voicing concern about noise, energy use and water use. Gemini's website says a fully built 500-megawatt campus using closed-loop cooling would use about as much water as two commercial car washes, and that the company, not existing customers, would pay for the electrical infrastructure the site needs. No end user has been named; Gemini says data center buildings would be built and run by a future operator. The project still has to clear the city's administrative process and could yet be denied, city planning director Jeff Eckhoff has said, while state lawmakers debate rules for data centers.

ft-497.text: The AI data center the Air Force offered to host at Arnold Air Force Base, near Manchester in Coffee County, Tennessee, has been cancelled. In a June 1, 2026 statement, the base said the Air Force Civil Engineering Center told local leadership that no developers would submit proposals for the land under the Enhanced Use Lease program for AI data centers, after the May 29 deadline passed. The Air Force had offered 274 acres at Arnold as one of five bases, along with Edwards in California, Davis-Monthan in Arizona, Robins in Georgia and Joint Base McGuire-Dix-Lakehurst in New Jersey, in response to executive orders President Trump issued in 2025. A qualifying project needed more than 100 megawatts of new load and at least $500 million in investment, with leases of up to 50 years, and companies had to pay fair market value for the land plus $250,000 to the government. "AI is transforming the modern world, and these data centers are crucial for America to remain at the forefront of innovation," said Robert Moriarty, the Air Force's deputy assistant secretary for installations. The plan drew doubts from the start: Stacie Pettyjohn of the Center for a New American Security said she had never heard of public land being leased to private companies this way, and raised the risk of espionage and sabotage. In Coffee County, the local Democratic Party launched a petition days before the announcement, saying: "We are not asking for the impossible. We are asking that it be done the right way, or not at all." Because the base is federal land, the decision rested with the Air Force, and with no proposals submitted there is nothing pending for Arnold.

ft-1780024884691-1880.text: The Hixson Data Center, a planned 25-megawatt AI data center in McMinnville, Warren County, Tennessee, cannot move forward for now after the city passed an 18-month moratorium on data center permits in June 2026. Its development director, McMinnville resident Alex Hixson, did not respond to questions about the project after the vote, the Tennessee Lookout reported. The project was announced in late May 2026 as a 96,065-square-foot, two-level campus built for Nvidia GB200 NVL72 systems, due to open in the first quarter of 2028. The developer said it was still seeking financing and a single tenant for all 25MW. It plans to run off the grid, with 30 MW of guaranteed power from Bloom Energy fuel cells running on natural gas, eight 4.4 MW diesel generators and a 25 MW battery system, according to the project's website. The website says the site is already owned and is industrial land next to transportation corridors and a railroad spur. Residents organized within days. A petition calling for a 12-month moratorium on new AI and large-scale data center approvals gathered more than 2,600 signatures, saying "This request is not about opposing technology or economic development." One signer wrote that "this town may never recover" if it went ahead. McMinnville resident Kai Sage, who lives near the planned site, said developers were targeting smaller places in Tennessee "because our land is so cheap, our laws are so lenient, the income isn't taxed like it is anywhere else." Sage told the Tennessee Lookout the city of 14,000, known for its plant nurseries, is not built for this kind of industry, citing electricity demand, water use, pollution and noise. WSMV noted that a new state law making data centers pay for their power infrastructure applies only to facilities with a peak demand of at least 50 megawatts, so a 25 MW project may fall outside it. The Tennessee Lookout reported that the same law lets data centers generate their own power, with gas turbines for example, without state or local oversight. The McMinnville Board of Mayor and Aldermen voted unanimously for the moratorium, which halts the acceptance and approval of land use, zoning, building, site plan and conditional use applications for data centers. "A moratorium is not a permanent ban. It is a responsible time-out," City Administrator Nolan Ming said. Any future data center will have to supply studies on infrastructure, environment, sound and utilities, and the city says the pause can be extended. No one from the Hixson Data Center attended the meeting. Nearby, Coffee County passed its own moratorium the same day, and Warren County commissioners passed their own moratorium on June 23. Nashville's council also advanced a moratorium bill in June. For the next 18 months the decision sits with the McMinnville Board of Mayor and Aldermen, which will use the time to rewrite its zoning and land use rules before any data center application can be accepted.

ft-1780860040054-4476.text: DC Blox, based in Georgia, bought a 24-acre site at 648 Grassmere Park in south Nashville, Davidson County, Tennessee, for about $23 million, planning to build a data center costing more than $700 million next to the Nashville Zoo. Nashville's Metro Council voted 27-5 on August 4, 2026 to authorize city attorneys to begin eminent domain proceedings to take the property, after passing new zoning rules and a moratorium on data centers in July. Under Tennessee's vested rights doctrine, a developer that filed for permits before local rules changed can claim the right to build anyway, and DC Blox filed before the new zoning law took effect. A petition against the project passed 540,000 signatures, and singer Brad Paisley and Senator Marsha Blackburn, who is running for governor, have come out against it. Nashville resident Adam Nicholson said: "The toll it takes on our grid and our water supply isn't sustainable. I think this is a step in the right direction to say this industry needs to be reined in." Mayor Freddie O'Connell called DC Blox's account of meeting him and the zoo to discuss safeguards "wishful thinking," even "divorced from reality." Councilmember Ginny Welsch, one of five no votes on the eminent domain measure, called it "a gross misuse of the power of condemnation." Metro would likely have to pay more than the $23 million DC Blox paid; the county assessed the property at $37 million, and a judge could set the final price if the two sides disagree. Pending zoning appeals against the project cannot be heard until the city's moratorium expires on December 1, 2026.

ft-1772678598263-1520.text: The data center at 147 Fourth Avenue North in downtown Nashville, Tennessee, is a 19,700-square-foot carrier hotel that H5 Data Centers and the investment firm Novacap took over from 365 Data Centers in early 2026. H5 and Novacap formed a joint venture, HyscaleIX Data Centers, to buy and run carrier hotels, and anchored it with three sites bought from 365 in Buffalo, Nashville and Tampa, DCD reported on Feb. 3, 2026. "Carrier hotels are highly sought-after data centers that perform a critical role in core network ecosystems," said Ted Mocarski of Novacap. The price was not disclosed, and H5 no longer lists a second Nashville facility it once had at 211 Commerce Street. Nashville has just written its first rules for the large data centers now being planned around the city. On July 21, 2026 Metro Council unanimously passed two bills from Councilmember Rollin Horton that ban data centers larger than 500,000 square feet, limit others to heavy industrial areas behind a special-exception process with a public hearing, and restrict them near homes, schools and parks. The council also passed Councilmember Courtney Johnston's moratorium on new data center permits through Dec. 1, 2026, which does not affect data centers already operating. The push followed news in May that the Atlanta company DC Blox planned a data center next to the Nashville Zoo, and Mayor Freddie O'Connell has moved to buy that property through eminent domain because DC Blox applied for permits before the new rules passed. "Passing this legislation is just the beginning of necessary restrictions," resident Emily Otnes said. The moratorium runs until Dec. 1 while Metro Council considers more legislation, including possible rules on decommissioning.
