ft-1779304944409-7202.text: Fisk University wants to build a data center that could draw 30 megawatts of power on its North Nashville campus in Davidson County, Tennessee, part of a $400 million plan called Quantum Leap, but a citywide moratorium on data center permits blocks new applications through December 1, 2026. The historically Black university announced the 100,000-square-foot Innovation Center, with a 70,000-square-foot data center shell, in May 2026, and has not yet named the partner that would run it. Fisk says it "strongly supports efforts to regulate" data centers in Davidson County. The five-acre site was once an athletics track, just west of Johnson Gymnasium at 17th Avenue North and Herman Street, a few blocks from Jefferson Street. Alumnus Winston Wright noted it sits right next to the Andrew Jackson Commons affordable housing development. Don Hardin, who is managing the project for Fisk, said Nashville Electric Service assured the university the facility would not overburden the area's power or raise residential bills, would use closed-loop cooling, and would use about as much water as 10 households. Neighbors and alumni pushed back quickly. "It could mean higher electric bills, unsafe drinking water, pollution and whatever else, and they're not even talking to the community about it," said Kaylynn Mourning, a North Nashville mother who circulated a petition against the plan. At a protest outside the campus gates on June 10, 2026, alumnus and public health expert Winston Wellington Wright said, "We are standing in a ZIP code that consistently ranks within the top three for the highest rates of asthma prevalence and emergency-department-related visits across the city." State Rep. Justin Jones, a 2017 Fisk graduate, told the protest: "If this project of AI data centers is not good for a zoo, then it's not good to build out of HBCUs, not good to build in the heart of a Black community." Nashville NAACP president Timothy Hughes asked Fisk to be more transparent, and a petition against the plan had gathered more than 6,000 signatures. Fisk said in June it "is aware of the proliferation of environmentally harmful data centers that have created issues in the communities where they exist" and has taken a "do no harm" approach. It told the Nashville Scene it is "in the process of identifying our partner for the Innovation Center." The historically Black university announced the 100,000-square-foot Innovation Center, with a 70,000-square-foot data center shell, in May 2026, and has not yet named the partner that would run it. Fisk says it "strongly supports efforts to regulate" data centers in Davidson County.

The five-acre site was once an athletics track, just west of Johnson Gymnasium at 17th Avenue North and Herman Street, a few blocks from Jefferson Street. Alumnus Winston Wright noted it sits right next to the Andrew Jackson Commons affordable housing development. Don Hardin, who is managing the project for Fisk, said Nashville Electric Service assured the university the facility would not overburden the area's power or raise residential bills, would use closed-loop cooling, and would use about as much water as 10 households.

At a protest outside the campus gates on June 10, 2026, alumnus and public health expert Winston Wellington Wright said, "We are standing in a ZIP code that consistently ranks within the top three for the highest rates of asthma prevalence and emergency-department-related visits across the city."

ft-502.text: Vantage Data Centers is building Frontier, a data center campus with 1,400 megawatts of power capacity, on about 1,200 acres in Shackelford County, Texas, near Albany and northeast of Abilene, as part of the Stargate expansion for Oracle and OpenAI. Vantage broke ground in December 2025 and said the first of 10 planned buildings, totaling about 3.7 million square feet, would go live in the second half of 2026. Vantage announced the $25 billion campus in August 2025, its largest investment to date, and Shackelford County commissioners approved it unanimously in July 2025 after a public hearing, creating a tax reinvestment zone. Under a 10-year abatement, Vantage agreed to pay the county $10 million a year instead of property taxes, which the Albany News said could raise the county's yearly budget by nearly 200 percent, plus $150,000 a year to local charities and 10 college scholarships. Company representatives told the county the project would create 250 full-time jobs paying $25 million a year, with up to 6,500 workers on site at the peak of construction. The company says the campus uses liquid cooling with a closed-loop chiller system that "requires minimal water," but filings with the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, cited by Construction Owners, show the contractor Voltagrid is cleared to run 210 gas generators on site with a combined 700 megawatts of capacity. Residents have raised traffic since: Twylia Waldon told commissioners in July 2026 that trucks run "all day, all night long" and "do not follow the speed limits," and Blaine Kayga said at an August town hall, "I have a cracked window just because of all the gravel trucks." A second project, Project North, is now before the county: Bolt Data and Energy wants to build on the Buck Nail Ranch about 16 miles west of Albany, an estimated $8.8 billion investment that would generate its own power. More than 100 people packed the Commissioners Court when it was introduced in July 2026, and in September commissioners unanimously accepted Bolt's tax abatement application and agreed to form a citizen advisory committee for the negotiations. The Shackelford County Hospital District has hired its own attorney, and trustee Mike Parsons said questions remain about the project's water needs and emissions. County Judge John Viertel, who leads the Commissioners Court handling both projects and begins a second term in January 2027, told KTXS: "We're not able to do a whole lot unless we do some abatement," adding, "which allows us to do some control and to set up terms." Gov. Greg Abbott called on June 30, 2026 for new AI data centers in rural Texas to be banned unless companies provide their own power and reuse their own water, a state policy that would affect any future expansion here.

ft-507.text: Fermi America and Texas Tech are building a data center and power campus, called Project Matador, on Texas Tech land next to the Pantex nuclear weapons plant in unincorporated Carson County, Texas. Fermi first announced the campus at 11,000 megawatts of power; its own website now calls Project Matador a 17,000 megawatt campus, with about 6,000 megawatts already permitted. Only a small first phase is under construction: a 222 megawatt data center leased to TensorWave. Amarillo's city council voted 4-1 in October 2025 to sell Fermi up to 2.5 million gallons of water a day for the project. Fermi says it holds groundwater leases in Carson County giving it access to up to 18.5 million gallons a day, and co-founder Rick Perry has said the first gigawatt would use about as much water as one irrigated cornfield. At a protest outside the old Potter County courthouse, Madison Boyle asked: "Why are we using ground water that farmers could be using for agriculture, for AI data center, where it's going to deplete a resource that's not really renewable?" The company's finances have wobbled: a prospective tenant pulled $150 million in funding in December 2025, the board fired co-founder and chief executive Toby Neugebauer in April 2026, and Fermi said it lacked cash for the year ahead without more financing. It has since signed its first binding customer, a 15-year, $6.5 billion lease with TensorWave, but that 222 megawatt data center still depends on financing and guarantees, with delivery targeted for the second half of 2027. Fermi has applied to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission for four AP1000 nuclear reactors that have no license yet, and the state approved air permits for up to 6,000 megawatts of gas-fired generation in February 2026 over objections. Texas ordered a state audit of large data center projects, including Matador, starting August 3, 2026, with no end date set. Amarillo considered a two-year moratorium on new data centers in May 2026, but it would not reach the campus, which sits outside city limits.

ft-1787746738289-7125.text: SpaceX's Terafab at Gibbons Creek Reservoir, in Grimes County, Texas, is mainly a chip factory rather than a data center, described in county documents as an integrated semiconductor manufacturing and advanced computing fabrication facility, and residents fought for months over what the county should demand before giving it a tax break. County commissioners approved the abatement on June 4, 2026, a month after SpaceX said it might come. A week before the vote, a Wyoming company called WIT TECH LLC, whose filings carry the signature of Musk's family office manager Jared Birchall, bought six parcels of more than 2,700 acres, including a pump station on the Navasota River and a one-acre parcel that is the river itself. Grimes County Citizens for Responsible Development asked the county to use the abatement to demand enforceable limits on roads, water, air emissions and nuisance, pointing to the county's own policy that an abatement may not be granted if it would be a hazard to public safety or health. "Our way of life here is about to change dramatically. We're just asking for that company to do something for us in return," said Marie Egyed, the group's director of operations. On August 6, SpaceX representatives faced residents at the commissioners court for the first time and said the state and school district agreements were signed and construction would start within months, with 3,000 permanent jobs in phase one. They said the plant would run on its own gas-fired power, that it would not raise electric bills, and that the Navasota pump station would divert stormwater into the reservoir: "We can't dry up the Navasota River. The amount of water we can take on an annual basis is limited," said Terafab's Riley Trennell. SpaceX's attorney Buck Brannon said the county abatement is about 78 percent rather than the reported 100, fixing payments to the county at $20 million a year for 35 years.

ft-1768501881634-3585.text: CleanSpark is proposing a 285-megawatt data center campus off Substation Road, about three miles outside Sealy in Austin County, Texas, where county commissioners have imposed a moratorium on new data centers while they write rules. CleanSpark announced in October 2025 that it had acquired rights to about 271 acres and signed power supply agreements for the full 285 megawatts, and it now expects to bring more than 200 megawatts online in the first half of 2027. Meta has signed a letter of intent for 885 megawatts across CleanSpark's Sealy and Brazoria sites, an SEC filing tied to a separate Meta lease in Sandersville, Georgia shows. On July 27, 2026, after nearly two hours of debate, the Austin County Commissioners Court in Bellville voted unanimously to impose a moratorium on battery storage systems and data centers across the county. Residents raised noise, water use, electrical demand, traffic and light pollution; one landowner near an existing battery site on Substation Road said she measured about 61 decibels on her property. "We are not going to lay down and take it. We are here to fight," resident Lisa Hicks said at a CleanSpark open house on August 14 that drew about 250 residents, the Sealy News reported. County officials say CleanSpark's substation work does not amount to approval for a data center, since no complete development permit application has been filed; CleanSpark says the substation on the land was always meant to serve one. County Judge Tim Lapham said the moratorium is one of the few tools the county has to set standards before more companies follow. On August 12, Gov. Greg Abbott said CleanSpark, Google and Rowan had agreed to comply with his data center standards, which require the Public Utility Commission of Texas and grid operator ERCOT to review each project's power, water and neighbor-impact plans. On September 21, Abbott went further, ordering the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to stop issuing new data center permits until ERCOT and the Texas Water Development Board finish auditing the industry. The Austin County moratorium has no fixed end date, and the Commissioners Court that adopted it will decide what permanent rules follow.

On August 12, Gov. Greg Abbott said CleanSpark, Google and Rowan had agreed to comply with his data center standards, which require the Public Utility Commission of Texas and grid operator ERCOT to review each project's power, water and neighbor-impact plans.

The Austin County moratorium has no fixed end date, and the Commissioners Court that adopted it will decide what permanent rules follow.

ft-1775786508153-1783.text: LandBridge gave PowerBridge the option to lease up to about 3,400 acres in Reeves County for its proposed Alpha Digital Campus, near the Waha natural gas hub. Their April 2, 2026, agreement allows PowerBridge to pursue site approvals and a long-term lease; it does not by itself establish a built data center or a signed customer. The companies described up to 2 gigawatts of initial power generation beside the campus, a planned supply figure rather than data-center power already in use. PowerBridge says it has filed an interconnection request for the generation facilities, supplied the associated data-center load details and ordered equipment for the power infrastructure. Its plan is to serve the campus through a private electrical network connecting the generation to future data halls. The companies forecast first power in 2027 and larger-scale generation in 2028, subject to regulatory work and commercial agreements. PowerBridge's wider development model includes mostly gas-fired power plants and possible reuse of water from oil and gas production. The Alpha Digital announcement, however, gives no site-specific water source or volume, fuel consumption, cooling plan or data-center customer. That announcement identifies Reeves County and proximity to Waha, but not the particular tract within LandBridge's holdings.

ft-555.text: Project Gladys is a planned 150-megawatt data center that the developer Soluna Holdings says will sit alongside a 226-megawatt wind farm in southeast Texas and draw on its power. Soluna, which builds data centers for Bitcoin mining and AI next to wind, solar and hydroelectric plants, announced the project in August 2025 and has not named the wind farm, the town or the county. It said only that the site is being developed with "a prominent U.S.-based independent power producer (IPP) managing over $40 billion in assets and more than 80 energy facilities nationwide." The project is named for Dr. Gladys West, the mathematician whose geospatial modeling work paved the way for GPS. At launch Soluna said it was still working on land acquisition, power contract negotiations and planning for a connection to ERCOT, the Texas grid operator. Its most recent public update, in April 2026, said it was still advancing land due diligence and power purchase negotiations for Gladys and two sister projects, Annie and Fei. In the same update Soluna said the three projects would move outside ERCOT's Large Flexible Load batch study, "leveraging the sub-75 MW interconnection pathway to accelerate development timelines." Soluna describes its business as turning surplus renewable energy into computing, and its projects page lists Gladys as a 150 MW wind-powered site in Texas; the company already operates other Texas data centers, including its Dorothy campus. Texas local governments have limited say over projects like this one: House Bill 2127, passed in 2023, blocks them from enacting policy that goes beyond state law. Gov. Greg Abbott has ordered regulators to audit the energy and water use of proposed data center developments statewide, and lawmakers are expected to take up data center rules in the session that begins in January 2027. Soluna says its next steps for Gladys are to complete power purchase agreements, land agreements and ERCOT planning.

ft-1768501547279-8324.text: CleanSpark, the Bitcoin mining company moving into AI hosting, plans a data center campus of up to 600 megawatts on 447 acres near Angleton in Brazoria County, Texas. The company closed the purchase in March 2026, saying the deal adds 300 megawatts of ERCOT-approved power to its Texas portfolio, with room to grow by another 300 megawatts. No tenant has been named yet, but Meta has signed a letter of intent for 885 megawatts across CleanSpark's Sealy and Brazoria sites, an SEC filing tied to a separate Meta lease in Sandersville, Georgia shows. Brazoria County's only operating data center, a 17-megawatt Giga Energy site near the town of Brazoria, has drawn noise complaints since it opened in March 2026. "The constant noise and vibration are still a daily nuisance," resident Wesley Burnett told commissioners. On June 9, 2026, Brazoria County commissioners unanimously passed a resolution opposing any future data center that does not protect the grid, water, farmland and public infrastructure. County Judge Matt Sebesta says the county cannot block a data center, only withhold tax abatements, which it will not grant. "We cannot stop this project," Sebesta said of a similar data center and gas plant proposed near Sweeny. "We do not have the tools." State Rep. Cody Vasut told The Facts he plans to push legislation next session on noise limits, water use and minimum distances from homes. On September 21, 2026, Gov. Greg Abbott ordered the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to stop issuing new data center permits until the state's grid operator, ERCOT, and the Texas Water Development Board finish auditing the industry's power and water use, a halt that now covers CleanSpark's Brazoria plans. The Legislature's next session begins in January 2027, and any tax abatement request for the project would still go to the Brazoria County Commissioners Court, which has said it will not grant one.

ft-1772136190912-7319.text: Viridien, the French earth data and technology company formerly known as CGG, plans what it calls a high performance computing center, a small data center, on 21 acres it owns at 2602 Longwood Drive in Brenham, in Washington County, Texas. The $100 million, 40,000-square-foot facility is meant to become the company's main U.S. operations center, moving employees from Houston. On January 8, 2026 the Brenham City Council voted 5-0 to deny it a tax break, refusing to create Reinvestment Zone No. 55. City Hall's chamber, which holds 75, overflowed into the lobby, and many residents said it was the first they had heard of a project the city had been discussing since around 2022. "They're headquartered in France. I don't understand why we are benefiting a French company, I don't understand," one resident said. Mayor Atwood Kenjura said the process of making the project public could have been handled differently but maintained it had not been rushed or concealed, and Councilmember Steve Soman asked the company, "Why should we grant you this that's going to cost the city millions of dollars?" Viridien's facilities manager James Whatley said the building would cool its servers by submerging them in mineral oil, with a closed water loop filled once: "Water for here will be zero for our compute." Local geologist Taylor Farmer doubted that would last, noting that deed restrictions on water-based cooling expire after 10 years, and questioned the company's promise that the center would not do large-scale AI work. "We will move forward with this project regardless of the decision," Whatley said. In April 2026 Viridien said the 40,300-square-foot building would draw 5 megawatts of power at first, up to 21 megawatts if it expands, with power from Bluebonnet Electric Cooperative and Viridien paying for any substation or transmission upgrades. It said construction would start early in 2026 and finish by the end of 2027, creating about 26 permanent jobs, and that it had applied for state tax incentives instead of the city's. The project now pays full city taxes after losing the reinvestment zone.

ft-1786570153211-1394.text: A proposal to convert a former Walmart and migrant children's shelter at 7480 Padre Island Highway in Brownsville, Cameron County, Texas, into a data center was withdrawn on July 29, 2026, about a week before its zoning hearing. The property owner, Randr Ventures LLC, pulled its request for a specific use permit, and Brownsville has since begun writing a 90-day moratorium on data centers. The plan would have converted a roughly 265,000-square-foot building on 32 acres near the Port of Brownsville and the airport. Built as a Walmart in 2004, the building most recently housed a shelter for unaccompanied migrant children run by Southwest Key Programs, and is appraised at about $10 million. The city has not said why the proposal was withdrawn or whether it could return. The plan drew opposition as the Rio Grande Valley's second major data center proposal, after a contested one near Harlingen. At a September 1 hearing on the moratorium, resident Leah Hollingshead told commissioners: "I truly cannot believe that the best use of my time in my one short life is to stand before you and state the obvious by telling you I don't want a data center in my backyard." Commissioners voted that day to start the moratorium and revive a task force to study its effects on power, water and neighborhoods. Under a new state law the moratorium needs three public hearings; Brownsville has scheduled a second hearing on October 6, a first reading of the ordinance on October 13 and a final vote on November 17. The pause would run from November 18 to February 16, 2027, with an option to extend to May 18, 2027, and the city commission must adopt data center rules before it ends.

ft-1787771173835-1270.text: EdgeConneX AUS02 is a $440 million data center at 8001 Wolf Lane in Cedar Creek, Bastrop County, Texas, where state and county records name the AI cloud company CoreWeave as the expected tenant. County officials said in June 2026 that the two-story, 578,000-square-foot building was expected to be finished that summer; Community Impact reported in August 2026 it was expected to open that month. No report since has said whether it opened, and its status stays under construction. Bastrop County approved a 10-year, 75% property tax abatement for the building in December 2024 and assigned that benefit to CoreWeave in October 2025. The Texas Comptroller certified the building for a 20-year exemption from state and local sales taxes on the equipment, electricity and cooling systems it uses. County documents projected about 60 permanent jobs and 400 to 600 daily construction jobs. EdgeConneX is also building two more, separate campuses nearby on FM 535: one of 951 acres and about $1.4 billion in planned buildings, and a smaller one still in early planning. Those campuses are apart from AUS02, and EdgeConneX has not sought tax abatements for them. Many neighbors say they only learned of the projects after county commissioners approved AUS02 in 2024; at a commissioner's request, EdgeConneX held town halls in three towns in June 2026 on water use and infrastructure. Residents packed a July meeting in Bastrop where state Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller called for a moratorium on data centers. "We chose Cedar Creek to build our homes, we have families, my six kids are supposed to be growing up in this area, next to a data center," resident Mary Santana said. County Judge Gregory Klaus has said the county has little power to stop such projects once they meet existing legal requirements, since Texas counties have limited zoning authority. Bastrop County commissioners held a public hearing on July 27 on new tax-abatement rules that would require future applicants to disclose environmental effects and create at least 25 jobs, a quarter of them filled by county residents. On August 10 commissioners again tabled a separate request asking the Texas Legislature for more authority over large industrial projects, with no new hearing date set.

ft-515.text: Childress, in Childress County, Texas, has been under a citywide boil water notice since September 8, 2026, while one of the largest data centers in the Panhandle runs on the edge of town. The data center is IREN's Childress campus: 750 megawatts on 576 acres, connected straight to the ERCOT grid through substations the company owns, which IREN calls its largest operational site. "We are having to buy bottled water. We can't use ice. We can't brush our teeth in the water," resident Jordan Farus said, adding: "Greenbelt is our water source, and it's been low for quite some time, even before the data centers got here." The city blames extreme heat, high ground temperatures and drought for disinfectant levels falling too low, Mayor Cary Preston declared a local state of disaster on September 11, and the town is under Stage 4 water restrictions. Nothing has tied the boil notice to the data center, and the city's problem is structural: it buys all its water from the Greenbelt Municipal and Industrial Water Authority, which relies on a shrinking lake and ten wells, and City Manager Kevin Hodges said, "we don't treat the water. We only distribute the water." The city is chasing up to $16 million from the state's drinking water fund for new wells and lines, though its contract with Greenbelt requires it to pay twice for any water it gets elsewhere. ft-514.text: Crusoe and Lancium announced on July 15, 2026 a 1-gigawatt AI data center campus on 270 acres Lancium owns in Childress, Childress County, Texas, with construction expected to begin in the third quarter of 2026. Under the partnership, Lancium owns the land, secures the power interconnection and manages the energy, while Crusoe designs, builds and operates the data center for what the companies call "a leading hyperscale technology company." Previous reports suggest Meta is set to lease capacity at the site from Crusoe, Data Center Dynamics reported. The companies say the grid-connected campus will add behind-the-meter solar and battery storage and use a closed-loop, non-evaporative liquid cooling system to limit water use. They say it will create thousands of construction jobs and more than 100 permanent positions in Childress County, and that they will invest directly in local water and other civil infrastructure and support housing, education and emergency services. It is the second campus the pair are building together, after their Abilene site, which Crusoe built for OpenAI via Oracle. "Working with Lancium again, in the same partnership model we built together in Abilene, made Childress an easy choice for our next site," said Chase Lochmiller, Crusoe's co-founder and chief executive. Lancium chief executive Michael McNamara said the companies are "deeply committed to working with local stakeholders to advance a model of development that addresses the broader needs of the community." Childress already hosts a data center campus from Iren, a former crypto miner, which is being leased to Microsoft. In the same week as the Childress announcement, Lancium said QTS will develop an 11-building campus at another Lancium site near Turkey, in Hall County. The announcement landed as Panhandle towns were weighing limits: in May and June, Amarillo, Childress, Clarendon and Quanah discussed possible moratoriums on data center development, and on new water meter connections, amid worries about the region's scarce water. Construction was due to start in the third quarter of 2026, but the state has since slowed new projects: on September 21, Gov. Greg Abbott ordered the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to stop issuing permits for data centers until state audits of their power and water use are complete.

ft-516.text: College Station's City Council unanimously rejected the sale of about 200 city-owned acres to Priority Power Management on September 11, 2025, blocking its Project Aggie plan for Midtown Business Park. The proposed site was along Corporate Parkway and Midtown Drive, behind Costco, and the land deal was valued at about $30 million. The developer's conceptual design showed two data-center buildings and two substations, with up to 600 megawatts of power at full buildout; none of that capacity was built. Residents objected to placing a large industrial campus near homes and to how little time they had to examine the deal. More than 75 people registered to speak at the council meeting, and opponents delivered a petition with 5,047 signatures. They raised noise, water and power concerns, while the city presented a proposed 600- to 900-foot planted buffer and said separate water and power agreements and a sound study would still be needed. The financial offer was substantial but contested. City officials estimated $10 million to $22 million a year in taxes and electric-fund transfers on top of the land price; their presentation projected 45 permanent jobs. Residents and Midtown developer James Murr questioned whether that was enough employment for 200 acres intended to support the wider business district. After nearly six hours of public discussion, the council voted down the sale, despite a staff recommendation to approve it. In January 2026, Mayor John Nichols said College Station had begun discussing rules for where future data centers could be placed, but KBTX reported no timetable for those rules. The rejected land agreement did not authorize Project Aggie to proceed on the Midtown site.

ft-1765423328545-1318.text: Riot Platforms' bitcoin mine and data center campus sits on FM 709, about seven miles outside Corsicana, Navarro County's seat. Corsicana had 25,109 residents at the 2020 census and sits 50 miles southeast of Dallas. The city announced the project on April 27, 2022: a 265-acre, 400-megawatt bitcoin mine promising about 150 jobs. Riot energized the first phase on April 18, 2024. Riot has since bought more land, including a further 238 acres in 2025, taking the site to around 890 acres. Riot says the Corsicana facility will have a total capacity of 1 gigawatt when fully developed. So far the site is equipped with 400 megawatts of power for bitcoin mining, and Riot aims to pivot at least part of it to AI and high-performance computing. In 2026 Riot filed with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation to add a new two-story data center building of 335,430 square feet, called Project Ditto, at the campus at 6980 FM 709; the $400 million project is set to run from April 2026 to May 2028. Riot's growth has come with a fight over tax breaks. In March 2024, Navarro County commissioners rejected a tax abatement for a planned $640 million, 256-acre expansion after residents packed the courtroom. Navarro County Commissioner David Brewer told DL News: "If you want to know my personal opinion about it, I don't think it's a good investment," adding, "I think that they created a lot of controversy out there." That October, on a 3-2 vote, commissioners approved a smaller abatement, and Brewer reversed his earlier opposition to vote yes. The rejected March proposal would have saved Riot nearly $14 million in property taxes over a decade and was tied to a promise of 180 full-time jobs. Riot said the expanded facility, once complete, would use enough electricity to power Navarro County's roughly 22,000 homes 34 times over. Opponents organized as the Texas Coalition Against Cryptomining, led by Jackie Sawicky, who had moved to Corsicana in 2018. On October 25, 2023, the coalition and Greenpeace USA protested outside the site with signs reading "No water for Riot." Greenpeace campaigner Joshua Archer said, "There's something worth fighting for in this county." Sawicky called Riot a multibillion-dollar corporation trying to avoid its tax obligations. Resident Theresa Hibbitts raised concerns about water scarcity during the drought. The facility draws about 1.5 million gallons of water a day at peak summer use, roughly an eighth of Corsicana's maximum daily use, from wells into the Woodbine Aquifer and an 18.5-acre rainwater retention pond. Sawicky disbanded the coalition in late 2024 and left Texas for New York. The site's next phase now faces a new state hurdle. On August 3, 2026, Governor Greg Abbott ordered the Public Utility Commission and ERCOT to pause approvals for data centers seeking new grid connections until they audit water use, power demand and tax incentives. Abbott's office said on August 18 that Riot Platforms had committed to comply with his standards, which include paying for its own grid upgrades and reusing its water rather than relying on taxpayer incentives.

ft-1768321303492-5854.text: The U.S. Army is offering underused land at Fort Hood, in Coryell County, Texas, for a commercial data center, one of four Army installations included in a request for proposals alongside Fort Bliss, Fort Bragg and Dugway Proving Ground. Bidders would lease the land for 50 years under the Army's Enhanced Use Lease program, a deal that lets a private company build on military land long-term, and proposals were due February 23, 2026. Contracting documents show the Fort Hood parcel lies "within ½ mile" of homes and businesses, and bidders must describe outreach to assess "local sentiment and any risks or opposition" to the project. University of Tulsa economist Jason Walter said the Fort Hood documents note that nearby Copperas Cove "will likely be affected as well as some of their water resources," and warned a data center on federal land "could be exempt or complicate local taxation while requiring more infrastructure." In late March 2026 the Army said it had "conditionally selected" investment firms to build data centers at Fort Bliss and Dugway, but it has named no developer for Fort Hood. Outside the gate, the City of Killeen was approached in December 2025 about a separate data center nearby, but city spokeswoman Torrie Bethany said no formal application had been submitted. The Department of the Army is still reviewing proposals for Fort Hood and has not named a winner.

ft-526.text: New Era Energy & Digital has signed a 20-year deal with Vistra's subsidiary Luminant for at least 207 megawatts of power to run the first phase of its Texas Critical Data Centers campus in Ector County, Texas. The data center campus is planned near Penwell in west Ector County, outside Odessa, next to Vistra's 1.1-gigawatt natural gas plant that will supply it, with power expected to start flowing in the third quarter of 2027. The project began as a joint venture between New Era Helium and the GPU cloud firm Sharon AI, first planned at 90 megawatts of power and then expanded to 250 megawatts with the potential to grow beyond 1 gigawatt. The partners bought 235 acres from GROW Odessa, an economic development corporation, in July 2025, and New Era, formerly New Era Helium, later bought out Sharon AI's stake for $70 million and closed on another 203 acres, taking the campus to 438 acres. In April 2026 it signed a non-binding letter of intent to form a joint venture with Stream Data Centers to develop and finance the campus, with equity from an unnamed institutional investor, and site plans suggest up to ten two-story buildings. No tenant has been announced; New Era's chief executive, Charlie Nelson, said the power contract made the site "an attractive opportunity to any quality tenant currently in the market," and said the company has construction permits in hand. Vistra gets a five percent non-voting interest in the data center once power starts flowing, and has also signed non-binding agreements for about 250 megawatts of on-site gas generation. In January 2026, Rosen Law Firm said it was investigating securities claims against New Era Energy & Digital over allegedly misleading business information, and the company's share price fell 6.9 percent. Opposition has reached the Ector County Commissioners Court. In June 2026, residents urged commissioners to be cautious about data centers, citing greenhouse gas emissions, strain on emergency services, noise and water use. County Judge Dustin Fawcett said the county was having its first formal meeting with a data center company. "We care about the environment and we will be asking all those questions," Fawcett said. At an August meeting, resident JoAnna Keese told the court it was being secretive and that land in the county was already cleared for a data center, and another speaker told commissioners not "to sell out and bow down you are elected to protect us." Commissioner Mike Gardner said he is not for tax abatements to lure data centers, but agreed with Fawcett that the county has no authority to tell landowners what to do with their property. The county has no ordinance-making authority, Fawcett said, but he told residents public meetings would be held before the county makes any agreement with a data center. Tom Manskey, director of economic development at the Odessa Chamber of Commerce, said in 2025 that three other data centers had expressed interest in the area.

The partners bought 235 acres from GROW Odessa, an economic development corporation, in July 2025, and New Era, formerly New Era Helium, later bought out Sharon AI's stake for $70 million and closed on another 203 acres, taking the campus to 438 acres.

In April 2026 it signed a non-binding letter of intent to form a joint venture with Stream Data Centers to develop and finance the campus, with equity from an unnamed institutional investor, and site plans suggest up to ten two-story buildings.

No tenant has been announced; New Era's chief executive, Charlie Nelson, said the power contract made the site "an attractive opportunity to any quality tenant currently in the market," and said the company has construction permits in hand.
Vistra gets a five percent non-voting interest in the data center once power starts flowing, and has also signed non-binding agreements for about 250 megawatts of on-site gas generation.

In January 2026, Rosen Law Firm said it was investigating securities claims against New Era Energy & Digital over allegedly misleading business information, and the company's share price fell 6.9 percent.

Opposition has reached the Ector County Commissioners Court. In June 2026, residents urged commissioners to be cautious about data centers, citing greenhouse gas emissions, strain on emergency services, noise and water use.
County Judge Dustin Fawcett said the county was having its first formal meeting with a data center company. "We care about the environment and we will be asking all those questions," Fawcett said.

At an August meeting, resident JoAnna Keese told the court it was being secretive and that land in the county was already cleared for a data center, and another speaker told commissioners not "to sell out and bow down you are elected to protect us."
Commissioner Mike Gardner said he is not for tax abatements to lure data centers, but agreed with Fawcett that the county has no authority to tell landowners what to do with their property.
The county has no ordinance-making authority, Fawcett said, but he told residents public meetings would be held before the county makes any agreement with a data center.
Tom Manskey, director of economic development at the Odessa Chamber of Commerce, said in 2025 that three other data centers had expressed interest in the area.

ft-1776916882527-1931.text: Meta's Project Seafox data center campus, at 7001 Stan Roberts Sr. Avenue in Northeast El Paso, has been under construction since Meta broke ground in October 2025. It is being built through Meta's subsidiary Wurldwide LLC and is set to deliver 1,000 megawatts of computing power, about 1 gigawatt, starting in 2028. A state filing for 12 more buildings and five substations puts the full campus at about 25.9 million square feet on roughly 600 acres, with work continuing to February 2029. Meta raised its planned investment to $10 billion in March 2026, then formed a roughly $14 billion joint venture in which BlackRock funds hold 80 percent, putting in $4.9 billion in cash against $2.3 billion in land and construction costs from Meta. The city and county had already granted an 80 percent break on property taxes for decades and $12.5 million for road repairs around the site. "I can say clearly, if I were voting on this today, I wouldn't support it," said El Paso City Rep. Chris Canales, who represents District 8 and voted for the tax break in 2023. "I wish we had voted differently in 2023, and I'm sorry for my role in it," he said. Part of the campus's power will come from 813 small gas-fired generators built onsite, totaling 366 megawatts. El Paso Electric says Meta will pay the full cost of that power for a bridge period of one to five years, after which the utility will fold the cost into rates paid by all customers. The generators would emit about 117 metric tons of nitrogen oxides a year, a smog-forming pollutant, according to figures from their maker, Enchanted Rock. Meta says more than 4,000 workers will build the campus and it will hire 300 full-time employees, though the city's tax deal requires only 50. El Paso Electric has asked the Public Utility Commission of Texas for permission to build the gas plant; its ruling will decide who ultimately pays for the power.

ft-527.text: Cawley Partners, a Dallas real estate firm, plans data centers and housing on South Creek Ranch, a 5,200-acre former cattle ranch it bought near Ferris, in both Ellis and Dallas counties about 20 miles south of Dallas. The firm closed on the land in late April 2025 and said development on the ranch's northern 2,000 acres, planned as a network of "digital commerce parks," would start that year, with the first buildings done in two or three years. Cawley has not released the size or number of data centers planned, and the company has said nothing more publicly about the project since that spring 2025 announcement. "The attributes of I-45, the future Loop Nine and the infrastructure the City of Ferris has, will help us develop a commercial park right away," said Tim Keith, who runs Cawley's land and digital commerce team. Ferris City Manager Brooks Williams told Fox 4 the project "is going to fundamentally change our city"; the town's population has doubled in five years, and officials expect new commercial tax revenue that could lower residents' property taxes. Any data centers built on the ranch would also have to clear new state rules: Governor Greg Abbott ordered the state's grid operator, ERCOT, and its utility regulator on August 3, 2026 to audit data centers seeking to connect to the grid and to deny connections to any that fail to comply.

ft-1768321818190-9332.text: The U.S. Army is planning a data center complex on 1,384 acres of Fort Bliss, Texas, to be financed, built and run by the Carlyle Group, which the Army conditionally selected in March 2026 to enter exclusive lease negotiations. By 2029 the Fort Bliss complex in far East El Paso would need 3 gigawatts of electricity, more than El Paso Electric's entire generating capacity of about 2.9 gigawatts, Deputy Undersecretary of the Army David Fitzgerald said. The project is part of the Army's Enhanced Use Lease program, which followed an executive order by President Donald Trump directing agencies to help data center projects; the February solicitation pointed to 50-year leases. The Army wants about 100 megawatts of computing running by late 2027, which Fitzgerald said means construction must begin soon. "AI is a strategic asset for the Army," Army Secretary Dan Driscoll said when the selection was announced. The Army says the developer will build its own behind-the-meter power and water systems, and that the Army Corps of Engineers will conduct an environmental review. Almost everything about how it would be powered and watered is still open. Army officials called combined-cycle natural gas turbines the "most likely" power source, which would add large amounts of carbon dioxide and particulate pollution in central El Paso. El Paso Electric said the Army has made no formal request for service and that whether the complex connects to the grid is still under review. The Army's own solicitation rates El Paso's water risk as "extremely high", and even water from Fort Bliss wells would come from the Hueco Bolson aquifer, the city's main source; Fitzgerald has promised the facility will be "water neutral" without saying how. A Carlyle representative at a community meeting did not answer questions about the facility or its power source. The complex would be the third giant in the region, after Meta's $10 billion data center in Northeast El Paso and the $165 billion Project Jupiter campus Oracle and OpenAI are building in Santa Teresa, New Mexico. El Paso Electric has asked Texas regulators for a special data center rate with a 20-year contract term and cash security, and said its projection of new data center demand does not include Fort Bliss. On July 20, 2026, the El Paso City Council unanimously adopted data center rules requiring a special permit with a council vote, 300-foot buffers from homes and plans for water, energy and emissions, but the rules do not apply to the Fort Bliss project on federal land. "Before, we didn't have any power," Mayor Renard Johnson said of the new framework. The decisions on Fort Bliss rest with the Army and Fort Bliss leadership: the Army must still finalize a lease with Carlyle, and El Paso Electric says questions about power will be decided by Fort Bliss leadership. As of July 2026, El Paso Matters reported, the Army had shared virtually no information about the project since unveiling it in April.

ft-528.text: Project Horizon, the data center campus Poolside Infrastructure Company is developing outside Fort Stockton in Pecos County, Texas, has lost the partner it launched with and shrunk on paper from two gigawatts to 400 megawatts of power. In an August 17, 2026 release naming a new chief financial officer, the Austin-based developer described Project Horizon as “a 400 MW data center in unincorporated Pecos County, Texas.” The project was first announced in October 2025 by the AI startup Poolside and the AI cloud company CoreWeave as a 2 gigawatt campus on 568 acres of the Longfellow Ranch, owned by the Mitchell family. CoreWeave was to be the lead customer for a first phase of 250 megawatts under a 15-year lease, expandable to 500 megawatts, with construction expected to finish in early 2027. The plan was to use natural gas produced in the Permian Basin. That partnership came apart. Data Center Dynamics reported in April 2026, citing the Financial Times, that the deal began to fail late in 2025 because Poolside could not get its first cluster of computer chips running on CoreWeave's timeline, and that Poolside's fundraising bid had also failed. A CoreWeave spokesperson said the companies “ultimately chose to pursue different paths for their own strategic and timing reasons.” Poolside then turned to other cloud providers, including Google, seeking commitments for up to 400 megawatts of construction, although a source told the Financial Times that Google was no longer in talks. The same report said the site could support up to 10 gigawatts and that Poolside aimed to build 2.5 gigawatts of solar and wind power there. Poolside Infrastructure Company, founded in 2026, is now carrying the project, led by chief executive Robert Bonar and chief financial officer Justin Lagasse, formerly of Avangrid. In a June 2, 2026 post, energy writer David Blackmon described the site as a 559-acre footprint next to the Longfellow Ranch, more than 25 miles outside Fort Stockton, buffered by ranchland. “Public resistance to data centers in other areas like Ohio and Pennsylvania is real and it's understandable,” Bonar told him. “Residents of those areas are being impacted, whether it be water usage, power rates, land prices and everything else. Looking at that, we believe there's a better solution here,” Bonar said. The county has also been asked for a tax break. The Pecos County Commissioners Court agenda for November 10, 2025 listed a tax abatement agreement with Poolside Inc. inside the Longfellow Renewable Energy Reinvestment Zone, a state tool that lets counties trade lower taxes for new investment, which the court created on January 13, 2025. The agenda does not say what the break is worth. Project Horizon is no longer the only large data center plan near Fort Stockton. In August 2026 Amazon Data Services filed plans for three buildings north of town, valued near $300 million each, and days later confirmed it had bought the 8,000-acre GW Ranch site in Pecos County for a separate gas-powered data center campus. Data Center Dynamics said it was unclear whether Amazon's plans involve Poolside. Tax abatements for projects in the county go before the Pecos County Commissioners Court, which meets at the county courthouse in Fort Stockton. Governor Greg Abbott has temporarily halted new data center approvals in Texas since August 2026, though that has not stopped facilities already cleared and building. The developer has not named a replacement lead customer for Project Horizon.

ft-1775093225991-3279.text: Blueprint Data Centers is building a 25-megawatt data center on about 10 acres off Westinghouse Road in Georgetown, Williamson County, Texas, a $160 million project of about 45,000 square feet. It is the smaller of the company's two Williamson County sites; the other is a planned 60-megawatt campus in Taylor, and Blueprint says the two together will deliver 85 megawatts by early 2027. The Georgetown City Council granted zoning and a 10-year, 50% property tax abatement for the project in September 2024, and the first phase was expected to operate by late 2026 with completion in early 2027, according to Hello Georgetown, citing the Austin Business Journal. Electricity would come from Georgetown Utility Systems, the city-owned utility, under a commercial rate structure, and in January 2026 the company said both Williamson County sites were moving forward on firm utility commitments and defined energization schedules. After the project was announced, Georgetown residents raised concerns about rate impacts, and Hello Georgetown later clarified that the tax abatement covers property taxes only, not the electricity or water rates, which the company pays at full commercial rates. Georgetown draws most of its water from the Brazos River Authority's lakes, and a project like this must pass a utility capacity review. Blueprint, founded in 2023, took a strategic investment from Northampton Capital Partners in April 2025; its founder and chief executive, Yaerid Jacob, has said, "In Texas today, megawatts on a slide don't mean much if you can't energize them in time." At its Taylor site, a separate lawsuit over the land's use as parkland was dismissed in October 2025, a ruling now on appeal. The company's January 2026 update still targeted power delivery in 2026.

It is the smaller of the company's two Williamson County sites; the other is a planned 60-megawatt campus in Taylor, and Blueprint says the two together will deliver 85 megawatts by early 2027.

The Georgetown City Council granted zoning and a 10-year, 50% property tax abatement for the project in September 2024, and the first phase was expected to operate by late 2026 with completion in early 2027, according to Hello Georgetown, citing the Austin Business Journal.

Electricity would come from Georgetown Utility Systems, the city-owned utility, under a commercial rate structure, and in January 2026 the company said both Williamson County sites were moving forward on firm utility commitments and defined energization schedules.

After the project was announced, Georgetown residents raised concerns about rate impacts, and Hello Georgetown later clarified that the tax abatement covers property taxes only, not the electricity or water rates, which the company pays at full commercial rates.
Georgetown draws most of its water from the Brazos River Authority's lakes, and a project like this must pass a utility capacity review.

Blueprint, founded in 2023, took a strategic investment from Northampton Capital Partners in April 2025; its founder and chief executive, Yaerid Jacob, has said, "In Texas today, megawatts on a slide don't mean much if you can't energize them in time."
At its Taylor site, a separate lawsuit over the land's use as parkland was dismissed in October 2025, a ruling now on appeal.
The company's January 2026 update still targeted power delivery in 2026.

ft-533.text: The Georgetown Data Center at 201 Blue Ridge Drive in Georgetown, Williamson County, Texas, is one of Citigroup's own data centers, a 304,700-square-foot facility the bank opened in 2008. Citigroup filed with the state in 2023 to convert existing equipment rooms into battery rooms, an estimated $500,000 renovation scheduled from March 1 to December 1, 2023, on private land for private use. Citigroup filed a matching $500,000 project at its South West Data Center in Roanoke, Tarrant County, also converting battery rooms into data hall space. The Georgetown building is LEED Gold certified; Citi once ran around 70 data centers and consolidated to about 20 by 2012. Williamson County has 30 operational or planned data centers on nine campuses, mostly along or east of Interstate 35, according to the Austin Free Press, and power availability along the stretch between Hutto, Taylor and the Samsung plant is the main draw, said Dave Porter, executive director of the county's economic development partnership. Governor Greg Abbott ordered a statewide pause on new data center grid connections on August 3, 2026 pending a state audit of the ERCOT queue, a step aimed at new projects rather than this operating Citi facility.

ft-1778016460822-2764.text: Pace, a new data center developer based in Austin, Texas, is planning the Lone Star Project, a data center in Glasscock County, Texas, with an initial 100 megawatts of power from natural gas generated on site. Founders Preston Stein and Chance Pressley announced the project in April 2026 and say the campus could eventually grow to 1 gigawatt of power, though they have not set a date for when it would open. The project is proposed and no vote is scheduled. Pace says it has already lined up the natural gas supply, land, water and fiber connections the project needs, and it will seek extra power from ERCOT, the Texas grid operator, for later phases. Stein, who comes from the oil and gas industry, said the project "is being built around speed to power, disciplined execution, and long-term scalability." Pressley said the goal is "to build a durable platform in Glasscock County grounded in real infrastructure site control, water, fiber, and substantial behind-the-meter gas positioning," meaning power made on site rather than drawn from the grid. Texas law leaves counties such as Glasscock with little power to regulate data centers, since a 2023 state law blocks local governments from imposing rules stricter than the state's, and Governor Greg Abbott has ordered a statewide audit of data centers' energy and water use.

ft-1770304491188-7235.text: The bitcoin mining data center that MARA Holdings, formerly Marathon, built in 2022 beside the Wolf Hollow power plant outside Granbury, in Hood County, Texas, has drawn noise complaints from its neighbors ever since. The site runs about 60,000 computers cooled by industrial fans that residents of the rural Mitchell Bend area say shattered their peace and quiet. Hood County Constable John Shirley measured 91 decibels coming off the site, a level the Centers for Disease Control estimates as roughly between a lawnmower and a chainsaw. Texas law treats 85 decibels as the limit for reasonable noise, and over 2024 Shirley documented more than 35 breaches of it. The CDC says two hours at 90 decibels can damage hearing. More than 40 residents reported illness, including hypertension, heart palpitations, chest pain, vertigo, tinnitus, migraines and panic attacks, with at least ten people seeking emergency or urgent care. Larry Potts, a retired pastor of 77, was rushed to the hospital in February when his heart gave out, kept alive by an external pacemaker and diagnosed with third degree atrioventricular block. Five-year-old Indigo Rosenkranz suffered a seizure on July 6 and was taken to the emergency room. German cardiologist Thomas Munzel, who studies noise and the heart, said the European Environment Agency "tells us that everything above 55 decibels is making us sick," and called levels of 70 to 90 decibels like torture. In 2024, the company said it would replace most of its air-cooled containers with immersion cooling by the end of that year, while acknowledging the risk of converting the technology at that scale. A sound wall built in 2023 at a cost of $1.9 million had made little difference by then. Shirley's fines of $500 each came to about $17,500, against Marathon's revenue of $165 million in the first quarter of 2024, and the company asked for a jury trial to overturn the citations. Since then MARA has built a taller, 24-foot wall and moved 67% of its cooling fans to a liquid cooling system, but residents say the noise remains disruptive. Because Texas counties lack authority to enforce noise limits, residents tried to incorporate the roughly two-square-mile community of about 600 people as the City of Mitchell Bend so it could pass a noise ordinance. MARA sued to block the election, a judge let it proceed, and on November 4, 2025, 62% of the 138 voters rejected incorporation. "We're pleased that Hood County voters saw through the sham incorporation effort and rejected it at the ballot box," a MARA spokesperson said. That leaves the courts. Citizens Concerned About Wolf Hollow, represented by Earthjustice, sued MARA in state court in October 2024 claiming the mine is a private nuisance. After the court rejected MARA's bid to dismiss, the group filed a motion in September 2025 to force the company to hand over its noise records; no ruling on that motion has been published.

ft-1771180842318-5355.text: Eneus Energy, a UK company, wants to build a 2,000 megawatt data center on 1,785 acres near Valley International Airport outside Harlingen, in Cameron County, Texas, with plans that project $14 billion in investment and about 1,000 jobs through 2045. Harlingen passed a 120 day moratorium on new data centers on May 23, 2026, and has since extended it through November 19, 2026 while it studies its ordinances. Eneus Energy is suing Cameron County and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton to block release of records on the project's timelines, water and power use, incentives and land deals. Amani Newman, 22, co-founded a civic group called the For The People Alliance, saying "local activism is going to help disrupt institutional systems that can silence us and keep us in the dark." Mayor Norma Sepulveda said there were "currently no proposed data center projects within Harlingen city limits" when the pause passed, and Commissioner Daniel Lopez said its purpose was "to make sure we as a community understand what's going on...and so that our ordinances reflect what the people of Harlingen want." A separate project, Fluidstack Cameron County, sits about 4 kilometers away at 27751 FM 106, a different address from Eneus Energy's airport-area site, so the two are not the same project. Cameron County has not scheduled a vote on the Eneus Energy project itself; Harlingen's extended moratorium on data centers runs to November 19, 2026.

ft-1784070682843-9282.text: Homebound Group LLC, a Google-linked entity, is building a data center campus that Haskell County calls Journey on 300 acres off Red Creek Road outside Haskell, Haskell County, Texas, under a 2025 county tax abatement. Google says it broke ground there in November 2025 as part of a $40 billion investment in three Texas data centers, two of them in Haskell County. The county abatement waives all county taxes except debt service, in exchange for a payment in lieu of taxes of 25 percent on phase one and a minimum $1 billion investment. "The advantages would be the growth of the economy that we could see here," Mayor Christina Isbell told KTXS, adding that "extra businesses create extra revenue for the city." County Judge Kenny Thompson said it would stay "a small-town atmosphere" once construction crews leave and credited the area's renewable energy for drawing Google. The county approved the Journey abatement alongside a second project, Thelma, in June 2025, and a third, Ranger, in April 2026. A state filing for the project shows an $11.68 million water treatment plant and fire protection system planned at US 380 and Red Creek Road, due to be built from August 2026 to November 2027.

ft-1778596768130-6523.text: Provident Realty Advisors has just under 300 acres under contract in north Hillsboro, in Hill County, Texas, for a data center campus, and the project cannot go ahead unless the city approves a development agreement. The land, the site of the former city airport, belongs to the Hillsboro Economic Development Corporation, is already zoned heavy industrial and sits inside city limits. No megawatt figure, tenant or cost has been published. Provident, a real estate firm, runs a data center platform, Provident Data Centers, with sites in eight states, including a 768-acre project in Dallas with PowerHouse. The development corporation extended Provident's pre-sale contract by four months to allow more due diligence before deciding whether to sell, with the contract running through November 2026 and closing about 45 days after the review period ends. The city has proposed a municipal management district through the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, under which the project would pay extra property taxes to fund its own infrastructure. "They pay the tax payments inside that district for that infrastructure," City Manager Megan Henderson said. "It's over and above the taxes they pay to the city." Residents turned out against it. A crowd packed Historic City Hall for a meeting with Henderson on April 28 that ran more than two hours, and many there opposed data centers. The city then proposed requiring data centers to obtain a specific use permit, which economic development director Jessica Trew said would make a development agreement mandatory. Without it, she said, a data center "could come into a heavy industrial zoned area without an agreement because they do not need a specific use permit." Linda Pauley, founder of Save Hill County, argued that writing data centers into the code would "open the flood gates for a data center." On May 11, after more than two hours of public comment, the Planning and Zoning Commission tabled the change to keep working on it. The county went further. On May 12, 2026, Hill County commissioners voted 3-2 for a one-year moratorium on new data centers in unincorporated areas, the first by a Texas county, with residents citing the Provident plan's noise, water and power use. "The data center folks have found a sweet spot in the state that has limited regulations, limited enforcement, limited code, and they're coming faster than we can keep up with," Commissioner Jim Holcomb said. County Judge Shane Brassell said at least eight data centers are in the works in the county. The county rescinded the moratorium a month later after a developer sued for $100 million. Statewide, Governor Greg Abbott ordered on August 3, 2026 that new data center connections to the ERCOT power grid wait for a state audit, and in September told the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to stop issuing data center permits until the audit is done. In Hillsboro, the decisions rest with the City Council, which must approve any development agreement and the proposed zoning rules, and with the Economic Development Corporation, which decides whether to sell the land. The contract runs through November 2026.

ft-535.text: Serverfarm's data center campus at 15555 Cutten Road in Houston, in Harris County, Texas, called HOU2, is a two-building campus near the former Compaq and HP headquarters in Cypress Creek. Manulife-owned Serverfarm bought the site, built and occupied by HP and later DXC, in 2024, and topped out its second building, the 60 megawatt CTX2, in February 2026. At full build-out the campus spans almost 500,000 square feet with secured customer capacity to scale to 100 megawatts using available grid power, Data Center Dynamics reported. ft-1782347848782-4491.text: Nexus Data Centers is building its Apex DFW campus outside Hubbard in Hill County, Texas, on about 2,000 acres between Highway 171 and County Road 3369. Filings with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation list two buildings at 357 HCR 3372, Nexus Apex DFW HB1 and HB2, each 491,380 square feet and $400 million, with construction running from January 2026 to October 2027 for the first and June 2026 to January 2028 for the second. The Financial Times has reported the campus is being built for Anthropic, with Google providing financial backing. When the plan surfaced in December 2025 it was described as a 600 megawatt natural gas-powered campus, with gas turbines running behind the meter, off the electric grid. An application to the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality describes natural gas engines at 880 State Highway 171 with a total generating capacity for the site of 612.93 megawatts, plus 152.75 megawatts of emergency diesel generation. The ambitions have since grown: by March 2026, citing the Financial Times, Data Center Dynamics described a 2,800-acre campus aiming for 500 megawatts later in 2026 and possibly around 7.7 gigawatts eventually, near a major gas pipeline. Nexus is backed by Transition Equity Partners, and its chief executive is Ivan Van der Walt, who has a background in the energy industry. At a February 2026 hearing on a reinvestment zone, the first step toward a tax abatement, residents asked about water use, environmental impacts, noise, jobs and the changing rural landscape. Amy Teal of Whitney asked why recording had not been allowed at Nexus's November town hall. Nexus said rainwater would be the primary water source, with treated effluent from Hubbard's wastewater plant of up to 100,000 gallons a day and a groundwater well as backup, and said it would design for noise of 65 decibels or less. In April 2026 Nexus withdrew from the tax break talks, and the project went ahead without them. Hill County Judge Shane Brassell has said the county is limited in what it can do since Nexus already purchased the land. The fight then widened to the whole county: on May 12, 2026, after nearly four hours of public comment, the Hill County Commissioners Court voted 3-2 for a one-year pause on new data centers, power plants and large batteries in unincorporated areas, with existing projects such as Nexus exempt. County Judge Shane Brassell said the pause would give officials time to study the effects of data centers before more projects move forward, and Brassell has said at least eight data centers are in the works in the county. RCM Hill, LLC, which is planning a separate 1,235-megawatt data center called Project Aquila on more than 800 acres elsewhere in the county, sued Hill County and the three commissioners who voted for the pause in federal court in Waco, calling the moratorium illegal. On June 4 the Commissioners Court unanimously rescinded the moratorium; one commissioner said, "Unfortunately, we tried." In August 2026 Gov. Greg Abbott ordered the Public Utility Commission of Texas and the state's grid operator, ERCOT, to audit data centers seeking new connections to the power grid before approving them, and said projects that fail to meet water, power and community impact requirements should be denied a connection. Nexus's power plant largely runs behind the meter, off the main grid, so it is unclear how directly the freeze affects the Hubbard project. Hill County has no zoning plan and requires no building permit in unincorporated areas, so most remaining decisions on Nexus rest with the state. The Hill County Commissioners Court, led by Judge Shane Brassell with Commissioners Jim Holcomb and Larry Crumpton among its members, is the body residents have continued to raise concerns with.

ft-1773979399544-6786.text: Iron Mountain is planning a data center campus called Taylor Meadows on about 500 acres on CR 404, just south of Samsung's chip plant, in Taylor's extraterritorial jurisdiction in Williamson County near Hutto, Texas. The proposed campus would have seven buildings, an electric substation and a retention pond, and Iron Mountain has asked the City of Hutto for sewer service in exchange for funding city projects. The Hutto City Council heard the pitch on March 12, 2026, and no further city action has been reported since. The land was part of a tract once approved for nearly 1,900 homes, whose developer will now build a smaller subdivision on the rest. Iron Mountain estimates the seven buildings would need about 30,200 gallons a day of sewer service, less than the homes would have used, because it plans a recycled closed-loop cooling system. "So really, the domestic water demand is limited to just toilets and sinks at that point," said Steven Walton, Iron Mountain's director of site selection. Walton said the facility does not intend to annex into any city, so it would pay no city property tax to Taylor or Hutto. Hutto's leaders were wary of serving a campus that would pay them no property tax. "Data centers are not popular with the people, for the large part," Mayor Pro Tem Dan Thornton said, adding that without property tax from the site, "I'm having a hard time making that case." City Manager James Earp said he would look into whether Iron Mountain could make a payment the city could use for debt service and lower tax or utility rates instead. Eastern Williamson County has become a data center hub because of the power infrastructure built for Samsung's plant; about 30 data centers are operating or proposed in the county, including 14 on three campuses in Taylor. Iron Mountain's would be the second project planned for the corridor around Samsung, after developer KDR's Project Comal on 210 acres nearby. Hutto has not set a date to decide on sewer service; because the site sits outside both Hutto and Taylor, neither city would collect property tax from it regardless of the outcome.

ft-1776265349414-9143.text: Zydeco Development withdrew its plan for a 70 megawatt data center at 450 Ed Schmidt Boulevard in Hutto, Williamson County, Texas, on April 17, 2026. It had sought to change the site from multifamily residential to heavy industrial zoning, and the city called off the April 20 planning and zoning meeting after the withdrawal. Residents organized a grassroots group called Stop The Hutto Data Center and gathered signatures from nearby property owners to trigger a state law requiring a supermajority City Council vote for the rezoning. The group said it had already secured a significant share of the signatures needed before Zydeco withdrew. "This is what happens when neighbors work together and get organized," said co-organizer Katie Martin. City staff had recommended against the zoning change because it conflicted with Hutto's growth plan, and it would have required amending both the future land use map and the SOAR 2040 comprehensive plan. Residents who objected to industrial zoning near their homes said they would stay involved in any future proposal for the land.

ft-537.text: Project Raptor is Colovore's data center at Hutto, Williamson County, Texas, and the first named tenant of an industrial park where State Highway 130 crosses West US 79. Hutto's city council approved it in December 2024 as a $500 million building of 180,000 square feet with 13,000 square feet of flex office, on the Ironwood Tract at 2351 Innovation Boulevard. The park around it is a joint venture of Velocis, Ironwood Realty Partners and MBK Industrial Properties, planned in two phases of three buildings each. Colovore bought its 30 acres in July 2025, inside the 118-acre park now called Hutto Crossing, and the price attached to the project has since come down to $280 million. The company was founded in 2012 to build for enterprises and startups, and is owned by King Street Capital Management. Colovore Austin 1 LLC registered the work with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation as a single story building of 192,694 square feet at 2401 Innovation Boulevard, designed by Ci Design of Dallas, running from December 1, 2026 to December 1, 2028. The halls are to draw 40 megawatts of power and are liquid cooled rather than air cooled, which is the business Colovore has built. The company is aiming the site at large cloud and AI computing firms, chipmakers, and autonomous vehicle, robotics and government customers. The neighboring tract could become a facility for Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos's space technology company. East Williamson County drew this wave of projects because Oncor's agreement to power Samsung's $17 billion semiconductor plant at Taylor brought new transmission capacity across the surrounding countryside. Bill Gravell, then the county judge, told commissioners on February 6, 2024 the county was "seeing tremendous movement in the data-processing center world," and predicted a billion-dollar facility in every one of its cities within two years. A roundup of area projects in December 2025 still described the Colovore building as 180,000 square feet and $500 million, with construction expected to start early in 2026. What is registered with the state is larger, cheaper and a year later; the city has already given its approval, so the next milestone is the December 2026 construction start.

ft-538.text: The Skybox PowerCampus at Hutto, in Williamson County, Texas, is under construction on 159 acres inside a 1,400-acre megasite, developed by Skybox Datacenters with Prologis and is the furthest-along and one of the largest data center projects in the county. Hutto's council approved preliminary annexation, a municipal services agreement for water, wastewater and waste collection, and light industrial zoning on 224 acres on Highway 79 on June 15, 2023; Prologis vice president JC Witt said "the city of Hutto is very attractive for its strong workforce, prime location and pro-growth mindset." On July 20, 2023 the council added a tax agreement exempting half the taxable value of the campus's personal property for ten years, against a minimum $100 million investment; Skybox has put its intended capital investment at $10 billion for 3.9 million square feet across six buildings drawing 600 megawatts of power. Power comes from two private 300-megawatt substations beside a 345 kV transmission line, with buildings designed at 24, 48 or 72 megawatts; the largest is three stories and 700,000 square feet. Skybox and Prologis are now planning a second campus of about 140 acres immediately west of the first, and have separately asked Round Rock to rezone land for another Skybox data center on Old Settlers Boulevard.

ft-540.text: The Mesone data center is proposed on 150 acres at 3911 County Road 305 in Jarrell, Williamson County, Texas, by Prominent Property Group with partners Savannah Developers and Power Infrastructure Partners. The $850 million campus would draw 200 megawatts of power at full build, with water recycled on site and some evaporation expected. Jarrell's city council approved the site's zoning on October 14, 2025, annexing the parcel, changing its land use to Business Park and rezoning it from agriculture to light industrial and warehousing. A dozen residents spoke against the project at a council meeting, among them Houston Brautigan, who moved to Jarrell from Ashburn, Virginia: "I moved 1,200 miles to get away from that. The last thing I want to do is to have one built half a mile from my house." The site sits behind the local high school, and a resident petition argues the campus "threatens to introduce constant noise pollution, heavy truck traffic, and significant water and power consumption" near students. ft-1777471887054-2686.text: OnMine's planned data center in south Killeen, Bell County, Texas, will not be built. The company withdrew its rezoning request for 2.6 acres at 6509 South Fort Hood Street in May 2026, before a Killeen City Council vote set for June 2 that would have needed a supermajority of six votes to pass. The Killeen Planning and Zoning Commission had recommended disapproval in April, after nearly 30 residents raised concerns about noise, water and electricity use; the company said its closed-loop cooling system would use less water. OnMine described its plan as "high-density computational research, AI-driven grid balancing and the operation of a Virtual Power Plant," and city officials asked to call it a "computing and energy research annex" instead of a data center. Five new council members, several of whom had campaigned against data centers, took office after a May 2 election, and incoming Mayor Joseph Solomon said during his campaign he would find it hard to support a project that "doesn't generate meaningful jobs or significantly enhance our economy." Councilman Anthony Kendrick said the applicant made a good decision to withdraw until the public is better educated about data centers: "There was a lot of misinformation out there in reference to data centers. We've got to do some forums and give them the information that they need so everyone understands."
