ft-1765432611408-8215.text: InfraKey Capital wants to build a 1,000 megawatt data center and gas-fired power plant, the Lacy Lakeview Data District, on more than 520 acres of farmland it bought near Elm Mott, north of Waco in McLennan County, Texas. The Lacy Lakeview City Council approved a memorandum of understanding with InfraKey on December 9, 2025 and passed an annexation resolution on January 13, 2026, but the project is still proposed: it still needs an agreement with Waco, which controls water and sewer service to the site, before construction can start. Water is the fight residents keep raising. InfraKey's memorandum of understanding says the finished data district would use and reuse 15 to 16 million gallons of water a day; by comparison, all of Lacy Lakeview bought just over 18.7 million gallons from Waco in the whole month of December, a small fraction of the project's daily need. Mayor Charles Wilson says the city has room: it uses only 20% of the 2.1 million gallons a day it already contracts from Waco, and plans to buy another 665,000 gallons a day of treated wastewater. County Judge Scott Felton was more cautious: "The amount of water needed is a big issue, and then also emissions, air quality. All those things have to be analyzed so that we're totally understanding what the consequence of operations would be besides the positive impacts of growing the tax base." At $10 billion of taxable value, the campus would become the county's largest taxpayer, well above Lacy Lakeview's current tax base of $649 million, with money also going to the Connally school district and McLennan Community College. Residents are not persuaded. A petition against the project reached nearly 3,000 signatures, and a Facebook group opposing it has about 2,500 members. Bob Beechner, a retired Waco firefighter who lives a quarter mile from the site, said he feared a "techno industrial zone" would consume his rural community: "That's a bombshell, man." Bryant Stanton, who runs a stained glass studio a mile away, said of the mayor: "For our mayor not to consider us, I take that as an affront. It's like, who cares about you guys?" The biggest obstacle is Waco, which owns the regional sewer system and holds the water service rights to the site. Lacy Lakeview would have to annex not just the data center property but a three-mile corridor 1,000 feet wide, and InfraKey would have to build a sewer plant to treat up to 2 million gallons a day of wastewater for reuse as cooling water. Waco City Manager Ryan Holt learned of the project from a news article in November 2025, and in April 2026 said his officials still lacked basic information: "If this is so urgent, wouldn't you think engineers would have been in the same room by now?" On May 2, 2026, Lacy Lakeview voters elected a data center opponent to the city council. Mayor Wilson said afterward he hoped to reach an agreement with Waco on the wastewater plan within weeks; no update on that agreement has been published since.

ft-1781208332343-1103.text: BaRupOn's data center near Raywood, in Liberty County, Texas, is part of a 701-acre campus the company calls the Liberty American Multi-Sourced Power and Innovation Hub, or LAMP, which is under construction and targets 3GW of on-site capacity, with an initial 240MW of generation under way. The California medical equipment maker says it broke ground in January 2025 on what began as a chemical plant, and plans to power the site with gas, geothermal, solar and advanced nuclear. "We call ourselves accidental data center builders," chief operating officer Balaji Tammabattula told the Houston Business Journal. The county says it was never told: County Attorney Matthew Poston said its subsidiary, QYK Brands, presented a project on Sept. 24, 2024, that "did not describe a data center as being a part of the project" and centered on plastics used in PPE. Commissioners had asked Poston to pursue enforcement against QYK for starting construction without permits, and he said the company cooperated briefly before renewing work "while failing to cooperate in the manner promised," with fines and fees accruing until final approval. On July 14, 2026, the Commissioners Court approved a preliminary plat for QYK's industrial park 3-1, with Precinct 4 Commissioner Gerald Kolarik dissenting. A proposed QYK concrete batch plant is also before state regulators, who extended the public comment deadline from July 27 to Sept. 11, according to state Rep. Janis Holt. Final county approval still waits on QYK paying the accrued fines and fees.

ft-547.text: Data Center THM1A is a 280,000-square-foot data center under construction at 10357 Loop Road in Haskell, Haskell County, Texas, built by Homebound Group LLC for an estimated $350 million. The state filing lists construction from June 18, 2025 to April 16, 2027, and describes the building as part of the THM campus, with no tenant named. THM stands for Thelma, a Google-linked data center campus in southern Haskell County; Data Center Dynamics reports that the county's tax abatement records tie Homebound Group to Google. A wastewater permit application for the Thelma campus describes five buildings, the first at 280,000 square feet and a second at 350,000 square feet. Google said in November 2025 that construction had begun on its Haskell County project, part of a $40 billion investment in Texas that includes three new campuses in Armstrong and Haskell counties. Homebound also has a second site in northern Haskell County, the Journey campus on Red Creek Road, where two buildings are registered at $400 million each, and a third Google-linked campus nearby got a county tax abatement in April 2026. Haskell County's abatement agreement with Homebound waives 100% of county property taxes on the Journey site for 10 years per phase, except the portion that pays county debt, in exchange for payments made in place of those taxes equal to 25% of what they would have been, at least 50 permanent jobs and a $20,000 yearly donation to local causes. The Haskell County Commissioners Court approved and oversees the abatements, with the county judge administering the agreements, and no hearing on further phases at either campus is currently scheduled.

ft-1783826724382-4737.text: HyperDataGrid, a Texas company, is building a data center outside Lufkin, in Angelina County, on the 40-acre site of the old Northern Chip Mill at Ben Dunn Road and Highway 103 West. Angelina County Judge Keith Wright said in July 2026 that the company had already secured electrical and water agreements and begun clearing land. A second, larger project, Amp Z Data Center, is proposed on the old Southland Paper Mill site on Highway 103 East, but as of July 2026 it had no construction activity and was still waiting on a power agreement with Oncor. "103 West is kind of out of sight, out of mind," Wright said. "But that's the one that's going to move forward first because they're already working on it," he said. Most people in the county did not know the HyperDataGrid project existed. County officials say they have no legal authority to stop either data center from being built; Texas counties do not have zoning power, and state law severely limits what counties can do about development. The county's only lever is a negotiated tax abatement, and only if a company applies for one. HyperDataGrid must still negotiate a road use agreement with commissioners, which the county plans to use to ask for concessions. Commissioners were also weighing a resolution asking the legislature for limited authority over data centers and other large industrial projects, and Wright said state senator Trent Ashby and state representative Rocky Thigpen were open to it. On August 3, 2026, Governor Greg Abbott ordered a statewide pause on new data centers connecting to the power grid pending an audit; HyperDataGrid had already secured its electrical agreement before then.

ft-1771179941512-6019.text: AmpZ Champion Data Center Holdings, of Denver, wants to build a data center on more than 1,000 acres of the old Southland Paper Mill site on State Highway 103 East outside Lufkin, in Angelina County, Texas, and the county cannot stop it. "We have no authority to do a moratorium or stop any type of development in the county," Angelina County Judge Keith Wright told a commissioners court meeting in June 2026, adding: "Texas legislators have consciously limited what counties can do, and they've done it on purpose. They don't trust us." The mill employed nearly 600 people before it stopped operating in 2004, and the site is classed as heavy industrial. The developer calls it Project Lufkin: about 175 megawatts of power in 2026, 1.1 gigawatts by 2028 and 2.1 gigawatts in the end, with up to a gigawatt of that from the proposed Longleaf Power Generation Plant nearby. The city of Lufkin's own fact sheet says the project is in the planning phase and has not been approved for construction, that it would bring about 500 construction jobs and 30 permanent ones, and that a closed-loop cooling system would use about 500 gallons of treated water a day, roughly what three homes use. Because the site is outside the city limits, it is not subject to city zoning or permitting, and Lufkin would get no sales or property tax from it. By July 2026 there was no construction at the site and AmpZ was still waiting on a power agreement with Oncor. Residents began organizing when news of the plan broke in February 2026, asking for transparency and for no tax abatements. In mid-May they rallied before a Lufkin city council meeting and were barred from speaking about it because the data center was not on the agenda; when the county put it on its own agenda in June, fourteen people signed up to speak on water, energy, noise, light and contamination. Shelley Tatum, a Democrat running for Texas House District 9 who grew up near the mill, asked commissioners to refuse any abatement: "That data center is not going to be operating in 10 years." A tax abatement is the county's only lever, and Wright said he would not bring one to the court unless the company first held a public meeting. If AmpZ applies, the county says it will press for noise limits at the property line, generator testing only in daytime and never on Sundays, written water and wastewater limits, a public project website, $250,000 a year for volunteer fire departments and a decommissioning bond. AmpZ did file a preliminary abatement application, which commissioners sent back asking for more detail, and Wright said in July that he had heard nothing from the company since. A second, separate data center is further along: HyperDataGrid is building on the site of the old Northern Chip Mill on Highway 103 West, has secured electrical and water agreements, and has begun clearing land, Wright said. "103 West is kind of out of sight, out of mind. Nobody is really seeing what's happening with that," Wright said. HyperDataGrid will still need a road use agreement with the commissioners court, which Wright said the county would use to ask for concessions, and in July 2026 the court put on its agenda a resolution asking the Texas Legislature to give counties limited regulatory authority over data centers and other large industrial projects.

ft-1771257374268-9257.text: Rowan Digital Infrastructure is building Project Cinco, permitted under the entity name North East Data Center LLC, a 300 megawatt data center campus on 440 acres in Medina County, Texas, west of Lytle. The campus is tailored, the company says, to the long-term needs of a top five US technology company. The site borders County Road 683 on the east and County Road 6712 on the west. Medina County commissioners unanimously approved an 80 percent property tax break for the first 10 years in December 2024. The Lytle City Council extended its extraterritorial jurisdiction over the site in January 2025 and made it a reinvestment zone by a 4-0 vote on March 26, with no public comment. The county deal requires 40 full-time jobs at 120 percent of the county's average wage, and Rowan has said it will ask Lytle to annex the site after the first phase. "Rowan's commitment to transparency, sustainability, and partnership shows what it means to be a good neighbor," Lytle Mayor Ruben Gonzalez said when construction began. Rowan's spokesperson told KSAT the campus will draw its water from the Edwards Aquifer, and aquifer authority general manager Roland Ruiz said the agency has no part in approving such developments. "A lot of times people will wonder, 'Why are you letting all these developments come in?' And, the answer is, we're not," Ruiz said. Natalia resident Rob Scholes, who lives within two miles of the site, said he learned of it only when neighbors were invited to an information session months before construction, after the land was bought. "If the place, a business, that affects all the residents in this area, then yeah, I think we should have some say in what happens and how that happens," Scholes said. Rowan broke ground in late summer 2025 and in February 2026 closed about $550 million of construction financing for the first phase, a 60 megawatt phase due online in 2026. The full 440-acre campus is expected to be fully operational in 2027.

ft-1781279595839-4992.text: Legacy Investing's planned 50-megawatt data center at 1000 Bolton Road, on the former San Antonio Karting Complex near Marion in Guadalupe County, Texas, was approved by Cibolo city staff without a council vote, and residents only learned of it months later. Cibolo's planning department administratively approved Legacy's site plan in April 2026 because the land is zoned for light industrial use, which allows data centers by right. Legacy, a Virginia-based real estate investment firm, plans a 243,000-square-foot building with more than 100,000 square feet of data halls on the 39-acre site, with room to expand to 150 MW, ready by the fourth quarter of 2027, built for AI inference with direct-to-chip cooling and closed chilled-water loops. Power would come from the Guadalupe Valley Electric Cooperative, which says it has more than enough, and water from the Green Valley Special Utility District; the projected water demand equals that of 33 single-family homes. District 4 Councilmember Katie Cunningham said the council had been told in 2025 that utilities lacked the power and water for a data center: "I'm angry about the process. Whether or not it was legally permissible to approve this administratively, the community and council should have known this was a real possibility, especially after being told it wasn't feasible." Place 3 Councilwoman Marissa-Ellen Patterson shared city and utility presentations with residents, saying her goal was "to make sure that the public has accurate information." A town hall on the project was scheduled for August 17, 2026 at Steele High School, followed by a special council meeting; no report on what happened there has been published. Cibolo's ordinance subcommittee recommended in July that the full council review the approval process and set development standards for water, energy use, pollution and noise; state law lets the project proceed where zoning already allows it, and a new state law, Senate Bill 6, only requires large loads of 75 MW or more to cover the cost of connecting to the grid. The decisions on Cibolo's data center rules rest with the City Council and its Planning and Zoning Commission.

ft-1783831945621-4547.text: Belltown Power plans a 1,500 megawatt data center, the Kahla Project, on private land near Marquez in Leon County, Texas. County Judge Byron Ryder said the company told him it would be a $15 billion project: "They were hoping to get half of it done in '26 and the other half in '27, like they were talking about tonight, speeding it up," he said at a January 2026 town hall. Ryder said the county has little power to stop a project on private land: "We can make it difficult for them, and we probably will make it difficult for them, but we really can't make, we can't keep them from coming if they want to come." Nearly 200 residents of the county, whose population is about 17,000, turned out for the January town hall, where Ryder said Belltown Power had given little explanation of the project's specifics. Resident Daniel McCoslin said, "We're hoping that the EPA and TCEQ can help file lawsuits against these companies because the quality of air that these data centers emit and the danger to the environment, we have 11 endangered species that exist in Leon County." He vowed residents would "make a stand until they run bulldozers through the pastures, and it's going to be a long, drawn-out fight for us." He also raised the toll on farms nearby: "it's going to be a huge detriment on ranchers in general. And we have a lot of chicken farms here. So the constant noise and lights will destroy our poultry business here as well." The county's main leverage is tax policy: Ryder said officials would withhold a tax abatement, "so that might discourage it right there." Officials also said they plan to form a 391 sub-regional planning commission to coordinate with other agencies on construction.

ft-548.text: Barrio Energy plans two 10-megawatt data centers in Matagorda County, Texas, and residents have organized against them. A petition from the group Matagorda County Against Data Centers had gathered more than 300 signatures by April 2026, and the county's economic development corporation has answered it point by point. Barrio said in August 2025 the first site would open by the end of 2025 and the second in early 2026; the project is still listed as proposed, with no report of either site opening. Barrio announced the two sites for advanced computing, modular data centers and cryptocurrency mining, both connected to ERCOT's South Zone, together totaling 20 megawatts. The county's economic development director described one as 10 megawatts sitting on 4 acres. Barrio, based in Houston and founded in 2022 by former Chevron team lead Ivan Pinney, runs similar sites in Monahans, George West, Lolita and Tyler, with clients including cryptomining operations. Residents say the county is the wrong place. "I'm not completely against data centers, but I believe data centers belong in a better place, not small rural communities," said Donna Howard of Matagorda County Against Data Centers. "How is this going to affect our water table? How is this going to affect our farmers?" asked Cheryl Wilkins, another member. "We should have a say so. We should have an opinion; our opinion should matter," said Angelica Hernandez. The petition says three data centers are seeking to locate in the county and warns of "significant noise, air, water, and light pollution" and higher electric costs, in a county on a major bird migration route. It claims a 10-megawatt data center uses as much electricity as 8,000 to 10,000 homes. The Matagorda County Economic Development Corporation disputes those numbers, saying a 10-megawatt facility equals about 2,500 homes under ERCOT standards and that Barrio's sites are flexible loads that power down when prices and demand spike. It says the projects would use "zero local water" with closed-loop cooling, would be about 37 decibels, and would not put upgrade costs on residents. "So this isn't a large data center," director Michael Ferdinand told ABC13, adding that ERCOT classifies large facilities as starting at 75 megawatts, and that the company had not approached the Lower Colorado River Authority for water. "10 megawatts is still large, I feel like they're downplaying," Howard said. Statewide, new data center approvals in Texas are frozen: Governor Greg Abbott ordered ERCOT and the Public Utility Commission in August 2026 to audit data centers in the grid queue before more move forward, and in September told the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to stop issuing permits for data center projects until that review is done. Ferdinand said ERCOT helps approve facilities like these based on the grid. "But at least we can voice as constituents what it is we want," Howard said.

ft-1785354243651-4603.text: Galaxy Digital's Project Merlin, a data center campus of more than $400 million on almost 500 acres in the city's industrial park in McGregor, McLennan County, Texas, has set off a petition to recall the town's mayor. The McGregor City Council approved the land sale to GXMG LLC, a Galaxy subsidiary, in a closed session at a special called meeting on June 22, 2026. Galaxy says the campus will start with 75 megawatts of grid power from 2028 and could grow into a multi-hundred-megawatt campus by 2030. Dennis Fehler, a fourth-generation McGregor native, started the recall petition in late June, calling the closed-door land sale "a noon special meeting" with "poor public notice (and) closed sessions." By mid-July more than 60 people had signed his petition; the recall movement needs at least 100 signatures before it can move toward changing city leadership. "He's the captain of the Titanic, and that's why we're going to get rid of him," Fehler said of Mayor Jim Lilley. Galaxy told the council each building would use about 3,000 gallons of water a day in closed-loop cooling, with a cap City Manager Kevin Evans said is written into the contract at "a total maximum of 30,000 gallons a day." "Any infrastructure upgrades that we need for our power, it's on us. We pay for that. It comes out of our pocket," Galaxy's Drew Luna told the council. The city says it made $7.5 million on the land sale and that Galaxy will pay property taxes on a $130 million base with no tax breaks, while building and paying for its own substation and any needed transmission upgrades. The closed-door approval follows years of water violations tied to SpaceX testing at the same park, where a groundwater district has cited the city three years running for overpumping wells and has demanded it obtain rights for the extra water and pay a fine. Governor Greg Abbott's statewide moratorium on new data center grid connections, ordered August 3, 2026 pending an audit of the ERCOT queue, could affect the timing of Project Merlin's first 75 megawatts. City leaders said construction would not begin for several months after the June vote.

ft-550.text: Experian's data center at 3400 South Stonebridge Drive in McKinney, Collin County, Texas, is a mostly underground building with 16-inch concrete walls built to hold consumer credit records, according to a 2014 report from inside it. Property records reviewed by Data Center Dynamics show a company called EvoDC McKinney Data Center LLC bought a 75,000-square-foot building at the same address in 2021, and DCD said the building was likely the same one, though it could not confirm the change with Experian or the buyer, Evocative. The building held nearly 1,000 servers and had round-the-clock guards, badge and hand scans and more than 10,000 intrusion sensors, with its data mirrored at a similar center nearby, and its monthly energy bill ran about $70,000, down from $100,000 after efficiency work. Evocative, which bought the VPLS hosting business that the 2021 sale record names, has not said publicly whether it now operates the McKinney building; that 2021 property record remains the newest information found on the question.

ft-1772656231892-1875.text: Project Pumpkin 2A is a $400 million, 761,000 square foot data center building registered at 8830 County Road 21 near Miami, in Roberts County, Texas, by IP Meitner Land LLC, an affiliate of the energy developer Intersect. It is part of the Meitner Energy Center, which Google and Intersect announced on June 4, 2026 as a Google data center built alongside more than a gigawatt of new wind, solar and battery storage across Gray and Roberts Counties. The state register lists work from February 6, 2026 to December 14, 2027, designed by HDR Engineering, and names the county as Gray. DCD called that a likely error, since Miami is in Roberts County, about 23 miles northeast of Pampa. Most of the site's power is to come from the co-located renewables from day one, with on-site gas firming a minority share, and Google says the building will be air-cooled with water limited to domestic uses such as restrooms. Google closed its purchase of Intersect in March 2026. Alphabet had announced the $4.75 billion cash acquisition in December 2025, and Meitner is the first project the two have announced since. "Our partnership with Google and Intersect has been instrumental in aligning this infrastructure initiative with our Gray County priorities," Gray County Judge Chris Porter said. Google is also setting up the Caprock Workforce Hub, an 800 acre camp for up to 3,500 construction workers in nearby Wheeler County. In Pampa, Mayor Mike Borger said Gray County commissioners required waterless cooling as a condition of the tax abatement, and that the county's tax base would grow from $1.6 billion to $4.6 billion in 10 years. Pampa Chamber of Commerce chief Cortnie Hale told KVII that residents' concerns about water are valid, and Google declined an interview about the project's economic impact and water use, providing a statement instead. Google said on June 4, 2026 that the data center had recently begun construction.

ft-551.text: FO Permian Partners and HiVolt Energy hold an option on 320 acres about 30 minutes southeast of downtown Midland, in Midland County, Texas, which they are marketing as an off-grid data center site powered by local natural gas. No data center company had signed on when the partners announced the site in September 2025. FO Permian co-founder Davis Farish said at the time, "we still have a steep hill to climb to attract a premier data center builder to West Texas." The first phase would offer 150 megawatts of power generated on-site rather than drawn from the grid, about what the whole city of Midland uses in its lowest-demand winter hours, according to the Midland Reporter-Telegram. HiVolt, an independent power producer, would run natural-gas engines backed by a battery system; the site is part of a larger 3,200-acre tract, and the partners say more than 5 gigawatts of gas supply stands behind it. Farish put the construction and hardware investment at nearly $4.5 billion. Both firms are based in Midland. HiVolt's chief commercial officer Andy Deck said that mattered: "A lot of times, big projects like this, people take a lot of value out of the Permian Basin. We liked the ability to keep value in the Permian Basin." Water is the local worry. The partners say the site has established industrial water supplies, and in May 2026 Midland Mayor Lori Blong said the city should not sell data centers municipal water: "I believe the only appropriate way for data centers to be developed in West Texas is for them to solve their own water solutions and their own power solutions, and that it be out away from neighborhoods and families." Midland County Judge Terry Johnson said three different data center groups, all describing closed-loop cooling and on-site gas generation, have approached the county. "These folks want to be good neighbors, so they're always trying to improve what they're doing," Johnson said. Midland's officials have set out conditions rather than rules: developers should bring their own power and their own water, and build away from homes. The next decisions are in Austin: the Public Utility Commission of Texas is collecting water-use data from data centers and must report to state leaders by the end of 2026, and data center power and water are expected to come before the Texas Legislature in 2027. On September 21, 2026, Gov. Greg Abbott ordered the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to stop issuing new permits for data centers until ERCOT and the Texas Water Development Board finish auditing the industry, a pause that would apply to this project if it moves toward construction.

ft-556.text: Soluna Holdings has secured land for Project Fei, its planned solar-powered data center near Childress, Texas, and said in July 2026 that it has begun raising money and designing construction; construction itself has not started. The project was announced in August 2025 as a 100-megawatt site colocated with a 240-megawatt solar farm. In its second-quarter results on August 13, 2026, Soluna said it had raised Fei's power to 240 megawatts to run AI computing. Fei is named after Dr. Fei-Fei Li, the computer scientist who founded the ImageNet data set. Soluna is still negotiating power contracts and working with ERCOT, the Texas grid operator, to connect the project; its July update said interconnection studies for Fei and for its Project Annie were nearing completion. Soluna's business puts data centers next to wind and solar plants that have more power than the grid can use; it said it was running about 192 megawatts across three sites as of August 1, 2026. Separately, Crusoe and Lancium announced a much larger, 1-gigawatt AI data center campus on 270 acres in Childress on July 15, 2026, expected to begin construction in the third quarter of 2026 and create more than 100 long-term jobs. What decides Fei's own timing is its ERCOT grid connection and the financing Soluna is still raising.

ft-557.text: Project Hedy is a wind-powered data center Soluna Holdings plans near Lyford, in Willacy County. Nothing has been built: in June 2026 Soluna said Hedy was still advancing through the interconnection and transmission process. In August it raised the planned size from 120 to 198 megawatts and redesignated the power for AI workloads. Soluna's own April 2025 announcement does not mention Lyford or Willacy County; it describes a site co-located with a 200 megawatt wind farm in neighbouring Cameron County, owned by a multinational conglomerate it did not name. At that point the company had signed only a term sheet for power, with the power purchase agreement, land agreements and ERCOT planning still to be finalized. DCD noted that both RWE and Duke Energy run 200 megawatt onshore wind farms in Cameron County, and that no development timeline was disclosed. Soluna's other Willacy County site, Project Kati, is the one that has moved: the Texas Tribune reported in October 2025 that the 166 megawatt campus beside the Las Majadas wind project was due to begin partial operation that December. "Value is how counties survive," Willacy County Judge Aurelio "Keter" Guerra told the Tribune. Cameron County's commissioners court adopted a resolution in April 2026 opposing open-loop evaporative cooling and other high-volume uses of drinking water in large data centers, while acknowledging that counties "do not possess general zoning authority."

ft-1786992679173-8336.text: Project Big Pine is a planned data center campus at the TexAmericas Center industrial park near New Boston in Bowie County, Texas, being marketed by the developer Potentia Development. In August 2026 Potentia, based in The Woodlands, said it was looking for a hyperscale, AI, neocloud or other data center operator to anchor the 450-acre site, and that it would power the campus with its own on-site generation rather than a grid connection. TexAmericas Center and Potentia first announced the project in April 2026, describing a campus of about 500 acres for data centers, AI and other power-intensive users. They put the investment at an estimated $3.5 billion at full buildout, with about 120 permanent jobs. Potentia says it can energize the site 20 to 30 months after a qualifying operator signs on, and that it has advanced natural gas delivery plans with interstate pipeline operators. A permanent grid connection is being pursued separately with the AEP utility SWEPCO; Potentia says a SWEPCO screening found room on an adjacent 345kV line for 300MW in 2032, 200MW more in 2034 and another 300MW in 2036, subject to Southwest Power Pool studies. TexAmericas Center executive director Scott Norton said at least six companies had shown interest, and that tenants would not draw power from the traditional grid. The companies also point to tax breaks at the site: Foreign Trade Zone No. 258, an Opportunity Zone designation and the Texas large data center sales and use tax exemption. "The first question serious users and infrastructure investors ask is simple: when can the power turn on?" Potentia CEO Carl Quesinberry said. No end user has been named. Big Pine arrives as opposition to data centers grows across Bowie County. Residents took their concerns to the Bowie County Commissioners Court in August 2026, and signs against the facilities have gone up around the county. Opponents call the Leary and Red Lick area "ground zero" for several proposed sites, and many say developers bought land under nondisclosure agreements. "This was something that we didn't know about because this was signed under an N.D.A., so we didn't have an opportunity to speak our concerns about this operation, and yes we are all very concerned," said Dr. Jamie Davis, who lives in that area. Nancy White of the Legislative Energy Action Foundation told commissioners that her group helped Van Zandt County adopt a moratorium, and said "We actually had four projects pull out since our moratorium with no legal recourse." On August 28, 2026 the commissioners approved the sale of roughly 582 acres for a proposed AI data center after more than two hours of heated public comment, the Texarkana Gazette reported. Big Pine itself does not go through the county. TexAmericas Center serves as the single local permitting authority for the project, which officials say shortens approvals. What decides whether it is built is whether Potentia signs an anchor operator, and its long-term grid supply depends on SWEPCO and the Southwest Power Pool's study process. Wider data center rules in the county rest with the Bowie County Commissioners Court, which took no action on the data center debate at its August 10 meeting.

They put the investment at an estimated $3.5 billion at full buildout, with about 120 permanent jobs.
Potentia says it can energize the site 20 to 30 months after a qualifying operator signs on, and that it has advanced natural gas delivery plans with interstate pipeline operators.

A permanent grid connection is being pursued separately with the AEP utility SWEPCO; Potentia says a SWEPCO screening found room on an adjacent 345kV line for 300MW in 2032, 200MW more in 2034 and another 300MW in 2036, subject to Southwest Power Pool studies.
TexAmericas Center executive director Scott Norton said at least six companies had shown interest, and that tenants would not draw power from the traditional grid.
The companies also point to tax breaks at the site: Foreign Trade Zone No. 258, an Opportunity Zone designation and the Texas large data center sales and use tax exemption.
"The first question serious users and infrastructure investors ask is simple: when can the power turn on?" Potentia CEO Carl Quesinberry said.
No end user has been named.
Big Pine arrives as opposition to data centers grows across Bowie County.
Residents took their concerns to the Bowie County Commissioners Court in August 2026, and signs against the facilities have gone up around the county.
Opponents call the Leary and Red Lick area "ground zero" for several proposed sites, and many say developers bought land under nondisclosure agreements.

"This was something that we didn't know about because this was signed under an N.D.A., so we didn't have an opportunity to speak our concerns about this operation, and yes we are all very concerned," said Dr. Jamie Davis, who lives in that area.

Nancy White of the Legislative Energy Action Foundation told commissioners that her group helped Van Zandt County adopt a moratorium, and said "We actually had four projects pull out since our moratorium with no legal recourse."
On August 28, 2026 the commissioners approved the sale of roughly 582 acres for a proposed AI data center after more than two hours of heated public comment, the Texarkana Gazette reported.
Big Pine itself does not go through the county.
TexAmericas Center serves as the single local permitting authority for the project, which officials say shortens approvals.
What decides whether it is built is whether Potentia signs an anchor operator, and its long-term grid supply depends on SWEPCO and the Southwest Power Pool's study process.
Wider data center rules in the county rest with the Bowie County Commissioners Court, which took no action on the data center debate at its August 10 meeting.

ft-562.text: CloudBurst is building a 1,200-megawatt data center campus at 2955 Francis Harris Lane, on the line between Hays and Guadalupe counties near New Braunfels, Texas, outside the city limits and extraterritorial jurisdiction of both San Marcos and New Braunfels. Guadalupe County, not Hays, holds jurisdiction over the site and its planned gas power plant, according to Hays County development services director Marcus Pacheco, and it was Guadalupe County commissioners who approved the project's development agreement and tax abatement. Guadalupe County commissioners first voted down a $500 million property tax abatement 3 to 2 on February 24, 2026, citing water concerns; Commissioner Stephen Germann said, "As a commissioner, I say we are out of water." On April 21, after nearly four hours of public comment, commissioners approved a development agreement and tax abatement 3 to 2, covering 706 acres and 90 percent of county taxes on improvements for five years, phasing down to 40 percent by year ten. "I do not oppose data centers overall, but there is no direct, articulable benefit" to locating one in a specific community, Commissioner Jacqueline Ott said, voting no. CloudBurst and partner Evolve broke ground on November 5, 2025, and the campus is to run on its own gas-fired power under a supply agreement with Energy Transfer, with the first 50-megawatt phase due online in the fourth quarter of 2026. On September 21, 2026, Gov. Greg Abbott ordered the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to stop issuing new data center permits until ERCOT and the Texas Water Development Board finish auditing the industry's power and water use, a hold that now applies to any further environmental permits CloudBurst needs for its remaining buildout.

ft-1784673433709-2419.text: About seven miles southeast of Vernon, in Wilbarger County, Texas, Google is building a data center campus that its state filings value at $1 billion. Two registrations with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation, Project Rise 1A and Rise 2A, each describe a $500 million, 991,000 square foot data center at FM 2897 South, owned by Planton Investments LLC and Platon Investments LLC at Google's Mountain View headquarters address. The filings put the work between March 31, 2026 and the end of March 2028. Vernon depends entirely on groundwater from the Seymour Aquifer, drawn from five well fields. In September 2026 the city asked customers to cut their use by 20 percent under Stage 2 of its drought plan, after the static aquifer level fell to 37.82 feet, about 3.8 inches above the point at which restrictions become mandatory. Google says the campus will be air-cooled, with water use limited mainly to domestic needs such as kitchens. On September 1 it gave the city $4.5 million to replace an aging water pipeline, but did not say which section, how long it is or when the work would happen, and the Vernon Daily Record noted the money is not an agreement to supply more water to the data center. "Without Google's support, this project would not have been possible," Mayor Pam Gosline said. The clearest public numbers about the people who will work there come from wastewater permits rather than from Google. Platon has applied to the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality for a plant near Oklaunion treating up to 130,000 gallons a day, sized for about 2,215 people on site across a 24 hour period, and for a second plant of 20,000 gallons a day sized for 440, which would discharge into Boggy Creek and on to Beaver Creek and the Wichita River. Neither application names Google or a data center, and the paper cautioned that the figures are engineering assumptions, not job commitments; Google has given no job figure for the site. Power is to come from generation that AES is building alongside the campus and will sell to it under 20-year agreements. County Judge Greg Tyra said the county had "worked closely with the Google and AES teams for the last couple of years" before the February 2026 announcement.

ft-563.text: APR Energy planned an 800-acre, 400-megawatt data center at Pampa, in Gray County, Texas, powered by natural gas turbines on site rather than the grid, with local business backing in June 2025 and a first phase originally slated for early 2026. The project's future is uncertain: Elon Musk bought APR Energy in a deal cleared by the Federal Trade Commission in May 2026, and Data Center Dynamics reported in July that it is unclear whether the Pampa data center will go ahead. APR, a Jacksonville, Florida company that deploys mobile gas turbines, said it picked Pampa for its access to water, fiber and natural gas, and that the data center could consume up to 1.5 million gallons of water a day. The Texas State Water Plan estimates new data centers statewide could lead to a nine million acre-foot water shortfall within a decade, Data Center Dynamics reported. Gray County commissioners required a different Pampa data center, Intersect's Meitner project, to use cooling that does not rely on water as a condition of its tax abatement, Mayor Mike Borger said; APR's plan makes no such commitment. On September 21, 2026, Gov. Greg Abbott ordered the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to stop issuing new data center permits until the state's grid operator, ERCOT, and the Texas Water Development Board finish auditing the industry. The new owner's record with gas turbines has drawn scrutiny elsewhere: Musk's xAI ran as many as 35 turbines without permits at its Memphis data centers, prompting a Clean Air Act lawsuit. As of July 2026, it remained unclear whether Musk's company would build the Pampa data center at all.

ft-564.text: Soluna's Project Annie is a proposed data center in northeast Texas, next to a solar farm built with a renewable energy developer the company has not named. The company now calls Annie a 74 megawatt Bitcoin hosting site being developed for a potential new customer, with capital raising and modular construction design underway, Soluna said in its June 2026 update. Soluna announced Annie in May 2025 as a 75 megawatt data center beside a 114 megawatt solar farm, its first project powered by solar rather than wind. It had signed a power procurement agreement and said its next steps were definitive power purchase agreements, land agreements and planning with ERCOT, the Texas grid operator. "It's our first project tapping solar energy, and it paves the way for sustainable computing that works in harmony with the sun," CEO John Belizaire said. The project is named after Annie Easley, the NASA computer scientist and mathematician. Soluna's project page still describes Annie as "designed for sustainable Bitcoin and AI compute." Its July 2026 update said capital formation and construction design had begun for Annie and Project Fei, another Soluna site in north Texas, and that ERCOT interconnection studies for both were nearing completion. Soluna places computing, including Bitcoin mining and AI, next to wind, solar and hydroelectric plants to use their surplus power, and it operated about 192 megawatts across three energized sites as of August 1, 2026. What decides Annie's timing now is the ERCOT interconnection study, Soluna's financing and whether its prospective customer signs. Gov. Greg Abbott ordered the Public Utility Commission and ERCOT on August 3, 2026, to audit every data center seeking to connect to the Texas grid before approving new connections, requiring disclosure of tax breaks, water and power use, cooling technology and ownership.

ft-574.text: The Pyote data center in Ward County, Texas, run by bitcoin miner Genesis Digital Assets, is being converted to work for artificial intelligence companies. Data center developer AiOnX bought a 77 percent stake in Genesis Digital Assets for $500 million in a deal that closed June 15, 2026, and plans to convert the site's computing power, now used to mine bitcoin, to run AI and heavy computing work instead. Genesis Digital Assets announced the West Texas site in November 2021 as a bitcoin mining operation with a planned capacity of 300 megawatts of power, drawing electricity from the Texas grid run by the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, known as ERCOT. By February 2025 the company had energized 195 megawatts at Pyote, adding two 20-megawatt buildings, and said on its website the site could expand to 370 megawatts. SWI Group, AiOnX's parent company, said Genesis Digital Assets operates 15 crypto data centers in the United States and Sweden with 1.3 gigawatts, or 1,300 megawatts, of power available, and that all of them will be converted for artificial intelligence and high-performance computing, the heavy calculations AI systems need. "Power connectivity is the most valuable commodity in digital infrastructure today, and converting legacy cryptocurrency mining infrastructure to AI and high-performance computing is the best and highest use of these assets," said SWI founder and chief executive Max-Herve George. AiOnX and SWI Group now control the decisions on converting Pyote to AI work. Neither company has said when construction at the site might start or named a customer for the converted capacity.

ft-583.text: The Cornerstone Southwest Data Center, this site's listing for Citigroup's South West Data Center at 931 Litsey Road in Roanoke, is one of the bank's own data centers in the Dallas-Fort Worth area, in Denton County, Texas. Citigroup's 2022 state filing for the building lists Tarrant County, but Census Bureau geocoding of the address places it in Denton County. The facility is operating. In 2023, Citigroup filed to convert existing battery rooms into data hall and support space at an estimated cost of $500,000, with work scheduled from March 1 to December 1, 2023; it filed a matching $500,000 project at its Georgetown Data Center north of Austin the same year. In 2017, Citi said the Roanoke site would be 50 percent powered by renewable energy from MP2 Energy. North Texas has become the nation's leading data center market, according to Cushman and Wakefield, and Fort Worth has adopted a moratorium, filing requirements and a task force for new data center projects, though the moratorium does not apply to projects already under construction.

ft-1788613407895-5221.text: Bitdeer, the bitcoin miner that runs AI cloud services through its Bitdeer AI subsidiary, has bought 200 acres of former Alcoa smelter land near Rockdale, in Milam County, Texas, to build AI data center infrastructure next to its existing Rockdale facility. The company announced on September 1, 2026 that it had paid about $100 million in cash for the parcel. The land was part of the Alcoa aluminum plant, a site of some 33,000 acres where smelting ended in 2008 and the plant shut completely in 2017. Pieces of it have since been sold, reportedly including 4,000 acres to SoftBank in June 2026, and SoftBank's energy arm SB Energy is building a data center elsewhere in Milam County that OpenAI will lease as part of its Stargate network. Bitdeer says its Milam County sites, including the new parcel, have about 563 megawatts of interconnected grid capacity, with plans to reach 742 megawatts, and a dedicated water supply. After the purchase it owns or operates about 255 acres in the county, and the company says it will keep mining bitcoin at the existing site while it develops the new land. "Rockdale is one of the best-connected locations in our portfolio, and we believe it is well positioned to receive additional power over the coming years", said chief financial officer Michael G. Potter. No tenant, building count or construction date has been announced. Growing beyond the current connection depends on the Texas grid, where new data center approvals are on hold. On August 3, 2026, Governor Greg Abbott ordered the Public Utility Commission and ERCOT to audit data centers in the grid's interconnection queue before any more are approved, and ERCOT paused its review of the first group of large projects. ERCOT was tracking more than 1,800 projects seeking about 474 gigawatts, more than five times the grid's record peak, and Abbott said about 90% of the requests were data centers. On September 21 he went further and told the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to issue no permits sought by data center projects until the audits are done, which ERCOT has said could run until December, according to Politico. During the pause ERCOT must verify that large projects are ready to be built, with a lease or deed and permits; the verification does not look at water use, noise or other effects on neighbors. ft-1768854703438-7754.text: Riot Platforms, a bitcoin mining company, is building AI data center capacity at its Rockdale, Texas, campus, and in August 2026 signed a $9.1 billion lease there with Anthropic. Rockdale is a city of about 5,300 people in Milam County, 41 miles west of College Station. Its economy was built around an Alcoa aluminum smelter that wound down between 2008 and 2014, cutting hundreds of jobs and shrinking the tax base. Riot Platforms, then called Riot Blockchain, built a bitcoin mining operation on the old Alcoa site, using the power substations and lines Alcoa left behind. The facility began construction in 2019 and started running in 2020. Rockdale Mayor Ward Roddam has credited the miners with reviving the town, saying they have invested more than $1 billion and become among the largest taxpayers in Milam County and its school district. Asked about the industry's critics, Roddam said: "Are these the actions of people who don't care about rural Texas? No." The Rockdale site is Riot's flagship, with 700 megawatts of developed capacity across seven buildings. The company says it has run bitcoin mining computers there around the clock using both air and immersion cooling. Greenpeace, which campaigns against bitcoin mining's energy use, has called Rockdale the most energy and carbon-intensive bitcoin mine in the U.S. In January 2026, Riot bought the 200 acres under the Rockdale facility outright for $96 million, funded by selling about 1,080 bitcoin from its own holdings. The company signed AMD as its first data center tenant: an initial 25 megawatts of computing capacity with room to grow to 200 megawatts, under a 10-year lease Riot valued at up to $1 billion if all extension options are used. Permits filed with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation describe a 40,000-square-foot addition at the site, called "Building G," with an estimated construction cost of $75 million. In August 2026, Riot disclosed a far larger deal: a 20-year lease worth $9.1 billion, running through June 2048, to supply 191 megawatts of computing capacity to a company it described only as a "leading frontier AI lab." Bloomberg later identified the counterparty as the AI company Anthropic. Riot said it would deliver 96 megawatts by December 2027 and the full 191 megawatts by June 2028, and that two five-year extension options could raise the deal's value to $16.1 billion. Riot financed the early construction with a $573 million loan from Morgan Stanley. Chief executive Jason Les said the Anthropic and AMD leases together gave Riot about $9.8 billion in contracted data center revenue, all signed within six months. On August 3, 2026, Governor Greg Abbott announced a moratorium on approving data centers until state regulators audit those seeking to connect to the Texas grid, including their tax breaks, power and water use and ownership.

ft-1783830765394-1466.text: Giga Energy plans a $384 million data center on County Road 2656 near Royse City, in Hunt County, Texas, on about 30 acres, calling it a micro data center for artificial intelligence computing. The project was first registered with the state on June 23, 2026 as BT Gateway Data Center LLC; in July, county officials said Giga Energy had taken it over, and state records now list the owner as Giga AFM LLC of Buna. Water has become one of the main worries for neighbors, company co-founder Brent Whitehead told the county commissioners court in July 2026. He said a closed-loop cooling system, filled once with water and glycol, would hold yearly use to about that of two and a half homes, mostly for restrooms and sinks. On noise, he promised ground-level equipment, a permanent sound wall and studies meant to keep road traffic louder than the finished plant. Whitehead said Hunt County was chosen because unused electrical capacity is already available through Farmers Electric Cooperative, so no new substation is needed, and that Giga would pay for any upgrades itself. The company is not seeking tax abatements, and estimates about $7.2 million a year in county property tax, 300 construction jobs and 20 to 24 permanent technical jobs. The state filing gives no megawatt figure, cooling method or water demand. Data Center Dynamics reported that BT Gateway Data Center LLC shares an address with Belltown Power, a Texas renewable energy developer that lists ten data center sites totaling 4.1 gigawatts, suggesting Belltown may have a bigger hand in the project than Giga has said. Giga held a town hall on July 30, 2026, at Smoke Sessions BBQ in Royse City; the company targets completion in mid-2027, and no report on the meeting has been published since.

ft-1767733844424-8213.text: Skybox Datacenters, working with the city as Skybox/Emergent, wants to build a data center campus on about 350 acres of city-owned land northeast of San Angelo, in Tom Green County, Texas, near U.S. Highway 67 North and City Farm Road. The San Angelo City Council approved rezoning for the project 6-1 on January 13, 2026, after residents raised concerns at a community meeting the month before. The campus is planned as six four-story buildings and would draw up to 600 megawatts of power, built in phases running from 12 to 18 months after groundbreaking through 2030. The council first authorized the city manager to negotiate a purchase and sale agreement with Skybox in May 2025, at $50,000 an acre, or about $17.4 million for the land. Michael Looney of the chamber of commerce said the campus could generate $27 million a year in franchise fees and, at an estimated $21 to $22 billion valuation, could nearly triple the city's $7.9 billion property tax base without city incentives. Power would come from the AEP Red Creek substation, which Looney said the city currently uses only about a tenth of, so the project would not take capacity meant for San Angelo. More than 20 residents spoke at the January 13 council meeting; one said, "There are significant water concerns that I and many other residents have regarding the data center," while another called it "a once-in-a-generation opportunity to shift and reduce the tax burden on our citizens." Council member Mary Coffey answered complaints about secrecy: "So just because you ask a question and we're not able to give you that answer does not mean it's a lack of transparency. It just means that we're still learning as we go." The council has since written rules for the project: land use regulations passed 6-0 on May 19, 2026, a sewer and discharge ordinance 5-1 on June 2, and a water usage ordinance 7-0 on June 16. The water ordinance requires closed-loop cooling and caps the initial fill at 8 gallons per square foot of building, which for a 250,000-square-foot building works out to roughly 2 million gallons once and about 60,000 gallons a year in make-up. Mayor Tom Thompson said: "If water use is not sustainable, it should not move forward." The city says it has received no development application yet, and any final project still needs council approval in an open meeting, along with a 380 agreement setting out community benefits and local hiring.

ft-607.text: The San Marcos City Council voted 5-2 early on February 18, 2026, to deny the rezoning that Highlander SM One LLC needed for a $1.5 billion data center on a 200-acre site at 904 Francis Harris Lane in San Marcos, Hays County, Texas. Four months later, on June 16, the council voted 4-3 to ban data centers anywhere in the city, the first Texas city to do so, and the ban stands unless the council reverses it or a court strikes it down. The site sits next to the Hays Energy power plant between San Marcos and New Braunfels. When the vote came at 2:14 a.m., the overflow room roared with cheers. At least 300 people attended the meeting, which ran past 2:30 a.m., and residents from across Hays County, where droughts have been felt for years, spoke overwhelmingly against the project. An earlier attempt to approve the project failed in August 2025, when the council lacked the supermajority needed to overturn the Planning and Zoning Commission's recommendation of denial. The campus would have had five buildings of 76 megawatts each, 380 megawatts in all, and a closed-loop cooling system needing a one-time fill of 60,000 to 70,000 gallons of water, from the Crystal Clear utility rather than the city. "We're working with the city to, first, cut water use in half, and then cut it in half again," said John Maberry, a managing partner at Highlander Real Estate Partners. "You are either going to greatly harm your relationship with your community or you're going to buckle down and work with us and come up with an alternative which we are all willing and eager to help you on," said Torrie Martin, who lives on a ranch next to the site. Mario Jimenez, whose family has lived on Francis Harris Lane since 1992, worried about a heat island effect on farmland and livestock. Mayor Jane Hughson said the question was less the data center's own cooling than "the water from the power generation." Union construction workers backed the project, and Matthew Gonzales of Laborers' Local 1095 told the council it offered "good, quality jobs on a construction project like this." The ban defines data centers in the city's land development code and makes them ineligible everywhere in the city. "I don't see how any business minded developer would want to reapproach, hoping they'll read the room," said Council Member Alyssa Garza. State Sen. Paul Bettencourt has said he will challenge the ban under state laws limiting local moratoriums and ordinances, while land use experts say the city's home rule powers give it a better chance than counties. Hays County, which cannot zone, voted in June to set up a water review board and suspend discretionary approvals such as tax abatements for data centers and other water-intensive projects through the end of 2026. Another developer, CloudBurst, is planning a data center south of San Marcos in the county.

Hays County, which cannot zone, voted in June to set up a water review board and suspend discretionary approvals such as tax abatements for data centers and other water-intensive projects through the end of 2026.
Another developer, CloudBurst, is planning a data center south of San Marcos in the county.

ft-608.text: Soluna Holdings' Project Kati is a 166 megawatt wind-powered data center campus on the site of the Las Majadas Wind Farm in the southeast corner of Willacy County, Texas. It is being built in two phases of 83 megawatts, the first for bitcoin hosting with Galaxy as the first customer at 48 megawatts, the second for AI and high-performance computing. Soluna's chief financial officer, John Tunison, asked the Willacy County Commissioners Court in Raymondville for a tax abatement on February 27, 2025, but no vote was taken because a quorum was not present. "The wind might be blowing, but they can't put it into the grid because the grid is either congested or doesn't need the power at that time," Tunison told commissioners, describing a data center connected behind the meter to take the power instead. He put the first phase at about $40 million for site work, buildings and electrical infrastructure plus up to $45 million of mining machines, said the AI phase would need $1 billion or more, and promised 12 full-time jobs in the first year rising to 18. He also told commissioners the project would add about $2.5 million of longer-term property tax and close to $1 million of school tax. County Judge Aurelio Guerra, a supporter, later said the county had hired a specialist tax abatement attorney and had largely agreed an abatement for phase one, with a second agreement for phase two expected within five years. "And yes, we're giving them an abatement. But needless to say, those abatements will go away in ten years and so, hopefully, we will have more new projects within those ten years," Guerra said. The groundbreaking was held on September 18, 2025, and Soluna says the air-cooled machines use no water for cooling. By April 2026 Soluna said Kati 1 had reached substantial completion ahead of schedule. In January 2026 it signed a partnership with the developer Metrobloks for Kati 2, on a separate campus just across from Kati 1, starting at more than 100 megawatts for AI and high-performance computing with a roadmap past 300 megawatts, and a possible neocloud tenant under a non-binding letter of intent.

ft-611.text: MSB Global Services broke ground on its Matrix data center campus outside Sulphur Springs, Texas, on June 13, 2025, on the site of a closed coal mine; the plan calls for up to 30 buildings and about 3,000 megawatts of power, built in phases over five years. On June 2, 2026, the city council voted to bring in a new developer to replace MSB Global; Mayor Tyler Law said a press release would follow, but the city has not named the new company. The land was given to the city by power company Vistra in 2019 with a deed barring it from ever being used to generate or store power, and MSB Global's plan needs about 3,000 megawatts of on-site generation to run. Vistra sued to block construction, and Hopkins County District Judge Dan Moore issued a temporary injunction on February 10, 2026 barring new construction tied to the covenant until trial. The trial was scheduled for September 2026; no result has been published. "I didn't find out from the city. I found out from a video that MSB Global had uploaded," said resident Jaime Mitchell, who runs a local transparency page. "This isn't just a data center. This is potentially one of the largest in the world. It's 30 buildings the size of Costco." The council added $1.2 million to its legal budget for the two lawsuits on May 5, 2026, on top of about $230,000 already spent; Mayor Law said the spending would not raise taxes. In December 2025 court filings, Vistra's lawyers asked that City Attorney Nate Smith be removed from the case, citing his past relationship with MSB Global's vice president of project development, Ganna Halvorsen; the city and MSB Global said the relationship had ended before the company had any dealings with Sulphur Springs. Residents held a national day of protest against data centers in downtown Sulphur Springs on July 18, 2026.

ft-1764028554679-9929.text: IREN, the Nasdaq-listed former bitcoin miner, is building the Sweetwater Hub, a 2,000-megawatt data center campus outside Sweetwater in Fisher County, West Texas. The campus has two sites, Sweetwater 1 and Sweetwater 2, set to total 2,200 acres; in early May 2026 IREN said it had turned on grid power to the 1,700-acre Sweetwater 1 site, with Sweetwater 2 expected to follow in 2028. IREN, formerly Iris Energy, was founded in 2019 and is winding down its bitcoin mining to put money into AI computing. Microsoft is its biggest named customer, with a five-year, $9.7 billion deal for access to IREN's Nvidia GPUs, deployed at IREN's other Texas campus, in Childress. David Shaw, IREN's chief operating officer, told KTXS that about 300 construction workers were on site at Sweetwater, that he expected that number to triple or quadruple within six months, and that the finished campus would employ more than 200 people. Shaw said Fisher County was picked for its cheap renewable power and its existing electrical lines: "We've switched it around and brought the data center out to the source of the power, where the infrastructure already exists." KTXS reported that some residents have raised concerns about traffic, power demands and the effect on rural communities as large AI facilities move into West Texas. IREN co-CEO Daniel Roberts wrote in August 2026 that the company's data centers "don't evaporate water for cooling; we recirculate it in a modern closed-loop system," and that IREN builds its sites with setbacks from homes. Sweetwater 1's power hookup came three months before Gov. Greg Abbott ordered a statewide audit of data centers seeking Texas grid connections on August 3, 2026. That audit does not touch a site already connected, and IREN expects to turn on power at Sweetwater 2 in 2028.

ft-1785353574775-1232.text: Flexential, a Colorado-based data center company, has bought 110 acres near Talty in Kaufman County, Texas, for a three-building data center campus, its fourth and largest in North Texas. The first phase is a 375,000-square-foot building of 36 megawatts of power, with room for two more the same size for 108 megawatts in all; site work is expected to begin in early 2027, with the first customers moving in during late 2028. The company announced the purchase at the end of July 2026. Flexential says the campus will serve business customers renting whole buildings or shared server space, support dense equipment racks, and use a closed-loop cooling system designed to use almost no water. "Dallas has the strongest combination of demand, infrastructure, and growth potential of any data center market in the country, and the development pipeline can't keep pace," said Ryan Mallory, Flexential's chief executive. Flexential already runs data centers in downtown Dallas, Plano and Richardson. Talty itself has no say over the project: city officials said the property was released from Talty's zoning authority earlier in 2026 under state law, after a landowner petition to Kaufman County, so the city has no regulatory power over it. Nearby, Forney is moving the other way. In April 2026 the Forney City Council raised the required setback for data centers from homes to 5,000 feet and required a conditional use permit, and on July 21, 2026 it directed staff to begin writing a zoning ban on data centers, which is expected to return for public hearings before a final vote. With no city review of the Talty site, the open questions are moving to the state. Gov. Greg Abbott has directed lawmakers to consider, in the 2027 legislative session, policies to keep residential customers from paying for new transmission lines built for data centers. On September 21, 2026, Abbott ordered the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to stop issuing new permits for data centers until the state's grid operator, ERCOT, and the Texas Water Development Board finish auditing the industry, a statewide pause that also covers this project.

ft-1775092815788-9591.text: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton said on September 17, 2026, that he is investigating the Blueprint Projects data center at 1601 Martin Luther King Jr. Drive in Taylor, Williamson County, Texas, because the land was deeded in 1999 "to be held in trust for future use as parkland." The company, BPP Projects LLC, plans a 135,000-square-foot, 30-megawatt data center there in three phases, with up to $1 billion invested over ten years and 20 to 30 jobs. In July 1999, members of the Cromwell family sold the 52-acre site to the Texas Parks and Recreation Foundation for $10 with a deed saying it was to be held in trust for future parkland. The parkland language dropped out of later deeds, and the city says the 1999 note was not a deed restriction; it says the land has been zoned industrial since 1970 and was designated an employment center in 2023. Pamela Griffin, who lives about 500 feet from the site and played on the land as a child, sued in 2025 with three siblings and a neighbor to enforce the deed. At the council's unanimous approval vote in July 2025, neighbors wore red X's in protest and complained of a "complete lack of transparency and meaningful communication." In October 2025 Judge Ryan Larson of the 395th District Court dismissed the case, ruling the residents lacked standing; they have appealed, and no action had been taken on the appeal by mid-September 2026. Paxton said, "If the Taylor data center development is unlawful, I will do everything in my power to stop it and hold those who have violated the law accountable," and added that he may seek court intervention. HALT co-founder Carrie D'Anna welcomed the probe but warned it would matter little without an injunction: "If he doesn't attach an injunction to this investigation, what he's doing is making a clear pathway for (the data center developers) to continue their work." The city said it would cooperate fully with the investigation; what happens next rests with the courts and the attorney general, on the residents' appeal and on whether Paxton goes to court over the deed.

ft-1775092501551-8874.text: Project Comal, a data center campus planned by the Dallas developer KDC next to Samsung's chip plant in Taylor, Williamson County, Texas, was approved by the Taylor City Council on March 26, 2026, over residents' objections. The council voted unanimously to annex the last 48 acres of the site and rezone it for the project. In July the council refused to act on a citizens' petition, signed by more than 1,400 residents, that would have paused data center approvals across the city. KDC plans six large buildings on the 220-acre site at 1051 County Road 401, next to Samsung's 1,200-acre chip campus. The site plan lists two substations, and Data Center Dynamics reported the project would offer 360 megawatts of power from the utility Oncor. The Taylor Press reported 180 backup generators, and KDC also plans about 10 acres of retail and office space fronting FM 973. Company officials have not named a tenant but told earlier meetings it is a "large brand name." The Taylor Economic Development Corp. estimated $145.9 million in net benefits to the city and $70.7 million to Taylor ISD over 10 years. Residents had fought the project since it reached the Planning and Zoning Commission in November 2025, filling the council chamber in March over rising utility bills and a lack of transparency. "We're not being heard," resident Carrie D'Anna told the council. To answer the objections, the city wrote custom zoning with KDC: a closed-loop cooling system capped at 5 million gallons per building for the first fill, 30 million gallons across six buildings, with more water needing the city manager's approval. It also requires a 300-foot landscaped buffer from the Castlewood South subdivision, a nighttime noise limit of 70 decibels at the property line and generator exhausts pointed away from homes, and KDC agreed to give $75,000 for parks and land for a future fire station. "I hear the request for moratorium, but we've got a developer who has not shied away from answering the questions," Mayor Dwayne Ariola said. The Halt Taylor Data Center Coalition submitted a citizen-initiated ordinance on June 11 that would have paused current data center projects and barred new ones until Taylor creates a dedicated zoning district for them. On July 9 the city said the council would take no action and would not put it on the ballot. "State law does not allow a city to enact or change its zoning by popular vote," Mayor Pro Tem Kelly Cmerek said. Organizer Sarah Winters called the handling of it "shady, shady business," and D'Anna said: "That's humiliating." Taylor's other data center project, Blueprint Data Centers, is planned for the southeast side of the city; the city says it is the only project it has given economic incentives. The rezoning does not finish Project Comal's approvals. KDC still must obtain water from the city or another provider and win approval of a site plan and a range of permits, the city says. The Taylor City Council has directed staff and the consultant Freese and Nichols to write an ordinance regulating data centers' water use, noise, light, air pollution and buffers from homes, to be shared for public input before adoption.

The Taylor Economic Development Corp. estimated $145.9 million in net benefits to the city and $70.7 million to Taylor ISD over 10 years. Residents had fought the project since it reached the Planning and Zoning Commission in November 2025, filling the council chamber in March over rising utility bills and a lack of transparency. "We're not being heard," resident Carrie D'Anna told the council.

To answer the objections, the city wrote custom zoning with KDC: a closed-loop cooling system capped at 5 million gallons per building for the first fill, 30 million gallons across six buildings, with more water needing the city manager's approval. It also requires a 300-foot landscaped buffer from the Castlewood South subdivision, a nighttime noise limit of 70 decibels at the property line and generator exhausts pointed away from homes, and KDC agreed to give $75,000 for parks and land for a future fire station.

"I hear the request for moratorium, but we've got a developer who has not shied away from answering the questions," Mayor Dwayne Ariola said. The Halt Taylor Data Center Coalition submitted a citizen-initiated ordinance on June 11 that would have paused current data center projects and barred new ones until Taylor creates a dedicated zoning district for them. On July 9 the city said the council would take no action and would not put it on the ballot.

"State law does not allow a city to enact or change its zoning by popular vote," Mayor Pro Tem Kelly Cmerek said. Organizer Sarah Winters called the handling of it "shady, shady business," and D'Anna said: "That's humiliating." Taylor's other data center project, Blueprint Data Centers, is planned for the southeast side of the city; the city says it is the only project it has given economic incentives.

The rezoning does not finish Project Comal's approvals. KDC still must obtain water from the city or another provider and win approval of a site plan and a range of permits, the city says. The Taylor City Council has directed staff and the consultant Freese and Nichols to write an ordinance regulating data centers' water use, noise, light, air pollution and buffers from homes, to be shared for public input before adoption.

ft-612.text: Rowan Digital Infrastructure is building its Project Temple data center campus in Temple, Bell County, Texas, on land at 1707 and 2351 Bob White Road that the city council approved in 2025. Rowan broke ground in January 2026 on the $700 million project, which it says could reach 300 megawatts of power at full build-out, with power secured through a partnership with Oncor and operations planned for 2027. On September 17, 2026, the Temple City Council approved new data center zoning rules and a set of agreements covering Rowan's next phase. In May 2026 Rowan secured nearly $3 billion in debt financing for the campus, and in July a state filing showed plans for a second building, AUS02 Building 2, a $780 million, 500,000-square-foot structure at 1855 Bob White Road under construction from August 2026 to August 2027. Rowan spokesperson Nathan Brown told the Temple Daily Telegram that Project Temple's 300 megawatts come from the power allocation of the company's earlier Moriah facility nearby, which was completed in 2023, lost its tenant in 2024, and is being converted into a warehouse. Rowan is also planning three more campus phases with six buildings in the Synergy Southeast Industrial Park, each phase worth $700 million and 40 jobs, city officials say. Phase 1B, called Project Lasso, sits on land Rowan bought to replace the site of the city's planned landfill expansion. Opponents cite a webpage of Rowan's parent, Quinbrook Infrastructure Partners, describing more than 1,350 acres and 1.6 gigawatts of planned capacity in the Temple area; Brown called that figure outdated. Meta already runs a data center in Temple's Industrial Park. Water is residents' first concern. City officials say Rowan's three new phases should average about 32,000 gallons a day combined, with a peak of about 78,200 gallons, and each building needs an initial 1.5 million gallon charge for closed-loop cooling. Under the infrastructure agreement approved September 17, Rowan will pay $38.5 million toward water and other infrastructure, including about $25 million for the South Temple Water Infrastructure Capital Program and a voluntary $13 million that includes $10 million for an aquifer storage project. The city caps each site's water use by meter, with no option to pay a fee to exceed the limit. The Temple Daily Telegram found the city has not commissioned independent studies of the projects' water use, grid impact or noise. City officials put Project Temple's own revenue at about $7 million a year during its 10-year tax abatement, rising to about $12 million after. Mayor Tim Davis instead cited the revenue once all six of Rowan's planned buildings are complete, about $42 million a year during the abatement period, rising to $56 million afterward, and rejected criticism that the deal was a "corporate giveaway." Residents organized as Stop the Temple Data Center, and after an April 2026 council vote to annex and rezone about 700 acres along Bob White Road for another $700 million data center, began collecting signatures to recall Mayor Davis, Mayor Pro Tem Jessica Walker and Councilman Mike Pilkington. "The water usage, the electricity usage, animals, the noise. We don't want them in Temple," resident Carly Byrd said. Davis cut off public comment at that meeting after five hours, saying, "I don't think one more question is going to move the needle on this." At a September 3 meeting, Temple Stands Together co-founder Joe Royer said the new zoning rules would not reach projects like Rowan's: "This is never going to apply because all these large data centers go through specially negotiated plan development agreements." The rules adopted September 17 require a conditional use permit for new standalone data centers in industrial districts, plus closed-loop cooling, buffering, traffic studies and noise mitigation, but apply only to future projects; Rowan's existing phases are instead governed by its own planned-development agreements. Resident Marcie Goodfleich said the rules' 200-foot setback from homes was inadequate. With the September 17 votes, the City of Temple now enforces Rowan's water and infrastructure limits directly through those agreements, and any further phases beyond Lasso would need their own council approval.
