ft-616.text: The data center at 507 Olive Street in Texarkana, Bowie County, Texas, is one of eight Windstream switch and data center buildings that JLL put up for sale as a portfolio in August 2024. JLL described the tenant only as a "major home Internet provider," and online listings for each address point to Windstream. The Texarkana building has been leased to that tenant since at least 2014, with the lease running through 2034. The eight buildings, in Texas, Kentucky, Colorado, Iowa, Arkansas, New Mexico and Georgia, total 379,000 square feet on 26 acres and bring in $5.7 million a year in rent combined. JLL said the buildings are critical infrastructure because they are interconnected transmission facilities that route the tenant's telecommunications traffic across its network. Windstream was formed in 2006 when Alltel's local telephone business merged with Valor Communications, and some of the buildings in the portfolio were once Alltel or Valor facilities. Windstream sold its separate data center business to TierPoint in 2015 for $575 million, and in 2024 it agreed to merge with Uniti Group to combine Uniti's fiber network with Windstream's fiber-to-the-home business.

ft-1782929726005-1713.text: Hood County commissioners approved the Comanche Circle data center campus without conditions, voting 3 to 1 on June 9, 2026, near Tolar and the Comanche Peak Nuclear Power Plant. Commissioner Nannette Samuelson cast the lone dissenting vote and Commissioner Dave Eagle was absent; developer Ryan Hughes, founder of Florida-based Sailfish Investors, did not attend, citing safety concerns. Commissioners dropped the conditions they had set at January's conditional-approval stage, saying engineering, drainage, water, wastewater and environmental questions would be worked out later, at the site development plan stage. "I am asking this court to show some backbone today," resident Joanne Thomas told the court. "Call a bad faith actor exactly what he is." Hood County Judge-elect Mark Lowrey asked how the county could trust a project whose representative "doesn't even have the respect or the courage to come in here," and resident Brian Crawford said, "Ryan Hughes is telling this court to pound sand." When a woman in the crowd asked commissioners how much they were being paid, County Attorney Matt Mills answered, "Not a dime," adding, "You're accusing people of being crooks. I'm tired of that." Texas counties have only the powers the legislature grants them and, unlike cities, no zoning authority, so Hood County cannot simply refuse a project like this. "Texas has always viewed counties as rural toddlers that can't be trusted with full powers," said Robert Paterson, a University of Texas at Austin professor of land use and environmental planning. Two attempts at a moratorium in Hood County have failed and developers have sued the county twice, in one case seeking no less than $250,000 in damages; state law has long favored development and property rights, Mills told the crowd. Eight data centers are proposed on more than 7,600 acres in Hood County, a rural county of about 62,000 people southwest of Fort Worth, with Comanche Circle's 2,100 acres the largest. A water district's minutes put Comanche Circle's request at 150,000 gallons a day after an initial 95-million-gallon "flush and fill" for construction, but Hughes told the Tribune that figure was wrong and his three data center proposals in the county combined would use less than 50,000 gallons a day of groundwater at full build.

ft-1785258427594-3902.text: Diode Ventures withdrew its plan for a data center near Trinidad in Henderson County, Texas, on July 22, 2026, after months of opposition from lake residents and pressure from Governor Greg Abbott. The company told the Texas Tribune it had decided not to advance the site beyond preliminary planning. Henderson County Commissioner Wendy Spivey said the site sat in the middle of a developed subdivision with hundreds of homes around it. The Fort Worth Star-Telegram reported the site was expected to take 12 years to build out and use 5 million gallons of lake water a day by its fifth year. Cedar Creek Lake supplies water to the Fort Worth area, and lake levels had been low this year with little rain. Save Cedar Creek Lake, a volunteer coalition formed in early 2026, gathered thousands of signatures demanding the project be dropped and stronger state rules for data centers. "I'm pro technology, but not at the expense of we, the people," resident Stacy Farmer said after the withdrawal. Governor Abbott said in a statement: "Data centers that want to do business in Texas must meet a clear standard. This project did not." Spivey said she did not think the fight was over, since the landowners were still looking for ways to sell or use the land. "There's not much the county can do," Spivey said. "We don't have zoning rules and regulations." Henderson County has signed a resolution asking state lawmakers for authority to regulate data centers, and Abbott has recommended the 2027 Legislature require closed loop water systems, make data centers pay their own grid costs, and end their tax breaks.

ft-1783830204354-4305.text: The Tyler Planning and Zoning Commission voted 5-2 on July 7, 2026 to deny Vulcan Core a special use permit for a 12-megawatt bitcoin mining data center at 1101 and 1105 West Erwin Street near downtown Tyler, in Smith County, Texas. On September 3, the city's Zoning Board of Adjustment ruled unanimously that it had no jurisdiction to hear an appeal from Barrio Resources LLC, which owns the site, because it was filed 364 days past the deadline. Vulcan Core, working with Barrio Energy, planned to reuse an existing building on about 1.8 acres, with eight 40-by-8-foot containers beside an electrical substation with available capacity, and said it would not use city water. The permit would have capped the 8,090-square-foot facility at 12 megawatts, with closed-loop cooling, outdoor dry coolers and no diesel generators. Barrio Energy announced in August 2024 that it had closed on the property. Twenty-six residents spoke against the data center and five for it, two of them from Vulcan Core, over three and a half hours. "In our technical review, the proposed activity is inconsistent with the Future Land Use Map (FLUM) and the Tyler Tomorrow Comprehensive Plan," said Kyle Kingma, the city's planning director, who recommended denial. Vulcan Core's community liaison, Mark Buntsev, said an independent sound study found the fans at full capacity would stay below the neighborhood's ambient level of about 45 decibels, and offered to sign 15 conditions, but commissioner David Hudson said the planning department still had questions that the noise "could be much higher than what they're hoping for." "We have to consider the overall benefit to our community with this just being seven to 10 jobs when you compare the potential impacts," said Phillip Olivares, who runs the building next door. Kathy Williams, who lives a block away, said: "We have entrusted the Planning and Zoning (Commission) to protect the public interest and we don't feel like this is in the interest of the public to have a data center there." Supporter Bob Westbrook said the project improves existing industrial property, expands the tax base and uses surplus grid capacity. The appeal went back to 2025, when Kingma ruled that bitcoin mining was an unlisted use needing a special use permit in the M-1 light industrial district. Barrio's attorney, Jason Mazingo, argued the city had given conflicting answers, pointing to a later email from a planning department employee saying a processing center did not need the permit; the city said only the planning director could make that call. "Barrio did not file its appeal in the 20-day statutory deadline, then you don't have the authority to hear this," City Attorney Steve Kean told the board. Barrio Resources had 10 days under state law to take the board's ruling to court. It also has a separate appeal of the July permit denial, filed on time and still pending, that would send the final decision on the data center to the Tyler City Council.
paragraphs: The Tyler Planning and Zoning Commission voted 5-2 on July 7, 2026 to deny Vulcan Core a special use permit for a 12-megawatt bitcoin mining data center at 1101 and 1105 West Erwin Street near downtown Tyler, in Smith County, Texas. On September 3, the city's Zoning Board of Adjustment ruled unanimously that it had no jurisdiction to hear an appeal from Barrio Resources LLC, which owns the site, because it was filed 364 days past the deadline.

Vulcan Core, working with Barrio Energy, planned to reuse an existing building on about 1.8 acres, with eight 40-by-8-foot containers beside an electrical substation with available capacity, and said it would not use city water. The permit would have capped the 8,090-square-foot facility at 12 megawatts, with closed-loop cooling, outdoor dry coolers and no diesel generators. Barrio Energy announced in August 2024 that it had closed on the property.

Twenty-six residents spoke against the data center and five for it, two of them from Vulcan Core, over three and a half hours. "In our technical review, the proposed activity is inconsistent with the Future Land Use Map (FLUM) and the Tyler Tomorrow Comprehensive Plan," said Kyle Kingma, the city's planning director, who recommended denial. Vulcan Core's community liaison, Mark Buntsev, said an independent sound study found the fans at full capacity would stay below the neighborhood's ambient level of about 45 decibels, and offered to sign 15 conditions, but commissioner David Hudson said the planning department still had questions that the noise "could be much higher than what they're hoping for."

"We have to consider the overall benefit to our community with this just being seven to 10 jobs when you compare the potential impacts," said Phillip Olivares, who runs the building next door. Kathy Williams, who lives a block away, said: "We have entrusted the Planning and Zoning (Commission) to protect the public interest and we don't feel like this is in the interest of the public to have a data center there." Supporter Bob Westbrook said the project improves existing industrial property, expands the tax base and uses surplus grid capacity.

The appeal went back to 2025, when Kingma ruled that bitcoin mining was an unlisted use needing a special use permit in the M-1 light industrial district. Barrio's attorney, Jason Mazingo, argued the city had given conflicting answers, pointing to a later email from a planning department employee saying a processing center did not need the permit; the city said only the planning director could make that call. "Barrio did not file its appeal in the 20-day statutory deadline, then you don't have the authority to hear this," City Attorney Steve Kean told the board.

Barrio Resources had 10 days under state law to take the board's ruling to court. It also has a separate appeal of the July permit denial, filed on time and still pending, that would send the final decision on the data center to the Tyler City Council.

The site was bought from Ballard Exploration Co., which lent the company about $64.5 million as part of the deal, according to county property records. Black Mountain has not said what it plans to build on the San Antonio land. Founded in 2007, the company invests mainly in oil and gas and lithium mining and is moving into battery storage, water, carbon capture and data centers. ft-618.text: A company has filed plans for a data center on about 217 acres at 900 East County Road 109 in Venus, Johnson County, Texas. The project's status with the city is proposed, and Texas counties have little authority over data center rezoning or permits, so state rules are the main hurdle it still faces. Land around Venus is being sold for data centers. A CBRE listing called Project Venus offers 700 acres nearby with a 345 kV transmission line through the site, an Oncor switching station under construction and a 12-inch gas pipeline, with Oncor requests pending to expand the site's available power. The listing tells buyers no rezoning, special use permit, comprehensive plan amendment or public hearing is required. In late 2024 about 3,700 acres near Midlothian in Ellis County and Venus in Johnson County went up for sale for data centers and energy companies, most of it owned by rancher and oilman Richard Miskimon. A broker said buyers wanted sites of 400 acres or more. Google built a $600 million data center near Midlothian in 2019. Statewide, Gov. Greg Abbott told the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality on September 21, 2026 to issue no permits sought by data center projects until audits by the state's grid operator and water board are complete. "Data centers must pay their own way, protect our grid and water, and complete the ERCOT and TWDB audits," Abbott said. For the Venus site, with little county authority to stop it, those state permits are the main checkpoint, and TCEQ must report to the governor's office on the pause by October 19, 2026.

ft-625.text: Genesis Digital Assets' Rowdy Data Center is operating as a bitcoin mine at the former Oklaunion Power Station near Vernon in Wilbarger County. GDA said in an August 2024 press release that the site opened running at 60 megawatts of power, supported by the Oklaunion Substation. Oklaunion Power Station board chair Tom Walker, who is also the Dallas Cowboys' chief financial officer, said in the release that "this project clearly demonstrates that Bitcoin mining creates entirely new dynamics for the energy industry." The Oklaunion plant closed in September 2020, and GDA said Rowdy brought back 12 permanent jobs and about 150 construction jobs. In February 2025 GDA added a 10 megawatt container at Vernon, bringing the site to 70 megawatts, as part of a 50 megawatt expansion that also grew its Pyote site. AiOnX bought a 77 percent stake in GDA for $500 million in June 2026 and plans to convert GDA's 15 bitcoin-mining centers to AI and high-performance computing, though its announcement gave no date for a change at Rowdy.

ft-1765215828092-6669.text: Crusoe's proposed AI data center campus covers 1,600 acres in Calhoun County, Texas, near the Port of Victoria, and would be powered by an advanced nuclear plant of up to 1.5 gigawatts that Blue Energy would build on a nearby secured site. Blue Energy says it would supply power from a natural gas bridge as early as 2028 and convert to nuclear generation by 2031. The data center site itself sits in Calhoun County, while the power plant and its tax question are being decided across the county line in Victoria County. On June 22, 2026, Victoria County commissioners voted only to receive Blue Energy's applications for six tax abatements covering about $6.5 billion of property, and as of late August no decision had been made. Residents asked for a delay because the meeting agenda had named the applicant as "Blue Ammonia," and Jewel Buchanan urged the county to wait while groundwater districts study the water demands of large AI data centers. "We have not yet made a decision to proceed," said Blue Energy's chief commercial officer, Tom O'Neill, who said the plant would supply the Crusoe data center but stay connected to the ERCOT grid. Blue Energy projects about 3,800 peak construction jobs and about 360 permanent ones, and $1.5 billion in local taxes over 25 years, and says it would buy desalinated water from a deep saline aquifer rather than use existing freshwater supplies. In August 2026, Victoria County Judge Ben Zeller said the application remained "under review with no new developments at this time," so no vote date has been set.

ft-627.text: The Willis Data Center at 606 State Highway 75 in Willis, Montgomery County, Texas, is a small Comcast cable facility, not a large campus: a 5,200-square-foot building for Comcast of Houston, LLC, estimated at $7.5 million, according to its Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation filing. The filing describes a power room, a headend room, a technician control room, a restroom and a vestibule, with no public access. It is finished and operating: the project was registered on August 20, 2024, construction ran from November 1, 2024 to December 15, 2025, and the state record now shows its accessibility inspection complete. Larger data centers are drawing more attention elsewhere in Montgomery County. On August 13, 2026, the Conroe City Council adopted rules for large data centers, requiring council approval after a public hearing, proof of water, sewer and electrical capacity, closed-loop cooling, noise limits of 5 decibels above ambient at the property line, and a 300-foot separation from homes, schools and parks. Those rules do not apply to the small Willis building, which is already built and in service; the state licensing filing remains the latest record for it.

ft-1784923186601-9665.text: Palomino Alpha LLC has proposed an 870-acre data center off Highway 123 near Zorn, in northern Guadalupe County, Texas. The project still has no water contract: the Crystal Clear Special Utility District board put off the company's request for up to half a million gallons a day at its August 27, 2026 meeting, saying they could not get answers about how the data center would work. The project is also covered by a statewide freeze Gov. Greg Abbott ordered on August 3, 2026, pausing new data centers' connections to the Texas power grid until regulators audit projects waiting in line. Project representatives "asked not to be placed on tonight's agenda" at the August 27 meeting, the utility district's attorney said, after missing three consecutive meetings they were supposed to attend. Board member Joseph Benavides said no one had told him how the system would work, how much water it needs or what chemicals it would use. "That unsettles me a lot because it really sounds like they're just telling us what we want to hear, and we're getting hoodwinked," he said. State Rep. Alan Schoolcraft urged the district to delay or deny the request. At an earlier meeting in June, the board tabled the same water agreement after hours of public comment. A consultant for Palomino Alpha, Thomas Dubel, told the board the project would "probably put a minimum of $400 million of tax, property tax revenue" into the Navarro ISD school system. Guadalupe County has already granted the project a tax abatement zone. The Commissioners Court approved it in December 2024 and, in February 2026, voted 3-1 to expand it with a buffer for neighbors; Commissioner Stephen Germann voted no. County Judge Kyle Kutscher abstained both times, saying his family owns nearly 200 acres in the project area next to the region's largest electrical substation, land that has been in his family since the 1930s. On July 20, 2026, the Data Center Action Coalition and residents sued the Guadalupe County Commissioners Court, claiming its approvals for Palomino Alpha and the nearby CloudBurst project broke the Texas Open Meetings Act, the Texas Tax Code and conflict-of-interest law. The suit says Kutscher and his family own 186 acres being sold to Palomino Alpha and that he lobbied for the approvals despite recusing himself from the formal votes. "What was happening in Guadalupe County was a pattern of meetings that didn't quite meet the standards required under state law," said Bobby Levinski, an attorney with the Save Our Springs Alliance. Residents have also raised concerns about water use, heat, noise, backup generator pollution and wastewater reaching tributaries of the San Marcos River. "The water bills, I don't want them to go up any higher," Seguin homeowner Cynthia told KSAT. "But if the data centers start draining the waters from the homeowners, what do we do?" The next decision is Crystal Clear's. Because the August 27 item was listed for discussion only, the board could not vote, and the district's notice says its board has not taken any action on the proposed Palomino Alpha service agreement. The lawsuit against the Commissioners Court is pending; Levinski said the plaintiffs will argue the approvals "should be considered void and should not be enforceable."

ft-1776265119432-8534.text: The Antelope Data Center, a 640-acre data center campus with its own natural gas power plant west of Cedar City, won a conditional use permit from the Iron County Planning Commission on June 4, 2026, in a unanimous vote. The developer is Pronghorn Development LLC, and the site is along Antelope Springs Road in unincorporated Iron County, Utah, roughly 15 miles northwest of Cedar City according to the company's application. The plan calls for five data center buildings and a gas-fired plant of up to 1.5 gigawatts, built in phases over an estimated eight to ten years. Iron County's description put the five buildings at about 1.35 million square feet. St. George News reported they could total up to 6.75 million square feet. The developer estimates it will finish the project in 2033, with the first 500 megawatts of generation done by 2028, and says the campus will support about 680 employees. Materials presented at the March hearing put the permanent workforce at about 175, roughly 35 for each of the five data hall buildings. No end user has been named. At the March hearing Cedar City resident Camilla Dorado asked, "What tech company will be owning the data center if the data center is built?" ft-630.text: BluSky AI, a modular data center company, signed a non-binding letter of intent in 2025 to buy 25 acres with up to 50 megawatts of power inside Creekstone Energy's Delta Gigasite, about 9 miles southeast of Delta in Millard County, Utah. Creekstone named BluSky one of the Gigasite's first major tenants, planning to install modular data centers there for AI computing. BluSky said it expected to finalize the purchase in the fourth quarter of 2025 and projected groundbreaking in late 2026. "This isn't just a land deal, it's a sign that Utah is ready to lead," Creekstone CEO Buford Ray Conley said when the tenancy was announced. Millard County had already changed the zoning and issued the conditional use permit for Creekstone's 1,143-acre campus around the Gigasite in summer 2025. The county has not said whether BluSky's 25 acres need a separate approval of their own. BluSky was a mining company called Inception Mining until it rebranded in April 2025, and it has been selling off its Clavo Rico gold mine in Honduras. Its chief executive, Trent D'Ambrosio, previously worked with RackScale Data Centers, a company Data Center Dynamics reported never delivered any data centers. BluSky has also signed a ground lease option on 51.6 acres in Milford, Utah, and a letter of intent to lease two acres in Wells, Nevada. In May 2026 BluSky launched a Regulation A+ offering to raise money for what it calls a network of more than 10 AI Factory sites with over 200 megawatts of potential capacity, and the offering did not name Delta. Its 2026 investor page lists Utah properties only as "North, UT" and "Southwest, UT," with none identified as Delta. Nothing has appeared since 2025 on whether the Delta purchase closed.

ft-628.text: Creekstone Energy's data center campus at Delta, in Millard County, is master-planned for more than 10 gigawatts on 4,000 acres at 11000 McCornick Road. The Millard County commission approved rezonings for Creekstone and for Joule Capital Partners, allowing both to start building once conditional use permits are finalised. Between them the two campuses would take about eight square miles of a county of 6,572 square miles, with 13,437 residents. The power plan is to leave the grid out of it. Both campuses would run on generators fed by natural gas lines rather than the local electricity network. Creekstone is already operating a 50 megawatt agreement with BluSky AI, and its campus is expected to produce up to $40 billion of economic activity for the region. Joule's launch capacity is expected in 2026, using Caterpillar generators and 1.1 gigawatt hours of grid-forming battery storage. The commissioners are enthusiastic and say they gave nothing away. No special incentives went to either developer, tax revenue is the expected benefit, and the commission expects little disruption to how the county runs. Commissioner Bill Wright said no other county in the United States "has the potential to produce power from six different resources," listing geothermal, solar, a little wind, coal, gas and nuclear on the horizon, and added: "If we're going to change, I love data centers compared to everything else." Vicki Lyman said worries about running out of resources could be put to rest.

ft-629.text: Creekstone Energy is building the Delta Gigasite, a data center campus master planned for 10 gigawatts, or 10,000 megawatts of power, on 1,143 acres about 9 miles southeast of Delta, in Millard County, Utah. Work on its natural gas power infrastructure is underway, and Millard County approved the rezoning and conditional use permit that let the project move ahead. Utah's rural tax incentive program has since credited the now-under-construction project with committing $17.1 billion in investment over 20 years. The site first came before the county in 2025 under the name Fibernet MercuryDelta, an Orem company that asked Millard County to rezone the land from agriculture to heavy industrial. The county commission approved the rezoning after the planning commission recommended it in May 2025, and issued a conditional use permit for the campus that summer; Creekstone says both passed unanimously. The company was co-founded by Fibernet CEO Lane Livingstone and Creekstone Capital CEO Ray Conley, who now leads Creekstone Energy. Creekstone describes a campus managing 10 gigawatts of power over a decade: 1.8 gigawatts from the Intermountain Power Project, 6 gigawatts from solar and 2 gigawatts from natural gas. In March 2026 the company said it had leased 13,000 acres of state trust land next to the campus for more than 1 gigawatt of solar, with county zoning approval, aiming for deliveries beginning in 2027. A company spokesperson told The Salt Lake Tribune the campus would use up to 200 acre-feet of water a year at full build-out, roughly what 400 households use annually, relying on a closed-loop cooling system the company calls essentially waterless. Conley said the site could also capture around 4,000 acre-feet a year of water condensed from the gas plant's exhaust, an idea the company has hired the University of Utah's Energy and Geoscience Institute to test. "If the results bear out, this could change the way the data center industry thinks about water," said Milind Deo, the institute's lead investigator. Not everyone in the county wanted the rezoning. At a June 2025 county commission meeting, resident Jarvis Jones said, "This land is currently zoned agricultural for a reason," warning the change was "a permanent shift in how this land and the land around it will be treated for generations to come." Resident Ron Larsen spoke in favor: "I think we ought to move forward with it." Commissioners Bill Wright and Vicki Lyman have said the county gave the project no special treatment or incentives. Wright called data centers a better way for the county to grow than a business that brings hundreds of workers needing new houses and schools. Lyman said the campuses will run on their own generators rather than the local grid. A second campus, Joule Capital Partners' project near Holden, broke ground in November 2025 on land the county rezoned in August 2025; together the two campuses would cover about 8 square miles of a county of 13,437 people. Creekstone expects the university's water test results by summer 2027 and says the data center will proceed whatever they show. Land use decisions rest with the Millard County Commission, which approved the zoning and the conditional use permit.

ft-1775655378279-3568.text: Joule's data center campus sits on 4,000 acres in rural Millard County, Utah. The land belongs to the family of co-founder Mark McDougal, who has farmed it for decades. The company, Joule Capital Partners, is based in Lehi and run by McDougal and David Gray. Millard County commissioners unanimously approved a conditional use permit for the project in August 2025. Joule broke ground on the site on Thursday, November 6, 2025. The first phase alone is 1.3 gigawatts, McDougal and Gray told the Deseret News. The company says it will generate its own electricity on site and will not draw power from the local utility grid. Gray said the family's decades-old water rights mean the project needs no new water allocation, and that it will use closed-loop cooling instead of evaporative cooling. "You can't have a neighborhood with a farm underneath it," Gray said. "We want to be wise stewards of the resources we have been given." "All of our generators are in the same area as our data center," McDougal said, adding that because the power use of large computing jobs rises and falls, "we can match the demand to the load." Emy Lesofski, director of the Utah Office of Energy Development, called the project's vision "commendable." Millard County held eight public hearings on Joule and a second nearby project, Creekstone, before commissioners signed off, according to KUTV. Critics told the station, in a report published June 3, 2026, that no environmental studies had been done before thousands of acres of farmland were approved for industrial use. "It feels that there's just a few of us that are screaming into the void," said Amanda Fahey, a Fillmore resident who has criticized the project. Commissioner Bill Wright told KUTV, "I'm not pushing data centers. The reason they're here is they have a right." At the November groundbreaking, Wright told the crowd, "I have a plan that every citizen will benefit from them being here." At the August commission meeting one resident, who said he moved to Millard County to avoid industrial zones, said: "We'd like to try and preserve that as much as we can." The county sheriff's office raised concerns about heavier traffic on rural roads used by children and animals.

ft-1772656712744-9213.text: Santaquin, in Utah County, approved the Summit Ridge data center from Orem-based Data Center Power Company before most residents had heard of it: the City Council amended land use in its commercial light manufacturing zone in October 2024, and site plans were approved in 2025. The 20-plus megawatt campus at 15372 S. Ridge Farms Road, off the Interstate 15 Summit Ridge Parkway exit, would run off-grid on natural gas engines with closed-loop cooling, and no construction start date has been set. Mayor Dan Olson said the city expects more than $3 million a year in sales tax and up to 100 six-figure jobs: "We need another fire station because from corner to corner, our city, it's 8 miles across it, and we need response times to save lives." Resident Kelsy Trane organized a rally at City Hall and a Change.org petition that passed 1,350 signatures, objecting to the site near the Sunroc gravel pit: "There's a ton of houses just right up on the ridge, and there's townhouses that are even closer and a city park where like all of our children play soccer." Olson said earlier public hearings were held and "nobody showed up," while Trane argued the postings never made clear a data center was being considered; resident Steven Johnson asked the council, "if this was such a great idea, why did nobody know about it, except you guys?" Olson said the city held 11 public meetings on the project, the last on January 6, 2026; with the land use change and site plans already approved, what remains before construction is a start date from the developer.

ft-1777347197406-6862.text: The Stratos project, including its eastern site along Interstate 84 at Hansel Valley Road near Snowville, would put hyperscale data centers and energy generation on up to 40,000 acres of largely undeveloped land in unincorporated Box Elder County, Utah. Celebrity investor Kevin O'Leary and the Military Installation Development Authority are leading the project on private, Utah National Guard and Hill Air Force Base land, which the Box Elder County Commission approved including on May 4, 2026. Utah Clean Energy estimated nine gigawatts of on-site combined cycle gas generation at full build-out would burn about 448 billion cubic feet of gas and emit 30.2 million tons of carbon dioxide a year, using 16.6 billion gallons of water. With reciprocating engines instead, the group put the figures at 41 million tons of carbon dioxide and 12,000 tons of nitrogen oxides a year, and said, "Utahns deserve more information and facts about this proposed project to fully understand its impacts." On April 27, 2026, the county commission delayed its vote after more than 80 people filled the meeting demanding a chance for public input, while state leaders sought a fast decision. A week later, at a contentious meeting at the county fairgrounds in Tremonton with sheriff's deputies controlling protesters, the Box Elder County Commission approved the project. Box Elder County commissioners approved a 180-day moratorium on new data centers and power plants on June 10, 2026, running from June 11 to December 8, 2026, but the already-approved Stratos project is unaffected by it.

ft-1777347134333-6528.text: The western half of the Stratos data center scheme sits on Locomotive Springs Road at Snowville, in Box Elder County, 21 kilometres from the eastern site. Stratos as a whole covers up to 40,000 acres of largely rural, undeveloped land in unincorporated Box Elder County, across private property, Utah National Guard land and Hill Air Force Base land, in three separate areas. The Military Installation Development Authority is leading it, and the documents describe energy generation, hyperscale data centers, advanced manufacturing, housing and commercial buildings. Private owners consented before the county was asked to approve the nonmilitary land. What makes the scale hard to picture is the power. Utah Clean Energy modelled nine gigawatts of on-site gas generation and found it would burn about 448 billion cubic feet of gas a year, one and a half times Utah's entire current consumption, if combined cycle turbines were used. Reciprocating engines, available sooner, would emit 41 million tons of carbon dioxide a year, raising state emissions by 75 percent, and 12,000 tons of nitrogen oxides, as much as Utah's whole oil and gas industry. Water ranges from 2 billion gallons a year for the engines, about 3,000 Olympic pools, to 16.6 billion for the turbines, about 25,000. The county delayed its vote on April 27, 2026 after more than 80 protesters asked for public input, and approved the project on May 4, 2026 at a contentious meeting in Tremonton with police present.

ft-1033.text: The Bull Church Data Center, a proposal to rezone land on Bull Church Road near Ladysmith in Caroline County, Virginia, for several data center buildings, is still in the county's technical review with no public hearing set. The applicant, NRD Retail, LLC, wants the land, owned by Mid Atlantic State Fund, LLC, rezoned from Rural Preservation to M-1 Industrial for a data center and supporting uses. The site, about 87.5 acres, lies east of the I-95 interchange at Ladysmith, next to the southern boundary of the old Virginia Bazaar. The plan is for data center buildings of up to 300,000 square feet each, 792,000 square feet in all. The development plan filed with the county shows a 10-acre substation on the site. NRD Retail's attorney, Ann Neil Cosby, invited neighbors to a community meeting at Lotus Academy in Ruther Glen in August 2024. No megawatt figure, tenant or cost has been made public. The land is zoned for rural preservation, so the project needs the Board of Supervisors to approve a rezoning after a Planning Commission hearing. The largest project at the Ladysmith interchange is CleanArc Data Centers' campus on 650 acres at the former Virginia Bazaar flea market, just east of I-95 at Exit 110. In August 2025 the Board of Supervisors approved a performance agreement for three 490,000-square-foot buildings there, with Bowling Green District Supervisor Jeff Sili the lone vote against, and the county will rebate part of the new taxes as annual grants. CleanArc needed no rezoning, because data centers were allowed by right on industrial land when it applied; the county changed that on December 10, 2024, and now requires a special exception permit for data centers on industrial parcels. On September 22, 2026, supervisors voted 4-2 to rezone 916 acres for Luck Stone's Carmel Technology and Enterprise Center, an industrial park with no named end user, over traffic concerns from Supervisors Jeff Black and Jeff Sili. Across the Fredericksburg region, residents are organizing: Cindy Staats of Safeguard Spotsy told a League of Women Voters forum that Spotsylvania has approved six data center developments with 10 more in the pipeline "all within a 15-mile radius," and said "We need to pause." Bull Church is one of several data center requests on the county's list: ADP Ladysmith Data Hub wants to rezone 140 acres on Green Road west of I-95, and Thornberry, LLC wants to rezone 657 acres on Carneal Lane for a data center campus, and neither has a hearing date. No hearing date had been set as of September 2026. When one is, the Planning Commission will hold a public hearing and make a recommendation, and the Board of Supervisors will vote. Caroline County's Board of Supervisors decides rezonings and special exceptions: Chair Clay Forehand, Nancy Long, Floyd Thomas, Reginald Underwood, Jeff Black and Jeff Sili. The site is in the Mattaponi District, represented by Supervisor Floyd Thomas.

ft-1045.text: Green Energy Ventures' King George Technology Center, a data center campus of 13 buildings on about 300 acres at the northwest corner of Kings Highway (Route 3) and Bloomsbury Road in King George County, was approved by the Board of Supervisors on February 17, 2026. The vote to rezone the land from agricultural to industrial was 3 to 2, with Cathy Binder of Shiloh and William Davis of Dahlgren against; Davis then joined the majority to let buildings rise to 65 feet at two stories and 90 feet at three, above the county's 50 foot limit. "You're asking us to make a vote on an unknown, and that bothers me," Binder said, because the project does not yet have a power source. Supervisor Ken Stroud answered that anything built in an industrial zone needs a lot of power: "So, regardless of what goes in there, there's going to be an issue of power." The approval allows 6.5 million square feet of data centers set back 250 feet from Route 3, forbids groundwater for cooling, allows only Tier 4 generators, and comes with 18 acres for the county, $3 million at the first building permit, $500,000 for public safety training and an aerial ladder truck. In March 2026 Horti-Group USA, whose 156.6 acre farm with 55 acres of greenhouses sits immediately next to the site, sued the board in King George Circuit Court, calling the decision arbitrary and capricious and a breach of the Chesapeake Bay Preservation Act and the county's own comprehensive plan. The farm grows 500,000 poinsettias and two million chrysanthemums a year, plants that need uninterrupted darkness, and says the campus's light and generator exhaust would imperil its crops and its workers' jobs; it asks the court to void the approval and stop all permits and construction. The site holds wetlands, a FEMA floodplain and a resource protection area, and in July 2025 the planning commission had voted 6 to 2 against recommending the height increase.

ft-1051.text: Ladysmith Technology Park, a data center and electrical substation planned by Mattan Ladysmith, LLC on Ladysmith Road just northwest of the I-95 interchange in Caroline County, Virginia, is under the county's technical review. The land is already zoned M-1 Industrial and B-1 Business, so Mattan filed a site plan rather than a rezoning, and no public hearing is required. The major site plan, prepared by Bowman Consulting Group and dated December 9, 2024, shows a first data center building and a substation yard of about 7.1 acres on the parcel, in the Port Royal district. No megawatt figure, tenant or cost has been made public. The timing matters. On December 10, 2024, the day after this plan was dated, the county began requiring a special exception permit for data centers on industrial land, which means a public hearing and a vote by supervisors. CleanArc, across the interchange, was allowed to proceed without one because it had applied before the change, and the county's list shows Ladysmith Technology Park still proceeding as a site plan with no hearing required. The largest project at the Ladysmith interchange is CleanArc Data Centers' campus on 650 acres at the former Virginia Bazaar flea market, just east of I-95 at Exit 110. On September 22, 2026, supervisors voted 4-2 to rezone 916 acres for Luck Stone's Carmel Technology and Enterprise Center, an industrial park with no named end user, over traffic concerns from Supervisors Jeff Black and Jeff Sili. Other data center requests near Ladysmith include the Bull Church Data Center rezoning on Bull Church Road and ADP Ladysmith Data Hub's rezoning of 140 acres on Green Road, both without hearing dates. As a site plan on land already zoned for industry, it is listed as needing no public hearing. The parcel is in the Port Royal District, represented by Supervisor Nancy Long. The latest county listing, from September 2026, still shows the plan in technical review.

ft-746.text: Project Hercules, a $3 billion data center campus that AVAIO Digital plans on 452 acres at 267 Industrial Park Lane in Appomattox, has split Appomattox County, Virginia, since residents learned of it in early 2026. The Appomattox County Board of Supervisors has voted for a performance agreement with AVAIO, the Lynchburg News & Advance reported on September 3, 2026, but the vote was not an approval of the data center itself, which is allowed by right at the site. The county's Economic Development Authority agreed in December 2024 to sell the vacant parcel in its industrial park to Avaio Digital Partners, of Stamford, Connecticut, for about $4.5 million, or $10,000 an acre. The site is reached from U.S. 460 and Virginia 26, just north of the town of Appomattox, and Avaio said then that it would have access to 300 megawatts of power from Central Virginia Electric Cooperative and Dominion Energy. The campus would have six buildings and, the EDA says, 200 to 250 jobs. AVAIO says the facility is projected to be energized in 2027; the company has several data centers in development but none yet running. The county estimates the project would generate approximately $17 million in tax revenue. Neighbors say the decisions were made before they knew. "Our announcement came by our local government after decisions had already been quietly made behind closed doors," said Susan Walton, who owns land next to the site. Carol Stratton, 75, who lives half a mile away, said residents rely on private wells and that her biggest fear is noise: "24/7, 365, droning from these mega data centers." Residents also pointed out that baseball fields, soccer fields and a playground are within half a mile, and that Appomattox buys its water from Campbell County under a contract that expires in 2029. A group of residents began raising money in February 2026 to hire an attorney. Hundreds attended an EDA information meeting on March 23, 2026, at which there was no public comment period. Resident Daniel Henry wants the jobs: "We need anything we can get as far as jobs go." Another resident, Harry Franklin Jr., said: "I'm afraid it might take too much water." AVAIO spokesperson John Delacio said the project would use less water and make less noise than local restrictions allow and would not raise residents' power bills, while EDA chair Garet Bosiger said one data center would use as much water as 15 houses. Dominion Energy would still have to supply an additional 250 megawatts, which will require new infrastructure. Robin Foutz, who lives a mile and a half away, put the residents' complaint about process this way: "We've elected you. We voted for you to make these decisions, and so I think that is where our area has missed the mark." Bosiger answered: "Now, you can't negotiate with businesses in the public." Because data centers are permitted by right at the site, the project needed no special permit or public hearing from the supervisors, and Board Chairman John Hinkle said they had no authority to stop it and focused instead on negotiating protections for how it would run. The performance agreement lets AVAIO receive annual payments based on the tax revenue the project generates once the county begins collecting it; Supervisor Trevor Hipps cast the only vote against it. Neighboring localities have moved the other way: Campbell and Amherst counties and Lynchburg have changed their zoning rules to require additional approvals for future data center projects. When the Appomattox deal was announced, AVAIO listed two other Virginia projects in development, at Ladysmith and Ruther Glen in Caroline County. The next chance for the public to weigh in is the state air permit: an AVAIO subsidiary has applied to the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality for a permit covering the backup generators planned for the site, with a public comment period scheduled to begin September 11, 2026 and a DEQ decision expected by mid-December. Locally, the county Economic Development Authority owns and sells the land and the Board of Supervisors controls the incentives, and the county has set up an email address, ADPquestions@appomattoxcountyva.gov, for residents' questions.

ft-716.text: WestDulles Properties of Reston is pursuing the Ironhorse East Ashland data center at 10171 East Patrick Henry Road, on the Hanover County and Ashland town line just east of Interstate 95, Virginia. The campus would span 180 acres and nine two-story buildings totaling 2.2 million square feet; Ashland's town council approved its share in 2024, and Hanover County is weighing a smaller, revised version of the rest. The Hanover Board of Supervisors has a public hearing on the rezoning set for November 10, 2026, according to the county's case file. Hanover rejected an earlier, larger version of the project in 2024. The new version is smaller in the ways neighbors asked for: building heights cut from 110 feet to 75, a 49-lot subdivision proposal dropped, one access point removed, wider buffers and eleven more acres of green space. Developer attorney Andy Condlin said the 2024 denial "was primarily, we feel, because of the residential, because of the height at 110 feet and because of the lack of transition from I-95 to the more rural area of the county," and that the new plan addresses each point. The same week in June 2026 that Hanover's planning commission deferred a decision on the project, the county's board of supervisors voted unanimously to reinstate its data center equipment tax at 45 cents per $100 of assessed value starting in the 2027 financial year. Supervisor Sue Dibble urged caution on the rate: "We need to fully vet this in a very comprehensive manner. This is probably a little premature as far as us effectively raising a tax any higher than our neighbors." The Hanover Planning Commission's August 20, 2026 hearing on the project was listed as a deferral request on the county's case file, and no result has been published. The request next goes to the Hanover Board of Supervisors, whose public hearing is scheduled for November 10, 2026, with WestDulles's affiliate Tradeport Hanover Land LLC as the applicant.

ft-1773977444756-3968.text: LS Power has withdrawn its zoning request for a data center campus at 10165 Old Ridge Road near Ashland in Hanover County, Virginia, next to the Doswell gas plant it used to own. The withdrawal came in a letter from the developer's attorney to the county in May 2026. It is not clear why LS Power pulled the plan, and no new zoning application had been filed as of late June 2026. The latest site plan called for three or four data center buildings on about 200 acres, south of Kings Dominion and the Doswell Energy Center, with a GE Vernova gas turbine and on-site solar. In 2025, LS Power asked federal regulators to let it sell about 300 megawatts of power from two gas units at the Doswell plant to a data center planned there, but the company has since sold Doswell to NRG Energy. It is unclear whether the land sale for the two parcels near Old Ridge Road is still pending. Hanover County supervisors voted 4-3 in May 2026 to deny Tract's 430-acre Mountain Road Technology Park nearby, with Supervisor Jeff Stoneman saying the water concern is valid. In August, the county planning commission voted 5-2 to recommend a separate project, WestDulles Properties' Iron Horse data center campus on East Patrick Henry Road, over objections from most of the dozens of residents who spoke. In Hanover, the planning commission makes a recommendation on each data center rezoning and the county Board of Supervisors makes the final decision, which is where Iron Horse goes next. LS Power has not said whether it will file a new plan for the Old Ridge Road site.

ft-1025.text: Pixel Factory is a small, locally run colocation data center at 9680 Atlee Commons Drive in Ashland, Hanover County, Virginia, just off I-95 north of Richmond. The company says it focuses on businesses the larger data centers do not typically serve, offering rented space, network connections and cloud access rather than the campus-scale computing going up elsewhere in the county. Pixel Factory says its network is fully redundant, with carrier-neutral cross connects to national Tier 1 providers and direct links to cloud providers including Google, Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services. It describes its approach as knowing customers personally, in contrast to the much larger data center campuses planned nearby in Hanover County.

ft-830.text: Brush Mountain Data Center runs a colocation and cloud computing facility in the Virginia Tech Corporate Research Center in Blacksburg, Montgomery County, Virginia. A division of Advanced Logic Industries, it has served businesses from the site since 2012, renting rack space with redundant power, cooling and fiber connections alongside private cloud, backup and disaster recovery services. The company markets itself to small and mid-sized businesses rather than the large campuses most of this site tracks. "We're not a distant hyperscaler. We're your neighbors in the New River Valley, reachable by phone, accountable for uptime, and invested in your success," its website says. It does not publish the size of its facility or how much power it uses. Both Brush Mountain and its parent company have long been tenants of the research park, which lets other tenants buy its services at special rates. The company has worked with Virginia Tech graduate engineering students on a cooling strategy meant to cut power use, according to the research park, which said Brush Mountain chose the location for the power and internet bandwidth available through the university's network.

Headwaters Site Development had applied to rezone about 68 acres on U.S. Route 28 north of Catlett, near Gaskins Lane in Fauquier County, from industrial park to business park, for up to five data center buildings 60 feet tall. In a letter dated July 15 to the county's chief planner, Adam Shellenberger, the company's attorney Tony Calabrese wrote that "after careful consideration, we have decided not to proceed with the rezoning." The planning commission hearing had been set for Thursday, July 18, and the application had drawn community objections about concrete buildings at the entrance to the village, noise and power lines. Supervisor Regan Washer said "I'm very upfront, and I'm not in favor of it at all," and board chairman Rick Gerhardt wanted to "rip the Band-Aid off it and move forward, and let the cards fall where they may." Chris Colvin, president of Protect Catlett, said afterwards: "We will continue to stay dialed in. We will keep a lookout for any future data center developers in Catlett, whether it be Headwaters or others." The Piedmont Environmental Council records the Catlett project as withdrawn in July 2024, describing it as 1.4 million square feet in three to five buildings on more than 60 acres, and notes it would have needed a three mile transmission line running into Prince William County. Fauquier is carrying a heavy pipeline behind this. Approved but unbuilt are a 220,000 square foot Amazon building at Warrenton and the 1,286,000 square foot Remington Technology Park, and proposed in the south of the county are Convergent Technology Park, Gigaland and SAMX. The council says the county's existing generation is maxed out and that four proposed rezonings would double the expected data center load, needing the power of more than 500,000 homes. The wiring is the part that reached beyond Catlett: Dominion Energy postponed its Morrisville line upgrade in April 2024, citing right of way limits, and has since asked for two new substation locations at Remington to serve complexes needing over 400 megawatts. A federal National Interest Electric Transmission Corridor designation, which would bypass state review, includes a segment through northern Fauquier near Fiery Run, and the council's recommendation is that the county build out only what is already permitted and approve nothing more.

ft-643.text: Diode Ventures, a subsidiary of Black & Veatch, withdrew its plan for a data center campus on about 515 acres in Charles City County, Virginia, after months of local opposition. The company told the county Board of Supervisors on August 18, 2025 that it was pulling its rezoning request and special use permits for the Roxbury Technology Park, and said it had no plans to refile there or anywhere else in the county. The 515-acre site, about 20 miles east of Richmond, sits on five parcels Diode wanted rezoned to Light Industrial; the campus's total power was never disclosed. Diode said it would not use groundwater for cooling and estimated 800 to 1,200 construction jobs and 50 to 100 permanent jobs. The planning commission recommended the project in May 2025, but the Board of Supervisors delayed its vote in June after residents raised noise, light pollution and a lack of transparency from the developer. Days before withdrawing, Diode filed revised plans turning about 100 acres of the site into a conservation buffer. The company said it was choosing "to shift our focus elsewhere based on the results of conversations with our local collaborators and analysis of the site's availability to be shovel-ready with power and municipal support." Any new plan for the Roxbury site would need a fresh rezoning request, a planning commission recommendation and a final vote by the Board of Supervisors. Charles City County adopted data center performance standards in 2024 that Diode had asked to modify for this project.

ft-1061.text: Balico LLC wanted to build a data center campus and a natural gas power plant on about 750 acres of farmland near the town of Chatham, in Pittsylvania County, Virginia. Its first application, filed in October 2024, covered 2,200 acres, 84 data center buildings and a 3,500-megawatt gas plant. Backers called it the largest gas plant in Virginia. CEO Irfan Ali told DCD the plant would draw on the Mountain Valley Pipeline: “MVP will provide us with all the gas we need, and it’s right there on our site.” Neighbors organized against it. Amanda Wydner, a cattle and livestock farmer who moved back to the county to raise her children there, and longtime resident Kathy Stump helped lead the opposition. Wydner said the fight drew together residents who were “Black and white, male and female, young and old,” united by fear the project would “irrevocably change the area.” Balico offered nearby landowners $30,000 up front and $50,000 every six months while it studied the land, payments large enough to divide neighbors. Dave and Amy Davis turned down an increased offer, saying “there's nowhere else” they wanted to live. Mike Ferrette and Mary Knapp had moved to the county from Fairfax to get away from exactly this kind of development. “I feel like I brought this down here with me like gum on my shoe,” Ferrette said. Balico withdrew that application in November 2024 and resubmitted a smaller version later that month: 12 data center buildings of 396,000 square feet each, with the same 3,500-megawatt plant. Ali said the first phase would be 300 megawatts. In January 2025 the county planning commission voted unanimously to recommend denial, saying not enough specifics had been provided. The board of supervisors then postponed its final vote twice, in February and March, at Balico's request. On April 7, 2025 Balico asked to withdraw its application, announcing the request the day before the board's scheduled vote. The board refused, voting 5-2 to deny the withdrawal request, then voted 6-1 on April 15, 2025 to deny the rezoning itself. Supervisor Tim Dudley, who represents the Hurt district, where the town of Hurt had agreed to supply the campus with water, cast the only vote for the project; Chairman Robert Tucker said he was not opposed to data centers but voted no because “we don't have community buy-in.” Supervisor Kenneth Bowman said the fight had divided the county: “It's going to take a long time to heal that pain. It may take a generation.” Resident Amy Davis told the board Balico would “threaten our communities in a negative way, impacting the region's air, water, noise, light quality.” Katie Whitehead, of the local opposition group, said the vote “shows respect for our comprehensive plan and concern for the many people whose health would be harmed by gas-fired power generation.” Morgan Butler, a senior attorney with the Southern Environmental Law Center, which had pressed concerns about the project, said residents had made clear that “Balico's gas plant and data center campus would upend the County's vision for this area.” The denial barred Balico from filing a substantially similar plan on the site for a year, a period that ended in April 2026. Company attorney Steven Gould said Balico would explore other uses for the land, including housing, and the company later called a residential subdivision on the 750 acres “a viable alternative,” though “not the ideal use we had envisioned.” No new application has been made public; any new plan would go back to the Pittsylvania County Board of Supervisors.

ft-645.text: Denver-based developer Tract withdrew its rezoning application for a data center park on 744 acres at 16100 Branders Bridge Road in Chesterfield County, Virginia, on July 1, 2025, after the county Planning Commission unanimously recommended denial. The site sits in southeastern Chesterfield near Colonial Heights, between Branders Bridge Road and Swift Creek. Tract said it intended to resubmit the application "in the coming months." Chesterfield's own list of data center projects, current as of July 2026, does not show a new filing at the Branders Bridge Road site. Tract had planned up to 11 data center buildings totaling about 2 million square feet on roughly 350 acres, with about 365 acres left as open space, and offered to cap water use, limit generator noise to 60 decibels, cap building heights at 110 feet and keep a 725-foot buffer along Branders Bridge Road. Planning commissioner Gib Sloan, who represents the Bermuda District, said the project's location, not its design, was the problem: "Inside the property lines, I feel like it's a good case. Where I have a real challenge is where it's located," he said, calling Branders Bridge Road "by every definition" a substandard road. Chesterfield's Board of Supervisors has since adopted a zoning ordinance that ends by-right development of new data centers, so a refiled Tract application would need a conditional-use permit, first from the Planning Commission and then a final vote by the Board of Supervisors.

ft-776.text: The whole of Culpeper County uses about 240 megawatts of power, and the XX Tech Park data center proposed at Brandy Station could need between 700 megawatts and 1.8 gigawatts. The applicant is Culpeper Acquisitions LLC, and the scheme is over 4.6 million square feet of data center space, which the Piedmont Environmental Council put at the equivalent of 25 Walmart Super Centers. The ground is farmland and battlefield. The site is less than a mile from the new Culpeper Battlefields State Park and near the Brandy Station Graffiti House. It would need a large substation and an imposing new transmission line through two to five miles of privately owned rural land. The same developer withdrew an earlier proposal at the same place, called AttoTek, in 2022, after fierce community opposition about the effect on the historic and agricultural resources of Brandy Station. The planning commission hearing was set for the evening of Wednesday, June 12. Culpeper has taken a lot already: eight data center campuses approved or built, and more than ten million square feet approved in recent years. Culpeper County wrote zoning limits on data centers on September 2, 2025, after this application went in.

ft-1779306466157-5974.text: STACK Infrastructure's planned AI data center campus at the Southern Virginia Megasite at Berry Hill, less than 10 miles west of Danville in Pittsylvania County, Virginia, is moving ahead after the Danville-Pittsylvania Regional Industrial Facilities Authority approved a local performance agreement on May 18, 2026. The agreement calls for $100 billion in investment and 2,500 jobs paying at least $80,500 over 30 years, the largest economic development announcement in Southside history. The company still has to close on the land and clear its own site-selection process before construction starts. In March 2026 the authority agreed to sell STACK's affiliate up to 2,990 acres, nearly all of the remaining land at the 3,528-acre megasite, at $238,000 an acre; the deal depends on securing 299 megawatts of power from Appalachian Power by the end of 2028. The land is being bought in phases, the first closing by June 2027 and the rest by June 2031. Pittsylvania and Danville bought the megasite together in 2008 and have spent more than $217 million preparing it. The performance agreement sets minimum local taxes of $16.25 million a year on the first 1,000 acres, rising to about $48.5 million once all 2,990 acres are bought, and requires payments if job targets are missed. Four residents spoke at the May meeting, three against the project over water use and transparency. "They say that they've got the water and power under control, the wells, but what happens if it goes wrong?" said Erin Hall, who lives four miles from the site. County economic development director Matt Rowe said the region has enough water for the project and that ratepayers will not see higher electric bills as a result. The Pittsylvania County Board of Supervisors is expected to set a separate tax on data center equipment of $1.62 per $100 of assessed value, and the county is giving no discretionary monetary incentives. Virginia's data center sales tax exemption, which the project depends on, runs to 2035 after the General Assembly kept it in place in June 2026; under a separate state deal the project is exempt from state retail taxes until at least 2040 if it invests at least $35 billion and creates at least 1,000 jobs.

sentences.t: STACK Infrastructure's planned AI data center campus at the Southern Virginia Megasite at Berry Hill, less than 10 miles west of Danville in Pittsylvania County, Virginia, is moving ahead after the Danville-Pittsylvania Regional Industrial Facilities Authority approved a local performance agreement on May 18, 2026.
The agreement calls for $100 billion in investment and 2,500 jobs paying at least $80,500 over 30 years, the largest economic development announcement in Southside history.
The company still has to close on the land and clear its own site-selection process before construction starts.

In March 2026 the authority agreed to sell STACK's affiliate up to 2,990 acres, nearly all of the remaining land at the 3,528-acre megasite, at $238,000 an acre; the deal depends on securing 299 megawatts of power from Appalachian Power by the end of 2028.
The land is being bought in phases, the first closing by June 2027 and the rest by June 2031.
Pittsylvania and Danville bought the megasite together in 2008 and have spent more than $217 million preparing it.

The performance agreement sets minimum local taxes of $16.25 million a year on the first 1,000 acres, rising to about $48.5 million once all 2,990 acres are bought, and requires payments if job targets are missed.
Four residents spoke at the May meeting, three against the project over water use and transparency.
"They say that they've got the water and power under control, the wells, but what happens if it goes wrong?" said Erin Hall, who lives four miles from the site.
County economic development director Matt Rowe said the region has enough water for the project and that ratepayers will not see higher electric bills as a result.

ft-779.text: OnePartner's ATAC data center in Duffield, Scott County, Virginia, has been operating for years as a colocation and disaster recovery site. The company says it was the nation's first commercial data center to earn Tier III certification from the Uptime Institute, and it has had no outages since it opened. The 4,000-square-foot facility grew out of a 2006 plan by Holston Medical Group of Kingsport, Tennessee, to store electronic health records, and it opened as OnePartner ATAC, the Advanced Technology and Applications Center, on the medical center campus. Announced with the Scott County Economic Development Authority, the project brought more than 40 technology jobs to Duffield. HMG founder Dr. Jerry L. Miller said at the time: "This will be a data center of excellence, a secure, high-availability repository for electronic medical records and data storage." OnePartner keeps round-the-clock staffed security with SOC 2 and SOC 3 compliance, and it says Scott County has never had even an F1 tornado.

ft-651.text: A data center campus is planned at the Mid-Atlantic Advanced Manufacturing Center, a 930-acre megasite near Emporia in Greensville County, Virginia. The county's Planning Commission voted unanimously on December 10, 2024, to recommend a special use permit for the project, sought by Arup Americas Inc. on behalf of the MAMaC Regional Industrial Facilities Authority, Milldam Public Relations reported. The Board of Supervisors, which decides special use permits, has not published a vote on that recommendation. Arup principal David Green described a four-building data center campus covering about 13 percent of the megasite, with parking, an electrical substation and buildings under 40 feet tall, screened by existing trees. More than 160 employees per 24-hour shift were expected, and the campus would likely use air-based cooling. The site sits in a Technology Overlay District the county created in June 2024 to encourage data center development. Greensville County needs the revenue. Its jobless rate is 6.6 percent, more than double the state average, and Emporia's 8.8 percent is Virginia's highest, after the Georgia-Pacific plywood mill in Emporia shut down last year, Cardinal News reported. County economic development director Natalie Slate said that without data center tax revenue for schools, courthouse renovations, first responder equipment and water and sewer lines, the county "would likely be forced to increase taxes on residents who are already facing substantial economic hardship." Virginia's tax break for data centers runs through 2035, and Senate Finance Chair Louise Lucas has pushed to end it early, which left the General Assembly without a budget for the new fiscal year. State Secretary of Finance Mark Sickles told the Senate Finance Committee in May 2026 that the uncertainty had led Compass Datacenters to halt its search for two data center sites in Greensville County or Emporia. Whether the tax break survives, and with it Greensville's data center hopes, is now up to the General Assembly.

ft-652.text: Black Chamber Partners, LLC, a Washington, D.C. private equity firm, paid $160 million in October 2025 for the 38-acre Merrifield Garden Center site at 6895 Wellington Road in Gainesville, Prince William County, Virginia, planning a data center there. The parcel sits inside the county's Data Center Opportunity Zone Overlay District, where data centers are allowed without a public hearing, so the project remains at the proposed stage with no vote required or scheduled. The sale, more than $4.2 million an acre, was a 500 percent premium on the property's 2025 assessed value of $26.5 million and a 6,857 percent premium on the $2.3 million the Warhurst family paid for the land in 2004. Black Chamber also paid $190 million in March 2025 for a 65-acre industrial site nearby in Manassas, and the firm expects the two sites together to produce more than 740 megawatts of power. Merrifield Garden Center had operated on the site since November 2008, with a 12,000-square-foot store and a 37,000-square-foot greenhouse, and closed December 31, 2025, with some staff moving to its Merrifield and Fairfax locations. Prince William Supervisor Tom Gordy said businesses in the data center zone are "at risk as long as the overlay continues to exist," calling the sale "a perfect example as to why the overlay needs to be removed." State Senator Danica Roem called losing "a garden center, where the business model is about plants and making sure people have greenery in their yards," so another data center could add to rising energy bills, "beyond parody." Board of Supervisors chair Deshundra Jefferson called Merrifield "unique and beloved," saying the county's local character "is not something we can put a price tag on." Science educator Katherine Conklin said the store drew monarch butterflies every migration season "because the plants and the flowers are available to the insects," and called the habitat loss "definitely a concern."

ft-1056.text: Trammell Crow wants to build a data center campus of three buildings, about 1.5 million square feet in all, on 181 acres along Olde Forge Drive in southern Stafford County, Virginia, across the Rappahannock River from Fredericksburg. The developer, TC Blaisdell of Delaware, applied in December 2024 to rezone 11 parcels from urban commercial and agricultural to heavy industrial. The application still needs approval from the Stafford Planning Commission and then the Board of Supervisors, and no decision has been reported since a March 2025 community meeting. At that meeting, the company's lawyer, Charlie Payne, said the campus would come online between 2028 and 2031, employ about 159 people at full buildout, and raise local tax revenue from $12.3 million in the first year to $35.9 million by 2031. Payne said the buildings would be air cooled and draw no water from the Rappahannock, and the company's proffers cap daytime noise at 55 decibels in residential zones, 65 in commercial zones and 79 in industrial ones. Neighbors were not convinced. Rebecca Malin, who works at Belmont, the nearby estate of the painter Gari Melchers, and said she lives in the house closest to the site, worried about noise and about who would pay for the power: "That's something that these guys never cover." Christina Mellors objected to the location: "But there's places for them to be placed, and that's places that already are heavy industrial." Payne said in March 2025 that the Board of Supervisors was unlikely to decide before 2026; the vote was expected in 2026, and no result has been published. By June 2026, Stafford County had roughly 18 data center proposals moving through its pipeline, county staff said at a Board of Supervisors meeting.

ft-1041.text: The Cranes Corner Data Center, proposed by GAM 403 Mountain LLC on about 46 acres east of U.S. 1 and about 1,400 feet north of Centreport Parkway near Fredericksburg, in Stafford County, Virginia, is one of five data center projects the county approved before tightening its rules that may still be built under the old ones. Its applicant, Jacob Manevich, also filed through GAM Stafford LLC for the larger Enon Road Technology Park nearby, planned for up to 2 million square feet of data center buildings. The rezoning, from agricultural and light industrial to heavy industrial, allows up to 900,000 square feet of data center buildings using air-cooled, closed-loop or other low-impact cooling that does not draw on public water. Stafford County's own financial forecast counts three buildings totaling 792,000 square feet at Cranes Corner, with two delivered in fiscal year 2030 and one in 2031. Unusually for a data center, Cranes Corner drew praise from a neighbor. AnnMarie Halterman, trustee for nearby land her family bought to build a house, told the Planning Commission in late August 2025 that she thought the data center would be quieter and better-looking than another industrial use, and "safer for my neighborhood... because of the extra security that's happening." The commission voted unanimously to recommend approval, and Garrisonville District Commissioner Laura Sellers said the project's impacts to local residents "are minimal." Elsewhere in Stafford the fight has been sharper. In October 2025 the Board of Supervisors required new data center buildings to sit 750 feet from homes, schools and the Rappahannock and Potomac rivers, up from 100 feet, then on December 2 voted unanimously to let Cranes Corner and four other approved projects continue under the earlier rules, narrowed so grandfathering covers only changes "directly attributable" to the approved project. The new rules also set a 55-decibel noise cap and 200-foot vegetative buffers that grandfathered projects do not have to meet. The next step is site plan review by Stafford County staff under the pre-October rules. The Board of Supervisors, chaired by Deuntay Diggs, would be involved again only if the developer sought changes beyond what is directly attributable to the approved project. No end user has been named.
