sentences.t: The Cranes Corner Data Center, proposed by GAM 403 Mountain LLC on about 46 acres east of U.S. 1 and about 1,400 feet north of Centreport Parkway near Fredericksburg, in Stafford County, Virginia, is one of five data center projects the county approved before tightening its rules that may still be built under the old ones.
Its applicant, Jacob Manevich, also filed through GAM Stafford LLC for the larger Enon Road Technology Park nearby, planned for up to 2 million square feet of data center buildings.

The rezoning, from agricultural and light industrial to heavy industrial, allows up to 900,000 square feet of data center buildings using air-cooled, closed-loop or other low-impact cooling that does not draw on public water.
Stafford County's own financial forecast counts three buildings totaling 792,000 square feet at Cranes Corner, with two delivered in fiscal year 2030 and one in 2031.
Unusually for a data center, Cranes Corner drew praise from a neighbor.

AnnMarie Halterman, trustee for nearby land her family bought to build a house, told the Planning Commission in late August 2025 that she thought the data center would be quieter and better-looking than another industrial use, and "safer for my neighborhood... because of the extra security that's happening."
The commission voted unanimously to recommend approval, and Garrisonville District Commissioner Laura Sellers said the project's impacts to local residents "are minimal."
Elsewhere in Stafford the fight has been sharper.

In October 2025 the Board of Supervisors required new data center buildings to sit 750 feet from homes, schools and the Rappahannock and Potomac rivers, up from 100 feet, then on December 2 voted unanimously to let Cranes Corner and four other approved projects continue under the earlier rules, narrowed so grandfathering covers only changes "directly attributable" to the approved project.
The new rules also set a 55-decibel noise cap and 200-foot vegetative buffers that grandfathered projects do not have to meet.
The next step is site plan review by Stafford County staff under the pre-October rules.
The Board of Supervisors, chaired by Deuntay Diggs, would be involved again only if the developer sought changes beyond what is directly attributable to the approved project.
No end user has been named.

ft-1060.text: The Enon Road Technology Park, a proposed data center campus of up to 2 million square feet on 162 acres south of Enon Road and west of Wyatt Lane, near Fredericksburg in Stafford County, Virginia, is still stuck in county staff review two years after it was filed, with its water and sewer plans not yet accepted. The Enon Road data center applicant is Jacob Manevich of GAM Stafford LLC, and the site lies just west of Interstate 95. The application, filed in July 2024, asks the county to rezone 162.36 acres in the Hartwood election district from agricultural (A-1) to light and heavy industrial (M-1 and M-2) for a technology park of data centers and infrastructure, according to the county's planning record. The county lists its status as incomplete, and no public hearing has been scheduled. In the first round of review in 2024, the planning, environmental, fire, historic, stormwater, utilities and zoning reviewers all failed the submission. Utilities staff asked for water use numbers for the data centers and for the proffers to say how the site would be sewered, noting the parcel is in the Claiborne Run sewer shed and would need to connect to the line along Route 1. Historic reviewers found county records showing a possible burial on one parcel and a possible family cemetery on another, which would likely need to be delineated. Another comment asked whether the noise of the data centers had been considered for wildlife and for a nearby park, and what happens to sound levels as more buildings come online. By the third round, completed on August 26, 2026, the planner and fire reviews had approved it, but the utilities review failed again. The same applicant is behind Cranes Corner, a data center of about 900,000 square feet on 46 acres just east of U.S. 1, filed under GAM 403 Mountain LLC. Cranes Corner is one of five Stafford data center projects the county grandfathered under its older rules when it tightened data center regulations in late 2025, along with the Stafford Technology Campus, Potomac Church Tech Center, Centreport Gateway/Pemberton and Vantage VA-4. Enon Road is not on that list, so it would have to meet the stricter rules, including the 750-foot setback from homes that the supervisors approved. Enon Road was one of five Stafford data center rezonings reported together in January 2025, alongside the GWV Data Center, Accokeek Center and Austin Ridge Logistics Center. Since then residents have pushed back hard. When the Accokeek Tech Park hearing was pulled an hour before it was to start in April 2026, Protect Stafford president Erin Sanzero called the move "unconscionable," and planning commission chairwoman Kristen Barnes said: "I felt the public's rage, and I agreed with them. I felt it, too." Accokeek Center later won a 4-3 planning commission recommendation in August 2026 over the objections of most of more than 50 speakers, and in July the supervisors deferred the Potomac Creek Campus over a cemetery believed to hold graves of enslaved people. Once county staff accept the application as complete, it goes to a public hearing before the Stafford Planning Commission and then to the Board of Supervisors, which makes the final rezoning decision. The site is in the Hartwood District, whose supervisor is Darrell English. The latest county review of the application is dated August 26, 2026.

ft-659.text: The Forest Lane Data Center, a plan to rezone 845 acres at the northeast corner of Kings Highway (Route 3) and Forest Lane near Fredericksburg in Stafford County, Virginia, for data centers, is still under county staff review. The applicant, Real Estate Pursuits 2 LC, is affiliated with the developer Peterson Companies and wants the land moved from agricultural and light industrial zoning to heavy industrial, with a conditional use permit for an electrical substation. When it was filed in the summer of 2025, it was the 16th active data center application in Stafford's pipeline, and little was known about the applicant. Army Corps of Engineers filings later tied Real Estate Pursuits 2 to Peterson, whose address and email addresses appear in the documents. The same affiliate has filed for Project Sisson nearby, off Kings Highway around Albion Lane on the banks of the Rappahannock River: 16 two-story buildings totaling 3.8 million square feet with four substations, cooled with water from the Little Falls Wastewater Treatment Plant. Peterson earlier developed the Stafford Technology Campus in Falmouth, since taken over by Stack. At the Board of Supervisors on June 2, 2026, residents raised air pollution and health. Washington District resident J.W. Swain, citing plans for about 11 million square feet of data centers along the Kings Highway assemblage, said: "I calculated based on tier 4 generators, which are the best you can get, 37,000 pounds of PM 2.5 and PM 10 material." He said schools lie 1.5 to 2 miles away and a park about 1,000 yards away. He added that state regulators cannot deny permits on the concentration of pollution sources alone: "You are the last stand for health, our health concerns." Kevin French, a George Washington District resident and former technology executive, urged supervisors to hire outside legal, financial and technical experts given the scale of the proposals; supervisors did not respond directly to the comments. Stafford is carrying roughly 18 data center proposals totaling tens of millions of square feet. In April 2026, county planning staff recommended deferring the Potomac Creek Campus off Eskimo Hill Road, where a cemetery holds the graves of 18 or more enslaved people, and denying the Accokeek Center near U.S. 1 as incompatible with nearby homes. At a League of Women Voters forum in September 2026, a University of Mary Washington professor described the Stafford Technology Center, being built near Eskimo Hill Road, as one of five data center projects Stafford has already cleared, and the group Protect Stafford is organizing residents. The rezoning needs public hearings before both the Stafford County Planning Commission and the Board of Supervisors, which makes the final decision. The Board of Supervisors adopted tighter data center rules in December 2025, Ordinance O25-29(R), after setback, buffer and noise recommendations from the Planning Commission. No hearing date has been set for Forest Lane; as of June 2026 the application remained under county staff review.

ft-660.text: King George County has approved one of the larger single sites in Virginia outside the Ashburn corridor. The Oasis Digital campus covers 485 acres on the north side of James Madison Parkway near Dahlgren, with ten data center buildings and 6.8 million square feet planned, and a year planned of 2028. The figures given for the county are 1,500 construction jobs, 50 to 60 permanent jobs per building once running, and $100 million to $120 million a year in tax. The land was assembled and pitched separately, under the name Dahlgren West. That project describes about 500 acres beside Route 301, zoned for a mix of commercial and industrial uses and formally designated a Technology District by the county. Its team held community meetings at the University of Mary Washington on April 17, 2024 and at the L.E. Smoot Library on October 30, 2024, and then submitted an application, after what it called over a year of conversations with residents, community leaders and stakeholders. It gives the same fiscal figure, about $100 million to $120 million a year at full build. Oasis co-founder Ross Likenhous said the choice was deliberate: "It's a tangible example of data centers being lured outside of Northern Virginia because of the shifting political winds and the shrinking appetite for additional data centers in Northern Virginia." His partner Nick Over was previously a principal at Potomac Development Group, which proposed a 9 million square foot campus on a 500 acre parcel off the same parkway in 2024, and Oasis has other projects in Russell, Wise and Greensville counties.

ft-655.text: Fredericksburg's city council turned down the Penzance Development data center twice over, in the early hours of Wednesday, August 26, 2026. It voted 7 to 0 to deny the rezoning that would have put two data center buildings on the 84 acre Hylton tract at 1500 Gateway Boulevard beside Interstate 95, then 7 to 0 again to deny the special use permit that would have raised them from 50 feet to 75. The developer was Penzance, through an affiliate called 1500 Gateway LLC. The application that went before the council had already been cut down. It was two buildings of about a million square feet, down from four and about two million; the generators had been turned to face the interstate; 44 percent of the site was to be left open; and the buildings were to be air cooled, with water limited to about 2,700 gallons a day for washrooms and fire suppression. Penzance raised its cash proffers to just over $40 million and signed a project labor agreement guaranteeing union construction. Its attorney, Charlie Payne, said: "I've never seen proffers of this nature in any data center industrial project, period." It did not turn on the money. Council members pointed to the Technology Overlay District the city adopted after a seven month public process, which confines data center development to about 3.8 percent of the city, near Celebrate Virginia South and the ballpark. Mayor Kerry Devine said development pressure on the Hylton tract is still on the table. The hearing ran past midnight and adjourned at about a quarter to one, with 51 speakers and 49 letters read into the record, against six speakers at the planning commission hearing in July 2025 and 51 at the December one. The planning commission had recommended refusal both times. Vice Mayor Chuck Frye, a Teamsters member, said the construction workers' concerns about union jobs were real, and urged his colleagues to apply the lessons of the project labor agreement to other city work.

ft-748.text: Sisson North is a proposed data center of about 1.1 million square feet on 106.48 acres along the north side of Kings Highway, near Layover Lane, in Stafford County, Virginia, filed by Jon M. Peterson of Real Estate Pursuits 2 LC, an affiliate of Peterson Companies. The company asks Stafford County to rezone the land from agricultural to heavy industrial and to allow an electrical substation; the application remains under staff review, with public hearings still to come before the Planning Commission and Board of Supervisors. Sisson North is part of Peterson's larger Project Sisson, which the company has described in federal filings as 16 two-story data center buildings totaling 3.8 million square feet with four substations on the banks of the Rappahannock River, with cooling water to come from the Little Falls Wastewater Treatment Plant less than two miles away. At the June 2, 2026 Board of Supervisors meeting, resident J.W. Swain said backup generators for the roughly 11 million square feet of data centers proposed along the Kings Highway corridor could release 37,000 pounds of fine particulate matter a year, with schools 1.5 to 2 miles away: "You are the last stand for health, our health concerns. You are the Alamo of our health concerns." Kevin French, a former technology executive, urged the county to hire outside legal, financial and technical experts: "Few local governments have ever been asked to simultaneously consider land use, water, utility, fiscal, legal and economic development implications on this scale." Stafford has roughly 18 data center proposals in its pipeline; the Planning Commission has recommended denial of the nearby Potomac Creek Campus over a historic cemetery on its site, while five large projects, including the Stafford Technology Campus, are grandfathered under the county's 2025 data center ordinance. The county held public meetings on June 18 and 22, 2026 to gather resident input on its five-year Comprehensive Plan update, which will guide where future data centers like Sisson North can go; no hearing date for the Sisson North rezoning itself has been published.

The company asks Stafford County to rezone the land from agricultural to heavy industrial and to allow an electrical substation; the application remains under staff review, with public hearings still to come before the Planning Commission and Board of Supervisors.

Sisson North is part of Peterson's larger Project Sisson, which the company has described in federal filings as 16 two-story data center buildings totaling 3.8 million square feet with four substations on the banks of the Rappahannock River, with cooling water to come from the Little Falls Wastewater Treatment Plant less than two miles away.

Swain said backup generators for the roughly 11 million square feet of data centers proposed along the Kings Highway corridor could release 37,000 pounds of fine particulate matter a year, with schools 1.5 to 2 miles away: "You are the last stand for health, our health concerns. ft-948.text: The Innsbrook data center at 4551 Cox Road in Glen Allen, in Henrico County outside Richmond, Virginia, now operates under Uniti Group, a fiber company that took it over through a corporate merger. Uniti and Windstream Holdings announced the merger in May 2024, combining Uniti's wholesale fiber network with Windstream's fiber-to-the-home business. The deal, unanimously approved by both companies' boards, was expected to close in the second half of 2025 and gives Uniti shareholders about 62% of the combined company, with Windstream shareholders getting $425 million in cash and $575 million in preferred equity. Uniti, based in Little Rock, Arkansas, owns fiber and wireless towers with about 138,000 fiber route miles; Windstream, also based in Little Rock, provides rural broadband and had been one of Uniti's biggest customers. The two companies were once the same business: Uniti was originally part of Windstream before they split in 2015 and renegotiated their lease agreement.

ft-664.text: HHHunt planned ten data center buildings, 3.9 million square feet, on the 410-acre Hunting Hawk Golf Club site near Glen Allen, north of Wyndham in Hanover County, Virginia, with its own substations, water and sewer systems. The county planning commission voted unanimously to recommend denial, and HHHunt withdrew its applications in a letter dated January 28, 2026, two weeks after that vote, Richmond BizSense reported on January 30. The project is now cancelled. More than 450 people packed a public meeting on the project in November 2025. Supervisor Sue Dibble said the plan clashed with the county's comprehensive plan, which recommends the site for homes: "this was simply not a good project in the right place." She said the public process behind that plan, which included "over 10 meetings in the South Anna District alone," "weeds out the bad projects." HHHunt's general manager, Jonathan Ridout, said the company had no comment on what it would do with the land. It was the second Hanover County data center project to run into organized resident opposition. Supervisors rejected the Tract Mountain Road Technology Park, a 427-acre proposal, by four votes to three, VPM reported June 1, 2026. Both projects were opposed by the group Friends of Hanover, whose organizer, Jennifer Corpus, said: "We really would love to stop playing whack-a-mole with data centers and instead get a data center ordinance, policy and guardrails passed in Virginia."

ft-973.text: A data center is proposed on 52 acres at 6321 Rockford School Road, Gretna, in Pittsylvania County, with no developer named. Fifteen kilometres away, a far larger plan was refused. Balico LLC proposed 84 data centers, each about twice the size of an average Walmart Supercenter, alongside a 3,500 megawatt gas fired power station, on 2,200 acres of rezoned farmland. It would have been the second largest gas plant in the country. Balico filed in September 2024, withdrew after community opposition, and came back in November 2024 on less land with the same gas plant in it. The planning commission unanimously recommended denial in January 2025, and on April 15, 2025 the board of supervisors refused the rezoning 6 to 1. The case that carried was health. A Harvard Data Science Initiative report found the plant would emit more than 326 tons of fine particulate matter a year, raising concentrations for more than 17,500 county residents, more than one in four, and creating about $31 million a year in healthcare costs. The Southern Environmental Law Center represented five local landowners, women it described as an unconventional group with contrasting political beliefs held together by mutual respect and love for their home, and teachers, farmers, pastors and business owners organised alongside them. Elizabeth Putfark, an SELC associate attorney, said: "Communities are a formidable force when they come together to fight large, high polluting projects like this one."

ft-758.text: The Cyber Integration Center at 139 Tyco Street, on a nearly 13-acre site off Main Street in north Harrisonburg, Virginia, is a data center that GI DC Harrisonburg LLC has owned since September 2014, when it bought the building from DBT-DATA for $59 million. The buyer registered a San Francisco address tied to GI Partners, a Menlo Park, California, private equity firm that invests in technology infrastructure. No expansion, sale or new filing at the site has been reported since the 2014 deal. DBT Data first bought the property in 2008, sold it to Harris Corp. for $41.6 million in 2010, then bought it back for $35 million in 2013 after Harris abandoned plans to run it as a cloud storage center. While DBT Data owned it, the company said the building held the only Tier III certification from the Uptime Institute in Maryland or Virginia at the time, plus LEED Silver certification and round-the-clock security staff. DBT Development's president, David Tolson, said demand for federal government and private sector data storage in the Washington, D.C. area was enormous, and that the site would be run to federal government standards.

ft-1784074174322-9081.text: The data center proposed for Hopewell is a study, not an application. Volterra Advisors, a technology consulting firm from Maryland, ran a feasibility case study with the city and the property owners on putting a data center at the former Green Plains ethanol plant at 701 6th Avenue, which closed in 2018 after making 60 million gallons of biofuel a year. The facility studied is 50,000 to 70,000 square feet drawing about 20 megawatts, which is the figure the record carries. For scale, the article set that against Google's three Chesterfield County data centers, about 285,000 square feet each and 200 to 300 megawatts when running. The attraction is the pipework left behind. Volterra's founder, Jeramy Utara, said: "There's potential to re-use the natural gas lines." NS Development Partners bought the 55 acre site about four months before the article appeared in July 2026, and has already leased seven acres to a manufacturer it has not named. The land had previously been looked at for a South Korean car customisation plant that would have employed 3,000 people. Hopewell city officials did not respond to requests for comment on the data center.

ft-665.text: EdgeCore Digital Infrastructure is expected to generate its own power for the 1.1 gigawatt data center campus it is building at the Shannon Hill Regional Business Park in southern Louisa County, Virginia, Louisa District Supervisor Manning Woodward said in June 2026, though the county has received no plans for it. "I would assume that they'll maybe be smaller gas plants or something, maybe small modular reactors," Woodward said; EdgeCore did not answer questions about how it would source its power. When supervisors rezoned the park in 2019 they made major utility service a by-right use, so EdgeCore can build a power plant there without a local public approval process, needing only state and possibly federal permits. The county marketed the site on its closeness to a Columbia Gas transmission line, and Columbia has written to landowners about expanding a section of the line through western Louisa between Boswells Tavern and Shannon Hill. Woodward said the campus would be cooled by a closed-loop air system and draw what water it uses from the James River rather than the Northeast Creek reservoir, central Louisa's only public drinking water source, through a line due by the fall of 2027. EdgeCore bought the 697 acres from the county's Industrial Development Authority for $42 million. It announced the purchase on June 25, 2025, for a 3.9 million square foot campus of more than 1.1 gigawatts and an investment of more than $17 billion. Its announcement named Rappahannock Electric Cooperative and its affiliate, Hyperscale Energy, as the power suppliers rather than Dominion. The land came from the county itself: Louisa County bought the Shannon Hill Regional Business Park for $2.6 million in 2018, zoned it for technology uses in 2019, spent $13.6 million in grants, $17 million in debt and $29.5 million on utilities getting it ready, and sold the 697 acres to EdgeCore for $42 million. Through EDI Louisa 1 LLC, EdgeCore has since applied to the Army Corps of Engineers for a second phase of three buildings and on-site substations on 187 acres between Shannon Hill Road and Parrish Road, which would affect 4.2 acres of wetlands and more than 6,300 feet of streams. By April 2026 construction work had begun at the Louisa campus, Virginia Business reported.

ft-1066.text: Oasis Digital Properties' Dahlgren West data center campus in King George County, Virginia, is fully approved and moving toward construction; residents who protested at the June 2, 2026 Board of Supervisors meeting were told the project is a done deal. The board approved the 1.2-gigawatt campus in August 2025, unanimously, for 10 buildings totaling 6.8 million square feet on 485 acres on the north side of James Madison Parkway near Dahlgren. No site plan had been submitted as of June 2, County Administrator Matthew Smolnik said. The wooded site sits off U.S. 301 about 3 miles south of the Navy base at Dahlgren, with access to 230,000-volt transmission lines, in an area the county designated a technology zone in 2023. Oasis projects 1,500 construction jobs, 50 to 60 full-time jobs per building and $100 million to $120 million a year in real estate and personal property taxes, and must pay the county $5 million toward schools once the first permit is granted. Residents of St. Pauls Road said no one had told them about the project before it was approved. "Would you build this 350 feet from your back deck?" Doug Cross asked the board. "We never got notification of this." Briana Morgan, who moved to the county in October 2025, said: "We bought our forever home. I've got little kids and I don't want a data center in my backyard." Residents came back on June 16, when Kenny Morgan said the campus "turns out it's 83 yards from the closest house's backyard" and told the board: "This won't be the end of us fighting it." Officials said the time to object had been the 2025 public hearings, and that the developer had sent letters, posted signs along Route 301 and advertised the hearings in the newspaper. "It's painful we're getting this months late," said Supervisor Ken Stroud. "This should've happened last year." Supervisor David Sullins, who voted for the campus, said on June 16 that it is "about a quarter mile from my house" and that "that vote was three years in the making." The county will not let Dahlgren West use potable water for cooling; developers are exploring treated wastewater and have asked about piping gray water from the county's wastewater plant at their own expense. Power will come from Northern Neck Electric Cooperative, which requires the developer to pay the entire cost of connecting. The next step is a site plan showing every building and paved surface, checked against state stormwater and buffer standards; wetlands there must be flagged with 100-foot buffers under the Chesapeake Bay Preservation Act, with no activity inside them.

Residents came back on June 16, when Kenny Morgan said the campus "turns out it's 83 yards from the closest house's backyard" and told the board: "This won't be the end of us fighting it."
Officials said the time to object had been the 2025 public hearings, and that the developer had sent letters, posted signs along Route 301 and advertised the hearings in the newspaper.
"It's painful we're getting this months late," said Supervisor Ken Stroud. "This should've happened last year."
Supervisor David Sullins, who voted for the campus, said on June 16 that it is "about a quarter mile from my house" and that "that vote was three years in the making."

The county will not let Dahlgren West use potable water for cooling; developers are exploring treated wastewater and have asked about piping gray water from the county's wastewater plant at their own expense.
Power will come from Northern Neck Electric Cooperative, which requires the developer to pay the entire cost of connecting.

The next step is a site plan showing every building and paved surface, checked against state stormwater and buffer standards; wetlands there must be flagged with 100-foot buffers under the Chesapeake Bay Preservation Act, with no activity inside them.

ft-666.text: Active Infrastructure wants data centers on 362 acres off Evergreen Mills Road in Leesburg, in the part of Loudoun County the county's own plan calls the Transition Policy Area. Loudoun Now described 3.25 million square feet across ten buildings up to a hundred feet tall, with three electrical substations and a backup power storage building, on 325 acres to be rezoned from Transitional Residential-10 to Industrial Park. The Loudoun Wildlife Conservancy put the plan at up to 3.5 million square feet on 362 acres, powered by natural gas hydrogen fuel cells with batteries on site. The land is not empty: the northern 150 acres is farmland, and the southern part is thirteen parcels of the Spring Valley subdivision, ten to seventeen acres each, with single family houses on them. The area also holds a Victorian style house of about 1880, a springhouse, a treehouse and a family cemetery. The conservancy's objection is the woods: mature forest on the banks of Goose Creek, next to the rural policy area and near the county's only nature preserve, and 325 acres of the Transition Policy Area gone. It argued no reduction in emissions could offset cutting down carbon-storing forest and destroying that habitat. The county's own planners opposed the rezoning too, calling it a fundamental departure from transitional residential policy and noting the nearest industrial zone is 2.3 miles away. Planning commission vice chair Michael Turner was blunter: "We have no business building data centers in the Transition Policy Area. It's the wrong place and the wrong time." On July 23, 2026, the commission voted unanimously to recommend refusal, following county staff, after a record number of speakers and written comments against it. The rezoning application is still moving through the county's process; the Board of Supervisors has not yet scheduled its own vote.

ft-793.text: Three data center buildings are approved for Tuscarora Crossing Landbay 3, a 37.6-acre site on Crosstrail Boulevard at the W&OD Trail near Leesburg, in Loudoun County, Virginia, but the substation they need for power is on indefinite hold. BlackChamber Group, a Washington private equity firm, bought the site for $64 million in 2021 and plans three two-story buildings of 233,800 square feet each, 701,400 square feet in all. In October 2025, the applicant, Tuscarora Landbay 3 LLC, asked the Loudoun County Board of Supervisors to defer its substation application indefinitely, after board chair Phyllis Randall decided to vote against it. The land was part of a 2012 rezoning of 250 acres for homes, shops and industry; data centers were allowed on it in 2015, and a 2019 change raised the permitted data center space to 1.4 million square feet. BlackChamber bought it from an entity controlled by Capretti Land. To win over neighbors, the applicant offered a partly enclosed substation, a 12-foot wall along Crosstrail Boulevard, evergreen screening, no gas turbines and cleaner generators, and county planning staff recommended approval. Residents of the Tuscarora Crossing neighborhood fought it. "If you approve this, you signal to every future developer they can plant substations and major utilities in residential areas and the board will look the other way," Brett Sposa told supervisors. Emily Kasabian said that when the land was rezoned for data centers, the applicant told the board no substation would be needed, and residents said they were never told a data center would be built nearby when they bought their homes. The Planning Commission had denied the substation permit; supervisors overturned that denial in July 2025, then split 4-4 on it, with Randall abstaining, on September 16. Nearby, supervisors voted 5-4 in July 2025 to approve the Cross Mill Center data center at Evergreen Mills Road and Crosstrail Boulevard, next to Bolen Park. On September 15, 2026, the Board of Supervisors voted 7-1 to pause new data center applications countywide for 12 months, effective immediately, with one supervisor abstaining and Leesburg's supervisor, Kristen Umstattd, voting against it. County staff are due to bring a formal resolution memorializing the pause to the board's October 20 meeting. The pause applies to new applications; it does not by itself restart the Tuscarora Landbay 3 substation case, which the applicant deferred and has not brought back. The Loudoun County Board of Supervisors will decide whether the substation is built if the applicant revives the case. No new hearing date has been set.

ft-672.text: Mesh Capital LLC's plan for three data centers on about 57 acres at U.S. 460 and Cabin Field Road, in the Concord district of Campbell County, Virginia, can go forward under the site's existing heavy industrial zoning, whatever the result of a resident's pending appeal. Supervisors voted 5-2 in October 2025 to reject Mesh Capital's bid to drop a proffer tying the land to a 2000 site plan, but the county's zoning administrator ruled the company's new concept plans meet that old plan, allowing the data centers by right. The original rezoning request would have dropped the proffer entirely, letting Mesh Capital build three data centers of 150,000 square feet each without being bound to a specific layout. The land was rezoned from agriculture to heavy industrial with that proffered plan in January 2000 and has never been developed. Little is known about Mesh Capital, whose representative has a Norfolk address; no end user has been named. The new plans include a 50-foot-wide internal road, up to 15 parcels and at least 14.4% of the property as common green space. Neighbors on Cabin Field Road raised concerns about noise, diesel generators, night lighting, traffic, water use of more than a million gallons a day, and blasting at a nearby quarry. Only 13 adjoining owners were notified, six of whom do not live on the road full time, residents said. "A lot of folks thought that we defeated data centers. That was really not the case," said Ashby Smith, who lives beside the property. Some neighbors with failing wells, though, wanted the water line the project would bring. Resident Ashby Smith petitioned the county to review the zoning administrator's finding, and the Board of Supervisors held a semi-judicial hearing on January 20, 2026 to affirm or reverse it. That hearing was the scheduled vote; no result has been published since. Either way, Mesh Capital can build under the 2000 zoning and proffers, though a reversal would send the company back to file formal site plans first.

ft-771.text: The Mid-County Industrial Park, a 64-acre data center project on Dumfries Road in Prince William County, Virginia, won a 5-3 rezoning approval from the Board of County Supervisors in June 2024 despite the Planning Commission's unanimous recommendation against it. The land, in Manassas, was then bought by the applicant, Minnieville Capital Acquisitions LLC, whose Seattle address in county property records is associated with a post office box used by Amazon. The approval rezoned about 40 acres in the Coles District from agricultural to industrial and added about 20 acres of the existing Colchester Industrial Park, for three data center buildings and an electric substation. The site lies about 250 feet northwest of the intersection of Dumfries and Minnieville roads, next to the Potomac Reserve community, inside the county's Data Center Opportunity Zone Overlay District. In September 2024 Minnieville paid $53.5 million, about $1 million an acre, for 16 of the park's 21 parcels; the rezoning allows buildings up to 95 feet tall. An Amazon spokesperson would not confirm the purchase, saying only that the company is "constantly evaluating new locations based on customer demand." Neighbors in Potomac Reserve fought the rezoning. "When we bought our house we were told that the [site] was agricultural and it was going to stay that way," said Noelia Gonzalez, who lives on John Mallard Drive, where seven homes sit about 100 feet from the planned substation. The developer's attorney said five of those seven homeowners supported the application. Supervisor Bob Weir told the applicant, "You've lost your credibility," over an email claiming the support of all adjacent homeowners who had raised concerns. Supervisor Kenny Boddye argued that part of the land was already zoned industrial, so a denial could have left a less restricted use: "If we vote no, there still could be an industrial use here without us being able to put any mitigations in place whatsoever." The developer promised more screening along Dumfries Road, reforestation, a 12-foot wall around the substation and a 75-foot height limit on the buildings closest to Route 234. It is the second Amazon-linked site in a new mid-county data center corridor, after Amazon's purchase of the former Parsons Business Park 2 miles to the north. Since then, supervisors have unanimously turned down the 2,000-acre Dulles South Innovation Center, in July 2026, days after the PW Digital Gateway ended. "Right now, we have data centers that are not operating because we cannot get power," Supervisor Tom Gordy said at that meeting. Supervisor Margaret Franklin urged the developers to keep nearby residents informed at each phase of construction, InsideNova reported.

ft-760.text: Amazon Web Services owns the former Parsons Farm on Dumfries Road (Va. 234) in the Independent Hill area of Prince William County, Virginia, after buying the land for $218 million in April 2024, a month after county supervisors voted to allow data center buildings up to 85 feet tall there. The Parsons Business Park LLC data center site, about 90 acres between Dumfries Road and the county landfill, sits in the county's data center opportunity zone overlay district, where data centers are allowed by right. A conceptual sketch filed with an early zoning application showed commercial buildings along Dumfries Road and four data center buildings at the rear, which could add roughly 800,000 square feet of data space. The land was rezoned in 2019 for a mix of commercial uses, including data centers up to 45 feet tall. The price came to about $2.4 million an acre, against a county assessment of $25.7 million before the height change. The height change passed 5-1 on March 19, 2024, over the Planning Commission's recommendation to deny it and objections from about a dozen neighbors. Residents had negotiated the 45-foot limit in 2019 and feared noise, security lighting glare and the view of concrete walls from their homes. "When the data center opportunity zone overlay district was created, it was not designed with the intent to build the tallest possible data centers maximizing all the available acreage into a concrete landscape. But that is exactly what it has become," said Rachel Ellis of Gainesville. At the hearing, the owner's lawyer, Mark Looney, said he did not know whether data centers would be built, saying the end use would be up to the new owner. Supervisor Yesli Vega, whose Coles District includes the site, voted yes, saying the application "checks all of the boxes"; Supervisor Bob Weir voted no, citing the stressed power grid. "Because they're always coming back for more and more and more and more and more," Weir said of developers. Further south on Dumfries Road, the proposed Mid-County Industrial Park planned three 95-foot data center buildings and a substation about 75 feet from homes in the Potomac Reserve subdivision. The rules around the site may change. Prince William supervisors are working on a zoning text amendment that would substantially shrink the data center overlay district and end by-right data center development, so that every new data center would need a special use permit from the Board of County Supervisors. Data centers already built or under construction, and those with a site plan past the county's quality control threshold, would stay in the overlay. On September 22, 2026, the Board of County Supervisors approved the amendment 8-0, ending by-right data center development countywide, with a 90-day grace period. A motion by Gainesville Supervisor George Stewart for no grace period, to head off what he called a "gold rush" of data center proposals, failed 3-5. County planners aim to bring a proposed setback from homes and schools to the Planning Commission in November, with a board hearing targeted for January.

The height change passed 5-1 on March 19, 2024, over the Planning Commission's recommendation to deny it and objections from about a dozen neighbors.
Residents had negotiated the 45-foot limit in 2019 and feared noise, security lighting glare and the view of concrete walls from their homes.

"When the data center opportunity zone overlay district was created, it was not designed with the intent to build the tallest possible data centers maximizing all the available acreage into a concrete landscape. But that is exactly what it has become," said Rachel Ellis of Gainesville.
At the hearing, the owner's lawyer, Mark Looney, said he did not know whether data centers would be built, saying the end use would be up to the new owner.
Supervisor Yesli Vega, whose Coles District includes the site, voted yes, saying the application "checks all of the boxes"; Supervisor Bob Weir voted no, citing the stressed power grid.
"Because they're always coming back for more and more and more and more and more," Weir said of developers.
Further south on Dumfries Road, the proposed Mid-County Industrial Park planned three 95-foot data center buildings and a substation about 75 feet from homes in the Potomac Reserve subdivision.
The rules around the site may change.

Prince William supervisors are working on a zoning text amendment that would substantially shrink the data center overlay district and end by-right data center development, so that every new data center would need a special use permit from the Board of County Supervisors.
Data centers already built or under construction, and those with a site plan past the county's quality control threshold, would stay in the overlay.
On September 22, 2026, the Board of County Supervisors approved the amendment 8-0, ending by-right data center development countywide, with a 90-day grace period.
A motion by Gainesville Supervisor George Stewart for no grace period, to head off what he called a "gold rush" of data center proposals, failed 3-5.
County planners aim to bring a proposed setback from homes and schools to the Planning Commission in November, with a board hearing targeted for January.

ft-781.text: The Roosevelt Building at 1755 and 1757 Old Meadow Road in McLean, Fairfax County, Virginia, is a two-story, 69,329-square-foot data center owned by Mapletree Industrial Trust, which lists the property as operating in the southwestern part of McLean. Fairfax County tightened its data center zoning rules in September 2024, adding a 200-foot setback from homes, pre- and post-construction noise studies and a one-mile setback from Metro stations for new projects. Facilities built or approved before July 2024, including the Roosevelt Building, are not subject to the new rules.

ft-677.text: Province Group's data center campus off Page Road near Midlothian has grown to 181 acres approved for about 2 million square feet of space, after the Powhatan County Board of Supervisors voted 5-0 in October 2025 to rezone another 61 acres on the Chesterfield County line. The campus was first approved in October 2024 on 119.9 acres at 1318 Page Road, partly bordering Chesterfield County; the county now describes it as a $3 billion data center on its eastern boundary. The first vote, in October 2024, was 3-2 for a rezoning from agricultural to light industrial and a permit for three data center buildings up to 75 feet tall totaling 1.525 million square feet, against the planning commission's recommendation to deny. Province Group, based in Newport Beach, California, estimated its investment at $3 billion, while county staff put it at $2.7 billion. The 2025 addition, from the Province affiliate Newport Equities LLC on land owned by JMS Investments LLC, allows up to four buildings, and county staff estimate recurring tax revenue of about $9.7 million a year at full build-out. The campus would need 300 to 400 megawatts of power and a new substation on 7 to 8 acres; equipment for it could take five to seven years to procure, and Dominion Energy has issued a will-serve letter but will not formally authorize service until it reviews final site plans. In 2024 residents and a supervisor objected that the project had no named end user and that, after 18 months, the proffers let the land be used for any of 45 other permitted uses. "In order to go to market, we need our zoning approval," Province Group CEO Mark Kerslake told the board. Supervisor Mark Kinney said then: "The $17 million is projected, and that's if all three buildings are built out, they get a user that wants all three [and] all three buildings are packed to capacity with servers." By 2025 Kinney was in favor: "I think this project will be a phenomenal addition to Powhatan and the future of this county." The county's case is its tax base. Residential property makes up just over 93 percent of Powhatan's property values, and the board wants commercial property to produce 15 percent of revenue. "It has very limited impacts with profound tax revenue," said Chairman Bill Donati Jr. The planning commission unanimously recommended denial of the 2025 addition on October 7, citing questions about proffers and impacts; county staff switched to recommending approval after the developer agreed to pay for on-site water and wastewater service, off-site line extensions and a share of upgrades at the Oakbridge Pump Station and Dutoy Creek Wastewater Treatment Plant. Supervisors asked to see any nondisclosure agreements that come up as data center users are recruited. With zoning in place, the next steps are site plans reviewed by Powhatan County staff, a utility agreement with the county before the first site plan is approved, and Dominion's formal authorization of service.

ft-785.text: The data center rezoning at Upper Magnolia Green is on the western part of the site, and the eastern part, which is where the record puts this entry, is being turned into a nature preserve. On Wednesday, May 28, 2025 the Chesterfield County board of supervisors rezoned nearly 980 acres at 4200 Moseley Road and the land adjoining it for data centers, part of more than 1,300 acres rezoned that day for two projects. Tract A, about 870 acres, is restricted to data centers and related uses; Tract B, about 100 acres, to offices, laboratories, pharmaceutical manufacturing and research. A separate proposal would make the eastern parcel, between Westerleigh Parkway and Duval Road where new school buildings are going up, a Swift Creek Preserve conservation area of at least 350 acres, taking away the residential development already approved there. The record holds the eastern part as a proposed data center of 744 acres at 18100 Duval Road, with no developer and no capacity figure. The conditions attached to the western rezoning are unusually specific. Buildings are capped at 110 feet, with a minimum 200 foot buffer around Tract A and a 750 foot setback from the existing houses on Moseley Road. Noise is capped at 75 decibels between six in the morning and eight at night, and 65 decibels overnight. Supervisor Mark Miller was categorical about the water: "We're never, ever going to put at risk our water as a result of a data center. We have one of the most extensive water proffers in place to ensure that we are walking into this with our eyes wide open." Vernon McClure, president of Main Street Homes, said not enough had been done about visibility and noise for the homes planned at his Dogwood Creek project. The board approved a second campus the same day, 350 acres of mostly undeveloped land at 750 Watkins Centre Parkway near Westchester Commons, also restricted to data centers.

ft-893.text: EdgeConneX runs NOR01, an edge data center at 3800 Village Avenue, Suite C, in Norfolk, Virginia, within four miles of downtown Norfolk. The EdgeConneX Norfolk data center has 750 kilowatts of power with N+1 redundancy, according to the company's data sheet. EdgeConneX says the carrier-neutral site was built to deliver content and applications to local consumers with the lowest possible latency, working with local network and cable operators. The company pitches it as a midpoint between the subsea cable landing station at Virginia Beach, the Richmond market and Northern Virginia. The building itself is a 100,000-square-foot, one-level structure at the corner of Village Avenue and Azalea Garden Road near the Interstate 264 and 64 interchange, in which EdgeConneX occupied about 20,000 square feet, according to a leasing flyer for the rest of the space. The flyer said a Cox Communications data center sits directly across from the building, and that power comes from Dominion Energy. EdgeConneX says the site can support anything from a single rack to a large custom cage or pod, up to a build-to-suit data center. Neighboring Virginia Beach and Chesapeake both stopped taking new data center applications in 2026 while they write rules, with Virginia Beach saying it wants to protect businesses tied to its subsea cable landings.

ft-1784758801593-2123.text: Menlo Digital, the data center arm of California real estate investor Menlo Equities, plans a four-building campus it calls MD-VA3 on 74 acres at 2255 Jamestown Drive in Petersburg, Virginia, offering 104 megawatts of power at full build-out, fed by a 300-megawatt substation built as part of the campus. Its site plan has not been approved: Petersburg's interim planning director, Jared Crews, said in July 2026 that comments on Menlo's latest submission went back to late April and an updated plan had not been resubmitted. Menlo's conceptual plan shows four buildings totaling 1.2 million square feet, and the company markets the project as "Richmond Virginia Data Center." An earlier 2024 staff memo to the planning commission described a proposal for two buildings totaling more than 1 million square feet and a substation. The land was zoned for agriculture until city council rezoned it for an initial version of Menlo's project in 2023, and Menlo Digital did not respond to requests for comment. After that rezoning, council changed the city's zoning code in 2024 to let data centers be built "by right," meaning without a council vote or public hearing, in its M-1 light industrial and M-2 heavy industrial districts. When Richmond BizSense reported four data center projects in the city's pipeline in July 2026, using records obtained under public records law, the mayor and several council members said it was news to them. "I read about them in the news," Mayor Samuel Parham told Councilman Charlie Cuthbert at the council meeting. Ward 1 council member Marlow Jones, whose district includes the Menlo site, said he also only learned about the projects that day. "We talk about transparency, and yet it's like we're in a cave with the lights out," said Cuthbert, who represents Ward 4. "From the get-go, I have thought that no data center should be allowed without a special-use permit," he told BizSense. Menlo's site is one of three data center campuses planned off U.S. Route 460 Business. Just south of it, NuVu Real Estate won the city's first data center site plan approval in February 2026 for a three-building, 75-acre, 300-megawatt campus estimated at $1.1 billion, and Wagner Properties' three-building, 73-acre project was approved in April. Warrenton Group's six-building, 175-acre campus went through council hearings, the only one of the three to do so. Menlo's next step is to resubmit its site plan to the city's planning office; NuVu and Wagner won their site plans at staff level, with no council vote or public hearing. Cuthbert has called the by-right zoning change "one of the problems" behind council's lack of knowledge about the projects. Gov. Abigail Spanberger's office dismissed the idea of a statewide data center moratorium in an August 2026 interview with the Petersburg Progress-Index.

ft-1784758454457-8638.text: NuVu Real Estate's approved data center campus at 2588 County Drive in Petersburg, Virginia, three buildings on 75 acres between Interstate 95 and County Drive, is a $1.1 billion, 300-megawatt project that never needed a public hearing. Petersburg amended its zoning code in 2024 to allow data centers by right in its M-1 light industrial and M-2 heavy industrial districts, so the Leesburg firm's site plan needed only staff approval, which it got in February 2026. An LLC tied to NuVu bought the land for $4.12 million in November 2025, and a NuVu representative said the layout works within M-1 zoning with no variances or wetland impacts and would use a closed-loop water system. As of late June 2026, interim planning director Jared Crews said NuVu had not yet applied for a land disturbance permit, its next step. NuVu's is one of at least four data center projects in Petersburg's pipeline, alongside Menlo Digital, Wagner Properties and Warrenton Group, which surfaced through records requests in July 2026. "I had no clue about any of this until 12 noon today," Ward 4 councilman Charlie Cuthbert said, adding, "We talk about transparency, and yet it's like we're in a cave with the lights out." Mayor Samuel Parham said he had not known about the other three projects either: "I read about them in the news." Cuthbert said he has thought from the start that no data center should be allowed without a special-use permit, but under the current code the City Council has no vote on NuVu's campus.

An LLC tied to NuVu bought the land for $4.12 million in November 2025, and a NuVu representative said the layout works within M-1 zoning with no variances or wetland impacts and would use a closed-loop water system.
As of late June 2026, interim planning director Jared Crews said NuVu had not yet applied for a land disturbance permit, its next step.
NuVu's is one of at least four data center projects in Petersburg's pipeline, alongside Menlo Digital, Wagner Properties and Warrenton Group, which surfaced through records requests in July 2026.
"I had no clue about any of this until 12 noon today," Ward 4 councilman Charlie Cuthbert said, adding, "We talk about transparency, and yet it's like we're in a cave with the lights out."
Mayor Samuel Parham said he had not known about the other three projects either: "I read about them in the news."
Cuthbert said he has thought from the start that no data center should be allowed without a special-use permit, but under the current code the City Council has no vote on NuVu's campus.

ft-1784758945221-2983.text: Wagner Properties' data center at 1161 Wagner Road in Petersburg, Virginia, won city site plan approval in April 2026 without a public hearing or a council vote, because Petersburg's zoning allows data centers by right on industrial land. The Petersburg data center would fill 27 acres of a 73-acre site with three buildings west of Wagner Road and alongside the railroad tracks, according to city documents obtained by Richmond BizSense. Wagner Properties, a Prince George company led by owner Joseph Wagner, is working with Legacy Engineering of Fredericksburg. The land is zoned M-2 heavy industrial and is owned by GFYA LLC, an entity tied to Jacob Manevich, a real estate agent in Potomac, Maryland; the LLC bought it from Wagner Properties Inc. in 2024 for $950,000. A Jacob Manevich is also the applicant for two data center rezonings in Stafford County, Enon Road Technology Park and Cranes Corner. The site plan was approved nearly two years after it was first submitted, and as of late June 2026 Wagner had not applied for the land disturbance permit that comes next, said Jared Crews, the city's interim planning director. Wagner Properties did not respond to requests for comment. Petersburg's council changed the zoning code in 2024 to allow data centers by right in the M-1 and M-2 industrial districts, after it rezoned land for Menlo Digital's campus in 2023. Wagner's project is one of four in the city's pipeline: NuVu Real Estate's $1.1 billion, three-building campus at 2588 County Drive between I-95 and County Drive, approved in February; Menlo Digital's four-building campus on 74 acres at 2255 Jamestown Drive; and Warrenton Group's six-building campus on 175 acres at the former CSX Collier Yard, 2233 Halifax Road. The Wagner, NuVu and Menlo sites all sit off U.S. Route 460 Business in Ward 1. City council members said they learned of the projects from the newspaper. "I had no clue about any of this until 12 noon today," Councilman Charlie Cuthbert said at the council's July 2026 meeting, holding up a printout of the BizSense report, and Mayor Samuel Parham said: "I read about them in the news." "We talk about transparency, and yet it's like we're in a cave with the lights out," Cuthbert said. Marlow Jones, whose Ward 1 includes the Wagner site, said: "This didn't have to go through us. It was already zoned and planned for, so some things slide under the cracks that we don't know until somebody posts it like this." Councilman Arnold Westbrook Jr. said the city can pursue growth while protecting quality of life: "I believe Petersburg can be both ambitious and responsible." Cuthbert wants the by-right rule reversed: "From the get-go, I have thought that no data center should be allowed without a special-use permit." Any change to the zoning ordinance would be up to the Petersburg City Council, but the Wagner site plan is already approved, and the next step is a land disturbance permit from city staff.

ft-1784759069969-4355.text: Warrenton Group, a Washington, D.C. apartment developer, has city approval for a six-building data center campus on 175 acres at 2233 Halifax Road in Petersburg, Virginia, the former CSX Collier Yard property that the city now owns. It is the one Petersburg data center project that council members said they knew about before July 2026, when a news report revealed three others. City Council gave the project zoning approval in 2025, then early in 2026 amended it to add three parcels for more access and room for wetland mitigation. Warrenton is developing the campus through its TWG Data arm, with engineering by Timmons Group. The city's interim planning director, Jared Crews, said in July that Warrenton had not submitted a site plan since the enlargement was approved, and no megawatt figure, tenant or cost has been published. Since 2024 Petersburg's zoning has allowed data centers by right on M-1 and M-2 industrial land, so three other projects won approval without public hearings or council votes: NuVu Real Estate's $1.1 billion, 300-megawatt campus at 2588 County Drive, Wagner Properties' three buildings at 1161 Wagner Road, and Menlo Digital's four-building campus at 2255 Jamestown Drive, whose site plan is under review. Council members said they were blindsided. "It was in that article that I learned there are three (more) data center sites moving forward in Petersburg," Councilman Charlie Cuthbert said at a July 2026 meeting, holding up the story; the Warrenton project was the only one he knew of. "From the get-go, I have thought that no data center should be allowed without a special-use permit," Cuthbert said. Councilmember Annette Smith-Lee said: "I didn't even know anything about it, and nobody came to us and presented anything to us about any data centers." Councilman Arnold Westbrook Jr., whose Ward 7 includes the Warrenton site, said he welcomes the interest: "I'm not pro-data centers; I'm not against data centers," he told council. Warrenton's next step is a site plan, which city planning staff will review. Whether Petersburg goes back to requiring special-use permits for data centers, as Cuthbert wants, is up to City Council.

ft-682.text: Convergent VA, LLC withdrew its rezoning application for the Convergent Technology Park, a data center campus planned on nearly 140 acres south of Remington in Fauquier County, Virginia, in late August 2026, and says it will build houses on the land instead. "Please be advised that we are withdrawing the above-stated rezoning application", Convergent VA manager Jeffrey Price wrote to the county, "and pursuing the by-right residential development of the property pursuant to its underlying residentially-zoned use." The land, two parcels south of the intersection of James Madison Highway (Route 15/29) and James Madison Street, has carried approval for a 198-home subdivision since 2003. The latest rezoning application asked to make about 104 acres a business park for roughly 1.584 million square feet of data center and office space, with about 35 acres for passive recreation; an earlier 2024 version called for four data center buildings costing more than $1 billion, needing 240 megawatts of power and up to 16 diesel generators per building set back 440 feet behind 12-foot berms. Scott District Supervisor Ike Broaddus said the withdrawal was "no surprise": "They've known for more than a year that they had no chance of approval for a data center." It was one of three Remington-area data center applications withdrawn within a month: Gigaland pulled its application on August 17 for the second time, and on September 17 the Remington Innovation Campus, backed by SDC Capital Partners and including land owned by Lee District Supervisor Daron Culbertson, was withdrawn hours before the Planning Commission was to consider it. On September 17 the Fauquier County Planning Commission unanimously recommended removing data centers as a permitted use in business park zones, limiting new ones to the Vint Hill area and requiring a special exception from the Board of Supervisors for each; county staff concluded there are "no appropriate areas for data center development" outside that district. That zoning change goes to the Fauquier County Board of Supervisors for a final vote, with no date yet set, while the Convergent land now proceeds as a by-right residential subdivision that needs no rezoning.

ft-680.text: Gigaland bought 202 acres near Remington, in Fauquier County, Virginia, for $4 million in October 2023, and sought to rezone the land from residential use to business park for an 800-megawatt, 2.2 million-square-foot data center campus. On June 18, 2025 the Fauquier County planning commission voted 4 to 1 to recommend refusing it. The Piedmont Environmental Council, which called it a seven-building, 2.2-million-square-foot campus, said the applicant promised water quality improvements even though the county water system already meets state and federal standards, and that the project would be one of four data centers proposed in the Lee District. The council also said the company actually behind Gigaland had never been publicly identified and would neither name itself nor provide proof it was more than a speculative real estate plan. The application included four substations, more than the council said appeared necessary, raising questions about where new transmission lines would cross private land. After losing the vote, the developers added a $15 million proffer to the county's Purchase of Development Rights program for farmland conservation. Two weeks before a September 2025 vote by the Board of Supervisors, the developers withdrew the 2024 application. Co-founder Art Lickunas said a new plan would shrink the campus to 847,400 square feet of one-story buildings with two substations instead of four. County officials assumed Equinix would be the end user, and Lickunas said half the site would be "more retail oriented, and the other will be more hyper scale operations." The Piedmont Environmental Council said even a scaled-down proposal leaves "the fundamental issues with data centers" in place, citing impacts on the county's air, water, land and historic resources. The revised application fared no better: in July 2026 the planning commission again recommended denial, 4 to 1, with commissioners citing harm to quality of life and arguing that the main benefit would be tax revenue. On August 17, 2026 Lickunas asked the county to "remove all four items from the September 10, 2026 Board of Supervisors agenda." Assistant community development director Adam Shellenberger said "there will be no further action" on the applications. "I do not know what their plans for the property are," Shellenberger said; any new proposal would have to go through the planning commission and the Board of Supervisors again.

ft-681.text: The Remington Innovation Campus, a six-building data center campus proposed on about 210 acres at Remington in Fauquier County, Virginia, was withdrawn on September 17, 2026, hours before the county Planning Commission was to consider it. The project was bankrolled by SDC Capital Partners of New York, and one of the landowners behind the application is Lee District Supervisor Daron Culbertson. At 7:16 that morning Ron Meyer, a former Loudoun County supervisor who is senior vice president of development at SDC Capital Partners, emailed the county asking to make the application inactive or, if not, withdraw it. The county has no inactive status, so it was withdrawn. Meyer declined to comment, and Culbertson did not respond. The application asked the county to add the 210.7-acre property to the Remington Service District, rezone about 182 acres from residential to business park, and allow three substations. When it was filed in May 2025, the plan showed copper-colored, barn-style buildings set back 250 feet from Remington Road, a 27-acre park, three substations and cooling with recycled water, and asked for a waiver to exceed the 45-foot height limit. The site sits near 230kV transmission lines, the Remington Power Station and the Remington Solar Power Facility. County staff flagged ponds, wetlands and floodplain on several parcels, and the site overlaps the Rappahannock Station I and II Civil War battlefields. County preservation planner Wendy Wheatcraft said it could have an adverse impact on historic resources. The application covered 11 parcels, including a 44.82-acre parcel at 11462 Remington Road that county records show Culbertson co-owns, and land owned by his sister and mother. Culbertson said the land had been under contract since December 2024. Residents called on him to step aside from data center votes. "You should recuse yourself from all data center votes, not just the one for your property," Denise Schefer of Protect Fauquier told the board in June 2025. Jeanne Ritchie, whose family farms near Remington, called his position "entirely unethical and a conflict of interest." Culbertson apologized "to any of the voters that felt like I misled them" and said: "My obligation has always been to the Lee District and the Remington community." In July 2026 he voted with the majority to allow a private natural gas fuel cell plant for the nearby Remington Technology Park. The withdrawal was the third for a major Remington data center in a month. Gigaland pulled its application for the second time on August 17, and Convergent VA dropped its Convergent Technology Park in late August to build houses on the land. "They've known for more than a year that they had no chance of approval for a data center," Supervisor Ike Broaddus said of Convergent. The approved but unbuilt Remington Technology Park nearby remains approved, and in July won permission for its own fuel cell power plant. The same evening the Innovation Campus was to be heard, the Planning Commission unanimously recommended a zoning change that would limit new data centers to land zoned for planned commercial industrial development, now only the Vint Hill area, and require every data center to get a special exception from the Board of Supervisors. Staff concluded there are "no appropriate areas for data center development" outside that zone. If the Board of Supervisors adopts it, a new application for this land would face those rules.

The site sits near 230kV transmission lines, the Remington Power Station and the Remington Solar Power Facility. County staff flagged ponds, wetlands and floodplain on several parcels, and the site overlaps the Rappahannock Station I and II Civil War battlefields. County preservation planner Wendy Wheatcraft said it could have an adverse impact on historic resources.

The application covered 11 parcels, including a 44.82-acre parcel at 11462 Remington Road that county records show Culbertson co-owns, and land owned by his sister and mother. "You should recuse yourself from all data center votes, not just the one for your property," Denise Schefer of Protect Fauquier told the board in June 2025.

Jeanne Ritchie, whose family farms near Remington, called his position "entirely unethical and a conflict of interest." ft-976.text: The Fauquier County Board of Supervisors has voted to let PointOne power its Remington Technology Park, a six-building, 1.8-million-square-foot data center campus in Remington, Virginia, with a private yard of natural gas fuel cells. The campus was first approved in 2018 but has not been built, and construction has been held up by trouble getting power to the property. PointOne, a Canadian company, applied in 2018 to build up to 1.8 million square feet in six buildings, and its website describes the Remington site as 300 megawatts and shovel-ready on 234 acres. A county staff presentation in July 2026 said the project's total energy demand could reach 600 megawatts, and noted the potential for a second 300-megawatt substation. Staff said the fuel cells were needed because of "Dominion Energy changes to delivery phases of electric power and energization schedule," and that without them construction would likely be delayed until at least 2030. How much power the fuel cells would generate, and for how long they would run, is still unknown. The Planning Commission had recommended denial 3-2 of an earlier version that used natural gas turbines. PointOne chief executive Colin Clish said the new proposal was "very different from the application" the commission saw. Supervisors Ike Broaddus, Daron Culbertson and chairman Kevin Carter voted for the rezoning, Regan Washer voted against, and Richard Gerhardt was absent. "Our grid is taxed, literally because of data centers," Washer said, adding that if a project needs "the equivalent power of several 100,000 houses to operate, maybe you're just not supposed to be there in the first place." "If we say no tonight, we're going to get the same data center," Broaddus said. "We're going to get it in four or five years delayed." He put the cost of that delay at about $100 million in lost tax revenue. Three residents spoke against it at the hearing, and Sumerduck resident Leah Cooper said the county lacks the "legal structure" to regulate a private power plant of that size. "When will it be enough?" she asked. "How many neighborhoods will be encroached on?" Remington Technology Park is the one data center already approved in the Remington area, which has drawn a string of other proposals. Those others have now fallen away. Just south of Lucky Hill Road, Gigaland proposed seven two-story buildings on 202 acres, which the Planning Commission voted 4-1 to recommend denying in June 2025. Gigaland withdrew its application for the second time on August 17, 2026, Convergent VA pulled its Convergent Technology Park in late August to build houses instead, and the Remington Innovation Campus was withdrawn on September 17. The county is now moving to shut the door on new projects like these. On September 17, 2026, the Planning Commission unanimously recommended a zoning change that would remove data centers as a permitted use in business park zones and limit new ones to land zoned for planned commercial industrial development, which today is only the Vint Hill area. Staff concluded there are "no appropriate areas for data center development" elsewhere in the county, citing the strain on the electrical grid, noise and air pollution. The change would also require every future data center to get a special exception from the Board of Supervisors. The recommendation goes next to the Board of Supervisors. It applies to future applications, and Remington Technology Park already holds its approvals.

ft-738.text: SAMX Data LLC wants to rezone 55.26 acres at 11825 Remington Road, near Remington in Fauquier County, Virginia, for a data center campus of two three-story buildings, 300,000 to 350,000 square feet each. The application, filed in October 2023, has not been resubmitted since SAMX asked for more time in 2024; the county had no new submission as of August 2025. On September 17, 2026 the Fauquier County Planning Commission unanimously recommended removing data centers as a permitted use in the business park zoning district SAMX is requesting. County staff raised concerns about the plan's consistency with its proffers, uncertain electrical service and its proposed use of groundwater, the Piedmont Environmental Council reported. Three other data center bids near Remington were withdrawn in the following weeks: Gigaland pulled its application a second time on August 17, a month after the Planning Commission voted 4-1 to recommend denial; Convergent VA withdrew its Convergent Technology Park in late August, saying it would build houses instead; and the Remington Innovation Campus applicants withdrew hours before a September 17 hearing. The neighboring Remington Technology Park, rezoned in 2018 for up to six data centers, had also stalled over power supply; on July 10, 2026 supervisors approved its developer's plan to run the site on natural gas fuel cells rather than wait years for grid capacity. The commission's new recommendation would limit new data centers in Fauquier to land near Vint Hill and require every project to get a special exception from the Board of Supervisors, which decides both that zoning change and any SAMX rezoning.

ft-744.text: CoreSite is expanding its Reston, Fairfax County, Virginia, data center campus at 12369 Sunrise Valley Drive with a three-story, about 215,000-square-foot, 75-foot-tall building called V3 Phase 2, which would replace a vacant one-story office building next to homes on Cocquina Drive. Fairfax County staff received the site plan, submitted June 20, 2025, and county rules let staff approve it 30 days after the notice to neighbors was postmarked; no report of that approval or denial has been published since. The building is part of a development plan the Board of Supervisors approved in 2018 for the former Sunrise Technology Park, which CoreSite bought from Brookfield Properties in 2016 for $60 million; when the full plan is built, CoreSite will have 1.3 million square feet of data centers in Reston. CoreSite already runs its VA1 and VA2 buildings at 12100 Sunrise Valley Drive, a former AOL site opened in 2008, and its VA3 campus at 12369 Sunrise Valley Drive, which includes two renovated 1980s office buildings and a two-story data center added in 2019. Most Cocquina Cluster residents learned of the plan only when a neighbor asked about it on a community Facebook group on June 16, 2025, after a notice letter listed the wrong address, 12098 Sunrise Valley Drive, across the street. "That feels, at best, careless," said Maggie Urbanik, president of the Cocquina Cluster Homeowners Association, who said at worst it was intentionally misleading. Resident Caitlin O'Dwyer called the existing building "an absolute blight" and said its evaporative cooling system is already having a visible effect on the neighborhood. CoreSite's mid-Atlantic general manager, Chris Lettiere, said the expansion would create about 300 construction jobs and 50 permanent jobs, and that the company is working closely with the county on permitting, without addressing residents' specific concerns. Fairfax County adopted new data center rules in 2024, including a ban on facilities within 200 feet of homes, but Hunter Mill District Supervisor Walter Alcorn's office confirmed they do not apply to CoreSite's already-approved plan.

ft-969.text: Infotel Systems, a VoIP telephone provider in the Richmond area, runs its own data center at 6008 Hermitage Road in the Lakeside area of Henrico County, Virginia, next to a Verizon facility. The building hosts the company's phone, video and data services for its customers and connects directly to Verizon's and Comcast's Virginia internet hubs. Henrico County has around 40 data centers of various sizes, most of them much larger, clustered in the White Oak Technology Park in the Varina District. The building has an hour of battery backup behind its main generator, alarm monitoring around the clock, and a reflective white roof installed in 2016. Infotel also keeps a second data center elsewhere and lists redundant generators with a 20 day supply of propane. Because data centers were once classified under the county's office or warehouse zoning, many small data centers were built in scattered locations across Henrico, and Varina Supervisor Tyrone Nelson said: "I am trying to keep... data centers from spreading all across the Varina District." The Henrico County Board of Supervisors adopted a data center amendment to its comprehensive plan on June 10, 2025, setting recommendations for new data center development countywide. The change means new projects go through a public process before the Board of Supervisors rather than being built by right, and any new data center in the county is now reviewed against those recommendations.

ft-684.text: Wagner Urban Logistics, tied to the Richmond firm Centra Logistics, proposed eight data center buildings totaling a million square feet on 200 acres off Darbytown Road in Varina, Henrico County, Virginia. The Henrico Planning Commission rejected the required permit before October 2025, Wagner withdrew the plan, and the county later denied its vested rights claim and rejected its appeal, leaving the site blocked for data centers. It was the first project filed under Henrico's rule, in effect since June 2025, requiring a provisional use permit for every data center instead of automatic approval. Planning director Joe Emerson denied Wagner's vested rights claim on December 10, 2025, finding Wagner did not own the property when it filed the claim and that state law grants vested rights only to landowners, not contract purchasers. Wagner had 30 days from the Dec. 10 letter to appeal to the county's Board of Zoning Appeals. Wagner closed on the 200-acre site on November 14, 2025, paying the pharmaceutical company Fareva $13.5 million for it, before the vested rights decision came down.
