ft-686.text: The data center Crusoe AI planned for Rocky Mount, Virginia will not be built. Franklin County Boone District supervisor Mike Meredith said in mid-August 2026 that the county had been told the Crusoe project, known as Project Flash, would not move forward: "Project Flash is not proceeding." The project was to be built by Crusoe AI in the Summit View Business Park, just north of Rocky Mount in Franklin County, with 50 to 100 megawatts of power on 150 acres, of which at least 95 were developable. Residents found out about the project on their own, through documents released in July 2026 under a Freedom of Information Act request. More than 100 people met at the Scruggs volunteer fire department to work out what it would mean for the county. Franklin County Community Coalition chair Kim Jones, who had pushed against the project for about six months, said: "It's hard to wrap your head around the magnitude of the whole thing." County officials had been negotiating with Crusoe for months and the company had been talking to electric provider Appalachian Power about the electricity it would need, but officials were bound by non-disclosure agreements. Resident Christine Sizemore said: "I think one of the issues, or primarily issue that I'm sensing really is the lack of transparency. This is a major infrastructure project that isn't just putting a factory up or another building somewhere." Neither the county nor Crusoe said why the project ended. Rocky Mount mayor Holland Perdue, who attended the community meetings, opposed the project: "Economic development is not something simply about attracting an investment. It is about attracting the right investment for the community." Resident Laura Carter said the fight was not over: "We won a battle, but we haven't won the war."

ft-1047.text: The Surry Green Energy Center, a data center and hydrogen campus that Green Energy Partners plans in Rushmere, next to Dominion Energy's Surry nuclear power plant off Hog Island Road in Surry County, Virginia, won its rezoning in 2024, but its developer went through Chapter 11 bankruptcy the same year. The company billed it as a first-in-the-nation data center and hydrogen fuel hub eventually powered by small modular nuclear reactors built on site. Surry County supervisors voted 3-2 on February 8, 2024 to rezone the land for 19 data centers on a 3 million-square-foot campus, with Supervisors Amy Drewry and Timothy Calhoun voting no after Drewry's motion to delay failed. The company's attorney, Greg Davis, described a $6.45 billion investment over a 13-year buildout that would by 2036 bring more than 1,300 permanent jobs and, by the company's analysis, $74 million a year in tax revenue. The data centers would first draw on existing grid power, with revenue paying for four to six small modular reactors, mini nuclear plants not likely to run for 10 to 15 years. The developer formed a joint venture with IP3 to develop the site. Opponents at the 2024 hearing questioned the reactors. "This is not a technology that's available as I stand here tonight," Davis himself said of them, putting them seven or 10 years away. Mike Eggleston, one of eight speakers against the project, called them an "unproven technology," and Daniel Shaye called the plan an "invasion by corporate interests" that "our rural, quiet, peaceful way of life will not withstand." A traffic study in the application projected daily weekday trips on the road would rise 93% to over 3,600, and Drewry called the company's proffers, including $950,000 of improvements to Hog Island Road, "vague." Court records show Green Energy Partners LLC filed for Chapter 11 in September 2024, listing more than $3 million in unsecured claims, and in February 2025 a bankruptcy judge approved assigning its $12 million contract to buy the land to a new company, Surry Green Energy Center LLC. Davis said it was "a reorganization, not a liquidation of Green Energy Partners, which is alive and well and continuing work on the Surry Green Energy Center." Drewry was not surprised: "I voted against the project because the proffers were not legally stringent enough to protect the citizens and county." To settle a lawsuit from neighboring landowner Cobham Bay Farms, the company had also agreed to buy another 248 acres across Hog Island Road if that land is rezoned. Surry County's economic development office said that "from a zoning standpoint, this private project may proceed." Any rezoning of the extra Cobham Bay acreage would go back to the Surry County Board of Supervisors, whose members in March 2025 were Chairman Robert Elliott, Vice Chairman Breyon Pierce, Tim Calhoun, Walter Hardy and Amy Drewry; no such application had been filed as of that report.

ft-690.text: ADP Ladysmith Data Hub, LLC wants to rezone 140.38 acres at 18577 Green Road, west of I-95 about 1.7 miles from the Ladysmith interchange in Caroline County, Virginia, for a data center campus, and the request is waiting for a hearing date. It asks for Planned, Innovation, Research and Technology zoning and a special exception for the data center, on land owned by Good Earth Horticulture, Inc. The generalized development plan, dated March 19, 2025, allows buildings up to 95 feet tall on two floors, with a substation area, 100-foot setbacks and at least 20% open space. It projects about 1,313 vehicle trips a day at full buildout and county water and sewer from Green Road. The plan lists the applicant at a Stamford, Connecticut address with a contact at AVAIO Capital, and its land use attorney is Ann Neil Cosby of GreeneHurlocker, who also represents the nearby Bull Church Data Center. No megawatt figure, tenant or cost has been made public. The county lists the request as requiring a public hearing. Since December 2024 Caroline has required a special exception permit for any data center on industrial land. The largest project at the Ladysmith interchange is CleanArc Data Centers' campus on 650 acres at the former Virginia Bazaar flea market, just east of I-95 at Exit 110. On September 22, 2026, supervisors voted 4-2 to rezone 916 acres for Luck Stone's Carmel Technology and Enterprise Center, an industrial park with no named end user, over traffic concerns from Supervisors Jeff Black and Jeff Sili. Also waiting are the Bull Church Data Center rezoning east of I-95 and Thornberry, LLC's request to rezone 657 acres on Carneal Lane for a data center campus. No hearing date had been set as of September 2026. The site is in the Mattaponi District, represented by Supervisor Floyd Thomas. Caroline County's Board of Supervisors decides rezonings and special exceptions: Chair Clay Forehand, Nancy Long, Floyd Thomas, Reginald Underwood, Jeff Black and Jeff Sili.

ft-689.text: The Airlee industrial and data center site is 184 acres at the intersection of Route 1 and CCC Road in Ruther Glen, Caroline County. Caroline County's application list shows a case from Airlee-Mattaponi, numbered RZ-06-2026 and SPEX-10-2026, over 191 acres between U.S. 1 and Interstate 95 in the Mattaponi voting district, deemed complete and forwarded for review. Almost everything else on that list is the same kind of thing. Thornberry wants 657 acres of a 1,001.5 acre parcel at Carneal Lane; ADP Ladysmith wants 140.38 acres at Green Road; Luck Stone Corporation wants 1,196.3 acres off Jericho Road under case RZ-06-2024; Avanti Management wants 1,658 acres at Ware Creek Road under RZ-05-2024; NRD Retail is still in technical review on Bull Church Road. CleanArc is the one that has actually been agreed, and it shows what the county is trading for. On August 12, 2025 the board of supervisors approved a performance agreement with CADC VA-1 LLC, a CleanArc subsidiary, over 650 acres in the Ladysmith area just east of Interstate 95 off exit 110, on the former Virginia Bazaar site, with Bowling Green supervisor Jeff Sili the only vote against. The agreement allows three buildings of 490,000 square feet each, with more possible on a further 87.5 and 126.6 acres, against a projected $8.8 billion at full build, 50 jobs paying 150 percent of the county's average wage, and more than $13 million a year in tax, about 17 percent of the general fund. The county offered better terms if the first building is finished by September 30, 2027.

ft-1065.text: The Carmel Church Data Hub, a data center planned for about 97 acres of the Carmel Church Station property next to Interstate 95 at Ruther Glen, in Caroline County, Virginia, won approval from the Caroline County Board of Supervisors in May 2024. The applicant, ADP Carmel Church Data Hub, LLC, asked to amend the proffers on land already zoned for planned mixed-use development under a 2009 rezoning so a data center could be built there in phases. The county planning commission had recommended approval. The 97 acres are part of a 253-acre parcel bounded on the east by I-95 and on the south by the CSX rail line, reached by Rogers Clark Boulevard, Route 207. The land is owned by Litt Thompson of Thompson Family Office, a Richmond investment firm, and was once meant for the DC South smart city and train station, approved in 2010 but never built. No size in megawatts, end user or construction date for the data center has been reported. The Carmel Church approval came weeks before the same supervisors voted 5-1 to reject a second Thompson-linked project, a 900-acre data center campus proposed by VALCO off Jericho Road along the North Anna River that residents had fought since January 2023. “I call it the zombie project,” said Ruther Glen resident Kevin Collins, “because it keeps popping up out of the grave on us.” Supervisors said there was plenty of land already zoned industrial, and county Planning Director Leon Hughes counted 1,848 undeveloped industrial acres east of the interstate in the Carmel Church Growth Area. Supervisor Clay Forehand, now the board's chair and a supporter of data centers, has argued that a single campus would bring as much tax as eight to 10 million-square-foot distribution centers without their truck traffic. By July 2025 the county had approved two data centers, one near the Spotsylvania line in Woodford and the one in Carmel Church, and three more by-right projects had site plans awaiting approval. That month the planning commission voted 4-2 to recommend denial of the Ladysmith Data Hub, a 140-acre campus off U.S. 1 from ADP Ladysmith Data Hub, LLC, after residents objected. The county's list of pending cases also includes the Thornberry Data Center Campus, a request to rezone 657 acres, and a Bull Church Road data center near the Ladysmith interchange. In September 2026 the supervisors voted 4-2 to rezone 916 acres near Carmel Church for Luck Stone's Carmel Technology and Enterprise Center, an industrial park with no end user named that the planning commission had recommended against. “We need to step back and ask a very basic question: ‘Does this project belong here?’” Collins told the board. No site plan approval or construction for the Carmel Church Data Hub has been reported; July 2025 reporting counted it as one of the county's two approved data centers, and any further approvals rest with Caroline County.

ft-1050.text: The applicant says this is not a data center. Luck Stone, a Richmond crushed stone and gravel producer, wants to rezone about 1,111 acres off Jericho Road in Caroline County from Rural Preservation to Industrial, across parcels between Jericho Road and U.S. Route 1 and along Zion and Oxford roads. Its attorney, Charlie Payne, told the planning commission: "It's not going to be data centers. We envision this to be your typical industrial park where you're going to have logistics, distribution, warehousing, and manufacturing." The zoning being asked for would permit data centers among the other industrial uses, which is why the site is on record at all. The county records the case as RZ-06-2024 from Luck Stone Corporation over 1,196.3 acres in the Reedy Church district; the record carries 1,196 acres. The commission heard it on Thursday, July 23, 2026 and, after a marathon meeting of long and heated public testimony, deferred its vote to August 27. Members of Oxford Mount Zion Baptist Church spoke for it, among them Bishop Duane Fields Sr., because Luck Stone has offered to help build a community centre and to assist Carmel Baptist Church's food pantry. Blake Morris, a recent Caroline High School graduate, said several children in the county have no mentors or role models at home, and that the centre "would give them a purpose and a reason to keep going in life to better themselves." Mark Atkinson, against, called the rezoning "a blank check that you're giving the developer in exchange for doing a few good things." Commissioner Mary Hodge questioned the proffers, including $50,000 towards a traffic light estimated to cost $700,000, and a $25,000 donation to the Musical Creations Foundation, a nonprofit run by the wife of another commissioner. The vote came on Thursday, August 27, 2026: 3 to 1 to recommend refusal. Mary Hodge, Richard Williams and Steve Rollins voted to deny, Lee Tingler to approve, Carol Horton was absent, and J.D. Young abstained because of the conflict of interest. Hodge's stated reason was the applicant's own wording: "Because the applicant is not forthcoming with any information about potential tenants on this property, I am very concerned with language in the GDP narrative which states the site will include storage warehouses and distribution facilities." Luck Stone has also offered to help Jericho Baptist Church and Carmel Baptist Church with ministry needs. The board of supervisors decides, and it had already voted 6 to 0 in August 2024 to change this land in the comprehensive plan from Rural Transition to Industrial.

The two acreages in circulation, about 1,111 acres in the rezoning as reported and 1,196.3 on the county's list, are unreconciled. ft-872.text: The Caroline Center for Innovation is a data center campus proposed through a pending rezoning application for parcels along Dry Bridge Road in Ruther Glen, Caroline County, Virginia, just south of the site of the Thornberry Data Center Campus. Thornberry's May 2025 filing described it as a pending zoning application that, together with Thornberry, would increase the area that can be developed for data centers by several hundred acres. Its current status is unclear: the county's list of pending rezonings includes Thornberry's case but no case under the Caroline Center for Innovation name. In December 2025, reviewing a separate data center nearby off W.C. Spratt Drive, Caroline County planners told the Planning Commission that 354 acres to the south of that site had been the subject of a rezoning request for a data center that was withdrawn in August 2025; the minutes do not name that project. The same planners warned that Dry Bridge Road is "a narrow secondary road with many tight curves." The area around Carmel Church has drawn several data center proposals. The Board of Supervisors expanded the Carmel Church Growth Area in September 2024 to take in properties along Dry Bridge Road and Carneal Lane and extended the technology land use designation there. Thornberry, LLC seeks to rezone 657 acres next door for a data center campus, a case still awaiting a hearing date. CleanArc Data Centers is developing a 650-acre campus at the former Virginia Bazaar near the Ladysmith interchange. On September 22, 2026, the supervisors voted 4-2 to rezone 916 acres for Luck Stone's Carmel Technology and Enterprise Center industrial park. Any data center rezoning here is decided by the Caroline County Board of Supervisors after a public hearing. The latest public record on data center projects in the area is from September 2026.

ft-687.text: The Caroline Center for Innovation-North, a data center campus proposed on 95.4 acres along W.C. Spratt Drive near Ruther Glen in Caroline County, Virginia, was withdrawn by its applicant, an affiliate of STACK Infrastructure, just before the Board of Supervisors was to vote on April 14, 2026. The county attorney told the board that the applicant's attorney had formally withdrawn the data center application and that the applicant would need to restart the process to bring it back. The applicant, SAC III Acquisition Co., LLC, sought a special exception, case SPEX-08-2025, for four two-story data center buildings of 375,000 square feet each, 1.5 million square feet in all, up to 95 feet tall, with a 10-acre substation to be built by Rappahannock Electric Cooperative. The land, owned by CCCII CDEFG, LLC and next to the M.C. Dean manufacturing plant in an industrial park zoned in 1989, lies about half a mile east of Colemans Mill Road and is designated for data centers in the county's comprehensive plan. The applicant's attorney, Charlie Payne, told planners his client was committing $5.3 billion in Caroline County and would own and operate the campus and lease it to tenants. On December 18, 2025 the Caroline County Planning Commission voted 4-1 to recommend approval, with Commissioner Steve Rollins voting no and a condition requiring closed-loop air cooling or a system approved under the county's data center water policy. Only two residents spoke. Mark Sandor of the Mattaponi district questioned where the power would come from and whether families would pay for it: "It's just not reasonable that working families should have to see that in their monthly utility bills." Mary Hodge of the Bowling Green district asked how the Mattaponi River and shallow wells would be protected and urged: "It is time for Caroline to say no." Planning Commission Chairman Robert Schwartz pressed the applicant on non-disclosure agreements, and Payne said the one his client had signed had expired. After the withdrawal, Reedy Church resident Kevin Collins told the supervisors he was pleased it was gone. Collins has fought data centers near his Jericho Road home since 2023; in 2024 the supervisors voted 5-1 against a comprehensive plan change for a 900-acre data center campus on the North Anna River there. Other large projects remain in the area. On the 1,001.5-acre parcel to the east, Thornberry, LLC has applied to rezone 657 acres for a data center campus, and ADP Ladysmith Data Hub is seeking a special exception for 140 acres on Green Road. In September 2026 the supervisors voted 4-2 to rezone 916 acres near Jericho Road and U.S. 1 for Luck Stone's Carmel Technology and Enterprise Center industrial park. Any new attempt on this site would start over with a special exception application, a Planning Commission hearing and a vote by the Caroline County Board of Supervisors, chaired by Clay Forehand. No new application for the parcel appears on the county's list of pending cases as of September 2026.

ft-688.text: CleanArc Data Centers is building its VA1 data center campus in Caroline County, Virginia, on the site of the former Virginia Bazaar flea market east of Interstate 95 at Exit 110 near Ruther Glen. The company broke ground in November 2025 on a 900 megawatt campus; the first 300 megawatts are due online in early 2027, a second 300 in 2030 and a third between 2033 and 2035. Gov. Glenn Youngkin called the $3 billion initial investment "the largest announced economic investment in the history of Caroline County." The 650-acre site will hold three data center buildings of 490,000 square feet each, with space leased to large cloud computing tenants. The land was zoned Industrial, so CleanArc did not need a special public rezoning vote; it built by right, meaning the use was already allowed under the existing zoning. The county later required new industrial projects to get a special exception permit, extra approval beyond zoning, but said CleanArc had already filed plans before that change. What the Board of Supervisors did vote on, in August 2025, was a performance agreement, under which the county pays back CleanArc and its tenants a share of the new tax revenue each year for 15 years. The Virginia Mercury reported the payback at 25% of the increased tax revenue, an estimated $13 million a year, equal to about 17% of the county's general fund budget. Bowling Green District Supervisor Jeff Sili cast the only vote against it. Water has been the main worry in a county where many homes rely on wells. The county will not supply drinking water for cooling, only for flushing and washing, and CleanArc said the water for cooling would be brought in and then recirculated. Then-chair Nancy Long said the county's rules include setbacks, noise limits, screening and a ban on using drinking water for industrial cooling. The three approved buildings need no further rezoning vote. Two more buildings planned for adjacent land would need the Board of Supervisors' approval; the next milestone is the first 300 megawatts of power, due online in early 2027.

ft-871.text: Thornberry, LLC has asked Caroline County, Virginia, to rezone 657 acres of its 1,001.5-acre parcel at 23202 Carneal Lane in Ruther Glen from Rural Preservation to the county's Planned Innovation, Research and Technology district for the Thornberry Data Center Campus. Its development plan, dated May 2025, shows up to 16 potential data centers totaling about 3.3 million square feet, built over several years with multiple substations. The county lists the case, RZ-03-2025, as complete and under review, with no public hearing date set, and the decision rests with the Caroline County Board of Supervisors. The land, a farm with a house, fields and timber, lies east of Coleman's Mill Road and north of Dry Bridge Road at the end of the public part of Carneal Lane, with the CSX railroad as its northern edge; the part north of the railroad would stay rural. Polecat Creek and Saddle Swamp, tributaries of the Mattaponi River, run through the property, and the applicant says wetlands and resource protection areas will be left as buffers. The applicant commits to noise at the property line of no more than 60 decibels by day and 55 at night. It cites a Mangum Economics study projecting 360 jobs and county revenue of about $24.4 million in the first year of operations, rising to $81.8 million in year three and settling at $65 million. The site falls within the Carmel Church Growth Area, which the Board of Supervisors expanded in September 2024 to take in properties along Dry Bridge Road and Carneal Lane for technology uses. ft-1769230835913-8005.text: VALCO sought to build a roughly 900-acre data center campus on Mount Airy Drive and Jericho Road at Ruther Glen, in Caroline County, Virginia, about 1,000 feet from Kevin Collins' home. The Caroline County Board of Supervisors voted 5 to 1 on June 18, 2024 to reject the comprehensive plan change the project needed, and VALCO withdrew its rezoning application that same night. It was the fourth time supervisors had turned the campus down, after two defeats at the planning commission and one earlier board vote. Collins had fought the project since January 2023 from a house off Jericho Road. "I call it the zombie project," he said, "because it keeps popping up out of the grave on us." VALCO, represented by attorney Ann Cosby, sought to rezone 250 acres of the site on Jericho Road for a data center park, tied to the wider plan change on Mount Airy Drive. Madison District supervisor Clay Forehand argued the campus would bring as much tax benefit as eight to 10 large distribution centers without their truck traffic. Bowling Green District supervisor Jeff Sili disagreed: "I cannot vote to approve a rezoning and comp plan change every time a developer finds a good deal on land in Caroline." The land is owned by Litt Thompson of the Thompson Family Office, a Richmond investment firm that also owns the Carmel Church land tied to the long-stalled DC South project. Planning director Leon Hughes told the board the county already had 1,848 acres of undeveloped industrial land east of Interstate 95, inside the Carmel Church growth area, that could hold data centers without touching the North Anna River site.

ft-994.text: Valo Park, at 7950 Jones Branch Drive in Tysons, in Fairfax County, is a two-tower office campus at the junction of I-495 and the Dulles Toll Road, and nothing published describes a data center there. The county rule that governs anything new here is recent. Fairfax County's board of supervisors adopted a data center zoning amendment on September 10, 2024, effective the next day, revising where data centers are permitted and to what standard. It caps them at 80,000 square feet and requires 200 feet between a data center and homes. Serverfarm is testing both limits about two kilometres from here. Its Vienna Cloud application, filed at the end of January 2026 for 7990 and 7980 Quantum Drive, is 316,228 square feet on 14.4 acres, up to 67 feet tall, and would stand 107 to 131 feet from apartments and townhouses. Serverfarm has since asked to be released from the Metro separation rule, the floor area caps and the 200 foot residential buffer. The planning commission hears it on November 18.

ft-691.text: Google's data center campus at the Botetourt Center at Greenfield near Daleville, Virginia, has been approved for grading: the company received a land disturbance permit from Botetourt County, and phased grading on the 312-acre site was set to begin in late summer 2026. The Google data center campus in Botetourt County is planned as three buildings of about 300,000 square feet each, with three electric substations and a 28,000 square foot office building. The county sold Google the land for $14 million in June 2025, and the developer, signing as Helio Capital LLC, agreed to invest at least $1 billion in each data center it builds, to pay local real estate taxes at once and to give $4 million to community projects over five years. Each data center is to employ at least 50 full-time workers at a median salary of $86,000. Google confirmed the plan in March 2026; its data center public affairs head, Amber Tillman, said each building takes 18 to 24 months to build and the campus will come in phases. The business park's zoning was changed to allow data centers in November 2024, and the project takes most of the park's remaining land. Power and water are the local questions. In a September 4, 2026 filing with the State Corporation Commission, Appalachian Power put Google's peak demand at about 300 megawatts, a figure not previously made public, and estimated $264 million in transmission and substation upgrades to serve it. The utility says the new load will bring in enough revenue that its other customers are not expected to pay more, and Google has cited the White House's Ratepayer Protection Pledge in promising to pay for the upgrades. Early estimates in an agreement between the county and the Western Virginia Water Authority put water use at two million gallons a day at first, rising to eight million, though Board of Supervisors Chairman Mac Scothorn said the chances of Google using two million gallons a day are "pretty low" and that the estimate reflects the hottest, most extreme weather. Google has said the 79 megawatts it buys from the Rocky Forge wind farm in the county will not cover the campus's needs. The Southwest Virginia Data Center Transparency Alliance has opposed the project's financial, health and environmental effects; its spokesperson, Hunter Hartley, raised water use, electricity costs, land disturbance, the buildings' looks and "ethical questions about what we do with our time and resources." Power company and water officials had signed nondisclosure agreements with the project before it was announced, the water authority's director as early as March 2024. Roanoke and Roanoke County have each asked for 15% of the tax revenue, and Scothorn said no revenue-sharing deal has been made. Under the county's permit, construction noise is barred from 9 p.m. to 7 a.m., blasting is regulated by the State Fire Marshal's Office, and Google has committed to on-site sound monitoring during construction and operation. Elsewhere in Appalachian Power's territory, Stack Infrastructure's Berry Hill project in Pittsylvania County has a commitment of at least 299 megawatts, and a developer in eastern Wythe County says its campus needs at least 1,000 megawatts. What remains is the State Corporation Commission's review of Appalachian Power's grid upgrades, state and federal environmental permits overseen by the Department of Environmental Quality, and further county plan approvals.

ft-695.text: Gateway Commerce Center is a proposed data center campus on about 203 acres on Hickory Ridge Road in Spotsylvania County, Virginia. Four Points, LLC, represented by attorney Charles Payne of the Hirschler law firm, filed rezoning application R23-0002 to reclassify the land from agricultural to industrial use, allowing up to 1,000,000 square feet of data center buildings in a first phase and as much as 1,066,040 square feet more in a future phase. The land is owned by Geoffrey Davis and by Thomas and Elise O'Keefe. The application has to meet rules that changed while it was pending: since February 24, 2026 every data center in Spotsylvania County needs a special use permit, with public hearings before the planning commission and then the board of supervisors. No hearing date for Gateway Commerce Center has been published; the county requires postcards to properties within 3,000 feet, a newspaper notice and signs on the property fifteen days before any hearing is held. County code bars the permanent use of drinking water for industrial cooling; a purple pipe system to supply treated wastewater instead is planned along a 13-mile corridor in the southeast of the county. Noise at the site would be capped at 65 decibels by day and 60 at night against residential areas, and backup generators must meet Tier 4 diesel standards. As of August 2026 the county had approved 15,469,908 square feet of data center space on 1,597 of the 2,701 industrial acres it has set aside for the use, part of a policy to reserve 45 percent of its industrial land for data centers. The county estimates a million square feet of data center generates about 750 vehicle trips a day, against 1,650 for a warehouse of the same size.

ft-1769231599872-1900.text: The SpotsyTech Campus, a 2.9 million square foot industrial and data center park on about 314 acres in Thornburg, Spotsylvania County, Virginia, won its rezoning in March 2023 on a 4-3 vote of the Board of Supervisors. SpotsyTechnoCampus LLC asked to rezone the land between U.S. 1 and Interstate 95 from agricultural to industrial; it borders Riverview Elementary and Thornburg Middle schools. The campus sits north of the Mudd Tavern and Morris Road intersection, on land that also borders Hickory Ridge Road and North Roxbury Mill Road. The first phase would be up to a million square feet in three warehouse and logistics buildings, and the second up to 1.9 million square feet in as many as nine two story industrial or data center buildings of 187,500 square feet each, with room for an on-site substation. The developer put the cost at $366.5 million and planned construction from 2023 to 2030. The land, formerly Pierson Farm, sold to SpotsyTechnoCampus for $6 million in 2022, and county documents list Matteo Coppola as the company's vice president. The developer said the campus could bring the county $4.5 million a year in taxes, and offered $3.4 million for road improvements on U.S. 1 and at Hickory Ridge and Roxbury Mill roads. No megawatt figure or tenant has been published. The vote was close. Supervisors Deborah Frazier, Kevin Marshall, Tim McLaughlin and David Ross voted for it; Chris Yakabouski, Lori Hayes and Jacob Lane voted against. At the February 2023 public hearing, several residents spoke against it over traffic and infrastructure, and the board delayed its decision to learn more about data centers first. The Planning Commission had recommended approval 5-1. Spotsylvania's rules have tightened since. The county banned permanent use of drinking water for cooling in November 2023, and since February 24, 2026 every new data center needs a special use permit and public hearings. Proffers accepted with a rezoning, such as SpotsyTech's road improvements, stay with the land if it is sold, and the county enforces them; SpotsyTech and other approved projects have committed to a 65 decibel noise limit.

The land, formerly Pierson Farm, sold to SpotsyTechnoCampus for $6 million in 2022, and county documents list Matteo Coppola as the company's vice president. The developer said the campus could bring the county $4.5 million a year in taxes, and offered $3.4 million for road improvements on U.S. 1 and at Hickory Ridge and Roxbury Mill roads. No megawatt figure or tenant has been published.

The vote was close. Supervisors Deborah Frazier, Kevin Marshall, Tim McLaughlin and David Ross voted for it; Chris Yakabouski, Lori Hayes and Jacob Lane voted against. At the February 2023 public hearing, several residents spoke against it over traffic and infrastructure, and the board delayed its decision to learn more about data centers first. The Planning Commission had recommended approval 5-1.

Spotsylvania's rules have tightened since. The county banned permanent use of drinking water for cooling in November 2023, and since February 24, 2026 every new data center needs a special use permit and public hearings. Proffers accepted with a rezoning, such as SpotsyTech's road improvements, stay with the land if it is sold, and the county enforces them; SpotsyTech and other approved projects have committed to a 65 decibel noise limit.

ft-995.text: Amazon Web Services is building a data center on Loisdale Road in southern Springfield, Fairfax County, Virginia, on the site of two office buildings demolished in June 2023. AWS is building a two-story, 120,000-square-foot data center on the 17.5-acre site, next to the Loisdale Estates and Newington neighborhoods. By March 2024 the Connection reported the first building was up near the Loisdale Road and Newington Road intersection, with more land being cleared on 23 acres in the Springfield Planning District, and no completion date was given. AWS said it has invested more than $51.9 billion in Virginia data centers and paid $334 million in personal property taxes in 2022. Fairfax County tightened its data center rules on September 10, 2024, requiring a 200-foot setback from homes, a noise study, and keeping new data centers out of a one-mile radius around Metro stations, though it grandfathered applications already filed. Springfield Supervisor Pat Herrity said data centers must be "properly located and screened to reduce the impact on our residents." The first building was up by March 2024, and any further construction on the site now falls under the county's 2024 rules unless it was already grandfathered. No newspaper account since March 2024 has said whether the project is finished.

ft-1043.text: NP Austin Ridge LLC, led by developer Nathaniel Hagedorn, wants Stafford County, Virginia, to rezone 183 acres at the end of Cedar Lane in Hartwood for a data center campus. The site sits about 2,000 feet south of Courthouse Road and west of Interstate 95. The plan covers roughly 2.1 million square feet of industrial space, including about 1.6 million square feet of data center buildings, and needs the county to rezone the land to M2, heavy industrial use. This is a separate project from the built Austin Ridge Logistics Center industrial park a short distance away on Austin Ridge Drive. NorthPoint Development of Kansas City broke ground there in June 2024 on five to seven buildings totaling 2.08 million square feet, aimed at logistics, warehouse and data center tenants, a $133.9 million investment the company said would create over 1,200 jobs. An October 2024 impact statement for a neighboring project, the 1,042-acre GWV data center campus off Ramoth Church Road, named Austin Ridge Logistics as already seeking the M2 rezoning to support data center use. After Stafford tightened its data center rules in October 2025, the developer of another nearby tract, Courthouse West LLC, told the Planning Commission in February 2026 that a data center there was now premature and dropped it from its own application. At that February hearing on the neighboring plan, Planning Commission chair Kristen Barnes noted the industrial zoning already nearby: "Our comprehensive plan and citizenry do not consider this to be an industrial area. The M1 we have there now [Austin Ridge Logistics] is plenty," she said.

ft-1782186463729-2086.text: Project Tallmadge, a data center campus that Takanock plans on 87 acres in the Strasburg Industrial Park near Interstate 81's Exit 296, would make its own power with on-site natural gas turbines, and it has drawn steady opposition in Strasburg, in Shenandoah County, Virginia. The town treats the data center as a use allowed by right, so Strasburg's council has no zoning vote on it, and residents have turned to the state's air permits instead. Data Center Dynamics reported that Takanock is proposing a 180MW campus and will bring 400MW of on-site natural gas generation, and its fact sheet puts the remaining permits and the start of construction in the third quarter of 2027. The Northern Virginia Daily reported the campus would cost $4.5 billion; the site plan reviewed by the town labels each of its two buildings a "160 MW-IT" data center, and the town expects Takanock to file a revised plan. Takanock was founded in 2023 by Kenneth Davies, founder of Google Energy, and is funded by DigitalBridge; Davies also co-founded Birch Infrastructure and its Rowan data center unit. Mayor Brandy Hawkins Boies has said Takanock bought the land in 2024, when "data processing" was permitted by right, and that "The by-right determination was not a policy decision made by this council". The council has since required special-use permits for data centers, effective July 1, 2025, but Project Tallmadge proceeds under the earlier ordinance. Former council member Seth Newman, who served when that ordinance was adopted, disputed the town's reading: "Back then, data processing meant an office building with a lot of cubicles," he said. "It did not mean an industrial 320-megawatt power plant." About 200 residents went through a bag search to attend a town forum at Strasburg High School on June 15, 2026, where an 11-member panel answered 56 questions chosen in advance. Takanock chief commercial officer Craig McKesson promised, "We are going to be a net supplier of power to your community," and said of the river, "It will not impact the Shenandoah River". The company's own water figures varied: a handout listed 2,000 to 4,000 gallons a day, a display board 4,000 to 8,000, and McKesson said the first fill of the closed-loop cooling would take about 300,000 gallons, down from an earlier estimate of about 4 million. Kyle Hart of the National Parks Conservation Association said: "You're essentially getting a natural gas plant at that site, which will operate full time". The fight has moved to the air permits. Resident Paula Knight said in July that she had filed an objection to Takanock's request that the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality treat the power plant separately from the data center, and that Takanock had applied for initial air permits for 80 diesel generators for the first data center. Knight argued that the 10-turbine gas plant "would not be constructed on this exact 86-acre lot in Strasburg but for the concurrent development of the adjacent data center," and asked DEQ to review the two as one source. At the forum, DEQ regional director Brandon Kiracofe said the state needs a form signed by the locality certifying whether the project suits the area before it acts on the turbines' air permit: "Until we have that form that's signed by the locality, we will not take any action on the air permit application". Shenandoah Valley Electric Cooperative said a new substation and distribution equipment would be needed, at the project's cost. At a July 2026 council meeting, 18 people spoke after Boies turned down calls to remove data centers from the zoning ordinance altogether, saying a blanket ban "is unlikely to withstand legal challenge". Zachary Walters said the opposition group had grown from 800 to 1,700 members in 25 days: "We will not stop until they cancel this project". Tammy Ruggiero asked the town to form a resident working group instead of relying on three-minute comments: "Sit down with people." What happens next: Takanock's revised site plan goes to the town's planning staff, DEQ decides the air permits, and the Strasburg Town Council, led by Mayor Boies, decides whether to sign the locality form DEQ needs for the turbines. Shenandoah County has said construction could start in late 2027 and finish around 2030.

ft-782.text: The data center at 1764A Old Meadow Lane in Tysons, Fairfax County, Virginia, is DataBank's IAD2, a colocation site with 40,690 square feet of raised floor and 3 megawatts of critical IT load. DataBank markets it as a disaster recovery site between Washington and the data center cluster at Ashburn, and says it runs on 100 percent renewable energy. New data centers in Fairfax County now face stricter rules: the board of supervisors adopted a data center zoning amendment on September 10, 2024, effective the next day. It limits data center buildings to 80,000 square feet and requires a 200-foot setback from homes, unless the county grants exceptions. The first real test of those rules is elsewhere in Tysons. At 7980 and 7990 Quantum Drive, the California operator Serverfarm filed at the end of January 2026 to replace the Tysons Technology Center with two data center buildings it calls Vienna Cloud. The buildings would stand 107 to 131 feet from the Reserve at Tysons Corner apartments and the Heritage Point townhouses that back onto the site. What Serverfarm has asked for since is to be let out of three of the rules. The ordinance requires a data center to sit at least a mile from a Metro station entrance, and the site is 0.9 miles from Tysons Corner. It asks to raise the first building from 80,256 to 95,014 square feet and the second from 202,500 to 221,214, and the site does not meet the 200 foot residential buffer either. Renee Grebe, the Northern Virginia conservation advocate for Nature Forward, said what a grant of those exceptions would mean: "If this gets passed, then I think it demonstrates that our zoning ordinance amendment is not as strong as it was touted to be by our board of supervisors." She pointed to round the clock noise and 28 diesel generators beside homes and sports facilities, against a comprehensive plan that calls for an active 24 hour environment of restaurants and shops. The planning commission set a public hearing for November 18, and supervisor Dalia Palchik said a community meeting would be arranged before it.

ft-780.text: Globalinx, which runs a cable landing station and colocation data center at the Corporate Landing Business Park in Virginia Beach, Virginia, is expanding: in August 2026 the Virginia Beach Development Authority agreed to sell it nine more acres there for $1.8 million. The land is for the third phase of the Globalinx Virginia Beach data center campus: an 85,000-square-foot building, a $65 million project to support more cable landing stations and carrier-neutral colocation, with no timeline given. Globalinx first agreed to buy land in the business park in 2016, planning a carrier-neutral data center near Telefonica's new cable landing station, as the Marea and Brusa subsea cables came to Virginia Beach. The first phase came online in 2019, and a second phase is under development. In January 2025 Globalinx said it had begun building an expansion of its 11-acre campus for four more subsea cables, alongside the three operating cables at the neighboring Telxius landing station, which connects to Globalinx in a meet-me room. The Brusa, Dunant and Marea cables land at Virginia Beach, with Confluence-1 due to join in 2026. A week after the development authority's vote, the Virginia Beach City Council voted unanimously for a 12-month pause on permits for new data centers, or until the city addresses data centers in its zoning. City officials have said they want to protect data center businesses tied to the subsea cable landing industry, and the moratorium is not expected to affect existing businesses. "This is an opportunity for us to take a pause to give us a chance to consider this topic in a thoughtful way," Councilmember Joash Schulman said before the vote. The city's planning commission chair had warned in May that data centers could be built by right in industrial districts because the zoning code does not define them. Neighboring Chesapeake adopted an eight-month data center moratorium and closed a zoning loophole in August 2026, after rejecting a 350,000-square-foot data center a year earlier. Globalinx is also planning a backup data center in Portsmouth and a cable landing station in Ocean City, Maryland, for Amazon's FastNet subsea cable.

ft-1064.text: CyrusOne's proposed Vint Hill data center campus would put four two-story buildings, about 870,000 square feet in all, on 47 acres at the southwest corner of Vint Hill Road and Vint Hill Parkway near Warrenton, in Fauquier County, Virginia. The site is in Vint Hill's Planned Commercial Industrial Development District, one of two zoning districts in the county where large data centers were allowed by right, and CyrusOne submitted its first site plan in March 2024. C1 Vint Hill, LLC, affiliated with CyrusOne, paid $89,383,312 for the 47.7 acres, nearly $2 million an acre and a Fauquier record, buying from a subsidiary of Zumot Real Estate Management that had paid $8.75 million in September 2021. County meeting notes suggested the buildings would be air-cooled, and a space directly south owned by NOVEC may hold a substation to power the complex; neither the drawings nor the notes said how much power it would use. Fauquier's Board of Supervisors voted 3-2 on March 15, 2024 to require a special exception permit for buildings over 50,000 square feet at Vint Hill, ending by-right data center construction there, but the change did not apply to CyrusOne's campus or an OVHcloud expansion already under way. CyrusOne had asked to be left out of the new rule, and the board included its project in a grandfathering provision. Supervisor Ike Broaddus noted that CyrusOne's buildings would be only 45 feet tall, while Vint Hill Conservancy president Chris Zumot called the new rule "an abomination that will only deter businesses from coming to Vint Hill." As of August 2024, county comments on CyrusOne's first site plan submission had been returned to the company. With the campus grandfathered, the county's site plan review is what remains before construction can start.

ft-974.text: OVHcloud runs its first U.S. data center at 6872 Watson Court in Vint Hill, near Warrenton in Fauquier County, Virginia, inside a former Army base, and the French cloud company is expanding it with a second building. On September 17, 2026, Fauquier's Planning Commission recommended limiting new data centers to the Vint Hill area and requiring a special exception permit and public hearing for each one; the Board of Supervisors will decide whether to adopt the change. OVHcloud bought the 84,200-square-foot building on 8.6 acres from real estate investor Rajai Zumot for $4.8 million in October 2016 and opened the data center in 2017. Governor Terry McAuliffe announced the project in 2016, with OVH planning to invest $47 million and create 54 jobs, backed by a $1.25 million state grant and county tax and infrastructure incentives. OVHcloud has bought 10.81 more acres nearby for a planned second building of 120,000 square feet, and the county has not said when it will take up that application. Neighboring developers want to grow too: CyrusOne has filed plans for a four-building, 870,000-square-foot campus on 47 acres at Vint Hill Road and Vint Hill Parkway, and Vint Hill Corners LLC proposes one or two buildings on about 50 acres at 4295 Aiken Drive. The Piedmont Environmental Council says the Vint Hill Planned Commercial Industrial District has already allowed 1.3 million square feet of data centers without a public hearing. In March 2024 the Board of Supervisors voted 3-2 to require a special exception permit and public comment for any data center building over 50,000 square feet in that district, though the OVHcloud expansion and the CyrusOne campus were exempted because they were already under way. Supervisor Ike Broaddus said OVHcloud had "proven itself to be a quiet neighbor," while Vint Hill Conservancy president Chris Zumot called the district's growth "an abomination that will only deter businesses from coming to Vint Hill." The Planning Commission's September 2026 amendment says the district "is not to become the 'Data Center District,'" and that data centers should stay "secondary and compatible" with other uses there. The Board of Supervisors has not yet set a date to vote on the recommendation.

ft-1003.text: Maple Tree Farm, a 145-acre family farm on the southeastern edge of Warrenton, in Fauquier County, Virginia, is being marketed as a data center site; its owners have never filed an application to build one. In September 2026 the county Planning Commission recommended zoning changes that would limit new data centers to the Vint Hill area, which would leave the farm outside the only district open to them. The farm belongs to the Dick and Leonard families and sits in a rough triangle bordered on the north by the Greenway extension and on the west by U.S. 15/29, the town's eastern bypass; once a dairy and cattle farm, it has lately hosted Christmas lights, a corn maze and a Halloween Haunted Hollow. In early 2023 the families asked Warrenton to take the farm into town limits, putting it on town water and sewer, so they could seek industrial zoning and a special use permit for data centers; a conceptual plan showed six buildings and a substation on 60 acres, and the land was priced at $950,000 an acre. "We really have hardly any residents around, so we think it's a good location," said Bill Chipman, the broker marketing the property. The Warrenton Town Council had already voted unanimously in January 2023 to rescind its own request to extend town limits, so the farm stayed outside town boundaries; it does not fall under the town's later ban on data centers. Julie Bolthouse of the Piedmont Environmental Council said "the proliferation of data centers around the town would be concerning." In December 2023 the Board of Supervisors adopted a data center policy that both sides called the strictest in Northern Virginia, limiting buildings to 45 feet and barring data centers and their power lines along scenic byways; U.S. 15, which the farm sits just off, is a National Scenic Byway. Chipman walked out of the committee that drafted it, and in January 2024 said of the farm's chances: "We have just a glimmer of hope." The zoning amendment the Planning Commission recommended in September 2026 would require every future data center to win a special exception from the Board of Supervisors, and would restrict new projects to the Vint Hill area; county staff told planners there are "no appropriate areas for data center development" elsewhere in the county. Fauquier has two data centers running, an Amazon Web Services facility at the Warrenton Training Center and OVHcloud in Vint Hill, with several more proposed nearby, including CyrusOne's 870,000-square-foot campus in Vint Hill. The Board of Supervisors has not yet voted on the Planning Commission's recommendation; that vote is the next decision affecting whether the farm could ever be rezoned.

ft-711.text: Vint Hill Corners LLC plans a data center campus of one or two buildings, up to two stories, on about 50 acres at 4295 Aiken Drive in Vint Hill, near Warrenton, in Fauquier County, Virginia. In May 2024 the Fauquier County Board of Supervisors voted 4-1 to exempt the project from Vint Hill's new, stricter zoning rules, so it can proceed without a special permit. The county is now reviewing the developer's site plan, the next step, which is decided by staff rather than at a public hearing. The exemption settled a dispute running since at least October 2023 over whether Vint Hill's zoning allowed a data center on the site. Under a compromise worked out by County Attorney Tracy Gallehr, the developer can choose 45-foot buildings, rooftop equipment included, or taller buildings with larger setbacks and smaller footprints. Supervisor Ike Broaddus, whose district includes Vint Hill, opposed it as too close to homes: "To them, it makes a very big difference whether we let them (be grandfathered) or not. It changes the land's value dramatically," he said. Vint Hill already hosts an OVHcloud data center, which plans a second building, and CyrusOne's 870,000-square-foot campus at Vint Hill Road and Vint Hill Parkway, both also exempt from the new rules. The Vint Hill district allows 1.3 million square feet of data center development by right, without public hearings, and the Piedmont Environmental Council has urged the county to build out only what is already approved. In September 2026 the county Planning Commission unanimously recommended zoning changes that would confine new data centers to that one district and require a special exception permit for every future one, saying it "is not to become the 'Data Center District.'"

ft-967.text: The Mineral Gap data center campus in Wise County, Virginia, is run by DP Facilities as a 65,000-square-foot, Uptime Institute Tier III certified facility on 22 acres in the Lonesome Pine Regional Business and Technology Park, built first to serve U.S. agency clients and their contractors. The company says it offers up to 45 megawatts of power and that future phases would add more than 200,000 square feet on more than 50 acres of adjacent land under option. Mineral Gap is powered in part by a 3.4-megawatt solar array built on former strip-mined land, which the Daily Yonder called the first abandoned mine land converted to solar in Virginia. DP Facilities lists armed security around the clock, anti-ram fencing and a blast berm among its security measures. Wise County officials are separately planning the Wise Innovation Hub, a roughly 2 million-square-foot data center complex with its own natural gas power plant, at the same business park. Red Post Energy signed a letter of intent in December 2025 to design that plant, and by April 2026 was studying whether to run it on hydrogen instead, Virginia Business reported. Brian Falin, Wise County's industrial development supervisor, said he does not expect the hub to be a heavy water user and that officials plan to increase public outreach this year. "We're not going to rush this. We fully understand that our community is going to need to be involved in this process," Falin said. A 2020 regional study named the park one of three prime coalfield sites for data centers, pointing to cooling with 51-degree water from old mines nearby.

Wise County officials are separately planning the Wise Innovation Hub, a roughly 2 million-square-foot data center complex with its own natural gas power plant, at the same business park.
Red Post Energy signed a letter of intent in December 2025 to design that plant, and by April 2026 was studying whether to run it on hydrogen instead, Virginia Business reported.
Brian Falin, Wise County's industrial development supervisor, said he does not expect the hub to be a heavy water user and that officials plan to increase public outreach this year.
"We're not going to rush this. We fully understand that our community is going to need to be involved in this process," Falin said.
A 2020 regional study named the park one of three prime coalfield sites for data centers, pointing to cooling with 51-degree water from old mines nearby.

ft-1786996756851-2319.text: Blue Fern Development's proposed 20-megawatt data center at its Bullfrog Flats development in Cle Elum, Kittitas County, Washington, prompted the city to pass a six-month moratorium on new data centers on July 31, 2026, just three days after the company unveiled the plan. The moratorium may not stop the project, though, because the site is covered by a 2002 development agreement, and the city has not decided whether a data center counts as an already-permitted use under it. Blue Fern plans a 100,000-square-foot data center costing about $200 million, using a closed-loop cooling system that would need about 80,000 gallons of water in its first year and much less afterward, and Puget Sound Energy said it could reliably serve the 20-megawatt project. Company representative Ben Paulus called it a "research sized data center" that would employ 20 to 40 people. Resident John Carlson, who has lived in Cle Elum for decades, said, "From what I understand with these data centers, they take a lot of electricity and power that we need to sustain our regular usage, and it is increasing rates across the country." Councilmember Steven Harper warned residents not to expect too much from the moratorium: "This is not a magical Band-aid that obviously fixes it." Kittitas County passed its own six-month moratorium on August 10 and scheduled a hearing on extending it for September 15, and the Cle Elum City Council scheduled its own hearing on the moratorium for September 8; both hearings were scheduled and no results have been published. The decisions rest with the Cle Elum City Council, Mayor Matthew Lundh and the Kittitas County commissioners, including whether a data center is allowed under the 2002 Bullfrog Flats agreement.

ft-1763416807013-1905.text: Keel Infrastructure, formerly known as Bitfarms, is converting its former bitcoin mine at 7906 Randolph Road NE in Moses Lake, Grant County, Washington into an 18 megawatt data center called Grant Node, its first full switch from cryptocurrency mining to AI and high performance computing. The company shut down mining there in April 2026 and is now demolishing the old site to build a single story data center with utility yards, parking and stormwater works on six acres supplied by the Grant County Public Utility District. Washington's Department of Ecology covered the construction under a stormwater permit that took effect June 1, 2026, and Keel is targeting commissioning in 2027. In June 2026 an Amazon Data Services job listing for a data center manager based in Moses Lake set off speculation that Amazon would be the tenant, but the listing named no facility and did not mention Keel; neither company has announced a lease, and as of August 10, 2026 Keel said it had prospective tenants negotiating at its priority sites but had not named a customer for Moses Lake. Keel's 2025 annual filing shows a $128.7 million agreement with Vertiv to fit out the building, and in August 2026 the company said the first Vertiv equipment had arrived on site. Keel projects the finished data center will run at a power usage effectiveness of between 1.15 and 1.35, a measure of how much of the power it draws goes to computing rather than cooling and other overhead. Keel chief executive Ben Gagnon said the site was worth converting because of the power already on hand there: "Power is the constraint. Everything else is downstream of it." The stormwater permit covers construction only and is not approval to build and energize the finished data center; Keel said in August 2026 that its final building permits were still being processed.

ft-1765226206392-3158.text: Atlas Agro, a fertilizer company, wants to build a data center beside the nitrate plant it is planning at Richland, in Benton County, Washington. It would put five buildings of 500,000 square feet each on about 275 acres in the Northwest Advanced Clean Energy Park, north of Horn Rapids Road and across from Framatome, at a cost of $500 million, employing more than 100 people, with construction starting in 2027. The fertilizer plant is the bigger half. Atlas Agro's $1 billion nitrate plant on 150 acres at the Horn Rapids Industrial Park would make 700,000 tons a year and need 320 megawatts, and it is meant to employ 200 people. Chief executive Petter Ostbo named the constraint on both: "It's the power that's the limiting factor, both for the fertilizer plant and for the potential data center." Dan Holmes, the company's president for North America, put the relationship between the two the other way round: "We don't see a data center as a separate business, but as a partner that helps us build the necessary power and utility infrastructure for the site," he told the council committee, adding that the approach "puts us on an expedited path to getting the fertilizer plant up and running." Both wait on Bonneville Power Administration grid upgrades expected within three years. Seven of the eight members present at Richland's economic development committee meeting on October 20 voted to recommend the agreement to the council. The council approved it unanimously on December 2, 2025: an option, not a sale, giving Atlas Agro a year to decide, against a nonrefundable fee of $250,000 and a price just under $24 million for the 275 acres at 2100 Horn Rapids Road if it goes ahead. Karl Dye, who runs the Tri-City Development Council, tied it to the Department of Energy's Genesis Mission and its seventeen national laboratories. What that option turned out to mean became clear in July 2026, when residents asked Richland for the kind of data center moratorium Pasco had adopted the day before. City manager Jon Amundson told them it was not available: "Because an option agreement is in effect, imposing a moratorium is not possible." Richland resident Kayla Madsen told the council its approach seemed to break the Atlas Agro question into small pieces to make it "sweet and palatable," and accused it of ignoring concerns about infrastructure, water, noise and utility rates. Amundson said federal deed restrictions already apply to the land and that the city meant to add binding conditions of its own, and that several steps remain before any sale: a purchase agreement back before the council, and building permits after that.

ft-1782349490474-2867.text: The owners of the Starbucks Center, the Sodo building that houses Starbucks' headquarters at 2401 Utah Avenue South in Seattle, have filed a conceptual site plan for a small data center in the building's empty ground-floor space. Colossus Data Center Advisors filed the plans in June 2026 for a roughly 20-megawatt data center sized just under the limit of the city's new data center moratorium; Starbucks itself is not the developer. The proposal would fill a former Amazon Fresh pickup site, empty since January 2024, using about 45,600 square feet in the building; it would not overlap the space Starbucks leases, which runs through 2038. Developer Kevin Daniels of building owner Nitze-Stagen said the filing was meant to test feasibility and that there is no tenant yet: "I actually resisted it, but one of my partners was aware of the fervor of the (data center) market and started to educate me on the issue." The filing came days after the Seattle City Council voted unanimously on June 9, 2026, for an emergency one-year moratorium on new data centers over 20 megavolt-amperes of power capacity, which can be extended six months. "Large AI data centers are popping up across the country, driving up utility costs for residents and small businesses while creating air, water, and noise pollution," said Councilmember Eddie Lin, the moratorium's prime sponsor. The moratorium followed a spring rush: in April, four companies approached Seattle City Light about five large data centers needing a combined 369 megawatts, roughly a third of what the city uses on an average day. After an outcry, one company canceled its plan and Sabey withdrew a 68-megawatt request at its Tukwila campus, leaving Equinix and Prologis with three proposals, two of them in Sodo. Because the Starbucks Center plan sits under the 20-megavolt-ampere threshold, the moratorium would not stop it on its own; it still needs the city's permits and power from Seattle City Light. The owners have not said whether they will pursue it, and Mayor Katie Wilson said she would sign the moratorium and work on "a long-term approach to these issues."

ft-1772675606659-3393.text: The Beaver Dam Common Council voted 11-3 in April 2026 to sell about 13 acres of city land at Highway 151 and Hemlock Road, in Dodge County, Wisconsin, to Oppidan for a proposed 90,000-square-foot edge data center, the second data center coming to the city. The sale price was $407,340, and Oppidan said construction was set to begin that summer with the facility going online in 2028. The council set a minimum taxable value of $41 million on a project Trent Campbell of the Beaver Dam Area Development Corporation expected to be valued near $72 million, with no other incentives in the deal. Residents filled the council chambers and hallway, some holding signs, and public comment was limited to 20 minutes. Former alder Kara Nelson told the council data centers put real demands on local water, power and land: "That means to manage their impact falls squarely on you." Alds. Frank Ferree, Elwood Flaherty and Jeff Bierman voted no; Flaherty called it a speculative investment: "I'm not against growth, by no means. But I'm against the wrong kind of growth." Alder Andrew Perkins voted yes with misgivings: "Why did a well dry up, right? Why are we having these issues, and can we resolve those? Because that does bother me," he said. In August 2026 the Dodge County Board of Supervisors voted 29-2 for an 18-month moratorium on data center development, citing changes residents reported in groundwater near the Meta and Oppidan sites. Beaver Dam resident Maily Kocinski told the county's public hearing, "For the last 14 months, I have been searching for answers because we have experienced changes in our groundwater." Supervisor Cathy Houchin said the county should study what the data centers are doing to land and water. The council's April vote cleared the land sale; Oppidan had set construction to begin in summer 2026, and no report of groundbreaking has been published since.

ft-1773463314386-4370.text: Cornmaze is the internal name for a data center campus of four buildings on more than 430 acres straddling the towns of Turtle and Beloit in Rock County, over 2 million square feet in all, which the developer compared to Soldier Field and Wrigley Field put together. The developer is Panattoni, of Irvine, California, and the cost is put at $1 billion. At its presentation on June 22, 2026 Panattoni said only that the end user will be an American company, and that specifics were not yet shareable. The Town of Beloit signed a pre-development agreement dated July 15, 2025 with Cambrin LLC, a Delaware company registered in Wisconsin the year before, whose president is listed as Pamela Gregorski. The land is an existing gravel pit on the northeast side of town. Filings Cambrin made with the Department of Natural Resources list a name and email address also used in documents filed by Degas, Meta's initial operating entity for its Beaver Dam data center, which is why Meta's name is attached, but Meta has not confirmed it. The agreement commits very little. It lets the developer apply to rezone, negotiate a development agreement and explore a tax increment financing district, and it requires Cambrin to reimburse the town up to $175,000 in costs so the town is not out of pocket if nothing happens. Town administrator John Malizio said the developer is in discussions with a land owner to buy the property and that in the meantime "there isn't anything going on besides a sewer and water study." No application, site plan or proposal had been put to town staff or elected officials, and the land purchase was not complete. If it advances there will be public hearings where residents can have their say. The project is marked proposed across 430 acres, with no capacity figure and Meta named as the developer flatly, which is further than the reporting goes. The Town of Beloit adopted a moratorium on data centers on August 18, 2026, Green County on July 15 and Jefferson County on May 19 and again on August 11. The Janesville proposal at the former GM plant is nine kilometres away. The Riverside and West Riverside gas plants, 530 and 697 megawatts, are three and four kilometres off. The numbers Panattoni did give were economic ones. Applied Analysis, working for the developer, put economic output at $636.7 million over a construction period of five to seven years and property taxes at $6.5 million a year, which would make the campus Rock County's largest principal taxpayer, ahead of Amazon by nearly double. On power it said demand could run to the hundreds of megawatts, and on water that a closed loop cooling system could need half as much as current facilities, without saying what that half would be. About fifty people protested outside. Philip Gorman questioned whether the private lunch meeting had breached Wisconsin's open meetings law, and said that whether you are invited "is really more of a sign of not whether you're a community leader, but whether you're supportive of data centers."

ft-1771256468378-6038.text: Cloverleaf Infrastructure has dropped its plan to buy land for a data center in the town of Carlton, in Kewaunee County, Wisconsin, after the town made clear it did not want one. The company scrapped the Carlton data center plan in late 2025, and Cloverleaf and town officials confirmed it in January 2026. Cloverleaf, founded in February 2024, is a powered land provider: it buys land for data center companies and works with utilities to upgrade the power supply. It had been trying to turn farmland outside Carlton into a site ready to host a data center. "The town chairperson said, 'I don't support data centers. I don't think this is a good fit,'" Cloverleaf chief development officer Aaron Bilyeu said. "We shook hands and said 'thank you.'" Carlton sits on the shore of Lake Michigan south of Kewaunee. It is an agricultural town of about 1,000 people that, its town board chair said, has more cattle than people. "I'm against big business," said town Chairman David Hardtke, who has pushed back against the idea for months. "People in the town of Carlton do not want the AI (data) center." Hardtke said data center companies and solar projects have been approaching the town to build near the nuclear site. "They're just crawling out of the woodwork right now, trying to eat up the farmland," he said. "Once they take land away, you know, it'll never come back," said Chris Kohnle, president of the Tisch Mills Farm Center. Others hoped for investment; Kewaunee County resident Dan Giannotti said an employer like that would bring new homes and businesses, "Because right now we're just stagnant." The draw is the Kewaunee Power Station, the nuclear plant in Carlton that closed in 2013. Its owner, EnergySolutions, is seeking Nuclear Regulatory Commission approval to bring nuclear power back to the site because it expects data centers and AI to raise the state's energy demand. The company told the town licensing could take three or four years and construction another eight to ten after that. Bilyeu said Cloverleaf is still looking for a data center site in northeast Wisconsin, and that it is not the only company looking. Carlton was the second Wisconsin site Cloverleaf walked away from; it also dropped a proposal near the village of Greenleaf in Brown County in January 2026 after community outrage. Neighboring Manitowoc County has since passed a data center moratorium, and a moratorium has been proposed in Brown County.

ft-1782690162364-4913.text: The Driftless Area Data Center, a proposed 400 to 500 megawatt data center in Cassville, Grant County, Wisconsin, is dead after residents voted 44 to nothing in late April 2026 to ban data centers in town. Two unnamed developers, one from the Northeast and one from the South, had offered 50 jobs and $5.5 million a year in taxes for a site of about 500 acres. The site would have used power from the Cardinal-Hickory Creek transmission line. The developers first met with Ron Brisbois, who runs the Grant County Economic Development Corporation, on November 6, 2025, and he announced the project publicly on December 3. Opposition grew through the winter; on March 8, 2026, opponents including Pete Moris and Melodie Betts held a rally with comedian Charlie Berens. By April 6 Brisbois still called the odds "better than a coinflip," but the developers stopped returning his calls soon after, and by late May the proposal was, in his words, only a memory. The town's vote was its first zoning regulation ever. The ordinance bans data centers for up to two years and requires town board approval for any change in land use. "This is the Driftless area for Christ's sakes," said resident John Hawn. "I suppose they didn't expect any problems coming into a small town." Town attorney Eric Hagen said the developers appeared to be "looking for the lowest-hanging fruit with the least amount of regulations." Melodie Betts, who opposed the project, said: "If we don't stop this now, we're going to lose everything that's precious in the Driftless Area." Brisbois said afterward: "I put a lot of time into this and lost a lot of sleep over it." Several other Grant County towns and the county board have since adopted their own data center moratoriums, and Wisconsin's Public Service Commission has moved to require data centers to pay the full cost of the power they use.

ft-1120.text: QTS Data Centers, of Virginia, wanted to build a $12 billion data center campus on about 650 acres in DeForest, Dane County, just north of Madison, Wisconsin, which would have required annexing roughly 1,600 acres from the neighboring town of Vienna. Village staff had been meeting with QTS and Alliant Energy since March 2025, seven months before the plan became public in October 2025, and the secrecy fed the backlash. On Tuesday, February 3, 2026, the DeForest Village Board voted 7-0 against the annexation, and QTS withdrew its rezoning and comprehensive-plan applications before the vote. The pre-annexation deal DeForest had reached with QTS would have guaranteed at least $1.2 billion of taxable value for 15 years, worth an estimated $12 million a year to local governments by 2031 and $1,772 a year off the tax bill on a $400,000 home. It also included $100,000 a year for 15 years for the Yahara River, $200,000 a year for affordable housing, money toward a planned interstate interchange, and QTS paying for the water, sewer and road work the site needed. "It's our job to provide the best package that we can get from our development, to benefit the population and the village," village administrator Bill Chang said. None of it was enough to keep the plan alive. "It has become clear that now is not the right time for our proposed project to move forward in DeForest," QTS said in a statement, adding it was disappointed with the outcome. Opposition had built around a Facebook group, No Data Center in DeForest, which grew past 4,100 members. Researcher Tyler Byrnes of the nonpartisan Wisconsin Policy Forum said the deal's public benefits went further than most: "You're not seeing these in other development agreements." The DeForest Village Board, which turned this annexation down, would decide on any future data center proposal there. Several other Dane County communities, including Cottage Grove, Middleton, Westport and Dane County itself, have since adopted their own moratoriums while they write data center rules.

ft-1767734064417-7029.text: Cloverleaf Infrastructure, a Houston-based data center developer, withdrew its plan for a roughly 500-acre data center campus in the Village of Greenleaf, Brown County, Wisconsin, in January 2026, days after residents packed an informational meeting. The company's chief development officer, Aaron Bilyeu, said Cloverleaf backed out after officials told it "the village of Greenleaf is now off the table" for such a project. The plan surfaced when residents were offered between $50,000 and $120,000 an acre for land between Highway 57 on the east, the East River on the west, Mallard Road on the north and Fair Road on the south; Cloverleaf was later revealed as the buyer. One resident said the offer came by phone, with word that some neighbors had already sold. Katrina Magnuson, who owns Ledgestone Vineyards and Gnarly Cedar, learned the facility would sit directly across from her business. "We are on wells out here. You hear the stories about those going dry. Our streams, our natural resources. We're right here on the Niagara Escarpment, which is a geological wonder," she said. Nearly 100 people attended a Stop the Data Center meeting that Jayne Black, a Brown County resident and field organizer for Moms Clean Air Force, helped organize, and Cloverleaf withdrew soon after. Bilyeu said Cloverleaf would not pursue projects in Greenleaf or the Town of Wrightstown, citing its preference for working with local leadership. "This is a great relief. We know the fight's not over," Magnuson said, and Bonnie Crossman, the Village of Greenleaf's board president, said the village's focus "will always be, what's best for this small community." Cloverleaf's interest then moved to the Village of Wrightstown, also in Brown County, where voters said no to an advisory referendum on supporting large-scale data center development, 1,033 to 151, on August 11, 2026. "We don't want a data center in this town at all," said Jason Stun, a Wrightstown village resident; the referendum does not bind the Village Board. Brown County's planning committee declined in June to pursue a countywide data center moratorium, reasoning that every town, village and city in the county already has its own zoning, so a countywide rule would not change anything.
