ft-1095.text: Janesville's plan for a data center campus on the former General Motors plant site, in Rock County, Wisconsin, is off for now. In June 2026 the city council voted unanimously to let its letter of intent with the developer, Viridian Acquisitions, expire, and the Janesville Gazette reported that the letter dissolved in July without the city or Viridian ever saying publicly whether the project would work at the site. The city owns the site, the former Janesville Assembly Plant at 1000 General Motors Drive, which General Motors operated from 1919 to 2008. The plant closed in 2009, and the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources considers the 250-acre brownfield contaminated. The deal had begun on Monday, November 10, 2025, when the council voted 5 to 2 for a non-binding letter of intent with Viridian Acquisitions LLC, of Colorado, which gave the city 120 days to negotiate. Viridian was weighing an eleven building campus or an eight building hyperscale one, drawing up to 800 megawatts, at a cost of more than $8 billion, with 1,200 construction jobs and 600 permanent posts. Viridian would carry out the cleanup under a plan approved by the Department of Natural Resources. More than twenty residents spoke against it at the hearing that night. Julie Backenkeller asked the council: "If data centers are so great, then why are so many communities fighting them?" Seth Lambert asked the council to "reject this data center project." Cassandra Pope said: "I don't trust these big, billion dollar corporations, and I don't trust our city government to hold these corporations accountable." Council member Heather Miller voted no: "Without being able to have input from someone about public health makes me concerned for the residents that surround this property." The opponents then went around the council. No Janesville Data Center gathered 3,927 signatures, twelve more than the 3,915 needed, and they were certified on January 21, 2026. On February 9, 2026 the council put the question on the ballot. On November 3, 2026 Janesville votes on whether any development costing more than $450 million on the undeveloped part of the GM and JATCO site must first be approved by the voters at a general or special election. If the measure passes and a plan is then rejected, the next plan needs another referendum. The question stays on the ballot even though the Viridian plan is gone. The same week it let the letter lapse, the council voted to develop guardrails on data center development and to study their impact on communities. "It would definitely provide a framework for what the council would deem necessary or acceptable for data centers, should they come to our community," said Nick Faust, assistant to the city manager. In September 2026 Forward Janesville, which had backed the letter of intent, formed Grow Janesville Responsibly to back a proposed data center moratorium and urge a no vote on the referendum, arguing that the city's GM/JATCO advisory board should guide the site plan. The referendum's backers are campaigning for a yes vote, and say they support a data center moratorium too.
paragraphs: Janesville's plan for a data center campus on the former General Motors plant site, in Rock County, Wisconsin, is off for now. In June 2026 the city council voted unanimously to let its letter of intent with the developer, Viridian Acquisitions, expire, and the Janesville Gazette reported that the letter dissolved in July without the city or Viridian ever saying publicly whether the project would work at the site.

The city owns the site, the former Janesville Assembly Plant at 1000 General Motors Drive, which General Motors operated from 1919 to 2008. The plant closed in 2009, and the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources considers the 250-acre brownfield contaminated.

The deal had begun on Monday, November 10, 2025, when the council voted 5 to 2 for a non-binding letter of intent with Viridian Acquisitions LLC, of Colorado, which gave the city 120 days to negotiate. Viridian was weighing an eleven building campus or an eight building hyperscale one, drawing up to 800 megawatts, at a cost of more than $8 billion, with 1,200 construction jobs and 600 permanent posts. Viridian would carry out the cleanup under a plan approved by the Department of Natural Resources.

More than twenty residents spoke against it at the hearing that night. Julie Backenkeller asked the council: "If data centers are so great, then why are so many communities fighting them?" Seth Lambert asked the council to "reject this data center project." Cassandra Pope said: "I don't trust these big, billion dollar corporations, and I don't trust our city government to hold these corporations accountable." Council member Heather Miller voted no: "Without being able to have input from someone about public health makes me concerned for the residents that surround this property."

The opponents then went around the council. No Janesville Data Center gathered 3,927 signatures, twelve more than the 3,915 needed, and they were certified on January 21, 2026. On February 9, 2026 the council put the question on the ballot. On November 3, 2026 Janesville votes on whether any development costing more than $450 million on the undeveloped part of the GM and JATCO site must first be approved by the voters at a general or special election. If the measure passes and a plan is then rejected, the next plan needs another referendum. The question stays on the ballot even though the Viridian plan is gone.

The same week it let the letter lapse, the council voted to develop guardrails on data center development and to study their impact on communities. "It would definitely provide a framework for what the council would deem necessary or acceptable for data centers, should they come to our community," said Nick Faust, assistant to the city manager. In September 2026 Forward Janesville, which had backed the letter of intent, formed Grow Janesville Responsibly to back a proposed data center moratorium and urge a no vote on the referendum, arguing that the city's GM/JATCO advisory board should guide the site plan. The referendum's backers are campaigning for a yes vote, and say they support a data center moratorium too.

ft-1778596114883-8026.text: Affordable Family Storage (AFS) withdrew its planned computing facility, widely called the AFS Milwaukee Midtown data center, from the former Walmart at 5825 W. Hope Ave. in Milwaukee, Milwaukee County, Wisconsin, on July 1, 2026, after weeks of opposition. Without it, the City Plan Commission unanimously cleared the rest of the redevelopment on July 20: indoor self-storage, a new Capitol Library branch, community space and about 200 affordable apartments on the parking lot. The plan put a 19,000-square-foot "computer research facility" in the rear of the 160,000-square-foot store, vacant since 2016, beside the self-storage. AFS co-owner Trent Overhue said it would run at an IT load of roughly seven megawatts plus about two megawatts of cooling, use a closed-loop system consuming less than five gallons of water a day, and serve tenants such as medical research firms. "You'll never know that we would exist in the back of this building," Overhue said. Residents were not persuaded. About 100 people came to a June meeting inside the empty store, and resident Kellie Momon, pleased by the library and housing, asked: "Why do we have to have a data center?" At a June 29 hearing that ran six and a half hours, several dozen speakers, many from the Party for Socialism and Liberation, opposed it; "You can call it whatever you want. It's still a data center," said Samantha Doucas. Opponents raised energy use, environmental impact, the outreach process and whether a majority-Black neighborhood was being asked to take a facility that would not be put elsewhere. The commission, unable to agree on conditions, held the matter over. Announcing the change, Ald. Mark Chambers Jr., who had backed the wider deal, said: "The decision to remove the computing research facility reflects what can happen when residents engage, local government listens, and all parties remain willing to find common ground." City Development Commissioner Lafayette Crump said the computing use would have produced three to five times more property tax per square foot than storage, and Overhue called losing it a "major loss" for his firm. Overhue is pursuing a larger data center in his home state of Missouri through Lumon Solutions. At the July 20 meeting Chambers accused opponents of spreading misinformation: "There is a difference between advocating for a community and speaking over one." Milwaukee has data center zoning rules pending, and the city attorney has told the council it cannot impose a moratorium because of changes in case law. Elsewhere in Wisconsin, Microsoft is building in Mount Pleasant, and large campuses are planned in Port Washington and, for Meta, Beaver Dam. The data center part of the Midtown plan is gone; any attempt to add computing back would need new zoning approval. The public can comment again when the library and community space designs come to the City Plan Commission, and the housing's tax incremental financing awaits the Milwaukee Common Council.

ft-1100.text: Balloonist LLC's proposed 324-acre data center along County Highway B in Dunn County, Wisconsin, cannot be built until the City of Menomonie finishes a new I-4 data center zoning district and Balloonist applies to rezone its land to it. The City Council read the draft I-4 ordinance, covering light and noise limits, water use, equipment setbacks and landscaping, on August 3, 2026 without a vote; it still must go to the Plan Commission and back to the council before Balloonist can apply. Mayor Matthew Crowe said in June 2026 that Balloonist had twice asked to meet him and that he had declined, so as not to be "unduly influenced regarding the project" before the council adopts the new zoning. Crowe has said the city cannot legally ban an industry, and the timeline depends on whether and when Balloonist applies. The land lies between 650th and 690th Avenue and was owned by the Town of Red Cedar; the city annexed and rezoned it for industry in August 2025 on an 8-3 council vote after the Plan Commission recommended it unanimously. Balloonist's renderings showed two data halls, an office building and a warehouse, and the city's FAQ put the investment at $1.6 billion in two phases over four to seven years. The city estimated the data center would use about 75,000 gallons of water a day, which would make it the fifth-largest user in the area. Few details about Balloonist are public; it was registered in 2024, a month before City Administrator Eric Atkinson signed a nondisclosure agreement on the project, and a council member said its end user was "one of the top tech giants." Residents say they learned of the project too late. A Facebook group, Stop the Menomonie Data Center, has more than 10,000 members, and many residents objected to the nondisclosure agreements and the secrecy. In September 2025 Mayor Randy Knaack told the council he would not negotiate a development agreement or tax increment district, and the city halted those talks, though Balloonist went on to buy the land days later. "For now, I'm not willing to negotiate a development agreement or TID district information," Knaack said then, while Ward 9 council member Sydney Brennan said the move gives "a big middle finger to companies that we are closed for business." Derek DeGross, who lives a couple of miles away, doubts the new rules will stop it: "that developer will be able to just cross off the checklist one by one, and then still build it." In January 2026 the council unanimously created a separate definition for data centers, with larger lot and setback requirements than a warehouse, meaning Balloonist would have to start its application over. "To Balloonist, if you want to be here and participate in my community honestly and truthfully, you are a data center, not a warehouse," resident Charles Warner told the council. An attorney for Balloonist, Douglas Buck, had urged the council to "please reengage with Balloonist."

ft-1104.text: Digital Power Optimization, a New York data center developer, told Wisconsin Rapids in July 2025 that it no longer intended to build the $200 million, 20-megawatt AI data center it had planned in the city, in Wood County, Wisconsin. A year later the city is weighing a far larger data center proposal from another developer on the former paper mill land next door, and its Plan Commission voted 7-0 on September 16, 2026 to recommend denying it. Digital Power Optimization had leased about 6 acres of a 15-acre parcel owned by Consolidated Water Power Company, a Billerud subsidiary, west of State 34 near the Wisconsin Water Quality Center, with interconnection rights to an energized substation and a lease of up to 50 years. The utility runs 32 megawatts of hydroelectric power and once powered the entire paper mill, leaving spare capacity after the mill idled. CEO Andrew Webber said in January 2025 that the modular facility would draw about 20 megawatts at peak, employ 12 to 20 people, and begin "initial energization" in 2026. Mayor Matt Zacher described the business model when the deal fell through: “They go in and lock up a contract, and then they go out and say hey we have 20mW of energy available any takers?” He said the city was now “more reluctant to give away 80MW of energy, and now we have no energy capacity to give to manufacturing, where you could employ 100- 200- 900 employees.” Digital Power Optimization did not reply to requests for comment. The new proposal, which Anton Voronkin of the New York developer PNK Group has taken over, would turn about 210 acres of the former mill into a data center campus. City staff recommended denying the application from DC Rapids LLC, citing missing pieces including approval from the electric utility, employment and shift projections, construction traffic details and the orientation of the buildings. “This city has been through enough. You all need to be better, you need to do better. That starts with denying this atrocity of an application. Thank you,” said Marissa Johnson of the South Wood County Neighbors for Responsible Development. Supporters of the trades urged a yes vote, and a representative of the applicant, Bill Griffith, said the company would keep working with the city on the conditions. Residents have raised water, electricity rates, air pollution and noise, and some have also objected to the developers' Russian backgrounds and business records, which Voronkin has dismissed. Zacher told Wisconsin Watch that perhaps 15 data center developers have explored the mill site, most concluding there was not enough electricity. The Wisconsin Rapids Common Council takes up the permit on October 20, 2026, and is the body that decides it.

ft-1774674122151-3553.text: Google has bought about 1,700 acres for a data center campus at 22272 Charleston Road, at the north end of the town of Buffalo near the Kanawha River, in Putnam County, West Virginia. Governor Patrick Morrisey's office announced the purchase on Friday, March 27, 2026, three days after the Department of Commerce received Google's application for certification as a high-impact data center. Google would not say what it paid or who sold the land, and the announcement gave no figure for the investment, the number of jobs, the emissions or the timing. Morrisey called it "a strong signal that our state is competing and winning for the jobs and industries of the future." A Google affiliate, Cumulus Group LLC, has applied to the Army Corps of Engineers for a permit for what it calls Project Avalon. The filing describes eight data center buildings on the 1,699 acre site, more than 2.2 million square feet, with construction disturbing about 1,254 acres and more than 14 miles of internal road. It would affect over 34 acres across 17 wetlands and more than 45,000 feet of 34 streams, and put 184 acres of spoil in the Kanawha River floodplain. Two 30 inch intake pipes would be installed by horizontal directional drilling for the project's water treatment plant, with 850 feet of permanent impact along the Kanawha shoreline. Nine federally protected species live in the range of the work, among them the Indiana bat, the northern long-eared bat, the tricolored bat, five freshwater mussels and the monarch butterfly. The Army Corps application went through a 30-day public comment period, and formal Endangered Species Act consultation will start once further bat and mussel surveys are received. The state Department of Environmental Protection estimates West Virginia has already lost 80 to 90 percent of its wetlands. Chad Minamyer, who had brain cancer in 2012, said he wants out: "We don't know the long-term health effects of living near something like that. Who knows what might happen to some of these people 20, 30 years from now if they don't move away." Mayor Conrad Cain said he was "tickled to death" and was waiting for more detail, while pointing out that the town now has Google to the north and Toyota to the south, the river on one side and a hillside on the other, and nowhere left to expand. Delegate Kathie Hess Crouse said that if the project goes ahead it will be at least a year before construction begins. Besides the Army Corps permit, Google's engineers filed applications dated June 15, 2026 with the West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection for a State Waters Permit and a Water Quality Certification, and those agencies decide whether the site work can go ahead.

The state Department of Environmental Protection estimates West Virginia has already lost 80 to 90 percent of its wetlands.

Chad Minamyer, who had brain cancer in 2012, said he wants out: "We don't know the long-term health effects of living near something like that. ft-1105.text: The Ridgeline Facility is a data center and gas fired power plant that Fundamental Data LLC wants to build between Thomas and Davis, in the corner of Tucker County, West Virginia known for Blackwater Falls and Canaan Valley. The first phase would add about 800 megawatts of gas power, nearly 1.3 gigawatts of solar and 14 data center buildings using more than 2 gigawatts, POWER magazine reported from the permit filings, with a second phase adding 3.1 gigawatts more. Fundamental Data targets 2028 for commercial operations. More than 300 people came to a June 30, 2025 public hearing on the project at Canaan Valley Resort State Park in Davis, and 100 to 150 of them spoke, pushing the meeting past midnight. Davis Mayor Al Tomson said no one spoke in favor: "There were no people that said, 'Build the data plant because I want worse air quality.'" State regulators issued air permit R13-3713 on August 15, 2025, and Appalachian Mountain Advocates appealed it for Tucker United, the West Virginia Highlands Conservancy and the Sierra Club; the state Air Quality Board upheld the permit in a February 5, 2026 final order. The groups then challenged whether Fundamental Data actually controlled the site when the permit was issued, and DAQ director Laura Crowder opened an inquiry on July 31, 2026. Fundamental Data handed over a redacted 2024 purchase agreement for the 291 acre tract, and on August 13, 2026 Crowder ruled the company had proven site control at the time the permit was issued. Fundamental Data's Casey Chapman defended the redactions: "Private is not the same thing as secret. The economics and negotiated terms of a private land transaction have nothing to do with what comes out of a stack." The Wall Street Journal reported the full complex could cover nearly 10,000 acres across Tucker and Grant counties, WV MetroNews reported. The project is moving forward under House Bill 2014, the Power Generation and Consumption Act that Governor Patrick Morrisey signed on April 30, 2025 to expand microgrid development using coal and natural gas. More steps remain, including interconnection terms, independent health impact modeling and continued community opposition, POWER magazine reported, before Fundamental Data can build toward its 2028 target.

ft-1778511860517-5615.text: Hog Lick Aggregates, which sells limestone and sandstone products, launched a feasibility study in May 2026 into a microgrid and data center on its quarry property in White Hall, near Fairmont, in Marion County, West Virginia. The company has 300 acres immediately available, with potential to expand to at least 1,500 acres, and its release says the full site could consume at least a gigawatt of power. Instead of drawing fresh water, it plans to use water from a nearby mine to create a geothermal cooling loop. President Brian Redmond was careful about it: "We need to validate that. We need to study it. We need to understand it. But, if we can prove that that's a viable alternative, there are a lot of abandoned coal mines in West Virginia filled with water." The release says Hope Gas and EQT can supply natural gas pipelines to support the potential gigawatt, which WDTV noted would mean burning a significant amount of gas. The company has said it remains open to proposals to develop the site for manufacturing or other commercial purposes instead. Company officials have argued the site could support the NOAA supercomputing facility being assembled at the I-79 High Tech Park nearby. "There's a whole high tech economy that's going to be built around the data center," Redmond said, but residents have raised concerns on Facebook and pointed out that most of the jobs would be short-term construction work. There is no timetable: Hog Lick would have to sell the site or partner with a data center developer before anything could be built.

ft-1778512141035-1060.text: NOAA's Environmental Security Computing Center, a federal supercomputing data center in the I-79 High Technology Park in Fairmont, Marion County, West Virginia, is operating and growing. The agency is installing a new research supercomputer called Rhea in a modular unit next to the existing center, adding about 30 petaflops of computing power, roughly 30,000 trillion calculations per second, to speed forecasts of weather, droughts, floods and wildfires. NOAA awarded $99.3 million to General Dynamics Information Technology to build Rhea, funded by the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law and the Inflation Reduction Act. As of May 2026, Rhea was still being installed. NOAA renewed its lease on the building with the West Virginia High Technology Foundation for another 20 years. Foundation president Jim Estep said the expansion is meant to draw more commercial weather and AI companies to the park, calling Rhea "one of the first big things that (the park) expansion was in preparation for." NOAA's design leaves room for several more modular data centers on the site later, and the center already houses NOAA's Hera supercomputer. In May 2026, Hog Lick Aggregates, next door in White Hall, said it is studying a private data center and microgrid on its 277-acre site that could support NOAA's computing work using geothermal cooling from a shuttered coal mine and local natural gas. Company president Brian Redmond called the study preliminary with no timeframe, and the proposal has drawn criticism on Facebook. Under West Virginia's 2025 law, House Bill 2014, the state certifies these "high impact" data centers and bars local governments from enforcing their own noise or pollution rules against them. In February 2026 the House voted down amendments that would have required water disclosures, 500-foot buffers from homes, schools and churches, and a local petition and vote. "I believe in local control," said Del. Laura Kimble, R-Harrison, who voted against those added rules.

ft-1106.text: TransGas Development Systems, a New York company, plans a gas-powered data center at the Harless Industrial Park near Holden and the Mingo-Logan county line, in Logan County, West Virginia. It is one of two identical campuses the company wants in the area; the other sits on the former Twisted Gun Golf Course in Wharncliffe, in neighboring Mingo County. The state Division of Air Quality issued air permits for both plants on October 2, 2025, after hearings in August and September where dozens of residents spoke against them, and the agency said the facilities "will meet all applicable state and federal air quality rules and regulations." Each power plant would run 117 gas engines and could generate more than 2,400 megawatts, the West Virginia Highlands Conservancy reported. The Ohio River Valley Institute reads the permits as allowing 2,457 megawatts per campus, together using more than 29.4 million megawatt hours a year, nearly as much as the 33 million megawatt hours the entire state of West Virginia consumes. The plants would be off grid, built to power the two campuses alone and supplying no one else in West Virginia; TransGas has said it wants to eventually expand its data center capacity to 9.8 gigawatts. Ten Mingo County residents sued in federal court in early December 2025, arguing the project needed federal environmental review, because of its effects on streams, mine-drainage channels and habitat used by federally protected species, before construction could continue. On December 23, 2025 U.S. District Judge Robert C. Chambers turned down their request for a temporary halt, ruling they had not yet notified the defendants and had not shown they were likely to win on the merits; their request for a permanent injunction was not addressed, so the state's air permits stand while the case continues.

ft-1107.text: The former Appalachian Power Company building at 1125 6th Avenue in downtown Huntington, in Cabell County, West Virginia, served as the utility's offices until the early 2000s, was bought by the Appalachian Transportation Institute in 2011 and has stood largely unused since. In October 2024 Alpha Technologies said it would turn it into a 60,000 square foot Tier 3 data center and its corporate headquarters. Founder and chief executive Doug Tate said work would start in mid-November with a first phase finished by March 2025, that Alpha would invest more than $20 million over the next few years, and that the building would employ 30 to 35 people, with a training center on the top floor. "Thirty-two percent of our population sits under the poverty line; another 16% of individuals ... live paycheck to paycheck," Mayor Williams said at the announcement, arguing that broadband and education are how the city lifts them up. The data center is anchored on a fiber network the city and Thundercloud are building to reach every home and business, part of the Huntington Innovation Project that won the $3 million America's Best Communities prize in 2017. Alpha already runs the state's largest data center, in South Charleston, serving governments, health care providers, schools and businesses.

ft-1764016151896-2450.text: QTS is planning a data center campus near Kearneysville on 300 acres split between Jefferson and Berkeley counties in West Virginia's Eastern Panhandle, with the first two buildings planned for the Berkeley County side. The Berkeley County Planning Commission signed off on the concept plan for those two Berkeley parcels in March 2025. The Berkeley land includes a 90-acre parcel for the two buildings, a guard shack, an electrical switching station, a water tank and stormwater ponds, plus a narrow parcel for access from Charles Town Road (Route 115). The third parcel, 191 acres in Jefferson County, is zoned industrial, and as of April 2025 the Jefferson County planning office had not received any plans for it. The F.O. Day Company sold the three parcels to IB10 Martinsburg LLC in July 2024; the land has access to a natural gas pipeline and two high-capacity transmission lines, and Berkeley County would provide water and sewer for the first phase, according to the plan documents. "We are in the initial stages of planning," a QTS representative told the Observer, adding that the company would communicate updates as it works to advance the project. QTS has not given a size in megawatts, an investment figure or a construction date for the site. The next step is a site plan filed with the Jefferson County planning office for the 191-acre parcel, which had not received one as of April 2025.

ft-1773464713880-3329.text: Penzance Management, a Washington and Northern Virginia real estate firm, plans a $4 billion data center campus, the Bedington Campus, on 548 acres it has bought in Falling Waters and Bedington, in Berkeley County, West Virginia. Governor Patrick Morrisey announced it on February 26, 2026 as the first project certified as a "high impact intelligence center" under House Bill 2014, and said he wants data centers called "intelligence centers" from now on. At full build the campus would cover about 1.9 million square feet with up to 600 megawatts of IT capacity, more than 1,000 construction jobs and at least 125 full-time jobs. It will likely connect to the existing grid, no tenant has been named, and the engineering and environmental plans Penzance filed with the state will likely not be made public. "We have already identified a significant opportunity to potentially utilize reclaimed water, which will lower costs for the company, save taxpayer money for the county, and preserve our vital natural resources," said Berkeley County Commission president Eddie Gochenour. ft-1764015083682-7528.text: The National Energy Technology Laboratory is building a 14,000-square-foot Computational Science and Engineering Center, a federal data center for its research supercomputers, on its Morgantown campus in Monongalia County, West Virginia. The lab calls it its largest construction project in more than a decade. The project is under construction and is funded in part by $150 million in Inflation Reduction Act money spread across NETL's three sites. The center will hold a server hall for NETL's computing systems, including current and future generations of its Joule supercomputer, a Wafer-Scale Engine chip system made by Cerebras Systems, and a visualization center. It will consolidate the Morgantown campus's data centers into one building so older, less efficient space can be shut down. Energy Secretary Chris Wright toured the site under construction in June 2025. The campus could also host something much larger. The Department of Energy has listed NETL's Morgantown site among 16 federal sites that could host AI data centers, citing about 50 acres with access to a transmission line and substation, and its nearness to West Virginia University. In July 2025 DOE picked its first four sites, Idaho National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, Paducah and Savannah River, and said it was still evaluating others; NETL was not among them. "You will see data centers built on national lab property," Wright said in Morgantown. Around Morgantown the debate is about state law. House Bill 2014, passed in 2025, created a certified microgrid program that exempts high-impact data centers from county and municipal zoning, noise rules and local building permits. "I think a lot of the counties had realized and noticed the changes that occurred, and took a lot of our local control away," said Monongalia County Commissioner Sean Sikora. The House voted down an amendment from Delegate Evan Hansen, D-Monongalia, that would have required developers to disclose water use, 23-70 in February 2026. Whether a private AI data center comes to the Morgantown campus depends on the Department of Energy, which said it would issue site-specific solicitations and could add more sites later. No solicitation naming Morgantown has been announced.

ft-1108.text: Nscale Global Holdings, a British company backed by Nvidia, Nokia and Dell, bought American Intelligence and Power Corp on March 16, 2026, taking over the Monarch Compute Campus data center project north of Point Pleasant in Mason County, West Virginia, on land that began as Fidelis New Energy's Mountaineer GigaSystem. The campus takes in up to 2,250 acres between the Ohio River, the CSX tracks and Route 62, and Nscale announced a letter of intent the same day to supply Microsoft with 1.35 gigawatts of AI computing power. The first phase, 2 gigawatts, or 2 billion watts, is due for installation across 2026 and 2027, with the campus running in the first half of 2028; full build is planned at 8 to 10 gigawatts. The power comes from onsite gas generators rather than the public grid: 2 gigawatts of fast-response units ordered from Caterpillar, delivered between September 2026 and August 2027, backed by batteries to absorb the swings an AI load makes. A 30-mile, 24-inch gas pipeline from Hope Gas, costing $250 million, will feed the plant, and cooling water will come from the Ohio River. The company says it will capture carbon to offset emissions and that its design uses less water with no effect on municipal supply or residential users. Permit filings describe a 2.16 gigawatt gas plant with 864 reciprocating engines, machines that burn gas on site to make electricity, powering three data centers. The Environmental Integrity Project ranked the plant second in the country for projected greenhouse gas emissions among planned data center gas plants, estimating 1,043 tons of carbon monoxide, 900 tons of volatile organic compounds, 506 tons of nitrogen oxides and 38 tons of fine particulate matter a year. State inspectors have cited the site four times since May 2026, on May 24, May 28, June 4 and June 10, for a broken silt fence, sediment-laden water discharging into the Route 62 culvert, a missing section of erosion control, earthwork done before it was approved, and sediment left in an unnamed tributary. Flooding over the weekend of May 23 and 24 reached about half a dozen Mason County homes, mainly damaging garages, crawlspaces and heating and air conditioning equipment. The company expects to employ more than 2,800 people, and Marshall University and Mountwest Community and Technical College have signed a training and apprenticeship agreement meant to give Mason County residents first call on the jobs. The West Virginia Economic Development Authority approved a $62.5 million forgivable loan for the project in 2023, of which $25 million has been paid out. More than 60 people met in Point Pleasant on March 17, 2026, at a gathering organized by West Virginia Citizen Action, the West Virginia Rivers Coalition and Fair Shake Environmental Legal Services. Morgan King, climate and energy program manager at WV CAG, told them the plant would need five million gallons of water a day, about what the city of Charleston uses, and said House Bill 2014 had stripped the county of power to regulate it. Mike Wooten, who lives near the site at Camp Conley, said he was not against the project outright but wanted "to be protected by the people [who are] supposed to protect me," naming the governor, legislators, the EPA and the permit process. Elaine Matheny, of Point Pleasant, offered to help organize residents and told them to read up on data centers built elsewhere, and King said: "You fight big corporations by building power in communities and by building up with numbers. That comes back to the organizing, getting together, talking with your neighbors."

ft-1109.text: TransGas Development Systems, a New York company, plans the Adams Fork Data Energy Center, a gas-powered data center campus on the former Twisted Gun Golf Course in Wharncliffe, Mingo County, West Virginia. It is one of two identical campuses TransGas wants in the county; the other sits at the Harless Industrial Park near the Mingo-Logan county line. TransGas has tried to build on this ground before: around 2010 it proposed a coal-to-gas plant there that was canceled in 2011, and in 2023 it announced what it called the world's largest ammonia plant on the site, permitted by the state in 2024; the data center is a third proposal for the same land. The Division of Air Quality took public comment at hearings in August and September 2025 and approved air permits for both plants on October 2, 2025, despite dozens of residents speaking against them, saying the facilities "will meet all applicable state and federal air quality rules and regulations." Each power plant would run 117 gas engines and could generate more than 2,400 megawatts, the West Virginia Highlands Conservancy reported; the Ohio River Valley Institute reads the permits as allowing 2,457 megawatts per campus, together using more than 29.4 million megawatt hours a year, nearly as much as the 33 million megawatt hours the entire state consumes. The gas plants would be off grid, built for the two campuses alone and supplying no one else in West Virginia; TransGas has said it wants to eventually expand its data center capacity to 9.8 gigawatts. Ten Mingo County residents sued in federal court in early December 2025, arguing the project needed federal environmental review, because of its effects on streams, mine-drainage channels and habitat used by federally protected species, before construction could continue. On December 23, 2025 U.S. District Judge Robert C. Chambers turned down their request for a temporary halt, ruling they had not yet notified the defendants and had not shown they were likely to win on the merits; their request for a permanent injunction was not addressed, so the state's air permits stand while the case continues.

ft-1782349093239-6541.text: Silicon Foundation's proposed Stokes Data Center at 74 Warwood Avenue in Wheeling, Ohio County, West Virginia, would reuse the 15-acre former Centre Foundry site on the Ohio River, with Stokes Inc. as the construction contractor. Early company posts described a 100 megawatt facility, which drew resident opposition; officials now say it would start at 10 megawatts and grow to no more than 50 megawatts, below the 90 megawatt line where West Virginia's House Bill 2014 takes over regulation. Twelve Warwood residents sued Silicon Foundry Energy LLC in Ohio County Circuit Court in July 2026, seeking an injunction and arguing the site's industrial zoning does not cover a data center. Attorney General J.B. McCuskey intervened to defend House Bill 2014, and the court granted the state's motion. "We don't want this data center, so we're just here to remind you of this," resident Natalie Miniard told City Council. Wheeling City Council was set to vote on September 15, 2026, on a memorandum of understanding in which Silicon Foundry Energy agrees not to build a high-impact data center, as the city plans a tax increment financing district on the property. The residents' attorney, J. Anthony Edmond Jr., urged a moratorium instead and criticized the short notice before the vote; city officials say they lack legal standing to pass one. No result of the September 15 vote has been published.

ft-1782186948504-7033.text: Prometheus Hyperscale wants a data center campus on 506 acres of ranchland 12 miles east of Evanston, in Uinta County, Wyoming, on the south side of Interstate 80. The ground is a ranch Trenton Thornock's family has worked for six generations, and the campus he wants on it would draw 1.25 gigawatts, more electricity than all the homes in Wyoming use. Thornock founded the company as Wyoming Hyperscale White Box, the name this project still carries, and renamed it Prometheus Hyperscale in September 2024 when he announced four more sites in Arizona and Colorado. The company puts the initial 1.25 gigawatts on a development path to 5 gigawatts. On May 26, 2026, Thornock took the plan to a packed room at the Roundhouse in Evanston. He argued the industry is wasteful and his design is not, saying of other operators that "they're using way too much power for the amount of compute that they're getting out and they're using way too much water for cooling." gemini-meta-lebanon.text: Meta is building a 13-building, 1,500-acre data center campus in Lebanon, Boone County, Indiana, inside the state's LEAP Research and Innovation District, confirmed at a groundbreaking on February 11, 2026 as a project of more than $10 billion designed to deliver 1 GW of power once operational. On September 14, 2026, a 33-year-old construction worker from Oklahoma was killed after being struck by a pickup truck on the site near County Road 400 West and State Road 32. The Boone County Board of Commissioners adopted a one-year moratorium on new data centers in unincorporated parts of the county on June 15, 2026, running to June 15, 2027, but it does not touch the Meta campus, because the state, not the county, made the land available: the Indiana Economic Development Corporation bought it for LEAP, had Lebanon annex and rezone it, then resold it to Meta. "We're dealing with, and subjected to, 24-hour construction noise, stadium lights and constant traffic," Leslie Hine, who lives half a mile from the site, told county commissioners in June, adding that her father-in-law's fields had flooded because of the construction. Meta says about 4,000 construction workers will be on site at peak and about 300 people will work there once it opens, with the first phase online in late 2027 or early 2028. The Lebanon City Council approved tax abatements for the first phase in 2024; Mayor Matt Gentry said that phase would generate more than $80 million in property taxes and more than $33 million in community impact payments over 15 years. Water is the biggest fight: Citizens Energy Group has a $550 million deal to pipe up to 25 million gallons a day from Indianapolis to Lebanon Utilities by 2031 for the LEAP district's two tenants, Meta and an Eli Lilly plant, and Meta itself asked in 2024 for up to three million gallons of water a day for the data center. After Indianapolis and Zionsville residents objected to LEAP's wastewater draining into Eagle Creek Reservoir, Lebanon Utilities said in May 2026 the discharge would not go inside Eagle Creek Park, and Zionsville's town council voted 7-0 on September 21, 2026 to ask Lebanon to drop plans for discharge into the town's own waterways; the final call rests with the Indiana Department of Environmental Management. Construction is going ahead; the open questions are where Lebanon Utilities will discharge LEAP's treated wastewater, which needs a state permit, and whether Boone County lifts its data center moratorium when it expires on June 15, 2027.

gemini-meta-social-circle.text: Meta runs a data center campus in Walton County near Social Circle, Georgia, the west campus of its larger Stanton Springs development, which spans Walton, Newton and Morgan counties. The east campus of that development, about 7 kilometers away in Newton County, is at the center of a lawsuit four Mansfield families filed in Gwinnett County court at the end of August 2026, accusing Meta of fouling their well water. The families say tree clearing, blasting and excavation for the campus disturbed the aquifer both campuses draw from. Meta's Georgia project was the state's first major data center, announced in 2018, when Governor Brian Kemp celebrated it with Facebook-branded shovels at the state Capitol. Meta said a study it commissioned found it "unlikely" that its data centers affected groundwater in the area, and the company has said it will keep defending itself against what it calls "baseless lawsuits." The lawsuit is moving through Gwinnett County court; no hearing date has been made public.

gemini-meta-davenport.text: Meta's planned data center on farmland in north Davenport, Scott County, Iowa, still had not broken ground by 2026, and neither Meta nor the city has said whether the project will go ahead. "Meta (Vemerald) purchased the land but has not announced any plans to build yet," Davenport's chief communications officer Denise Hnytka told the Quad-City Times; the company had said it would break ground in late 2025 if it went ahead. Meta's subsidiary Vemerald LLC proposed two data halls and other buildings totaling 715,000 square feet on 328 acres near Hillandale Road and Enterprise Way, after paying $21 million for 355 acres across 10 parcels in 2024 and 2025. The Davenport City Council backed a property tax exemption in May 2024, and the Iowa Economic Development Authority board then granted a High Quality Jobs award for an $800 million investment and 35 jobs paying at least $28.76 an hour. The exemption covers 60 percent of property taxes for 20 years, which the Quad-City Times put at about $161 million; the city estimated the finished campus would still pay about $107 million in property taxes over 20 years to the city, Scott County and Davenport schools. How much water and power the campus would use is not public. Iowa American Water declined to answer questions, citing a nondisclosure agreement with Meta, and MidAmerican Energy declined to give the expected electricity demand, citing state rules protecting customer information. MidAmerican said it does not expect the data center, if built, to increase customer rates, because large-load customers must cover the cost of the infrastructure that serves them. The city and state incentives are already in place, so whether the campus gets built is now Meta's decision; Meta did not respond to the Quad-City Times' request for comment.

gemini-meta-etna.text: Etna is a township in Licking County, Ohio, on the edge of the New Albany corridor, and the Meta data center campus recorded there is powered by a gas plant that will never touch the public grid. The Ohio Power Siting Board approved the Socrates South Power Generation Project on June 9, 2025 to supply the Meta campus exclusively. Will-Power OH, a subsidiary of the Williams Companies, is building it at an expected $1.6 billion, starting at 200 megawatts and later expanding to 400, with commercial operation targeted for the third quarter of 2026. Meta's local affiliate, a company called Sidecat, owns a 740 acre industrial campus in the New Albany Business Park. Licking County already has more data centers than any other county in Ohio, with Meta, Google, Amazon, QTS and Edged Energy at New Albany, three Microsoft sites under construction and eight more announced by Cologix at Johnstown at a cost of $7 billion. Intel's $20 billion semiconductor plant sits next to the cluster and is due to operate in 2028. The county has not produced the organised opposition seen in some smaller Ohio counties, though residents still raise electricity rates and the loss of farmland. Since July 23, 2025 AEP Ohio's data center tariff has required any facility above 25 megawatts to pay for at least 85 percent of the capacity it subscribes to each month, and school districts that abate these buildings give up property tax revenue for 30 years. Nearby townships have gone further: Sunbury passed a moratorium on April 16, 2026, Jackson Township followed on May 29, 2026, and St Albans Township banned new data centers outright from March 10, 2026.

gemini-openai-stargate-do-a-ana.text: Project Jupiter, the OpenAI Stargate data center campus in Santa Teresa, is being built on a 1,400-acre site in Doña Ana County, New Mexico, near the Texas border. It is under construction for Oracle and OpenAI to train artificial intelligence models, built by BorderPlex Digital Assets and STACK Infrastructure, and it has dominated public comment at county commission meetings for 11 months. The project began as a "digital infrastructure campus" that Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham announced in February 2025 with BorderPlex Digital Assets, promising 1,000 new jobs. Epoch AI puts its planned capacity at 2.2 gigawatts, with completion targeted for the end of 2028. The county's money is at the center of the fight. On September 19, 2025, after a closed meeting, Doña Ana County commissioners voted to pledge $165 billion worth of industrial revenue bonds for the project, and the county issued a grading permit on October 2. Under the bond contract the county holds title to the project properties and leases them to the developer. Residents and groups have gone to court over how that was done: the Empowerment Congress of Doña Ana County sued over the tax incentives in October 2025, and the Foundation for Open Government sued in June 2026 over records the county withheld. In July 2026 the state Department of Justice opened an investigation into fraudulent public comments submitted in support of the project, and the commission voted unanimously to end County Manager Scott Andrews' contract. Power and water are the other fights. The developers now plan to run the campus on natural gas fuel cells by Bloom Energy rather than gas turbines, a change announced in April 2026 that would still emit about 10.1 million tons of greenhouse gases a year. State Land Commissioner Stephanie Garcia Richard denied right-of-way permits for part of the gas pipeline across state trust land in March and again in July. gemini-openai-stargate-port-washington.text: Port Washington is a Lake Michigan city of about 12,000 people in Ozaukee County, Wisconsin, north of Milwaukee. In October 2025, Vantage Data Centers announced a $15 billion data center campus there as part of the Stargate initiative, working with OpenAI and Oracle. Epoch AI put the planned capacity at 1.3 gigawatts, with construction beginning in early 2026 and completion targeted for the end of 2028. At the April 2026 spring election, Port Washington voters passed a referendum by roughly a two-to-one margin, making it the first city in the country to require voter approval before local officials can grant a data center developer more than $10 million in tax incentives. The vote does not stop the Vantage campus itself, which was already under construction; it only limits future incentive deals. The measure was organized by a local group called Great Lakes Neighbors United, formed after Vantage's initial announcement. Mayor Ted Neitzke, who had approved the project, faced an unsuccessful recall effort afterward. The Metropolitan Milwaukee Association of Commerce sued to block the referendum, arguing it violates state law, a challenge that could freeze the measure while it plays out in court. Vantage and its partners say 70 percent of the project's power will come from zero-emission sources and that the developers, not ratepayers, are funding the electrical upgrades the campus needs; Oracle has promised no increase to local energy bills. Residents have raised concerns locally over the strain the campus will put on the regional grid.

gemini-microsoft-south-central.text: Mills County, Texas, is a rural county of a few thousand people whose seat is Goldthwaite, and it is listed as the site of a 450 megawatt Microsoft data center. No local news report, permit record or hearing has been found that mentions such a project, and the one source cited for it carries no usable content. Texas froze new data center connections to the state grid on August 3, 2026, after an audit ordered by Governor Greg Abbott, covering roughly 1,800 projects in the queue, though a project that generates its own power on site can bypass it.

gemini-microsoft-licking-county.text: Microsoft's data centers in Licking County, Ohio, are finally going up: site work began in February 2026 at Hebron, about 30 miles east of Columbus, with AMES Construction grading the ground from February to November and the bulk of the work between March and August. A second site at Heath is on the same schedule, and a third at New Albany is due to be finished late in 2027. Work at Heath and Hebron resumed after about a year's pause. For the neighbours at Hebron, Microsoft's own construction updates set the terms: work Monday to Friday from 7am to 7pm and on Saturdays and some Sundays from 8am to 5pm, tree removal along the perimeter in March, and a permanent construction road on the east side of the property. The company says truck traffic through the summer and into the fall will vary with the work, and that vertical construction will follow the site preparation at the end of the year. What the county gives up for the three sites is the argument a campaigning group has made. It puts a 15 year, 100 percent sales tax exemption on them at $72.5 million, about $1 million of foregone tax revenue for every job, and says Microsoft turned down real estate tax abatements at Heath and Hebron, leaving that revenue with the Lakewood Local School District. The group says the three sites carry a combined $1 billion commitment on more than 700 acres, and that Microsoft uses waterless cooling at its existing campuses. AEP Ohio's data center tariff, in force since July 2025, makes any facility above 25 megawatts pay for at least 85 percent of the capacity it subscribes each month.

gemini-microsoft-west-des-moines-iv.text: Microsoft has built five data center campuses in West Des Moines, Iowa, since opening the first in 2012, and the city council approved an agreement for a sixth campus last year. The company has invested an estimated $5 billion to $6 billion in its West Des Moines data centers, Wisconsin Public Radio reported. The campuses used 68.5 million gallons of water from West Des Moines Water Works in 2024, about 2.62 percent of the utility's total, and Microsoft was its biggest customer that year, said general manager Christina Murphy. An agreement lets Microsoft use up to 5 million gallons a day, and the company has funded about $25 million in water system upgrades, including a 2 million gallon tank finished in 2023 that serves both the data centers and residents. Mayor Russ Trimble said Microsoft's arrival has transformed the city, which is now third in Iowa for property valuation, behind only Des Moines and Cedar Rapids. He said the region cannot support more data centers until its power infrastructure catches up with demand. The city has spent more than $200 million on public infrastructure for the campuses, economic development director Ryan Moffatt said. Neighbors are not all pleased. David Roach, a 62 year old network engineer who lives across from the site of the newest campus, said of the light at night: "I like to refer to it as they're really polluting my dark." Margaret VanGinkel, whose farm faces an existing campus, said: "That's the thing. They just keep building all the time." Construction on the sixth West Des Moines campus is set to start in 2026, Moffatt said.

gemini-microsoft-leesburg.text: Microsoft's Leesburg data center is one of the buildings that make Loudoun County, Virginia the densest concentration of them in the world, operating at about 180 megawatts. As of March 1, 2026 the county counted about 233 data center buildings built or under construction, roughly 56.5 million square feet, and the taxes they pay came to $1.2 billion in the 2026 financial year, 39 percent of the whole county budget. Dominion has proposed raising residential electricity rates 14 percent in 2026, citing data center growth and AI demand. What people who live among them complain about is noise and diesel fumes. After a power failure on July 16, 2026 set backup generators running across the county, one homeowner said: "I always know when they're running their diesel generators because it irritates my throat and my lungs, and I've even woken up at night." County chair Phyllis Randall was due to meet residents living near the data centers that week. In Sterling, Greg Pirio measured 60 decibels at his property line while a Vantage Data Centers site ran its generators for about 24 hours after that same failure, and left home: "I had to go to my daughter's house because it was hurting my lungs." Virginia DEQ director Michael Rolband said the agency had no power to stop emergency generators running under the rules as they stand, and Sterling district supervisor Koran Saines said he would put an initiative to the board directing county staff to find a way to regulate them. The county's zoning ordinance caps sound at 55 dBA at the property line of a residential property, and every data center must file a noise assessment before building and another within a year of occupancy. The rules say nothing about tonal or low frequency noise, and the language to cover it is not expected until amendments to the comprehensive plan and zoning ordinance in spring or summer 2027. Most of the backup diesels in the county are still Tier 2 units, some retrofitted with filters, and from July 1, 2026 Virginia requires Tier 4 equivalent emissions standards only for new or modified generators at data center sites.

gemini-microsoft-chicago.text: The data center fight in Logan County, in central Illinois, is over Hut 8's proposed 500 megawatt, $5 billion campus on 250 acres of farmland in Laenna Township near the village of Latham. About 250 people turned out at a county meeting to raise noise, water supply and the loss of farmland, and the zoning board held its public hearing on January 8, 2026. On May 19 the county board voted 6 to 4 for a moratorium, but the state's attorney ruled it invalid, and Hut 8 then asked Latham to annex the site so that the village, not the county, would decide. "We believe the proposed structure would more directly connect the project's economic benefits with the village located closest to the project," said Gregory Irwin, a Hut 8 senior vice president. Latham's village president, Theodore Allen, who had opposed the project earlier in the year, said: "If we can improve our little town, I'm all for it. Our community could use a lot of upgrades." "I think it is vile. They're just as sleazy as we thought they were," said Rachel Strechman, who founded Logan County Indivisible, and Amanda Maxheimer of Sustain Logan County Communities said: "It just seems like a lot of risk for the village of Latham." The village board set a public hearing and vote on the annexation, rezoning and a community benefit agreement for August 3.

gemini-microsoft-kilby.text: Microsoft plans a data center campus of about 2 gigawatts outside Pecos, in Reeves County, Texas, powered by a dedicated natural gas plant, Project Kilby, that Chevron will build next to it. Chevron's subsidiary Energy Forge One signed a 20-year agreement on June 22, 2026 to supply power from Kilby, which is expected to deliver about 2.67 gigawatts. The site spans more than 2,000 acres near Pecos, Quartz reported, citing The Wall Street Journal. Microsoft calls it a multibillion-dollar investment over five to seven years, with more than 6,000 construction jobs at peak and hundreds of permanent ones. The power plant will not connect to the electric grid; it will run on gas from Chevron's own Permian Basin wells, using large turbines from GE Vernova and Solar Turbines. Chevron says the plant will use non-potable, salty groundwater instead of fresh water, with controls to cut emissions and noise. Microsoft says its data centers will use closed-loop cooling that needs water only once, not continuously. Chevron's subsidiary applied to the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality for air permits, filed October 17, 2025, covering carbon monoxide, greenhouse gases, nitrogen oxides and other pollutants. The agency's staff made a preliminary finding that the emissions will not break state or federal air rules and drafted a permit. The commission held a public meeting on the permits in Pecos on June 10, 2026, and people affected by the plant's emissions can ask for a contested hearing, similar to a civil trial, before final approval. Energy Forge One applied for a state school tax break for large projects, and the Pecos-Barstow-Toyah school board approved it in February 2026; the state covers the cost, not the district. State documents show the break could save the company more than $227 million over 10 years, Wired reported. Wired's analysis found the plant could emit more than 11.5 million tons of carbon dioxide equivalent a year. Greg LeRoy of Good Jobs First noted that Microsoft's pledge to pay its "full and fair share of local property taxes" does not mention tax abatements. Reeves County Judge Leo Hung, the county's top elected official, welcomed it: "We are excited to welcome Microsoft to Pecos." Chevron puts the project's benefit at more than $10 billion in state and local tax revenue and almost 2,000 jobs. The next decisions are the state air permits and Chevron's final investment decision, expected by the end of 2026.

microsoft-microsoft-alviso-milpitas.text: Microsoft broke ground in June 2026 on its Alviso data center campus at 1657 Alviso-Milpitas Road in northern San Jose, Santa Clara County, California, its first self-owned and operated data center in the city. The first phase will offer 48 megawatts of computing capacity, according to the contractor building it. In a filing with the California Energy Commission, Microsoft listed the campus's maximum electrical load at up to 99 megawatts of power, with an estimated everyday load of 77 megawatts. The campus is due for completion in 2028, with an estimated 600 construction jobs and 100 jobs once it is running. Microsoft bought the 64-acre site along Highway 237, next to the Los Esteros Energy Center, in 2017 for $73.2 million. The plan calls for two single-story buildings of about 397,000 square feet in total and a new electrical substation; 79 trees are to be removed and 273 planted. The San Jose Planning Commission approved the project in April 2025, after an earlier version filed in 2019 had stalled; the site had been used as a homeless encampment, and people living there were reportedly told to leave in April 2025. "You need this backbone of infrastructure to power the modern world," Mayor Matt Mahan said at the groundbreaking. Many San Jose residents disagree. At an April 2026 council session on the city's push to attract a dozen large power users, Ellina Yin of the Dreaming Collaborative said, "There has been an incredible push from the city to bring data centers for AI, however there has been little to no meaningful community engagement on what that means for San Jose residents living within and around these data centers." Alviso is also the site of a larger proposal: Prologis is in talks with the city for a 159-acre site for more than 1 million square feet of data center space across four buildings. "A lot of this is being pretty much pushed on the community," said Marcos Espinoza, president of Alviso in Action, who said residents worry about noise, air pollution and nearby burrowing owl habitat. San Jose city staff are drafting data center review standards covering air quality, noise, greenhouse gas emissions and public outreach, which are expected to go to the City Council in December 2026. Those rules would apply to future projects; the Microsoft campus already has its approvals and is under construction, with contractor HITT Contracting putting the build at about 18 months.

gemini-google-cerrillos.text: Google's plan for a second data center in Cerrillos, in southwest Santiago, Chile, was stopped in court over water, and the company has said it will start again without groundwater. In December 2020 fourteen residents of the Cerrillos commune and the municipality itself challenged the project's environmental permit before Chile's Second Environmental Court. The project would have drawn 228 litres a second from three wells in the Santiago central aquifer, more than 7.2 billion litres a year, which one account compared to 40,000 households. By the end only one resident was still in the case, and on September 26, 2024 the court partly upheld the claim, ordering the Environmental Assessment Service to redo the evaluation and take account of climate change. The tribunal said the original assessment had not properly weighed the effect on water or applied precaution about the aquifer, citing doubts from the General Directorate of Water and Chile's mega drought. Google has since said it will switch to air cooled condensers and use no groundwater, and that a new process will start from scratch. Chile has been in drought since 2010, and Tania Rodríguez of the Mosacat movement said of Santiago: "It's turned into extractivism. We end up being everybody's backyard." Microsoft won environmental approval for a Santiago project in early 2023 and Amazon in early 2024.

gemini-google-changhua.text: Google's data center in the Changhua Coastal Industrial Park, in Changhua County on Taiwan's west coast, has been running since 2013 on a 15-hectare site, and Google says it has invested more than $1.6 billion in Taiwan since arriving. Google picked the Changhua site in September 2011, when the project was billed as a US$100 million-plus data center and one of the most efficient in Asia. The facility cost $600 million by the time it opened in 2013, DCD reported, and Google later added a second Taiwanese data center in Tainan. In 2020 Taiwanese papers reported that Google was also behind a land purchase in a Yunlin County industrial park for a third, though the company did not confirm it. Water is the local question. In 2016 a Taiwanese newspaper reported that Google's expansion in Changhua had stalled for lack of water, which the economic ministry rejected. The Water Resources Agency said that when Google came to build in 2013, officials and Taiwan Water found a way to meet its demand for 6,000 cubic meters of water a day, and that the data center was then using only 700. Taiwan Water said it was spending NT$1.64 billion on projects to raise Changhua's water supply, including a purification plant on the Fuma Canal. A March 2026 Taipei Times commentary said Google had since shifted its Changhua cooling to non-potable industrial water and begun investing in local water stewardship programs. The pressure on Taiwan's water and power has grown with the AI build-out: during the 2021 drought about 74,000 hectares of rice paddy went dry as water was rerouted to industry, the commentary noted. Google signed Taiwan's first corporate geothermal power purchase agreement, with Baseload Capital, and backed a citizen solar plant in Changhua's Beidou Township that began operating in 2024. The commentary's author, Romain Blachier, called for binding water-efficiency rules for Taiwan's data centers and a public record of what each new facility draws from the grid and aquifers.

gemini-google-eemshaven.text: Google's Eemshaven data center sits in the seaport of Eemshaven, in the municipality of Het Hogeland in the province of Groningen in the Netherlands, where the transatlantic fiber cable linking the United States and Europe comes ashore. Google announced it at a ceremony to break ground led by Economic Affairs Minister Henk Kamp, saying it would spend about 600 million euros over four years and employ 150 permanent workers. The data center opened at the end of 2016, and in March 2018 Google said it would put another 500 million euros into expanding it, bringing its investment in the region to almost 1.5 billion euros. In June 2019 Google announced a further Eemshaven expansion on top of the 2018 one, alongside a new site at Agriport in Hollands Kroon, with a combined investment of more than 1 billion euros and 350 people to work at Eemshaven once it was running. The site is part of Google's europe-west4 cloud region, and Google invested 45 million euros in a water treatment plant that takes water from the Eemskanaal and supplies it to companies in the port for cooling, including its own data center, DCD reported. Water and jobs have been the local questions. When Groningen province and Het Hogeland briefed councillors in 2021 on expanding the Eemshaven for new businesses, some parties said data centers were not their first choice because they create few jobs, and raised concerns about drinking water being used to cool servers. Google's Petran van Hugten told them the company was looking at using wastewater from sewage treatment plants as cooling water, and said Google aimed to stay and grow in the Eemshaven. The latest complaint is light: in August 2026 Google switched the data center's outdoor lighting on and off at night to measure how much light the site gives off, partly in response to residents who said the lights of large companies in the port bothered them. Google said the measurement was coordinated with the Omgevingsdienst Groningen, the environmental agency that supervises light emissions for the municipalities, and no date has been set for publishing the results. The port is filling up around Google: QTS is building a second hyperscale data center, EEMSDC2, on Kwelderweg as part of a 1.4 billion euro expansion that doubles its Eemshaven capacity and adds 130 jobs. Google also opened a data center in Winschoten, elsewhere in Groningen province, in November 2025 to add capacity to the same cloud region, and broke ground on another at Westpoort in the municipality of Groningen in April 2024. What comes next at Eemshaven is the result of the light measurement, which the Omgevingsdienst Groningen oversees for the municipalities. Room for more data centers in the port depends on the expansion that Groningen province and Het Hogeland intend, and on how the Provinciale Staten and the Het Hogeland council weigh it.

Google said the measurement was coordinated with the Omgevingsdienst Groningen, the environmental agency that supervises light emissions for the municipalities, and no date has been set for publishing the results.

The port is filling up around Google: QTS is building a second hyperscale data center, EEMSDC2, on Kwelderweg as part of a 1.4 billion euro expansion that doubles its Eemshaven capacity and adds 130 jobs.

Google also opened a data center in Winschoten, elsewhere in Groningen province, in November 2025 to add capacity to the same cloud region, and broke ground on another at Westpoort in the municipality of Groningen in April 2024.
What comes next at Eemshaven is the result of the light measurement, which the Omgevingsdienst Groningen oversees for the municipalities.
Room for more data centers in the port depends on the expansion that Groningen province and Het Hogeland intend, and on how the Provinciale Staten and the Het Hogeland council weigh it.

gemini-google-fredericia.text: Google's Fredericia data center sits at Taulov, in Fredericia Municipality, Denmark, and Google opened it in November 2020 after more than two years of construction and a cost of 4.5 billion Danish kroner. Google bought the 73.2-hectare plot in June 2017 and announced the build in November 2018, saying it expected 150 to 200 staff when it opened. Google paired the opening with five new solar parks around Denmark, which it said more than offset the data center's power use. "Data centers are frontrunners when it comes to innovation - this is where we develop the most energy-efficient solutions and new, green technology", said Malou Aamund, then Google's Danish director. A Copenhagen Economics report for the opening credited the project with 2,600 jobs from 2018 to 2020 on top of construction staff, with about 150 people to be employed at the site. The question now is a second phase. Fredericia Municipality has granted an environmental approval and a section 25 permit for an expansion with three new data center halls, internal roads, parking and more utility buildings, with no objections from residents or authorities during the hearing period, Electronic Supply reported in May 2026, citing Fredericia Dagblad. At that point Google said no final decision had been taken, and its Nordic data center policy lead, Niels Martin Andersen, called the site work under way a natural part of preparing the area. On June 30, 2026 Fredericia Dagblad reported that Google would double the data center in Prinsessens Kvarter, with up to 1,200 workers building the expansion, 100 more permanent jobs, and the new servers assured power from the grid. Water is the local issue: the expansion would raise demand for cooling water, and the municipality is working to set up a company to produce technical water as an alternative to drinking water, with Google asking for its timetable. The municipality is also discussing a greenhouse project that would run on the data center's waste heat, possibly at Tuevej, according to Fredericia Dagblad's reporting. The next decisions sit with Fredericia Municipality, on the technical water company and the heat project, and with Google, on the pace of construction.

gemini-google-ghlin.text: Google's data center campus at Saint-Ghislain, in the province of Hainaut in Wallonia, Belgium, was the company's first data center in Europe, and Google has built five data centers and a solar plant on the 90-hectare site since 2009, DCD reported in 2023. Google does much of its business in Belgium through a company called Crystal Computing, which files the permits for the site at Baudour, a section of Saint-Ghislain next to Mons and Quaregnon. The campus keeps growing: in November 2024, with a sixth building barely started, a planning permit was filed for a seventh on a plot along the rue des Roseaux, filling the last empty area of land Google owns there. The application covers a hall for servers, transformers, backup generators and batteries, air coolers and cooling towers, an electrical substation, a water tank, diesel tanks of more than 250 cubic meters and a new storm basin. In October 2025 Google announced a further 5 billion euros for 2026 and 2027 to expand the campus and add 300 full-time jobs, along with new carbon-free energy agreements. "This development makes us a dynamic innovative ecosystem, creating opportunities for other businesses too", said Saint-Ghislain Mayor Florence Monier. Neighbors are less sure. Anne More, 68, lives 200 meters from the data center across the rue des Roseaux and told the Belgian magazine Médor in summer 2026 that the extension being built causes noise, and that she bought a headset so she would not hear it. "On ne sait rien. Google construit, agrandit, et on a à peine été consulté", she said. Médor reported that Google's growth in Wallonia raises questions about pressure on the power grid, a lack of transparency and unclear economic benefits. In the 2024 public inquiry, neighboring Quaregnon's mayor Damien Jenart said the town would not oppose the extension but regretted that it receives no tax revenue from Crystal Computing, while Saint-Ghislain declined to comment so as not to influence its residents. Google is spreading across Hainaut and beyond: it has filed for a three-building campus at the Ecopôle park in Farciennes and bought a 36-hectare site in Ecaussinnes, near La Louvière. Each new building needs a single class 1 permit, which goes to a public inquiry in Saint-Ghislain and the neighboring municipalities; for Quaregnon, the opinion it gives is only symbolic.

gemini-google-hamina.text: Google converted a former paper mill in Hamina, in Finland's Kymenlaakso region, into a data center in 2009, and the site has used seawater to cool its servers for 15 years. On September 9, 2026, Google announced a 13 billion euro investment in digital infrastructure, clean energy and local partnerships across Finland over the next two years, its largest single investment in Europe. Google has not said how much of that money goes to Hamina or how much new capacity the site will get. Hamina is also where Google first piped waste heat off site, into a district heating system run by Haminan Energia that serves homes, schools and public buildings. Google said the heat would cover 80 percent of the network's needs for free. "It feels good to be the hometown of Google in Finland," Hamina mayor Ilari Soosalu said. Google says it has invested 3.5 billion euros in the region to date, and bought 50 acres next to the data center in 2022 for a possible expansion. It has signed a 22-year deal to help extend the life of the Loviisa nuclear plant, is adding wind power, and has contracted a new 94-megawatt battery system to help steady the grid during cold, windless spells. Google says construction in 2027 and 2028 will support more than 37,000 jobs nationwide, and it plans 31 million euros over four years for education and community projects in Hamina, Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala, including AI training for more than 4,400 workers.

gemini-google-henderson.text: Google's data center at 560 West Warm Springs Road in Henderson, in Clark County, Nevada, used 352 million gallons of water in 2024, about what 2,700 average households get through in a year. It is the only data center in Henderson. Southern Nevada banned evaporative cooling for new data centers in 2023, because the water authority cannot recycle what that method consumes; this site opened in 2020 and uses it. The Nevada Independent describes it as one of the state's thirstiest. In June 2026 Henderson's council voted to consider a 180 day moratorium on new data centers, with a final decision set for July 21. Mayor Michelle Romero, who proposed it, explained her reasoning simply: "I'm not an IT expert, I'm not a data center expert." On the night the council rejected the pause and told staff to rewrite the standards instead, so that any future data center would need an individually negotiated development agreement with the city. City attorney Nicholas Vaskov said a moratorium "is temporary to some degree, they are only defensible for up to a certain point, usually that's up to 12 to 18 months." About 20 residents spoke, on energy use, noise and the environment. "... it alarms me how little time we've been given to prepare the proper regulations to protect people," said resident Drake York. What is queuing behind that decision is large. NV Energy has had requests to serve 39 proposed data center projects drawing 16,530 megawatts between them, against a state peak load of 8,241 megawatts. A 300 acre data center campus proposed by Trammell Crow has already been approved in eastern Henderson under a conditional use permit, and Clark County has 43 data centers in all. John Entsminger, who runs the Southern Nevada Water Authority, told lawmakers in March that data centers "can be built without consuming any more water." Tray Abney of the Nevada Data Center Alliance put the industry's view of the argument: "For some reason, data centers are the boogeyman of the day." Google bought the 64 acre site on Warm Springs Road for $19 million through an entity called Jasmine Development LLC. The company said it would invest at least $600 million over 20 years, and later said it planned to invest more than $400 million in Nevada in a single year for its cloud and data center infrastructure. The state gave a $25 million tax abatement, and Google said it would hire 50 employees within five years at an average salary of $65,000. Any future data center in Henderson will now need an individually negotiated development agreement with the city, a route the Sierra Club said "falls far short of the temporary pause residents requested."
