gemini-google-inzai.text: Google's first data center in Japan is in Inzai, a city in Chiba Prefecture east of Tokyo, and Google opened it in March 2023. Google chief executive Sundar Pichai announced the Inzai data center in October 2022 as part of a $730 million investment in Japanese infrastructure running from 2021 through 2024, which also paid for the Topaz subsea cable linking Japan with the west coast of Canada. Before Inzai, Google's cloud regions in Tokyo and Osaka ran in colocation buildings operated by partners such as Equinix, DCD reported. Pichai said the data center would give people in Japan faster, more reliable access to Google's tools and services and support economic activity and jobs. Google cited a skilled local workforce and good digital infrastructure among its reasons for choosing Inzai. Inzai is crowded with data centers. The area around Chiba New Town Chuo and Inzai Makinohara stations on the Hokuso Line is known as the data center Ginza, and the city and Chiba Prefecture told Jiji Press they had not gone out to recruit data centers, pointing instead to firm ground, low flood and earthquake risk and the 40-kilometer distance from central Tokyo. The city's fixed asset tax revenue rose from 7.9 billion yen in fiscal 2015 to 12.6 billion yen in fiscal 2022, according to Jiji. Tokyo Electric Power Company Power Grid estimated that data center demand in the Inzai area would grow to about eight times the whole area's late-2010s load by the early 2030s, and began building a new Chiba Inzai substation in August 2021. The build-out has started to meet resistance: when a six-story, 52.7-meter data center was planned beside Chiba New Town Chuo station, Mayor Kengo Fujishiro wrote that a data center was not the right facility for that spot, and residents of a neighboring apartment building raised concerns about lost sunlight, Nikkei reported. City officials told Nikkei there was little they could do to stop a private project on private land, and about 50 complaints about the view and noise reached the city. Fujishiro has said his top job is to attract industries other than logistics and data centers, and that he wants city rules for development next to residential areas. Those rules would be set by Inzai's city government; Google's own site is not among the disputed projects.

gemini-google-spade.text: Google's Project Spade data center is planned on nearly 2,000 acres south of Interstate 70 near New Florence, a town of fewer than 700 people in Montgomery County, Missouri. The site replaces Hoette Farms and Nursery, and Amazon is already building its own data center, Project Green, across the interstate. The county proposed a 70 percent abatement of personal property tax on Google's equipment in return for $10 million a year for 20 years, $500,000 a year each to High Hill, New Florence, the Gasconade County School District, Wellsville and Middletown and the rest for the county. Residents who asked at a May 6 meeting why there had been no public vote were told by presiding commissioner Ryan Poston: "That's not how this works." "When we first heard about the data center plans, we put a lot of public pressure on county commissioners. They were not paying attention to us," said Tom Westhoff, a co-founder of Preserve Montgomery County. gemini-google-mica.text: Google is building Project Mica, a data center campus of five buildings on nearly 500 acres at the northeast corner of Interstate 435 and U.S. Highway 169 in Kansas City's Northland, in Clay County, Missouri. Google confirmed in February 2026 that it is behind the project, at 12701 N Arrowhead Trafficway. Construction is already underway, Google said. The campus would total 1.56 million square feet and draw nearly 700 megawatts at full build-out, supplied by the adjacent Nashua Power Station and on-site substations, according to Port KC. Port KC authorized up to $10 billion in taxable revenue bonds for the project in July 2025, with a 25-year, 75% property tax exemption and full exemption from local and state sales taxes on construction materials and equipment. In return Google committed $1.5 million upfront to the nearby Smithville School District and $250,000 to the Northland Career Center. Google's Trystine Payfer declined to give a completion date but said its data centers usually take 18 to 24 months to build. The site was first marketed by Diode Ventures in 2023 as the Rocky Branch Creek Technology Park; QTS had been set to develop there before pulling out over power timelines. Power is the main public question. Google says it will cover the full energy costs of powering both of its Kansas City campuses, and it is the first customer to qualify for Evergy's Large Load Power Tariff, approved by the Missouri Public Service Commission in November 2025, which requires long-term contracts, direct cost recovery and a premium rate for users of 75 megawatts or more. Residents across the region have raised the tax breaks and possible effects on utility bills, KCUR reported. Platte County Presiding Commissioner Scott Fricker has criticized Port KC's tax breaks for the separate Project Kestrel campus near KCI: "Port KC has no obligation to tell us anything, and we're just left guessing." Mica is Google's second campus in the Northland; its first, a $1 billion project near Worlds of Fun, broke ground in March 2024 and is still under construction. Meta's Northland campus is operating, and a $100 billion campus called Project Kestrel is proposed near Kansas City International Airport. Kestrel would have six data centers on 379 acres, with a 35-year tax abatement from Port KC. The main public decisions on Mica have been made: Port KC granted the bonds and tax breaks, and the Missouri Public Service Commission approved the Evergy tariff under which it will buy power; the finish date is up to Google.

gemini-google-detroit-edge.text: Isabella County, Michigan, near Mount Pleasant, is recorded as the site of a proposed 1,000 megawatt Google data center under the name Detroit Edge, and nothing published describes such a project there. There is a 1,000 megawatt data center at a Mount Pleasant, but it is in Wisconsin. That one belongs to Microsoft, which announced a $4 billion addition to its campus at Mount Pleasant in Racine County on September 18, 2025. The only data center in Mount Pleasant, Michigan is a small colocation facility run by CMS Internet at 131 South Main Street.

gemini-google-clarksville.text: Google's data center in Clarksville, in Montgomery County, Tennessee, has run since 2019 on the former Hemlock Semiconductor site, and it is now the benchmark for new county rules written because local officials doubt the area could support another one its size. By September 2026 the Clarksville-Montgomery County Regional Planning Commission had approved the county's first data center zoning rules and sent them to the County Commission. Google announced that it had bought the Hemlock site, roughly 1,300 acres, and would invest $600 million and create 70 jobs in what was then its eighth U.S. data center. Governor Bill Lee opened the site on November 6, 2019. Google said it would reuse many of the existing office buildings, and the state said the site would be powered by renewable energy under an arrangement with the Tennessee Valley Authority. Google later signed a deal with TVA for 413 megawatts of solar power from new farms in Tennessee and Alabama to serve the Clarksville site and its Jackson County, Alabama data center. Google says it has invested more than $6 billion in Tennessee since the Montgomery County data center was built. The Google site has largely avoided controversy. "It's got a lot of buffer from the community around there. It's kind of set out of the way, and that one doesn't seem to bother anybody," said Jeff Tyndall, director of the regional planning commission. But when another major technology company recently explored a large facility in the county, officials decided the zoning rules needed work, and the project did not go ahead. "I don't think at this point our community would have the water infrastructure to support another site the size of Google," Tyndall said. County Mayor Wes Golden said he would have concerns about another large data center "because of the amount of resources". The proposed amendment would allow data centers only in industrial districts through a review process, on sites of 10 to 100 acres, with a noise mitigation plan, noise limits at neighboring property lines, disclosure of water sources and use, and confirmation from electric and gas providers that capacity exists. Tyndall said noise appears to be the largest complaint about data centers. The rules would not apply to Google's existing operations, but any future expansion of the Google site would have to meet them if they are adopted. The Montgomery County Commission is expected to vote on the amendment at its next formal meeting.

gemini-google-delhi.text: Google's data center in Delhi, India, is the company's Google Cloud data center region for India's National Capital Region; it opened on July 15, 2021, as Google's second cloud region in the country after Mumbai. The project is operating and was announced in 2020. Google Cloud chief executive Thomas Kurian said at the launch that the company was expanding its local infrastructure in response to customer demand, and that a second data center in India gave customers more choice to store their data inside the country. Each of the two Indian regions has three availability zones, meaning three physically separate locations each with its own power, so a customer's service can keep running if one zone fails. Google said the two regions also sit in different seismic zones so customers can use one to back up the other. HDFC Bank, the online brokerage Groww and Dr. Reddy's Laboratories were among the customers Google quoted welcoming the region.

gemini-google-dublin.text: Google's data center at Grange Castle Business Park in Dublin, Ireland, has operated since 2012, after being announced in 2011, and employs about 150 people. In August 2024 South Dublin County Council refused planning permission for a new Google data centre on the same site, a 72,400 square metre building with data halls and a high voltage compound. The council cited insufficient national grid capacity, a lack of renewable energy commitments, unclear engagement on power purchase agreements, no connection to a district heating network, and inadequate detail on how the plant would affect the power supply once operational in 2027. The decision issued on September 2, 2024 also took issue with the design in relation to its surroundings, and Google had four weeks to appeal. Google had sought ten year permission, and told the council that without the project meeting customer demand for its cloud services would become difficult. Google appealed on September 18, 2024, the last day allowed; the expansion is the third phase of its Grange Castle campus and would bring 800 construction jobs and 50 permanent ones, RTÉ reported. "We have filed an appeal to the recent decision by South Dublin County Council to reject the expansion of our existing data centre in Ireland," a Google Ireland spokeswoman said. Councillor Madeleine Johansson said councillors had previously voted to ban further data centre development in the area, but the government overturned that decision. Teachta Dala Gino Kenny said data centres are expected to use 27 percent of Ireland's electricity by 2028. Behind the refusal is a national power problem. Ireland had halted new data centre grid connections since 2021, after a surge in electricity demand from the sector. Data centres now take almost a quarter of Ireland's electricity, more than all urban households put together, against about 5 percent a decade ago. On December 12, 2025 the Commission for Regulation of Utilities ended the ban. A new data centre must now install generation or battery storage on site able to meet its full electricity demand and give power back to the grid when needed, and at least 80 percent of each facility's annual electricity must come from new renewable projects, with annual reports on renewable use and carbon emissions. The government planned legislation to let data centres generate power independently of the grid, which at present only the grid operator may transmit. Industry groups had argued through the freeze that Ireland was missing out on global capital during a building boom. The decision on Google's expansion now rests with the national planning appeals board, An Bord Pleanála, since renamed An Coimisiún Pleanála, which lists Google Ireland as the first-party appellant in case 320852.

gemini-google-frankfurt.text: Google's Frankfurt-area data center stands on Marie-Curie-Strasse in the Wolfgang technology park of Hanau, a city in the Main-Kinzig district of Hesse, Germany, and it was the first cloud data center Google owned in Germany when it opened in October 2023. The four-story building holds about 10,000 square meters of computing space and serves Google's Frankfurt cloud region, which is about 20 kilometers from the DE-CIX internet exchange. The developer NDC-Garbe built the first building and sold it to Google, which in 2021 bought the whole 20,000-square-meter plot, leaving room for two more data centers of the same size, according to the city of Hanau. The site replaced a plutonium bunker, a leftover of the industry that once gave Hanau the nickname "Atomdorf". Mayor Claus Kaminsky argued at the 2021 handover that if Hanau turned such projects away, neighboring towns would build them anyway and Hanau would feel the effects without any say or share of the benefits. Google said at the opening that at least 80 percent of the site's energy would be carbon-free, that air-based cooling would keep water use as low as possible, and that it was studying whether its waste heat could supply neighboring buildings in the Wolfgang industrial park. Now the site is growing. In November 2025 Google said it would invest 5.5 billion euros in cloud and AI infrastructure in Germany, mainly in a new data center in Dietzenbach, in Offenbach district, and in expanding Hanau. Google broke ground on the Hanau expansion on April 28, 2026, with the Hesse state government saying the site would create at least 100 direct jobs and that Google was working with 44 German suppliers, 16 of them from Hesse. "Hessen ist das Herz des europäischen Datenverkehrs und bildet das Rückgrat der digitalen Wirtschaft in Europa", said Minister-President Boris Rhein at the groundbreaking. Google also bought land years ago in Erlensee, also in Main-Kinzig, and in Babenhausen, and has not said whether it will build there, hessenschau reported. The Hesse state government backs the build-out through its regional data center strategy, Digital Minister Kristina Sinemus said. Hanau's city hall has welcomed the site, with the local paper noting the business tax income it expects. Construction of the expansion is now under way on the Wolfgang plot; the open questions are whether Google fills the rest of it and whether the waste heat plan for neighboring buildings goes ahead.

Jens Gröger of the Öko-Institut argues that operators should have to publish absolute figures for both water and electricity so that councils can decide with the numbers in front of them. gemini-google-jakarta.text: Google opened its Jakarta cloud region, its Google Cloud data center presence in Indonesia's capital, on June 24, 2020, with three zones. Google says it was the first major cloud provider to launch a cloud region in Indonesia. In May 2025 Google said it was still expanding the region's computing capacity to meet demand, without saying by how much. Indonesian customers had used Google's cloud regions in Singapore and Sydney before Jakarta opened. XL Axiata's chief information and digital officer, Yessie Yosetya, said at the launch that having the infrastructure at home would let the telecom company meet data compliance rules and manage its latency needs. Google says the region added the equivalent of 55 billion dollars in economic value to Indonesia over its first five years and expects to add about 88 billion dollars more over the next five. Demand for data centers in Indonesia is growing fast; nearly 200 facilities were operating across the country by March 2026, according to IDNFinancials. Indonesia's Ministry of Investment says it is offering special regulatory treatment and incentives to attract more investment, modeled on the Nongsa Digital Park special economic zone in Batam.

gemini-google-koto-ku.text: Google's data center capacity in Tokyo, Japan, runs through its asia-northeast1 cloud computing region, which opened November 8, 2016, but Google has not said which Tokyo ward holds its servers, so there is no confirmation that any of its buildings sit in Koto City. DCD reported that Google's Tokyo and Osaka cloud regions are hosted in colocation buildings, meaning buildings built and owned by another company, such as those run by Equinix, not by Google itself. Koto City has tightened its rules for large data centers since April 2025, requiring builders to post signs 120 days before construction instead of 90 and to show where outdoor air conditioning units will go. On February 1, 2026 the ward added a stronger guideline covering any building taller than 10 meters and larger than 3,000 square meters that is mostly data center, requiring advance consultation with the ward, a residents' briefing within 15 days of posting a sign, and disclosure of waste heat, noise, vibration, fuel storage and security plans. The rule's first test is a five-story, 51-meter data center planned by Singapore-based Empyrion Digital in Sengoku 3-chome, about 500 meters from the ward office, where residents have raised concerns about heat, noise and roughly 1.2 million liters of heavy fuel oil planned for underground storage in a flood-prone area. Ward Mayor Tomoka Okubo has said Japan's Building Standards Act does not define data centers and no law regulates where they can be built, so the ward's only tools are guidance and required briefings, not the power to block a project. Whether Google's own Tokyo servers would ever fall under those rules depends on Google and its colocation partners, which have not said where the servers are located.

gemini-google-lenoir.text: Google's data center at 708 Lynhaven Drive in Lenoir, Caldwell County, North Carolina, has operated since 2007, when Governor Mike Easley promised 210 jobs for people in and around the town. State records show Google withdrew in December 2008 from the Job Development Investment Grant those jobs were tied to, and many residents say the jobs never came. "That seems really unfair," said Brittany Parsons, who has lived in Lenoir all her life. "If I'm a poor business and they're a trillion-dollar business, why won't they uplift me?" asked Duke Dula, who has cut hair in the town for 22 years. Google paid about $5.2 million in property tax in 2025, nearly 10 percent of Caldwell County's total property tax collections, in a county the state ranks among its most economically distressed. On October 22, 2024 the Caldwell County Board of Commissioners and Lenoir City Council approved incentive grants of 50 percent of real property taxes and 85 percent of personal property taxes over 20 years for about 60 acres of expansion land, and Google agreed to put $6.8 million into the city's water system to supply it. Under a 2024 confidentiality agreement with the county and city, Google's energy use, water and sewer use and its exact employee count are kept secret, though media reports have put the headcount at about 400. Google has since said it will spend $1 billion over two years to expand the Lenoir campus, with at least 30 new jobs anticipated, and it has started a $2 million energy fund with Blue Ridge Community Action, Blue Ridge Energy and Advanced Energy for weatherization and community solar. State Rep. Pricey Harrison has said officials should also track "residents' health impacts and quality of life" as the state weighs data center growth.

gemini-google-lok-yang-way.text: Google's Lok Yang Way data center is operating in Jurong, in western Singapore. It was the company's third data center in Singapore when it began operating in August 2022, following facilities announced in 2011 and 2015, as part of a long-term investment Google put at $850 million. Google has disclosed no specifications or power figures for its Singapore data centers. When it announced this site, the company pledged $1 million to the conservation group Mandai Nature. "Singapore is a regional hub for our network of data centers, cloud regions and subsea cables," Google said. Singapore controls new data center growth tightly. The government reopened applications for capacity in 2022 after a three year pause, and on August 21, 2026 its Economic Development Board and Infocomm Media Development Authority gave a second round of new capacity, 200 megawatts of power, to four operators: Digital Realty, Equinix, Keppel Data Centres and ST Telemedia Global Data Centres, out of more than 20 proposals. Google was not among them. Those new data centers must draw more than half their power from green sources and will sit in a low-carbon data center park JTC is developing on Jurong Island. Any further Google capacity in Singapore would need approval from the same two agencies, which plan to review within 18 to 24 months whether to hold another application round.

google-google-jurong-west.text: Google's Jurong West data center sits on land the company bought in western Singapore in 2011. Its first building opened in 2013, a second came online in 2015, and in 2018 Google began a third, multi-story facility "just down the road" from the first two, 9to5Google reported. That third building started operating in 2022, bringing Google's long-term Singapore data center investment to 850 million dollars. Google says it uses recycled water to cool its Singapore data centers. A fourth facility was completed in 2024, taking Google's technical infrastructure investment in the country to 5 billion dollars, the company says. Google has disclosed no specifications or power figures for any of its Singapore data centers. Singapore reopened applications for new data centers in 2022 after a three-year pause, with rules meant to limit power use and environmental impact. On August 21, 2026 the Economic Development Board and the Infocomm Media Development Authority provisionally picked Digital Realty, Equinix, Keppel Data Centres and ST Telemedia Global Data Centres to split 200 megawatts of new capacity from more than 20 proposals; Google was not among them. The winners must draw more than half their power from green sources and will build in a low-carbon data center park on Jurong Island. The two agencies said they would review whether to open another call for applications in 18 to 24 months.

gemini-google-london.text: Google's London data center capacity is its Google Cloud region europe-west2, which opened in July 2017, and Google does not say where in or around Greater London, in the United Kingdom, its data centers are. "We don't say for a number of reasons, but one is that our customers are actually really keen on not having people know exactly where their application is hosted," Google engineering vice president Benjamin Treynor Sloss told DCD at the launch. Some reports have suggested the region is hosted in Equinix facilities in Slough, but that has not been confirmed, DCD reported in 2024. Sloss said Google typically offers three data centers in a region, close enough together to replicate data with latency under a millisecond but far enough apart that no normal physical event would hit more than one. The region, formed of three zones, was Google's tenth worldwide and its second in Europe after Belgium. The europe-west2 region went down during the summer 2022 heatwave. Google's own UK data center is north of London. Google began building on a 33-acre site in Waltham Cross, in the borough of Broxbourne, Hertfordshire, in January 2024, on land it bought in October 2020, and said it would invest $1 billion there. Chancellor Rachel Reeves opened that data center on September 16, 2025 as part of a two-year, £5 billion UK investment by Google, which said the building uses air cooling to limit water use to domestic needs and is equipped to send waste heat off site. Most London-area data center building is to the west, around Slough, Hayes and Iver, and a large campus planned in nearby Havering faces strong opposition, DCD reported.

gemini-google-melbourne.text: Google's Melbourne data center capacity is its Google Cloud region australia-southeast2 in Melbourne, Victoria, Australia, which opened in July 2021 as Google's second Australian region after Sydney. Google says the region has three availability zones but has not said which buildings in greater Melbourne host it. "One of the big factors that was driving this [region] is the idea of building disaster recovery and business continuity across Australia," Google's Matt Zwolenski said at the launch. Australia Post, Bendigo and Adelaide Bank and Optus were named as early customers. Victoria has just set out new rules for data centers. On September 22, 2026 Premier Ben Carroll announced that new data centers must supply their own renewable energy, may not use drinking water for cooling, may not be built near schools or childcare centers, and must sit at least 150 meters from homes. "Data centres must power themselves, protect homes and pay their way," Carroll said. The rules will not apply to planning applications already cleared or to eight now before the planning minister, and Carroll gave no date for the planning changes. Data Centres Australia chief executive Belinda Dennett called the changes "disappointing", while the Greens, who want a moratorium, called them a win for communities. About 50 data centers already operate in Victoria, mostly in Melbourne's west, where residents fought high-voltage power poles for NextDC's West Footscray data center until the distributor Jemena halted the work in September 2026. The state has sent several data center applications straight to the planning minister under its Development Facilitation Program, bypassing local councils. Victorians vote in a state election on November 28, and a Senate inquiry into AI and data centers was scheduled to hold hearings in Melbourne on September 23; Google has not said whether it plans more capacity in the state.

gemini-google-middenmeer.text: Google's data center in Middenmeer, North Holland, in the Netherlands, went into operation in December 2020, the company's second in the country after Eemshaven, DCD reported. It sits at Tussenweg 8 on the Agriport A7 industrial estate in the municipality of Hollands Kroon. Google says it has invested more than 500 million euros in the Middenmeer site. A Google spokesperson told DCD at the opening that the data center is air-cooled and reuses its waste heat to warm the office space for its 125 employees. Google said it would be powered through four renewable energy supply agreements representing around 130MW, including wind and solar in Delfzijl and wind farms in Zeeland. The municipality describes Google's Tussenweg site and Microsoft's, at subarea B1, as two of the largest data centers in the Netherlands, together providing more than 500 permanent jobs and 200 to 300 temporary ones during construction. The water is the part the municipality is careful about. Cooling water comes from PWN, the drinking water company, and the municipality notes that PWN puts households ahead of industry; one operator has built rainwater recycling at another site, and new buildings must be fitted with waste heat connections in case that heat is ever used. The Hoogheemraadschap Hollands Noorderkwartier issues the permits for discharging water and watches its quality, and the Omgevingsdienst Noordzeekanaalgebied checks that permit conditions are kept. Both sites run on contractually fixed renewable electricity from the national grid through TenneT, with emergency diesel generators under safety rules overseen by the regional safety authority and the environmental service. After pressure the municipality agreed stricter requirements for new buildings: more greenery, better landscaping and screening, and buildings set further back from the motorway. The province of North Holland had objected to the plan west of the A7, over traffic safety rather than water or power. It withdrew the objection on October 27, 2022, after the municipality agreed changes to the Agriport-N239 junction and to the crossings of the N239 with the A7 slip roads. The province set conditions on energy supply, water use, waste heat and how the building sits in the landscape, to be written into the permit, which had not been applied for at that point. LTO Noord's Hollands Kroon branch, the farmers' organisation, has opposed such projects over the loss of agricultural land. The company says it runs an apprenticeship programme with local schools, has given 6.1 million euros in grants to the area between 2017 and 2022, and pays a nonprofit called Agrotheek to farm a demonstration plot next to the data center. Permits for new data center buildings at Agriport come from Hollands Kroon, with the water board and the regional environmental service overseeing water discharges and permit conditions.

gemini-google-milan.text: Google's Milan data center capacity is its Google Cloud region europe-west8 in Milan, in the Lombardy region of Italy, which Google opened in June 2022 as the first of two Italian cloud regions. It was built with Telecom Italia (TIM), whose data centers host it. At the launch, TIM's Elio Schiavo said "our network of data centers, designed and built according to eco-sustainability criteria, will allow significant CO2 savings." The region launched with three cloud zones, and Google said a second Italian region would follow in Turin. Google cited a University of Turin economic impact report finding that the two regions could generate up to €3.3 billion and support up to 65,000 new jobs in Piedmont and Lombardy. "This new region is a strong step towards building regional capacity that meets the needs of the Italian digital economy, from availability and data residency, to digital sovereignty and sustainability," said Fabio Fregi, Google Cloud's country manager for Italy. In July 2026 Intesa Sanpaolo, Italy's largest banking group, said it had finished moving a fundamental part of its core IT systems onto the Milan and Turin regions, migrating more than 800 applications. Lombardy has since become the first Italian region with its own law on data centers. The regional council's law, reported by GreenPlanner in June 2026, raises urbanization fees by up to 200% for data centers built on green or farm land, requires new data centers to use only renewable energy, and bans drawing water from public aqueducts for cooling. It cuts construction fees by 10 to 30% and speeds permits for data centers on disused industrial land, and gives municipalities a year to update their plans and map such brownfield sites. About half of the roughly 30-gigawatt pipeline of data center requests across Italy is concentrated in Lombardy, according to regional assessor Sertori. A steering group of the Lombardy Region, ANCI Lombardia, the environmental agency ARPA, universities and the provinces will oversee how the law is applied.

gemini-google-moncks-corner.text: Google's data center campus in the Mount Holly Commerce Park at Moncks Corner, Berkeley County, South Carolina, was established in 2007, the company's first in the state. In September 2024 Google said it would invest $1.3 billion to expand the Berkeley County campus, and in October 2025 it announced $9 billion more for its South Carolina data centers, to be spent in 2026 and 2027 on the Berkeley County expansion and two new campuses under construction in neighboring Dorchester County. The campus is best known locally for a fight over water. In 2016 Google applied to triple its permitted withdrawal from the Middendorf Aquifer, from 183 million to 549 million gallons a year to cool servers, then withdrew the request after strong opposition. It applied again in February 2019. The aquifer, about 1,600 feet down, also supplies Mount Pleasant, Sullivan's Island and Isle of Palms. "This aquifer is ... a primary source of water supply not only to 80,000 citizens of Mount Pleasant but also the surrounding Charleston County area," said Mount Pleasant town councilman Mark Smith, who called the plan "a threat to public health and safety." A regional Council of Governments advisory committee recommended denial, but the state Department of Health and Environmental Control approved the 549-million-gallon permit in October 2019. "Our customers ask me all the time, why would DHEC take groundwater away from the citizens of Mount Pleasant and give it to Google to cool computers. Unfortunately, I don't have a good answer for that," said Clay Duffie, general manager of Mount Pleasant Waterworks, whose own groundwater draw faced a deep proposed cut. The state required Google to reduce its regular groundwater demand, keep it for peak use or backup, and develop other sources. Google also buys surface water from Berkeley County Water and Sanitation for cooling, but has refused to say how much, calling it a trade secret, according to the Coastal Conservation League. Google's facilities manager, Paul Carff, said the permit would build the data center's sustainability and that the company is committed to responsible water stewardship.

gemini-google-montreal.text: Google's Montreal data center capacity is its Google Cloud region northamerica-northeast1 in Montreal, Quebec, Canada, which opened on February 1, 2018 as Google's first cloud region in Canada. Google says the Montreal region's three zones sit in one or two physical data centers and that it is expanding to at least three, but it has not said where in the Montreal area they are. Google announced the region in March 2017, and its Quebec managing director, Marie-Josée Lamothe, tied the choice to Montreal's AI research, including the Google Brain centre and a $4.5 million grant to the Montreal Institute for Learning Algorithms. Hydro-Québec welcomed the region, with chief executive Éric Martel pointing to the province's green energy and the lowest electricity rates in North America. Google said at launch that hosting in Montreal could cut latency by up to 90% for users there, and it offered dedicated connections to its cloud through Cologix in the city. Those cheap power rates are now changing. In February 2026 Hydro-Québec asked the provincial energy board, the Régie de l'énergie, to approve a new tariff for large data centers averaging 13 cents per kilowatt-hour, about double the current large-power rate, to take effect in the second half of 2026. Existing data centers would move to the new rate over five years, and the utility said it expects data center consumption in Quebec to grow sevenfold by 2035. "These tariff changes aim to recognize the contribution of our renewable electricity and promote responsible consumption," Hydro-Québec chief executive Claudine Bouchard said, in the English rendering DCD published. Large projects must also still go through Hydro-Québec's selection process before they get power. The Régie de l'énergie decides whether the tariff takes effect, and Hydro-Québec's selection process decides which new data centers in Quebec get electricity; Google has not announced a new Quebec site.

gemini-google-mumbai.text: Google's Mumbai data center is a cloud region called asia-south1, a linked cluster of data centers, in Mumbai, Maharashtra, India. It opened on November 1, 2017 as Google's first cloud region in India, built from three data centers whose exact addresses Google has not made public. Google said hosting in Mumbai would cut latency by 20 to 90 percent for users in Chennai, Hyderabad, Bangalore and Mumbai compared with its Singapore region, and it offered private network connections at GPX Mumbai and Tata's Mumbai data center. A second Indian cloud region followed in Delhi in 2021, and in April 2026 Google broke ground on a much larger AI hub near Visakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh. Around Mumbai, the data center boom has reached residents: in Thane's Balkum area, people have protested an Amazon Web Services data center over noise, heat and water use. In September 2026 the Maharashtra Pollution Control Board said it was drafting the state's first data center policy with IIT Bombay. "Environmental problems being caused due to upcoming data centres in the state is a matter of concern but while addressing it, we want to also address the issue wherein we want new investment to come in Maharashtra," board chairman Siddhesh Kadam said. The policy, which the board says will set buffer zones around homes and require recycled or treated wastewater for cooling, is expected to be finalized within a few months and would govern where Mumbai's next data centers can go.

gemini-google-osaka.text: Google's Osaka data center capacity is its Google Cloud region asia-northeast2 in Osaka, Osaka Prefecture, Japan, which Google opened in May 2019 as its second cloud region in Japan after Tokyo. Google does not own the Osaka buildings: DCD reported that it colocates the region in Equinix's OS1 and NTT's Telepark Dojima Building 2. "Two cloud regions in-country provide improved business continuity planning with distributed, secure infrastructure needed to meet IT and business requirements for disaster recovery," Google Cloud chief executive Thomas Kurian wrote at the launch. Asahi Group Holdings was among the customers Google quoted welcoming the region. Google's first owned data center in Japan opened later, in Inzai, Chiba Prefecture, in 2023. Other companies are now building AI capacity near the city. In January 2026 KDDI opened its Osaka Sakai Data Center, an AI data center built in about six months on the former Sharp Sakai plant site, reusing the plant's high-capacity power and cooling systems. KDDI said the site would provide GPUs and on-premises services for Google's Gemini AI model to pharmaceutical, manufacturing and other customers, and that it runs on 100% renewable energy. Google says the Osaka region's three zones sit within one or two physical data centers and that it is in the process of expanding to at least three.

gemini-google-osasco.text: Google's Osasco data center capacity is its Google Cloud region southamerica-east1, which Google opened on September 19, 2017 as its first cloud region in South America, serving São Paulo, Brazil, with three zones. Google said the region could cut round-trip latency by 80 to 95 percent for customers in Chile, Argentina and Brazil compared with its U.S. regions, and let customers pay in Brazilian reais. Dotz, Contabilizei and Movile were among the Brazilian companies Google quoted at the launch. Brazil is now writing national rules for data centers. On September 1, 2026 the Senate passed bill PL 278/2026, which creates the Redata tax regime and removes federal taxes on imported electronic and IT components for data centers; the Chamber of Deputies had already passed it, so it goes to the president for signature. In return, companies must use clean or renewable energy, keep water use for cooling at or below 0.05 liters per kilowatt-hour, invest 2% of the value of tax-free purchases in Brazil, and reserve 10% of their data center services for the domestic market. The government estimates the tax break at about R$5.2 billion in 2026 and R$1 billion in each of the next two years. Civil society groups criticized the bill as not debated enough, arguing in a joint note that "Soberania não se resume a instalar servidores em território nacional". The next decision is the president's signature on Redata, which would set the terms for any new Google capacity in Brazil; Google has not announced one.

gemini-coreweave-phoenix.text: No CoreWeave data center in Phoenix, in Maricopa County, Arizona, has been reported by the company or by anyone covering it; CoreWeave leases space in other companies' buildings, and none of the American sites that can be traced to it is in Arizona. What Phoenix has done is write rules: Ordinance G-7396, adopted on July 2, 2025, brought data centers into a special permit framework in named commercial and industrial districts, with standards for siting, noise, design and public safety. On August 31, 2026 Attorney General Kris Mayes asked the legislature and Governor Katie Hobbs to stop approving new data centers statewide, on the ground that they are heavy users of both power and water. The federal government had cut Arizona's Colorado River allocation by close to 30 percent, and a 2025 analysis by Ceres projected data center water demand across greater Phoenix rising by 450 percent.

gemini-coreweave-raleigh.text: No CoreWeave data center at Raleigh, North Carolina, or in nearby Chatham County, has been reported; the company's North Carolina presence that appears in listings is at Winston-Salem, about 170 kilometres away. North Carolina would be a difficult place to add one now: at least 93 data centers operate in the state, more than 20 projects have been announced since the start of 2025, and dozens of local governments have passed moratoriums. The most recent was Charlotte, whose council approved a 150 day pause unanimously in front of a packed room. The pressure there came from a door-knocking campaign in the neighbourhood beside one of the projects; Dana Alhasan, who ran it, said many residents had not known it was there at all.

gemini-coreweave-santa-clara.text: CoreWeave's reported data center presence in Silicon Valley, near Santa Clara, California, is networking and inference equipment in Equinix's SV1, SV5 and SV10 interconnection centers in San Jose, according to DGTL Infra's survey of the AI cloud company's sites. Santa Clara itself, in Santa Clara County, is one of the most grid-stressed data center markets in the country. Two finished data centers in the city, built by Digital Realty and Stack, stood empty in late 2025 because the city's utility, Silicon Valley Power, could not yet connect them, Bloomberg reported. Digital Realty won planning permission for its building in 2019 and still had no grid connection six years later, and Stack's finished facility was in the same position. "SVP is undertaking a $450 million system upgrade to meet the needs of these and other customers, and the project is currently on schedule to be completed in 2028", utility spokesperson Janine de la Vega said. The report prompted questions at the Santa Clara City Council during a discussion of a major Silicon Valley Power expenditure. "Have we overpromised and underdelivered?" Vice Mayor Kelly Cox asked in November 2025. Santa Clara has 57 data centers active or under construction, Bloomberg reported, and until the upgrade is done new and existing data centers compete for limited power. CoreWeave's reported U.S. deployments beyond its large campuses include sites in Ashburn, Virginia; Atlanta; Chicago; Secaucus, New Jersey; and San Jose. Any new data center load in Santa Clara depends on Silicon Valley Power's upgrade, and the utility gives regular public reports on its progress.

gemini-vantage-frontier.text: Vantage Data Centers' Frontier campus in Shackelford County, Texas, near Albany, has put gravel trucks on the county's rural roads, and they will be there through early 2027. The campus is in Shackelford County, not in Mills County, where some data center trackers place it. In December 2025 the Albany News reported the site in its mobilization phase, with crews laying civil infrastructure, underground utilities, earthwork and concrete, and vertical construction expected to begin early in 2026. "Roadway safety is paramount for the construction team and the traveling public," a Vantage spokesperson said, adding that the company coordinates with the state highway department and local law enforcement at shift changes. It is Vantage's largest campus anywhere: 1,200 acres, ten single-storey buildings totalling 3.7 million square feet and 1.4 gigawatts, at more than $25 billion, broken ground for OpenAI as part of the Stargate programme Oracle is building out. Vantage says the first data center is due in the second half of 2026 and the campus complete in 2028, cooled by a closed-loop chiller system it says needs almost no water.

gemini-vantage-lighthouse.text: Vantage Data Centers is building Lighthouse, a $15 billion data center campus for OpenAI and Oracle, on 672 acres on the north side of Port Washington, Wisconsin, in Ozaukee County. Vantage broke ground in December 2025; the campus will have four single-story data centers totaling 902 megawatts across 2.5 million square feet, scheduled to be finished in 2028. The project is part of Stargate, the $500 billion OpenAI initiative, and Vantage expected about 3,500 workers on site in 2026 and 5,000 in 2027, according to filings with the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources. On April 7, 2026, Port Washington became the first city in the United States to put data center tax breaks to a public vote, and about 66 percent of voters said no. The referendum requires city leaders to get voter approval before granting a developer tax incentives over $10 million; it was put on the ballot by residents and a local group called Great Lakes Neighbors United, and came too late to affect Lighthouse. The $458 million tax incremental financing district the city authorized for Lighthouse in November 2025 is unaffected, but business groups including the Metropolitan Milwaukee Association of Commerce have sued to have the referendum ordinance struck down, a case that could void it entirely. Vantage says We Energies will supply the campus's power, with 70 percent from zero-emission sources including solar, wind and battery storage, and that a closed-loop cooling system will use about 11,000 gallons of water a day. At the December groundbreaking, Vantage North America president Dana Adams said the campus would use about 1.3 gigawatts of power without raising other customers' rates: "We're paying our own costs, including infrastructure upgrades that benefit everyone." The business groups' lawsuit over the referendum ordinance is the open legal question in Port Washington, while construction of the campus continues toward its 2028 completion date.

developers3-stack-hillsboro-por01.text: STACK Infrastructure's POR01 data center at 3145 NE Brookwood Parkway in Hillsboro, Washington County, Oregon, is one of three STACK campuses in the city, now marketed as an 80 megawatt campus on 18 acres with two buildings. Hours before the Hillsboro City Council adopted a 120-day moratorium on new data centers on July 27, 2026, STACK applied to revise an existing land-use approval for a three-phase campus the city approved in 2014. Because the filing came in before the vote, state law requires the city to review it under the rules that were in effect that morning. The council adopted the moratorium unanimously with only a day's public notice; Mayor Beach Pace said it was meant to "prevent a rush of applications from data centers." Through November 24, 2026, the city will not accept, process or approve new data center or battery storage proposals, including expansions to existing facilities. Backlash had built after residents learned data center campuses had secured decades of property tax breaks; Hillsboro approved 15 of 17 enterprise zone applications before a statewide moratorium on new data center tax breaks took effect in June. City Councilor Kipperlyn Sinclair joined a June lawsuit seeking to overturn those tax breaks. "While our residential electricity rates have risen by nearly 50%, data centers continue paying less than half the rate per kilowatt-hour that we do," she said in April. The city's water director, Niki Iverson, has said data centers account for about 1.8% of Hillsboro's annual water demand. STACK was not the only late filer: Wagon Data Center, Corny Data Center and Aligned Data Centers all filed applications in the days and hours before the moratorium, and most proceed under the old rules. On October 6, 2026, the city council holds a public hearing on its first permanent data center rules, recommended by the Planning Commission in September. They would allow standalone data centers only in the Industrial Park and Industrial Sanctuary zones, cap them at 215 and 310 acres, bar them within 1,000 feet of schools, and require a public hearing instead of staff approval for new facilities. About 12 and 17 acres remain available in those zones under the caps.
paragraphs: STACK Infrastructure's POR01 data center at 3145 NE Brookwood Parkway in Hillsboro, Washington County, Oregon, is one of three STACK campuses in the city, now marketed as an 80 megawatt campus on 18 acres with two buildings. Hours before the Hillsboro City Council adopted a 120-day moratorium on new data centers on July 27, 2026, STACK applied to revise an existing land-use approval for a three-phase campus the city approved in 2014. Because the filing came in before the vote, state law requires the city to review it under the rules that were in effect that morning.

The council adopted the moratorium unanimously with only a day's public notice; Mayor Beach Pace said it was meant to "prevent a rush of applications from data centers." Through November 24, 2026, the city will not accept, process or approve new data center or battery storage proposals, including expansions to existing facilities. Backlash had built after residents learned data center campuses had secured decades of property tax breaks; Hillsboro approved 15 of 17 enterprise zone applications before a statewide moratorium on new data center tax breaks took effect in June.

City Councilor Kipperlyn Sinclair joined a June lawsuit seeking to overturn those tax breaks. "While our residential electricity rates have risen by nearly 50%, data centers continue paying less than half the rate per kilowatt-hour that we do," she said in April. STACK was not the only late filer: Wagon Data Center, Corny Data Center and Aligned Data Centers all filed applications in the days and hours before the moratorium, and most proceed under the old rules.

gemini-copt-van-meter.text: COPT Defense Properties' planned data center campus at Van Meter, in Dallas County, Iowa, is stalled on power: chief executive Stephen Budorick told investors on the company's April 28, 2026 earnings call that COPT is "at an impasse on power" and does not expect to move for three to four years. COPT bought the 365-acre parcel near Des Moines in late September 2024 for $32 million, saying the land could hold about 3.3 million square feet of data center buildings supported by an estimated 1 gigawatt of power. The existing zoning already allows data centers, COPT said, and the site could total 15 buildings of 220,000 square feet each and two substations, built for an unnamed Fortune 100 cloud computing tenant, according to Data Center Dynamics. COPT plans to build the site in phases and self-fund the work, Budorick said when the land purchase was announced. "No real update. We are at an impasse on power," Budorick told analysts on the April call, adding that the economic terms to move forward had been too burdensome: "We elected to step aside, let others lead in that market, and wait for the power company to adjust to the elevated demand for power for data in the market." Because the zoning already allows data centers, what happens next turns on COPT signing a tenant and securing power rather than on a rezoning vote; any site plan would still need approval from the Van Meter City Council.

gemini-percheron.text: Rowan Digital Infrastructure plans the Percheron Data Center, a 300-megawatt campus on Tower Road southwest of Boardman, in Morrow County, Oregon, near the former coal plant and the Carty gas plant. The company describes the site as about 275 acres and says it closed on the land in 2024 after Morrow County approved rezoning in 2023. Rowan's stated target is a phased buildout by 2030; the 300 megawatts of power describe planned campus capacity, not power already in use. The county rezoned the parcel from farmland to industrial use with an overlay limiting it to a data center. Rowan argued that the former Threemile Canyon Farms land had not been irrigated or cultivated and was poorly suited to farming. Its original concept called for four buildings totaling about 1.1 million square feet, but the county findings said the number and size of buildings could change with final design. Water and road work remain important local details. Rowan told the county that industrial use and cooling could require 20 million to 60 million gallons of water a year; it was evaluating existing water rights or supply from a planned Port of Morrow treatment facility. The proposal also called for a new power line along an existing Tower Road corridor and on-site backup power, while county public works recommended an agreement for Rowan to pay to chip-seal eight miles of Tower Road after construction. The 2023 application projected at least 35 full-time operational jobs and described recycling industrial wastewater on site, with a retention pond for water that could not be reused. Morrow County's planning director said in April 2026 that industrial-site data centers still go through site-plan review with public notice, including checks of roads and utilities. Rowan's current portfolio gives the 2030 completion target but does not state that the full campus is operating.

gemini-sabey-umatilla.text: Sabey Data Centers is building a 714,540-square-foot campus on Wanapa Road in Umatilla, Umatilla County, Oregon, designed to draw more than 150 megawatts of power. The company marked the site's steel-raising with a ceremony on July 15, 2026, and the first of its two data halls is due online in April 2028. Sabey picked Umatilla for the Columbia River corridor's hydroelectric power and its cluster of data centers already operating or under development across 10 campuses in neighboring Morrow County, mostly around Boardman. Sabey president Tim Mirick said, "We believe Umatilla is a perfect spot." Executive director John Sabey acknowledged what he called anxiety about AI, saying "that anxiety is manifesting itself in a little bit of pushback toward data centers." Critics have focused on water use. Sabey says its closed-loop cooling system recirculates sealed liquid rather than losing water to evaporative cooling towers, and uses significantly less water than companies such as Amazon. Umatilla City Manager Dave Stockdale said, "There really isn't a lot of water impact compared to farming or golf courses." In March 2026 Amazon agreed to pay $20.5 million to settle a lawsuit over nitrate-contaminated well water tied partly to data center wastewater spread on farm fields in neighboring Morrow County. State Rep. Bobby Levy, who attended the ceremony, said, "Investments like this create momentum." Stockdale said the project should draw related businesses such as fiber optics and pipefitting firms to Umatilla. The next milestone is the first data hall, due to open in April 2028.

gemini-atnorth-swe04.text: atNorth, a Nordic data center company, has bought about 50 hectares at Hamre Industrial Park in Långsele, Sollefteå Municipality, Västernorrland County, Sweden, for SWE04, a data center campus of up to 300 megawatts of power that it aims to open in 2028. The municipal council voted for the sale on February 23, 2026, and the contract was signed that same evening. The municipality says the price, 175 million kronor, is based on an independent land valuation from January 2026. In May 2026, atNorth and grid operator E.ON Energidistribution agreed to a 200-megawatt grid connection, which requires a new substation at Hamre and an overhead power line of about five kilometers to the national-grid station at Nässe. atNorth says the site will support direct liquid cooling and up to 1 megawatt per rack, and that it will seek partners to reuse the campus's waste heat. "Our Sollefteå campus represents a significant milestone for the company and demonstrates our commitment to building data center ecosystems that deliver both technical excellence and long-term value for local communities," said chief executive Eyjólfur Magnús Kristinsson. atNorth first secured land at Hamre in 2024, then describing an initial 200-megawatt mega site. atNorth was acquired by Equinix and the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board in a $4.2 billion deal; the municipality's own site tells residents atNorth will keep the same local Nordic focus despite the change in ownership. The municipality expects about 100 to 150 direct jobs and several hundred more during construction, and says it gives no grants or subsidies to the project. Before construction, atNorth needs a building permit from Sollefteå Municipality and an environmental permit from the Västernorrland County Administrative Board covering cooling methods and water use, while E.ON handles permitting for the new power line.

gemini-yotta-greater-noida.text: Yotta runs a 30-megawatt data center campus in Greater Noida, in Gautam Buddh Nagar district, Uttar Pradesh, India, and the company says it is operating and expanding. In March 2026 Yotta said it would invest more than $2 billion to deploy 20,000 Nvidia Blackwell Ultra chips there, with more capacity planned at its Navi Mumbai campus. Gautam Buddh Nagar has become one of India's busiest data center corridors, with 17 facilities operating or planned, among them AdaniConneX, Yotta, Nxtra, CtrlS and STT. By June 2025, proposed data center capacity across Uttar Pradesh had reached 644 megawatts of power. The Central Ground Water Board's 2023 assessment found groundwater extraction across the district running at 104.79 percent of what is naturally replenished each year. Uttar Pradesh's 2021 data center policy set out to attract Rs 30,000 crore in investment and build a 900-megawatt industry, promising that development authorities such as Noida and the Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority will ensure "24x7 uninterrupted water supply" to data center units. Down To Earth found the policy has no plan for sustainable water use, and officials could not say how much the facilities consume. Vishwajeet Singh, an executive engineer in the district's ground water department, said it grants permits "only if companies commit to recharging two litres of groundwater for every one litre extracted." The department says most of Gautam Buddh Nagar is a notified area where extraction is restricted.

Vishwajeet Singh, an executive engineer in the district's ground water department, said it grants permits "only if companies commit to recharging two litres of groundwater for every one litre extracted."
The department says most of Gautam Buddh Nagar is a notified area where extraction is restricted.

gemini-yotta-navi-mumbai.text: Yotta's Navi Mumbai data center park sits in the 600-acre Hiranandani Fortune City area of Panvel, Navi Mumbai, Maharashtra, India, where Yotta, a Hiranandani Group company, opened its first building, NM1, in July 2020. NM1 holds about 7,000 server racks and runs on 52 megawatts of power, and Yotta says it is India's only Tier IV data center open to multiple tenants, the industry's highest reliability rating. Yotta has since turned NM1 into a computing site for artificial intelligence: it runs 1,024 Nvidia L40 and 8,192 Nvidia H100 chips there for its Shakti Cloud service, Data Centre Magazine reported in June 2026. The company's next Navi Mumbai building, the planned 75-megawatt NM2, is meant to add 36,000 newer chips on a campus Yotta says can scale to 2 gigawatts of power, and the company plans more than 80,000 chips across its sites by fiscal 2027-28. Frost & Sullivan named Yotta its 2026 Indian Company of the Year in AI infrastructure in June 2026. "This honour belongs to our customers, partners, and teams who share our vision of positioning India among the world's leading AI and digital infrastructure hubs," said Sunil Gupta, Yotta's co-founder and chief executive. The Mumbai region's data center boom is drawing state rules. In September 2026 the Maharashtra Pollution Control Board said it was drafting a state data center policy with IIT Bombay that would set buffer zones from homes and require recycled or treated wastewater for cooling, after residents in Thane protested an Amazon data center. The Maharashtra Industrial Development Corporation is also planning pipelines of treated sewage and desalinated seawater for four data center clusters in the Mumbai region, including TTC Navi Mumbai and Taloja, according to documents reported by CarbonCopy. How NM2 is cooled and powered will fall under whatever rules the pollution board finalizes, which it expects within a few months.

gemini-cdc-brooklyn.text: CDC Data Centres formally opened its Brooklyn data center campus in Melbourne's western suburbs, Victoria, Australia, in February 2026, its first campus in the Melbourne region. The campus, at 594 Geelong Road in Brooklyn, has two data center buildings, has been operating since 2024, and is expected to reach more than 350 megawatts of power when finished, according to CDC. Then-Premier Jacinta Allan opened the campus alongside ministers Danny Pearson and Daniel Mulino, and CDC founder and chief executive Greg Boorer told about 150 government and industry leaders at the event that "what we have built here is not only critical digital infrastructure, it is long-term economic infrastructure and job creation for Victoria." CDC says its investment there has generated more than 5,000 jobs in construction, engineering, skilled trades, security and operations, and the campus hosts Monash University's AI supercomputer, MAVERIC. CDC's Melbourne page says the Brooklyn campus's first building, BK1, is fully operating while the rest of the campus and CDC's second Melbourne campus, at Laverton North, are still under construction; together the two campuses are set to give CDC more than 780 megawatts of capacity in Victoria. CDC says its LiquidCore closed-loop cooling system does not use water for the campus's primary cooling. On September 22, 2026, Victorian Premier Ben Carroll, who succeeded Allan, announced new rules requiring data centers built in the state to supply their own renewable energy, stop using drinking water for cooling and stay at least 150 meters from homes. The rules will not apply to projects already approved, so they do not affect the Brooklyn campus.

gemini-cdc-laverton-north.text: CDC Data Centres' Laverton campus, on Leakes Road in Laverton North, in Melbourne's south-west, Victoria, Australia, is under construction as the company's second Melbourne data center campus. CDC broke ground on February 17, 2025, on what it then called a 150 megawatt campus; the company's Melbourne page now says the finished campus will add more than 400 megawatts of capacity. Wyndham City Mayor Mia Shaw, Laverton MP Sarah Connolly and federal MP Tim Watts joined CDC founder and chief executive Greg Boorer at the groundbreaking; Boorer said he was "delighted to expand our presence in Melbourne and offer more customers access to our secure, reliable, sustainable and connected data centre solutions." CDC says the project will put more than $2.7 billion into the economy during construction and, combined with the company's Brooklyn campus, will give CDC over 780 megawatts of capacity across Melbourne. On September 22, 2026, Victorian Premier Ben Carroll announced new rules requiring data centers to supply their own renewable energy, stop using drinking water for cooling and sit at least 150 meters from homes. The rules are not retrospective, so the Laverton campus and eight other applications already before the planning minister would not have to meet them; Greens MP Sarah Mansfield called the changes "a huge win for communities," while Data Centres Australia chief executive Belinda Dennett called them "disappointing."

gemini-applied-digital-adair.text: Applied Digital proposed a 200-megawatt data center in 2024 for the 1200 block of Fallow Avenue near Adair, Iowa, next to a NextEra Energy substation, but at a September 23, 2026 hearing Adair County supervisors said no developer has approached the county with plans to build one. The county is instead writing its own data center ordinance, with the next public hearing set for October 14 at 9:15 a.m. Draft Ordinance #41 would keep data centers at least 1,000 feet from property lines and 2,600 feet from occupied homes, set noise standards, and require permanent foundations and decommissioning plans for any data center or cryptocurrency mine built in unincorporated Adair County. Supervisor Jodie Hoadley, who presented the draft, said it "would not keep developers out" but would set restrictions to deal with environmental and quality-of-life concerns. The fight began in April 2024, when Applied Digital's Nick Phillips and Lance Cummins told supervisors they hoped to start construction that summer or fall, before Adair County had any zoning ordinance covering data centers. Residents pushed back over the unknowns, and the board passed a first ordinance setting setbacks of 300 feet from property lines and 1,200 feet from homes; the 2026 draft more than doubles the home setback. Adair County adopted a moratorium on data centers on April 18, 2026 while it drafts final rules, and Hoadley has shared the ordinance draft with neighboring Union and Madison counties, which are working on similar rules of their own; she said Union County plans its own moratorium. The Board of Supervisors decides whether Ordinance #41 is adopted, and its next hearing is October 14, 2026.

gemini-edged-energy-pottawattamie.text: Edged is building a two building data center campus at College Road and East Kanesville Boulevard in Council Bluffs, in Pottawattamie County, Iowa, known inside the company as Project Lola. Each building runs to about 285,445 square feet and the site is reported at around 200 megawatts; Edged broke ground in October 2025 and topped out the first building in June 2026, with the second due in September. The land had been approved for a logistics park in 2021 and never built on. Turner Construction is the general contractor, and Edged, formerly Edged Energy, is part of Endeavour, set up by Aligned's founder Jakob Carnemark. The company sells itself on waterless cooling, and the plans have moved. The letter of intent Edged put to the city council described carbon neutral, zero water cooling systems that use no water; the revised plans include a row of modular cooling towers and two 60 foot makeup water tanks. The buildings shrank as well, from two of 80 feet totalling 900,000 square feet to two of 36 feet 3 inches, with an administrative building alongside. Rather than draw from a MidAmerican Energy substation, Edged is installing two substations of its own, a switchyard and overhead electrical infrastructure.

research-google-franklin-township.text: Google withdrew its rezoning request for Project Flo, a planned data center campus on 468 acres of farmland along I-74 and Post Road in Franklin Township, Indianapolis, Marion County, Indiana, on September 22, 2025, just before the City-County Council was expected to deny it. "I was given notice by our council attorney that Google is withdrawing their petition," Councilor Michael-Paul Hart told residents in an overflow room, who erupted into applause. The request was filed in March 2025 by Deep Meadows LLC, an affiliate whose link to Google was confirmed in July, and site plans showed four buildings. Google would have received tax cuts for 10 years, and the Metropolitan Development Commission had backed the rezoning 8-1 in August 2025. "We have withdrawn the rezoning application for the proposed data center development in Franklin Township", a Google spokesperson said. Neighbors organized as Protect Franklin Township, fearing the data center would drain or contaminate local water and raise electric bills. They launched petitions, ran digital ads and bought billboards, said Meredith Sharp, a mother of three who lives blocks from the site. Residents also objected to the lack of transparency, including that Hart had signed a nondisclosure agreement about the project, which he said he did so as not to be shut out of the discussions. "We're going to be vigilant," organizer Andrew Filler said after the withdrawal, noting Google could refile in three months. Across Indiana, the Citizens Action Coalition counted nearly 30 active data center projects in October 2025, with at least 11 withdrawn. Data centers and Google are not finished in Indiana: a Google data center is being built in Fort Wayne. Two Republican councilors, Josh Bain and Derek Cahill, have said they would consider a data center in their districts. If a data center plan returns to the site, a rezoning goes first to the Metropolitan Development Commission's hearing examiner and the commission, and the district councilor can call it down to the City-County Council, where 15 councilors must vote against it to block it. Residents can write to city planners at PlannerOnCall@Indy.gov or contact their councilor.

research-aws-japan-expansion-tokyo.text: Amazon Web Services says it is putting up new data centres in the Tokyo region, but nothing it has published places one at Higashishinagawa in Shinagawa ward, Tokyo, where trackers list one under construction. The new Tokyo building it has described is being built by Takenaka Corporation with a concrete that replaces 60 to 70 percent of the cement with blast furnace slag. Behind it is Amazon's January 2024 plan to spend 2.26 trillion yen, about 15.24 billion dollars, on its Tokyo and Osaka cloud regions by 2027. The limit in Tokyo is the grid. The pipeline of data centre projects around Tokyo comes to roughly 10 gigawatts, about 17 percent of peak load and more than double the supply expansion expected in the next few years, and about 7 trillion yen of grid reinforcement between regions stands behind it. Japanese data centre electricity use is forecast to triple to 66 terawatt hours by 2034, about 60 percent of the country's growth in power demand.

research-vantage-jnb1-waterfall-city.text: Vantage Data Centers' Johannesburg I (JNB1) data center campus in Waterfall City, near Midrand, Johannesburg, South Africa, is being built out to 120 megawatts of power across three buildings. In September 2026, South Africa's Competition Tribunal cleared the sale of the first building, JNB11, to a fund managed by African Infrastructure Investment Managers, w.media reported. The second building, JNB12.1, has been completed, according to Attacq, the real estate company that developed it with Vantage. Attacq and Vantage formed a 50:50 partnership to build the unfinished shell of that second building, a four-hall facility of 10,363 square meters under a 20-year lease, DCD reported in March 2025. Attacq valued its half of the building at about R628 million and said JNB12.1 would support an initial power load of 12 megawatts, rising to 16 megawatts over time. gemini-google-leesburg.text: Google's data center near Leesburg, in Loudoun County, Virginia, sits on a 57-acre property in the Stonewall Business Park that the company bought for $31 million in 2017, just west of Ashburn's Data Center Alley. Google confirmed the purchase alongside a 91-acre site in Arcola, shifting from leasing wholesale data center space in Northern Virginia to building its own campuses there. "We've purchased property in Northern Virginia to increase our capacity and meet the growing demand for Google's services in the area," Google public affairs manager Liz Schwab said at the time. The site anchors a cluster of data center campuses south of the Leesburg Executive Airport. TA Realty's campus next door grew from a planned 300 megawatts to a 430-megawatt lease of five buildings and 1.9 million square feet, signed with a single cloud provider in 2023. "This was probably the last remaining large parcel where you can build a campus," TA Realty's Allison O'Rourke said of her firm's site. Loudoun has the highest concentration of data centers in the world, and data centers paid $1.2 billion in county property taxes in fiscal 2026, 39 percent of the county's budget. In March 2025 the Board of Supervisors voted 7-2 to end automatic approval of new data centers, so new projects now need a special exception with public hearings. On September 15, 2026, the board voted 7-1-1 to have staff draft a resolution pausing new data center applications for up to 12 months; the pause is not yet in force. Leesburg's own supervisor, Kristen Umstattd, voted against it, and Catoctin's Caleb Kershner abstained. The pause would apply only to new applications, and the board is expected to take a final vote on it on October 20, 2026.

google-google-loudoun-county-ashburn.text: Google's data center on Goose Landing Lane in Ashburn, in Loudoun County, Virginia, is one of about 250 in the county, and nothing has been published about the building itself. The county has decided it has enough of them for now. On September 15, 2026 the board of supervisors voted to direct staff to draft a resolution pausing new data center and substation applications for 12 months, and the pause took effect immediately, carried 7-1 with one abstention. County attorneys had warned that an outright, indefinite moratorium would be illegal under Virginia law, so the board is pursuing a time-limited pause instead, with a formal resolution due back at the October 20 meeting. The county had already stopped allowing data centers as of right, and is looking at whether it can withdraw that status from projects previously grandfathered in. The money makes it a hard habit to break. Data centers supplied 38 percent of Loudoun County's general fund revenue in the 2026 budget, money the county has used to build parks, schools and recreation centers. Some residents told reporters the tradeoff is still not worth it. "For years, I have been pushing for Loudoun County to get a handle on data center growth," said Juli E. Briskman, the Algonkian district supervisor who brought the motion. "Now we have the breathing room required to complete the critical work of revising our regulations to protect our communities."

google-google-elmina-business-park.text: Google's first data center in Malaysia is under construction at Sime Darby Property's Elmina Business Park in the City of Elmina township, Sungai Buloh, Selangor, outside Kuala Lumpur. Google expects the data center to start operating within nine months, a Google infrastructure executive told Media Selangor in August 2026, though no exact date has been set. "Development has been progressing very well. Construction has been very good," said Ken Siah, Google's Asia Pacific global infrastructure principal. Google has not published the site's power or water use, but Bernama reported in August 2025, citing an investment bank research note, that the first phase is designed for 100 megawatts of power and a second phase could add 200 to 250 more megawatts. Air Selangor confirmed Google had asked for a water supply allocation for the facility, which its chief executive called "a substantial demand," and Google requested treated potable water, Bernama reported. "Diverting significant amounts of treated water to industrial facilities such as data centres may compromise water security for other consumers, particularly in high-demand areas," said Ahmad Faizal Abdul Rahman, chief executive of the National Water Services Commission. "I'm worried that the needs of this mega project may be prioritised as they may have been promised uninterrupted water and electricity supply," said Mohd Faris Mohd Razali, who lives in the nearby Elmina Green neighborhood. In September 2026, Selangor Menteri Besar Amirudin Shari said the state would not approve any data center project without enough water and electricity supply. The data center is part of a $2 billion investment Google announced in May 2024, which also covers its first Malaysian Google Cloud region, and Google projects more than $3.2 billion in economic impact by 2030. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim attended the groundbreaking on October 1, 2024, and Sime Darby Property then targeted completion in early 2026. Sime Darby Property is building the data center to Google's specifications and leasing it for 20 years to Pearl Computing Malaysia, a Google-affiliated company, W.Media reported. The first project covers 49 acres, and a second Google data center of 77 acres, worth RM5.6 billion and due by 2027, was announced for the same park in December 2024. Google says the site will use water cooling, which it says uses less energy than air cooling, and as part of its water stewardship it will work with the Global Environment Centre and Petaling Jaya City Council to restore Taman Aman Lake. Siah said construction alone is expected to create about 4,200 jobs, and Sime Darby Property expects the whole Elmina Business Park to create about 35,000 jobs by the time it is completed in 2035.
