google-google-canelones.text: Google's Uruguayan data center is in the Parque de las Ciencias in Canelones, on Route 101 near Carrasco International Airport outside Montevideo. The zone lies beside Colonia Nicolich. For years nobody outside the government knew how much water the plant would take, because Google had written confidentiality clauses into its agreement with Uruguay and the state agreed to keep the environmental projections classified. Two researchers, Daniel Pena of the University of the Republic and Enol Nieto Jiménez of the BETA Tech Center, sued the Ministry of Environment together with the water groups CNDAV and Coordinación por el Agua to force the figures out, citing the article of the constitution that requires public participation in water management. On World Water Day, March 22, 2023, more than forty organisations and over 3,000 people marched through central Montevideo against the data center and other projects they said privatised water. After they won in court, the documents showed the plant would need about 2 million gallons (7.6 million litres) of water a day to cool its servers, equivalent to the domestic daily use of 55,000 people. Montevideo declared a water emergency in June 2023. On March 25, 2024 the Movimiento por un Uruguay Sustentable and Amnesty International opened a public campaign before the comment period closed on April 5. They asked the Ministry of Environment to make Google account for the carbon behind its electricity demand, for its waste, and for taking the plant apart at the end of its life, and noted that the company had promised 50 jobs on a site that pays no tax. Google redrew the project. It shrank from about 30 hectares to about 10 and swapped the cooling towers for a closed air-cooled system that uses no water and produces no wastewater. The revised campus was still reckoned to draw the electricity of about 200,000 households a year. Work began on August 30, 2024, with Google putting about US$850 million into the site. The Intendencia de Canelones gave the campus about 400 permanent jobs and 800 workers at the peak of construction. Eduardo López, who runs Google Cloud in Latin America, said the talks had begun in 2018 and the project was settled in 2020. President Luis Lacalle Pou and the intendente of Canelones, Marcelo Metediera, were both there. Critics pointed out that the site sits in a free trade zone and pays no tax, and that the environmental summary expected it to breach air quality standards for PM10 and NO2 during operation. The environmental authorisation came in June 2024 from then environment minister Robert Bouvier, with seven conditions, among them that Google drop drinking water for cooling in favour of chillers. In April 2026 President Yamandú Orsi toured the site and said the works were "muy avanzadas, más de lo que suponíamos" (very advanced, more than we assumed). Now the neighbours have gone to law. On July 29, 2026, four families living less than 100 metres from the site filed an appeal with the Ministry of Environment asking it to annul the authorisation granted to Eleanor Applications SRL, the company behind the Google project. The environmental study had identified them as sensitive receptors, one as the most vulnerable neighbour for noise, but they say they were never contacted, and they complain of industrial lighting and noise from night-time pipe flushing, load bank tests and generators. La Mañana reported that the permit file models the campus's 27 generators exceeding Uruguay's legal limit for nitrogen dioxide 17 times over if all run at once in a power cut. The appeal asks the ministry to annul the authorisation or, failing that, to change it to deal with the impacts; the ministry decides, and meanwhile construction goes on. Orsi met Google's global head of government affairs, Karan Bhatia, at the United Nations in September 2026, and the data center was one of the topics.

microsoft-microsoft-bergheim-inka-terra-.text: Microsoft broke ground on March 12, 2026 on a data center cluster in the Rhineland coal region of North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, with sites in Bergheim, Bedburg and Elsdorf, and building permits granted for Bedburg and Bergheim. Bergheim's data center, on the INKA terra nova industrial estate at Paffendorf, is under construction, and the current fight there is over its backup power. On August 19, 2026 the Cologne district government held a public hearing in Bedburg on objections to the emergency power supply for the first Bergheim-Paffendorf building, where Microsoft plans a plant of 36 diesel engines outside the building, Radio Erft reported. The objections come mainly from conservation groups, and BUND, the German conservation federation, says the diesel units would emit large amounts of CO2 and take up a great deal of farmland. Microsoft plans to keep up to 3,400 tonnes of diesel on the site as an emergency reserve and to install solar panels there, Radio Erft reported after questions from the local SPD. The city said Microsoft may draw only as much power as the operation needs, keeping supply in Bergheim and neighbouring towns stable, and the Greens want the waste heat used for a planned swimming and health centre, the ErftOase. Bergheim mayor Volker Mießeler called the groundbreaking a significant moment for the city. Critics doubt the jobs, since data centers are highly automated and few permanent posts remain after construction, and they question how Bergheim and the other host towns will share in the business tax; Germany's national data center strategy, adopted in March 2026, proposes a special allocation rule that still needs legislation. A similar hearing on 66 diesel engine units for the planned Bedburg data centers is due in November 2026, before the Cologne district government decides on permits for both towns' backup power.

microsoft-microsoft-grange-castle-dublin.text: Microsoft's Grange Castle data center campus, on Nangor Road in south Dublin, Ireland, is getting its own gas-fired power station, because Dublin's grid has no room for new data centers. When The Irish Times toured the campus in February 2026 it counted 13 data centers there, and Noelle Walsh, president of Microsoft cloud operations, said the company would get back to expanding now that the Dublin moratorium on new data centers had been lifted, pointing to "pent-up demand from the pause." Two buildings there, DUB14 and DUB15, won planning permission in 2021 and together cover 56,246 square meters, part of a 900 million euro development. In December 2022 Microsoft applied to Ireland's Environmental Protection Agency for an industrial emissions licence, the permit that lets a facility legally release pollution, to run a 170 megawatt gas-fired plant and 21 emergency diesel generators, telling the agency the new buildings sat in an area constrained for electrical capacity. The constraint is formal: EirGrid will accept no new data center grid connection applications in Dublin until 2028, a refusal that pushed Interxion to pause its expansion and preceded Dataplex going into voluntary liquidation after being denied power contracts. The Environmental Protection Agency granted the licence, and the plant, reported at about 100 million euro, is licensed to run eight hours a day every day of the year to meet the energy regulator's flexible demand policy, which requires standby generation that can be called on when the grid is stretched. The plant may not export power and is backed by up to 150 diesel generators if it fails; the plan also includes a 75 megawatt fuel cell installation. "The gas engines and generators will be used solely for the purpose of generating power for the installation," the agency said. Madeleine Johansson, a People Before Profit councillor, objected: "The plan for a private gas power plant is clearly a way for Microsoft to circumvent the new stricter criteria for data centres in the Dublin Region." Gas, she said, "is a fossil fuel and needs to be phased out", and while the plant does not add to grid congestion it adds to Irish emissions. Eoin Doherty, Microsoft's head of data center operations in Europe, the Middle East and Africa, told The Irish Times the campus serves governments, small businesses and large global companies. The gas plant remains Microsoft's answer to Dublin's grid constraint, which EirGrid does not expect to ease before 2028.

microsoft-microsoft-middenmeer.text: Microsoft's data center campus on the Agriport A7 business park near Middenmeer, in the municipality of Hollands Kroon, North Holland, Netherlands, is operating, and Microsoft wants to grow it from ten data center buildings to sixteen. Microsoft presented its expansion plan to the Hollands Kroon council in September 2025, after buying 50 hectares across the road for six more buildings, and expects to file its final application, covering an environmental permit and impact assessment, in the second half of 2026. The existing halls used 1.17 terawatt hours of electricity in 2025, more than one percent of all power used in the Netherlands, the national enterprise agency RVO reported in July 2026. From the start of construction until mid-2025, Microsoft invested nearly 12.5 billion euros at the site, about 5 billion in land and buildings and 7.5 billion in servers and other equipment, its Dutch data center unit's latest annual accounts show. Those accounts showed 458 full-time employees at Microsoft's data center arm in 2025, a year in which it paid 27 million euros in corporate tax. Water use has caused trouble before: in 2021 the regional paper Noordhollands Dagblad found the campus had used 84 million liters of drinking water, 75 million of it for cooling, after Microsoft and the municipality had told residents it would need only 12 to 20 million liters a year. Microsoft said the figure covered the water-heavy construction phase, and that cooling switches from outside air to water only above 25 degrees Celsius, which happened on six days in 2021. Microsoft also built ahead of its permits once before: NRC reported in November 2020 that it had started a second large data center without the required environmental permit, and farmers' group LTO argued the province, not the municipality, should decide because of the site's heavy emergency generators. Hollands Kroon granted the building's permit, for a hall called Het Venster, in January 2021, after setting aside nearly all of 64 objections over horizon pollution, a lack of public participation and high energy use. A November 2022 Council of State ruling still forced Microsoft to seek after-the-fact approval for nitrogen released during that construction, which NRC reported was still unresolved in February 2023, more than a year after building began. Robert Leever, a Hollands Kroon alderman, said Microsoft's earlier plan had come as "a great shock" to residents, and Nick Hengelman, who runs Microsoft's Dutch data centers, said the company had "learned from last time" and wanted to be transparent about its plans early on. In June 2026 Microsoft paid 44 million euros for 37.5 hectares of farmland in Middenmeer next to a site where grid operator TenneT is considering a new high-voltage substation, and has already applied for a grid connection there, NRC reported from land registry records. Hollands Kroon's coalition agreement says no new data centers will be allowed outside the existing Agriport A7 area, and only on two sites already zoned for it. A municipal spokesperson said the new farmland parcel is zoned for agriculture and greenhouses with no rezoning application under way, and that the municipality had earlier stopped a data center CyrusOne wanted to build on the same parcel, citing too many big developments for public participation to keep up. Microsoft says it has no data center plans for the new parcel yet, though it would like to build there one day; its final application for the six-building expansion is expected in the second half of 2026.

microsoft-microsoft-boydton.text: Microsoft's data center campus at Boydton, in Mecklenburg County, Virginia, has been operating since 2010 and hosts the Azure US East 2 region; its taxes now pay for about a quarter of the county's budget. Dominion supplies the power, and the Mid-Atlantic Broadband Cooperative's fiber network was described as a key reason Microsoft chose the county, which has taken about $2 billion of investment, the Richmond Times-Dispatch estimated. The campus exists because of a tax break written for Mecklenburg County: in 2008 Delegate Tommy Wright introduced a bill exempting data center equipment from sales tax, aimed at a county where unemployment was 6 percent and had lately been nearly twice that, and it passed the House 97-2 and the Senate 40-0, with a fiscal note estimating the state would forgo $1.54 million. Microsoft arrived two years later. Tax revenue from the complex now covers about a quarter of Mecklenburg's budget, has helped pay for a new high school and let the county cut its property tax rate; median household incomes, once slightly below neighboring Halifax County's, are now about 5 percent higher. Statewide, the exemption Wright's bill created now costs about $1.6 billion a year against $9.1 billion of annual economic activity from data centers, a figure the state comptroller's report put before the General Assembly in January 2026. Microsoft said it had created 300 jobs in the county by 2019, when a sixth expansion was announced with another 100 expected, and in May 2018 it bought 315 megawatts from Virginia solar projects, at the time the largest single corporate solar purchase in the United States. On June 29, 2023 Constellation Energy agreed to supply up to 35 percent of the campus's power from nuclear plants, matched hour by hour against what the data center actually draws rather than against an annual total.

microsoft-microsoft-columbia-quincy.text: Microsoft's data center campus in Quincy, a farming city on the Columbia River in Grant County, Washington, is one of eight in town whose taxes have rebuilt local services. Microsoft began building what was called one of the world's largest data centers there in 2006, drawn by cheap hydroelectric power, and twenty years later the company holds Quincy up as its national model. In January 2026 Microsoft promised to ask utilities to charge data centers enough to cover their own power and network upgrades without raising household bills, to cool new buildings with closed-loop water rather than local supply, and to take no local tax incentives. "If you want to visit what's probably the nicest high school in the state of Washington, you don't go to the neighborhood where Microsoft's headquarters is based," said company president Brad Smith. "You don't go next door to Amazon, you go to Quincy." Quincy collected $9.8 million in taxes in 2018 and $20 million in 2024. Total city revenues rose from $6 million in 2006 to $47 million in 2024, and state representative Alex Ybarra, who grew up there, says data centers now pay 57 percent of all the tax the city collects. The population has grown from 5,300 to 8,200, with a new library, police station, medical center, fire and ambulance stations and high school. The eight campuses around town, run by Microsoft, Sabey, Vantage, H5, CyrusOne, NTT Data and Oath, use 37 percent of the Grant County Public Utility District's power generation. Each building can run with 50 employees or fewer, but former mayor Patty Martin says the benefits may not hold up. "What about 10 years, 20 years from now, and these facilities are still here and the electrical grid, because now there's more people, there's more electric cars, there's not as much water running in the river because the snow packs aren't there," she said. In 2012 the state Pollution Control Hearings Board ordered Microsoft and other Quincy data centers to study the health impacts of diesel particle pollution from their backup generators. Martin, who pushed for the air quality rules over a decade ago, said she still does not think the permit limits are being enforced, and that she can see a Microsoft facility from her kitchen window. Microsoft, the largest of the Quincy operators, employs about 400 people there and marked its 20th year in town by donating $200,000 to local nonprofits. The company's pledge to keep other ratepayers' bills from rising now depends on the utilities that set rates, and in Quincy that is the Grant County Public Utility District.

microsoft-microsoft-cheyenne-logistics-d.text: Microsoft has run data centers in Cheyenne, in Laramie County, Wyoming, since 2012, and its Logistics Drive campus is adding on-site backup power. On April 3, 2026, Wyoming's air quality regulators approved a permit letting Microsoft install 30 natural gas fired engines and two emergency diesel generators there. That followed a July 2025 permit for 128 diesel emergency generators and 128 diesel storage tanks of 13,853 gallons each at the same site. Eleven days later, on April 14, 2026, Microsoft said it would roughly triple its Cheyenne footprint by buying 3,200 acres southeast of downtown, split between 3,000 acres of raw land and a 200-acre parcel on Wapiti Trail in Bison Business Park. It has also applied to the city for a 385-acre site east of College Drive and a 35-acre site south of Happy Jack Road. Rima Alaily, Microsoft's vice president and general counsel for infrastructure legal affairs, said the company was "really at the very start of the process and still working on the acquisitions." Microsoft held a public information session at Laramie County Community College in late May 2026, days after city leaders defeated a proposed pause on development. Resident Holly Spagnol asked about emissions, air quality, water and the heat the buildings give off. Company representative Jonathan Noble told the room, "We're taking this responsibility to build out this infrastructure very seriously." Noble said Microsoft works to make sure infrastructure costs for water or power are not shifted onto other ratepayers. Microsoft says it is not seeking tax incentives for the expansion, pays about $11 million a year in local taxes as the city's largest taxpayer, and that about 500 Cheyenne residents work for it full time. On April 3, 2026, Wyoming's air quality regulators approved a permit letting Microsoft install 30 natural gas fired engines and two emergency diesel generators there. That followed a July 2025 permit for 128 diesel emergency generators and 128 diesel storage tanks of 13,853 gallons each at the same site.

Eleven days later, on April 14, 2026, Microsoft said it would roughly triple its Cheyenne footprint by buying 3,200 acres southeast of downtown, split between 3,000 acres of raw land and a 200-acre parcel on Wapiti Trail in Bison Business Park. amazon-aws-hilliard-i-hayden-run.text: Amazon Web Services' first Hilliard data center sits at 5109 Hayden Run Road in Franklin County, Ohio, west of Columbus; construction began in 2015 and the campus opened AWS's first Ohio cloud region in 2016. The campus grew to five buildings, and in 2022 Hilliard's economic development director David Meadows said the fifth and final building there was being finished. Amazon has since built two more Hilliard campuses, one between Cosgray and Leppert roads and one on Scioto Darby Road, and in 2023 said it would spend an estimated $7.8 billion over six years on central Ohio data center operations, after $6.3 billion invested there since 2015. Hilliard offered Amazon a 15-year, 100 percent property tax abatement in 2019, Signal Ohio reported. The newer fight over power in Hilliard involves a natural-gas fuel cell plant planned for the Scioto Darby Road campus, a separate site with its own zoning and permit history from the Hayden Run buildings.

amazon-aws-hilliard-ii-cosgray-road.text: Amazon Web Services' second Hilliard data center campus sits on 104 acres between Cosgray and Leppert roads in Franklin County, Ohio, planned as a $200 million development; Amazon bought the site around October 2020 for about $14.5 million. By September 2026 the Cosgray campus had four buildings, WOSU Public Media reported, and the site sits directly across from a residential neighborhood. AWS assembled the site in two land deals, $11.76 million with the city and $2.8 million with the Hilliard City School District. The city's economic development director said in 2021 that construction would begin by the end of that year, and in May 2022 said Amazon planned to begin construction that fall. The city says AEP Ohio has told it the utility lacks the electrical capacity to serve all the data center buildings planned across Hilliard, a constraint that applies to the Cosgray campus as well as the newer Scioto Darby Road site. Power plants large enough to solve that shortfall are decided by the Ohio Power Siting Board and permitted by the Ohio EPA, not by Hilliard.

amazon-aws-hilliard-iii-scioto-darby.text: Amazon's third Hilliard data center campus stands on 142 acres at Scioto Darby Road and Interstate 270 in Franklin County, Ohio, where a 2022 plan calls for seven data center buildings and an American Electric Power substation. AEP Ohio wants to install 228 natural gas fuel cells on the site, a 72.9-megawatt power plant on about six acres to run the buildings. State law gives the Ohio Power Siting Board sole authority over a power plant that size, not the city of Hilliard. The Ohio Power Siting Board's approval of the fuel cell plant took effect September 22, 2025, and AEP withdrew its request for a city hearing that October, cancelling a Planning and Zoning Commission hearing that had been set for November 13, 2025. Amazon holds a 15-year, 100 percent property tax abatement on the campus, granted in 2019, and City Councilman Les Carrier said the fuel cells were never part of that deal: "They changed our agreement. I certainly did not approve a tax abatement for a fuel cell operation." Neighbors in the subdivision next door organized as Rise Up Hilliard. Resident Annette Singh told Signal Ohio: "I was unaware that putting in a data center meant putting in a mini gas power plant and all these other things with it." The Ohio EPA's air permit for the plant allows up to 1.45 million pounds of carbon dioxide a day, which the city compared to the output of 66,000 cars, and the campus also has 158 diesel backup generators. Hilliard appealed the Ohio EPA permit, arguing it was issued without notice to the city, then withdrew that appeal in September 2026. "From the beginning, we knew this would be an uphill battle because state law intentionally gives local communities very limited authority over facilities like this," City Council President Emily Cole said, adding that withdrawing the appeal was not an endorsement. The city plans to test air quality once the fuel cells are running.

amazon-aws-new-albany-beech-road.text: AWS New Albany Beech Road is an operating Amazon data center campus at 3180 Beech Rd in New Albany, Licking County, Ohio, on land Amazon began assembling in April 2020 when it bought 112 acres at Beech Road NW and Jug Street for about $21.8 million. City records show two buildings, Building B and Building E, totaling about 516,740 square feet. In August 2025 the city and AWS said the campus had finished two buildings, with the rest expected operating by end of 2025. Amazon is not done on Beech Road. In December 2022 it bought about 400 more acres along the road for $116.6 million, and filings with the Ohio EPA described up to 29 more data center buildings on both sides of Beech Road NW. In September 2023 the New Albany City Council approved a $3.5 billion tax deal for the first five of those buildings, on about 85 acres, with construction expected from 2025 through 2030. Amazon gets a 100% tax break for 15 years and 75% for 15 more on the new buildings, but must pay the city at least $352,000 a year, an amount that rises over time. "It's been an incredible easy place to do business", said AWS public policy manager Merle Madrid. The land Amazon bought in 2020 carried its own 15-year property tax abatement, approved separately by the city council. Tax deals for new buildings on Amazon's Beech Road land go to the New Albany City Council, and wetland permits for the expansion go to the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency.

amazon-aws-new-albany-crosby-court.text: Amazon Web Services' Crosby Court data center campus is a group of five buildings at 6645 to 6685 Crosby Court in Dublin, Ohio, in the Columbus area, which the directory Data Center Map lists as part of AWS's US East (Ohio) cloud region. Crosby Court lies in Franklin County. Amazon does not publish the locations of its data centers; the directory says its AWS listings are built from property records, permits, construction applications and news coverage. The Dublin buildings are separate from the five-data-center campus Amazon is building in New Albany, in Licking County, which the New Albany City Council cleared in 2023: 1.25 million square feet on 85 of the 439 acres Amazon bought along Beech and Miller roads, with construction running from 2025 to 2030. That $3.5 billion New Albany investment comes with a 30-year tax break, under which Amazon pays money directly to the city instead. Statewide, Amazon says it has invested more than $19.7 billion in AWS data centers in Ohio since 2015 and expects its planned investment to pass $23 billion by 2030, according to the City of New Albany.

amazon-aws-jerome-township-industrial-pa.text: Amazon's AWS Jerome Township data center campus sits on Industrial Parkway in Jerome Township, Union County, Ohio, just outside Plain City, one of two Amazon campuses in the township; the township approved the rezoning in 2021. Amazon's two Jerome Township campuses called for fire and emergency services 84 times in four years, and firefighters told the Columbus Dispatch they were often met by security guards and made to wait outside the gates for up to an hour. Two construction workers have died at Amazon's Jerome Township sites, one crushed at the nearby Warner Road campus and one in a fall at Industrial Parkway, and an April 2025 fire at Industrial Parkway occupied firefighters for 30 hours and caused $50 million in damage. Amazon said it and its contractors have "implemented additional mechanisms to further improve health and safety of their sites," and put the gate delays down to contractors' own background-check rules. On September 3, 2025 Jerome Township's trustees voted unanimously to halt new data center applications for nine months, catching four projects already filed. "We're finding now that we're experiencing data centers in real time, it is not tolerable for our residents," trustee Wezlynn Davis said. The halt did not cover applications already filed before the vote, and trustees later approved permits for some of those pending projects, the Columbus Dispatch reported. Davis said the pause would let the trustees move data centers from a permitted use to a conditional one, giving the township more oversight of future projects. Amazon's two campuses in the township carry 10-year tax abatements approved by Union County, so the township collects less commercial tax from them than it otherwise could. Jerome Township's trustees decide the township's zoning and are weighing the shift from permitted to conditional use for future data center projects.

amazon-aws-warner-road-union-county.text: Amazon Web Services' data center campus at 8657 Warner Road in Jerome Township, Union County, Ohio, near Plain City, is under construction. It is one of two AWS campuses in the township; the other is at 8619 Industrial Parkway, and each is reported to have four buildings. Trustees paused new data center approvals for nine months in September 2025 after complaints about noise from Amazon's buildings. Amazon's two data centers in the township hold 10 year tax abatements approved by Union County, so Jerome Township collects less commercial tax revenue than it otherwise would, Trustee Wezlynn Davis said. Amazon said it paid $1.1 million in Union County property taxes in 2024 and supports an average of 2,360 full time equivalent jobs a year in the county. “They feel like they're footing the bill for a mega-corporation,” Davis said of residents, since township police and fire serve the campuses. Trustees received complaints about a persistent “industrial buzz,” and Davis said: “According to the way that the noise is measured, it may be in compliance, but it still is not pleasant.” Amazon said it was surprised by the moratorium and pointed to “multi-million-dollar investments in engineering solutions that further reduce sound.” Davis said an April 2025 fire tied up firefighters for upwards of 30 hours, and she wants data centers to bring their own power generation and become a conditional rather than a permitted land use. Civil Solutions filed plans in April 2025 for two more campuses, 11 buildings on about 215 acres directly north and east of the Warner Road site. The township denied both zoning certificates on September 3 for failing its noise and nuisance rules, and Civil Solutions appealed; those applications predate the moratorium, which does not apply retroactively. The nine-month moratorium was due to run through June 2026, and no result on what the township adopted afterward has been published.

amazon-aws-jefferson-township-columbus.text: Amazon Web Services plans a data center campus in Jefferson Township, outside Jeffersonville in Fayette County, Ohio, next to the Honda and LG electric vehicle battery plant near Interstate 71 and U.S. Route 35. Amazon Data Services bought 589.8 acres in two parcels from the Martin Land Co. in January 2025 for $102.4 million, and AWS says it will invest an estimated $5 billion in Fayette County by 2030. The project remains proposed, and Amazon has not said when construction would begin. AWS vice president Roger Wehner said the campus would generate more than a hundred AWS jobs over five years, and the building trades council expects up to 1,500 union construction jobs. The Fayette County Commissioners granted AWS a Community Reinvestment Area agreement with a 30-year, 100 percent tax exemption on new structures at the site, and the county and Jefferson Township changed their zoning codes to list data centers as a permitted use on industrial land. At an April 2026 briefing for the commissioners, Ohio State University researcher Gabriel Lade said a new AES power station in Jefferson Township was built to support the Honda and LG plant and the coming AWS data centers, and that a separate gas-fired plant is planned in the township to power the servers off the grid. Lade told commissioners that data centers usually employ fewer people than manufacturing plants for the money invested, and commissioners said the county must remain "prepared, informed, and managed responsibly." Amazon has kept further project details, including a construction timeline, under wraps. Any further local approvals would run through the Fayette County Commissioners and Jefferson Township, which have already rewritten their zoning to allow data centers on industrial land.

amazon-aws-marysville.text: Amazon Web Services is building a $1 billion data center campus, known as Project Cosmo, on 55 acres at 14684 Industrial Parkway in the US 33 Innovation Park in Marysville, Union County, Ohio. Site preparation began in early 2026, with construction to follow through 2027, according to the City of Marysville. AWS plans two data center buildings totaling about 500,000 square feet. The Marysville City Council approved a reinvestment area agreement on March 10, 2025 that gives AWS a 30-year, 100 percent property tax exemption on the value of the data centers. In return AWS agreed to provide $15 million a year to the Marysville Exempted Village School District and the city over 15 years, according to Data Center Dynamics. The city says the abatement covers only the buildings, not the land, and that the company makes a payment in lieu of taxes each year the abatement runs. "We are proud to reinforce our long-term commitment to the state of Ohio with plans to expand AWS cloud infrastructure in the city of Marysville," said Roger Wehner, AWS's vice president of economic development. The city's data center FAQ gives no water figure for the campus; it says water use "will depend on the cooling system specified in the plan details" and that on-site wells are not allowed. It says utility upgrades are paid for by the developer and that the facility must comply with local noise ordinances. A second, larger data center is also approved in Marysville. Following a first reading on November 10, 2025, the City Council approved a reinvestment area agreement with Anadonna, LLC for a data center on about 600 acres known as Marysville South, south of the Union County Airport and west of Industrial Parkway, with 750,000 to 1 million square feet of buildings and more than $1 billion of investment. A Change.org petition started in March 2026 asked the Marysville City Council to reject "the proposed data center," citing water consumption, and closed with 5,757 supporters. AWS is also building elsewhere in central Ohio, with a five-building campus in New Albany and a planned $2 billion campus in Sunbury. The city expects infrastructure work, including a planned overpass, to run through 2026 and 2027 alongside the AWS construction. Tax and incentive agreements for Marysville data centers go before the Marysville City Council.

amazon-aws-sidney-galaxy.text: Amazon is building Project Galaxy, a $3 billion data center campus on the north side of Millcreek Road in Sidney, in Shelby County, Ohio. Sidney City Council approved a 30-year, 100 percent property tax abatement for it on October 27, 2025, and in April 2026 approved water and development agreements for the site. As of April 2026, City Manager Jon Crusey said the site plan was still under review and would be approved by city staff, not council. The tax break is worth between $180 million and $350 million over 30 years, or $2.4 million to $4.6 million for each of the 75 permanent jobs it is meant to bring. "That is not a fair trade for Sidney taxpayers, especially given the 30-year duration of the abatement," resident Maria Cera wrote in the Sidney Daily News. Two resident groups formed in response, Sidney Citizens for Responsible Development and Sidney Citizens Data Center Watch. In April 2026 the council approved a water agreement letting the campus draw up to 1 million gallons a day, though its projected use is 12,600 gallons a day, and a deal for Amazon to put up to $8 million toward widening Millcreek Road. At the meeting, resident Anne Abbott said the project was "approved without the proper research, health studies." Resident Kristin Allen has a separate public records dispute with the city over redacted agreements, pending before the Ohio Court of Claims. The city's site plan review, handled by staff rather than the council, is the next step before construction can begin.

amazon-aws-wilmington-ohio.text: Amazon has proposed a $4 billion data center, known as Cosler Farm, on a 471 acre site on the south side of Wilmington in Clinton County, Ohio. The plan calls for nine buildings totaling about 1.9 million square feet, and Amazon has promised the city $25 million in infrastructure upgrades, including a 1 million gallon water tower, plus 100 permanent jobs with an $8 million annual payroll. Homeowners near the site sued the city, alleging improper rezoning and a lack of public notice; the case later moved to federal court. On August 20, 2026, a federal judge's order forced Wilmington City Council to follow Ohio's open meetings law and give residents proper notice, leading to a special meeting on three data center ordinances. Council passed a generator noise ordinance 6 to 1 with emergency language, but a rezoning ordinance failed because it needed 75 percent approval, and council tabled it until September 3. “The silence was deafening on the council's part. They had an opportunity to ask us questions. They did not,” resident Brenda Shobe said. On September 3, 2026, council passed the rezoning with an emergency clause, which under Ohio law takes effect at once and blocks a referendum. Rachel Mary Brooks, whose home is near the site, sued in Clinton County Common Pleas Court to block it: “I asked the city's representatives if there was any actual harm in waiting the normal 30 days. They could not provide an answer.” The city agreed at a hearing not to act on the rezoning for a week and not to interfere with residents gathering signatures. Separately, residents Quintin Koger Kidd and Susan Croutwater had filed a citizen petition in July 2026 for a ballot measure setting limits on data center noise, lighting, emissions, water use and heat, and letting residents sue operators directly for violations. The Clinton County Board of Elections voted not to certify the petition, and on September 18, 2026 the Ohio Supreme Court ruled 5-1 that the measure could not appear on the November 3 ballot because it improperly let residents sue directly, a power cities do not have.

amazon-aws-pickaway-county.text: Amazon Web Services owns 234 acres on State Route 104 in Pickaway County, Ohio, for a possible data center, land it bought for $49.1 million in a deal that closed December 28, 2023, outside Southern Point between Commercial Point and Lockbourne. AWS has not filed a building plan, timeline or permit for the site since the purchase, and no work has been reported there. AWS said in April 2024 only that it was "constantly evaluating new locations based on customer demand" and "performing due diligence in exploring possible data center locations." The purchase is part of $7.8 billion AWS has committed to central Ohio data centers through 2029, and the company already runs campuses in nearby Franklin and Licking counties. In September 2023 Amazon also opened a 2,000-acre solar farm spanning Pickaway and Ross counties. A separate data center fight in Pickaway County involves a different company: EdgeConneX's planned campus in the village of Ashville, where in April 2026 the village council fast-tracked approval by declaring an emergency. In August 2026 the Ohio Supreme Court ruled the council's stated reasons for that emergency declaration were not valid, putting residents' referendum petition back on track for the Pickaway County Board of Elections to decide.

amazon-aws-hermiston.text: Amazon Web Services is building its first Hermiston data center campus on Livestock Road in Umatilla County, Oregon, with two buildings under construction as of September 2025, Oregon Public Broadcasting reported. The Hermiston City Council was scheduled to vote on September 14, 2026 to finalize a wastewater and domestic water agreement with AWS. No result of that vote has been published. The council approved a 25-year water service agreement with Amazon in February 2025, under which Columbia River water is pumped from October to March and stored about 1,500 feet underground in the basalt aquifer to cool Amazon's campuses. AWS pays to treat and inject at least 100 million gallons a year beyond its own cooling needs for the city's use, and Assistant City Manager Mark Morgan said AWS pays all construction costs and the same water rates as other customers. "A lot of people think (data centers) use a lot more water than they actually do," Morgan told the council. In August 2025 the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality fined Amazon $10,400 for violations at its Hermiston and Boardman sites, saying the Hermiston facility failed to monitor recycled water in 2024 and began building a new wastewater pond before submitting the plans for approval. The council also approved a sewer main project in Feedville Road and Highway 207 in March 2026, funded 73.6 percent by AWS, after annexing 800 acres south of Feedville Road with a hyperscale data center designation in fall 2025. The Hermiston City Council makes the local decisions on Amazon's water and sewer deals, meeting at City Hall, 180 NE Second St.

amazon-aws-boardman-olson-road.text: Amazon operates a data center campus on Olson Road in Boardman, Morrow County, in eastern Oregon, over an aquifer that supplies about 45,000 people, most of them through private wells. Amazon arrived in the county in 2008 and opened its first data center there in 2011; the Olson Road campus is operating, and Amazon has since built seven data centers in the county with five more under construction. Decades of fertilizer and dairy runoff had already pushed nitrate levels in basin wells above safe limits before Amazon arrived, and cooling water that evaporates at its data centers returns to farmland more concentrated, an investigation published November 25, 2025 found. Water entering Amazon's data centers measured 13 parts per million of nitrate; the wastewater leaving averaged 56, against Oregon's limit of 7. County commissioner Jim Doherty, a cattle rancher, began testing tap water in 2022 and declared an emergency that June after finding widespread illness in homes he visited; voters recalled him and a fellow commissioner that November. Resident Kathy Mendoza's well tested at up to 55.7 parts per million: "How can you live with yourself knowing that the water you put in people's houses is causing miscarriages or cancer?" Amazon has denied causing the contamination and on March 31, 2026 agreed to pay $20.5 million to settle a federal lawsuit, Pearson v. Port of Morrow, without admitting wrongdoing. The case continues against the Port of Morrow, Lamb Weston and other farms and companies, with plaintiffs seeking class-action status and a state-backed cleanup and health monitoring program.

amazon-aws-boardman-bombing-range.text: Amazon Web Services is building a data center on the west side of Bombing Range Road near Boardman, Morrow County, Oregon, south of the Highway 730 and Interstate 84 interchange. County filings from 2022 described four single-story buildings of 215,461 square feet each, plus a water treatment building, storage tanks and a security building, and the project cleared county zoning that March. The campus is under construction; filings said the first phase would build one data center and ancillary buildings, with Umatilla Electric Cooperative building an on-site substation. Amazon has been building data centers in Boardman since about 2011 and said in 2022 its Morrow County sites employed 461 people at an average wage of about $75,000. In May 2023 the Port of Morrow approved enterprise zone tax breaks worth about $1 billion for five new Amazon data centers, including this one. The deal exempts Amazon from nearly three-quarters of the property taxes other businesses pay, while the company pays about $5 million in community fees per project at construction and about $110,000 a year per data center to local schools and emergency services. Two Port of Morrow commissioners who owned Windwave Communications, a fiber supplier to Amazon's data centers, voted on the incentive deal; state ethics staff later sought penalties against three former officials over the conflict. Morrow County Commission chair David Sykes has defended the tax deals as a way to diversify an economy that lost its sawmill jobs and the Boardman coal plant. Amazon has not publicly said when each Bombing Range Road building will be finished.

Amazon already has about 800 acres of data centers running or being built around Boardman. Oregon lawmakers passed a law in 2025 meant to keep households from paying for the electricity that supplies data centers like this one.

amazon-aws-arlington-oregon.text: Amazon Data Services has bought about 376 acres at the Arlington Mesa Industrial Park, above the Columbia River town of Arlington in Gilliam County, Oregon, for a future AWS data center campus, and was buying another 30 acres from the Port of Arlington. The Arlington City Council agreed on August 7, 2024, to sell 375.605 acres to Amazon for $10,111,000; the port parcel was priced at $3 million. Amazon has said the campus is years away while it pursues permits, electricity and tax breaks, and that it plans 13 years ahead when choosing sites. Kevin Miller, Amazon's vice president of data centers, said the site sits close to the company's campuses in Morrow and Umatilla counties: "I think it could be equivalent to what we would have in nearby locations." The City of Arlington, the Port of Arlington and the Gilliam County Court signed a non-disclosure agreement with Amazon in 2022, and when the Times-Journal requested the sale agreement, the city released a redacted copy and charged attorney fees. Across Oregon, Amazon receives nearly $100 million a year in tax breaks on its data centers, far more than the $50 million it pays in local taxes and fees, and County Judge Cris Patnode said Gilliam County would instead negotiate under the Strategic Investment Program. "It's going to be an enhanced growth spurt for us and we're actually quite excited about it," Mayor Jeffery Bufton said. Judge Patnode said officials hope to put tax revenue into housing, schools, daycare and parks, while the port plans a workforce housing subdivision.

amazon-aws-wallula-gap.text: Amazon Data Services has proposed a data center campus at the Port of Walla Walla's Wallula Gap Business Park in Burbank, an unincorporated community in Walla Walla County, Washington. The company filed plans in May 2026 for what it calls the Attalia Data Center Campus, and the county ruled the application substantially complete on August 24, 2026. The first phase covers a 134 acre parcel and calls for three 220,000 square foot buildings, an industrial water facility and a pad for a future electrical substation. Amazon held a public open house on August 11, 2026, at Columbia High School in Burbank, and the atrium filled with attendees, many wearing shirts opposing data centers. Roger Wehner, Amazon's vice president of economic development, told the crowd that any major industrial project should draw questions, and that “we need to have this broader conversation.” Kennewick resident Bonnie Wescott compared the pace to the region's history with the Hanford nuclear site: “They went into Hanford real quickly and didn't have all the information.” Daniel Brown, a Walla Walla protestor at the open house, said, “There's multiple sides to this story, not just what Amazon says.” Amazon told the crowd the campus would use water equal to about 6 percent of the site's annual allocation, roughly a quarter of what local agriculture uses on the same acreage. Port officials have said the project would grow the county's tax base by half as it is built out over four phases. Public comment on the permit is open until 5 p.m. on October 12, 2026. After that, Walla Walla County's Community Development Department will issue a threshold decision on whether the project needs a full environmental impact statement, opening a second comment period before the county makes its final call on the application.

amazon-aws-lake-anna-tech.text: Amazon Web Services is building its Lake Anna Technology Campus, a data center campus on 153 acres at the corner of Kentucky Springs Road and Haley Drive in Louisa County, Virginia, next door to Dominion's North Anna nuclear station. AWS plans seven standard data centers, two specialty ones and an administration building, about 1.7 million square feet, drawing a minimum of 420 megawatts. Two 300 megawatt substations will serve it, one owned by Dominion and one by Rappahannock Electric Cooperative. Earthmoving began in mid-November 2024, after state agencies granted a memorandum of understanding and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers approved a wetlands permit. By the fall of 2025 the first data center shell was up and work on the support buildings was well underway, with Clark Construction as general contractor and the campus expected to be completed by 2027. The questions residents keep asking are about water and electricity. The campus is water cooled and will average 630,000 gallons a day at full build. Water comes from wells on the site, where the storage tanks are complete, until a pipeline from the county-owned Northeast Creek Reservoir is built. The raw water line was scheduled for January 2027. That reservoir has a safe yield of 3.2 million gallons a day and its current users take about 300,000, peaking at 500,000. Cuckoo District Supervisor Christopher McCotter said the build had been tolerable so far: "For the most part, so far this construction process has been bearable for Cuckoo residents. When there were issues like rocks on the road or muddy runoff into the lake, I can make a phone call to Clark and they work quickly to address the situation." Andy Wade, the county's economic development director, estimated a single data center here could return just over $2 million a year in tax revenue over a 15-year period. Elsewhere in Louisa County, a homeowner living across the road from AWS's Northeast Creek campus sued the company in federal court in August 2025 over dust, night noise, light and well water that turned brown, and a judge let the nuisance claim proceed. The campus sits in one of the Technology Overlay Districts the Louisa County Board of Supervisors created for data centers, whose standards the county calls its most restrictive, with limits on decibel levels and required buffers and setbacks. Under the county's process the performance agreement with Amazon came before the Board of Supervisors for public consideration three times, and the board is where residents take problems with the build. For the Lake Anna site that means McCotter, who represents the Cuckoo District.

amazon-aws-northeast-creek-technology.text: Amazon Web Services is building its Northeast Creek Technology Campus, 10 data center buildings on Jefferson Highway (Route 33) in Louisa County, Virginia, with construction that started in March 2025 and is due to finish in 2031. The campus, permitted by right in the county's Technology Overlay District, is now the subject of a federal nuisance lawsuit from a neighbor whose case a judge let move forward in July 2026. Austin Newsom, who lives on the district's border and runs a boat repair business, Central VA Marine, next to his home, told county officials that construction brought loud noise, clouds of dust and tap water that turned brown starting in March 2025. His lawsuit says construction vibration is cracking his house's foundation and is devaluing his home and disrupting drainage. "(My well has) made it through four major droughts we've had since the '50s and never had an issue with it," Newsom said. Amazon argued in court that the brown water, noise, air quality and light pollution "are each insubstantial," but U.S. District Judge Jasmine H. Yoon let the nuisance claim proceed while dismissing a separate injunction claim. A preliminary hearing in the case was scheduled for August 19, 2026; no result has been published. Board of Supervisors Chair Duane Adams said he had been in contact with the Newsoms several times and worked to get some of their concerns addressed. The county has pushed back on further AWS growth nearby: in July 2025 Amazon withdrew an application for a third campus near the Northeast Creek Reservoir after residents objected over water, farmland and schools. In January 2026 Amazon bought about 1,920 acres near the reservoir for about $72 million, and Adams said he would move to strip the Technology Overlay District designation from that land. "I have been very clear since June of 2025 that I'm opposed to any data center development on that property," Adams said.

amazon-aws-desper-creek-technology.text: No Amazon data center campus called Desper Creek appears in any filing or report found in Louisa County, Virginia; Desper Creek is the stream that bounds Amazon's Northeast Creek Technology Campus, which sits east of it off Jefferson Highway. That campus is under construction, and it is where the trouble is. Austin Newsom lives across the road from Northeast Creek and runs a boat repair and detailing business there. When construction started in March 2025 he began reporting problems to the county: trucks throwing up clouds of dust, noise late into the night, and light from the site coming into his children's bedroom. Then his tap water turned muddy brown, on and off, for months. The well had come through four major droughts since the 1950s without going bad. Newsom sued Amazon in August 2025 in the US District Court for the Western District of Virginia, at Charlottesville. He says construction vibration cracked his foundation, that drainage was disrupted, and that buyers walked away once they learned what was going up across the street. Amazon argued that the brown water, the noise, the diminished air quality and the light pollution were "each insubstantial and thus require dismissal of the entire nuisance claim," and says it has run street sweepers and water trucks to hold the dust down. Judge Jasmine H. Yoon let the nuisance claim go forward and threw out a separate claim for an injunction, with a preliminary hearing set for August 19, 2026. Duane Adams, who chairs the county board of supervisors, said he had treated the Newsoms as he does all his constituents and tried to be responsive, to help address issues affecting them and to help mitigate the circumstances. "One person can make a difference," Newsom said. Northeast Creek is Amazon's second campus in Louisa County and is planned at ten buildings with three substations, finishing in 2031.

Amazon argued that the brown water, the noise, the diminished air quality and the light pollution were "each insubstantial and thus require dismissal of the entire nuisance claim," and says it has run street sweepers and water trucks to hold the dust down.
Judge Jasmine H. Yoon let the nuisance claim go forward and threw out a separate claim for an injunction, with a preliminary hearing set for August 19, 2026.

Duane Adams, who chairs the county board of supervisors, said he had treated the Newsoms as he does all his constituents and tried to be responsive, to help address issues affecting them and to help mitigate the circumstances.
"One person can make a difference," Newsom said.
Northeast Creek is Amazon's second campus in Louisa County and is planned at ten buildings with three substations, finishing in 2031.

amazon-aws-louisa-county-third.text: Amazon Web Services withdrew its application for a third data center campus in Louisa County, Virginia, in late July 2025, two months after filing it. The plan would have put up to 7.2 million square feet of buildings on 1,370 acres of timberland near the Northeast Creek Reservoir, outside Mineral, an area TechTarget described as more than 1,000 football fields. AWS pulled the permit after strong pushback from residents and from Duane Adams, the supervisor for the Mineral District. Neighbors raised concerns about construction traffic on the area's narrow roads and the risk to the reservoir that supplies drinking water to central Louisa. AWS attorney Charles W. Payne Jr. said in a statement, "We have heard the community and appreciate the desire for more robust input in any future projects that may be brought forward in the county." In January 2026 AWS bought about 1,920 acres in central Louisa for about $72 million, including most of the withdrawn campus's land, most of it previously owned by Fisher Chewning L.C. Amazon told a reporter the purchase was "to help support water infrastructure needs in the area" and that future development "would involve community input, coordination with local leaders, and transparent public processes." Adams said he did not learn of the purchase until after it closed. Supervisors voted in January 2026 to ask the planning commission whether to remove the purchased land, along with the nearby Cooke Rail Park, from the county's Technology Overlay District, which would make a future data center harder to approve. The planning commission has pulled the public hearing on that question twice, most recently in April 2026 after a closed session on what it called "specific legal matters," and no new hearing date has been set.

amazon-aws-stevensburg-culpeper.text: Amazon Web Services is building a $500 million data center campus on 243 acres along Route 3 in Stevensburg, in eastern Culpeper County, Virginia, on a former horse farm. The Board of Supervisors approved rezoning the land from agricultural to light industrial in April 2022, by a 4 to 3 vote, after the Planning Commission recommended denial. The approved plan calls for two buildings totaling about 445,000 square feet, a six-acre Dominion substation and a new transmission line. Nearly 40 people spoke against the project at the supervisors' hearing. "We're here to protect peoples' investments," said Supervisor Susan Gugino, who voted no. Neighbors then sued in Culpeper County Circuit Court, arguing the rezoning was illegal spot zoning; landowner Alan Davis said he would go from "looking at horses in pastures" to "a 50-foot building with lights and security fencing." The circuit court had not ruled on the case as of the last local reporting. The State Corporation Commission has final approval of the new transmission line; supervisors asked Dominion in 2023 to use a shorter southern route to spare farmland. Gugino later said the county had approved the rezoning "in a most expedited fashion" without weighing its effects. County planning director Sam McLearen said Amazon has built a berm along most of Route 3 as required, with landscaping still to come. The site borders Salubria, an 18th century manor on the National Register of Historic Places, and sits across Route 3 from the Brandy Station battlefield; the Piedmont Environmental Council said the project would significantly alter the historic landscape. Construction on the first building was under way by October 2024, with Amazon hiring technicians who need Top Secret security clearances.

amazon-aws-manassas-tanner-way.text: AWS Manassas Tanner Way is an operating Amazon data center complex on Tanner Way, outside the City of Manassas in Prince William County, Virginia, about 400 feet from Great Oak, a 291-home subdivision. Residents there have complained since the spring of 2022 that the rooftop air conditioning units, not the servers, run without pause and keep them awake. "It's like being on a tarmac with an airplane engine running constantly," said Fred Kurst, who lives in Great Oak. Residents pressed the county for two years, taking their own decibel readings and asking supervisors to update a noise ordinance written in 1989. A county advisory group studied the problem starting in July 2023; its experts proposed limits of 52 decibels by day and 47 at night in residential areas. On October 30, 2025, the Board of County Supervisors instead voted 5 to 2 for looser limits, 73 decibels by day and 68 at night in industrial areas, above the 67 and 62 its own paid consultants had recommended. "It (the new ordinance) doesn't provide any meaningful relief at all," said Kathy Kulick, a Gainesville resident who served on the advisory group. Amazon's Sarah Georgiades, the company's head of community engagement, said a completed sound study "demonstrates that (Amazon Web Services') efforts have significantly reduced sound, and that AWS is in compliance with applicable law." Enforcement of the new limits falls to Prince William County, which set aside $219,000 to hire two engineers to check compliance; officials estimate some facilities could take one to two years to comply.

amazon-aws-manassas-innovation-drive.text: The data center at 9680 Innovation Drive in Manassas, Prince William County, Virginia, is a single 213,320-square-foot building on a 31-acre lot. County records compiled by the Coalition to Protect Prince William County in February 2024 show the building is owned by STACK Innovation Holdings LLC, an affiliate of STACK Infrastructure, not Amazon. Amazon Data Services sold land nearby, an 81-acre property at 9650 Innovation Drive and a parcel on University Boulevard, to STACK Innovation Holdings for $87.4 million in December 2021, according to county records reported by Data Center Dynamics. Amazon had bought both plots in 2018 for $29 million; no source confirms Amazon Web Services as the building's tenant. Prince William County had 45 operating data center buildings covering about 8.6 million square feet, according to that February 2024 compilation. On September 22, 2026 the Board of County Supervisors voted 8-0 to end by-right data center development countywide, so future projects need a special use permit from the board, though buildings already built or under way, including this one, are unaffected. Rachel Ellis of the Coalition to Protect Prince William County called the new rule "smoke and mirrors" and said "there's no teeth to this." The county kept a 90-day grace period before the new rule takes effect.

amazon-aws-manassas-vulcan-lane.text: Amazon Web Services owns 113 acres at 8401 and 8501 Vulcan Lane outside Manassas in Prince William County, Virginia, beside the Vulcan Materials quarry, zoned for a data center but with no site plan yet filed. Amazon Data Services bought the land in January 2024, along with 27 acres nearby on Century Park Drive, about 140 acres in all for roughly $152 million, according to the Washington Business Journal. On September 22, 2026 the Prince William County Board of Supervisors voted 8-0 to end by-right data center development countywide, ending the fast, no-vote permitting that had covered Vulcan Lane. New projects will instead need a special use permit, with a public hearing and a board vote, after a 90-day grace period for pending plans. Supervisor Tom Gordy, who pushed the change, said in June 2026 it would stop "land grabs that displace our existing small businesses and the jobs they bring." The county's new noise rules will also apply to anything built on Vulcan Lane. In late October 2025 supervisors voted 5 to 2 to cap industrial-area noise at 73 decibels by day and 68 at night, below the previous 79 and 72 but above the 67 and 62 recommended by consultants the county paid about $2 million. "It (the new ordinance) doesn't provide any meaningful relief at all," said Kathy Kulick, a Gainesville resident who sat on the county's data center ordinance advisory group. Land already finished, being built, or with a site plan past the county's quality control check keeps by-right status. Vulcan Lane's undeveloped parcels do not, so any Amazon proposal there now goes before the Board of County Supervisors for a special use permit vote.

amazon-aws-manassas-nokesville-road.text: Amazon Web Services is building a 250,000-square-foot data center at Dean Drive and Wellington Road in the city of Manassas, Virginia. AWS bought the two vacant parcels, at 9720 Dean Drive and 9811 Nokesville Road south of Wellington Road and Route 28, in 2021 for a combined $6.6 million, and plans a three-building complex with access from Dean Drive. The project can be built by right under the site's industrial zoning and includes an additional electric substation. The city estimates it will bring $4 million to $6 million a year in tax revenue. "There were no incentives used by city council to attract these facilities, so this is all net new revenue to our community," said Patrick Small, the city's economic development director. Small said the city pressed AWS on the building's design because the site is an entryway to the historic downtown: "I know the planning department and my department spent a lot of time with AWS, insisting that...it needs to be one of the nicer looking data centers they've ever built." The city said in January 2025 that construction had begun. No report since has given a completion date or the building's power capacity in megawatts.

amazon-aws-stafford-potomac-church.text: Amazon's Potomac Church Tech Center stands on 49.9 acres on Old Potomac Church Road in the Falmouth district of Stafford County, Virginia, near U.S. 1 and Stafford Hospital. The first of its two data center buildings received a certificate of occupancy on May 1, 2026, and is now in service; the second is targeted for July 2028. Supervisors voted 7 to 0 for an incentive agreement with Amazon in January 2024, projecting a $6 billion investment in the county. Amazon is paying about $75 million for a reclaimed water plant at the county's Aquia Wastewater Treatment Plant so treated wastewater, rather than drinking water, cools the buildings. Until that system is running, the first building uses drinking water and the second building's occupancy is limited. An Amazon spokesperson said ten years of data show the campus needs cooling water only about 4 percent of the year, in the hottest months. In August 2026 supervisors voted 4 to 2 to amend the project's terms after complaints about road damage, generator emissions and water sharing. Amazon dropped a request for more drinking water and replaced its duty to build road improvements with a $10 million cash payment, against about $3 million in road work county staff said was needed. Supervisor Tinesha Allen asked that the money go first to a stretch of Old Potomac Church Road that speakers said construction trucks had buckled. The campus's diesel generators were approved in March 2025, before stricter state emissions rules took effect on July 1, 2026, and county staff said replacing them would delay the second building two to four years. A daycare sits about 400 feet from the nearest building; resident Jeff Eastland told supervisors the generators' emissions were a health risk that close to it. Amazon's attorney said the generators run only for emergencies and testing under state air permits.

amazon-aws-cosner-tech-spotsylvania.text: Amazon's Cosner Tech Campus, a 1.9 million-square-foot data center on 329 acres off Massaponax Church Road near Fredericksburg in Spotsylvania County, Virginia, was approved by the county's Board of Supervisors in 2023 and is under construction, not yet operating. It is the only one of Spotsylvania's approved data centers to commit to a 55-decibel noise limit measured at the property line, tighter than the county's standard 65. The campus has already drawn state enforcement. The Virginia Department of Environmental Quality fined Amazon Data Services $72,067.80 after a May 2025 power outage during commissioning started backup diesel generators whose pollution controls failed, pushing nitrogen oxide emissions over the permitted limit. An Amazon spokesperson said the equipment failed before the company had taken occupancy, that Amazon reported it within the required window, and that the generators are now in compliance. Spotsylvania bans data centers from using drinking water for cooling on a permanent basis, so Cosner is one of three approved sites allowed temporary water from the public system until a privately financed wastewater-reuse system is ready, which the county has scheduled for Cosner in the 2028-2029 cooling season. Opposition to data centers has grown since Cosner was approved. amazon-aws-carter-s-store-tech.text: Amazon's Carter's Store Tech Campus, a proposed data center campus of about 2.6 million square feet on 313 acres along Flippo Drive east of Interstate 95, south of Fredericksburg in Spotsylvania County, Virginia, has its rezoning but no construction schedule. Amazon Data Services filed to rezone 314 acres at 8432 Flippo Drive from Rural to Industrial-1 for data centers and a substation, to be built in phases by 2035. Carter's Store is one of four campuses Amazon filed for in 2023 around the Carter's Store area, with Summit Crossing, Cosner and Orrock, and documents suggested an investment of around $1 billion in each. The land is mostly undeveloped woodland. In October 2024 the county said there was no construction schedule yet, "but preliminary discussions are underway to begin proffered construction traffic studies," which must be done before a site plan can be approved. Spotsylvania has since turned more skeptical of data centers. In February 2026 the Board of Supervisors began requiring a special use permit for every data center, ending by-right development even on industrial land, and the county does not let data centers use drinking water or dig wells for cooling. In August 2026 the board voted 4-2 for a resolution urging Gov. Abigail Spanberger to enact a statewide moratorium "in order to allow the Commonwealth to study and determine whether data center development should continue to be permitted and, if so, under what conditions." Supervisor Drew Mullins, who voted no with Deborah Frazier, called the idea that Richmond would solve the problem "a pipe dream" and said: "We can be the moratorium. Each applicant comes before us, and we scrutinize what they're doing." Supervisor Jacob Lane said he was voting for the constituents protesting the industry, including the group Safeguard Spotsy. Later in August the supervisors voted 3-2 to amend the Comprehensive Plan so that data centers take up no more than 45% of the county's industrial land. The county has approved eight data centers occupying 1,756 acres, with 10 more applications pending. "I think it does send a clear message that we want to pump the brakes a little bit," said Supervisor David Goosman. Carter's Store already has its zoning, so the next step is Amazon's site plan, which needs the proffered traffic studies before county staff can approve it; the Spotsylvania County Board of Supervisors decides any new data center permits and rezonings. No construction start at Carter's Store has been reported; the latest county-wide reporting is from August 2026.

amazon-aws-summit-crossing-tech.text: Amazon's Summit Crossing Tech Campus covers about 232 acres in Spotsylvania County, Virginia, near the Caroline County line. The county rezoned the land from rural to industrial in October 2023, one of four Amazon rezonings approved that night, so Amazon Data Services could build a data center campus there. By January 2026, Amazon had buildings going up on the site. Unlike two of Amazon's other Spotsylvania campuses, Summit Crossing will not get temporary drinking water for cooling while the county builds a wastewater reuse system; county officials say it "will not be needing bridging." Its permit caps noise at 65 decibels, with a test required before each building can open, and it calls for cleaner Tier 4 diesel backup generators, the standard the county now requires of every approved project. Under a 2024 performance agreement, Spotsylvania pays Amazon back 60 percent of the added tax revenue from its data centers, up to $93.3 million against a projected $207 million increase over 15 years, in exchange for at least $6 billion of investment countywide by 2040. County spokesperson Michelle McGinnis said in January 2026 there was not yet enough information to say when that tax revenue would start being collected. In August 2026 supervisors voted 3 to 2 to cap data centers at 45 percent of the county's industrial land in its draft comprehensive plan, below the 55 percent county staff had recommended. Approved projects already total about 15.5 million square feet; supervisors are to revisit the limit once construction starts on three quarters of that or at the next five year plan update.

amazon-aws-mattameade-orrock-tech.text: Amazon's Mattameade Tech Campus, also known as the Orrock Tech Campus, sits in Woodford on Orrock Lane and Stonewall Jackson Road, on the line between Spotsylvania County and Caroline County. Amazon Web Services plans 11 two-story data center buildings and a central administration building on about 1,143 acres southeast of the Interstate 95 and Mudd Tavern Road interchange, with at least 770 megawatts of capacity by 2027. The buildings go on the Caroline side, about 916 acres that Caroline supervisors rezoned on October 24, 2023 into a Planned Innovation, Research and Technology district. Caroline created that district two weeks earlier to allow data centers while keeping out uses common in the county such as distribution centers. The Spotsylvania piece, 158 acres on the east side of Mallard Road about half a mile south of Mudd Tavern Road, was rezoned from agricultural to light industrial on October 10, 2023 for the utility buildings that will serve the campus. No one spoke at that hearing, and Spotsylvania supervisors approved it 5 to 2. Caroline has no water or sewer capacity in that part of the county, so Spotsylvania will supply both, and in exchange the counties split every local tax the campus produces, 57.5 percent to Caroline and 42.5 percent to Spotsylvania. Spotsylvania supervisors approved the joint resolution on their consent agenda on November 12, 2024, and Caroline's board followed on November 14. The Free Press reported a 40 year projection of $371.1 million for Spotsylvania. The state Commission on Local Government found in December 2024 that the deal was likely to support both counties' growth; it runs for 40 years after the first million square feet is built, which the counties expected in 2027, so sharing would last to about 2067. The counties projected the campus would average about $22.4 million a year after its tenth year, $12.9 million for Caroline and $9.5 million for Spotsylvania. Spotsylvania's ban on drinking water for permanent data center cooling applies to Amazon here even though the buildings stand in Caroline. The campus is designed to be cooled with recycled water pumped from Spotsylvania's Massaponax Wastewater Treatment Plant, which Amazon agreed to fit with a Level 1 reuse system. Until that is done Spotsylvania will supply drinking water as a bridge, and the county's schedule has reuse water reaching Mattameade for the 2029 to 2030 cooling season, a year after Cosner Tech and Powerhouse 95. Bridging water across the county's data center sites is projected to peak at about 1.1 million gallons a day in 2028. Amazon applied to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers in February 2025 for permits covering wetland and stream impacts, offering to buy 6.48 wetland credits and 2,346 stream credits. The plans include three substation pads, stormwater ponds, a water treatment plant, and pickleball and basketball courts. Sargent Corporation, doing the earthwork on what it describes as a 1,300 acre site, calls the job the largest in its history, with phase one under way and overall completion targeted for March 2027. Spotsylvania lists Whiting-Turner as the contact for neighbors of the Mattameade sites, at 804-215-6653. The rezonings, incentive agreements and revenue split are settled; what remains is Amazon's Army Corps of Engineers permit for wetland and stream impacts. Recycled cooling water from Spotsylvania's Massaponax plant is scheduled to reach the campus for the 2029 to 2030 cooling season. Sargent, the most recent to report on the site, puts overall completion at March 2027.

amazon-aws-birchwood-king-george.text: Amazon's Birchwood project covers 869 acres at the site of the former Birchwood Power Facility, north of the Rappahannock River on the east side of Fredericksburg, in King George County. Amazon told Virginia officials it planned to invest up to $6 billion in 17 data centers there, according to a report on the resulting court case. On December 19, 2023, the King George Board of Supervisors approved a performance agreement and zoning changes clearing the way for the project. Amazon says it then bought the property for almost $169 million and spent $6 million advancing the project. A newly elected board majority took office and rescinded that agreement at its first meeting, on January 2, 2024. Supervisor Cathy Binder, who had voted for the rezoning despite concerns about the company's control of a water intake on the Rappahannock, asked the new board to reconsider it. Amazon sued the county in circuit court in May 2024, arguing it had vested property rights under the approved rezoning and that the county's zoning administrator had missed a legal deadline to certify those rights. Curry Roberts, the retired president of the Fredericksburg Regional Alliance, asked: "What company is going to build in a county that doesn't honor an approved performance agreement?" Judge J. Bruce Strickland ordered limited discovery in the case in January 2026. King George has tried to use a new state law, in effect since July 1, 2026, to limit what Amazon can obtain in discovery; Amazon argues the law should not apply retroactively. A trial was scheduled for September 2026, after an earlier date in May 2026 was pushed back.

amazon-aws-devlin-technology-park-bristo.text: Amazon Web Services bought 189 acres in the Devlin Technology Park in Bristow, Prince William County, Virginia, where it plans to build data centers. The $700 million sale from Stanley Martin Homes closed in November 2025, on land zoned for up to 3.5 million square feet of data center space after county supervisors approved the rezoning in November 2023. Amazon has not said what it will build there or when construction might start. The rezoning followed a fight that lasted through an overnight Board of Supervisors meeting in November 2023, when the board voted 5 to 3 in favor. Residents challenged the vote in court and lost, both at trial and on appeal. "There's been pushback since day one. People are not happy about this whatsoever. This is like the last straw," said nearby resident Catherine O'Connor, who said she worries about truck traffic, water and the power grid. The county board has grown more skeptical of the industry since the vote. Chair Deshundra Jefferson, who took office afterward, said of Amazon: "[Amazon] paid an eye-popping sum of money for that land. Surely, they can pay more in taxes." Supervisor George Stewart, elected in November 2025 after campaigning to limit data centers, said residents should not end up "paying their energy bill." Amazon already owns or leases more than 50 data centers around Prince William and nearby counties. The Devlin land is zoned and ready, but no construction has been reported since the sale closed. The next lever residents have is the county board, which sets the tax rate on data center equipment and, under Jefferson, has pushed to raise it.
