The rezoning followed a fight that lasted through an overnight Board of Supervisors meeting in November 2023, when the board voted 5 to 3 in favor.
Residents challenged the vote in court and lost, both at trial and on appeal.

"There's been pushback since day one. People are not happy about this whatsoever. This is like the last straw," said nearby resident Catherine O'Connor, who said she worries about truck traffic, water and the power grid.
The county board has grown more skeptical of the industry since the vote.
Chair Deshundra Jefferson, who took office afterward, said of Amazon: "[Amazon] paid an eye-popping sum of money for that land. Surely, they can pay more in taxes."
Supervisor George Stewart, elected in November 2025 after campaigning to limit data centers, said residents should not end up "paying their energy bill."
Amazon already owns or leases more than 50 data centers around Prince William and nearby counties.
The Devlin land is zoned and ready, but no construction has been reported since the sale closed.
The next lever residents have is the county board, which sets the tax rate on data center equipment and, under Jefferson, has pushed to raise it.

amazon-aws-erin-s-run-sterling.text: Amazon's Erin's Run data center campus consists of three buildings at 23825 Erin's Run Drive in Sterling, just west of Dulles International Airport, in Loudoun County, Virginia, according to the Baxtel data center directory. The directory lists the buildings as IAD-120, IAD-121 and IAD-122, part of Amazon Web Services' US East region in Northern Virginia. No hearing, dispute or complaint naming this campus has been reported. Loudoun County has more than 200 data centers operating and 100 more in the pipeline, and data center tax revenue pays for 45 percent of the county's budget, according to WJLA. On the same road, Prologis owns a 94-acre site including 23845 Erins Run Drive with three data centers built around 2019, totaling 475,000 square feet, and in 2024 asked Loudoun to rezone it so a warehouse complex could be replaced with more data centers up to 100 feet tall. A Prologis spokesperson said the aim was "future-proofing our buildings", and the Business Journal reported the company may have been trying to lock in data center zoning amid a county crackdown on by-right use. Elsewhere in Sterling, neighbors of data centers have flooded the Board of Supervisors with complaints about noise and generator fumes. After a power failure on July 16, 2026 sent Vantage Data Centers' Ashburn II campus on Glenn Drive in Sterling onto diesel backup generators, one homeowner told WJLA: "This data center has been a curse on our life here." Vantage said the state environment department had reviewed its operating data and confirmed emissions had stayed well below permitted levels. Dominion Energy has warned the county board that backup generator use may become more frequent because of growing demand on the grid. Land use decisions for data centers in Loudoun rest with the Board of Supervisors, whose chair, Phyllis Randall, was set to meet residents living near the Vantage campus in late July 2026.

amazon-aws-reeds-farm-lane-dulles.text: Amazon Web Services plans three data centers on its 90-acre parcel at 42139 Reeds Farm Lane in Sterling, in the Stone Ridge area of Loudoun County, Virginia, southwest of Washington Dulles International Airport. The buildings would be two or three stories tall; total square footage has not been disclosed. Amazon's data center arm bought the parcel in July 2019 for $116.4 million from an affiliate of White Peaks Capital, which had paid $98.67 million for it hours earlier the same day. Amazon bought two more parcels nearby at the end of 2021 for $146 million, and Microsoft owns a large tract between the two Amazon sites. The Northern Virginia Electric Cooperative bought land at the site from the Inova Health Foundation in May 2022 for $7 million for a substation and applied to the county for a permit that September. Loudoun County has since tightened how data centers get approved: supervisors voted 7 to 2 in March 2025 to end by-right development, so new projects now need a special exception and a public hearing, while letting 22 applications already filed continue under the old rules. On September 16, 2026 the board voted 7-1-1 to direct staff to draft a resolution pausing new applications for up to 12 months; the pause is not yet in force, and a final vote is due at the October 20 meeting. Supervisors Juli Briskman and Laura TeKrony have separately proposed ending the 2025 grandfathering, which would send pending applications to public review; the board is due to take that up October 6.

amazon-aws-pathfinder-plaza-sterling.text: Amazon Web Services' data center campus at 45900 Pathfinder Plaza in Sterling, Loudoun County, Virginia, has been running since 2017; Amazon Data Services bought the 33-acre site for $135.75 million on June 24, 2024. The purchase covered three one-story buildings totaling about 442,000 square feet, known as TransDulles Centre 2. The seller was a CBRE Investment Management fund that had bought the buildings in 2018 for about $111 million, when the site was already leased to what CBRE called a "global cloud computing platform." An AWS spokesperson said only that the company is "constantly evaluating new locations based on customer demand." Amazon owns 26 parcels totaling 514 acres in Loudoun County, not counting land it leases through affiliates. More than 200 data centers operate in Loudoun County, and supervisors say data center taxes fund 45% of the county's budget. On September 16, 2026 the Board of Supervisors voted 7-1-1 to direct county staff to draft a resolution pausing new data center applications for up to 12 months; the pause is not yet in force, and a final vote is due at the board's October 20 meeting. "This pause is a major step forward. Now we have the breathing room required to complete the critical work of revising our regulations to protect our communities," said Algonkian District Supervisor Juli Briskman, who brought the proposal. The pause would not reach buildings already operating, like Pathfinder Plaza, and no expansion or new filing for this site has been reported.

amazon-aws-renaissance-technology-park-h.text: Amazon Web Services is the end user of Renaissance Technology Park, a 60-acre data center campus that Starwood Capital Group is building on Redskin Drive in Herndon, in Fairfax County, Virginia. Amazon Data Services filed for state air permits in 2024 for its first two buildings there, IAD-500 at 13860 Redskin Drive and IAD-501 at 13876 Redskin Drive, asking to install 72 stationary engine generators and two transitory generators. The Fairfax County Board of Supervisors approved Starwood's special exception on July 19, 2022, for four data center buildings totaling about 2.1 million square feet, a 6-acre electrical substation and support buildings, with the first building up to 102 feet tall. That makes it the largest data center campus in Fairfax County. Starwood bought the warehouse park for $134.1 million in 2019 and began demolishing the 1970s and 1980s warehouses in 2021. The building permit for 13860 Redskin Drive was approved in February 2024, and the later buildings are to follow as "market conditions" allow. The campus is growing. In June 2023 a Starwood affiliate paid $25 million for the nearly 30-acre former Word of Grace Christian Church property at 13832 Redskin Drive, once part of a Washington Commanders training facility, which the Renaissance park surrounds. Its air permit application describes two more data centers there, a 60-megawatt Building E of about 406,000 square feet and a 32-megawatt Building F, with 62 generator engines. County staff approved the site plan on November 19, 2025, and a county planner found the site "suitable" and "fully consistent" with local ordinances. Fairfax County's permit record shows the building permit for Building F, at 2850 Towerview Road, was issued on August 28, 2026. The school next door is the new concern. The Word of Grace site is less than a mile from the former King Abdullah Academy campus, which Fairfax County Public Schools planned to reopen as a high school, and FCPS said it was "monitoring" the data center project. That school, Skyview High School, opened this fall at 2949 Education Drive, the county's first new high school in nearly two decades. County rules adopted in 2024 require data centers to be at least 200 feet from residential property lines, but set no such distance from schools. Those rules also require noise studies before and after construction and keep backup generators 300 feet from homes. Starwood's generator permits go through the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality, which approves the air permits for the diesel engines. The Fairfax County Board of Supervisors sets the county's data center rules, which it tightened after residents raised noise, water, air pollution and energy concerns.

amazon-aws-mallory-drive-chantilly.text: Amazon Web Services' data center at 3980 Virginia Mallory Drive in Chantilly, in Virginia's Fairfax County, sits on part of the 46.4 acres Amazon bought in early 2021 for $55.9 million. County records showed AWS was granted building permits for the data center, and for its plumbing and gas, in April 2022, with an investment of around $30 million; a separate support building at 3980A Virginia Mallory Drive was still awaiting its permit. The site lies between Route 50 and a group of office buildings, just south of Dulles International Airport, a few minutes west of the Sully Historic Site. The permit filings did not include building specifications. Neighbors raised objections at a Sully District council meeting on June 28, 2023. Carol Anne Ohrnberger of the Pleasant Valley neighborhood said she had paid a premium for a lot backing onto land she was told was zoned for parkland: "Now I'm hearing that zoning can possibly change. How is that possible?" "The area that's parkland is going to stay parkland," replied Sully District Supervisor Kathy Smith, who said the applicant would use about 12 acres at the front of the property and hoped to donate most of the rest to the park authority. Residents also asked about the water needed to cool data centers. "I'm getting the feeling that people want to hear me say, 'I'm gonna stop this.' That's not my legal responsibility," Smith said. Amazon already has several data centers in Chantilly and a large footprint across Northern Virginia. Across Route 50, the developer Penzance broke ground in November 2025 on a 45-megawatt, 240,000-square-foot data center at 4151 Auto Park Circle that Amazon Web Services will lease, due to open in the first half of 2027. In September 2024 the Fairfax County Board of Supervisors voted 8-2 to tighten its data center rules after a four-hour meeting with more than 50 speakers. The amendment requires data center buildings to be at least 200 feet from residential property lines and backup generators 300 feet, requires cooling and other equipment to be enclosed or screened, keeps data centers at least a mile from Metro stations, and requires noise studies before and after construction. The Fairfax County Board of Supervisors, including the Sully District supervisor, sets the county's data center rules, and larger data centers outside the I-5 and I-6 districts now need its special exception approval. By November 2025, Northern Virginia Magazine described Amazon Web Services as operating a cluster of three data centers on Virginia Mallory Drive, which it called the Virginia Mallory Campus.

amazon-aws-haymarket.text: Amazon Web Services operates a data center campus on John Marshall Highway in Haymarket, Prince William County, Virginia, across from the Novant Health UVA Haymarket Medical Center near Interstate 66. One building was already operating by 2017, and a second was completed on adjacent land by 2018; no more recent count of buildings or expansions has been reported. The campus set off one of the region's longest power line fights. Dominion Energy needed a six mile transmission line to serve it, first proposed as overhead wires along the Rural Crescent and estimated at $51 million; residents fought the plan for years over property values and the historic landscape. "In our judgment, the root problem is the Haymarket location for the Amazon data center," state Del. Bob Marshall and Sen. Richard Black wrote to Amazon founder Jeff Bezos in 2015. The fight ended in 2018 when Dominion agreed to bury three miles of the line, and the final project cost $221 million, more than four times the original overhead estimate, the Prince William Times reported. Data center fights in Prince William County have grown since. Regional grid operator PJM is now weighing 14 new transmission proposals affecting the county, worth $16.7 billion combined, driven largely by data center demand. "It's very clear that the whole reason the grid needs to expand is the data center load," said Karen Sheehan of the Coalition to Protect Prince William County.

Regional grid operator PJM is now weighing 14 new transmission proposals affecting the county, worth $16.7 billion combined, driven largely by data center demand.
"It's very clear that the whole reason the grid needs to expand is the data center load," said Karen Sheehan of the Coalition to Protect Prince William County.

amazon-aws-kline-township-schuylkill.text: Kline Township supervisors have until September 30, 2026 to decide on Amazon Web Services' land development plans for a proposed data center campus off Lofty Road south of McAdoo in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, after granting Amazon an extension to answer comments from the township's engineers and consultants. The Amazon data center, dubbed Project Brewster, would put nine data centers plus administration, water and security buildings, 2.1 million square feet in all, on the former Brewster Development land across from van Hoekelen Greenhouses, which had been approved for warehouses. At the township planning commission's first hearing on June 30, 2026, Amazon development executive Evan Caso said the campus is about 1 million square feet smaller than the Brewster warehouse plan, and Amazon would realign Lofty Road near Route 309 and add a traffic light at its own cost. Amazon's Becky Ford said the campus would bring 400 to 500 full-time jobs, and the company will pay for upgrades to the Kline Township Municipal Authority's system and to PPL's. PPL's Jane George said customers should not see a rate increase and that "we are forecasting that customers will actually see a decrease in their rates." The planners and the public pressed on water and noise. Caso said the site may draw up to 15,000 gallons a day for workers and restrooms, and on cooling: "We use water for cooling less than 2% of the year," he said. "If we're allowed 100,000 gallons per day, that doesn't necessarily mean we're drawing 100,000 gallons per day every day." Neither Caso nor Ford could estimate yearly water use, and the authority's representatives said a new water main through Haddock would be needed. Amazon also wants its diesel backup generators exempted from the township noise ordinance, and its representatives gave varying answers on how often they would be tested. "I beg this committee to not approve their request to be able to exceed the decibels," said Jackie Joyce, the closest neighbor to the site. "I'm kind of appalled by the lack of specificity in a lot of questions that were ask for the answers of them," said Dan Krivenko of Lofty. Crowds have followed the project from the start: an overflow crowd forced the township to cancel its December 2025 meeting, and the June hearing was held under heavy security because of "a credible threat." At that hearing, where comment was limited to township residents and property owners, police removed former House Majority Leader Todd Eachus of Drums by force as he tried to speak. Felony assault charges against Eachus were later withdrawn, and misdemeanor charges were sent to county court; he pleaded not guilty. In August 2026 Gov. Josh Shapiro removed all data centers from the state's Permit Fast Track Program, which had accepted the Kline project on May 22, 2025, saying fast-track permitting is "not right for this kind of development." The same week the planning commission held its third public hearing on the plans. The Kline Township Board of Supervisors decides the preliminary and final land development plan, now due by September 30, 2026, and numerous other approvals are still required, though basic site preparation has begun under the earlier Brewster permits.

amazon-aws-homer-city.text: Amazon wants to buy about 2,200 acres of the Homer City Energy Campus, in Center and Blacklick townships near Homer City in Indiana County, Pennsylvania, and build 39 data centers there, next to the 4.5-gigawatt natural gas power plant that Homer City Redevelopment is building on the site of the old coal plant. On September 9, 2026, the Indiana County Planning Commission tabled Amazon Data Services' preliminary master land development plan for the data center campus after more than 100 people packed the courthouse, and commissioners said they might bring in county or outside engineers to assess it. Amazon's project narrative describes 39 two-story data centers about 70 feet tall, each with a footprint of about 112,500 square feet, on six sites: Bruner, Green and Rura in Center Township and Helen, West and Harvey/Gaston in Blacklick Township. Construction would start in December 2026, subject to permits, and finish in 2036. Power would come from FirstEnergy, backed by the new gas plant, and Amazon says it would use existing water-withdrawal rights and return non-contact cooling water to the Homer City station for reuse. The company projects 1,500 to 2,000 permanent jobs paying $80,000 to $100,000 on average, says it will not seek local or county tax incentives, and has offered a community benefits agreement. Amazon has pledged at least $20 billion in Pennsylvania, and a spokesman said in August that it had no definitive agreement with Homer City Redevelopment. The gas plant is being built on a 3,200-acre site and is due online in 2028; the old Homer City Generating Station, a 2-gigawatt coal plant, ran from 1969 to 2023. Homer City Redevelopment CEO Corey Hessen said more than 1,800 people were building it in August. Environmental groups including PennFuture, the Clean Air Council, the Sierra Club and Earthjustice asked the state Department of Environmental Protection to reconsider its approval of the plant, saying it would be the largest source of carbon dioxide pollution in Pennsylvania. The plant's proposed wastewater permit would allow 6.84 million gallons a day into Blacklick Creek, a stocked trout stream, at up to 110 degrees, and the Mountain Watershed Association says that could be more than 30% of the creek's flow in summer. That permit covers the power plant only, not any discharge from the data centers. Residents learned of Amazon's interest from a public records request: Concerned Residents of Western Pennsylvania said the request brought to light an August 2025 email exchange between an Amazon economic development manager and Gov. Josh Shapiro's office. At the planning commission, residents raised noise, water damage and unanswered questions, and one speaker used the meeting "to directly tell Amazon that Indiana County does not welcome you." Another speaker said a project map showed dashed lines across their property although they had never been contacted or signed any agreement. A third welcomed the prospect of jobs for her son: "Thank you for bringing hope to people here, to the students that are graduating from our school system." California attorney J. Byron Fleck and supporters in Indiana County have again pushed a proposed county ordinance to ban non-disclosure agreements. Amazon is asking the Indiana County Planning Commission to approve a preliminary master land development plan for a six-phase campus, and the commission has tabled it while it keeps asking questions. Amazon also says it will follow Gov. Shapiro's data center standards, under an executive order that has the Department of Environmental Protection review permit applications only from developers who commit to them.

amazon-aws-hobart-indiana.text: Amazon is building an $11 billion data center campus near 61st Avenue and Colorado Street in Hobart, Lake County, Indiana, part of a $15 billion Amazon investment across northern Indiana. The Hobart City Council approved a 10-year, 100 percent property tax abatement and a 35-year exemption for Amazon's IT equipment in January 2026, and the city issued a fill permit for site grading that February. Amazon paid the city a $47 million community enhancement payment, with another $55 million due once building permits are issued and construction begins. Mayor Josh Huddlestun said the money would help fix roads, fund public safety and education, and avoid tax increases: "We sought to find good, strong development to kind of offset those losses, so that we didn't have to turn to our residents and put everything back on the backs of our residents." Four residents, Angelita Soriano, Albina Venegas-Roman, Barbara Koteles and Joseph Conn, sued the city's plan commission and council over roughly 700 acres rezoned from residential to light industrial for the project, saying their due process rights were violated. "We don't know what type of generators are going to use in these buildings we want transparency before approvals happen not after," Soriano said. Amazon has not released renderings or a final building count, and its consultant told the Hobart Plan Commission in February 2026 that a site plan was still three to four months away. Huddlestun said the campus could have up to 25 buildings and target completion by 2028. The Hobart Plan Commission's review of that site plan and the residents' lawsuit against the city are both pending.

amazon-aws-wheatfield-rise.text: Amazon Web Services' Project Rise, a $7 billion data center campus approved by Jasper County officials in June, is being built on 304 acres of NIPSCO land beside the Schahfer Generating Station in Wheatfield, Indiana. NIPSCO owns the land next to its coal plant, built in the 1970s; the utility once planned to close it, but in December 2025 the Trump administration ordered the remaining two coal units to stay open. The tenant is Amazon. Dozens of residents filled a planning commission meeting on December 15, 2025, and the commission voted 8 to 1 against rezoning the land for the project. The county commissioners approved it anyway on February 2, 2026, voting unanimously. “We can say no today and we're still gonna get a data center,” commission president Rein Bontreger said after the vote. “This is a bunch of garbage!” said Barb Deardorff, a teachers' union organizer whose family has farmed the county for five generations. NIPSCO's own groundwater monitoring around the coal ash landfill next to the site has found raised levels of molybdenum, lithium, cobalt and arsenic; the company says the contamination has not moved beyond the plant site. Sameer Doshi of Earthjustice said the landfill “is likely leaking and endangering the groundwater and health of everyone who lives around the Schahfer facility.” The county's approval came with nine commitments, including $98 million paid to the county in advance, $25 million toward expanding the water supply and 250 jobs. The next decision belongs to the state: the Indiana Department of Environmental Management is renewing the Schahfer plant's wastewater discharge permit, which would authorize discharges from the coal and gas plant “as well as an adjacent data center” to Davis Ditch, Stahlbaum Ditch and the Kankakee River. IDEM will hold a virtual public hearing on October 7, 2026, and written comments are due by October 22, 2026.

amazon-aws-covington-georgia.text: Contractors for Amazon Web Services are building a data center near Highway 142 and Alcovy Road, inside Covington city limits in Newton County, Georgia. Amazon Data Services paid $36 million for about 430 acres along Interstate 20 in three deals that closed December 22, 2023. On December 15, 2025, the Covington City Council approved agreements under which Amazon will build a $100 million water reuse plant and hand it to the city, which will sell the reclaimed water back to Amazon for cooling; the data center's projected demand is 1.9 million gallons of water a day. "We will never issue a contract until that money is in the bank," city attorney Frank Turner Jr. said of Amazon's payments. Local governments expect more than half a billion dollars over 16 years from payments Amazon makes in place of property taxes through the county's industrial development authority. Construction stopped for several weeks this summer after a city inspector found the site was not following erosion-control rules; the stop-work order was lifted in August, subject to conditions, with no fines set. The council adopted a 180-day moratorium on new data center requests on January 20, 2026, and voted the same night to deny an annexation that would have brought more than 1,500 acres off Elks Club Road into the city for another data center. The moratorium, originally set to expire October 20, 2026, was lifted early on August 31 after the council adopted a new ordinance that sorts data centers by size and raises the required buffer from residential zoning to at least 250 feet.

amazon-aws-butts-county-i-75.text: Amazon Data Services, the company's data center arm, paid about $270 million for 984.89 acres on the west side of Interstate 75 in Lamar County, Georgia, off High Falls Park Road near Exit 198 outside Barnesville. The sale closed on July 25, 2025, and at well over $270,000 an acre it was the largest real estate deal by dollar value in the county's history. The land was part of the Legacy 75 Trade Center, an industrial park its developer, High Falls 75 LLC, planned to grow to 19 million square feet. The tract had been rezoned earlier in 2025 for warehouses and distribution centers with some retail and commercial use, and it takes in every foot of I-75 frontage on the western side of the interstate in the county, with heavy transmission lines crossing it. The rezoning carried a covenant capping buildings at 125,000 square feet, which at first looked like a bar to a data center. Barnesville Buzz found the cap covers only about 35 acres zoned commercial along High Falls Park Road; the other 950 or so acres are zoned industrial and allow up to 19 million square feet of buildings, room for a large data center campus. Other covenants still protect land near High Falls Lake on the east side of the interstate. Amazon has not said what it will build. "We are constantly evaluating new locations based on customer demand. We recently purchased land in Lamar County, Georgia, and are performing due diligence in exploring possible data center locations," the company said after the sale. Commission chairman Ryran Traylor said Amazon would lay out the nature and scope of its plans at pre-construction meetings with the county, and that the county was committed to ensuring the project brings "the minimal possible disruption" to neighbors. "The big concern is that yes, this could be a big project that would financially take some burden off the people in our community but also that it's the least impactful on the neighbors that are around," Traylor told WGXA in September 2025. Barnesville resident Makalyn McGuire worried about pollution and the effect on wildlife at High Falls State Park. "It disrupts the ecosystem, and when they have decided that it's over," she said. "They can just pick up and leave. Who was here left to deal with the consequences of what they've built?" Chris Manganiello, water policy director for the Chattahoochee Riverkeeper, warned that rising water and power rates tied to data centers would weigh heaviest on Black residents and others who struggle to make ends meet. In September 2025, two months after the sale, Lamar County commissioners passed a moratorium that covers data centers. Planning and zoning director Anita Buice said the pause was mainly to rewrite commercial and industrial zoning rules untouched since 2010: "Our code does not currently have the term 'data center' in it." Data centers dominated the commission's March 17, 2026 meeting, and commissioners voted unanimously to extend the moratorium.

amazon-aws-richmond-county-nc.text: Richmond County commissioners in North Carolina negotiated the sale of land for Amazon's data center under the code name Project Blue Marlin without telling the public who the buyer was. The county drafted a confidential agreement in March 2025 to sell 646 acres in Hamlet, rezoned the site to heavy industrial in April, and voted in May 2025 to sell the parcels for $26 million; officials did not confirm Amazon was the buyer until June 4, 2025, the same day they approved its tax breaks. "I don't recall any public hearing," Lee Quick, who lives across the road from the property, told state regulators. Shaun Ingram, who co-leads the Richmond County Coalition for Justice, called it "shameful to sign away public trust while residents are left to ask basic questions about our energy, wells, water, wildlife and our health." The deal gives Amazon a 50% property tax break on its buildings and a 65% reduction on machinery and equipment for 20 years, for a $10 billion project planned as 21 buildings of 200,000 square feet each, with the first building expected to be running by 2027. County officials said they chose the data center over nearly 50 competing industrial proposals because it would use less water and electricity than most manufacturing alternatives and pay for its own infrastructure upgrades. The plan calls for 592 diesel backup generators at Amazon's buildings, plus 57 temporary generators Duke Energy wants to run until new transmission lines are finished, which state regulators estimated could emit close to 250 tons a year of pollutants. At a July 30, 2026 hearing, resident Luis Balli, who has worked with diesel engines, said the emissions would be dangerous for the elderly and people with medical conditions: "The toxins will be harmful, let's put it that way." The state Department of Environmental Quality approved air permits for all 649 generators on September 1, 2026, saying its authority was limited to whether each application met air-quality rules, not where the data center is built or how it gets power.

amazon-aws-vicksburg.text: Amazon Web Services' $3 billion data center campus is under construction in its early stages in Vicksburg, on what it calls the U.S. 61 South Warren site along U.S. Highway 61, with its main entrance road off Old Cain Ridge Road, AWS said in April 2026. The AWS data center, known locally as Project Steamboat, is the largest private-sector investment in Warren County, Mississippi's history. Gov. Tate Reeves announced the project in November 2025, promising at least 200 full-time jobs at the campus and about 300 more across the county. The state authorized $44 million in incentives under the Mississippi Major Economic Impact Act, Warren County is also investing, and Entergy Mississippi has promised to supply the power. It is Amazon's second data center campus in Mississippi, after the $10 billion Madison County investment announced in 2024. Reeves said the Vicksburg Warren School District will receive millions of dollars a year through a fee-in-lieu arrangement. Roger Wehner, AWS's vice president of economic development, told the Vicksburg-Warren County Chamber of Commerce in April that "The construction mobilization is kicking off," with about $3 million of initial infrastructure and site work to deal with the land's topography. He said 1,000 to 1,250 workers are expected on site at the peak of construction, and permanent jobs will average $70,000 to $80,000 a year. Power will come from the $1.2 billion Vicksburg Advanced Power Station that Entergy is building nearby, and Wehner said AWS pays the full cost of its energy use and related infrastructure. Residents have raised water, energy and environmental concerns, and Reeves's announcement drew comments worried about utility rates. Wehner said AWS modeling shows the campus would use water for cooling about 9 percent of the year: "So it's probably 30 days out of the year, and I bet everybody in this room can guess what 30 days that is? Probably somewhere around August." He promised to limit traffic, noise and daily disruption for neighbors. "Those disruptions are temporary," he said. "The benefits are not." The Mississippi Free Press noted that watchdog groups warn such centers consume large amounts of power and water, and that residents near new data centers elsewhere have faced rising energy costs. The county's part is under way. On July 6, 2026 the Warren County Board of Supervisors approved a $20 million Mississippi Development Authority loan for infrastructure tied to the project, a right of way for a new Entergy 500kV line from the power station, and engineering for road work on Highway 61 South to connect the entrance road. It also approved an agreement under which AWS would cover the county's loan payments if they come due before revenue from the project arrives; Pablo Diaz of the Vicksburg-Warren Economic Development Partnership said this was not a sign of any delay: "The project is going on schedule as planned." Elsewhere in Mississippi, Compass Datacenters is building a facility in Meridian and Avaio has announced a $6 billion campus in Rankin County. The Warren County Board of Supervisors, led by President Kelle Barfield, and the Vicksburg city government are AWS's local partners, and the supervisors vote on the county's agreements for the project. No completion date has been announced.

amazon-aws-clinton-mississippi.text: Amazon Web Services is turning the old Delphi Packard Electric plant at 1001 Industrial Park Drive in Clinton, Hinds County, Mississippi, into a data center. A quitclaim deed moved the 99-acre site to Amazon on February 13, 2026, when the project was valued at $750 million. Amazon Web Services marked the opening of its fourth Mississippi data center with a ribbon cutting on June 9, 2026, an investment the company said could bring more than 100 jobs. "This is an exciting day in Mississippi," said Roger Wehner, AWS vice president of economic development, adding that the Clinton building uses newer approaches to operations, including not using water coolants. More than three months after the AWS announcement, the Board of Aldermen had drafted a separate ordinance on buffers, screening and setbacks for future data centers, though it had not yet voted on it as of July 2026. The board had already changed Clinton's zoning so data centers are a conditional use in industrial areas, and any new project must go through a public hearing before the Planning Commission; neither rule applies retroactively to the Amazon building, which still must meet existing zoning and noise rules.

amazon-aws-resilient-technology-park-shr.text: Amazon Web Services announced on August 18, 2026 that it will invest $6 billion in a data center campus at the Resilient Technology Park in west Shreveport, Caddo Parish, Louisiana, to be built by STACK Infrastructure, after a court fight over the site's permit. It is the third AWS data center campus in the Shreveport-Bossier area, bringing Amazon's planned investment there to $18 billion. The 313-acre park sits off Greenwood Road next to Interstate 20. The data center's address is 7340 Greenwood Road, inside the Shreveport city limits. STACK has said the Shreveport campus will be roughly the same size as its other two, about 1.3 million square feet. A STACK representative put completion of construction in the middle of 2028. AWS says the campus will create about 210 direct jobs and some 2,250 construction jobs, and that it will pay for the water and wastewater work and fund new power infrastructure with Southwestern Electric Power Company. The companies have not disclosed the campus's power capacity or number of buildings. The site needed a special use permit because it is close to a residential subdivision. The Shreveport Metropolitan Planning Commission denied it on December 3, 2025, and after a long and contentious meeting on December 18 the City Council voted unanimously to overturn that denial. In January 2026 Mooringsport Mayor Tyler Gordon and two Caddo Parish residents, Michael Craft and Mary Blakemore, sued Mayor Tom Arceneaux and the city, arguing leaders failed to provide "sufficient transparency" and to consider "environmental impacts." "I would love to see development here that benefits us but we just need to do it in a way that won't harm long-term water security," Gordon said. Because of the suit, the site was left out of Gov. Jeff Landry's February 23 announcement of Amazon's first two campuses. On April 20 District Court Judge Ramon Lafitte dismissed the petition and upheld the council's decision. The plaintiffs' attorney, Jake Bailey, said the case had put much more on the record and asked the city to stop "blindly rubber stamping this process," adding that the data center will now have diesel generators he believes were not in the original plans. "The problem is that once the permit's approved, it's approved," Bailey said. In May the Sierra Club announced that the plaintiffs would appeal Lafitte's ruling. The other two campuses are already moving: STACK is building near Benton in Bossier Parish and at the Stateline site near Blanchard in Caddo Parish, where residents protested outside a March 2026 community meeting. At that meeting STACK's Kevin Greer said the Stateline center's 57 million gallons of water equals the use of 530 homes, and SWEPCO's Paul Pratt said STACK and AWS had committed to pay for all needed electrical upgrades. The parishes' incentive term sheets cut the property tax rate further if the company builds three or more projects, and three more term sheets have been signed for undisclosed locations. What happens next: the Resilient Park data center must meet Shreveport's noise ordinance, the plaintiffs' appeal would go to Louisiana's 2nd Circuit Court, which one of their attorneys, Clay Garside, called the most obvious route, and Bailey has said his firm is preparing nuisance claims in case residents suffer noise, air pollution, vibration or flooding. The Shreveport City Council and Mayor Arceneaux made the local decision.

The Shreveport Metropolitan Planning Commission denied it on December 3, 2025, and after a long and contentious meeting on December 18 the City Council voted unanimously to overturn that denial.

In January 2026 Mooringsport Mayor Tyler Gordon and two Caddo Parish residents, Michael Craft and Mary Blakemore, sued Mayor Tom Arceneaux and the city, arguing leaders failed to provide "sufficient transparency" and to consider "environmental impacts."
"I would love to see development here that benefits us but we just need to do it in a way that won't harm long-term water security," Gordon said.
Because of the suit, the site was left out of Gov. Jeff Landry's February 23 announcement of Amazon's first two campuses.
On April 20 District Court Judge Ramon Lafitte dismissed the petition and upheld the council's decision.

The plaintiffs' attorney, Jake Bailey, said the case had put much more on the record and asked the city to stop "blindly rubber stamping this process," adding that the data center will now have diesel generators he believes were not in the original plans.
"The problem is that once the permit's approved, it's approved," Bailey said.
In May the Sierra Club announced that the plaintiffs would appeal Lafitte's ruling.

The other two campuses are already moving: STACK is building near Benton in Bossier Parish and at the Stateline site near Blanchard in Caddo Parish, where residents protested outside a March 2026 community meeting.

At that meeting STACK's Kevin Greer said the Stateline center's 57 million gallons of water equals the use of 530 homes, and SWEPCO's Paul Pratt said STACK and AWS had committed to pay for all needed electrical upgrades.
The parishes' incentive term sheets cut the property tax rate further if the company builds three or more projects, and three more term sheets have been signed for undisclosed locations.

What happens next: the Resilient Park data center must meet Shreveport's noise ordinance, the plaintiffs' appeal would go to Louisiana's 2nd Circuit Court, which one of their attorneys, Clay Garside, called the most obvious route, and Bailey has said his firm is preparing nuisance claims in case residents suffer noise, air pollution, vibration or flooding.
The Shreveport City Council and Mayor Arceneaux made the local decision.

amazon-aws-blanchard-state-line.text: Amazon Web Services is building the State Line data center, a reported 1.3 million square foot campus on Stateline Road near Blanchard in Caddo Parish, Louisiana, with developer STACK Infrastructure. Gov. Jeff Landry announced the project on February 23, 2026 as part of more than $12 billion Amazon plans to invest in three interconnected campuses across Northwest Louisiana. The campus is under construction, and on August 31, 2026 the Caddo Parish Commission voted 6-4 against a resolution asking planners to consider pausing data center construction in the parish. STACK, a Denver-based company, will own the facility, with Amazon as the tenant. Amazon plans to hire 540 employees and to spend $400 million on public water systems in the Caddo-Bossier area, and it has promised to pay 100% of its own electricity costs, including upgrades to SWEPCO's substations and transmission lines. Amazon's Roger Wehner said the Northwest Louisiana data centers will use water for cooling "less than 13% of the year." The project became public on December 9, 2025, when Blanchard agreed to sell 1.5 million to 5 million gallons a day to the site from Caddo Lake, which also supplies Mooringsport and Oil City. Commissioner Chris Kracman's proposal for a one-year moratorium on large water users, pending a lake study, failed to reach the commission agenda. Resident Mary Stahl May, who organized her own community meeting in January, said: "They shoved it down our throats. So now we're going to make sure that they do what they say they're going to do." Commissioner John-Paul Young, whose resolution failed, said: "We have approved a tax plan for one data center in Caddo Parish and that is probably enough." The parish has zoning authority only within five miles of Shreveport, so a moratorium there would have to start at the Planning and Zoning Commission, the parish attorney said. The Caddo Parish Commission and the Town of Blanchard, which sells the water, are the local bodies with a say over what happens next.

amazon-aws-bossier-parish.text: STACK Infrastructure is building a data center campus for Amazon Web Services on 1,089 acres west of Louisiana Highway 3, north of Benton in Bossier Parish, called the Highway 3 Technology Park. The Bossier Parish Police Jury approved the project's final plat unanimously on March 20, 2026, for six buildings totaling more than 1.3 million square feet, with Haskell of Jacksonville, Florida, as general contractor. Gov. Jeff Landry announced the $6 billion project on February 23, 2026, part of an $18 billion Amazon investment across three Louisiana campuses. Much of the groundwork happened before residents knew what it was for: rezoning, tax breaks and a water agreement with Bossier City all went to votes without public confirmation the projects were data centers, since police jurors and parish administrator Ken Ward had signed nondisclosure agreements. A public hearing on March 18, 2026 drew two hours of questions about health, water, noise, drainage and the secrecy. "The people in this country have a really big distrust of government right now," said Dr. Richard Harrell, who lives near the site. STACK expects the campus to use about 57 million gallons of water a year under an agreement letting it draw up to 13.5 million gallons a day from Bossier City, which will get about $12 million a year and fixed water leaks from the deal, parish administrator Ken Ward said. SWEPCO's Amanda Nottingham said the utility is "committed to ensuring that our ratepayers do not feel the impacts" of the new construction, with Amazon and STACK paying for new power lines. STACK projects 500 construction jobs and 270 permanent jobs at the Bossier campus, with Ward expecting the first building finished in 2028.

amazon-aws-spectrum-hood-county.text: Amazon Web Services has withdrawn Project Spectrum, its planned 21-building data center campus at 2300 Coates Road near Granbury in Hood County, Texas, telling 60 Minutes before its September 20, 2026 broadcast: "We ultimately decided to not build in Hood County, and we received no incentives from the county." Hood County commissioners had approved the project 3-0 on May 26, 2026; 60 Minutes reported the project is now moving forward in a neighboring county that gave AWS the tax rebate it wanted, without naming which county. Amazon had asked Hood County for up to 90% in property tax rebates for 30 years, according to a pitch obtained by 60 Minutes. "They basically came in here to razzle dazzle me," said Commissioner Dave Eagle, who voted against the project and said company representatives would not say exactly what they wanted to do. The land was unzoned, undeveloped agricultural property, and plans from Bohler Engineering showed the campus drawing electricity from the nearby Comanche Peak Nuclear Power Plant. The May vote was contested: commissioners had set conditions in January requiring a drainage plan, traffic assessments, an endangered species report and water-use information, then found in May that Amazon had met them, with two commissioners absent. "That is our position. We are exempt from your regulations, with all due respect," Amazon's attorney, Jonathan Vinson of Jackson Walker, told the commissioners. Statewide, Gov. Greg Abbott ordered a moratorium on new data center grid connections on August 3, 2026, pending an ERCOT audit, and his Democratic opponent in November, Gina Hinojosa, is calling for her own temporary moratorium. With Amazon gone, no application is pending before the Hood County Commissioners Court; the county's development commission was still weighing its own moratorium on industrial development as of a May 28, 2026 meeting.

amazon-aws-bastrop-county-cedar-creek.text: Amazon Data Services bought 1,229 acres in Bastrop County, Texas, on May 1, about three miles southwest of the EdgeConneX data center campuses at Cedar Creek. The company told Community Impact it "has not made a final development decision" about the land. It would be arriving into an argument already under way. EdgeConneX has three campuses planned at Cedar Creek: 112 acres and a $440 million, 578,000 square foot building now under construction, a second of 951 acres and $1.4 billion, and a third of 400 acres with nine possible buildings. County commissioner David Glass asked the company to hold three town halls, on June 16 at Elgin, June 17 at Smithville and June 18 at Bastrop. EdgeConneX chief marketing officer Phillip Marangella said the projects would mean more than 200 permanent jobs on a payroll of about $16 million a year. Residents have organized across party lines. A meeting run by the League of Independent Voters of Texas was co-sponsored by the county's Republican Club, its Democratic Party and the Texas Forward Party. Merrie Santana, who lives in Cedar Creek, said: "I am for economic development as long as it is responsible. But this location right here, where you see all of those communities, where you see all of those families, that location is not suitable for a data center of that magnitude." She asked when the air quality, groundwater and noise studies would be done. Elgin attorney Nick Lealos proposed a framework he calls the Bastrop Bill of Rights, and Texas agriculture commissioner Sid Miller told the meeting: "Just stop. Hold up. This is getting away from us. We have got to put some guardrails around this industry, or we're gonna be in a huge train wreck." The county has little power here. A draft policy would require companies seeking tax abatements to disclose their effects on air and water quality, runoff, wetlands, waste and noise, and to hire at least 25 full time workers with a quarter of them from the county. Commissioners tabled a resolution on August 10 that would have declared the county's limited authority and asked the Texas legislature for more. The county hired PFM Group Consulting in March 2026 to work out what all this actually costs and returns.

amazon-aws-eagle-boling.text: Amazon Web Services is building Project Eagle, a $10 billion data center campus on nearly 3,000 acres in unincorporated Wharton County outside Boling, Texas, a town of fewer than 400 people about 55 miles southwest of Houston. Amazon bought the land in March 2026 and, with county permits in hand, is moving dirt on a site now planned for 10 buildings of 189,060 square feet each, about $3 billion in listed construction. The company has not disclosed the campus's electricity needs, but Amazon confirmed it is in ERCOT's new review process for large customers, which sets a 75-megawatt minimum at peak demand. Amazon says the first buildings will be air-cooled and will not use groundwater for cooling, though the Lower Colorado River Authority says the company expects to use about 500 acre-feet, roughly 163 million gallons, of surface water a year as the site grows. The company promises at least 150 permanent jobs by mid-2027. Water and secrecy are the local fight: red yard signs across the highway from the site read "You can live without data, but you can't live without water," and County Judge Philip Spenrath signed a non-disclosure agreement restricting what the county can say about the project's design and finances. "We don't have any zoning, so all of that adds to a ripe place for a corporation like Amazon to exploit," said David Rodriguez, a goat farmer who lives about six miles away. Earlier in 2026 the Coastal Bend Groundwater Conservation District delayed permits for two larger wells for the project after community objections. Statewide, Gov. Greg Abbott ordered a moratorium on new data center grid connections on August 3, 2026, pending audits of tax breaks, power use and water use, and ERCOT has said approvals will be delayed while it complies. Spenrath is negotiating a binding county agreement that would bar groundwater for cooling and require Amazon to protect roads, drainage and water resources, and County Attorney Trey Maffet said none has been finalized: "We don't know if there is going to be one." That agreement, the county's remaining permits and the groundwater district's decision on the well permits are the next steps ahead for Wharton County.

gemini-google-doha.text: Google's cloud region in Doha, Qatar, Google's first in the country, has been in service since 2023, running on data centers in Qatar. Google opened the region with three availability zones in the spring of 2023, three years after first announcing it in March 2020, but did not share specifications for the facilities. A cloud region is a complex that houses at least two data centers, The National explained, and this one was built with Qatar's Ministry of Communications and Information Technology and the Qatar Free Zones Authority. More than 2,700 people attended the official launch at the Qatar National Convention Centre in May 2023, according to the free zones authority. Research commissioned by Google projected that the region would add $18.9 billion to Qatar's economic output between 2023 and 2030 and create 25,000 jobs in 2030 alone. "This new region is a strong step towards building regional capacity that meets the needs of the Qatari digital economy, from availability and data residency, to digital sovereignty and sustainability," said Ghassan Kosta, Google Cloud's Qatar country manager. Microsoft opened its own Qatar cloud region with the local firm Meeza in August 2022. Google Cloud opened a Center of Excellence for training at the Business Innovation Park in the Ras Bufontas Free Zone in December 2024. At a Google Cloud Summit in Doha on September 22, 2026, which marked three years of AI adoption and regional innovation, the company announced a national program of more than 50,000 AI learning opportunities. A ministry official said Qatar's framework agreement with Google Cloud underpins the government's use of cloud and AI, and that more than 40 AI projects are being developed or put in place across government and other sectors.

sentences.t: Google's cloud region in Doha, Qatar, Google's first in the country, has been in service since 2023, running on data centers in Qatar.
Google opened the region with three availability zones in the spring of 2023, three years after first announcing it in March 2020, but did not share specifications for the facilities.

A cloud region is a complex that houses at least two data centers, The National explained, and this one was built with Qatar's Ministry of Communications and Information Technology and the Qatar Free Zones Authority.
More than 2,700 people attended the official launch at the Qatar National Convention Centre in May 2023, according to the free zones authority.
Research commissioned by Google projected that the region would add $18.9 billion to Qatar's economic output between 2023 and 2030 and create 25,000 jobs in 2030 alone.

microsoft-microsoft-woodlands-singapore.text: Microsoft's Woodlands data center at 1 Woodlands Industrial Park E9 in Singapore is a nine-story building with offices, utility support areas and its own substation, built as Microsoft's SG2 data center project. Its air-conditioning contractor dates its part of the work from December 2012 to April 2014. It is one of three data centers Microsoft says it operates in Singapore, which together employed about 120 people as of 2025. Microsoft opened its Singapore Azure cloud region in 2010 with three availability zones. Microsoft says water-cooled chillers at its Singapore facilities use reused water all year, and that its practices include noise and light reduction. In 2024 it signed a 20-year power purchase agreement with EDP Renewables for power from the 200MWp SolarNova 8 rooftop solar project. Microsoft is growing in Singapore. In 2023 it was one of four operators given a share of 80MW of new data center capacity as Singapore began easing its moratorium on new data centers, and in April 2026 it said it is on track to invest $5.5 billion in Singaporean cloud and AI infrastructure by 2029. "Our ongoing investment in cloud and AI infrastructure reflects Microsoft's long-term confidence in Singapore as a global digital leader," said Microsoft president Brad Smith. Singapore had a moratorium on new data centers from 2019, and in December 2025 the government opened a second call for at least 200MW of capacity, requiring new facilities to be at least 50 percent powered by green energy. New data center capacity in Singapore is allocated by the Economic Development Board and the Infocomm Media Development Authority.

amazon-aws-bridgefield-tech-center-ashbu.text: George Washington University sold its Ashburn campus in Loudoun County, Virginia, the Virginia Science and Technology Campus, to Amazon Data Services for a data center project, in a sale of $427.3 million that closed on March 2, 2026. Amazon filed a site plan on July 28, 2026 for what it calls the Bridgefield Tech Center: four two-story data center buildings and three parking garages totaling more than 800,000 square feet, proposed under a 1972 zoning ordinance that would let the project skip Planning Commission review and public hearings. On July 30, 2026, the county's zoning administrator, Teresa Miller, ruled that an older policy treating data centers as office uses was obsolete, a step that could affect Amazon's by-right claim. Loudoun supervisor Juli Briskman opposed the plan, saying it would be "a profound loss for our community," and vowed to fight it because it sits too close to homes, Bles Park and the Potomac River. Resident Miriam Musau said of the data centers: "They are invading and making this area like a concrete jungle." Loudoun's economic development director, Buddy Rizer, a longtime supporter of data center growth, said in March 2026 the campus was never an area the county anticipated for data centers. Supervisors voted 6-1 in July 2026 to study a temporary pause on new data center applications, and on September 15, 2026 the board voted 7-1-1 to direct staff to draft a resolution pausing new applications for up to 12 months; the pause is not yet in force. County staff are due to bring a formal resolution memorializing the pause to the board's October 20, 2026 meeting. Amazon has said construction would not start until GW has fully left the campus, and it noted it has paid more than $2.1 billion in property taxes and fees in Loudoun County since 2016.

amazon-aws-gw-ranch-pecos-county.text: Amazon Web Services is building a data center campus on GW Ranch, 8,400 acres in Pecos County, Texas, about 17 miles north of Fort Stockton. The campus is under construction as three buildings, A, B and C, at a stated cost of $300 million each, with work underway since August 2026. Pacifico Energy is building a 7,650 megawatt natural gas plant on the same ranch to power the campus off the Texas grid. The gas plant would use 35 turbines and could emit up to 33 million tons of carbon dioxide a year under the air permit Texas issued in January 2026, more than the country's largest coal plant. Because the plant counts as a separate business from the data centers, the data centers themselves need only minor air permits as low-level polluters. Amazon's link to the project became public in early August 2026, when it filed three construction permits with the state. The energy newsletter Cleanview then reviewed satellite imagery and found land clearing already underway at the site described in GW Ranch's air permit records; Amazon confirmed it had bought the site and would buy power from Pacifico Energy's plant. Amazon says the campus is "powered by new on-site generation that won't raise electricity costs for Texas families" and is designed to shift to grid power later; Pacifico Energy plans up to 750 megawatts of solar and 1.8 gigawatts of battery storage on site. On August 3, 2026, Governor Greg Abbott ordered a statewide moratorium on approving new data centers until regulators audit projects seeking grid connections, though GW Ranch is being built off the grid.

amazon-aws-horizon-junction-floydada.text: Amazon Data Services has filed with the state to build three data center buildings, together called Horizon Junction, on County Road 241 in Floydada, the seat of Floyd County, Texas, about 45 miles northeast of Lubbock. State filings list each building at 189,060 square feet and $300 million, built from August 2026 to April 2027, on land that is now a nine-hole golf course. County officials describe a bigger project, worth more than $1 billion, that could hold seven buildings on about 485 acres. Texas counties cannot zone land or ban development, so the Floyd County Commissioners Court says its only real leverage is a Chapter 312 tax break, an agreement that trades a property tax discount for conditions the county sets. The court says it will offer that break only if the data center cools itself with air instead of water, to save groundwater, and generates all the electricity it needs so it never competes with residents and farmers for power. In an August 2026 open letter, commissioners wrote that the data center issue had been "thrust upon us, early this year" and was not on their radar before January. The town's own water system has been under strain: in late July 2026 the city of Floydada asked residents to cut back on lawn watering as its wells worked harder in triple-digit heat, and in mid-September it asked residents to stop all irrigation while crews repaired one of the city's wells. Gov. Greg Abbott ordered ERCOT on August 3, 2026 to audit new large power users, including data centers, before they can connect to the Texas grid; the order does not cover data centers that bring their own power. Floyd County commissioners discussed a possible tax abatement with Amazon Data Services on July 13, 2026 but took no action after meeting with their lawyers in closed session. The commissioners say they have not signed, and will not consider, a nondisclosure agreement on the project.

amazon-aws-san-antonio-bitter-blue.text: Amazon Data Services has filed to build a two story data center called Bitter Blue at 12807 Donop Road in Elmendorf, on the far Southeast Side of San Antonio, in Bexar County. The Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation filing describes 119,407 square feet costing $65 million, designed by Gensler, with work set to start December 3, 2026, and finish February 9, 2029. The state received the filing on March 15, 2026. Amazon bought the land in October 2020 from the San Antonio developer Bitterblue, and separately built an earlier, smaller Amazon data center nearby at 11625 Old Corpus Christi Highway. The rest of the roughly 200 acre tract was rezoned in 2021 for a mixed use project of homes, apartments, retail and a 50 acre industrial site, inside a special tax zone that runs until 2046. San Antonio is writing new data center rules that would keep buildings at least 500 feet from homes, schools and hospitals, with the Zoning Commission expected to finish them in September 2026 and the City Council able to adopt them in October. Council members are also weighing a moratorium of up to 180 days, though at least 12 projects already negotiating for utility service would be exempt, city Development Services director Amin Tohmaz said. CPS Energy and the San Antonio Water System told the council in March they can handle the added demand, but residents worry about water use during drought and about noise. Statewide, Gov. Greg Abbott on August 3, 2026 ordered state regulators to audit data centers seeking to connect to the Texas grid and to deny connection to any that fail the review. "My biggest concern is the 500-foot setback," said Deedee Belmares of Public Citizen.

amazon-aws-mesa-pecos-road-phx065.text: Amazon's Project PHX65 is a proposed two-building data center campus on 71.3 acres on the north side of Pecos Road, east of Signal Butte Road, in southeast Mesa, Maricopa County, Arizona. Amazon Data Services filed site plans for two data center buildings with 264 parking spaces, and the Mesa Design Review Board discussed the project's look and landscaping on May 14, 2024. The two data halls would each be about 227,000 square feet. Amazon bought the Pecos Road site in December 2021 for slightly more than $18 million, near the Legacy Park sports complex; it had earlier been considered for a last-mile delivery hub, a plan that was shelved. Amazon filed nearly identical plans for a second site, 42.9 acres next to the Apple data center at Signal Butte and Elliot roads. Pecos Road is filling with data centers. At Pecos and Crismon roads, NTT won a 4-0 Planning and Zoning Board recommendation for a seven-building, 2.3 million square foot campus with closed-loop cooling and an on-site substation, after buying 170 acres from Pacific Proving for $300 million. Mesa created a 5-mile technology corridor between Signal Butte and Hawes roads in 2014, where Apple, Google, EdgeCore, Meta and Novva already operate. Amazon's site plans still need approval from Mesa's Planning and Zoning Board and city council. No construction start has been reported for PHX65, and the most recent reporting on the project dates from 2024.

amazon-aws-mesa-elliot-road.text: Mesa's Planning and Zoning Board approved the site plan for Amazon Web Services' AWS Mesa Elliot Road, two buildings totaling 458,608 square feet on 42.9 acres south of Elliot Road and west of Signal Butte Road in the Eastmark community of Mesa, Maricopa County, Arizona, at its March 26, 2025 meeting. The site sits next door to Apple's Mesa data center. The 4-0-1 vote cleared the way for construction despite opposition from Eastmark's master developer. The board also approved a special use permit cutting parking to 152 spaces from the 512 normally required, and a 6,933-square-foot security building near the Elliot Road entrance. The fight was over who reviews the design: the board dropped a requirement for final approval from the Eastmark Design Review Committee before any building permit, leaving only the city's own review. "There's a regulatory requirement for this process," said Susan Demmitt, a lawyer for master developer DMB Mesa Proving Grounds, calling it a break from 14 years of precedent. Gary Hayes of Ryan Companies, the developer, said Brookfield Residential had rejected its revised design submittal after giving conditional approval: "We can't get building permits because they rejected our submittal after they gave us a conditional approval." Amazon bought the land in December 2021 for $16.9 million; it had earlier been planned for an Amazon logistics facility. Arizona's mood on data centers has shifted since. On August 31, 2026, Attorney General Kris Mayes asked the legislature and Gov. Katie Hobbs to stop approving new data centers, saying "the only sane thing to do is to pause the approval of new data centers." With the site plan approved, the next step is building permits from the City of Mesa; no construction start had been reported as of the most recent coverage, in April 2025.

The site sits next door to Apple's Mesa data center.
The 4-0-1 vote cleared the way for construction despite opposition from Eastmark's master developer.
The board also approved a special use permit cutting parking to 152 spaces from the 512 normally required, and a 6,933-square-foot security building near the Elliot Road entrance.
The fight was over who reviews the design: the board dropped a requirement for final approval from the Eastmark Design Review Committee before any building permit, leaving only the city's own review.
"There's a regulatory requirement for this process," said Susan Demmitt, a lawyer for master developer DMB Mesa Proving Grounds, calling it a break from 14 years of precedent.

Gary Hayes of Ryan Companies, the developer, said Brookfield Residential had rejected its revised design submittal after giving conditional approval: "We can't get building permits because they rejected our submittal after they gave us a conditional approval."

amazon-aws-laveen-phoenix.text: Amazon Data Services paid $277 million for 220 acres near Loop 202 and Dobbins Road in Laveen, in southwest Phoenix, Maricopa County, Arizona, as a potential data center site. The deal closed in October 2024; an AWS spokesperson said only that the company was "constantly evaluating new locations based on customer demand," with no data center plans announced since. Amazon paid more than $1.2 million an acre, according to land records and the Tempe real estate database Vizzda. The seller, IDM Companies, had assembled the site for about $100.9 million, and the land sits in an industrial corridor the city wants to build into a technology center. Salt River Project is adding power to the corridor through its South Mountain Transmission Project, a new substation and transmission lines that a state siting committee cleared in December 2024. Since July 2, 2025, Phoenix has required a special permit for any data center, reviewing grid reliability, fire risk, emergency access and noise before construction can begin. Any data center AWS builds on the Laveen land would need that permit from the City of Phoenix. Mayor Kate Gallego said growth "must be balanced and not ignore public safety or potentially negative impacts upon the community." AWS has shared no plans for the site since the 2024 purchase.

amazon-aws-gilroy.text: Amazon Web Services' data center in Gilroy, under construction on a 56-acre site at 8050 Camino Arroyo in the northeast of the Santa Clara County city, is untouched by the temporary moratorium on new data centers the Gilroy City Council passed unanimously on September 14, 2026. The Gilroy data center was approved at staff level on July 3, 2025 as a site and architectural application for two single-story data center buildings and a security building totaling about 438,500 square feet, plus a substation and switchyard. The first building, of about 218,000 square feet, needs a 49-MW connection to PG&E and would be backed by twenty-five 2.5-MW diesel generators; the second building would use battery or fuel cell backup instead of diesel. The city's environmental impact report found two significant and unavoidable impacts, and its comment period closed on September 26, 2024. The city says the first phase will use about 23 acre-feet of drinking water a year, under 1% of the city's use, falling to about 2 acre-feet once Amazon pays for a recycled water connection expected by 2030, and that the site will use evaporative cooling. The city expects about $40 million in new revenue over the first ten years and says it gave Amazon no tax abatements; Amazon is paying for a dedicated substation and must buy carbon-free power from Silicon Valley Clean Energy. Residents objected that the project got through with no public input. Some alleged the land violated the state Subdivision Map Act before Amazon owned it, which city officials said they looked into and found no violation. In August 2026 the council began requiring community meetings and mailed notices for large commercial projects and Planning Commission review for any project needing an environmental impact report. "As this data center is getting constructed, we are looking to ensure that there is independent and public oversight to make sure that Amazon is keeping true on the promises they've made," said Britt Smith, founder of Gilroy Community Action, which is also working on a ballot initiative. The 45-day moratorium bars the city from accepting or approving applications for new data centers while staff write zoning and operating standards on water use, electrical demand, noise and generator emissions. It halts a possible second Amazon data center at Highway 152 and Camino Arroyo, which is only at the pre-application stage. "Our residents have asked for a greater voice in decisions about major development in Gilroy, and we are listening," said Mayor Greg Bozzo. The moratorium expires October 29, 2026 unless the Gilroy City Council extends it, which state law allows in stages up to two years, and residents are pushing for the full extension; the Community Development Department and Planning Commission will recommend the new standards.

amazon-aws-santa-clara-mission-college.text: Amazon Web Services is building a data center campus on Mission College Boulevard in Santa Clara, Santa Clara County, California, on land it bought for about $100 million in December 2019. Plans filed with the California Energy Commission call for two three story buildings totaling 490,000 square feet, 43 diesel backup generators, and a new substation to be built and run by the city's own utility, Silicon Valley Power. The utility could not supply enough power over its existing lines, so in July 2024 the Santa Clara City Council voted 6-0 for a 15-year deal in which the city buys power from Bloom Energy fuel cells and resells it to Amazon, letting the company add power faster for a second building. Amazon pays all the costs, at about 50 percent above the utility's usual industrial rate, with renewable energy credits used to offset the gas-fired power. "We have been working very hard to try to get additional transmission capacity and grow the system," the utility's chief electric officer, Manuel Pineda, told the council, adding that at least four other customers wanted a similar deal. Santa Clara has 58 data centers, the most of any city on the West Coast, is spending $459 million to double its power grid, and collects an estimated $29.5 million a year from them, a September 2026 report found. Most of the city's data centers use recycled water, but residents have complained about noise, height and appearance since one went up on Memorex Drive. The Santa Clara City Council, which owns Silicon Valley Power, decides on the utility's power deals and rates.

amazon-aws-green-new-florence.text: Two data center campuses are going up side by side along Interstate 70 between New Florence and High Hill, and they have split Montgomery County. Amazon's Project Green sits north of the interstate and Google's Project Spade to the south, together covering about 1,900 acres. Project Spade replaced Hoette Farms and Nursery, which moved to Jonesburg. Both projects were announced in mid-2024. Amazon's administrative review finished in November 2024, the project was presented and approved at a Montgomery County Commission meeting in December 2024, construction permits went in that February and ground was broken on April 1, 2025. Residents formed a group called Preserve Montgomery County after the announcement and later sued to halt Amazon's project, saying the public notice was insufficient and the consequences were never properly weighed. "When we first heard about (the data center plans), we put a lot of public pressure on the county commissioners," said co-founder Tom Westhoff. "They were not paying attention to us. They basically ignored us." Co-founder Sabrina Cope said the water study "was conducted by Amazon in 2020, before data centers had reached the scale of these projects," and that no study had been done by an independent source. Montgomery County resident Brenda Buechele said: "I feel like we win little battles every day, all day long." The county commission heard public comment on the Amazon project on Monday, January 12, 2026, with Presiding Commissioner Ryan Poston and commissioners Dave Teeter and Doug Lensing present. Resident Janette Seper told the commission: "I have a lot of personal concern with noise, pollution, water usage, electrical usage, and I'm concerned about the data center coming in." J. Hardin, from High Hill, was more cautious than opposed: "I think it's reasonable to be concerned about anything new that comes in that a community is not used to." Commissioner Teeter said of the delay in answering residents: "We couldn't answer some of the questions until we received accurate information." Amazon, which plans 17 buildings on the site, said tax revenue could range from $401 million to $1.8 billion over the next 25 years. On water, Amazon says cooling will draw on water about 6 percent of the time, with air cooling the rest, and that the effect on aquifer recharge will be small. The lawsuit is going ahead. Preserve Montgomery County sued the county and the Missouri Department of Economic Development in February 2026, arguing that neither posted proper public notice of the project or gave enough information about the data centers' water and electricity use, and that residents were not fully told the terms of the tax abatement. On September 18, 2026, Cole County Circuit Judge Cotton Walker refused to dismiss most of the case, ruling that the group has standing, though he dropped the Department of Economic Development as a party. No further hearings had been scheduled, and the county and state say there is no factual evidence for the claims.

amazon-aws-becker-minnesota.text: Amazon Web Services suspended its planned data center in Becker, Sherburne County, Minnesota, in May 2025, saying its timeline for permits and utility agreements had grown more uncertain than first projected. Amazon owns 348 acres in Becker and had considered up to 600 megawatts of standby generation for the site. Two things changed first: Minnesota's Public Utilities Commission turned down Amazon's request over backup diesel generation, and the 2025 legislative session repealed the sales tax exemption on electricity for data centers. The same session extended the exemption on hardware and software to 2042 or 35 years, whichever is later, replacing the old 2042-or-20-years rule; Amazon soon announced data center plans in North Carolina and Pennsylvania instead. City Administrator Greg Lerud said: "Amazon did tell the city that they are suspending their activities in Minnesota, which includes the property they own in Becker." The city sits beside the closing Sherco coal plant, which provides about $5 million of the school district's $12 million budget; the data center's tax income would have nearly filled that gap, Lerud had said. Mayor Mark Kolbinger called the cancellation a gut punch, comparing the lost project to Xcel Energy's arrival in the 1970s, which he said remade the community. Representative Shane Mekeland estimated the project would have meant 6,000 to 8,000 union construction jobs over a decade and about 1,900 permanent jobs counting Microsoft's nearby plans. Amazon still owns the Becker land and says it continues to evaluate the location. If it returns, state regulators have ruled Amazon must prove it needs the 250 backup diesel generators it had planned, not be exempted from that requirement.

amazon-aws-dublin-mulhuddart.text: Amazon Web Services has permission to build three data centers on Cruiserath Road in Mulhuddart, Blanchardstown, County Dublin, Ireland, with a combined power load of 73 megawatts. An Coimisiun Pleanala approved the project on December 26, 2025, after Fingal County Council had approved it in 2023 and five appeals delayed the final decision for two years. The appeals, from Friends of the Earth and four other objectors, argued the project's carbon footprint was too high. Consultants estimated the three buildings would emit 213,840 tonnes of carbon dioxide in 2025, falling to 132,164 tonnes by 2030 as Ireland's electricity grid gets cleaner. The commission concluded the project "would have no unacceptable impacts on the environment or on property in the vicinity." Permission carries one condition: before the data centers can switch on, Amazon must sign a contract to buy renewable electricity matching everything the buildings use, known as a corporate power purchase agreement. That mirrors new rules Ireland's energy regulator set in December 2025 when it lifted a four year freeze on new data center grid connections in the Dublin area, requiring on-site backup power and at least 80 percent renewable supply. No start of construction has been reported since the December 2025 approval. The next step is for Amazon to sign that renewable power contract before it can begin operating the site.
