No start of construction has been reported since the December 2025 approval.
The next step is for Amazon to sign that renewable power contract before it can begin operating the site.

amazon-aws-drogheda.text: Amazon Web Services runs a 48 megawatt data center at the IDA Business and Technology Park on the Donore Road, just outside Drogheda in County Meath, near the border with County Louth. Amazon has permission to build a second, identical 48 megawatt data center next to it, and Meath County Council approved the first building in February 2020. The first data center has been operating since construction finished in 2021. The council approved the second building in June 2021, but the heritage group An Taisce appealed, arguing that planning authorities were granting data centers "on a case-by-case basis without adequately addressing the cumulative impacts of energy use." An Bord Pleanala granted permission for the second building in April 2022, finding it would not significantly affect climate or national emissions targets. At approval, the second building was expected to be finished by June 2026, a date that has now passed with no report of it opening. Each building was expected to bring about 50 jobs, with up to 400 people on site during construction, and the second was to add its own substation and rooftop solar panels. AWS has told planners that three phases planned for the park would together draw up to 144 megawatts. The most recent report on progress at the second building is from April 2022, and nothing more recent has been published.

amazon-aws-greenhills-tallaght.text: Amazon Web Services runs three two-story data centers on a 7.72 hectare site off Greenhills Road in Tallaght, County Dublin, Ireland, and has been operating there since 2014. The closest homes, in Tymon North Green and Tymon North Lawn, sit about 50 meters from the site boundary, according to Amazon's 2022 filing with the Environmental Protection Agency. The campus runs 50 diesel backup generators and fire pumps, meant only for power cuts or testing and expected to run under 500 hours a year. Amazon's air modeling found the generators would keep nitrogen dioxide within air quality limits, and the data halls are cooled mostly with outside air. The site uses about 23,912 cubic meters of water a year, and rainwater drains through six outfalls into the Tymon River, which the Environmental Protection Agency rates as poor ecological quality, on its way to the Poddle and the Liffey. In July 2026 Amazon applied to build a new security building and gatehouse at the site's entrance, with a vehicle checkpoint and new perimeter fencing. Ireland's energy regulator froze new data center grid connections in the Dublin area from 2021 until December 12, 2025, when it lifted the freeze on condition that new sites cover their own peak demand and get at least 80 percent of their power from new renewable projects. No further expansion at this site has been reported since the July 2026 filing.

amazon-aws-offaly-eco-energy-park.text: Amazon Web Services plans to develop data centers at Bord na Móna's Eco Energy Park in County Offaly, in Ireland's Midlands about 100km west of Dublin, as the first business to join the park. The partnership, announced on April 30, 2024, is subject to regulatory and planning consent, and the number, size and timing of the data centers have not been shared. AWS would draw power from Bord na Móna's renewable developments under a long-term power purchase agreement. The Eco Energy Park, announced in 2021, is planned on 3,000 hectares of Bord na Móna land close to the M6 motorway at Rochfortbridge in Westmeath, taking in parts of counties Offaly and Meath. The park is to host low to zero-carbon generation from wind, solar and gas, along with energy storage. As part of the deal AWS signed a 105-megawatt power purchase agreement for the 21-turbine Derrinlough Wind Farm in west Offaly and pledged to back an 800-megawatt pipeline of new renewable projects in Ireland. "We can co-locate these large companies with our renewable energy assets to offer a sustainable pathway to grid capacity that is backed up with Flexible Technology power as required," said Bord na Móna chief executive Tom Donnellan. Ireland's energy regulator ruled in 2025 that future data centers must meet 80 per cent of their energy needs from additional Irish renewable plants, a rule AWS's Ireland lead Niamh Gallagher said creates long-term demand for new green power. Most of Ireland's data centers are around Dublin, where Amazon has campuses in Clonshaugh, Blanchardstown and Tallaght and has reportedly held back some projects because of a moratorium on new grid connections. In May 2026 Gallagher said the Derrinlough deal was among AWS's Irish renewable agreements, part of its 800-megawatt goal for new generation.

amazon-aws-didcot.text: Amazon Web Services plans four data centers on the site of Didcot A, a coal and oil power station in Oxfordshire, England, that shut down in March 2013. RWE, which owned the land, sold about 100 acres to Amazon for roughly 197 million pounds in a deal that closed in November 2025. Amazon filed a reserved matters application for the four data center buildings, with a decision due January 27, 2026; that date has passed and no decision has been published. The site already has permission for a smaller scheme nearby. In June 2021, Vale of White Horse District Council unanimously approved two data centers on 16 hectares there for an applicant later tied to Amazon, Willow Developments, and South Oxfordshire District Council approved it in September 2021. Councillor Ben Mabbutt called the smaller scheme "a good use of the land... that won't tax our heavily populated travel network." Didcot and Sutton Courtenay parish objected that landscaping would not shield neighbors from light, noise and movement, and that the plan did too little for public transport, cycling and walking. RWE separately won permission in July 2025 for a wider 197,000 square meter data campus on the same brownfield site, and Amazon counts its Didcot plans toward a pledge to spend 8 billion pounds on UK data centers from 2024 to 2028. The Environment Agency also consulted on a backup generator permit for what Amazon calls the Didcot North Data Center Campus, through January 19, 2026. The reserved matters decision on the four data center buildings, due January 27, 2026, is the next step, and it has not been published.

amazon-aws-bracknell.text: Amazon Web Services' data center at Amen Corner, on Cain Rd in Binfield, Bracknell Forest, Berkshire, England, is operating on the former UK head office site of Hewlett Packard Enterprise. Bracknell Forest Council approved the single story building, 139 meters long and just over 12 meters high with 8,692 square meters of floor space, under planning application 21/00239/FUL on March 3, 2021. McLaren Construction built the data center, which it says has a capacity of about 20 megawatts across four phases of fit-out, for a client it does not name. The applicant behind the planning permission, Mount Elbert Edgecore Services LLC, did not mention Amazon by name, though its planning statement referred to staff hired directly by AWS; the Register later reported that AWS used Delaware shell companies for planning applications at Bracknell and at Burderop near Swindon. The approved plans include ten 3 MVA emergency generators plus one smaller backup unit, tested briefly every two weeks and at full load twice a year in daytime, and Amazon Data Services UK Limited applied to the Environment Agency in September 2021 for a permit covering them. The site's water use was expected to stay under 1,000 cubic meters a year, about what eight average UK households use. West of the data center, land at Amen Corner South is approved for 725 homes, a neighborhood center and a primary school.

amazon-aws-houghton-regis-linmere.text: Two data centre buildings are planned for the Linmere Island site at Houghton Regis in Central Bedfordshire, an 8.7 hectare plot boxed in by the A5 Dunstable bypass, Chantry Way, Woodside Link and Sundon Road. The campaign group Foxglove identifies Amazon Web Services as the operator behind the applicant, Colliers Properties LLC. The officer report describes about 51,300 square metres of floorspace in two buildings with a substation compound between them, an attenuation pond and an entrance from Chantry Way. The buildings would be about 20 metres tall, with lift shafts and plant reaching 25 metres, and the developer's consultation put the operating workforce at 70 to 100 people. The report counted at least 350 construction jobs over three to five years and 70 permanent jobs, and said the scheme was part of the applicant's plans to invest 8 billion pounds in the UK data centre market. The land lies in Linmere, the Houghton Regis North urban extension whose 2014 outline permission allowed up to 5,150 homes and a data centre; in January 2025 the council removed the data centre and the island site from that permission. Chalton Parish Council objected that the scheme broke with the employment zone agreed for Linmere, that 70 highly technical jobs offered little to local people, and that the applicant had not said how much power its 43 emergency generators would produce. The parish estimated the campus would draw between 50 and 100 megawatts from the Sundon substation over a 132 kV connection. Anglian Water objected to a connection into its foul sewer over capacity and pollution risk; the connection turned out to be into Thames Water's network, and officers proposed settling it by condition. At the development management committee in early July 2025, Keith Featherstone of Chalton Parish Council said: "This site has been selected only because it's close to the Sundon substation." He estimated that 40 to 50 per cent of the energy supplied would leave as waste heat from 222 extraction fans and put carbon dioxide emissions at more than 12,000 tonnes a year. Tim Squirrell, head of strategy at Foxglove, said similar data centres "tend to consume between four and 19m litres of water a day" for cooling, and that it was unclear how much Affinity Water would need to supply. Houghton Regis Town Council backed the parish objections. Nick Finney, the planning agent, said the buildings would be air cooled and that "Affinity confirmed it can supply sufficient water." The committee approved the plan subject to conditions, including one on a district heating network, and a Section 106 agreement. No decision notice had been issued when, in March 2026, a solicitor for a third-party objector wrote to the council arguing that the climate and renewable energy measures it had relied on were not secured by condition and that the draft Section 106 agreement had not been published. The letter indicated that a judicial review might follow, and on legal advice the council sent the application back to committee. On May 6, 2026 the committee approved it again, with condition 24 reworded and the draft Section 106 agreement published. Featherstone told the meeting that the sustainability statement was the original one and covered the two buildings but not the equipment inside that makes the heat: "It's madness to invest in an increased grid capacity and then allow most of the energy to add to global warming." Finney said the site would use no water to cool servers for about 97 per cent of the year, and that heat export depended on "the availability of a potential heat network and a specific customer." The permission is not final until the Section 106 agreement is completed and Central Bedfordshire Council issues its decision notice; in May the council's principal planning officer told the committee that "the Section 106 agreement is being finalised and no decision notice has been issued to date."

amazon-aws-villanueva-de-gallego.text: Amazon Web Services' data center at Villanueva de Gallego, in the Poligono Industrial San Roque north of Zaragoza in Spain's Aragon region, has been operating since 2022 and is one of three AWS sites in the region now being expanded. AWS plans 11 interconnected data center complexes across Aragon by 2030. In January 2026 two civil society groups, Tu Nube Seca Mi Rio and Ecologistas en Accion, filed an administrative appeal against the regional government of Aragon over the fast track approval of Amazon's expansion. The High Court of Justice of Aragon accepted the appeal weeks later, in what campaigners call Spain's first court case over a data center approval, argued by the Barcelona firm Fons de Defensa Ambiental. “They turn a deaf ear to concerned citizens and bypass democratic processes,” said Aurora Gomez of Tu Nube Seca Mi Rio, whose campaign raised 15,000 euros through crowdfunding to pay for the case. The objection is scale: one of the eleven planned complexes alone is expected to use 16.5 percent of the region's total energy, and the combined output of all of them would exceed current demand for all of Aragon. Campaigners say Amazon has resisted publishing water use figures for its Spanish sites. Amazon says it now replenishes more water in Aragon than its data centers use, has raised its regional water spending to more than 21 million euros, and that leak detection with FidoTech in Villanueva de Gallego's pipes has saved 33 million litres of water a year. The appeal is now before the High Court of Justice of Aragon, which is reviewing the case file on the regional government's fast track approval of Amazon's expansion.
paragraphs: Amazon Web Services' data center at Villanueva de Gallego, in the Poligono Industrial San Roque north of Zaragoza in Spain's Aragon region, has been operating since 2022 and is one of three AWS sites in the region now being expanded. AWS plans 11 interconnected data center complexes across Aragon by 2030.

In January 2026 two civil society groups, Tu Nube Seca Mi Rio and Ecologistas en Accion, filed an administrative appeal against the regional government of Aragon over the fast track approval of Amazon's expansion. The High Court of Justice of Aragon accepted the appeal weeks later, in what campaigners call Spain's first court case over a data center approval, argued by the Barcelona firm Fons de Defensa Ambiental.
“They turn a deaf ear to concerned citizens and bypass democratic processes,” said Aurora Gomez of Tu Nube Seca Mi Rio, whose campaign raised 15,000 euros through crowdfunding to pay for the case.

The objection is scale: one of the eleven planned complexes alone is expected to use 16.5 percent of the region's total energy, and the combined output of all of them would exceed current demand for all of Aragon. Campaigners say Amazon has resisted publishing water use figures for its Spanish sites.

amazon-aws-huesca-walqa.text: Amazon Web Services is building a new data centre campus, known as Walqa 2, on about 69 hectares of former poultry farms beside the Walqa Technology Park outside Huesca, in the province of Huesca in Aragon. The company put the investment at 714.6 million euros, and site work began in late April 2025. The plot is bounded by the technology park to the west, the railway to the north-east and the N-330 to the south-east. Plans described at the time showed 127,888 square metres of buildings, including data halls, a water treatment plant, two electrical substations, an administration building and fire water tanks, to be built over four years to 2029. Walqa will be Amazon's second site near Huesca, after its data centre at the Plhus logistics park. The campus is being approved under a Project of General Interest of Aragon, or PIGA, a category the regional government reserves for investments of special significance to the region. The planning stage of Amazon's second PIGA ran from 2024 to August 2025, and the basic infrastructure was approved in November 2025. In early May 2026 the first cabinet meeting of the new regional government gave final approval to the building projects for Walqa and two campuses at Villanueva de Gállego, moving the work from site preparation to construction. At Walqa the approval covers four large data centre buildings and one smaller one, up to 20 metres high, with ponds holding recycled water and surface runoff for cooling, storm tanks and solar panels. Work has to start within nine months and finish within four years. Regional minister Octavio López said the approval showed Aragon's commitment to becoming the leading technology hub of southern Europe. In June 2025 Amazon paid almost 1.5 million euros for a 1.4 kilometre underground line from the Plhus substation to the site, running under the A-23 and the N-330. A larger connection followed: about 20 kilometres of buried high voltage lines, two double 220 kV circuits and two double 132 kV circuits, from Red Eléctrica's Esquedas substation through La Sotonera, Lupiñén-Ortilla, Almudévar, Chimillas and Huesca, with a metering centre at Plasencia del Monte. INAGA, the Aragon environmental agency, issued a favourable environmental impact statement for the lines in October 2025. Amazon's filings put Walqa's water needs at 152,890 cubic metres a year, from three new wells, the municipal supply fed by the Valdabra reservoir, and rainwater. Amazon says its Aragon data centres return about 15 litres to the local water system for every litre they use, and it has paid to restore nearly 5.4 kilometres of historic pipeline at San Julián de Banzo in Huesca province. The groups Tu Nube Seca Mi Río and Ecologistas en Acción are challenging the regional government's August 2025 approval of Amazon's expansion plan, which covers five complexes, before the High Court of Justice of Aragon. The court admitted the appeal a few weeks after it was filed in January 2026 and later rejected Amazon's argument that it had been lodged too late. Aurora Gómez, the founder of Tu Nube Seca Mi Río, said the authorities ignore worried residents and sidestep democratic process, pointing to the shortened public comment periods under the PIGA.

amazon-aws-el-burgo-de-ebro.text: Amazon Web Services runs a 15 megawatt data center at the El Espartal industrial estate in El Burgo de Ebro, near Zaragoza, Aragon, Spain, which has been operating since 2021. A second, larger campus is planned on 43 hectares nearby; Aragon's environmental agency approved its environmental permit in May 2026, and the regional government gave final approval in June 2026. The new campus would have six main buildings plus a substation, backup generators and 8,736 solar panels mounted over its water reservoirs. It would use nearly 115,000 cubic meters of water a year, most of it drawn from the Canal Imperial de Aragon in summer, plus about 80,000 cubic meters of stored rainwater for cooling. Amazon is paying 3.73 million euros to seal 25 kilometers of open irrigation ditches on the canal, which it says will save water for the region. Two environmental groups, Tu Nube Seca Mi Rio and Ecologistas en Accion, are challenging the regional government's approval of Amazon's wider Aragon expansion, which includes this campus, before the High Court of Justice of Aragon. The court admitted their appeal in January 2026 and rejected Amazon's argument that it had come too late. The regional Council of Government approved the project as one "of general interest" to Aragon; the latest report on the campus is from June 2026, and the court has not yet ruled.

amazon-aws-la-cartuja-zaragoza.text: Amazon Web Services plans a data center in La Cartuja Baja, on the edge of Zaragoza in Aragon, Spain. In June 2026 Spain's grid operator authorized the project's electrical connection, one of the last steps before construction can begin, Data Center Dynamics reported. AWS already runs data centers elsewhere in Aragon, at El Burgo de Ebro, Villanueva de Gallego and Huesca, and the La Cartuja site is part of the company's wider expansion in the region. Grid connections have become one of the biggest obstacles for new data centers in Spain, especially in Aragon, where so many projects have strained the available capacity. Aragon has become one of southern Europe's biggest data center markets, and AWS plans to spend tens of billions of euros there over the next decade. Construction can go ahead now that the connection is authorized, though AWS has not said when it will start.

amazon-aws-la-puebla-de-hijar-teruel.text: Amazon Web Services plans its largest data center campus in Aragon, Spain, on 70 hectares beside the N-232 highway in La Puebla de Hijar, a Teruel village of 935 people. Amazon chose the village because substations around Zaragoza have reached capacity, and the site has 100 megawatts of power guaranteed through Endesa's grid, connected at the Hijar substation. Construction is due to start in autumn 2027, and technology-industry sources put the investment at about 5 billion euros. The fight here is over water. The campus needs 350,000 cubic meters a year for cooling, and Amazon wants to draw it directly from the Ebro River. Talks with the Gaen irrigation community have been stuck for months, with irrigators saying they will not put the area's water future at risk. Counting the neighboring municipality of Azaila, the Teruel campus covers about 329 hectares, most of it at La Puebla de Hijar, 2.3 kilometers from the village and 51 kilometers from Zaragoza. Aragon has drawn more than 47 billion euros of data center investment in total, and two environmental groups, Tu Nube Seca Mi Rio and Ecologistas en Accion, are challenging the fast-track approval process used for Amazon's projects in the regional High Court. A new national rule could change the picture: on September 11, 2026 the Government of Aragon filed objections to Spain's draft decree on data centers, and economy minister Eva Valle warned that none of the region's currently planned centers would comply with it as drafted. Amazon declined to comment on the decree.

amazon-aws-massen-niederlausitz.text: AWS Massen-Niederlausitz is an Amazon Web Services data center under construction at Massen, near Finsterwalde in the Elbe-Elster district of southern Brandenburg, Germany. By May 2026 earthworks were visible across the site, temporary surfaces had been laid for construction and logistics, and a container village had gone up to house the workers. The site is planned for about 200 megawatts of power, one of the largest data center projects in southern Brandenburg. The Elbe-Elster district building authority issued the construction permit after about four months of review. One step is still outstanding: approval for the substation planned on site to supply the campus had not been fully granted as of the May 2026 report. Massen is one of two Brandenburg sites carrying the first region of the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, a service for European public bodies and regulated industries that opened January 15, 2026. AWS says it has committed more than 7.8 billion euros to the program in Germany and expects it to support an average of 2,800 full time jobs a year. Brandenburg's economics minister, Daniel Keller, said the state is on course to become Germany's leading data center location after the Rhine-Main region. Brandenburg now counts 15 data center projects, and many of its districts show up on independent mapping of groundwater stress, with the regional power network described as nearing its limits given the number of connection requests. Permits for what is still outstanding at Massen, the on-site substation, come from the Elbe-Elster district building authority.

amazon-aws-baruth-mark.text: Amazon Web Services plans a 100-megawatt data center in Baruth/Mark, in the Teltow-Fläming district of Brandenburg, Germany, for its AWS European Sovereign Cloud, the regional news site Niederlausitz aktuell reported in January 2026. It is one of two AWS sites planned in the region, alongside a 200-megawatt data center in Massen near Finsterwalde, part of 7.8 billion euros of planned AWS investment in Brandenburg. AWS launched the European Sovereign Cloud in Potsdam on January 15, 2026, and the Brandenburg economy ministry said AWS would first use existing colocation data centers before building its own in the state. AWS says the sovereign cloud is kept physically and logically separate from its other regions, run only by EU residents, with all data, including metadata, kept in the EU. Water is the local worry: in September 2026, as the Baruth town council cleared a development plan for a separate factory project in the area, the environmental group Ressourcen-Bündnis Baruth asked how the region's water supply would hold up in dry years if all the planned large users drew water at once. Brandenburg's economy minister Daniel Keller has said up to 30 billion euros could be invested in data centers in the state in the coming years. Any AWS project in Baruth would go before the same town council that voted 12 to 2 to approve the nearby factory plan in September 2026.

amazon-aws-schoeneck.text: Amazon Web Services has bought a 7.4-hectare plot in the Kilianstadten Nord II business park in Schoneck, in the Main-Kinzig district of Hesse, Germany, for a data center, and will pay the town more than 220 million euros for it, Mayor Carina Wacker announced in August 2026. amazon-aws-maintal-west.text: Amazon Web Services' planned data center in the Maintal-West industrial area of Maintal-Bischofsheim, Hesse, Germany, near Frankfurt, is still at the start of the building permit process, and at a public information evening in May 2026 AWS would not say how much power or computing capacity it will have. The AWS data center is on the former DHL site in Maintal-West, and AWS aims to have it running within five years. The event was AWS's first public information market of its kind in Germany, and many residents came. AWS manager Thomas Blood said grid power is already secured by contracts with the network operators, though it is not yet decided whether the new line will run above or below ground, and that climate studies, including on the effect on the nearby housing estate, are still missing. AWS says the site will be cooled by air alone 95 percent of the time, and that when water is needed, up to 93 percent of it will be collected rainwater used several times; it cites a global average power usage effectiveness of 1.15 for its data centers but gave no figure for Maintal. Maintal already fought one data center. EdgeConneX's plan in the Doernigheim district came with its own gas power plant, and the protest against it, led by aerospace engineer Thomas Schadt and former ship's captain Mark Behrend, drew national coverage and stalled the project pending further studies. Schadt said he is less critical of the AWS plan because it has no gas plant, but still asked what happens if there is not enough rain for the cooling system. One visitor, told no megawatt figure, said he did not feel taken seriously. Mayor Monika Boettcher, an independent, expects a billion-euro investment and does not expect protests like those against EdgeConneX, because grid power is available. She wants to join Hanau and Dietzenbach in calling for a new way of calculating business tax for data centers so more money stays with the host towns. The city says an agreement for Maintal-West rules out any further data center in the newly developed industrial area. The building permit process and the missing climate studies come next, with the Maintal city council and the permitting authorities deciding.

amazon-aws-tnuvot.text: Amazon Web Services' 12 megawatt data center at Tnuvot, east of Netanya in Israel's Center District, is already operating. In November 2025 AWS signed a letter of intent to lease a nearby 10.5 acre lot from Rotshtein Real Estate for a second data center of 35 to 40 megawatts, the business paper Globes reported. A data center that size would roughly double AWS's processing capacity in Israel, probably by 2030, according to Globes. The Tnuvot site is one of three data centers behind the AWS Israel Region, which launched in August 2023 after AWS leased facilities at Tnuvot, Shoham and the Har Tov industrial park near Beit Shemesh. AWS announced the region in June 2021 after it and Google won a $1.2 billion tender to provide cloud services to Israeli government agencies under Project Nimbus. In January 2025 Globes reported that AWS had ended its search for more Israeli data center sites, as many local companies preferred to keep their data abroad. The November 2025 lease deal at Tnuvot revived those expansion plans. Under the letter of intent, AWS would pay the landowners, led by Rotshtein Real Estate with the Yehuda Levy Group and Moshav Tnuvot, 15 million shekels a year for up to five years while it decides, and could walk away with an exit penalty of up to 25 million shekels. Globes reported AWS had not yet ordered equipment or committed to building the data center, and put the possible investment at $600 million to $800 million. AWS can hold that option for up to five years before deciding whether to build the second Tnuvot data center.

amazon-aws-padre-hurtado-santiago.text: Amazon Web Services' Padre Hurtado data center, the company's first built data center campus in Chile, sits on an 18.7-hectare site in the Padre Hurtado district, in the Santiago Metropolitan Region. The $205 million, two-stage project cleared Chile's environmental review in January 2024, and its first building was due to be finished in 2025, with a second building scheduled for 2028. The first stage was a data center of 4,630 square meters; the second adds 3,470 square meters, according to BNamericas as reported by DCD. The campus includes 12 diesel backup generators and what Amazon describes as low-water-consumption cooling, air conditioning and fire control systems; its capacity has not been disclosed. The Santiago Metropolitan Region's Environmental Evaluation Commission backed the project unanimously, The Clinic reported, and it is meant to serve local users of Amazon's cloud. The worry around Santiago is water. Chile has been in a national drought since 2010, expected to last until 2040, and a small data center using water-based cooling at one megawatt needs about 25 million liters of water a year, Rest of World reported. "It's turned into extractivism," said Tania Rodríguez of the activist group Mosacat. "We end up being everybody's backyard." Activists want companies to file full environmental impact studies rather than self-assessed declarations; an AWS spokesperson said the company had complied with all the requirements of its environmental impact declarations for Padre Hurtado and Huechuraba. Amazon's second Santiago project, in Huechuraba, drew almost 50 citizen observations in 2023. In April 2026 Chile's Second Environmental Court turned down residents' claim against that project's environmental approval, finding it did not need to be assessed together with a high-voltage line that had been dropped. The court said any future high-voltage project would need its own environmental assessment, including the cumulative impacts alongside projects already cleared, such as the Amazon data center. Google's second Santiago data center, authorized to draw 228 liters of water a second, was halted by the environmental tribunal until Google reassessed its impact, after protests by Mosacat. Environmental approvals in Chile are handled by the Environmental Evaluation Service, and its approval rate for evaluations is 94%, its executive director has said. In May 2025 AWS committed more than $4 billion to a Chile cloud region with three availability zones, to launch by the end of 2026, and said its data centers in the country would be largely air-cooled, using water for cooling only around four percent of the year. Padre Hurtado's second building is the next stage, scheduled for 2028.

amazon-aws-hyderabad-chandanvelly.text: Amazon Web Services' Chandanvelly data centre sits inside the state industrial corporation's park at Chandanvelly, in Shabad mandal of Rangareddy district, about 26 kilometres from Hyderabad's Shamshabad airport and 8 kilometres from Shabad town. Amazon Data Services India built it on a plot of 137,034 square metres, about 34 acres, spread over survey number 190 of Chandanvelly village and 195 of Hythabad village, with the hamlet of Anthareddyguda half a kilometre away. The site was one of two data centres, together worth 11,624 crore rupees or about 1.6 billion dollars, that Amazon put before Telangana's environmental regulators in early 2020; the other was at Meerkhanpet in Kandukur mandal. The State Expert Appraisal Committee recommended clearance on January 31, 2020, a step required for any building over 20,000 square metres. Amazon's environment management plan for Chandanvelly described 66,003 square metres of floor space in two buildings: the first drawing 5 megavolt-amperes from the grid, the second, covering phases two and three, drawing 48 megavolt-amperes through its own substation. It put the total cost at about 5,821 crore rupees, of which about 5,115 crore was computer equipment and machinery and about 24 crore was land. The plan said the finished site would take 159 kilolitres of fresh water a day from the corporation's pipeline next to the plot, draw no groundwater, and treat its sewage on site for toilet flushing and gardening. Amazon launched its Hyderabad cloud region in 2022, and by the end of 2025 had invested more than 1.3 billion dollars in cloud infrastructure there. The company says 250 students have gone through its data centre training programme in Telangana, and 110 of them were hired into its operations teams; the latest group of 51 graduated from Vardhaman Engineering College in Shamshabad. Near Hyderabad, it says, it paid for the rehabilitation of ten storage ponds and the digging of 100 new ones across 12 villages with the nonprofit SEARCH, which it counts as about 86 million litres of water a year. The park itself was carved out of farmland. In January 2024 families displaced by it told Deputy Chief Minister Mallu Bhatti Vikramarka that the previous BRS government had forcibly acquired more than 1,000 acres at 15 lakh rupees an acre when the market price was 1.5 crore, and that officials surveying survey number 190 had paid compensation to people who did not own land there while passing over the real owners. Bhatti promised an inquiry that would spare no official or broker found to have cheated the farmers, and jobs for local people in the park's new industries. Chandanvelly is now part of a much larger Amazon build. On July 15, 2026, Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy was to lay the foundation stone for Amazon's largest data centre campus in Bharat Future City, and the state has allotted 300 acres for the project, 202 in Future City and 98 at Chandanvelly. The plan is worth about 60,000 crore rupees, with a first phase due within 24 months and the rest over ten years. Telugu outlets reported in December 2025 that Microsoft was also building near Chandanvelly in Shabad, and that land prices in the area were expected to climb. Anurag Khilnani, AWS director of data centre delivery, said: "The support of the State Government of Telangana has been essential to fast-tracking the build of India's digital backbone in Hyderabad." The pace worries some. In July 2026 Donthi Narasimha Reddy, an environment and public policy expert, urged that data centres face mandatory environmental impact assessments and public hearings, pointing to a hyperscale complex proposed at Chandanvelly and neighbouring Manchanpally with a projected demand of 645.07 megawatts and 200 kilolitres of water a day. Summer temperatures in the area run between 40 and 44 degrees Celsius and reach 45 in May, and he argued that the heat these buildings shed into the air sets them apart from the townships they are classified alongside. "This entire cluster is expected to come up in Chandanvelly, Bharat Future City, Fab City, and the proposed Chevella data centre city," he said. Environmental clearance for large data centre buildings in Telangana runs through the State Expert Appraisal Committee, which recommended Chandanvelly's in 2020.

Bhatti promised an inquiry that would spare no official or broker found to have cheated the farmers, and jobs for local people in the park's new industries.
Chandanvelly is now part of a much larger Amazon build.

On July 15, 2026, Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy was to lay the foundation stone for Amazon's largest data centre campus in Bharat Future City, and the state has allotted 300 acres for the project, 202 in Future City and 98 at Chandanvelly.
The plan is worth about 60,000 crore rupees, with a first phase due within 24 months and the rest over ten years.
Telugu outlets reported in December 2025 that Microsoft was also building near Chandanvelly in Shabad, and that land prices in the area were expected to climb.
Anurag Khilnani, AWS director of data centre delivery, said: "The support of the State Government of Telangana has been essential to fast-tracking the build of India's digital backbone in Hyderabad."
The pace worries some.

In July 2026 Donthi Narasimha Reddy, an environment and public policy expert, urged that data centres face mandatory environmental impact assessments and public hearings, pointing to a hyperscale complex proposed at Chandanvelly and neighbouring Manchanpally with a projected demand of 645.07 megawatts and 200 kilolitres of water a day.

Summer temperatures in the area run between 40 and 44 degrees Celsius and reach 45 in May, and he argued that the heat these buildings shed into the air sets them apart from the townships they are classified alongside.
"This entire cluster is expected to come up in Chandanvelly, Bharat Future City, Fab City, and the proposed Chevella data centre city," he said.
Environmental clearance for large data centre buildings in Telangana runs through the State Expert Appraisal Committee, which recommended Chandanvelly's in 2020.

amazon-aws-navi-mumbai-taloja.text: Amazon Web Services has filed for environmental clearance to build a data center campus that trade coverage describes as near Taloja in Navi Mumbai, though the land Amazon bought from Lodha actually sits in the Palava township area of Ambernath, in Thane district. Amazon Data Services India's April 2026 filing describes six buildings on about 49 acres: four seven-story data center blocks and two buildings for electrical and water equipment, with 473 megawatts of power. The investment is reported at nearly 4,000 crore rupees, about 430 million dollars, in Hindustan Times reporting cited by The Tech Capital and StorageNewsletter. Amazon bought the land in two parcels from Macrotech Developers, the listed Lodha company: 38.18 acres registered on November 12, 2024 for more than 450 crore rupees, and 10.6 acres registered on May 26, 2026 for 125.13 crore rupees, according to SiliconIndia and Lodha's own account of the project. Lodha is developing the surrounding land as what it calls a Green Digital Data Centre Park, backed by a 30,000 crore rupee agreement with the Maharashtra government, and names Amazon Web Services and STT Global Data Centres as buyers in the park. No date has been given for construction to start at the Amazon site, and the environmental clearance was still pending as of the most recent reporting.

amazon-aws-thane.text: Amazon Web Services plans a large data center on a 53-acre plot at Balkum, in the Majiwada area of Thane, Maharashtra, close to the Balkum, Kolshet and Dhokali housing societies. Amazon Data Services India bought the land from Ananta Landmarks, a Kalpataru Group company, in October 2022 for more than 1,800 crore rupees, with the finished campus estimated to cost about 47,000 crore rupees. The Thane Municipal Corporation granted permits for the site, its roads and its entrance in 2024, and tree clearing and site work are already under way. In July 2026 the Marathi daily Saamana counted 112 trees cut on the site, including 39 mango trees, eight tamarinds and a banyan, more than the 239 trees Amazon says its permit allowed it to fell. Thane's member of parliament, Naresh Mhaske, asked for construction to stop pending an independent review and accused the company of cutting more trees than permitted. Amazon rejected the allegations and said it holds valid permits and clearances. Amazon says the campus will use only 125 kiloliters of water a day, split between drinking water and treated sewage water for landscaping, and will not draw on the community's drinking supply. Residents point instead to the Thane Municipal Corporation's agreement to supply the site with 12 million liters a day of recycled sewage water, in a city that already runs about 30 million liters a day short, with many housing societies relying on tanker trucks. Dayanand Nene of the Satark Nagrik Foundation has asked the Maharashtra state cabinet to review and cancel the site's layout permissions. On September 9 Aaditya Thackeray said the campus would use far more water than Amazon claims for only about 75 jobs across two shifts. The permissions still stand, and the decisions residents are pressing for rest with the Thane Municipal Corporation and the state government.

amazon-aws-cyberjaya.text: Amazon Web Services' first data center in Malaysia is being built on Persiaran APEC in Cyberjaya, Selangor, according to a project signboard photographed in August 2024. The signboard showed a multi-phase project, including the data center itself, offices and other buildings, overseen by the Sepang municipal council, with no construction start or completion date given. AWS launched its Malaysia cloud region, based in this area, on August 22, 2024, and pledged to invest $6 billion in the country by 2037. The company said the investment would add about $12.1 billion to Malaysia's economy and support an average of 3,500 jobs a year at outside businesses through 2038. Cyberjaya is one of Malaysia's three main data center hubs, along with Kuala Lumpur and Johor, and the operator NTT also has a data center on the same road. As of the most recent published report, in August 2024, the timeline and size of the AWS building itself remained unknown.

amazon-aws-ulsan-sk-group.text: SK Group and Amazon Web Services are building an AI data center in the Mipo National Industrial Complex in Ulsan, on South Korea's southeastern coast north of Busan, on a site formerly operated by SK Chemicals. SK Telecom and SK Ecoplant broke ground on August 29, 2025, and the facility is to reach 103MW at completion, with 41MW available by November 2027 and the whole facility by February 2029. The project is set to house 60,000 GPUs, and Korea's Ministry of Science said it would bring 7 trillion won ($5.11bn) of investment to the region. SK Gas will supply liquefied natural gas to SK Multi Utility, whose combined heat and power plant will provide the electricity, and SK Ecoplant is leading the design and construction. The GPU racks are designed to draw 20 to 40 kilowatts each, cooled by a hybrid air and water system. SK Telecom and SK Broadband bought the roughly 36,000 square meters of land from SK Chemicals for 28.3 billion won, according to Construction Review Online. "This project is not just about putting up a building, but about laying the foundation of Korea's digital economy and building its future," SK Supex Council Chair Chey Chang-won said at the groundbreaking. Ulsan's city government expects the project to create jobs and spread AI uses such as digital twins and smart factories in local manufacturing, and Ulsan Mayor Kim Doo-gyeom attended the ceremony. The plan has since grown: SK Telecom has said it will expand the Ulsan site to gigawatt scale as part of a push for up to 15 gigawatts of AI data centers, with 5 gigawatts to come online in stages from 2029. In September 2026, SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won said at the Ulsan Forum that the site was nearing 900 megawatts of planned capacity and that talks with global technology companies were moving quickly. "I am worried if we make huge investments, but there is not much return," Chey said at the same forum. In August 2026, SK Telecom moved its data center assets, including the Ulsan project, into a new company, SK Horizon, in which KKR and an IMM-led consortium agreed to invest 3.08 trillion won. The next milestone is the first 41MW phase, due in November 2027.

amazon-aws-cobblebank-melbourne.text: Amazon Web Services is planning a data center on a 13.47-hectare site at 54-80 Ferris Road in Cobblebank, a suburb of the City of Melton about 40km west of central Melbourne, Victoria, Australia. Amazon paid AU$60.5 million for the land, 150 percent more than the previous owner paid for it as a business park site in 2021. The site sits next to Harness Racing Victoria's Tabcorp Park Melton at a Western Freeway interchange, within walking distance of a train station. Melton City Council said in July 2026 that it is aware of three data center proposals in the municipality: the Cobblebank site, already under construction, and two more in nearby Truganina still in the planning phase. The council said its role is limited to providing feedback through the state planning process, run by the state's Department of Transport and Planning. The council also addressed community discussion about a proposed data center in Plumpton, saying it had not received formal notification of any such project from the state government.

amazon-aws-kutanegara-west-java.text: Amazon Web Services runs a data center in Kutanegara, part of Karawang Regency in West Java, Indonesia, one of the buildings behind AWS's Asia Pacific (Jakarta) Region. It sits on Jalan Surya Utama inside the Suryacipta City of Industry estate, about an hour from Jakarta by toll road. West Java won the project in 2019, after governor Ridwan Kamil said in June that year that Amazon had committed to a data center investment of about 1 trillion rupiah in the province. The province offered three sites and Amazon chose Karawang; by December 2019 the regional government had signed off on the plan, and its labor department was already running cloud computing training with AWS. AWS told reporters in November 2019 that the Jakarta region would have three availability zones, each with at least one data center. The region opened on December 14, 2021, with a pledge of $5 billion, about 71 trillion rupiah, over 15 years, which AWS estimated would support 24,700 jobs a year. The Suryacipta estate, which hosts the Kutanegara site, says on its own website that Amazon has spent 35 trillion rupiah on data centers in its Karawang industrial park.

apple-apple-maiden.text: Apple is adding another 237,600-square-foot data center building at its campus off Startown Road in Maiden, Catawba County, North Carolina, a $175 million project reported in April 2025 on land the company already owns. The campus, which Apple began building in 2009, spans about a million square feet and has drawn around $4 billion in investment, Data Center Dynamics reported. In 2015, a chemical leak at the campus sent five people to the hospital. The campus runs entirely on renewable energy, Data Center Dynamics reported, from Bloom Energy biogas fuel cells, two solar arrays and direct clean-energy purchases. Apple's 2024 environment report put the site's use at 453 million kilowatt-hours, 82 percent of it from solar and 12 percent from wind. The Maiden expansion is part of the $500 billion U.S. investment Apple announced in February 2025, which also grows data centers in Iowa, Oregon, Arizona and Nevada. With a drought raising concerns about local water supplies, Catawba County says the Maiden site draws water from the City of Hickory, along with other data centers in the county, and is projected to use a small share of the city's daily production capacity once fully running. Apple opened its first North American data center campus in Maiden more than a decade ago, Catawba County says. The company has since begun shipping American-made servers from a new factory in Houston, some of which will be installed at Maiden as part of the current expansion.

apple-apple-mesa.text: Apple's Mesa data center in Mesa, Arizona, in Maricopa County, is the company's global data command center, housed in the 1.3-million-square-foot former GT Advanced Technologies plant that was meant to make sapphire glass for Apple before GT went bankrupt in 2014. Apple announced in February 2015 that it would invest $2 billion to turn the building, which it had bought in 2013, into a command center for its global networks. The state said the site would employ 150 full-time Apple workers and bring 300 to 500 construction and trade jobs, and Apple pledged to power it entirely with renewable energy. The plant was operating as a data center by 2017, and a handful of staff at a time work 10-hour shifts monitoring the company's operations, according to a 2018 Arizona Republic tour reported by 9to5Mac. Apple said it partners with the Salt River Project for clean energy and planned solar panels on the parking lot. Mesa's Elliot Road Technology Corridor has since filled with data centers, from Google, EdgeCore, CyrusOne, Digital Realty, NTT and EdgeConnex among others. Water has been the argument: when the city council backed a development agreement for a large data center there in 2021, Vice Mayor Jenn Duff objected, "Data centers are not a responsible use of our water and it's time to stop and allow other forms of manufacturing and technology to infill in this area." Apple has said it plans to keep expanding data center capacity in Arizona as part of its $500 billion U.S. investment commitment. In August 2026, Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes asked the Legislature and Gov. Katie Hobbs to pause approvals of new data centers, citing a federal plan to cut Colorado River water and rising energy costs. Any new Mesa data center agreement would go to the Mesa City Council, as the 2021 vote did; a statewide pause would need the Legislature and the governor.

Apple said it partners with the Salt River Project for clean energy and planned solar panels on the parking lot.

Mesa's Elliot Road Technology Corridor has since filled with data centers, from Google, EdgeCore, CyrusOne, Digital Realty, NTT and EdgeConnex among others. Water has been the argument: when the city council backed a development agreement for a large data center there in 2021, Vice Mayor Jenn Duff objected, "Data centers are not a responsible use of our water and it's time to stop and allow other forms of manufacturing and technology to infill in this area."

Apple has said it plans to keep expanding data center capacity in Arizona as part of its $500 billion U.S. investment commitment. In August 2026, Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes asked the Legislature and Gov. Katie Hobbs to pause approvals of new data centers, citing a federal plan to cut Colorado River water and rising energy costs. Any new Mesa data center agreement would go to the Mesa City Council, as the 2021 vote did; a statewide pause would need the Legislature and the governor.

apple-apple-prineville.text: Apple's data center campus in Prineville, in Crook County, Oregon, sits beside Meta's much larger campus in a town two tech companies have reshaped. Apple has released far less about its Prineville site than Meta has, and did not respond to The Source's questions for a July 2026 story on the town's data centers. Apple's arrival was reported in April 2012, when the company, under the code name Maverick, struck a deal with the city and county exempting the project from most of its property taxes. In return Apple committed a minimum investment of $250 million and at least 35 jobs, after paying $5.6 million for 160 acres. In 2015 Apple halted plans for a second data hall during a legislative fight over a data center tax, then went ahead once Governor Kate Brown signed a bill ending that threat. Both companies negotiate their tax exemptions with city and county leaders through Oregon's long-term rural enterprise zone program. In exchange, the city collects utility fee revenue, which has risen from about $430,000 in 2011 to nearly $11 million, close to three times the city's annual property tax take. Crook County Schools gave up $10 million in local revenue to corporate tax exemptions in 2019, and by 2024 that had nearly tripled. City leaders are pleased with the trade-off. City Councilor Steve Uffelman said, "We are more financially stable now than we have ever been because of the revenue generated by the data center." Not everyone agrees: Karl Wilkerson, co-owner of the downtown diner Dad's Place, said, "To me it hurts the economy, it doesn't help the economy. It's not like it's benefitting us from having that up there." Prineville leaders say they likely won't offer a full property tax break to the next data center that comes around. City Manager Steve Forrester told Governor Tina Kotek's Statewide Data Center Advisory Committee on June 26, 2026 that the city will roughly double its property tax revenue once Meta's first exemption expires. In March 2026, state lawmakers blocked new data center projects from enterprise zone tax breaks until the summer of 2027, and the advisory committee is due to report its recommendations by October 2026.

apple-apple-reno-sparks.text: Apple's data center at Reno Technology Park in Sparks, Washoe County, Nevada, is expanding again: in August 2024 the company won about $62 million in tax abatements for the project. The site sits across the Truckee River from the Tahoe Reno Industrial Center, on the river's path from Lake Tahoe to Pyramid Lake. Apple is to make nearly $992 million in capital equipment investment over 10 years and create 10 jobs at an average hourly wage of $32.51 within five years, the Northern Nevada Business Weekly reported. Apple was the first company to build at Reno Technology Park, starting in 2012 with a campus code-named Project Mills, planned at 14 buildings. By January 2016 it had filed for a second campus, Project Huckleberry, after the site's power supply neared capacity, a Washoe County planner said. The expansion is expected to generate about $279 million in new taxes over the abatement period. Nevada's data center tax breaks can cut property tax up to 75 percent for a decade or two, and the state says Apple, Google and Vantage will still produce nearly half a billion dollars in tax revenue. The build-out has raised alarms among water experts: the Truckee River, the region's main water source, ends at Pyramid Lake, on the tribe's reservation. "It's completely tied into us as a people," said Steven Wadsworth, chairman of the Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe. Other companies including Google, Tract, Switch, Novva and Vantage are also building or expanding nearby in the Tahoe Reno Industrial Center, and public filings show a dozen area data center projects seeking large new blocks of electricity over the next decade. Apple's expansion filings go to Washoe County planners, while the state's Governor's Office of Economic Development tracks the tax returns the project has promised.

apple-apple-waukee.text: Apple's Waukee data center, on about 2,000 acres at Hickman Road and S Avenue in Waukee, in Dallas County, Iowa, has one building running, opened in October 2024 seven years after Apple announced the $1.3 billion project. The building serves North American users of iCloud, the App Store, Apple Music and iMessage, Apple told the Des Moines Register. Apple first said the data center would be online in 2020, later won an extension from the Iowa Economic Development Authority to August 2027, and filed for planning permission in February 2022. Filed plans show one 315,773-square-foot data center building with administration, maintenance and network buildings; future data center buildings, possibly up to five, would each need further site plan approval. In July 2025 the Waukee City Council approved site plans for more parking, mechanical units, a storm shelter, a materials storage building and a logistics building to assemble components for future projects on site. Asked whether the improvements could pave the way for more data centers, City Administrator Brad Deets said that would not be an "inaccurate conclusion." The deal has not always paid the city what it expected. Under the 2017 agreement Apple has a 20-year abatement on the buildings, with a minimum taxable value of $52.2 million per data center set in a 2023 agreement. When Dallas County calculated a year's valuation without applying that abatement, the correction left the city with $3.4 million less than planned, and the school district and county with less too. The city said the loss would not affect its operating budget but was making it re-evaluate the timing of infrastructure projects in its capital plan. Waukee reportedly offered about $214 million in local and state incentives in 2017, and Apple committed $100 million to a public fund and $4 million toward Triumph Park. The city receives $500,000 a year per building under its deal with Apple, AppleInsider reported. Any further data center buildings on the campus need separate site plan approval from the City of Waukee.

apple-apple-viborg.text: Apple's data center near Foulum, about 8 kilometers outside Viborg in central Jutland, opened in 2020 as a 6.3 billion kroner (Danish currency) project covering 166,000 square meters, the largest foreign investment ever placed in Denmark when it was announced in February 2015. It serves the App Store, Apple Music, iMessage and Siri across Europe, drawing power from two 150-kilovolt lines and backed by 14 diesel generators, with its usage matched by a solar array in Thisted and two large wind turbines near Esbjerg. Apple promised from the start to send the site's waste heat into Viborg's district heating network, but Danish tax on surplus heat made the deal uneconomic for years. That changed after the government abolished the price ceiling on surplus heat on January 17, 2025; the district heating company, Viborg Varme, had already approved a 266 million kroner plan in April 2024 to build an energy hub of heat exchangers and pumps at Foulum with a 4.5-kilometer line into the city. Chairman Kristian Brøns Nielsen said the plan could cut the bill for an ordinary detached house by 3,000 to 4,000 kroner a year. Construction of the heat hub began in early 2026, with the first stage, about 12 megawatts of heat, due in the first half of 2027; the line is sized for as much as 69 megawatts, and Viborg Varme expects the project to cover at least half the city's heating. In July 2025 Apple confirmed a further expansion at Foulum without saying how large, and Mayor Ulrik Wilbek said the extra heat would feed the network. Neighbors complained to the Viborg Folkeblad in November 2018 about light and noise from the site during construction. A decade after the announcement, the center employs about 80 people, and former mayor Torsten Nielsen admitted the jobs had fallen short of what he had talked about, calling it a steep learning curve.

apple-apple-gui-an.text: Apple's first data center in China, built jointly with Guizhou-Cloud Big Data Industry Co (GCBD) in the Gui'an New Area of Guizhou province, has served iCloud customers on the Chinese mainland since May 2021, DCD reported, citing the state news agency Xinhua. GCBD operates the data center and uses it to store Chinese customers' iCloud data inside the country. Apple first announced plans for a data center in China in 2017, promising $1 billion of investment. The move followed a 2016 cybersecurity law requiring customer data to be stored on local servers, and Apple signed an agreement with the Guizhou government in 2017; construction began in March 2019. GCBD took over as operator of Apple's Chinese iCloud service in 2018, and Apple began moving data to the facility shortly afterward. The arrangement has drawn privacy criticism. Under its agreements in China, GCBD is the legal owner of Apple iCloud data there, which lets Chinese authorities demand data from GCBD rather than Apple, AppleInsider reported. Apple maintains that only it has access to the encryption keys, but security experts say physical access to the servers makes that hard to guarantee. Apple's support pages say iCloud in China mainland is operated by GCBD, which Apple identifies as AIPO Cloud (Guizhou) Technology Co. Ltd, and that iCloud data there is subject to GCBD's terms and conditions. Apple has also been developing a second Chinese data center in Ulanqab, in the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. Chinese rules require foreign cloud firms to work through domestic partners; AWS's data centers there are operated by Beijing Sinnet and Microsoft's services by 21Vianet.

neoclouds-coreweave-kenilworth-nest.text: Construction is underway on CoreWeave's $1.8 billion AI data center at the former Merck & Co. headquarters on Galloping Hill Road in Kenilworth, Union County, New Jersey, and residents are still asking borough officials to take another look. A council meeting on June 16, 2026 ran nearly five hours as residents filled the room and lined the hallway, and it ended with no vote or action to change the project's approvals. CoreWeave is converting an existing 284,500 square foot lab and manufacturing building known as 11 NEST and adding 108,100 square feet of new construction, for a 392,600 square foot data center planned at 250 megawatts. The company first leased the site in 2024 and in August 2025 bought the facility and 27 adjacent acres for $322 million; the state awarded the project a $250 million tax credit in exchange for 143 jobs kept in New Jersey over ten years. The Planning Board signed off on the project in May 2025, and it drew little notice until word spread on social media in spring 2026: "Social media, that's the only way you'll hear about it here even though we're only 200 yards from the location," Union County resident Brent Krueger told News 12. At the June meeting, resident Toni Johnson, who said she relies on an oxygen tank, told the council: "If they put any air pollution more than what we have into the air, I'm gonna be dead by Christmas." A residents' group, the Union County Residents Alliance Coalition, says borough records describe 31 backup generators and a cooling yard of 29 chillers, and that no redevelopment agreement had been signed as of June 2026. Mayor Linda Karlovitch has defended the project, telling News 12 that CoreWeave is "using a closed loop cooling system and it avoids continuous use of local water," and that the company is paying for a substation so its costs are not passed on to residential ratepayers. CoreWeave says an acoustics study it commissioned expects 42 to 49 decibels at nearby homes in normal operation, and that the cooling loop needs about 310,000 gallons of water only once, at startup. New Jersey lawmakers moved to end the tax credit program that funded Kenilworth's award, and Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed the End Data Center Tax Credits Act on August 27, 2026, but it leaves CoreWeave's $250 million award in place because it ends only the program's uncommitted credits. With local approvals granted, borough officials say their role now is mainly to make sure the project follows the plans as it is built, and the state award can be paid out over five years starting in 2027 if CoreWeave meets its requirements.

The Planning Board signed off on the project in May 2025, and it drew little notice until word spread on social media in spring 2026: "Social media, that's the only way you'll hear about it here even though we're only 200 yards from the location," Union County resident Brent Krueger told News 12.

At the June meeting, resident Toni Johnson, who said she relies on an oxygen tank, told the council: "If they put any air pollution more than what we have into the air, I'm gonna be dead by Christmas." A residents' group, the Union County Residents Alliance Coalition, says borough records describe 31 backup generators and a cooling yard of 29 chillers, and that no redevelopment agreement had been signed as of June 2026.

Mayor Linda Karlovitch has defended the project, telling News 12 that CoreWeave is "using a closed loop cooling system and it avoids continuous use of local water," and that the company is paying for a substation so its costs are not passed on to residential ratepayers. CoreWeave says an acoustics study it commissioned expects 42 to 49 decibels at nearby homes in normal operation, and that the cooling loop needs about 310,000 gallons of water only once, at startup.

New Jersey lawmakers moved to end the tax credit program that funded Kenilworth's award, and Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed the End Data Center Tax Credits Act on August 27, 2026, but it leaves CoreWeave's $250 million award in place because it ends only the program's uncommitted credits. With local approvals granted, borough officials say their role now is mainly to make sure the project follows the plans as it is built, and the state award can be paid out over five years starting in 2027 if CoreWeave meets its requirements.

neoclouds-coreweave-lancaster.text: CoreWeave's data center at 216 Greenfield Road in Lancaster, Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, is under construction and due to open in summer 2027, and no hearing was ever held on whether a data center belongs there. The city's zoning officer classed it as wholesale trade and storage, a use already allowed in the Suburban Manufacturing district, so only land development plans needed approval. "They are not the same thing, and should never ever have been called the same thing," said resident Frank Arcoleo, who appealed that ruling in August 2025, but in December 2025 Lancaster County Judge Thomas B. Sponaugle ruled against him on procedural grounds. Council President Amanda Bakay said she wanted every data center project to come before council or the zoning board, and council is drafting data center rules, though they will not cover this site or a second CoreWeave building planned at 1375 Harrisburg Pike because of a community benefits agreement already signed with the developer. Chirisa Technology Parks, the site's co-developer, agreed as part of that community benefits agreement not to cool the facility using large volumes of water, and commissioned an acoustic study that found a neutral noise impact, which the city said it was checking independently. Two more buildings are planned: a second at Greenfield Road in late 2027 and one at 1375 Harrisburg Pike in 2029, on a site that held the old LSC Communications and R.R. Donnelley printing plants. CoreWeave announced the project in July 2025 at a Pennsylvania energy summit attended by Governor Josh Shapiro, putting the cost at up to $6 billion, starting at 100 megawatts of capacity with room for 300, and projecting 600 to 1,000 construction jobs and 150 permanent positions. The city has so far collected $327,345 in real estate transfer tax and about $7.8 million in phase one building permit fees. The city council, which is drafting the data center rules that will not apply to this project, next takes the zoning ordinance amendment to a public hearing before the full council.

neoclouds-coreweave-plano.text: CoreWeave's first Texas data center is a converted corporate campus at 1000 Coit Road in Plano, Collin County, once the North American headquarters of the French telecom company Alcatel. The $1.6 billion, 454,421-square-foot facility on a 23.8-acre site became operational at the end of 2023 inside Lincoln Property Company's Lincoln Rackhouse building. The campus passed from Alcatel to Westmount Realty Capital in 2004, then to Countrywide Financial, which Bank of America took over in the 2008 financial crash before selling the site during a data center consolidation. CoreWeave signed a six-year agreement with Lincoln for up to 30 megawatts of computing power, worth more than $260 million, with two two-year renewal options. The site holds four 14,000-square-foot data halls and 50,000 square feet of shell space for later expansion. The Plano City Council voted unanimously on July 24, 2023 to approve a tax rebate agreement requiring CoreWeave to invest at least $800 million a year for two years; half of the $1.6 billion minimum spent on improvements is to be returned to the company in 2025 and 2026. Mayor John B. Muns said the city was "thrilled to partner with CoreWeave as the company invests in its first data center in Texas." CoreWeave chief executive Michael Intrator said the company was pleased to partner with Plano and would "create new jobs."

neoclouds-coreweave-cheyenne-related-dig.text: Related Digital broke ground on October 7, 2025 on a $1.2 billion data center campus for CoreWeave on 115 acres at the Cheyenne Business Parkway in Cheyenne, Laramie County, Wyoming. CoreWeave has leased the first 88 megawatts of the campus, and it is planned for up to 302 megawatts in all. The land came from three men who grew up together in grade school, John and Jim Volk and Mickey Powers, who spent about 30 years developing lots nearby as the Campstool Land Company. "We decided we will only build self-contained cooling systems that do not use water," Related chief executive Jeff Blau said at the groundbreaking, adding that most water on site would go to about six bathrooms. Gov. Mark Gordon said, "This demonstrates that we can build data centers that aren't going to use water." Blau also gave $3.5 million toward a 184-unit affordable housing project the city had struggled to pay for, and Mayor Patrick Collins said Cheyenne faces a shortage of 5,000 to 7,000 homes by 2030. "We're going to change the lives of 184 families, because now they're going to be looking at 30% of their salaries going to rent," Collins said. Related projects more than $250 million in tax revenue for the state and city over the first 15 years, and 40 permanent jobs. By June 2026 more than 400 construction workers were on site, with more than 700 expected at the peak, and crews had laid 80,000 feet of chiller pipe and 40,000 feet of medium voltage conduit. The halls use closed loop, direct-to-chip liquid cooling that needs almost no makeup water, and batteries carry the load for about seven minutes in an outage before generators start. Cowboy State Daily reported that Related expects the campus eventually to deliver up to 420 megawatts for CoreWeave, more than the 302 megawatts in the original announcement, with the first 184,000 square foot building due to finish in late 2026.

neoclouds-coreweave-cambridge-ontario.text: CoreWeave runs an AI data center in north Cambridge, Ontario, in the Region of Waterloo, where the Canadian AI company Cohere is a customer. The building, on Vondrau Drive, belonged to BlackBerry until 2017, and French company OVHcloud is also a tenant. Real estate records link the property to TowerBrook Capital Partners, a private equity firm with offices in New York and London, which has partnered with the American developer Related Digital. A zoning application to the City of Cambridge in July 2024 showed the owner planned to turn the warehouse part of the building into a new data center. In August 2025 CPP Investments committed $225 million to the construction loan for a 54 megawatt expansion by Related Digital, TowerBrook and Ascent, with Deutsche Bank as lead lender and the space pre-leased long term to a GPU-focused AI cloud provider. Cohere's use of the site is tied to federal money: Ottawa announced in December 2024 it would give the company up to $240 million for computing. Cohere chief executive Aidan Gomez said putting the computing power on Canadian soil would help more Canadian researchers, startups and companies compete globally. On July 19, 2026, the province was called about an "odorous, milky white substance" in the stormwater pond across from the data center, on property co-owned by Ascent and Related Digital. The province said the substance had reached West Creek and the Speed River, which flows into the Grand River, and Brantford took precautions to protect its drinking water. Related Digital blamed a "bacterial bloom" from stagnant water and heat, and preliminary samples showed "no evidence of contaminants of concern," but the Region of Waterloo said the investigation into the source was continuing. Local government is now catching up. In August 2026 regional councillors unanimously asked staff for an overview of data centers' effects on water, power, the economy and the environment, due in early 2027. Cambridge council unanimously directed its own staff to identify appropriate locations and policies for any future data centers, with a report expected in early 2027. On August 25, 2026 it also asked Ontario to speed up a provincial framework for judging data center proposals. "So many municipalities in North America and around the world are getting caught because we don't have guidelines in place," Mayor Jan Liggett said. "There's nothing out there to protect the residents."

neoclouds-coreweave-barcelona-merlin-edg.text: MERLIN Edged runs a data center in Barcelona's Free Zone in Catalonia, Spain, that hosts the AI cloud company CoreWeave; in its first, roughly 15 megawatt phase, CoreWeave is running 10,224 Nvidia H200 chips, its computer processors for AI work, connected by a fast network called InfiniBand. Barcelona Mayor Jaume Collboni inaugurated the facility on May 13, 2025 with Albert Tort, the Catalan government's secretary of telecommunications and digital transformation. "This asset represents the realization of a shared vision: to transform Barcelona into a true digital port in the Mediterranean," Collboni said. MERLIN Edged is a joint venture formed in 2020 by the Spanish real estate company MERLIN Properties and Edged Energy, and also runs data centers in Madrid and Bilbao. "This is our southern Europe region, which gives us the ability to feed any metro in the south within 20 to 30 milliseconds," CoreWeave's international general manager Mike Mattacola told DataCenterDynamics. The companies say MERLIN Edged data centers use no water for cooling, run on renewable electricity, and are designed to waste very little power, with what the industry calls a power usage effectiveness of 1.15, close to the 1.0 of a perfectly efficient facility. The Barcelona site is part of CoreWeave's plan to spend about $2.2 billion on data center infrastructure across Europe. A second phase at the site, expected to use Nvidia's newer Blackwell chips, has not started; Mattacola said in 2025 the company would decide on it "a little bit closer to the time when we plan to launch capacity," and no update on that decision has been published since.
