developers-vantage-va2-ashburn-ii.text: Vantage's VA2 data center on Glenn Drive in Sterling, in Loudoun County, Virginia, is the only Vantage campus in the state that runs full time on its own gas turbines rather than the grid. Eight turbines in one building power it around the clock, and at an August 24, 2026 town hall, Vantage told residents the campus is not expected to get grid power until 2040. Vantage bought 17 acres on Glenn Drive for $46 million in October 2021, and filings by Loudoun County Economic Development put the finished campus at up to 96 megawatts across 800,000 square feet. "There was this constant, just like a buzzing in your head ... And this is just not pleasant to listen to every day, all day," said Lindsay Shaw, who welcomed the project when she first heard about it and changed her mind once it went online. "One, sometimes it wakes me up. You can hear it in my house," said Greg Pirio, who has organized neighbors to press their case in public. Kasey Hatch told Loudoun Now the loud days grew more frequent as the weather warmed, and described anxiety and broken sleep she now takes medication for. Loudoun's ordinance caps noise at 55 decibels, and county readings at homes next to the site have never exceeded that limit, Supervisor Koran Saines said, adding that new zoning enforcement officers would give residents real-time responses to complaints. The county has since set up a working group to look at how turbine noise is measured and whether the ordinance needs changing. The Piedmont Environmental Council commissioned a study, built on Vantage's own state permit, estimating the emissions could cause three to six additional deaths a year in the area, and 17 to 33 over five years. "It's associated with asthma and increased cardiovascular impacts on especially vulnerable populations and the elderly," said Julie Bolthouse of the council. Vantage's Adam Shalapin said the permit figures are maximums rather than day-to-day reality, and that "the VAT facility operates well below those permitted limits and emits significantly less pollution." A power failure on July 16, 2026 put the campus onto its diesel backup generators and brought a fresh round of complaints; one homeowner described diesel fumes that irritate the throat and lungs and wake them at night, and property values undercut by the noise. Phyllis Randall, chair of the county board, arranged to meet the affected residents. What happens next is up to the Loudoun County Board of Supervisors: Saines said the county's work group will review its authority and options on data center problems, and residents such as Hatch want the noise ordinance to set limits per octave rather than on overall volume.
paragraphs: Vantage's VA2 data center on Glenn Drive in Sterling, in Loudoun County, Virginia, is the only Vantage campus in the state that runs full time on its own gas turbines rather than the grid. Eight turbines in one building power it around the clock, and at an August 24, 2026 town hall, Vantage told residents the campus is not expected to get grid power until 2040.

Vantage bought 17 acres on Glenn Drive for $46 million in October 2021, and filings by Loudoun County Economic Development put the finished campus at up to 96 megawatts across 800,000 square feet. "There was this constant, just like a buzzing in your head ... And this is just not pleasant to listen to every day, all day," said Lindsay Shaw, who welcomed the project when she first heard about it and changed her mind once it went online.

"One, sometimes it wakes me up. You can hear it in my house," said Greg Pirio, who has organized neighbors to press their case in public. Kasey Hatch told Loudoun Now the loud days grew more frequent as the weather warmed, and described anxiety and broken sleep she now takes medication for.

Loudoun's ordinance caps noise at 55 decibels, and county readings at homes next to the site have never exceeded that limit, Supervisor Koran Saines said, adding that new zoning enforcement officers would give residents real-time responses to complaints. The county has since set up a working group to look at how turbine noise is measured and whether the ordinance needs changing.

The Piedmont Environmental Council commissioned a study, built on Vantage's own state permit, estimating the emissions could cause three to six additional deaths a year in the area, and 17 to 33 over five years. "It's associated with asthma and increased cardiovascular impacts on especially vulnerable populations and the elderly," said Julie Bolthouse of the council. Vantage's Adam Shalapin said the permit figures are maximums rather than day-to-day reality, and that "the VAT facility operates well below those permitted limits and emits significantly less pollution."

A power failure on July 16, 2026 put the campus onto its diesel backup generators and brought a fresh round of complaints; one homeowner described diesel fumes that irritate the throat and lungs and wake them at night, and property values undercut by the noise. Phyllis Randall, chair of the county board, arranged to meet the affected residents.

What happens next is up to the Loudoun County Board of Supervisors: Saines said the county's work group will review its authority and options on data center problems, and residents such as Hatch want the noise ordinance to set limits per octave rather than on overall volume.

developers-vantage-va3-ashburn-iii.text: Vantage Data Centers is building its VA3 campus on 134 acres at 19509 Belmont Ridge Road in Ashburn, in Loudoun County, Virginia, and now advertises seven buildings there. It bought the land in 2022 for $180 million from Barcroft Associates, an entity controlled by Charles B. DeLashmutt, and gives the finished campus 2.3 million square feet and 288 megawatts of power. The county's board of supervisors voted 7-1 in September 2026 to pause new data center applications for 12 months, and county staff are due to bring a formal resolution on the pause to the board on October 20, 2026. The pause took effect immediately; the county had already removed data centers as a by-right zoning option and is exploring removing by-right status from projects that were grandfathered in. The Army Corps of Engineers received a joint federal and state permit application for the site in early 2023, covering ground west of Belmont Ridge Road and south of Harry Byrd Highway. The filing said the work would affect just over two acres of wetlands and 3,551 linear feet of stream channel, which Vantage proposed to offset by buying wetland credits from the Northern Virginia Stream Restoration Bank and stream credits from The Nature Conservancy of Virginia. The site plan filed with it showed four buildings and a substation, three fewer buildings than the company now lists. Cooling is a closed-loop chilled water system fed by air-cooled chillers with economizer capability, which Vantage says brings water use to near zero liters per kilowatt hour. Dominion, the local utility, is spending $50.1 billion on capital projects between 2025 and 2029, including the Golden to Mars 500/230 kilovolt transmission line and the Evergreen Mills project, both of which run through this area. Michael Turner, vice chair of the county board's transportation and land use committee, counted 199 data centers operating in Loudoun with another 117 in development.

developers-vantage-fredericksburg.text: Vantage Data Centers is building VA4, a $2 billion, 192 megawatt data center campus in Stafford County, near Fredericksburg, Virginia. Construction began November 6, 2025, on 82 acres, with three two-story buildings totaling about 929,000 square feet, and the first one is scheduled to open in late 2027. VA4 got its permits before Stafford tightened its data center rules in October 2025. On October 21, 2025, Stafford County supervisors widened the required buffer between data center buildings and nearby homes, schools and the Rappahannock and Potomac rivers from 100 feet to 750 feet. On December 2 they voted unanimously to let five projects filed before the change, including VA4, continue under the old rules. After residents objected, supervisors limited later changes to those "directly attributable" to the approved project, not any "related" change. The Stafford County Board of Supervisors would decide anything more restrictive that affects VA4 directly. VA4 is Vantage's fourth Virginia campus and its first outside Northern Virginia's Data Center Alley, about an hour away, bringing the company's statewide capacity to 782 megawatts. The project is expected to create 1,100 construction jobs and 50 permanent jobs, and Vantage plans a closed-loop chilled water system to limit the water needed for cooling.

developers-vantage-new-albany-oh1.text: Vantage Data Centers is building a 192-megawatt data center campus in New Albany, Licking County, Ohio, inside Lincoln Property Co.'s Silicon Heartland Innovation Park on Horizon Court. Vantage broke ground in October 2024 on three buildings totaling more than 1.5 million square feet, investing more than $2 billion, with the first building due to open by December 2025. The campus remains under construction; no report has confirmed that any building has opened. American Electric Power Ohio supplies the power, and Turner Construction is the general contractor. New Albany Mayor Sloan Spalding welcomed the company, saying its "values align closely with ours." Vantage also partnered with the New Albany Community Foundation and the Columbus State Community College Foundation on workforce training. AEP Ohio's data center tariff, which requires big power customers like Vantage to commit to monthly billing minimums, has cut the utility's demand forecast from 30,000 megawatts to about 5,700 megawatts, and manufacturers are challenging the rule at the Ohio Supreme Court.

developers-vantage-quincy.text: Vantage Data Centers finished its Quincy data center campus in Grant County, Washington, in October 2023, when it opened WA13, the third and last building on the 68-acre site. The campus now totals 89 megawatts of power across nearly 775,000 square feet, and Vantage says it has invested more than $1 billion there since entering Quincy in 2011. Power comes from the Grant County Public Utility District, which runs two hydroelectric dams on the Columbia River, and Vantage credited the state's rural data center tax incentive with spurring the industry there. Grant County projected the Quincy area's 2024 assessed value at over $8 billion, more than half of it from data centers; Sabey, Yahoo, NTT, Microsoft and CyrusOne also run data centers in Quincy. Quincy is a majority Hispanic farming community of about 7,500 people, and the tax money has paid for a new high school and hospital. Microsoft president Brad Smith has pointed to the town: "If you want to visit what's probably the nicest high school in the state of Washington, you don't go to the neighborhood where Microsoft's headquarters is based, you don't go next door to Amazon, you go to Quincy." City Administrator Pat Haley has said hydropower and water in Grant County are maxed out, and the utility district has 79 pending applications in its queue, most of them for data centers. Former mayor Patty Martin said: "What about 10 years, 20 years from now, and these facilities are still here and the electrical grid, because now there's more people, there's more electric cars, there's not as much water running in the river because the snow packs aren't there."

developers-vantage-reno.text: Vantage Data Centers is building a 224-megawatt data center campus, NV1, in Sparks near Reno, in Storey County, Nevada, inside the Tahoe Reno Industrial Center. The company is investing nearly $3 billion in four multistory buildings totaling about 1.1 million square feet, with the first scheduled to open in the second quarter of 2026. No report has confirmed that any building has opened, and the campus remains under construction. The first two buildings are already fully leased, though Vantage has not named the tenants. Filings for two of the buildings, NV11 and NV12, at Electric Avenue and USA Parkway, list investments of $150 million and $254 million, and Vantage was granted Storey County tax abatements in November 2024. NV Energy supplies power through a private 500-megawatt substation built for the site. Storey County manager Austin Osborne said: "Their arrival marks another important milestone in the growth of our region's digital infrastructure." Vantage joins PowerHouse, Google, Apple, EdgeCore, Novva and Tract building data centers in Storey County; no public dispute over the Reno campus has been reported.

developers-vantage-santa-clara-i.text: Vantage Data Centers' Santa Clara I data center campus, at 2820 Northwestern Parkway in Santa Clara, Santa Clara County, covers 21 acres. Six multi-story buildings hold more than 335,000 square feet and 77 megawatts of power. Vantage says the campus is the largest LEED Platinum certified data center campus in North America, cooling with a chilled water loop and reclaimed water from a water treatment plant. Santa Clara owns its electric utility, Silicon Valley Power, which charges 18.2 cents a kilowatt hour, 57 percent less than neighboring PG&E, and the city says it collects about $29.5 million a year from its data centers. That revenue funds police, parks, libraries and other resident services. "Our bills are about $130 for the electricity, the garbage and the water," a resident of Santa Clara Square, an apartment complex surrounded by data centers, told the New York Post.

developers-vantage-santa-clara-ii.text: Vantage Data Centers' Santa Clara II data center campus, known as CA2, sits on 9 acres on Mathew Street in Santa Clara, Santa Clara County, less than two miles from the company's first Santa Clara campus. The campus has more than 541,000 square feet in three four-story buildings with 75 megawatts of power, served by Silicon Valley Power through three on-site 50-megawatt transformers. Vantage broke ground in 2018, and the first building, 21 megawatts and 175,000 square feet, was due in 2019. Santa Clara has more standalone data centers than any other California city, and Silicon Valley Power, the city-owned utility, has hit its limit. In 2025 the utility had requests to add 500 megawatts of load on top of a peak of about 720, its chief operating officer Nico Procos said, and two new data centers built by Digital Realty and Stack stood finished but empty while they waited for power. Silicon Valley Power says its $450 million system upgrade to add capacity is on schedule for 2028.

developers-vantage-santa-clara-iii.text: Vantage Data Centers plans a third Santa Clara data center campus, CA3, at 2590 Walsh Avenue in Santa Clara, Santa Clara County, within two miles of its first two campuses and close to San Jose International Airport. The nearly 8-acre site will hold 486,000 square feet in one four-story building with 64 megawatts of power, run on renewable electricity from Silicon Valley Power, Vantage says. Vantage bought the plot, a 1980 warehouse of 113,600 square feet, for $40 million in 2021, then borrowed $350 million from Societe Generale in 2022 to convert it. Vantage's own site still describes CA3 in future tense, saying it "will include" the new space, and no report says construction is finished or the building has opened. Two other new Santa Clara data centers, built by Digital Realty and Stack, stood finished but empty in late 2025, both waiting for Silicon Valley Power to connect them. Santa Clara collects about $40.9 million a year from its data centers in taxes and utility payments, the city's economic development director Reena Brilliot has said.

Two other new Santa Clara data centers, built by Digital Realty and Stack, stood finished but empty in late 2025, both waiting for Silicon Valley Power to connect them.
Santa Clara collects about $40.9 million a year from its data centers in taxes and utility payments, the city's economic development director Reena Brilliot has said.

developers-vantage-berlin-i.text: Vantage Data Centers' Berlin I campus sits on Uferring 5 in Brandenburg Park, Ludwigsfelde, south of Berlin in Brandenburg, Germany, and is the company's second site in Germany after Frankfurt. The campus opened its first building in June 2022 and is planned, once built out across all four buildings, to hold 56 megawatts of power across 25 acres (10 hectares). At the 2022 opening the campus was described as 13 acres, with the first building alone offering 32 megawatts across 250,000 square feet; the fuller 25-acre, 56-megawatt figure is the plan for all four buildings together. "Data centers are the backbone of our digitalized world and therefore also an important part of the success of the industries based in Ludwigsfelde," Ludwigsfelde mayor Andreas Igel said at the opening. A second building later opened at 16 megawatts across 12,000 square meters, and Vantage's president for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, Antoine Boniface, said the company had grown quickly and was continuing to build across the region. A 110 kilovolt substation on the campus, with backup redundancy, draws power from the utility E.DIS, and cooling runs on a closed-loop chilled water system with air-side economizers that the company says keeps water use near zero liters per kilowatt hour. Solar panels supply part of the power for offices and other non-critical areas, and waste heat from the campus is fed into district heating.

developers-vantage-berlin-ii.text: Vantage Data Centers' Berlin II campus is in Mittenwalde, just south of Berlin in Brandenburg, Germany, where the first of two planned buildings has been running since November 2022, offering 16 megawatts of power. The five-hectare campus is meant to hold two such buildings at full build-out, for 32 megawatts across 24,000 square meters, about 20 kilometers from Vantage's Berlin I campus. Mittenwalde lost a much bigger data center plan in 2025. Google had bought a 30-hectare plot near Schenkendorf, between the L30 and A13 highways, in 2022, but withdrew in July 2025 after what a spokesperson called "a thorough review of feasibility, general market developments, and our business priorities." The regional paper Markische Allgemeine Zeitung reported that local power availability was not suited to AI computing needs, and that even Google's original, smaller plan would have needed the power grid expanded. Vantage's own campus has an on-site substation rated at 45 megawatts, fed by the regional utility E.DIS, and a closed-loop chilled water system using air-cooled chillers; the company broke ground in late 2021 and is backed by DigitalBridge.

developers-vantage-frankfurt-ii-raunheim.text: Vantage Data Centers' Frankfurt II campus in Raunheim, Germany, southwest of Frankfurt between Rüsselsheim and Hattersheim, is operating with 56 megawatts of computing power, about a 10-kilometer drive from Frankfurt International Airport. The company completed its first building there, a four-story structure accounting for 40 of the campus's 56 megawatts, in November 2022, after breaking ground on a second, 16-megawatt building, FRA22, that July. "The data center industry provides services that are indispensable for a digital and sustainable future," said Raunheim mayor Thomas Jühe, who also pointed to the company's energy partnership with the city. Vantage says the campus draws power through its own on-site substation and uses a closed-loop cooling system designed for near-zero water use. Vantage's first Frankfurt-area campus, a 55-megawatt site in Offenbach about 30 kilometers away, brings the company's total planned capacity around Frankfurt to 111 megawatts.

developers2-cyrusone-chandler-phoenix.text: CyrusOne runs a data center campus along South Ellis Street in Chandler, Maricopa County, Arizona: eight buildings the company puts at 2 million square feet of technical space and 169 megawatts of power. None of the eight buildings uses water to cool; the campus draws about 180,000 gallons a year only for humidification, which CyrusOne calls the first net positive water data center in its portfolio. Arizona's data centers together were expected to use about 905 million gallons of water in 2025, roughly what 10,000 Phoenix-area homes use in a year and less than a tenth of one percent of the state's water. Chandler has limited a data center to 115 gallons a day per 1,000 square feet since 2015, with anything more brought in from outside the city supply. The city also wrote zoning rules for data centers before most American cities had considered them: an ordinance adopted in 2022 and in effect since January 5, 2023, confining the use to certain zoning and requiring resident notification, a baseline sound study and limits on testing backup generators. "Unlike energy, using water to cool a data center is a choice, not a requirement," said Alex Setmajer of Equinix. CyrusOne says its newest data centers, built from 2024 onward, use zero-water cooling company-wide.

developers2-cyrusone-yorkville.text: Construction is under way on CyrusOne's 228-acre data center campus at the northeast corner of Faxon and Eldamain roads in Yorkville, Kendall County, Illinois, the first of three data center projects the city has approved along its Eldamain Road corridor. Work began in spring 2026, and by July the access drive lined up with Menards had been built and the site's electrical substation was largely developed. The campus now calls for eight single-story buildings totaling 1,854,805 square feet, no taller than 50 feet 10 inches, down from the nine two-story buildings of about 2.45 million square feet originally approved. The substation, originally planned at 800,000 square feet, has been cut by half along with the buildings; CyrusOne has a full allocation of 480 megawatts from ComEd, with the site due to be energized by the end of 2027. The developers said the first building should be running by the end of the first quarter of 2028. In July 2026 the city council approved a new development agreement: CyrusOne will pay Yorkville $15 million up front when the first building permit is issued, and its water use is capped at 40,000 gallons a day, down from the 500,000 once projected, with penalties for going over. The developer is paying to rebuild Faxon and Beecher roads and a railroad crossing, and the city says it is no longer giving CyrusOne tax incentives. The new noise rules, adopted after residents raised concerns about a construction period that could run 10 to 20 years, require CyrusOne to predict its noise before each building permit, install monitoring devices, and pay penalties if the campus exceeds the city's limits of 60 decibels by day and 50 at night in residential areas. Alderman Craig Soling said he and residents he has spoken to are "skeptical about estimates" from CyrusOne, pointing to its Aurora data centers, which it is now spending tens of millions of dollars to fit with sound attenuation. The separation from the two nearest homes grew from 732 feet to 833 feet under the new layout. The next milestones are the first building permit, which triggers the $15 million payment, and road work due by November 30, 2027.

developers2-cyrusone-council-bluffs-ocb1.text: CyrusOne's OCB1 data center in Council Bluffs, in Pottawattamie County, Iowa, near Omaha, is a colocation building the company markets for its low-latency cloud connectivity. The company gives it 216,000 square feet, of which 120,000 is raised floor, and 9 megawatts of IT capacity, and lists 420,000 square feet of technical IT space. Each cabinet is rated to 17 kilowatts. CyrusOne says the building is cooled by four 500 ton chillers per data hall in an air cooled plant at N+2 redundancy, with minimal water use for humidification and maintenance. In June 2026 Mayor Jill Shudak asked the city council for a year-long pause on data center projects that had not yet started or come before it, to review the rules the city first wrote for data centers in 2007: "we're running very high at capacity for both water and sewer," she said. Public Works Director Matt Cox compared a large data center's wastewater to that of roughly 4,000 homes: "So when we get a request, it's not for 100,000 gallons a day. It's for a million gallons a day or two million gallons a day. So it only takes one or two big projects and we're at capacity." At a special meeting the council rejected the moratorium unanimously. Councilman Doug Rew said a pause would make the city look closed to developers: "They see a red stop sign and say, 'that's what we're going to do' and I'm not sure that's the message as a community that we would want to send right now that we're not open for business." Council members agreed a wastewater management plan was the better next step, and Cox put the cost of a new, expanded treatment plant at $200 million to $300 million. Council members said they could write new data center zoning rules without a moratorium and sort out issues case by case in negotiations with developers, which has been the city's approach so far.

developers2-cyrusone-whitney-hill-county.text: CyrusOne is building a data center campus with 400 megawatts of power near Whitney, in Bosque County, Texas, on 270 acres below the Lake Whitney dam and next to Calpine's gas-fired Thad Hill Energy Center, which will feed it power directly. The first building, DFW10, is under construction and the companies expect it to be operating by the fourth quarter of 2026. Calpine agreed in July 2025 to supply 190 megawatts to the campus, with the two companies putting the investment at $1.2 billion. State construction filings describe five single-story buildings: DFW10, a $750 million, 250,000-square-foot building; DFW11, at $400 million and 88,875 square feet; and DFW17, DFW17B and DFW17C, budgeted at a combined $1.3 billion, with construction windows running into April 2027. The Bosque County Commissioners Court agreed in November 2024 to a 10-year, 30% tax abatement for CyrusOne, which company officials called the smallest incentive they have received. County officials say the first two phases would raise the county's tax base by about 120% and bring an estimated $70 million over 30 years to the county, Clifton ISD, the Bosque County Hospital District and others. Since August 2025, nearly 6,000 people have signed a petition claiming Lake Whitney's level could drop because of the project and a planned water reallocation. The Brazos River Authority says its study of reallocating the lake's hydropower storage would not lower lake levels and that it has no agreements or discussions with any data center for water. At a January 2026 town hall in Clifton, CyrusOne president John Hatem said the campus would use a closed-loop cooling system filled once every 15 years with trucked-in water, that wastewater would be trucked out rather than discharged into the Brazos River, and that up to 500,000 gallons a year would be needed for plumbing and about 40 employees. CyrusOne is seeking well water permits from the Middle Trinity Groundwater Conservation District for the campus's plumbing needs, and the district decides those. The Bosque County Commissioners Court controls any future tax abatement.

developers2-cyrusone-allen.text: CyrusOne's Allen campus at 2300 Chelsea Boulevard in Allen, a Dallas suburb in Collin County, Texas, holds its operating DFW3 and DFW4 data centers, which the company says provide 77 megawatts of computing power on a 90-acre site it calls the largest data center campus in Texas. The campus is planned for 976,000 square feet of building space at full build-out, with a third site, DFW5, held as land for future development, and the buildings use a closed-loop, water-free cooling system. CyrusOne first announced the campus in 2017, and in 2023 filed with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation to invest $31.5 million in DFW4, a 126,000-square-foot building, with construction running from January to September 2024. CyrusOne, based in Dallas and jointly owned by KKR and Global Infrastructure Partners, operates more than 60 data centers across the US and Europe and named longtime executive John Hatem its chief executive in July 2026. On September 21, 2026, Gov. developers2-cyrusone-san-antonio-westove.text: CyrusOne operates a data center on Westover Hills Boulevard in San Antonio, Texas, part of Bexar County's Council District 6, the section of the city with more data centers than any other. The buildings hold 295,785 square feet of technical space and 36 megawatts of total IT capacity, built in 18-megawatt redundant power blocks, with eight Detroit Diesel generators rated for 48 hours of running and sixteen uninterruptible power supplies. Cooling is a closed loop chilled water system that uses no water. Councilman Ric Galvan says his district has the highest concentration of data centers in San Antonio. CPS Energy and the San Antonio Water System briefed the city council on what that growth means for power and water; CPS put the energy needs of data centers already in its pipeline at around 26,000 megawatts. On August 25, 2026 the council debated two options: a moratorium on new data centers or permanent changes to the city's development code. City staff recommended the code changes, which would confine data centers to certain zones, keep them at least 500 feet from homes and schools, and bar them from the Edwards Aquifer recharge zones. A moratorium could last only 90 to 180 days, would not stop projects already under way, and would take until year's end to enact. A council vote is possible by mid-October 2026. "So it's a patch. It's not gonna fix the problem; it's gonna slow down the development right now," development services director Amin Tohmaz said. Councilman Jalen McKee-Rodriguez backs a moratorium, saying the city has "a very clear and present moral obligation to take action." Councilwoman Misty Spears disagreed: "San Antonio has a major economic opportunity in front of us, and a moratorium sends a concerning message." Galvan, who pushed for both the pause and the new rules, said he does not want to block every future data center but wants council approval required for each one, with "transparent community meetings with the neighbors around them."

developers2-cyrusone-broadlands-ashburn.text: CyrusOne is building a five-building data center campus on 57.6 acres at the Belmont Ridge Road and Dulles Greenway interchange in Broadlands, Ashburn, Loudoun County, Virginia. The company bought the land for $47 million in December 2022 and said at the time it would develop it "consistent with the existing zoning." In September 2026 residents launched a petition asking the county to stop the project, which they say has not yet moved forward. The land had long been fought over: a 165-bed hospital planned two decades ago was never built, and a later plan for more than 700 homes drew objections over traffic and schools. Because a data center was already approved and permitted under the existing zoning, CyrusOne needed no rezoning or public hearing to proceed. The petition, started by resident Dominika Cadotte, says CyrusOne "secured administrative, by-right approvals without any opportunity for public hearing" for a nearly 1-million-square-foot industrial data center near homes and schools. It warns of high-voltage power lines and constant mechanical noise, and urges residents to write to Broad Run District Supervisor Sylvia Glass and Gov. Abigail Spanberger. On September 15, 2026, the Loudoun County Board of Supervisors voted 7-1-1 to have staff draft a resolution pausing new data center applications for 12 months; the county attorney said an indefinite moratorium would not be legal. The board is expected to take a final vote on the resolution in October 2026.

developers2-cyrusone-sterling-ridgetop.text: CyrusOne's NVA1, NVA2 and NVA3 data centers sit on a 14-acre campus at 21111 Ridgetop Circle in Sterling, Loudoun County, Virginia, about eight miles from Dulles International Airport. The company says the campus has 420,000 square feet of technical space and 44 megawatts of IT capacity, cooled with a zero-water system. CyrusOne opened its first Loudoun County data center in 2015, and by early 2023 said it operated 10 data centers at five campus locations in the county. Loudoun is home to 233 data centers, the largest concentration in the country, and their spread has been contentious. On September 15, 2026 the Board of Supervisors voted 7-1-1 to have staff draft a resolution pausing new data center applications for 12 months, with Leesburg's Kristen Umstattd voting no and Catoctin's Caleb Kershner abstaining. The pause would apply only to new applications; the county attorney said an indefinite moratorium would not be legal. Residents have complained about health problems from living close to data centers, and about the high-voltage transmission lines the power demand brings near homes, schools and backyards, while the construction industry has argued the projects bring needed jobs. The Board of Supervisors still has to take a final vote on the resolution, due back on October 13, 2026.

developers2-cyrusone-quincy-pnw1.text: CyrusOne's PNW1 data center stands along D Street Northwest in Quincy, Grant County, Washington, a farming town that has become one of the country's best-known data center hubs. The Wenatchee World reported in October 2024 that the operating campus was nearing completion. Quincy's data centers, owned by Microsoft, Sabey, Vantage, H5 Data Centers, CyrusOne, NTT Data and Oath, used 37% of the Grant County Public Utility District's power generation, the PUD says. Data centers pay 57% of all taxes collected in Quincy, according to state Rep. Alex Ybarra, and city tax revenue rose from $9.8 million in 2018 to $20 million in 2024, helping pay for a new high school, library, police station and hospital. Grant County PUD is now near its maximum power load, and new data center construction has slowed. Its $260 million Quincy Transmission Expansion Plan would add six new transmission lines by 2029, including a 32-mile line from the Wanapum switchyard, and the PUD is using eminent domain against landowners who refused its offers. "People say the data centers have done a lot of good for Quincy as far as our tax base, and we've got a new hospital," said homeowner Jacque Rasmussen, who turned down $7,400 for a strip of her land. "But now it's starting to impact people's homes," she said. Those landowners have asked the Grant County Superior Court to throw out the PUD's condemnation suit.

developers2-cyrusone-frankfurt-wilhelm-f.text: CyrusOne is building its FRA6 data center at Wilhelm-Fay-Strasse 31-37 in the Sossenheim district of Frankfurt, Germany, next to its operating FRA1 through FRA4 sites. The company plans 90 megawatts of power across eight data halls and four floors, backed by two power feeds totaling 108 megavolt-amps. CyrusOne bought the 27,500-square-meter Europark site in December 2022, then describing FRA6 as a 72-megawatt data center, the German trade site connect professional reported in July 2023. The site lies in an area Frankfurt's city data center plan designates as suitable for the use, which CyrusOne said gives it planning certainty. CyrusOne is aiming for a BREEAM Excellent sustainability rating, a widely used green-building certification, a closed-loop water cooling system, and an efficiency target below 1.3, meaning the site would use less than 1.3 units of total power for every unit that reaches its computers. Next door, CyrusOne's FRA3 building offers 22 megawatts of power in two attached towers, connected to the high-voltage grid through its own substations and cooled with outside air rather than water.

developers2-cyrusone-dublin-dub1.text: CyrusOne operates its DUB1 data center in Grange Castle Business Park in west Dublin: three buildings with 22,854 square meters of technical space and 14 megawatts of power. It is cooled by closed-loop water systems, backed by two separate power feeds capable of 80 megavolt-amps combined, and CyrusOne says it runs entirely on renewable electricity. South Dublin County Council granted planning permission for the 400 million euro campus in October 2018: about 349,000 square feet across two buildings on nearly 15 acres, expected to employ close to 70 people once finished. In July 2023 CyrusOne asked the council to extend that permission, which it granted on November 8, 2023. The extension covers a second building on the site of a house called Erganagh, with 32 standby generators, an on-site substation and 32 sound-insulated chillers. When Data Center Dynamics reported the filing in 2023, it noted that Ireland's grid operator, EirGrid, had said it would grant no new connection requests in the Dublin area until 2028, and had refused two neighboring proposals over grid capacity. That freeze began in 2021, when regulators had EirGrid halt new data center connections across the Dublin area over the risk of rolling blackouts. It was lifted on December 12, 2025, on new conditions: on-site power backup able to meet full demand, at least 80 percent renewable electricity, and annual reporting on energy and emissions. Data centers now take close to a quarter of Ireland's electricity, up from about 5 percent a decade ago. South Dublin County Council still decides any new planning applications at Grange Castle, now under the regulator's December 2025 conditions on new grid connections.

It was lifted on December 12, 2025, on new conditions: on-site power backup able to meet full demand, at least 80 percent renewable electricity, and annual reporting on energy and emissions.
Data centers now take close to a quarter of Ireland's electricity, up from about 5 percent a decade ago.
South Dublin County Council still decides any new planning applications at Grange Castle, now under the regulator's December 2025 conditions on new grid connections.

developers2-cyrusone-milan-mil1.text: CyrusOne broke ground in March 2026 on MIL1, its first Italian data center, under construction on Via Reggio Emilia in the Redecesio area of Segrate, a town just east of Milan. The Dallas-based developer says the three-story building will deliver 27 megawatts of power in three 9-megawatt sections, with the first nine megawatts running by the third quarter of 2027. The site is the former Cise research center, empty since 2003 and used for years as a shelter by homeless people; about 50 old buildings were demolished before construction began. Italy's environment ministry screened the project's backup generators and has since reviewed CyrusOne's compliance with its conditions, most recently in June 2026. As part of the deal, CyrusOne bought a 658,628-square-meter farmland plot known as the Golfo Agricolo and gave it to the town, which had long fought to keep it undeveloped. "This is an important day for all of us in Segrate. At last, the Golfo Agricolo is ours," Mayor Paolo Micheli said in 2024. CyrusOne is spending more than 6 million euros on local roads, including turning Via delle Regioni into a boulevard with cycle paths, and plans solar panels on public school buildings. The groundbreaking set off weeks of debate on local social media during the town's spring 2026 election campaign, the Giornale di Segrate reported. Answering residents' questions in that paper, CyrusOne said about 150 trees removed for the project would be replaced with 170 new ones, and that its closed-loop cooling system uses no continuous daily water after the first fill. CyrusOne also plans a second, 54-megawatt Milan data center, MIL2, near Linate Airport, drawing power from the same expanded electricity substation.

developers2-cyrusone-halfweg-ams1.text: CyrusOne operates its AMS1 data center at Linieweg 1 in Halfweg, Netherlands, on the PolanenPark business park between Haarlem and Amsterdam, about 15 minutes from Amsterdam and 10 from Schiphol Airport. The campus is designed for 54 megawatts of power across two buildings of 27 megawatts each, with 29,350 square meters of technical space, according to the company. CyrusOne bought 6.3 hectares of land at PolanenPark from the Schiphol Area Development Company, which said the site would hold about 72 megawatts across two buildings. The Belgian contractor Cosimco began building the first building, a three-story, 27,000-square-meter shell, in December 2018 and made it wind and watertight within five months. CyrusOne, the city of Haarlem, the province of North Holland, and local utilities Waternet and Alliander DGO studied whether the data center's waste heat could feed a heating network in Haarlem; as of 2019 those talks were still ongoing. The project is part of the European Green IT innovation initiative Catalyst. Halfweg was CyrusOne's second large expansion in the Netherlands, after a partnership with Agriport A7 in Middenmeer, 40 kilometers north of Amsterdam, for a 270-megawatt campus.

developers2-stack-port-washington.text: STACK Infrastructure's own list of locations includes no site in Wisconsin, and the data center being built in Port Washington, in Ozaukee County, is Vantage Data Centers' Lighthouse campus for OpenAI and Oracle. Vantage broke ground in December 2025 on 672 acres on the north side of the city, planning 1.3 gigawatts at first and up to 3.5 gigawatts later, at a cost of $15 billion, with completion in 2028. It told the state it expected 3,500 construction workers in 2026 and 5,000 in 2027, and about 300 permanent staff afterwards, with 700 more from the tenants. On April 7, 2026, Port Washington became the first city in the United States to put data center tax breaks to a public vote, and about 66 percent of voters backed the new limit. The referendum requires city leaders to get voter approval before granting a developer tax incentives of more than $10 million. It was put on the ballot by residents and a local group called Great Lakes Neighbors United. It did not touch the $458 million tax incremental financing district the city had approved in November 2025 for the Lighthouse campus, and business and trade groups have gone to court to strike it down. Oracle said the project would put $175 million into local infrastructure including water and wastewater systems, and officials had to move meetings to fit the crowds turning up to object over energy and water use, environmental effects, and the way the city had gone about it.

developers2-stack-new-albany-cmh01.text: STACK Infrastructure operates its NAL01 data center campus in New Albany, Ohio, east of Columbus in Franklin County, where two buildings sit on 40 acres with 60 megawatts of critical capacity. NAL01A holds 11 megawatts in 116,000 square feet and NAL01B holds 51 megawatts in 332,000 square feet; the company says 48 megawatts of that capacity is new, with secured utility power. STACK markets the campus for AI, machine learning and cloud workloads, citing its low-latency reach to Chicago, New York and Northern Virginia. The campus draws power from AEP Ohio, whose new data center tariff requires large customers to commit to monthly billing minimums and exit fees; the utility said in February 2026 that the rule had cut its forecast of new Ohio data center demand from 30,000 megawatts to about 5,700. The Ohio Manufacturers' Association is challenging the tariff at the Ohio Supreme Court, arguing inflated forecasts are already raising ordinary customers' bills: "We need proof from AEP, not more claims." The Public Utilities Commission of Ohio has approved AEP's billing plan, and the manufacturers' appeal is now pending before the Ohio Supreme Court.

developers2-stack-atlanta-lithia-springs.text: STACK Infrastructure's ATL02 data center campus in Lithia Springs, Douglas County, west of Atlanta, spans 64 acres and now offers 160 megawatts of power, according to STACK's own site. STACK first filed with the Georgia Department of Community Affairs in 2024 for two three-story data centers at 808 Factory Shoals Road, a $380.9 million project with completion listed for May 2026. A later filing added two more buildings, of 196,030 and 227,260 square feet, and STACK had marketed the land as a build-to-suit site since at least 2021, when it listed 39 acres and 48 megawatts. STACK's first Atlanta facility, ATL01, was one of eight data centers seeded to the company by IPI in 2019 and offers 7 megawatts. Lithia Springs and Douglasville have become a center of Atlanta's data center growth, with Digital Realty, CoreSite, Switch, Google, Microsoft, Flexential, H5 and QTS also building in the area. The campus was reviewed by Georgia as a Development of Regional Impact, a state process for large projects, rather than through a contested local vote.

developers2-stack-chicago-elk-grove.text: STACK Infrastructure's CHI01 data center stands at 1441 Touhy Avenue in Elk Grove Village, Cook County, Illinois, in the village's business park near O'Hare, and STACK counts it among its operating campuses. The building used to belong to T5 Data Centers, which bought it in 2016 before T5 combined facilities with IPI Partners in 2019 to form STACK. In March 2025 STACK announced a second Elk Grove campus, CHI02, a two-story data center on 18 acres about a mile away with closed-loop cooling; Mayor Craig Johnson welcomed it as "the kind of investment that drives our local economic growth while rejuvenating valuable industrial real estate." Elk Grove Village has 20 operating data centers and 19 more in the pipeline, the second-highest concentration in the country after Northern Virginia. In May 2026 more than 500 people filled a village town hall on data centers, where Johnson argued that claims about water and electricity use were unfounded and said generator noise is shielded from homes. Residents asked the village to ban gas-powered generators at data centers and to cap how many can be built, and questioned the power demands of AI data centers, the incentives offered to companies and how few jobs data centers create; the village says data center taxes paid for $400 credits on residents' water bills.

developers2-stack-dallas-lancaster-tx.text: STACK Infrastructure's DFW01 data center campus on Pinecrest Drive in Plano, in Collin County north of Dallas, Texas, offers 80MW of critical capacity across 45 acres, according to the company. STACK lists two buildings at the Plano data center campus, DFW01A with 21MW in 318,000 square feet and DFW01B with 11MW in 156,000 square feet, and an adjacent expansion, DFW01C, with 48MW in 332,000 square feet. The company markets DFW01 for its low-latency connection to the Dallas Infomart interconnection hub. STACK's second Dallas-area campus, DFW02, is much larger: it spans 193 acres in Lancaster, south of Dallas, where the company offers up to 500MW. Statewide, Gov. Greg Abbott ordered the Public Utility Commission of Texas and ERCOT on August 3, 2026, to audit data centers moving through ERCOT's interconnection queue, saying any that fail should be denied connection to the grid. On September 21 he told the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to issue no permits sought by data center projects until the ERCOT and Texas Water Development Board audits are complete.

developers2-stack-phoenix-avondale.text: STACK Infrastructure is building its PHX01 data center campus on 100 acres at Litchfield and Lower Buckeye roads in Avondale, Arizona, in Maricopa County west of Phoenix; the city says the first of three planned buildings, totaling about 1 million square feet, is expected to be completed in 2027. STACK's own listing gives the campus 225 megawatts of power, with closed-loop cooling to cut water use. STACK announced the project in June 2020 as a 150-megawatt data center on a 79-acre site in the Avondale Techplex, with a 10-year tax waiver and state and local sales tax rebates on data center equipment and labor. "The access to power, fiber, and land provides outstanding opportunity for scale, and the State of Arizona and City of Avondale teams are true partners," said Brian Cox, then STACK's chief executive. Avondale residents raised water use first, followed by the size and look of the buildings, the city says; Avondale was among the first cities in the region to restrict water-cooled data centers and now allows only closed-loop, air-cooled facilities. Avondale's water utility, like Mesa's and Phoenix's, caps water use for industrial facilities and requires developers to buy supplemental water to go over the cap. Two more data center campuses are coming to Avondale: Prime Data Centers broke ground in May 2026 at Avondale Boulevard and Lower Buckeye Road, and QTS plans an eight-building campus of about 3.2 million square feet. The city reviews each data center project for utility capacity, traffic, noise and neighborhood fit before it moves forward, and STACK's first building is due to open in 2027.

developers2-stack-milan-siziano.text: STACK Infrastructure's data center campus in Siziano, near Milan, Italy, has been operating since 2016 and now has three buildings with more than 50 megawatts of power live, after the third building, the 10-megawatt MIL02, opened in July 2022. STACK also holds expansion land at the site for more than 80 megawatts of total power. In April 2025 STACK agreed to sell its European colocation business, including its Milan data centers, to funds managed by Apollo, and it has not said publicly which of its Milan buildings, including MIL02, were part of that sale. The campus began as Supernap Italia, a venture between the US company Switch and the ACDC Holdings fund; STACK says it chose the Siziano site in 2015 for its access to highways and railways, low seismic risk and room for electrical substations. IPI Partners bought Supernap Italia in March 2021 and rebranded it under the STACK name a year later; the second building opened in November 2021, bringing the campus to 40 megawatts. Under the Apollo deal, Sherif Rizkalla, chief executive of STACK's EMEA colocation business, will lead a new, independent company for the sold data centers, one that will not carry the STACK name or logo. STACK, owned by Blue Owl Digital since October 2024, said it would keep operating in Europe with a focus on hyperscale clients, and it still runs multiple campuses in Milan. DCD reported in April 2025 that it had asked STACK which of its European data centers, including any in Siziano, were part of the sale; no answer had been made public as of that report.

digitalrealty-buildings-digital-realty-3.text: Digital Realty operates the YYZ10 data center at 371 Gough Road in Markham, Ontario, just north of Toronto, Canada, a single-story building of about 104,500 square feet on a 10-acre site. The company bought the property, then a partly leased warehouse and office building, for C$8.65 million in 2013 and converted part of it for data center use. It is built with backup power and cooling systems designed so one set can fail without cutting off customers, and it holds LEED Silver certification for energy efficiency. When Digital Realty bought the building it was 48 percent leased to two tenants, about 17 miles north of Toronto's financial district. "We have been tracking a significant amount of demand for enterprise-quality data center space with very limited supply in the Toronto market," then-chief executive Michael Foust said at the time. The company said the building could support about 5.4 megawatts of power for customer computing equipment across four ready-to-lease suites. The building now operates as leased colocation space within Digital Realty's cluster of Toronto-area data centers, which also includes its sites in Vaughan and downtown Toronto. Digital Realty markets the space to companies that need computing capacity near Toronto's fiber routes, rather than serving a single corporate tenant.

digitalrealty-buildings-ascenty-fortalez.text: Ascenty's Fortaleza 1 data center sits in Maracanau, in the Brazilian state of Ceara on the country's northeast coast, with 10 megawatts of power, 97,000 square feet of total area and room for 1,900 racks. Ascenty says the building is directly connected to the landing stations of the submarine cables at Praia do Futuro, which is why the company chose the site. It is far smaller than ByteDance's data center now being built nearby at the Pecem port complex in Caucaia, also in Ceara, planned at 300 megawatts per phase across four phases. That larger project is now facing a federal lawsuit: prosecutors and public defenders asked courts on September 14, 2026 to halt it until a fuller environmental review and consultation with the neighboring Anace indigenous community is carried out, saying its permitted water use rose from 19,700 to 144,000 liters a day.

digitalrealty-buildings-ascenty-queretar.text: Ascenty's Queretaro 2 data center stands at kilometer 17.5 of State Highway 100 in the municipality of Colon, in the Mexican state of Queretaro, and opened on July 1, 2022 together with its Queretaro 1 building, the company's first two data centers in Mexico. Queretaro 2 covers 24,000 square meters with 31 megawatts of power, and Ascenty, a joint venture of Digital Realty and Brookfield, opened it with 20 percent of its space already taken by clients. Founder Chris Torto said Queretaro is attractive for its location near the industrial Bajio region and Mexico City, its low risk of earthquakes or hurricanes, and its reliable power supply. Governor Mauricio Kuri has led the drive to bring data centers to Colon, which has drawn $10 billion in investment from Microsoft, Google and Amazon while the area has lived through more than two years of drought. Guadalupe Hernandez, 68, who sells blackberries to tourists, gets water only every 15 days: "I have lost 60% of my crop. With no crop, there's no money." On August 31, 2026 Oxfam Mexico and Oxfam Intermon published a report saying data centers in Colon and El Marquez are stripping residents of public goods, and that the state government has exempted the companies from filing environmental impact statements. Water concessions come from the National Water Commission, CONAGUA, which told reporters it had granted no new concessions in Queretaro and that Microsoft had bought its concession from another owner.

digitalrealty-buildings-digital-realty-p.text: Digital Realty runs PDX10, a two-story, 48,000-square-foot colocation data center at 3825 NW Aloclek Street in Hillsboro, Oregon, which the company pitches for low-latency links to Asia-Pacific. Washington County, where Hillsboro sits, has grown into a major data center hot spot in Oregon, and residents are pushing back against more expansion. Digital Realty says the PDX10 data center is LEED Gold and Energy Star certified and runs on 100% renewable energy. In July 2026 the City of Hillsboro adopted a four-month moratorium on approving new data centers and the large battery storage systems that supply them, acting on a day's notice so developers could not rush in applications first. The city had earlier used enterprise zone agreements to extend tax breaks for large data centers before a state moratorium on those breaks took effect in June. In April 2026 City Councilor Kipperlyn Sinclair started a petition for a pause: "A moratorium is not a permanent ban. It is a pause for accountability." "There's data centers being finished here in Hillsboro that have no power, and they're being told three to five years before you get power," said Hillsboro Herald editor Dirk Knudsen. Under Oregon's POWER Act, Portland General Electric proposed in June 2026 to raise rates 29% for data centers and other customers using more than 20 megawatts, while cutting residential rates 1.3%. The Oregon Citizens' Utility Board has said households paid more than twice as much per kilowatt-hour as data centers under the old rates. Farmer Jacob Roloff said the math on data centers "isn't mathing" as farmland is cleared for them. The Hillsboro City Council decides what happens when its four-month moratorium on new data centers, adopted in July 2026, runs out.

digitalrealty-buildings-ascenty-paulinia.text: Ascenty's Paulinia data center, at Avenida Prefeito Jose Lozano Araujo 4545 in Paulinia, in the Campinas area of Sao Paulo state, has been running since 2019 with 8,000 square meters, 1,300 racks and 14 megawatts of power. It is certified Tier III in design and facility, built with three power lines serving each data hall, a dual coil chilled water cooling system, and two diesel tanks holding 48 hours of fuel. Ascenty chose the town for the same reason the petrochemical industry did: it sits on the highway cutting across the city, with quick access to Sao Paulo and the rest of the region. Paulinia has since become a data center hub: CloudHQ held a groundbreaking there in March 2023 for its first Latin American campus, announced at 228 megawatts across up to six buildings and more than 3 billion dollars. About a third of Brazil's data centers are in Sao Paulo state, which went through an acute water crisis about a decade ago, and that history is why the buildout worries residents there.

digitalrealty-buildings-digital-realty-p.text: PAR13 is a Digital Realty data center at 14 rue de l'Orme à Moineaux in Les Ulis, in France's Essonne department, and its second phase, delivered by the contractor Equans in July 2024, brought it to 20MW of IT capacity, DCD reported. Digital Realty lists the address and a total building size of 16,800 square meters. Plans for the data center were first announced in June 2023, when the site was said to be expandable to 80MW. A second building, PAR14, is expected on the same site, bringing the total to 54,000 square meters. The engineering firm Terrell Group, which worked on the project, says the two buildings will be built in phases to a total of 80MW, 30MW in PAR13 and 50MW in PAR14, each with two levels of data halls, its own substation and an outdoor generator platform. Equans said the building uses prefabricated piping, ceiling containment and a lean distribution system. Digital Realty says PAR13 runs on 100% renewable and carbon-free energy, with N+1 cooling redundancy. Digital Realty has twelve other data centers in Paris, including the four buildings of its Paris Digital Park. Its next large campus is the Dugny Digital Hub on a former French Air Force site northeast of Paris, where construction of the first building, PAR15, began in December 2025, DCD reported in May 2026; the three buildings are planned to provide 176MW of IT capacity.

digitalrealty-buildings-digital-realty-m.text: A Digital Realty company, Digital Milan 1, has asked Abbiategrasso, southwest of Milan, Italy, to let it turn the disused Ropal industrial site and the neighboring Vigevanese area, about 138,800 square meters in all, into a data center campus. The proposal, filed on August 5, 2026, is now with the town's technical offices and must go through a strategic environmental assessment in which residents and associations can comment. Mayor Cesare Nai said the company had confirmed the servers would be cooled in a closed loop, so that no groundwater would be drawn continuously and the aquifer would not be warmed. The filing describes three buildings up to 21 meters high with 120 megawatts of electrical capacity, and about 10 million euros for the town in fees and environmental compensation. Il Giorno reported in July a 1.3 billion euro campus of four data centers and 94 megawatts, the first 8 megawatts running from 2028, employing 150 to 200 people. Milan already has 68 data center facilities, the densest concentration in Italy. Lombardy alone has 166 new requests for grid connection totaling more than 44 gigawatts, and across Italy the operator Terna has 529 requests for roughly 95 gigawatts. Data centers account for less than 2 percent of Italy's electricity demand today, and in the highest growth scenarios could reach 12.7 percent by 2035. Towns around Milan have begun organizing. More than 2,200 people signed a petition against a data center at San Bovio, in Peschiera Borromeo, over energy and water consumption, noise, how close it sits to houses and to the Gambarone spring, groundwater drawn from shallow aquifers, and carbon dioxide from burning diesel. Residents of the southwest Milan area have kept up protests since a sit-in in July against a planned campus at Lacchiarella, and committees are forming ahead of the first national demonstration, set for October 10 in Milan.

ft-4.text: DC BLOX's Huntsville data center, at 333 Diamond Drive NW in Cummings Research Park, Madison County, Alabama, is an operating Tier III colocation facility that opened with a ribbon cutting on October 3, 2018. DC BLOX designed it to serve executive branch agencies, defense contractors and others handling Controlled Unclassified Information, near Redstone Arsenal and the Marshall Space Flight Center. At the opening, Huntsville Mayor Tommy Battle called DC BLOX "one of those companies that we need to have in our area," and U.S. Rep. Mo Brooks said employment would "start out a little on the low side." The company offers up to 7,400 square feet of tenant office space and markets the site as a disaster recovery location for businesses in Nashville, Birmingham, Greenville and Chattanooga. State Sen. Sam Givhan said a poll he ran found 55 percent of respondents in his Madison County district opposed more data center development. In August 2026 the Tennessee Valley Authority's board approved a new rate structure for data centers, effective October 1, under which they are expected to pay about 10 percent more for power, and new or expanding data centers needing more than five megawatts must pay a capacity commitment charge. ft-48.text: Cielo Digital Infrastructure's Hudson data center is listed as a planned campus on 500 acres in Weld County, Colorado, but no filing, hearing or local report on it has been published. If it goes ahead it will face Weld County rules written this year: on April 6, 2026 the county commissioners voted 4 to 1, with Commissioner James against, to add data centers to the county code. The code bans data centers from agricultural zones, sends those in light industrial zones through use by special review and those in medium and heavy industrial zones through site plan review, and requires an electricity will-serve letter, proof of water supply and a 65 dBC noise limit at the property line. More than 25 residents spoke at the hearing, most about water. Ellie Andrews of Greeley said: "I'm disappointed to see this move forward without clearer limits to the impacts on our water resources." Garrett Helzer of Windsor said: "These data centers can drink a river dry. We need to protect water for agriculture and future generations."

ft-77.text: Intero Systems runs a data center at 1800 Phoenix Boulevard, Suite 201, near College Park and the Atlanta airport, in Clayton County, Georgia. The company rents server space to other businesses for a monthly fee and describes the building as an enterprise class facility with secured entry, backup cooling and power, fire suppression and fiber connections. Intero says it has more than 25 years of experience in telecommunications and network infrastructure. Clayton County has had a moratorium on new data center applications and construction in unincorporated areas since September 2025, extended three times since then, though Intero's building predates it. Commissioner DeMont Davis said at a July 2026 town hall: "We have to put policies in place that are going to dictate the locations where they can be and where they cannot be." In nearby Lovejoy, developers withdrew a 15 building, 403 acre data center campus planned across the street from two schools after residents objected.

ft-86.text: No Coloblox data center is listed at 2812 Spring Road SE in Cobb County, Georgia, where trackers place one under the name Marietta. The only Marietta in the company's own list of Atlanta facilities is 56 Marietta Street, a meet-me room in downtown Atlanta about 20 kilometres from the city of Marietta, alongside colocation suites at 1100 and 900 Circle 75 Parkway. The city of Marietta and the county around it have both shut the door on anything new. Marietta council passed a six month moratorium on new data centers running to the end of December, and on August 11, 2026 Cobb County commissioners extended their own by a further six months, to February 24, 2027, on the ground that they had not settled on rules. Atlanta itself moved earlier and differently. Two ordinances approved on September 2, 2024 keep data centers out of the Beltline overlay and away from within half a mile of a MARTA rail station, after the city's pipeline rose from more than 235 megawatts in the first half of 2023 to more than 730 in the second, which the legislation likened to the output of a typical gas plant.

ft-113.text: FOGO Solutions runs an operating data center at its headquarters, 340 Tom Reeve Drive in Carrollton, Carroll County, Georgia. The bunker-style facility offers colocation and cloud computing to West Georgia businesses, with backup power, cooling and around-the-clock monitoring. It is already up and running; no new permit or vote is required for it. Carroll County has barred new data center, battery storage and solar farm permits since March 2026, after heavy opposition to a large data center proposed elsewhere in the county. Commissioners adopted a 100-day moratorium in early March 2026 and extended it on June 3 for another 100 days, through September 11. The moratorium covers only unincorporated parts of the county and does not apply to municipalities such as Carrollton.

ft-120.text: JMF Solutions lists its IXP Farm data center at 8 Corporate Ridge Parkway in Columbus, Georgia, with 50,000 square feet of raised floor, backup generators and two battery rooms, according to its directory listing. The Columbus, Muscogee County site is the kind of data center that hosts local networks and servers rather than a hyperscale campus: JMF describes it as having an internet exchange point on site and cross-connects to more than 30 providers. In that listing JMF calls the building, which it names DLI ONE, the centerpiece of its network and says it was built to meet Tier 4 and SOC 2 criteria and once handled more than 30 percent of VISA's payment processing. JMF Solutions is a holding company for telecommunications, cloud and blockchain businesses, including IXP Farm, which it says uses federal and state broadband funds to build a middle-mile network for rural and underserved areas. A far larger project is the one Columbus is arguing about. Project Ruby, a planned hyperscale data center, would sit on 865 acres in northeastern Muscogee County bordering Harris and Talbot counties, with four buildings on the eastern side near high-voltage transmission lines and a substation, according to a map released by Choose Columbus in 2026. Habitat Real Estate Partners formed Muscogee Property 1 LLC to manage the property, Choose Columbus chief executive Missy Kendrick told the Ledger-Enquirer. At an August 2026 town hall, residents raised concerns about higher energy bills, and Columbus resident Ric Rivera said: "I just don't see that promise as being believable". No data center has received approval there, only the land, WTVM reported, and District 8 Councilman Walker Garrett said the county would seek limits on noise and testing of water and air if one comes. Garrett said the potential property tax revenue is one of the biggest selling points for the city council; for the existing IXP Farm building no public dispute has been reported.

ft-215.text: Red Wolf DCD Properties wants to build a 1.2 million square foot data center with an on-site electrical substation on 148.2 acres at the southeast corner of Georgia Highway 20 West and Rocky Creek Road, outside Hampton in Henry County, Georgia. The applicant of record, 0 Rocky Creek Road LLC of Wilmington, Delaware, asked the county to rezone the land from residential agricultural to office institutional and to change its comprehensive plan; the end user has not been named. Red Wolf is also behind a second data center proposal off Simpson Mill Road nearby, and county planners recommended approval of Rocky Creek with a 60 foot buffer after a state Development of Regional Impact review. Accounts of the zoning advisory board's November 14, 2024 vote conflict: the Henry Reporter said it recommended approval of Rocky Creek and denial of Simpson Mill, while WSB-TV reported the opposite and added that the county commission has the final say. Henry County commissioners pulled both requests from their November 19, 2024 agenda and put them off into 2025. As of March 2025, when Hampton approved a separate 133 acre data center campus in the Henderson Farms development, the Rocky Creek and Simpson Mill requests were still awaiting a commission hearing that had not been scheduled.

ft-225.text: Cielo Digital Infrastructure, a Texas company that finds and sells sites for data centers, is marketing a 150 megawatt (a measure of power) site in Des Moines, Polk County, Iowa, that it calls Des Moines 1. The site is 166 acres, with 145 acres usable for construction. No data center has been approved or built there, and Cielo has not named a buyer or end user for the site. Cielo was founded in 2023 and previously developed a large campus in Culpeper County, Virginia, that it sold to Edgecore. It calls itself a site developer rather than an operator: "We identify and negotiate sites ready for data center development," its website reads. Its backer, the Texas investment firm Arroyo Investors, lists its investment in Cielo as realized in March 2026. As of its most recent property listing, from March 2026, Cielo was still marketing the Des Moines site alongside a second Iowa site, Middle Creek, at 343 acres. No local vote or hearing has been reported for the Des Moines site because no government body has yet taken up a proposal for it.

Equinix will also reimburse the village for water and sewer lines it ran under Interstate 80 up to Holt Road and over to Ridge Road.

ft-247.text: Cielo Digital Infrastructure lists a 300 megawatt, 141-acre data center campus in New Lenox, Will County, Illinois, on its website, but no application has been filed with the village. At the New Lenox Village Board meeting on August 10, 2026, Mayor Baldermann said there is false information that a data center is coming: "This is not true and we are not entertaining any data centers," the minutes record him saying. Cielo, founded in 2023 and owned by the Texas investment firm Arroyo Investors, lists projects in several states, including a second Illinois site at Minooka. It sold an earlier campus in Culpeper County, Virginia, to Edgecore, and announced a $2.1 billion, 300 megawatt campus in Gaffney, South Carolina, in June 2025. Residents have raised the issue anyway. At the same August meeting, Terry Nolan told the board he opposes data centers in New Lenox. In March 2026, Janet Diaz of Joliet told trustees she opposed "the new data center that is proposed to be constructed" and said she would join a protest, the minutes say. Any data center proposal would go to the New Lenox Village Board, led by Baldermann with Trustees Christopherson, Scalise, Madsen, Wilson, Gugliuzza and Reiser. Public comment is taken at its regular meetings at Village Hall, One Veterans Parkway. The mayor's August 2026 statement is the latest word on the project.

It sold an earlier campus in Culpeper County, Virginia, to Edgecore, and announced a $2.1 billion, 300 megawatt campus in Gaffney, South Carolina, in June 2025.
Residents have raised the issue anyway.
At the same August meeting, Terry Nolan told the board he opposes data centers in New Lenox.
In March 2026, Janet Diaz of Joliet told trustees she opposed "the new data center that is proposed to be constructed" and said she would join a protest, the minutes say.
Any data center proposal would go to the New Lenox Village Board, led by Baldermann with Trustees Christopherson, Scalise, Madsen, Wilson, Gugliuzza and Reiser.
Public comment is taken at its regular meetings at Village Hall, One Veterans Parkway.
The mayor's August 2026 statement is the latest word on the project.

ft-254.text: The DartPoints data center at 2425 Technology Boulevard in Columbus, in Bartholomew County, Indiana, was built in 2008 and first run by Data Cave, which Immedion bought in 2018; DartPoints took it over when it acquired Immedion in May 2021. The 86,400 square foot building is leased long term to DartPoints, its only site in Indiana, and was sold for $8.3 million to an unnamed institutional investor. DartPoints says it has 2.5 megawatts of utility power, 300 tons of cooling, six network providers on site, and a building engineered to withstand an EF-5 tornado. The Republic, the Columbus newspaper, reports that it houses some of the city's own IT infrastructure. In September 2025 DartPoints said it would rebuild the inside of the building to take much denser equipment, with liquid cooling, after the investment firm Nova Infrastructure bought a majority stake. Chief executive Scott Willis said the center handled a little over one megawatt and would handle close to 10 by the end of 2027: "We've got an underutilized asset from a space perspective. We're going to construct that out within the building." DartPoints has 20 employees across its Midwest sites, and Willis said the work might bring a few more hires but not significantly more jobs. He said public backlash was something the industry had to face: "How do we develop ecosystems and data centers in a way that is very favorable for all parties involved?" Columbus moved first: on July 8, 2026 the city council unanimously made data centers, which the zoning code calls a "communication service exchange," a conditional use needing case by case approval and a public hearing before the Board of Zoning Appeals. The planning department had received no applications, and assistant planning director Melissa Begley said an outright ban could be legally problematic.

ft-1787597977129-3250.text: Sphere 3D, a cryptocurrency mining company, plans a 50 megawatt data center in Hopkinsville, in Christian County, Kentucky, and wants to convert the 15 megawatt bitcoin mine it already runs in the city to AI and high performance computing. Its subsidiary North Campbell Land Co. put both proposals to a July 27, 2026 public hearing on the city's first data center zoning rules, and neither has been approved yet. The existing mine is 22 modular units that have run for about three years inside Hopkinsville Electric System's Holland Substation, and residents' discovery of it pushed the city toward writing its first rules. It takes part in a flexible load program, so its power can be cut back or stopped when the Tennessee Valley Authority system is under strain. The new 50 megawatt data center would go on a separate site the company has not disclosed. North Campbell has offered to pay for a new 65 megawatt substation for the utility, estimated at $8 million to $10 million, with the 15 megawatts left over available to other customers. Jeff Hurd, the utility's general manager, told council members that the Tennessee Valley Authority could supply the extra power without affecting service to its roughly 13,000 customers, and that the substation could be ready in six to 12 months. North Campbell became part of Sphere 3D when it bought Cathedra Bitcoin in June 2026, and the company reported a second quarter net loss of $13.8 million with $2.8 million in cash at the end of June. In September it raised $5 million in a private placement, agreed to sell its Iowa site and about 5,500 mining machines, and said it had secured a land option in Hopkinsville for the new data center. Thomas Masiero, speaking for North Campbell, told the hearing: "To the best of my knowledge, there has not been a noise or water complaint against our facility during the three years of operation." Hurd said the utility, about 80% of whose customers are households, needs the income: "To avoid future rate increases on the backs of our customers, HES is constantly looking for additional revenue to offset these costs." The company's attorney, Robert Ison, said the draft rules went too far: "Make no mistake, if you adopt the more restrictive ordinance, you will effectively ban data centers in the city of Hopkinsville." Sherry Byerline of Pembroke said she can already hear industrial machinery running several miles from her home. "Once they get in and get a foothold, they pretty much do what they want to do, and this creates continuous pollution," she said. Becca Hostilo of Hopkinsville asked the city to require closed loop cooling, to consider capping the number of data centers, and to "make sure that Little River and Lake Barkley are kept safe." The company's representatives said the new building would use a closed loop system that recirculates water. The July draft would have allowed data centers under 75 megawatts and 50,000 square feet, set 1,000 feet back from homes and public property, and banned anything bigger as hyperscale; the existing mine would keep grandfathered status. By September 18 the planners had reworked it: data centers would be sorted by footprint, from small at up to 25,000 square feet to hyperscale at 150,000 or more, confined to the I-1 and I-2 industrial districts with a conditional use permit. The committee cut the setback for large facilities from 300 to 150 feet and the buffer from non-industrial land from 1,000 to 500 feet after Community and Development Services president Tom Britton said the old figures left few properties in the city where a large data center could go. The new draft also caps waste heat at a 5 degree Fahrenheit rise at the property line and requires decommissioning within 24 months of a site shutting down. Planning commission chairman Dan Thomas said no moratorium is needed, because a use not listed in the city's zoning, including data centers and cryptocurrency operations, cannot locate in Hopkinsville without a zoning amendment first. The second public hearing is at 6 p.m. on September 28, 2026, in the Hopkinsville Community College auditorium. Comments there could change the draft again before it goes to the full planning commission and then to the Hopkinsville City Council, which has the final say.
