ft-1784673966393-6863.text: Diversified Gas and Oil Corp. and a real estate company called Maverick Holdings hold an option to buy 100 acres in the Gateway Industrial Park near Jenkins, in Letcher County, Kentucky, to build a 100 megawatt gas fired power station; the developers hope the power would draw a data center or a large manufacturer as a tenant, but no data center project has been proposed for the site yet. The Appalachian Industrial Development Authority, a board appointed by the judge-executives of Letcher, Floyd, Knott and Pike counties, signed a joint development agreement with the two companies in March 2026, starting an 18 month window to seek grants and market the site to users including hyperscale data centers. Diversified owns a 20 inch interstate gas pipeline running through the 260 acre park, a reclaimed surface mine, with a large compressor station, and Colby Kirk of the regional development group One East Kentucky said it makes more sense to burn that gas locally than pay to repressurize it for the trip north to Pittsburgh and Cleveland. "Power grids are strained nationwide, so speed to power is becoming more and more important," Kirk said. Byron Gary of the Kentucky Resources Council said the local utility is the bigger problem: "Kentucky Power Co. has been capacity shy for a number of years now. They don't have enough capacity to serve their current customers." The authority met privately with Diversified at Jenkins City Hall for 30 minutes on January 21, 2026, and offered non-disclosure agreements to its private sector board members; Kirk said he signed one, while Jeffery Justice of the Pine Mountain Partnership said none of the appointed members did. The judge-executives of Letcher, Floyd and Pike counties said in July they had not been briefed, and the city of Jenkins said on Facebook it was not involved in the planning, though city officials sit on the authority that approved the agreement. Jenkins, a former coal company town of 1,700 people, runs water and sewer lines laid in the 1960s under a century old dam, and Kirk said it remains unclear whether the town's wastewater system could handle a hyperscale data center. The park has drawn other bidders before: MD Squared Power proposed a $1.2 billion AI data center there but has since moved to Pikeville, and HyForest LLC pitched two campuses of up to 200 megawatts for about $2 billion. Kirk called the Diversified plan the most attractive of the three but said it is still in due diligence: "I'm hopeful that they can find something that maybe works, but, you know, we have to be realistic when it's in this early stage. I'm not holding my breath."

ft-1785381367484-2023.text: The Department of Energy announced on July 29, 2026 that Brookfield will develop and run a data center campus at the former Paducah Gaseous Diffusion Plant in Kevil, McCracken County, Kentucky, with more than $100 billion of private money involved altogether. NextEra Energy will build 2 gigawatts of gas-fired power and 2.6 gigawatts of battery storage alongside it, which the companies say would make it the largest gas-fired power plant in Kentucky. The campus could reach up to 1.8 gigawatts of utility capacity and more than 1.2 gigawatts of computing capacity, with construction due to finish in 2031. Big Rivers Electric, Jackson Purchase Energy Cooperative and Paducah Power System are also partners, and the companies say the developers will pay for the power and transmission so other customers are not billed for it. Governor Andy Beshear's office said he had not been briefed on the deal: "The Governor hasn't been briefed by any of the companies or agencies involved, and thus has a number of questions related to power, environmental impact, jobs and whether the project will pay the community its fair share of taxes," spokesperson Jack Richter said. The project's power contract still needs approval from the Kentucky Public Service Commission. The plant, built in 1952 to enrich uranium and later fuel for power plants, closed in 2013 and is still owned and being cleaned up by the Department of Energy. It has been a Superfund site since 1994 because of decades of soil and water contamination, and cleanup of the roughly 3,550-acre site is expected to run until 2065 at a cost of about $17 billion. Paducah Mayor George Bray calls it the ideal site for a data center: "When we enriched uranium there, all the infrastructure around that power is still available," he said. "Plus, we've got you know tremendous water capacity out there." Protect McCracken County, a residents' group that includes people living beside the site, wants an independent environmental review before building goes ahead. "Our biggest concern with all of these projects is that you're doing it on a Superfund site," said Erica Moore, who helped start the group. Byron Gary of the Kentucky Resources Council said permits for building on the contaminated land or drawing on the water beneath it must not be skipped: "There shouldn't be a justification to get around that and end up potentially dumping a lot more burden on a rural community that can't afford it."

ft-308.text: Cielo Digital Infrastructure, founded in 2023 and owned by the Texas investment manager Arroyo Investors, said in June 2025 that it aims to develop 157 acres in Chisago, Minnesota, into a 300-megawatt data center campus. The Chisago site appeared in a list of Cielo's planned projects published alongside its 300-megawatt plan for Gaffney, South Carolina, with no address, timeline or investment figure given for Minnesota. In spring 2026 residents came to the Chisago City Council, in Chisago County, Minnesota, twice asking for a moratorium on data centers. The council had earlier said a company once explored building a data center in the city but dropped it after Xcel Energy said the local power grid was inadequate. City Administrator John Pechman said the Minnesota Supreme Court has deemed it illegal to arbitrarily exclude a legitimate business, so a one- or two-year moratorium could only let the city decide where and under what conditions data centers could go. Mayor Jeremy Dresel said the city had heard no current proposals and that Xcel had no plans to expand the area's grid for them; the council said it does not sign nondisclosure agreements with prospective businesses. In August 2026 the Chisago County Board, after a public hearing, voted to impose a one-year moratorium on applications for data centers, or high utility use developments. Assistant County Attorney Jeffrey Fuge said it need not run the full year: whenever the planning commission has an ordinance ready to recommend, the commissioners can call a hearing. paragraphs: Cielo Digital Infrastructure, founded in 2023 and owned by the Texas investment manager Arroyo Investors, said in June 2025 that it aims to develop 157 acres in Chisago, Minnesota, into a 300-megawatt data center campus. The Chisago site appeared in a list of Cielo's planned projects published alongside its 300-megawatt plan for Gaffney, South Carolina, with no address, timeline or investment figure given for Minnesota.

In spring 2026 residents came to the Chisago City Council, in Chisago County, Minnesota, twice asking for a moratorium on data centers. The council had earlier said a company once explored building a data center in the city but dropped it after Xcel Energy said the local power grid was inadequate.

City Administrator John Pechman said the Minnesota Supreme Court has deemed it illegal to arbitrarily exclude a legitimate business, so a one- or two-year moratorium could only let the city decide where and under what conditions data centers could go. Mayor Jeremy Dresel said the city had heard no current proposals and that Xcel had no plans to expand the area's grid for them; the council said it does not sign nondisclosure agreements with prospective businesses.

In August 2026 the Chisago County Board, after a public hearing, voted to impose a one-year moratorium on applications for data centers, or high utility use developments. Assistant County Attorney Jeffrey Fuge said it need not run the full year: whenever the planning commission has an ordinance ready to recommend, the commissioners can call a hearing. The moratorium covers only the parts of the county where the county holds zoning authority.
County planners are to use the pause to define data centers and draft conditions to control their effects, and the commissioners can end it early once the planning commission recommends an ordinance.

ft-354.text: The Bellevue Data Center at 1001 Fort Crook Road North in Bellevue, Sarpy County, Nebraska, is TierPoint's Omaha (Bellevue) facility, an operating data center offering colocation and managed services. TierPoint calls it a telecommunications hub for the central United States and links it by high-speed connection to its other regional data centers, including its Omaha (Midlands) site. ft-357.text: TierPoint runs its Midlands data center at 11425 South 84th Street in Papillion, Sarpy County, Nebraska, an operating colocation facility also known as Omaha (Midlands). TierPoint says the building has LEED Gold and Energy Star certification, was built to withstand winds of 250 mph, and has more than 63,000 square feet, including over 15,000 square feet of raised floor. It runs on two separate power feeds backed by redundant backup generators with at least 48 hours of runtime, and links by private network to TierPoint's Bellevue, Kansas City and St. Louis data centers. Sarpy County, south of Omaha, already hosts far larger data centers, including Meta's Sarpy campus, first announced in 2017 and expanded in 2022 into a planned nine-building, 4 million-square-foot site.

ft-365.text: The bigbyte.cc Corp. data center at 123 Central Avenue NW in downtown Albuquerque, Bernalillo County, New Mexico, is an operating colocation and business continuity facility. bigbyte.cc describes a "Colo-Neutral" environment with network redundancy through multiple providers, disaster recovery services, and on-demand office, training and conference space for clients' staff. The company has also promoted the launch of ABQ-NET, New Mexico's node of Qunnect's quantum network. On February 10, 2026, the Bernalillo County Commission approved a rule requiring data centers that seek county incentives such as industrial revenue bonds to cover their own electricity and water, fully offset their water use, pay permanent workers at least 120% of the area median salary, and prioritize New Mexican construction workers. "We cannot ask our community to subsidize costs for multi-million-dollar companies," said Commissioner Eric Olivas, who sponsored the resolution, while opponents called the rules too restrictive.

ft-431.text: The Cherokee Data Center at 7400 N. Lakewood Avenue in Tulsa, Tulsa County, Oklahoma, is a nearly 430,000-square-foot data center at Cherokee Industrial Park that has operated since 2001. Hewlett-Packard has owned it since 2014, when it bought the building for $150 million from BNP Paribas Leasing Corp., the Tulsa World reported, and a June 2026 Tulsa news roundup still lists it as HP-owned and operating. Sabre Inc. built the original 245,200 square feet in 2001; much of the building is underground and designed to withstand a tornado, with walls up to 22 inches thick in places. Electronic Data Systems took over the site in 2002 and added a 184,700-square-foot building in 2008, the same year HP bought EDS for $13.9 billion. The 2014 purchase may have been the largest real estate deal in Tulsa County's history, said Keith Hulsizer, the county's chief deputy assessor. The property was assessed at $170.2 million, and HP employed about 800 people there at the time. Google and Beale Infrastructure are now building a much bigger neighbor: Project Clydesdale, a 506-acre data center campus in unincorporated Tulsa County near Cherokee Industrial Park, just west of Owasso, which is expected to bring a new power substation and 1.5 miles of water lines.

ft-1769720540856-8663.text: Fezzik Energy, a group that includes land developer Chuck Betters, attorney Jonathan Kamin and Joanna Doven, is trying to bring a data center to a 27.82-acre former J&L Steel parcel in Aliquippa, Beaver County, Pennsylvania, the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette reported in February 2026. In March 2025, Aliquippa City Council was asked to adopt a resolution declaring a data center a permitted use on the parcel; city records do not show whether the council adopted it, and no developer has been named in the city's own notice. The city's March 2025 notice described "a data center, information processing and computer facility" that "will operate on a 24-7 basis and will generate its own energy for the facility." It proposed to treat the project as a permitted use under the zoning ordinance on the ground that its operations "qualify as a laboratory devoted to research, design, experimentation, and/or processing." A separate Wall Street Journal report in July 2025 described a $2 billion plan to turn the same mill site into "a power plant and data centers" to support artificial intelligence. Mayor Dwan Walker, who is also Midland's borough manager, said developers should be upfront with residents: "When you come into somebody's house, you wipe your feet, introduce yourself, shake hands." He also said early talks stay private: "In the beginning, you're cloak and dagger." Near the site, coffee shop owner Barb Michna said a data center would help her business, but her customer Jacob Wild disagreed: "The constant humming, the bright light, it's not going to be nice to live next to." Joanna Doven, of the Pittsburgh-based AI Strike Team and a Fezzik partner, said "former industrial sites abound in Beaver County" and it is up to local communities to decide "if this is an investment that they want." Any data center on the Aliquippa parcel still needs a conditional use hearing and zoning approval from Aliquippa City Council, which has not confirmed a formal proposal or developer for the site.

ft-1764686543728-5747.text: Ascent Data, a Pittsburgh IT company, runs an operating data center at 90 Beta Drive in RIDC Park, just outside Pittsburgh in Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, as part of its managed IT and cybersecurity business. The company says its data center holds SOC 2 Type 2 certification, audited by the Pittsburgh accounting firm Schneider Downs, runs on seven bandwidth providers, and promises 100% uptime with staff on site around the clock. The bigger data center fight in the county is over a much larger project a few miles away in Springdale, where Allegheny DC Property Company plans a data center on the site of a former power plant; borough council approved a permit for it in December 2025. Allegheny County is writing a model zoning ordinance defining data centers for its 130 municipalities, but county sustainability director Brittany Prischak said it will not be legally enforceable, since zoning for new data centers is set by each municipality. On August 25, 2026, members of Allegheny County Council introduced a bill to ban data center construction on the roughly 30,000 acres of county-owned property, and it went to the council's sustainability committee.

On August 25, 2026, members of Allegheny County Council introduced a bill to ban data center construction on the roughly 30,000 acres of county-owned property, and it went to the council's sustainability committee.

ft-1763749832975-3977.text: Lumen's Pittsburgh 2 data center, formerly a Level 3 facility, is an existing colocation building at 200 Technology Drive in Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania. Mayor Corey O'Connor told TribLive: "I would not support a data center happening in the city of Pittsburgh." The city has no zoning ordinance regulating data centers, so the zoning administrator or the Zoning Board of Adjustment would have to find the closest comparable use if an application came in, zoning administrator Carolyn Ristau said. After a divided Springdale Borough approved a contentious data center project nearby, advocates turned to Allegheny County to regulate the industry, PublicSource reported. On August 25, 2026, county council members introduced a bill to ban data center construction, including backup generators and cooling towers, on county-owned properties, nearly 30,000 acres of land. Allegheny County Council voted unanimously on September 24, 2026 to approve the ban on "hyperscale" data centers on county land; the rule excludes private land and existing internet infrastructure, and County Executive Sara Innamorato's office said she will sign it. Innamorato had not signed the county-land ban as of the September 24 vote, though a spokesperson said she is expected to. The county's next step is a model zoning ordinance covering privately owned land, expected to be finished by the end of the year, though sustainability director Brittany Prischak said it will not be legally enforceable.

ft-1763752475494-7249.text: Centre WISP Venture Company runs SCDC1, a small colocation data center at 2038 Sandy Drive in State College, Centre County, Pennsylvania. As of May 2026, no plans for a new data center had been submitted anywhere in Centre County, StateCollege.com reported. Local governments in the area are writing rules in case one is proposed. College Township became the first Centre Region municipality to adopt conditional use zoning for data centers in February 2026, giving it about 120 days to review any application and attach conditions such as buffer zones and energy and water use standards, assistant manager Mike Bloom told WJAC. In May 2026, Ferguson Township's supervisors voted to have the planning commission write similar conditional use rules and to explore a shared land use agreement with another municipality, after 16 residents spoke during an 80-minute hearing. "You cannot go two miles in any direction without coming across two or three data centers," said Tim Stedman, who moved to the township from Northern Virginia and called the prospect "an absolute disaster." Dave Gibbons, who owns a commercial building in the township, warned that "a blanket 'no' on data centers will be really detrimental to Ferguson Township" because local tech businesses along the Science Park Road corridor already rely on data centers of their own. Snow Shoe Township has also amended its zoning rules for data centers, and Rush and Half Moon townships are working on their own, county planning director Ray Stolinas said.

ft-487.text: Cielo Digital Infrastructure, a Texas data center developer, plans a $2.1 billion campus of four buildings at 000 Ford Road in Gaffney, Cherokee County, South Carolina, with up to 300 megawatts of power at full build-out. Cherokee County announced the project in June 2025 and its council finalized a tax incentive deal, with the campus expected to open by the end of 2028. Cielo, founded in 2023 and owned by the Texas investment firm Arroyo Investors, previously developed a campus in Culpeper County, Virginia, that it sold to Edgecore. Ken Moon, director of the county's development board, would not give the size of the tax breaks when the deal was signed, saying "the paperwork has not been finalized." By the time residents came to the county council to object, in January 2026, the decision had already been made. "The idea that we need a data center in Cherokee County to be on the forefront of progress and growth is nonsense," said resident Courtney Smith, who also pointed to a 16% rise in her property taxes. Moon said the Ford Road project is a data storage center, not an energy-intensive AI facility, and that it would fund about a third of the county's budget in taxes. "No, absolutely we're not seeking out any more data centers," he said, adding that any future project would have to bring its own power. Gaffney resident Denise Maista has asked for community liaisons so residents who cannot attend meetings learn "what is going on and what can and cannot be done." No construction has begun on Ford Road, and no further council vote on the project has been reported. Cherokee County Council, which signed the incentive deal, would set terms for any data center project that follows it.

ft-489.text: DC BLOX's Greenville data center at 33 Global Drive, in the Global Business Park off Interstate 85 in Greenville, Greenville County, South Carolina, is an operating Tier III colocation facility that opened in January 2022. The initial 25,000-square-foot building holds more than 400 cabinets and 3MW of power, and DC BLOX plans 54,000 square feet of white space and 18MW at full build-out. "We have seen robust pre-leasing activity as the Upstate is thriving," DC BLOX chief executive Jeff Uphues said at the opening. Mark Farris of the Greenville Area Development Corporation called the data center "yet another key selling point for businesses considering investment in the Upstate." Larger data centers are now meeting resistance across South Carolina, where the Legislature has not passed statewide rules. In June 2026 Spartanburg County Council took a first unanimous vote on a one-year moratorium, Greenwood County began a 12-month pause, and Chesterfield and Newberry counties enacted their own. DC BLOX's growth has met resistance elsewhere in the region: in June 2026 its plan for a two-building, 24-acre data center next to the Nashville Zoo drew a petition with more than 391,000 signatures and a zoning appeal from the zoo, and Nashville's Metropolitan Council was considering a moratorium that could block it.

ft-493.text: DC Blox's Chattanooga data center, CHA1, at 807 East 16th Street in Chattanooga, Hamilton County, Tennessee, is an operating Tier III colocation facility linked directly to the city's Smart Grid, which reroutes power around outages. DC Blox markets the site to businesses in the "Gig City" and as a disaster recovery location for companies in Atlanta, Memphis, Knoxville and Nashville, with up to 2,000 square feet of tenant office space and carrier-neutral cross-connects. On July 15, 2026, the Hamilton County Commission unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on new data centers in the county's unincorporated areas, running through July 15, 2027. County Mayor Weston Wamp said the goal is zoning restrictive enough to keep data centers out, telling commissioners that based on his talks with local utilities, data centers are not the right fit for Hamilton County. The moratorium covers unincorporated parts of the county, not the City of Chattanooga, where DC Blox's facility sits, so it does not apply to this site.

ft-495.text: Cielo Digital Infrastructure, a data center developer owned by the Texas investment manager Arroyo Investors, lists a 350-megawatt campus on 107 acres in Clarksville, Montgomery County, Tennessee, among the projects on its website. But as of September 2026 no data center had actually been proposed in the county, Clarksville Now reported, and Cielo has not said where in Clarksville the campus would go. Asked in September 2026 whether any data center was proposed, Montgomery County planning director Jeff Tyndall said the short answer was no. "But we believe there was some interest recently," he said. "We currently don't have the electrical (and) water capacity to support another mega center like Google. And that's only going to keep them at bay for so long." NewsChannel 5 reported that a major technology company had recently explored a large facility in the county before the project did not move forward, prompting planners to look again at zoning rules; it did not name the company. Montgomery County already hosts a roughly 400-acre Google data center operating since 2019, and Tyndall said, "I don't think at this point our community would have the water infrastructure to support another site the size of Google." The Montgomery County Regional Planning Commission responded by approving new rules on September 22, 2026 that would let a data center locate only in M-1 or M-2 industrial zones, on 10 to 100 acres, with a noise plan, proof of its water supply, and written statements from TVA and local utilities on power and gas. The developer, not ratepayers, would pay for the utility upgrades the project needs, under a new state law. The Montgomery County Commission, which makes the final decision, is next to vote on the rules, and Tyndall said a similar ordinance could follow for the City of Clarksville. If Cielo or anyone else files for a campus the size Cielo lists, it would first need a public hearing before the county's Board of Zoning Appeals.

ft-508.text: Tesla runs an AI training data center, which it calls Cortex, at Gigafactory Texas outside Austin in Travis County, and the Giga Texas data center more than doubled its computing power in the first half of 2026. Tesla's Q2 2026 report showed on-site AI training capacity in Texas rising from roughly 115 megawatts at the end of 2025 to about 260 megawatts by the end of June, with a goal of nearly 400 megawatts by the end of the year, according to Not a Tesla App's reading of the report's chart. The first Cortex cluster, 50,000 Nvidia H100 chips, came online at the Austin factory in the fourth quarter of 2024, according to Tesla's shareholder deck. "Cortex helped enable V13 of FSD (Supervised)," the deck said. Musk said on the company's earnings call in January 2025 that the training needs for the Optimus humanoid robot are "probably at least 10x of what is needed for the car to get to the full range of useful roles." The expansion now under way is Cortex 2.0; state construction filings describe new construction for it on Robotic Avenue on the Austin campus. "Cortex 2 supports the development of both vehicle and humanoid robot autonomy software and will ramp further over the rest of the year to ensure we have sufficient compute resources," Tesla said in its Q2 2026 report. Gigafactory Texas covers 2,500 acres and employs 16,500 people, who build electric vehicles and batteries and are adding lines for robots and new products. Tesla is also building a facility there for chip refining and packaging for its Terafab semiconductor project, whose main plant is planned in Grimes County. Terafab's state agreement lists a December 1, 2026 construction start in Grimes County and completion by the end of 2028. Little about the data center is public. Tesla did not respond to the Austin American-Statesman's requests for interviews or visits, and a lawyer for the company recently called the site "essentially Fort Knox." In Travis County, Tesla recently had part of its tax rebate withheld for not complying with its economic development agreement.

ft-1768857701845-3484.text: Texas Solar Works withdrew its request to rezone 936 acres off Northeast Loop 289 and East Municipal Drive in northeast Lubbock, Lubbock County, Texas, for a hyperscale data center in January 2026, after the city's Planning and Zoning Commission voted 4-3 against it. Hugo Reed and Associates, for the company, had asked to change the mostly low-density single-family land to general industrial, with a specific use permit for power generation, transmission and distribution. The data center would have drawn on large lines connecting to ERCOT, solar power and gas generation. About 10 people spoke against it at the Jan. 8 commission meeting, many from north and east Lubbock neighborhoods that say they already carry heavy industrial burdens. "Gas turbines, pollution, noise. No, absolutely not," Fabian Mata said. John Osborne of the Lubbock Economic Development Alliance said the developer had committed to moving the energy portion to 500 adjacent acres it planned to buy in the county, and that the site was being built for a buyer not yet known. Osborne said the builder planned to adjust the request to be "more in line with what the community has requested" and resubmit it with a site plan. Residents then gathered more than 3,900 verified signatures for an 18-month moratorium on high-water and high-energy data centers, which the council accepted on Aug. 25, 2026. On Sept. 22 the council let the 18-month version fail without a second and voted 5-2 to start a 90-day moratorium on rezoning, permits and annexations for large data centers, which needs two public hearings before it takes effect. "No one's coming to Lubbock in the next year anyway with a data center," Mayor Mark McBrayer said. Any resubmitted rezoning would go before the Lubbock City Council, which has the final say.

ft-558.text: Project Ellen is a 100 megawatt data center that Soluna Holdings plans on a 145 megawatt wind farm in Cameron County, Texas, for bitcoin mining and artificial intelligence work. In May 2026 County Judge Eddie Treviño Jr. said county engineers had held only preliminary talks with two unnamed data center firms, and that "no permit applications for data center construction or development have been submitted to the county." The Albany, New York, company said in April 2025 that it had signed a term sheet to buy power from a 145 megawatt South Texas wind farm, owned by a partner it did not name, for a 100 megawatt data center built in two phases, with the power purchase agreement, land deal and grid planning still to come. By June 2026 it said Ellen was moving through the interconnection and transmission process. In August it raised the planned size to 145 megawatts and designated the site for AI workloads. Chief executive John Belizaire told investors that at sites including Ellen the land is identified and the power agreements signed, while listing new power purchase agreements for Ellen among the goals for the rest of 2026. Treviño said in May that the county was not willing to offer tax abatements to data centers, and in April the commissioners court asked the Legislature to give counties more authority to regulate such industries. "If they meet the requirements with regards to the engineering and the model rules, or what have you, we're bound to approve that application or that permit," Treviño told KRGV, because counties lack the zoning power cities have. The county has since issued a worksite permit for Fluidstack's separate 1,100 acre data center along FM 106 near Rio Hondo, where residents such as Isaac Newman have questioned what it will do to limited water. Soluna has not disclosed which wind farm in Cameron County would host it, and the listings that fill the gap disagree. Data Center Map files Ellen under Harlingen and places it inside the Palmas Altas wind farm, whose 145 megawatts match Soluna's figure. Compute Atlas files it under Rio Hondo. Palmas Altas itself is Acciona's 46-turbine farm in Cameron County, put into service in December 2019 with a 10-person operations crew.

ft-559.text: Project Rosa, a wind-powered data center that Soluna Holdings plans in South Texas, has grown on paper to 242 megawatts, but it has not been built. In August 2026 the company said it had redesignated Rosa's power for AI workloads, raising it from 187 to 242 megawatts. Soluna, based in Albany, New York, puts its data centers beside renewable power plants. Its pitch is to use wind power that would otherwise be wasted, which happens largely because Texas lacks the transmission lines to carry it, according to the renewable energy group Advanced Power Alliance. It announced on February 25, 2025 that it had secured a purchase agreement for 60 acres for Rosa, beside a 240-megawatt wind farm in Texas that it did not name. At the time Rosa was planned for bitcoin mining and AI, in two phases. "Securing these land agreements is a critical achievement for Soluna," chief executive John Belizaire said then. Data Center Dynamics noted that details on where Rosa will be located were not shared. Rosa is still in development. As of August 1, 2026, Soluna said it operated about 192 megawatts across three energized sites, with 14 more megawatts under construction at Project Kati 1, and counted the rest of its pipeline, including Rosa, as planning and development. Soluna has not named a tenant, and no local approvals or hearings for Rosa have been reported. Soluna's other Rio Grande Valley projects give a sense of what Rosa would look like. Project Kati 1, a $50 million, 166-megawatt bitcoin mining site on the Las Majadas wind farm, is under construction just north of the Cameron County line in Willacy County, and a second campus there, Kati 2, is planned with Metrobloks for AI. Willacy County Judge Aurelio Guerra welcomed Kati 1 for its taxable value: "Value is how counties survive". Soluna also plans two more data centers at unnamed wind farms in Cameron County, the 100-megawatt Project Ellen and the 120-megawatt Project Hedy. In August 2026 it raised those to 145 and 198 megawatts. What happens next depends on the Texas grid. Since August 3, 2026, new data center connections to the ERCOT grid have been on hold while state regulators audit the projects in the queue, on Governor Greg Abbott's order. Data centers that take power straight from their own generation can fall outside that pause. When it bought the land, Soluna said the next step was working out plans for Rosa with ERCOT, the grid operator.

ft-569.text: Skybox Atlantic Station is a planned 100 megawatt build-to-suit data center campus that Skybox Datacenters is marketing with Prologis on the former NTT Data Services site at 2300 West Plano Parkway in Plano, Collin County, Texas. Prologis still lists it as available, describing a second phase "designed to facilitate up to 4 mission critical data centers" on the 64-acre site. The campus could hold up to 1 million square feet of data center space, with an on-site substation that had 25 megawatts available when Skybox first listed it in April 2023. Skybox says the substation is privately owned, that the site sits in Oncor's deregulated power territory and that build-to-suit projects can be delivered in 12 to 24 months. The land has a long history as a technology campus. It was the former Perot Systems complex, which Dell bought in 2009 for $3.9 billion and sold to NTT Data in 2016 in a deal valued at more than $3 billion; NTT sold the million-square-foot complex to GI Partners in early 2019 and leased it back, including two data center buildings. Parts of the campus were demolished in 2021, and a Prologis affiliate bought the 64 acres at the end of that year. The first phase of Prologis Atlantic Station is three industrial buildings, of about 160,000, 110,000 and 122,000 square feet, with dock doors and build-to-suit office space. Plano residents have started asking the city for data center rules. At a June 2026 City Council meeting, resident Kyle McGinn urged officials to explore a data center moratorium or add a special zoning category for data centers to the Unified Development Code the city is rewriting. "I can recruit people. I can call people. I can block walk for these people", resident Shirley Lawson said, noting several council members face reelection in 2027. The council did not discuss data centers at that meeting. Elsewhere in Plano, Overwatch Capital bought a 30 megawatt data center in Legacy West in 2025 and planned to begin operations there in the fourth quarter of 2026. Skybox says zoning allows data centers by right on the campus, so a data center there would not need a rezoning. Any new city rules on data centers would come from the Plano City Council, which residents have asked to act through its Unified Development Code rewrite.

ft-560.text: Soluna's data center campus just south of Silverton, off Highway 207 in Briscoe County, Texas, runs on the wind: the company says it has built 98 megawatts of what it calls renewable computing there. The first two buildings, Dorothy 1A and 1B, have a combined 50 megawatts and are used for bitcoin hosting and mining. In April 2026 Soluna bought the 150 megawatt Briscoe Wind Farm that feeds the site for $53 million, then paid $16.5 million for Spring Lane Capital's stake in Dorothy 1A to own it outright. "With Briscoe secured and Dorothy 1A now fully owned, we have the foundation for what comes next: a vertically integrated AI campus, from energy generation to compute infrastructure, that we control end to end," chief executive John Belizaire said. The company says the campus will move from bitcoin mining to AI as its main workload over the medium term. "We've had for a couple of years a bitcoin mining facility, and it's filled in a gap of when we lost our abatement, our pilot money from the wind farms," County Judge Rank Cogdell told KVII in July 2026. With a larger data center planned, the county is weighing a tax abatement as a way to put safeguards in place, and commissioners were working with the company on a town hall where residents could ask questions. "It might even create more income for other businesses to come in, and of course our town is struggling; the whole county is struggling at this time," said Danny Francis, the Precinct 3 commissioner. That next phase, Dorothy 3, is an AI campus of up to 300 megawatts on 397 acres Soluna bought beside the existing buildings, across from the wind farm's substation.

ft-561.text: Project Dorothy 2 is the second phase of Soluna's data center campus off Highway 207 just south of Silverton, in Briscoe County, Texas, and with Dorothy 1 it brings the site to 98 megawatts of what Soluna calls renewable computing. Dorothy 1 and Dorothy 2 have capacities of 50 MW and 48 MW, and both run on the 150 MW Briscoe Wind Farm next door, which Soluna bought in April 2026 for $53 million. Soluna, based in Albany, New York, builds data centers for artificial intelligence and bitcoin mining, and says it owns and operates about 192 MW of energized capacity at wind- and solar-powered sites in Texas and Kentucky. The campus is named after NASA mathematician Dorothy Vaughan. "Moving on to build a data center, we've got the wind farm that we now own here as a permanent power source and were able to develop this data center with the existing 150-megawatt wind farm that we have," said Karl Shinn, Soluna's regional lead. Soluna is planning a much larger third phase. In August 2026 it closed on 397 acres next to the wind farm and Dorothy 1 and 2 for Dorothy 3, an AI data center campus with a potential capacity of 300 MW, also to be powered from the wind farm's substation. No construction or operating timeline has been given for Dorothy 3, and no partner has been named. Chief executive John Belizaire said: "Dorothy 3 is a site we control end to end, and that is what turns a development project into something a customer can plan around." For Briscoe County the question is money. County Judge Rank Cogdell said the bitcoin mining facility "filled in a gap of when we lost our abatement, our pilot money from the wind farms". The county is weighing tax abatements for the new data center plan, which Commissioner Danny Francis said might bring more income for other businesses: "our town is struggling; the whole county is struggling at this time". Cogdell said: "Everybody has an opinion, and the best thing that can happen is to be informed." Decisions on abatements rest with the Briscoe County Commissioners Court, which in late July 2026 was working with the data center's representatives on a town hall where residents could ask questions. The court is County Judge Rank Cogdell and commissioners Ross Estes, Jack Wellman, Danny Francis and John Burson.

Dorothy 1 and Dorothy 2 have capacities of 50 MW and 48 MW, and both run on the 150 MW Briscoe Wind Farm next door, which Soluna bought in April 2026 for $53 million.

Soluna, based in Albany, New York, builds data centers for artificial intelligence and bitcoin mining, and says it owns and operates about 192 MW of energized capacity at wind- and solar-powered sites in Texas and Kentucky.
The campus is named after NASA mathematician Dorothy Vaughan.

"Moving on to build a data center, we've got the wind farm that we now own here as a permanent power source and were able to develop this data center with the existing 150-megawatt wind farm that we have," said Karl Shinn, Soluna's regional lead.
Soluna is planning a much larger third phase.

In August 2026 it closed on 397 acres next to the wind farm and Dorothy 1 and 2 for Dorothy 3, an AI data center campus with a potential capacity of 300 MW, also to be powered from the wind farm's substation.
No construction or operating timeline has been given for Dorothy 3, and no partner has been named.
Chief executive John Belizaire said: "Dorothy 3 is a site we control end to end, and that is what turns a development project into something a customer can plan around."
For Briscoe County the question is money.
County Judge Rank Cogdell said the bitcoin mining facility "filled in a gap of when we lost our abatement, our pilot money from the wind farms".

The county is weighing tax abatements for the new data center plan, which Commissioner Danny Francis said might bring more income for other businesses: "our town is struggling; the whole county is struggling at this time".
Cogdell said: "Everybody has an opinion, and the best thing that can happen is to be informed."

Decisions on abatements rest with the Briscoe County Commissioners Court, which in late July 2026 was working with the data center's representatives on a town hall where residents could ask questions.
The court is County Judge Rank Cogdell and commissioners Ross Estes, Jack Wellman, Danny Francis and John Burson.

ft-1768321516004-3014.text: CyrusOne's proposed Dugway Proving Ground data center would cover about 1,201 acres of the Army base near Dugway in remote Tooele County, Utah, under a project the Army announced in March 2026, with initial operation expected in fiscal 2029. The Army entered exclusive negotiations with CyrusOne, a Dallas firm held by funds managed by KKR and BlackRock, through its Enhanced Use Lease program, and no deal had been finalized when the choice was announced. The Army says the developer will finance, build and run the data center at no upfront cost to taxpayers, with its own behind-the-meter power and water systems, and that the Army Corps of Engineers will conduct an environmental review. The Skull Valley Band of Goshute Indians, a tribe of 134 enrolled members based in Grantsville, opposes the project over groundwater. "The hyper-scale data center will have an extreme impact on the quality and quantity of groundwater available to ensure the tribe's survival, potentially contaminating the tribe's sole source of water and the area's fragile ecosystem," the band said. The band says the facility would use 500 megawatts of electricity and discharge up to 250,000 gallons a day of salt-heavy wastewater, and that Tooele County's groundwater is already over-allocated. It sent a letter of opposition to Gov. Spencer Cox without getting a response, and is also fighting an EnergySolutions plan to bring 1.31 million cubic yards of low-level radioactive waste from Canada to the county's Clive facility. The tribe has asked Tooele County officials to oppose any zoning or land-use requests tied to the project. The project goes ahead only if the Army and CyrusOne finalize a lease, which the Army's solicitation suggested could run 50 years.

ft-1077.text: Equinix runs SE4, a one story data center at 6906 South 204th Street in Kent, King County, Washington, with 75,003 square feet of colocation space connected to carriers including CenturyLink and Verizon. The site has N+1 backup power and generators rated for at least 30 hours at full load, and Equinix says it uses free cooling, hot and cold aisle containment, and was matched with wind and solar renewable energy certificates in 2025. Washington's Utilities and Transportation Commission is writing rules so large power users like data centers do not shift costs onto other electric customers, after a bill to regulate data centers' power use died in the state legislature. Kent itself has not passed a moratorium, unlike nearby Seattle, Burien and Federal Way, and the commission's rate guidelines were still being drafted as of August 2026.

ft-1078.text: TierPoint runs SPO03, one of its two Spokane-area data centers, at 23017 East Mission Avenue in Liberty Lake, Spokane County, Washington, with more than 16,500 square feet, including 9,900 square feet of raised floor. TierPoint's spec sheet lists 2,500 kilowatts of backup power with two full redundant systems and 15,000 gallons of fuel on site, and says the facility can support GPU and AI computing at up to 85 kilowatts per cabinet with liquid cooling. In August 2026, Spokane County commissioners voted unanimously to pause new large data center permits from August 18 to December 15, and the county's planning director said the eight data centers already operating in the county, including SPO03, would not be affected. The pause followed paused talks between Avista Utilities and an unnamed company seeking 125 megawatts of power within two years, growing to 500 megawatts, and draft county rules would apply to any data center project needing more than 20 megawatts and steer new projects to land zoned for heavy industry. "I just really want this four months to be used extremely wisely," said Brittany Anderson, a Spokane resident who used a public records request to uncover a commissioner's talks with a data center developer. Washington's Utilities and Transportation Commission is separately writing statewide guidelines so large power users like data centers, including customers of Avista, the utility serving Liberty Lake, do not pass extra costs onto other ratepayers. The Spokane County Commission plans to adopt permanent data center zoning rules at its final meeting of the year on December 15, 2026, when the pause is set to expire.

ft-1082.text: The State Data Center sits inside 1500 Jefferson, a six-story, 240,594-square-foot building on the State Capitol Campus in Olympia, Thurston County, Washington. The state agency WaTech runs it as the primary site for state agencies' servers, backed by a second site in eastern Washington, built to Tier 3 standards with redundant power, cooling and network links. The building opened in July 2011, the first major construction on the Capitol Campus in two decades. The state financed the building with tax-exempt bonds through a private development team, and the National Development Council owns it on the state's behalf. About 950 people work there, according to WaTech's chief financial officer, Judy Fitzgerald. WaTech has moved state agencies' computer systems into the building, its Quincy backup site or outside cloud services, and some agencies have needed waivers when moves ran late. Washington's Utilities and Transportation Commission is writing rules on how much of large data centers' power costs get passed to other customers, after a bill to regulate that died in this year's legislative session. "There will be indirect impacts on cost, and those are really hard to quantify," Commissioner Ann Rendahl said in August 2026.

A resident searching for a data center in Jefferson County will find a company selling connections, not a campus.

aligned-aligned-waddell-phx-12-13-14.text: Aligned Data Centers is building a 100-acre data center campus on North Reems Road in Waddell, in Maricopa County, Arizona, where it broke ground on the first of four planned buildings, PHX-13, in April 2025. PHX-13, at 8805 N. Reems Road, is a 72-megawatt data center, and the campus is also planned to hold PHX-12 and PHX-14. Aligned bought the 100 acres at 8785 N Reems Road in December 2024 for $86.5 million from LXP Industrial Trust, according to Cushman and Wakefield. The site was once a rose farm. A City of Glendale economic development official described the campus as having over 1 million square feet of data hall space. Aligned's PHX-07, also on North Reems Road at 8785, was due to go live in 2025. Power for the campus will come over a new 230-kilovolt transmission line from Arizona Public Service. Aligned says it will cool PHX-13 with its Delta3 air cooling arrays and a closed-loop system that recycles water, and that turning the rose farm into a data center campus cuts annual water use by more than 73%. The company says it kept the site's unused well rights, so the groundwater stays on-site. Glendale Mayor Jerry Weiers welcomed the project at the groundbreaking. "This project and all the benefits it will bring are exciting for our Glendale community," he said. West Glendale has more data centers coming, and not all of them have been welcomed. In April 2026 the Glendale City Council voted unanimously for a pre-annexation development agreement for Project Baccara, two data center buildings north of Olive Road and half a mile west of Litchfield Road near Luke Air Force Base, which the City of Surprise says will be powered by natural gas generators. Luke Air Force Base officials wrote that the project is not compatible with the base's noise and accident potential unless certain conditions are met. "The noise of this 24/7 is nothing like the 10–15 seconds that a jet makes when it goes over," said Dave Krause, who lives nearby. On May 6, 2026, the Maricopa County Board of Supervisors voted 4-1 to issue that project a military compatibility permit after its developer agreed to conditions set by the base commander, with Supervisor Steve Gallardo voting no.

microsoft-microsoft-boyd-farms-maiden.text: Microsoft is building its Boyd Farms data center off Zeb Haynes Road in Maiden, Catawba County, North Carolina, one of four data centers it promised in 2022 to develop in the county for at least $1 billion. Construction began on April 1, 2024, and in a May 2026 update Microsoft said crews were making steady progress on the foundations, underground utilities and infrastructure, with the first slab pour planned for early June 2026; Microsoft has not published a newer update on the site since. The general contractor is now Clark Construction, and Microsoft's May 2026 update said it may need controlled blasting to remove underground rock, a request that was under review at the time, with neighbors to be notified in advance and the work taking about two to three months once it begins; no decision on the blasting request has been published since. Microsoft slowed construction at its Catawba County sites in 2025, but the county's economic development president, Scott Millar, said in April the projects remained on track, since the company has until 2032 to meet the investment and job terms of its tax incentives. As data centers became part of a broader national debate, Catawba County, the cities of Conover and Hickory, the Town of Maiden and the county's economic development corporation answered questions about the project's impact with a joint statement on June 23, 2026. "The current drought brings local water capacity into sharp focus and raises legitimate questions about what industries local leaders are trying to attract," the statement said, adding that the City of Hickory supplies water to all the county's data center sites and expects them, once running, to use about 1% of Hickory's daily water production capacity because they will rely mainly on less water-intensive cooling. The statement also said Microsoft's sites will pay property tax on the full value of their buildings and equipment, and that the local incentive agreements are being amended to reflect that. Maiden already hosts Apple's first North American data center campus, opened more than a decade ago, and the region also has Google in Lenoir and Meta in Forest City; Microsoft's other Catawba County sites are along Tate Boulevard in Hickory, in Conover and along Stover Court in Newton.

microsoft-microsoft-nova-caledonia.text: Microsoft withdrew its Project Nova data center plan for 244 acres in Caledonia, Racine County, Wisconsin, in October 2025, days before the village board was due to vote, after more than 2,000 people signed a petition against the rezoning. "Based on the community feedback we heard, we have chosen not to move forward with this site," a Microsoft spokesperson said of the Caledonia data center. The site, on County Line Road and State Highway 32 southwest of We Energies' Oak Creek Power Plant, was surrounded by farmland and homes. Microsoft needed the land rezoned from agriculture to a light manufacturing and office district; the village plan commission approved the rezoning in September 2025, and the Village Board was to take it up on October 14. The company expected 40 to 50 jobs after construction. County Executive Ralph Malicki said Microsoft had not sought local development incentives for the site. At the plan commission in September, 40 of the 49 people who spoke opposed the plan, worried about noise, air quality, electric bills and how few jobs it would bring. "Why do we have to subsidize a company making billions of dollars a year?" resident Mike Kirchner asked. Village Trustee Fran Martin said the board was being asked to approve the zoning without enough detail: "And why it was done in such a secretive fashion and then rushed forward is not clear to me." Trustee Nancy Pierce, who voted against the rezoning on the plan commission, said she learned of the withdrawal from a media report. Village President Tom Weatherston said he was disappointed: "We want Microsoft here." A Microsoft spokesperson said the withdrawal did not affect its other Wisconsin projects in Mount Pleasant and Kenosha. Microsoft and Racine County officials said they would look for another site in the county, possibly in Caledonia, and Pierce said she had asked about alternatives including the former South Hills Golf Course property and land near Seven Mile Road. By January 2026, Prescott Balch, who played a key role in the Caledonia opposition, was sharing what he learned with communities across Wisconsin and around the country, Spectrum News reported.

google-google-west-memphis.text: Google has its first Arkansas data center under construction on about 1,100 acres in the industrial park south of West Memphis, in Crittenden County, a $4 billion investment through 2027; work began in October 2025. Google's subsidiary Groot LLC bought 1,117 acres of farmland from Bollinger Brothers Inc. for $16.5 million in November 2024, and an Army Corps of Engineers notice puts the whole data center site at 1,178 acres. Google has confirmed plans for two buildings with room for up to five, and a spokesperson said initial build-out typically takes 18 to 24 months, with hundreds of permanent jobs and thousands in construction. The West Memphis City Council approved up to $60 billion in industrial development bonds over 30 years for the project, $10 billion for real estate and $50 billion for equipment. Mayor Marco McLendon called the announcement the biggest day in the city's history. Google has pledged a $25 million energy efficiency fund for local households, and applied in September 2025 for a Clean Air Act permit for backup generators, which it says are only for the rare event the grid goes down. The fight is over who pays for the power. Entergy Arkansas, not the city utility, will serve the campus, partly from Cypress Solar, a $1.6 billion solar project. Documents Entergy says were accidentally released show Google paying $526 million upfront, about a third of the solar project's cost, with the rest funded by a nearly $6 monthly increase for Entergy ratepayers over 20 years. Entergy went to federal court to stop the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette from publishing further details, and a judge refused. At a legislative hearing in September 2026, Sen. Mark Johnson, co-chair of the Joint Energy Committee, held up his own Entergy bill with an added $22.81 from the new rider, and Sen. Matt McKee asked Entergy to explain why ratepayers pay for Cypress Solar if Google covers its costs: "Help me understand the process of why that benefits ratepayers, because unfortunately I don't think that's how most ratepayers look at that." Entergy says the rider only shifts the timing of costs and saves customers financing charges. A Google spokesperson said that in the long run the project will lower overall costs for residents. West Memphis Utilities says Google's infrastructure costs will not be passed on to its own customers. Local leaders contrast Google with xAI across the river in Memphis, where gas turbines drew an NAACP lawsuit. "They had no air permits. They did no community focus groups," West Memphis Utilities general manager Bob Atkins said of xAI, adding, "that is not what happened here at all." Atkins said Elon Musk had planned a Tesla data center on the same West Memphis land before pulling out in 2024. The cost questions now sit with the Arkansas Public Service Commission, which approved the rider under the Generating Arkansas Jobs Act of 2025, and with state lawmakers on the Joint Energy Committee.

microsoft-microsoft-person-county-mega-p.text: Microsoft plans a data center on the 1,385-acre Person County Mega Park in Woodsdale Township near Roxboro, in Person County, North Carolina, on the Virginia border, which it bought for $26.85 million in 2024. County officials confirmed on February 24, 2026 that the site would be the future home of a data center, and Microsoft said it would begin permitting through Person County this year. About 400 of the site's acres are wetlands. The secrecy started early. County officials signed nondisclosure agreements for what emails called "Project Energy", and by the time the buyer was public, the land had been sold, a section of Country Club Road through the site had been closed, and Duke Energy was already permitting a new gas plant to power it, The Assembly reported. Commissioner Kyle Puryear said in September 2024 that only four people knew the company was interested and that he had never seen a company this secretive in all his years as a commissioner. Neighbors are frustrated. "The road closure really is a detriment to emergency service," said Tina Clayton, 71, who lives a few miles from the site. "It takes EMS 11 minutes to go around now," she said. Roxboro restaurant owner Kendall Phelps welcomed Microsoft but said: "They shut our road and they shut my business down by a third of it by shutting the road down. And I'm hoping that we'll get something in return." At a Microsoft meeting with neighbors in June 2026, residents asked about energy, water and noise. Roxboro City Councilor Kendra Coggins, whose main worry is how much water the campus would draw from the city, said: "It feels like we got a lot of canned responses, but I'm appreciative that Microsoft came out." Olive Burress of the Sierra Club said Microsoft's commitments are voluntary. An Elon University poll that spring found just 24 percent of North Carolinians support a data center in their community. Microsoft says it will pay for its own infrastructure so utility rates do not increase, reduce water use while replenishing more than it consumes, and invest in local workforce training. Commission Chairman Kyle Puryear said the project would "enhance community well-being through strategic investment, job creation, and responsible stewardship of resources." The next step is permitting through Person County; County Manager Katherine Cathey has said Microsoft is developing its site plans for that process, with development expected to take several years.

google-google-spring-tulsa.text: Google's Project Spring, a data center campus on the 827-acre former Ringle Ranch near Oklahoma 97 and 56th Street North in Sand Springs, now belongs to a Google subsidiary, and in August 2026 a Tulsa County judge dismissed, for now, a residents' lawsuit against its rezoning. Sand Springs is a Tulsa suburb of about 20,000 people, and the Google data center site lies several miles outside town. The Sand Springs City Council annexed the land in June 2025 at the owners' request and voted 6-1 in February 2026 to rezone it from agriculture for the data center. In May the council approved a development agreement with Horizon Land Development LLC and Design LLC, acting for Google, and on July 1 the Ringle family sold the ranch; a day later it passed to Horizon Land Development, which City Manager Mike Carter described as a Google subsidiary. Project Spring would have at least one data center and as many as three. Construction is slated to begin in 2027, with operation planned for 2029. City officials expect at least 1,000 construction jobs and 200 permanent jobs; Google did not confirm those figures. The fight has been over how the land came into the city. Neighbors of the site live in Osage County, outside the city, and cannot vote in city elections. Rick Plummer, whose 165-acre horse ranch fence line is about 300 feet from the property, said his real estate agent warned him to prepare for a seven-figure loss in property value. "Nobody protected the poor ag guy," Plummer said. "You cannot just keep it a secret from the whole town and then drop it in their laps," said Kyle Schmidt, president of the Protect Sand Springs Alliance. Mayor Jim Spoon told the crowd at the February vote that it was a yes-or-no choice because Sand Springs would not get another chance at a data center. A campaign to recall city councilors failed in April 2026 when the city found the petitions did not have the required number of verified signatures, with many signers not registered in the right ward or living outside Sand Springs. Three lawsuits are in play: one challenging the annexation, one by the Alliance challenging the rezoning, and one in Osage County by Land Legacy. Land Legacy, a Tulsa-based land conservation nonprofit, alleges the landowner violated a land agreement by letting the city use the property for the data center. In August 2026, Tulsa County District Judge Tracy Priddy dismissed the Alliance's rezoning suit for lack of standing but gave the plaintiffs 20 days to amend it. "The case was only dismissed in its current form, and we have the opportunity to amend our petition, which we will do," Schmidt said. The land has been sold, Carter said, and "there's just a couple pieces of litigation to go through and then we think the project will start." The next decisions are in the courts, in the amended rezoning case, the annexation case and the Land Legacy suit.

ft-1782942807947-6996.text: The Loring LiquidCool Data Center, planned by Minnesota-based LiquidCool Solutions in a former Air Force warehouse in Limestone, Aroostook County, Maine, is expected to be the state's first large-scale AI data center. It is proposed to start at five to six megawatts and grow to 50 megawatts at full capacity. Governor Janet Mills vetoed a statewide bill in April 2026 that would have capped new data centers, including this one, at 20 megawatts, and the Legislature did not override her veto. Northern Maine has its own small, independent power grid with a peak load of about 150 megawatts, so a 50-megawatt data center could use more than a third of the region's power. "Adding 50 megawatts to such a small, isolated grid is huge," said Hepeng Li, an engineering professor at the University of Maine. The developers say the site will run on hydropower from New Brunswick, but New Brunswick Power told a reporter it has no supply agreement or memorandum of understanding with the project. Maine Public Utilities Commission Chairman Philip L. Bartlett II said: "Part of the challenge with data center development we've seen throughout the country is we see a lot of PR statements before real commitments and contracts." The developers also plan diesel backup generators on a site that borders the Mi'kmaq Nation and the Aroostook National Wildlife Refuge. LiquidCool signed a long-term lease in October 2025 with Green 4 Maine, which owns 450 acres of the former base, for the warehouse at the corner of Florida and Kansas roads. The building already has two megawatts of power, and the company has a will-serve agreement with Versant Power for 24 more. It would likely operate as a colocation center, renting server space to other companies, using immersion cooling that LiquidCool says will eliminate water use for cooling the servers. The bill Mills vetoed, LD 307, would have barred approvals for data centers using more than 20 megawatts until November 2027, and Zien said the company "can live with that" if the cap had passed. Mills said she agreed a pause was warranted given the effect of large data centers on the environment and electricity rates in other states, but that she would have signed the bill with an exemption for a separate project in the town of Jay. Zien said in March 2026 that he hoped to finish financing within a month and have the center running about six months after that: "We believe that this one will move forward, but nothing is 100% until the money is in the bank, as they say." No update on the financing has been published since.

sentences.t: The Loring LiquidCool Data Center, planned by Minnesota-based LiquidCool Solutions in a former Air Force warehouse in Limestone, Aroostook County, Maine, is expected to be the state's first large-scale AI data center.
It is proposed to start at five to six megawatts and grow to 50 megawatts at full capacity.
Governor Janet Mills vetoed a statewide bill in April 2026 that would have capped new data centers, including this one, at 20 megawatts, and the Legislature did not override her veto.
Northern Maine has its own small, independent power grid with a peak load of about 150 megawatts, so a 50-megawatt data center could use more than a third of the region's power.

google-google-dawson-charleston.text: Google is building a data center campus on about 231 acres at the Pine Hill Business Campus in Ridgeville, Dorchester County, South Carolina, a project it pursued under the code name Project Dawson before confirming its identity. It is one of two Google campuses under construction in Dorchester County, alongside one at Winding Woods Commerce Park in St. George. Dorchester County agreed to sell the county-owned Pine Hill land to Autumn Timber LLC, a Google shell company, for $5.84 million and approved tax breaks and a water-service agreement. Autumn Timber LLC used the Project Dawson name on a state environmental permit, and Mallard LLC appeared in Dominion Energy's filings with the state Public Service Commission before Google confirmed its role. Google announced the two Dorchester campuses in September 2024 as a $2 billion investment with 200 operational jobs, part of $3.3 billion that also expands its Moncks Corner campus in Berkeley County. In October 2025 it announced a further $9 billion in South Carolina for 2026 and 2027, including more development of the two Dorchester campuses. Dominion's filings described Project Dawson as a "substantial load" with its own new substation. The Post and Courier reported Google was offered an economic development electricity rate of 6 cents a kilowatt hour, about half what residential customers pay, while the site's planned capacity was redacted from the filings. County leaders have backed the project for its tax revenue. "This is the way life is, if you turn a light switch on it's gonna go through a data center," then-council chairman Todd Friddle said in 2024. Current council chairman David Chinnis said the investment "provides significant funding towards both school districts in Dorchester County each year." Google said in 2024 it expected the Dorchester campuses to be running within 12 to 18 months, and its South Carolina website now says it has opened its newest data center in Dorchester County without naming which of the two campuses. No source has confirmed the Ridgeville campus itself is finished, so it remains listed here as under construction. Any rate agreement for its power is reviewed by the South Carolina Public Service Commission, and land, tax and water terms rest with Dorchester County Council.

google-google-little-rock-port.text: Google's planned $1 billion data center at the Port of Little Rock, in Pulaski County, Arkansas, known as Project Boar, would put five industrial buildings totaling 1.43 million square feet, two office buildings and an electrical substation off Zueber Road, just east of Harper Road in Sweet Home. Google told the Little Rock Board of Directors in June 2026 that it has not yet decided to build. In April 2025 the board approved a memorandum of understanding to sell 380 acres at the port to Willowbend Capital LLC, the front company Google uses for the project, and the land has since been rezoned for heavy industry. Google was not revealed as the developer until an Arkansas Democrat-Gazette report in January 2026, and city and economic development officials say they signed nondisclosure agreements. Under the memorandum, Google would pay $300,000 a year, plus $200,000 for each additional data center, and receive a property tax abatement of at least 65% for 30 years. The project's permit notice from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers says it will likely draw more than 100 megawatts, and the developers want to fill about 16 acres of wetlands near Fourche Creek. Google plans to offset the wetland loss by buying mitigation bank credits. The filing does not say how much water or electricity the campus would use. Entergy Arkansas plans about 2,600 megawatts of new generation over five years, in part for data centers, and much of that cost will fall on its customers; the terms of Google's deal with the utility have not been disclosed. At a nearly five-hour board meeting on June 2, 2026, residents criticized the project and asked for a moratorium instead of new rules. "They're immediately going to think about the mayor and the board of directors that let it happen", resident Tobias Peoples said of rising utility rates. George Wise of the local Sierra Club said of Entergy's promise that bills would not rise: "What's a pledge? What's a pledge? I don't believe it". The board approved Mayor Frank Scott Jr.'s data center regulations for the city's industrial zones by voice vote that night. Scott said the rules could be strengthened, and that a 2023 state law, Act 851, keeps local governments from banning data centers outright. "A final decision to build is only made after all diligence and public reviews are complete, and, candidly, we have not reached that point," said Google representative Laurel Brown. Five hyperscale data center projects are in development across central and eastern Arkansas. A similar $1 billion project in Conway was filed by Forgelight Ventures LLC, whose incorporator, Michael Montfort, also incorporated Willowbend, and Google has committed $4 billion to its Project Pyramid campus in West Memphis. Pulaski County, which lacks Little Rock's zoning rules, tried to pass a data center moratorium in late May, but officials later said it had not passed because of a vote-counting error. What happens next depends on the Army Corps wetlands permit, which the port's director said could take two to six months, and on Google's own decision to build. The Little Rock Board of Directors sets the city's data center rules.

microsoft-microsoft-la-porte.text: Microsoft broke ground on June 17, 2026, on its data center campus off Boyd Boulevard on the south side of La Porte, in LaPorte County, Indiana, a $1 billion project on 489 acres. Phase one is six buildings, the first due by spring 2029 and a third by winter 2029, and after the city annexed more land for the project in spring 2026, the campus could grow to 17 buildings. "Soon you'll see cranes here, you'll see construction here and you'll see building go up fast," said Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith. Microsoft first announced the project in June 2024; the original site is in the Radius Industrial Park, and Microsoft promised about 200 jobs. Smith said the company would not seek local property tax breaks: "Don't give us a reduction in the local property taxes; charge us what we owe." The city has committed 15 percent of the data center's revenue to the LaPorte Community School Corporation. Smith said Microsoft would cover its share of electricity and water costs: "We won't use local communities water anymore than say a local restaurant does on an annual basis." The expansion drew opposition: at an April 13, 2026 hearing on annexing land in Pleasant Township, south of Boyd Boulevard between County Road 250 South and State Road 2, council chambers overflowed as union workers backed the plan and neighbors objected. "I put 30 years in here and bought properties, and I didn't buy them to be around a data center," one resident said. LaPorte County Commissioner Joe Haney said the county was "kind of in the dark" without the city sharing information. At a Microsoft information session later in April, which hundreds attended, the company's Jonathan Noble was cautious about electricity bills: "What we can say is that it is not our intent for our development to have any impact on that." "We're awfully close and we were never given an opportunity to talk about it before it was already a done deal," said LaPorte County resident Lary Campbell. The LaPorte City Council voted unanimously on May 18, 2026, to allow a second campus, running along Highway 35 south to County Road 250. Haney said the county was working to put Microsoft's promises on berms, landscaping and lighting into a formal document, and the third phase-one building still needs permit approval.

microsoft-microsoft-lyle-creek-catawba-c.text: Microsoft's Lyle Creek data center campus on Highway 16 in Conover, Catawba County, is under construction, and in September 2026 Microsoft said the first building's exterior was in its final stages. Mechanical and electrical work on that building has begun, and work is starting on other building areas for later phases. Lyle Creek is one of four data centers Microsoft agreed in November 2022 to build in Catawba County, investing at least $1 billion over 10 years with Conover, Hickory, Maiden and the county's economic development corporation. Microsoft began building at the 220-acre site, known as Project Agate, in March 2024, first with contractor Morgan Corp, which excavated and crushed rock, at times with controlled blasting in the early afternoon. By February 2026 Whiting-Turner had taken over as general contractor and began site preparation once weather allowed, with foundation work starting in mid-March. By May 2026 underground work and foundations were complete on several buildings and steel had started going up; construction runs Monday to Friday, 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. Conover has been under Stage 2 mandatory water restrictions since May 1, 2026, and the current drought "brings local water capacity into sharp focus and raises legitimate questions about what industries local leaders are trying to attract," the county, its towns and the economic development corporation said in a joint statement on June 23, 2026. The City of Hickory supplies water to the county's data center sites, and Microsoft's are expected to rely mainly on other cooling methods and, once running fully, to use about 1% of Hickory's daily water production. Microsoft has committed to "replenish more water than it withdraws in the communities where it operates," the statement said, and its Catawba County sites will pay property taxes on the full value of their buildings, equipment and infrastructure under incentive agreements now being amended to reflect that. Scott Millar, president of the county's economic development corporation, said Catawba is not chasing more data center investment: "We're not actively chasing that sector for new investment... We're going to go off and pursue other sectors." Lyle Creek is not the county's only site; Microsoft broke ground in 2024 on its Boyd Farms campus in Maiden, about 10 miles south, where Apple opened North America's first Apple data center more than a decade ago. The four data centers cost Microsoft a combined $909 million according to construction permits, and the county says growth will be managed through local permitting. The amended incentive agreement reflecting Microsoft's higher property-tax commitment is still being finalized.

google-google-peanut-chester.text: Project Peanut, Google's first data center campus in Chesterfield County, Virginia, is planned as three buildings totaling nearly 856,000 square feet on a 300-plus-acre site on Bermuda Hundred Road in Chester, next to Meadowville Technology Park. WWBT reported the site was already under construction in July 2026, when hundreds of people came to Google's open houses on its three Chesterfield campuses. Google bought the land in 2020 for $18.1 million from the Chesterfield Economic Development Authority, and filed its site plan in November 2025, with AECOM as architect and Bohler as civil engineer; its megawatt capacity has not been disclosed. The project was revealed in August 2025 as part of a $9 billion Google investment in Virginia. All three Google projects have county agreements freezing the data center equipment tax at 24 cents per $100 of assessed value for 30 years. Residents have faulted the Board of Supervisors for approving all three projects in a public vote while Google's involvement was concealed. Clover Hill Supervisor Jessica Schneider said nondisclosure agreements signed in 2018, when talks on Project Peanut began, were the reason. "I want to have clarity from our local government," said University of Richmond professor Mary Finley-Brook, a Chesterfield resident who has filed Freedom of Information Act requests. "Who is responsible for paying for this infrastructure, and what commitment did they make to Google about the construction of the water infrastructure?" At the July open house, Google gave no project-specific figures for water or power, and spokesman Clay Allsop said: "Once it's operational we disclose that." Google says it will pay for any infrastructure improvements the projects need. Google's other two Chesterfield campuses are Project Skye, four buildings on 848 acres on Moseley Road, and Project Loch, three buildings on 334 acres on Watkins Centre Parkway. The project was revealed in August 2025 as part of a $9 billion Google investment in Virginia. All three Google projects have county agreements freezing the data center equipment tax at 24 cents per $100 of assessed value for 30 years.
