google-google-stillwater.text: Google is building a data center campus in Stillwater, Payne County, Oklahoma, on 400 acres at Perkins and Richmond roads, in a project reported at up to $3 billion. Neighbors across Perkins Road in Park View Estates sued Google and its contractors in August 2025, saying runoff from the construction site polluted their pond. The city of Stillwater named Google in March 2025 as the buyer, after months in which the applicant was known only as a subsidiary, Kipper LLC; plans first shared in 2024 described a six-building campus. Under the tax incentive deal, Google will make payments in lieu of property taxes that in the first phase will bring almost $900,000 to public schools, Meridian Technology Center, Payne County government and the health department, according to a report from KOSU. Every local taxing body approved the 25-year incentive except Payne County Commissioner Rhonda Markum, who voted no, saying, "I have several constituents that are not in agreement with the 25-year tax deferment." The agreement covers up to six data centers, but the city council has cleared only the first two phases, and going further would require substantial investment in the city's water supply. The Park View Estates Homeowners Association's lawsuit, filed in Payne County District Court, names Kipper LLC, Manhattan Construction Group, Olsson Inc. and Emery Sapp & Sons, and claims mass grading was done without required stormwater pollution controls. "I feel like they just came in and hurt our little piece of paradise," said HOA president Doris Al-Harake, who worries about what could happen once the data center is running. The association is seeking more than $75,000 in damages; the case is before Judge Michael Kulling. In April 2026 OG&E said it would supply three new Google data centers in Stillwater and Muskogee, with Google paying all the costs of connecting them to the grid; the Oklahoma Corporation Commission must still approve those agreements. No update on the pond lawsuit has been published since the case was filed in August 2025.

google-google-rumble-road-macon.text: Google owns about 950 acres off Interstate 75 and Rumble Road in Monroe County, Georgia, between Forsyth and Macon, where it has said only that it plans to build a data center, with no confirmed timeline. "While we do not have a confirmed timeline for development for the site, we want to ensure we have the option to further grow, should our business demand it," a Google spokesperson told The Telegraph after the company paid about $42 million for the land in September 2025. Monroe County commissioners have passed a moratorium on new data center permits, effective December 3, 2025 with no set end date, as they draft tighter rules for the industry. The county rezoned the land to C-1 commercial in November 2024 so it could be sold to a tech company for a data center; before Google bought it, developer David Aldridge had pitched the site as a $1.2 billion campus of up to 12 buildings. In November 2025 Google asked the county to sign a nondisclosure agreement on the project; county attorney Ben Vaughn advised against it, and commissioners voted unanimously not to sign, to loud applause from a packed chamber. Joshua Pruitt, whose family has 10 acres on Rumble Road, said the earlier rezoning vote had caused an "erosion of public trust." "If Google wanted to go into this non-disclosure agreement, why did they not send their representative," Forsyth homeowner Carol Edge asked. Monroe County has turned down a data center before: in August 2025 commissioners unanimously denied rezoning more than 900 acres near Bolingbroke after hundreds of residents objected, and the owners sued the county. A proposed amendment to the county's development rules, drafted for an April 2026 commission meeting, would limit data centers to the M-1 district by special use, require 900-acre minimum sites, 500-foot building setbacks, public water and sewer instead of private wells, and a 65-decibel limit at the property line. The amendment was drafted for the county commission's April 2026 meeting; no result of that vote has been published.

google-google-evergreen-dorchester-count.text: Google is building a data center campus, first known as Project Evergreen, on 206 acres at the Winding Woods Commerce Park along U.S. Highway 78 near St. George in Dorchester County, South Carolina, one of two new Google campuses in the county. At a packed community meeting in St. George on May 28, 2026, Google said the work was on schedule and that portions of the two data centers should be running later this year. Google bought the Winding Woods land in early 2024 under the aliases Project Evergreen and Gannett Enterprises LLC, and said at first it would hold it for future needs while developing its Pine Hill site near Summerville. In September 2024 it announced a $3.3 billion South Carolina investment and broke ground on both Dorchester County campuses, which it valued at $2 billion together. Google has said the two campuses will create more than 200 full-time jobs and that it wants to hire locally. Water has been the fight at St. George. Dorchester County, which supplies the water, had agreed at Google's request to keep the site's usage secret, until Mount Pleasant resident Frank Heindel sued under the state Freedom of Information Act; in a January 2025 settlement the county agreed to publish the site's daily and monthly water use and pay $10,000 of his legal fees. Heindel said the agreement gives the St. George site first priority for uninterrupted water, so rural residents could be restricted in a crisis while the data center keeps running: "a monopolist, like Google, should not control a secret portion of the public's daily water supply." For comparison, Google's older Berkeley County data center withdrew 847 million gallons in 2023. At the May meeting Google's Lilyn Hester said the company pays for its own power and water: "The water's coming from Lake Marion," she said. "We are not relying on an aquifer to get our water." St. George resident George Felder raised flooding: "Because we already have a flooding issue. And then with them coming in, they're adding more to that flooding problem." Harleyville resident Timothy Lewis asked what Google would do for the community, while Town Council member and mayor pro tem Betty Walker Collins said she hoped it would add jobs and invest in "major issues" on that end of the county. The county gave Google's Pine Hill site some of the largest tax breaks it has granted, fixing its property taxes at 4 percent of assessed value for at least 40 years, and Dominion Energy agreed to power that site at a special rate less than half what residential customers pay. Hester said Google receives incentives and that the county's tax revenue check from the company begins next year. Google says it will keep holding community meetings and takes questions at south-carolina@google.com; oversight of the county's water deal and incentives rests with Dorchester County Council.

google-google-franklin-furnace.text: Google's Project Dazzler, a planned data center campus in Franklin Furnace, Scioto County, Ohio, has divided Green Township since the company was confirmed early in 2026 as the business behind a 500,000-square-foot, $1 billion project on the Ohio River. Its identity came out after the Scioto County Commission gave the data center a 75 percent tax abatement for 15 years, with a payment in lieu of taxes of $500,000 a year plus more once it is built. The project was filed by Tilted Gate LLC, first described only as a "Fortune 100 tech company." Google's project website places it more than 1,000 feet east of Gallia Pike (Old U.S. 52), with a new electrical substation to be built separately by AEP Ohio, and schedules construction setup in 2026, major site work in 2026 and 2027, building shells in 2027 and interior and electrical work through 2029. Google says it will pay the full cost of the electricity and the AEP Ohio infrastructure the campus needs, and that its Ohio facilities send wastewater through public sewers rather than discharging it. County commissioners have said they had no authority to stop the landowners selling or to block a data center there. "Our decision was based on the partner, not the project," Commissioner Scottie Powell said, pointing to Google's water conservation work and its plans to protect wetlands on the site. In May the commissioners unanimously backed an agreement under which Google will pay the county's $4 million local match for a project to fix the bridge-strike area where Green Township traffic crosses US-52. At a May 2026 open house at Green High School, protesters outside held signs reading "No data centers" and "No blank check for big tech." Audrey Dotson, a resident, said her main concern was noise: "We have autistic children that live in this neighborhood and go to this school and they can't stand to have the noise." Vina Colley, president of Portsmouth-Piketon Residents for Environmental Safety and Security, said: "The people are tired of it. They're tired of being sick. They're tired of being ran over by corporate." Google's Timothy Chadwick said several protected wetlands on the campus will be preserved, and Commissioner Merit Smith said Google's people admitted they should have shared information sooner. Across Ohio, 18 communities vote on data center measures this November, and a statewide petition to ban the largest data centers missed its July signature deadline, with organizers now aiming for 2027. Asked about a possible statewide vote, Chadwick said: "If that's the decision that the voters in the state of Ohio go, we're going to respect it completely." By late July 2026 crews had begun clearing ground, and Commissioner Merit Smith said building construction would start before the end of the year, that two buildings are now planned, and that the builder expects about 3,500 construction workers on site at the peak. The wetlands permits sit with state and federal regulators, AEP Ohio builds the substation, and the Scioto County Commissioners, who granted the abatement, will take public input on the bridge project before it is final.

The site runs roughly from Keller Hill Road south to State Road 42, and from West Union Church Road east to North Antioch Road. google-google-loch-richmond.text: Google's Project Loch, a three-building data center campus on 334 acres at 750 Watkins Centre Parkway in Midlothian, Chesterfield County, Virginia, is one of three Google campuses in the county, alongside Project Peanut in Chester and Project Skye on Moseley Road. The project is waiting on a U.S. Army Corps of Engineers permit because it would be built next to Tomahawk Creek, which feeds the Chesapeake Bay watershed. Google shared its plans for the Moseley and Westchester Commons-area sites in August 2025, the same day it announced a $9 billion Virginia investment, but said they were longer-term plans that would follow the Bermuda Hundred Road project and were not part of that $9 billion. Project Peanut is already under construction, and Loch's own construction timeline depends on the permitting. In its application, Google and its consultant Timmons Group said the site plan avoids perennial streams and resource protection areas but would affect roughly 3,000 feet of intermittent and rain-dependent streams and 4 acres of wetlands, and proposed building about 11 acres of wetlands and preserving 34.2 acres elsewhere in the South Anna River watershed. Google says it will pay for any infrastructure improvements the projects need. Residents say Google's involvement in all three Chesterfield projects was kept under nondisclosure agreements while the Board of Supervisors approved them in public votes, and an online petition demands more accountability from the board. At Google's July 2026 open house, which drew hundreds, the company explained water and power use only in general terms. "What we are being told is incomplete information," said Mary Finley-Brook, a University of Richmond professor and Chesterfield resident. Zach Xavier, another Chesterfield resident, said he was frustrated that he had no way of knowing whether concerns he raised individually with Google staff would be recorded or acted on. Clover Hill Supervisor Jessica Schneider, who voted for Loch and Skye, has said she will not support any more data center rezonings in the county. With zoning approved, Loch still needs the Army Corps permit and further county approvals before construction can begin.

google-google-chateauroux.text: Google's planned data center in Etrechet, near Chateauroux in the Indre department of France, has cost the small town its mayor. Florence Laurent resigned on September 15, 2026, saying the council had been told days earlier that the project would go ahead regardless of residents' concerns, after her three deputy mayors and a councillor had already quit in protest. The data center would rise on about 195 hectares of the Ozans business zone, with eight to ten buildings and new high-voltage power lines, and would need more than 500 megawatts of power. Laurent listed visual nuisance, water contamination from PFAS chemicals, falling home values and road traffic as issues still without firm commitments from the developers. Four Etrechet councillors who resigned a day earlier said the project escapes any real decision by the town while bringing heavy risks to water, the power grid and daily life, and questioned the independence of studies done on it. They said Gil Averous, president of the Chateauroux metropolitan area, had warned he would not take account of an unfavorable result in any local referendum on the project. Google's subsidiary Tricolore Computing signed a five year promise to buy the land from Chateauroux Metropole on July 5, 2025, for a reported 58.5 million euros, with construction meant to start in 2029. Grid operator RTE plans to double the high-voltage line between the Eguzon dam and Marmagne to supply enough power, a nearly 300 million euro project not expected to start before 2032. Google told the Multinationals Observatory the project remains in its very early stages, with no details yet on its timeline, cooling technology or energy sources. About 250 people protested outside Chateauroux city hall on June 30, 2026, as metropolitan councillors voted to double the power line serving the site. The regional Green party's climate vice president, Jeremie Godet, has warned that air cooling could use PFAS-emitting refrigerants and create a heat island near the Chateauroux forest; Averous says the waste heat could instead warm market garden greenhouses and dry alfalfa. Averous says the Ozans project has always had the backing of Etrechet and the metropolitan area's other towns whenever it came up for a vote. France's National Commission for Public Debate named the guarantors for a preliminary public consultation in April 2026; Averous expected it to happen in October 2026. A public inquiry follows later in the process, and Google has said it will not proceed before obtaining building permits.

google-google-skien.text: Google's first data center in Norway has been under construction since February 2024 at Gromstul, just north of Skien in Telemark, with 240 MW of power allocated to the first phase of the 600 million euro project. Google said in 2024 the plant would run on more than 99 percent carbon-free power because of the make-up of the Norwegian grid and would be operating in 2026; no opening has been announced. Google bought about 200 hectares at Gromstul, roughly 85 miles southwest of Oslo, around 2019; local press named the seller as Leopold Lovenskiold, one of Norway's largest forest owners. The data center is designed to be ready to supply its waste heat, and a Deloitte study commissioned by Google estimated 6.7 billion kroner of value creation in Norway from the investment between 2024 and 2025. Power has drawn the most debate. Before construction began, some reports suggested the campus could eventually need up to 860 MW, a figure Skien's mayor, Marius Roheim Aarvold, called a long-term prediction for the whole Gromstul area, saying Google's first phases would be 20 MW and then 100 MW, with a further 120 MW toward 2030. "We have been waiting anxiously for Google to make the decision to start construction of its first data center here in Skien," Aarvold said at the 2024 announcement. Skien municipality promotes Gromstul as a new regional site for data center operations and says there has been high building activity around it since construction began.

microsoft-microsoft-busan-pus05.text: Microsoft runs two data centers in the International Industrial Logistics City in Gangseo-gu, Busan, South Korea: its first, completed in 2020, and a larger second one, the Miumsandan data center, which Microsoft and the city unveiled on September 23, 2024. The two together total 85 megawatts of power, and Microsoft is now preparing a third, larger building nearby. Edaily reported on June 1, 2026 that Microsoft's Korean data center company, 5673 Korea, plans a 125-megawatt building on land it bought from the city's development corporation in the Mieum area, with construction due to start in October 2026 and finish in October 2031. Edaily put the third building's cost at more than 2 trillion won and reported that Microsoft was looking to lease neighboring land to speed up construction, with more than 100 megawatts planned beyond that once power supply is settled, for a cluster of over 400 megawatts at Mieum. Busan Mayor Park Heong-joon, Gangseo District Mayor Jin Gyo-hoon and representatives of KEPCO and the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy attended the September 2024 completion ceremony for the second data center, and Microsoft said it worked with the city, the trade ministry, KEPCO and the National Heritage Administration to secure a stable power supply. "Microsoft's investment aligns with our vision of making Busan a global hub for technology and innovation," Park said at the ceremony. The city is also training workers for the site: Busan's Microsoft Data Center Academy graduated its second cohort of 35 trainees in September 2026, and 14 of them are to start internships at Microsoft's Busan data center in early November. From the first cohort, six trainees became interns at the data center and one was hired full time.

microsoft-microsoft-koge-cph03.text: Microsoft's Koge data center, southwest of Copenhagen in Koge Municipality, Region Zealand, Denmark, is one of three campuses in the company's new Denmark East cloud region, which Microsoft has opened for customers. A second construction phase at the Koge site began on March 9, 2026, and is due to finish in April 2028. Microsoft first said in December 2020 that it would build data centers in Denmark; Koge was its second site after Roskilde, with the contractor Exyte preparing the ground and starting excavation for phase one. Details about the size and capacity of the Koge data center have not been made public, DCD reported. Microsoft says its Danish data centers use no water for cooling, run backup generators on renewable diesel where available, and are designed for a power usage effectiveness of 1.16. Long-term power purchase agreements in Denmark provide 130 megawatts of renewable energy, including the 27 megawatt Svinningegarden Solar Park in Holbaek Municipality, and waste heat will go first to district heating in Hoje-Taastrup, enough for about 6,000 homes, "with future expansion planned in Koge," Microsoft says. Koge Mayor Ken Kristensen said the opening showed Koge was "an attractive location for large, future-proof projects," and that he was pleased the data center would over time send surplus heat to the local district heating network. For the second phase, Microsoft directs neighbors with questions about the construction to its main contractor, SISK, and says it is following guidance from Koge Municipality.

microsoft-microsoft-quilicura-scl03.text: Microsoft's SCL03 data center in Quilicura, in Santiago's northwest, is a $317 million project on a 6.8-hectare site that Microsoft filed with Chile's environmental evaluation service in January 2022. The plans call for one data center building split into two units, COLO1 and COLO2, plus an administration building and a 26MVA substation, with the first phase estimated to take 17 months, which would put completion around mid-2023. SCL03 is part of Microsoft's Chilean cloud cluster, which spans three Santiago-area locations. Quilicura is a dense data center hub that also has Google's only operating data center in Latin America. In June 2025 President Gabriel Boric said the cluster would generate more than 81,000 jobs, a figure Microsoft said includes indirect jobs at clients and partners. Rest of World reported in November 2025 that permit filings for 17 Chilean data center projects, including Microsoft and Google sites, show a combined potential of no more than 1,547 full-time operations jobs. Quilicura councilwoman Alexandra Arancibia told the outlet the specialized jobs "can't be filled locally." Environmental activist Tania Rodríguez of the group Mosacat said "data centers are like warehouses filled with machines and cables, and there's little need for workers." Santiago residents have also objected to the water and energy the data centers use. Chile's investment agency InvestChile says 32 more data centers are planned by 11 international firms by 2028, and most of Chile's 67 planned and operating data centers are in the Santiago region.

microsoft-microsoft-staffanstorp.text: Microsoft's Staffanstorp data center, near Malmö in Skåne County, Sweden, is one of three sites in the company's Sweden Central cloud region, which opened in late 2021 alongside facilities in Gävle and Sandviken. Microsoft said in September 2021 that the Staffanstorp data center was up and running, would open to customers in November 2021, and employed more than 60 people. The site became a local fight over backup power. According to Sydsvenskan, the building was described in its original permit as a warehouse, not a data center, and only after it was finished did Microsoft apply to the Skåne County Administrative Board for a permit for about nine diesel units, DCD reported. Residents and local groups fought the plans and hoped to have existing permits revoked. In August 2022 Microsoft withdrew its application to add backup power for a planned 70MW of extra capacity, saying it needed a larger data center in the region than Staffanstorp could hold and would look for a new site in southern Sweden. "We can already state that even if we expand in Staffanstorp to the maximum capacity, it will not cover the needs we have in the region," Microsoft Sweden's communications head Andreas Wingren told Sydsvenskan, adding that local opposition was not part of the decision. Microsoft said it would keep operating and expanding in Staffanstorp using only the backup units already in place. It then equipped the building's interior from late 2022 to spring 2023, and said it did not intend to use more backup power capacity than was already installed and permitted. Microsoft says its Swedish backup generators run on HVO fuel from Preem and that the region is powered by 24/7 carbon-free energy matched with Vattenfall. In June 2024 Microsoft announced it would spend 33.7 billion Swedish crowns, or $3.2 billion, over two years to expand its Swedish data centers in Gävle, Sandviken and Staffanstorp, including 20,000 new GPUs for AI. Permits for backup power at the Staffanstorp site come from the Skåne County Administrative Board, which handles permits for environmentally hazardous operations.

google-google-jackson-county-bridgeport.text: Google announced in June 2026 that it will spend $1.5 billion over 2026 and 2027 to expand its data center campus near Bridgeport, in Jackson County, Alabama, on the site of the Tennessee Valley Authority's retired Widows Creek coal plant. The campus began operating in 2019. When Google chose the Widows Creek site, it planned a $600 million data center on 350 acres of TVA land and 75 to 100 initial jobs, the first project recruited under Alabama's data center incentives. "The idea of repurposing a former coal generating site and powering our new facility with renewable energy, especially reliable, affordable energy that we can count on 24/7 with the existing infrastructure in place, was attractive", Google's Gary Demasi said then. TVA had voted to close the coal plant, in operation since 1952, citing new federal coal ash rules. The expansion is expected to bring more than 1,000 contract workers during construction, on top of hundreds of full-time jobs already at the campus. "This is probably one of the largest announcements that have been made in Jackson County," said Alabama House Speaker Nathaniel Ledbetter. "It's generational change." Google says it will pay for all the electricity the site uses and the infrastructure costs tied to its operations, so costs are not shifted to residential ratepayers. "One of our points, as we always do, we pay our way," said site lead Thomas Gamble. Google also announced a $2 million Energy Impact Fund with TVA and the Community Action Agency of Northeast Alabama for weatherization of homes and schools, and $550,000 for STEM kits in Jackson County schools. Google says it has contracted for more than 300 megawatts of new generation in the Tennessee Valley, joined TVA and Kairos Power in a 2025 deal for up to 50 megawatts of advanced nuclear power, and reduces its electricity use when demand on the grid peaks. Data centers can use up to 5 million gallons of water a day, and Google points to its pledge to replenish more water than it uses by 2030 and its support for restoring the Paint Rock River watershed. Alabama lawmakers this year passed a bill reducing tax abatements for large data centers and another requiring the facilities, not neighbors, to pay for the energy they consume. Alabama voters are split: in one statewide survey, 22% said data centers were good for the state, 25% bad and 37% a mixed bag.

microsoft-microsoft-malaga-wenatchee.text: Microsoft's first data center campus in Chelan County, on Malaga Alcoa Highway in Malaga, Washington, is partly running, with a second building under construction and a third planned. Microsoft has filed permits for three buildings on about 102.5 acres at 5375 Malaga Alcoa Highway and could build up to six, depending on demand. Microsoft bought the land in 2022, including the 72.5-acre former Lojo property for $6.6 million, and began clearing the site in 2023; the land once held orchards, near the Alcoa Wenatchee Works aluminum smelter that closed in 2021. One building permit describes a one-story, 244,440-square-foot building valued at about $56.8 million, with 72 workers on site at peak shift; Microsoft's presence in North Central Washington began about 20 miles away in Quincy in 2006. Water is the question neighbors keep asking. In July 2026 Malaga residents raised concerns at a public meeting on a $50 million expansion of the Malaga Water District's system, which Microsoft is paying for. "Nobody knows exactly how big the Malaga aquifer is and how much water is in it; separate from the one in the Columbia River," said resident Lois Munro. "We made an agreement with the port, and with Microsoft, and with us, to give them water," said water district commissioner Staci Shearer. "But we can shut their water off at any given time because our residents need it, and our residents are going to come first." Microsoft's Lisa Karstetter said the three buildings will use "6 million gallons of water annually, for a total of about 18-19 million gallons per year at full buildout," compared with about 129 million gallons a year the orchards once used. The first three buildings use an older direct evaporative cooling system; later buildings could use closed-loop or air cooling, though those plans are not final. Microsoft says the three buildings will draw up to about 150 megawatts of power at full buildout, and a Chelan County PUD contract covers up to 288 megawatts of power for the site through 2040 as more buildings are added. Microsoft declined to give figures on its state tax incentives; Washington exempts data center server equipment and power infrastructure from sales tax. Microsoft paid $1.5 million, a third of the cost, to renovate the Malaga fire station, which reopened in 2025, and is funding three of its firefighter positions. The water district's commissioners control the water supply, and the Chelan Douglas Regional Port Authority manages the water system work on the district's behalf. Microsoft's second building, toured by Chelan County officials on September 17, 2026, is expected to be operating by January 2028, with a third building expected by late 2028.

google-google-winschoten.text: Google's Winschoten data center, at Hoogebrug 3 in Winschoten in the municipality of Oldambt, Groningen province, the Netherlands, opened in November 2025 as Google's third Dutch data center location, after Eemshaven and Middenmeer. Google began construction in December 2023 with a planned investment of 600 million euros, and the building adds capacity to Google's europe-west4 cloud region. Oldambt alderman Jurrie Nieboer said at the 2023 start that he had been closely involved in bringing the 13-hectare data center to the town. The regional development agency NOM was involved from the start in choosing the site, and the municipality said it valued the jobs for technicians as well as for cleaning and grounds staff. Google says the building has solar panels on the roof, uses air cooling to limit water use to domestic needs, and is equipped to send waste heat into a heat network for future users such as local homes, schools or businesses. "This means several dozen jobs on a structural basis, in various roles, from technicians to security," alderman Erich Wunker said at the opening. Google also announced a partnership with Oldambt, WerkPro, Afeer and Cosis for a Circular Centre across from the data center, a two-story, 196-square-meter building to repair and dismantle electrical appliances, with about 10 full-time workers once running. Elsewhere in Groningen province, residents near Google's Eemshaven data center have complained about light from the port's large companies, and Google measured its outdoor lighting there in August 2026. Whether the Winschoten heat reaches homes depends on a heat network and future buyers, which Oldambt and Google have not yet named.

google-google-aabenraa.text: Dapsi International ApS, Google's Danish subsidiary, has applied to build a four building data center campus, Data Center Kassø, on farmland near Rødekro in Aabenraa Municipality, Denmark. Google has owned the site since 2017 without building on it, and the municipality issued its scoping statement for a required environmental impact assessment on April 27, 2026. The next steps are the company's environmental report, a draft permit and a further public hearing. The plan covers about 105 hectares next to the Kassø high voltage transformer station, in an area zoned for industry and data centers. The four large buildings would mainly hold server halls, with a central office, cooling plant, a switching station and up to 185 emergency generators, built in stages over about six years. About 400 people are expected to work at the site once it is running, with up to 220 heavy vehicles a day at the busiest point of construction. Google bought the 131 hectare site in November 2017, saying it had no current plans to use it but wanted room to expand in Europe. Then mayor Thomas Andresen said the purchase put Aabenraa on the world map. Apple dropped plans for a data center next door in 2019, and SAP bought nearby plots at Kassø and Padborg in 2020 without building. At a public hearing on the assessment's scope, held from February 27 to March 27, 2026, Kassø residents said year round homes west of the site had been left out of consideration and would be heavily affected, especially by traffic. They asked the assessment to treat the wider Kassø industrial park as one combined impact, covering noise, air pollution, dust, vibration and light, but the municipality said only concrete, planned projects can be included in that combined review. Energinet, the grid operator, asked that an accident at the data center must not affect the nearby substation.

Google has owned the site since 2017 without building on it, and the municipality issued its scoping statement for a required environmental impact assessment on April 27, 2026.
The next steps are the company's environmental report, a draft permit and a further public hearing.
The plan covers about 105 hectares next to the Kassø high voltage transformer station, in an area zoned for industry and data centers.
The four large buildings would mainly hold server halls, with a central office, cooling plant, a switching station and up to 185 emergency generators, built in stages over about six years.
About 400 people are expected to work at the site once it is running, with up to 220 heavy vehicles a day at the busiest point of construction.
Google bought the 131 hectare site in November 2017, saying it had no current plans to use it but wanted room to expand in Europe.
Then mayor Thomas Andresen said the purchase put Aabenraa on the world map.
Apple dropped plans for a data center next door in 2019, and SAP bought nearby plots at Kassø and Padborg in 2020 without building.

At a public hearing on the assessment's scope, held from February 27 to March 27, 2026, Kassø residents said year round homes west of the site had been left out of consideration and would be heavily affected, especially by traffic.

They asked the assessment to treat the wider Kassø industrial park as one combined impact, covering noise, air pollution, dust, vibration and light, but the municipality said only concrete, planned projects can be included in that combined review.
Energinet, the grid operator, asked that an accident at the data center must not affect the nearby substation.

google-google-farciennes.text: Google is building its second Belgian data center campus at the Ecopôle business park in Farciennes, in the province of Hainaut, Belgium. Construction began in April 2024 on a campus of three buildings covering about 53,000 square meters on 53 hectares, part of a €1 billion investment that also expands Google's existing campus at Saint-Ghislain. The first stone was laid on April 5, 2024, with Mayor Hugues Bayet, Secretary of State Thomas Dermine and Energy Minister Tinne Van der Straeten, according to the town, which developed the project with the intermunicipal agency Igretec. Local press first reported Google's interest in Farciennes in 2019, and the company bought the land that year; plans were officially announced in July 2023, and grid operator Elia said capacity in the 200-to-300-megawatt range would be available at the site. The permit requires rooftop solar panels, 90 percent carbon-free energy on site by 2025 and 95 percent by 2030, a switch from water-based to air cooling, and a connection to a local district heating network. DCmag reported that the permit also called for 350,000 cubic meters of fill to be moved by waterway, and for shared bike and scooter stations at the Farciennes and Aiseau-Presles train stations. Google does much of its business in Belgium through the company Crystal Computing. "Once this new data centre is operational, we are thinking of about 100 permanent jobs," Google's Michiel Sallaets said, naming server technicians as well as catering, maintenance and security staff. Farciennes is Wallonia's poorest municipality, The Brussels Times noted. The Ecopôle, spread over more than 150 hectares along the Basse-Sambre road on former heavy-industry land, has a bypass road so that heavy trucks no longer cross the town center, according to the municipality. In March 2026, about a hundred delegates of the socialist union FGTB staged a protest at the construction site, asking to meet the posted workers employed there and check that labor laws were respected, but their request was refused, La DH reported. Two socialist members of the European Parliament, Estelle Ceulemans and Johan Danielsson, took part. When work began in April 2024, The Brussels Times reported that construction of the new campus "will take several years," alongside the expansion at Saint-Ghislain.

google-google-kajaani.text: Google plans a new data center at Otanmäki in Kajaani, in Finland's Kainuu region, one of three new Finnish data centers in a €13 billion investment the company announced on September 9, 2026. Google called the program, which also expands its existing Hamina data center and adds sites in Vaala and Muhos, its largest single investment in Europe, with construction expected in 2027 and 2028. The regional paper Kainuun Sanomat reported that a data center and a battery system would be built at the Otanmäki site within two years. Google contracted a new 94-megawatt battery system near its Kajaani-region operations, due to start in late 2027, to help balance the Finnish grid. Google bought land in Kajaani and Muhos for more than €27 million in November 2024; the Otanmäki plot is about four times the size of the nearly 200-hectare site where XTX Markets is building in Kajaani, Yle reported. Data Center Map lists the site on Ryynäsentie in Otanmäki. In April 2026, a planner from the consultancy Sweco told a public meeting on the site's zoning plan that Google had dropped plans to cool the data center with water from Lake Oulujärvi, Kainuun Sanomat reported. In September 2026, Finland's Licensing and Supervision Agency began examining whether logging at Google's Kajaani and Muhos sites broke environmental rules, after the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation raised concerns. The agency asked Google's Finnish project company Tuike Finland Oy, Muhos municipality and the city of Kajaani for information, as forestry work had started at the sites months earlier while environmental impact assessments were unfinished. Google communications manager Michiel Sallaets said trees on Google-owned land in Muhos and Kajaani were felled in full compliance with the Forest Act, and the company said areas of environmental value were protected. Google also plans a €31 million community fund for Hamina, Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala over four years. The environmental impact assessments for the Kajaani and Muhos sites were still unfinished when the agency opened its review. The zoning plan for the Otanmäki site was still going through public meetings in April 2026. "This means jobs, lots of jobs for Finns across Finland," Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said at the announcement.

google-google-kronstorf.text: Google is building its first data center in Austria in Kronstorf, in the Linz-Land district of Upper Austria, and broke ground on April 23, 2026. The first phase covers 42,000 square meters, 29,000 of them data center space, on a site Google bought about 18 years earlier, and groundwork had been under way since at least August 2025, DCD reported. The data center under construction is designed for a maximum of 150 megawatts, with a planned second stage of up to 500 megawatts, ORF reported. In July 2026, only months after the groundbreaking, Google applied to the municipality and the Linz-Land district authority to build out the whole campus of about 50 hectares. Upper Austria's economy minister Markus Achleitner said the full build-out would raise the site's yearly power demand from 1.31 terawatt-hours to as much as 4.4, that Google would pay for its own grid connection, and that permits could be finished in the second half of 2027. The state calls it the largest single investment in Upper Austria's history, worth several billion euros. Google says the site will offer its waste heat free of charge once a taker is found, will have a green roof with solar panels, and will create 100 direct jobs. Opposition has grown. On July 17, 2026, more than 200 people joined a protest near the construction site called by the citizens' group Bürgerinneninitiative Rechenzentrum Kronstorf, which wants all contracts disclosed and full reviews of noise, traffic and grid security, ORF reported. Critics point to the sealing of about 50 hectares of good farmland, the power demand, and cooling plans that would draw millions of cubic meters of water a year from wells and discharge much of it into the Enns River at up to 30 degrees Celsius. Upper Austria's Green environment minister Stefan Kaineder said the most fertile farmland was being paved over and that a project of this size should have an environmental impact assessment. After a review ordered by Kaineder, the state confirmed in September 2026 that its 2020 ruling that no environmental impact assessment is needed is final and covers both stages. Kronstorf Mayor Christian Kolarik said Google bought the land 18 years ago for step-by-step development and that is now happening, and the town noted that all four parties on its council backed the needed decisions unanimously.

google-google-muhos.text: Google plans a data center campus at Pyhansivu-Leppiniemi in Muhos, a town of about 9,000 people in North Ostrobothnia, Finland, one of three new Finnish sites in a 13 billion euro investment Google announced September 9, 2026. Its Finnish project company, Tuike Finland, plans nine server halls on about 571 hectares roughly 4 kilometers northeast of the town center, between the Oulujoki River and the Oulu-Kontiomaki railway. Heavy earthworks are under way, but construction cannot begin until an appeal against the zoning plan is resolved by the court. A private individual appealed the zoning plan, which the municipal council adopted in early March 2026, arguing the nature impacts were not studied enough and that Google's land deal had steered the zoning. Under that August 2025 deal, Tuike Finland will pay the municipality 26 million euros once the plan takes legal effect, and will protect about 255 hectares of forest as compensation. Google has already cleared forest and reinforced roads and stormwater structures on the site; a request to halt that work was turned down, the regional paper Kaleva reported. The Finnish Association for Nature Conservation says more than 300 hectares have been cleared at Leppiniemi and wants the Licensing and Supervision Agency to halt construction until a full environmental impact assessment is done; that assessment report is still pending. Depending on the cooling method it uses, the data center could draw up to about 20 million cubic meters of water a year from the Oulujoki River, according to the 2025 assessment program. Google says the tree felling on its Muhos land complied with Finland's Forest Act. Muhos municipal manager Kimmo Hinno says the town strongly supports the project; the land deal also includes about eight kilometers of new roads, a junction with Highway 22 and a rail underpass. Google spokesperson Michiel Sallaets told Kaleva that further work depends on the zoning plan being finalized and permits being obtained.

google-google-valer.text: Google is considering a data center at Gylderåsen, an industrial area in Våler in Østfold county, Norway, and has applied for a 480-megawatt grid connection for it. The application was made through the company WS Computing AS in the NO1 power region, for a project in the Moss region, and the amount equals the power used by about 200,000 homes, Nettavisen reported, citing Digi.no. Google has made no investment decision, Google Norway communications head Sondre Ronander said in December 2025, and whether it builds depends on getting power. In September 2026 the technical weekly TU reported that Google had secured the 480-megawatt connection, while Ronander stressed that no development had been decided. The site is being developed by KI Våler AS, owned 96 percent by Østfold Energi and 4 percent by Våler municipality, which has given Google the rights needed to develop the project. Våler's municipal director Ivar Nævra said it was realistic that construction could start in 2030, and that the area is an extension of an existing industrial area and not very attractive for hiking or recreation. The idea dates to a 2017 study for Østfold county by Cowi and Smart Innovation Norway that picked out Gylderåsen as a possible location for large data centers, and the municipal council backed the main project unanimously that October. The council adopted a zoning plan for power-intensive industry at Gylderåsen in December 2022 after objections from the county governor, neighboring Vestby municipality and the county's cultural heritage office. The umbrella group Forum for Natur og Friluftsliv appealed in January 2023 on behalf of six nature and outdoor groups, including BirdLife Norway's Østfold branch and Naturvernforbundet in Østfold, and the county governor upheld the plan that December, making it legally binding. Østfold has a power deficit of about one terawatt-hour, and the business federation NHO warned that more generation and faster grid building are needed to keep prices in check. Google is also building a data center campus in Skien, its first in Norway.

microsoft-microsoft-la-muela.text: Microsoft plans the largest of its three proposed Aragon data center campuses on 146 hectares in Phase 5 of the Centro Via industrial estate in La Muela, near Zaragoza, Spain. The Aragon government declared the La Muela campus a project of regional general interest in December 2023, and gave initial approval in November 2025 to Microsoft's overall plan, called Region MSFT, for campuses in La Muela, Villamayor de Gallego and Zaragoza. The La Muela site would hold two single and two double data center buildings plus an administration building, at an estimated cost of 2,179 million euros, according to the plan as summarized by Hoy Aragon. The three campuses together would cover 283.79 hectares and cost more than 5.3 billion euros to build, with 1,000 to 2,000 construction workers per site and about 900 permanent jobs once all three are running. "Following its final approval, we will begin simultaneous construction of the first phase of the project at the three planned locations in La Muela, Villamayor de Gallego, and Zaragoza," a Microsoft spokesperson said after the initial approval. Microsoft planned to begin construction at the end of 2026 and have the first phase running in 2030, with work on the full campuses continuing for another six years, El Espanol reported in March 2026. The same report said Amazon Web Services and Microsoft were competing for space at the same grid connection point, Penaflor 220, and that power availability would govern how fast Aragon's many data center projects come online. El Espanol reported local opposition to data centers in Aragon over their use of water and energy. The plan has not yet had final approval: in an order dated July 24, 2026 and published July 30, the Aragon government amended its initial approval to add Microsoft's environmental impact study, approved that study initially, sent it to the regional environment agency INAGA for assessment, and opened a new public comment period on it.

microsoft-microsoft-naas.text: Microsoft is developing plans for a data center campus at Jigginstown, near Naas in County Kildare, Ireland, on land that Kildare County Council zoned for data centers in the Naas Local Area Plan 2021-2027. The 54.55-hectare site, known locally as P2, backs onto Primrose Garden and carries an exclusive "P - Data Centre" zoning, but more than three years after Microsoft confirmed its interest in 2023 it has not lodged a planning application, the Kildare Nationalist reported in August 2026. Microsoft held a public event on its early concepts at the Osprey Hotel in Naas in November 2023, and in July 2024 said contractors were carrying out ecological surveys and ground investigations on the site. When it confirmed the plan, Microsoft did not give the campus size or capacity, and said its preferred solution was 100 percent renewable energy through corporate power purchase agreements. "The selection of Naas will also help to build its reputation as a regional digital hub at the forefront of Ireland's digital economy," the company said. Local opposition has grown in 2026. Campaigners want councillors to start a formal variation of the local area plan to remove the data center zoning before any application is made. "We're not against data centres as such. We're against a development of this scale, this close to people's homes, on land that could support a broader range of employment uses with less strain on water, gas and the electricity grid," said campaign spokesperson Sorcha O'Neill. More than 200 people attended a meeting on Naas data center plans at the Osprey Hotel on September 3, 2026, where speakers pointed to noise complaints from residents living near a data center in Clondalkin, The Irish Times reported. Naas Municipal District mayor Bill Clear told the crowd he had visited the Clondalkin site the day before, and said the whistling noise he heard "was almost like if you had tinnitus." At the district meeting on September 8, 2026, Clear proposed that the council consider varying the plan to review the Jigginstown/Maudlins zoning, and the motion was referred to the full county council meeting on September 28. In a written response, senior planner Amy Granville said there was no evidence of a material change in circumstances since the plan was adopted, and so no basis for changing the zoning. On the neighboring P1 site, Kildare County Council granted permission in August 2025 for a separate six-building, gas-powered data center campus, a decision under appeal by both the developer and third-party objectors, the Kildare Nationalist reported. That €3 billion campus, proposed by Herbata Ltd next to the M7 motorway, awaits a ruling from An Coimisiún Pleanála, which is expected by January, The Irish Times reported. The full Kildare County Council is due to take up Clear's motion on September 28, 2026. Clear has said he doubts a vote can reverse the zoning: "I will do it, but it will not work," he told the Kildare Nationalist in August.

sabey-sabey-decatur-township-indianapoli.text: Sabey Data Centers is building a $4.3 billion data center campus on 130 acres at 6400 Kentucky Ave. in Decatur Township, on the southwest side of Indianapolis in Marion County. It will have two buildings totaling 1,062,500 square feet and an on-site substation able to supply up to 250 megawatts of power. On September 16 the Metropolitan Development Commission approved more than $240 million in tax breaks for it, and Sabey expects to finish construction by 2031. The commission approved the plan in March after months of objections over noise, power, water, jobs and home values. Because Sabey asked only for variances, not a full rezoning, the district's city-county councilor could not call the vote to the council. "It does not belong in the middle of these residences," said Pat Andrews of the Decatur Township Civic Council. Andrews and other residents are suing to block the project. The tax breaks cut real estate taxes 60% over 10 years, passed 6-1, and equipment taxes 90% over 15 years, passed 5-2. Sabey and its tenant will still pay nearly $53 million in taxes during those periods, and Decatur Township Schools will get $31 million over 15 years. The company says it will create 75 jobs averaging $50 an hour, use a closed-loop cooling system and pay $5 million for road improvements.

developers3-qts-york-county.text: QTS is building a data center campus near Hands Mill Highway and Campbell Road by Lake Wylie in unincorporated York County. The company says its approved plan has nine buildings across three phases, starting with four buildings on about 109 acres. QTS expects to begin construction on the second phase in early 2027. Neighbors have described blasting, early morning construction noise and bright lights near their homes, and a resident petition had nearly 800 signatures by February 2026. QTS says it is considering staggered work shifts to reduce traffic on Hands Mill Highway. The company says the buildings will use air-cooled, closed-loop cooling after an initial water fill and that it does not plan to drill wells at the site. York County Council voted 6-0 in July to pause new data center approvals for nine months in unincorporated areas. Previously approved site plans are exempt only within their approved scope and subject to existing conditions. QTS says its current nine buildings are approved, while any expansion would require a new review. County staff are studying noise, water and power use before recommending zoning changes. The pause runs into April 2027 unless council extends it.

fluidstack-fluidstack-cameron-county-har.text: Fluidstack has started construction on a data center campus in Cameron County, Texas, on more than 1,100 acres near Rio Hondo, east of Valley International Airport and west of the Port of Harlingen. The $4 billion first phase is expected to create more than 2,500 construction jobs and several hundred permanent jobs, Fluidstack said when it broke ground in September 2026. The project follows directives from Gov. Greg Abbott, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, the Public Utility Commission of Texas and a Cameron County resolution on data centers, Fluidstack said, and the company is developing community benefit agreements with local leaders. The groundbreaking came a week after Harlingen city commissioners tabled a drainage agreement that would have let Fluidstack route stormwater into a city-owned canal. Fluidstack spokesperson Kate Franko said the company received a worksite permit from Cameron County instead and will pursue alternative plans for wastewater discharge, using closed-loop cooling supplied by the East Rio Hondo Water Supply Corporation. Harlingen Mayor Norma Sepulveda said on social media the project was moving forward "with or without the city of Harlingen." "It was not located in Harlingen. It was not asking Harlingen for permission to build. We did not have the authority to stop it," Sepulveda said, adding that Cameron County approved Fluidstack's drainage permit and that $20 million once proposed for Harlingen infrastructure will instead go to the county. Fluidstack says it will cover all energy, infrastructure and water costs, with nothing passed on to residents, and that the project comes with no local property tax breaks while adding millions of dollars a year to the local tax base. Cameron County Commissioner David Garza, whose precinct includes the site, welcomed the project: "They are investing in and paying for their own energy and infrastructure, ensuring those costs do not fall on our residents." Not everyone is satisfied. U.S. Rep. Vicente Gonzalez said data centers are "energy-intensive and large water consumption facilities that will place significant new demands on already strained communities," and that he opposes new data centers "until we have an abundance of water, a reliable energy grid, and a well-thought-out plan for the future." Cameron County's worksite permit lets construction continue while Fluidstack finalizes its wastewater plan; the company says further project details will be released as agreements with local leaders are completed.

ntt-ntt-phoenix-mesa-ph1-ph7.text: A seven-building, 2.3 million square foot data center campus proposed by NTT Global Data Centers is planned on 170 acres at Pecos and Crismon roads in southeast Mesa, Maricopa County, Arizona. The Mesa Planning and Zoning Board voted 4 to 0 in May 2026 to recommend the city council approve rezoning, a use permit and a site plan; council action was expected in July 2026 but was pushed to later that summer, and no result has been published since. NTT, a Japanese company, bought the 170 acre site from Pacific Proving LLC in 2025 for 300 million dollars. The seven two-story buildings, each 310,000 to 400,000 square feet, would use a closed-loop water cooling system filled only once, with no evaporative cooling, a design NTT says avoids the up to 5 million gallons a day that large data centers can use. Two residents who attended a neighborhood meeting last October raised concerns about noise from the substation and generators near their homes; NTT said it would use low-noise fans and equipment. A different data center had permission on the same site in 2024 for another company, but it was never built, and the current plan is allowed under older, less strict rules because it was submitted before the city's stricter data center ordinance took effect last July.

amazon-aws-tucson.text: Beale Infrastructure is building the Project Blue data center south of Tucson in Pima County, Arizona. Construction vehicles began clearing the desert by April 2026 as residents protested outside the site near the county fairgrounds. Tucson voted against annexing the land, which stopped Beale from using Tucson Water, but the developer continued the project through Pima County. Amazon Web Services had been the intended end user, and the Tucson Sentinel reported that it seemingly backed out after the cooling plans changed.

cipher-cipher-stingray-andrews.text: Cipher Digital is developing its Stingray data center project on a 250-acre site west of Andrews in Andrews County, Texas, with up to 100 megawatts of power capacity. The company has leased 70 megawatts of critical IT load at the site to AWS and funded the project with an $810 million bond offering. At a town hall, Cipher described a plan to treat brackish water from a deep aquifer for the facility, and residents questioned water use, electricity demand and noise. Cipher had targeted energization in the second quarter of 2026, but its own investor materials now target rent starting April 1, 2027 for the site's network hall and May 1, 2027 for its data hall.

meta-meta-sturgeon-county.text: Meta proposed a data center complex east of Gibbons in Sturgeon County, Alberta, Canada. The project was announced in July 2026 with an estimated cost of $13 billion. A separate natural gas-fired power plant was planned to help serve it. Hundreds of residents protested outside county offices in Morinville over the proposal. Some residents said they were concerned about electricity and water costs. Sturgeon County had made data centers a permitted land use in 2025, and the mayor said the county had not required public open houses for this kind of project. The Globe and Mail reported a planned capacity of one gigawatt.

ntt-ntt-tokyo-inzai-shiroi-tky12-shr1.text: NTT Global Data Centers is developing the Tokyo TKY12 data center campus in Shiroi, Chiba Prefecture, Japan. The six-building campus is designed for about 200 megawatts of computing capacity. Its first phase is expected to enter service in 2030 or later, after utility power connections are complete. TKY12 is planned beside NTT's TKY11 data center, which the article says is a separate 50-megawatt site scheduled to open in April 2027. NTT said the timing of TKY12's first phase depends on securing grid power. The company is coordinating the development with Shiroi City and local stakeholders.

PowerHouse Data Centers and Pennsylvania Data Center Partners are behind the wider project. The approval moved the first phase toward construction. Residents protested the plan and asked the supervisors to delay the vote until a vacant board seat was filled. Don Geistwhite Jr. and Phil Neiderer approved the agenda items with a two-person quorum. developers3-qts-denver-aurora.text: QTS operates and is expanding its Aurora data center campus at 1160 North Gun Club Road in Arapahoe County, Colorado. The 65-acre campus is planned for at least 160 megawatts of capacity. One of its three large data centers was complete by July 2026, while work continued on the others. QTS applied to add 98 diesel backup generators to 40 already installed at the campus. Residents raised noise and air pollution concerns at an Aurora town hall, and QTS representatives attended. The company said the additional engines would have pollution controls and its cooling system would recirculate water.

developers3-qts-porter-county.text: QTS withdrew its plan for a data center campus in Union Township, Porter County, Indiana. The company had sought to rezone about 800 acres near Wheeler High School for the project. Residents opposed the plan, and QTS withdrew the rezoning request. Hundreds of residents attended a county meeting and raised concerns about power use, environmental effects and public health. QTS said it would not proceed because the conditions made the development economically difficult. County commissioner Jim Biggs said he wished the proposal had received a full county hearing.

keppel-keppel-dc-dublin-1-citywest.text: Keppel DC Dublin 1 is an operating data center at Unit 4033-4035, Citywest Business Campus, Naas Road, Dublin 24, Ireland, owned by Keppel DC REIT. The building sits on a 218,236 square foot leasehold site and holds 125,044 square feet of floor space rented out to 24 tenants under colocation leases. It was 96.5 percent occupied as of the end of 2025 and brought in about 23.2 million Singapore dollars in rental income that year. Keppel DC REIT values the facility at 171.4 million Singapore dollars, more than the 102.8 million dollars it paid to acquire it. Power remains the main constraint on new data centers around Dublin, where regulators now require new projects to bring their own on-site generation and locate outside the congested grid near the city.

keppel-keppel-dc-singapore-1-serangoon.text: Keppel DC Singapore 1 is an operating data center at 25 Serangoon North Avenue 5, owned by Keppel DC REIT, on a leasehold site running to September 2055. It has 225,945 square feet of gross floor area and 17 tenants, but was only 53.3 percent occupied at the end of 2025, the lowest of Keppel's five Singapore buildings. Singapore has capped new data center construction since a 2019 moratorium, and new projects now must meet strict energy efficiency rules under the government's Green Data Centre Roadmap.

The first phase in Japan is set to deliver 18 megawatts of capacity, with a planned 36 megawatts across the full two-building campus. NTT DATA's own newsroom said the first facility is slated to open in fiscal year 2027, which would bring the company's Osaka-region count to three data centers totaling about 70 megawatts. chinamobile-china-mobile-harbin-intellig.text: China Mobile operates this intelligent computing data center in Hanan Industrial New Town, part of the Harbin High-tech Industrial Development Zone in Pingfang District, Harbin. The site covers about 1,294 mu (86 hectares), with a planned total floor area near 600,000 square meters and more than 160,000 square meters already built, providing 18,000 equipment racks. China Mobile has certified it as a national green data center and a five-star facility within its own network. The center runs what China Mobile calls the largest single-cluster AI computing operation among telecom operators worldwide, with 6.93 exaflops of computing power across an 18,000-chip cluster and a power usage effectiveness rating of 1.2. It serves more than 40 Heilongjiang provincial government departments along with banks and tech companies including Baidu, Alibaba, Tencent and ByteDance, according to Heilongjiang Daily. Two more buildings, B04 and B05, were due to finish by the end of June 2026, bringing the site's total designed IT power to more than 61 megawatts; that date has passed and no report of their completion has been published.

chinamobile-china-mobile-international-h.text: China Mobile International operates this data center, its global network center at 3 Chun Cheong Street in the Tseung Kwan O Industrial Estate, Hong Kong, which opened in November 2014. The data center covers about 9,700 square meters of land with roughly 24,000 square meters of floor space and had 1,920 equipment racks online at opening. It is China Mobile's largest international network center and the first cable landing station built outside mainland China by a Chinese carrier. The site works as a cable landing station, global network operations center and internet data center, carrying services such as IP transit, mobile roaming and cloud computing for China Mobile's international customers. Dr. Tiger Lin, then chairman of China Mobile International, said the center "strengthens the position of Hong Kong as the global communications hub."

chinamobile-china-mobile-international-l.text: China Mobile International opened this 10 megawatt data center at 536 Ipswich Road in the Slough Trading Estate, England, in December 2019. The facility holds about 1,600 equipment racks and has Tier III certification of design from the Uptime Institute. It connects to European and Asian fiber routes including the Transit Europe-Asia networks, giving it links to more than 300 cities across 31 Chinese provinces and regions. China Mobile International chairman Li Feng said the opening reflected the company's "commitment to promoting secure and reliable high-speed connections around the world." The site works alongside newer China Mobile International facilities in Singapore and Frankfurt as part of the company's expansion across Europe and Asia.

cyrusone-cyrusone-frankfurt-fra7.text: CyrusOne is building the FRA7 data center at its Frankfurt Westside campus in Germany, where local politicians celebrated the groundbreaking at the end of 2024 as a sustainability flagship project. Barely a year later, CyrusOne struck a deal with energy supplier E.ON to expand the Germany site's power from 84 megawatts to the 126 megawatts on record here, using gas-powered generators. CyrusOne added the gas generators because Frankfurt's power grid could not supply the extra energy; grid operator Mainova says new large connections in the city have no chance until the 2030s. Marina Kuhn of the Federal Environment Agency said such on-site gas plants "occur frequently in the Frankfurt area," while economist Claudia Kemfert warned of the noise, fine dust and carbon emissions that come with them.

google-google-north-weald.text: Epping Forest District Council approved Google's outline plans in December 2025 for a data center on North Weald Airfield in Essex, calling it a "nationally significant and sustainable development." Google is paying 88 million pounds for the North Weald land, which currently hosts the area's Saturday market. Councillor Alan Lion said the site was already allocated for development in the district's local plan and called Google's arrival "something of an advantage to Epping Forest." The council says the project will add 62 million to 123 million pounds in economic value and create 830 to 1,660 construction jobs, plus 100 to 200 permanent jobs once it opens. The market, which draws around 300 stalls, will lose nearly a hectare of trading space, and its parking will convert to data center use for at least five years.

huawei-huawei-cloud-ulanqab.text: Huawei operates its Ulanqab Cloud Data Center in the Chahar High-tech Industrial Development Zone, calling it its largest computing hub in northern China. Huawei began the Ulanqab partnership in 2013, and the first of four planned construction phases opened in 2016. The site's average annual temperature is only 4.3 degrees Celsius, cool enough to run on outside air most of the year, which Huawei says keeps its year-round power usage effectiveness below 1.26, well under the industry average near 1.8. The center runs Huawei's government cloud, which the report says connects nearly 200 business systems across dozens of local agencies.

huawei-huawei-wuhu-jiangbei.text: Huawei Cloud opened its East China data center in Wuhu's Jiujiang District on June 14, 2024, completing the national layout of hub nodes for its computing and storage network. Huawei says the planned campus covers about 6,000 mu, roughly 988 acres, with room for up to 3 million servers. Huawei calls it the core node for its cloud business in northern China, with about 50,000 square meters of floor space and room for 4,500 server racks, Leiphone reported in 2018. ntt-ntt-hemel-hempstead-hh1-hh4.text: NTT Global Data Centers operates a campus of data centers in Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire. The company says it runs six data centers in the town in total. Hemel Hempstead 2 has 2,275 square meters of IT space and 5.8 megawatts of power. Hemel Hempstead 3 offers 8,960 square meters of IT space with up to 20 megawatts of power. NTT opened its newest building, Hemel Hempstead 4, in December 2021 as its seventh London-area data center site, with the first phase delivering half of its capacity. Fully built out, Hemel Hempstead 4 is designed to reach 9,600 square meters of IT space and 24 megawatts of power. NTT has said the investment could more than double its London-area capacity to over 120 megawatts once Hemel Hempstead 4 and its London 1 site in Dagenham are both fully built.

ntt-ntt-hillsboro-hi1-hi5.text: NTT Global Data Centers opened the first data center building on its Hillsboro, Oregon, campus, HI1, on February 23, 2021, with 36 megawatts of power on a 47-acre site at the heart of the Pacific Northwest technology hub. NTT says the completed campus, with five buildings (HI1-HI5), will deliver 126 megawatts of power and more than one million square feet of data center space. The campus runs on optional carbon-neutral IT and 100 percent renewable energy, and earned a Level 3 certification, the highest level, from the Cleaner Air Oregon program. NTT's Americas data center chief, Doug Adams, said opening Hillsboro and a sister campus in Chicago was just the beginning of that year's expansion, which also included new campuses planned for Silicon Valley and Ashburn, Virginia. NTT DATA said in 2026 that it had acquired more land in Hillsboro for an additional 216 megawatts of capacity, bringing its total planned capacity in the Hillsboro market to 354 megawatts.

ntt-ntt-london-1-dagenham.text: NTT Global Data Centers opened its London 1 data center in Dagenham, East London, in 2020, with 12,800 square meters of server space; the first phase delivers 32 megawatts of critical IT power, growing to 64 megawatts once the site is fully built out. The site sits about 10 miles east of London's city center, near the Docklands internet hub that carries most of the London Internet Exchange's traffic. NTT has said it could more than double its London-area capacity to over 120 megawatts once London 1 and its Hemel Hempstead 4 site are both fully built out.

Talen Energy bought out TeraWulf's 25% stake in the Nautilus joint venture in October 2024 for about $85 million cash plus mining equipment, giving Talen full ownership. A trade publication has named it one of the most beautiful data centers in the world, and the building connects to a dense fiber network with dual, redundant power feeds. Texas Governor Greg Abbott ordered a freeze on new data center grid connections statewide on August 3, 2026, requiring the Public Utility Commission and grid operator ERCOT to audit projects before they can connect to the power grid.
